title: Closing arguments set for Monday after testimony wraps in Candlewood Place murder trial
description: After four days of testimony coming from law enforcement, forensic experts and neighbors who overheard the fatal shooting that took McGarland "Mack" Walker VI's life on March 8, 2024, closing arguments are expected to start Monday, May 4.
_full_text:
After four days of testimony coming from law enforcement, forensic experts and neighbors who overheard the fatal shooting that took McGarland "Mack" Walker VI's life on March 8, 2024, closing arguments are expected to start Monday, May 4. 

Luke Birch, 23, of Rapid City, is charged with first-degree murder and, in the alternative, second-degree murder for Walker's death. Walker was shot and killed inside Candlewood Place, an apartment building in west Rapid City. Birch can only be convicted of one of the charges, not both.

After the state rested, Birch's attorney Ole Oleson called upon one last resident from the apartment building. The resident was not among the state's witnesses. He was the lone witness to testify for the defense. 

The man said he was heading to bed around 4:30 p.m. when he heard consecutive loud knocks. He said he was wondering if it was gunshots, but his wife said that was impossible because they lived in a good neighborhood. Minutes later, the man said there were police cars surrounding the building. 

Oleson asked if there were any pauses between the shots. He said there wasn't and that it was in quick succession to one another. 

The man testified he was contacted by the state's attorney's office about whether he heard a pause in the shots, and he told them no. 

"It did appear they (the state) were attempting to pressure me to try to remember if there was a long pause or not," the man testified. 

Under Oleson's questioning, he said the state did not pressure him to change his testimony. 

On Tuesday, April 28, the jury also heard testimony from other residents inside Candlewood Place, all of whom testified to hearing two men arguing, followed by a volley of gunshots, then silence.

 Luke Birch
Birch 

One resident said he watched from his window a man dressed in all black running north towards Wilderness Park, before retrieving his own handgun and investigating the hallway.

He said he found Walker laying on his back unresponsive and another resident calling 911. Together, they reported the shooting, and he told the operator about the fleeing man.

Afterward, he went back to his apartment, where he put on a bulletproof vest and pulled out his rifle. He then waited out in the hallway "to be a sentry," until law enforcement arrived.

He relinquished his guns to the police and spoke with them. His guns were later returned to him.

Another resident testified to seeing a man wearing all black and a partial face covering rushing past with what looked like a handgun. He said he went into his apartment debating to call 911, until he heard the gunshots.

Each of the neighbors who testified on Tuesday said they heard a pause between the first flurry of shots and the second.

On Friday, May 1, Deputy State's Attorney Adam Shiffermiller asked if the man's own personal guns were confiscated by police. He said yes, one from his bedroom and another on his person. 

Shiffermiller referenced a police report where a female officer interviewed the man, asking if he recalled telling her he heard four to five shots and one to two shots slightly after that. The man said he doesn't remember telling anyone there was a pause between the shots. 

Birch's trial is set to continue Monday at 8:30 a.m.

title: Recital season keeps Rapid City florists on their toes
description: The bevy of local dance recitals, along with graduations, weddings and Mother’s Day, turn May into a beautifully busy month for Rapid City florists.
_full_text:
The bevy of local dance recitals, along with graduations, weddings and Mother’s Day, turn May into a beautifully busy month for Rapid City florists.

Recitals mean a demand for hundreds of bouquets and gifts to congratulate the dancers after their performances. While dancers are rehearsing, flower shops including Flowers by LeRoy and Victoria's Garden are stocking up for recitals days and weeks in advance.

“We try to know when all the recitals are. We try to be prepared by having some designs already made that people can go ahead and buy. A lot of people pre-order,” said Vicki Bierman, owner of Victoria’s Garden. “We try to match costume colors or characters and try to create a theme for them.”

 Victoria's Garden (copy)
A floral designer at Victoria's Garden creates an arrangement in this file photo. Rapid City florists are stocking up and planning ahead for the increased demand for gifts and flowers for dance recitals and Mother's Day in May. All five Rapid City dance schools hold their recitals in May. 

Victoria’s Garden, for example, partners with Prima School of Dancing every year to provide a pop-up shop outside the Fine Arts Theater during Prima’s four recitals, which will be at The Monument on May 9.

“We have done that so many years. We find out the theme of the dance and we pack flowers and fun little gift items,” Bierman said. “This time of year, we stock up on any fun little accents. We can add lots of jewels and butterflies and ladybugs and glittery things. We’re little girls at heart so it’s fun for us, too.”

“We love doing the flowers for dance recitals. I just think it’s so cute they come off the stage and they’re greeted with flowers or a gift. I love that tradition,” she said. “The dancers have worked so hard.”

Often, Bierman said the young dancers stop by the pop-up shop with their parents before the show to choose the flowers or gifts they want. Bierman said she carries items ranging in price from $5 or $10 to about $75 to fit everyone’s budget, and to help ensure every dancer can receive a gift or flowers as a reward for their months of practice.

“If you dive into what goes on behind the scenes — the rehearsal, the prep rooms — it is hustle and bustle and so much organization and planning,” Bierman said of the work the dance schools' staffs and students put into each recital. “It’s overwhelming to me. It’s really something.”

Prima School of Dancing's recitals fall on Mother’s Day weekend, so the pop-up flower shop is a chance for moms to choose their Mother’s Day gifts, too — and many of them do, Bierman said.

Bierman and a team of about four staff members will be at the Prima recitals pop-up shop, and she has extra staff at Victoria’s Garden to keep up with Mother’s Day weekend demand.

title: Rapid City company wins a top honor in world's largest condiment competition
description: Kinzie Foods , a small-batch barbecue sauce business that opened 18 months ago in Rapid City, is taking the world of condiments by storm.
_full_text:
Kinzie Foods, a small-batch barbecue sauce business that opened 18 months ago in Rapid City, is taking the world of condiments by storm.

Kinzie Foods’ Dubai Chocolate BBQ sauce took first place in the Specialty category at the American Royal World Series of Barbecue contest in April in Kansas City, Kansas. It is the largest condiment competition in the world. This was Kinzie Foods’ first time entering the competition.

“The Specialty category was the one we wanted to win. … It was a big deal to us to be put up against the biggest brands in the world,” said Kinzie Foods founder Walter Kinzie.  

“Every condiment company in America was in this thing, and we beat them all,” he said.

Among other recognitions the company won, Kinzie Foods’ Fiery sauce took third place in the American Royal World Series of Barbecue’s Vinegar Sauce category.

 Walter Kinzie - Kinzie Foods
Walter Kinzie, founder of Kinzie Foods in Rapid City, holds bottles of the company's small-batch barbecue sauce. Locally, the sauce is available at locations including Boyd's at Baken Park, Ace Hardware stores throughout Rapid City and the Black Hills, RC Hardware, Breadroot Co-op, and Lynns Dakotamart stores in the Black Hills. 

Kinzie Foods also won the Black Hills Stock Show chili cookoff earlier this year.

Kinzie Foods is establishing its niche in the barbecue sauce market by producing small-batch sauces that can be eaten at every meal. While most barbecue sauces are marketed for use when smoking or grilling meat, Kinzie said he wants his products to be a condiment customers use every day.

Kinzie’s prize-winning Dubai Chocolate BBQ sauce, for example, is a versatile topping that can pair equally well with vanilla ice cream, tater tots, French fires, and more, Kinzie said. Chefs and online creators have developed recipes for breakfast, lunch, dinner, appetizers and desserts that are on the Kinzie Foods website to educate consumers about how to use the sauces.

Kinzie Foods produces five black-label flavors that are available year-round at locations throughout the Black Hills and nationwide. The company creates limited edition special flavors, too, that are announced each month through online launch events on the company’s website and social media.

The unusual flavors, such as Pistachio that dropped in April, as well as the sauces’ versatility and the monthly launch events for new flavors, are a hit with customers.

“We’re 18 months into this and every month we’re doubling our revenue,” Kinzie said. “We have a small but loyal and rabid fan base.”

Kinzie Foods also plans local sampling events this spring. Follow Kinzie Foods on social media, including Facebook, Instagram and TikTok, for more information.

“I’ll be out there. You can meet me and try all of our flavors. We’re very involved in the community. Sampling events will become a bigger part of our future,” Kinzie said.

Kinzie Foods’ product line started with a family recipe from Kinzie’s aunt. Before taking the leap into specialty foods, Kinzie produced large-scale events that ran the gamut from concerts with Garth Brooks to a presidential inauguration to corporate events.

The homemade sauce was a gift Kinzie gave to some of his clients, many of whom were celebrities.

“I started getting calls from celebrities asking, ‘Where can I buy this in Los Angeles, New York, Nashville?” said Kinzie, who initially gifted his clients more.

When that became prohibitively expensive – and Kinzie was spending much of his free time making sauce to keep up with requests for it — he started selling it and discovered a demand for it. That inspired the creation of Kinzie Foods.

A talent for big ideas

Thinking big and building businesses has been Kinzie’s lifelong passion. Growing up in a small town in Kansas, he acquired his first business loan — $125 — from a local bank to purchase a pig he entered in the county fair. His father co-signed the loan.

Walter Kinzie moved on to cattle and by age 18, he had a head of about 40 head of cows and calves. When a rare disease sidelined Kinzie, he needed a kidney transplant that required him to be hospitalized for much of a three-year period. He sold his cattle to pay for his surgery.

 Kinzie Foods sauce and burger
Kinzie Foods in Rapid City created five black label sauces that are available year-round, plus new limited edition flavors that are introduced every month.  

After recovering his health, Kinzie went to work for Mattress Firm in Texas. There, he started and ran a division of the company. At Mattress Firm, Kinzie also met his wife, Clara, who grew up in Fort Pierre.

He’d also started an experiential marketing firm, producing concerts and live events. That quickly became more lucrative than his Mattress Firm job. When Kinzie switched to producing live events as his full-time job, Mattress Firm was one of the clients that hired him for corporate events.

"I was helping bring people together for dynamic experiences that drove passion and excitement. … Ultimately, I got to do some really big stuff. I worked for every living president and a couple who aren’t with us – Jimmy Carter and George H.W. Bush,” Kinzie said. “That has been a fascinating experience.”

When the COVID-19 hindered large-scale events like the kind Kinzie had been producing, he eventually decided to pivot and learn how to build a small-batch barbecue sauce business.

“This is a chance for me to combine all my knowledge and grow something very welcoming. … I had massive retail experience and I understood how retail worked, and I had massive experience bringing people together for a shared experience and creating memories that were impactful and lasted a lifetime,” Kinzie said.

“What better way to bring people together than a meal? That’s where fun and fellowship and opportunity and discussion. All the things that matter intellectually and emotionally oftentimes happens over a meal," he said.

During the pandemic, the Kinzie family had moved to Rapid City to be near Clara’s family in Fort Pierre. The Kinzies are happy to be raising their daughters Piper and Poppy here.

Kinzie Foods currently manufactures its sauce in Denver. On April 29, Kinzie Foods marked the first anniversary of opening a warehouse in Rapid City. Within a year, Kinzie’s goal is to completely move production of Kinzie Foods sauces to Rapid City.

“We’re able to do this at a place that is home, and that’s Rapid City for us. This is where we are raising our daughters and we’re going to thrive right here in Rapid City. This is our home,” Kinzie said.

title: What are the weapons detection system being installed in Rapid City high schools?
description: Rapid City Area Schools announced on Monday, April 27, it will be installing weapons detection systems at Central High School and Rapid City Alternative Academy. But what are they and how much did they cost?
_full_text:
Rapid City Area Schools announced on Monday, April 27, it will be installing weapons detection systems at Central High School and Rapid City Alternative Academy. But what are they and how much did they cost?

The systems, set to go into operation on May 4, were purchased for $200,000 through a federal COPS (Community Oriented Policing Services) grant, secured through collaboration between RCAS and the Rapid City Police Department. The $500,000 grant was awarded in 2023.

"The implementation of the system will help us partner with the RCAS and their security personnel in continued efforts to promote safety within our area schools," the department said.

Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson told media at a press conference on Wednesday, April 29, that although she doesn't fully understand the technology, "it's similar to a metal detection system, in that it senses the object and then alerts us if there is a potential weapon." 

Thompson could not provide a list of items the system is designed to detect. Brendyn Medina, spokesperson for the police department, declined to comment on the system. 

"The RCPD/SROs (school resource officers) will not be operating the system so I’ll defer to the RCAS to address those specifics," he wrote the Journal in an email. 

According to CEIA USA, the Ohio company that makes the system and other metal detection and security screening products, OpenGate is "capable of detecting a wide range of metallic threats, from single-shot micro-pistols to high-caliber assault weapons, enabling schools and districts to detect exactly what their threat environment warrants, to help ensure student and staff safety."

 Thompson
Rapid City Area Schools Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson speaks at a press conference on April 29 about the new weapons detection systems in two Rapid City high schools. 

The metal detectors come in the form of 25-pound pillars set across from each other. They are battery-powered, portable and designed to handle high volumes of students without the need for them to take off personal items, according to CEIA USA. According to the company, the detection and signaling parameters can be set through the OpenGate app.

"In a few days, this should become very routine for students. They just have to walk through the system," Thompson said. "If the alarm were to alert us to something, then they would be taken to a more discreet location where there would be a secondary screening, either through a metal detection wand or asking students to empty their pockets, that type of thing. But our focus will always be on maintaining the dignity and the privacy of the student that's being screened while also maintaining overall safety for all of our other students."

Thompson said the goal is to eventually install systems at Stevens High School, but it's not conducive to do so at this point because of the number of entrances.

"However, that is part of our broader plan. Once we are able to do some construction and some remodeling of that building, we'll be able to add weapons detection systems there as well," Thompson said.

Asked about timeline, Thompson said it will depend on whether or not the bond issue passes, which can't be predicted.

A $107 million Rapid City Area Schools bond question is set to appear on the Nov. 3 ballot. The tax levy will be dedicated to school improvements and construction, including $20 million in safety and security improvements at Stevens.

"I don't feel like Stevens is unsafe by any stretch of the imagination. I feel like the students there will be fine with the protocols and the relationships that we have with kids, but when we're able to take further precautions, we will," Thomspon said.

The superintendent added the district is not putting the systems in place as a disciplinary action or because of any one action within the community or schools. 

"It's not that we don't feel our schools are safe at this point, we just want to make sure we're continuing to increase our safety precautions," she said.

The efforts are, Thompson said, part of a wider district effort to improve safety in its schools, including adding secure entrances to every school in the district.

title: Organizers say occupation of 2 drilling sites in the Black Hills will continue over the weekend
description: On Friday afternoon, May 1, various local leaders from Remember the Children, Black Hills Clean Water Alliance and NDN Collective held a press conference for the media giving an update on the occupation of the two Rochford Mineral Exploration Drilling Project sites in the Black Hills, citing plans to continue blocking drill sites over the weekend.
_full_text:
On Friday afternoon, May 1, various local leaders from Remember the Children, Black Hills Clean Water Alliance and NDN Collective held a press conference for the media giving an update on the occupation of the two Rochford Mineral Exploration Drilling Project sites in the Black Hills, citing plans to continue blocking drill sites over the weekend. 

 Occupation in Black Hills
From left to right: Amy Sazue, Lilas Jarding and Foster Hogan speak at a press conference on the current occupation of two drill sites in the Black Hills. 

Amy Sazue executive director of Remembering the Children, said the press conference was to bring more attention and understanding of the importance of Pe’ Sla to the Indigenous community and non-tribal members.

"It's not activists and advocates and actors that are here. It's community members, it's moms and brothers and nephews and uncles and aunties that are here, protecting and fighting for this land, because it is that important to us," Sazue said.

The press conference took place outside of the Black Hills Mystic Rangers office in Rapid City. The office was closed for the day.

On the morning of May 1, members of NDN Collective, Oglala Lakota Youth Council and other community members restrained their arms on the drilling machinery to prevent workers from continuing their operation and conducted ceremonies at the sites. 

Valeriah Big Eagle, director of He Sapa initiatives at NDN Collective, told the Journal no one was working the sites when the group arrived.

Over an estimated dozen members are still onsite and are prepared to stay over the weekend, Foster Hogan, bison coordinator at NDN Collective said.

Hogan read a message from one of the members on site of the drilling pads, "We are standing in prayer to protect our sacred places and clean drinking water for all. Every single person has a moral duty to protect our world from harm. The illegal drilling activities of Pete Lien & Sons is a threat to us all. We ask for the immediate halt of all drilling activities, that a full EIS (Environmental Impact Study) be completed, along with proper consultation with tribal nations. We ask for expanded community support so that we can work toward a better future for all people and Mother Earth.” 

 Occupation in Black Hills
Zachary Martinez with NDN Collective holds an eagle staff at the press conference on May 1. 

"There's a lot going on right now, and I know that it's important that everybody be updated on activities. Black Hills Clean Water Alliance focuses on protecting water resources in the Black Hills from new large-scale mining and a graphite mine in the headwaters of Rapid Creek, which supplies water for all of us in Rapid City and Ellsworth Air Force Base and beyond," Dr. Lilias Jarding, executive director of the Black Hills Clean Water Alliance (BHCWA) said. "It's just an idea that should be nipped in the bud for that reason."

 Occupation in Black Hills
Lilias Jarding with Black Hills Clean Water Alliance shares information on the concerns of water contamination from drilling and mining in the Black Hills.  

Pe' Sla (Bald Spot) is an area in the Black Hills marked by a rocky peak overlooking a large meadow, according to the National Park Service. It sits in the Black Hills west of Rapid City. 

According to a press release by NDN Collective, 10 drill pads are actively operating and claim some are within the 2-mile buffer zone protected by a memorandum of understanding between the U.S. Forest Service and Lakota Tribes.

 Pe Sla
Community members protesting an exploratory drilling project located near Pe’ Sla in the Black Hills on Friday, May 1. 

The exploratory drilling by Pete Lien & Sons was permitted by the U.S. Forest Service on Feb. 27, for a large mineral exploration drilling project on USFS-managed public lands near Rochford in west Pennington County. The permit allows the company to use its federal mining claims to look for graphite in the area. 

The Forest Service granted the permit. A decision memo from the Forest Service allows for 18 boreholes at a maximum depth of 1,000 feet.

 Pe Sla
A protester at a drilling machine in the Black Hills. 

Access to the drilling land would be made by USFS roadways and roughly 5,060 linear feet of new, temporary overland access trails. "Water used for drilling will be sourced from approved municipal supplies and recirculated on-site using infiltration galleries or tanks. No water will be withdrawn from streams or wetlands," the Forest Service said in the memo.
NDN Collective said in a press release the drilling in the area has started despite public opposition, no environmental review, and the active lawsuit against the Black Hills Forest Service filed by NDN Collective, Black Hills Clean Water Alliance, and Earthworks.
The hearing for the lawsuit is slated for Monday, May 4.
On April 29, the organizations against the project filed motions for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction in the lawsuit, asking a judge to stop the drilling. The defendants have not yet filed a response, according to federal court records.
Additionally, all 9 federally recognized tribes in South Dakota filed a joint lawsuit against the U.S. Forest Service on April 30. The tribes are asking the court to suspend drilling operations until the hearing and decisions on the case is made.
Petel Lien and & Sons has not responded for comment.
The U.S. Forest Service declined to comment on both the occupation and the lawsuits filed against them.
Earlier on Friday morning, community members stood outside of the Pete Lien and Sons main office building with signs voicing concern about the drilling project, Jarding said.
Jarding told the Journal this was to bring awareness to shed light on what Pete Lien & Sons is doing in the Black Hills.
In a statement to the Journal on Friday, May 1, the Pennington County Sheriff's Office said, "We have a law enforcement presence. We are simply focused on keeping everyone safe. Continuing to work with our partners on the criminal investigation regarding shutting down the legally permitted drilling operation."
The statement continued, saying this is now a federal investigation on federal land and sheriff officers are not blocking access to Pe’ Sla. 
Sazue said the Seven Hills Road to get to the drilling pads is being blocked off and only permitted to local traffic.
Zachery Martinez, facilities manager at NDN Collective said, "They (sheriff's deputies) have a checkpoint right down the road from the access point, and yes, they're asking for IDs when everybody trying to pass that road."
He said this restricts tribal members from praying on the sacred land of Pe’ Sla.
"There are hundreds of historical sites within Pe’ Sla and the surrounding areas, including the buffer zone. Where these drilling pads are in the U.S. Forest Service was obligated to include Pe’ Sla and the surrounding lands with the two-mile buffer zone recognized in the memo of understanding between the great Sioux Nations, tribes and the forest service. (They) failed to recognize this and allowed the drilling to commence," Hogan said. 
A 2014 Memorandum of Understanding between the U.S. Forest Service and representative tribal nations of the Oceti Sakowin (meaning seven council fires made up of the Lakota, Nakota and Dakota tribes) acknowledged and agreed that Pe’ Sla was of great cultural and religious importance to the Oceti Sakowin, the lawsuit claims.

Sazue said, "I understand that there is a disconnect between our local community and understanding the history of this place and the people that have been here. And we're here to remind everybody that Pe’ Sla is important and that we will always fight for the Black Hills. We will always fight for our sacred sites."
The press conference concluded with a plea for support via calling the U.S Forest Service, showing up at the drill site signing an online petition and a letter for support.

title: Rapid City police trying to identify man reported walking around Cathedral parking lot with a gun
description: The Rapid City Police Department said officers were dispatched to the Cathedral of Our Lady of Perpetual Help parking lot on Sunday, May 3, for a report of a man walking around with a shotgun.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Police Department said officers were dispatched to the Cathedral of Our Lady of Perpetual Help parking lot on Sunday, May 3, for a report of a man walking around with a shotgun. 

"This caused a lot of concern for church-goers, and police are currently working to identify the man," the department said on Sunday evening. 

 Man in Cathedral parking lot
Police are looking to identify this man who was reported walking around the parking lot at the Cathedral of Our Lady of Perpetual Help on Sunday, May 3, in Rapid City. 

The man is described as an older Caucasian man, about 6-feet tall with gray hair, khaki pants, and a blue long-sleeve shirt. 

Police ask anyone with information about his identity to contact police at 605-394-4131. An anonymous tip can be submitted by texting the letters "RCPD" and the information to 847411.

title: No one injured in structure fire in rural Box Elder
description: The Box Elder Volunteer Fire Department said no one was injured in a garage fire in rural Box Elder on Sunday, May 3.
_full_text:
The Box Elder Volunteer Fire Department said no one was injured in a garage fire in rural Box Elder on Sunday, May 3.

The department said it responded to a report of fire and smoke visible from a detached garage in the 4900 block of South Sunnyside Drive around 1:35 p.m.

 5-3-2026-NM.jpg
A garage burned down in rural Box Elder on Sunday, May 3. 

Firefighters arrived to find a free-burning fire with heavy smoke coming from the single-story structure with fire extending into the ceiling, roof assembly and adjacent grass.

Rapid attack by firefighters contained the fire to the structure of origin, stopping the spread of the flames to nearby structures and infrastructure, the department said. About 1/4 of an acre of grass was burned as well.

The fire department said there were no reports of injuries to firefighters, civilians or domestic animals.

 5-3-2026-NM-1.jpg
The Box Elder Volunteer Fire Department said no one was injured in a garage fire in rural Box Elder on Sunday, May 3. 

"Please maintain your smoke and CO detectors, keep them clean, free of dust and dirt. When you change your clock, change detector batteries. Replace the entire detector after 10 years or (if) you suspect they are failing or faulty," the department said in a release.

title: Judge rules to halt Rochford drilling operations until further hearings are held
byline: SHALOM BAER GEE and MADISON WILLIS Journal staff
description: After a hearing that stretched on for more than three hours at the federal courthouse in Rapid City, a judge ruled to halt operations at the Pete Lien & Sons Rochford Mineral Exploratory Drilling Project until further hearings are held.
_full_text:
After a hearing that stretched on for more than three hours at the federal courthouse in Rapid City, a judge ruled to halt operations at the Pete Lien & Sons Rochford Mineral Exploratory Drilling Project until further hearings are held.

 Project Pe'Sla Now! sign
About a 100 people gathered at the Andrew W Bogue Federal Building United States Courthouse to sit in the motions hearing held on May 4. The courtroom was full, and staff opened another courtroom to stream the proceedings. Inside, people sat on the floor. Outside, people stood with signs advocating for the protection of Pe' Sla.  

At the beginning of April, NDN Collective, Black Hills Clean Water Alliance, and Earthworks filed a lawsuit to block the project. On April 29, the plaintiffs filed a motion for a restraining order to stop drilling until the case can be heard. U.S. District Court Judge Camela Theeler approved that request. 

The U.S. Forest Service permitted the drilling on Feb. 27 for a large mineral exploration drilling project on USFS-managed public lands near Rochford in west Pennington County. The permit allows the company to use its federal mining claims to look for graphite in the area.

 Tribal leaders gather in front of federal court
Several tribal leaders gathered in front of the federal courthouse to address the courts decision in approving the temporary restraining order to stop exploratory drilling near Pe'Sla.   

A decision memo from the Forest Service allows for up to 18 boreholes at a maximum depth of 1,000 feet. Attorneys at the Monday hearing said drilling has been underway at seven of the 18 sites. 

The drill sites are within 2 miles of tribally owned land of Pe' Sla, a sacred area to the Lakota people. The plaintiffs argue the drilling is a disruption of their religious practices and that the Forest Service unlawfully granted the permit without proper environmental review and without consultation of the tribes. The Forest Service argues it followed the law, reached out to the tribes and that the project is not disruptive. 

 Close up on tribal leaders
The temporary restraining order will apply until the next evidentiary hearing on May 20 and 21. Tribal leaders shared the news to the crowd who sat outside during the May 4 motions hearing.

title: Rapid City man found guilty of murder for killing his 'best friend'
description: After about six hours of deliberation, a Pennington County jury on Monday, May 4, found 23-year-old Rapid City man Luke Birch guilty of second-degree murder after he shot and killed his best friend , McGarland "Mack" Walker VI, at Candlewood Place apartments on March 8, 2024 in Rapid City. He was 24.
_full_text:
After about six hours of deliberation, a Pennington County jury on Monday, May 4, found 23-year-old Rapid City man Luke Birch guilty of second-degree murder after he shot and killed his best friend, McGarland "Mack" Walker VI, at Candlewood Place apartments on March 8, 2024 in Rapid City. He was 24. 

Birch was charged with first-degree murder and, in the alternative, second-degree murder for Walker's death. 

 Luke Birch
Birch 

During jury instructions, the state also added first-degree manslaughter in the alternative to the other two charges. The jury ultimately landed on second-degree murder. 

Jurors went into deliberations around 11:51 a.m. Monday morning after hearing four days of testimony. During the trial, the state played a recording on an interview with law enforcement, during which Birch said, "I shot and killed my best friend."

The shooting was after an argument between the two men. Birch's defense attorney characterized it as self defense during closing arguments. 

“Luke had an impossible decision to make with no time to think,” the attorney, Ole Oleson, said. “... It's a desperate act of a man trying to survive.”

The state's argument, however, ultimately prevailed with the conviction. 

"Killing someone for angry words is not reasonable. Killing someone for pushing and shoving is not reasonable," said Adam Shiffermiller, the prosecutor on the case during closings on Monday.

title: Time is running out as the Bills home since 1973 gets closer to a methodical demolition
byline: By Mike Petro News Business Reporter
description: The former home of the Buffalo Bills has taken a major step toward becoming a thing of the past.
_full_text:
The former home of the Buffalo Bills has taken a major step toward becoming a thing of the past.

But it will not go out with a bang.

 Highmark Stadium excavator (copy)
An excavator is parked outside Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park. With power shut off to the venue as Friday, the start of the mass demolition of the Bills' home of 53 years has officially started.  

Power was officially turned off to Highmark Stadium Friday. It is considered the start of the stadium’s mass demolition and is a significant milestone for the project as the new stadium nears completion.

While the actual demolition isn’t scheduled to be done until next spring, work to ready the site to decommission the stadium is already occurring.

An increase in heavy construction machinery activity and noise and dust is expected at the current stadium site on Abbott Road, across from where the new Highmark Stadium is being built and will open for the 2026 season.

The final stretch: The journey to a new Buffalo Bills stadium

Explosives and implosions that have marked the end of other historic stadiums nationwide will not be used by the Bills, the team said.

The demolition will be mechanical, and the stadium will come down piece by piece. Crews will use heavy equipment such as bulldozers, excavators and wrecking balls. 

The Bills plan to keep their old administration building, behind the current stadium, and will be using parking lots next to and around the current stadium during the 2026 season as the excavation process occurs.

“Demolition is underway, and as part of the process, power was disconnected at the former stadium, as scheduled, on May 1," the Bills confirmed in a statement. "The project is slated for completion by March of 2027."

The beginning of the end of the stadium started in February, when Brandon Steiner’s CollectibleXchange began taking down signs and goal posts, and then ripping up seats and benches from the concrete. The turf and other items around the stadium followed. The items were put up for sale to fans wanting a piece of the stadium where the Buffalo Bills played for 53 years. 

Steiner's company was retained by the Bills and Erie County to salvage any stadium elements with resale value. They will split the proceeds with the county, which is expected to take in more than $1 million.

CollectibleXchange was expected to be done harvesting stadium items in April, likely setting the stage for some of the more significant work to take apart the stadium to begin this month.

 Highmark demo (copy)
Workers are seen on March 31 as they prepare Highmark Stadium for demolition, which will be mechanical as opposed to being imploded. 

The current stadium hosted its final game Jan. 4. Its footprint is a little over 900,000 square feet, and it is about 830 feet wide and 930 feet long. It seats around 70,000 fans, and the multi-level bowl rises about 140 feet above grade.

The project includes decommissioning of the current stadium, demolition, abatement, and disconnecting and removing existing utilities so the site can be filled to grade. It will likely be turned into a parking lot, although the Bills have talked about the potential for other uses.

Much of the fill will come from the dirt and soil lifted to create the hole for the new stadium. That is being stored next door to the SUNY Erie Community College campus on Southwestern Boulevard.

Harvesting collectibles from Bills stadium marks start to demo phase

Arc Building Partners is the project lead for demolition. Breeze National of Long Island is expected to be a major player in the effort to deconstruct the stadium through the demolition and asbestos abatement process. The downstate company led the demolition of Shea Stadium in Queens in 2009.

The latest NFL stadium being demolished is RFK Stadium in Washington, D.C., as the Commanders prepare to start building a new stadium, expected to be open for the 2030 season.

It is also being taken down piece by piece, rather than a quickfire implosion. The removal of the stadium’s structural steel has been completed, and the demolition of the remaining concrete structure and sorting of metal and concrete is nearly done over a year after the project started. 

 Highmark demo (copy)
Breeze National excavation equipment is set up at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park on Tuesday, March 31, 2026. (Joed Viera/Buffalo News) 

The Georgia Dome in Atlanta was one of the latest NFL stadiums to be imploded in 2017 to make way for Mercedes Benz Stadium – the home of the Falcons. A few years earlier, Candlestick Park in San Francisco was taken down piece by piece over multiple months after a plan to implode the stadium was scrapped amid concerns the blast might create health problems for people living nearby.

Originally part of the planned demolition in Orchard Park, the Bills had a change of heart about its old administration building, which was constructed with the current stadium in 1973 to house the team’s football and administrative offices.

Bills want to hold onto their old admin building when stadium is demolished

Although close to the stadium, it is structurally independent from it. The old administration building is at the east end zone of the current stadium toward Big Tree Road and across from the field house.

Much of the team’s staff and operations were moved to the newer administrative building attached to the field house, which was built in 1995 and went through major renovations more than a decade ago. But the older administration building continued to be used daily.

It now serves as office space for about 25 staff members and as a hub for staff check-ins, game production, IT infrastructure and event command operations. The first floor was used on game days for food and beverage operations, but that will move over to the new stadium.

title: Jury in deliberation after hearing closing arguments in Rapid City homicide trial
description: A Pennington County jury went into deliberations Monday, May 4, after hearing closing arguments from the state and defense for a Rapid City man who allegedly shot and killed his best friend McGarland "Mack" Walker VI at Candlewood Place in March 2024 in Rapid City.
_full_text:
A Pennington County jury went into deliberations Monday, May 4, after hearing closing arguments from the state and defense for a Rapid City man who allegedly shot and killed his best friend McGarland "Mack" Walker VI at Candlewood Place in March 2024 in Rapid City.

Luke Birch, 23, is charged with first-degree murder and, in the alternative, second-degree murder for Walker's death. Walker was shot and killed inside Candlewood Place, an apartment building in west Rapid City. Birch can only be convicted of one of the charges, not both.

 Luke Birch
Birch 

During jury instructions, the state also added first-degree manslaughter in the alternative to the other two charges.

The jury went into deliberations around 11:51 a.m. Monday morning after hearing four days of testimony.

Deputy State's Attorney Adam Shiffermiller began his closing arguments using Birch's own words during his interview with police after the March 8, 2024, incident. Shiffermiller quoted Birch describing Walker as a person who wants to resolve a conflict with a friend immediately and in person.

Shiffermiller said several witness testimonies and pieces of evidence, followed by Birch's own words with law enforcement, shows this case is not self-defense but an unjustifiable killing.

"He not only lied, he hid evidence, deleted text messages, he is doing everything he can to conceal what happened," Shiffermiller said. "... Killing someone for angry words is not reasonable. Killing someone for pushing and shoving is not reasonable."

Shiffermiller said Walker and Birch were arguing in finding a time to hangout, and through not being able to come to an agreement Shiffermiller acknowledged Walker proceeded to send angry texts to Birch.

Birch's attorney Ole Olson argued the texts were more than just angry messages, they were blatant threats. The jury was able to review the text where Walker swore on his children's life to harm Birch and texted “come out side an(d) shoot (explicitive).”

He highlighted how Walker came to Birch's apartment after work dressed in his work clothes, while Birch answered the door with "a ski mask and a gun."

Oleson said Walker also had a gun during the time of the incident. Shiffermiller said witness testimony showed Walker was known to carry a concealed firearm whenever he went to work and the gun never left the holster at the time of the shooting.

Shiffermiller said it was Birch who let Walker inside and that there was no evidence Walker forced his way inside or was committing any forceful felony that justified the shooting.

“It’s not a crime to be in an argument with your friends,” Shiffermiller said.

Oleson argued Birch may have unlocked the door to speak with Walker and de-escalate their argument, but he had no intention of letting him inside. He claimed Walker pushed and shoved Birch and himself further inside, continuing to threaten Birch.

Shiffermiller criticized how Birch told police that his first few shots “didn’t do s---” even though the autopsy report revealed none of the six shots were minor and nearly all of them were labeled fatal.

He said Walker never pulled out his gun, not even after being shot the first time. Shiffermiller quoted Birch when he described Walker transforming to an "aggressive," "angry" and "demonic" person he didn't recognize after being shot. Shiffermiller said he couldn’t imagine the hurt, the sadness and anger that came over Walker after being betrayed by his best friend.

“The last person to see McGarland Walker alive was the man who was supposed to be his friend,” Shiffermiller said.

Oleson said Walker was the one who brought violence to Birch’s doorstep and the evidence will show that this was clearly a case of self-defense.

“Luke had an impossible decision to make with no time to think,” Oleson said. “... It's a desperate act of a man trying to survive.”

Oleson acknowledged Birch did run after the shooting, hid evidence and initially lied to law enforcement, but not because of motivation to plan a murder, but because fear and trauma pushed him to do so.

Oleson said when Birch opened that door for Walker he was hoping to calm the situation down and that it was Walker who continued to push and shove, while threatening him.

“Luke is not a murderer, he’s a survivor of a tragedy he never asked for,” Oleson said.

Oleson said Birch had put his hand over his holster, warning Walker to calm down, that is when Walker said, "I'll show you how do that (explicative) for real," before he allegedly reached for his own gun. Birch, however, was able to pull out his gun first and fire.

“Either Mr. Birch has the fastest hands in the west or his gun was already drawn,” Shiffermiller said after highlighting a neighbor’s testimony seeing a young man dressed in all black with a face covering and holding a gun in hand.

Oleson decried the state and law enforcement for not doing a more thorough investigation after Birch told police about his self-defense case. Testimony from one of the lead investigators confirmed they did not contact Walker’s workplace or coworkers about his demeanor that day.

Additionally, Oleson said nowhere in Walker’s personal phone did it show if there were any problems between Walker and Birch prior to 4 p.m. on March 8, 2024. He criticized the state for not searching Walker’s work phone to see if there was any evidence of Walker’s motivation that day.

Shiffermiller argued defense has the same power and resources as the state to search and acquire evidence.

During closing arguments, Shiffermiller said Birch denied having a face cover to police, despite it being found with other pieces of evidence he had allegedly scattered around Wilderness Park. Oleson said Birch cannot be faulted for forgetting minor details.

Oleson called this case a tragedy, but there would be a bigger one if the jury didn’t carefully consider the facts of the case.

“The final tragedy would be a unanimous jury determining that self-defense in your own home is not justifiable in this city,” Oleson said.

Shiffermiller said the facts of the case will only point to one thing — that “Luke Birch is guilty of murder.”

“You have a really cool power today,” Shiffermiller said to the jury. “You get to be McGarland Walker’s last words.”

title: South Dakota Mines names new provost, CEE Department head
description: Two respected leaders at South Dakota Mines are stepping into new roles this spring.
_full_text:
Two respected leaders at South Dakota Mines are stepping into new roles this spring.

Jim Stone, Ph.D., current department head of civil and environmental engineering (CEE), has been appointed the university’s next provost and vice president for academic and student affairs. He succeeds Lance Roberts, Ph.D., who is stepping down to pursue opportunities outside higher education. Stone will begin his new role on May 22, 2026.

 jim stone.jpg
Jim Stone, Ph.D., current department head of civil and environmental engineering (CEE), has been appointed the university’s next provost and vice president for academic and student affairs. 

Stone previously served as interim provost during the 2025 university presidential search, a period when Roberts was serving as interim president.

In addition, Marc Robinson, Ph.D., professor and associate CEE department head, will step into the role of department head.

“Jim Stone and Marc Robinson are both highly respected leaders who have made lasting contributions to South Dakota Mines through their dedication to students, research and the success of their department,” said Mines President Brian Tande, Ph.D. “I look forward to working with both of them in their new roles.”

Stone has been a fixture at South Dakota Mines for more than 20 years. He earned undergraduate and master’s degrees at Virginia Tech before working for five years in industry, designing environmental remediation systems. Stone joined the Mines faculty in 2003, following the completion of his doctorate at Penn State University in 2002.

“Dr. Stone brings a thoughtful, collaborative approach and deep understanding of our institution to his new role as provost,” Tande said. “I am confident he will help guide Mines forward as we prepare students to meet the complex challenges of the future.”

As a professor, Stone’s research focused on a range of collaborative, interdisciplinary projects on sustainability and the environment. His work delved into issues around agriculture and environment, uranium mining, water quality and bioenergy production. Stone worked with environmental-focused students on relevant, real-world case studies and assignments to better prepare them to handle tomorrow’s complex environmental problems.

He has been CEE department head since 2020.

“It’s an honor and privilege to be considered for this leadership position at South Dakota Mines,” Stone said. “I’m looking forward to working with our talented faculty and staff across campus to help train our current and future science and engineering students for the grand challenges that await them in their future careers.”

In his free time, Stone enjoys everything outdoors - hiking, biking, snowboarding, camping. He recently completed the Dakota 5-0 mountain bike race, a challenging singletrack race in Spearfish, with his son Zander, a freshman civil and environmental engineering major at Mines.

Robinson joined the Mines faculty in 2009. He earned his undergraduate and master’s degrees from Utah State University. He worked at ABS Consulting, where he focused on the design of new buildings and the seismic retrofitting of existing structures. In 2008, he earned his doctorate in structural engineering from the University of California, San Diego.

 blur soil walkway with many trees in the park,place to exercise and relax. abstract, blur background
Marc Robinson, Ph.D., professor and associate CEE department head, will step into the role of department head. 

“Dr. Robinson’s leadership, industry experience and commitment to excellence make him exceptionally well-suited to lead the civil and environmental engineering department,” Tande said.

Robinson has advised numerous undergraduate and graduate students in a variety of research areas during his nearly two decades at Mines.

“I have been part of the CEE department at South Dakota Mines for 17 years, and I look forward to coming to work every day because of our outstanding students, faculty and staff,” Robinson said. “I’m excited to build on the strong foundation already in place as we continue to support our CEE family in achieving their professional goals.”

title: Rapid City Council to match up to $10,000 of funds raised by Bowl of Hope fundraiser
description: The Rapid City Council voted to approve authorization of using council contingency funds of up to $10,000 for the Bowls of Hope Fundraiser in partnership with St. Vincent de Paul.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Council voted to approve authorization of using council contingency funds of up to $10,000 for the Bowls of Hope Fundraiser in partnership with St. Vincent de Paul.

"I hope your offer to match funds will help our loving, caring community take on this challenge to match your $10,000 when a family is in need has a sudden emergency (and) they have to choose what bills to pay," said Eileen Desmond, vice president of the Society of St. Vincent de Paul Rapid City.

The Rapid City chapter of the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul, a Catholic charity, will manage and distribute the funds. The society helps people with rent, housing, utilities, groceries, gas and spiritual and emotional needs. 

 Bowls of Hope
Society of St. Vincent de Paul Rapid City Vice President Eileen Desmond speaking to the Rapid City Council at a meeting on Monday, May 4. 

The council voted 9-0 to authorize the funds at the May 4 council meeting. Councilman Rod Pettigrew (Ward 5) was absent at the meeting.

According to City Finance Director Daniel Ainslie, the city has done this same action in 2025 and wants to continue the donation this year on May 19, at the Dahl Arts Center.

According to city documents, the fundraiser event is a partnership between the city and St. Vincent de Paul, with the city's Public Works Department hosting soup events in exchange for donations. 

From previous reporting, this is a part of the city's program called, "City Utility Assist," aiding in raising funds through donations going directly toward helping eligible residents who are struggling to keep up with their city utility bills.

The event will be held on Tuesday, May 19, from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m., Rapid City inside the Dahl Arts Center. The event is free to attend with reservations for tickets available on Eventbrite. 

 Bowls of Hope
Council members Josh Biberdorf (Ward 1) and Lindsey Seachris (Ward 2) make up two of the 9 council members who voted on Monday, May 4, to approve of up to $10,000 of council contingency funds for the Bowls of Hope fundraiser. 

Council member Lindsey Seachris (Ward 2) said, "So I just wanted to commend our city staff for their work in bringing forward this effort ... Utilities can amplify a crisis situation pretty quickly. I'm going to be supporting this. I think our city staff have done a great job, and I'm just really proud of the city and have been observing this over the last year."

Councilman Stephen Tamang (Ward 1) posted on Facebook bringing awareness to the event, saying, "This is a simple idea with a real local impact: enjoy a bowl of soup, gather as a community, and help support Rapid City residents who are struggling with utility bills."

title: Mayor Salamun recognizes 2026 as the sesquicentennial anniversary of Rapid City
description: Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun declared 2026 the city's sesquicentennial (150th) anniversary at the Monday, May 5, Rapid City Council meeting.
_full_text:
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun declared 2026 the city's sesquicentennial (150th) anniversary at the Monday, May 5, Rapid City Council meeting.

 Salamun
Mayor Jason Salamun, right, reads a proclamation on behalf of the City of Rapid City recognizing 2026 as the 150th anniversary of the city's founding as Councilman Stephen Tamang, right, listens. 

"Rapid City is looking pretty good for our age, 150 years young," Salamun said.

 Darell Shoemaker
Public Information Officer for the City of Rapid City Darrell Shoemaker holds the proclamation recognizing the city's sesquicentennial milestone. 

He read aloud the proclamation, saying, "Whereas in February, 1876, John Brennan and Samuel Scott led a small party of discouraged gold prospectors to the banks of Rapid Creek on the hillside across from Founders Park, where they laid out a square mile business district. Within six months, more than 100 people called Rapid City home."

 Rapid City painting
A painting of early Rapid City inside The Journey Museum. 

Salamun continued, "And whereas the city's founders built a community as a gateway to the Black Hills, and it quickly lived up to the moniker. Originally known as Hay Camp, Rapid City soon became a staging ground for wagon solid supplies to miners in the Black Hills."

From previous reporting, On Feb. 22, 1876, a party of seven miners led by John Brennan left Palmer Gulch for Rapid Valley. They intended to found a town they envisioned as “the next Denver." After exploring the area, they camped at present-day Founders Park.

On Feb. 25, the original one-square-mile town site was laid out by Sam Scott and several others using a tape and a pocket compass. By the 1890s, Rapid City had surpassed Deadwood as the largest town in the Black Hills.

Salamun said the city has celebratory events to highlight this momentous occasion, a new exhibit in the Journey Museum dedicated to Rapid City opened in February, opening of a time capsule from 1976, and a new time capsule to buried and opened in 2076.

 Time capsule
City staff had to use electric tools like a saw to get the box open. 

A community photo for the new time capsule will be taken on May 22 at 1:30 p.m. at Main Street Square, and will be buried on May 29, at Founders Park.

City officials said list of items to be buried in the capsule include an article from the Rapid City Journal, a letter from the mayor and a print of the community photo.

City spokesman Darrell Shoemaker said the city will announce details of further items to be places in the capsule later this week. 

 Darell Shoemaker
Public Information Officer for the City of Rapid City Darrell Shoemaker holds the proclamation recognizing the city's sesquicentennial milestone.

title: Rapid City man who shot family member and broke into a stranger's home sentenced to prison
description: A Rapid City man was sentenced to 15 years in prison after shooting his family member twice and then breaking into a Rapid Valley home while fleeing from law enforcement.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man was sentenced to 15 years in prison after shooting his family member twice and then breaking into a Rapid Valley home while fleeing from law enforcement. 

Travis Chipps, 20, appeared for his sentencing before Circuit Court Judge Jeffery Connolly at the Pennington County Courthouse Tuesday, May 5. 

Chipps pleaded guilty in March to one count of aggravated assault, one count of first-degree burglary and one count of simple assault against a law enforcement officer for an "sliming" incident that occurred inside the Pennington County Jail. 

According to court documents, Chipps was initially indicted for attempted first-degree murder for shooting a man on Oct. 4, 2024.

Authorities were called to the 4200 block of Apple Tree Road around 12:15 a.m. that morning for a report of a man knocking on doors asking for help after being shot. The victim was later found with gunshot wounds. An investigation led officials to believe he had been shot at a different location. He was sent to the hospital and declared stable.

During the investigation into the shooting, an attempted burglary was reported around the 6200 block of East Highway 44.

The state said the shooting occurred earlier in the day, while the separate burglary incident happened later that evening.

In exchange for Chipps' guilty pleas, the state agreed to dismiss all other charges and request a 15-year sentence.

Deputy Pennington County State's Attorney Braedon Houdek said Chipps had shot his family member once in the face and once in backside before leaving the scene. 

While evading law enforcement, Houdek said Chipps broke into a stranger's home to hide. While incarcerated, Chipps threw a bag of bodily fluids at a corrections officer, which resulted in the simple assault charge. 

"Taken together, these acts show a person who is not just dangerous, but someone who has no regard for human life, no respect for authority and no basic decency," Houdek said. "He shot a family member in the face, invaded a home while fleeing and then assaulted a corrections officer in one of the most vile ways imaginable." 

Chipps attorney Paul Brankin highlighted Chipps young age and said he is "the product of the environment." 

Brankin requested the court for a partially suspended sentence so that Chipps has the opportunity to make a brighter future for himself. 

Connolly sentenced Chipps to 15 years in prison for aggravated assault, 15 years for first-degree burglary and two years for the jail incident. The sentences will run concurrently.

title: Project aimed at bringing Missouri River water to western South Dakota estimated at $4 billion
description: An estimated $4 billion project aimed at bringing water from the Missouri River to Western South Dakota is being spearheaded by the nonprofit Western Dakota Regional Water System.
_full_text:
An estimated $4 billion project aimed at bringing water from the Missouri River to Western South Dakota is being spearheaded by the nonprofit Western Dakota Regional Water System.

On Friday, April 25, Hay Camp Brewery hosted a panel discussion on the pipeline and water conservation in West River.

 Water
From left to right: Senior Project Manager with AE2S Jim Jones, Water Whys Irrigation and Landscape design owner Molly McDowell and Senior Public Director for Elevate Rapid City Garth Wadsworth 

The panel included state Rep. Nicole Uhre-Balk, D-32, Rapid City Water Superintendent Eric Boyda, Senior Public Director for Elevate Rapid City Garth Wadsworth, Senior Project Manager with AE2S Jim Jones, Water Whys Irrigation and Landscape Design owner Molly McDowell and Assistant Professor of Industrial Engineering at South Dakota School of Mines and Technology Rich Burgess.

 Water
From left to right: Assistant Professor of Industrial Engineering at South Dakota School of Mines and Technology Rich Burgess, Rapid City Water Superintendent Eric Boyda and state Rep. Nicole Uhre-Balk, D-32. 

The panel discussion started with information on the inception and goals of WDRWS. Jones said a 2019 study by researchers at the South Dakota School of Mines showed Rapid City could face water shortages during a prolonged drought period.

Jones said since the 1970s, Pennington County and the city have had future use permits for Missouri River water and given the results of the 2019 study, the municipalities should continue to pay for the permits as water conditions in Western South Dakota become questionable.

 Water
Slide of the current feasible water pipeline map and dimensions that could cost $4 billion to construct. 

"During extreme drought conditions in western Pennington County, there is already additional or more use than what aquifer recharge and surface water can support," Jones said on the study's findings.

He continued saying that if a drought of five years or longer were to occur the area would need further water access.  

"We have some concern. I wouldn't say it's a panic, but it is a concern that as populations increase, as more groundwater is tapped, there's potential that during extreme drought conditions, even today, that we might not have the capacity available," Jones said.

He said since 2021, WDRWS has been looking into the feasibility and funding of a pipeline of around 175 miles from Lake Oahe — which sits next to the Missouri River behind the Oahe Dam — to Rapid City.

 lake Oahe
Lake Oahe is the fourth-largest reservoir in the United States, stretching across over 200 miles. 

Lake Oahe is the nation’s fourth-largest reservoir according to South Dakota Department of Game, Fish and Parks. 

Similar developments already exist within the Missouri River, including the Mni Wiconi and Lewis and Clark projects, which bring water into other parts of the state.

Jones stated the current stage of a WDRWS feasibility study suggests the project could cost $4 billion, up from the $2 billion previously reported in 2024 by South Dakota Searchlight. South Dakota Congressional delegation is working to bring $10 million to the state for the feasibility study.

Jones said the price tag may change after the feasibility study is completed.

Wadsworth said the additional costs may also come from the long construction timeline for such a development.

"You've got the physical factors, you've got the length of the pipeline and the size of the pipeline, but then the time it takes to actually build it is a huge factor ... You get 10 years into a project, something happens. You run into roadblocks, you get delayed, and now you have to reinitiate, and it lands up costing more, not because the pipeline is more or the size of it is different, it's just the time it takes," Wadsworth said.

Funding for the pipeline

While the feasibility study continues, state officials are seeking funding to bring the project to life.

Uhre-Balk said she has been having conversations at the state level to secure funding for additional environmental and water projects. 

She said the passing of Senate Bill 231 established a water infrastructure development fund to aid in projects like the pipeline. The fund will have $3 million transferred from the state's general fund to the water infrastructure fund.

"That's a hard number to swallow, and in fact, there's no way that the state could do it at the state level. So, if the feds don't approve it, then it's, it's a non-conversation, even with the state of South Dakota. So for me, it does feel like (it) just depends on what happens with the feds," Uhre-Balk said.

Water conservation

Boyda said water conservation efforts by Rapid City are helping. In March Rapid City officials announced water restrictions, which started April 1. Also on April 1, the city elevated the storage condition status for Pactola Reservoir from “normal status” to “concern status.”

The restriction was due to current water levels and inflows at Pactola Reservoir. The reservoir level was at 47,532 acre feet, which is below the “concern status" threshold of 48,950 acre feet. The lower water level, coupled with the lack of snowpack remaining in the Pactola watershed areas, led to the restrictions.

 Water
A graph of both average Rapid City water usage and max day of water usage dating back to 1950. 

These measures limit residents' water usage from April through the end of September. No watering is allowed between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. daily. Odd-numbered addresses are allowed to water, outside those time restrictions, on odd-numbered calendar days. Even-numbered addresses are allowed to water on even-numbered calendar days. No outside watering is allowed on the 31st day of any month.

Manual watering with a handheld hose or with a bucket, sprinkling can or other similar container is allowed at all times.

This is the second consecutive summer Rapid City officials have instituted early water restrictions. Last summer, City officials implemented water conservation measures May 1, a month ahead of the annual water restriction period of June 1-Aug. 31.

 Water study chart
This chart shows that the estimated water supply in western Pennington County is already insufficient to cover demand in a dry period and will eventually be unable to meet the rising need for water in an average year. 

Boyda previously told the Journal the Rapid City water portfolio is made up of a mix of surface and stored water at 83%, and groundwater making up just 13% of the water the city uses.

Since the 1990s, the City of Rapid City has instituted mandatory water conservation measures, generally implemented June 1-Aug. 31 each year under "normal status" conditions. Status conditions include normal, concern, alert and critical stages and are determined by the water levels and inflows to Pactola Reservoir.

The “concern status” designation means whenever Pactola Reservoir contains less than 48,950 acre feet of water or the inflow to Pactola Reservoir is less than 90% of the mean monthly average, conservation measures will be implemented earlier and continue through Sept. 30.

Under the "alert status" designation, water conservation measures shall apply throughout the entire year and under the "critical access" designation, no outside watering is permitted. The status designations are determined by water levels and inflows at Pactola Reservoir.

Boyda, at the panel discussion, presented slides of the national average gallons of water compared to the city's usage.

"I just want to emphasize that right now people in Rapid City are using approximately the national median gallons per capita today," Boyda said.

Wadsworth said water restrictions for bigger cities with water limitations are already being used, like Las Vegas, which he said continues to grow despite these similar concerns.

"It's the quintessential desert, and they push water conservation reduction to its limit, and so it can conceivably reduce average households water consumption by 80%," Wadsworth said. "Us drinking the water is not the problem. It's everything around us ... The restrictions do not apply (to) the guy out there with the hose. We can think of all kinds of green spaces, that is where the majority of the residential water use goes."

"I would go ahead and add to that if we apply water to the landscapes as it's needed, and not uneven distribution, uniformity and over watering some areas, underwatering some other areas ... if we apply the water more evenly, there's a bigger picture that we could conserve and save in the fertilizer applications needed, and all of those other costs of that maintenance that goes along with maintaining the landscape," McDowell, the Water Whys Irrigation and Landscape Design owner, said about additional possible conservation efforts.

title: Man arrested for threatening others with gun at Planet Fitness in Rapid City
description: The Rapid City Police Department said it arrested a man who allegedly threatened people at Planet Fitness with a gun.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Police Department said it arrested a man who allegedly threatened people at Planet Fitness with a gun.

Around 12:50 p.m. on Saturday, May 2, officers were dispatched to 1845 Haines Avenue, Planet Fitness, for a report of a male threatening others with a firearm in the parking lot. The department said police located the suspect on arrival. Officers arrested Garrett Beu, 32, of Rapid City on two counts of aggravated assault.

An investigation determined that Beu was inside the gym and began to grow irate toward other patrons and staff, police said. At one point, Beu allegedly went out to his car, retrieved a handgun and walked back toward the entrance of the business. Employees locked the door and he was unable to get inside, police said.

Beu remains at the Pennington County Jail with no bond set, according to jail records. He's due in court at 10 a.m. on Tuesday, May 5.

title: 'Our church is the land': A look inside the camp occupying drill sites in the Black Hills
description: PE' SLA — At the end of a rough, one-lane Black Hills road, winding through ponderosa pines and framing cloudy skies, sits a camp of tents and tipis. Signs tied to trees and tents read: "Our church is the land," "Landback" and "Protect Pe' Sla."
_full_text:
PE' SLA — At the end of a rough, one-lane Black Hills road, winding through ponderosa pines and framing cloudy skies, sits a camp of tents and tipis. Signs tied to trees and tents read: "Our church is the land," "Landback" and "Protect Pe' Sla."

"We would never want to go into somebody's church and start drilling," said Wizipan Garriott, citizen of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe and president of NDN Collective, as he stood in front of a drilling machine at Site No. 1. Not far from the drill bit sat sage. The bit has yet to penetrate the earth, but at seven other sites like it, drilling looking for graphite has been underway.

 "Our church is the land"
A banner stating "Our church is the land" hangs at the Pe' Sla campsite.  

Pe' Sla means "the bald spot" in English. The high mountain prairie stands out among the treed areas surrounding it. In 2012, the Great Sioux Nation purchased Pe' Sla, 1,900 acres of land north of Deerfield Lake considered by the Lakota as the "center and heart of everything," the Journal reported. In 2014, the tribes purchased 437 additional acres. 

Garriott said, however, that it's not just the prairie area that's considered Pe' Sla, and if the tribes could have purchased more land in the area, they would have. But the surrounding area is owned by the U.S. Forest Service.

The drill sites are within a 2-mile radius around that tribally-owned land. Opponents claim those 2 miles are a designated buffer zone under a Memorandum of Understanding to protect Pe' Sla.

 Judge rules to halt Rochford drilling operations until further hearings are held
The U.S. Forest Service permitted the drilling on Feb. 27 for a large mineral exploration drilling project on USFS-managed public lands near Rochford in west Pennington County.

The memorandum wording is as follows: "Parties will discuss potential stewardship agreements with land management goals for the Black Hills National Forest that could include: (among other points listed in the document), co-stewardship of Black Hills National Forest lands, including lands within 2-mile radius of Flag Mountain and Pe'Sla Tribal Trust land."

Garriott, and other opposing the drilling, also point to the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 as establishing rights to the land.

The treaty recognized the Sioux Nation's rights to the Black Hills. After gold was discovered in the hills, the federal government broke the treaty in 1877. In 1980, the United States Supreme Court ruled in United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians that the treaty had been violated and ordered compensation. The tribes rejected the compensation and many people continue to fight for land reclamation today.

 Garriott
Wizipan Garriott, citizen of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe and president of NDN Collective, stands in front of a drilling machine at Site #1. 

"When we see drilling and destruction, it's impacting us on a very deep and personal level," Garriott said, adding the sacred places extend above, on and below the ground.

Garriott, community members, environmental organizations and all nine of South Dakota's tribes are joining in an effort to protect what they consider a threat to the sacred area, an exploratory graphite drilling project.

The camp sprung up near two Pete Lien & Sons Rochford Mineral Exploratory Drilling Project sites on Thursday, April 30, in an effort to prevent drilling. Those on site at the camp said they didn't encounter anyone drilling when they arrived, but drilling machinery and equipment sit on location. Garriott emphasized the group is not destroying any equipment.

Surrounded Bear, with the Oglala Lakota Youth Council, told the Journal on Monday. May 4, he had been at the camp since Thursday, April 30.

"It's been very beautiful. We started this in ceremony, and we've been in ceremony ever since because this is one of our most sacred sites located within the Black Hills," Standing Bear said. "In our origin stories, this is the center of the center. Pe' Sla is located right in the center of the Black Hills. 

 Drill
A drill with flags calling for the protection of Pe' Sla and landback on Monday, May 4.  

He continued, "And in our stories from the Lakota people, the Black Hills is the heart of Turtle Island, of this continent. So for us, this is the center of the whole continent. So this is like, literally the heart. And this is why we do as much as we could, to protect it, to preserve it, because this place isn't just land. It's our church, it's a hospital, it's a school, it's our home, it's everything."

The U.S. Forest Service permitted the drilling on Feb. 27 for a large mineral exploration drilling project on USFS-managed public lands near Rochford in west Pennington County. The permit allows the company to use its federal mining claims to look for graphite in the area.

A decision memo from the Forest Service allows for up to 18 boreholes at a maximum depth of 1,000 feet. 

At the beginning of April, NDN Collective, Black Hills Clean Water Alliance, and Earthworks filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Forest Service to block the project. The day before the camp formed, the organizations filed motions for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction in the lawsuit, asking a judge to stop Pete Lien & Sons from going forward with the project until the case can be heard. 

 Bald spot
Pe' Sla as seen from a ridge above drill sites.  

The plaintiffs argue in their filing the federal government violated the National Environmental Protection Act by incorrectly using a "categorical exclusion" to avoid factoring in concerns from tribal communities, clean water organizations and others. 

In response to public comment opposing the project, the Forest Service wrote, "The USDA Forest Service has fulfilled its tribal consultation responsibilities consistent with applicable legal and policy requirements. The proposed drilling exploration would not occur on Tribal Trust lands or private property. The Forest Service has conducted multiple government-to-government consultation meetings throughout 2025, including ten separate engagements with Tribal Government Representatives to discuss the proposed project."

The agency defended the categorical exclusion, arguing a short-term project of less than 12 months with incidental support activities allow for the categorial exclusion.

In addition to the NDN and partners lawsuit, all nine federally recognized tribes in South Dakota filed a joint lawsuit against the U.S. Forest Service on April 30, asking the court to suspend drilling operations until further hearings on the case are held. 

Garfield Steele, Oglala Sioux Tribe council member representing the Wounded Knee District, was also on site of the camp on Monday, May 4. He said the effort is about protecting the land for generations to come. He, and others, expressed concerns about the impact on water. 

 Garfield Steele
Garfield Steele, Oglala Sioux Tribe council member representing the Wounded Knee District, was also on site of the camp on Monday, May 4.  

"The water is the first medicine given to our people, and without water, there's no life," Steele said.

Director of He Sepa Initiatives at NDN Collective Valeriah Big Eagle, Hunkpati Dakota, said the efforts are about protecting the land for generations to come. 

The lawsuits stack onto the efforts at the drill sites, a demonstration at Pete Lien & Sons office in Rapid City on Friday, May 1, and an overwhelming turnout at the court hearing on Monday, May 4, where a judge heard arguments on the restraining order.

 Valeriah Big Eagle
Valeriah Big Eagle, director of He Sapa Initiatives at NDN Collective, speaks with media at the campsite.  

A Journal reporter waited an hour in line to get into the federal courthouse in Rapid City, where the hearing was held. The courtroom was full, and staff opened another courtroom to stream the proceedings. Inside, people sat on the floor. Outside, people stood with signs advocating for the protection of Pe' Sla.

U.S. District Court Judge Camela Theeler ruled to block any drilling until an evidentiary hearing is held on May 20 and May 21. Also at the hearing on Friday, the tribal lawsuit and the NDN and partners lawsuit were joined together. 

The Pennington County Sheriff's Office has called the activities of those gathering at the sites illegal. However, no one at the site has been arrested.

 NDN Collective, partners get temporary restraining order to stop drilling in the Black Hills
About 100 people gathered to the Rapid City federal courthouse to listen to the motions hearing. The judge heard arguments on the restraining order and ruled to block any drilling until evidentiary hearing held on May 20 and May 21. 

 Memorandum of Understanding
This Memorandum of Understanding between the Great Sioux Nation Tribes and the U.S. Forest Service was filed in a lawsuit against the Forest Service as proof of a 2 mile boundary around the Pe' Sla trust lands. 

 Photos from the camp in opposition of Rochford drilling project
The camp sprung up near two Pete Lien & Sons Rochford Mineral Exploratory Drilling Project sites in an effort to block drilling opponents said impact Pe' Sla, a sacred site to the Lakota people.
