title: Rapid City Community Cleanup yields 970 tons of trash, materials for landfill
description: More than 1,000 volunteers — young people, seniors, business teams, service club groups, city department directors, elected officials — picked up trash from fence lines, ditches, roadsides, creek beds and gullies in late April. Homeowners cleaned out garages, attics and basements of items no longer needed or wanted.
_full_text:
More than 1,000 volunteers — young people, seniors, business teams, service club groups, city department directors, elected officials — picked up trash from fence lines, ditches, roadsides, creek beds and gullies in late April. Homeowners cleaned out garages, attics and basements of items no longer needed or wanted.

When it was all tallied up, Rapid City residents picked up, bagged up, collected, hauled and delivered 970 tons of garbage to the Rapid City Landfill during the annual Cleanup Week April 20-25.

 Rapid City Journal cleans up
From left, Rapid City Journal staff members Tanya Manus, Frank Espinoza (foreground), Madison Willis and Shalom Baer Gee pick up trash in a marshy drainage area on Thursday, April 23, as part of Community Cleanup Week. 

This April’s yield of discarded items and trash materials easily surpassed the nearly 850 tons of garbage during the 2025 Community Cleanup Week and the 895 tons collected from the 2024 community effort.

In terms of vehicles, a total of 2,694 vehicles dropped off garbage during this year’s cleanup activities, compared to 2,315 in 2025. Including residential, yard waste and commercial traffic, a total of nearly 4,000 (3,971) vehicles passed through the Landfill scales in just one week.

A total of 80 volunteer teams, averaging 12-15 people, participated in this year’s cleanup activities April 20-24, with Community Cleanup Day on April 25. Some teams cleaned three to four areas. Of the tonnage collected, nearly five tons of waste was picked up by the volunteer teams.

“It was simply a spectacular effort by everyone,” said Rapid City Solid Waste Outreach Coordinator Ria Hannon. “Once again, teams were committed to the effort. They look forward to this week of cleanup each year. And the number of people hauling trash materials and items to the Landfill was definitely impressive.

“The community, from fence lines and ditches to home and garages, looks so much better.”

Hannon said community cleanup efforts are not just dedicated to one week of each year.

“We can commit ourselves to cleaning up our community throughout the year, one fence line, one volunteer team effort at a time,” Hannon said. “We can dedicate ourselves to picking up litter, taking a bag with us on an evening walk or working with colleagues once a month to cleaning up a specific area.”

For more information on what items can be dropped off at the Rapid City Landfill, visit www.rapidcityrecycles.org .

 PHOTOS: Rapid City Journal sets down keyboards, picks up trash for Community Cleanup Week
Rapid City Journal staff members picked up trash in a portion of the greenway along Rapid Creek on Thursday, April 23, as part of the 54th annual City-Wide Cleanup Week.

title: Pennington County proclaims May 3 through May 9 as Corrections and Care Campus Week
description: The Pennington County Board of Commissioners proclaimed the week of May 3 through May 9 as Corrections and Care Campus week, honoring correctional officers, nurses, teachers and mental health professionals working for the county.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Board of Commissioners proclaimed the week of May 3 through May 9 as Corrections and Care Campus week, honoring correctional officers, nurses, teachers and mental health professionals working for the county.

 County
The Pennington County Board of Commissioners proclaimed this is Corrections and Care Campus Week, and recognized the staff for their work. 

Commissioner Ron Weifencbach (District 2) declared at the May 5 meeting, "Now, therefore, we, the Board of Commissioners, County of Pennington County, South Dakota, do herby proclaim the dates of May 3, through May 9, as recognition of our professionals in corrections and Care Campus."

Weifenbach read and signed the proclamation to celebrate and give recognition to staff of the Pennington County Jail, Juvenile Services Center and Care Campus.

Pennington County Law Enforcement Division Chief Deputy Mark Hughes said, "Today is a pretty exciting month for us in corrections. We get to celebrate our correctional officers, our nurses, our mental health individuals and our teachers."

More than 10 staff members from both corrections and the Care Campus attended and gave their names and title to the commission. 

Pennington County Jail Commander Corey Brubakken said, "I just want to tell you how much we appreciate you taking this time to acknowledge our staff. It means a great deal to them and for the work that they do every day. It's very demanding, and it occurs behind the secure doors, so there's a little bit of publicity on that, but what they do is absolutely essential to the safety and success of our operation on daily basis."

Pennington County Jail Capt. Casey Munsch told the commission he has worked for the county at the jail for 20 years, Sgt. Kurt Clark said he has been with the county for 14 years.

 County
Joe Guttierez, commander of the Western South Dakota Juvenile Services Center, spoke at the meeting. 

Joe Guttierez, commander of the Western South Dakota Juvenile Services Center, has been with the county for 15 years.

Juvenile Services Center Sgt. Heather Heinert said she has been working for the county for 26 years.

"I appreciate everything you guys do. It's a reflection on our leadership that so many of you have invested so much time and I appreciate that. I appreciate that you make this county your home," Weifenbach said.

Guiterez said the week will celebrate staff and employees with various food dishes on each day, and on Friday, May 8, they will be saying goodbye to two retiring staff members at the Juvenile Services Center.

Commissioner Ron Rossknecht (District 1) said, "Thank you for your service. I've toured the facilities years ago I was really amazed at how well it was running, and how important it is to our community that help these folks get reset and get out and live a good life going forward."

 County
Commissioner Ron Rossknecht (District 1) stands with staff of corrections and Care Campus, recognizing their work for the county. 

Commissioner Deb Hadcock (District 4) said, "I agree with Corey (Brubakken), you guys don't get a lot of publicity, but you do a lot of hard work make Pennington County look successful and be successful. That takes a good team and takes some good leaders. Pennington County has the best so with your experiences ... it makes Pennington County a better place to work and live."

Commissioner Gary Drewes (District 5) said he appreciates the hard work the staff does. 

Commissioner Jerry Derr (District 4) said he commends their work field as he said it takes a special person to work in corrections.

title: Dancers' destination: Black Hills Dance Boutique moving to centrally located shop downtown
description: Black Hills Dance Boutique will soon celebrate its debut in downtown Rapid City when it moves to a new location.
_full_text:
Black Hills Dance Boutique will soon celebrate its debut in downtown Rapid City when it moves to a new location.

After ensuring the region’s dancers are ready for local recitals throughout the month of May, Black Hills Dance Boutique will open its new shop on June 8 at 429 Kansas St., Suite 1A.

 Black Hills Dance Boutique owner
Lindsay Ulmer, owner of Black Hills Dance Boutique, stands in her shop that's stocked with supplies and gifts for dancers in local recitals throughout the month of May. Black Hills Dance Boutique is moving and will open its new location, 429 Kansas City St., Suite 1A, on June 8. 

The move allows the boutique, which is currently at 3448 Sturgis Road, to be more centrally located for dancers and dance studios in Rapid City and the surrounding area. Black Hills Dance Boutique is the only independently owned dancewear store in western South Dakota.

Owner Lindsay Ulmer spent her life as a dancer and dance teacher before opening Black Hills Dance Boutique in March 2023. She performed with the Rocky Mountain Dance Ensemble, the Colorado Youth Ballet Company and Praise Dance Ensemble, Colorado Ballet Society, and the California Ballet, among others.

 Black Hills Dance Boutique accessories
An assortment of accessories dancers need for performances are displayed on a vintage tray at Black Hills Dance Studio in Rapid City. 

When she and her husband relocated to Rapid City from Denver, Lindsay saw a need for a local boutique that sold dancewear and shoes.

She brings expertise in dance, while her husband has a background in business and sales. The two took a leap of faith in opening Black Hills Dance Boutique, Ulmer said, and received a warm welcome from the local dance community.

 Black Hills Dance Boutique shoes
Ballet shoes are displayed at Black Hills Dance Boutique in Rapid City.  

“I get customers from all five studios (in Rapid City). I have had customers from North Dakota, Wyoming, Montana and Nebraska,” Ulmer said. “We reach a pretty really wide radius because as of right now, the only other independently owned dancewear store is either in Sioux Falls or Denver.”

In its new location, Black Hills Dance Boutique will continue to provide all of the essentials needed for classes, performances and competitions, Ulmer said. The boutique carries a variety of accessories, books, gift items, leotards, gymnastics wear, and more. New brands will be added when boutique moves downtown.

Black Hills Dance Boutique’s new location allows for better inventory storage and potential for growth.  

 Black Hills Dance Boutique shop
Shoes and leotards are on display at Black Hills Dance Boutique in Rapid City. The boutique is moving and will open its new location downtown on June 8.  

“I think with our move, I’m looking forward to meeting more dancers from around the area, especially the local dance community,” Ulmer said. “It’s really been a joy to establish our business here and just to see the community support that we have received. We have lots of very, very loyal customers. A lot of people have really expressed gratitude for the fact that we’re here and available, so that’s always very heartwarming.”

Having access to a local boutique that sells dancewear — especially shoes — is vitally important for dancers, Ulmer said. Dance shoes sometimes use European sizing that can be confusing for customers.

“I have gotten a lot of wonderful feedback — people that tell me, ‘Thank you. This is so convenient.’ It eliminates them needing to order things online and wondering about the sizing,” Ulmer said.

Ulmer said she’s learned to especially stock up on shoes as dancers prepare for their recitals.

 Black Hills Dance Boutique mirror
Black Hills Dance Boutique owner Lindsay Ulmer transformed a vintage mirror from her great-uncle into a one-of-a-kind sign for her business.  

“It’s definitely a busy season. Recital season can be a little bit hectic but it’s also really great to see some of the behind-the-scenes hard work that helps to bring the performances to life and being able to provide dancers with everything they need for a successful performance,” Ulmer said.

“There’s so much I enjoy (about recital season). One of my favorite things is getting the little tiny dancer in here that it’s going to be her very first time performing. They just love to come in here for their new shoes for the stage and get fit and talk to me all about what their costume is going to look like and how excited they are to be on stage,” Ulmer said.

Black Hills Dance Boutique’s new location will maintain its regular business hours: Monday and Wednesday 2 to 6:30 p.m., Tuesday and Thursday 2 to 6 p.m., and Saturday 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Follow Black Hills Dance Boutique on Facebook and Instagram for updates.

 Black Hills Dance Boutique cards
Handmade, locally crafted cards at Black Hills Dance Boutique in Rapid City are ready for recitals and other special occasions.

title: Update: 3 juveniles face consequences for damage Mary Hall Park restrooms
description: The restroom facilities at Mary Hall Park in Rapid City are closed indefinitely after considerable damage was discovered at the west side park Wednesday, May 6.
_full_text:
The restroom facilities at Mary Hall Park in Rapid City are closed indefinitely after considerable damage was discovered at the west side park Wednesday, May 6.

The facilities were among many opened for the summer season last Friday in the city’s park system.

In an afternoon update, the Rapid City Police Department said three juveniles have been identified as being involved in the vandalism. An investigation into the vandalism remains active the juveniles "will be held accountable through the appropriate channels of the juvenile justice system."

Toilets and sinks were damaged beyond repair and debris was strewn throughout the facilities.

 Mary Hall Park restroom damage #1
Damage to the bathrooms at Mary Hall Park discovered on Wednesday, May 6, is extensive.  

“There was serious and considerable damage to the restrooms. Sadly, we encounter issues with damage and graffiti in our City parks on a regular basis,” said City Parks Division Manager Scott Anderson. “This incident is one of the most substantial and serious instances of destruction I’ve seen.”

Restroom facilities in the city’s parks are checked and cleaned on a daily basis. City park rangers are also utilized to monitor conditions in the parks and greenway areas. Parks officials have closed various facilities in the past for various durations of time while repairs are made. Some facilities are not reopened due to continued issues with vandalism.

“The park facilities are a city asset and it will take considerable city resources to repair the damage,” said Anderson.

Officials are asking the public’s assistance and to report if they witnessed any suspicious activity at the park Wednesday afternoon.

 Mary Hall Park restrooms damage
Aside from the debris strewn about, toilets and sinks in the Mary Hall Park restrooms were damaged beyond repair. The damage was discovered on the afternoon of Wednesday, May 6. 

“We have increased our monitoring and efforts in the parks but it’s important for the public to step up and share if they see any suspicious activity in our parks. If they see something, say something,” Anderson said.

Mary Hall Park is located in west Rapid City off Sioux San Drive. It is one of more than three dozen parks in the city system.

Anyone with any information about the incident can call 605-394-4131. An anonymous tip can also be submitted by texting the letters "RCPD" and the information to 847411.

title: Authorities look for missing 9 week old last seen in Rapid City
description: South Dakota has issued an Endangered Missing Advisory for a 9-week-old boy last seen in Rapid City.
_full_text:
South Dakota has issued an Endangered Missing Advisory for a 9-week-old boy last seen in Rapid City.

According to an alert from the state, Melinko Ivan Bagola is Native American, has brown eyes and brown hair. The baby is 2 feet tall and weighs 12 pounds.

The alert said the baby was last confirmed to be seen in mid-April and is believed to have last been in the care of one of his parents, Tyler Slow Bear, 33, or Denitra Bagola, 31.

The alert said authorities know Slow Bear and Denitra Bagola's whereabouts and are only searching for Melinko.

Anyone with information is asked not to take action to rescue the child but to instead call 605-773-3536.

title: Rhoden activates South Dakota Drought Task Force
description: The South Dakota Drought Task Force held its first meeting on Thursday, May 7.
_full_text:
The South Dakota Drought Task Force held its first meeting on Thursday, May 7.

Gov. Larry Rhoden activated the task force earlier this week. The latest U.S. Drought Monitor shows moderate to extreme drought present throughout the lower third of South Dakota, with abnormally dry conditions across central parts of the state, the governor's office said in a release. Counties in northern South Dakota remain under normal conditions.

According to the monitor, the southern strip of Pennington County is in extreme drought, as is all of Custer and Fall River counties, and most of Shannon County.

The rest of Pennington County, save for the northeast panhandle, is in severe drought. The southern edge of Lawrence and Meade counties is also in severe drought.

“My administration is committed to protecting our farmers, ranchers, and communities across the state. While recent rainfall has provided some relief, drought is still impacting parts of South Dakota,” Rhoden said in a release. “The Drought Task Force will help us closely monitor conditions and respond quickly if needed.”

 050826-nws-drought-p1.png
The U.S. Drought Monitor for South Dakota, as of data from Tuesday, May 5, released on Thursday, May 7. 

The Drought Task Force coordinates the exchange of drought-related information among government agencies and partners to assess potential impacts on agriculture, fire management, and water supplies, the governor's office said.

"Through this collaboration, the Task Force can more effectively monitor drought conditions, assess drought severity, evaluate impacts, and review available drought-response resources," the office said in the release. 

State agencies represented on the Drought Task Force include the Governor’s Office, Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources, Department of Public Safety, Department of Game, Fish and Parks, South Dakota National Guard, Department of Social Services, Department of Tourism, and the Department of Tribal Relations. Additional partners include USDA’s Farm Service Agency and Natural Resource Conservation Service, South Dakota State University Extension and School of Mines climatologists, the National Weather Service, and South Dakota Rural Water.

Because of the dry conditions, the public is urged to use caution with open burns and other activities that could start fires.

title: Rapid City Hall serves as permanent donation location for 911 cell phones, other electronics
description: The Rapid City Hall lobby is now serving as a permanent drop-off location for the public to drop off cell phones, tablets, chargers and cords for the 911 Cell Phone Bank.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Hall lobby is now serving as a permanent drop-off location for the public to drop off cell phones, tablets, chargers and cords for the 911 Cell Phone Bank.

The City of Rapid City is coordinating the effort with the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office Victim’s Specialist Program. In December and January, the City Hall lobby served as a drop-off location for cell phones and related items A total of 419 phones were donated by the public and Victim’s Specialist Program turned the items over to the 911 Cell Phone Bank.

It was the second consecutive year the City of Rapid City participated in the holiday donation program. City Hall will now serve as one of the permanent donation locations for the program.

 Donation location
A donation box at Rapid City Hall accepts cell phones and other electronics for the 911 Cell Phone Bank. 

The used items will be repaired, refurbished, recycled and securely erased, then provided to partnering agencies to be given to victims of violent crimes.

“We are pleased to serve as a permanent location for donations of cell phones for this worthwhile effort,” said Kelly Langenbau with the City of Rapid City. “The phones are literally a life line for victims of violent crimes. We are encouraging the public to drop off the phones, tablets and accessories they no longer will use and know the items will continue to provide a great service.”

Donations are also accepted at the Public Safety Building, 300 Kansas City Street.

For more information, contact Rebecca Elger or Jeanne Mann with the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office at 605-394-6115.

title: A closer look at the federal ruling to halt Pe' Sla drilling
description: On Monday, May 4, U.S. District Court Judge Camela Theeler imposed a temporary restraining order blocking an exploratory graphite drilling project within an area in the Black Hills that is sacred to several Native American tribes.
_full_text:
On Monday, May 4, U.S. District Court Judge Camela Theeler imposed a temporary restraining order blocking an exploratory graphite drilling project within an area in the Black Hills that is sacred to several Native American tribes.

The U.S. Forest Service permitted the drilling on Feb. 27 for a large mineral exploration drilling project on USFS-managed public lands near Rochford in west Pennington County. The permit allows the company to use its federal mining claims to look for graphite in the area. A decision memo from the U.S. Forest Service allows for Pete Lien & Sons to drill up to 18 boreholes at a maximum depth of 1,000 feet. Drilling has occurred at seven sites. All 18 sites are within 2 miles of tribally-owned land known as Pe' Sla, which means "the bald spot" in English. 

 Project Pe'Sla Now! sign
About a 100 people gathered at the Andrew W Bogue Federal Building United States Courthouse to sit in the motions hearing held on May 4. The courtroom was full, and staff opened another courtroom to stream the proceedings. Inside, people sat on the floor. Outside, people stood with signs advocating for the protection of Pe' Sla.  

The high mountain prairie stands out among the surrounding treed areas. In 2012, the Great Sioux Nation purchased Pe' Sla, 1,900 acres of land north of Deerfield Lake considered by the Lakota as the "center and heart of everything," the Journal reported. In 2014, the tribes purchased 437 additional acres.

Opponents of the drilling state it's not just the prairie area that's considered Pe' Sla, however. The areas surrounding it are also of religious and cultural significance.

At the beginning of April, NDN Collective, Black Hills Clean Water Alliance, and Earthworks filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Forest Service to block the project. The nine federally-recognized South Dakota tribes filed their own suit. 

Theeler's ruling came after a three-hour hearing at the federal courthouse in Rapid City. On Tuesday, May 5, Theeler signed the official order. The 11-page document explains her legal reasoning. The restraining order is in response to both the nonprofits' lawsuit and the tribes' lawsuit. 

When a judge is considering a temporary restraining order, they must consider four factors:

The threat of irreparable harm to the movant (the party or parties requesting the order)
The balance between that harm and the injury that granting the injunction will inflict on the other parties
The probability of success on the merits
The public interest

Probability of success

In her analysis, Theeler determined the cases are likely to succeed on one particular issue: The U.S. Forest Service choosing not to make a report on how the project would impact the human environment. Theeler tackled this issue first in the analysis portion of her order.

The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) requires federal agencies, such as the U.S. Forest Service, to prepare Environmental Impact Statements (EIS) for proposed undertakings that will have significant effects on the human environment. Agencies must prepare Environmental Assessments (EA) for proposed undertakings whose effects on the human environment are uncertain. 

There are, however, exceptions in situations that do not have a significant effect on the human environment. If that's the case, agencies can issue Categorical Exclusions (CE) and bypass the environmental evaluations. 

One of the situations that allows for a categorical exclusion is a short-term (one year or less) mineral, energy or geophysical investigation and their incidental support activities. 

The U.S. Forest Service argues the project near Rochford fits into that exception. The judge disagreed.

The project includes post-drilling reclamation, including revegetation, noxious weed monitoring and treatment, and field inspections. The noxious weed monitoring and treatment will continue for two to three years after the drilling, with inspections ongoing for three years. Theeler noted another federal court explained in a 2024 case that exploration and reclamation are viewed as a single proposed project, which pushes the project over the one-year exception. 

Regarding the categorical exclusion used in this case, Theeler wrote, "...the Forest Service’s reliance on CE-8 (the categorical exclusion rule) was arbitrary and capricious because project operations, taken as a whole, will not be completed within one year."

Because of her finding on that issue, Theeler did not analyze the other claims in the case with respect to the temporary restraining order. 

Irreparable harm 

Theeler found the plaintiffs in both the tribal and nonprofit cases have established they'll suffer irreparable harm if the court did not act. That harm comes in the form of impact to sacred land and traditional, cultural and religious practices at Pe' Sla; harm to the water quality and drinking water resources; ecological harm to a rare landscape; and permanent loss of procedural rights under NEPA and the Historical Preservation Act.

"The harms described by plaintiffs are not speculative or generalized — many have already occurred," Theeler wrote, clarifying that harm includes impact on ceremonies that must be done during this season at Pe' Sla. 

She also wrote the plaintiffs suffered procedural harm by the elimination of the NEPA process that would review potential harms before the project approval. 

Equities and public interest

Theeler wrote she does not discount the interests Pete Lien & Sons and the public has in mineral exploration, but the damage to sacred cultural sites, disruption of religious ceremonies and risk to a unique ecosystem are significant and already recurring. 

She added the public has interest in the enforcement of NEPA, "which exist to ensure that federal agencies make informed decisions about projects affecting public lands and resources."

"The public interest in mineral development does not override the public interest in ensuring that development occurs only after lawful environmental review," Theeler concluded on that issue.

Bond

Theeler set a $10,000 bond in the case, meaning both groups of plaintiffs — the tribes and the nonprofits — must submit $10,000 to the court. If it's found Pete Lien & Sons or any other party is wrongfully affected by the restraining order, that money would go to them.

title: Brad Thomson
description: January 3, 1958 - January 8, 2026
_full_text:
January 3, 1958 - January 8, 2026

Brad A Thomson, age 68, passed away on January 8, 2026, at his home in Lake Wales, Florida.

He was born in Casper, Wyoming, and raised in Rapid City, South Dakota. In his early years, he served United States Marine Corps, PVT- a Vietnam Veteran, a role he carried privately and without fanfare. He was a father of three, and a man whose life moved through distinct chapters.

Over the course of his life, he walked many paths- known fully to some and only partially to others. To those who loved him early on, he was Dad- a role that carried meaning, memory, and emotion that changed over time.

Life did not unfold simply, and relationships evolved in ways that were sometimes distant and sometimes quiet. Still, he remains part of the story of those who came from him. There are memories-some clear, some faded- held with a mix of gratitude, sadness, and reflection. Even when time and circumstance created space, the connection was never entirely erased.

He is remembered not only for who he was, but for the impact of his presence, however brief or complicated it may have been. His life reminds us that families are imperfect, that love can be layered, and that remembrance does not require full understanding.

He is survived by his children Dawn (Rick) Tiegs, Brad Jr. (Carrie) Thomson, & Derricka (Joe) Hansen; Grandchildren Justice (Emma) Miller & ShawnMarie (Gavin) Lubovinsky, Austin Gieswein & Wyatt Thomson, Clair, Thomas, Alice & Benjamin Hansen; Great Grandson River Lubovinsky; siblings' Donna (Pat), Wendt, Debbie (Don) Morgan, Sky (Libby) Thomson, & Greg (Peggy) Thomson; as well as many nieces and nephews.

He will be laid to rest July 20, 2026, at 2:30 pm with a Military Honors Service held at the Black Hills National Cemetery, with family and others whose lives intersected with his in ways known only to them. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that time be taken to reflect on the complexity of human relationships, and the grace it takes to carry them forward.

title: Pete Lien & Sons pulls out of Rochford drilling project near Pe' Sla
byline: SHALOM BAER GEE and MIKE BROWNLEE Journal staff
description: An exploratory graphite drilling project in the Black Hills that opponents said threatens Pe' Sla, an area sacred to several Native American tribes, appears to have come to an end.
_full_text:
An exploratory graphite drilling project in the Black Hills that opponents said threatens Pe' Sla, an area sacred to several Native American tribes, appears to have come to an end.

NDN Collective said in a Friday, May 8, press release the nonprofit was notified that Pete Lien & Sons sent a letter U.S. Forest Service withdrawing their plan of operations for the Rochford Mineral Exploratory Drilling Project. The letter, a copy of which was provided to the Journal by NDN, Pete Lien & Sons Chief Operating Officer Brian Tidemann told the Forest Service the company withdraws its Plan of Operations for the site.

At the beginning of April, NDN Collective, Black Hills Clean Water Alliance, and Earthworks filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Forest Service to block the project. The nine federally recognized South Dakota tribes filed their own suit.

"It's is a great day for all people who live in the Black Hills," Wizipan Garriott, president of NDN Collective, told the Journal. "It shows what can happen when the community and community members step up to say no against illegal mining that threatens cultural and sacred sites and places."

In a release, Garriott called the effort, "the result of courageous land defense by the community, strategic legal action, and collective prayer."

"We celebrate, but we also understand that there's a lot more work ahead," Garriott told the Journal, "because there are many other places that are being threatened by mining activities in the Black Hills."

The Journal left a message with Pete Lien & Sons that wasn't immediately returned. In the letter to the Forest Service, Tidemann said the company does not plan to apply again for exploratory drilling at the site.

Messages to the U.S. Forest Service communications team in Washington DC weren't immediately returned. USFS Mystic District Ranger James Gubbels, who was named in the lawsuit along with the U.S. Forest Service and U.S. Department of Agriculture, said he was unable to comment because of the pending litigation.

Other efforts against the drilling included a multi-day occupation of two drill sites at the project.

“From the very beginning of this battle, our ancestors were with us – we felt prayers coming to Pe’ Sla from all over Turtle Island,” Valeriah Big Eagle, director of He Sapa Initiatives at NDN Collective, said in the release. “When we ground together in truth and what is right, led by our spiritual leaders and the next generation of warriors, we are unstoppable. This is just the beginning.”

The Friday news comes at the heels of a Monday, May 4, federal court ruling from U.S. District Court Judge Camela Theeler, who imposed a temporary restraining order blocking the drilling, citing procedural issues and the cultural significance of the site.

 drill
A drill at one of the Rochford project sites on Monday, May 4. 

The U.S. Forest Service permitted drilling on Feb. 27 for a large mineral exploration drilling project on USFS-managed public lands near Rochford in west Pennington County. The permit allowed Pete Lien & Son to use its federal mining claims to look for graphite in the area. A decision memo from the U.S. Forest Service allows for Pete Lien & Sons to drill up to 18 boreholes at a maximum depth of 1,000 feet. Drilling occurred at seven sites.

 IMG_8428.png
The letter from Pete Lien & Sons to the National Forest Service. 

All 18 sites are within 2 miles of tribally-owned land known as Pe' Sla, which means "the bald spot" in English.

Pe’ Sla is sacred to the Lakota, who have visited the site for thousands of years, the NDN Collective release noted, adding, "It is actively utilized for prayer, ceremony, and cultural activities — and with today’s victory, will be the site for many more ceremonies to come."

“This victory reaffirms a critical human truth — that we all have a right to clean drinking water,” Lilias Jarding, executive director of the Black Hills Clean Water Alliance, a part of the lawsuit with NDN Collective, said in the release. “Community engagement and action forced an extractive company off our shared land. Today is a reminder that not only do we all have a duty to protect the Black Hills from harmful drilling and mining projects — but that we have the ability to win.”

Garriott said the next step on the lawsuits he expects would be the removal of the temporary restraining order so Pete Lien & Sons can begin the reclamation process at the land. Pete Lien & Sons confirmed its reclamation plans in the letter.

"It's going to take a while for that work to be completed so that the land can be fully reclaimed," he said, noting preliminary work for the drilling included adding drill pad sites and roads.

 Photos from the camp in opposition of Rochford drilling project
The camp sprung up near two Pete Lien & Sons Rochford Mineral Exploratory Drilling Project sites in an effort to block drilling opponents said impact Pe' Sla, a sacred site to the Lakota people.

title: Rapid City father arrested for alleged murder, hiding body of missing infant
description: A father was arrested Friday morning after police found the body of his missing infant son at an undeveloped outdoor location in Rapid City overnight.
_full_text:
A father was arrested Friday morning after police found the body of his missing infant son at an undeveloped outdoor location in Rapid City overnight.

Tyler Slow Bear, 33, of Rapid City was arrested Friday, May 5, on suspicion of second-degree murder and improper disposal of a body.

 Tyler Slow Bear
Tyler Slow Bear 

The Rapid City Police Department was originally called to Slow Bear's residence at around 9:05 on Thursday, May 7, for a welfare check after someone called with concern for baby Melinko Bagola's safety. 

Bagola was left in Slow Bear's care, however, when the reporting party attempted to make contact with the baby, he was nowhere to be found. Bagola was last seen on April 19.

Police made contact with Slow Bear and could not find the infant at the residence. Slow Bear told police a family member was watching the 9-week-old baby, but it was later discovered the family member lived on a different side of the state and did not have the baby. 

 Melinko Bagola
Melinko Bagola 

Slow Bear was brought in for further questioning about the infant's disappearance. During the interview, it was determined that Slow Bear assaulted Bagola and the infant died at some point following the assault. 

Following the infant's death, Slow Bear concealed Bagola's body at an undeveloped outdoor location in Rapid City. Police searched the location overnight and found the infant's remains. 

"The work our officers poured into this case is a testament to their diligence and dedication," Rapid City Chief of Police Don Hedrick said in a release. "Our team, in collaboration with our local law enforcement partners, worked to thoroughly progress this case from a welfare check to a homicide arrest in less than 24 hours. The loss of a child in our community is never easy, and our hearts ache for those who loved baby Melinko. We will continue to work tirelessly to ensure Rapid City is a safe place for every child." 

 050926-nws-missing-p1.pdf
This Endangered Missing Advisory was issued on Thursday, May 7, and later canceled that evening.

Slow Bear has a prior 2019 conviction for possession of a controlled substance, where he was sentenced to five years in prison, according to South Dakota court records. He was released on parole and violated it in 2021, where he was found guilty and was given a suspended sentence. Slow Bear has several other convictions from 2022 to 2025 for domestic simple assault, resisting arrest and obstructing police, jailer or firefighter, jail records show.

An autopsy has been scheduled in the ongoing investigation into Bagola's death. As of Friday morning, Slow Bear is being held at the Pennington County Jail with no bond.

title: Water worries: Billions needed to keep South Dakota taps flowing
byline: BART PFANKUCH South Dakota News Watch
description: Compared to several states to the west, South Dakota is not even in the conversation of places in danger of experiencing a water crisis.
_full_text:
Compared to several states to the west, South Dakota is not even in the conversation of places in danger of experiencing a water crisis.

Arizona, New Mexico, California and Colorado are increasingly in panic mode trying to find reliable sources of drinking water to quench the thirst of growing populations and future generations.

Over its 137 years of statehood, South Dakota has relied on rivers and reservoirs but mostly on underground aquifers to provide high-quality fresh water in quantities sufficient to accommodate slow but steady population, agricultural and industrial growth.

But that comfort level is quickly evaporating, and signs of ongoing or potential water shortages are popping up in all corners of the state. Among them:

The WEB Water system in Aberdeen has declared several portions of its service area as "moratoriums" in which no further water taps can be added until system capacity increases.

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers recently announced that ongoing drought has lowered Missouri River water levels, potentially affecting barge traffic, hydro-electric generation and recreational activities.

Facing declining water levels in the Big Sioux Aquifer, the Minnehaha County Water Corp. in Dell Rapids has turned away potential high water use industrial employers to maintain service to existing residential and municipal customers.

A 2025 federal geological survey showed that some of the "sub-aquifers" that provide fresh water to northern Black Hills communities are not recharging as fast as they are being depleted.

Due to low water levels in Pactola Reservoir and a forecast of continued drought, Rapid City officials in April enacted summer water use restrictions two months earlier than usual.

Looking 40 years into the future

While those impacts are not seen as harbingers of an immediate or near-term crisis in the state, they are generating concern over what could happen if South Dakota waits too long to begin finding future reliable sources of water.

"Statewide, water managers are seeing this and realizing we need to start making plans now for 40 or 50 years into the future," said Shane Phillips, executive director of the WEB system that provides 6 million gallons of water a day to nearly 40,000 people and hundreds of farms and businesses in north-central South Dakota. "If you wait until the need is there, you're already way behind."

In response, local, regional and state water officials are pushing forward with water projects that will surely cost billions of dollars and increasingly tap into one of the world's greatest sources of fresh water and the longest river in the U.S. — the mighty Missouri River.

"There's a tsunami of water projects underway or under discussion in South Dakota right now," said Troy Larson, executive director of the Lewis & Clark Regional Water System, a massive South Dakota-based provider of water to much of the state's southeastern quadrant and parts of Iowa and Minnesota.

 2026-4-10 Big Bend Dam.jpeg
The Missouri River is shown at the Big Bend Dam near Fort Thompson, S.D., on April 10. 

To grasp the scope of the proposals, News Watch reviewed documents and conducted interviews to gain an understanding of ongoing or planned major water projects in the state. The four largest:

Lewis & Clark has nearly copleted its $711 million "base system" that serves 20 communities, including Sioux Falls, with 44 millions of gallons per day (MGD). An expansion to 60 MGD is underway, with a second expansion to 155 MGD planned after that, all with a price tag of unknown billions of dollars.

WEB water and its new WINS cooperative serving Aberdeen and communities to the east has made $20 million in improvements since 2016. The system is spending $82 million to expand its treatment plant and add a new 50-inch pipeline upgrade.

Western Dakota Regional Water System representatives recently testified before Congress to seek approval of a feasibility study for a 165-mile, 71-inch pipeline from the Missouri River to Rapid City and more than 50 communities and systems in the Black Hills region. If approved, the project is estimated to cost at least $3 billion and take decades to construct.

The Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System Inc. is also seeking congressional approval of a feasibility study on an ambitious project to pump Missouri River water to almost the entirety of East River South Dakota and parts of Minnesota and Iowa. The project could include a 96-inch main pipeline and a price tag of up to $10 billion.

"Experts have shown us that we’re straining our aquifers in South Dakota, and we need to act now so our future generations don't have to react," said Kristen Conzet, director of the Western Dakota system. "The cheapest time to do any of this is now if not yesterday."

Larson said the need for water is being driven mainly by population growth and a long-range drought in many areas of the state.

 2026-3-19 Missouri River near Vermillion.jpeg
Due to a lingering drought, the Missouri River was running low on March 19, 2026, at this major bend south of Vermillion, S.D. This image was taken from the Mulberry Bend Overlook in northern Nebraska. 

Other water managers said the state needs to be prepared to sustain existing industries such as agriculture production and ethanol and be ready to accommodate new businesses including data centers or other employers that may locate in South Dakota in the future.

Major water projects are paid for through a variety of sources. In a typical example, the $711 million Lewis & Clark base system was funded at 80% from the federal government, 10% from the three states serviced and 10% from customers, Larson said.

A shift to regional systems and the Mighty Mo

For generations, and currently in many regions, South Dakota homes, farms and municipalities mostly tapped into underground aquifers with individual wells to obtain fresh water.

But as the state has grown, and water pipeline and treatment technologies have evolved, the state has moved to a model known as "regional water systems" in which a main provider of water taps a river or reservoir and installs underground pipes for distribution.

The origin of the model dates back about 50 years to a heated battle that took place over how to obtain water from the Missouri River in the north-central part of the state and what to use it for.

The proposed Oahe Irrigation Project was a federal government effort to build a series of canals to provide Missouri River water to agricultural producers in a 190,000-acre area in Brown and Spink counties. But it faced opposition — largely from landowners who opposed the forced taking of their land — and caused heated division among residents, farmers, and local, state and federal officials.

After extensive lobbying of federal officials, and gaining control over a regional water board, opponents halted the project and its federal funding in 1978.

 2026-3-17 Troy Larson with photo.jpeg
Troy Larson, executive director of the Lewis & Clark Regional Water System, points to a photo in the system's headquarters in Tea, S.D., on March 17. 

Roger Schuller, a third-generation farmer from Claremont, was a vocal opponent of the irrigation canals and has since become a historian of South Dakota water projects.

“We were trading a billion-dollar project for a lot less expensive project that would service thousands of people instead of a smaller amount of recipients who farmed,” Schuller, 82, told News Watch. “It changed the direction of water development in South Dakota.”

As the irrigation effort was unraveling, the WEB rural water system was taking shape as its replacement. The pipeline system, which carries fresh water to a wide swath of northeastern South Dakota, remains in operation and is now undergoing a large expansion.

“The WEB project, to my mind, was the start of the rural water revolution as we see it now in this state,” said Schuller, adding that the project fueled both population growth and the development of the ethanol industry in the region. “Water is the key for human consumption and for any industry you want. But you can expect controversy to arise around almost any water project.”

Internal, external race for water system capacity

From a broad perspective, South Dakota is in a race to obtain more Missouri River water on two separate fronts.

First off, the state needs to make investments now and begin building pipeline infrastructure because major systems can take 30 to 50 years to complete, said Kurt Pfeifle, 66, executive director of the Dakota Mainstem project.

 South Dakota News Watch logo

"I probably won’t be around when this project gets built," said Pfeifle, 66, who formerly was head of South Dakota Association of Rural Water Systems. "If you’re going to do these big things, you need to start now because it’s not going to get done quickly or be any cheaper than it is now."

But the state is also eager to build new water systems in order to get ahead of other states that could potentially try to tap into the Missouri River as a source for desperately needed water.

The threat of Colorado or New Mexico possibly building a pipeline to the Missouri is a topic that South Dakota water managers approach with caution because they don't want to legitimize a concept with a low likelihood of becoming reality.

But at the same time, it's one they must confront.

While no firm proposals are being considered, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation did consider a proposal in 2012 backed by several Western states to tap the Missouri River. The idea never took hold, but it called for an $11 billion, 670-mile pipeline to provide water to 1.2 million customers in seven arid states that rely on the faltering Colorado River for water.

 2026-3-20 Clay water system.jpeg
Rural South Dakota relies heavily on small water systems, but plans are underway to expand capacity through a handful of major water providers. The Clay Rural Water System, shown on March 20, 2026, operates near Wakonda. 

Phillips, director of WEB Water, said he has heard estimates that if the city of Denver implemented an additional 1% sales tax, the city could quickly afford to build a pipeline to the Missouri River. If other states tap the Missouri, it could reduce water availability for states that already rely on the river, including South Dakota.

"We have one of the greatest water resources in the world, the Missouri River, running right through our state. And if we don’t think of ways to utilize it properly, the concern is that other states will figure out a way," Phillips said. "It’s a cautionary tale and a reminder that we need to plan for the future now."

 Water conservation
Public Works Director Mike Theis discusses water conservation efforts in Rapid City during an Elevate Rapid City Critical Issues Luncheon on Thursday, May 7, at the Rushmore Hotel in Rapid City.

title: Lee Enterprises reports sharp Q2 gains, digital revenue leads growth
_full_text:
Lee Enterprises, the Davenport, Iowa-based publisher of the Rapid City Journal, Casper Tribune and other publications nationwide, on Thursday, May 7, reported sharply improved second-quarter results.

 

The company said adjusted EBITDA — or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization — increased $7 million, or 95%, from the prior-year quarter. That marks Lee’s fourth consecutive quarter of year-over-year adjusted EBITDA growth on a comparable basis.

 

Net loss narrowed to about $2 million during the quarter ended March 29, compared with a loss of roughly $12 million during the same period a year earlier.

 

Other company results released Thursday include:

Total operating revenue was $122 million.

Total digital revenue was $68 million and represented 56% of Lee’s total operating revenue.

Revenue from digital-only subscribers totaled $22 million, an increase of 17% annually over the past three years. Digital-only subscribers totaled 591,000 at the end of the quarter.

Total print revenue was $54 million.

“In the quarter, we continued to take proactive steps to align our cost structure with the ongoing shift in our revenue mix,” President and CEO Nathan Bekke said.

 

“These actions include further optimization of our operating footprint, streamlining of workflows, reduction in corporate overhead, and continued prioritization of investments that support digital growth,” Bekke said. “As a result, we are realizing meaningful efficiencies while maintaining our focus on delivering high-quality local journalism and content.”

 

The earnings report comes months after investor David Hoffmann led a $50 million investment in the company that reduced Lee’s borrowing costs.

 

Under the agreement announced in December, the company’s interest rate on roughly $455 million in debt was reduced from 9% to 5% for five years, a move Lee says is expected to save about $18 million annually in interest expense. Hoffmann became chairman of the board following the deal’s closing.

Lee’s portfolio includes more than 70 publications in 25 states. Other titles include the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, Omaha World-Herald, Richmond Times-Dispatch and Wisconsin State Journal.

 

The earnings report Thursday also referenced insurance reimbursements tied to a cyberattack last year that disrupted billing systems, vendor payments and other operations. Lee said approximately $4 million in business interruption recoveries contributed to quarterly adjusted EBITDA.

 

Excluding those reimbursements, the company said underlying operating performance still drove adjusted EBITDA growth of 45% year over year.

The $455 million in debt is outstanding under its credit agreement with BH Finance. The financing includes a 25-year maturity, a fixed annual interest rate, no fixed principal payments and no financial performance covenants.

Lee finished the quarter with $53 million in cash, up $49 million from a year earlier.

 

“This improved liquidity, combined with lower interest expense, positions us well to accelerate our strategic priorities and further strengthen our balance sheet over time,” Bekke said.

title: 4 big water projects underway in South Dakota
byline: BART PFANKUCH South Dakota News Watch
description: VERMILLION — In a wooded site along the west shore of the Missouri River, an engineering marvel was taking shape one afternoon in March that will eventually help provide fresh water to hundreds of thousands of people.
_full_text:
VERMILLION — In a wooded site along the west shore of the Missouri River, an engineering marvel was taking shape one afternoon in March that will eventually help provide fresh water to hundreds of thousands of people.

Contractors hired by the Lewis & Clark Regional Water System had positioned 16-foot concrete rings above a structure known as a Ranney well that will draw water from an aquifer 140 feet below the surface. To form the sides of the giant well, workers jam several of the sleeves into the caisson structure that collects water through a series of pipes that extend outward at the bottom.

The construction is part of a wide-scale increase in water service capacity now underway in South Dakota, where water managers of several systems are implementing plans to serve the state for the next 40 to 50 years.

To ensure a steady supply of high-quality drinking water, four major projects are in progress to take more water from the Missouri River.

Headquartered in Tea, the Lewis & Clark Regional Water System was authorized by Congress in 2000 and began delivering water in 2012.

The base system is nearly completed at a cost of $711 million to provide 44 million gallons of treated Missouri River water per day to 20 communities in southeastern South Dakota, including Sioux Falls, and in Iowa and Minnesota.

 2026-3-18 L&C operator Jim Auen.jpeg
Jim Auen, operations manager for the Lewis & Clark Regional Water System, stood on March 20, on the roof of the water treatment plant that is under expansion just north of Vermillion. 

The system uses wells positioned on the banks of the Missouri River to capture aquifer water that is treated and then shipped through a 54-inch main underground pipeline.

The first expansion began in 2022 and will cost an estimated $150 million to increase the water flow to 60 million gallons per day (GPD) by 2030. The project includes an expansion of the water treatment plant, addition of a new storage facility and construction of a new water collection well along the Missouri River near Vermillion.

The second expansion, now in the feasibility study stage, could increase water flow to 165 million GPD.

The Water Investment in Northern South Dakota (WINS) project is a regional collaborative that includes the WEB Water system, the BDM Rural Water System and the city of Aberdeen.

 2026-3-18 L&C new Missouri well.jpeg
A concrete sleeve was ready on March 20, 2026, to be pushed down into a new Lewis & Clark collector well on the banks of the Missouri River near Vermillion. 

WEB, the main portion of the project, was launched in 1975 to tap the Missouri River to initially serve the counties of Walworth, Edmunds and Brown in north-central South Dakota.

Since 1986, the system has taken Missouri River surface water at a point on Lake Oahe south of Mobridge, treated it to drinkable status and then shipped it through 688 miles of underground pipe heading east and north.

The system now provides up to 11 millions of gallons of water per day to 18 counties, 15 of them in South Dakota and three in North Dakota.

WEB has spent $20 million on improvements since 2016 to strengthen delivery systems, even though those projects have not expanded capacity to allow for more users.

To accommodate expected growth and increase area water needs, WEB is in the midst of an $82 million upgrade that will include 14 miles of 49.5-inch parallel pipeline and an expansion of its treatment plant from a capacity of 11 million GPD to 17 million GPD.

 2025-4-25 WEB water construction.jpeg
o expand water capacity, WEB Water has added a new 50-inch pipeline from the Missouri River to this location at the intersection of U.S. 12 and state Highway 83 south of Selby, S.D., shown in April 2025. 

The Western Dakota Regional Water System was formed in September 2021 largely to pursue a 72-inch pipeline about 161 miles from the Missouri River to the Black Hills region.

The system is pursuing a $13 million feasibility study that is a requirement of a large project under the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation.

So far, 56 municipalities or water systems from Winner to Fort Pierre to Rapid City have signed on as partners.

The pipeline would supplement the many existing West River water systems that draw from aquifers, which are slowly depleting..

The Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System is also in the planning stages and would provide water to a huge swath of eastern South Dakota and parts of Minnesota and Iowa.

 2025-4-21-Pactola-sign-goose-low-1.jpg
Sand bars not normally seen on Pactola Reservoir, S.D., in the Black Hills of South Dakota were visible in April 2025 due to unusually low water levels. The reservoir is a water source for the Rapid City region. 

So far, 57 potential members have signed on to the plan to build a pipeline up to 96 inches in diameter to carry treated water taken from Missouri River aquifers near Yankton. The project could take more than 20 years to build and cost as much as $10 billion.

Dakota Mainstem officials were set to attend their own feasibility authorization hearing before Congress on April 29.

 Mike Theis water discussion
Rapid City Public Works Director Mike Theis discusses levels at Pactola Reservoir during an Elevate Rapid City Critical Issues Luncheon on Thursday, May 7, at the Rushmore Hotel in Rapid City.

title: Red Ribbon Skirt Society pushes for 'Feather Alert' System for South Dakota
description: On Tuesday, May 5, the Red Ribbon Skirt Society held a memorial for Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women by gathering outside of the Journey Museum, honoring two recent MMIW cases and pushing for a state-wide alert system for missing Indigenous people.
_full_text:
On Tuesday, May 5, the Red Ribbon Skirt Society held a memorial for Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women by gathering outside of the Journey Museum, honoring two recent MMIW cases and pushing for a state-wide alert system for missing Indigenous people.

"I think it's critical that we put that in place, not only to help our missing and murdered, but to find our people. As a state, we're always talking about building relationships, we're always talking about reconciliation," said Red Ribbon Skirt Society founder Lily Mendoza, Lakota.

 MMIW
On Tuesday, May 5, National Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women/People Awareness Day, Red Ribbon Skirt Society held a memorial outside the Journey Museum in Rapid City. 

The gathering was held on National Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women/Persons Awareness Day — Tuesday, May 5. The event included prayers, songs, and the placement of red handprints on a tipi to raise awareness and remembrance for victims and their families.

The local nonprofit, based in the Black Hills, serves victims' relatives and loved ones, striving to bring a sense of healing.

 MMIW
A red dress placed on a tree outside the Journey Museum holds victims' names to bring awareness to MMIP in Rapid City. 

The state-wide alert system they are advocating for is the "Feather Alert," which would work much like the national Amber Alert system by enabling law enforcement to act when an Indigenous person goes missing.

According to the Justice Department website, the requirements to issue an Amber Alert include:

The child is 17 years or younger.
Reasonable belief by law enforcement that an abduction has occurred.
Law enforcement agency believes that the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury or death.
Sufficient descriptive information about the victim and the abduction for law enforcement.
The child's information is entered into the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) system.

South Dakota also has an "Endangered Missing Advisory" system if the circumstances fail to meet the criteria for the Amber Alert. This includes when the individual is missing under unexplained, involuntary or suspicious circumstances; in danger because of age, health, mental or physical disability, environment or weather conditions; in the company of a potentially dangerous person that could cause injury or death and there is enough descriptive information that could assist the public in the safe recovery of the endangered person.

Alert systems for Indigenous people already exist in other states, including North Dakota's "Feather Alert." The North Dakota "Feather Alert" requires:

The missing/abducted individual to be Indigenous
The individual is 18 years of age or older
The individual is believed to be in grave danger of serious bodily harm or death,
There is enough descriptive information about the adult and/or the abductor, and/or the suspect's vehicle to assist with the safe recovery of the victim and/or the apprehension of the suspect
There is enough information that immediate broadcast will provide the public enough with descriptive information to help locate the adult, the suspect, or the suspect's vehicle

The specifics on the "Feather Alert" system are still subject to discussion, Mendoza said.

Mendoza hopes to bring the Feather Alert to South Dakota by collecting signatures to bring to the Attorney General's Office and the Governor's Office.

 MMIW
Sahela Sangrait-Dubray, Lakota, was allegedly murdered in August 2024 on Ellsworth Air Force Base.  

"As far as runways go, there's the misconception that they have to wait so many hours before they can start looking ... I really believe that we could find our people faster," Mendoza said.

She said when it comes to missing Indigenous people, waiting for the requirements of enacting an Amber Alert can be too long.

According to the Bureau of Indian Affairs, a 2016 study by the National Institute of Justice found that more than four in five American Indian and Alaska Native women have experienced violence in their lives, including 56.1% who have experienced sexual violence. Overall, the study found that 1.5 million American Indian and Alaska Native women have experienced violence in their lifetime.

As of May 7, the South Dakota Missing Persons Clearinghouse reports there are 112 American Indian and Alaskan Native missing persons cases.

Say her name

Included in the May 5 memorial gathering were family members of Sahela (Different Cheyenne Woman) Sangrait-Dubray, a 21-year-old Cheyenne River Lakota woman who was allegedly murdered on Aug. 11, 2024, at Ellsworth Air Force Base.

Her body was later found on March 4, 2025, outside of Hill City, 40 miles from Box Elder.

 MMIW
McKenna Wendel, 14, Lakota, of Sioux Falls was discovered dead on March 19 in Brookings just an hour north of her home in Sioux Falls. Her death is still under investigation. 

Quinterius Charles Chappelle, a 24-year-old airman, is charged with first-degree murder in federal court. His jury trial is scheduled to begin at the federal courthouse in Rapid City on Nov. 2. According to federal court documents, Drew Durand of Rapid City is charged with accessory after the fact and misprision of a felony in connection with the case.

"They kept her remains for quite some time to do whatever they needed to do with DNA and all of those sorts of things. So, they kept her for quite some time. We were sort of anxious to get her home. Now she's home," Mendoza said.

An evening wake service took place on Friday, April 17, with a funeral service of Sahela's remains taking place on Saturday, April 18.

 Red Ribbon Skirt Society
Members of the local nonprofit Red Ribbon Skirt Society held a memorial for MMIW/MMIP awareness, which included prayer, songs and printing of hands on a tipi, on Tuesday, May 5. 

Mendoza also spoke about 14-year-old McKenna Wendel, Lakota, of Sioux Falls, who was found dead on March 19 in Brookings.

"With McKenna (Wendel), hers is a big case over in Sioux Falls. The case is still open and is still pending. They're doing investigations right now. If I understand correctly, whoever's going to be charged, it's going to be over in the state of Iowa," Mendoza said.

"For us, we have a lot of mothers who have gone through the same thing, but we all felt it would be a good thing for us just to really do strong prayers for them today and remember them with the kids today," Mendoza said of the vigil.

title: 4th annual Healing with Horses Camp in Rapid City empowers youth, fosters community
description: The fourth annual Healing with Horse Camp, supported by the Great Plains Tribal Health Board, aims to bring cultural connections for the Indigenous community in Rapid City through traditional services, amenities and events and connection building with "šúŋkawakȟaŋ" — "horse" in the Lakota language.
_full_text:
The fourth annual Healing with Horse Camp, supported by the Great Plains Tribal Health Board, aims to bring cultural connections for the Indigenous community in Rapid City through traditional services, amenities and events and connection building with "šúŋkawakȟaŋ" — "horse" in the Lakota language.

"We ask them to help us reconnect, to be Lakota and reconnect to who we are as Lakota people. That's why if there were no horses, we wouldn't have a camp. I wouldn't do it," said Delaney Apple, Lakota, organizer of the Horse Camp.

 Horse Camp
Community members are able to connect with horses as a positive experience by Healing with Horses Camp.   

The camp started on Thursday, May 7, and will go on until Sunday, May 10. The four-day event will be filled with games, songs, crafting and some horsing around.

"It takes us to a good place, a safe place, a comforting place, a place to be invited. We want to bring it just right here to the community, so people can look out the window and be reminded that we're Lakota," Apple said.

The Horse Camp is set up in the Lakota Homes neighborhood, in the area of 719 Wambli Drive, to bring cultural identity to youth who grow up in Western society, Apple said.

 Horse Camp
Volunteers with Horse Spirit Society brought their horses for the community to connect with.  

"The horses are going to knock us into a good way of thinking, shake us up, and say, 'Hey, remember you're Lakota!' Then we're going to turn around and look at the fire and we're going to look at the tipis and we're going to smile and remember who we are," Apple said.

Apple said the horse is a relative in Lakota society, in which a person can build a personal connection with the mighty steed.

 Horse Camp
The fourth annual Healing with Horses Camp is at Lakota Homes in Rapid City. 

On May 7, around 15 horses arrived at the camp coming from the nonprofit Horse Spirit Society based on the Pine Ridge Reservation. The nonprofit also works in the same cultural connection effort as the Horse Camp.

The youth are able to interact with horses with the supervision of members of the Horse Spirit Society, getting hands-on experience and building a connection with the horses. In addition, they also rode through the camp on Friday.

Apple said the days of events are meant to disconnect the youth and adults from modern living and bring a sense of community with participants.

 Delaney Apple
Delaney Apple (on the right) is the lead organizer for the Healing with Horses Camp in Rapid City 

"Most times we get here, we're still thinking about the Xbox or the season I'm on, what episode am I on, or I got all these emails to catch up on," Apple said on the initial mindset of participants.

He continued saying that those who stay for all four days have a tendency to leave the outside world behind.

The camp has tipis set up for youth to spend the night in, chaperoned by volunteers. The youth are encouraged to bring a sleeping bag, blankets and cots. Bringing your own chair is also strongly advised.

Hand games

Jeremiah Moreno is a volunteer at the camp, providing oversight of the games throughout the event.

Moreno spoke with the Journal about the popularity of hand games, also known as stick games, within the Lakota community.

"That'd be cool if hand games could help us start talking in our language again. I think that's for the future," Moreno said on the games, exposing the youth to the Lakota language.

He said he learned the game from his grandmother and later learned more about the game from his uncle Wilmer Mesteth.

Moreno credits Mesteth with helping to bring the popularity of the game back to the youth. Mesteth was a Lakota elder who taught at Oglala Lakota College.

"Wilmer had a class, and in his class, he talked about hand games for like three hours. He went over songs and even drew a diagram on the board. He said we only played one game at a time, and had four judges, and they all had these staffs with no feathers, just the stick, and they'd hold them. Two judges would watch one team, and the two judges would watch the other team, and if they saw anything, they put that stick down in the middle and then stop the game, and they would take care of the discrepancies," Moreno said.

 Bones
Hand Games are popular at the Horse Camp event.  

Moreno said the games are played by many tribal groups, with intertribal being the most popular to play across the different communities. The size of the two teams can vary, with the games consisting of a pair of small bones, one striped and one not striped.

The point of the game is to guess which hand hides the stripped bone, in the Lakota-style game. Each time has a head guesser and a hider of the bones.

If the guesser fails at the guess, then the other team gains a stick. The total number of sticks can vary and whoever collects all the sticks or most of the sticks wins the game.

Moreno said while members play, songs in Lakota are sung, one of the ways the youth are exposed to their language. He said the game has been played for hundreds of years, prior to colonization.

In the past, wages were horses and other high-value items, now, he said, groups can win up to thousands of dollars in tournaments across the U.S.

"One time we went to this tournament in Washington, it was $150 bucks a team, and the payout was $10,000 for first place," Moreno said.

Moreno reflected, saying that during the early reservation period for the Lakota culture, activities such as hand games were illegal; now, it's a well-known game across tribal communities. He hopes this can occur with other Lakota games.

"So that's one reason that I was pumped up about this. Maybe, like, in about four years, we can start bringing those horse games back. We got high hopes for this," Moreno said.

 PHOTOS: Healing with Horse Camp  in Rapid City
The camp at Lakota Homes in Rapid City continues through Sunday, May 10.

title: A Mother's Day chapter: IGNITE and Rapid City Library partner for family reading program
description: For Krista Licht, the hushed aisles of the Rapid City Public Library have always been a sanctuary, driven by a passion for everyone to enjoy and explore the wondrous worlds books provide.
_full_text:
For Krista Licht, the hushed aisles of the Rapid City Public Library have always been a sanctuary, driven by a passion for everyone to enjoy and explore the wondrous worlds books provide. 

Through a new partnership between the Pennington County Sheriff's Office IGNITE (Individual Growth Naturally and Intentionally Through Education) Program, Friends of the Library and the library, the online resources librarian and mother traded in the library's organized book shelves for the stark concrete of the Pennington County Jail. 

 Reconnecting Families through Reading
Reconnecting Families through Reading began in November 2025, and with Mother's Day around the corner the Pennington County Sheriff's Office IGNITE Program and the Rapid City Public Library wanted to make this recording session special.  

There, the metallic chill of the facility is softened by a sound rarely heard within its walls — the steady, loving cadence of a mother's voice as she reads a story to her child in preparation for Mother's Day. 

"It's been very rewarding," Licht said. "It's a great way to be able to connect parents with their kids even though they're apart."

The program is called Reconnecting Families through Reading. Inmates at the jail can apply to be a part of the program. From there, participants fill out a form about particular characters or subjects their kids might be interested in, and the library staff picks a book and records the parent reading it. The recording and the book is then sent to the child, where they can read along while listening to their parent's voice. 

 Reconnecting Families through Reading
An inmate in the program said she was grateful for the chance and it has shown her that the community actually cares for those who are incarcerated.  

IGNITE Coordinator Jessica Afrank said a participating inmate has to be staying at the jail longer than 60 days and have a child or children under the age of 8 to be accepted into the program.

This is one of many programs within IGNITE centered around community collaboration to help provide programs within the jail, as well as connect former inmates to job opportunities. 

"The whole purpose of IGNITE is to provide resources and continue connections that they have with the community and surrounding communities," Afrank said. 

The idea came to her after a meeting in the summer of 2025 with other IGNITE Programs across the nation. She drew inspiration after speaking to one of the other coordinators who was hosting a similar reading program. 

 Reconnecting Families through Reading
Online resources librarian Krista Licht said she jumped at the chance to be a part of the program.  

Afrank said the goal of the program is to keep families together while someone is incarcerated.

Licht said she learned about the program when her boss sent an email asking if anyone was interested in participating. Licht jumped at the chance, sympathizing as a fellow parent and wanting to unite families. 

"I thought it was a really neat program. It's a great way to extend library services everywhere in the community, not just those who can physically visit the library," Licht said. "I'm a mom myself and so I thought having that chance to help another parent connect with their child is very important to me." 

After going through a background check and several trainings, Licht was able to do her first recording session with a group of 14 incarcerated parents on Nov. 5, 2025, with the goal of their families having the recordings by Thanksgiving.

 BRIGHT SIDE LOGO.jpg
Sharing the good news: We’re looking for upbeat stories and shout-outs worth celebrating. Send your story ideas to the Journal newsroom, news@rapidcityjournal.com, with "Bright Side" in the subject line. 

They hosted their second recording on Valentine's Day and are about to send out their recordings for this upcoming Mother's Day on Sunday, May 10. Licht said they plan to do another round for Father's Day as well. 

"From the library's standpoint, it's a great way to build literacy for not only the kids but the adults as well," Licht said.  

Afrank said there has been a lot of support to continue the program. 

"It generates a lot of excitement because we don't have any other programs like that currently offered at the jail, so it's very unique and it's very positive," Afrank said. "There's a lot of support from the community, the families and also the inmates themselves." 

Like many incarcerated individuals, the weight of missing one's family hung heavy on one female inmate's shoulders. The woman and the jail asked that her name not be used.

"The program is to provide books for our children at home and also for us to give an incentive to our kids," the woman said. "What I love about the program it's allowing us to reach out to our kids from a place that seems like nowhere." 

The inmate said she was informed about the program a couple weeks before the recording session set for April 28 and knew she had to reach out to her children. 

"I just decided to join because of the fact that there's no other way I can reach my children at this moment," the woman said. "So this would be a good way for them to know that I still care."

In the stark white room, the mother read "I've Loved You Since Forever" and "Chicka Chicka I Love Mom" for her 7-year-old and 17-month-old children. Her fingers gently flipped through each page as she read aloud to the microphone, a smile finding its way to her lips as her voice carried all the love and warmth of a mother. 

The woman said she is grateful for this program and it has shown her that the community actually cares for those who are incarcerated.

title: Rapid City hosting 4th annual Cardboard Boat Races on June 20
description: One of Rapid City Parks and Recreation Department’s most popular events is back for another year with the fourth annual Cardboard Boat Races. The event will be held Saturday, June 20 at the 50-meter outdoor pool at the Roosevelt Swim Center.
_full_text:
One of Rapid City Parks and Recreation Department’s most popular events is back for another year with the fourth annual Cardboard Boat Races. The event will be held Saturday, June 20 at the 50-meter outdoor pool at the Roosevelt Swim Center.

Boat check-ins are at 9 a.m. with the boat launch slated from 9:30-11:30 a.m.

Registration deadline for two-person teams is June 15. The racing event includes a kids division for youth between six and 13 years of age with awards provided for fastest boat, best design and titanic award. There is an adult division for a second consecutive year, featuring an award for fastest sinking boat.

 Boat races
Kids take part in the Cardboard Boat Races on June 8, 2024, at the Roosevelt Swim Center’s 50-meter outdoor pool. 

“The cardboard boat races is becoming one of our more popular events, with kids, adults and families getting involved,” said City Recreation Special Events Coordinator Lindsey Myers. “It’s a fun event with a lot of interest, no matter whether the cardboard boat makes it to the finish line, sinks at the starting line or somewhere in between.”

Teams can be assisted by a land crew, which can consist of two adults who can help with getting the boat in the water and participants in the boat. No push-offs will be allowed.

There is $5.00 entry fee for teams and the event is open to the public. Participants are asked to wear bathing suits and shorts, no denim.

Teams are encouraged to dress in the theme of their boats. Boats will race half the length (25-meters) of the Swim Center’s 50-meter pool and the teams must begin and finish the race with the two-person crew intact. Boats must be made of only cardboard and duct tape. Boats can be propelled with the use of arms or cardboard paddles.

Rules and regulations are available at https://rapidcity.activityreg.com . For more information or anyone with questions, contact Lindsey Myers at 605-394-4175.
