title: Newsrooms, journalists honored for excellence in SDNA contest
description: A reporter who covers education issues in South Dakota was named Outstanding Young Journalist for 2025 by the South Dakota NewsMedia Association.
_full_text:
A reporter who covers education issues in South Dakota was named Outstanding Young Journalist for 2025 by the South Dakota NewsMedia Association.

Morgan Matzen, a reporter for the Sioux Falls Argus Leader, received the recognition during SDNA’s convention on Friday, May 1, in Deadwood. Journalists under the age of 30 are eligible for the Outstanding Young Journalist Award.

 Morgan Matzen-2.jpg
Morgan Matzen 

“Morgan Matzen is the only full-time education reporter at any news outlet in South Dakota. She tackles the beat relentlessly, with fervor and resiliency, time and time again,” Argus Leader News Director Shelly Conlon wrote in her nomination letter. “Ms. Matzen reports in a way that makes people care about broad topics many often tune out unless they’re directly affected. Her work regularly commands attention from all kinds of readers and changemakers.”

SDNA also presented awards in various categories for the best journalism and best advertising on Friday, May 1, in Deadwood. General Excellence Awards were presented to the best overall news media outlets. Sweepstakes Awards went to news organizations winning the most awards in their respective divisions.

The SDNA General Excellence winners for 2025 include:

Division 1 (cities under 3,000): Hamlin County Republican, Castlewood

Division 2 (cities 3,000 to 15,000): Madison Daily Leader

Division 3 (cities over 15,000): Aberdeen Insider

The SDNA Sweepstakes winners for 2025 include:

Division 1 (cities under 3,000): Hamlin County Republican, Castlewood

Division 2 (cities 3,000 to 15,000): Madison Daily Leader

Division 3 (cities over 15,000): Black Hills Pioneer, Spearfish

The association also presented awards to winners in two specialized contests.

The “Strengthening Civil Society Award” for journalism about non-profits in South Dakota is sponsored by the John T. Vucurevich Foundation in cooperation with the Black Hills Area Community Foundation. The award was established in 2025 by Eric Abrahamson and Lois Facer in recognition of Abrahamson’s dedicated service to the Vucurevich Foundation board of directors.

A first-place award and $500 checks were presented to South Dakota News Watch journalists Carson Walker and Bart Pfankuch for their comprehensive coverage of housing shortages in the state and the role of non-profit organizations helping to solve those problems.

Honorable mention awards and cash prizes were presented to Wendy Pitlick ($250) of the Black Hills Pioneer at Spearfish and Randy Dockendorf ($125) and Cora Van Olson ($125) of the Yankton Daily Press & Dakotan. Pitlick reported on the finances of a non-profit organization providing recreational services for the city of Lead. Dockendorf and Olson reported on the financial struggles and challenges for various non-profit organizations in the Yankton community.

The A-Mark Prize for Investigative Journalism, sponsored by the A-Mark Foundation, was awarded to four journalists and the news organizations for which they work.

Joshua Haiar of South Dakota Searchlight won first place in the A-Mark contest for his investigative reporting about an extraordinary set of connections between the state of South Dakota and a company receiving a large amount of government financial assistance. The A-Mark Foundation awarded $5,000 to Haiar and $2,500 to South Dakota Searchlight.

Morgan Matzen of the Sioux Falls Argus Leader, a former Rapid City Journal reporter, won second place for her reporting about private funds and taxpayer money used by universities and associated foundations to purchase property in and outside of South Dakota. The A-Mark Foundation awarded $3,000 to Matzen and $1,500 to the Argus Leader.

Luke Hagen of the Mitchell Republic and Patrick Lalley of Sioux Falls Live won third place in the A-Mark competition for their ongoing reporting about criminal charges and other issues related to Legion baseball in Mitchell. The A-Mark Foundation awarded $1,000 each to Hagen and Lalley and $1,000 to the Mitchell Republic and Sioux Falls Live.

A complete list of contest results can be found at www.sdna.com.

South Dakota NewsMedia Association, based in Brookings, represents more than 100 newspapers and digital news outlets in South Dakota.

title: Kinder-gardeners try their hands at horticulture in Rapid City elementary classroom
description: Curious gardeners want to know: "How does a seed hatch?" "How do you make big flowers?" "How do you make seeds?"
_full_text:
Curious gardeners want to know: "How does a seed hatch?" "How do you make big flowers?" "How do you make seeds?"

Rapid City Greenhouse Specialist John Berglund said the questions are his favorite part of the plants class he taught to kindergarteners at Grandview Elementary School on Friday, May 8.

"That's always fun," he said.

 Lily
Lily, a kindergarten student at Grandview Elementary School on Friday, May 8, holds up her flower she planted a class on plants held by the City of Rapid City's greenhouse specialist.  

The class was complete with an activity where the tiny green thumbs got to plant their very own snapdragons. The flowers made their way into pots with the students' names on them to go home with them just in time for Mother's Day. 

Berglund told the noon class they could keep the flowers themselves or give them to someone special. One boy said, "I will make my mom so happy!" as he held up his plant. 

"It happens to be always before Mother's Day, so they get a plant to take home to their mom or special someone, so it's always an exciting time for us," Berglund said. "...It's a great outreach and a great thing to provide for the kids."

He said he hopes the kids' excitement will continue. 

 Meredith
Meredith, a kindergarten student at Grandview Elementary School on Friday, May 8, holds the flower she planted during a class on plants held by the City of Rapid City's greenhouse specialist.  

"It's the ultimate reward, as far as being able to teach somebody and see that excitement, and hopefully that fosters some more excitement for keeping on with growing and horticulture," he said. "Maybe this will lead one day to coming to work for us. Maybe it leads to them going into a college degree in horticulture. I mean, it's just a great thing, and knowing that you're just a little piece of that puzzle that helped them get to where they want to be when they grow up."

 Berglund
John Berglund, Rapid City Greenhouse Specialist, explains plants to a kindergarten class at Grandview Elementary School on Friday, May 8. 

Berglund works for the city's Parks and Recreation Department. He is part of the team that plants thousands of flowers in the city's parks and green spaces.

About 22,000 flowers are growing in the city's greenhouse. Berglund said he's aiming to plant before Memorial Day, weather pending. He tends to wait for consistent 50-degree nights. 

 Helping plant
The children each received a pot to place their flower in with their name on it during an event with Rapid City Greenhouse Specialist John Berglund at Grandview Elementary School on Friday, May 8. 

"We provide a great service to the city by sprucing up our parks, providing gardens, flowers, maybe give people ideas. Maybe they come out and see a different plant that they haven't seen yet. They take that idea and they go home and they grow the same thing in their yard. So it's a great thing," he said.

 Grandview flower planting - Meredith
Meredith, a kindergartener at Grandview Elementary School on Friday, May 8, talks about her experience with the class on plants held by the City of Rapid City's greenhouse specialist. 

 Grandview flower planting - Berglund
John Berglund, Rapid City greenhouse specialist, talks about teaching a class on plants for kindergarteners at Grandview Elementary School on Friday, May 8. 

 Photos of kindergartners planting flowers at Grandview Elementary School
On Friday, May 8, Rapid City Greenhouse Specialist John Berglund held a class on seeds and plants at Grandview Elementary School. The kindergartners also got to plant their own flowers ahead of Mother's Day to give to someone special or to keep for themselves.

title: Pennington County Sheriff's Office, Box Elder PD to launch K9 programs thanks to civil forfeiture funds
description: The Pennington County Sheriff's Office and the Box Elder Police Department will soon have K9 officers.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Sheriff's Office and the Box Elder Police Department will soon have K9 officers.

The South Dakota Attorney General's Office announced a pair of grants to the departments to stand up drug-detection dog programs. The AG's Drug Control Fund will disperse up to $60,000 to the sheriff's office and up to $93,000 to the Box Elder department.

"This is an exciting opportunity for us," sheriff's office Lt. Casey Kenrick said during a media availability on Monday, May 11. "This is something that (we've) wanted to do for many years."

The Attorney General’s Drug Control Fund consists of drug forfeiture monies and is to be used for drug control and apprehension purposes. So far this year, the fund has distributed $221,565.38 to seven law enforcement agencies statewide, the AG's Office said.

 Pennington County Sheriff's Office Lt. Casey Kenrick
Pennington County Sheriff's Office Lt. Casey Kenrick discusses a grant that'll allow the office to launch a K9 program on Monday, May 11, at the Law Enforcement Building on Kansas City Street in Rapid City. 

Kenrick explained Pennington County Search and Rescue, which is under the purview of the sheriff's office, has search dogs, but this will be the first time the office has had a drug-detection K9 unit. The office will procure two dogs and designate which deputies will serve as dog handlers. From there, the team will complete initial training with the state before hitting the streets. Box Elder plans to get one dog.

The Rapid City Police Department has had a K9 unit for years, Kenrick noted.

"That's what we've relied on for many years. With the growing population, everyone knows how much drugs have become a fuel for violent crimes and all kinds of different crimes. The sheriff thought this was a good time to step up and take on this responsibility in Pennington County," Kenrick said.

The lieutenant noted that people often think of police dogs as German shepherds or Belgian Malinois, which agencies like Rapid City also use to clear a building or space before humans enter, among their duties. But the sheriff's office plans to use its dogs as "purely drug-detection dogs," with an eye toward some search-and-rescue training down the road, Kenrick said.

"So they're probably going to be what people would consider a 'non-traditional' (police) dog, maybe a Lab, maybe some other (breed), what we refer to as floppy ear dogs," he said.

In a release, Pennington County Sheriff Brian Mueller said, "three additional K-9s is a force multiplier with the existing Rapid City Police K-9 program. Methamphetamine is the No. 1 driver of violence in our community. This is something we have wanted to do for some time.”

“Enforcement alone will not solve the drug problem. As a community, we hope to receive additional opioid settlement dollars to help on the treatment and prevention fronts," he said.

Kenrick said the K9 officers will be used in a variety of drug-related efforts, including during traffic stops. When deputies believe there's probable cause to look for drugs, the dogs will do a sniff to help their handlers.

"We can use these drug dogs in a way less intrusive search, and then it'll just let us know if that's a vehicle or that's a person that we need to spend additional time with," Kenrick said. "And there are rules and laws on how we can use those dogs and when we can use those dogs, and we're going to comply with all that to be a good partner for our citizens."

"I don't want our people searching vehicles that they don't need to be searching," Kenrick said later in the interview. "I don't want to tie people up any longer than they need to. I want to do the right thing. This is another tool to help us do the right thing."

In the release, Box Elder Police Chief Bob Connell said, "We are grateful for the efforts of the Division of Criminal Investigation and the support from the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office in helping make this program a reality."

“Having this asset available within our own department will increase our efforts to eradicate illegal drugs in the City of Box Elder, Pennington County, and Meade County," Connell said.

The agencies will select K9s and handlers throughout the summer with training completion planned for early this fall.

title: Passenger tries to force his way into cockpit of flight bound for Rapid City
byline: SHALOM BAER GEE and MIKE BROWNLEE Journal staff
description: A man tried to force his way into the cockpit of a plane inbound to Rapid City, the Rapid City Police Department said.
_full_text:
A man tried to force his way into the cockpit of a plane inbound to Rapid City, the Rapid City Police Department said. 

The department said on Monday, May 11, it was advised of the incident around 9:15 p.m. on Saturday, May 9.

Police arrived at the airport and made contact with airline staff at the gate. Police boarded the aircraft, and airline staff identified the passenger as 30-year-old Krish Mishra of Rosemont, Illinois.

 IMG-0154.JPEG
A passenger provided this photo of a man being detained after a flight landed at Rapid City Regional Airport around 9:30 p.m. on Saturday, May 9. 

Staff informed police Mishra had also refused multiple requests to stay in his seat, even after the plane had landed. He was escorted off the aircraft by police and arrested on suspicion of disorderly conduct before being transported to the Pennington County Jail. The report for the incident has been forwarded to the Department of Homeland Security for further investigation, police said.

A passenger on the flight told the Journal the plane came from Chicago. She said the detainment was "not very dramatic," as law enforcement entered to take the man away. 

"We had no idea anything was happening until we were told we had to wait to get off (the plane) due to a 'security issue,'" she said.

The police department said no one was injured in the incident. As of Monday afternoon, Mishra was not listed on the jail roster. The Journal reached out to the airport for comment on the situation, but did not immediately hear back.

title: Woman arrested as accessory to Oxford Apartments murder in Rapid City
description: A 25-year-old Rapid City woman has been arrested on an accessory to first-degree murder warrant in connection to an August 2025 murder at Oxford Apartments.
_full_text:
A 25-year-old Rapid City woman has been arrested on an accessory to first-degree murder warrant in connection to an August 2025 murder at Oxford Apartments. 

The Rapid City Police Department arrested Kylee Red Bear at a residence at 737 E. Anamosa Street on Friday, May 8. She is currently being held at the Pennington County Jail on a $50,000 cash-only bond. Red Bear joins 30-year-old Kane Youngman, of Pine Knot, Kentucky, as a defendant in the case. Red Bear is charged with first-degree murder and other charges for the Aug. 27, 2025, shooting death of 29-year-old Monte Gakin.

 Monte Gakin memorial (copy) (copy)
A memorial for Monte Gakin, 29, of Rapid City, who was murdered on Aug. 27, at an apartment complex on East Watertown Street in Rapid City. 

Youngman was arrested on Friday, March 13. His arrest was nearly seven months after the shooting. Red Bear was arrested nearly nine months after. Her warrant was filed in court on April 29. 

Police told the Journal in January 2026 investigators had conducted dozens of interviews, reviewed hours of video footage and analyzed and examined numerous pieces of evidence. The primary persons of interest in the case had been identified, police said at the time, noting there wasn't an ongoing threat to the public.

Officers were called to the scene where Gakin died around 7:15 p.m. on Aug. 27, 2025, on a report of gunshots heard in the building, police said. Officers found Gakin suffering from gunshot wounds inside an apartment. Police rendered emergency first aid to Gakin but he ultimately died at the building.

Over the course of the investigation, investigators established Youngman’s involvement in the shooting through physical evidence recovered from the scene and ongoing forensic testing and analysis, police said.

Red Bear's arraignment is scheduled for 2:15 p.m. on May 18 at the Pennington County Courthouse. Youngman pleaded not guilty to his charges on April 14. He's set to appear in court for a status hearing on at 9:45 a.m. on May 19 at the Pennington County Courthouse. As of Monday, May 11, he is held at the Pennington County Jail on a $1 million cash-only bond.

title: Rapid City man pleads not guilty to allegations he abused 2 children
description: A 47-year-old Rapid City man on Tuesday, May 12, pleaded not guilty to allegations of child abuse in Pennington County Court.
_full_text:
A 47-year-old Rapid City man on Tuesday, May 12, pleaded not guilty to allegations of child abuse in Pennington County Court. 

Kyle Soltesz is charged with two counts of child abuse. The first charge is a Class 3 felony because the alleged victim is under 7. The other charge is a lesser felony, a Class 4, because the child in question in over the age of 7 but still a minor. South Dakota law defines child abuse as abuse, exposure, torture, torment or cruel punishment of a minor in a manner that does not constitute aggravated assault.

Soltesz, if he is convicted, could face up to 15 years in prison and up to a $50,000 fine for the first charge and up to 10 years in prison and up to a $20,000 fine for the second. If the state applies his past criminal history, which includes felony DUIs, he could face up to 25 years in prison for the charge and up to 15 years for the second charge. 

Court records show Soltesz was arrested on April 10 for abuse the state alleges happened from Oct. 4, 2025 through March 15, 2026.

Less than a week after his arrest, on April 16, Soltesz posted a $5,000 bond. He is currently out of custody. At the end of April, Circuit Court Judge Jeffrey Connolly denied Soltesz's request to travel to Nicaragua on a personal trip this week. Connolly approved travel within the United States for work purposes. 

Soltesz's South Dakota criminal history dates back 25 years, court records show.

In 2001, he as sentenced to five years suspended for marijuana distribution. In 2006, he picked up a DUI and received a 30-day suspended jail sentence. In 2007, he was once again convicted of a DUI. He received a 90-day jail sentence with 75 days suspended. In 2008, he was convicted of driving without a license. Also in 2009, he was convicted of his third DUI and driving with a revoked license, and sentenced to two years in prison, all suspended, as well as probation.

In 2011, he was convicted of disorderly conduct and sentenced to 30 days suspended in jail. In 2016, Soltesz was convicted of another DUI and sentenced to two years in prison, all suspended, and two years of probation. In 2021, he was convicted of failing to use the proper child passenger restraint system and fined $25.

Soltesz also currently faces a pending small claims case, a collections case and a misdemeanor case alleging he drove without a license or insurance on April 21.

title: Rapid City Council candidates in 3 wards talk population growth, public schools, crime and addiction
description: More than 25 residents of Rapid City sat in for a City Council candidate forum hosted by the Black Hills League of Women Voters at the Dahl Arts Center.
_full_text:
More than 25 residents of Rapid City sat in for a City Council candidate forum hosted by the Black Hills League of Women Voters at the Dahl Arts Center.

During the two-hour event, candidates vying to represent Ward 1, Ward 3 and Ward 5 discussed population growth, public school infrastructure, crime and safety and addiction treatment.

The current seats up for election on June 2 are held by Josh Biberdorf (Ward 1), Lindsey Seachris (Ward 2), Kevin Maher (Ward 3), John Roberts (Ward 4) and Rod Pettigrew (Ward 5).

 Council candidates
Rapid City Council candidates for Ward 1, Ward 2, and Ward 5 attended a forum hosted by the Black Hills League of Women Voters on May 7 at the Dahl Arts Center. 

Pettigrew is the only council member not seeking reelection.

Those throwing their hat in the race who are not currently on the council are Murray Lee (Ward 1), Christopher Vanderhoof (Ward 2), Andrea Schaefer (Ward 3), Valeriah Big Eagle (Ward 4), Pat Roseland (Ward 5) and Laura Armstrong (Ward 5).

Biberdorf did not attend the Thursday, May 7, forum at the Dahl.

Introductions

Ward 1:

Lee said he grew up in Rapid City but moved away for a period. He said a background in working in the corporate and nonprofit field.

"I'm really just about bringing people together, having conversations that are sometimes tough, and working on solutions," Lee said.

Ward 3:

Maher said he is from Huron and has a background in banking.

"I've always been interested in community involvement," Maher said.

 Kevin Maher
Current council member representing Ward 3, Kevin Maher, who is seeking re-election, speaks at a candidate forum held at the Dahl Arts Center on May 7. 

Schaefer said she moved to Rapid City in 2007 and has owned two businesses. She said through her business ventures, she feels a deep sense of community needs from local leaders.

"What I have that maybe a lot of people already sitting on council don't have is a unique point of view that comes from running a small business for almost 25 years," Schaeffer said.

Ward 5:

Roseland said he has lived in the city for over 35 years and is a retired, certified registered nurse anesthetist.

"I have been involved in many different organizations and committees and commissions over the 30 years that I've been here in Rapid City, which basically gave me a good overview of what I think Rapid City needs," Roseland said.

 Pat Roseland
Candidate for Ward 5 Pat Roseland speaks at the forum. 

Armstrong noted she has previously been on the City Council for Ward 5 for two terms and is running again to tackle issues on infrastructure, development, educational partnerships, accessibility for everyone, and shared social spaces.

"We didn't push historically expensive TIFs (Tax Increment Financing District) onto our taxpayers and regular working folks weren't being taxed at every turn just for basic city services," Armstrong said of when she was on the council.

Q&A

The Black Hills League of Women Voters opened the forum to questions from the public.

One person asked about handling population growth without overextending city resources.

Roseland said he wants to provide affordable housing to families in the city.

 Laura Armstrong
Laura Armstrong, who is running for a Ward 5 seat on the Rapid City Council, speaks at a candidate forum held at the Dahl Arts Center on May 7. 

Roseland said, "I think the main problem we have in Rapid City at this point is not enough affordable housing and workforce housing. To me, that's a big problem. What we have here is short-term rentals in Rapid City."

Maher said he's most concerned about keeping the quality of life for current and future residents in the city.

"We have this tremendous bike trail, 13 miles long, going through the city. We have tremendous parks and rec facilities. We spend $15 million a year in our parks and rec, and I think that's very important to take care of the people that live here," Maher said.

Armstrong said this same challenge is affecting a lot of other communities across the U.S.

"That's why we need to focus on our comprehensive plan and invest in our community development. I truly believe in priority-based budgeting, because that ensures that we're spending and our decisions are aligned with what the community actually wants," Armstrong said.

School infrastructure

A member of the public asked whether the candidates would support current school infrastructure efforts.

Lee said he would support any actions by the City Council that would aid in the efforts to support public schools.

 Andrea Schaefer
Rapid City Council candidate Andrea Schaefer, running to represent Ward 3, speaks at a forum held at the Dahl Arts Center on May 7.  

"I myself went to Wilson (Elementary) School, so I would hate to see Wilson School go away. You know, getting out in the community, meeting with the school board, finding out ways that we can support as the city, seeing what that looks like. Seeing if there's reasonable, efficient and productive ways that we could support the schools and the things that they need," Lee said.

Schaeffer also agreed she would support this effort if elected.

"When I started this run, I was also told that the City Council doesn't really have much to do with schools, but I'm very involved with teachers and obviously, I was a teacher for 20-some years, not in the schools, but still working with children and families. I think we could incentivize universities to offer more training for teachers and paraeducators. We have a massive para shortage right now," Schaeffer said.

Crime and safety

A question was posed on how candidates would tackle crime and safety in the community.

Maher said when he was voted to the council, the Rapid City Police Department was down an estimated 30 officers, and now they are nearly full-staffed. He credits the police department with championing the increased safety in the community. He also said the city is working to address mental strain on the officers to have a capable workforce.

"You've got to do one neighborhood at a time, and we have to protect our people. Everybody has the freedom of speech. You can't stop somebody from panhandling downtown in Rapid City, but you can have officers walking down the streets that are available at a moment's notice," Maher said. 

After a stabbing in the 400 block of Sixth Street in April of 2025, where a man was stabbed and died from his injuries, the city has increased patrols in the downtown area.

 Murray Lee
Murray Lee, who is running to represent Ward 1 on the Rapid City Council, speaks at a candidate forum at the Dahl Arts Center on May 7. 

Armstrong said she comes from a law enforcement family and said the city has been reacting to crime rather then working in crime prevention.

"Since we're talking about the quality of life unit in 2017, when it started, I was on the council. In addition, I was on a founding board as president for Journey On, so law enforcement can focus on crime and not harass homeless people, and let social (workers) work with those that are houseless. And I was very proud to be on the hiring committee that hired Don Hendrick as our police chief," Armstrong said.

Schaeffer said she met with Lt. Tim Doyle with the Rapid City Police Department to get a perspective on crime in the city. She also said that as a business owner in the downtown area, she has noticed an improvement of safety.

"I think that we're doing a good job. I think there's holes, and we need work, but I think we're doing a good job. He did mention that crime moves, that they kind of like saturate one neighborhood, and then it'll move. And I asked him do the community gardens work?' He said 'Yeah, it works," Schaeffer said. "So, I would believe in funding these groups. People are already, you know, doing the work in some of these small grassroots organizations."

Addiction

A question was asked on the opioid settlement funds and how that can be used by the city.

Per previous reporting by the Journal, Tamang, Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun and Pennington County Sheriff Brian Mueller sent a letter on Sept. 11, 2025, to South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley requesting $25 million from the state's opioid funds.

The South Dakota Department of Social Services opioid settlement fund dashboard shows the state has received nearly $33 million since disbursement. Of that, $9.6 million has gone to local governments. Rapid City and Pennington County have received a combined $1.5 million and reported about $300,000 in spending. The majority of the funds, 70%, are under the state’s purview. 

Armstrong said she would talk with residents and medical professionals to better address the needs of the community. She said as a medically-based speech language pathologist, she's seeing the long-term effects of addiction.

"I work primarily with people with brain injuries, and I'm seeing now chemical brain injuries, before they were physical brain injuries, strokes, but now these opioids are literally scrambling brains. These are our neighbors and people that are in our community, and we need to talk about this," Armstrong said.

Schaeffer said she has lost two family members who were facing addiction. She said after speaking with many nonprofits in the city helping in this cause, she would provide further funding.

"I would give it to the people who are already doing the work. We have people who are doing the work, and I think that they do recognize where the gaps are. I think before we spend any of that money, we need to maybe put together a task force so that we have somebody looking at all of it at the same time and make sure that communication is happening between all these wonderful organizations," Schaeffer said.

Roseland said the city currently lacks long-term care for addiction, a gap he said he would work toward filling.

"We need $20 million so we can build at least two treatment centers and alcohol treatment centers and drug treatment centers so that we can get people off the streets and not just see them back on the streets again. They need to have treatment and so that they can get out and live a normal life," Roseland said.

Maher said the city, along with Councilman Stephen Tamang (Ward 1), have been working on a local opioid settlement committee to address the needs of the community — they just need the state to trickle down more of the funding.

"We need to get that money to Sioux Falls and Rapid City. Build the treatment centers and use the experts. We do have a committee that Stephen Tamang sits on, and he's really our subject matter expert on the Council," Maher said.

Lee said addiction is a very complex issue that is not a one-size-fits-all solution.

"You may have to develop facilities. You're going to have to bring in qualified people to treat people in those facilities' competitive wages ... It's just this very complex, comprehensive body of work that would need to take place. Boots on the ground, (working) diligently on it to accomplish the things that need to be done," Lee said.

Voting information

Absentee voting began on Thursday, April 24, after a delay because of ballot printing issues, and continues until 4 p.m. on Monday, June 1, at the Pennington County Administrative Building at 900 Concourse Drive.

The delay was a result of state law timelines and was not caused by the Pennington County Auditor’s Office.

The voter registration deadline is May 18, ahead of the June 2 election day.

title: James (Jim) Dark
description: September 6, 1947 - February 4, 2026
_full_text:
September 6, 1947 - February 4, 2026

SUMMERSET - James (Jim) William Dark, Summerset, S.D. (formerly of Sundance, Wyo.), passed away on February 4, 2026, at Ft. Meade Veteran's Hospital in Sturgis, with his wife, Donna, by his side.

Jim was born on September 6, 1947, in Nevada, Mo., to Clarence and Wilma (Wallis) Dark. He grew up on a farm near Metz, Mo., where he learned to love the outdoors. During high school he was a star athlete and especially enjoyed playing baseball and basketball. He graduated from Metz, Mo., where he developed a love for the great outdoors fishing and hunting birds accompanied by one or more faithful canine companions.

In high school he was a star athlete enjoying baseball and basketball. He graduated from Metz High School in 1965. Following graduation, he joined a sister and brother-in-law, Jim and Mary Ellen Murray, in California. Jim entered the U.S. Air Force in 1966 and completed the "Electrical Power Production Specialist Course" at Sheppard Air Base in Texas in 1967. In April he was relocated to the 731st radar squadron, Sundance Air Force Station near Sundance, Wyo. He reported daily to the PM-1 nuclear power plant atop the Bear Lodge Mountains working in specialty of power supply and was induced into the "Order of the Nervous Neutron".

In March of 1968, he met Donna Hayward at the Sundance bowling alley and asked her to go out. They dated for three months before Jim received orders to report an 18th month tour at Clark Air Force Base in the Philippines. Anticipating the possibility that Donna could join him, they were united in marriage at Ellsworth Air Force Base on July 6, 1968.

Upon arrival at Clark AFB, however, Jim was placed in a temporary support group that would travel to numerous combat locations in SE Asia. His most frequent assignment was to a small base in the mountains above the demilitarized zone in Korea where the military was constructing power lines and all airmen were required to always have armed bodyguards.

Jim returned to Sundance and was honorably discharged in August 1972. Upon his return to Sundance, he joined his father-in-law, Calvin Hayward, in his electrical contracting business. A daughter, Darby, was born in 1973, and another daughter, Jayme, joined the family in 1980. Jim was a patient and loving family man and father.

Jim and Donna later purchased the appliance portion of the Hayward business which they operated as Sundance Appliance for 35 years. Jim was also well known in the surrounding towns of Newcastle, Upton, Hulett and Moorcroft, where he had many faithful customers before retiring and moving to Summerset, S.D.

A loving and devoted man, Jim was always available to his family, friends and customers. He loved sports and enjoyed playing as well as watching. His true passion was God's great outdoors where he spent endless hours fishing, hunting, playing baseball, camping and hiking accompanied by family and again, those faithful canine companions. He enjoyed working in his business and always appreciated the time spent at customers' home making conversation and friendships.

Jim was preceded in death by his parents, Clarence and Wilma (Wallis) Dark; a sister, Mary Ellen Murray. He is survived by his wife of 57 years, Donna Dark; daughters, Darby (Jason) Smiley of Rapid City, S.D.; and Jayme (Brock) Buresh of Maryville, Tenn.; grandchildren, Jacob and Olyvia Smiley of Rapid City, S.D., and Brynn Buresh of Maryville, Tenn.; sisters, Rosalee (Bob) Craig of Olney, Texas, and Carol (Leonard) Ayres of Leavenworth, Kan., and numerous nieces and nephews.

Funeral services will be Wednesday, May 27, 2026 at 10:30 a.m. at Grace United Church, 10060 Foothill Drive in Piedmont, S.D. Burial will follow at Black Hills National Cemetery at 1:30 p.m.

Those attending funeral wear casual attire to include your favorite sports team shirts or the color red.

In lieu of flowers, please consider donating to Pheasants Forever or the Veteran's Administration.

title: Rapid City woman who killed her mother sentenced to probation; judge says she's 'worth saving'
description: It's not common for a judge to show emotion on the stand. But on Wednesday, May 13, Presiding Seventh Circuit Court Judge Heidi Linngren fought back tears after hearing an uncle say he forgives his niece, who killed her own mother with a pair of scissors.
_full_text:
It's not common for a judge to show emotion on the stand. But on Wednesday, May 13, Presiding Seventh Circuit Court Judge Heidi Linngren fought back tears after hearing an uncle say he forgives his niece, who killed her own mother with a pair of scissors.

"That was one of the most powerful statements I've heard to date," Linngren told Jon Little Wound in a Pennington County courtroom. Little Wound is the uncle of 27-year-old Taylor Bird Horse, of Rapid City, and the brother of Karri St. John, who died at 45 years old.

"I wasn't prepared for Mr. Little Wound's statement," the judge said. 

On April 7, 2026, Bird Horse stabbed St. John — her mother — in the leg with a pair of scissors. St. John developed an infection and died three days later. 

Bird Horse was arrested Monday, April 14, 2025, on suspicion of first-degree manslaughter in relation to her mother’s death. She pleaded no contest on April 2 this year to second-degree manslaughter, almost a year after the stabbing. 

The charge carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and up to a $25,000 fine. Under the initial charge, Bird Horse would have faced up to life in prison and up to a $50,000 fine. 

Little Wound took the stand at Bird Horse's Wednesday sentencing and provided a window into the impact the incident has had on the family. 

"This incident tore our families apart," he said. "...Taylor's not gonna have a mom anymore."

Instead of asking for punishment, Little Wound offered forgiveness and support to his niece, who he said he babysat as a little girl. He described her as "a comical little girl." He said as an adult, she was still comical.

Little Wound said from the witness stand as he looked at Bird Horse, wearing a jail uniform, sitting next to her defense attorney, "You are a good person.

"You can go far in life ... That's what I want to see for you here on out," he said.

Little Wound said St. John would want someone to be there for her daughter. 

"I was mad at the situation. I was sad at the situation ... but I think that with the right guidance, Taylor can turn her life around and make better choices," he said. " ... "I'll always be there to support her because she's my niece."

Referencing letters submitted to the court ahead of sentencing, Linngren said family members wrote they believe St. John would forgive her daughter. 

Addressing Bird Horse, Linngren told her, "I think that you're worth saving."

Linngren, as well as Bird Horse's defense attorney Kyle Beauchamp, said she was on the path to drinking herself to death.

Reading from a letter Bird Horse submitted to the court, Beauchamp said, "Alcohol robbed me of my potential and of my mom's life."

Beauchamp said Bird Horse, at the age of 27, has learned a lesson people much older than her haven't: "You can't outrun addiction."

It's unfortunate, Beauchamp said, that the lesson came after her mother's death. 

"Nonetheless, your honor, she has learned that," he said. 

Speaking for herself, Bird Horse said alcohol ruins lives and apologized to her family.

"I am sorry. I still need my mom. She was the glue in my life," she said. "...For my mom, I will continue to try."

As for the state, prosecutor Kevin Krull said Bird Horse blames her actions on alcohol and is back-and-forth about taking responsibility. He noted she initially told law enforcement a friend of her mother's stabbed her before admitting it was her. 

"She's got a terrible problem with alcohol," Krull said before asking the judge to sentence Bird Horse to 10 years in prison, the maximum for the charge. 

Beauchamp, however, argued the best interest of justice is to allow Bird Horse a chance on probation. He said she wants to attend treatment.

That argument landed with Linngren. She sentenced Bird Horse to 10 years suspended and 10 years of probation, but not without a warning. 

"You have to make this work," Linngren said, emphasizing probation would be "no tolerance."

The judge then promised Bird Horse she would send her to prison for 10 years if she did not comply with the terms of probation, which include keeping a job or attending school and staying away from drugs and alcohol. She also ordered grief counseling and other treatment. 

"This is designed to get you some help," Linngren said.

title: Pedestrian seriously injured in crash on Omaha Street in Rapid City
description: The Rapid City Police Department said an investigation continues after a pedestrian struck by a vehicle suffered serious injuries.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Police Department said an investigation continues after a pedestrian struck by a vehicle suffered serious injuries.

The department said alcohol use by the pedestrian is believed to be a factor.

Officers were called to the intersection of Sixth Street and Omaha Street around 9:35 p.m. on Tuesday, May 12, on a report of a vehicle vs. pedestrian crash, the department said.

A medical unit took the pedestrian to the hospital with serious injuries.

After speaking to witnesses, police determined the vehicle was eastbound along Omaha Street and entered the intersection of Sixth Street with a green light when it struck the pedestrian in the roadway.

The crash remains under investigation by the RCPD’s Critical Accident Reconstruction Team (CART). Police told the Journal there are no charges related to the crash but that could change after the investigation.

title: SD tourism leader: High gas prices could hold 'silver lining'
byline: BART PFANKUCH South Dakota News Watch
description: KEYSTONE — Members of the Foley family of Green Bay, Wisconsin, are the quintessential visitors that tourism officials and operators hope will push South Dakota to a successful 2026 tourism season.
_full_text:
KEYSTONE — Members of the Foley family of Green Bay, Wisconsin, are the quintessential visitors that tourism officials and operators hope will push South Dakota to a successful 2026 tourism season.

The family of four drove 12 hours from home for a weeklong tour of the Black Hills of South Dakota in late April and refused to let high gas prices, inflation or a soft national economy delay or postpone their visit.

 2025-9-23 Dignity statue.jpeg
A woman walks in September 2025 near the Dignity statute, a cultural tourist attraction located at the Interstate 90 welcome center near Chamberlain. 

The Foleys usually fly to a beach destination each spring but chose to drive somewhere this year, mostly because their 15-year-old dog named Doc Holliday couldn't be left at a kennel. They settled on the Black Hills because it is a drivable destination with a wide range of sights and experiences.

"It's our family trip, so if we needed to pay a little more for gas, it's no big deal," said Ryan Foley, who had just finished a scenic helicopter flight in Keystone with wife Alexis and daughters Amelia and Mabel.

While it may seem counterintuitive, South Dakota tourism secretary Jim Hagen said the Rushmore State's extensive travel industry could actually benefit from higher gas prices.

In an interview with News Watch, Hagen said South Dakota has outperformed other states in prior years when gas prices were high or rising.

Furthermore, recent national surveys show that 90% of Americans said they will travel this summer despite higher costs, and that many are considering driving to a destination rather than flying, Hagen said.

"They want to travel regionally, and they're opting for that over more expensive, long-haul air travel trips or more expensive, longer road trips," he said. "They're going to travel to destinations that are closer to home. And the silver lining is that South Dakota is seen as a regional drive market and because we really are the ultimate road trip destination."

After their trip to the state, the Foleys appear to agree.

 2026-4-30 Keystone Bria Dillavou.jpeg
Bria Dillavou, owner of Mackabee Boutique in Keystone, S.D., was preparing shirts for display during the upcoming tourism season on April 30, 2026. 

Ryan Foley owns a real estate firm and Alexis is a school counselor, so the Foleys had a solid but not extravagant spending budget. In the Black Hills, they were able to pack a ton of experiences into their visit, including stops at Wind Cave National Park and Mount Rushmore National Memorial, and scenic drives on the Needles Highway and through Custer State Park.

They stayed in an Airbnb rental, ate at local restaurants and "received good value for our dollar," Ryan Foley said.

"It's been affordable, but the most important thing was being together with the family, and seeing all this," he said. "These are memories we're going to have forever."

Nation's birthday a potential tourism driver

The 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, also known as the country's semiquincentennial, will be celebrated across the state this summer.

As a result, Hagen sees strong tourism potential for South Dakota, both by residents and visitors.

Surveys show a majority of potential travelers are interested in American history, and that visitation to national parks is up 18% so far this year, which bodes well for a state with a patriotic vibe and several parks and monuments.

Rapid City, which promotes itself as the City of Presidents, will capitalize on the country's 250th anniversary with the Real America Birthday Bash planned for downtown on July 1-4. The U.S. Air Force Academy band will play on July 1, drone shows are slated for July 2-3, and a parade and fireworks show are on the calendar. The festivities will include vendors, food trucks, a beer garden and live music shows.

 2026-4-30 Tourist family helicopter.jpeg
Wisconsin tourists Ryan and Alexis Foley and their daughters, Amelia and Mabel, pose for a photo after taking a scenic helicopter ride with Black Hills Helicopters in Keystone, S.D., on April 30, 2026. 

The Black Hills region as a whole hopes to benefit from the nation's big birthday, including the fireworks show planned for Mount Rushmore on July 3. Gov. Larry Rhoden has invited President Trump, but no official announcement has been made.

"With the 250th and the fireworks, we're hoping for a good season," said Keystone clothing store owner Bria Dillavou.

With some uncertainty looming for summer 2026, Dillavou ordered the typical number of products for the two stores she owns with husband Corey — Mackabee Boutique and Mount Rushmore T-shirts — in the Keystone Mall just down the hill from Mount Rushmore.

"In general, vendors nationwide have been offering a lot more patriotic gear and souvenirs this year," she said as she unpacked shirts in her store.

Dillavou said she hears from a lot of tourists from the East who stop in Sioux Falls and the Black Hills on their way to points west, including Yellowstone National Park.

"Our experience has been that people are still taking family trips, especially if they can drive to their destination," she said.

Major events across the state in 2026

While the Black Hills may benefit from the 250th and, as usual, from the 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally on Aug. 7-16, tourism operators elsewhere across the state are optimistic for a strong year.

Sioux Falls is increasingly seen as a strong regional tourism market for shoppers and “foodies” who enjoy varied cuisines, said Teri Schmidt, CEO of Experience Sioux Falls.

The city and the rest of eastern South Dakota are attractive for visitors who want a family-friendly place to attend a wide range of annual events, including the Rock the Country Music Festival in late June, and the Sioux Falls Airshow and Hot Summer Nites car show in July.

 2026-5-4 Hagen at Rushmore.jpeg
South Dakota tourism secretary Jim Hagen, shown at Mount Rushmore National Memorial on May 4, 2026. Hagen and Gov. Larry Rhoden were at the memorial to announce distribution of $200,000 from the Tourism Advertising Promotion program that provided grants from $1,000 to $10,000 to 40 entities that operate festivals and other tourism events across South Dakota. 

Hunting, fishing, camping and other outdoor activities remain major draws for other East River locales, including the Glacial Lakes area in the northeast and the Missouri River in the central and southeast parts of the state.

Travel South Dakota, the tourism agency led by Hagen, spent most of its roughly $13 million advertising budget on neighboring states or markets that have shown success in the past, such as Chicago. Visits by Canadians remain down for the second year amid an ongoing trade war and vows by President Donald Trump about annexing the nation's northern neighbor.

South Dakota had what would be considered a so-so year for tourism in 2025, with 15 million visitors spending an estimated $5.2 billion, a 1.1% increase in revenues over 2024.

Other than the COVID-19 slowdown in 2020, when the state saw 12.6 million visitors spend $3.4 billion, South Dakota has seen a slow but steady rise in both categories over the past decade.

Visit South Dakota touts the fiscal power of the state tourism industry with a list of data points on its website. The agency said tourism generated 4.7% of the state's overall economy and 16.5% of all state sales tax collections last year, a total of $406 million. The agency said that tourism supports more than 59,000 jobs and that without tourism, each South Dakota household would have paid $1,121 more in taxes in 2025.

 051326-nws-travel-p6.png

Hagen said that last year, economic concerns caused trepidation among tourists, a sentiment not shown in traveler surveys this year.

"This year, I think people are like, 'We've had it. Let's get out, let's go have fun, let's travel, even if they'll be looking for good value along the way," he said.

And yet, some concern over gas prices

Schmidt said she and other tourism officials are keeping a wary eye on the national economy, which has been soft.

“The things that worry us are gas prices, airline prices and the overall economic condition of the country,” Schmidt said. “If gas goes to 5 bucks a gallon, we don’t know how people are going to respond and we could be looking at a much different situation.”

Schmidt said tightening consumer budgets could prompt some visitors to shorten planned visits or cull back typical spending levels. The early months of 2026 have been flat or only slightly up for visits and tourism spending, which will put more pressure on tourism businesses to have a strong summer to raise revenues into the black, she said.

 South Dakota News Watch logo
Learn more about South Dakota News Watch at sdnewswatch.org. 

Experience Sioux Falls has broadened its marketing efforts beyond the typical five-state neighboring region and more into the national market to potentially attract new tourists in addition to those who have visited in the past. Sioux Falls and South Dakota overall provide very good value for the tourism dollar, which will help during a challenging economy, she said.

“Our marketing has been strong, if not stronger than ever, but the competition for the tourism dollar also remains strong,” Schmidt said.

To date, visits to the Experience Sioux Falls website have been up, providing Schmidt and others with some hope. “Are we concerned? Of course we are. But we’re also very optimistic,” she said.

A boost in the spring and fall?

Michelle Thomson, CEO of the Black Hills & Badlands Tourism Association, said the high cost of living and rising fuel prices could drive more tourists to travel in the spring and fall shoulder seasons, when they anticipate lower prices.

Travelers are also more indecisive and are waiting longer to make reservations, which can add stress to tourism operators who like to see things booked out well in advance.

Rapid City and the Black Hills should see a strong year for revenue, with the Sturgis rally and the nation's 250th birthday leading the way, Thomson said.

"With the 250th, we have the potential to bring in people from across the country because we have such a patriotic experience here, and that's not just the fireworks," she said.

 2026-5-6 Wall tourist cars.jpeg
This May 6, 2026 photo of the iconic Wall Drug in Wall, S.D., shows cars from Iowa, New Hampshire, Colorado and South Dakota all parked out front. 

Thomson said national research shows that potential visitors are aware that the price of a vacation is rising but also that they aren't overly concerned.

"People are anticipating spending more, but they want to have those experiences and are willing to pay a little bit more for it," Thomson said.

title: Christopher Baumgartner running for state Senate in District 33
description: Christopher Baumgartner of Rapid City is the Democratic candidate for state Senate in District 33, which consists of several Rapid City neighborhoods as well as Black Hawk and Summerset.
_full_text:
Christopher Baumgartner of Rapid City is the Democratic candidate for state Senate in District 33, which consists of several Rapid City neighborhoods as well as Black Hawk and Summerset.

"South Dakota needs a strong two-party system," Baumgarner said in a release. "From groceries to gas to housing, South Dakotans are being squeezed. Home prices in the Rapid City area have surged, pushing home ownership out of reach and straining renters. We need policies that encourage affordable housing. To accomplish positive results, we need a diversity of viewpoints in Pierre."

 Christopher Baumgartner
Christopher Baumgartner 

Baumgartner is a graduate of Central High School and Northern State University in Aberdeen, with a degree in international business. He has worked in a variety of private businesses and is currently a contract employee for an immigration law firm. He was an Eagle Scout and is a member of the Knights of Columbus.

"Having lived with a disability my entire life, I know what it means to navigate systems and spaces that weren't designed for people like me," Baumgartner said. "South Dakota must do more to ensure full and equal access to public spaces, employment, healthcare, education, and state services. I hope to bring my lived experience to the Senate."

 Christopher Baumgartner
Christopher Baumgartner speaks during a Pennington County Democrats campaign announcement event on Monday, April 27, in Box Elder. 

Baumgartner said he believes South Dakota should reduce addiction by investing in treatment centers instead of incarceration. "We have the highest women's incarceration rate in America, which is not an effective response to the addiction crisis."

Baumgartner is also an advocate for affordable healthcare and for preserving rural hospitals. "I'm running for the State Senate because the status quo is no longer acceptable."

title: Eagle Butte man convicted of sexual abuse for incident on Pine Ridge Reservation
description: An Eagle Butte man faces up to life in prison after a jury convicted him of sexual abuse without consent and sexual abuse of a minor.
_full_text:
An Eagle Butte man faces up to life in prison after a jury convicted him of sexual abuse without consent and sexual abuse of a minor.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for South Dakota announced a jury returned a verdict for Emanual Semon, 24, on May 7, following a three-day trial.

The charges carry a maximum penalty of life in prison and/or a $250,000 fine, five years of supervised release and a $200 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

Semon was indicted by a federal grand jury in July 2024, the U.S. Attorney's Office said.

The convictions stem from an incident that occurred at a residence in the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in July 2024. At trial, the evidence established that on the afternoon of July 3, 2024, Semon engaged in sexual activity with a juvenile female without her consent. Semon stopped when an adult entered the room and interrupted him.

The crime was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian country be prosecuted in federal court as opposed to State court.

This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety. Supervisory Assistant U.S. Attorney Kirk Albertson prosecuted the case.

This case was brought as a part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorney’s Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc.

A presentence investigation was ordered and sentencing will be scheduled at a later date. Semon was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Updated: No threat found during search of Central High after bomb threat spurs evacuation
description: A bomb threat to Rapid City Central High School prompted law enforcement to evacuate the building on Thursday, May 14.
_full_text:
A bomb threat to Rapid City Central High School prompted law enforcement to evacuate the building on Thursday, May 14. 

In an update posted to Facebook around 6 p.m., the Rapid City Police Department said local law enforcement, in conjunction with explosives detection K9 officers from Ellsworth Air Force Base, found no threats during a search of the school.

"We are aware of similar hoax bomb threat calls that have been made across the nation in recent weeks. Even though there is no evidence to suggest a credible threat, today's public safety response to the location and swift evacuation of students/staff is a clear example of the priority local first responders place on the safety of our classrooms," the department said in the post. "We will continue to work with our federal law enforcement partners to identify the source of the initial call and will do everything in our power to ensure appropriate accountability for the person(s) responsible."

The police department said it was made aware of the threat shortly before 1 p.m.

The department said around 1:20 p.m., "Numerous law enforcement units have responded to the school and are currently working to assist with an evacuation of the building. Student and staff safety is the priority as law enforcement works to investigate the credibility of the threat."

A spokesperson for Rapid City Area Schools District said shortly before 2 p.m. that students are out of the building.

"Waiting on law enforcement to do their thing," she said.

In a video posted at about 2:25 p.m. on the Rapid City Police Department Facebook page, Police Chief Don Hedrick, RCAS Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson and Rapid City Fire Department Battalion Chief Calen Maningas provided an update on the situation.

Hedrick said something like this generates "a very quick and immediate response" from first-responders to get students to safety. Hedrick said he is proud of the quick and safe response that occurred. He said everything is locked down and students are staff are out of the building. 

"Now we're calling in all of our partners to help us investigate," Hedrick said,

That includes the Criminal Investigation Division, which is made up of law enforcement from both the Rapid City Police Department and the Pennington County Sheriff's Office. Hedrick added the department is calling in help from state and local partners, including Ellsworth Air Force Base, which is bringing dogs to help clear the building.

"We've caught people that have done this in the past, and we're gonna do everything we can to hold those accountable that did this here today," Hedrick said. 

Thompson said she's grateful for the quick response from law enforcement and staff to evacuate students.

"We had a very thorough response, and I am thankful all of our students and staff are safe," she said, also extending gratitude for the patience of parents.

Maningas said the fire department is staged on scene in the event of fire or injuries. 

The threat comes exactly two weeks after a bomb threat at Douglas High School prompted an evacuation. Law enforcement determined it was a hoax.

Just two days before the Douglas threat, two north Rapid City elementary schools were briefly placed on secure status after a report of a man in the neighborhood with a gun. The man was arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm with a prior felony drug conviction and receiving stolen property.

title: Campaign fact check: Rhoden voted for failed gas tax increase, but didn’t raise concealed carry fees
description: A claim in a political ad that South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden “increased the gas tax” is wrong, although he did vote for a failed increase, while a claim that he then “targeted your guns, increasing fees on concealed carry permits” is false.
_full_text:
A claim in a political ad that South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden “increased the gas tax” is wrong, although he did vote for a failed increase, while a claim that he then “targeted your guns, increasing fees on concealed carry permits” is false.

The claims are in ads paid for by the Rushmore Principles political action committee, chaired by Hadyn Smith of Mountain Brook, Alabama. Smith’s email address in campaign finance documents indicates he’s affiliated with the Crosby Ottenhoff Group, which describes itself as “focused on building strategic, quality services for political committees.” Smith did not respond to requests for comment.

 Rhoden Announcement Rhoden.JPG
Gov. Larry Rhoden announces his bid for a full term on Tuesday, Nov. 18 at the Alex Johnson Hotel in Rapid City. 

Because Rushmore Principles was formed in March and doesn’t face a campaign finance reporting deadline until next week, nothing is publicly known about the committee’s funding sources.

One of Rushmore Principle’s ads says “Rhoden raised fees on plumbers, nurses, miners, barbers, and even on assisted living facilities that care for seniors. And he increased the gas tax, the cell phone tax, and fees on milk. Then Rhoden targeted your guns, increasing fees on concealed carry permits and hunting licenses.”

Rhoden’s campaign singled out the two claims that he raised the gas tax and increased fees on concealed carry permits as false, and demanded that broadcasters pull the ad. A broadcast official contacted by Searchlight indicated that the ads are under review and have not been pulled, and Fury did not respond when asked whether he knew of broadcasters pulling the ads.

Rhoden campaign manager Ian Fury called the claims “patently false” and said Rhoden “has cut taxes his entire career.” Fury said the last state gas-tax increases happened in 1999 and 2015, when Rhoden was not serving in the Legislature or the executive branch. Before being elevated to governor last year when then-Gov. Kristi Noem departed for a job in the Trump administration, Rhoden had been lieutenant governor since 2019. He previously served 16 years in the Legislature.

As a state senator in 2009, Rhoden voted for Senate Bill 201. The version of the bill that came to the Senate would have increased the gas tax by 3 cents per gallon. The bill was amended on the Senate floor to an increase that amounted to a tiny fraction of a penny. The bill’s primary sponsor, Sen. Mike Vehle, R-Mitchell, proposed the amendment in an attempt to keep the bill moving.

“I want to keep this bill alive,” Vehle told fellow senators in the Senate chamber.

 Dusty Johnson
U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson speaks to a crowd at the David Lust Accelerator Building at Elevate Rapid City on Monday, June 30, as he announces his run for governor. 

Rhoden voted for the amended version of the bill, but it failed. Fury said the description of the vote in the ad was inaccurate.

“The ad doesn’t say ‘voted to raise gas tax,’” Fury told Searchlight in a statement. “It says he raised it.”

Regarding the concealed carrying of pistols, the Noem-Rhoden administration eliminated fees for concealed carry permits in 2022. South Dakota Searchlight was unable to find evidence of Rhoden increasing fees on concealed carry permits. He did cast a vote in 2017, while serving as a state representative, for a bill that created an easier renewal process for concealed-carry permits and set the renewal fee at $10, but that fee was unchanged from the prior reapplication process.

A broader Rushmore Principles claim that Rhoden raised “400 taxes and fees” was not fully documented. Fury told Searchlight that he highlighted the gas-tax and concealed-carry claims because those were “patently false,” while describing other claims as “twisting the facts.”

“There are certainly other false claims in Dusty’s ads,” Fury said, referring to Republican U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, who is running against Rhoden for the Republican nomination for governor in the June 2 primary election. State House Speaker Jon Hansen and businessman Toby Doeden are also running.

Johnson disclaimed any connection to the Rushmore Principles ads.

“I did not approve these ads, but it’s clear this PAC supports me and opposes the governor’s history of tax and fee increases,” Johnson said. “Every other candidate has a PAC supporting them and this is no different.”

 Johnson, Lt. Doyle talk accountability
Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, who is running for governor, and Rapid City Police Lt. Tim Doyle, talk about offender accountability.

title: 21-year-old pleads not guilty to charges related to incident that left woman with a gunshot wound
description: Neves Blue Legs, a 21-year-old Rapid Citian accused of involvement with a shooting that left a woman with a leg injury, pleaded not guilty in Pennington County Court Thursday, May 14, to one additional and one adjusted charge added to his case.
_full_text:
Neves Blue Legs, a 21-year-old Rapid Citian accused of involvement with a shooting that left a woman with a leg injury, pleaded not guilty in Pennington County Court Thursday, May 14, to one additional and one adjusted charge added to his case. 

The shooting occurred on Dec. 12, 2024, per court documents and the Rapid City Police Department. When officers arrived at 110 E. Watertown St. that day, they found a woman with a gunshot wound to the leg after a bullet entered the residence from the outside. The woman was treated on scene and then taken to the hospital. Multiple people were seen running from the scene, police said.

They found the group at a convenience store nearby and detained them. Ultimately, the then 19-year-old Blue Legs was arrested. 

A grand jury charged him on Jan. 15, 2025, with aggravated assault, discharge of a firearm at a motor vehicle, possession of a loaded firearm while intoxicated and possession or consumption of alcohol by a minor. The first three charges are Class 3 felonies with a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison at up to a $30,000 fine. The alcohol charge is a Class 1 misdemeanor with a maximum of one year in prison and up to a $500 fine. He pleaded not guilty on Feb. 6, 2025. 

A document called a Part II Information labels Blue Legs as a habitual offender for a November 2023 first-degree burglary conviction. If that's proven or Blue Legs admits it is accurate, the maximum penalties for the first three charges would increase to 25 years in prison and a $50,000 and the misdemeanor alcohol charge would increase to a Class 5 felony, which carries a maximum penalty of 5 years and up to a $10,000 fine. 

On Thursday, Blue Legs maintained his existing not guilty pleas and his denial of the Part II information. He also pleaded not guilty to possession of a firearm by one with a prior violent crime conviction, a charge added onto a superseding May 14 indictment.

He also entered a not guilty plea to an adjustment on the discharge of a firearm charge. The adjustment added the wording about the discharge of a firearm at an occupied structure. Discharge of a firearm at an occupied structure or a motor vehicle are governed by the same statute. 

Blue Legs is held in the Pennington County Jail on a $10,000 cash only bond. He is held on no bond for an alleged probation violation in the burglary case. 

He is scheduled to appear in court for a status hearing at 2:15 p.m. on June 11.

title: Rapid City police: Officer uses stun gun on man holding metal rod who refused commands
description: A Rapid City Police Department officer Tased a man holding a metal rod who didn't comply with commands during a disturbance at Hainesway Apartments in Rapid City.
_full_text:
A Rapid City Police Department officer Tased a man holding a metal rod who didn't comply with commands during a disturbance at Hainesway Apartments in Rapid City.

The department said officers were called around 9:30 p.m. on Wednesday, May 13, to an apartment at 1330 Atlas Street for a report of an in-progress disturbance. When officers knocked on the door of the residence, a woman inside told them to enter. As police opened the door, they encountered a man, Benjamin Long Wolf, 43, of Rapid City, standing in the entryway who allegedly threatened officers with a large metal rod he was holding over his head.

The man refused multiple commands to drop the rod, according to the department. A responding officer deployed a stun gun, police said. The man complied after that.

Officers detained the man and, in accordance with department policy, called a medical unit in to evaluate the suspect post-Tasing.

Police arrested Long Wolf on suspicion of aggravated assault on law enforcement and on several outstanding warrants. Long Wolf remains at the Pennington County Jail, with no bond set for the assault charge as of early afternoon on Thursday, May 14, according to jail records.

South Dakota court records show Long Wolf has a pending case in Fall River County on a driving under the influence-second offense charge and driving with a suspended license.

On the assault charge, Long Wolf made his initial appearance in court Thursday morning and has a preliminary hearing scheduled for 9 a.m. on May 29.
