title: Gillette man sentenced to prison in SD after he survives fentanyl overdose, but family member dies
description: On New Years Eve in 2020, Christopher Ray Lara, of Gillette, Wyoming — who is now 32-years-old — obtained pills in Pennington County he thought were oxycodone and shared them with a family member. Both took the pills, which were actually fentanyl, and overdosed. Lara lived, the family member died.
_full_text:
On New Years Eve in 2020, Christopher Ray Lara, of Gillette, Wyoming — who is now 32-years-old — obtained pills in Pennington County he thought were oxycodone and shared them with a family member. Both took the pills, which were actually fentanyl, and overdosed. Lara lived, the family member died. 

On Thursday, May 14, Lara appeared in court for his sentencing on a possession of a controlled drug or substance charge, which he pleaded guilty to on April 22.

Deputy Pennington County State's Attorney Olivia Siglin asked the judge to sentence Lara to three years in prison for the charge, which carries a maximum of five years in prison and up to a $10,000 fine.

She said the state could not charge Lara with distribution resulting in a death because no exchange was made. If he had been charged with that, depending on the circumstances, Lara would have faced from up to 25 years to up to life in prison. 

Matthew Rappold, Lara's defense attorney, said his client is sorry his relative passed away. He asked the court for a sentence that would allow Lara to return to Wyoming to finish out a sentence he's serving there. After that, he would go to California. 

Presiding Seventh Circuit Court Judge Heidi Linngren honored Siglin's request. She noted there are mitigating factors, such as Lara attending treatment, but the aggravating factors are significant. 

She and Siglin noted Lara picked up three new felony charges in Wyoming since the death of his family member.

"He continued to commit felony crimes," Linngren said before imposing the 3-year sentence. 

Fentanyl is a potent synthetic opioid drug approved by the FDA for pain relief and as an anesthetic, according to a fact sheet from the Druge Enforcement Administration It's 100 times more potent than morphine and 50 times more potent than heroine.

According to the DEA, overdose deaths involving synthetic opioids, excluding methadone, were involved in roughly 2,600 drug overdose deaths each year in 2011 and 2012, but from 2013 through 2021, the number of drug overdose deaths involving synthetic opioids, excluding methadone, increased dramatically, to more than 71,000 in 2021. The total number of overdose deaths for this category was greater than 260,000 for 2013 through 2021. These overdose deaths involving synthetic opioids is primarily driven by illicitly manufactured fentanyl, including fentanyl analogs.

title: DIY delight: Frenchies Haus in Rapid City a hub for creative adults, kids
description: Lexi Privitt loves making the world a happier, more beautiful place. This spring, she opened a The Parfum Bar in Rapid City where locals and tourists can use their creativity to craft signature scents.
_full_text:
Lexi Privitt loves making the world a happier, more beautiful place. This spring, she opened a The Parfum Bar in Rapid City where locals and tourists can use their creativity to craft signature scents.

Privitt is the owner and hair stylist at Graceful Glamour salon, and the owner of Frenchies Haus. Frenchies Haus is a creative hub that offers DIY charm bracelets and necklaces, customizable trend accessories, custom slime for kids, and now The Parfum Bar. Privitt’s side-by-side businesses at 4447 S. Canyon Road Suites 2 and 3 are uplifting havens for Privitt and her customers.

 Frenchies Haus owner Lexi Privitt
Frenchies Haus owner Lexi Privitt holds a stand with a newly completed charm bracelet on it. Frenchies Haus is a DIY destination in Rapid City where people can make their own custom jewelry, perfume, and kids can make their own slime.  

“I have always loved crafts and making art,” Previtt said. “Last year, I had the passion to share that with my community. Seeing other individuals come in and make art, I love that. … Being able to have a space and seeing kids play with slime, and seeing moms and daughters or best friends come in and make matching charm bracelets is very nostalgic for me. I love seeing the joy it brings my community.”

Appointments are highly encouraged for The Parfum Bar, Charm Haus and Slime Haus at Frenchies Haus. Frenchies Haus hours are 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., or by appointment, Friday through Sunday.

 Frenchies Haus The Parfum Bar
The Parfum Bar opened in April at Frenchies Haus in Rapid City. The Parfum Bar allows customers to create personalized fragrance blends.  

“I wanted people to feel like, ‘What should we do on a Friday or Saturday? We should go to Frenchies and add to our charm bracelets or make our new perfume or getting the kids together and letting them make slime,’” she said.

“I wanted to know my community and to have recurring guests come back so I could know them. I love connections. I love knowing who lives in my city and the cities surrounding. That’s been very exciting,” Privitt said.

The Parfum Bar

The Parfum Bar debuted in April. It’s the latest addition to Frenchies Haus, which Privitt opened in December 2025. The Parfum Bar offers customers an assortment of cosmetic-graded fragrance oils they can use to create signature scents and customizable perfume bottles.

 Frenchies Haus perfume bottles
The Parfum Bar at Frenchies Haus in Rapid City gives customers the opportunity to paint or engrave bottles to hold the custom-blended scents they create. Frenchies Haus owner Lexi Privitt holds hand-painted perfume bottles. 

Inspiration for The Parfum Bar came from Privitt’s hair salon customers who said they wanted more “different and cool and fun” experiences for older teens and women in Rapid City. When Privitt learned about custom mobile perfume bars at weddings in California, she adapted the idea for Frenchies Haus.

“I’ve always loved perfume, but I couldn’t justify spending $100-plus on perfume that I don’t get to refill,” Privitt said.

At The Parfum Bar, every fragrance oil’s name is an affirmation such as Strength, Grace, Rejoice and She Flourishes. Each customer can choose three oils to blend for their own signature fragrance.

“I think affirmations are very powerful, and what we are clothing ourselves in, what we’re spraying on ourselves, what we tell ourselves is very powerful, whether it’s positive or negative. I wanted this to remind people who are building (their fragrances) that they’re worthy. They are loved, that they’re cared for. They’re important,” Privitt said.

A brief, fun personality quiz can further guide customers as they concoct each signature perfume. With paint and engraving, customers can create distinctive bottles for their fragrances. In The Parfum Bar’s first weeks in business, it’s attracted customers who want scents for everyday wear, date nights and special occasions, Privitt said.

 Frenchies Haus bracelets
An array of bracelets is displayed at Charm Haus at Frenchies Haus in Rapid City. The bracelets can be customized with hundreds of charms.  

“We had a bridal party from Nebraska (come to The Parfum Bar). The bride created a custom scent and engraved her new last name on the bottle,” she said.

The Parfum Bar keeps a record of each customer’s fragrance blend so it’s easy for people to return and blend refills of their fragrances.

Charm Haus

Charm Haus invites customers to select necklaces or bracelets to adorn, with hundreds of charms to choose from. All the bracelets are non-tarnishable and waterproof for longevity. Customers can opt for premium charms, which are $8 each and made to be more long-lasting, or signature charms, which are $3.

The premium charms come in an array of specific themes. The signature charms offer fun, budget-friendly options.

People love the opportunity to choose charms that are personal and meaningful, Privitt said.

 Frenchies Haus putting charms on a bracelet
Frenchies Haus owner Lexi Privitt add charms to a bracelet at Charm Haus, part of Frenchies Haus in Rapid City.  

“I have not met anyone who has not been able to find to find something that they’re looking for,” she said. “They’re creating their story with it. That takes the longest.”

Frenchies Haus also carries an assortment of colorful decorative “icings” customers can use to adorn sunglasses, handheld mirrors, phone cases, bookmarks, hair clips, picture frames, jewelry boxes and more. Resin or silicone-based mixtures are used to adhere beads and charms to accessories and to create fanciful textures that resemble icing.

“That has been very popular for people to create their own fun accessories, whether they wear it or they use it every day,” Privitt said.

Slime Haus

Squishies, toys that give kids sensory experiences are “a phenomenon,” Privitt said. Squishies are silicone-wrapped sensory toys. In January, Privitt introduced Slime Haus at Frenchies Haus where kids have hands-on opportunities to create their own squishy, colorful, accessorized slime-filled squishies.

Squishies’ silicone wrapping can break, especially with rough play, so Frenchies Haus offers non-toxic slime to go inside squishies.

 Frenchies Haus trend accessories
DID trend accessories are popular with kids and adults at Frenchies Haus in Rapid City. Resin or silicon-based mixtures that resemble icing are used to adorn accessories with beads and charms.  

“Kids love to customize their own things. They can come here and make their own (squishies), filling with slime. We’ll fill the squishie and seal it. If it breaks, they have the slime inside they can play with, so it’s kind of like a two-for-one,” Privitt said.

Justice Raven joins Privitt to teach slime classes and help kids make their creations.

“We teach them how to mix it together. We give kids a slime master certificate and it’s signed and dated. We send them home with a goody bag and activator spray that helps make the slime not so sticky,” Privitt said.

Storage jars are available for the slime in case the silicone wrapping breaks.

The slime and squishes have been “a huge hit,” especially with Privitt’s nephew, Alkai, 10, and niece is Shyheir, 4.

“When I started doing the slime, they were actually my little guinea pigs,” Privitt said, chuckling. “They were testing it out and touching it and adding all the things, so they know when they come to Auntie’s, they get to play and make their own slime.”

 Frenchies Haus ice cream slime
It looks like ice cream but it's actually non-edible slime, a toy kids can create at the Frenchies Haus mobile cart. 

For the littlest creatives younger than 4, Slime Haus has cloud dough, similar to PlayDoh, for children don’t know how to play with slime’s unique texture yet.  

This summer, watch for Frenchies Haus’ mobile cart, where kids will be able to make slime that looks remarkably like real ice cream but isn’t edible.

Frenchies Haus will host classes and special events like birthday parties and bridal showers. For more information, follow Frenchies Haus on Facebook, Instagram and TikTok.

title: Graceful Glamour: Frenchies Haus sister business a salon to pamper you
description: Lexi Privitt, owner of Frenchies Haus in Rapid City, started her journey as an entrepreneur two years ago by opening a hair salon, Graceful Glamour .
_full_text:
Lexi Privitt, owner of Frenchies Haus in Rapid City, started her journey as an entrepreneur two years ago by opening a hair salon, Graceful Glamour. 

Graceful Glamour, at 4447 S. Canyon Road Suite 2, sits next door to Frenchies Haus. While Frenchies Haus is a place for people to express their creativity, Graceful Glamour is a place where Privitt helps her customers look and feel better.

Privitt, 27, has been a hair stylist for eight years. At her salon, she specializes in giving her clientele personalized care in a peaceful setting. She trained at Paul Mitchell in Dallas for her aesthetics license (skin care, waxing, lash extensions) and she earned her cosmetology license at Black Hills Beauty College where she trained as a hair stylist, and for waxing and facials.

 Graceful Glamour
Graceful Glamour in Rapid City is a peaceful salon during its business hours. After business hours, a portion of the salon is designated for birthday parties and special events. Graceful Glamour is a sister business to owner Lexi Privitt's Frenchies Haus next door.  

“I wanted my own shampoo room that could provide that unique and relaxing experience,” Privitt said. “I really love the art of shampooing hair.”

Graceful Glamour offers hair cuts and styles, coloring and waxing. What sets the salon apart most, though, are Japanese head spa treatments.

“I think I was the first one (in Rapid City),” Privitt said, saying that learning how to offer Japanese head spas was a fulfilling experience.

A Japanese head spa is “a very relaxing experience where a lot of sensory (stimulation) is going on on the scalp. There is a (round, over-the-bowl) fountain stimulating the scalp. It feels like a waterfall on the scalp. I massage with oils on the scalp and you have that waterfall on the scalp, and it is a series of stimulation using tools like guasha combs,” Privitt said.

The result is an experience that can help with hair growth. The Japanese head spas also can alleviate dry, flaky scalps that may be made worse by a lack of humidity and hair product build-up.

“I’ve had clients come in with recurring migraines, and the pressure points and massaging (involved in Japanese head spas) relieve tension that people don’t even realize that they have in their scalp,” Privitt said.

 Lexi Privitt Graceful Glamour and Frenchies Haus owner mug
Lexi Privitt 

“In general, you come in and the moment a stylist is touching you, there is this bond that’s undescribable,” she said. “You’re helping someone just escape their reality for a moment being a nurturing place. … There’s something about the human touch and a caring human touch that makes such a difference.”

Offering a nurturing atmosphere for clients is one of Privitt’s favorite aspects of Graceful Glamour.

“The older I get, the more I have this feeling of wanting to be (out in the) community,” she said. “I love to serve. I feel like that’s my purpose here.”

Graceful Glamour is open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday through Thursday. Appointments can be booked online at lexiprivitt.glossgenius.com. Follow Graceful Glamour on Facebook and Instagram for more information.

title: Businesses urge power merger, while consumers cite cost, reliability concerns
description: If NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills Corp merge, the deal could mean as much as $16 million for CEO Brian Bird, and a total of nearly $30 million for the top five executives of the Montana utility.
_full_text:
If NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills Corp merge, the deal could mean as much as $16 million for CEO Brian Bird, and a total of nearly $30 million for the top five executives of the Montana utility.

Bird is CEO of NorthWestern, and if the Montana Public Service Commission approves the proposed merger, and the deal goes through, Bird would head the new company, Bright Horizon Energy, or get the “golden parachute.”

Tuesday, the Montana Public Service Commission’s hearing on the $15.4 billion merger started, with ratepayers calling for more transparency when it comes to data centers, and business representatives pushing for approval of the deal in a quest for reliable power.

In opening statements, lawyers for the utilities argued the merger will “deliver long-term value to customers” —  but one attorney representing a couple of third parties said it would be a “betrayal” of Montanans.

“Everyone at the table negotiating this deal loved it,” said lawyer Monica Tranel, with 350 Montana and the Montana Farmers Union. “They all can make a lot of money from it. But who wasn’t there? The people of Montana.”

In questioning, Tranel showed NorthWestern would have less control if the merger is approved; Black Hills would account for 56% of the parent company overseeing the merged entity, while NorthWestern would account for 44%, and Black Hills would have six board seats, while NorthWestern would have five.

But lawyer Sarah Norcott, with NorthWestern Energy, said a merged company would still be under the oversight of the Montana Public Service Commission. Additionally, Norcott said the utility would be better equipped to weather market volatility and have easier access to capital to invest in infrastructure.

“Our Montana utility operations will remain exactly where they are today,” Norcott said.

In August 2025, NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills announced the proposed deal, which requires approval from regulators, including the Montana Public Service Commission. The PSC is made up of five elected officials, currently all Republican, with two seats up for election this year.

The proposal under consideration includes four settlement agreements, including with the Montana Consumer Counsel, which advocates for customers, but ratepayers and conservation watchdogs have raised questions about the merger.

For example, a filing in the case has estimated labor “savings” at $36 million, with ensuing concerns about employee cuts in Montana. Also, on an investors call, Bird pitched the merger as a chance to “really capture data center opportunities,” but NorthWestern has blacked out most of the details in documents about those deals.

Tuesday, the hearing started with public comment, and many Montanans pointed to Bird’s remarks about the “capture” of data center businesses. Leah Nuese-Yaker, a recent graduate of the University of Montana, said the deal is for shareholders and tech companies, not Montanans.

“It is not for Montana families. It is not for rural communities who are already feeling the squeeze of rising utility costs,” Nuese-Yaker said.

Sarah Lundquist, with Families for a Livable Climate, said in other states, data center demand is leading to reliability concerns and “pressure on electricity costs,” with residential customers needing protection.

“Montanans should not be asked to shoulder these risks without clear protections and full public transparency,” Lundquist said.

But representatives of the business community asked the Public Service Commission to approve the merger to ensure companies in Montana can count on electricity to run operations into the future.

John Iverson, with the Treasure State Resources Association, said energy intensive businesses in timber, oil, gas, transportation and construction make investment decisions years, even decades in advance.

In doing so, Iverson said they need to know power will remain affordable and reliable.

“Without that, we don’t have these large-scale operations in Montana,” Iverson said. “We simply can’t support them.”

State Rep. Gary Parry, R-Colstrip, urged support for the merger. Parry, who represents a community with NorthWestern’s coal-fired plant and sits on Gov. Greg Gianforte’s energy task force, also said the question before the PSC isn’t about data centers.

“From my perspective, this merger is fundamentally about reliability, long-term infrastructure investment and ensuring Montana has a utility capable of meeting the growing demand, energy demands, of our state and region,” Parry said.

In opening statements, Norcott, on behalf of NorthWestern, said nothing in the merger diminishes the Public Service Commission’s authority, weakens regulatory protections, or shifts risk onto customers.

“Montana will remain the largest jurisdiction after the merger closes,” Norcott said. “Rates will remain unchanged because of the merger. Today’s exceptional service by these two utilities will remain.”

On behalf of Black Hills, lawyer Wiley Barker said the utilities are “natural” partners, serving some of the same territory, and sharing strong commitments to their respective communities and customers.

“This is not an acquisition. It is a true merger of equals,” Barker said.

On behalf of a couple of intervenors, however, Tranel said the people crafting the deal all have something to gain, from bankers who will get as much as $60 million in transaction fees to shareholders who already own both companies and will get a 5% to 7% higher return.

A Securities and Exchange Commission filing outlines the potential wins for NorthWestern executives should the merger close without positions for them, including $16 million for Bird, $5.3 million for Crystal Lail, $2.9 million for Shannon Heim, $2.5 million for John Hines (he retired after the filing, according to NorthWestern), and $2.6 million for Bobbi Schroeppel.

By comparison, Tranel said a credit for customers in a settlement with the Montana Consumer Counsel is $10 million, which she said some will argue is a good deal. But Tranel said that amount translates to about $18 a household — “not a customer, a household.”

Tranel also said if the merger is approved, the utilities together would control a span of  land covering 20% of the United States, “a multistate area that covers the prime agricultural land in this country,” and a deal she said is designed to serve data center demand.

In its early days, Montana saw the Copper Kings enrich themselves in the state at the expense of clean rivers and workers, and some members of the public said they worried the merger would bring more of the same.

“If the Public Service Commission approves this merger, you will be creating a whole new modern-day robber-baron class … that will once again get filthy rich at the expense of our water, our Earth, our paychecks and generations to come,” said Patty Ames.

Mark Brastrup spoke about more recent history. Brastrup said he’s a journeyman lineman who has worked on the electrical grid in Montana for 30 years, and he sees firsthand what it takes to keep the electricity flowing.

Brastrup said the merger should be approved as a practical matter. He said Montana is a big state with tough weather and infrastructure that requires constant upkeep and investment, and a larger utility will mean more access to capital and resources.

“Keeping the system reliable takes people, materials, money and consistency over time,” Brastrup said. “What I’ve seen over the years, when the investment falls behind, the grid falls behind. Repairs take longer. Equipment ages out. The job gets harder and less safe for the crews working it. That’s where I see the benefit.”

The hearing is expected to resume at 8:30 a.m. Wednesday and conclude Friday.

A recent news release from the utilities about the merger said the deal still requires approval from regulators in Nebraska and South Dakota, and the companies expect to close the second part of 2026.

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to note the payout for NorthWestern executives takes place if the merger closes and they do not have positions in the new company, and to note Hines retired following the SEC filing.

title: Woman dies, another injured in 2-vehicle crash west of Rapid City on U.S. Highway 16
description: A Rapid City woman died from injuries suffered in a two-vehicle crash west of Rapid City.
_full_text:
A Rapid City woman died from injuries suffered in a two-vehicle crash west of Rapid City.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol said the two-vehicle crash occurred on Thursday, May 14, on U.S. Highway 16 near the 58-mile marker, about 6 miles west of Rapid City. The patrol did not provide the time of the crash.

The patrol did not release the names of those involved pending notification of family members.

A preliminary investigation determined a 56-year-old Rapid City woman driving a 1996 Toyota Corolla entered the intersection on US 16 from Busted Five Court when a westbound 2019 GMC Sierra driven by a 58-year-old Newcastle, Wyoming man on US 16 collided with the Corolla.

The Corolla spun onto the north shoulder, ejecting the passenger, a 76-year-old woman from Rapid City. Neither woman in the Toyota was wearing a seat belt. Medics took both women to Monument Health Rapid City Hospital with life-threatening injuries and the passenger later died, the patrol said.

The Wyoming man suffered minor injuries. He was wearing a seat belt, according to the patrol.

The patrol said an investigation into the crash continues.

title: Larry Blote
description: October 6, 1934 - May 11, 2026
_full_text:
October 6, 1934 - May 11, 2026

After a short courageous battle with cancer, Larry Blote died peacefully on May 11, 2026, at the Hospice House in Rapid City, his family at his side. He was 91 years old, diagnosed only 3 months ago, and was still going to work daily until that point at the family business, First Stop Gun.

Larry was born on October 6, 1934, to Otto and Leona Blote. His only sister, Gloria, joined the family 8 years later. The two siblings cherished their childhood years in their hometown of DeSmet, South Dakota, the famed setting of "Little House on the Prairie."

Larry married Patricia Kovarik in 1956 at the Church of St. Anthony, in Red Owl, SD, at which time he joined the Catholic Church. They were blessed with three sons, Mark, Mike, and Steve. After graduating from Black Hills State College as a busy dad, Larry built a successful career in banking and finance. He was involved in the family gun store for almost 50 years.

Larry was working daily for the last three decades as an integral part of the family businesses.

An avid traveler, Larry visited many countries on 6 continents and loved to take in theatre productions from Rapid City to New York to London.

Active in his community, Larry served on the Rapid City Common Council, the YMCA board, Downtown Rapid City BID board and the Savings and Loan National Association board. He was also a member of the Rapid City Chamber of Commerce, Kiwanis, and the Moose Lodge.

Above all, Larry could best be defined as a man who deeply loved his family and friends.

He is survived by his wife Patricia and his 3 sons, Mark (Debra Watson) Blote, Mike (Laura) Blote, and Steve (LaRae) Blote. Larry's six grandchildren, RoseMarie, Brigit, Teresa, John, Emily, and Grace were his pride and joy. Larry is also survived by his beloved sister, Gloria (late Allen) Wienk, as well as many loved family members and dear friends.

In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation in Larry's name to Hospice House (% Stacey Lenards, 224 Elk St, Rapid City, SD 57701) or your favorite charity.

title: Dr. Bert Corwin
description: Dr. Bert Clark Corwin was born on October 4, 1930, in Rapid City, SD to Meade Carpenter and Adeline Clark Corwin. On May 10, 2026, at the age of 95, he peacefully passed away at home, surrounded by his loving and devoted family, to be with his Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. His passing was the result of metastatic melanoma.
_full_text:
Dr. Bert Clark Corwin was born on October 4, 1930, in Rapid City, SD to Meade Carpenter and Adeline Clark Corwin. On May 10, 2026, at the age of 95, he peacefully passed away at home, surrounded by his loving and devoted family, to be with his Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. His passing was the result of metastatic melanoma.

At the age of three, Bert experienced a profound tragedy when a fire at the family home in 1933 claimed the lives of his mother and infant brother, James, and severely injured his father Meade. Following the tragedy Bert lived with his paternal grandparents, Bert Noyes and Fannie Carpenter Corwin, on their farm near Forestburg, SD. Sharing his grandfather's name, he was affectionately known as "Buddy."

At age 9, after his father married Opal Barber, Bert returned to live with his father and stepmother on the family farm in Meade County, where he worked alongside his father and developed the strong work ethic and resilience that would define his life.

Bert began his education in a one-room rural schoolhouse, riding his horse to and from school each day. He graduated from New Underwood High School, where he served as captain of the football team. He went on to earn a degree in Agriculture from South Dakota State University before being accepted to the Illinois College of Optometry. After receiving his Doctor of Optometry degree, he began what would become a distinguished 60-year career in optometry, specializing in contact lenses, low vision, and Primary care. He remained licensed until 2026, always furthering his knowledge and education.

Bert met the love of his life, Lydia Forehand, on a blind date while waterskiing at Sheridan Lake in 1958. They were married in 1959 and celebrated their 66th wedding anniversary last October. Together they built a beautiful life and family, welcoming two children: Bert Clark "Clark" Corwin II and Kelley Linette Corwin.

Dr. Corwin enjoyed an extraordinary and highly respected career in optometry. His professional memberships included the South Dakota Optometric Society, the American Optometric Association, the American Academy of Optometry, the American Academy of Optometry Foundation, and the International Society of Contact Lens Specialists. He was a Diplomate of the Cornea and Contact Lens Section of the American Academy of Optometry. Throughout his career, he held numerous leadership positions, including President of the South Dakota Optometric Society, President of the South Dakota State Board of Examiners in Optometry, President of the American Academy of Optometry, and President of the American Academy of Optometry Foundation.

His dedication to the profession earned him many honors and awards, including Optometrist of the Year from both the South Dakota Optometric Society and the American Optometric Association, induction into the American Academy of Optometry Hall of Fame, Honorary Life Memberships in both the American Academy of Optometry and the International Society of Contact Lens Specialists, and recognition as a Distinguished Practitioner of the National Academy of Practice in Optometry.

Dr. Corwin was equally devoted to serving his community. He was a charter member and past president of the Rushmore Lions Club, a member of the NAJA Temple Shrine and the Masonic Lodge for 72 years, former President of the Rapid City Regional Airport Board, and a faithful member of Faith Community Church. He also gave back extensively to his profession through research and education. He participated in FDA clinical investigations of new contact lens products and lectured regionally, statewide, nationally, and internationally on contact lenses, pharmacology, low vision, and practice management.

Bert pursued his leisure activities with the same enthusiasm and passion that he brought to his profession. He learned to fly in 1947 at the age of 17 on the family farm in Bonita Springs, where he and his father, also a pilot, maintained a grass runway and hangars on their property. Flying remained one of his lifelong passions, and he continued piloting aircraft for 79 years, taking his final flight on March 20, 2026.

An avid waterskier, Bert was a longtime member of the Black Hills Water Ski Club beginning in 1960. He competed in slalom, trick skiing, and jumping events and participated in ski shows on Canyon Lake. He took his final ski ride at the age of 93. Bert also loved snow skiing, a passion he pursued for more than 75 years after beginning in the mid-1950s. He made his last run in March 2026.

Growing up in rural South Dakota instilled in him a lifelong love of hunting deer, antelope, and pheasants, and he rarely, if ever, missed a season. He also continued branding cattle from his teenage years until the age of 95. Reflecting those country roots, he loved John Wayne movies, Gunsmoke, and western music.

Bert and Lydia shared a deep love of travel and adventure. Together they visited 69 countries and all seven continents. In 2000, they were among a select group of travelers who flew around the world aboard the Concorde jet.

Above all, Bert was known for his kindness, compassion, generosity, and unwavering faith. He was a remarkable husband, father, grandfather, mentor, and friend whose life positively impacted countless people. He will be deeply missed by all who knew and loved him.

He is survived by his beloved wife, Lydia; his son, Clark (Julie) Corwin; his daughter, Kelley Fromm; grandsons Chase, Jake, and Nick Fromm; granddaughters Kaylee, Lexi, and Trinity Corwin; step-grandsons James Kielhorn and Dominic Frein; and cousins Gary Pearson, Dean Clark, Tom Clark, Kay Deane, and Marge Lindemann. He was preceded in death by his grandparents, Bert N. and Fannie Corwin; his parents, Meade and Adeline Corwin; his stepmother, Opal Barber; his infant brother, James; and his half-sister, Arla.

Visitation will be held Sunday, May 17, 2026, from 5:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. at Kirk Funeral Home. Funeral services will be held Monday, May 18, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. at Canyon Lake United Methodist Church. The burial location is the Pine Lawn Cemetery. Memorial donations in Bert's honor may be made to the Bert C. and Lydia M. Corwin Ezell Fellowship Award at the American Academy of Optometry Foundation or to Faith Community Church in Rapid City, South Dakota.

title: Indian rodeo: Documenting 1 of South Dakota's oldest traditions
byline: MOLLY WETSCH South Dakota News Watch
description: The massive hand-painted sign, hung on a fence at a bull riding event in Kyle, certainly illustrates the rough-and-tumble nature of South Dakota's official state sport: “Not responsible for accidents or thefts.”
_full_text:
The massive hand-painted sign, hung on a fence at a bull riding event in Kyle, certainly illustrates the rough-and-tumble nature of South Dakota's official state sport: “Not responsible for accidents or thefts.”

Even more so when you consider the fact that this sign is smack-dab in the middle of one of the most remote regions of the state — no hospitals for about 50 miles. And when you see a young man with one hand flung in the air next to it, holding on for dear life, you've got yourself a true Wild West rodeo.

So, of course, Jeremiah Murphy had to take a photo of it.

 Murphy - Three Mile Creek.jpg
A rider on the back of a bull at the Three Mile Creek Easter Egg Hunt and Bull Riding event in Kyle, S.D., on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation on Apr. 11, 2026. 

Murphy, a lobbyist by trade, began photographing the Indian rodeo circuit in South Dakota and surrounding states about 15 years ago. He describes stumbling into it after a lifetime of dabbling in photography. It was the Crazy Horse rodeo in 2011 that really drew him in, and it was full-steam ahead from there, he told News Watch.

"I just sort of shot rodeos one day at a time, and then one day I looked up and said, 'You shoot a lot of rodeos,'" Murphy said of a conversation he had with himself a few years into his hobby.

Grew up in Sioux Falls, attended OG

“Indian rodeo” refers to the events that take place across the country on tribal lands and in Native communities.

Some are massive and draw in crowds by the thousands, like the annual Crow Fair in Montana or the Rosebud Wacipi, Rodeo and Fair. Some, like the event in Kyle and dozens of others throughout the year, are a bit rougher around the edges, which is just how Murphy likes it.

 Murphy – CJ Jewett, 2023 Owl Bonnet Rough Stock Shoothout, St. Francis, SD.jpg
C.J. Jewett on the back of a bucking bronc at the Owl Bonnet Rough Stock Rodeo in St. Francis, S.D., on the Rosebud Indian Reservation in 2023. 

He gets to know the people on the circuit, even if he doesn't get many chances to chat. He describes himself as "bad company at rodeos" because he's always behind the camera, and building trust with them is a critical part of his job. Many times, he's capturing people in either life-or-death moments or the best moments of their lives.

Sometimes, it's both.

Murphy’s not a country boy himself and doesn't even look the part, really. He was born and raised in Sioux Falls, attended the private O'Gorman High School and frequented the Minnehaha Country Club. One of his oft-told stories is about getting kicked out of a Deadwood rodeo for not having a cowboy hat on.

Murphy said that a conversation with a bull rider at a rough stock show in Kadoka helped him understand why these communities let him in to their spaces.

"I said, 'People really treat me well here.' And then he smiled bigger and he said, 'Cowboys like to have their pictures took,'" Murphy said.

Telling the story of those not in the spotlight

Murphy can read these people as well as any born-and-raised rodeo lover, though, and doesn't treat them with the delicate eye of an outsider. His photos illustrate the haphazard nature of rodeo’s most perilous events. But they also have another crucial element — the residents of South Dakota, ones who don’t live in major cities or along the I-90 corridor.

"It was embarrassing that there's this whole side of South Dakota that as the Sioux Falls and Rapid City resident I was really ignorant of. These rodeos will take you to places in Kyle or Red Scaffold, and it's great. There's great stuff out there," Murphy said.

 South Dakota News Watch logo
Learn more about South Dakota News Watch at sdnewswatch.org. 

His photos certainly do not shy away from the difficult parts. Not every rider is wearing a brand-new Stetson hat and a pearl-button shirt. Some are sun-weathered, some are sweating, some are in pain. That's what makes Murphy's photos what they are.

 2026-4-30 Murphy profile.jpg
eremiah Murphy, who has been photographing the Indian rodeo circuit for over a decade, in Rapid City, S.D., on Apr. 30. 

"There are a lot of rough ranch kids. There's plenty of rough city kids, too. But that toughness is really, really revered in the real ranching world," Murphy said. "It's hard work. Rodeos are hard. Ranching is hard. I mean, there's a number of people at rodeos in wheelchairs, or missing limbs or missing fingers."

These people, some of whom live in the most difficult economic conditions in the country, are genuine celebrities in Murphy's images. They are not treated as something to pity — because they aren't.

He describes one woman in a photo of his: mouth full of chew, close-cropped hair and large sunglasses perched on her head as she wrangles a horse. She is, to Murphy, "Audrey Hepburn in South Dakota."

Featured in national magazine

Last year, Murphy's photographs were featured in The New Yorker magazine, along with a full profile of his life and work, showcasing his photos to a global audience for the first time.

Murphy said that not much has changed in his life since the story published — he still lives in Rapid City and makes it out to every rodeo he can. But he has certainly seen more of a general interest and appreciation for art that captures the modern American West. A print of one of his photos is now hanging in the office of an architecture firm in New York City's Flatiron Building.

 Murphy - Kyle, S.D. 1.png
A young rider lies on the ground beneath a bull after being bucked off. 

Because of the ongoing success of his photos, Murphy said he's begun looking into exhibitions and has also started selling prints of his popular work. He has quite a bit to go through — he's been to more than 100 rodeos since he began documenting them.

"I'm still trying to look at myself as a photographer. You know, really, I know I'm a lobbyist. I did it for so long, but I'm still working on becoming a photographer," Murphy said.

Murphy's photos are, of course, modern in nature. Some elements, like vests decorated with sayings like "STRAIGHT OUTTA RIDGE" (a reference to rap group NWA), help viewers understand that these photos are not historic — they illustrate a very-much alive tradition in South Dakota.

 Murphy - Kyle, S.D. 2.png
A young rider heads for the fence after getting back up in Kyle, S.D. 

His strict use of black-and-white, though, can't help but call back to days long gone. After all, horses and bulls have bucked people off of them in the same way for hundreds of years. He said that, in his photos, he is primarily drawn to elements that connect viewers to the past and demonstrate the long-standing traditions that make up rodeo. He sees Indian rodeo as the best place to do that, where everything is a bit more off the beaten path.

“I've actually lived long enough that I've seen big structural changes in ways that I don't think we're going back," Murphy said. "But boy, this history, it's so intertwined. I thought, this is as close to what happened 100 years ago as you can get, which was, 'Let's all just meet at Joe's pasture Saturday afternoon and see who's got what.'"

Rodeo community's future uncertain

Also present in his photos is the sense of community that one feels at a rodeo.

While a rider gets on the bull or bronc alone, there's almost always people in the background cheering them on. Most of the time, it's their competitors, which Murphy said is part of what makes Indian rodeo special.

"It's sort of amazing. You know, you've got six or eight guys going for the same pot (of prize money), and they'll be yelling for every single guy. Never mind the fact that if his ride keeps going that well, he's going to knock your 78 off, and you're going to move to second," Murphy said, referring to rodeo scoring systems for bull and bronc riding.

 Murphy – Porshia Zimiga.png
Porshia Zimiga, who starred in 2025 film "East of Wall," barrel racing at the Hunter Memorial Rodeo in Kyle, S.D., on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation. 

"There's a camaraderie, I think, for doing it. I think being willing to do that work sort of overcomes a lot of other stuff."

Murphy does worry, though, about the future of this rugged rodeo circuit.

It doesn’t have the same commercial value as the Professional Bull Riders tours that fill arenas in Sioux Falls and Rapid City. By his own observation, there are fewer and fewer people in the grandstands every summer — mostly girlfriends, parents, siblings and friends of the riders.

“I fear I'm documenting the end of something,” Murphy said.

He said that it can be difficult to get people who aren't from the area to find interest in the sport. Though his photos are popular, and he encourages people to come to rodeos themselves, some of the events are struggling to sell tickets and generate enough revenue to keep running year-after-year.

"To this date, I've never run into anybody at a rodeo from Rapid (City) who said, 'Murph! ... You were right, this is great. I came to the rodeo. I'm so glad.' That has not happened once," Murphy said.

The sheer magnitude of young people involved, though, would give anyone hope for a bright future in the sport.

Bull riders are young by nature, and plenty of ranch kids are deeply involved in rodeo. "East of Wall," a 2025 film that highlighted a ranching family in South Dakota, featured at least half a dozen teens that found themselves drawn to the discipline and hard work of rodeo.

 Murphy- Eagle Butte.png
Two women wrangle a horse at a rodeo in Eagle Butte, S.D., on the Cheyenne River Indian Reservation. 

Murphy sees that just about every rodeo, too. He describes younger children who watch their older siblings competing with a sort of awe. One has to assume that they will also be up on that horse someday.

One set of Murphy's photos illustrates just how much the reckless bravery of youth is on display at these events. In the first, a young boy, just 14 is in a pair of shorts, looking like he just might be crushed by a thousand-pound bull. The next, he's up, helmet off and ready to shake the hand of a wrangler.

"A lot of people like the second picture more than the first. I thought that was interesting and sort of spoke well of people," Murphy said. "You get a little bit of relief from seeing that. Watching it through my camera, it just about turned my stomach."

Murphy has read and witnessed lots of discussions about the death of the West. Some of those conversations are rooted in reality — just look to his own observations of declining attendance and low ticket sales.

His photos, though, are a certain reminder that at least for those who know South Dakota and what this sport means, cowboys will never truly die.

"There's a lot about the declining cowboy culture, which is true, but boy it clings, you know. It clings," Murphy said.

title: Rapid City releases list of items to be stores in time capsule burial ceremony on May 29
description: More than 20 items will be stored inside the Rapid City time capsule meant to be opened in 2076. Items included in the capsule will be a community photo, letter from the mayor and a paper clipping of the Rapid City Journal.
_full_text:
More than 20 items will be stored inside the Rapid City time capsule meant to be opened in 2076. Items included in the capsule will be a community photo, letter from the mayor and a paper clipping of the Rapid City Journal. 

 Newspaper clip
A newspaper clip from the Rapid City Journal about the original 1976 time capsule burial. 

As part of the city's celebration of Rapid City's founding 150 years ago in 1876, a community photo is scheduled for 1:30 p.m. (assemble by 1:15 p.m.) on May 22 at Main Street Square and a time capsule burial ceremony on May 29. 

 Darell Shoemaker
Rapid City Public Information Officer Darrell Shoemaker holds the proclamation recognizing the city's sesquicentennial milestone. 

According to a release by the city, more than 20 items listed to be placed in the capsule include a community photos, letter and coin by Mayor Jason Salamun, Native American cultural items, local newspaper clippings, 2076 predictions of the future, a 2025 minted penny, a used smartphone, pictures of the 1972 Rapid City flood, a Rush hockey puck, a Post 22 baseball and America 250 challenge coin.
Some of the items may be subject to change.
The time capsule burying ceremony will be conducted at 1:30 p.m. on Friday, May 29, at Founders Park.
The ceremony will include remarks from Salamun, Public Information Officer Darrell Shoemaker, City Council members and local faith community members , while there will also be a Lakota honoring and blessing. 
The city previously honored the sesquicentennial anniversary with a new exhibit in the Journey Museum dedicated to Rapid City, which opened in February, and the opening of a time capsule from 1976.

title: Mission man sentenced for assaulting a federal officer
description: A Mission man was sentenced to time served after a conviction for assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer.
_full_text:
A Mission man was sentenced to time served after a conviction for assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer.

U.S. District Judge Eric C. Schulte has sentenced Duane Rouillard, III, 37, to time served through April 22, 2026, equal to approximately three years and one month in custody, followed by three years of supervised release, the U.S. Attorney's Office for South Dakota said in a release.

Rouillard was indicted by a federal grand jury in Feburary 2023. He pleaded guilty on Feb. 19, 2026.

In December 2022, Rouillard was in custody at the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Adult Correctional Facility, in Todd County, South Dakota. On the evening of Dec. 29, 2022, Rouillard assaulted a corrections officer by punching him multiple times in the head and face with a closed fist, the U.S. Attorney's Office said.

This case was investigated by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services. Supervisory Assistant U.S. Attorney Kirk Albertson prosecuted the case.

Rouillard was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Pennington County judge gives 20-year-old convicted of statutory rape a chance on probation
description: A Pennington County judge opted to sentence a 20-year-old convicted of rape to probation — with a decade of prison time and couple weeks of jail time hanging over his head — because the judge would "much rather have him supervised by probation" than send him to prison and have no control over what supervision he receives when he's let out.
_full_text:
A Pennington County judge opted to sentence a 20-year-old convicted of rape to probation — with a decade of prison time and couple weeks of jail time hanging over his head — because the judge would "much rather have him supervised by probation" than send him to prison and have no control over what supervision he receives when he's let out. 

A judge can set specific terms for probation, but they don't have control over parole, which falls under the executive branch of the state.

"They may not supervise him at all,"  Circuit Court Judge Jeffrey Connolly said at the Friday, May 15, sentencing of Melvin Desersa of Rapid City. 

With the probationary sentence and suspended sentence, Connolly said, "I have 10 years to work with, which is significant." The five years of probation "get him to 25 (years old)," which the judge noted should be enough time to determine whether Desersa will commit more crimes or make improvement.

Desersa pleaded guilty on Feb. 27 to fourth-degree rape, which is sexual penetration with someone who is between 13 and 16 years old and three or more years younger than the perpetrator. Initially, a grand jury indicted Desersa with third-degree rape and, in the alternative, fourth-degree rape. Third-degree rape is sexual penetration with someone who is incapable of consent, due to intoxication or other factors. 

Chief Deputy Pennington County State's Attorney Gina Nelson said the victim was found in a pile of mud intoxicated "out of her mind." 

"He is the adult in this situation," Nelson said, emphasizing Desersa had a duty to know she was 13 years old. 

Desersa's defense attorney, Brittany Cook-Oleson, rebutted, "I think there was an actual lack of knowledge." 

Cook-Oleson said the two were in a relationship, the girl spent time with his roommates, and he met her mother. She said the victim seems older and Desersa seems younger. 

"He wasn't grooming a child or being a predator," Cook-Oleson said.

The defense attorney said Desersa has been working, seeking counseling and engaging in social activities while out on bond. He spent 162 days in the Pennington County Jail before posting a $10,000 surety bond through a bondsman on March 2. Since then, he has been out on an ankle monitor with no issues, his defense attorney said.

"I've finally taken myself a lot more seriously," Desersa told the judge, adding he wants to focus on his job and taking care of his mom. 

"I have so much to repay her for staying by my side," he said. 

Connolly's sentence, in addition to the probation and 10 years of suspended prison time, included a 180-day jail sentence. Connolly applied the 162 days of time served and suspended the remaining 18 days. If Desersa fails at probation, Connolly could impose those suspended sentences.

The conditions of probation include Desersa being required to register as a sex offender, have no contact with the victim or anyone else under 18 and stay away from drugs and alcohol. 

He left it up to the probation office whether they want to add a requirement barring Desersa from dating apps. Nelson said Desersa met the victim on a dating app and requested the requirement. 

Nelson initially requested a prison sentence for Desersa, but after discussion with the judge about the supervision probation could offer, she agreed, "Probation is probably the answer." Cook-Oleson asked for one year in jail and five years of probation.

title: Rapid City police: Suspect arrested after he threw rock through windshield, assaulted man
description: A Rapid City man faces charges after an assault.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man faces charges after an assault.

The Rapid City Police Department said officers were dispatched around 8:15 p.m. on Thursday, May 14, to the 500 block of East North Street for a report of a physical altercation that was happening in the parking lot.

On arrival, police encountered a man, later identified as 35-year-old Shawn Marrowbone of Rapid City, actively assaulting another man on the ground. Officers were able to pull Marrowbone away from the other man and detain him in handcuffs, police said.

An investigation determined Marrowbone had allegedly thrown a rock through the windshield of a vehicle parked in the 400 block of East North Street. The vehicle owner confronted Marrowbone, at which point Marrowbone began assaulting the victim prior to police arriving on the scene, the department said.

Officers arrested Marrowbone on suspicion of aggravated assault, felony vandalism and on a parole hold before being taking him to the Pennington County Jail.

Marrowbone is being held on a $100,000 bond, according to jail records. Marrowbone made his initial court appearance on the morning of Friday, May 15, and is due back in court for his preliminary hearing at 10 a.m. May 29, according to South Dakota court records.

According to court records and the South Dakota Department of Corrections, Marrowbone was sentenced to five years in prison, with three years suspended, in October 2020 in connection to an incident in Minnehaha County. As part of a deal, Marrowbone pleaded guilty to two counts of simple assault against a law enforcement officer and driving under the influence-first offense, per court records.

His parole term was set to expire on Dec. 30 of this year.

title: 47-year-old Rapid City man sentenced to prison for sexual contact with a child under 16
description: A 47-year-old Rapid City man was sentenced to 15 years in prison on Thursday, May 14, a couple months after a jury found him guilty of three counts of sexual contact with a child under 16.
_full_text:
A 47-year-old Rapid City man was sentenced to 15 years in prison on Thursday, May 14, a couple months after a jury found him guilty of three counts of sexual contact with a child under 16.

Court records show Treon Middletent was charged on May 14, 2025 with four counts of sexual contact with a child under 16. After a two-day trial in March of this year, a Pennington County jury found him guilty on three of the counts and acquitted him on one. 

Exactly a year after the indictment was filed in Pennington County Court, Middletent appeared for sentencing before Fourth Judicial Circuit Judge Gordon Swanson. According to a Pennington County State's Attorney's Office release, the state argued for three consecutive 15-year sentences. The maximum for each charge is 15 years. Swanson opted for three concurrent 15-year sentences.

In the release, the state said the incidents occurred between December 2020 and May 2022, beginning when the child was 10 years old. Middletent knew the victim.

Pennington County Jail records on Friday, May 15, show Middletent remains in at the jail, where he was booked on May 16, 2025. He awaits transportation to the state penitentiary.

title: Rapid City man sentenced to more than 2 years in prison for felony ammunition possession
description: A Rapid City man faces more than two years in prison on drug charges.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man faces more than two years in prison on drug charges.

U.S. District Judge Karen Schreier sentenced Bradley Two Eagle, 27, to two years and six months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, according to the U.S Attorney's Office.

The sentencing took place on May 8 in Rapid City.

Two Eagle was indicted for possession of ammunition by a prohibited person by a federal grand jury in November 2025. He pleaded guilty on Jan. 28, 2026.

On Oct. 17, 2025, the Rapid City Police Department responded to an emergency call reporting that gunshots had been fired. Law enforcement spoke with Two Eagle, who gave a false identity and then fled from the officers. As Two Eagle ran, he threw ammunition to the ground. Law enforcement caught Two Eagle. They recovered his discarded ammunition and also found a methamphetamine syringe on him. Two Eagle had previously been convicted of a felony offense. Possessing ammunition or firearms after such a conviction is a federal felony. It is also a federal felony to possess ammunition or firearms while actively engaged in the use of a controlled substance such as methamphetamine.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and the Rapid City Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Schroeder prosecuted the case.

Two Eagle was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Meet the candidates running for legislature in the Rapid City area
description: More than 20 candidates looking to take seats in the South Dakota Legislature attended a Meet the Candidates forum hosted by the Black Hills Home Builders Association and Elevate Rapid City inside the Dahl Arts Center in Rapid City.
_full_text:
More than 20 candidates looking to take seats in the South Dakota Legislature attended a Meet the Candidates forum hosted by the Black Hills Home Builders Association and Elevate Rapid City inside the Dahl Arts Center in Rapid City.

 BHHBA
Candidates running for the South Dakota Legislature, Rapid City Council and Pennington County Commission attended the meet and greet on Tuesday, May 12. 

"Decisions made locally and at the state level directly affect housing affordability, infrastructure, workforce development, growth (and) economic opportunities. Always stay engaged, research your candidates and always, always get out and vote," BHHBA Executive Board member Daene Boomsma said during the Tuesday, May 12 event.

Residents at the event had the chance to speak to legislative, Rapid City Council and Pennington County Commission candidates. 

Boomsma introduced candidates one by one to speak for one minute.

"Tonight is only about engagement and getting to know each other," Boomsma said.

Meet the candidates 

South Dakota has 39 Legislature districts, with two representatives and one senator from each representing constituents at the Capitol in Pierre.

District 30:

District 30 includes all or portions of Custer, Fall River and Pennington counties, including Custer State Park and most of the Southern Hills.

Amber Hulse (Republican) said she is seeking re-election as senator representing District 30 and has a background as an attorney.

"Two of my big passions in legislation is election integrity and property tax reform. I'm looking forward to continuing to give the Southern Hills a voice again in the Senate, and continuing to be an effective voice," Hulse said.

Julie Frye-Mueller (Republican), who is also running for the Senate for District 30, was not in attendance.

 BHHBA
Members of the community and candidates attended the meet and greet forum by the Black Hills Home Builders Association on May 12, inside the Dahl Arts Center. 

Stephen Saint (Republican) said he is an Army veteran with a law enforcement background working as a deputy sheriff. He owns Fort Welikit Campground in Custer. He is running for representative of District 30.

"I'm running on the platform of property taxes, property rights and veterans' well-being. I'm a big proponent of all those (and) changing some of these things. I've spent the last six years as a citizen in the state capitol (lobbying) for various bills, for and against them," Saint said.

Trish Ladner (Republican) said she has served as a representative for District 30 for six years and is a champion of property tax relief.

"I'm the voice for the people in District 30. I'll call home and ask experts about our building bills. 'What's your opinion?' 'What's your voice?' Educate me. We can't be good at everything, so we need everybody in this room to join with us. I'm a common-sense voice in Pierre," Ladner said.

Tim Goodwin (Republican) and Bret Swanson (Democrat), both running for representative of District 30, were not in attendance.

District 32:

District 32 includes downtown Rapid City, much of north Rapid City and its southeast corner extends to Cambell Street.

Jeff Shelton (Democrat), a candidate for senator in District 32, said he has a background in archeology and is a local homeowner in Rapid City, which he said gives him a unique perspective as a candidate.

"I definitely want to make sure that we can keep Rapid City as a great, affordable place for all sorts of folks. I'm really looking forward to putting my name in the hat, and I am looking forward to a very, very eventful year," Shelton said.

 Daene Boomsma
Daene Boomsma is a member of Black Hills Home Builders Association Executive Board. 

Helene Duhamel (Republican) is running for re-election as senator for District 32. Duhamel was not at the forum.

Nichole Uhre-Balk (Democrat) said she is seeking re-election as representative for District 32, after what she said was a productive first term.

"I want to continue to focus on education. Protecting the Black Hills (has) been a big part of my platform, and of course, affordability (and) housing. As a voice of reason, I'm looking forward to another year and another session," Uhre-Balk said.

Karen McNeal (Republican), a candidate for representative District 32, said she was born and raised in Rapid City and has a background in science. She said she is a strong proponent of education for the youth.

"When I've looked at the roster of state legislators that we have, we have no scientists, we have a few teachers, we've got a doctor, mostly attorneys, business owners. But I think we need some more people with science backgrounds. I'm very good at analyzing data. I think we have a spending problem in this state, not a revenue problem, and that's something I want to work on," McNeal said.

Rep. Steve Duffy and challenger Zach Martin, both Republicans running for representative for District 32, were absent at the forum.

District 33:

District 33 includes Silver City and Johnson Siding, along with Summerset and Black Hawk on the west side of Interstate 90, with the district boundary including land inside Pennington and some Rapid City neighborhoods.

Christopher Baumgartner (Democrat), a candidate for senator for District 33, said he is not a politician but a neighbor, as he grew up in Rapid City. He said he graduated from Northern State University.

"With the values of trustworthy, loyal, helpful, kind, brave, (these) are all good descriptions for any state senator in South Dakota ... I spent my whole career advocating for people left out for the conversations, and that's what a politician should do," Baumgartner said.

David Johnson (Republican), who is running for senator for District 33, said he grew up in Rapid City with his family running their own business, and later served in the U.S. Air Force. He previously served in the legislature.

"You can look up my record in Pierre. What you'll find is that I have been successful in passing multiple legislative efforts in Pierre that have helped the citizens of Rapid City and the citizens of South Dakota," Johnson said.

Sen. Curt Voight (Republican), running for re-election, said he is a Vietnam veteran and worked as an assistant fire chief and a school administrator. 

"I would appreciate your consideration and my responsibilities in the Senate. At this point, I have been the vice chair of (the) Senate Education (Committee). I've been on the Ag (Agriculture) Committee, Health and Human Services (Committee), and I was appointed to Senate State Affairs," Voight said.

Rep. Curt Massie (Republican) said he has worked in the state's department of revenue and is seeking a third term as a representative for District 33.

"I tell people, if you want to maximize your property tax reduction, you need to vote for me, because there are ways that we can ensure that these big out-of-state corporations are paying their fair share, so we as South Dakotans can pay less," Massie said.

Jeff Marlette (Republican) said he comes from the agricultural community and his prior work experience as a school administrator and a combat veteran in Iraq make him an ideal candidate for representative in District 33.

"What I would ask you to consider is proven leadership, somebody that's run organizations from the smallest 15 people up to over 4,600 employees. I understand what it takes to get things done, and I understand that it takes to work with people. I hate to use the word I, because I didn't do all those things. I had great teams, and together, we did some really good things," Marlette said.

Sandra Comer (Republican) a candidate for representative for District 33, said she is a businesswoman, a mother of five and a military wife who has spent years serving the community.

"As I traveled ac directly with families, I keep hearing the same concerns (of) rising property taxes, housing pressures, infrastructure challenges and the feeling that everyday people are being ignored while government keeps growing. I don't believe in showing up empty handed and asking for your vote, I believe in earning it with real solutions," Comer said.

Rep. Phil Jensen (Republican), who's seeking re-election, and challenger Kari Hall (Democrat) were both not in attendance.

District 34:

District 34 includes western Rapid City and extends into rural Pennington County.

Jason Green (Republican) said he grew up in Lead and worked in the Rapid City Attorney's Office for more than 10 years. He is running for senator for District 34.

"I think one of the most important things that we need to get done in the state legislature is to assure that we have a friendly and welcoming climate for businesses in our communities, growing our economic pie .... Obviously, we need to address inappropriate spending, fraud and waste," Green said.

Taffy Howard (Republican) is seeking to be re-elected as senator for District 34 and said she is an Air Force veteran and currently serves as the Senate Chair of Government Operations and Audit Committee. 

"I'm a lifelong Republican because I believe in the Republican Party platform. I believe in limited government, lower taxes, less regulation (and) individual responsibility. I believe in putting the citizens first, not special interests, and I built a record in Pierre fighting for those principles," Howard said.

Michael Calabrese (Democrat) is the owner of Black Hill Vinyl, a record shop in downtown Rapid City. He said he has a background in operations and revenue for a local tech company, making him a strong candidate for senator for District 34.

"We need to really focus on tax reform that benefits families that are helping to grow this community and workforce. Housing that keeps the talent that we're attracting, schools and childcare that make staying easier than leaving. I'm running because none of that built itself, and the people deserve a senator who's committed to building the future of our community," Calabrese said.

Becky Drury (Republican) said she is a former Rapid City Council member and representative for District 34. She said these experiences make her a qualified candidate.

"There's a couple things that really drive me when I'm in Pierre. Making sure that we're not taking jobs away from our City Council, away from our school boards, away from the county commissioners. Let them do their job, and then we'll do our job in Pierre. They should mesh just fine, because we should be talking to each other," Drury said.

Rep. Mike Derby (Republican) said he is running for re-election as representative for District 34, based on his background in growing up in the community and as a business owner for 40 years.

"Rapid City is a special place. This will be me finishing up my sixth term. I'm running for one more term, and then I'm termed out. I am focused on running for the House of Representatives for District 34 and I'd appreciate your vote," Derby said.

Rep. Heather Baxter (Republican) and Victor Dominques (Democrat), both running for representative for District 34, were not at the forum.

District 35:

District 35 includes Box Elder, Rapid Valley and parts of eastern Rapid City.

Sen. Greg Blanc (Republican) is seeking re-election in District 35. He said he's been a resident of Rapid City for 25 years and has worked as a contractor for 15 years.

 Greg Blanc
Greg Blanc (Republican) is running for state Senate in District 35.  

"In the last two decades, I have watched our midsize city expand into one of the fastest-developing cities in the Midwest. We all realize that Rapid City is going through a unique season of growing pains, and my role as a legislator is to be the voice for the people who elected me. Lower property taxes and affordable housing are not just buzzwords to me. My voting record proves that," Blanc said.

Nicole Mitzel (Republican), a senate candidate, said she is a board member for the Black Hills Home Builders Association and is the general manager at Mind by Design, a local stone fabrication shop and showroom in Rapid City.

 Nicole Mitzel
Nicole Mitzel (Republican) is running for state Senate for District 35. 

"I'm running because I want to make sure that we keep South Dakota free, affordable, safe and opportunity-driven. I'm going to support things that make our business climate more stable. I'm all about responsible growth that creates jobs, less regulation, better pay and a better quality of life for the hard-working people of South Dakota," Mitzel said.

Dale Bartscher (Republican) is running for representative in District 35. He siad he was born and raised in South Dakota and a self-described Christian Conservative Republican.

"I grew up in a contractor's home. My dad worked hard to feed 10 of us children. When I was old enough to carry a brick or a two by four, I went to work. I worked through middle school, high school, and college, and I'm grateful that my dad taught us a work ethic. I'm proud to work and live and work in a state that understands the work ethic," Bartscher said.

Emmett Reistroffer (Republican) is one of the founders of Genesis Farms, a medical marijuana dispensary, and is running for representative for District 35.

"I want to deliver results for my people. That's who I am fighting to represent. We need partnerships with the business community. We need someone who knows how to coordinate between state government and local government, and how to listen to the people. Through my experience working on maybe a controversial issue, I learned how to bring people together," Reistroffer said.

Jace West (Republican) said he served in the U.S. Air Force at the Ellsworth Air Force Base and attended the South Dakota School of Mines. He hopes to retain graduates of the school by promoting job growth in the area. West is running for representative for District 35.

"I'd really love to retain some of those graduates. I would really. I grew up in a broken home, and one of the things that is really important to me is the drug problem that we have. I know we've got meth and fentanyl problem in the area, and I would really love to work with our local law enforcement," West said.

Jason Fleeming (Republican), a candidate for representative for District 35, said he served in the U.S. Air Force, is the owner of a construction business and a member of the Builders Association. 

"I am a proud member of Black Hills Home Builders Association. I know the industry. So, what I will do is I will make sure I keep the developers developing, the builders building and the realtors selling," Flemming said.

Ken Jeakins (Democrat), who is running as a representative for District 35, was not at the forum.
