title: Jury finds Parmelee man not guilty of assault
description: A federal jury found a Parmelee man not guilty of assault with a dangerous weapon, assault resulting in serious bodily injury and using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence.
_full_text:
A federal jury found a Parmelee man not guilty of assault with a dangerous weapon, assault resulting in serious bodily injury and using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence.

Joey Kills Plenty, 26, was found not guilty on May 7, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for South Dakota.

Kills Plenty was indicted by a federal grand jury in November 2025.

The case was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office. The investigation was conducted by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services.

title: Former President Joe Biden to speak in South Dakota
description: The South Dakota Democratic Party announced that former President Joe Biden will serve as the keynote speaker for the party's McGovern Day Dinner on Friday, June 5, at the Best Western Plus Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls.
_full_text:
The South Dakota Democratic Party announced that former President Joe Biden will serve as the keynote speaker for the party's McGovern Day Dinner on Friday, June 5, at the Best Western Plus Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls.

“It is an honor to welcome President Biden to South Dakota, especially during such a critical time for our country,” party Chair Shane Merrill said in the announcement, issued on Saturday, May 16.

Per a release from the party: At 29, Biden became one of the youngest Americans ever elected to the U.S. Senate. Over 36 years representing Delaware, he played a leading role in addressing major domestic and international issues, including authoring the Violence Against Women Act.

 051726-nws-biden-p1.png
Former President Joe Biden will serve as the keynote speaker for the party's McGovern Day Dinner on Friday, June 5, at the Best Western Plus Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls. 

In 2008, Biden was elected vice president alongside President Barack Obama. Together, the Obama-Biden Administration passed the Affordable Care Act, helping millions of Americans gain access to affordable health insurance.

In 2020, Biden was elected the 46th president of the United States. The party said "during one of the most challenging moments in modern American history," his administration led the nation through the COVID-19 pandemic, accelerated vaccine distribution and "helped drive an economic recovery that created more than 16 million jobs."

 051726-nws-biden-p1.png
Former President Joe Biden will serve as the keynote speaker for the party's McGovern Day Dinner on Friday, June 5, at the Best Western Plus Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls. 

“It is an absolute privilege to welcome President Biden to South Dakota and have him speak to people from across the state who want a brighter future,” Merrill said in the release. “This is a historic moment for McGovern Day, and we are honored to host someone who knew and served alongside leaders like George McGovern, Tim Johnson, and Tom Daschle.”

“President Biden’s Administration played a crucial role in helping South Dakota recover from the economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic,” Merrill continued. “His policies delivered millions of dollars in investments for rural housing, broadband expansion, infrastructure, and agriculture. As a farmer, I appreciate that President Biden prioritized rural communities, supported sustainable agricultural practices, and worked to strengthen our food supply. I’m excited for President Biden to share his perspective with Democratic candidates and supporters from across South Dakota. This will be an incredible evening as we celebrate the future of our state.”

Tickets for the McGovern Day Dinner are now on sale. The deadline to purchase tickets is Monday, May 25.

title: America 250 commission for South Dakota and Rapid City share behind the scenes planning before July 4 celebration
description: South Dakota's America 250 Commission has been working since 2023 to encourage municipalities to host celebratory events leading up to the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States.
_full_text:
South Dakota's America 250 Commission has been working since 2023 to encourage municipalities to host celebratory events leading up to the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States. 

Commission Chair Dr. Ben Jones also sits as chair for the South Dakota State Historical Society. Jones said the commission was born out of the executive order by then-Gov. Kristi Noem in 2023, with the goal of promoting events across South Dakota by working with organizations, groups and municipalities.

The South Dakota America 250 website states the commission is a nonpartisan initiative working to engage every citizen "to pause and reflect" on the nation's history, honoring contributions of all Americans, and looking toward the future for the next generations.

Jones said the state commission has been meeting every other month for more than three years to spread the word amongst community groups.

Commission members total 18, including South Dakota Department of Tourism Secretary James Hagen, Department of Tribal Relations Secretary Algin Young, Historical Society Foundation Chief Executive Officer Catherine Forsch and Department of Veteran Affairs Secretary Jeremiah Schneider.

"We've been really spreading the word amongst community groups on economic development, tourism and veterans to say, 'Hey this year is going to be a very special Independence Day,'" Jones said. "There's going to be a lot of activities going on at the national level, and your town ought to be doing something."

South Dakota, and every state in the nation, is working with America250, a nonprofit supporting organization to the U.S. semiquincentennial commission.

According to America250's website, they work with commissions across the country to facilitate robust public-private partnerships that bring the vision for America250 to life.

The organization's website says all 50 states have a commission that is aiding in this national celebration effort.

Jones said over 150 organizations and groups have signed on to participate in the South Dakota's celebration.

Statewide municipality celebrations include the Boots and Roots celebration in Pierre on July 1 through July 5the , Mount Rushmore fireworks show on July 3, Sioux Falls' Independence Day celebration on July 4, and Rapid City's Real America Birthday Bash from July 1 through Independence Day.

Jones said the commission tried to work with every community group in South Dakota to participate, including tribal organizations and nations.

"Tribal governments have not responded in a way that indicated they want to participate in anything. On the individual level though, we have received some interest in that," Jones said.

He said in 2024 as a commission they honored the 100th anniversary of the Indian Citizenship Act (also known as Snyder Act) signed on June 2, 1924. The event was a panel discussion in partnership with the University of South Dakota. The Indian Citizenship Act gave Native Americans citizenship status and rights. 

For more information about events happening across the state visit americas250th.sd.gov.

Rapid City Birthday Bash

Rapid City will be honoring the national anniversary and the city's 150th anniversary (since its founding) this year.

In 2025, the city approved the 2026 budget, which included $250,000 to put toward the celebration of America 250.

Rapid City Chief of Staff Leah Braun previously told the Journal the America 250 steering committee and citizens committee have been planning the celebration, including working with other local organizations, like Visit Rapid City.

 Journey Museum
Inside The Journey Museum in Rapid City, a new exhibit dedicated to the history and founding of the city is now on display for the public. This is an effort in partnership with the city to celebrate the 150th anniversary of the city's founding. 

She said she has been working with the state's commission group in productive talks with other municipalities across the state to work together on hosting the best events for each community.

"I have been attending the state of South Dakota's planning meetings, which are held monthly, and it's really a collaborative effort. There are about 50 different municipalities on the call. Really what we do during that time, we share what's being planned, to kind of give each other ideas. If (a) city's not quite as far in the planning process as we are, we'll share and exchange ideas, and then anything that the state is doing, we are welcome to participate in," Braun said.

She said the city has been working to include the Indigenous community to participate in the July celebration by inviting dance groups, drum groups and crafting demonstrations highlighting the community in the city.

"We want everybody to feel welcome to not only participate in the festival, but to contribute ideas and to bring in different cultural aspects of the things that make the Rapid City community a really great place to live ... We do want people to feel that they have a place at the festival and with the festivities, and so that is, that's why we're working hard to ensure we include kids and cultural components and something for everyone, something for all ages, something for all different interest levels," Braun said.

She said members of the city's steering committee have made these efforts to reach out to local Indigenous talents and artists for a more inclusive celebration.

She said the steering committee consists of 16 members from various entities, including Visit Rapid City, HomeSlice Media, the Rapid City Council, The Monument, the city's finance office, Black Hills & Badlands Tourism Association, a state representative and South Dakota Public Broadcasting.

The city was able to secure a drone show from Sky Elements Drone Shows. Sky Elements has worked with brands like MLB, Disney Studios, Marvel, The Seattle Seahawks, and Coca-Cola, according to their website. 

Rapid City Public Information Officer Darrell Shoemaker said a multi-day celebration for Independence Day hasn't occurred in Rapid City since 1991, during celebrations for the 50th anniversary of Mount Rushmore.

Anticipated for this year's celebration, in addition to the festivities, is an emphasis on safety.

Recently, Mayor Jason Salamun announced country artist Chancey Williams will headline the July 4 music show.

To learn more about this summer’s “Real America Birthday Bash” events, visit www.realamericabirthdaybash.com or call at 605-718-8484 or 800-487-3223.

 Photos from Rapid City's announcement about 150 celebrations
Rapid City announced plans for 150th anniversary celebrations throughout 2026 during a media event on Monday, Feb. 2. On display were a number of artifacts and photos from Rapid City's yesteryear.

title: Design dilemmas: New project reveals original plans for Mount Rushmore, national landmarks
description: What would Mount Rushmore look like if Gutzon Borglum’s initial plans had been realized? A new visual project reveals the surprising, lesser-known original designs for some of the nation’s most iconic landmarks.
_full_text:
What would Mount Rushmore look like if Gutzon Borglum’s initial plans had been realized? A new visual project reveals the surprising, lesser-known original designs for some of the nation’s most iconic landmarks.

Astrak US, a national supplier to the construction and heavy machinery industries, has created a series of visual interpretations showing how five famous landmarks might have looked. By using their original blueprints, Astrak US’s project shows side-by-side comparisons of what was planned versus what was actually built.

 Mount Rushmore original conception
Using original blueprints for the design of Mount Rushmore, Astrak US has created an illustration showing what the mountain might have looked like if Gutzon Borglum's original vision for it had been accomplished. 

As the United States celebrates its 250th anniversary, this series of illustrations focuses on five instantly recognizable national landmarks. Reshaped by budget constraints, political delays, engineering limitations and changing ambitions, the original designs for familiar landmarks were often more complex than the final results.

Astrak US’s visual project highlights Mount Rushmore National Memorial, the Statue of Liberty, the U.S. Capitol Building, the Washington Monument, and the Golden Gate Bridge. Along with before-and-after images, Astrak US explains how modern construction might have been able to achieve the original designs.

 Mount Rushmore
Mount Rushmore National Memorial, carved out of the Black Hills near Keystone. 

“By reimagining these landmarks as they were first conceived, we can get a fascinating glimpse into how different some of America’s most recognizable sights might have been,” said Calum Mair, commercial director at Astrak US. “That construction history is full of bold ideas that had to be scaled, reshaped, or rethought along the way.”

According to Astrak US, early designs featured larger structures, more architectural elements, or more elaborate artistic details. Practical challenges, especially construction costs, engineering limitations, and project timelines, forced architects and planners to simplify their visions so the projects could realistically be completed.

Mount Rushmore National Memorial

Borglum’s initial vision for Mount Rushmore was far more ambitious than the final 60-foot faces of four presidents. Borglum planned to carve full-body or waist-up sculptures of George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln, along with a monumental Hall of Records to house important documents from American history.

Borglum selected those four presidents because, from his perspective, they represented the most important events in the history of the United States.

Creating Mount Rushmore with dynamite blasting and carving took 14 years, from Oct. 4, 1927, to Oct. 31, 1941, and ultimately required the efforts of nearly 400 men and women.

 Mount Rushmore before and after
Before and after: Astrak US created illustrations of what Mount Rushmore might have looked like if Gutzon Borglum had achieved his original design for it, left, versus the finished monument, right.  

Funding limitations during the Great Depression, technical challenges of carving the granite mountain, and time constraints forced the project to be scaled back. According to the nonfiction book “Love Letters from Mount Rushmore,” spring blizzards, summer heat, and Borglum’s unpredictable moods also affected the progress.

Astrak US believes technology available in the 21st Century might have made Borglum’s original vision more achievable. Borglum carved the mountain by relying primarily on dynamite blasting. 

Today, precision drilling, controlled blasting and 3D laser scanning could allow sculptors to map and carve granite with far greater accuracy and safety. Heavy-lift equipment, drones, and digital modeling might also help plan and execute complex carvings across difficult terrain. These tools might make it possible to safely create the larger full-figure sculptures Borglum originally imagined, according to Astrak US.

Statue of Liberty

French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi first proposed a colossal figure, “Egypt Carrying the Light to Asia,” for the Suez Canal. After that project fell through, Bartholdi reworked the idea for the United States as “Liberty Enlightening the World,” transforming the 305-foot statue’s symbolism while retaining the iconic torch-bearing form.

 America 250 logo

The Statue of Liberty is the only national landmark that was not made in the United States. The statue was constructed in France between 1875 and 1884, disassembled into 350 individual pieces, and the pieces were packed in 214 wooden crates that were transported by ship to the New York Harbor.

Dedicated on Oct. 28, 1886, the Statue of Liberty was designated as a National Monument in 1924. The Statue of Liberty has undergone two major renovations: in 1936 for its 50th anniversary, and a multi-year renovation from 1982 to 1986 ahead of the statue’s 100th anniversary.

U.S. Capitol Building

Architect William Thornton’s original design featured a modest copper dome appropriate for the early federal government. As the House and Senate wings were added in the 1850s, architect Thomas U. Walter replaced it with the much larger cast-iron dome that defines the Capitol’s silhouette today. The dome was completed during the Civil War, crowned by the Statue of Freedom that dominates the Capitol’s silhouette.

Washington Monument

Architect Robert Mills envisioned the Washington Monument as an obelisk surrounded by a decorative colonnade and statues, possibly including an equestrian statue of George Washington. Funding issues, political challenges, and the Civil War delayed construction, and the monument was ultimately completed in 1884 as a simpler, taller obelisk.

Golden Gate Bridge

Engineer Joseph Strauss’s early concept was far heavier and more industrial-looking than the sleek Golden Gate Bridge that has become an indelible symbol of San Francisco. Collaborative input from other engineers and architect Irving Morrow led to the streamlined suspension bridge that was completed in 1937, with sweeping cables and slender towers replacing the bulkier truss elements of the original concept.

title: One injured as fire destroys house in rural Keystone
description: The Battle Creek Fire Department responded Friday, May 15, to a reported structure fire in the 13000 block of Lost Cave Road in rural Keystone.
_full_text:
The Battle Creek Fire Department responded Friday, May 15, to a reported structure fire in the 13000 block of Lost Cave Road in rural Keystone.

The Battle Creek volunteer department said first-arriving firefighters found a free-burning fire with heavy smoke coming from the interior of a single-story residential structure, with fire extending into the ceiling and roof assembly.

Additionally, fire extended to adjacent trees, vegetation and agricultural shelters, causing smoke, heat and fire damage.

Rapid attack by firefighters contained the structure fire, stopping further threats to population and damage to infrastructure and other improvements and the wildland fire was stopped at 1/10 of an acre, the department said.

The fire was reported around 3:17 p.m.

There were three people in the residence and one was treated and released at the scene, the department said. One firefighter suffered minor injuries.

 5-15-2026 Lost Cave Rd.jpg
One person was injured in a house fire on Friday, May 15, in rural Keystone. 

The American Red Cross Serving Central and Western South Dakota, family and neighbors are assisting the residents. No injuries to domestic animals were reported.

Responding agencies: Pennington County 911, Battle Creek Fire Department, Town of Keystone, Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, Southern Hills Water, Rockerville Volunteer Fire Department, Rapid City Fire Department, Hill City Volunteer Fire Department, Rapid Valley Volunteer Fire Department, Black Hills Electrical Cooperative, Johnson Siding Volunteer Fire Department, Whispering Pines Volunteer Fire Department. North Haines Volunteer Fire Department, Keystone Ambulance Service, Custer Volunteer Fire Department, South Dakota Wildland Fire, local friends and neighbors.

title: Mission man sentenced to more 3 years in federal prison for assault
description: A Mission man faces more than three years in prison on an assault charge.
_full_text:
A Mission man faces more than three years in prison on an assault charge.

U.S. District Judge Eric C. Schulte sentenced Jacob Wright, 31, to three years and five months in federal prison after his conviction of assault resulting in serious bodily injury, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for South Dakota.

Wright was indicted for assault resulting in serious bodily injury by a federal grand jury in December 2025. He pleaded guilty on Jan. 26, 2026.

According to the U.S. Attorney's Office:

On April 23, 2025, Wright and the victim were consuming alcohol at a residence south of Okreek, South Dakota. The two argued while outside the residence but eventually separated, with Wright going into the residence. The victim entered the residence later.

As the victim crossed the threshold, Wright struck the victim on the left side of the head and in the chest with a metal bar. The blow to the head caused a skull fracture and subdural hematoma. The head trauma required surgical intervention, specifically, removal of a portion of the right side of the skull to reduce the pressure created on the left side of the brain.

The sentencing took place on April 21.

This matter was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian Country be prosecuted in federal court as opposed to state court.

This case was investigated by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services. Assistant U.S. Attorney Abby VanDenBerg prosecuted the case.

Wright was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Kyle man sentenced to federal prison for stealing checks
description: U.S. District Judge Camela C. Theeler has sentenced a Kyle man convicted of larceny to a year in prison.
_full_text:
U.S. District Judge Camela C. Theeler has sentenced a Kyle man convicted of larceny to a year in prison.

Lyle Dean Misun Tibbits, 33, was sentenced to one year in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release. He was further ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund and $9,880.00 in restitution.

Tibbits was indicted for larceny by a federal grand jury in November 2025. He pleaded guilty on Jan.9, 2026.

In June 2025, Tibbits, while working on a ranch in Kyle, stole several blank checks belonging to his employer. Between June and July 2025, he unlawfully wrote several checks totaling nearly $10,000.00 to himself and another person and then cashed the checks and used the proceeds for his own personal gain.

Theeler sentenced Misun Tibbits on April 20 at the federal courthouse in Rapid City.

The matter was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian Country be prosecuted in federal court as opposed to state court.

This case was investigated by the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety. Supervisory Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Patterson prosecuted the case.

Tibbits was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Rapid City teen accused of murder faces new charge; defense works to argue transfer to juvenile court
description: Omariraine Red Bear is a Rapid City teen facing a first-degree murder charge in Pennington County. He was 17 when he was arrested. Since turning 18, he's been transferred from a juvenile detention center to the Pennington County Jail, faces a new charge and is being held in administrative segregation. At the same time, the process in underway for a judge to consider whether to transfer his case to juvenile court.
_full_text:
Omariraine Red Bear is a Rapid City teen facing a first-degree murder charge in Pennington County. He was 17 when he was arrested. Since turning 18, he's been transferred from a juvenile detention center to the Pennington County Jail, faces a new charge and is being held in administrative segregation. At the same time, the process in underway for a judge to consider whether to transfer his case to juvenile court.

In court on Friday, May 15, Red Bear pleaded not guilty to the new charge —assault with bodily fluids. The incident allegedly took place on April 3 in the Pennington County Jail. It's a Class 6 felony with a maximum penalty of two years in prison and up to a $4,000 fine. When he entered his plea, he wore a red-and-white jail uniform, an indicator he's held in administrative segregation either for his own safety or the safety of others.

Red Bear's murder charge stems from the May 17, 2025 fatal shooting of Dakota Britthouer at an apartment in the 1500 block of Wood Avenue in north Rapid City. Police found Britthouer outside the apartment building with a gunshot wound. He was declared dead at the hospital. 

Police said at the time it's believed Red Bear and Britthouer knew each other, "and the incident was not random in nature." Red Bear was arrested the same day.

A month after the shooting, Red Bear's attorney filed a request for a transfer hearing before a judge to argue the case be moved to juvenile court. When a charge is severe enough — such as first-degree murder — and the minor charged with it is 16 or 17, the case is automatically referred to adult court. From there, the burden is on the defense to argue it's in the public interest for the case to be heard in juvenile court. 

Friday's hearing was scheduled to address the transfer request. Red Bear's defense attorney, Gregory Sperlich, requested that the hearing be canceled and ultimately rescheduled once more information is gathered. 

Sperlich said a psychologist is working to review Red Bear's Department of Social Services record as she writes a report. The psychologist, Brenna Tindall out of Fort Collins, Colorado, works across criminal, civil, and domestic relations courts, providing expert psychological and forensic evaluations for attorneys, government agencies, and court systems, according to her website.

On Red Bear's arrest warrant for the murder charge, it lists the Department of Social Services office as his address. In court Friday, Red Bear said the furthest he went in school is fifth grade.

Seventh Circuit Court Judge Jeffrey Connolly presided over the Friday hearing. He scheduled a status hearing in the murder case on June 23 at 10:45 a.m. The hearing will also function as non-evidentiary motions hearing in the new case.

If the defense is ready for a transfer hearing before that date, Connolly asked Sperlich to reach out so one can be set. 

Although first-degree murder carries a mandatory minimum of life in prison in South Dakota, if a crime is committed when someone is under 18, they cannot be sentenced to life. A judge can sentence them to "a term of years," per South Dakota law.

title: Judge sentences 3 defendants for separate federal gun crimes in Rapid City
description: U.S. District Court Judge Camela C. Theeler has sentenced three individuals for separate gun crimes. The individuals were sentenced on April 20, the U.S. Attorney's Office for South Dakota said.
_full_text:
U.S. District Court Judge Camela C. Theeler has sentenced three individuals for separate gun crimes. The individuals were sentenced on April 20, the U.S. Attorney's Office for South Dakota said.

Oscar Ortiz-Romero, 34, a Mexican national, was convicted of possession of a firearm and ammunition by a prohibited person and sentenced to time served after having been held for over a year.

Ortiz-Romero was pulled over by the Box Elder Police Department on March 15, 2025, for speeding. He was driving while intoxicated. Ortiz-Romero is in the United States unlawfully and is expected to be deported. In the vehicle, Ortiz-Romero had a loaded pistol and, in his pocket, ammunition. It is unlawful for an undocumented immigrant to possess a firearm or ammunition. Ortiz-Romero was immediately turned over to Immigration and Customs Enforcement authorities.

Avalon Gayton, 23, of Rapid City, was convicted of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person and sentenced to four years in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

On Sept. 5, 2025, Rapid City police officers initiated a traffic stop on Gayton’s vehicle. Gayton had a pistol in her possession. She had been previously convicted of a crime punishable by over a year in prison. It is a federal felony to possess a firearm or ammunition after such a conviction.

Ashton Shaw, 20, of Rapid City, was convicted of receipt of a firearm while under indictment and sentenced to five years in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

On June 12, 2025, Rapid City police officers responded to a report of shots fired from a vehicle. Law enforcement found the vehicle and determined Shaw had been inside it moments earlier. Officers found a stolen pistol with an extended magazine inside the car. Shaw received and possessed this pistol after being indicted with a felony in South Dakota State Circuit Court. It is a federal felony to receive a firearm while charged for such a crime.

“These cases reflect this administration’s ongoing commitment to reducing gun violence and keeping our communities as safe as they can possibly be,” U.S. Attorney Ron Parsons said in a release. “It is illegal under federal law for a convicted felon to possess a gun or ammunition, for an illegal alien to possess a gun or ammunition, and for someone under indictment for a felony to acquire a gun or ammunition. If you are aware of a felon in possession of a gun, or any other violation of federal gun laws, please report it to law enforcement right away. You can do so without giving your name and you may well be saving someone’s life.”

The first case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, and the Box Elder Police Department. The second and third cases were investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and the Rapid City Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Schroeder prosecuted these cases.

All three individuals were immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Law enforcement: Buckle up, buttercup
description: Law enforcement near and far is pushing people to buckle up and buckle up correctly.
_full_text:
Law enforcement near and far is pushing people to buckle up and buckle up correctly.

The Pennington County Sheriff’s Office and Rapid City Police Department said it’s partnering with South Dakota Department of Public Safety-Office of Highway Safety, and U.S. Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to urge drivers to buckle up.

The Click It or Ticket seat belt safety campaign is a national high-visibility seat belt enforcement effort, which coincides with the Memorial Day holiday, running through May 11-31.

Seat belt use should be an automatic habit for drivers and passengers alike, law enforcement said. During the Click It or Ticket campaign, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office and the Rapid City Police Department said in a joint release on May 18. They are working with fellow law enforcement officers across local and state lines to ensure the message gets out to drivers and passengers. Not buckling up could mean a ticket, or worse, risk a life.

In 2024, there were 9,758 unbuckled passenger vehicle occupants killed in traffic crashes, according to the pair of local departments.

“The national seat belt use rate in 2024 was 91.2%, which is good — but it can be better,” the release read. “The other 8.8% still need to be reminded that seat belts save lives. Participating law enforcement agencies will be taking a no-excuses approach to seat belt law enforcement, writing citations day and night.”

One of the focuses of the Click It or Ticket seat belt campaign is nighttime enforcement. NHTSA data shows a higher number of unrestrained occupant fatalities happen at night (56% between the hours of 6 p.m. and 6 a.m.). Of the males killed in crashes in 2023, more than half (53%) were unrestrained. For females killed in crashes, 41% were not buckled up.

Buckle up the right way

Place the shoulder belt across the middle of the chest and away from the neck.

Lay the lap belt across the hips and not the stomach.

Never place the seat belt behind the back or under arms.

Front seat and back, child and adult — everyone needs to remember to buckle up.

For more information on the Click It or Ticket seat belt enforcement campaign, visit NHTSA.gov/ClickIt and https://drivesafesd.com

title: Rapid City police reminds public not to use cars as gun safes after recent burglary

_full_text:
The Rapid City Police Department is reminding the public to not store their firearms inside their vehicles after a recent car burglary. 

At around 8:20 a.m. on Saturday, May 16, police responded to a residence in the 2200 block of Philadelphia Street for a report of a vehicle burglary. 

The reporting party told police that their truck was burglarized and a loaded firearm was taken from inside the car. Police noted no signs of forced entry to the pickup. 

"A vehicle is not a viable gun safe," The Rapid City Police Department wrote in a press release. "Responsible firearm ownership starts with maintaining 24/7 accountability for all owned firearms."

The department reported 10 firearms have been stolen from vehicles in Rapid City over the past year.

title: Box Elder man arrested less than 12 hours after being released from prison
description: A Box Elder man was arrested Friday night, less than 12 hours after being released on parole from prison.
_full_text:
A Box Elder man was arrested Friday night, less than 12 hours after being released on parole from prison.

Diego Perez, 20, was arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm by a felon, receiving stolen property and open container in a motor vehicle. Perez was previously convicted of possession of a controlled substance and was sentenced to one year and six months in prison.

At around 10:30 p.m. on May 15 police responded to the 3500 block of Black Fox Drive for a report of a suspicious incident. 

The reporting party told police they were outside of their home when an unknown pickup truck pulled up and asked them for a cigarette and invited them into the car. They refused and the occupants of the truck allegedly became confrontational. 

Police later found the truck and initiated a traffic stop, during which they identified Perez as one of the occupants. Several open alcohol containers were found in the truck, along with a loaded revolver that was reported stolen in August 2025 during a vehicle burglary.

Perez was determined to be on parole and police learned he had been released from prison earlier that day.

As of Monday, May 18, Perez is being held at the Pennington County Jail with a $10,000 cash-only bond.

title: Manderson man sentenced to life for fire that killed one, injured another
description: A Manderson man was sentenced to life in prison for the death of 42-year-old Tanya White Butterfly and the injury of his brother after he set a residence on fire in 2024.
_full_text:
A Manderson man was sentenced to life in prison for the death of 42-year-old Tanya White Butterfly and the injury of his brother after he set a residence on fire in 2024.

Reno Rondeau, 52, was found guilty on Feb. 5, 2026, by a jury for first-degree murder, assault with intent to commit arson, assault resulting in serious bodily injury and arson. 

Rondeau appeared for his sentencing before U.S. District Court Judge Camela Theeler at the Andrew W. Bogue Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse in Rapid City on Monday, May 18. 

Evidence at trial established Rondeau lit his brother's house near Manderson on fire on Oct. 19, 2024, by first igniting items inside a wheelbarrow and then dumping the fire onto the home's wooden porch. The government said at the start of the trial Rondeau was upset his brother had the house. The brother tried everything he could to save White Butterfly's life, but he wasn't able to.

Rondeau's niece, his brother's daughter, said during trial she arrived at the fire and could hear White Butterfly "murmuring" inside as her brother and father removed window screens and tried to put the fire out with a garden hose in an effort to save her.

Rondeau's attorney, Paul Winter, declined to rediscuss the facts of the case and acknowledged that first-degree murder has a mandatory minimum of life in prison. When the court asked if Rondeau had anything to say, he said he will be filing a notice of appeal. 

Assistant United States Attorney Paige Peterson highlighted the recent celebration of Mother's Day on Sunday, May 10, and how Rondeau denied White Butterfly's family the ability to celebrate with her ever again. 

White Butterfly's cousin said White Butterfly was the glue that held their family together, always offering a helping hand. 

"Tanya, my cousin, was genuinely a good person," he said. 

He said since losing White Butterfly there has been a void in the place she once filled with warmth and care. He said he is heartbroken knowing she won't be able to attend his daughter's graduation, and that this is a pain they will continue to face.

White Butterfly's obituary states she left behind three children and three grandchildren.

During sentencing, Theeler emphasized the "very sad circumstances" of the case. Theeler acknowledged Rondeau's criminal history of substance abuse, theft and simple assault. 

Theeler sentenced Rondeau to life in prison for first-degree murder and 10 years each for the other remaining charges. All charges will run concurrently to the life sentence.

title: Hearing on proposed Black Hills uranium drilling opens with hours of opposition testimony
description: HOT SPRINGS — Persistent, drizzling rain didn’t keep dozens of people from rallying against a proposed uranium drilling project in the southern Black Hills on the first day of a weeklong hearing to decide on a permit application.
_full_text:
HOT SPRINGS — Persistent, drizzling rain didn’t keep dozens of people from rallying against a proposed uranium drilling project in the southern Black Hills on the first day of a weeklong hearing to decide on a permit application.

Law enforcement officers and vehicles flanked the parking lot and theater doors Monday at the Mueller Civic Center, where the hearing took place.

Opponents cited concerns about Craven Canyon, which is near the proposed drilling sites and is marked with ancient Native American petroglyphs. Opponents said they’re also concerned about the potential to contaminate underground water, and to negatively affect the state’s agriculture and tourism industries.

 052026-nws-sl-mining-p1.jpg
Elizabeth Lone Eagle (far right) speaks to the South Dakota Board of Minerals and Environment at the first day of a hearing on an exploratory drilling permit on May 18, 2026, at the Mueller Civic Center in Hot Springs. 

“A lot of the people in this room don’t live near Craven Canyon, but that doesn’t mean that you ditch the responsibility to protect it,” said project opponent Anissa Martin. She then referenced the Lakota name for the Black Hills. “So I ask you, where will we go when the He Sapa are uninhabitable, when we have no water in the Black Hills? And I ask you, what water will you drink?”

The hearing drew public testimony from not only residents of the Black Hills, but also from Wyoming, Minnesota and Pennsylvania. People who spoke Monday during the hourslong public comment period were all in opposition to the project.

The company proposing the drilling has maintained that it has gone through all the necessary steps in the permitting process, and the project will not harm the nearby canyon.

The state Board of Minerals and Environment can deny an application to explore for uranium for several reasons, including negative impacts on historical, archaeological or recreational aspects of an area, if those impacts outweigh the benefits of the exploration. The board can also deny the permit if it will negatively affect the productivity of aquifers.

In March 2024, Clean Nuclear Energy Corporation and its Canada-based parent company Nexus Uranium filed an application to drill exploratory holes in search of uranium near Craven Canyon, 7 miles north of Edgemont.

The company plans to use 50 sites to drill holes as deep as 700 feet on state-owned land, according to its application. Each hole will take approximately two weeks to drill.

The company has additional drilling plans on federally owned land. That portion of the project is under review by the U.S. Forest Service, which estimates it will issue a decision next month.

Besides taking public testimony, the state board dealt with several preliminary matters Monday.

 052026-nws-sl-mining-p2.jpg
A view of Craven Canyon in the southern Black Hills. 

The board’s hearing chairman, Bob Morris, declined to require the state’s commissioner of school and public lands to testify in person. That office manages the state land at the proposed project site.

Bruce Ellison, an attorney and project opponent, sought to require the commissioner’s in-person testimony. Ellison said he didn’t receive sufficient evidence from a records request about the commissioner as to “how he did his job.”

Morris said there is written material from the commissioner in the case file, and Morris doesn’t see “how it’s relevant” to question the commissioner.

The board also failed to produce a Lakota interpreter for the hearing, after agreeing to provide one. A staff member for the state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources said potential interpreters had conflicts of interest or scheduling conflicts that prevented them from accepting the role.

The board decided to have a discussion Tuesday morning about whether to continue the hearing without an interpreter. The hearing is scheduled to continue through Friday.

The proposed drilling near Craven Canyon is separate from another proposal to mine uranium in the Edgemont area that’s been pending since the early 2000s. That proposal, from Texas-based enCore Energy, has met staunch opposition from Native Americans and environmental activists and has been in regulatory and legal limbo. Last year, the federal government’s Permitting Council selected enCore’s project for inclusion in FAST-41, a process intended to improve coordination among permitting agencies and hold them accountable to deadlines.

Uranium is a metallic, radioactive element used as fuel in nuclear weapons and nuclear power plants. Interest in uranium exploration and mining has risen recently, in response to nuclear energy’s potential to meet the growing electricity demands of data centers handling the computing needs of artificial intelligence.

The hearing in Hot Springs comes on the heels of a victory for opponents of another drilling project in the Black Hills. Rapid City-based company Pete Lien & Sons recently withdrew from an exploratory graphite drilling project that was underway near Pe’ Sla, also known as Reynolds Prairie, a sacred site for Lakota people in the central Black Hills. The withdrawal came after two lawsuits from opponents challenging the project and the formation of a protest camp at the drilling site.

title: 'Save Our Tail' celebrates Deadwood's history and the West's fierce women
description: “Save Our Tail,” a four-day celebration of Western history, storytelling, preservation and remarkable women, starts Wednesday in honor of Deadwood’s 150th anniversary.
_full_text:
“Save Our Tail,” a four-day celebration of Western history, storytelling, preservation and remarkable women, starts Wednesday in honor of Deadwood’s 150th anniversary.

“Save Our Tail” takes place May 20 through 23, with a series of presentations, performances and special events. All events are free but donations are welcome.

Throughout “Save Our Tail,” award-winning author and historian Chris Enss will bring stories of bold, unconventional women of the West to life, giving presentations in full period costume.

Enss is a New York Times bestselling author who has written about women of the Old West for more than 30 years. She has penned more than 50 published books on the subject. One of her most recent books is “An Open Secret: The Story of Deadwood’s Most Notorious Bordellos,” exploring the history of houses of ill repute such as The Gem. It was owned and operated by Al Swearengen, who opened The Gem shortly after arriving in Deadwood in 1876, the year the town was founded.

 1980 Deadwood brothel raid (copy) (copy)
Deadwood townspeople parade in support of brothels in this July 1980 Journal file photo. A story in the July 18, 1980, edition of the Journal says "Signs in a raucous 'Bring back our ladies' parade read: 'Pro Pros,' 'Have a heart - preserve our wildlife' and 'Save our tale (sic).'" A highlight of the "Save Our Tail" festivities May 20-23, 2026, in Deadwood will be a reenactment of this impromptu procession.  

“Save Our Tail” opens with a family-friendly program for adults and children at 4 p.m. May 20 at Deadwood Public Library, 435 Williams St. Enss will highlight trailblazing women physicians and teachers who defied expectations and shaped frontier communities.

On May 21, “Save Our Tail” features a presentation by Enss at noon at the Homestake Adams Research and Cultural Center, 22 Van Buren St. Enss will discuss her book “The Widowed Ones: Beyond the Battle of the Little Bighorn,” an intimate look at the seven wives of U.S. Army officers killed at the battle. The presentation explores their shared grief, financial hardships, and resilience that helped them rebuild their lives.

 Chris Enss
Author and historian Chris Enss will give presentations throughout "Save Our Tail" May 20-23, 2026, in Deadwood. She has written more than 50 books about women in the West.  

On May 22, activities begin at 1 p.m. on Main Street with a reenactment of the 1980 “Save Our Tail” impromptu procession. Enss will appear in period costume as Madam Dora DuFran for the reenactment. The original “Save Our Tails” procession was sparked by the infamous, historic “bust of the brothels” that closed Deadwood brothels.

At 2:30 p.m., Justin Koehler will screen his documentary, “Nita: Hotbed in Deadwood” in the Eagle Bar beneath The Brothel Deadwood, 610 Main St. The screening will be followed by a discussion with Koehler. He is an award-winning director, producer, videographer, and screenwriter who lives in South Dakota.

 Nita documentary poster
South Dakota filmmaker Justin Koehler will screen his documentary “Nita: Hotbed in Deadwood” as part of "Save Our Tail" festivities May 20-23, 2026, in Deadwood. This documentary delves into the story of Nita Celaya and her pivotal role in Deadwood’s 1980 brothel raid.  

“Nita: Hotbed in Deadwood” delves into the story of Nita Celaya and her pivotal role in Deadwood’s 1980 brothel raid. The documentary explores tensions between tradition, morality and survival. Through a rare interview and a 1980 FBI tape, Celaya’s voice brings this controversial chapter to life.

"Save Our Tail" events on May 22 conclude with live acoustic country-rock by the Johnny Lonesome Band from 4 to 5 p.m. at the Eagle Bar, and from 8 to 10 p.m. at The Nugget Saloon, 604 Main St.

“Save Our Tail” concludes on May 23 with book signings from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at The Brothel Deadwood, featuring Enss’ books including “An Open Secret,” “Wicked Women,” and other titles. Brothel tours will be available throughout the day for $12 per person.

Enss will present talks about “Wicked Women” and “An Open Secret” at noon, 2 and 4 p.m. and will deal Faro for book prizes throughout the afternoon.

“Save Our Tail” helps commemorate Deadwood’s start in 1876. After gold was discovered in the northern Black Hills, miner staked their claims and set up camp in a gulch full of dead trees, and Deadwood was born. In April 1876, the city of Deadwood was officially laid out. Dance halls, gambling establishments, saloons and brothels were built on both sides of lower Main Street in May.

In July 1876, Deadwood residents celebrated the United States’ centennial, even though South Dakota was not a state. South Dakota became part of the United States in 1889.

title: Rapid City man sentenced after 2024 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally sex trafficking sting
description: A Rapid City man was sentenced to five years in federal prison followed by five years of supervised release for attempted receipt of child pornography.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man was sentenced to five years in federal prison followed by five years of supervised release for attempted receipt of child pornography. 

Eli Poorman, 21, appeared for his sentencing before U.S. District Court Judge Camela Theeler at the Andrew W. Bogue Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse in Rapid City on Tuesday, May 19. 

Poorman was one out of seven men arrested in a multi-agency sex trafficking operation during the 2024 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally designed to apprehend people attempting to arrange sexual encounters with underage children. The operation began on Aug. 2, 2024 and continued through Aug. 8, 2024.

Poorman pleaded guilty on Feb. 4 to attempted receipt of child pornography through a plea agreement with the government. Poorman was initially indicted with attempted commercial sex trafficking of a minor and attempted transfer of obscene material to a minor.

In the plea agreement, the government agreed to dismiss those charges and both sides agreed to ask for five months in prison followed by five years of supervised release.

According to the factual basis statement — which is a document that establishes the basis of a guilty plea and is signed by both the government and the defendant — Poorman messaged who he thought was a 13-year-old girl, but was actually a Homeland Security Investigations agent, asking sexual favors in exchange for money. He also sent several photos of himself during the interactions and invited the girl to his apartment in Rapid City, where he was met with law enforcement instead. 

Poorman's attorney Gregory Erlandson said his client is taking responsibility for his actions while seeking out treatment for his lengthy medical history. 

Erlandson described the plea agreement holds Poorman not only accountable but ensures he can flourish afterwards.

Poorman told the court he's learned a lot from this experience, and learned he's been taking advantage of a privilege for some time – his freedom. 

Poorman's grandmother and mother testified on Tuesday, describing Poorman as "a great young man." They both expressed concerns in Poorman getting the proper resources to treat his health issues and his relative safety in prison. 

Poorman's mother expressed her discontent with the State of South Dakota, highlighting he would never harm a child. Poorman’s case is federal, but local enforcement participates in the sting.

"It's not right that the State of South Dakota can do these sting operations and label my son as a predator," she said.

Theeler acknowledged Poorman's young age, medical history and history with drugs and alcohol. Since being arrested, Theeler said Poorman has taken strides to better himself and learn from the experience by getting clean and seeking out his GED. 

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Gregg Peterman said the five-year supervised release will require Poorman to be honest and candid as he seeks out treatment. 

"It's up to you if you can come out better, and I think you're capable of that," Theeler said before sentencing.

title: Rapid City police arrest two juvenile males after finding sawed-off shotgun
description: A gunshot call led to discovery of a sawed-off shotgun and the arrest of two juvenile males on Monday, May 18, Rapid City police said on Tuesday, May 19.
_full_text:
A gunshot call led to discovery of a sawed-off shotgun and the arrest of two juvenile males on Monday, May 18, Rapid City police said on Tuesday, May 19.

According to the department, officers responded to a dispatch call around 12:30 a.m. on May 10 to the area of 600 Lindbergh Avenue, the address of Ridgestone Mobile Home Park just off of Haines Avenue.

Officers nearby also reported hearing gunshots as well. As officers arrived, they began searching the area. At one point, police located several spent shotgun shells. A short time after locating the spent shells, police observed two subjects in dark clothing enter an awaiting passenger vehicle.

The vehicle began driving away from the location, and police pulled it over in the area of Holcomb Avenue and Anamosa Street. As police spoke to the driver, they saw two juvenile males in the back seat. Police also saw a shotgun sitting on the floor near their feet.

The males were told to exit the vehicle but refused, police said. Officers were forced to physically remove the males from the backseat, and they continued to resist. Despite their resistance, police were ultimately able to detain both males in handcuffs.

They were both identified as the males responsible for the earlier gunshots call. Police found the shotgun to be loaded and illegally-shortened. Both juvenile males have since been placed in the appropriate channels of the juvenile justice system. The Rapid City Police Department said one was on parole and the other was on probation. The juvenile justice system is closed to the public, so the Journal is unable to confirm that information or look up the cases underlying any parole of probation for juveniles.

title: Three men conduct citizens’ arrest on unruly gas station visitor
description: A hectic situation at a Rapid City gas station on Monday, May 18, started with a man becoming confrontational with employees and concluded when police arrived to find three men holding him down on the ground, the Rapid City Police Department said on Tuesday, May 19.
_full_text:
A hectic situation at a Rapid City gas station on Monday, May 18, started with a man becoming confrontational with employees and concluded when police arrived to find three men holding him down on the ground, the Rapid City Police Department said on Tuesday, May 19.

Police were dispatched to the Circle K at 1610 Caregiver Circle at around 5:20 p.m. on Monday for a report of a man attacking customers. When they arrived, they found Carlos Ambriz, 37, of Sioux Falls, being held on the ground by the three men. Witnesses told police that when Ambriz became confrontational with employees, one customer tried to de-escalate the situation and Ambriz assaulted him. At that point, several customers took Ambriz to the ground and held him there.

The police department highlighted Ambriz is on parole but that his parole agent didn’t want him placed on a parole hold. Officers ultimately arrested him on suspicion of disorderly conduct and failure to vacate, and took him to the Pennington County Jail. As of Tuesday, May 19, Ambriz was not listed on the jail roster and no new charges had been filed against him, per South Dakota court records.

South Dakota Department of Corrections records show Ambriz was sentenced on June 6, 2024, to three years in prison for third-degree burglary. The judge suspended the entire sentence and applied 78 days of time served to the three years. Ambriz pleaded guilty to the charge on the same day. South Dakota law defines third-degree burglary as when someone enters or remains in an occupied structure with intent to commit a crime unless the person is legally allowed to be there.

title: Nigerian man accused of embezzling funds from Pine Ridge casino
description: A federal grand jury has indicted Kenneth Godwin, a Nigerian man, for conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud and unauthorized access to a protected computer in furtherance of fraud related to the attempted scamming of Prairie Wind Casino & Hotel in Pine Ridge, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for South Dakota.
_full_text:
A federal grand jury has indicted Kenneth Godwin, a Nigerian man, for conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud and unauthorized access to a protected computer in furtherance of fraud related to the attempted scamming of Prairie Wind Casino & Hotel in Pine Ridge, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for South Dakota.

The maximum penalty upon conviction is up to 20 years in custody and/or a $250,000 fine, three years of supervised release, and $100 to the Federal Crime Victims Fund. Restitution may also be ordered.

Between May 2023 and March 2026, Godwin, while believed to be living in Nigeria, conspired with others to embezzle funds from the Prairie Wind Casino & Hotel in Pine Ridge, South Dakota, in order to enrich themselves, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said. The grand jury indicted Godwin in March 2026.

According to court documents, in June 2023 Godwin allegedly gained unauthorized access to the Prairie Wind Casino's general manager's email credentials, including the general manager's official Prairie Wind Casino & Hotel email address and password.

“After obtaining access to the general manager's email account, the defendant and others unknown to the grand jury directed emails using the general manager's account to others, authorizing wire transfer payments to what appeared to be businesses, but were in fact accounts unrelated to those businesses,” the indictment document says.

Allegedly, Godwin and others later fraudulently obtained more than $270,882 through the scheme, according to the indictment.

“No agency on earth is better at this than the FBI,” U.S. Attorney Ron Parsons said in a release. “They will track down those who steal from and commit fraud against the people of the United States wherever those offenders may be.”

“This international business email compromise (BEC) scheme caused substantial financial damage to a business owned and operated by the Oglala Sioux Tribe on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota,” said FBI Minneapolis Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson. “This indictment is an example of how the FBI operates every day to dismantle and disrupt criminal enterprises in Indian Country and across the United States that target businesses and citizens in communities. The message is clear; we will work with our partners to hold fraudsters accountable.”

The investigation is being conducted by the FBI. Assistant U.S. Attorney Ben Patterson is prosecuting the case, according to the release.

title: Rapid City Council Q&A with Ward 2 candidate Christopher Vanderhoof
description: Name, age, occupation
_full_text:
Name, age, occupation

Christopher Vanderhoof, 56, Sr. Engineer for Identity Access Management

Why are you running?

I’m running to serve our community. Our residents deserve to be engaged and heard. Too many people feel disconnected from the decisions that are shaping our city. My commitment is to be a steady, accessible voice for people, someone you can rely on to listen to, communicate clearly, and keep you informed.

 Christopher Vanderhoof
Christopher Vanderhoof 

I will establish regular times and locations where residents can meet with me to discuss priorities, ongoing issues, and upcoming proposals. I understand that not everyone can attend City Council meetings, and navigating the city’s website can be challenging. I’ve experienced those frustrations myself. I intend to make information easier to access by sharing clear updates and providing direct links to important documents so the public can stay informed.

Rapid City needs stronger communication and genuine accountability in local government. My goal is to ensure the public is never left out of the conversation and always have a seat at the table. I will work every day to make sure your voice is heard and your concerns are represented with honesty, stability, and respect.

What are the top three issues Rapid City faces that you would work to address on the council? Is there anything specific to your ward?

The top three issues I hear most from our residents, especially while walking Ward 2, are roads, housing, and homelessness. These concerns reflect real challenges our city must address.

First, our roads need serious attention. People are frustrated with potholes, deteriorating streets and slow repairs. Reliable infrastructure is a basic expectation, and we need a more consistent, accountable plan for maintaining and improving our road system.

 Elections

Second, housing affordability is a growing concern for both young families and our aging population. Residents want options that fit their budgets without being pushed out of the neighborhoods they love. We need to support responsible development, encourage a range of housing types, and make sure existing neighborhoods remain livable and attainable.

Third, homelessness continues to be an issue nationwide. People want to see compassionate and effective solutions that improve the welfare of those struggling while also addressing the impacts on neighborhoods and public spaces. This requires coordination, education and a focus on long-term outcomes.

These are a few of the issues that are important, where residents want to feel heard and see real progress. We need to bring practical, community-driven solutions forward and ensure the voices of the city are part of every decision.

What approach to Tax Increment Financing would you bring to the council?

My approach to Tax Increment Financing is simple: bring fresh eyes, ask direct questions and make sure the public is never left out of the process. TIF’s can be a useful tool, but only when it’s used responsibly and with a clear outcome.

Residents deserve to know exactly what’s being proposed, how long the TIF will last, what the public gets in return, and whether the project would still happen without taxpayer support. Too often, people feel decisions are made without them. We need to keep the community informed and involved at every step.

How should the city approach growth?

The city must approach growth with vision, innovation and strong leadership. Rapid City is changing, and we need to embrace that change with thoughtful planning and a clear understanding of the opportunities it brings. With comprehensive information and responsible decision‑making, we can adapt to growth in a way that strengthens our community and protects our quality of life.

We have the people, the talent, and the resources to move Rapid City forward. Our region’s diverse strengths, from technology and education to the unique assets of the Black Hills. This gives us advantages that many communities simply do not have. By leveraging these strengths, we can position Rapid City as a leader in sustainable, well‑managed growth.

What is working and what needs to be fixed in the city’s approach to homeless people?

Homelessness is one of the most complex issues facing Rapid City, and it’s clear that we need a balanced, compassionate, and effective approach. Before making decisions, we need to find where the gaps still exist and address them. Our homeless neighbors are part of our community, and any long term solution must reflect that.

Moving forward, the city needs a more coordinated strategy that focuses on safety, accountability, and support. That means working with service providers, law enforcement, neighborhoods, and most importantly the public to make sure we’re addressing both the immediate challenges and the root causes. Transparency will be essential, so residents understand what’s being done and why.

We need to help build an approach that improves outcomes for those experiencing homelessness while also protecting the health, safety, and quality of life in our neighborhoods.

What can the city do to make living in Rapid City more affordable?

Making life more affordable in Rapid City starts with strengthening our local economy and investing in the needs of our residents. That means focusing on the basics: reliable infrastructure, attainable housing, and services that support working families. While also attracting the kinds of employers that create stable, good-paying jobs.

We should be looking at opportunities to bring in tech companies and medium to large employers, that can diversify our economy and expand career options for residents. When people have access to better jobs and a stronger economic base, affordability improves across the board.

At the same time, the city must stay focused on smart investments that directly benefit the community. When we balance economic growth with responsible planning, we create a Rapid City where families have more opportunities and a better chance to thrive.

What should the city’s role be in addiction services and how should the city use opioid settlement funds toward fulfilling that role?

The city has an important role to play in supporting addiction services, especially when it comes to coordination, vision, and making sure resources are used effectively. Addiction affects families across Rapid City, and we need to approach it with both accountability and compassion.

We need to understand what services currently exist, where the gaps are, and how we can strengthen partnerships with healthcare providers, nonprofits, and regional treatment programs. The city shouldn’t try to replace medical professionals; we need to be a leader in the standard of care for addiction services, along with investing in quality care providers.

One of the biggest gaps residents talk about is the lack of long-term, structured treatment options. Many people feel that short-term or revolving door approaches don’t give individuals enough time or stability to begin recovery. Exploring ways to support or attract an inpatient rehabilitation facility, one that offers extended stays and evidence-based therapies, is something worth evaluating as part of a broader strategy.

As for the opioid settlement funds, those dollars should be used responsibly and transparently, and only for programs that directly address addiction, recovery and prevention. That could include expanding access to treatment services, supporting prevention and education efforts, improving coordination between service providers, and ensuring people have access to quality therapeutic support.

Our goal is to make sure every dollar is used in a way that strengthens our community, supports recovery, assists with prevention and improves outcomes for the people who need it.

title: Rapid City Council Q&A with Ward 2 candidate Lindsey Seachris
description: Name, age, occupation
_full_text:
Name, age, occupation

Lindsey Seachris, 42, Development Coordinator at Black Hills Center for Aging

 Lindsey Seachris
Lindsey Seachris 

Why are you running?

I’m running for Rapid City Council because I care deeply about Rapid City and its future. As a working mother raising my children here, I have a long-term investment in making sure Rapid City remains a place where families, businesses, and residents can thrive.

Through my experience in private industry, local government, and higher education, I’ve seen both the opportunities ahead of us and the challenges we face — especially affordability, infrastructure, public safety, responsible growth, and retaining local talent. I also bring a perspective rooted in the experiences of working families and everyday residents.

I believe local government works best when leaders focus on practical solutions, thoughtful planning, and listening to the people they serve. We don’t have to agree on everything to work together and move Rapid City forward. I want to continue bringing a balanced, common-sense approach that respects taxpayers, plans responsibly for the future, and keeps Rapid City a strong, welcoming place to call home.

What are the top three issues Rapid City faces that you would work to address on the council? Is there anything specific to your ward?

One of the biggest issues facing Rapid City is affordability. Housing costs, rent, utilities, and property taxes have increased faster than many residents’ incomes, especially impacting young families, seniors, and working people. We need to support attainable housing, workforce development, and economic opportunities that allow people not just to live here, but to build a future here.

The second issue is growth and infrastructure. Rapid City is growing whether we like it or not, and roads, water systems, traffic planning, and public safety services must keep pace. I support thoughtful growth that prioritizes infrastructure, responsible infill development, revitalization of existing neighborhoods, and protection of the quality of life that makes Rapid City special.

A third challenge is public safety and issues tied to addiction, mental health, and homelessness. Residents deserve to feel safe in their neighborhoods and public spaces. These are complex issues that require coordination, compassion, and accountability, and while the City cannot solve them alone, it plays an important role in supporting first responders, partnerships, and long-term solutions.

In Ward 2 specifically, I continue to hear concerns about road conditions, public safety, and making sure development includes the infrastructure necessary to support our neighborhoods. Residents want to feel informed and heard before decisions are made, and I will continue working to improve communication between residents, developers, and the City.

What approach to Tax Increment Financing would you bring to the council?

I believe Tax Increment Financing (TIF) can be a valuable economic development tool when used carefully, strategically, and with a clear public benefit. TIF should primarily support projects involving infrastructure improvements, workforce housing, redevelopment of underutilized areas, or projects that would be difficult to accomplish without public-private partnership.

A strong example is the Homestead Street Overlay, which is helping fund a joint Fire/Police substation and Homestead Park. This investment improves emergency response times, supports proactive policing, and creates new recreational opportunities for families.

 Elections

At the same time, taxpayers deserve transparency and accountability. TIF should not become a routine subsidy for projects already financially viable on their own. I have voted against several TIF proposals in recent years after carefully reviewing the details. Any use of public financing tools should include strong oversight, measurable outcomes, and clear communication about community impact.

How should the city approach growth?

Rapid City should approach growth with long-term planning and intentional decision-making. Growth should support growth.

That means making strategic investments in roads, water infrastructure, utilities, and public safety while protecting the quality of life that makes Rapid City a great place to live. Growth done well should strengthen neighborhoods, improve infrastructure, and create economic opportunity.

I believe we should prioritize thoughtful infill development, support workforce and attainable housing, preserve parks and open spaces, and encourage development that fits the character of existing neighborhoods. People should feel informed, heard, and included in decisions that impact their neighborhoods and daily lives.

What is working and what needs to be fixed in the city’s approach to homeless people?

Rapid City has many organizations, churches, nonprofits, first responders, and volunteers doing important work to help individuals experiencing homelessness, and these partnerships are essential.

In 2026, the City invested approximately $2.41 million into organizations supporting the homeless population, but these challenges cannot be solved by government alone. We need stronger coordination and a better long-term strategy, including addressing gaps such as transitional housing.

We also need continued collaboration between law enforcement, mental health providers, addiction services, housing organizations, and nonprofits because these issues are interconnected. The focus should be on prevention, recovery, and pathways toward stability rather than simply managing the problem.

At the same time, residents deserve to feel safe in their neighborhoods, parks, downtown, and public spaces. I believe we can approach these issues with both compassion and accountability by supporting public safety while also creating opportunities for treatment, housing assistance, job support, and recovery services.

What can the city do to make living in Rapid City more affordable?

Affordability is one of the biggest challenges facing Rapid City, and the City has an important role in helping keep our community accessible for working families, young professionals, and seniors.

We need to support a wider range of housing options, encourage workforce and attainable housing, and streamline development processes where appropriate while maintaining quality standards and responsible planning. Getting infrastructure in place ahead of growth can also help reduce long-term costs for taxpayers.

Affordability is about more than housing — it also includes utilities, transportation, childcare access, and overall cost of living. That’s why I believe the City must manage taxpayer dollars responsibly, prioritize essential services, and avoid unnecessary tax burdens whenever possible.

What should the city’s role be in addiction services and how should the city use opioid settlement funds?

Addiction impacts every part of our community, including public safety, healthcare, families, businesses, and overall quality of life. The City has an important role in supporting partnerships, coordinating resources, and helping connect people to treatment and recovery services.

I believe opioid settlement funds should be used strategically, transparently, and in ways that produce measurable long-term results. Priorities should include expanding access to addiction treatment, mental health services, recovery support programs, prevention efforts, and programs that reduce repeat emergency and law enforcement interactions.

I also support collaborative efforts that bring together healthcare providers, schools, nonprofits, law enforcement, and recovery organizations. The goal should be long-term recovery, stronger families, and safer neighborhoods — not simply managing the problem in the short term.

title: Judith “Judy” Kaye (Knighton) Simon
_full_text:
April 8, 1954 - May 4, 2026

Judith "Judy" Kaye (Knighton) Simon, age 72, of Sturgis, South Dakota, peacefully passed away on May 4, 2026, at her sister Teresa's home in New River, Arizona, surrounded by her loving family and her faithful dogs, Ruger and Jack. Judy left behind a legacy of resilience, vibrant western heritage, and deep devotion to her family after facing complications from a stroke.

Born on April 8, 1954, in Columbia, South Carolina, to Kenneth and Helene (Price) Knighton, Judy's childhood journey quickly moved to the wide-open spaces of South Dakota. After a brief time in the historic community of Igloo, the family settled in Pierre, where Judy grew up as an energetic tomboy. She excelled in track and field at TF Riggs High School, setting several school records, and famously spent her days swimming the Missouri River alongside the local Boy Scouts, playing baseball, and riding bikes.

Her enduring passion, however, belonged to horses and dogs. As a young girl, she bought her first pony in Pierre and spent endless hours riding between the Pierre and Fort Pierre communities and assisting local ranches. Her horse sense even earned her a spot as a rider swimming horses across the Missouri River in the iconic Casey Tibbs film Born To Buck. One of Judy's favorite memories to tell was giving horseback rides to the band members of Three Dog Night after they performed in concert in Pierre.

Judy's life was deeply rooted in the ranching traditions of South Dakota. While living at her grandparents' ranch near Zeona and Hoover, she met Jerry Simon. The two married on September 1, 1970, and were blessed with their daughter, DeLynn, in 1974. On the Simon ranch, Judy truly shone as a skilled horse trainer and rodeo competitor. Known for being "as ranchey as they came," she successfully trained numerous arena horses and competed for many years in the SDRA finals. She also bred and trained high-caliber Australian Shepherds that sold throughout the US.

Following her divorce in 1987, Judy moved to Sturgis and enrolled at Black Hills State University. It was there that she met Steve Sander. The two formed an instant connection, becoming inseparable best friends right from the start. Their shared drive and spirit of adventure soon took them out of South Dakota, relocating to Las Vegas and Arizona for work opportunities. Judy's natural leadership and handiness allowed her to do many jobs ranging from managing crews installing massive commercial curtain systems in newly constructed Las Vegas hotels to managing an Appaloosa Ranch in Arizona.

In the spring of 1990, Judy and Steve returned to their roots in the Midwest, sharing a beautiful life together as they moved between Sturgis, Fort Pierre, and Beulah, Wyoming. Though they never officially married, Steve was the absolute true love of Judy's life. For decades, they built a home centered on the things they loved most: fishing on local waters, embracing nature, target shooting, raising Rat Terriers, and listening to rock & roll, and old country music. They also shared an incredible circle of friends, building a close-knit "family" at the Pyramid in Sturgis.

When Steve passed away in February 2020, Judy lost her anchor. She felt his absence deeply, carrying a profound loneliness and missing him every single day.

For many years, Judy was a beloved fixture at the Broken Spoke Saloon as a bartender during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Her warm personality and sharp character drew rally visitors back to her bar year after year, including lifelong friends Bud and Duck Weiser.

Judy was also an exceptionally gifted craftsman who could fix or build almost anything. She mastered minor electrical work, plumbing, and mechanics. Her creative talents shone through exquisite beadwork, handmade western belts, breast collars, sewing, needlework, and leather work. Her patience and connection to the earth also led her to become a certified Master Gardener through the SDSU Extension program. Judy could also cook, can, or bake anything!

In her later years, Judy found immense comfort in her family. Starting in the fall of 2020, she and her daughter DeLynn began a treasured seasonal tradition, driving together back and forth between South Dakota and Arizona. Judy loved these road trips—viewing the country, laughing, and jamming to music alongside her daughter.

She spent her winters soaking in the Arizona warmth next door to her sister Teresa, finding peace under the morning sunshine. Above all, she was fiercely proud of her grandchildren, Chase and Timber, tracking their sporting wins and celebrating their unique futures.

Judy was preceded in death by her beloved partner, Steve Sander; her parents, Kenneth and Helene Knighton; and her older brother, Riley Knighton. She is survived and dearly missed by her daughter, DeLynn (Bryan) Hanson; her grandchildren, Chase (Shannon Bailey) and Timber Hanson of Fort Pierre, SD; her sisters, Teresa (Todd) Witte of New River, AZ, and Lynda Tucker of Sioux City, IA; her aunt, Lois Cornish of Mesa, AZ; and a wide, loving circle of nieces, nephews, cousins, and friends.
