title: David Ray Hodgson
_full_text:
April 13, 1949 - May 8, 2026

David Ray Hodgson was born April 13, 1949, and he died May 8, 2026 at home with family and caregivers at his side. David died from complications related to frontotemporal dementia. Above all, David is remembered for kindness and humility, a unique sense of humor, love for family and friends, and lifelong dedication to public service in emergency medical services (EMS) as a paramedic, firefighter, and educator.

David was born in El Paso, TX to Edward (Ray) and Loretta Hodgson. His parents raised their family in Boulder, Colorado where he graduated from Boulder High School in 1967 and attended the University of Colorado. From 1970-1974, he served in the United States Air Force as Fire Protection Specialist and Staff Sargeant for the 44th Civil Engineering Squadron, Ellsworth Air Force Base. He was a Fire Protection Inspector at EAFB from 1974-1976. Hodgson launched his EMS career in Rapid City and completed the Rapid City Regional Hospital Paramedic Program in 1979. He worked for Rapid City Pennington County Emergency Medical Service, EmergiCare, and AMR ambulance services. He served with Rapid City Fire Department as Firefighter Paramedic from 1988-1996. Hodgson was dedicated to peer support of colleagues facing the trauma of EMS work through the Katharsis Critical Incidence Stress Management (CISM) Team. He received the South Dakota "Star of Life" award for exemplary service to his EMS community.

Hodgson and his family moved to Saint Paul, MN in 1999 where he worked for Regions Hospital as an EMS Clinical Supervisor for Saint Paul Fire Department. David connected with firefighters, EMTs, and Medics as an educator. He appreciated the common spark of vocation, dedication to serve, and awareness of the challenges of working the streets in EMS. He could spin a good story with subtle wit. David retired from his 40-year career in EMS in 2015.

David was an avid reader and enjoyed subjects from Minnesota history to Catholic mysticism. He collected Superman comic books. . .and tattoos. He shot thousands of photos, hunted for fossils, researched ancestry, and made it to kids' hockey games and events. David loved riding his Harley in the Hills, sweetening the ride with a stop for pie and ice cream.

Hodgson is survived by his children, Joshua Hodgson, Michelle Hodgson (died in infancy), Michaela Hodgson (Seattle), Aedan Hodgson (Chicago), his former wife, Mary Healy, and his siblings, Karen and Noel Hodgson. Thanks to Becky and David Gallati for loving care of David in their home. Services celebrating Hodgson's life will be held in Saint Paul in July, 2026 (TBD). He will be buried at Black Hills National Cemetery July 16, 2026 at 10:00 a.m.

title: Dr. Janette Kay Murray
_full_text:
July 19, 1942 - May 18, 2026

Janette K. Murray, born July 19, 1942, died peacefully at her home May 18, 2026, attended by her husband, Arthur Amiotte while under the auspice of Rapid City Monument Health Home Hospice Care.

She is survived by her daughter, Leslie Murray, of Pine, CO; stepson, Andrew Amiotte of Chadron, NE: sister, Judy Trautman and nephew Tim Trautman of Moorhead, MN niece, Tamara Trautman Bowersock (Haas, Douglas) of Wichita Falls, TX and three grand-nephews, Landon and Collin Bowersock and Tyler Trautman.

She was preceded in death by her parents, Edwin and Berna (Schwandt) Juntunen, formerly of Moorhead, MN.

She was proud of her large extended family of past and present Finnish Juntunens and German Schwandts nationwide.

Having received her Ph.D in education from University of North Dakota in 1974, she was an accomplished educator, administrator, grants writer and advocate of Midwest Native American college, higher education and the arts.

During the late 1990s, employed as a grants writer and programmer for the development department of the administration of Rapid City Regional Hospital she and local community committee members and volunteers established the very first prototype of home hospice care in Custer, S.D.

She, her husband Arthur, an artist, and community participants sponsored arts-related events and generously contributed to the funding of this pilot endeavor which eventually became the present Monument Health Hospice Program, Black Hills wide.

The family sincerely thanks the Rapid City and Custer Monument Health medical caregivers over the years, the Fountain Springs Health Facility, Rapid City, special neighbor-friend Charlotte Johnson, Custer and the Custer Chamberlain McColley Funeral Home.

At Jan's request, no formal funeral service will be held.

Visitation at the Custer Chamberlain McColley Funeral Home will be from 4-6 p.m. Thursday, May 21, 2026.

Condolences may be sent to Box 471, Custer, S.D. 57730

No memorials have been designated.

title: Nebraska becomes first state to sign off on Black Hills-NorthWestern Energy merger
description: The proposed merger of Rapid City-based Black Hills Energy with a Montana-based utility took another step forward Tuesday.
_full_text:
The proposed merger of Rapid City-based Black Hills Energy with a Montana-based utility took another step forward Tuesday.

The Nebraska Public Service Commission unanimously approved the merger between Black Hills Corp. and NorthWestern Energy at its meeting Tuesday, making Nebraska the first state to sign off on the deal. Regulators in Montana and South Dakota, as well as the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, must approve the merger before it can be finalized, according to a PSC news release.

The merger is expected to close later this year, according to a Black Hills news release.

Black Hills, which is based in Rapid City, South Dakota, announced its intent to merge with NorthWestern Energy in August to create an electric and natural gas utility company that would serve about 2.1 million customers. The two would merge stocks and have a combined market value of about $7.8 billion, with Black Hills shareholders owning 56% and NorthWestern shareholders owning 44%.

As part of the merger, a moratorium would be placed on rate increases in Nebraska until May 1, 2027, for NorthWestern customers and May 1, 2028, for Black Hills customers. The companies will also be prohibited from passing on merger transaction costs to customers, according to the PSC release.

PSC spokesperson Jason McFarley said regulators will enforce protections through ongoing regulatory oversight, including review in future rate proceedings and required reporting by the utilities.

"The commission undertook a thorough and careful review of this request to ensure it serves the public interest," said Tim Schram, chair of the Nebraska Public Service Commission. "Approval of the merger, subject to the terms of the settlement agreements, will support continued safe, reliable natural gas service for Nebraskans while maintaining responsible regulatory oversight and customer protections."

Black Hills provides services across six states — Wyoming, Colorado, Kansas, Iowa, Arkansas and Nebraska — where it serves about 350,000 Nebraska customers, including in Lincoln, Columbus and Scottsbluff. They also provide electric utilities in Wyoming, South Dakota, Montana and Colorado.

The company has more than 8,700 miles of natural gas pipeline mains, about 327,300 service lines and more than 1,300 miles of pipelines in Nebraska.

NorthWestern operates in Montana, South Dakota, Wyoming and Nebraska, with services in Grand Island, North Platte and Kearney. 

Black Hills CEO Linn Evans is expected to continue in his role until the merger, when he will retire. NorthWestern's CEO and president, Brian Bird, is expected to lead the new company, which will be based in Rapid City.

"We believe this merger will create a stronger, more resilient company, better positioned to safely, reliably and cost-effectively meet customers’ evolving energy needs," Evans said. "By joining forces, we will have the added scale to make us a financially stronger, more resilient utility better equipped to meet the challenges of a rapidly changing energy landscape."

The proposed merger comes after Black Hills implemented a rate increase due to inflation affecting the company's maintenance and operating costs. 

At a four-day hearing about the merger in front of the Montana Public Service Commission, climate action organization 350 Montana raised concerns that the deal was really about data centers in Montana. 350 Montana co-chair Jim Parker referenced quotes from NorthWestern leadership, saying the company would be in a better position to capitalize on data center interest and worried it could lead to rate increases in the state, Montana TV station KTVH reported.

Sarah Norcott, NorthWestern’s director of regulatory corporate counsel, said the hearing should not be focused on data centers.

“Do we expect the merger will allow us to effectively serve new large loads? The answer is yes,” she said. “Was it the primary reason that NorthWestern and Black Hills decided to merge? The answer is no. Questions about service to data centers will exist whether this merger is approved is not.”

Brandy Johnson, Black Hills' senior manager of public affairs, said data center development was "not the primary driver" for the merger.

The Montana PSC will hold another hearing about NorthWestern's plan for serving "large load" customers like data centers later this year.

title: Explaining his absence, Rapid City Council president says daughter was in danger in Middle East
description: Rapid City Council President Rod Pettigrew (Ward 5) reminded the public to be kind to one another as he emotionally reflected on the reason he's been absent from recent meetings — a family member was in danger due to conflict in the Middle East.
_full_text:
Rapid City Council President Rod Pettigrew (Ward 5) reminded the public to be kind to one another as he emotionally reflected on the reason he's been absent from recent meetings — a family member was in danger due to conflict in the Middle East.

 Rod Pettigrew
Rapid City Council President Rod Pettigrew addresses his recent absence at city meetings at the Monday, May 18, council meeting at City Hall. 

"I just wanted to address things here that I think are getting out of control. I've been absent the last two or three council meetings, I'm very much aware of that. I'm kind of a private guy, and I didn't share much with anybody," Pettigrew said during the Monday, May 18, City Council meeting.

He said his daughter, a teacher at New York University in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, was in imminent danger as the U.S.-Iran conflict erupted in late February. She was placed in a bomb shelter near campus before she escaped to a nearby country and later to France where Pettigrew joined her.

On Feb. 28, the United States and Israel began striking Iran in a campaign that killed the nation's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and other Iranian officials, according to Reuters. 

In retaliation, Iran began targeting U.S military assets in the region, including in the United Arab Emirates. 

"I talked to the mayor and said family first, and he agreed 100%. I talked to Vice President Stephen Tamang (Ward 1) over the situation. He said family first," Pettigrew said.

Pettigrew continued saying, "but I got some very disturbing comments, and I guess (that's) the state of our world today. One gentleman sent me an email, he said I voted for our increase in wages, and that I'm not showing up, and I'm probably sitting on the beach in Hawaii ... Another gentleman left me a nasty email saying he's going to do everything he can to make sure I don't get re-elected (Pettigrew is not running to retain his seat).”

“And today (Monday), on my drive back from Denver, I got (a call) and hung up on the guy. He says he hopes he sees my stuttering ass at tonight's council meeting," he continued.

Pettigrew was not at the July 2025 meeting where the council voted to increase their wages 67% (from $12,929.57 to $21,582.50), with Pat Roseland (Ward 5) and John Roberts (Ward 4) voting no.

"This has to stop. My daughter lives in the region over by Iran as a private citizen and bombs are flying. It took us two weeks to get her out of the country. She's a refugee. She left with a suitcase for herself with clothes and my granddaughter," Pettigrew emotionally said to the public. "As a parent, it's my job to make sure they're safe."

Pettigrew spoke to the Journal, further explaining the situation.

He told the Journal his daughter had been living in Abu Dhabi for 12 years as a teacher for the NYU campus there, when in late February she called Pettigrew alerting her of bombing at a nearby port.

"She said when she would look out her window when this all started, she could see bombs and drones hitting the port and things blowing up," Pettigrew recounted.

Thereafter, she and her family were placed in a bomb shelter for two weeks, before she decided to flee with her daughter to the nearby country of Oman, an estimated 10-hour drive.

Pettigrew said his daughter's husband is still in Abu Dhabi in fear of losing his job.

Pettigrew said he communicated with Sen. John Thune's office about help for his family, but no immediate answers to help his daughter were given.

Local businessman Hani Shafi, who is from Palestine, offered to help Pettigrew's family by suggesting safer routes to escape the region. Pettigrew said Shafi has family in Gaza that he has been helping since the conflict with Israel escalated in 2023.

Pettgirew said his daughter managed to escape the region safely on her own and is now residing in France, without a home and her husband. 

"When she was driving to Oman, she said there were missiles and bombs going over them. That's pretty intense," Pettigrew told the Journal. "I just gave her and my daughter a big hug and cried."

Pettigrew said he rented a short-term apartment to help her get settled, as she is still required to teach remotely. He said he traveled to France for two weeks to serve his daughter and granddaughter, cooking, cleaning and taking care of his granddaughter.

"I missed the Legal and Finance and Public Works meetings, but I watched them online, so I knew what was going on. Vice President Tamang was communicating with me and told me nothing's going on, to take care of myself. I communicated with the other council members. I didn't let any of my obligations as a council person, (get) neglected, but I had other things on my plate as well," Pettigrew said.

"For France, her life stuff is still tough, but I don't want to make it sound bad. She's teaching, she's got her hands full, her husband is still with Abu Dhabi ... he's hoping this war is going to end soon," Pettigrew said.

title: Man sentenced for stabbing visitor at Wounded Knee Memorial site
description: A man was sentenced to eight years and one month in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, for a June 12, 2025, stabbing at the Wounded Knee Memorial site on the Pine Ridge Reservation.
_full_text:
A man was sentenced to eight years and one month in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, for a June 12, 2025, stabbing at the Wounded Knee Memorial site on the Pine Ridge Reservation. 

Raymond Eagle Hawk, Jr., 19, appeared for his sentencing before U.S. District Court Judge Camela Theeler at the Andrew W. Bogue Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse in Rapid City on Tuesday, May 19.

According to the factual basis statement filed in the case, Eagle Hawk, who was 18 at the time, was intoxicated and panhandling at the Wounded Knee cemetery parking lot. A 71-year-old man and his wife traveled from Texas to visit the site.

At the memorial site, Eagle Hawk asked the man for money. The man gave him $10 and a bottle of water, however, Eagle Hawk demanded more and when the man refused, Eagle Hawk stabbed him in the throat with a knife. 

Assistant U.S. Attorney Kathryn Rich said the only reason the man survived that day is because he rushed to his truck and plugged a koozie into the wound and refused to lay down when people insisted he lay down. The man attempted to also get his gun from his car, afraid Eagle Hawk would attempt to hurt his wife, but his hands were too bloody to get a hold of it.

Rich said Eagle Hawk had severed the man's jugular vein, leaving the man with permanent damage in his neck area.

After the incident, Rich said Eagle Hawk fled the scene and attempted to carjack a woman nearby, but failed. 

Eagle Hawk was indicted for assault with intent to commit murder, which carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in federal prison. He pleaded guilty on Oct. 5, 2025.

Eagle Hawk's attorney, William Hustead, said this was an unusual case due to Eagle Hawk not having a violent past. Rich argued that was incorrect, stating there were two violent incidents when he was a juvenile. Theeler said one incident involved Eagle Hawk assaulting his father with a shovel.

The juvenile justice system is closed to the public, so the Journal is unable to confirm that information or look up facts of either of those cases.

Hustead highlighted how Eagle Hawk was raised in an abusive and unstable environment, and had an extensive history with substance abuse and drinking. Hustead requested the court to consider a lesser sentence so Eagle Hawk can get treatment for his addiction and maintain sobriety.

Rich said if it wasn't for the victim's quick thinking, this case would have been a first-degree murder case.

Rich said Eagle Hawk has been grasping to become an adult through violent acts for some time, highlighting his gang involvement, alleged juvenile charges and addictions. She said since being arrested, he has damaged property and has been disrespectful to jail staff. 

"Although he is young, he needs to be treated as the adult he keeps trying to be," Rich said.

Theeler said she couldn't help but describe the case as anything but "shocking and horrific" and agreed Eagle Hawk was a great concern for community safety. 

"It doesn't matter how young you are, this violent nature, especially against a stranger who tried to help you at this sacred site, is astonishing," Theeler said.

Before sentencing him, Theeler said she hopes Eagle Hawk will take this time to learn from his mistakes and make strides to improve himself for his future.

title: Black Hawk homeowners stuck in 6 years of sinkhole limbo
byline: BART PFANKUCH South Dakota News Watch
description: BLACK HAWK — Six years ago, a huge sinkhole opened in a residential neighborhood in this unincorporated town that serves largely as a bedroom community for Rapid City.
_full_text:
BLACK HAWK — Six years ago, a huge sinkhole opened in a residential neighborhood in this unincorporated town that serves largely as a bedroom community for Rapid City.

After all that time, the homeowners directly affected and those put at risk by the sinkhole have received no financial relief for their ongoing or potential losses.

 RCJ sinkhole file shows tunnel.jpg
The sinkhole that opened in the Hideaway Hills neighborhood in Black Hawk, S.D., is shown shortly after the collapse in April 2020. 

Meanwhile, the immediate area around the sinkhole in the northeast end of the Hideaway Hills subdivision — easily visible from nearby Interstate 90 — has an almost apocalyptic appearance.

Chain-link fences surround the roughly dozen properties where residents were forced to flee almost immediately in April 2020, unable to return over fears of further collapse of the underground mine upon which their houses were built.

 2026-5-12 sinkhole neighborhood sign.jpeg
The Hideaway Hills subdivision in Black Hawk, where a large sinkhole opened in 2020, has roughly 160 moderately priced homes but is at risk of further geological settling. Many of the streets in the subdivision, shown on May 12, are buckled or cracking. 

Their homes and many of their belongings have since been left to rot, and their properties are virtually worthless. Tall grass and weeds have overgrown their yards. A vehicle sits stalled in one driveway. Children's playground equipment is abandoned nearby.

Those families and about 150 other neighboring homeowners have pinned their hopes for help on a lawsuit against the state now pending before the South Dakota Supreme Court. They allege that the state, which previously owned and mined gypsum on the site, is responsible for monetary damages of more than $60 million.

"If the Supreme Court rules against us, we're pretty much done," said Carolyn Lorge, a retiree who lives with husband Mike on East Daisy Drive in Black Hawk, just two houses away from the condemnation area. "I mean, you can still move, you can still try to sell your home, but as for being compensated for your loss, you're pretty much out of luck."

 South Dakota News Watch logo
Learn more about South Dakota News Watch at sdnewswatch.org. 

The origins of the sinkhole date back to the early 1900s, when a company called Dakota Plaster dug underground mine shafts in a search for gypsum, which is used to slow the hardening of concrete.

When the state of South Dakota opened its own concrete plant in Rapid City in 1925, it began mining for gypsum, including in the future subdivision site in the 1980s. Lawyers for the state said mining was done only on the surface and that no underground mining was undertaken, though blasting did occur.

 2026-5-12 Sinkhole fencing.jpeg
Fences and signage warn people to stay away from the immediate area around the sinkhole in the Hideaway Hills subdivision in Black Hawk, S.D., shown on May 12. 

In the 1990s, the state ended mining operations, reclaimed it for grazing and sold it in 1994 to a private owner. That owner lived and ranched on the land before selling it to a developer who obtained permission from Meade County to build a subdivision in the early 2000s.

The presence of the mine was noted at several points during the land transactions, though homebuyers were not told, according to court documents. Terra Larson, a Pierre attorney representing the state in the Supreme Court case, said the developer disclosed the mine location to the home builder, "who fraudulently concealed it to all the people who would be living there."

As early as 2008, Hideaway Hills homeowners began reporting shifting in the foundation of their homes, and in April 2020, the sinkhole opened in the northeast edge of the subdivision. No one was injured.

 2026-5-12 Sinkhole neighbor.jpeg
Carolyn Lorge of Black Hawk, shown on May 12, 2026, said the sinkhole that opened near her home has not prevented her from being an active gardener and landscaper who has beautified her property despite its reduced value. 

In July 2024, a class-action lawsuit was filed against the state, arguing that the gypsum mining operation was not properly reclaimed when it sold the land. A circuit judge ruled in favor of the state in September 2024, and the homeowners appealed the case to the Supreme Court.

The homeowners argued that the state improperly filled in areas where it had mined with overly soft materials that have worn away and led to the sinkhole.

The state said it did not open any tunnels during its surface mining operations, and argues largely that the lawsuit is technically a "tort" from which the state has sovereign immunity that blocks such legal actions.

 RCJ sinkhole photo side view.jpg
In this May 2020 photo, a sinkhole on East Daisy Lane in Black Hawk exposes that part of the Hideaway Hills community was built over an abandoned gypsum mine. 

Underground mines once used to take coal or gypsum are the biggest culprits of sinkholes in the Mountain West region of the United States, said Paul Santi, a sinkhole expert and professor at the Colorado School of Mines.

Unlike South Dakota, Colorado has an extensive mine mapping service and a geological survey agency within state government, which helps avoid disasters like the one in Hideaway Hills, Santi said.

“I would think that an engineer or geologist who had access to that information could have seen this problem beforehand,” he said.

 sinkhole 5 jpeg.jpg
Exposed earth in the backyard of a Hideaway Hills property shows the bumper of a vehicle in this June 2021 photo.

title: RCAS: Central High School bomb threat came from the East Coast
description: A bomb threat called into Rapid City Central High School last week came from a group on the East Coast, Rapid City Area Schools Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson said at the Tuesday, May 19, school board meeting.
_full_text:
A bomb threat called into Rapid City Central High School last week came from a group on the East Coast, Rapid City Area Schools Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson said at the Tuesday, May 19, school board meeting.

“Central High School was the victim of a swatting situation. Swatting is a dangerous hoax in which someone makes a false emergency report, such as a bomb threat, to trigger a large law enforcement response. The goal of swatting can be to create fear, disruption, or to get publicity,” Thompson said.

On Thursday, May 14, an afternoon bomb threat called into the school prompted an evacuation of the high school and an extensive law enforcement response. The Rapid City Police Department heard word of the threat shortly before 1 p.m. that day. Students and staff evacuated the building. Local law enforcement and explosives detection K9 officers from Ellsworth Air Force Base searched the school and found no threats.

Although the call was traced back to the East Coast, Thompson said, “that does not in any way diminish the disruption or the stress that it caused in the moment. I am very grateful for the quick action that was taken by our staff, our administration, our SROs (School Resource Officers) as well as first responders, such as the fire department and the police department.”

Thompson said the event reinforced the importance of having strong safety protocols in place, practicing those procedures on a regular basis and having a strong partnership with law enforcement.

Board member Jamie Clapham said she is impressed and pleased with law enforcement and administration.

“I don't think it probably could have gone smoother. The fact, honestly, that I did not get a lot of extra calls tells me that people were informed,” she said. “Obviously, it's not an ideal situation, but I think it very much showed the way our staff works as a team, and that you (Thompson) led with calm, and that everybody else followed, and so it worked like it was supposed to.”

The threat came exactly two weeks after an April 30 bomb threat at Douglas High School prompted an evacuation. Law enforcement determined it was a hoax.

Just two days before the Douglas threat, two north Rapid City elementary schools were briefly placed on secure status after a report of a man in the neighborhood with a gun. The man was arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm with a prior felony drug conviction and receiving stolen property.

The Rapid City Police Department said they cannot confirm the information that the threat came from the East Coast or comment further on the case, but that the FBI is investigating the incident. An FBI representative told the Journal the FBI received information from Rapid City police about a bomb threat they determined was a hoax.

“The threat appears to be part of a disturbing trend of similar hoax incidents happening around the country,” the FBI said in an email response. “Knowingly providing false information to emergency services about a threat to life is a crime under state and federal law. It drains public safety resources, wastes taxpayer money, and, most importantly, puts innocent people at risk. The FBI takes these incidents seriously and will refer offenders for prosecution when appropriate. If anyone has information about this or other similar incidents, they should report it to tips.fbi.gov or 800-CALL-FBI.”

The representative declined to comment on whether the threat originated from the East Coast, stating, “By longstanding Department of Justice policy, I am unable to offer further comment on matters which may be under investigation.”

title: Man arrested after allegedly throwing rock through window of Rapid City business
description: A Rapid City man with a history of misdemeanor damage to property was arrested on felony vandalism after allegedly throwing a rock through a glass door of BreakRoom Billiards and Darts on Monday, May 18.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man with a history of misdemeanor damage to property was arrested on felony vandalism after allegedly throwing a rock through a glass door of BreakRoom Billiards and Darts on Monday, May 18.

According to the Rapid City Police Department, 34-year-old Wade Bull Bear “engaged in a disturbance” with another man outside the building when they arrived. Police detained Bull Bear. After talking to witnesses, police determined he was the one who through a rock through the glass door, shattering it.

In 2022, Bull Bear was convicted of misdemeanor intentional damage to property valued between $400 and $1,000. He pleaded guilty and a judge sentenced him to 30 days in jail, all suspended. In 2023, Bull Bear was once again convicted of misdemeanor intentional damage to property, with the property valued at $400 or less. He received a 30-day suspended jail sentence in that case as well.

From the BreakRoom incident, Bull Bear faces a Class 5 felony of intentional damage to property valued between $2,500 and $5,000. The maximum penalty is up to five years in prison and up to a $10,000 fine.

The Pennington County Jail roster does not list Bull Bear. Court records show he appeared in court on Tuesday, May 19. No bond is listed.

title: Rapid City tourism in 2025 brought in $776.2 million
description: Visit Rapid City CEO Ally Formanek said "2025 was a record year for tourism in Rapid City" during a recent presentation.
_full_text:
Visit Rapid City CEO Ally Formanek said "2025 was a record year for tourism in Rapid City" during a recent presentation.

Formanek highlighted key points from the organization's 2025 Tourism Economic Impact Report during a presentation to the Rapid City Council during its meeting on Monday, May 18. She noted 3.9 million visitors came to Rapid City and spent $776.2 million in sales revenue.

The study was produced by Tourism Economics, a business that provides economic data on popular tourism destinations, Formanek said. No action was taken at the meeting as this was a presentation-only item on the agenda.

Visit Rapid City is the official Destination Marketing Organization for Rapid City, aimed with the mission of bolstering the tourism industry in the area.

According to the report, 2025 marked a 1.3% increase in annual visitors, with 3.93 million visiting, compared to the 2024 total of 3.87 million.

Formanek said 2025 was an impactful year, as it matched the post-pandemic numbers of 3.93 million visitors in 2021.

"We're building on a strong post-pandemic recovery, and 2025 was no different," Formanek said.

 City Council
Rapid City Council members listen as Visit Rapid City CEO Ally Formanek presented during the Monday, May 18, meeting. 

According to the presentation, visitor spending totaled $776.2 million, with $527 million contributing directly to local businesses in the food, lodging and recreation industries. A 2.9% increase to 2024's $513 million.

This supported 7,704 tourism jobs, meaning one in 10 jobs in Rapid City is tied to a visitor activity either directly or indirectly, Formanek said.

She said the tax revenue generated totaled $117.3 million, which contributed $61.8 million to federal taxes, $25.4 million to state taxes and $30.1 million to local taxes.

"(This) is sales tax, property tax and other local government revenue. Put in a different way, each Rapid City household would need to pay an additional $1,700 in taxes to replace the revenue that our visitors bring into Rapid City. Our visitors are in fact subsidizing some of our city services for our residents here, roads, parks, infrastructure," Formanek said.

She continued, "Tourism dollars help get those things done, and when this council invests in tourism, you're also protecting the revenue streaming that offsets the tax burden on your constituents."

 Ally Formanek
Visit Rapid City Ally Formanek CEO presented a 2025 tourism report to the Rapid City Council during its meeting on Monday, May 18, at City Hall. 

Councilman Bill Evans (Ward 2) asked how the data was quantified and whether the city of Box Elder has influenced tourists away from Rapid City.

Formanek said the data was quantified in more than 10 different data sources that Tourism Economics uses.

According to data shared by Visit Rapid City, Tourism Economics uses a compilation of visitor statistics, including industry data, government data, visitor spending by category and economic impact modeling.

She also said yes about Box Elder taking some tourism dollars away, but they are trying to continue to get visitors to stay and spend in Rapid City.

Formanke said for 2026, which marks the celebration of the country's founding 250 years ago on July 4, she expects a record-breaking turnout.

"Rapid City is a very Americana iconic destination, so 2026 we think it's going to be a banner year for tourism. We saw April numbers looking positive already, so we're, we're hoping it's going to be a very busy summer for us.," Formanek told the Journal.

No other comments were made at the meeting.

title: Eagle Butte man sentenced for threatening federal official
description: U.S. District Judge Eric C. Schulte has sentenced an Eagle Butte man after his conviction for threatening a federal official.
_full_text:
U.S. District Judge Eric C. Schulte has sentenced an Eagle Butte man after his conviction for threatening a federal official. 

Joseph Lafferty, 68, was sentenced to four years of probation and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for South Dakota.

A grand jury indicted Lafferty in August 2025. A jury convicted the man following a trial in federal district court in January 2026.

According to the U.S. Attorney's Office:

The evidence presented at trial established that on July 21, 2025, Lafferty threatened to get his gun and kill a federal official employed by Indian Health Service, an agency of the United States Department of Health and Human Services. The defendant made the threat in Eagle Butte, in the Cheyenne River Sioux Indian Reservation.

This case was investigated by the FBI and Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services. Assistant U.S. Attorney Wayne Venhuizen prosecuted the case.

The sentencing took place on April 20, 2026.

title: YMCA announces Summer Feeding Program sites and times
description: The Rapid City YMCA has announced its Summer Feeding Program meal site locations for 2026.
_full_text:
The Rapid City YMCA has announced its Summer Feeding Program meal site locations for 2026.

Any child aged 18 and under (and their adult caregiver) will be provided a complimentary meal for breakfast and lunch. The program runs Monday-Friday from June 1 – August 7 at the Y Courtyard Café and Main Street Square, downtown Rapid City. Meals are served on-site, and a seating area is provided. The YMCA will also provide meal prep box distribution at the Liberty Center YMCA in Box Elder 2 days per week. The YMCA is an equal opportunity provider, and summer serving times and locations are as follows:

Rapid City Y Café – 815 Kansas City Street (age 18 & under/adult caregiver)

Breakfast Monday-Friday: 7:45AM-8:45AM (June 1 – August 7)

Lunch Monday-Friday: 11:45AM-1PM (June 1 – August 7)

Main Street Square – 512 Main Street, Downtown Rapid City (age 18 & under/adult caregiver)

Lunch Monday-Friday: 11:45AM-1:30PM (June 1 – August 7)

Liberty Center YMCA – 401 Main Street, Box Elder (Families with children age 18 & under)

Meal Prep Boxes available Tuesday and Friday: 3PM - 5PM (June 1 – August 7)

 2026 Summer Food Program Facebook-X 940x788x2 - 2

“The Y Summer Feeding Program provides any child aged 18 or under with a free, healthy meal option in an enriching environment over the summer months,” James Jackson, YMCA of the Black Hills Food Service Director states. “Thanks to the generosity of the Black Hills Area Community Foundation, this year we are also able to provide meals for a child’s adult caregiver. This program helps strengthen our community by improving the health and well-being of people of all ages.”

According to Feeding South Dakota in 2025, 12.1% of residents, or 1 in 9 Adults and 1 in 6 Children in South Dakota, struggled with food insecurity - meaning they did not have enough food at times to live a healthy, active and full life. In addition, approximately 34,000 residents in our area with low income live in a “food desert” – meaning they have limited access to grocery stores, often living over half a mile from a store location. The YMCA is part of the Friends of Food Security Group facilitated by the Black Hills Area Community Foundation, where members focus on identifying needs and developing solutions to address food insecurity together.

Questions? Please contact the Y at 605-718-9622, via email to events@rcymca.org or visit https://ymcabh.org/food-program/

title: Craven Canyon project opponent files federal lawsuit, uranium drilling hearing paused
description: The status of a hearing on an exploratory uranium drilling permit was left uncertain Wednesday, May 20, after a state board adjourned until further notice, following a private session to discuss legal matters.
_full_text:
The status of a hearing on an exploratory uranium drilling permit was left uncertain Wednesday, May 20, after a state board adjourned until further notice, following a private session to discuss legal matters.

The permit application is from Clean Nuclear Energy Corporation, which is seeking to drill dozens of holes up to 700 feet deep on state land. The proposed site is near the rim of Craven Canyon in South Dakota’s southern Black Hills.

Dozens of people and some organizations have raised formal complaints about the project to the Board of Minerals and Environment, which will decide on the permit. Opponents have said the drilling could disturb ancient Native American petroglyphs on the canyon’s walls, disrupt Lakota ceremonies and potentially contaminate groundwater, among other concerns.

On Monday, the board started a hearing in Hot Springs on the permit application. The hearing was scheduled to continue through Friday.

On Wednesday, the third day of the hearing, project opponent Elizabeth Lone Eagle filed a federal lawsuit against the board, the state’s Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources, Clean Nuclear Energy and state employees involved in evaluating the permit application, alleging violations of due process. Lone Eagle filed the lawsuit herself, without representation by an attorney.

 052026-nws-sl-mining-p2.jpg
A view of Craven Canyon in the southern Black Hills. 

Lone Eagle, along with six other people, including five described as Lakota first-language speakers, are listed as plaintiffs in the suit. The suit alleges “systematic, ongoing, and deliberate denial of meaningful participation to Lakota first-language speaking” project opponents.

Lakota is spoken by western South Dakota tribes, which once controlled the Black Hills as part of the Great Sioux Reservation. The board agreed prior to the hearing that the state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources would provide a Lakota interpreter for the proceedings. The department failed to provide an interpreter on Monday, but provided interpreters Tuesday. At times on Tuesday, project opponents objected from seats in the audience when parts of the hearing proceeded without interpretation.

The lawsuit also alleges that a “significant multi-jurisdictional law enforcement presence” creates an “atmosphere of intimidation” at the hearing.

The board did not provide a date to resume the hearing, which was being held at the Mueller Civic Center in Hot Springs, a little more than 20 miles from the proposed drill site. Several project opponents who’d been attending the hearing told South Dakota Searchlight on Wednesday evening that they were going home to await a further announcement.

Neither the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources nor Clean Nuclear Energy immediately responded to Searchlight’s requests for further information.

title: Rapid City Council Q&A with Ward 3 candidate Andrea Schaefer
description: Name, age, occupation:
_full_text:
Name, age, occupation:

Andrea Schaefer, 49, Self-Employed

Why are you running?

I am a longtime resident of Rapid City and the Black Hills, a small business owner for 20 years and a mother of a freshman at Stevens. I have long wanted to see representation on the Rapid City Council of everyday locals like me. As former owner of Barefoot Dance Studio, 2007-2023, and now a downtown business owner, I am connected to the community in a unique way. Not only in the hundreds and hundreds of children that I have taught, but small business ownership has connected me to so many other small business owners. We need each other to succeed. The relationships between us are important, and I hear their needs in a real way.

 2SGE3583.jpg
Andrea Schaefer 

What are the top three issues Rapid City faces that you would work to address on the council? Is there anything specific to your ward?

Affordability is the number one topic discussed during my door-knocking in Ward 3. While the council's influence is limited by the legislature, there are opportunities for negotiation that can lead to positive change. Supporting regulatory and zoning ordinances that benefit low-income families is a crucial first step. I will prioritize encouraging infill development to revitalize areas of town, bringing in tax revenue and jobs for current residents and creating new activity centers to improve overall quality of life. This includes downtown, the area east of Fifth Street, The Uptown Mall area, and the East New York Street area, among others.

I will work to make sure that data centers stay out of Rapid City and the Black Hills until we have answers to all of our myriad of concerns. The moratorium bills that did not pass at the state level shouldn't give Rapid City the green light. I would propose a similar measure at the city level so that all parties can come to the table, the community can be informed and heard, and any and all safeguards can be thought out. Although some may rationalize these projects based on revenue opportunity, there are so many other factors to consider and standards to set. There are different kinds of data centers with different levels of concerns, and although the one that has been approved already is argued to be less evasive, I'm not convinced that we are prepared for every outcome whether that be power outages, antiquated equipment or extreme weather events that put us in harm's way.

 Rapid City Christian School

Transparency is an overused word right now, so I've given considerable thought to what it looks like in a realistic and effective way. I believe it starts with my personal accountability, acknowledging that I don't have all the answers. I believe this job requires me to find them by being consistently available to my constituents, listening to their concerns, and going directly to the source of those who are knowledgeable. I will ensure that what I learn is shared back with the community, and then I will listen again. I believe it's the responsibility of leadership to create an informed community. An informed community fosters trust, trust creates participation, which drives positive progress that improves our lives. I will hold regular office hours at coffee shops or the library so that real conversations can inform my decisions.

What approach to Tax Increment Financing would you bring to the council?

I am excited to be a voice on the Rapid City Council that has high standards for any new development and especially TIF development. If incoming contracts are not serving Rapid City at a high standard, I will champion negotiations that push for more. Transportation, police/fire services paid for and immediate housing needs considered should be non-negotiable. I believe we can offer incentives or streamlined permitting to work with developers to get more of what's good for the most people in Rapid City.

How should the city approach growth?

Growth should be a practice of balance. Balancing new development with effective infill development will be a top priority for me. I will also focus on balancing tax revenue with the quality of life that new projects bring to town, which is often difficult to quantify but can be gauged through conversations with constituents and by voting in line with community desires. As a small business owner, I am concerned about the balance between supporting local businesses and incentivizing outside interests, and I am committed to being a reasonable and balanced voice on these issues. I also intend to work on balancing the drive towards tourist dollars with investment in year-round concerns.

What is working and what needs to be fixed in the city’s approach to homeless people?

Many things are working! There are extraordinary people working for extraordinary non-profits, big and small. Cornerstone, One Heart, Care Campus, Complete Health and so many more organizations are doing the work but they are fighting for funding and community engagement to keep up the good work. A task force that brings all of these groups to the table is needed. A task force would facilitate broader conversations that can make the gaps in services more identifiable. When the gaps are identified we can begin conversations about how to fill them and relieve the pressures on existing organizations to take on more than they are designed for. We have so many people in this town that truly care and have real world solutions. They need to be heard and they need to be funded.

What can the city do to make living in Rapid City more affordable?

Beyond what I already discussed above, I think that diverse representation on the Rapid City Council gives us the best chance at making sure that no one is left behind. Ensuring that the community is engaged in the discourse protects us from special interests taking the lead. I have real life experience with hardship. I have real life experience of having to lean on organizations that support those in need. I know the realities of living paycheck to paycheck, choosing groceries over bills, or ignoring health concerns for fear of costs. With a little help from my community I have been able to step out of this cycle and find success and stability. These experiences will inform my decisions.

What should the city’s role be in addiction services and how should the city use opioid settlement funds toward fulfilling that role?

I have lost two siblings to addiction-related deaths. I can’t pretend to know the complexities of how our community could have helped prevent it. But I do know that there are people and organizations fighting for solutions. When this funding is released, I will listen to the professionals in the field for guidance. I will make sure I am listening to a broad number of perspectives and work with my colleagues to fund those doing the work to reach more people in need.

title: Rapid City Council Q&A with Ward 3 candidate Kevin Maher
description: Name, age, occupation
_full_text:
Name, age, occupation

Kevin Maher, 68, retired from banking.

Why are you running?

I have loved living, working, and raising my family in Rapid City, and I have always believed in giving back to the community. During my three years on the council, I have gained valuable experience serving in 12 committee and liaison roles, which has given me a strong understanding of city operations and long-term planning.

 Kevin Maher
Kevin Maher 

Rapid City continues to grow, bringing both opportunities and challenges. I want to continue working to ensure we make fact-based decisions that improve quality of life, maintain strong public safety and infrastructure, and ensure growth pays for the services and infrastructure our residents need

What are the top three issues Rapid City faces that you would work to address on the council? Is there anything specific to your ward?

Affordable housing remains a major challenge in Rapid City. We should continue supporting developers who are building workforce and affordable housing. I would also like to bring home builders and Community Planning together to identify building code or permitting issues that add unnecessary time and cost to projects.

Infrastructure and road improvements continue to be important, e specially in Ward 3. Following completion of the Sheridan Lake Road project, several major projects remain, including the Chapel Valley bridge reconstruction, Wonderland Drive, and Carriage Hills Drive improvements. These projects are essential for safety, traffic flow, and long-term growth.

Public safety and quality of life must remain priorities. We need continued support for police, fire, parks, and recreation services to keep Rapid City a safe and attractive place to live and raise a family.

What approach to Tax Increment Financing would you bring to the council?

TIFs should be used carefully and only when they provide clear public benefit and needed infrastructure improvements. It is important for council members to fully understand the financial details and long-term impacts of each project.

 Elections

Recent TIF projects have helped deliver important community investments, including a new police precinct in north Rapid and a new fire station and park development in east Rapid City. These projects help support growth while improving public safety and quality of life.

How should the city approach growth?

Rapid City should continue planning responsibly for long-term growth. The city’s Comprehensive Plan and Metropolitan Planning Organization help coordinate transportation and infrastructure planning with neighboring communities, counties, and the state.

Growth should pay for the infrastructure and services it requires, so existing residents are not unfairly burdened with additional costs.

What is working and what needs to be fixed in the city’s approach to homeless people?

The Care Campus has become an important community resource and demonstrates what can be accomplished through partnerships between the City of Rapid City, Pennington County, nonprofits, and service providers.

The Rapid City Police Department’s Quality of Life Unit and local nonprofit organizations work every day to connect people with services while also addressing public safety and neighborhood concerns. We should continue supporting programs that balance compassion, accountability, and community safety.

What can the city do to make living in Rapid City more affordable?

The city should focus on responsible spending, improving efficiency, and supporting economic growth that creates good-paying jobs. We should also continue looking for ways to modernize city operations and use technology, including AI tools where appropriate, to improve services and reduce costs.

What should the city’s role be in addiction services and how should the city use opioid settlement funds toward fulfilling that role?

South Dakota is expected to receive approximately $99 million in opioid settlement funding over several years through 2038. Rapid City and Pennington County should continue working with the local task force and community partners to ensure those funds are used effectively for opioid remediation, treatment, recovery, and prevention efforts.

Long-term treatment options remain a significant need in our community. In the meantime, funding for naloxone access, outreach, and recovery support can help save lives and connect individuals with treatment services.

title: Rapid City Council Q&A with Ward 5 candidate Pat Roseland
description: Name, age, occupation
_full_text:
Name, age, occupation

Patrick Roseland, 76, retired Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetist. U.S. Navy veteran, 22 years of service.

Why are you running?

I am running for re-election because my heart has always been about community, giving back and my love of Rapid City. I served three years on the council, attended 84 of 86 meetings, and served as Vice President. I currently serve the community on the Rapid City Zoning and Planning Commission and the Historic Preservation Commission, as well as vice chair of both Journey On and the Journey Museum. I know how the council works and I know the issues facing Ward 5. Good government starts with listening, showing up, and putting the community first. I want to continue that work.

 Pat Roseland
Pat Roseland 

What are the top three issues Rapid City faces that you would work to address on the council? Is there anything specific to your ward?

First, infrastructure. The city must provide infrastructure where we want to grow, then invite growth, not the other way around. We spend millions of dollars reacting to where developers want to build instead of leading with a plan. Infill development, where the infrastructure already exists, is key to decreasing sprawl and decreasing costs.

Second, housing. Rapid City is lacking in affordable and workforce housing. The Planning Department must work with developers, contractors, and the council to find ways to provide housing our working families can afford.

Third, public safety and quality of life. Our parks are becoming harder for residents to enjoy. Benches and tables are being removed, restrooms are closed due to vandalism and safety hazards, and businesses deal with graffiti, theft, and panhandling every day. Our police and fire departments are doing their best, but they need our full support.

In Ward 5 specifically, we have aging neighborhood streets and stormwater issues that need attention, and residents want development that fits the character of their neighborhoods.

What approach to Tax Increment Financing would you bring to the council?

TIF is a useful tool for development, but it needs to be used carefully. Every TIF proposal should show a clear public benefit, not just a private one. I want to see what jobs are being created, what infrastructure is being built, and what happens if those things do not come through. The council should look at each TIF on its own merits and not just go along with every request.

How should the city approach growth?

I would like to see responsible growth, a city where families and businesses alike would want to move to and thrive, with high-paying jobs, great schools, and a vibrant downtown. But growth has to be strategic. The city should focus on infill development first, where infrastructure already exists. When we do expand, we need infrastructure in place before the rooftops go up. Sprawl without planning just shifts the cost to taxpayers.

 Elections

The Planning Department should be streamlined so that contractors and developers get timely feedback instead of waiting months for answers. Growth should enhance what we have, not overwhelm it.

What is working and what needs to be fixed in the city's approach to homeless people?

Rapid City is a compassionate and giving community. Organizations like One Heart and the Care Campus, along with our police and fire departments, are doing good work. Journey On provides teams that connect people with services rather than just cycling them through the system. Those partnerships are working.

 Elections

What needs to be fixed is the daily reality. The point-in-time survey may show a decrease, but our residents see something different. Parks are harder to enjoy. Businesses deal with graffiti, theft, and related problems every day. We need to ask an honest question: are we helping people or enabling them? We need programs that move people toward getting back on their feet, not just manage the problem.

What can the city do to make living in Rapid City more affordable?

The biggest thing is housing. We need more affordable and workforce housing, and that means the city has to make it easier to build. Streamlining permitting, supporting infill development, and working with builders to cut unnecessary costs all help bring prices down. The city also needs to be careful about not passing costs along to taxpayers when we let sprawl get ahead of infrastructure. Keeping tax rates competitive while funding essential services takes discipline, and it starts with smart budgeting.

What should the city's role be in addiction services and how should the city use opioid settlement funds toward fulfilling that role?

Rapid City has a huge addiction and alcohol problem that we are all aware of. We know what the issues are and we know what is needed to help, and that is programs that help in prevention and addiction treatment. What we are doing is not working, not because of a lack of trying.

Our local opioid committee is working to get the state to release the settlement funds in a large sum rather than a little at a time. A large amount of that money coming into Pennington County and Rapid City would give a real boost to the programs that are working to help those with addiction and substance abuse. The city should support treatment and prevention, work with the county and nonprofits, and make sure those dollars reach the people who need them. If there is no treatment, there is no cure.

title: Rapid City Council Q&A with Ward 5 candidate Laura Armstrong
description: Name, age, occupation:
_full_text:
Name, age, occupation:

Laura Armstrong, 56, Speech Language Pathologist, Interim Executive Director for Minneluzahan Senior Center and engaged community member.

 Laura Armstrong
Laura Armstrong 

Why are you running?

I’m running for Rapid City Council again because I believe our city deserves leadership that listens, collaborates, and puts the public first. During my time on the council, I worked to make local government more accessible through town halls, community engagement, and open dialogue. I believe people deserve a voice in the decisions that shape their neighborhoods and daily lives.

In recent years, I’ve become increasingly concerned about the direction of City Hall: less transparency, less collaboration, and too many major decisions being made without meaningful public input. We’ve seen growing frustration from residents who feel unheard on issues that directly affect their quality of life.

I’m running to bring experienced, transparent leadership back to the table. I understand how city government works; but more importantly, I understand who it works for. I believe in smart development, responsible infrastructure planning, fiscal accountability, and making sure growth benefits the entire community, not only a select few.

This campaign is not about politics or titles. It is about service. I care deeply about this city, and I’m willing to do the work again to help restore trust, strengthen communication, and ensure residents always have a seat at the table.

What are the top three issues Rapid City faces that you would work to address on the council? Is there anything specific to your ward?

The biggest issues facing Rapid City are all interconnected. I believe the top priorities are infrastructure, connected development, and accessibility/community investment.

First, infrastructure is critical. Roads, water, sewer, and landfill planning are essential to supporting both current residents and future growth.

Second, we need forward-thinking development which balances growth with transparency, neighborhood input, and responsible planning so taxpayers and residents benefit.

 Elections

Third, we need stronger investment in accessibility, education, and community spaces that improve quality of life, strengthen the workforce, and help people stay connected to their community. These issues all work together, and our city needs collaborative, long-term solutions rather than short-term fixes.

What approach to Tax Increment Financing would you bring to the council?

Tax Increment Financing can be a useful tool when used carefully and transparently, but it should not become the default solution for every development project. I believe TIFs should be focused primarily on blighted areas and infill development where investment can help revitalize existing parts of the city, strengthen infrastructure, and make better use of land and services already in place.

My approach would emphasize transparency, fiscal responsibility, and public input. Residents deserve to understand how incentives impact taxpayers, infrastructure, and long-term city priorities before decisions are made. I also believe stronger accountability measures are needed to ensure projects deliver meaningful public benefit and follow through on commitments made to the community.

How should the city approach growth?

Rapid City should approach growth in a thoughtful and sustainable way that prioritizes long term planning over rapid expansion. I believe the city should focus more on infill development and mixed use models that make better use of existing infrastructure while creating neighborhoods where people can live, work, and access services more efficiently.

Growth should also emphasize better interconnection between neighborhoods, businesses, schools, and public spaces through improved street design, walkability/bikability, and transportation planning. Public transit must be part of that conversation as well because a growing city needs accessible and reliable transportation options that serve residents of all ages, abilities and income levels. Smart growth is not just about expanding outward. It is about building a more connected, accessible, and financially sustainable community.

What is working and what needs to be fixed in the city’s approach to homeless people?

I was proud to help bring forward the concept of Journey On and serve as the inaugural president of its board of directors. That experience reinforced my belief that homelessness is a complex issue which cannot be solved through policing alone. Coming from a law enforcement family, I understand that being homeless is not a crime and should not be treated as such.

There are many factors that contribute to homelessness, including mental illness, trauma, addiction, and economic hardship. I believe models like The Care Campus and OneHeart are making a positive impact by providing coordinated services and support within our community. At the same time, more work is needed. We need stronger access to mental health care, addiction services, affordable housing, and social services, along with greater focus on education and early intervention as preventative measures. The city must continue working collaboratively with our nonprofits, healthcare providers, and schools to create compassionate, practical, and long term solutions.

What can the city do to make living in Rapid City more affordable?

To make living in Rapid City more affordable, the city should focus on attracting and supporting businesses that are willing to invest not only in our economy, but also in our residents. We need to encourage employers to provide livable wages, healthcare benefits, and provide support for challenges many working families face, including childcare and transportation.

The city should also prioritize smart growth, workforce development, and housing policies that help working families remain in the community. Affordability is not just about lowering costs. It is also about creating opportunities for people to build stable, sustainable lives here in Rapid City.

What should the city’s role be in addiction services and how should the city use opioid settlement funds toward fulfilling that role?

Rapid City has an important role in supporting addiction services by helping coordinate resources, partnering with local organizations, and investing in prevention, treatment, and recovery efforts that improve public safety and quality of life. Addiction impacts families, neighborhoods, healthcare systems, law enforcement, and businesses, so it requires a collaborative community response.

I believe opioid settlement funds should be used strategically for long term solutions rather than short term gaps. That includes expanding access to mental health care, addiction treatment, recovery programs, transitional housing, and early intervention services. Funds should also support education, prevention efforts, and programs that help individuals reconnect with employment, transportation, and stable housing. I also believe accountability and transparency are critical. Residents deserve to know how these funds are being spent and whether the investments are producing measurable outcomes for the community.

title: This fashion-forward new footwear brand is trending
byline: Sponsored content by Karin Dawsinna, Brand Ave. Studios contributing writer
description: When Kelley Powell Williamson envisioned her debut footwear collection, she set out with a clear intention: to create shoes that felt elevated, fashion-forward and aligned with the way modern women truly want to dress, without sacrificing ease of wear.
_full_text:
Kelley Kouture Footwear - Karma Color Shot.png

When Kelley Powell Williamson envisioned her debut footwear collection, she set out with a clear intention: to create shoes that felt elevated, fashion-forward and aligned with the way modern women truly want to dress, without sacrificing ease of wear. 

With Kelley Kouture, she has done exactly that. 

Officially launched in spring 2026, the Richmond, Virginia–based brand introduces a refined new perspective in luxury footwear. Crafted in Italy and available nationwide through kelleykouture.com, the collection blends directional design with thoughtful construction, offering women shoes that feel as exceptional as they look. 

Williamson reinterprets key runway influences seen throughout Milan and Paris with a more wearable, enduring approach. Architectural heels, sculptural silhouettes, rich textures and expressive colorways define the collection, yet every detail is designed with movement, balance and versatility in mind.  

Central to the brand is the proprietary “K Heel,” a signature two-piece sculptural heel developed to bring greater stability and fluidity to the wearer while maintaining a striking visual identity. It reflects the philosophy behind the brand as a whole: Luxury footwear should support the woman wearing it beautifully. 

Throughout the collection, Italian craftsmanship meets intentional design. Custom lasts were developed to move more naturally with the foot, while cushioned leather insoles, supple napa leathers, plush suedes and flexible materials create a more refined wearing experience. 

 HOME-product-beauty-shot_updated-3-16-2 (1).jpg

The collection moves effortlessly between occasions and moods. The Mia ballerina flat (offered in metallic woven finishes like modern turquoise and gunmetal) captures the rise of elevated everyday dressing, while the Kismet pump in black flocked velvet over mesh delivers evening sophistication with versatility beyond formalwear. 

Elsewhere, sculpted slingbacks, soft peep-toes, sleek sandals and statement pumps balance fashion and functionality with a distinctly modern sensibility. The Cheeky sandal introduces vibrant color through scarlet red and bright yellow paired with delicate adjustable straps, while styles like the Cherish mule and Karma pump showcase the brand’s emphasis on texture, shape and rich saturated tones. 

 Beverley-Models_1920.jpg

While color and silhouette define the visual language of Kelley Kouture, restraint and proportion remain equally important. Williamson’s designs embrace clean lines and thoughtful architecture over excess, reflecting a broader shift in luxury fashion toward pieces that feel modern, intentional and enduring rather than overtly trend-driven. 

Discover the collection at kelleykouture.com.
