title: Man sentenced to federal prison for sexually exploiting a minor
description: A 24-year-old man who persuaded a minor girl to send him explicit photos and threatened to share the images with others if she didn’t comply was sentenced at the federal courthouse in Rapid City on Tuesday, May 19, to 15 years in prison and five years of supervised release for sexual exploitation of a minor.
_full_text:
A 24-year-old man who persuaded a minor girl to send him explicit photos and threatened to share the images with others if she didn’t comply was sentenced at the federal courthouse in Rapid City on Tuesday, May 19, to 15 years in prison and five years of supervised release for sexual exploitation of a minor.

Deshawn Pourier pleaded guilty to the charge on Feb. 11. He initially faced several other charges — receipt of child pornography, possession of child pornography and distribution of child pornography. The government dismissed those charges as part of a plea deal.

A document filed in the case that Pourier, the government and his defense attorney signed established the facts to support Pourier’s guilty plea. In the document, written in Pourier’s point-of-view, he admitted to creating a fake Facebook account to obtain and collect pornographic images of minor girls. He persuaded the victim in the case to send him naked images, despite him knowing she was a minor. Initially, Pourier pretended to be another female.

“I then repeatedly messaged (her) and told her to send me more nude images, or else I would expose her by showing others the pornographic images she had already sent me,” the document reads, adding Pourier would instruct the girl how to pose and make her retake photos if he “did not like the resulting images.”

He used the account between June 1, 2022 and January 23, 2025, the date he was arrested and booked in the Pennington County Jail on a federal warrant. Pourier also contacted and exploited the girl over Snapchat.

Law enforcement discovered hundreds of images of the girl on Pourier’s digital accounts.

Pourier admitted, “I persuaded (her) to engage in sexually explicit conduct for the purpose of producing visual depictions of such conduct. I did so knowingly and willfully.”

The case landed in federal court because the social media interactions constituted interstate commerce.

title: Rapid City Fire Department begins annual Fill the Boot drive before Memorial Weekend
description: Usually fighting against fire and smoke to keep the community safe, Rapid City Fire Department members are strapping their boots to help in a different way. The department's annual "Fill the Boot" fundraising drive to support the Muscular Dystrophy Association began on Wednesday, May 20 just before Memorial Weekend.
_full_text:
Usually fighting against fire and smoke to keep the community safe, Rapid City Fire Department members are strapping their boots to help in a different way. The department's annual "Fill the Boot" fundraising drive to support the Muscular Dystrophy Association began on Wednesday, May 20 just before Memorial Weekend.

"This helps raise money for the families that are affected here in South Dakota. As well as help with the research around the country," Rapid City Fire Department Firefighter Paramedic and IAFF Local 1040 President Jonny Knutson said.

 Firetruck at Safeway
Firefighters will be present with boots ready for donations on May 21 and May 22 from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. and 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. 

Firefighters will be present with boots ready for donations on Thursday, May 21, and Friday, May 22, from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. and 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. at Walmart on North Lacrosse Street, Walmart on Stumer Road, Family Fare on East Saint Patrick Street, Family Fare at Baken Park, Safeway on Mountain View Road and Sam's Club on Eglin Street. 

The effort is part of a 70-year tradition by the International Association of Fire Fighters, which has successfully raised funds to help advance research, care and advocacy for families affected by muscular dystrophy, ALS and related neuromuscular diseases.

"We've been doing it for decades here in Rapid City and it's really a great cause," Knutson said. 

 Woman donates money to the cause
A woman with a grocery cart walked up to one of the firefighters to donate some money for the cause while shopping at Safeway on Wednesday, May 20, in Rapid City. 

Last year, the Rapid City Fire Department collected more than $47,000 for MDA in just three days. In 2024, they raised more than $54,000, in 2023 it was $60,000 and 2022 was a record-breaking year with $67,000 donated. All of the money donated goes to the Muscular Dystrophy Association. 

"We're one of the top earners in our district, which is the Dakotas, Minnesota and Wisconsin. We're usually in the top five," Knutson said. "Great support from the community and I know the families that this helps really appreciates it." 

Residents can also contribute online at https://filltheboot.donordrive.com/team/rapidcityfire.

title: Larry A. Weitzenkamp Ph.D./M.D.
description: October 28, 1940 - May 15, 2026
_full_text:
October 28, 1940 - May 15, 2026

RAPID CITY - Larry A. Weitzenkamp Ph.D./M.D., 85, of Rapid City, South Dakota passed away May 15, 2026, at West Hills Village in Rapid City.

Larry was born October 28, 1940 in Craig, Nebraska on a farm to Alvin and Lily Weitzenkamp but grew up in West Point, Nebraska. In high school he was involved in FFA and played the piccolo. After graduating from high school, he went on to University of Nebraska, where he majored in electrical engineering. After undergraduate and graduate work there he received a Ph.D. He served as assistant professor of electrical engineering at South Dakota School of Mines and Technology for five years.

On April 10, 1966, he was united in marriage to Carol Towne. To this union, three children were born: David, Mark, and Janet. In 1973, he attended medical school at University of South Dakota under an Air Force scholarship, and was a member of the first four-year class to graduate from the school in 1977.

Larry took his family practice residency training for three years at Carswell Air Base in Texas, after which he spent four more years in the Air Force as a flight surgeon and family physician. During that time he had the opportunity to live in Germany for three years as a flight surgeon for an F15 Squadron, and spent his last year of active duty at Ellsworth Air Force Base. Larry and Carol separated in 1991.

Larry began private practice in Rapid City. He moved to Martin, South Dakota, seven years later in April 1991. Audrey White joined his life in October 1993 and they moved back to Rapid City in 2000. He spent five years working at Maniilaq Health Center in Kotzebue, Alaska before returning to Rapid City in 2009 and retiring in 2011.

Larry and Audrey enjoyed traveling around the country and off the beaten path on road trips. They often visited family in Rapid City, Denver, Colorado, and Seattle, Washington, and every corner of the country including the Redwood National Park in California, Everglades National Park in Florida, and more.

Another particular interest of Larry was in Earth Watch research projects. He joined a group for three weeks of research on a volcano in far east Russia, two weeks of research on glaciers in the Himalayas, as well as others in Norway, India, and more. Together, Larry and Audrey have taken several road scholar trips.

Larry was known by loved ones as quiet, always thinking, kind, and always preparing for the opportune moment to joke. He enjoyed watching NASCAR, the Nebraska Huskers, and hockey, taking skiing trips, and recounting stories of his many life experiences. Around friends in West Hills Village, he was also known as a puzzlemaster and often helped others. To Audrey, Larry was known as a gentle, thoughtful partner, eager to go on new adventures. Each night, they fell asleep holding hands.

He is survived by his life partner of 33 years, Audrey White; brother Roger (Diane) Weitzenkamp, sisters Dorothy (Frank) Bay and Leta Searcy; sons David and Mark Weitzenkamp, daughter Janet (David) Grundstrom; grandsons Michael (Shaina) Grundstrom and Dylan (Bellamy) Grundstrom; great grandson Theodore Grundstrom; along with numerous cousins.

In lieu of flowers memorial donations may be given to the University of South Dakota School of Medicine.

His Celebration of Life Visitation will be held between 4:00 to 6:00 PM Wednesday, May 27th at Osheim & Schmidt Funeral Home. There will be a Private-Family Only Burial Service at a future date.

title: Paul James
description: November 16, 1951 - May 19, 2026
_full_text:
November 16, 1951 - May 19, 2026

Paul Eugene James, 74, of Rapid City, South Dakota, passed away peacefully at his home on May 19, 2026, surrounded by his loving family following a recent diagnosis of liver cancer.

Paul was born on November 16, 1951, in South Bend, Indiana, to Herbert and Freida (Waggoner) James. He later lived in Indianapolis and graduated from Lawrence Central High School in 1969. After briefly attending college, he enlisted in the United States Air Force on May 14, 1970.

During a distinguished 22-year Air Force career, Paul worked primarily on B-52 and B-1 aircraft, serving as a Line Chief and later Superintendent of Flight Safety. He retired from Ellsworth Air Force Base on September 30, 1992, with the rank of Master Sergeant. His military decorations included the Meritorious Service Medal, Air Force Commendation Medal, and Air Force Achievement Medal.

Following his military retirement, Paul attended National American University, earning a Bachelor of Science degree in Computer Information Systems in 1998. He then worked as a Network Administrator for the Civil Engineer Squadron until retiring in 2004.

Paul married Cynthia Morgan on April 4, 1971, and together they welcomed two sons, Robert and Daniel. The couple later divorced. He married Alice Karas on March 10, 1997. During retirement, Paul and Alice enjoyed spending winters in Arizona until her passing in 2015. Paul continued to pursue his love of travel, visiting family throughout the country and around the world. His final trip was during Christmas 2025, when he spent the holidays with family in Louisiana.

Paul enjoyed hunting, computers, technology, all things aviation related, and learning how things worked. Known for his intelligence and curiosity, he was often the person family members called when something needed to be fixed. More than anything, he cherished time spent with family. Whether helping his son Dan with his race car, repairing electronics, or teaching a grandchild something new, Paul found joy in sharing his time and knowledge. He especially treasured supporting his great-grandson Jesse at sporting events and activities and was immensely proud of him.

Paul was preceded in death by his parents, Herbert and Freida James; his former wife and mother of his children, Cynthia "Cindy" James; and his second wife, Alice James.

He is survived by his sons, Robert James (Nikki) of Okmulgee, Oklahoma, and Daniel James (Debra) of Kaiserslautern, Germany; stepson Joe Karas (Rose); stepdaughter Susan Peterson (Dave); sister Diana James of Fishers, Indiana; brother Tim James (Sherry)of Indiana; and sister Sue Richards Walker of Lebanon, Indiana. He is also survived by grandchildren Bailey James, Rebecca Brimmer (Richard), Alyssa Rolen (Austin), Kyle James (Tuesday), Taylor James, Joshua Peterson, Avery James, Jason Karas, Aiden Peterson, Samantha James, and Olivea James; great-grandchildren Jesse James, Lydia Brimmer, Leila Brimmer, Theodore Rolen, and Anastasia James; as well as numerous nieces, nephews, cousins, extended family members, and friends.

Funeral services will be held at 12:30 p.m. on Wednesday, May 27, 2026, at Kirk Funeral Home. Visitation will be held one hour prior to the service. Interment with military honors will follow at Black Hills National Cemetery.

In lieu of flowers, the family requests memorial contributions be made in Paul's memory to the Wounded Warrior Project. Donations may be made online at Wounded Warrior Project or mailed to Dan James, 118 E. Texas St., Rapid City, SD 57701, for forwarding to the organization.

Paul will be remembered for his dedicated service to his country, his love of learning, his willingness to help others, and his unwavering devotion to his family. He will be deeply missed by all who knew and loved him.

title: Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity receives $87K grant for affordable housing
description: Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity in Rapid City has received an $87,500 grant from Federal Home Loan Bank of Des Moines and Black Hills Federal Credit Union .
_full_text:
Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity in Rapid City has received an $87,500 grant from Federal Home Loan Bank of Des Moines and Black Hills Federal Credit Union.

The funds, provided by the Member Impact Fund matching grant program, support affordable housing and community development in South Dakota, as well as Alaska, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.

“I am so grateful to Black Hills Federal Credit Union and to the Federal Home Loan Bank of Des Moines for this generous gift,” said Scott Engmann, Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity’s executive director. “We share a commitment to making a tremendous impact on the lives of homeowners. This work affects health, environmental and educational outcomes, civic and social engagement, the financial stability of Habitat families, and helps to build local economies.”

 Raising the first Wall (copy)
Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity volunteers raise the first wall of a house in this May 2021 file photo.  

In South Dakota, the income needed to purchase a median-priced home is $115,000, according to a news release from Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity. However, as of October 2025, the median income in Rapid City is $65,712, per demographic data compiled by HomeSnacks from the U.S. Census, FBI, OpenStreetMaps, and dozens of other sources.

The disparity between local home prices and income makes homeownership difficult for many citizens in the Black Hills. The $87,500 grant will help finance and build affordable single-family homes, townhomes, and fund home repairs for qualifying families.

Grant recipient organizations, including Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity, were selected based on the needs for grant funding to strengthen their ability to fulfill affordable housing or community development needs, such as job training, financial literacy, food banks and youth programs.

Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity’s vision is that everyone deserves a decent place to live. Founded in 1990, Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity has served more than 715 people through affordable homeownership and home repair.

“As a Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity Board Member, I have the privilege of witnessing the passion this organization brings to addressing the affordable housing need in our community,” said Holli Edwards, VP Marketing at BHFCU. “Their impact goes beyond providing just a home. Partner families invest time into their homes and are given the opportunity to build equity and a solid future for their families.”

FHLB Des Moines provides funding solutions to more than 1,200 members to support mortgage lending, economic development and affordable housing in the communities they serve.

title: South Dakota Mines research team works with first graders to create new STEM toys
description: When it comes to designing new, effective learning tools, the best ideas come directly from the people who will use them most – especially when those users are curious, candid and creative first graders.
_full_text:
When it comes to designing new, effective learning tools, the best ideas come directly from the people who will use them most – especially when those users are curious, candid and creative first graders.

A new initiative at South Dakota Mines is reimagining how young children learn engineering by bringing elementary students, families, teachers and university faculty and students together to design mechanical engineering toys from the ground up.

 Wilson Elementary - Playtime Observation
A new initiative at South Dakota Mines is reimagining how young children learn engineering by bringing elementary students, families, teachers and university faculty and students together to design mechanical engineering toys from the ground up. 

The project “Designing Engineering Toys Through School-University Co-Design: A Pilot for Inclusive Learning,” partners researchers and engineering students at Mines with first-grade teacher Ashley Whitehead and her students at Wilson Elementary School to create hands-on toys that introduce foundational engineering concepts through play.

The idea came from Cristian Vargas Ordóñez, Ph.D., assistant professor in Mines’ Leslie A. Rose Department of Mechanical Engineering, and is funded through a National Science Foundation E-CORE Grant led by Black Hills State University. The effort aims to make engineering education more accessible, engaging and culturally responsive for young learners while strengthening connections between local schools and higher education.

 Wilson Elementary - Playtime Observation
The project “Designing Engineering Toys Through School-University Co-Design: A Pilot for Inclusive Learning,” partners researchers and engineering students at Mines with first-grade teacher Ashley Whitehead and her students at Wilson Elementary School to create hands-on toys that introduce foundational engineering concepts through play. 

Oftentimes, toys and other products are designed with a “top-down” approach, with the expert deciding what and how something needs to be created. “My philosophy is more the co-design way where all those who are going to be impacted or affected are involved in the process – asking everyone their perspective on what they want to bring to the conversation,” Vargas said. “With this, kids will be the final users, why not get them involved in the process?”

Vargas and his graduate and undergraduate students worked closely with Whitehead and her first-grade class, visiting several times throughout the semester to better understand how young children interact with STEM toys. The project began with the Mines team bringing two-liter bottle rockets for the students to experiment with.

During later visits, the researchers asked the children what they liked and disliked about different toys before setting up cameras in the classroom to observe students playing with a variety of STEM toys featuring mechanical engineering concepts. The team also gathered input from parents about the types of toys their children enjoy, what they avoid and what families hope children learn through play.

 Wilson Elementary - Playtime Observation
Vargas and his graduate and undergraduate students worked closely with Whitehead and her first-grade class, visiting several times throughout the semester to better understand how young children interact with STEM toys. 

Ayomide Oladele, a mechanical engineering graduate student at Mines, said his goal with the project is to help make engineering more exciting and approachable for young learners. “As a young kid growing up in Nigeria, when you heard engineering, it was very technical,” he said. “My point is to make engineering more accessible and one way to do this is to make true toys. If kids are interacting with them through play, they are gathering some knowledge.”

Oladele said his favorite part of the project has been watching the students simply play. “It was fun to see the kids’ reaction to the toys we brought in, what they played with and what they did with the toy,” he said. “They are giving us insights and ideas we never thought of originally. This is all helping us make not just a toy, but a meaningful toy that helps kids learn something.”

 Wilson Elementary - Playtime Observation
The researchers asked the children what they liked and disliked about different toys before setting up cameras in the classroom to observe students playing with a variety of STEM toys featuring mechanical engineering concepts. 

Whitehead said her students loved serving as the focus group for the pilot project and were constantly asking when the Mines team would return. The collaboration also aligned perfectly with her spring curriculum, which explored inventions and included reading about a toy inventor.

Soon, her first graders will be able to say they helped in creating a new toy.

Using insights gathered from classroom video footage, parent feedback, students’ drawings and simple conversation with the students, the Mines team will spend the summer designing and building two new interactive toys centered on mechanical engineering concepts.

Scott Bormann and Dale Burks, both freshman mechanical engineering majors at Mines, are charged with creating the toys - one built from wood and another created through 3D printing.

 Wilson Elementary - Playtime Observation
The idea came from Cristian Vargas Ordóñez, Ph.D., assistant professor in Mines’ Leslie A. Rose Department of Mechanical Engineering, and is funded through a National Science Foundation E-CORE Grant led by Black Hills State University. 

The completed toys will then be brought back to Whitehead’s new class of first graders to test out. The toys will also be shared with their co-designing second graders.

“It’s really neat that they get to make a tangible toy that they helped design and create and get to play with,” she said.

The completed toys, along with open-access lesson plans and teacher guides, will remain with the classroom for continued use and future student learning.

Vargas said the long-term goal is to establish a scalable model for engineering toy co-design that can support early engineering identity development and inspire more students to see themselves as future engineers.

title: Black Hills State wins national awards for website, enrollment campaign
description: Black Hills State University earned national recognition in the 2025 Collegiate Advertising Awards (CAA), receiving a Gold Award for the redesign of the BHSU website and a Silver Award for its “Not Too Far from Close to Home” enrollment campaign. This recognition marks BHSU’s second consecutive year of national honors from the CAA program.
_full_text:
Black Hills State University earned national recognition in the 2025 Collegiate Advertising Awards (CAA), receiving a Gold Award for the redesign of the BHSU website and a Silver Award for its “Not Too Far from Close to Home” enrollment campaign. This recognition marks BHSU’s second consecutive year of national honors from the CAA program.

The CAA is an elite program recognizing higher education organizations for excellence in communications, marketing, advertising, and promotions of their schools across the nation, BHSU said.

 BHSU website
Black Hills State University earned national recognition in the 2025 Collegiate Advertising Awards, receiving a Gold Award for the redesign of the BHSU website and a Silver Award for its “Not Too Far from Close to Home” enrollment campaign. 

BHSU’s website redesign earned a Gold Award, placing it among the top 5% of entries nationwide. The “Not Too Far from Close to Home” campaign, developed in partnership with Sioux Falls-based agency Fresh Produce, earned a Silver Award, placing it in the top 12% of entries.

“Being recognized on a national stage is a testament to the talent and creativity behind our work,” Becca Walters, senior director of Marketing and Communications at BHSU, said in a release. “The enrollment campaign alongside Fresh Produce and our website redesign shows how BHSU is telling its story authentically and connecting with students in compelling ways.”

The 2025 CAA program received entries from small colleges and large universities across the United States and Canada. Submissions were evaluated by a national panel of industry experts and scored on a 100-point scale. BHSU’s entries competed against similar-sized organizations in their specific groups and categories.

“National recognition like this is a proud moment for Black Hills State University and a reflection of the commitment our campus community brings to everything we do,” said BHSU President Steve Elliott. “These awards highlight not only the strong creative work, but how effectively we are sharing the BHSU story and strengthening connections with future students.”

title: Rapid City area Republican Legislature candidates talk education, property taxes, veterans
description: Several dozen people sat in for a Republican candidate forum and luncheon by the Pennington County Republican Woman at the The Park 707 Event Center, in Rapid City.
_full_text:
Several dozen people sat in for a Republican candidate forum and luncheon by the Pennington County Republican Woman at the The Park 707 Event Center, in Rapid City.

During the hour and a half event on Thursday, May 21, candidates vying to represent District 30, District 32, District 33, District 34 and District 35 discussed education funding without raising property taxes.

"Our purpose is to get Republicans elected and that's what here to do today," PCRW Interim President Lauri Davis said. 

One resident asked the candidates with prior service about a psychedelic drug called Ibogaine being used to help veterans with PTSD, the general consensus was the issue is beyond their ability to determine what medications are available through the V.A.. However, the candidates agreed that as a community we should strive to support veterans.

 Group Photo
During the hour and a half event, candidates vying to represent District 30, District 32, District 33, District 34 and District 35 discussed education funding without raising property taxes. 

Davis gave each candidate three minutes to introduce themselves, followed by a Q&A open to the audience. Afterward, residents were invited to speak to the legislative candidates. 

Meet the candidates 

South Dakota has 35 Legislature districts, with two representatives and one senator from each representing constituents at the Capitol in Pierre. Two House candidates will advance out of each political party's primaries with more than two people running.

District 30: 

Republicans Stephan Saint, Tim Goodwin and Trish Ladner are running for House District 30. District 30 includes all or portions of Custer, Fall River and Pennington counties, including Custer State Park and most of the Southern Hills.

District 32: 

Republicans Steve Duffy and Zachary Martin are running for House District 32. District 32 includes downtown Rapid City, much of north Rapid City and its southeast corner extends to Cambell Street.

District 33: 

Sandra Comer, Jeff Marlette, Phil Jensen and Curt Massie are running for House District 33. District 33 includes Silver City and Johnson Siding, along with Summerset and Black Hawk on the west side of Interstate 90, with the district boundary including land inside Pennington and some Rapid City neighborhoods.

District 34:

Becky Drury, Mike Derby and Heather Baxter are running for House District 34. District 34 includes western Rapid City and extends into rural Pennington County.

District 35: 

Dale Bartscher, Jace West, Emmett Reistroffer and Jason Fleming are running for House District 35. District 35 includes Box Elder, Rapid Valley and parts of eastern Rapid City.

Education and property tax 

The event allowed enough time for two questions to the Republican candidates, in which each candidate had an option to commit or not. Davis led the second question by asking the candidates about their thoughts on how the state can revive the education system without raising property taxes. 

 Becky Drury
Becky Drury (Republican) running for District 34 said there has been recent debates on how the education funding formula is broken and it needs tweaking, however, she said she feels we as a community has lost sight in valuing our educators and it is costing our children's education in the long run. 

Drury said there have been recent debates on how the education funding formula is broken and it needs tweaking, but said she feels as a community we've lost sight of valuing our educators and it is costing children's education in the long run. 

"We've lost some respect for that professional on the line that I think we need to glean back, but its all gonna start with us and it's gonna start with the parents," Drury said. "... We really need to focus on what we can do for the kids and what's best for them."

 Heather Baxter
Rival candidate for District 34 Heather Baxter (Republican) echoed Drury's thoughts saying "she hit the nail on the head."  

Drury said the highest priority should be giving the best resources available to the children, even it "isn't always what best for us."

Rival candidate for District 34 Heather Baxter echoed Drury's thoughts, saying "she hit the nail on the head." 

"Our funding formula is very broken and we do need to find a way to focus on our kids and the more we have educated successful kids then that means less prisons that we have to continue to build," Baxter said. 

Saint said he has no problem spending about $12,000 of his property taxes to local schools. However, said he agrees with the other candidates that it seems the community isn't doing enough for their educators and children need to learn to respect them.

"These teachers are educating our children and they have our children and teachers need to have our backing as parents so that when they're in that classroom and they have to control that classroom, we're not tying their hands with education and discipline in the classroom," Saint said. 

 Stephan Saint
District 30 candidate Stephan Saint (Republican) said he has no problem spending about $12,000 of his property taxes to local schools. however, he agrees with the other candidates that it seems the community isn't doing enough for their educators and children need to learn to respect them.  

Saint said he doesn't believe in throwing money at everything, but sees how it can be beneficial to give more money to educators so the future generation can be better supported and educated. 

None of the other candidates responded to the question.

title: Pennington County approves zoning change, will return for vote on June 16
description: The Pennington County Commission voted 3-2 to add amendments to the county's zoning ordinance that ban utility-scale wind and solar on agricultural land. The proposed changes also provide restrictions for personal-use wind and solar and ban all battery storage units.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Commission voted 3-2 to add amendments to the county's zoning ordinance that ban utility-scale wind and solar on agricultural land. The proposed changes also provide restrictions for personal-use wind and solar and ban all battery storage units.

Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voted no on the amendments to the ordinance at the commission's Tuesday, May 19, meeting.

According to Pennington County Planning Director Brittney Hand, because the county voted on substantial changes to the ordinance, the ordinance must be re-advertised in accordance with applicable public notice requirements.

The first reading will be voted on again on June 16, with a second reading scheduled for July 7.

 Ron Rossknecht
Commissioner Ron Rossknecht (District 1) voted no against restrictions for utility-scale wind and solar developments in agriculturally zoned land in Pennington County. 

The county's proposed changes to Section 317 of the county's zoning ordinance, which governs wind and solar, include regulations for pitched-roof-mounted systems.

"For all roof-mounted systems, the elevation must show the highest finished slope of the solar collector and the slope of the finished roof surface on which it is mounted ... The panels will not be extended beyond the roof ridge line and must meet Pennington County height restrictions for the zoning district," the proposed ordinance change states.

Additionally, ground-mounted systems for solar panels must not exceed 15 feet.

This comes as the public's interest on the matter led to the county forming a task force on solar and wind energy after it passed a moratorium on utility-scale wind and solar developments. The task force group researched the topic and considered future county regulations.

 Eileen Peterson
Eileen Peterson, a member of the county's task force on wind and solar, spoke to the commission on March 3, about the agricultural community and outside communities supporting rezoning changes.  

The task force members include Commissioner Jerry Derr (District 4), attorneys, an appraiser and individuals from the ranching community, local government and the energy sector.

Resident and task force member Eileen Peterson spoke to the commission, saying she had further setbacks she wanted to include on the county's amendments.

"If we're going to continue to go down the road of allowing them (battery storage units), there is a matter of setback being inadequate in more populated areas where there's potential for being close to schools and businesses and if there's a fire," Peterson said.

The county adopted all recommended changes she submitted to the county, including a property line setback to 1,000 feet and a buffer zone of 50 feet for solar panels. Wind turbines have a setback for property lines of 1.2 miles and a 50-foot buffer zone.

County staff recommended solar have a setback of 50 feet from property lines and a 25-foot buffer zone. Wind turbines were recommended to be setback at three times the height of the turbines and a buffer zone of 25 feet.

Resident John Henderson said he agreed with Peterson's setback recommendations and agreed barring utility-scale wind and solar projects on ag land is warranted. 

"The more restrictions that you put on any of this, I think, would benefit the county in the future, and certainly the residents," Henderson said.

 Jerry Derr
Commissioner Jerry Derr (District 4) voted in favor of barring utility-scale wind and solar project on agriculturally zoned land in the Pennington County Zoning Ordinance.  

Derr said, "I'm going to make a motion to approve this ordinance with the following amendments: that we adopt a setback as set by in the document that's on the agenda by Eileen Peterson, and then we put a clause in here that no battery storage is allowed for discussion."

Deb Hadcock (District 3) said, she agreed with the motion and wanted sound considerations be put into the ordinance.

Previously, on March 3, the commission laid the groundwork to ban wind and solar on agricultural land after residents on the east side of the county expressed concerns about projects near New Underwood.

The first step was an amendment to Comprehensive Plan-View to 2040, which passed with a 3-2 vote. Rossknecht and Drewes voted no. Utility-scale wind and solar systems are set to be permitted in industrial districts in the plan. 

The county's comprehensive plan is defined as a guide for government officials, residents and developers in regard to "decision-making" for current and potential future development within the county. The plan specifically provides a framework for land-use decisions, public service expansions, economic development, resource management and the general growth of the county.

The Pennington County zoning ordinance serves as a regulatory framework indicating land use and development within the county, ensuring that land is utilized in a manner that aligns with community standards and environmental considerations.

It establishes specific zoning districts and outlines permitted uses, building height restrictions and setbacks, thereby promoting orderly development and mitigating potential conflicts between different land uses.

Julian Arcoren, 37, was sentenced to time served through April 20, equal to approximately 15 months in custody, followed by three of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for South Dakota.

A federal grand jury indicted Arcoren in June 2024. He pleaded guilty on March 4.

According to the U.S. Attorney's Office:

On Jan. 3, 2024, in St. Francis, Arcoren distributed methamphetamine, a Schedule II controlled substance.

This case was investigated by Rosebud Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services. Supervisory Assistant U.S. Attorney Kirk Albertson prosecuted the case.

title: Rooting for recovery: How flowers are reshaping the Pennington County Jail through IGNITE Program
description: The gray concrete of the Pennington County Jail gives way to vibrant purples and golds as inmates plant a new garden.
_full_text:
The gray concrete of the Pennington County Jail gives way to vibrant purples and golds as inmates plant a new garden.

Inmates, through the Pennington County Sheriff's Office's IGNITE Program, started work on Friday, May 22. 

Amidst the fresh blooms, Andrew Fletcher pauses to wipe sweat from his brow, a wide smile on his lips. Dressed in a bright yellow shirt with IGNITE emblazoned across his back, Fletcher and his fellow inmates in the program aren't just turning soil, they're claiming their lives back by one step at a time. 

 Pennington County Jail gardening 4
The PCSO IGNITE Program is centered around community collaboration to help provide programs within the jail, as well as connect former inmates to job opportunities.  

"It's actually a really good program," Fletcher said. "I enjoy coming out and working with the community. It's showing me a lot of different avenues for recovery and for what I'm gonna do when I get out." 

The IGNITE Program, which began in 2024, is an initiative to provide education and job skills training to incarcerated populations at the Pennington County Jail, Western South Dakota Juvenile Services Center and Care Campus.

IGNITE (Individual Growth Naturally and Intentionally Through Education) began in Genesee County, Michigan. Sheriff Christopher R. Swanson started the program, and now the National Sheriffs' Association helps other jails replicate it.

The program was launched in South Dakota in the spring of 2023.

 Pennington County Jail gardening 7
Andrew Fletcher has been in the program for 28 days and says he's happy that there are still people who care for those who are incarcerated.  

This innovative initiative aims to offer the judicial system more flexibility in sentencing, allowing individuals initially facing 30 to 90 days in custody to maintain employment, develop valuable skills, pursue education and facilitate their entry into the workforce.

The program involves work assignments within and around city and county facilities. Successful completion of their sentences may lead to potential job offers with participating businesses.

On Friday, the sheriff's office partnered with the Rapid City Parks to get participants outside and make the city a beautiful place.

Jail corrections officer and IGNITE Coordinator Sherin Harris said the inmates are not only in charge of planting the flowers but also maintaining it through the summer. She said they're expected to be done with the project on Tuesday, May 26.

"We help them get their documents as far as IDs so they can get a job when they get out," Harris said. "We take them to different job sites two days a week, we do community service for the city two days a week, community service for the county and on the fifth day they have an education day." 

For Fletcher, he said this program has given him another chance to start anew and break the cycle.

 Pennington County Jail gardening 2
Cyril Black Spotted Horse held flowers as members of the PCSO IGNITE Program determine the best spot to put them in front of the Pennington County Jail.  

"I want to get more involved in the community. I want to get clean," Fletcher said. "A lot of us in here are recovering addicts and we're looking for a better avenue and this helps us get involved with the community and to do something with our time."

Another participant, Cyril Black Spotted Horse, echoed Fletcher's thoughts, adding how excited he was to learn new things, such as CPR (he's certified).

"It feels good preparing yourself for a brighter future," Black Spotted Horse said. "It really opened my eyes in what a sober and clean life could be."

title: Rapid City Parks crews set to plan 20,000 flowers this week
description: Rapid City Parks crews will be busy this week planting thousands of flowers in city parks and frontage areas.
_full_text:
Rapid City Parks crews will be busy this week planting thousands of flowers in city parks and frontage areas.

The parks will get a quick splash of color as the plants have been enjoying the comfy confines of the City greenhouse in recent weeks. Greenhouse specialist John Berglund and his crews have been in a holding pattern as frost and freeze conditions were evident as late as last week.

Forecasts now have Rapid City in Berglund’s "safe zone."

“It’s not unusual to be out planting the week before or after the Memorial Day holiday,” Berglund said. “Last year, we were out the week after the holiday as the threat of frost or freeze can hover around until the last half of May.

“We are ready, the flowers are ready and we’ll be busy getting everything planted.”

Crews will plant flowers in numerous areas, including Halley Park, Wilson Park, the Sunken Gardens area behind McKeague Field on Canyon Lake Drive, the William Noordermeer Formal Gardens at Sioux Park and Otto’s Corner on the northwest corner of Omaha Street and West Boulevard.

Berglund said crews will be planting numerous varieties of flowers with an emphasis this year on colors reflecting Rapid City’s celebration of the nation’s 250th birthday. He also says the popular gargantuan banana plants will be making another appearance, observing their 10th year of display in Rapid City.

As the spring and summer progress, Berglund says hail is always a concern. He keeps a number of flowers in reserve to plant and replace damaged flowers.

title: Rapid City teen sentenced for shooting at group in Scheels parking lot
description: An 18-year-old Rapid City man was sentenced to eight years in prison after firing multiple gunshots at a group of teenagers in the Scheels parking lot on March 4, 2025.
_full_text:
An 18-year-old Rapid City man was sentenced to eight years in prison after firing multiple gunshots at a group of teenagers in the Scheels parking lot on March 4, 2025. 

Connor Allen appeared for his sentencing before Presiding Circuit Judge Heidi Linngren on Friday, May 15, at the Pennington County Courthouse. Allen pleaded guilty to two counts of aggravated assault on Thursday, March 5. 

"This case involved an extremely dangerous act of violence that could have easily ended in tragedy," Pennington County Chief Deputy State's Attorney Gina Nelson said in a statement after sentencing. "While Mr. Allen's age was a factor considered during plea negotiations, accountability remained critically important given the seriousness of the offense and the risk posed to multiple victims and the community."

Allen was 17 at the time of the shooting, but his case landed in adult court because of the severity of the charges. In South Dakota, minors who are 16 or 17 and charged with severe felonies are tried in adult court automatically unless the defense requests a transfer hearing and convinces a judge it's in the public’s best interest for the case to be transferred to juvenile court.

Allen was initially indicted on four counts of attempted first-degree murder, two counts of aggravated assault and one count of discharge of a firearm from a moving vehicle. Attempted first-degree murder is a Class 2 felony, the lowest level felony that moves a juvenile case to adult court.

Through a plea agreement with the state, Allen pleaded guilty to two counts of aggravated assault. The state agreed to dismiss all other charges and recommend 25 years in prison with 15 suspended. 

In South Dakota, aggravated assault is a Class 3 felony with a maximum sentence of 15 years in prison and a $30,000 fine.

To provide factual basis for his guilty plea in March, Allen testified he saw his ex-girlfriend walk out of Scheels. and he began to get angry. That is when he decided to shoot at the group.

Police were dispatched to the area for a report of a group of people who had been shot at by a passing vehicle.

No one was injured in the incident. The person who called police said they recognized the driver, Allen, inside the vehicle when he began firing.

Police were able to associate the vehicle to an address in Box Elder. A short time later, the Box Elder Police Department located the car and Allen and detained him.

Per a Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office press release, two victims, along with the parents of another victim, addressed the court during sentencing about the lasting emotional impact the shooting has had on their lives. One victim told the court, "we could have died.”

Linngren noted that the offense was not an isolated incident, but part of what she described as a pattern of escalating violent behavior, according to the release. Linngren said Allen was on probation at the time of the shooting. Due to Allen being a juvenile before the incident, criminal records of juveniles are not public record and the Journal was unable to access this information. 

While acknowledging Allen's young age, Linngren said his actions demonstrated he posed a danger to society.

title: Two parolees arrested after Roosevelt Park gunshot call leads to foot chase
description: Two Rapid City parolees were arrested Sunday, May 24, after gunshots at Roosevelt Park Pond led to a short foot pursuit.
_full_text:
Two Rapid City parolees were arrested Sunday, May 24, after gunshots at Roosevelt Park Pond led to a short foot pursuit. 

Tommy Blue Bird, 37, and Jon Caldwell, 39, were placed under arrest on parole holds. Caldwell was also arrested on suspicion of obstruction. Police said they anticipate state and federal firearm charges are forthcoming for Blue Bird and Caldwell. As of Wednesday, May 26, court records do not show recent charges against either man.

Blue Bird was previously convicted of forgery and given a suspended sentence of three years and one month. Caldwell was previously convicted of receiving/transferring a stolen vehicle and was given a suspended sentence of five years and one month. 

Blue Bird and Caldwell’s arrests came after police were called around 7:40 a.m. on Sunday, May 24, to Roosevelt Park at 300 Omaha Street for a report of a man firing a handgun near the pond. 

Officers quickly converged on the area and located Blue Bird. Upon arrival, another man fled from police along a bike path and discarded the firearm. After a short foot pursuit, Caldwell was detained.

The firearm has since been recovered and no injuries were reported as a result of the gunfire. The investigation is still ongoing.

“This is the second incident in less than a week’s time in which Rapid City police have apprehended a parolee after they recklessly discharged a firearm within one of our city’s neighborhoods,” Rapid City Police Chief Don Hedrick said, referencing the May 19 arrest of two juveniles in Rapid City after a report of gunshots in the area of 600 Linbergh Ave.

According to police, one of the minors was on probation and the other was on parole. Police found a sawed-off shotgun in the vehicle where they found the boys. No one was injured in the incident.

Hedrick continued in his statement following the Roosevelt Park arrests, “We refuse to allow this type of dangerous behavior to become normalized, and it’s clear that work needs to continue at the state level in order to ensure the parolees released into our community by the State Department of Corrections are appropriately supervised to ensure they do not continue to create new victims as they are allowed to serve their sentences outside the penitentiary setting.

"I’m extremely thankful no one was hurt by the suspect’s dangerous actions, and for the quick response of our officers that resulted in the swift apprehension of the two men involved.”

As of Tuesday, May 26, Blue Bird and Caldwell were being held at the Pennington County Jail with no bond.

title: Rapid City police remind public about safe gun storage after Memorial Day weekend vehicle burglaries
description: The Rapid City Police Department once again reminds the public to not use their cars as gun safes after two vehicle burglaries resulted in two firearms being stolen over the Memorial Day weekend.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Police Department once again reminds the public to not use their cars as gun safes after two vehicle burglaries resulted in two firearms being stolen over the Memorial Day weekend. 

"A vehicle is not a viable gun safe. Responsible firearm ownership starts with maintaining 24/7 accountability for all owned firearms. Firearms and other valuables should not be left unattended in a vehicle," police said in a release.

On Friday, May 22, at around 7:40 a.m., police responded to a report of a vehicle burglary which took place overnight in the 800 block of N. Spruce Street.

The reporting party said their pickup had been burglarized and a loaded handgun was taken from inside the car. Police noted no signs of forced entry and the reporting party said the car was left unlocked overnight. 

On a separate call, on Saturday, May 23, at around 7:30 a.m., police responded to a vehicle burglary in the 2700 block of Oak Avenue. 

The reporting party in this incident said three of their cars were left unlocked overnight and all three were burglarized. A loaded handgun was taken from one of the cars. 

Both cases have been forwarded to the RCPD's criminal investigations division for further follow-up.

title: Rapid City police discover 4 guns, arrest a teen and two juveniles during gunshot call response
description: A Rapid City teen was arrested on Monday, May 25, in Rapid City, allegedly with three guns on him. Police spotted him while investigating a separate gunshot call nearby that resulted in officers arresting two minors.
_full_text:
A Rapid City teen was arrested on Monday, May 25, in Rapid City, allegedly with three guns on him. Police spotted him while investigating a separate gunshot call nearby that resulted in officers arresting two minors.

At around 2 a.m. Monday, police responded to 100 Surfwood Drive, Sage Place, for a report of gunshots heard in the area.

During the investigation, police saw a boy walking through the area where the gunshots were heard. As police attempted to make contact with him, he refused to stop and went inside a nearby apartment building. 

Police followed him and heard him discard something in the hallway. Police detained him and identified him to be a juvenile. The item he discarded was a loaded pistol magazine which was missing several rounds. 

Two girls were nearby, one of them with a pistol, police said. The pistol was determined to match with the magazine the boy attempted to discard. Police said it was determined that the boy gave the girl the gun just prior to contact with police. The firearm was stolen. 

The boy and one girl were both arrested and placed in the channels of the juvenile justice system, which is closed to the public.

While investigating that incident, police saw a man wearing a ski mask and dark clothing running through the parking lot of 105 E. Knollwood Drive. Police said he was seen reaching for his waistband. 

As officers began to exit their patrol car to speak with him, they heard a gunshot come from the area where he was located. Police told him to show his hands, however, he continued to resist officers, reaching for his waistband. 

Once detained, police said they found three firearms on his person and noted the smell of alcohol coming from him. Jaycias Flying Horse, 18, was placed under arrest on suspicion of obstruction, resisting arrest, receiving stolen property, underage consumption of an alcoholic beverage and possession of a loaded firearm while intoxicated. Police said one of the guns was stolen.

Flying Horse is being held at the Pennington County Jail with no bond.

title: Rapid City municipal pools to open Friday
description: With school out for the summer, the collective whistle is ready to be sounded signaling the official start of the summer outdoor pool season in Rapid City.
_full_text:
With school out for the summer, the collective whistle is ready to be sounded signaling the official start of the summer outdoor pool season in Rapid City.

Friday, May 29, is the opening day for city pool facilities at Horace Mann, Parkview and Jimmy Hilton Sioux Park pools. The 50-meter outdoor pool at Roosevelt Park Swim Center opened last Friday.

Pools at Parkview, Horace Mann and Jimmy Hilton will be open from noon to 6 p.m. daily except on July 4 when all city pools will be open from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. for Independence Day.

Roosevelt’s 50-meter outdoor pool will be open from 8 a.m.-7:45 p.m. Monday-Friday, 8 a.m.-5:30 p.m. Saturdays and Noon to 5:30 p.m. Sundays.

Daily swim passes are $8 for adults and youth, and $7 for senior citizens 62 years and older. There are 20-punch passes also available for adults and youth, seniors, and families.

Among the special events and offerings this summer:

‘Quick Dip Hour Passes’, half-price passes offered at Parkview, Sioux Park and Horace Mann pools from 5-6 p.m.

Sunday for Funday: Four people admitted for $16

Teen Night Pool Party: this free event for youth ages 10-17 is scheduled July 29 at Horace Mann Pool from 6:30-8 p.m. offering food, drinks and music with special guest DJ Jeremy Waddell

Glow Swim Pool Party: June 18 at the Parkview Pool from 7-9:30 p.m. for an evening of glowing fun

Family Fun Nights: June 11 at the Jimmy Hilton Pool and July 22 at the Parkview Pool, from 6:30-8 p.m. featuring games, music and prizes

Cardboard Boat Races: Back for the fourth consecutive year, the event is scheduled for Saturday, June 20 with check-in at 9 a.m. and boats launching from 9:30-11:30 a.m. at the Roosevelt Park 50-meter outdoor pool. Entry fee is $10 with a youth division for youth ages 6-13 along with an adult division

A total of 88,270 admissions were recorded last summer at the Sioux Park, Parkview, Horace Mann and Roosevelt Park Swim Center pools, a big spike in numbers over the summer of 2024 when 81,025 admissions were recorded and from 2023 when 73,097 admissions were tallied. As with last summer, the City plans to keep two pools open later this season. Horace Mann and Parkview pools will close Aug. 20 with Jimmy Hilton Sioux Park staying open until Sept. 6 and the 50-meter outdoor pool at Roosevelt Swim Center staying open until Sept. 26.

title: Rapid City Council Q&A with Ward 1 candidate Murray Lee
description: Name, age, occupation
_full_text:
Name, age, occupation

Murray Lee, age 53, consultant for a local nonprofit (He Sapa Otipi) 

Why are you running?

 Murray Lee (copy)
Murray Lee 

Because, through it’s best and it’s worst, I love this city. It’s as simple as that.

I was raised here, and I have seen Rapid City at its best, neighbors helping neighbors, people stepping up when someone is struggling, and families (like mine) building a life here because for lack of a better explanation, it simply feels like home. A real home. But I’ve also experienced racism. I’ve seen families, like my own, struggle with affordability and jobs and livable wages. I’ve watched people do their best and still feel unheard or uncared about. And I want to do what will be in my power as a City Council member to change the bad and make the good even better.

I’m not running because I want a title. I’m running because I care deeply about this community, and I want people to feel like their local government is listening to them. I want them to feel heard. And I want to contribute what I can toward practical solutions.

What are the top three issues Rapid City faces that you would work to address on the council? Is there anything specific to your ward?

Well, the first issue is affordability and housing. Too many people are working multiple jobs and still barely making it each month. Rent, groceries, fuel, childcare, property taxes…everything feels heavy and expensive right now. We need more truly affordable housing, smarter development, and policies that help regular families stay in Rapid City long term.

The second is infrastructure and responsible growth. Growth is coming. It just is. And the question is if we are planning for it wisely. Roads, water, traffic, public safety, schools, and neighborhoods all matter. We can’t just chase a patchwork of expansion without making sure the basics keep up.

The third thing is addiction and mental health. Including all the peripheral issues that come along with them. A lot of folks are affected by this. And it can be devastating to families and frustrating for others. So, we need accountability, compassion, treatment options, and better coordination between the city, nonprofits, healthcare systems, and law enforcement. Ignoring it, or approaching it without compassion, doesn’t help anybody.

 Elections

For Ward 1 specifically, I hear a lot about neighborhood quality of life, traffic, safety, aging infrastructure, and wanting growth that keeps the neighborhood feel of each area intact. People want common sense solutions and they want balance.

What approach to Tax Increment Financing would you bring to the council?

I think TIF can be a useful tool when it’s used carefully and transparently. I really do.

But the question I always think about is, does this project genuinely benefit the public long term, or are taxpayers taking on risk without enough return? I’m very supportive of projects that create real community value. Things like housing, infrastructure improvements, revitalization, good jobs, quality-of-life investments, especially in areas that otherwise would struggle to develop.

And I also firmly believe that the public deserves clear communication and accountability. People should understand where the money is going, why it matters, and what the long-term impact will be.

How should the city approach growth?

Well, in a word…thoughtfully.

I don’t think most folks are against growth itself. I think they’re worried about losing the things they love about Rapid City. The pace matters. The planning matters. The infrastructure matters. All of it.

Growth should improve the quality of life for the people already living here, not just benefit short-term gains for a few. That means protecting green spaces, thinking long term about water and infrastructure, supporting local businesses, investing in public safety, and making sure working families aren’t pushed out as the city expands.

I think we all want Rapid City to grow in a way that still feels like Rapid City. Just larger.

What is working and what needs to be fixed in the city’s approach to homeless people?

I think we have a lot of folks and organizations that genuinely care and are doing incredible work. I never want to dismiss the work being done by nonprofits, shelters, outreach workers, churches, volunteers, healthcare providers, or the folks in public safety.

But I also think the current system sometimes feels reactive instead of coordinated.

So, I think that we could work on better coordination between agencies, continue to focus more on mental health and addiction treatment, more pathways into stability and housing, and clearer expectations around public safety and accountability.

And we need to create larger pipelines of providers for things like mental health and addiction treatment, so that we can have the capacity to offer an appropriate level of support for the folks who can benefit from this.

What can the city do to make living in Rapid City more affordable?

We need to think seriously about workforce housing, smart infrastructure planning, childcare access, wages, and supporting local businesses.

I also think the city should be careful about passing unnecessary costs onto residents whenever possible because people are already stretched thin.

One thing I hear over and over is that people don’t want Rapid City to become a place where only higher-income households can comfortably live. Teachers, nurses, tradespeople, service workers, young families, and seniors should all still be able to build a life here. They just should. That matters to me a lot.

What should the city’s role be in addiction services and how should the city use opioid settlement funds toward fulfilling that role?

Addiction is hurting a lot of families here. It’s not abstract. It’s real. And it’s personal for a lot of people. Addiction has even touched my life. It can be incredibly painful.

I think the city’s role is to help coordinate partnerships and invest in solutions that actually help people recover and regain stability. The city can’t solve addiction alone, but it can help connect systems more effectively.

As for opioid settlement funds, I believe they should go toward evidence-based solutions with measurable outcomes. Things like treatment access, recovery support, mental health services, detox capacity, youth prevention efforts, supporting outreach teams, transitional support, and programs that help people stay out of the addiction cycle long term.

I also think the public deserves transparency in how those funds are spent and whether the programs are truly helping people. This is huge.

title: Rapid City Council Q&A with Ward 1 candidate Josh Biberdorf
description: Name, Age, Occupation
_full_text:
Name, Age, Occupation

Dr. Josh Biberdorf, 52, chiropractor and entrepreneur

Why are you running?

 Headshot.png
Josh Biberdorf 

I am running because I believe Rapid City deserves a council member who puts families first. I have been active in state and local politics for 25 years and have learned how to be part of the solution rather than part of the problem. As a Christian conservative and business leader, I want to bring a solutions-first approach to our community as we continue to grow. My priority is to keep Rapid City a premier, safe place to raise a family while supporting quality growth and fiscal responsibility.

What are the top three issues Rapid City faces that you would work to address on the council? Is there anything specific to your ward?

The three issues I am most focused on are public safety, responsible growth, and homelessness. Rapid City must remain a safe place for families and businesses alike. As our city grows, we need to be intentional about ensuring that growth expands our tax base and attracts quality investment without sacrificing the character of our neighborhoods. Addressing homelessness is also critical. Having served on the Cornerstone Rescue Mission board, I understand the importance of balancing genuine compassion with personal accountability to keep our community safe and vibrant. In Ward One specifically, maintaining the quality of our neighborhoods and ensuring strong public services for residents remains a top concern.

What approach to Tax Increment Financing would you bring to the council?

I believe Tax Increment Financing should be used strategically and transparently. As Rapid City's budget grows beyond $200 million, we must be careful stewards of taxpayer dollars. TIF can be a valuable tool when it is used to catalyze genuine economic development that would not otherwise occur, but it must come with strong accountability measures and clear metrics for success. I will always look for innovative ways to use taxpayer money efficiently and ensure that TIF decisions are made with full transparency to the public.

How should the city approach growth?

Rapid City should pursue responsible, quality growth that expands our tax base, attracts new investment, and creates good-paying jobs for families. Growth should not come at the cost of public safety or the character of our community. I want to keep Rapid City an excellent place to do business while ensuring that development supports rather than strains city services. We need to plan thoughtfully so that growth benefits all residents, particularly families who choose to make Rapid City their home.

What is working and what needs to be fixed in the city's approach to homeless people?

Rapid City has made meaningful investments in organizations like Cornerstone Rescue Mission, and that work matters. However, effective help for people experiencing homelessness must balance genuine compassion with personal accountability. What is working is our community's commitment to providing services. What needs improvement is ensuring those services move people toward self-sufficiency rather than enabling long-term dependency. The city should work in partnership with nonprofit organizations and require measurable outcomes for the resources it invests. Keeping our neighborhoods and public spaces safe for all residents must also remain a priority alongside efforts to help those in need.

 Elections

What can the city do to make living in Rapid City more affordable?

Affordability starts with keeping Rapid City a great place to do business so that employers can offer good-paying jobs. The city should reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up the cost of housing and construction. Supporting responsible growth that increases the housing supply is essential to keeping home prices accessible for working families. The city must also be disciplined about spending so that property taxes remain manageable. Transparency and accountability in how taxpayer dollars are spent directly impacts the affordability of life in our community.

What should the city's role be in addiction services and how should the city use opioid settlement funds toward fulfilling that role?

The city has a responsibility to its residents to address addiction thoughtfully and effectively. Opioid settlement funds represent a significant opportunity to make a lasting difference, and they must be invested in proven, outcome-based programs rather than simply expanding existing infrastructure.

The city should partner with established faith-based and nonprofit organizations that have a track record of success in recovery services. Any investment should prioritize long-term recovery and reintegration over short-term management of symptoms. Accountability and transparency in how these funds are deployed is non-negotiable.

title: William Kenneth Hinchley
description: October 5, 1945 - May 6, 2026
_full_text:
October 5, 1945 - May 6, 2026

William "Bill" Kenneth Hinchley, 80, of Smith Center, Kansas, passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Wednesday, May 6, 2026. Graveside services will take place on June 13, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. at Marsland Cemetery in Marsland, Nebraska. Bill was born on October 5, 1945, to Hank and Opal Hinchley of Marsland, Nebraska. He attended grade school in Marsland and graduated from the University of Nebraska School of Agriculture in Curtis, Nebraska, in 1964. After graduation, he enlisted in the United States Army and proudly served for three years before being honorably discharged.

Later in life, Bill found his true calling when he began working at the Osborne Schools. He became a friend, mentor, and familiar smile to countless students. He had a special way of connecting with children, and they adored him in return. When he retired, the school honored him with a special parade, a fitting tribute to someone who was a friend to all.

A devoted husband and father, as well as a loving grandfather and great-grandfather, Bill's legacy lives on through his family. He is survived by his wife of 56 years, Billie Hinchley of Smith Center, Kansas; daughter, Mickie (Kirk) Hilzer of Greeley, Colorado; and sons, George Hinchley of Osborne, Kansas, Eric Dahlman of Buena Vista, Colorado, and Mark Dahlman of Smith Center, Kansas. Also surviving Bill are thirteen grandchildren and thirty-six great-grandchildren. He is also survived by his sisters, Harriet Glover of Wilber, Nebraska, and Wanda (Pete) Michelena of Farmington, New Mexico; brothers, Earl (Pennye) Hinchley of Aurora, Colorado, and Dennis (Laura) Hinchley of Eaton, Colorado; and many other extended family members. Bill will be deeply missed by all who knew and loved him.

title: Summer Nights makes a comeback Thursday: A summer staple for Rapid City hopes to create memories for community
description: After a year of uncertainty, Summer Nights returns Thursday, May 28, on Sixth Street, with the stage on Kansas City Street.
_full_text:
After a year of uncertainty, Summer Nights returns Thursday, May 28, on Sixth Street, with the stage on Kansas City Street.

"I think it creates a real sense of community for a lot of people, and that's where the memories come from. It doesn't matter what walk of life you come from, when everybody comes to Summer Nights, everybody's just friends," Summer Nights President Sandy Schwan said.

 Sandy Schwan
Summer Nights President Sandy Schwan addresses public concerns and city officials' questions about the return of Summer Nights during the March 16, 2026, Rapid City Council meeting. 

Starting May 28 and going through August, Summer Nights will run every Thursday from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. on Sixth and Kansas City streets. The area will be filled with food trucks, ice-cold beverages and live musical performances. 

The headliner for Thursday's show is the Brandon Jones Band, who will be performing on the Coca-Cola stage, one of the sponsors for the event.

Schwan said it was a touching moment to plan and set up Summer Nights again.

"We spent an entire day at our warehouse cleaning the trailers, another entire evening stocking the trailers, and just fixing canopies and tables and things that need to be done. A lot of it was just the planning; everything had to be dusted off and made sure it was working, since it's all been in storage for almost two years," Shwan said on setting up again after more than a year.

The event was hosted in the heart of downtown Rapid City every Thursday night from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m. from Memorial Day to Labor Day for 17 years — until last year. In early 2025, the Summer Nights board announced the series would pause, citing the Rapid City Council's denial of their permit for their preferred location and an inability to find a new location during negotiations with city staff.  

Council members cited safety concerns regarding the closure of St. Joseph Street for the event, and several businesses expressed frustrations with Summer Nights reportedly affecting business by deterring locals from the downtown area and consolidating commerce to food trucks and vendors at Summer Nights.

In January 2026, Summer Nights secured a special event permit to hold the event at a new location — on Sixth Street, with the stage on Kansas City Street. Summer Nights previously suggested the location in 2025, but city staff turned it down because of the active construction of Block 5, which is now complete.

The event core was previously at the intersection of Saint Joseph and Seventh streets, with the stage on Seventh Street.

 Summer Nights
Summer Nights, a free summer concert series in downtown Rapid City that ran for 17 seasons, cancelled its 2025 season. To fill the void and meet the public's increased desire for new and different things to do, businesses have added live music, DIY classes and events to bring people downtown.  

The Rapid City Council was split, voting 4-4, on the approval of the special event liquor license for the event — Mayor Jason Salamun cast a tie-breaking "yes" vote for approval — during the council's March 16 meeting. As he broke the tie, Salamun said Summer Nights should cooperate with concerned business owners.

Hay Camp Brewery co-owner Karl Koth at the March council meeting cited concerns about the economic impact to his brewery. Schwan said they have tried to address all the concerned businesses. 

"After a lot of work with the city officials, we managed to figure out a way in which patrons can go into Hay Camp and purchase a beverage if they prefer, and bring it out into the event. We will also obviously be there with beer trailers, but Hay Camp will be able to sell to the patrons as well," Schwan said.

She cited food vendors that will be at Thursday's kickoff include Eddie's Tacos and Ugly Graffiti, as well as popcorns and lemonade vendors.

This year Summer Nights has partnered with the Central States Fair to do ticket giveaways every Thursday.

Schwan also cited safety measures have increased this year, with the implementation of barriers set up at every entrance. She reminded the public to not bring any weapons, pets, large bags, backpacks or outside food and drinks. Service animals, small purses and clear bags are allowed.

"There are a couple that met at Summer Nights and are still together today. There's another couple that met at Summer Nights that are married and have a child," Schawn said, reflecting on the community aspect of Summer Nights. "So that's always fun."

title: Mines physics lecturer earns national recognition as Outstanding Chapter Advisor
description: For years, Michael Dowding, senior lecturer in the physics department at South Dakota Mines, has inspired and mentored countless students both inside and outside the classroom. Now, that dedication has earned him national recognition from the Society of Physics Students.
_full_text:
For years, Michael Dowding, senior lecturer in the physics department at South Dakota Mines, has inspired and mentored countless students both inside and outside the classroom. Now, that dedication has earned him national recognition from the Society of Physics Students.

Dowding has received the 2026 Outstanding SPS Chapter Advisor Award, the organization's most prestigious award. He was also a finalist for the award in 2019.

SPS is a professional association designed specifically for students and their advisers, helping students become contributing members of the professional community. Membership in the collegiate chapters is open to anyone interested in the physical sciences. Aside from physics majors, the Mines chapter includes students in a variety of other majors, including astronomy, chemistry, computer science and engineering.

“Having had the pleasure of advising SPS chapters, I can truly say I am impressed by the depth and personal nature of the comments in your support letters,” said Earl Blodgett, Ph.D., the interim director for SPS and Sigma Pi Sigma.

 RileySinger-3-an-ice-cream-photowalk_P1-Riley Singer-2025-07-12.jpg
Michael Dowding, a senior lecturer in the physics department at South Dakota Mines, has been named the 2026 Outstanding Society of Physics Student Chapter Advisor, the organization's most prestigious award. Dowding’s hands-on involvement has become a defining part of the chapter’s culture. 

According to his nomination, Dowding represents the best of what advising can achieve. “Through sustained commitment, thoughtful mentorship, and a genuine passion for student development, Mr. Dowding has created an SPS chapter that not only enriches the undergraduate experience but also helps shape the next generation of the workforce,” his nomination said.

The nominators also added, “Through his unwavering logistical and financial support, his dedication to our professional development, and his genuine care for our community, he empowers us to grow not just as physics students but as future leaders in the scientific community.”

Dowding began serving as the university’s SPS advisor in 2013, helping to create a recognized chapter at Mines. With the department’s growth, physics majors wanted an official chapter to better participate in and network with other physics students and organizations around the world.

He is humbled and honored by the recognition, adding that it is as much an honor for the students. “There are generations of student members from our campus chapter that have been building an organization from the ground up to one that now receives national recognition for their efforts,” Dowding said.

The Mines SPS chapter has a history of national recognition. For eight consecutive years, the Mines SPS student chapter received the Outstanding Chapter Award, a designation awarded to fewer than 10 percent of all SPS chapters in the United States and internationally. In 2016, the chapter also received a Distinguished Chapter Award.

 240713-NeutrinoDay2024-0318.jpg
Dowding and the students participate in educational outreach and community service projects, including the annual Neutrino Days at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead. 

The organization’s success is rooted in a three-tier mission focused on the chapter, the department and the broader community. Members hold monthly meetings and informal gatherings, from study sessions to game nights, to strengthen relationships, host socials with physics staff, faculty and other campus departments, and participate in educational outreach and community service projects, including the annual Neutrino Days at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead.

At the center of it all is Dowding, whose hands-on involvement has become a defining part of the chapter’s culture.

“As an advisor, I don’t want to be someone who just shows up for meetings or signs off on paperwork,” Dowding said. “I share ideas and recommendations for activities, help guide them through the rules and make myself available to work alongside them in everything they do.”

Dowding will receive the award during the American Association of Physics Teachers annual meeting this July in Pasadena, Calif. The honor also includes $6,000 for the South Dakota Mines SPS organization and physics department.

title: Rapid City man pleads guilty to second-degree rape
description: A Rapid City man pleaded guilty to second-degree rape.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man pleaded guilty to second-degree rape. 

Hayden Czerwonka, 23, appeared for his change of plea hearing before Circuit Court Judge Jeffery Connolly at the Pennington County Courthouse on Wednesday morning, May 28.

Czerwonka was initially indicted for two counts of first-degree rape with an 11-year-old child for incidents that took place between July 12, 2021 and June 7, 2022. 

Through an agreement with the state, Czerwonka pleaded guilty to one count of second-degree rape, with all other charges dismissed and the Part II information that labeled Czerwonka as a habitual offender removed. Both sides are free to comment at sentencing.

According to the Part II information, Czerwonka was convicted in March 2022 for violating a protection order-stalking. 

In South Dakota, first-degree rape is a Class C felony that carries a maximum sentence of life in prison with a mandatory minimum of 15 years in prison. Second-degree rape is Class 1 felony which carries a maximum sentence of 50 years in prison and a $50,000 fine. 

Czerwonka's sentencing is set for July 20 at 9 a.m.
