title: Out of the greenhouse, into the ground: Rapid City crews plant thousands of flowers
description: City crews are working on planting about 22,000 flowers around Rapid City this week, an annual effort to zhuzh up the town as the spring heat sets in.
_full_text:
City crews are working on planting about 22,000 flowers around Rapid City this week, an annual effort to zhuzh up the town as the spring heat sets in.

“It’s just the summer kick-of for us. We’re finally getting the flowers out of the greenhouse, getting them in the ground. Hopefully the cold weather’s behind us,” Rapid City Greenhouse Specialist John Berglund told the Journal at Halley Park on Wednesday, May 27, as he waited for another truck-full of flowers to arrive for planting. The flowers came from the city’s new greenhouse, which debuted about a year ago.

Crews are planting in numerous areas, including Halley Park, Wilson Park, the Sunken Gardens area behind McKeague Field on Canyon Lake Drive, the William Noordermeer Formal Gardens at Sioux Park and Otto’s Corner on the northwest corner of Omaha Street and West Boulevard. About 8,000 to 10,000 of the plants were grown in the city’s greenhouse from seed and the rest came as plants.

 Berglund
Rapid City Greenhouse Specialist John Berglund holds a tray of flowers in each hand. 

Berglund said the plants include salvias, dahlia, zinnias, marigolds and snap dragons. The city’s five gargantuan banana plants are celebrating 10 years with the city. Berglund grew three from seeds and bought two from Rapid City Hardware.

“I like to choose a lot of plants that can handle our drought-tolerant weather that South Dakota gets,” Berglund said. “…With the water restrictions, I don’t want to be the one that’s wasting water out there.”

The City of Rapid City implemented water restrictions two months early this year, starting on April 1 rather than in June.

Those measures affect residents' watering usage from April through the end of September. No watering is allowed between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. daily. Odd-numbered addresses are allowed to water, outside those time restrictions, on odd-numbered calendar days. Even-numbered addresses are allowed to water on even-numbered calendar days. No outside watering is allowed on the 31st day of any month. Manual watering with a handheld hose or with a bucket, sprinkling can or other similar container is allowed at all times.

 Flowers in the dirt
A crew members packs dirt around a freshly-planted flower. 

A crew of about 15 high school and college students are aiding Berglund in the planting task.

“Without them, we couldn’t get our work done. There is no way I could personally do all that work by myself, so it’s great to have them help. I get ideas. I learn from them as much as they learn from me.”

Berglund said the city went with a patriotic theme for the flowers this year in celebration of America’s 250th birthday and Rapid City’s 150th birthday.

“This particular park here, at Halley Park, you’re gonna see a lot of red and white and purple, kind of mimic the blue. And then you’ll see an American flag at Otto’s Corner, which we’ll be planting tomorrow (May 28),” Berglund said. “…After that we’ll probably start in the Formal Gardens and then we did a Native American medicine wheel at Sunken Gardens, so we’ll be finishing that up this afternoon hopefully.”

title: Community photo will be placed in Rapid City time capsule to be opened in 2076
description: A crowd of more than 80 people gathered in Main Street Square in Rapid City for a community photo that’ll be placed in a time capsule to be opened in 2076. Among the crowd were Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun, Gov. Larry Rhoden and state legislators.
_full_text:
A crowd of more than 80 people gathered in Main Street Square in Rapid City for a community photo that’ll be placed in a time capsule to be opened in 2076. Among the crowd were Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun, Gov. Larry Rhoden and state legislators.

"What's a better thing to have in the time capsule than the smiling faces of the folks who live here? While everybody couldn't be here today, we had people from all walks of life, all ages represented here today to be a part of history, and for me, that's what it's all about," Salamun told the Journal.

 Community photo
A crowd of more than 80 people gathered on Friday, May 22, at Main Street Square in Rapid City for a community photo that’ll be placed in a time capsule to be opened in 2076. 

The gathering occurred at Main Street Square on Friday, May 22, where the city used a drone to take two photos. One photo had the crowd facing the main stage. For the second photo, the group faced toward the intersection of Sixth Street and Main Street.

The day marked the start of Memorial Day weekend and the first day of the season for the square’s water fountains, which were switched on for children to play in.

"We do a lot of things right in South Dakota, and I think that's because of the people, and that's why I enjoy so much getting out to events like this, just visiting with the people of South Dakota, and reminding people of what makes us special," Rhoden said.

 Selfie
Community members take a selfie with a smartphone, just before the community photo.  

Rhoden said he’s contributing a challenge coin to the time capsule, but is unable to attend the Friday, May 29 burial. 

"I'm old enough, I remember our bicentennial celebration and how we celebrated that. I'm looking forward to this, especially with the Mount Rushmore fireworks," Rhoden said of the upcoming America 250 celebrations.

This year marks the semiquincentennial (250 years) of the founding of the United States, with statewide municipal celebrations including the Boots and Roots celebration in Pierre on July 1 through July 5 , Mount Rushmore fireworks show on July 3, Sioux Falls' Independence Day celebration on July 4, and Rapid City's Real America Birthday Bash from July 1 through Independence Day.

 Jason Salamun
Mayor Jason Salamun, center, flanked by Gov. Larry Rhoden, left, and Sen. Helene Duhamel (R-Rapid City), right, smile at the community photo event on Friday, May 22, 2026. Salamun thanked community members for attending. 

Rapid City is also celebrating 150 years since its founding in 1876. The city previously honored the sesquicentennial anniversary with a new exhibit in the Journey Museum dedicated to Rapid City, which opened in February, and the opening of a time capsule from 1976.

The new time capsule is a part of the city's continued celebration of its founding.

The city is planning on placing more than 20 items inside the capsule, including the community photo, a letter by Mayor Jason Salamun, Native American cultural items, local newspaper clippings, 2076 predictions of the future, a 2025 minted penny, a used smartphone, pictures of the 1972 Rapid City flood, a Rush hockey puck, a Post 22 baseball and an America 250 challenge coin.

 052826-nws-community-photo-p12.JPG
Derek Mann, a traffic crash reconstructionist with the Rapid City Police Department, took the community photo. 

"We'll have some marketing materials for our America 250 celebration, so they can see what we did to celebrate America's independence, because 50 years from now, they'll be celebrating 300 years of American independence and 200 years since Rapid City's founding. They'll have their own celebrations then, so it'd be cool for them to see how we celebrate it in this time," Salamun said.

Officials and dignitaries will bury the time capsule at 1:30 p.m. on Friday, May 29, at Founders Park.

The ceremony will include remarks from Salamun, Public Information Officer Darrell Shoemaker, City Council members and local faith community members, while there will also be a Lakota honoring and blessing. 

Words for the future

Salamun told the Journal he hopes values of God, family and country will carry the country to a prosperous future in 2076.

"I certainly hope that is true. In the next 50 years, we will have a great nation. Family is the building block of society, and it's all thanks to our creator, so I hope that is true. If they're guided by those same timeless eternal principles, we'll be in good shape," Salamun said.

 052826-nws-community-photo-p13.JPG
People wave to the drone camera as Rapid City community members gathered for a group photo on Friday, May 22, at Main Street Square in Rapid City. 

Salamun pondered the influence technology will have on our lives and as a society, cautioning the future as either being "like the Jetsons or the Flintstones."

Despite his half-joking remark, Salamun said he hopes life's simple pleasures continue to ring true for future generations.

"We couldn't have imagined what life would be like today 100 years ago. It's hard for us to picture what life will be like 100 years from now," Salamun said. "What I hope is still true is that people love one another, that kids are cared for, that people fall in love and get married and have babies and pursue their purpose with their skills and talents and gifts God gave them. That they work to make this community a better place to live, that they leave it better than they found it."

 052826-nws-community-photo-p11.JPG
"What's a better thing to have in the time capsule than the smiling faces of the folks who live here? While everybody couldn't be here today, we had people from all walks of life, all ages represented here today to be a part of history, and for me, that's what it's all about," Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun told the Journal. 

He described what the community of Rapid City is like in 2026 as family-rooted. Saying he doesn't always make decisions as mayor based on politics, but on the children's future.

"If I could bottle this up and send it to you 50 years from now, I wish I could. What I'm going to tell you, you will not go wrong investing in the next generation. We stand on generations that invested in us, and right now we will continue to invest in the next generation, and so that should always be true, and so I pray that that will always be true 50 years from now and beyond," Salmaun said.

 Community photo
Rapid City Journal Assistant Editor Shalom Baer Gee with her daughter and husband.  

 Larry Rhoden
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden was in attendance for the community photo. 

 Community photo
Residents gather to get ready for the community photo taken on Friday, May 22, at Main Street Square in Rapid City. The city will place the photo in a time capsule set to be buried on Friday, May 29, and opened in 2076. 

 Mike Derby
Rep. Mike Derby R-34, smiles at the community photo event. 

 Drone
Rapid City used this drone to capture photos of the participating community members.

title: Loren Doyle
_full_text:
March 6, 1945 - May 24, 2026

RAPID CITY - Loren Eugene Doyle passed away Sunday, May 24, 2026, at the Fort Meade, VA Health Care, at the age of 81.

Loren was born in Rapid City, SD, on March 6, 1945, to Daniel and Auguste Doyle joining a brother Arnold and sister Joyce. He attended school at St. John's Elementary, North Junior High and Rapid City High School.

After graduating, Loren began a career in concrete construction with Stanley Johnson Concrete. He was then drafted to serve the Army for the Vietnam War. While Loren was stationed at Fort Carson, Colorado, he met the love of his life in Donna Hutson. They were soon married, a relationship that lasted nearly 56 years. They have one son David. Upon his return from the Army, Loren went back to work for Stanley Johnson.

In 1980, Loren and Donna started Loren Doyle Concrete. They built a successful business serving many satisfied customers until retiring in 2007. Retirement allowed him to enjoy traveling and spending many summer days at the Elks Golf Course.

Throughout his life, Loren enjoyed the outdoors, hunting, fishing, and great friends. A natural athlete, he enjoyed watching, and especially playing many sports from his school days through participating in the Senior Olympics.

Loren was preceded in death by his parents and siblings.

He is survived by his wife Donna; son David (Lisa); two granddaughters, Madison and Macy Doyle; several nieces and nephews and his sister-in-law, Diane Hutson.

Visitation will be from 5:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026 at Osheim & Schmidt Funeral Home with a Vigil at 7:00 p.m.

Funeral Mass will be offered at 11:00 a.m. on Monday, June 1, 2026 at the Cathedral of Our Lady of Perpetual Help with Fr. Brian Christensen presiding.

Burial will follow at Pine Lawn Memorial Park.

The family would like to extend their heartfelt gratitude to the staff at the Ft. Meade VA for the exceptional care and compassion shown to Loren throughout his time there. They are also deeply thankful for the many kindnesses extended to their family. There are far too many people to thank individually, but please know your support and care were truly appreciated.

Memorial donations may be made to the Humane Society of the Black Hills in memory of Loren.

Brooks Lee Hanna of Spearfish, SD, passed away on Sunday, May 24, 2026, at the age of 80 years old.

Brooks was born June 13, 1945, in Williston, ND to Claude and Fay Hanna. He was raised in Watford City, ND, graduating from high school in 1964. He spent much of his younger years with his beloved Uncle Lee. He met the love of his life, Elaine Berget and married her on December 28, 1964.

Brooks was 'pedal to the metal' whether at work or play. He was at home on the basketball court, both as a player and as a referee, cementing many friendships. Over the years, he owned and managed multiple award-winning car dealerships in ND, SD, WY, MT. He was beloved by his employees, customers, and business partners. He loved to fly his airplanes, appreciating the earth and inhabitants beneath his wings. He was just as comfortable on the ground, becoming an avid golfer. Brooks was a long-time supporter of BHSU athletics, attending many sporting events and contributing time and money to the programs.

Of all his accomplishments, the most important thing to Brooks was the relationships he fostered. He loved life and loved meeting people, lighting up the room wherever he went.

Brooks is survived by his beloved wife and companion Elaine; four children, Holly (Hank) McClurg, Chad (Mieka) Hanna, Shane Hanna, and Scott (Krista) Hanna; five grandchildren, Blake, Brook, Bryn, Reese, and Cooper; and two sisters, Beverly Olheiser, and Cindy (Peter) Ostman.

He is preceded in death by his parents, in-laws Olaf & Pearl Berget, and brothers-in-law Bruce Berget, Ron Olheiser, and Harley Wright.

title: Rapid City commemorates 150th anniversary at 2076 time capsule ceremony
description: One hundred and fifty years ago, in 1876, Founders Park was no more than a campsite for gold prospectors looking to establish a settlement within the Black Hills. Today, the land flourishes with trails and a park for those who call the area home.
_full_text:
One hundred and fifty years ago, in 1876, Founders Park was no more than a campsite for gold prospectors looking to establish a settlement within the Black Hills. Today, the land flourishes with trails and a park for those who call the area home. 

Friday afternoon, May 29, dozens of people gathered at Founders Park for the 2076 time capsule burial ceremony to plant another seed of history at the park and commemorate the 150th anniversary of Rapid City.

 Time Capsule Photo 1
Some of the items in the time capsule are winning entries from a Rapid City 150th youth art contest.  

"We are here because of generations that have gone before. There are other people that have sacrificed to make this city special. We didn't make it special on our own, others did," Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun said. "Now we are stewards to ensure it's special for the next generation. That's what we're called to do and that's what we intend to do." 

At the ceremony, attendees heard remarks from Salamun, Public Information Officer Darrell Shoemaker, who gave a brief rundown of Rapid City's history, City Council members and local faith community members. There was also a Lakota prayer song blessing the people and the land, led by Pastor of Grace City Church, Quincy Good Star. 

 Time Capsule Photo 5
Friday afternoon dozens of people gathered at Founders Park for the 2076 time capsule burial ceremony to plant another seed of history at the park and commemorate the 150th anniversary of Rapid City.  

In March and April, Rapid City residents were surveyed about which items should be placed in the 2076 time capsule and about their predictions for what life will be like in 50 years.

Items placed in the time capsule include:

The Friday, May 22, community photo from Main Street Square showcasing local residents.

A letter from Mayor Jason Salamun.

Challenge coins from the mayor and South Dakota Governor Larry Rhoden.

Fact sheets displaying the average cost of goods and demographic information about Rapid City in 2026.

Winning entries from a Rapid City 150th youth art contest.

A small smudge kit and dream catcher from Prairie Edge Trading Post.

A Post 22 baseball.

A Rapid City Rush hockey puck.

Copies of the Rapid City Journal and Rapid City Post.

Items from the Journey Museum, Visit Rapid City, Dinosaur Park and Storybook Island.

A booklet featuring 1972 Rapid City flood information and photos.

1926 and 2025 pennies.

A smartphone from the mid-2020s.

“Then and Now” photos of the Valentine McGillycuddy home.

A Black Hills Symphony Orchestra program.

A Rapid City Youth Council coloring book.

 Time Capsule Photo 10
Mayor Jason Salamun said he hopes that same level of care, passion and sense of community finds its way to Rapid City in the next 50 years.  

The time capsule also includes predictions for Rapid City in 2076 supplied by Rapid City residents. Those predictions include:

Rapid City’s population could grow significantly, with estimates ranging from 100,000 to over 300,000.

Concerns about overcrowding, rising costs of living, strained public resources.

Increased automation could reduce the need for human labor, leading to more leisure time.

The area will become part of a larger regional or “mega-city.”

Potential increases in crime, poverty and infrastructure challenges if growth is not managed well.

Access to essential resources, like potable water, may become more limited or regulated.

Increased walkability, expanded parks and new community amenities are envisioned.

Ongoing global change, including environmental and economic instability

The gig economy may dominate the workforce with fewer traditional homeowners.

A shift toward subscription-based living, even for physical goods.

Development of cultural centers and tourism destinations.

The time capsule will never be opened.

The running joke at Friday's ceremony was whether the time capsule is up to the task of properly containing these items, but Salamun and Shoemaker assured that City Hall has taken extra precautions to ensure everything remains intact. 

Though the park hummed with laughter and excitement for the event, Salamun said it is important to cherish the timeless moments we share with our loved ones and our community. Salamun said he hopes that same level of care, passion and sense of community finds its way to Rapid City in the next 50 years. 

"What's really going to matter in 50 years is what's always mattered," Salamun said. "That we love God, that we love people and I hope that is true 50 years from now." 

 PHOTOS: Rapid City 2076 Time capsule ceremony
Dozens of people gathered at Founders Park on Friday, May 29, to witness the Rapid City 2076 time capsule burial ceremony.

title: Dusty Johnson discusses taxes, ads, public education during Hill City stop
description: HILL CITY — Just days away from the primary election, gubernatorial candidate Dusty Johnson made a stop in Hill City to speak with residents, breaking bread with a breakfast meal and a cup of coffee.
_full_text:
HILL CITY — Just days away from the primary election, gubernatorial candidate Dusty Johnson made a stop in Hill City to speak with residents, breaking bread with a breakfast meal and a cup of coffee.

"I got to tell you, you got to show up, and more than that, you've got to tell your friends and neighbors about the differences between the candidates. I think we need an energy and a vision to have the kind of South Dakota that we really need for my kids, for your kids, for your grandkids," said Johnson, currently the state’s representative in the U.S. House. "I think doing the same old same old is not going to get us in the right direction."

Johnson held the event at Hill City Cafe on Friday, May 29, where more than 20 residents gathered in the Ranger Room. Nine of those in attendance posed questions over Johnson's sales tax ads and public education.

Johnson previously served on the South Dakota Public Utilities Commission in 2004 and left the commission in 2010 to become then-Gov. Dennis Daugaard's chief of staff. Thereafter, he was elected to the House in 2018 and re-elected in 2020, 2022 and 2024.

The Republican governor's race primary is contested with South Dakota House Speaker Jon Hansen of Dell Rapids, businessman Toby Doeden of Aberdeen and Gov. Larry Rhoden of Union Center, who took over in January after then-Gov. Kristi Noem was confirmed as Department of Homeland Security secretary.

Democrat Dahn Ahlers is also running for governor and is unopposed in the primary.

 Dusty Johnson
South Dakota gubernatorial candidate Dusty Johnson made a stop in Hill City on May 29 to speak with residents ahead of the Tuesday, June 2 primary election.  

The primary election is on Tuesday June 2, and the GOP gubernatorial race winner needs to earn at least 35% to avoid a runoff. If that threshold isn’t met, a runoff election will be held on July 28. The general election on Nov. 3.

Johnson kicked off the meet-and-greet in Hill City by making his opening remarks to the eager crowd before he took questions from the public.

"I love this state. I think this is a great state, but if we're being honest, there are some key areas where we're falling behind," Johnson prefaced before addressing three points. 

He said he wants to address recidivism rates among parolees, expand job opportunities to address wage increases and tackle the decline in test scores in public education.

"I know we're a small state, but we used to know that we were capable of great things. Where are the bold plans on any of these issues? What are you hearing from your state government? What consensus have they built about these major leaps forward that we're going to make together," Johnson said.

Per previous reporting, Johnson said if elected he would create a task force on to address recidivism and incarceration rates. He said this task force would be co-chaired by former long-time Pennington County Sheriff Kevin Thom and Minnehaha County State's Attorney Daniel Haggar. 

According to the Sentencing Project, South Dakota's imprisonment rate is 370 per 100,000 people, 15th in the country and higher than the national rate of 355 per 100,000.

South Dakota was one of 14 states where recidivism increased between 2011 and 2021 when the state went from 42% to 50%. The Justice Center estimates that the state's recidivism costs $44 per person — the ninth highest rate in the country, South Dakota Newswatch reported, based on data from the Justice Center.

National Assessment of Educational Progress report assesses reading and math for 4th and 8th graders across the country every two years, found in their most recent report of 2025, South Dakota reading scores dropped in both grades, but both remained at or above the national average.

Questions from the public

One member asked Johnson about his recent online ads that state Gov. Larry Rhoden has increased sales tax to a South Dakota historic amount, without clarifying this increase in sales tax was to offset property tax.

Johnson defended his ads by stating they are not, "allegations."

"We still have the 38th highest property taxes in America, which is to say we're in the bottom third or the top third most affordable. It doesn't mean that I'm comfortable with where we're at. It does mean that we want to have that in some context. You're putting into place property tax relief, you're getting a little more than half of South Dakotans a tax increase, a tax relief, while charging everybody more, and that's going to have some impacts, particularly on lower costs, lower income South Dakota," Johnson said.

 Dusty Johnson
Residents of Hill City were able to ask U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, who’s running for governor, questions during a meet-and-greet. 

The 2026 South Dakota Legislature session featured multiple bills aimed at reducing property taxes that Rhoden signed. Rhoden has defended those bills, tellings South Dakota News Watch assertions about the historic increase are “unquestionably false, and people know that."

Senate Bill 96 provides counties the ability to increase sales tax by up to 0.5% (including on cities within the counties), with the proceeds dedicated to reducing property taxes on owner-occupied properties. 

As part of the rollout of the property tax relief bills, the Governor's Office released an interactive map showing the savings from the bills.

As an example of the property tax relief provided by the bill, if a home in Pennington County were assessed at $325,000, its property taxes would decrease by 22%.

The 2026 levy rate for Pennington County is 2.488 and a home valued at $325,000 would have a property tax of $808.60. The estimated 22% decrease in property tax brought on by SB 96 would then decrease the cost to roughly $603.70.

A mill levy is a property tax based on the assessed value of a property. One mill is equal to one dollar per $1,000 of assessed value. The levy is calculated by determining the amount of revenue each jurisdiction needs to fund its budget for public services, such as schools, parks and libraries.

According to reporting by South Dakota Searchlight, Senate Bill 245 would capture $114 million in ongoing annual revenue from next year’s scheduled increase of the statewide sales tax rate from 4.2% to 4.5%.

This funding would then be used to reduce local school district property taxes on owner-occupied homes.

Additionally, $56 million would be taken from state reserves to get the effort started before the sales tax rate increase.

In the same interactive map from the Governor's Office, a home in Pennington County valued at $325,000 would pay $547 in property taxes that would go to the school, saving an estimated 13%.

 Dusty Johnson
South Dakota gubernatorial candidate Dusty Johnson speaks with an attendee of his meet-and-greet on Friday, May 29, at the Hill City Cafe. 

Additionally, the passing of Senate Bill 1245 allowed municipalities the option to raise sales tax by 1% to fund capital projects. 

From previous reporting, Finance Director for Rapid City, Daniel Ainslie said, "Essentially, what it does is authorize a different funding mechanism for projects in a community. And so specifically, the legislation says that it can be a project the city owns, or a project the city would turn over to the county, or project the city would turn over to the schools. It needs to be something kind of unique and kind of solitary identifiable."

As defined by the bill, a municipality will have to create a five-member capital improvement board to review and vote on project proposals. A project can be selected and will be taken to a public vote (requiring a minimum of 60% voter approval).

Ainslie said then it would need to be referred to the electorate for an election.

The money raised by the tax would go into a special capital fund, for a maximum duration of five years, or until the collections exceed the needed amount.

 Dusty Johnson
Dusty Johnson discussed taxes, education and more during a campaign stop in Hill City. 

Municipalities cannot impose another such tax within 24 months after the collection of funds for the special project.

"This would be an opportunity to say here's another funding stream, that way sales tax could generate money not just from the residents, but also from tourists and people coming into your community and have them offset some of the costs," Ainslie said.

"In my example, it's a $40 million project. So once $40 million is collected, then the tax goes away, and then it can't be brought up again for at least two years. So it can't just be an ongoing 1% extra tax," Ainslie explained.

"It's remarkable when you've got affordability as the number one biggest problem in our state, you hear it about everything. You hear from the ranchers, you hear from the farmers, you hear from the manufacturing companies, you hear it from everyday South Dakotans. So go once, twice, three times to new sales taxes to solve the problem," Johnson said. 

He said of the three sales tax increases, two of the three are geared toward property tax relief. Johnson said former governors have lowered property taxes without increasing sales taxes for residents.

Education

Blake Gardner, the superintendent of the Hill City School District, asked Johnson for his ideas to aid and push public education in South Dakota.

"Our educators are working as hard as they ever have, and I'm not blaming them at all. I think our school boards and administrators do an incredible job, but we need to acknowledge that we have not had the types of gains, gains that Texas, and Alabama and Mississippi have, and I don't think a school district on their own can execute those kinds of turnarounds," Johnson said.

In one of those states, the “Mississippi Miracle” came after education laws passed in the state helped schools teach kids to read at the appropriate level and help keep kids on track. According to the Associated Press, Mississippi ranked the second-worst state in 2013 for fourth-grade reading and made a turnaround to 21st in 2022. 

"In Mississippi, there was tremendous state investment into that ‘Mississippi Miracle.’ School districts couldn't do it on their own. The failure of where we have been in the last few years is not at the local level. It is on a total lack of leadership from state government in giving you guys the resources you need for phonics, science, reading," Johnson said.

The Education Scorecard report ranked South Dakota near the bottom nationally for post-pandemic academic recovery, ranking the state as 30th in math recovery and 31st in reading recovery. The report analyzed student growth from 2022 through 2025. The data showed reading scores in the state have declined since 2022.

title: Pennington County Commission Q&A with District 3 candidate Randy Decker
description: Name, age, occupation
_full_text:
Name, age, occupation

Randy Decker, 63, Pennington County Public Defender’s Office (Investigator)

Why are you running?

I believe District 3 and all of Pennington County, deserve commissioners that are willing to listen to all sides of an issue. Then work with the citizens and fellow commissioners to find a solution that works best for everyone. I am the candidate that will research, listen to, and understand the issues. My personal call to civil service began when I entered the military and law enforcement, and then continued to work in government services as a South Dakota Correctional Officer and currently as an Investigator for the Pennington County Public Defender’s Office. I remain active in several civic/veteran organizations in a voluntary-service status.

 Randy Decker
Randy Decker 

What are the top three issues Pennington County faces that you would work to address on the council? Is there anything specific to your ward?

A primary issue that I am concerned with is the county budget, and not simply balancing it, but also reducing it. Reductions, however, cannot negatively impact the county, so I would strive to manage it in a way that provides the most cost-efficient success for each department.

County employees and property: Making sure everyone is treated fairly and equally so that we are able to retain the best employees for our departments and that property is being managed and cared for in the best interest of the citizens.

Public safety: Work with all agencies and provide the necessary tools to protect and serve all citizens.

Should the county zoning plan allow wind and solar projects on agricultural land? Why or why not?

I believe industrial zones are the proper location for those facilities, but there is a procedure in place to adjust zoning regulations and descriptions and to change from one type of zoning district to another. That gives multiple county boards/departments and the Board of Commissioners the opportunity to review each proposal on a case-by-case basis. Everyone’s property rights have to be accounted for, not just the person who wants to put something on their property.

Should the county institute the state-approved 0.5% sales tax for use toward property tax relief? Why or why not?

Yes. I believe it is a good start with the guidelines in place to assist homeowners in reducing their property taxes. Hopefully, it will be able to expand and help compensate for commercial and agricultural land, also.

What approach to Tax Increment Financing would you bring to the commission?

My approach entails ensuring that the plans follow the laws, rules, and regulations that are in place. Proposed projects must also benefit the people of our county. Therefore, these plans should be thoroughly analyzed and vetted in order to maximize the benefits that they can bring.

 Elections

What are your goals with the 2027 county budget?

My goal is to not only balance the county budget, but to also reduce it wherever possible while maintaining that departments are not lacking in funds they require. I also intend to account for individual department needs through meetings with department heads, etc., to ensure that budget cuts, allocations, and more make sense for real-time operations.

After the county 2026 budget was passed, residents had concerns over budget cuts to public services like the public library. What are your thoughts on such cuts by the county?

Some cuts may be necessary, but they have to be looked at in terms of “returns on investment." If a funding source is only bringing in X amount of money, we can’t invest more in those projects unless we find another source for the money, and is the outcome worth the investment?

title: Green vs. Mulally: A contentious Pennington County Auditor race
description: The Pennington County Auditor's race is contested this year with current Auditor Sabrina Green and Rep. Tina Mulally, R-District 35, going to bat for the position. Green’s relied on her experience at the office and Mulally’s pointed to her own track record while dredging up Green’s financial past and bumps in the road at the office.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Auditor's race is contested this year with current Auditor Sabrina Green and Rep. Tina Mulally, R-District 35, going to bat for the position. Green’s relied on her experience at the office and Mulally’s pointed to her own track record while dredging up Green’s financial past and bumps in the road at the office.

Cindy Mohler had been the county auditor from 2018 until she announced her early retirement in October 2025. She told the Journal the reason for her resignation is to mark a new beginning in her life.

Green has worked at the Auditor's Office since 2018 and served as deputy auditor under Mohler. The Pennington County Board of Commissioners appointed Green to the auditor position to finish out Mohler's term, which is set to end March 2, 2027. The election is on Tuesday, June 2. 

According to the county website, the auditor’s office is responsible for auditing all accounts and maintaining all financial records for the county, including payroll, preparing the annual budget, establishing levies and apportioning all tax collections. The office also conducts elections and maintains all records of voter registration and election history. The county auditor position is a four-year term. 

Meet the candidates

 Sabrina Green
Sabrina Green 

Green told the Journal she is running because she values accuracy and transparency in the Auditor's Office.

"There is no room for fabrication or cutting corners. I learned under the previous auditor that the office demands a standard of honesty, which is why I’m proud of both endorsements," Green said.

"I don’t get to decide whether I like the outcome. My job is to make sure the process is clean and the count is right. We saw that play out recently with the Libertyland vote. That was a closely watched, emotionally charged election, and when the results came in, they stood up to scrutiny because the process was sound," Green said about election integrity. 

The Destination District Tax Increment Financing District was a $125 million TIF for infrastructure needed for the development of a mixed-use development including Libertyland USA, an America themed amusement park. This was taken to a public vote in January, where Rapid City residents voted to deny the TIF.

 Tina Mulally
Tina Mulally 

Mullaly has been a state representative for District 35 since 2018 and has served on the House Appropriations Committee for eight years, according to her website.

"I’m running for Pennington County Auditor because the county needs a change. The Auditor’s Office oversees taxpayer dollars, elections, voter registration and public records. When the office fails, taxpayers and voters pay the price," Mullaly said.

"My approach is different. On appropriations, I reviewed budgets line by line and asked questions when numbers didn’t add up. As SDGOP (South Dakota Republican Party) Treasurer, I uncovered neglected accounts, unexplained expenses and recurring charges no one had questioned. I fixed the problems instead of ignoring them," Mulally said on her experience.

Mulally claims

Mulally has criticized Green's ability to properly manage the Auditor's Office, pointing out Clinton and Cristen Brink, who were attacked and killed in Arkansas in July of 2025, were still listed as active voters in Pennington County until recently.

"State law requires voter registrations to be canceled upon notice of death. Voters should not have to question whether voter rolls are accurate or procedures are being followed. Pennington County deserves an Auditor’s Office that is accurate, organized and accountable. That is why I am running," Mulally said.

Green said after it was brought to the office's attention, the office confirmed their obituary details and removed them from the rolls. Green said their records found the Brinks last voted on Nov. 5, 2024, in the general election the year before they died.

The South Dakota Secretary of State's Office confirmed neither Clinton or Cristen Brink listed as active voters as of May 26.

"Voter removal is governed by the state law and requires documentation. If the death certificate is filed in the state of South Dakota the system will run through the database and we are able to un-register anyone that is deceased," Green said. 

Mullaly has also claimed a six-day delay in the availability of primary election absentee ballots in Pennington County is the fault of Green's office. South Dakota Searchlight reported auditor's offices in counties throughout South Dakota experienced the delay, including Codington and Harding counties.

Under South Dakota law, absentee voting is scheduled to begin 46 days prior to an election, which is April 17. Absentee ballots in Pennington County were not made available until April 23.

State law as it currently stands places the candidate filing deadline on the last Tuesday of March. This year, that was March 31, which is 17 days before absentee voting is set to begin. Generally, the last Tuesday rules allows for more time to print the ballots.

Per Searchlight, lawmakers earlier this year declined to heed warnings from county auditors and apply a fix for this year’s election, citing concerns about changing the laws governing a candidate petition process that was already underway.

"The truth is that auditors across the state for two years traveled to Pierre or testified over the phone during legislative sessions to try and stop the problem before it would happen," Green said.

 County building outside
The June 2 election season includes Sabrina Green and Tina Mulally running for county auditor in Pennington County. 

House Bill 1095, which moves the filing deadline to the third Tuesday of March to provide more breathing room, passed in the 2026 legislative session. Mulally voted against the bill, which doesn’t go into affect until July 1, 2026. Green pointed out Mulally's no vote.

Mulally also pointed out that under the current Auditor's Office, Pennington County paid more than $87,000 in IRS penalties tied to payroll tax errors.

Per previous reporting by the Journal, the penalty occurred in 2019 under then-Auditor Julie Pearson, who served as the auditor for 32 years until Mohler was elected to the position in November 2018. The issue came when county employees were paid once per month, but were the given the option of receiving a mid-month paycheck.

Employees who participated in the mid-month draw received one payment on the 15th each month and the end of each month. The county did not withhold payroll taxes from the mid-month checks. Instead, the county waited until the end of each month to withhold payroll taxes from employees' total monthly pay.

The county was found to be late each month in remitting federal payroll taxes that should have been withheld from mid-month checks. The payroll errors occurred from 2016 through 2018.

More than half of the county’s employees participated in the program, Mohler said at the time.

Green joined the Auditor's Office in 2018.

Mulally has also targeted Green for filing for Chapter 7 bankruptcy nearly a decade ago, saying in a Facebook post, “… when you’re asking voters to trust you with public finances, accuracy and transparency matter.”

Per U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of South Dakota records, Green and her husband jointly filed the petition for Chapter 7 bankruptcy on Oct. 18, 2017, listing $255,612 in liabilities. The debts included over $71,000 in student loans, just shy of $25,000 in other debts (banks and some medical) and $159,342 in claims on property. That property was $155,000 owed on their house, $11,000 owed on a 2010 Chevy Traverse and $6,000 owed on a 2005 Chevy Trailblazer.

The Greens both completed credit counseling, as evidenced by certificates filed with the court, also on Oct. 18, 2017. They also completed financial management courses. Those certificates were filed on Dec. 1, 2017. The case was closed on March 2, 2018.

Green addressed the assertions directly in a Facebook post on May 20, “Over the past several days, campaign mailers have been sent discussing a difficult period in my personal life from almost 10 years ago. There have been several misleading statements made regarding my past bankruptcy.

“To be clear, my student loans were not discharged in bankruptcy, and my home loan obligations were not simply erased. Like many families facing hardship, we worked through a legal financial process during a difficult period in our lives.

“I understand voters have questions, and I respect that. But I also believe this election should focus on qualifications, experience, integrity, and who is prepared to serve as County Auditor on day one.

“Since 2018, I have worked in the Auditor’s Office serving the residents of Pennington County, and I remain committed to doing this job professionally, ethically, and with transparency.”

Green told the Journal, "In the end, I am a wife and a mother who worked her way through getting an education and a career while raising a family. Every family has good times and bad times in life and I am proud of the way I have worked through my lean times. I have a long history of accuracy and integrity. If elected, I will continue to do the job of being the Pennington County Auditor."

Addressing Mullaly’s approach, Green said, “I would encourage you to look at her campaign record in previous elections, and you will see a trend. This is how she campaigns. There is also a record of my opponent’s miscalculations, hostile rhetoric and negative campaign tactics."

Who won in 2020?

Both Green and Mulally were asked their thoughts on the 2020 presidential election. President Joe Biden won the election, with multiple courts striking down multiple attempts by President Donald Trump to overturn the results based on unfounded claims of fraud.

“With the 2020 election, it brought increased public attention to the election process across the country, and with that came more questions about voter integrity and election security. In South Dakota, our elections are administered locally with multiple safeguards in place, including public testing of equipment, bipartisan election boards, chain of custody procedures and canvassing processes designed to ensure accuracy and accountability,” Green said.

Mulally said, “As for the 2020 election, Joe Biden served as president. My focus is not relitigating national politics. My focus is Pennington County — running accurate elections, maintaining clean voter rolls and restoring confidence in the process here at home.”

Election

The county set the minimum yearly salary for the auditor to $110,000 annually in January. Green currently earns $112,000 per year. Mohler's final salary before retirement was $131,934.40. 

Absentee voting began on Thursday, April 23, after the delay because of ballot printing issues, and continues until 4 p.m. on Monday, June 1, at the Pennington County Administrative Building at 900 Concourse Drive.

June 2 is Election Day.

title: Pennington County Commission Q&A with District 1 candidate Mike Mueller
description: Name, age, occupation
_full_text:
Name, age, occupation

Mike Mueller, 63, Retired Mechanical Engineer

Why are you running?

Twenty-three years of my career was spent in public service and the other 14+ was in the private sector. I have seen both the taxpayer and tax spending side of the equation. I believe that the insight from my career of facilities and construction management along with decades of volunteer service will serve me well as a commissioner. I like to solve problems and am dedicated to make government both efficient and effective. I would also like to introduce one evening Board of Commissioners meeting each month to allow our constituents (taxpayers) to attend, just as both school boards and city councils meet now.

 Mueller 905 2022 full res (1).jpg
Mike Mueller 

What are the top three issues Pennington County faces that you would work to address on the council? Is there anything specific to your ward?

1. Property taxes

2. Necessary funding of all first responders

3. Overall budget review

Specifically, I have heard that ambulance service may be in jeopardy for volunteer fire districts with regard to funding.

Should the county zoning plan allow wind and solar projects on agricultural land? Why or why not?

No. I appreciate the recent ordinance change proposed by Planning and Zoning to remove agricultural land and to utilize only Industrial Zoned Sites for these projects. (SECTION 317 – ALTERNATIVE ENERGY AND BATTERY ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS, Section C.8.a) I would like to see as much agricultural land stay in production as possible. As the saying goes: KNOW FARMS, KNOW FOOD --- NO FARMS, NO FOOD.

Should the county institute the state-approved 0.5% sales tax for use toward property tax relief? Why or why not?

No. This becomes a tax shift and even though Pennington County may gain revenue from neighboring counties, those neighboring county’s will then be overtaxed by paying extra sales tax here and still have the same tax burden in their home county.

 Elections

Also, if implemented, when does any new tax ever go away? When the state sales tax went up from 4.0% to 4.5% for teacher pay, two things occurred. One: the tax quickly went into the general fund instead of a dedicated teacher pay fund. Two: The anticipated tax revenue was less than the proportional tax increase because people didn’t spend at the same rate as before.

What approach to Tax Increment Financing would you bring to the commission?

TIF’s should be used in a very limited way. The spirit of the law is to use TIF’s for truly blighted areas. Too many times the public (tax dollars) are used or leveraged to show a private entity that we want them to join our community. That intent is outside the proper use of a TIF and more scrutiny of the use of public funds (tax dollars) to subsidize investors is needed. I believe the TIF related statutes need to be reviewed and tightened up.

What are your goals with the 2027 county budget?

It would be great to find ways to reduce the county budget. I want to introduce Zero Based Budgeting for every county department. This means that each department starts with a blank budget sheet and builds each component of the budget to layout a realistic budget. Major components would include personnel, equipment, consumable supplies, leases, and major purchases. By starting at Zero (0) every budget cycle would prevent us from past practices of “use it or lose it” and then just adding the maximum percentage allowable to the previous budget.

Another aspect of county spending relates to looking at Constitutional and Statutory requirements of the county as the highest priority, then carefully evaluate programs beyond that scope.

After the county 2026 budget was passed, residents had concerns over budget cuts to public services like the public library. What are your thoughts on such cuts by the county?

I believe every part of the budget needs to be scrutinized and justified as the steep increase in property taxes, which funds approximately 50% of this county’s budget, has put many homeowners at risk of losing their homes. Auxiliary services may need to come up with other means of funding or scale back on the services. We need to concentrate on essential services, such as first responders (ambulance and firefighters), law enforcement, and maintaining safe roads.

title: Rapid City Council Q&A with Ward 4 candidate John Roberts
description: Name, age, occupation
_full_text:
Name, age, occupation

John Roberts, 60, real estate Broker/Owner, The Real Estate Group.

Why are you running?

The reason I decided to run again is that I am in the middle of some important city projects that I want to see finished, Like the new maintenance facility which I have worked with staff on to cut millions of dollars out of their projected project costs, new fire dept which I helped the city to determine a location and funding sources, new water tower and multiple street projects in my ward.

 John.RobertsMug.jpg
City Council Ward 4 Candidate John Roberts

What are the top three issues Rapid City faces that you would work to address on the council? Is there anything specific to your ward?

The three most important things I have heard from my constituents are crime, affordable housing, and the cost of living (utility rates and property taxes being the two major issues). In my ward I worked with and helped the city to locate and purchase our new police precinct

In Ward 4, which will be paid for thru the Marshall Heights Tract Tax Increment Financing District, I have helped bring hundreds of units of affordable housing to Rapid City, and with the utility rates I was opposed to and voted against the rate increases as I believed there were other more affordable options and we are currently working on some that may reduce some of those future increases.

What approach to Tax Increment Financing would you bring to the council?

My entire career on the City Council I have been pro-TIF, we have had many good TIFs, like Rushmore Crossing, Buffalo Crossing and Shepard Meadows. It is one of the few tools we have to fund the city’s infrastructure and create growth, I have been very supportive of the city using the TIF but I have also stopped many TIFs. One of the most recent was the Robbinsdale overlay TIF that would not have been good for the Residents of Rapid City and would have raised taxes.

How should the city approach growth?

I think the city’s primary focus on growth should be in our core and finding ways to use the tremendous amount of infill properties we have. A few years ago I helped create the East of 5th zoning district that has helped with some infill projects like the Elements Apartment retail building, I think that zoning can be a fantastic tool to spur growth and help with affordability, I also believe that we need to focus more on the industrial/manufacturing sector to create more higher-paying jobs to help keep more of our children from moving elsewhere.

What is working and what needs to be fixed in the city’s approach to homeless people? What should the city’s role be in addiction services and how should the city use opioid settlement funds toward fulfilling that role?

The homeless issues is a very complex issue that the city invests millions of dollars a year into and I think a positive step forward that I have advocated for many years for is a West River mental health / long term addiction center I believe this will have to partnership with the State for long term funding and the hospitals and I believe this would be a good investment of our opioid settlement money.

 Elections

There are a few things that I am currently working on to help with the affordability issues we have in Rapid City as most people know I was not in support of the huge utility fee raises and voted against them but since they have already started we are looking for ways to offset some of those future increases with other funding and better newer technology also working on ways to make it more affordable to build housing in Rapid City through some zoning changes.

Thank you for your support and I hope I have earned your vote in the upcoming June 2nd election.

title: Vendors Emporium and Curiosities tenants told to vacate by former South Dakota senator
byline: SHALOM BAER GEE and TANYA MANUS Journal staff
description: After about a year and a half of Vendors Emporium and Curiosities operating in Rapid City adjacent to the city’s first cat cafe, the owner of both businesses — former South Dakota Sen. Jessica Castleberry — notified vendors their leases will not be renewed and threatened legal action against them and her son, her former business partner.
_full_text:
After about a year and a half of Vendors Emporium and Curiosities operating in Rapid City adjacent to the city’s first cat cafe, the owner of both businesses — former South Dakota Sen. Jessica Castleberry — notified vendors their leases will not be renewed and threatened legal action against them and her son, her former business partner.

The Emporium is located at 315 B E. St. Patrick St. in the Robbinsdale neighborhood, accessible only through Coffee and the Cats, which opened in spring 2024 featuring adoptable cats. The Emporium opened in spring 2025 under a vendor model, with multiple booths offering art, hand-crafted items, locally-baked goods and troves of trinkets.

 The ever-changing Emporium
This March 2025 photo shows merchandise for sale at the Vendors Emporium and Curiosities. 

Castleberry, who has previously provided Kersey as her last name to the Journal in a story about the emporium, owns both businesses.

In December 2019, then-Gov. Kristi Noem appointed her to finish out Lyndi DiSanto’s term in the Senate, effective Jan. 1, 2020. Voters then elected Castleberry to the position in November 2020 and November 2022. In August 2023, Castleberry resigned from her seat in the Senate after a South Dakota Attorney General’s Office investigation found Castleberry improperly received COVID-19 stimulus funds for her preschools in Rapid City, violating the state’s constitution.

South Dakota Public Broadcasting reported Castleberry defaulted on her payments to return nearly $500,000 on Nov. 4, 2024, a few weeks before shutting down both Little Nest Preschool locations on Nov. 27, 2024, due to "unforeseen catastrophic circumstances.”

Castleberry’s 20-year-old twin children, Lukas Linn and Claire Linn, previously co-owned Coffee and the Cats with their mother.

The Linns sold their shares to their mother in July 2025 because of financial issues, disagreements and feeling “exploited,” Lukas Linn told the Journal over the phone, before later writing an email stating, “I have not been served a formal cease and desist, but I have been threatened legal action by my mother if I continue to speak on the Vendor Emporium situation. I will respect her order.”

South Dakota Secretary of State business records show on July 31, 2025, a filing put the business in Castleberry’s name. Castleberry did not respond to a request for comment about her children leaving the business. The Emporium has been under Castleberry’s name alone since its initial filing with the state in March 2025. Per Journal reporting in March 2025, the Emporium was created by Castleberry and Lukas Linn. However, Lukas is not listed officially on business documents with the state.

On Friday, May 17, Emporium vendors received the first email stating they have until 6 p.m. on June 3 to clear out of the space. The next day, they received a second email signed “Vendor Emporium Management.” It threatened legal action “if slanderous public statements are not removed online and/or continue.” A post on the Rapid City subreddit by someone claiming to be a vendor received traction.

The first email to vendors, signed “Jessica,” explained “due to a recent change in our lease, we are no longer permitted to sublet vendor space.” The email said all April sales will be fully accounted for and paid out no later than May 31, and all May sales will be fully accounted for and paid out no later than June 30.

“We are committed to making this transition as smooth as possible. If there’s anything you need during this time, please let us know. Thank you for being part of this space and for everything you’ve contributed – it truly has meant a lot,” the email continued.

Castleberry told the Journal over text message, “The Emporium is not closing. Vendors were there on a month-to-month lease with the understanding that either party could terminate the lease before the 20th of the month. Vendors were notified on the 18th that their leases would not be renewed according to those terms.”

Castleberry did not confirm the emails, but her comments reflected the information contained in them. She also highlighted she granted a grace period up to June 3, even though leases are up at the end of May, “as a courtesy to remove their items and to enable them to sell fully through the 31st (of May).”

“We received 17 days' notice. That’s pretty quick to change your business model,” a vendor speaking anonymously said.

A vendor speaking anonymously said the Vendors Emporium had served as their business’ storefront, noting that being left without a storefront just as tourist season is beginning is particularly stressful.

“We depend on our (income), even if it’s less than $100. That’s still money in our pocket that pays our bills, feeds our families,” the vendor said.

Vendors have confirmed with the Journal the lease terms were in fact month-to-month and did not provide for a 30-day notice.

When asked about the reason for the change and future business model, Castleberry said, “Several factors came in to play when making this decision. This is one of the benefits of having a month-to-month lease because it provides flexibility for both parties as needs change. The plan is to continue the Emporium with a retail and event space where the community can continue to gather.”

 Vendor Emporium Reddit post
This Reddit post from a person claiming to be a vendor at Vendors Emporium and Curiosities in Rapid City garnered attention from the local community. 

 Vendor Emporium Email, May 17
This May 17 email informing tenants at the Vendors Emporium and Curiosities their leases will not be removed was provided to the Journal by a vendor on the condition of anonymity. 

 Vendor Emporium Email, May 18
This May 18 email telling tenants at the Vendors Emporium and Curiosities they could face legal action for comments made publicly was provided to the Journal by a vendor on the condition of anonymity.

title: What state law says about Rep. Heather Baxter running for 2 offices at same time
description: Rep. Heather Baxter, R-Rapid City, is taking an either-or approach to public service.
_full_text:
Rep. Heather Baxter, R-Rapid City, is taking an either-or approach to public service.

She is on the June 2 primary ballot, seeking re-election to represent District 34 in the South Dakota House of Representatives. She is also running for South Dakota Secretary of State. The Journal reached out to the Pennington County Republican Party and the South Dakota Republican Party and reviewed the law to learn more about a candidate’s ability to run for legislative and constitutional offices at the same time.

"I am running for both, so at one position or another, I can continue being a public servant for South Dakotans. It's not about me, but what do the people of South Dakota want when they elect me to either position? I want to continue to be a voice for South Dakota and what the people are asking for in whichever position they elect me," Baxter told the Journal.

There are 35 legislative districts in South Dakota, each with one senator and two representatives. All 70 House seats and all 35 Senate seats are up for election this year for two-year terms. District 34 includes western Rapid City and extends into rural Pennington County.

The primary election for legislative races is on June 2, with potential runoff elections taking place on July 28, with winners advancing to the November ballot. The South Dakota State Republican Convention runs from June 25 through the 27 in Rapid City. At the convention, either Baxter or incumbent Monae Johnson will be nominated for South Dakota Secretary of State.

In the GOP primary election, Baxter is competing against Becky Drury and incumbent Mike Derby for two of the party’s slots on the general election ballot in Nov. 3.

Baxter said she has been open and transparent about running for both a legislative and a constitutional seat. 

Law allows Baxter to run for both, but what happens if she wins both?

According to SDCL 12-6-3, a candidate cannot appear on the primary election ballot for more than one public office (such as in the legislative races), but can be a candidate for constitutional offices.

Legislative seats are positions in the House and the Senate. The state’s constitutional offices are Attorney General, Secretary of State, State Auditor, Treasurer, and Commissioner of Public Schools and Lands, as laid out in the state constitution. The respective political parties nominate their candidates for constitutional offices at their conventions before the November election.

Pennington County Republican Party Chair Amy Wagner said if Baxter wins in the legislative primary and is nominated for the constitutional office, she will have to choose which seat to pursue. If she chooses South Dakota Secretary of State, the Pennington County Central Committee will have to fill her primary slot on the general election ballot. If she chooses to withdraw from the constitutional office instead, the state party central committee could pick a replacement.

 Heather Baxter
Heather Baxter is a Republican candidate running for re-election to represent House District 34 and for the party’s Secretary of State for South Dakota nomination. 

This withdrawal would have to be made on or before the date on which the Secretary of State candidate receives the state party certification, according to state law. SDCL 12-8-6 states, "Nominations by party committee to fill vacancies occurring in nominations made in primary elections and certificates of nomination to be filed with the secretary of state and those to be filed with the county auditor shall be filed not later than the second Tuesday in August at 5 p.m. or mailed by registered mail by that date and time prior to the election."

The law clarifies that if the individual is a current legislator, they are not resigning in their current role as a legislator, as the person would not take office in the constitutional position until being sworn into the office in January 2027.

"I have only been through this once and never this scenario, so I believe that it would be a central committee nomination, and then we would have a central committee meeting, where the nominations would come from, and then they would be voted on by the central committee," Wagner said.

Candidates for nomination could be anyone in District 34, not just the candidates who ran in the election for the same seat, Wagner said.

If she does not get picked for a House, Baxter is still able to be nominated for Secretary of State. If she is picked for the House seat, and not nominated for the constitutional office, then she can still appear on the November ballot.

Baxter said she has no preference for which position she appears on the ballot for and said she would prefer the people decide. She didn’t answer a question about which she’d choose, though she’ll have to if she wins the primary and is nominated at convention.

State party chair ‘wouldn’t like to see a whole of’ running for two offices

Jim Eschenbaum, the chair of the South Dakota Republican Party, said this strategy of running for two offices is rare and has caused discussion within the party.

"I don't know if it's a moral or ethics question, but I certainly would say I wouldn't like to see a whole lot of it," Eschenbaum said.

Eschenbaum said this dual running is legal and does happen every couple of election cycles, but he has gripes with the strategy in general. 

The Journal asked Baxter if she has addressed concerns by her constituents.

"I heard one precinct person from the east side of the state who said to me I shouldn't run for both offices, and I saw one Political Action Committee postcard that showed disdain for my choice for running for both positions. The Republican bylaws allow Constitutional Officers to run for two positions; I'm not the first to do it. I would suggest the precinct person or the PAC (Political Action Committees) change the bylaws if they don't like them. I will continue to stand for and support wherever they elect me in our state, where 'Under God People Rule.’”

title: Green vs. Mulally: A contentious Pennington County Auditor race
description: The Pennington County Auditor's race is contested this year with current Auditor Sabrina Green and Rep. Tina Mulally, R-District 35, going to bat for the position. Green’s relied on her experience at the office and Mulally’s pointed to her own track record while dredging up Green’s financial past and bumps in the road at the office.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Auditor's race is contested this year with current Auditor Sabrina Green and Rep. Tina Mulally, R-District 35, going to bat for the position. Green’s relied on her experience at the office and Mulally’s pointed to her own track record while dredging up Green’s financial past and bumps in the road at the office.

Cindy Mohler had been the county auditor from 2018 until she announced her early retirement in October 2025. She told the Journal the reason for her resignation is to mark a new beginning in her life.

Green has worked at the Auditor's Office since 2018 and served as deputy auditor under Mohler. The Pennington County Board of Commissioners appointed Green to the auditor position to finish out Mohler's term, which is set to end March 2, 2027. The election is on Tuesday, June 2. 

According to the county website, the auditor’s office is responsible for auditing all accounts and maintaining all financial records for the county, including payroll, preparing the annual budget, establishing levies and apportioning all tax collections. The office also conducts elections and maintains all records of voter registration and election history. The county auditor position is a four-year term. 

Meet the candidates

 Sabrina Green
Sabrina Green 

Green told the Journal she is running because she values accuracy and transparency in the Auditor's Office.

"There is no room for fabrication or cutting corners. I learned under the previous auditor that the office demands a standard of honesty, which is why I’m proud of both endorsements," Green said.

"I don’t get to decide whether I like the outcome. My job is to make sure the process is clean and the count is right. We saw that play out recently with the Libertyland vote. That was a closely watched, emotionally charged election, and when the results came in, they stood up to scrutiny because the process was sound," Green said about election integrity. 

The Destination District Tax Increment Financing District was a $125 million TIF for infrastructure needed for the development of a mixed-use development including Libertyland USA, an America themed amusement park. This was taken to a public vote in January, where Rapid City residents voted to deny the TIF.

 Tina Mulally
Tina Mulally 

Mullaly has been a state representative for District 35 since 2018 and has served on the House Appropriations Committee for eight years, according to her website.

"I’m running for Pennington County Auditor because the county needs a change. The Auditor’s Office oversees taxpayer dollars, elections, voter registration and public records. When the office fails, taxpayers and voters pay the price," Mullaly said.

"My approach is different. On appropriations, I reviewed budgets line by line and asked questions when numbers didn’t add up. As SDGOP (South Dakota Republican Party) Treasurer, I uncovered neglected accounts, unexplained expenses and recurring charges no one had questioned. I fixed the problems instead of ignoring them," Mulally said on her experience.

Mulally claims

Mulally has criticized Green's ability to properly manage the Auditor's Office, pointing out Clinton and Cristen Brink, who were attacked and killed in Arkansas in July of 2025, were still listed as active voters in Pennington County until recently.

"State law requires voter registrations to be canceled upon notice of death. Voters should not have to question whether voter rolls are accurate or procedures are being followed. Pennington County deserves an Auditor’s Office that is accurate, organized and accountable. That is why I am running," Mulally said.

Green said after it was brought to the office's attention, the office confirmed their obituary details and removed them from the rolls. Green said their records found the Brinks last voted on Nov. 5, 2024, in the general election the year before they died.

The South Dakota Secretary of State's Office confirmed neither Clinton or Cristen Brink listed as active voters as of May 26.

"Voter removal is governed by the state law and requires documentation. If the death certificate is filed in the state of South Dakota the system will run through the database and we are able to un-register anyone that is deceased," Green said. 

Mullaly has also claimed a six-day delay in the availability of primary election absentee ballots in Pennington County is the fault of Green's office. South Dakota Searchlight reported auditor's offices in counties throughout South Dakota experienced the delay, including Codington and Harding counties.

Under South Dakota law, absentee voting is scheduled to begin 46 days prior to an election, which is April 17. Absentee ballots in Pennington County were not made available until April 23.

State law as it currently stands places the candidate filing deadline on the last Tuesday of March. This year, that was March 31, which is 17 days before absentee voting is set to begin. Generally, the last Tuesday rules allows for more time to print the ballots.

Per Searchlight, lawmakers earlier this year declined to heed warnings from county auditors and apply a fix for this year’s election, citing concerns about changing the laws governing a candidate petition process that was already underway.

"The truth is that auditors across the state for two years traveled to Pierre or testified over the phone during legislative sessions to try and stop the problem before it would happen," Green said.

 County building outside
The June 2 election season includes Sabrina Green and Tina Mulally running for county auditor in Pennington County. 

House Bill 1095, which moves the filing deadline to the third Tuesday of March to provide more breathing room, passed in the 2026 legislative session. Mulally voted against the bill, which doesn’t go into affect until July 1, 2026. Green pointed out Mulally's no vote.

Mulally also pointed out that under the current Auditor's Office, Pennington County paid more than $87,000 in IRS penalties tied to payroll tax errors.

Per previous reporting by the Journal, the penalty occurred in 2019 under then-Auditor Julie Pearson, who served as the auditor for 32 years until Mohler was elected to the position in November 2018. The issue came when county employees were paid once per month, but were the given the option of receiving a mid-month paycheck.

Employees who participated in the mid-month draw received one payment on the 15th each month and the end of each month. The county did not withhold payroll taxes from the mid-month checks. Instead, the county waited until the end of each month to withhold payroll taxes from employees' total monthly pay.

The county was found to be late each month in remitting federal payroll taxes that should have been withheld from mid-month checks. The payroll errors occurred from 2016 through 2018.

More than half of the county’s employees participated in the program, Mohler said at the time.

Green joined the Auditor's Office in 2018.

Mulally has also targeted Green for filing for Chapter 7 bankruptcy nearly a decade ago, saying in a Facebook post, “… when you’re asking voters to trust you with public finances, accuracy and transparency matter.”

Per U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of South Dakota records, Green and her husband jointly filed the petition for Chapter 7 bankruptcy on Oct. 18, 2017, listing $255,612 in liabilities. The debts included over $71,000 in student loans, just shy of $25,000 in other debts (banks and some medical) and $159,342 in claims on property. That property was $155,000 owed on their house, $11,000 owed on a 2010 Chevy Traverse and $6,000 owed on a 2005 Chevy Trailblazer.

The Greens both completed credit counseling, as evidenced by certificates filed with the court, also on Oct. 18, 2017. They also completed financial management courses. Those certificates were filed on Dec. 1, 2017. The case was closed on March 2, 2018.

Green addressed the assertions directly in a Facebook post on May 20, “Over the past several days, campaign mailers have been sent discussing a difficult period in my personal life from almost 10 years ago. There have been several misleading statements made regarding my past bankruptcy.

“To be clear, my student loans were not discharged in bankruptcy, and my home loan obligations were not simply erased. Like many families facing hardship, we worked through a legal financial process during a difficult period in our lives.

“I understand voters have questions, and I respect that. But I also believe this election should focus on qualifications, experience, integrity, and who is prepared to serve as County Auditor on day one.

“Since 2018, I have worked in the Auditor’s Office serving the residents of Pennington County, and I remain committed to doing this job professionally, ethically, and with transparency.”

Green told the Journal, "In the end, I am a wife and a mother who worked her way through getting an education and a career while raising a family. Every family has good times and bad times in life and I am proud of the way I have worked through my lean times. I have a long history of accuracy and integrity. If elected, I will continue to do the job of being the Pennington County Auditor."

Addressing Mullaly’s approach, Green said, “I would encourage you to look at her campaign record in previous elections, and you will see a trend. This is how she campaigns. There is also a record of my opponent’s miscalculations, hostile rhetoric and negative campaign tactics."

Who won in 2020?

Both Green and Mulally were asked their thoughts on the 2020 presidential election. President Joe Biden won the election, with multiple courts striking down multiple attempts by President Donald Trump to overturn the results based on unfounded claims of fraud.

“With the 2020 election, it brought increased public attention to the election process across the country, and with that came more questions about voter integrity and election security. In South Dakota, our elections are administered locally with multiple safeguards in place, including public testing of equipment, bipartisan election boards, chain of custody procedures and canvassing processes designed to ensure accuracy and accountability,” Green said.

Mulally said, “As for the 2020 election, Joe Biden served as president. My focus is not relitigating national politics. My focus is Pennington County — running accurate elections, maintaining clean voter rolls and restoring confidence in the process here at home.”

Election

The county set the minimum yearly salary for the auditor to $110,000 annually in January. Green currently earns $112,000 per year. Mohler's final salary before retirement was $131,934.40. 

Absentee voting began on Thursday, April 23, after the delay because of ballot printing issues, and continues until 4 p.m. on Monday, June 1, at the Pennington County Administrative Building at 900 Concourse Drive.

June 2 is Election Day.
