title: Air Force Academy Band to kick off Rapid City's America 250 celebration
description: The United States Air Force Academy Band has released its 2026 summer tour. Entitled “Freedom 250”, the tour will include a concert to kick off Rapid City’s America 250 Birthday Bash.
_full_text:
The United States Air Force Academy Band has released its 2026 summer tour. Entitled “Freedom 250”, the tour will include a concert to kick off Rapid City’s America 250 Birthday Bash.

The Air Force Academy Band’s concert is scheduled for Rapid City’s Memorial Park Band Shell Wednesday, July 1 at 7 p.m. The event is part of Rapid City’s Real America Birthday Bash of events July 1-5.

“We are extremely excited to kick off the multi-day Real America Birthday Bash with the US Air Force Academy Band,” said Visit Rapid City CEO Ally Formanek. “The concert will set the patriotic tone to several days of celebration in Rapid City and we are pleased the group is making Rapid City a part of their summer tour.”

The US Air Force Academy Band’s summer tour includes stops at Colorado Springs, CO, Broomfield, CO, Casper,WY, Belle Fourche, Rapid City and Mount Rushmore.

 USAF Academy Band -7.1-IG-1080x1080.jpg

The USAF Academy Band is made up of 60 premier active-duty musicians. Audiences will enjoy a vibrant musical program to honor America from the Revolution to the 21st century and beyond featuring patriotic favorites, American classics and modern selections across genres – including jazz, pop, country and beloved film scores – all performed by world-class musicians.

Admission is free and concerts are open to the public. No tickets are required but early arrival is strongly encouraged. Attendees are asked to bring a lawn chair or blanket and enjoy an evening of music.

In addition to the academy band concert, the “Real America Birthday Bash” will also include a patriotic drone show, community parade, downtown festival spanning multiple days, a Mount Rushmore fireworks display viewing party from Main Street Square, a performance by country singer Chancey Williams, events in Memorial Park, the City’s fireworks display, a Kids’ Zone, a 5K Freedom Run, interactive exhibits, performances by local and regional bands, historical reenactments and patriotic readings.

To learn more about this summer’s “Real America Birthday Bash” events, visit www.realamericabirthdaybash.com or contact Visit Rapid City at 605-718-8484/800-487-3223.

title: Local money flows to Virginia PAC before landing in Rapid City Council race
byline: FRANK ESPINOZA and MIKE BROWNLEE Journal staff
description: A local gas station ownership group has funneled $31,000 through an out-of-state super PAC to a quartet of candidates in the Rapid City Council race.
_full_text:
A local gas station ownership group has funneled $31,000 through an out-of-state super PAC to a quartet of candidates in the Rapid City Council race.

PSA PAC Inc., a Virginia-headquartered super political action committee, made the contributions. The PAC is solely funded by Rapid City-based Moyle Petroleum Company — which owns Common Cents gas stations in South Dakota, Nebraska, Wyoming and Utah — according to Federal Election Commission records.

According to FEC filings, Moyle Petroleum donated $377,500 to the super PAC from July of 2025 through March of 2026. Super PACs are also known as independent expenditure-only PACs.

The Rapid City Council race contributions, according to candidate filings with the city:

Challenger Pat Roseland, $11,500

Councilman Josh Biberdorf, $5,000

Councilwoman Lindsey Seachris, $5,000

Councilman Kevin Maher, $10,000

Biberdorf (Ward 1), Seachris (Ward 2) and Maher (Ward 3) are seeking re-election on June 2. Roseland previously served on the council from 2022 to 2025 for Ward 5 and is seeking a return to the council.

Other challengers are Murray Lee (Ward 1), Christopher Vanderhoof (Ward 2), Andrea Schaefer (Ward 3), Valeriah Big Eagle (Ward 4) and Laura Armstrong (Ward 5).

Ward 4 candidate Ardin Cychosz announced on April 15 that he would be dropping out due to work-related schedule conflicts, but his name appears on the ballot.

PSA PAC Inc.’s treasurer is Chris Marston, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Marston works at Virginia-based Dunlap, Bennett & Ludwig and focuses his practice on political and election law, providing financial and compliance services, “to Republican campaigns and party committees, conservative political action committees, tax-exempt organizations, and corporate and trade association PACs,” according to the firm’s website.

The organization has given to candidates in other Rapid City races in the past, including $5,000 apiece to Roseland and Councilman Lance Lehmann during the 2025 council race.

Other contributions

The Rapid City-based Free Republic PAC gave $7,000 apiece to Councilman John Roberts and Maher and $2,000 apiece to Seachris, Roseland and Biberdorf, according to its pre-primary filing with the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office. Maher is listed as the PAC’s treasurer.

The PAC’s pre-primary filing shows Craig Mount of Rapid City and Atlantis LLC both gave $10,000 to the PAC.

Paul J. Bradsky is listed as the registered agent for Atlantis LLC, according to South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office business records. Its address is 927 Main St., home of Bradsky, Bradsky & Bradsky law firm. Mount is a local entrepreneur and co-founder of the multi-million dollar company Nerdy Nuts.

The Pennington County Democratic Party PAC gave $600 to Armstrong, $1,250 to Big Eagle and $905 to Schaefer, according to its pre-primary filing. The PAC is chaired by Ranee Haglund, the county’s Democratic Party chairwoman. Lee received a combined donation of $2,000 from Ranee and Brian Haglund.

Democracy in Action PAC contributed $1,000 apiece to Armstrong, Lee, Vanderhoof, Big Eagle and Schaefer, according to its pre-primary filing. DIA is a Rapid City-based PAC that lists retired school nurse Susan Kelts as committee chair.

Rapid City Finance Director Daniel Ainslie told the Journal city ordinance does not prohibit super PAC participation. Asked if super PACs can give directly to candidates, a South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office official pointed to state law on the matter. That section of code, SDCL 12-27-7, notes there is no limit on donations political action committees can make. The law does not address super PACs.

title: Pine Ridge man pleads not guilty in deadly crash after a pursuit
description: A Pine Ridge man pleaded not guilty to first-degree manslaughter and second-degree eluding for a Rapid City car crash that left four other people injured and one dead.
_full_text:
A Pine Ridge man pleaded not guilty to first-degree manslaughter and second-degree eluding for a Rapid City car crash that left four other people injured and one dead. 

Torry Ghost Bear, 31, appeared for his arraignment before Circuit Court Judge Joshua Hendrickson at the Pennington County Courthouse Monday, June 1. 

Ghost Bear is indicted for first-degree manslaughter, a Class C felony with a maximum sentence of life in prison and a $50,000 fine, second-degree eluding, a Class 6 felony with a maximum sentence of two years in prison and a $4,000 fine and false personation, which is Class 1 misdemeanor that carries up to one year in jail and a $2,000 fine. 

The state also filed Part II information, labeling Ghost Bear as a habitual offender. According to the information, Ghost Bear was previously convicted in March 2020 for sexual abuse of a minor. In April 2023 he was convicted of possession of a controlled drug or substance and in November 2024 he was convicted of failure to register as a sex offender. 

The Department of Public Safety said the preliminary information indicated that during an attempted traffic stop on Feb. 5, for not having a license plate Ghost Bear failed to pull over and initiated a pursuit with law enforcement. 

Ghost Bear then allegedly drove past a stop sign, entering the intersection of North Cherry Avenue and East North Street and was struck by a 2022 Ford F350 traveling eastbound on East North Street. 

Four occupants of Ghost Bear's vehicle, a 2012 Jeep Liberty, sustained serious injuries and were transported to the hospital. One of the passengers, Mia Lane Carpio, 22, died Feb. 12 from her injuries. The driver of the Ford also sustained injuries and was transported to the hospital. 

Ghost Bear's next motions hearing is set for June 22 at 3:15 p.m.

title: Deibert wins in Senate District 31: South Dakota election live updates
description: Voting has wrapped up throughout South Dakota .
_full_text:
Voting has wrapped up throughout South Dakota.

The ballot for Republican primary is full of contested races from U.S. Senate and House to Pennington County Commission. In Rapid City, voters in each of the five wards will choose between a pair of candidates. Two council members represent each ward, making for a total of 10 seats, half of which are up for grabs.

And the South Dakota Legislature features a number of contested races on the GOP side. There are no contested Democratic races in the Rapid City area.

A South Dakota Legislature result

10:33 p.m.: Sen. Randy Deibert of Spearfish will look to retain his seat in November and seems destined to as there’s no candidate on the Democratic side in District 31. Deibert beat challenger John Teupel, 56% to 44%, according to unofficial results from the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office. Deibert received 2,692 votes to Teupel’s 2,077.

District 31 covers Lawrence County, including Spearfish, Lead and Deadwood. Deibert first won election to the state Senate in 2022.

Update to Rapid City Council race results

9:23 p.m.: Councilman Josh Biberdorf seems poised to take the Ward 1 race. Biberdorf’s at 1,181 votes (72%) against Murray Lee (457 votes, 28%) with all five precincts partially reporting results, according to unofficial results from the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office.

In Ward 2, Councilwoman Lindsey Seachris (241 votes, 56%) leads Chris Vanderhoof (193 votes, 44%) and in Ward 3, Councilman Kevin Maher (572 votes, 62%) leads Andrea Schaefer (354, 38%). In Ward 4, Councilman John Roberts (458 votes, 50%) leads Valeriah Big Eagle (417 votes, 46%) and in Ward 5, Laura Armstrong (1,338 votes, 55%) leads Pat Roseland (1,079 votes, 45%).

Rapid City Council absentee voting results

8:23 p.m.: As of about 8 p.m., absentee ballots are in from the Rapid City Council election, the city said in an alert. It’s the first race since 2002 with contests in each of the city’s five wards. Here are the candidates who are in the lead, listed by ward. In-person votes are still being counted and the races are not over.

Ward 1

Josh Biberdorf has 71% of the counted votes with 568 in his favor. Murray Lee has 233 votes, 29% of the counted vote. Biberdorf is the incumbent.

Ward 2

Lindsey Seachris has 208 votes, 56% of those counted. Christopher Vanderhoof has 164 votes, 44% of those counted. Seachris is the incumbent.

Ward 3

Kevin Maher has 572 votes, 62% of those counted. Andrea Schaefer has 354 votes, 38% of those counted. Maher is the incumbent.

Ward 4

John Roberts has 214 votes, 65% of those counted. Challenger Valeriah Big Eagle has 122 votes, 35% of those counted. Ardin Jay Cychosz, who dropped out of the race in April, has 14 votes, 4% of the votes counted. Roberts is the incumbent.

Ward 5

Laura Armstrong has 413 votes, 54% of the votes counted. Pat Roseland has 345 votes, 46% of those counted. Armstrong and Roseland are vying for the seat to be vacated by Council President Rod Pettigrew, who is not running for re-election.

Associated Press calls U.S. Senate, U.S. House primaries

 Mike Rounds
Rounds 

The Associated Press has called the U.S. Senate and U.S. House Republican primaries for Sen. Mike Rounds and current South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley, respectively. Rounds beat Jeremy McNeal of Rapid City, while Jackley beat James Bialota of Rapid City.

 jackley mug (copy)
Jackley 

Rounds, of Pierre, is seeking his third term after winning elections in 2014 and 2020. In the November general election, the former South Dakota governor will face Democrat Julian Beaudion, a Sioux Falls nonprofit leader and former state trooper, and Independent Brian Bengs, an Air Force veteran who lives in Hot Springs.

Jackley, of Sturgis, advances to take on Democrat Nicole "Nikki" Gronli of rural Dell Rapids, who led USDA Rural Development in South Dakota from 2022 to 2025.

Personal connection a factor for voter

7:13 p.m.: At First Assembly of God Church on Rushmore Road in Rapid City, voter Michael Goodhope said he’s from Sturgis (and lives in Rapid City now) and knows Marty Jackley, a Republican candidate for U.S. House who’s currently the South Dakota attorney general.

The other important race, Goodhope said after casting his ballot around 6 p.m., was the Republican race for governor.

 060326-nws-election-live-mfb-p6.JPG
A man walks into vote at First Assembly of God Church on Rushmore Road on Tuesday, June 2, in Rapid City. 

“It was a tough choice because (Gov.) Larry Rhoden’s from Meade County. Ultimately, (I voted) for Dusty Johnson,” he said. “He has the Washington experience. I thought we needed that.”

“If you don’t vote, you can’t complain,” Goodhope said about the importance of voting, adding with a chuckle, “You can still complain if you vote. But you need to weigh in on it.”

The church is in Rapid City Council Ward 3, a race between Councilman Kevin Maher and challenger Andrea Schaefer.

Polls closed at 7 p.m.

7 p.m.: The polls are now closed across South Dakota.

West Middle School the location for two precincts

6 p.m. West Middle School Community Center at 1003 Sioux San Drive is the location for two voting precincts, 5-3 and 5-5. Just shy of 1,000 voters had cast their ballots by 4 p.m., with 366 voters from Precinct 5-3 and 628 from Precinct 5-5.

Both precincts are in Ward 5 for the municipal election and fall under District 34 in the legislative races. Poll workers told the Journal nearby construction on Sioux San Drive had been a common complaint amongst voters, but they were unsure if it deterred anyone from casting a ballot.

The Ward 5 municipal race is between Pat Roseland and Laura Armstrong, both former council members who represented Ward 5 in the past.

For the House race in District 34, Republicans Mike Derby, Heather Baxter and Becky Dury and Democrat Victor Diego Dominquez have thrown in their hats. Two Republicans will advance, as will Diego Dominquez, who is unopposed.

For the Senate seat in District 34, incumbent Taffy Howard is up against Jason Green in the primary. Michael Calabrese is the Democratic candidate who’ll advance to the general election in November.

Carrie Jeannie, 50, said about why she's voting, “The political stuff that's going on is really important these days, because there's just so much bad stuff that's happening in our country.”

Elections are, “giving us the opportunity to make our voices heard,” she said.

“We feel like we have more of an impact on local elections than really big statewide ones, so they do really matter,” Jeannie said.

Amber Tjeerdsma, 45, said, “This is our community, and if you want to be a part of the community, you have to contribute, and voting is just one small way that we can contribute.”

 West Middle School
West Middle School housed voting for both Precinct 5-3 and Precinct 5-5. 

Voting at Grandview Elementary School

3:53 p.m.: Construction at Grandview Elementary School and a slight relocation of the voting site in the school did not deter voters at Precinct 1-5. The precinct is located in Ward 1 for the municipal election and District 32 in the legislative races. Josh Biberdorf and Murray Lee are competing for the Ward 1 position on the council.

By 2 p.m. Tuesday, poll workers reported that 306 people had voted and there had been a continuous stream of voters arriving all day. Kathe Strand, superintendent of Precinct 1-5, arrived at Grandview at 6 a.m., where she was joined by four poll workers. Two ACLU volunteer observers were at the school as well, and they said voting had gone smoothly.

“It’s been very steady and it’s awesome,” Strand said. “It has been (all ages) and it’s awesome because you can’t gripe and moan and groan if you’re not going to vote.”

Husband and wife Don and Doneen Grimm of Rapid City have been lifelong voters. Doneen, 85, said voting is a habit.

“I always believe it’s a patriotic thing. We should always vote,” said Don, 91. “I wanted to vote for our governor and some other ones that I thought was good.”

Being a lifelong voter is a value Martha Rossiter of Rapid City wants to instill in her daughter. Martha, 47, brought her almost-10-year-old daughter, Theodora Rossiter, with her to vote at Grandview Elementary School. Theodora proudly wore an “I Voted” sticker even though she’s not yet of voting age.

“I always try and bring her voting so that she knows the importance of it, and knows how to do it and how easy it is and how important it is,” Martha said. “I think it’s important to vote every election opportunity because that’s the only way that we have a voice a lot of times.”

“In this particular voting session, it really it just important to vote. There weren’t issues that I necessarily got to weigh in on presently. It’s just another opportunity to come out and tell everybody I’m a Democrat and I’m here loud and proud about it.”

 Theodora and Martha Rossiter
Theodora Rossiter, left, accompanied her mother, Martha Rossiter, to vote at Grandview Elementary School on Tuesday, June 2, in Rapid City. Theodora will soon celebrate her tenth birthday. Martha brings her daughter to the polls to demonstrate the importance of voting. 

Checking in at the Moose Lodge

2:25 p.m.: 130 voters cast their ballots at Precinct 2-5, located at the Loyal Order of Moose Lodge at 841 E Saint Patrick St., as of around 12:45 p.m. The precinct is located in Ward 2 for the municipal election and District 32 in the legislative races. Lindsey Seachris and Christopher Vanderhoof are competing for the Ward 4 council seat up for election.

Voter and Rapid Citian Helen Walker, 70, said she usually votes early but due to life events and conflicting schedules she decided to vote on Tuesday, June 2. Walker said her experience voting on Tuesday was “excellent” and appreciated how informative the poll workers were.

Walker said there were two items on the ballot important to her; the governor's race and the Rapid City Council race.

Walker highlighted the importance of community voting.

“Voting is one of the main reasons we still have a democracy,” Walker said. “And if we want to continue to have a democracy, we need to vote. We need to care. We need to have our voice heard.”

 All smiles at the poll
A poll worker helps a woman prepare to vote at the Loyal Order of Moose Lodge on Tuesday, June 2.  

Governor’s race

12:46 p.m.: South Dakota Republicans will choose their gubernatorial candidate today.

Gov. Larry Rhoden faces U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, state Speaker of the House Jon Hansen and businessman Toby Doeden in the race.

Most polls heading into the election have had Johnson in the lead, though the latest, from Emerson and KELO Land, showed Doeden in first place. If none of the candidates receive 35% or more of the vote the top two will head to a runoff election in July.

“Surreal doesn’t even come close to conveying it. Never in my wildest dreams would I have imagined that a poor kid from Groton would have the opportunity to run for the highest office in our state,” Doeden said in a Twitter post earlier Tuesday. “South Dakota has made me who I am today. I look forward to fighting for each and every person who calls this place home.”

Johnson posted, “The next 20 years can be the best 20 years in South Dakota’s history. But that is not going to happen by accident. It takes energy, vision, and determined leadership. And that’s what I will bring as Governor.”

Rhoden also took to Twitter, posting “VOTE TODAY to keep building a South Dakota that’s strong, safe, free, and Built to Last!”

“Don't forget to get out and vote TODAY for Jon Hansen for Governor,” Hansen posted on Facebook today.

Voters turn out to Bethel Church, candidates take to the streets

9 a.m.: About 60 voters had cast their ballots at Precinct 4-2, located at Bethel Church at 122 N Maple Ave., by 9 a.m. The precinct is located in Ward 4 for the municipal election and District 32 in the legislative races.

One voter, 52-year-old Rapid Citian Danny Nagel, said was reminded by someone to vote.

“It’s close to the neighborhood,” Nagel said of the polling place.

Nagel said there were no specific issues that stuck out to him when he cast his vote, “other than just familiarity with people on the ballot.”

The only race on Nagel’s ballot was the Ward 4 Rapid City Council race between John Roberts and Valeriah Big Eagle. South Dakota is a closed primary state, so only registered Republicans can vote in the Republican primary.

In District 32, Helene Duhamel and Karen McNeal are going head-to-head for the Republican party nomination to advance to the General Election in November. Jeff Shelton is the Democrat running for the Senate. In the House race, Steve Duffy and Zachary Martin are running on the Republican ticket. Nicole Uhre-Balk is the Democrat running for one of the district’s two seats in the House. In Pennington County, Sabrina Green and Tina Mulally are competing in the Republican primary for Pennington County Auditor.

Republican voters in the district will also be able to cast votes in the U.S. Senate and House races and in the South Dakota governor race.

8 a.m.: Candidates and supporters stood at Rapid City street corners advocating for residents to vote, including in Halley Park between West Main and Saint Joseph streets.

 Bethel Church
Poll workers at Bethel Church, the polling place for Precinct 4-2, on Tuesday, June 2. 

 Candidates at Halley Park
Rapid City area candidates and supporters stand with signs encouraging citizens to vote during the primary and municipal elections held on Tuesday, June 2.

title: You might see some media at your polling place, and yes, it’s legal
description: On Tuesday, June 2, a poll worker at a voting precinct in Rapid City told the Journal it could not take photos on the property, per an official’s request. Here’s what happened and what the law says about conduct at the polls:
_full_text:
On Tuesday, June 2, a poll worker at a voting precinct in Rapid City told the Journal it could not take photos on the property, per an official’s request. Here’s what happened and what the law says about conduct at the polls:

Around 8:30 a.m., the Journal was taking photos outside Bethel Church building of signs directing voters to the church atrium, where voting booths are located, but was told photography inside was prohibited. The church, located at 1202 North Maple Ave. is the polling place for Precinct 4-2.

The Journal reached out to Rapid City lawyer Jim Leach after talking with a poll worker. Leach, who — among other work — offers guidance on media law, advised that polling places are public and it is within the press’ rights to take photos at them.

 Vote Here
A “Vote Here” sign hangs in the window of Bethel Church on June 2. The church is the polling place for Precinct 4-2 in Rapid City. 

Per state law, as laid out in 12-18-3, no person may within 100 feet of a polling place, “use any communication or photographic device in a manner which repeatedly distracts, interrupts, or intimidates any voter or election worker.” The law does not ban taking of photographs or media coverage of the polls.

Among the activities prohibited under the statute are campaigning, signature gathering, or any practice that interferes with the voter’s free access to the polls or disrupts the administration of the polling place.

The media routinely cover the polls during elections across the country, including here in Rapid City.

After speaking to Leach, the Journal entered the church atrium and informed the poll worker that the polling place is public and subject to unobtrusive media coverage. The poll worker did not attempt to prevent the Journal from briefly taking photos. Speaking to the Journal, a pastor said they’d reversed the directive and would not attempt to prevent news gathering.

The pastor declined to comment on the record about the reasoning behind the initial decision or its timing, other than to say, “We support our community.”

 Bethel Church
Voters fill out ballots on June 2 at Bethel Church, the polling place for Precinct 4-2 in Rapid City.

title: After several delays, Rapid City man pleads not guilty for death of his father
description: After four initial appearances and five rescheduled arraignments, the Rapid City man accused of murdering his father pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity on Tuesday, June 2.
_full_text:
After four initial appearances and five rescheduled arraignments, the Rapid City man accused of murdering his father pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity on Tuesday, June 2.

Nicholas Selig, 31, was finally arraigned before Circuit Court Judge Jeffrey Connolly at the Pennington County Courthouse on the fifth date the hearing was scheduled. Selig was indicted on a first-degree murder charge in connection to the death of his father, Vernon Selig. 

 Nicholas Selig
Nicholas Selig 

Selig has had multiple court appearances rescheduled due to "uncooperative behavior" and waiting for the mental health competency evaluation by Rapid City psychologist Dr. Kari Scovel, according to court documents. 

In South Dakota, first-degree murder is a Class A felony with a mandatory life sentence and up to a $50,000 fine. Depending on the circumstances, first-degree murder can be death penalty eligible.

Case background

Vernon Selig was reported missing to the Rapid City Police Department on Tuesday, Aug. 26, 2025, at 5:54 p.m.

About an hour earlier, around 4:34 p.m. on Tuesday, Aug. 26, 2025, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office was called to the area of Victoria Lake Road and First Thunder Road, just outside Rapid City, where they found Vernon Selig dead in a rural wooded area with a gunshot wound to the head.

At a press conference on Wednesday, Aug. 27, 2025, authorities said they were looking for Nicholas Selig through the night and into the morning. Around 10:45 a.m. on Thursday, Aug. 28, 2025, Selig was spotted on Jackson Boulevard in Rapid City in front of an auto shop, and law enforcement took him in for questioning. He was then placed under arrest a few hours later.

Selig was originally scheduled for his initial appearance at the Pennington County Courthouse at 10 a.m. Tuesday, Sept. 2, 2025. At an initial appearance, the judge informs the accused of their rights in the case, and the state reads the charges and a brief description of the events. The state and the defense then present bond arguments, and the judge sets bond.

Due to Selig being uncooperative that day, the hearing was continued to Wednesday, Sept. 3, 2025. That hearing had a similar result. As Magistrate Judge Scott Bogue attempted to explain Selig's charges that day, he continually interrupted, yelling out a random assortment of numbers and phrases. Delays continued in the case until Tuesday, June 2.

title: RCAS hires Director of Indian Education and School Improvement
description: After a restructuring of the role and a several-month gap, Rapid City Area Schools District’s Director of Indian Education and School Improvement started on Monday, June 1.
_full_text:
After a restructuring of the role and a several-month gap, Rapid City Area Schools District’s Director of Indian Education and School Improvement started on Monday, June 1.

The Rapid City Area Schools Board voted unanimously on April 7 to hire Gina Curran to the position at a $120,000 a year salary. RCAS Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson introduced Curran to the Rapid City Area Schools Board on Monday.

“We are very glad to have her and glad that she made it through the day. That’s a good sign,” Thompson quipped as she introduced Curran to the school board at its Monday meeting.

Thompson said Curran has a master’s degree in elementary administration, a minor in Lakota leadership and management and a specialist degree in school district superintendent. She has served as the high school principal for St. Francis Indian School, an elementary principal/superintendent at Marty Indian School and has taught elementary and middle school at Crazy Horse School and Wounded Knee School.

“A lot of experience,” Thompson said.

Following the resignation of the Title VI Indian Education manager in January, the district created the new director position. The position is a combination of the Title VI Indian Education manager position and the Title 1A position, which provides funding to schools with high concentrations of poverty to close achievement gaps and improve outcomes for students who need additional support. The restructuring also added school improvement under the new director’s purview.

“This allows us to place a stronger emphasis on improving outcomes for our Native students and on our building level school improvement efforts.  Our goal is to reduce achievement gaps for our Native students and our students who come from disadvantaged or poverty backgrounds,” Thompson said.

Recent and historic state testing data shows Native American students and students living in poverty routinely test considerably lower than their counterparts in the district. For example, in RCAS elementary schools, 14.2% of Native students tested at or above grade-level expectations in English language arts in 2024-2025, compared to 42.8% of non-Native students.

Board Member Walt Swan congratulated Curran on the new position. Board Member Angela Rafferty thanked her for saying “yes” and accepting the position. Board President Troy Carr said it is always good to have someone from the outside to help the district go where it wants to go.

The superintendent also thanked district staffers Kit Veit for temporarily taking on the Title VI duties and Jen Roberts for temporarily taking on the Title IA duties until Curran started.

“This was a lot to ask of them, but they handled it with professionalism and grace,” she said.

title: Joan Pillen
_full_text:
Aug 18, 1963 - May 23, 2026

Joan (Haugan) Pillen was born on August 18, 1963, to Dr. Haakon and Helen Haugan on a blazing hot summer day in St. Paul, Minn. Soon afterward, the family moved to Rapid City, S.D., in the beautiful Black Hills, where Joan's adventurous spirit began to flourish.

As a child, Joan loved ballet, gymnastics, and most of all, horses. A gifted rider, she excelled in dressage and jumping competitions, winning numerous awards with her beloved horse, Chief's Smokey, whom she trained herself. Fearless and creative, Joan approached life with enthusiasm, curiosity, and a daredevil spirit.

Joan graduated from the South Dakota School of Mines and Technology with a Bachelor of Science degree in Geological Engineering and an MBA from USD. After working in industry, she returned to Rapid City, where she met the love of her life, Jubal Pillen. The two were married on September 7, 1999, in the Bahamas — fittingly, another grand adventure in a life full of them.

Together, Joan and Jubal built a life and business in Sturgis, where they owned an J & J Optical, with their two cheerful poodles greeting customers at the door. Joan also poured her creativity and passion into her wedding business, the Sturgis Hitchin' Post.

An avid storyteller with a deep love for horses, the Black Hills, and authentic living, Joan went on to write the Prairie Magic series, four award-winning novels that reflected her imagination, insight, and love of life. She had a gift for connecting with people through stories, laughter, wit, and genuine warmth.

Joan's life was filled with gratitude, dear friendships, and deep love. She will be profoundly missed by all who knew her. She would want to be remembered with her signature smile, charm, resilience, and grace — dancing through life on her own terms.

Joan was preceded in death by her father, Dr. Haakon Haugan; mother-in-law, Bonnie Pillen, and her brother-in-law, Paul Pillen.

She is survived by her husband, Jubal Pillen; her mother, Helen Ackerson; her stepfather, Ronald Ackerson; her sisters, Ruth Haugan and Mary (Alan) Anderson; father-in-law, Gary Pillen (Kathy); sisters-in-law, Shannon Madison and Kari Smith (Jake); brother-in-law, Mike Pillen (Carissa), and her nephews, Haakon Anderson, Henry Anderson, and Holden Anderson.

A Celebration of Life ceremony will be held at 1:30 p.m. on Friday, June 5, 2026 at Kinkade Funeral Chapel. Interment will follow at Bear Butte Cemetery. Please visit: www.KinkadeFunerals.com.

title: Drury grateful for support; Baxter won’t seek recount
description: Former legislator Becky Drury could get past the Tuesday, June 2, Republican primary for the House District 34 seat.
_full_text:
Former legislator Becky Drury could get past the Tuesday, June 2, Republican primary for the House District 34 seat.

“I feel great about winning. I’m very happy the vote turned my way and I’m just so grateful for the support and the voters in District 34,” she told the Journal on Wednesday. “I can’t do this all by myself. It involves my family, my friends, the supporters. It’s not my win. It’s our win.”

Drury previously served in the South Dakota Legislature before losing to Reps. Heather Baxter and Mike Drury in the 2024 primary. Drury finished just ahead of Baxter in Tuesday’s election — Drury received 1,861 votes (29%) while Baxter received 1,815 votes (28%), within the legal allowable threshold for a recount. A legislative candidate may ask for a recount when the margin between two candidates is five votes or less, or 2% or less of the overall vote.

But Baxter told the Journal she’s not going to seek a recount.

“It’s been awesome to be a public servant for District 34. I’m grateful for the chance to serve and be a voice for the people. Congratulations to Rep. Mike Derby and former Rep. Becky Drury,” Baxter said.

Drury ran for a seat in the House again because she missed serving, and said he believes the state legislature would benefit from “a voice of reason.”

 Becky Drury
Becky Drury (Republican) running for House District 34, speaks during a candidate forum. 

“I felt like we were missing a voice of reason in Pierre in more than one district, and I felt like I knew I could provide that for Rapid City,” Drury said.

As she campaigned and went door-to-door to talk to people, Drury said her support for families, children and economic development were issues that seemed to resonate most.

“Economic development means smart growth. It does not mean mega data centers, but it doesn’t mean shutting down and letting no one move to Rapid City, or to the Hills,” she said. “It means smart growth. We always have to protect our natural resources, and we should be protecting them.”

Drury is looking forward to a break before campaigning begins for the general election in November. She said voters need a break, too, but she encourages voters to stay focused on the runoff election for governor between Toby Doeden and Gov. Larry Rhoden, set for July 28.

title: Derby ‘very happy’ after handily winning District 34 primary
description: In the Republican primary for two District 34 House seats, on Tuesday, June 2, Mike Derby advanced.
_full_text:
In the Republican primary for two District 34 House seats, on Tuesday, June 2, Mike Derby advanced.

“I’m very happy and proud to once again be selected to go into the general election for District 34,” Derby told the Journal on Wednesday, June 3. “It’s a district I grew up in, and it is always an honor to represent it.”

Derby and a second Republican will face Democrat Victor Diego Dominquez in the general election in November. If Derby wins a House seat, he will serve his seventh and final term in the South Dakota Legislature.

Derby won the primary with 42% of the vote (2,710) votes, finishing ahead of challenger Becky Drury (1,861 votes, 29%) and Rep. Heather Baxter (1,815 votes, 28%). With such a small margin between second and third place, a recount is possible.

Derby previously served three terms under Gov. Bill Janklow from 1997 to 2002, then took an 18-year break before returning to the state legislature in 2021.

 Mike Derby
Rep. Mike Derby R-34, smiles at the community photo event on May 22 in Rapid City. Derby won in the June 2 election for a chance at a seventh term in the South Dakota Legislature. 

Derby said he returned to politics because he’d had a number of people tell him they believed the Legislature had lost institutional knowledge.

“I had served on the appropriations committee for three terms (1997-2002) and I came back and got back on appropriations to chair it, so my institutional knowledge of (the) appropriations process proved to be very valuable,” Derby said.

Additionally, Derby said he heard concerns about a lack of civility and decorum in the Legislature, and “I felt I could offer that.”

During this year’s legislative session, Derby said he’s proud he helped guide what he called the largest property tax cut in South Dakota history. He’s also proud of helping get a new prison in Rapid City “fully funded and right-sized. That was a big deal, too,” he said.

Derby said he’s looking forward to a peaceful summer for himself and voters before campaigning begins again for November’s election. He also thanked the voters, and the candidates who ran for office.

“Everybody should run for some office sometime in their life just to crystallize their belief system and be a part of the process. I really appreciate anybody that stepped forward and entered the arena into the election process,” Derby said. “I’m very happy at this moment.”

title: District 29: Meirose 'looking forward' after primary victory, Deering and Cammack express excitement
description: William Meirose has a straight shot to the Capitol in Pierre in the November elections after Tuesday, June 2, primary.
_full_text:
William Meirose has a straight shot to the Capitol in Pierre in the November elections after Tuesday, June 2, primary.

Meirose beat Sen. John Carley. Meirose received 2,280 votes (51%) to Carley's 2,151 (49%), according to the unofficial results from the South Dakota Secretary of State's Office.

"I'm looking forward to it," Meirose said. "A little anxious, a little excited to see what's gonna take place. Anxious because I want to do a real good job." 

Meirose said his main plan during the summer months is to take time to listen to the people in Meade County and fully address their most pressing issues and figure out a legislative solution. 

In the House, challenger Gary Deering took first place with 2,198 votes (28%). He'll be joined on the general election ballot by former Rep. Gary Cammack, who's seeking to regain his seat after losing in the 2024 primary. Cammack received 2,135 votes (27%) in Tuesday's election.

Sitting Rep. Kathy Rice and Rep. Terri Jorgenson came in third and fourth with 1,957 (25%) and 1,572 votes (20%), respectively.

Cammack said he was thankful for Tuesday's results. During the race, Cammack said he prioritized having more opportunities to support future generations within South Dakota. Another issue Cammack said is important to him is property taxes. 

"Of course, there will be an ongoing discussion about property tax, and I think we need to be a bit creative when it comes to that," Cammack said. "... The best way to reduce property tax is to broaden the base, so if we can get some of these enterprises in then we'll make some significant contributions in the form of taxes." 

Deering said he feels pretty good about the primary election results. He said he's always been a strong property rights and local control advocate. 

"We're seeing issues that come from top down from the state. Mining issues in Piedmont is a prime example, that skipped some of the local processes because some of the statutes we have in place," Deering said. "So local control has always been a big issue for me, and limited government." 

Deering said there's no other county like Meade County and he is excited to head into the capital to figure out the state's budget. 

There are no Democrats running in District 29, meaning the trio is poised to advance in the general election.

title: Tina Mulally says it’s time to ‘get to work’ after winning Pennington County Auditor GOP primary
description: Outgoing state Rep. Tina Mulally, R-District 35, will be the Republican nominee for Pennington County Auditor in the November general election. Mulally beat current Auditor Sabrina Green by 656 votes.
_full_text:
Outgoing state Rep. Tina Mulally, R-District 35, will be the Republican nominee for Pennington County Auditor in the November general election. Mulally beat current Auditor Sabrina Green by 656 votes.

Mulally and Green received a total of 12,878 votes, with Mulally garnering 6,767 votes (53%) and Green bringing in 6,111 (47%), according to unofficial results from the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office. 

"(I'm) pleased with the results, and thankful to all the people that supported me. You know, I look forward to what's in store. … I just want to dig in deep and make sure everything's on the up-and-up," Mulally said on the future.

 Tina Mulally
Rep. Tina Mulally, R-District 35, secures the seat for Pennington County Auditor after the June 2 election results.  

Mullaly has been a state representative for District 35 since 2018 and has served on the House Appropriations Committee for eight years, according to her website.

She told the Journal she did not pay attention to the election until early on the morning of Wednesday, June 3. When she was notified, the votes were fully counted.

"I was like, ‘That's great, a new chapter in my life. Now let's get to work,’" Mullaly said.

Mullaly will be unopposed on the general election ballot.

According to the Pennington County website, the auditor’s office is responsible for auditing all accounts and maintaining all financial records for the county, including payroll, preparing the annual budget, establishing levies and apportioning all tax collections. The office also conducts elections and maintains all records of voter registration and election history. The county auditor position is a four-year term. 

 Sabrina Green
Pennington County Auditor Sabrina Green. 

Cindy Mohler had been the county auditor from 2018 until she announced her early retirement in October 2025. She told the Journal the reason for her resignation is to mark a new beginning in her life.

Green has worked at the Auditor's Office since 2018 and served as deputy auditor under Mohler. The Pennington County Board of Commissioners appointed Green to the auditor position to finish out Mohler's term, which is set to end March 2, 2027.

Green did not immediately respond to the Journal's inquiry for comment.

title: Mueller reacts to win in Pennington County Board of Commissioners District 1 primary
description: Mike Mueller, a retired mechanical engineer and husband to former District 30 state Sen. Julie Frye Mueller, has secured his name on the general election ballot in November after beating Zach Bush in the District 1 Republican primary by 619 votes.
_full_text:
Mike Mueller, a retired mechanical engineer and husband to former District 30 state Sen. Julie Frye Mueller, has secured his name on the general election ballot in November after beating Zach Bush in the District 1 Republican primary by 619 votes.

Both candidates totaled 3,1915 votes with Mueller securing 2,267 votes (58%) and Bush tallying 1,648 votes (42%), according to unofficial results from the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office.

Mueller said he spent election night picking up election signs in Rapid City and in southern Hill City.

District 3 covers most of the western side of Rapid City and Pennington County.

 Mike Mueller
Mike Mueller 

"Since I ran four years ago, I'm happy to have prevailed to get to the general election, and now that I'm retired, I've got more time on my hands, and I'd like to help people in Pennington County whenever way I can," Mueller said.

Commissioner Ron Rossknecht has previously served District 1 since 2019. Rossjnecht did not seek re-election.

County Commissioners serve for a four-year term.

Mueller said he is hoping to bring a change in the county by advocating that Board of Commissioners meetings be moved from the first and third Tuesdays of every month, starting at 9 a.m., to evenings to allow more taxpayers to participate.

 Zach Bush
Zach Bush ran for the Pennington County Board of Commissioners District 1 seat. 

He added he would also like to see zero-based budgeting be utilized when the county is managing its budget, meaning every item that is included int the budget is justified before being added in.

Mueller has served on the South Dakota Mines Hardrock Club and Mechanical Engineering Industrial Advisory Board, the American Society of Heating, Refrigeration, and Air Conditioning Engineers Regional and Chapter Service, Rapid City Elks Lodge Board of Trustees and with South Dakota Citizens for Liberty.

Mueller also served as an elected official for four years on the West Dakota Water Development District.

According to a release, Bush is a veteran. He did not immediately respond to the Journal's inquiry for comment.

title: Howard wins in District 34, vows to fight for people over special interests
description: In the Republican primary for Senate District 34 , Sen. Taffy Howard won on Tuesday, June 2.
_full_text:
In the Republican primary for Senate District 34 , Sen. Taffy Howard won on Tuesday, June 2.

“First and foremost, I’m just so grateful to the people of District 34 that they put their trust in me and voted for me for another two years,” Howard said. “I’m going to keep fighting for them. I’ve said from the beginning the people come first, not the special interests.”

Howard will face Democrat Michael Calabrese in the general election in November. If elected in November, Howard will serve her fifth term in the Legislature. She has served three terms in the South Dakota House of Representatives and one in the state Senate.

 Taffy Howard.jpg
Taffy Howard 

She believes her work on property taxes and TIFs are among the issues that resonated with voters.

“They know how hard I’ve worked on property taxes, I hope. It’s also issues such as TIFs. I think I gained a lot of support because I helped defeat the Libertyland TIF, which was just too far,” Howard said. “The City Council did not listen to the people in that matter.”

Howard also said she’ll work for “common sense guardrails” at the state level for data centers that provide guidelines under which cities and counties can operate.

 031726-nws-sl-developers-p2.jpg
Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, speaks in the South Dakota Senate on Feb. 11, 2026, at the Capitol in Pierre. 

“I think the state needs to take the lead and have common sense guardrails around issues like that,” she said. “If the community would like to have data centers, that’s fine. That’s local control. I believe we need to address the water, the noise, the setbacks, which we did partly last year with the Data Center Bill of Rights, but that doesn’t go far enough.”

“I know that resonated with people because we’re looking at having the first data center come into Rapid City. Just from what’s happening all around the country, it’s very much a hot issue now.”

Howard said she has been saddened by negative attacks that have occurred against candidates at all levels throughout this election cycle, and she is grateful for the trust voters put in her.  

“I always say it’s one of the greatest honors of my life to serve the people of this district,” she said.

title: District 32: Duhamel 'delighted, thrilled, thankful' to ring in primary victory
description: State Sen. Helene Duhamel won the Republican Party nomination on Tuesday, June 2, to advance to the general election ballot in the District 32 Senate race. She beat challenger Karen McNeal.
_full_text:
State Sen. Helene Duhamel won the Republican Party nomination on Tuesday, June 2, to advance to the general election ballot in the District 32 Senate race. She beat challenger Karen McNeal.

Duhamel won with 1,316 votes (63%) against McNeal’s 759 (37%), according to unofficial results from the South Dakota Secretary of State's Office. Duhamel was appointed to the seat by former Gov. Kristi Noem in 2019 and won elections in 2020, 2022 and 2024.

"I'm just delighted, thrilled, thankful for my hometown support," Duhamel said. 

Duhamel said she's always been advocating for nonpartisan issues such as water, quality education, good-paying jobs and providing opportunities for future generations. 

"For far too long we export our best and brightest because it's hard to make a living here," Duhamel said. "I think we have to continue to focus on good-paying jobs, smart growth." 

 Duhamel
Sen. Helene Duhamel, R-Rapid City, who also works as the Public Information Officer at the Pennington County State's Attorney's Office, explains why the legislature shot down a bill that would have put $2.7 towards a nonprofit rehabilitation program within the prison system during an event in Rapid City. "It's very hard to get legislators to want to spend money on anything, and especially something like this," she said. 

This is the second time Duhamel has competed against McNeal and won, after beating her in the 2024 general election when McNeal ran as an independent. Duhamel said she is grateful for anyone who puts their hat in the ring and actively wants to make South Dakota a better place. She said it takes a lot of courage to run. 

"The goal is to serve the best we can, to represent the people of our cities and our state," Duhamel said. 

Now that she has passed the recent hurdle of Tuesday's elections, Duhamel said she will continue to prioritize what she's always prioritized. She said the perks of being in office for so long is that she’s starting to see her hard work about addressing water issues resonate with the Legislature. 

"I'm going to continue to advocate for us making plans and investments now for clean, reliable drinking water," Duhamel said. "I think the whole nation is thirsty, I think we have to get on board and start making those plans fast."

Duhamel will go up against Democrat Jeff Shelton in the general election.

title: Rapid City Ward 4: Roberts ‘honored’ for opportunity to serve another 3 years
description: Rapid City Councilman John Roberts said he’s, “honored that the people of North Rapid gave me the opportunity to serve as a council person for another three years, so I’m looking forward to it. I hope it’s as good as the last three years.”
_full_text:
Rapid City Councilman John Roberts said he’s, “honored that the people of North Rapid gave me the opportunity to serve as a council person for another three years, so I’m looking forward to it. I hope it’s as good as the last three years.”

The Rapid City Council election held on Tuesday, June 2, resulted in Roberts retaining his Ward 4 seat with 870 votes (52%). He beat Valeriah Big Eagle (737 votes, 44%). Ardin Jay Cychosz, who announced he was dropping out of the race months ago but still appeared on the ballot, received 65 votes (4%). There were contests in all five of the city’s wards for the first time in over two decades.

 JohnRoberts.jpg
John Roberts, City Council Ward 4 candidate

On the competition between himself and Big Eagle, Roberts said on Wednesday, June 3, “I was very happy with it. It was a nice, clean campaign as far as I saw. And that was my goal. I didn’t want to be negative like the governor’s race. There was just enough negative crap out there. We didn’t need it locally, too.”

Roberts said there’s a “tremendous amount” of infrastructure projects in the works, and he wants to see some of the bigger projects finished in the next three years.

“I’m just looking forward to Rapid City growing more,” he said.

A request for comment from Big Eagle was not immediately returned.

Roberts is set to be sworn in for his new term at the July 6, 2026, council meeting.

title: Rapid City Ward 1: Biberdorf ‘grateful’ for another term on City Council
description: Rapid City Councilman Josh Biberdorf said he’s thankful to head into another term in office.
_full_text:
Rapid City Councilman Josh Biberdorf said he’s thankful to head into another term in office.

“Just grateful for all the people that came out with the resounding ‘yes’ vote and voted for me,” Biberdorf told the Journal on Wednesday, June 3. “It gives us confidence in the direction of what we've been doing, and to continue that work moving forward.”

 Josh Biberdorf
Councilman Josh Biberdorf (with mic) speaks during a Citizens for Liberty City Council candidate forum. At Biberdorf’s left is Murray Lee. Biberdorf beat Lee in the Tuesday, June 2, council election. 

In the Rapid City Council Ward 1 race, Biberdorf received 1,881 votes (71%) against challenger Murray Lee (770 votes, 29%).

Looking to the future, Biberdorf said, ”Our messaging has always been ‘families first.’ So, how do we make Rapid City a great place to raise a family? And a couple of those things are: make sure that we commit to safety, invest in our police, invest in our fire. … Making sure that we're protecting our parks and community areas for all the citizens throughout the city to make sure that we are taking care of our families.”

 Headshot.png
Josh Biberdorf 

He also said a focus will be on continuing “to make sure that Rapid City is open for sustainable and responsible economic growth.”

What does “responsible” growth look like to Biberdorf?

“Have growth pay for growth, so if we can bring economic development to this area we can partner with (entities) where it spurs sales tax revenue for the city, so that every citizen in the city can win by using that sales tax to improve our infrastructure in our town,” he said. “That’s No. 1. No. 2, if there's growth that's going to help with workforce housing and low-income housing, that would be really good as well.

 Murray Lee
Rapid City City Council candidate Murray Lee speaks during a press conference. 

Biberdorf said he has the utmost respect for Lee and the campaign was clean.

“We had lots of great conversations,” he said. “Very civil, very nonpartisan, no negativism on either side of the campaign. So I’m just grateful for a good opponent and somebody who is a very respected individual.”

A message to Lee wasn’t immediately returned on Wednesday.

title: District 33: Phil Jensen ‘pleased I won'; runoff possible between Massie, Marlette
description: In the race for House District 33, Rep. Phil Jensen won to run in November for what would be his final term. Jensen has served 18 years in the South Dakota Legislature. Another win would give him two more years in the legislature.
_full_text:
In the race for House District 33, Rep. Phil Jensen won to run in November for what would be his final term. Jensen has served 18 years in the South Dakota Legislature. Another win would give him two more years in the legislature.

“I’m pleased I won,” Jensen told the Journal on Wednesday, June 3. “I didn’t think I was going to lose, but I’m very happy that the people of District 33 chose to put me back in for my final two years in the House.”

Property taxes and government corruption were issues voters seemed particularly interested in, he said.

“People are shocked when I tell them that South Dakota ranks No. 3 (of the) most corrupt state governments in the country,” Jensen said.

Data from cato.org/blog/public-corruption-state supports Jensen’s statistic about corruption among state government employees.

“A lot of it has to do with transparency and a lack thereof. I will continue as I have in the past (when I was in the Senate) I pointed out how South Dakota ranked No. 3 most corrupt state governments, and I said it again on the House floor this past March. I think that’s why I have so many enemies on the House floor and in the Senate, because I call it the way it is,” Jensen said.

“We’ve got some new people coming in, that’s exciting, good conservatives,” Jensen said of the election winners. “I’m looking forward to working with them.”

Second and third in the race were Rep. Curt Massie, who beat challenger Jeff Marlette by five votes — 1,988 to 1,983 -- which rounds to 27% for each candidate.

The race is close enough a recount is possible for the second spot, according to state law. A legislative candidate may ask for a recount when the margin between two candidates is five votes or less, or 2% or less of the overall vote. The race between Massie and Marlette meets both thresholds.

Massie did not immediately respond to the Journal’s request for an interview.

Marlette said Wednesday he hadn’t yet decided whether to pursue a recount.

Jensen and the second-place finisher will face Democrat Kari Hall in the general election, after which two of the three will serve in the legislature.

David Johnson won the race for the District 33 Senate seat. He did not respond to the Journal’s request for an interview by press time. Johnson will face Democrat Christopher Baumgartner in the general election.

title: 'I just play like we're going to lose:' Deb Hadcock wins Pennington County Commission District 3 primary
description: Pennington County Commissioner Deb Hadcock is set to retain her seat representing District 3 on the Pennington County Board of Commissioners after beating Republican primary challenger Randy Decker by 490 votes.
_full_text:
Pennington County Commissioner Deb Hadcock is set to retain her seat representing District 3 on the Pennington County Board of Commissioners after beating Republican primary challenger Randy Decker by 490 votes.

 Randy Decker
Randy Decker 

The vote count totaled 2,110, with Hadcock securing 1,300 votes (62%) and Decker receiving 810 (38%), according to unofficial results from the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office. Both candidates are registered Republicans.

Hadcock heads to the November general election, where she’ll be unopposed on the ballot. No Democrats are running for the District 3 seat.

District 3 spans much of downtown and eastern Rapid City.

Hadcock told the Journal she spent election night with her family, unsure if the results would turn in her favor.

"I just play like we're going to lose," Hadcock said of her approach to campaigning.

Hadcock has served as the commissioner for District 3 since first being elected in 2015. County commissioners serve a four-year term. She said she is going to continue to "hit the ground running" with her likely re-election.

 Deb Hadcock
Deb Hadcock secures her re-election for Pennington County Board of Commissioners for District 3. 

Her background includes owning multiple businesses in the hair salon and hotel industries in Rapid City.

Decker is a veteran in the U.S. Marines and Army and has a law enforcement background. He currently serves as an investigator for the Pennington County Public Defender’s Office.

Decker posted to Facebook on June 3, saying, "This isn't how we wanted this journey to end, but life goes on. To those of you who supported and encouraged me on this journey the last 7 months, Thank you! Your words and generosity mean the world to me. Now on to the next adventure, whatever that may be!"

Decker did not respond to the Journal's inquiry on the election at the time of publication. 

Reflecting on the race, Hadcock said Decker played a clean campaign for the seat.

title: Rapid City Ward 5: Armstrong ‘it feels good;’ Roseland will ‘keep on keeping on’
description: The Rapid City Council election held on Tuesday, June 2, is over . There were contests in all five of the city’s wards for the first time in over two decades.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Council election held on Tuesday, June 2, is over. There were contests in all five of the city’s wards for the first time in over two decades.

In Ward 5, former Councilwoman Laura Armstrong (1,589 votes, 56%) beat former Councilman Pat Roseland (1,229 votes, 44%) for the seat Council President Rod Pettigrew is set to vacate. Armstrong will be sworn in to the office for a three-year term at the Monday, July 6, council meeting, but as far as she’s concerned, “today is day one,” she told the Journal on Wednesday, June 3.

“It feels good to have the opportunity to serve this community again,” Armstrong said. “I’m already hearing from council members that they’re excited to work with me. They know that we are going to focus on the important issues for our constituents. I’ve got a record of tangible results and they know that we’re gonna work well together.”

 Laura Armstrong
Laura Armstrong 

Before she’s sworn in, Armstrong said she wants to meet with the city’s department directors to get to know their personal perspective on their departments , what’s going well, what could be done better and the challenges they face. She added she also wants to get her hands on the budget, even though it’s in draft mode.

“I just want to see where we’re at. That’s really important. Fiscal responsibility is critical to this role,” she said, adding she also wants to improve her relationships with council members that she doesn’t know very well. “You can only move forward at the speed of trust.”

Armstrong described the campaign between herself and Roseland as “positive” and “productive.” The two spoke over the phone the morning after election night. Armstrong said they had a good talk, and they’ll continue to work together as Roseland is on the Planning and Zoning Commission.

Roseland confirmed he reached out to Armstrong to congratulate her.

“Hopefully we can work together in the near future while she’s on council and make the best of what we have,” Roseland said.

 Pat Roseland
Pat Roseland 

As for his reaction to the results, Roseland said, “My team and I did the best we could do. I think we worked really hard. We all had the same goal in mind, to get me back on City Council, which did not work. I had a lot of support from friends and neighbors and supporters throughout Ward 5 … I’m gonna keep on keeping on and do what I feel is best for Rapid City. I’m not sure what that is at this point, but I won’t be hiding under a couch at all. I’ll be out there doing my thing.”

Roseland is also a member of the Historic Preservation Commission.

title: Rapid City Council swears in new City Attorney Carla Cushman
description: On Tuesday, June 1, the Rapid City Council voted to appoint interim City Attorney Carla Cushman as the director for the attorney's office, officially replacing former City Attorney Joel Landeen.
_full_text:
On Tuesday, June 1, the Rapid City Council voted to appoint interim City Attorney Carla Cushman as the director for the attorney's office, officially replacing former City Attorney Joel Landeen.

But two council members shared grievances about the hasty hiring process by the city.

The city council voted 10-0 to appoint Cushman as the City Attorney.

 Carla Cushman
Carla Cushman 

This comes after Mayor Jason Salamun on April 1, fired Landeen as city attorney.  Landeen had served in the city attorney’s office since 2004 and as city attorney since 2012.

In April, city Public Information Officer Darrell Shoemaker told the Journal Landeen's last day with the city was March 31. He said Salamun was looking for leadership changes in city government but did not specify what prompted this decision.

“We would like to thank Joel for his many years of public service to the City of Rapid City,” Salamun said in a statement on Wednesday, April 1. “We wish him well in his future endeavors.”

 Former City attorney Joel Landeen
Rapid City Attorney Joel Landeen's last day in the position was March 31. 

 Swearing in
Carla Cushman was voted in and sworn in by the city on June 2. 

Salamun told the Journal, "It was my decision to make a change in leadership in the City Attorney’s Office," confirming Landeen did not resign. "I determined it was time to bring fresh perspective, renewed energy and stronger execution to our priorities."
Landeen told the Journal, "It wasn't antagonistic. I know everybody always wants to make this like there's some conspiracy, or there's something going on. A lot of times this stuff is a lot more benign than people think, and there isn't any hard feelings or animosity."
According to the Rapid City Human Resources Department, Landeen was making $182,988 a year as of late 2025.
Cushman, who served as deputy city attorney, assumed the role of interim city attorney immediately after Landeen's departure.
Cushman is a graduate of Augustana College and the University of South Dakota Knudson School of Law, and has been with the city attorney’s office in Rapid City since 2012.
In a press release, Salamun said the recommendation of Cushman as city attorney came after a detailed search for candidates that began in early April.
At Monday's council meeting, Councilman Greg Strommen (Ward 3) said he participated in her interview process and supported her appointment.
"I think it's important that we know these people are appointed because they're qualified," Strommen said.
According to SDCL 9-14-3, "Such officers as needed and provided for by ordinance shall be appointed. Each appointive officer of a municipality governed by a mayor and common council shall be appointed by the mayor with the approval of the council, and in other municipalities, each officer shall be appointed by a majority vote of the members elected to the governing body, except as provided in the city manager law and subject to the provisions of the civil service applying to employees, police, and firefighters. Such officers shall be appointed annually or at intervals determined by the governing body."
Strommen continued, saying the previous city attorney would respond to inquiries by Strommen saying he works on behalf of the mayor. Strommen said this statement was not true. 
"The mayor (Salamun) does have appointing power, but state statue says the attorney shall provide professional services as sent to his or her office as may be required by the ordinance or directive by governing body. We are the governing body," Strommen said.
He said Cushman understands this.
Strommen also shared grief over the city's hasty online posting for the position.
"I think it's important that the city does more than a two-week posting. I know the mayor was quoted as saying we had a detailed process that began in April. That wasn't a detailed search process," Strommen said.
He congratulated Cushman, but said he would've liked to see a larger pool of applicants.
Council President Rod Pettigrew (Ward 5) agreed with Strommen's claims.
"I have noticed since Carla has been in there, there's a change in the City Attorney's Office, and it's positive," Pettigrew said about Cushman's leadership. 
Neither Cushman or Salamun made any comments at the meeting.

title: Local South Dakota Legislature races: Duhamel, Derby and Howard among winners
description: The South Dakota Legislature primary race results are in. All contested races were on the Republican Party side.
_full_text:
The South Dakota Legislature primary race results are in. All contested races were on the Republican Party side.

Here’s a look at who advanced, according to unofficial results from the South Dakota Secretary of State's Office. One Senate candidate and two House candidates from each race advance to the general election. 

District 29:

Challenger William Meirose beat Sen. John Carley. Meirose received 2,280 votes (51%) to Carley's 2,151 (49%). There's no Democrat in the Senate race, meaning Meirose has a clear path to the Capitol in Pierre in the November election.

In the House, challenger Gary Deering took first place with 2,198 votes (28%). He'll be joined on the general election ballot by former Rep. Gary Cammack, who's seeking to regain his seat after losing in the 2024 primary. Cammack received 2,135 votes (27%) in Tuesday's election.

Sitting Reps. Kathy Rice and Rep. Terri Jorgenson came in third and fourth with 1,957 (25%) and 1,572 votes (20%), respectively.

District 29 includes all of Meade County, including Sturgis.

District 30:

In the Senate, Sen. Amber Hulse, won against former Sen. Julie Frye-Mueller, who Hulse also beat in the 2024 GOP primary.

Hulse received 4,139 votes (67%) to Frye-Mueller's 2,084 (33%). Hulse will be unopposed in the general election.

In the House, Reps. Tim Goodwin and Trish Ladner advanced to the general election, where they'll be joined by Democrat Bret Swanson on the ballot, with two advancing to Pierre.

In Tuesday's primary, Goodwin was first with 3,708 votes (39%), followed by Ladner at 3,450 votes (36%), with challenger Stephan Saint in third at 2,313 votes (24%).

Saint lost to Goodwin and Ladner in 2024.

District 30 includes all or portions of Custer, Fall River and Pennington counties, including Custer State Park and most of the Southern Hills.

District 31:

Sen. Randy Deibert of Spearfish will look to retain his seat in November and seems destined to as there’s no candidate on the Democratic side in District 31. Deibert beat challenger John Teupel, 56% to 44%, according to unofficial results from the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office. Deibert received 2,692 votes to Teupel’s 2,077.

District 31 covers Lawrence County, including Spearfish, Lead and Deadwood. Deibert first won election to the state Senate in 2022.

District 32:

Sen. Helene Duhamel beat challenger Karen McNeal and will face Democrat Jeff Shelton in the general election.

Duhamel received 1,316 votes (63%) to McNeal's 759 (37%).

Duhamel beat McNeal, who ran as an independent, in the 2024 general election.

District 32 includes downtown Rapid City, much of north Rapid City and its southeast corner extends to Cambell Street.

District 33:

Former state Sen. David Johnson is seeking to retain his seat and beat Sen. Curt Voight on Tuesday after losing to him in the 2024 primary.

Johnson won with 2,409 votes (52%) on Tuesday, to Voight's 2,240 (48%). Johnson will face Democrat Christopher Baumgartner in the general.

In the District 33 House race, Rep. Phil Jensen advances to the general election with 2,285 votes (31%).

Second and third in the race were Rep. Curt Massie, who beat challenger Jeff Marlette by five votes — 1,988 to 1,983, which rounds to 27% for each candidate.

The race is close enough a recount is possible for the second spot, according to state law. A legislative candidate may ask for a recount when the margin between two candidates is five votes or less, or 2% or less of the overall vote. The race between Massie and Marlette meets both thresholds.

Jensen and the second place finisher will face Democrat Kari Hall in the general election, after which two of the three will serve in the legislature.

District 33 includes Silver City and Johnson Siding, along with Summerset and Black Hawk on the west side of Interstate 90, with the district boundary including land inside Pennington and Meade counties and some Rapid City neighborhoods.

Since District 33 includes more than one county, if Massie or Marlette want a recount, one will have to file the request with the Secretary of State within three days of the official state canvass.

District 34:

In the Senate, Sen. Taffy Howard beat Jason Green again, receiving 2,334 votes (57%) to Green's 1,760 (43%). The pair also squared off in 2024, with Howard winning.

Howard will face Democrat Michael Calabrese in the general.

A recount is also possible for the second spot in House District 34.

Rep. Mike Derby won handily, with 2,710 votes (42%). The second slot is tight.

Former Rep. Becky Drury and Rep. Heather Baxter are separated by 46 votes. Drury received 1,861 votes (29%) to Baxter's 1,815 (28%). The race meets the 2% or fewer margin requirement for a recount.

Derby and the second-place finisher will face Democrat Victor Diego Dominquez in the general. 

District 34 includes western Rapid City and extends into rural Pennington County.

The trio faced off in the 2024 GOP primary, with Derby and Baxter advancing and, eventually, being elected to the Legislature.

Because District 34 is located entirely within Pennington County, a request for a recount must be filed with the county auditor within three days after the state election canvas.

District 35:

In the Senate, Sen. Greg Blanc received 1,289 votes (52%) to beat challenger Nicole Mitzel, who received 1,180 votes (48%).

In the House, Dale Bartscher was first (1,241 votes, 34%), followed by Jason Fleming (1,205 votes, 33%). Both advance.

Jace West finished third (744 votes, 20%) and Emmett Reistroffer was fourth (484 votes, 13%).

District 35 includes Box Elder, Rapid Valley and parts of eastern Rapid City.

title: Man hit by vehicle on Saint Joseph Street in Rapid City
description: A man was apparently struck by a vehicle heading east on Saint Joseph Street on the evening of Thursday, June 4.
_full_text:
A man was apparently struck by a vehicle heading east on Saint Joseph Street on the evening of Thursday, June 4.

The Journal arrived on the scene at about 6:25 p.m. to find an ambulance parked outside the front of the Hyatt Place in Block 5. Medics inside the ambulance appeared to be treating someone in the back.

A bystander, 14-year-old Will, said he saw a man get out of a vehicle parked in the diagonal spaces on the south side of the street. When he got out, he was struck by the vehicle heading east on Saint Joseph.

The Journal overheard a Rapid City Police Department officer say that the other occupants in the parked vehicle told him the man got out of the vehicle and fell to the ground before being struck. The ambulance left the scene at 6:34 p.m. with the man still in the back.

“I’ve seen a lot of car wrecks, but never this bad,” Will told the Journal.

Will said he was downtown for summer nights when he saw the incident.

The condition of the man is unknown at this time.

A firefighter shields the view of man being treated by medics after he was struck by a vehicle on Saint Joseph Street in Rapid City on Thursday, June 4.
