title: Republican voters once again opt to oust incumbents from South Dakota Legislature
description: After 14 incumbent South Dakota lawmakers lost their seats in the 2024 Republican primary, 16 lost on Tuesday, according to unofficial results from the Secretary of State’s Office.
_full_text:
After 14 incumbent South Dakota lawmakers lost their seats in the 2024 Republican primary, 16 lost on Tuesday, according to unofficial results from the Secretary of State’s Office.

The 2024 shakeup was described as “an earthquake” by Spearfish Rep. Scott Odenbach, a Republican incumbent who won his own primary that year and was elevated to majority leader of the House of Representatives with support from the newcomers. 

Ousted incumbents, 2026 Republican primary
Rep. Logan Manhart, R-Aberdeen
Rep. Al Novstrup, R-Aberdeen
Rep. Dylan Jordan, R-Clear Lake
Rep. Kent Roe, R-Hayti
Rep. Tim Czmowski, R-Sioux Falls
Rep. Bobbi Andera, R-Sioux Falls
Rep. Tony Kayser, R-Sioux Falls
Rep. Terri Jorgenson, R-Rapid City
Rep. Kathy Rice, R-Black Hawk
Rep. Heather Baxter, R-Rapid City
Rep. Josephine Garcia, R-Watertown
Rep. David Kull, R-Brandon
Sen. Carl Perry, R-Aberdeen
Sen. Tamara Grove, R-Lower Brule
Sen. John Carley, R-Piedmont
Sen. Curt Voight, R-Rapid City

In the 2026 primary, those former newcomers made up the majority of the ousted incumbents.

Sioux Falls Mayor Paul TenHaken’s South Dakotans for Common Sense political action committee reported raising $340,500 and spending $214,000 since the beginning of the year. Much of that money went to support an organized effort to retake both legislative chambers at the state Capitol from the 2024 insurgents.

TenHaken was happy on Wednesday.   

“South Dakotans are looking for practical, common-sense leaders who focus more on solving problems than scoring political points,” he said. “I’m encouraged by the results and optimistic about the direction our legislative makeup is heading.”

Odenbach, who had no primary opponent on Tuesday and whose own political action committee offered financial backing to his supporters in the Legislature, did not respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

New leadership

Results are unofficial until canvassed, and several races are marked as potential recounts.

South Dakota Retailers Association President Nathan Sanderson said that based on his count, it’s a “near certainty” that new House and Senate leadership will be elected.  

Several of the lawmakers who lost their seats in the 2024 primary regained them on Tuesday, and several of 2024’s victors won’t return to Pierre.

Lobbying groups like the Retailers Association, political action committees associated with U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson’s gubernatorial campaign and others aligned with South Dakota business interests spent heavily on legislative primaries involving those candidates. 

 060526-nws-sl-incumbents-p1.jpg
The South Dakota Senate meets on Feb. 11, 2026, at the Capitol in Pierre. 

Some current Republican state leaders, both inside and outside the Legislature, directed their campaign dollars toward efforts to defend the seats of the candidates whose victories two years ago helped create the largest freshman class of state lawmakers in more than three decades.

Many of the 14 lawmakers ousted in 2024’s primary had supported legislation that sought to regulate, rather than defeat, a proposal for a five-state carbon capture pipeline proposed by Iowa-based Summit Carbon Solutions that would have run through eastern South Dakota. 

Opponents of the legislation — expressing concern about the private property rights of landowners along the route — referred it to voters, who rejected it in the 2024 general election. Opponents also won enough legislative seats in 2024 to replace the Republican legislative leadership team and ultimately pass legislation banning eminent domain for carbon pipelines — a law that has so far kept the pipeline out of the state. 

Pendulum swings away from 2024 winners

Some of Tuesday’s clearest wins for those dissatisfied with the 2024 primary’s outcome came in the state Senate. Katherine Washnok defeated Senate Assistant Majority Leader Carl Perry in Aberdeen. Like Odenbach, Perry was both an incumbent and pipeline opponent in 2024, and secured a leadership position in 2025. 

Former legislator David Johnson of Rapid City, meanwhile, defeated incumbent Sen. Curt Voight.

Sen. Glen Vilhauer defeated Rep. Josephine Garcia for a Watertown Senate seat. Garcia is a member of the South Dakota Freedom Caucus, which describes itself as “for liberty, limited government, and conservative values” and supported anti-eminent domain legislation.  

Only one member of the Freedom Caucus’ nine publicly listed members will return to Pierre. Three did not run this year, and five others lost their primary races: Sen. John Carley and Reps. Dylan Jordan, Logan Manhart, Heather Baxter and Tony Kayser, although recounts are possible in Baxter’s and Kayser’s races. Baxter told the Rapid City Journal she doesn't plan to pursue a recount.

Freedom Caucus Chairman Rep. Phil Jensen, R-Rapid City, remains. 

Some former lawmakers return

Sen. Michael Rohl, R-Aberdeen, identifies with the faction that retook some seats. He also expects new legislative leadership to be elected.

“The 2027 and 2028 sessions are going to feature some really talented public servants,” Rohl said.

The Senate wins for Rohl’s preferred colleagues were mirrored in the results for the House of Representatives. Ryan Kohl and former legislator Fred Deutsch led a five-candidate field in the Watertown area, with Freedom Caucus’ Dylan Jordan finishing fourth. 

In Sioux Falls, Rep. Taylor Rehfeldt and former legislator Tyler Tordsen led their House race. That race is flagged for a recount, because Tordsen leads Kayser by 52 votes, within the recount margin.

In a district encompassing parts of the northeastern Black Hills and nearby rural areas, Gary Deering and former legislator Gary Cammack finished ahead of Reps. Kathy Rice of Blackhawk and Terri Jorgenson of Piedmont, who both received support from Odenbach’s Liberty Tree PAC.

Candidates supported by Odenbach’s PAC also had some successes: 

Rapid City Sen. Taffy Howard defeated Jason Green of Rapid City. 

Sen. Mykala Voita of Bonesteel defeated former Sen. Erin Tobin of Winner. 

Sen. Lauren Nelson defeated former Sen. Jean Hunhoff in Yankton.

title: Brookings man found dead at Deerfield Lake in Pennington County
description: A 68-year-old Brookings man was found dead Thursday, June 4, at Deerfield Lake in Pennington County.
_full_text:
A 68-year-old Brookings man was found dead Thursday, June 4, at Deerfield Lake in Pennington County.

At about 10:30 a.m., Thursday, emergency responders responded to Deerfield Lake for a report of an individual in distress. Upon arrival, first responders found a man named Terry Olson. 

Despite response efforts of emergency personnel, Olson was pronounced dead at the scene. Preliminary information indicated the death may have resulted from a medical emergency, the Pennington County Sheriff's Office said. 

The sheriff's office said there is no indication of suspicious circumstances and the incident remains under review.

title: District 35 House primary: Pair of newcomers, Bartscher and Fleming, secure slots
description: In the District 35 Republican primary on Tuesday, June 2, first-time candidates Dale Bartscher and Jason Fleming took the party nominations. Bartscher pulled in 1,241 votes (34%), and Fleming received 1,205 (33%). They beat out Jace West and Emmett Reistroffer, who received 744 votes (20%) and 484 votes (13%), respectively.
_full_text:
In the District 35 Republican primary on Tuesday, June 2, first-time candidates Dale Bartscher and Jason Fleming took the party nominations. Bartscher pulled in 1,241 votes (34%), and Fleming received 1,205 (33%). They beat out Jace West and Emmett Reistroffer, who received 744 votes (20%) and 484 votes (13%), respectively.

“It’s feeling absolutely wonderful,” Bartscher told the Journal on Wednesday, June 3. “I’m more than grateful for the many who came out and put their trust in me to trust me with their vote. I’m ready for the challenge of this November. I’m going to go into it with a great amount of gusto.”

Bartscher and Jason Fleming will face Democrat Ken Jeakins for the District 35 House seat in the general election in November. Democrat Greg Blanc, who did not respond to the Journal’s request for an interview by press time, will run unopposed for the District 35 Senate seat.

Fleming said he joined the race late and put in a lot of work and door-to-door campaigning to get in front of voters.

“It paid off. We’re excited,” Fleming told the Journal on Wednesday, June 3. “I’ve always been involved in politics and followed politics and (serve on a lot of) boards in the community. I figured I’d throw my hat in the ring and see what happens.”

Fleming and Bartscher will face Democrat Ken Jeakins for a District 35 House seat in the general election in November.

Bartscher believes his South Dakota roots and his values appeal to voters.

“Voters really appreciated the fact that I have been a lifelong South Dakotan, born and raised here in this great state. I’ve raised my children here. My wife, Jan, and I have lived in District 35 for over 30 years,” he said.

“They’ve also appreciated the fact that I stand for conservative Christian values and I’m a Constitutionalist. Voters appreciated hearing that,” Bartscher said.

 Jason Fleming
Jason Fleming won in the primary election Tuesday, June 2, for the District 35 House seat. 

Bartscher also said voters liked his positive campaign.

“They’ve had enough of the negative. They’ve appreciated everything they’ve seen come out to be very issue-oriented and positive,” he said.  

He plans to remain “in campaign mode 24/7” leading up to the general election.

“I will continue to visit with people one on one, continue to get my name out there and speak to people about those issues that matter to them,” Bartscher said.

 Dale Bartscher
Dale Bartscher (Republican) is running for representative in District 35 

Concerns about money were the top issues Fleming heard about from voters as he campaigned.

“The most important thing, in talking to voters, was money. Property taxes – where is the money going in the state and why are taxes so high?” Fleming said. “We’ve definitely got to address it. I’m not for eliminating property tax, but we have to work on property tax. We definitely need to figure out something and cut it, and really look at the budget and see where we can make sure there’s no wasteful spending.”

A day after his primary election win, Fleming said he’s “taking it all in” and in a few months he’ll start gearing up for the November election.

Republican Sen. Greg Blanc, who did not respond to the Journal’s request for an interview by press time, will run unopposed for the District 35 Senate seat. Blanc (1,289 votes, 52%) beat challenger Nicole Mitzel (1,180 votes, 48%).

title: 21-year-old arrested for manslaughter after Rapid City apartment shooting
description: A 21-year-old Rapid City man is in custody after another man was shot and killed at south Rapid City apartment.
_full_text:
A 21-year-old Rapid City man is in custody after another man was shot and killed at south Rapid City apartment.

Around 12:30 a.m. Thursday, June 4, the Rapid City Police Department received a report of a shooting at 3350 Palm Drive, Vista Pointe Apartments.

When officers arrived, they found 21-year-old Christopher Tromp, of Rapid City, in the parking lot. Police said Tromp was identified as the shooter. Other officers went into the apartment building and found a man who was shot and “obviously deceased.”

Police transported Tromp to the Public Safety Building on Kansas City Street to be interviewed by detectives. Following the interview, Tromp was placed under arrest on suspicion of first-degree manslaughter.

The name of the victim is being withheld until proper notification of next-of-kin can be accomplished. The investigation into the shooting remains active and ongoing.

Court records show Tromp has traffic violations and a use or possession of drug paraphernalia conviction on his record, all from 2023.

Tromp is currently held at the Pennington County Jail on no bond. He is set to appear in court at 10 a.m. on Friday, June 5.

title: Meade County Sheriff's Office finds body of missing Black Hawk man
description: The Meade County Sheriff's Office reported finding the body of a 23-year-old man on Tuesday, June 3 at 3 p.m.
_full_text:
The Meade County Sheriff's Office reported finding the body of a 23-year-old man on Tuesday, June 3 at 3 p.m. 

Following an extensive three-day search involving numerous agencies and volunteers, authorities said Jonah Temple of Black Hawk, who was reported missing on Sunday, May 31, died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

During the initial investigation, Temple's vehicle was located on U.S. Forest Service property at the far west end of Peaceful Pines Road. The sheriff's office extended its deepest condolences to Temple's family and loved ones during this difficult time. 

"The efforts demonstrated over the past three days are a testament to the spirit of service and cooperation that we rely upon throughout the Black Hills," Sheriff Pat West said. "This search effort and the eventual recovery of Mr. Temple would not have been possible without the countless hours contributed by our partner agencies and volunteers. We are sincerely grateful for their commitment and support."

The investigation remains ongoing, and final determinations will be made by the appropriate authorities.

title: Ward 2: Seachris ‘deeply honored’ to win another term
description: Rapid City Councilwoman Lindsey Seachris will keep her seat.
_full_text:
Rapid City Councilwoman Lindsey Seachris will keep her seat.

In Ward 2, Searchris (775 votes, 54%) beat challenger Chris Vanderhoof (652 votes, 46%) in the Tuesday, June 2 election. Council members serve three-year terms.

“I'm just deeply honored and grateful for the opportunity to continue serving and representing Ward 2,” Seachris told the Journal. “It was a narrow margin. I really commend Christopher for running a clean campaign. It was a fair process. I think we both ran the clean campaigns, and, especially in City Council, local government, that's so important that these races remain nonpartisan and remain focused on issues, community and vision and our future.”

“So I think he did a great job, and really commend his efforts, and I think it's healthy and great to have good candidates step forward,” Seachris continued.

 Forum
From left, Rapid City Council candidates Josh Biberdorf, Murray Lee, Christopher Vanderhoof, Lindsey Seachris, Andrea Schaefer and Kevin Maher speak during the Citizens for Libery candidate forum. 

Looking to the future, Seachris said focusing on the basics is important.

“We need to really prioritize our roads and infrastructure. I know we heard that throughout the campaign. It really is a huge need and priority of our community, especially in Ward 2,” she said. “We have a lot of traffic challenges.”

Seachris is the council’s liaison to Rapid City Parks and Recreation and she said she’ll work with city staff and fellow council members on more funding sources with an eye toward long-term stability.

 Lindsey Seachris
Lindsey Seachris 

“Right now, we allocate a very small portion of our general fund to the operations of Parks and Rec … We have about $2 million in deferred maintenance annually with our parks system,” she said. “I’m a huge advocate for neighborhood parks,” she said, noting the need to recognize that “planned development and quality of life are tied into our park system, and we need to figure out how we can sustain that better.”

Vanderhoof told the Journal, “The people picked what they wanted, so that’s how it goes,” and noted he’d posted a reaction on Facebook.

“Thank you to everyone who cast their vote yesterday. It was truly an honor to speak with the people of Ward 2 and across our city. The right to vote and to have our voices heard is what makes this country strong. While this election did not end in my favor, I respect the outcome and want to formally congratulate and concede to the winner. Serving this community is a great privilege, and I am grateful for the support, conversations, and trust so many of you placed in me,” he said in the post. “Elections remind us that there are different perspectives, strong convictions, and people willing to stand up for what they believe is right. That is something worth respecting and protecting. This is not the end of my commitment to our community, but it is a new beginning.”

Seachris said, “Thank you to everyone who supported me throughout this process. It's been a humbling experience. I've learned a lot about myself and my community, and I'm really grateful for the opportunity. And I take nothing for granted. I'm going to work hard for all of us.”

title: Rapid City Ward 3: Maher ‘happy with the results;’ Shaefer plans to run again

_full_text:
The Rapid City Council election held on Tuesday, June 2, is over. There were contests in all five of the city’s wards for the first time in over two decades. In Ward 3, Councilman Kevin Maher (1,921 votes, 58%) beat challenger Andrea Schaefer (1,392, 42%). Maher, who currently holds the seat that he just won, will be sworn in for another three-year term at the Monday, July 6, council meeting.

On Wednesday, June 3, Maher told the Journal, “Of course I’m happy with the results. My opponent and I … we got along pretty good during the campaign, and she did very well for first time candidate.”

 Kevin Maher
Kevin Maher 

Maher said he’s looking forward to the council with Councilman Josh Biberdorf (Ward 1) and Councilwoman Lindsay Seachris (Ward 2) returning for another term and former Councilwoman Laura Armstrong set to rejoin on July 6 to represent Ward 5.

“I’m looking forward to a fresh start in July,” Maher said. “We have a lot of big things coming up.”

Maher noted a transportation TIF to extend East Anamosa Street to Elk Vale Road, the next budget, continuing to take care of public safety and “some ideas about what to do with some of our homeless issues.”

On the campaign, Schaefer said, “I’m proud of my campaign and grateful for all the support and the voters that showed up. I’ve learned so much about myself and this great city, and I intend to run again in the future.”

Andrea Schaefer

title: Dr. Michael Wayne Kadrmas, M.D.
_full_text:
May 7, 1967 - May 29, 2026

Michael Wayne Kadrmas, 59, passed away peacefully on May 29, 2026, at his home in Rapid City, South Dakota, surrounded by the family he loved and devoted his life to serving.

Michael was born on May 7, 1967, to Wayne and Shirley Kadrmas in Hettinger, North Dakota, and grew up in Sheridan, Wyoming, where the Bighorn Mountains shaped his boyhood and never let him go. It was there that he earned the nickname "Maddog Kad" on the football field and met Kari Lidahl — his high school sweetheart and the partner of everything that followed.

From an early age, Michael felt called to a life of service, shaped in part by a childhood medical emergency that revealed the difference a physician could make. Through the Air Force Health Professions Scholarship Program, he completed his medical degree at the University of Washington in 1994 then served as a General Medical Officer in the United States Air Force. His service took him to England, where he supported contingency operations, embassy evacuations, and Space Shuttle alternate landing sites, and to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where he ran toward a burning airplane after it crashed on the runway and extracted numerous crew members from the wreckage — an act of courage for which he was awarded the Airman's Medal for Heroism, and which he spoke of rarely.

After training in Orthopedic Surgery at Duke University, Michael joined Black Hills Orthopedic and Spine Center in Rapid City, where he spent nearly three decades as an orthopedic trauma surgeon. He understood that distance is its own kind of suffering and dedicated his career to ensuring that families across western South Dakota, Wyoming, North Dakota, and Nebraska could receive high-quality trauma care close to home.

A phrase Michael returned to often — the right thing is rarely the easy thing — was less a motto than a self-portrait. He was humble, steady, and led entirely by example. Outside of medicine, he was most himself in the Bighorns, bringing his family to the same trails and campsites he had loved as a boy, and finding in them something worth passing on.

Michael is survived by his wife, Kari Kadrmas, whom he married on June 29, 1991, and cherished for nearly 35 years. He is also survived by his three children and their families: his son Caleb, daughter-in-law Megan, and grandchildren Warren and Emma Kadrmas of Alexandria, Virginia; his daughter Alyssa, son-in-law Chandler, and grandson Oliver Brooks of Rapid City; and his son Warren Kadrmas of Rapid City. He is further survived by his mother, Shirley Kadrmas of Sheridan, Wyoming, and his in-laws, Larry and Karen Lidahl of Sheridan, Wyoming. He was preceded in death by his father, Wayne Kadrmas, and his beloved brother, Warren Kadrmas.

To those who offered comfort, care, and presence over the past five years, the family is profoundly grateful.

All are welcome to attend a Celebration of Life from 5:30-8:30 p.m. on Monday, July 6, 2026 at Pine Haven Venue and Lodging, 13514 US-16, Rapid City, SD 57702.

In lieu of flowers, the family welcomes expressions of sympathy in a form that reflects how Michael lived — in service to others.

At this time, the family requests you share your condolences through the funeral home's online guestbook. Sympathy cards may be sent to the funeral home or brought to the Celebration of Life.

Arrangements with Kirk Funeral Home.

title: Robert J Clements
_full_text:
August 4, 1952 - May 30, 2026

Robert "Bob" Clements was born August 4, 1952 in Quinn, SD to John F and Colleen (Buchholz) Clements. Bob grew up on his parents ranch 14 miles north of Philip, SD until moving to Wall, SD in 1967. After attending his elementary years at a country school near the ranch, he spent his Freshman year at Philip High School and the remaining high school years at Wall High School before graduating in 1970.

Robert attended art school and lived most of his life as an artist and gallerist. He owned the Robert Clements Gallery and framing business in Portland, ME eventually moving that business to Belle Fourche, SD and finally to Mineral Point, WI.

In February 1988 Robert and Ellen Mugar were united in marriage in Minneapolis, MN. To this union, a daughter, Lydia Louise was born in 1991. Lydia followed in her dad's love of both art and rocks. He was noted as saying, "I never met a rock I didn't like". Robert also had a great love of the prairie whether driving or hiking around, he was at home.

Surviving Robert are his daughter, Lydia Clements and her husband Elijah Melanson from Raleigh, NC; his sister Connie Richards, IA; his brother David Clements, WY; and his sister, Nancy Clements, WI. In addition, Robert is survived by several nieces and nephews and many cousins.

He was preceded in death by his parents.

A Celebration Life Gathering will be June 23 from 1-4 pm in Wall, SD. Location is pending and information soon to be announced.

title: Former U.S. president Joe Biden takes the mic in Sioux Falls
description: SIOUX FALLS — Amid a battle with stage four cancer, former president Joe Biden served as the keynote speaker for the South Dakota Democratic Party's McGovern Day Dinner on Friday, June 5, in Sioux Falls.
_full_text:
SIOUX FALLS — Amid a battle with stage four cancer, former president Joe Biden served as the keynote speaker for the South Dakota Democratic Party's McGovern Day Dinner on Friday, June 5, in Sioux Falls.

During his speech, Biden called President Donald Trump, "the most corrupt president in the history of the United States" and urged the crowd to vote Democrat in the upcoming general election to shift the tide of the state and country. Among the most notable races for South Dakotan democrats include Dan Ahlers' run for state governor, Julian Beaudion's bid for U.S. Senate and Nikki Gronli's campaign for the state's U.S. House seat, who all spoke after Biden. 

"From the bottom of my heart," the 46th president said at the Best Western Plus Ramkota Exhibit Hall, "There's no better place to start than right here in South Dakota."

According to Jessica Meyers, vice chair of the South Dakota Democratic Party, the event sold out within 72 hours and sold a record-breaking 1,200 tickets. 

 060726-nws-bidenphotos-p13.JPG
Former U.S. President Joe Biden delivered the keynote address at the South Dakota Democratic Party's McGovern Day Dinner on Friday, June 5, at the Best Western Plus Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls. 

It was Biden's first Rushmore State appearance since providing the eulogy at George McGovern's funeral in 2012. McGovern, a Democrat born in Avon, represented South Dakota in both the U.S. Senate and House during his lifetime. Biden, according to previous reporting by Politico, said McGovern's outspoken anti-Vietnam War stance provided the then-29-year-old Biden the "courage" to run for a Delaware Senate seat in 1972. He won despite being considered a heavy underdog at the time. 

Speaking in the late senator's home state once again, Biden reflected on McGovern's life and legacy, calling McGovern "a good friend."

The 83-year-old Biden's keynote address on Friday comes as he's fighting stage four metastatic prostate cancer that has spread to his bones. On June 1, Biden's wife, Jill, told NBC's "Today" the 46th president was "doing OK" despite his circumstances.

Considering his ongoing battle, Laura Armstrong — who was elected on Tuesday, June 2, to represent Ward 5 on the Rapid City Council — called it an "inspiration."

 Laura Armstrong
Laura Armstrong, who secured a seat to represent Ward 5 on the Rapid City Council, speaks at a candidate forum held at the Dahl Arts Center on May 7. Armstrong attended at the South Dakota Democratic Party's McGovern Day Dinner on Friday, June 5, at the Best Western Plus Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls where former president Joe Biden spoke. 

"Here he is battling cancer and other things going on. It just shows that, 'you know, what's your excuse?'" said Armstrong, who will take her spot on the council on July 6. "He's still in the game, he wants other people to be engaged in the game. He wants people to stay engaged, regardless of the tumultuousness that's going on. He wants to unify people. He wants to inspire people, and it's really important just to stay engaged, regardless."

 060726-nws-bidenphotos-p11.JPG
Rep. Nicole Uhre-Balk, D-32, smiles for a photo at the South Dakota Democratic Party's McGovern Day Dinner on Friday, June 5, at the Best Western Plus Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls. 

Rep. Nicole Uhre-Balk, who is a Democrat running for re-election to represent Rapid City’s District 32 in the South Dakota House, said, "It's just such an honor to have a former president, come and be here, and to take time, and to say hello to South Dakotans, because oftentimes we're flyover country, and so it is a really big deal to have someone who has had that position come and be here."

Biden was diagnosed on May 2, 2025, nearly one year after he ended his re-election campaign — on July 21, 2024 — because of health concerns. 

But Biden's roughly 20-minute speech appeared to be a stark contrast from his infamous debate performance against Trump that first prompted calls for him to step down. As he flipped through his notes at the lectern, he rarely stumbled, his voice carried through the room and he looked toward the audience while unloading barbs toward Trump. 

 060726-nws-bidenphotos-p5.JPG
Former U.S. President Joe Biden gives a thumbs up to the crowd after delivering the keynote address at the South Dakota Democratic Party's McGovern Day Dinner on Friday, June 5, at the Best Western Plus Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls. 

After criticizing Trump's ambitions to "tear down the East Wing of the White House" and "building an arch that will dwarf the Lincoln Memorial."

Toward the end of his speech, the audience rallied around Biden when he listed a Trump criticism — increasing gas prices for example — and followed it by booming into the mic, "vote Democrat."

As the crowd applauded, Biden mentioned the swelling support he had seen during speaking engagements he's made across the country. 

"The same thing happened in Delaware. We had over 1,000 people for our dinner. It was the biggest thing we've ever had," Biden said. "In a situation where I'm doing Maryland's dinners, I'm doing North Carolina, the crowds are enormous, not because of me, but because so much is at stake, so much is at stake."

"We have a chance to right so many wrongs very quickly, very quickly. We got to step up," he said, before exiting the lectern on his own volition to a rousing applause. 

 060726-nws-bidenphotos-p8.JPG
Former U.S. President Joe Biden exits the stage after delivering the keynote address at the South Dakota Democratic Party's McGovern Day Dinner on Friday, June 5, at the Best Western Plus Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls.

title: It’s official: Pennington County Commission canvasses June 2 election, GOP turnout over 35%
description: The Pennington County Commission made official the votes cast within the county in the Tuesday, June 2, election.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Commission made official the votes cast within the county in the Tuesday, June 2, election.

Pennington County Auditor Sabrina Green presented the results to the commission on Thursday, June 5.

The canvass recognized the election results for the Republican primaries for South Dakota governor, the legislature, Pennington County Auditor, three Pennington County Commission races and state’s congressional seats, as well as races for Republican party precinct committee members. Also included in the audit is the Custer School District Board races, and the mayoral race and city council races in Hill City and Rapid City.

The council voted 4-0 to approve the canvass. Commissioner Ron Rossknecht (District 1) was absent at the meeting.

The results showed 20,321 Pennington County residents voted in the election out of the 87,871 registered. This marks a voter turnout of 23.13%.

There are 45,967 registered Republicans and 41,904 registered nonpartisan voters in the county. Of those nonpartisans, 9.19% (3,894) voted in the election. As for the registered Republicans, 35.82% (16,472) of those registered voted in the election. South Dakota has a closed primary election, and the bulk of races in Pennington County were for the Republican primaries. The municipal and school board elections were open to all parties.

Green said a post-election precinct audit, which is usually done during a canvass, could not take place Thursday because a recount has been requested for a precinct, exempting the office from conducting the precinct audit.

An auditor's office staffer told the Journal this was due to Tonchi Weaver having filed a recount for the Republican Precinct Committeewoman for Precinct 5-3. She is opposed by Leigha Carsrud, who received 151 votes. Weaver received 149, just two fewer than her opponent.

Here’s a snapshot of some of the results that came out of Pennington County:

The county’s voters favored Toby Doeden in the governor’s race, with 5,810 (35.82%) voting for him in the primary. Gov. Larry Rhoden came in second place with 4,714 (29.07%) of the county’s vote. Statewide, Rhoden received 34,379 votes (25%) and Doeden received 41,791 (31%). Since neither candidate cleared the 35% threshold statewide to secure the party nomination (Doeden cleared it in Pennington County), they’re headed for a run-off election on July 28. The other two Republicans vying for governor, were pushed out by Doedon and Rhoden with Rep. Dusty Johnson garnering 31,925 votes (23%) and Jon Hansen pulling in 28,390 (21%). Democrat Dan Ahlers will face off with the Republican pick in the November election.

In the Republican primary for the state’s seat in the U.S. Senate, Pennington County followed suit with the vast majority of that in choosing Sen. Mike Rounds. Rounds received 101,471 (76%) of the vote statewide and 11,629 votes (72.51% in Pennington County. His opponent Justin McNeal received 32,412 votes (24%) statewide and slightly more support — 4,409 votes (27.49%) — in Pennington County. Rounds will face Democrat Julian Beaudion in the November general election.

South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley also received the overwhelming support of Pennington County voters and voters across the state in his bid for the Republican nomination for the U.S. House race. He received 103,290 votes (79%) statewide and 12,026 votes (76.63%) in Pennington County. His opponent James Bialota pulled in 3,668 votes (23.37%) in Pennington County and 27,140 (21%) statewide. Jackley will face Democrat Nicole “Nikki” Gronli in the general election.

State Rep. Tina Mulally received 6,767 votes (53% of ballots cast) to beat Auditor Sabrina Green, who received 6,111 votes (47%).

In the Pennington County races: State Rep. Tina Mulally received 6,767 votes (53% of ballots cast) to beat Auditor Sabrina Green, who received 6,111 votes (47%). In District 1 for the Pennington County Commission, Mike Mueller beat Zachary Bush. Mueller received 2,267 votes, good for 58% of ballots cast. Bush received 1,648 votes (42%). In District 3, Commissioner Deb Hadcock received 1,300 votes (62%) to beat challenger Randy Decker, who received 810 votes (38%). There are no Democrats or independents running for auditor or in the commission districts.

title: 21-year-old makes court appearance for death at Rapid City apartment
description: A 21-year-old Rapid City man made his first court appearance after 22-year-old Gavin Price died at a south Rapid City apartment.
_full_text:
A 21-year-old Rapid City man made his first court appearance after 22-year-old Gavin Price died at a south Rapid City apartment. 

Christopher Tromp appeared for his initial appearance before Magistrate Court Judge Scott Bogue at the Pennington County Courthouse Friday, June 5. 

Tromp is charged with first-degree manslaughter, which is a Class C felony that carries a maximum penalty of life in prison and a $50,000 fine. There is no minimum sentence.

In court, Tromp and his family fought back tears as Bogue read Tromp his rights. Senior Deputy States Attorney Braedon Houdek requested Tromp's bond be set to $1 million cash only, stating there was numerous times Tromp admitted to law enforcement that, "he shot and killed Gavin Price." 

Houdek said there was also substantial amount of evidence and witness testimony that placed Tromp in an apartment at 3350 Palm Drive (Vista Pointe Apartments) during the time of the shooting. 

When officers arrived, they found Tromp in the parking lot. Police said Tromp was identified as the shooter. Other officers went into the apartment building and found Price who was shot and “obviously deceased.”

Police transported Tromp to the Public Safety Building on Kansas City Street to be interviewed by detectives. Following the interview, Tromp was placed under arrest on suspicion of first-degree manslaughter. Bogue entered a not guilty plea on Tromp’s behalf at the hearing. Magistrate judges cannot accept guilty pleas on felonies and its customary a not guilty plea is entered on initial appearances.

Court records show Tromp has traffic violations and a use or possession of drug paraphernalia conviction on his record, all from 2023.

Before considering bond, Bogue credited Tromp having no previous violent convictions and having strong support from family in the courtroom, however, he said the first-degree manslaughter is "one of the most serious offenses." 

Tromp's bond was set to $750,000 cash only and his next court appearance is yet to be determined.

title: Pennington County approves of Black Hills Marketplace TIF, in partnership with Rapid City
description: A Tax Increment Financing District (TIF) that includes land within Pennington County and Rapid City limits is moving forward.
_full_text:
A Tax Increment Financing District (TIF) that includes land within Pennington County and Rapid City limits is moving forward.

The Pennington County Board of Commissioners voted 4-0 on Tuesday, June 2, to approve the Black Hills Marketplace Tax Increment Financing District, which carries a value of $68 million for future major retail and restaurant developments, as well as single and multi-family residential developments. The TIF area is about 192 acres located generally south of Catron Boulevard, west of Fifth Street and east of Black Hills Boulevard. The project site is approximately 172 acres.

The Rapid City limits section is on Catron Boulevard and accounts for less than 5% of the TIF’s acreage, Rapid City Finance Director Daniel Ainslie estimated in April.

The Black Hills Marketplace Development Team submitted the TIF request to the commission on Tuesday, June 2. The county board’s vice chair Ron Rossknecht (District 1) was absent from the meeting. 

The Rapid City Council in April approved allowing the city land to be included in the TIF. Pennington County Commission Office Director Jordan Neeb told the Journal the county plans to annex the county’s portion of the TIF to the city. Hadcock asked Hand about the details of an area within the TIF that is intended to be used by the county. Hand said it is planned for six to nine acres to be allocated to the county for future needed space.

Hand clarified to Journal, “anytime that a property abuts Rapid City limits, when they plot it, (it) automatically gets annexed, and also Rapid City is providing the water and sewer service, so they'll be annexed based on that.”

Some council members posed skepticism about the level of oversight the city has over the TIF.

Rapid City Finance Director Daniel Ainslie previously told the Journal the city would have some oversight of the project. He said the city still controls the planning and zoning aspects of the project that’s within the city limits.

Pennington County Planning Director Brittney Hand presented to the board a brief outline of the TIF.

 Ron Weifenbach
Commissioner Ron Weifenbach (District 2) carefully reads the project plans for the Black Hills Marketplace $68 million TIF. 

The TIF will be used for improvements to the general area for the future erection of structures. These improvements include extension of Black Hills Boulevard and Fifth Street, adding turn lanes on Catron Boulevard and an extension of internal commercial roadway, water and utility infrastructure other improvements.

Project details for future construction include 400,000 square feet of retail, hospitality and restaurants, a 500-unit multi-family development and 130 single-family residential homes. Plans include sites for future retail and restaurants and industrial.

 Brittney Hand
Pennington County Planning Director Brittney Hand presented an overview of the proposed TIF. 

Hand said after the erection of structures in the area is complete, the estimated value of the development will be more than $500 million.

She said the project will add 900 full-time jobs and 2,000 construction-related jobs.

The current property value of the land is $74,600, with an estimated property value of $214.6 million after development is complete.

Commissioners Ron Weifenbach (District 2) and Deb Hadcock (District 3) said they approved the TIF as it would provide needed infrastructure and improvements for the area.

 Jerry Derr
The Pennington County Board of Commissioners voted 4-0 to approve the TIF request. Commissioner Ron Rosskencht was absent at the June 3 meeting.

title: Rapid City warns of email scam seeking funds transfer on application fees
description: City of Rapid City officials are warning the public of an email scam requesting immediate wire transfer of funds to the City’s Planning Commission to process development applications.
_full_text:
City of Rapid City officials are warning the public of an email scam requesting immediate wire transfer of funds to the City’s Planning Commission to process development applications.

Officials were notified Thursday morning, June 4, by a local business official, who shared an email that appeared to have been sent by the City’s Planning Commission. The detailed email included the City’s seal and indicated the correspondence was from the City of Rapid City – Planning Commission; with an invoice number, date, and indicating fees were due upon receipt. The correspondence included an invoice with line items of various fees totaling $5,000 and indicating failure to immediately remit payment would delay final administrative, processing, scheduling and approval actions with the application.

“This correspondence appears legitimate with the use of the City’s seal and details that appear official in nature,” said Vicki Fisher, Director of Rapid City’s Community Development Department. “This is a scam. The City’s Planning Commission does not e-mail or send out correspondence seeking payment. Although there are various fees associated with City permits and applications from the City’s Community Development Department, we would never seek immediate wire transfer of funds or threaten to delay work on the processing of applications without the wire transfer of funds.”

City officials advise the public that legitimate e-mail messages from Rapid City government departments and staff will contain @rcgov.org (City offices), @rcplib.org (Rapid City Public Library) or @themonument.live (The Monument) as part of the sender’s address. Official correspondence will never be sent from the Rapid City Planning Commission. As a general rule, do not open links or attachments from unknown sources. In addition, anyone receiving the Planning Commission wire transfer e-mail request is advised to contact Community Development. Department staff are available to discuss the status of individual permits and applications with City customers.

title: Pennington County grants sheriff’s request to increase law enforcement wages
description: Pennington County Sheriff Brian Mueller took to the podium on Wednesday, June 3, standing before the Pennington County Board of Commissioners, and requested a 3% increase to law enforcement wages, and the commission was receptive.
_full_text:
Pennington County Sheriff Brian Mueller took to the podium on Wednesday, June 3, standing before the Pennington County Board of Commissioners, and requested a 3% increase to law enforcement wages, and the commission was receptive.

The commission voted 4-0 to approve the increase. Commissioner Ron Rossknecht (District 1) was absent at the meeting.

Current wages starting wages:

Deputy I: $30.46

Deputy II: $31.56

Sergeant: $38.42

Lieutenant: $45.38

Captain: $51.38

Chief Deputy: $58.02

New starting wages to go into effect on July 5:

Deputy I: $31.37

Deputy II: $32.51

Sergeant: $39.57

Lieutenant: $46.74

Captain: $52.89

Chief Deputy: $59.76

Mueller expressed to the commission the importance of competitive wages in markets that include the Rapid City Police Department.

"I talked to Commissioner (Jerry Derr) yesterday, instead of asking for the motion to be a cost of living adjustment, to ask it to be a market adjustment, which is really what it is ... Part of it is our main competitor with Rapid City Police Department has really gotten out ahead of us with wages,” Mueller said."

RCPD wages:

Officer: $33.88

Officer II: $34.07

Senior Officer: $36.47

Sergeant: $50.31

Lieutenant: $53.22

Captain: $59.90

Assistant Chief: $61.70

To balance this increase with the sheriff’s office budget, Mueller said he will return to the county in late June with reductions of their overall budget.

Before voting, Commissioner Ron Weifenbach (District 2) said, "I just want to thank the sheriff and Jerry (Derr) for the hard work. I don't think anybody understands some of the hard work that goes in here. I think it's easy to throw rocks at somebody that's digging into this stuff, but I know that Commissioner Derr has worked diligently on giving us proper information, and Brian (Mueller) has delved in and said, ‘tell me what you want and let's work together to make something happen.’"

title: Update: Fairgrounds shooting suspect dead after officer-involved shooting on Pine Ridge
description: Law enforcement is looking for this man, John Lee, of Rapid City, after a June 7 shooting at Central States Fairgrounds. Law enforcement believe he has since shaved his face.
_full_text:
John Lee
Law enforcement is looking for this man, John Lee, of Rapid City, after a June 7 shooting at Central States Fairgrounds. Law enforcement believe he has since shaved his face. 

The man who is accused of shooting another man at the Central States Fairgrounds on Sunday, June 7, is now dead.

The Pennington County Sheriff’s Office provided an update just after 2 p.m. on Sunday and said 58-year-old John Troy Lee, of Rapid City, is dead after an officer-involved shooting on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation.

The Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety said the agency was informed on Sunday that Lee was possibly headed toward the reservation. After a search and coordinated law enforcement response, Lee was found on the southwest portion of the reservation after local residents tipped off OSTDPS. During the encounter, Lee shot at officers, hitting and injuring one, according to the law enforcement agency. During the encounter, Lee was killed.

“There is no further threat to public safety,” the sheriff’s office said. “The Rapid City Police, South Dakota Highway Patrol, Rapid City Fire, US National Park Service, and Oglala Sioux Tribal law enforcement are assisting with this ongoing investigation.”

Earlier Sunday, law enforcement had asked for the public’s help in locating Lee after a shooting at the fairgrounds in Rapid City that left another man injured. He remains hospitalized as of the afternoon update. His name and condition are not being released at this time.

Before he was found, law enforcement released photos of Lee and noted he was driving a white GMC pickup. Lee left the area, and law enforcement said he was believed to be armed and dangerous and he may have dyed his hair black and shaven his beard.

 John Lee
Police are looking for this man who is wanted for a shooting at Central States Fairgrounds on Sunday, June 7. 

From earlier:

“If you happen to see him or somebody you believe may be our bad guy, then please call us. Again, he’s probably armed and dangerous,” Rapid City Police Department Capt. Christian Sigel said Sunday, urging people not to approach Lee or to try to get involved in any way but to call law enforcement.

Pennington County Sheriff’s Capt. Casey Kenrick said around 8:45 a.m. Sunday law enforcement responded to the Central States Fairgrounds for the report of shooting. When law enforcement arrived, they found a man who had been shot.

“And that’s why we’re looking for John,” Kenrick said earlier Sunday.

Sigel said numerous resources from different agencies were dedicated to restoring order at the fairgrounds and finding Lee. Kenrick thanked the U.S. Forest Service for their help and noted, in addition to the sheriff’s office, the Rapid City Police Department, Rapid City Fire Department and the South Dakota Highway Patrol responded to the fairgrounds.

According to the Central States Fair website, there are two events underway on Sunday, June 7, the Scottish Collie Preservation Society 10 Year Anniversary and Boots and Saddles Playdays.

 John Lee
Lee is believed to be driving a white GMC pickup.

title: Rapid City cancels hydrant parties, citing drought and water restrictions
description: Due to drought conditions and water restrictions, Rapid City’s popular hydrant parties have been cancelled after a three-year run. Last year, one of the parties was rescheduled and then ultimately cancelled due to cold weather. This year, it’s the opposite.
_full_text:
Due to drought conditions and water restrictions, Rapid City’s popular hydrant parties have been cancelled after a three-year run. Last year, one of the parties was rescheduled and then ultimately cancelled due to cold weather. This year, it’s the opposite.

Two hydrant parties, hosted by the Rapid City Parks and Recreation Department, were scheduled this year for June 17 at Sioux Park and July 8 at College Park. The events include fire department personnel spraying water on participants from fire hoses and also include participation from the Rapid City Police Department, Rapid City Public Library and Solid Waste Division.

 Hydrant Block Party
Some families brought water guns and water balloons to fight off the summer heat at a hydrant party in Sioux Park on June 18, 2025. 

“The Splish Splash fire hydrant parties are very popular and the kids and families love them, but under the circumstances, due to the severe drought conditions and water restrictions, we need to cancel this summer’s events,” said City Recreation Special Events Coordinator Lindsey Myers.

The city implemented water restrictions two months early this year, on April 1, rather than in June. The decision came after the water storage condition status at Pactola Reservoir was elevated from “normal status” to “concern status” in March.

Through the end of September, no watering is allowed between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. daily in the city. Odd-numbered addresses are allowed to water, outside those time restrictions, on odd-numbered calendar days. Even-numbered addresses are allowed to water on even-numbered calendar days. No outside watering is allowed on the 31st day of any month.

Myers encourages families to participate in a number of special events planned at the city pools this summer. Visit the City’s Parks and Recreation Facebook page for more details.
