title: Marilyn Beaton
description: September 25, 1935 - April 3, 2026
_full_text:
September 25, 1935 - April 3, 2026

Into God's eternity, Marilyn Beaton, 90, passed away peacefully in her sleep on, April 3rd, 2026 (Good Friday Morning). Marilyn "Dolly" was born September 25, 1935, on the family farm 2 miles east of Ryder, ND. She was the youngest of 6 children born to Elmer and Florinda Hansen.

Growing up, Marilyn attended church every Sunday with her Mom and siblings at the Church of God in Ryder, ND. She had many stories to share about helping her mom and dad on the farm. She could often recall the specific chores that each day would bring on the family farm which also included early mornings and late afternoon's milking the cows. Monday's included baking bread, buns, occasional cakes, cookies, and pies and anything else involving flour. Tuesdays is when the cream was delivered to the creamery in Ryder, Wednesdays were clothes washing day, Thursdays were meant for candling and cleaning the eggs which were then taken to market in Ryder, and Fridays were "going to town (Minot) day" making milk and egg deliveries to family members who had moved to town.

As a teenager, Marilyn worked as a waitress and car hop at her brother Joe's – Hansen's Diner in Minot. This is where she met the love of her life and future husband Lyle (Sonny). Dolly and Sonny's love grew with their friendship, and they continued to date while Marilyn attended Minot Business College for a 2-year associate's degree. They were married on Valentine's Day, February 14th, 1956, and began their family of 5 children on a farm north of Minot. In 1968, they moved the family to Rapid City, SD where they raised their five children.

Marilyn started a career with Northwestern Bell Telephone Company (Ma Bell) in Rapid City during the late 60's. After retiring from Northwestern Bell 20 years later Marilyn began managing the office and agents of Ideal Financial Services Insurance Agency, which she and Lyle built over 40 years. She enjoyed their many travel adventures while in the insurance business to see the US, Mexico, Australia and Europe. In that time, Marilyn and Lyle were also Founders of Pioneer Credit Counseling with their daughter Laca Ossenfort. Marilyn continued to help with Pioneer up until her mid-80's where she would love to come and "work", which meant - visit the team at the office.

Marilyn's life revolved around God and family. Both Marilyn and Lyle's Motto was to 'Work Hard and Play hard". There were many family fishing and camping expeditions in the Black Hills and South Dakota Rivers and Lakes! Being the best grandma around, she was very involved with all the grandchildren's lives and wouldn't miss an opportunity to go to any school/sporting events.

Through the years, Marilyn always had the gift of Hospitality and loved to host many dinners and family gatherings which included the traditional King Crab on Christmas Eve. Family was always important to her and her biggest desire was that her children, grandchildren and great grandchildren would all know and love Jesus as their personal savior.

Marilyn and Lyle moved into the Spearfish Edgewood community when they were 82 years old and several years after Lyle's passing in 2020 Marilyn moved to the Good Samaritan Society in New Underwood, SD for memory care. Now Dolly is together with her loving Sonny in their Heavenly home.

Marilyn is survived by her children, grandchildren and great grandchildren, Stacy Beaton/Florida; Drew (Becky) Beaton-Eli, Taylor, Lucas Beaton-Liam, Medora, Seth Beaton, McLain Beaton, Tabb (DeVona) Beaton/Alaska; Tabitha (Adam) Carmody, Sarah (Marcus) Spencer-Dimitri, Naomi, Charlotte, Annie (Max) Edwards/Rapid City; Laca (Matt) Armitage-Brady, Stella, Josh Edwards, Laca (Todd) Ossenfort/Rapid City; Danielle (Scott) Oldfield-Eleanor, Noah, Jacob Ossenfort, Sidney Ossenfort, Rebecca (DJ) Lancaster/Texas; Journai Lancaster, Lillia Lancaster. Marilyn is also survived by cousins, nieces, nephews.

title: Update: Manufactured homes burn in Black Hawk
description: Several manufactured homes on the site of a dealer in Black Hawk were decimated by fire on Tuesday, June 17. On Wednesday, June 18, the damage to the homes at Centennial Homes of Rapid City was evident.
_full_text:
Several manufactured homes on the site of a dealer in Black Hawk were decimated by fire on Tuesday, June 17. On Wednesday, June 18, the damage to the homes at Centennial Homes of Rapid City was evident.

The Black Hawk Volunteer Fire Department said in a Wednesday press release the department responded to fire at about 6:19 p.m. on Tuesday. When they arrived, one of the manufactured homes was “fully involved” with flames spreading to nearby structures.

Due to the absence of fire hydrants in the area, additional resources were immediately requested. Water tenders and personnel responded from Piedmont, North Haines, Rapid City, Box Elder, Whispering Pines, Rapid Valley, Doty, Johnson Siding, and Ellsworth Air Force Base to support fire suppression operations.

Initial crews focused on exposure protection to prevent the fire from spreading further.

Firefighters worked to contain the fire and protect surrounding properties until the incident was brought under control.

In total, seven nearby structures sustained damage or ignited as a result of the primary fire. Three homes suffered significant or moderate damage.

The fire is under investigation by the South Dakota Fire Marshalls office.

An employee at the business, located at 11910 J B Rd Suite A in Black Hawk, directed questions to the company’s corporate office.

A representative at the office said Wednesday afternoon staff is working on gathering more information.

 Siding melting
Melted siding on a manufactured home damaged by fire a Tuesday, June 16 fire in Black Hawk, as seen on Wednesday, June 17. 

 Centennial Homes
Centennial Homes of Rapid City is located on J B Road in Black Hawk.

title: Federal agencies and tribe partner to clear Pine Ridge Reservation’s ballistics testing backlog
description: Federal law enforcement agencies and the Oglala Sioux Tribe have partnered to add the ammunition casing signatures of more than 500 firearms seized in criminal investigations on the Pine Ridge Reservation into a federal weapons database .
_full_text:
Federal law enforcement agencies and the Oglala Sioux Tribe have partnered to add the ammunition casing signatures of more than 500 firearms seized in criminal investigations on the Pine Ridge Reservation into a federal weapons database.

In clearing the backlog of untested firearms, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of South Dakota hopes to find clues in unsolved cases on the reservation.

Every entry in the database could help move investigations toward closure for families who’ve lost loved ones, according to Ron Parsons, U.S. attorney for South Dakota. 

 061826-nws-sl-ballistics-p2.jpg
Christopher D. Dotson, special agent in charge, FBI Minneapolis Field Office, speaks on June 16, 2026, in Rapid City, South Dakota. Behind him, from left, are Jason Lone Hill, chief of police, Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety, and Jessica Four Bear, attorney general for the Oglala Sioux Tribe. 

The FBI investigates felony-level crimes that occur on tribal land; U.S. attorney’s offices prosecute the cases. Parsons spoke of the high number of missing and murdered Indigenous people cases in South Dakota, and said the ballistics testing will help the FBI and his office meet their obligation to attend to them.

“The full weight of federal forensic capability is being brought to bear on cases that have waited far too long for answers,” Parsons said on Tuesday.

Parsons’ comments at a federal law enforcement facility in Rapid City came one day after agents with the FBI began to fire off hundreds of rounds of ammunition on the Pine Ridge Reservation, work that will continue for the next few weeks. The casings were given to a mobile Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives lab for entry into that agency’s National Integrated Ballistic Information Network.

The network has resulted in more than a million investigative leads on unresolved gun crimes, according to a press release from the FBI.

The initiative, dubbed “Operation Ballistic Backlog,” is part of a larger-scale expansion of federal policing resources in tribal areas called “Operation Steadfast Promise.” Among other efforts, the latter put 70 FBI agents into rotation for temporary detail in tribal areas across the U.S. and stepped up efforts to prosecute fraud involving tribal dollars.

Ballistics like a fingerprint

Firearms leave the equivalent of fingerprints on spent ammunition casings, according to Spence Burnett, assistant special agent in charge for the St. Paul field office of the ATF.

The microscopic marks left when guns are fired can be used to match casings to firearms seized by law enforcement and cataloged by the ATF’s National Tracing Center, and can then serve as evidence in criminal trials. 

“No two firearms are the same,” Burnett said.

The network was launched in 1999, but Burnett said after the press conference that not every seized firearm logged in the National Tracing Center database is linked to a shell casing signature in the network.

There’s no cost to enter 3D images of casing signatures into the network’s database, or for law enforcement agencies to access the information. But for signatures to be logged, agencies first need to fire the weapons, collect the casings and send them in for inclusion. That can be a logistical challenge for any agency, he said, particularly ones with heavy caseloads. 

 061826-nws-sl-ballistics-p1.jpg
Ron Parsons, center, U.S. attorney for the District of South Dakota, speaks on June 16, 2026, in Rapid City, South Dakota, with Jessica Four Bear, left, attorney general for the Oglala Sioux Tribe, and Christopher Dotson, special agent in charge for the Minneapolis field office of the FBI. 

The initiative brought ATF agents to the reservation, as well as FBI agents to fire the weapons, and the federal agencies provided the ammunition.

The Oglala Sioux Tribe has filed multiple lawsuits against the federal government over policing, alleging that the U.S. has failed to uphold its treaty obligations to provide public safety by underfunding law enforcement.

The litigation was not addressed at the press conference. Parsons did, however, acknowledge that local police have been taxed by high crime.

“For years, a great many firearms and other ballistic evidence, potentially tied to serious crimes on the reservation, have sat unexamined, not for any lack of will, but because caseloads have been overwhelming, and laboratory testing capacity has been stretched thin,” Parsons said.

Jason Lone Hill, the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety’s chief of police, and Jessica Four Bear, the tribe’s attorney general, were present for the press conference. They did not speak, but both were quoted in a press release sent shortly before the event.

“Working with our federal partners strengthens our ability to protect the community with our limited resources,” Lone Hill said in the release.

Tribal consultation led to backlog-clearing efforts

The idea to step up ballistics testing came through consultations with the tribe, according to Christopher Dotson, special agent in charge for the Minneapolis field office of the FBI.

“Getting out to the lands, meeting with the tribal councils, the chiefs, the police departments, is a priority, not only in South Dakota, but in other states in the nation who have Indian Country in their jurisdiction,” said Dotson, whose office oversees the agents operating at the Rapid City regional FBI facility.

Last week, the FBI announced a reward of $50,000 for information leading to an arrest in the 2022 murder of 6-year-old Logan Warrior Goings, killed in his home in a drive-by shooting in the community of Oglala. Shell casings recovered from the scene were linked through the database to a weapon recovered in another part of the state.

Dotson told reporters gathered for the press conference on the ballistics testing that the database was used to help prosecute the men who killed Vincent Von Brewer III outside Pine Ridge’s SuAnne Big Crow Boys and Girls Club in 2016. A pair of men from Denver were convicted of that murder in 2021.

Dotson said the collection of ballistics evidence, folded into unsolved criminal cases, is meant to show that the agency is committed to addressing the high number of unsolved violent crimes in places like Pine Ridge.

“We will never stop seeking justice for victims of gun violence,” Dotson said. “We are committed to solving every murder, every assault, and bringing violent criminals to justice, no matter how long it takes.”

title: Board standardizes late work deadlines across Rapid City Area Schools District
description: The Rapid City Area Schools Board voted unanimously Tuesday, June 16, to pass the first reading of a revised policy that standardizes the deadline for late work submissions throughout the district’s schools.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Area Schools Board voted unanimously Tuesday, June 16, to pass the first reading of a revised policy that standardizes the deadline for late work submissions throughout the district’s schools.

The revisions were made in an effort to “establish consistent expectations for missing assignments and make-up opportunities while promoting regular attendance, timely completion of assignments, student accountability, and effective classroom instruction and learning,” per the policy language.

The revised policy states students will be given as many school days as they were absent, plus one additional school day, to complete and submit missed assignments for full credit for excused and exempt absences. If a student misses that deadline, they could see up to a 40% reduction to their earned grade.

Students who miss school without an excused absence or are present in class but don’t complete the work in time, may also see up to a 40% reduction for the late work. If students complete work ahead of the unexcused absence, they’ll receive full credit.

All late or missing work must be submitted no later than one week prior to the end of the term (each semester consists of two academic terms).

It’s a move away from a fairly bare-bones policy that stated individual arrangements for the completion of work may be made through teachers. Teachers still have the ability to set the initial deadlines for work and can provide an alternative assignment or assessments at their discretion. The up to a 40% reduction on a late-work grade remains consistent between the old and new policy language.

Board Member Jamie Clapham noted the policy revisions connect to the district’s strategic plan to make sure students are educated and prepared with the skills to succeed.

“And we’ve really gotten a lot of feedback from our secondary teachers, especially that you have students that turn in 35 assignments with one week to go, and the reality is, is that’s not the best way educationally for those students,” Clapham said, adding that late work doesn’t allow time for feedback.

“It’s not just about the workload for the teacher, but also what’s best for the student,” she said.

Board Member Katy Urban said adding deadlines to the policy “makes a lot of sense.” Urban also said the up to 40% reduction rule may need to be looked at in the future because grade reductions for late work aren’t applied uniformly between schools.

“I know there are some schools that do that, some that don't, because they operate under different philosophies,” Urban said.

In the vein of consistency in grading, board members and RCAS Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson discussed the grading system differences between Central High School and Stevens High School. For students at Stevens, 80% of their final grade is from projects and assessments, 10% is from finals and 10% from assignments. The school used a 0-100 grading scale.

At Central, 90% of final grades are based on projects and assessments and 10% from final tests. The school is moving to a 1-4 grading scale with freshman and sophomores under the new scale during the 2025-26 school year. During the 2026-27 school year at Central, freshmen, sophomores and juniors will be under the new scale. By the 2027-28 school year, all grades at Central will use the new scale.

Board President Troy Carr said he finds it “odd” the two high schools have different systems.

“A true evidence-based grading would be 100% projects and assessments, and the 1-4 grading scale, but most schools aren't strictly adhering to evidence-based grading, they're determining what works best for their students, families and teachers, and going with that,” Thompson said, adding research shows evidence-based grading is the most accurate, but there’s not definitive research on one grading method being better for learning or achievement.

Addressing a question from Board Member Angela Rafferty, Thompson said if a student transfers from one high school to the other, there is a conversion chart to translate their grades.

The superintendent added that if the board wants two consistent grading strategies, it could be looked at. However, “It will create angst among teachers and families because everybody has their own belief about what that should look like, and neither high school at this point really wants to make a change.”

Urban said, “I would say our current policy does call for uniformity, whether that's right or not, I don't know.”

Board Member Walt Swan was not present at Tuesday’s meeting, so he did not cast a vote on the policy change.

title: Rapid City Council adopts changes to Tax Increment Financing guidelines to comply with new state law
description: After state lawmakers passed legislation with additional regulations for municipalities using the Tax Increment Financing District tool, Rapid City has adopted changes into its policy.
_full_text:
After state lawmakers passed legislation with additional regulations for municipalities using the Tax Increment Financing District tool, Rapid City has adopted changes into its policy.

On Monday, June 15, the Rapid City Council voted 9-0 to approve revisions of certain TIF statutory provisions that are set to go into effect on July 1. Councilman Rod Pettigrew (Ward 5) was absent from the meeting.

The numerous changes to the financing tool include a decrease in the amount a local government can add to an existing TIF, down to 25% after previous law allowed 35%.

How does a TIF work?

When a Tax Increment Financing District is established in a defined area, the value of the district is calculated. When infrastructure is improved or a development is added to the district, the value of that land increases. The property taxes generated beyond the base value are the increment. Rather than the city collecting those property taxes, the additional funds are diverted to pay for infrastructure, development or other costs. There are four TIF categories in South Dakota. Per the South Dakota Department of Revenue’s summary of the law, they are:

Local: Local classification is the default classification. Unless the TIF district meets the definition of an Industrial, Economic Development, or Affordable Housing TIF district, it is a Local TIF district. Examples include public infrastructure improvements for housing that does not meet the Affordable Housing requirements. The projects usually benefit the local government instead of having a regional or statewide benefit.

Industrial: Industrial classification includes an area where activities are recognized as industrial by zoning authorities. Examples include an animal processing plant or an ethanol plant.

Economic Development: Economic development classification includes any area where there is or will be one or more businesses engaged in any activity defined as commercial or industrial by the governing body that has zoning authority over the land contained within the TIF district. Examples include public infrastructure improvements for commercial or retail development.

Affordable Housing: Affordable Housing TIF examples include housing developments and workforce housing. The classification includes an area where:

The original selling price of any house in the district will be at or below the first-time homebuyer purchase price limit being used by the South Dakota Housing Development Authority as of the date the house is sold; OR

The monthly rental rate of all multifamily housing units in the district will be at or below the calculated rent for the state's eighty percent area median income as of the date the district is created, for a minimum of five years following the date of first occupancy.

 TIF example
This chart from the South Dakota Department of Revenue shows how a TIF works. 

State Law Changes

SB 228 adds more guidelines for a TIF to follow before approval, including:

A joint resolution is required for overlapping districts, including cities and counties.

Updated definition of contiguous geographic area requirement for a district.

An application is to be submitted, and any comments from any other local government entity with the power to levy taxes on property within the district are to be incorporated.

An additional public hearing to receive input from any affected taxing district.

The developer is now required to have an independent fiscal feasibility review completed at least 21 days prior to a Planning Commission meeting addressing the TIF.

TIFs with grants need to specify the purposes for which the grant will be used.

The TIF amount approved to apply for an additional 35% has been reduced to a 25% increase.

Part of the changes include the opportunity for the Pennington County Board of Commissioners and the Equalization Department, the Rapid City Area School District, and any other local government entity with the power to levy taxes on property located within the proposed district to provide comments on the submitted request for a TIF District.

The comments received will be given to the Rapid City Planning Commission.

Prior to the Planning Commission meeting addressing the TIF, the city is required to facilitate a public meeting so that any affected taxing district may provide input. These entities may comment but do not hold the power to approve or reject the application.

Additionally, at least 21 days prior to the Planning Commission hearing, an independent fiscal feasibility review is now required. After the review is submitted, the taxing district public hearing is conducted, and the 45-day staff review timeframe, the application will be placed on a Planning Commission agenda.

No discussion or comments were made on the revisions at the meeting.

title: Nebraska South Fork Fire update: Blaze affects more than 39,000 acres
description: The South Fork Fire was “generally quiet” on Tuesday, fire officials said.
_full_text:
The South Fork Fire was “generally quiet” on Tuesday, fire officials said.

In a Wednesday, June 17, update, Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 2, which is spearheading firefighting efforts, said several areas of heat were discovered. Ash devils were seen from Highway 20 near Crawford. The activity posed no threat to surrounding communities, the team said.

The fire affects 39,057 acres and is 80% contained. The team said 482 personnel are assigned to the fire.

On the west side of the fire, areas of heat were detected adjacent to the line and were extinguished. Fire managers ordered an infrared flight to check the area for hot spots. Officials use drones with thermal imaging to map active wildfires, locate hotspots and “provide critical fire intelligence.”

 South Fork Fire
Fire crews continue work on the South Fork Fire in northwest Nebraska. 

“Firefighters are closely watching the area of burning cottonwood trees on the south end of the fire in Division Alpha, south of Highway 20,” officials said in the update. “They are allowing the fire to slowly consume the trees.”

Operation Section Chief Nathan Hallam said mop-up continues in multiple areas within the fire.

“There was no significant fire growth last night … so looking really good throughout the night operation,” Hallam said during an operational update video posted to the South Fork Fire Nebraska Facebook page. Discussing Wednesday’s activities, he said, “We have our resources all engaged on the line. Patrol for areas of heat.”

Those east side efforts continue today, while firefighters are also taking care of any hazardous trees that could fall on trails in Fort Robinson State Park.

 061826-cha-news-fireupdate-p2.jpg
From the South Fork Fire Nebraska Facebook page, this fire progression maps show how a wildfire grows over time by displaying the fire perimeter for each day in a different color. 

The northern point of the fire has an uncontained line portion, and firefighters will be focusing on that area as well.

“That’s pretty adverse terrain, steep ground. We’re looking really good through this area currently. Drones (are) looking for hot spots,” Hallam said.

Hallam said crews are also ready to help local fire departments if there are any new fire starts in the area.

Lastly, he mentioned “suppression repair” will begin in the interior of the fire. That includes efforts to return the land to pre-fire conditions, with Hallam noting the initial attack included the creation of a number of bulldozer lines.

“Now it’s time to go in and repair some of these areas,” he said, noting they won’t be focusing on the fire line yet.

From the team’s morning update: (Wednesday), a strong cold front early morning will produce gusty northwest winds of 45-55 mph through sunset. A fire weather watch remains in effect through 9 p.m. today for low relative humidity and gusty winds. Lines will be tested, as the fire is expected to encounter the strongest winds. Any new start outside the fire footprint has the potential to be very similar to the fire behavior at the start of the South Fork fire.

This article has been updated to correct what day it is today. Our apologies.

title: Proposed Black Hills uranium mine gets approval to start building infrastructure on portion of site
description: A controversial uranium mining proposal on the edge of the Black Hills received approval from the federal Bureau of Land Management to begin constructing “ancillary infrastructure,” according to a press release from the agency Monday, although the project lacks permission to begin mining.
_full_text:
A controversial uranium mining proposal on the edge of the Black Hills received approval from the federal Bureau of Land Management to begin constructing “ancillary infrastructure,” according to a press release from the agency Monday, although the project lacks permission to begin mining.

Uranium is a metallic, radioactive element used as fuel in nuclear weapons and power plants. The Dewey-Burdock project near Edgemont, in southwest South Dakota, has been in the proposal stage for nearly two decades and still requires additional permits. The Trump administration picked the project last year for an expedited permitting process known as FAST-41.

Monday’s approval from the Bureau of Land Management gives Powertech, a subsidiary of Texas-based enCore Energy, the green light to build infrastructure including access roads, four groundwater monitoring wells and overhead power lines on the section of the project site that’s managed by the bureau, according to the press release.

 061726-nws-sl-mining-p1.jpg
Monday’s approval from the Bureau of Land Management gives Powertech, a subsidiary of Texas-based enCore Energy, the green light to build infrastructure including access roads, four groundwater monitoring wells and overhead power lines on the section of the project site near Edgemont. 

About 240 acres, roughly a third of a square mile, of the project site are on public lands that the bureau oversees. The entire project area is 10,580 acres, or about 16.5 square miles.

“The Dewey-Burdock Project still requires several additional approvals from other federal and state agencies, including a license renewal currently under review by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission,” said a bureau spokesperson.

EnCore Energy did not immediately provide a response to South Dakota Searchlight questions.

Opposition to project

In April, the bureau published a draft of its environmental assessment and opened it for public comment until May 15. In that monthlong span, the agency received 764 submissions, according to Monday’s press release, “including comments related to groundwater, cultural resources, tribal concerns, environmental justice, and compliance with federal laws.”

The bureau published its final environmental assessment Monday, as well as a finding of no significant impact. If the project receives all other necessary permits, the bureau estimates a start date for the project within the next five years. Infrastructure will remain at the site for 20 years after the implementation of the project, which the environmental assessment describes as the mine’s lifespan.

The environmental assessment is vague about groundwater pollution concerns and impacts on cultural resources in the area such as Native American historic sites, according to Lilias Jarding, a project opponent and executive director of the Black Hills Clean Water Alliance.

“The process was rushed. It’s only been a few weeks between the end of the comment period and this decision coming out in its final form,” Jarding said. “The Bureau of Land Management was being, what I would consider, irresponsible in this situation.”

EnCore Energy plans to use a method known as “in-situ” mining to extract uranium from underground. As opposed to open pits and tunnels, the method involves drilling wells to inject a water-based solution underground, dissolve uranium and pump it to the surface. The water would be pulled from local aquifers and then treated and pumped back underground after being used for mining, causing opponents to fear pollution of local groundwater sources.

“I don’t think the company understands the depth of public opinion against uranium projects in the Black Hills,” Jarding said.

The Black Hills Clean Water Alliance and other project opponents have also been working against another, nearby uranium exploratory drilling project in the southern Black Hills, proposed by Clean Nuclear Energy Corp. and its Canada-based parent company Nexus Uranium.

The decision on Clean Nuclear Energy’s exploration permit is in the hands of the state Board of Minerals and Environment. A hearing on the permit application was paused last month after a project opponent filed a federal lawsuit against the board, the state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources and Clean Nuclear Energy Corp.

The lawsuit remains pending, and no date has been scheduled to resume the permit hearing.

title: Rapid City reminds truckers to cover load in Air Quality Control Zone
description: Rapid City Environmental Planner Morgan Twombly is reminding the public all truck loads must be covered for drivers passing through the City’s Air Quality Control Zone.
_full_text:
Rapid City Environmental Planner Morgan Twombly is reminding the public all truck loads must be covered for drivers passing through the City’s Air Quality Control Zone.

It is a violation of Rapid City Municipal Code to transport materials that have the potential to emit fugitive dust without a covering. All vehicles used for transporting such materials must be equipped with a tarp.

“This requirement applies to those passing through Rapid City on the interstate as well as those hauling material outside the City but within the Air Quality Control Zone,” Twombly said. “The zone is a 10x10 mile area around all of Rapid City, excluding the portion which is located within the city limits of Box Elder. Truckloads, no matter how small, must be covered, and large material is not exempt.”

Twombly said the issue greatly impacts Rapid City’s air quality.

“This is an issue that has persisted for quite some time and directly contributes to Rapid City’s air quality,” Twombly said. “Contractors, in particular, are well aware of the requirement.”

Contractors are advised that covering truck loads is a stipulation of approval for air quality permits, and failure to cover loads will result in fines up to $500 per day of violation or 30 days in jail.

For more information, contact the City’s Air Quality Office at 605-394-4120.

title: 'They just won't listen:' Rural South Dakota nears postal breaking point
byline: MOLLY WETSCH South Dakota News Watch
description: PHILIP — At Petersen's Variety store, there are no less than three signs in the window advertising that residents of Philip can ship, pick up and drop off packages via UPS. The store is just a block away from the town's post office.
_full_text:
PHILIP — At Petersen's Variety store, there are no less than three signs in the window advertising that residents of Philip can ship, pick up and drop off packages via UPS. The store is just a block away from the town's post office.

Philip residents may be forgiven for choosing the — often more expensive — private shipping company over the nation's postal service: Long delivery times and unreliable service have led to growing distrust and dissatisfaction with the United States Postal Service's operations in rural South Dakota.

In early 2024, USPS downgraded a distribution facility in Huron to a local processing-only facility. The service had also initially planned to downsize its Sioux Falls distribution facility but later said that the plan had been paused.

USPS spokesperson Tara Jarrett offered a few details on the impact of those changes in a statement to News Watch.

 2026-05-02 Petersen_s variety.jpeg
Petersen's Variety in Philip on May 2, 2026. The store advertises that residents can deliver and pick up mail from UPS at the site. 

"Local mail continues to be processed in our Sioux Falls (570-571 ZIP Codes), Dakota Central (572-575 ZIP Codes), and Rapid City (577 ZIP Codes) plants, and that mail does not leave the state for additional processing if it is staying in that region. Mail in the 576 ZIP Codes continues to be served by our Bismarck, ND plant."

The organization has also recently begun rolling out its reduced service of rural post offices, stopping delivery vehicles at rural sites once a day, rather than twice.

The moves, which are part of USPS’s Delivering for America plan, aimed to “modernize the nation’s aged and neglected postal network.” But for thousands of people across the state, including dozens of local newspaper publishers, that effort has significantly hindered day-to-day life and operations.

West River publisher sees dramatic changes

Don Ravellette’s family has been publishing papers out of Philip for nearly 50 years through the company Ravellette Publications. The Philip Pioneer Review, the company's primary imprint, now publishes news from Murdo, Wall, Bison, Kadoka and Faith.

The Pioneer Review is a true community paper: Recent stories include the details of a new lighted stop sign in Philip, the results of the Harding County regional high school rodeo and a story about how Murdo residents rallied together to clean up a city planter with new soil and flowers.

Ravellette said that for the past two years, he's been having a harder time making sure that news is delivered to subscribers in a timely manner. He's also chosen to regularly direct employees to drive to Wall to deliver papers. Ravellette said the town's 577 ZIP code — compared to Philip's 575 — means that subscribers receive papers in a timelier manner.

"More and more publishers have had to do that, this exceptional dispatch, where they're literally doing the work of what the post office used to do, in terms of taking these bundles to surrounding post offices. Just to try to get them to expedite the delivery, particularly in the local area," Dave Bordewyk, executive director of the South Dakota NewsMedia Association told News Watch.

Ravellette told News Watch he is experiencing more frustration than ever before with the postal service.

"It's common talk from the coffee shops to the business owners that the post office is still unreliable. It's not even funny," Ravellette said. "And when we send out 1,000 livestock catalogs, it's sad when the out-of-state ones get delivered before the ones you mail out 25 miles from your house, from your post office."

In rural areas, the postal service is a lifeline because it is legally mandated to provide delivery and mail services to every ZIP code in the country. That means that routes cannot be discontinued or disrupted if they aren't used frequently or are not profitable.

Ravellette said that many of his subscribers do not see the value in having a weekly subscription to the newspaper when they can't expect it will arrive on time.

 2026-05-02 Ravellette Publications.jpeg
Ravellette Publications, which publishes the Pioneer Review, in Philip on May 2. 

"They were saying, 'Well, we might just have to quit our subscription, maybe we'll just stop in and buy a paper whenever we can.' So there goes 50 bucks. And if you get 100 of those, you do the math," Ravellette said.

Ravellette said that he feels like decisions are being made at the national level that aren't considering the needs of rural America.

"They just won't listen. They just won't," he said.

Delivery worsened for 65% of newspapers

Ravellette is not the only publisher frustrated with the postal service.

Bordewyk recently sent a survey to members of the South Dakota NewsMedia Association, which includes 109 newspaper publishers and digital media outlets from across the state.

The organization received 64 responses to the survey, of which about 65% said deliveries of their newspapers had worsened in the past year. Just 7% said deliveries had improved. Common complaints issued through the survey were inconsistencies with delivery times, struggles retaining advertisers and subscribers not receiving papers at all.

On June 4, Bordewyk met with the USPS Inspector General's office to discuss commonly expressed issues with the state's mailing system. He said that he thought the meeting went well and that the office seemed alarmed at publishers' complaints.

 South Dakota News Watch logo
Learn more about South Dakota News Watch at sdnewswatch.org. 

But he expressed concern at the organization's ability to fix what has already been broken.

"There's no good news here. It's all bad news when it comes to the future, in terms of what they've done to the system, what it's costing, where they're at. And Congress is reluctant to do anything about it," Bordewyk said.

USPS data shows meandering routes, longer delivery times

USPS’ Service Performance Dashboard provides data about on-time delivery rates for four types of mail shipped through the service: First Class Mail, newspapers and periodicals, marketing mail and bound printed matter, media and library mail.

A News Watch analysis of the data found that at the ZIP3 level, which is the first three numbers of a ZIP code, the percentage of on-time inbound delivery for newspapers and periodicals varies greatly across the state.

Inbound delivery times illustrate the average time it takes for papers and periodicals to arrive to addresses in a specific ZIP code. Just 57.81% of papers arriving to 575 ZIP codes arrived on time in the second quarter of 2026, compared to 86.37% in 570 ZIP codes. The ZIP3 code 575, where Philip is located, also sees the slowest average delivery time at 4.3 days this year.

 2026-05-02 Philip postbox.JPG
Long delivery times and unreliable service have led to growing distrust and dissatisfaction with the United States Postal Service's operations in rural South Dakota. 

Outbound delivery, though, which measures the timeliness of mail being sent from a specific ZIP code, is a reflection of the on-time rate that local papers can expect when sending their publications to subscribers from their town's post office. In the 575 ZIP3 code, the average delivery time for outbound newspapers this year is 5.3 days.

"All the newspapers mail us copies of their paper to the (SDNA) office here in Brookings," Bordewyk said. "One-hundred newspapers are sending them to us. It used to be by the end of the week, by Friday — because most weeklies would be printing and mailing on a Tuesday or Wednesday — we would see more than 90% of the newspapers. Today, by Friday, less than half of them are showing up."

Newspapers see much lower on-time delivery rates and more days to deliver than other tracked USPS mail types like First-Class Mail or marketing mail.

Ravellette shared a tracking number with News Watch for a package received by a rancher near Quinn, in western South Dakota. The package, which was shipped on July 28, 2025, from Phoenix, was received on Aug. 12, 2025.

The archive tracking statement for the package shows that it made its way through 14 cities on its way to Quinn. It notably ended up in Omaha, Nebraska, and Sioux Falls twice — once after making the 600-mile trip out to Billings, Montana.

The roughly 1,300-mile trip from Phoenix, the package's original destination, to Quinn turned into a 3,600-mile odyssey under USPS' care.

USPS maintained in its statement to News Watch that its delivery performance in South Dakota is above average.

"USPS delivery performance in South Dakota is strong. About half of all First-Class Mail is delivered early. In the Sioux Falls area specifically, for the week ending 5/22/26, 92.6% of incoming mail was delivered on time, above our national target of 89%," Jarrett said.

The organization did not address questions about whether it is aware of issues in rural South Dakota and if there are any plans to speed up service in those areas.

South Dakota U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds told News Watch that he was unsatisfied with notions that the service in South Dakota was up to par.

"I know there's information out there suggesting that we have good service in South Dakota. I reject that," Rounds said. "I think the clear evidence is that the mail service is terrible in South Dakota."

Members of Congress looking for action

Rounds has previously been vocal about his dissatisfaction with USPS' performance in the state.

In a press release in December 2025, he said the service has “deteriorated to critical levels” in South Dakota. He also said that the Postmaster General David Steiner had "downplayed such issue existed in South Dakota."

Rounds called for an investigation into the service in the state. The USPS field operations review audit website does not currently display any former or active audits of processing or distribution centers in South Dakota.

Rounds told News Watch, though, that he is aware of ongoing investigations in South Dakota. On June 11, he sent a letter to chairman Sen. Rand Paul and ranking member Sen. Gary Peters of the Senate Homeland Security Committee. In that letter, he said he would reject any nominations to four open postal service positions until a plan was in place to fix issues in South Dakota.

"I would, at this point, remind South Dakotans that your local postal employees are trying to help us," Rounds said to News Watch. "This is a systemic problem, and it has to be fixed with a systemic change."

The impact of slow USPS delivery extends beyond birthday cards and bank statements.

U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson said in a column in January that he had surveyed 4,000 South Dakotans and held a roundtable in Sioux Falls where constituents shared issues with the postal service.

Many spoke of financial consequences, concerns with delayed medical prescriptions and other problems that have significantly impacted their day-to-day lives, he said.

"I heard from folks like Susan from Faulkton who incurred a $2,700 late fee because her check took 25 days to get to Sioux Falls. There’s a business in Bath whose customers often don’t receive their checks or get them two months late. And some people like Mary bought Christmas presents early, only to have them travel to nine different states before being delivered to Huron — 10 days late and after Christmas," Johnson wrote in the column.

Bordewyk said that while conversations with the Inspector General's office were generally reassuring, newspaper publishers across the state will still have to reckon with the fact that the system may never go back to the way it was — and be willing to make changes.

"The question for all of us is, will the postal service decide to walk back these system changes that they made?" Bordewyk said. "I understand your audience, your subscribers want that printed product, and that still serves a predominant need. But the move to a digital delivery is just going to be more and more necessary for even our smallest newspapers going forward. In order to survive, that's what's going to be necessary."

title: South Fork Fire update: Containment at 64%
description: Chadron Fire Chief Branden Marten said his department had nine trucks and about 25 firefighters fighting the South Fork Fire on Wednesday, June 10. Marten said so far a small shed is the only structure that has been burned up.
_full_text:
Chadron Fire Chief Branden Marten said his department had nine trucks and about 25 firefighters fighting the South Fork Fire on Wednesday, June 10. Marten said so far a small shed is the only structure that has been burned up.

The South Fork Fire remains at 38,914 acres with containment increasing to 64%, officials said the evening of Monday, June 15.

Amy Landreth Ormseth, a native of Chadron and now the Acting Forest Supervisor of the Bighorn National Forest headquartered at Sheridan, Wyoming, said the firefighters serve 16-hour shifts on the fire lines. She noted that there are probably 500 tents set up in Chadron and Crawford for the firefighters to use.

She also noted that drones are being used to search for hot spots that are apt to break out. During a briefing on Monday morning, June 15, at Chadron State, one of the spokesmen urged the firefighters to keep an eye on cottonwood trees because they often have hot spots following a fire that can burst into flames.

Ormseth said emphasis is placed on checking out the perimeters of the fire to keep it from spreading.

Things were treacherous near the end of last week when the wind shifted directions several times. Progress was made in containing the fire Saturday and Sunday when temperatures were cool and winds were light. But it’s supposed to be hotter and windier at midweek. That’s a reason so many firemen are remaining on the job.

Here’s some data that KCSR radio had Monday:

Aircraft have dropped 42 loads of retardant totaling 170,000 gallons on the fire while “scooper planes” made 36 water drops totaling 58,000 gallons. The water is being taken from Box Butte dam that is on the Niobrara River in southern Dawes County.

 Map of fire _0782.JPG
A map of the South Fork Fire. The first notch at the bottom going to your left is Fort Robinson. Crawford is just out to the right of the map by the grid. As of Monday morning, the fire had burned 38,914 acres. Much of the terrain in this map is the most rugged in Nebraska. 

Of course, the fire is mostly a result of the extremely dry conditions in the entire region. Much less than an inch of precipitation per month has been received in most of Dawes and Sioux counties during the past 8.5 months. According to KCSR Radio, Chadron received 2.13 inches of precipitation last August and 2.75 in September, giving the community 15.13 for the first nine months of the year, but Chadron had only 16.81 inches at the year’s end.

 Fire--tents on campus .JPG
There are about 500 tents set up in Chadron, including at Chadron State, pictured, and Crawford for firefighters to use. 

There was just 1.64 inches of moisture in Chadron in 2026 through May 29 before a 2.4 inch downpour occurred on the 30th, but that was primarily only in Chadron and hardly any other places in the vicinity got more an inch and much of the area got almost nothing.

 South Fork WIldfire
The Mitchell Volunteeer Fire Department sent six personnel and three rigs to help fight the South Fork Wildfire on June 9, 2026. 

Here are some facts and figures pertaining to the fire. It’s official name is the South Fork Fire.

It started the afternoon of Tuesday, June 9 about halfway between Harrison and Crawford not far from Highway 20. The highway was closed the rest of that day and Wednesday. After lightning started the fire, it quickly moved to the east through rugged Smiley Canyon and toward Fort Robinson. Local fire crews worked feverishly to prevent the fire from burning the dozens of structures on the state’s largest and most scenic state park. But much of the grass in the pastures in the 22,000-acre park was burned.

Nearly all of the regional volunteer fire departments responded immediately to help. More help soon arrived. Officials at the Incident Command headquarters established at Chadron State College said there were 340 people involved in fighting the fire and providing support services. By Monday that number had grown to 581 from 13 states.

Management of the fire is being shared by the State of Nebraska and the U.S. Forest Service with support being supplied by the Department of Interior, contractors, the National Guard and volunteer firemen who have remained on duty. It has been helpful that there are no other large fires in the surrounding states at this time. Ormseth said, “This is the one we’re focusing on.”

title: Update: Rapid City Council codifies code of conduct, removes abstention reason requirement
description: Update: The Rapid City Council approved the ordinance changes uninmously, with no discussion.
_full_text:
Update: The Rapid City Council approved the ordinance changes uninmously, with no discussion.

Original story: The Rapid City Council is considering a lengthy list of municipal code updates and revisions geared towards the council and the mayor. The changes include the implementation of code of conduct rules and rules governing the handling of complaints, which include the requirement that the person filing the complaint maintain confidentiality or the council may dismiss the complaint.

Assistant City Attorney Kinsley P. Groote told the Journal many of these changes were made in response to recent bills passed by the South Dakota Legislature.

This includes SB 146, which updates SL 2017, ch 56, § 9, cleaning up language for alderman responsibilities and procedures. 

SB 167 amended sections of SDCL 9-6-1 through SDCL 9-12-9, revising, removing and updating various municipal codes.

A SDCL 9-8-5 revision states, "The council is the judge of the election and qualification of its members. The council may, by ordinance, determine its rules of procedure and code of conduct, and may punish its members for disorderly conduct while performing the duties of office, and, with the concurrence of two-thirds of the aldermen, may expel a member.”

SB 167 tweaks language regarding the removal of an elected official convicted of bribery.

The law now states that if an alderman or mayor is convicted of a crime that involves bribery, they are automatically removed from office from the moment they’re convicted.

“State law has changed some of the sections and this is really just an update so that we make sure that the municipal code is reflective of (state law provisions),” Groote said.

The 16-page ordinance at hand — Ordinance No. 6717 — goes before the council for a second reading at tonight’s (Monday, June 15) council meeting.

Municipal codes are used by cities for the power to create and enforce local regulations that must comply with both state and federal laws. A municipal code is a rule book for the city to follow and provides residents, businesses, and visitors with guidelines of legal obligations and community standards.

It also sets enforceable actions when violations of guidelines are made.

Reason for abstention no longer required under new language

Regarding abstention, current code reads, "No member of the council who is present may abstain from voting unless he or she states on the record the reason for his or her abstention." Among the changes the council will vote on is the removal of the requirement for council members to state a reason for their abstention. They will still have to declare that they are abstaining.

The rule was not customarily followed and council members routinely abstain without giving a reason.

Abstention means when a person chooses not to vote in a decision. 

The change also removes language that counted abstention votes with the majority vote.

The section has now been updated according to SDCL-6-1-17, stating, "No county, municipal, or school official may participate in discussing or vote on any issue in which the official has a conflict of interest. Each official shall decide if any potential conflict of interest requires such official to be disqualified from participating in discussion or voting. However, no such official may participate in discussing or vote on an issue if the following circumstances apply: The official has a direct pecuniary (monetary) interest in the matter before the governing body; or at least two-thirds of the governing body votes that an official has an identifiable conflict of interest that should prohibit such official from voting on a specific matter.”

The law continues to say that if an official with a conflict of interest gives input on the discussion or votes, their sole vote is invalidated.

“It's one of those where it just doesn't seem like it's particularly necessary … If there's a conflict of interest they (council members) can absolutely state it if they want to. It's just that it's not going to be required," Groote said.

She said the city didn’t enforce the procedure before when a council member failed to explain his or her reasoning. She said the change came from the City Attorney’s Office after they determined it was not necessary.

Complaints filed against council members

The council will vote on adding a code of conduct for council members to city law. The rules were already on the books as a policy, but the ordinance change will codify the rules.

Complaints filed against a council member can be dismissed by the council. Per state law, SDCL 9-8-5, the council is the sole judge of the election and qualification of its members and it can determine its rules of procedure and code of conduct and may punish its members for disorderly conduct while performing the duties of office. It takes a two-thirds majority for a council to expel a member for disorderly conduct.

Another section that has seen updates is for investigations and complaints made toward council members. 

Upon receiving a complaint, the City Attorney’s Office, or an independent investigator hired by the city, shall review the complaint and related submitted evidence.  The investigation will seek an unbiased review of documents, statements and such other information to determine if violations were broken, according to the ordinance.

After the completion of the investigation, a copy of the report shall be provided to the members of the Common Council at an executive session. 

According to the ordinance, "Under SDCL § 9-8-5, the Common Council is the judge of the qualification of its own members. Any sanction available under state law shall be available to the Common Council in judging its members."

The following actions can be made if an investigation determines a violation occurred.

Public reprimand: A public declaration made by resolution of the common council announcing that an elected official’s conduct was improper and describing the impropriety under the Code of Conduct.

Public censure: An official public condemnation made by resolution of the common council denouncing an elected official’s conduct as a violation of the Code of Conduct and the reasons therefore.

Expulsion: The removal of the elected official from office by resolution of the common council following a finding that the elected official’s conduct in violation of the Code of Conduct is significant and/or egregious.

A complaint must remain confidential, if a complaint is determined by the council to have breached any confidentiality provisions, then the council has the ability to dismiss the complaint altogether.

Councilman Lance Lehmann (Ward 4) said this language was already used in the city's Code of Conduct Procedures but is now being adopted into the Municipal Code to reflect their already practiced procedures. 

"We changed those several years ago, and I think they're just making a match, of what we changed in the (Code of Conduct Procedures),” he said.

The Journal previously obtained confidential documents regarding a complaint filed against Councilman Bill Evans (Ward 2) and an independent investigation the city outsourced to seek Code of Conduct violations made by Evans. The investigation found Evans acted inappropriately at a meeting where he was a council liaison to the Historic Preservation Commission.

Thereafter, an executive session was scheduled, during which Evans stepped down as council vice president and removed himself from other committee responsibilities.

title: Sr. Teresa Hinker
_full_text:
June 4, 1934 - June 12, 2026

Sr. Teresa Hinker, age 92, died on Friday, June 12, 2026, at Good Samaritan Village where she resided.

Sr. Teresa was born on June 6, 1934, the seventh of ten children of Edward and Lena (Watznauer) Hinker of Watauga, S.D. Her childhood was spent on a farm that straddled the North Dakota/South Dakota state line. Summer catechetical sessions introduced her to the Sisters of Loretto of Toronto, Canada and nourished her desire to join them.

Sr. Teresa entered the sisters of Loretto community on September 8, 1949, made temporary vows on May 31, 1952, and her Perpetual vows on August 15, 1958. She was one of three daughters to enter religious life. In her time with the Loretto Sisters she ministered in many capacities including housekeeping, cooking and baking. Much of her time was spent caring for the sick sisters and she was eventually sent to Rapid City, S.D. to obtain her degree in nursing.

While working on her nursing degree, Sr. Teresa lived at St. Martin Monastery and began discerning a possible transfer to the Benedictine Sisters. This transfer took place on August 25, 1990. Sr. Teresa ministered as their health care supervisor for many years. In later years, she also supervised the Monastery kitchen. She enjoyed making many kinds of jams, jellies and pies and also enjoyed reading and crocheting.

Sr. Teresa was a deeply spiritual woman and had a love of prayer. As a Benedictine sister, she was faithful to the Liturgy of the Hours and found great solace there. She loved her family and community with all her heart. She had a gentle spirit and all felt at home in her presence.

She is survived by her Benedictine community, her sister, Sr. Margaret Hinker, a sister-in-law and numerous nieces and nephews.

Services will be held on Friday, June 19, 2026, in Holy Cross Chapel at the Terra Sancta Retreat Center (2101 City Springs Rd.,) beginning with the greeting of the body at 9 a.m., Morning Prayer, at 9:15 a.m. followed by visitation from 9:45 to 10:45 a.m. Her Funeral Mass will be held at 11 a.m. Burial will follow in St. Martin Cemetery. There will be a lunch held at Terra Sancta Retreat Center following burial.

Arrangements are with Osheim & Schmidt Funeral Home; www.OsheimSchmidt.com.

title: Rapid City man sentenced to 40 years for fatal downtown stabbing
description: During the sentencing hearing for her son's killer, Henrietta Nelson remembered 45-year-old Francis Tobacco as a natural guardian.
_full_text:
During the sentencing hearing for her son's killer, Henrietta Nelson remembered 45-year-old Francis Tobacco as a natural guardian.

"He was a protector, he was a warrior. He always helped the people around him," Nelson testified, recalling her son, who was fatally stabbed in downtown Rapid City.

Diontea Eagleman, 23, appeared for his sentencing hearing before Circuit Court Judge Matthew Brown at the Pennington County Courthouse Monday, June 15, where he was sentenced to 40 years in prison.

Tobacco, died at the hospital after a stabbing that occurred around 7 p.m. in the 400 block of Sixth Street in downtown Rapid City on April 1, 2025. Eagleman was arrested on suspicion of first-degree murder, according to the Rapid City Police Department, after an investigation.

Through an agreement with prosecutors, Eagleman pleaded guilty on April 24 to first-degree manslaughter. 

Per the plea agreement, Eagleman pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter and the state agreed to request 40 years in prison at sentencing.

In South Dakota, first-degree manslaughter is a Class C felony with a maximum sentence of life in prison and a $50,000 fine.

Assistant Chief Deputy State's Attorney Olivia Siglin said Tobacco was stabbed once in the neck and another time in the forehead. She said evidence showed Tobacco was also unarmed during the incident. 

During the sentencing, multiple members of Tobacco's family told the court how Tobacco was a protector and often went out of his way to help those in need. Each family member echoed the same sentiment in that Tobacco "didn't deserve what happened." 

The family asked the court to consider the maximum sentence for first-degree manslaughter, stating it isn't fair that Eagleman can continue his life when Tobacco's was taken from him too soon. 

Siglin said the state's recommendation reflected the seriousness of Eagleman's actions while also taking into consideration his acceptance of responsibility through his guilty plea and him writing an apology letter within hours after the stabbing incident in 2025. 

"Throughout this case, we have never lost sight of the fact that a family lost a loved one," Siglin said. "Today's sentence reflects the seriousness of this crime and ensures that Mr. Eagleman is held accountable for taking a life." 

Eagleman's attorney, Matthew Skinner, requested that the court consider a 25-year sentence with about half suspended. He highlighted Eagleman's remorse about the incident and how he gave the police a letter detailing his remorse and admitting to the stabbing. 

Skinner said Eagleman has had a tough upbringing and been out on his own since the age of 14. He said while Eagleman battled homelessness, he also dealt with years of drug and alcohol abuse. Despite these factors, Skinner said Eagleman viewed Tobacco as a friend and didn't intend to kill him. 

"This is a tragedy, a sad situation on all accounts,' Skinner said. 

Skinner said the toxicology report also showed both Eagleman and Tobacco were intoxicated. Additionally, he said Eagleman was high on methamphetamine at the time of the incident. He said after the stabbing Eagleman he washed the knife with a water bottle and stuffed it in his pocket. The knife was later retrieved by police. 

Before sentencing, Brown sympathized with Tobacco's family, while also acknowledging the efforts Eagleman has taken to own up to his actions.  Brown characterized the killing as both "senseless" and "grievous" and agreed to follow the plea agreement.

title: Man throws bottle at Runnings employee, brandishes knife before arrest
description: The Rapid City Police Department arrested a 19-year-old man on Sunday, June 14, after he allegedly caused a ruckus at Runnings that ended with bystanders holding him on the ground until police arrived.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Police Department arrested a 19-year-old man on Sunday, June 14, after he allegedly caused a ruckus at Runnings that ended with bystanders holding him on the ground until police arrived.

At around 5:15 p.m. Sunday, police arrived at Runnings at 1020 N. LaCrosse St. for a report of an assault with a weapon.

Witnesses told police the man — who officers identified as 19-year-old Destin Rencountre of Rapid City — entered the liquor store and told employees that he was not going to pay for the liquor he grabbed from the shelf, before throwing the bottle at an employee and brandishing a knife. A customer and employee took Rencountre to the ground and got the knife away from him.

When police arrived, they found Rencountre being held down by bystanders and then handcuffed him. Police noted the strong smell of an alcoholic beverage on Rencountre.

Court records show Rencountre is held on three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and one count of simple assault. He is at the Pennington County Jail on a $8,000 cash only bond.

This is the second time within a month bystanders have stepped in to pin down someone in Rapid City until police arrived. On May 19, three men held down an unruly gas station patron at the Circle K at 1610 Caregiver Circle.

title: Rapid City Hall lobby features ‘I love America because…’ table
description: The lobby of Rapid City’s City Hall has been transformed and all decked out in celebration of America’s 250th anniversary, including a display table inviting building visitors and staff to share sentiments of why they love America.
_full_text:
The lobby of Rapid City’s City Hall has been transformed and all decked out in celebration of America’s 250th anniversary, including a display table inviting building visitors and staff to share sentiments of why they love America.

 PHOTO America Display table3.jpg
“It’s a simple way to share a feeling or sentiment about America,” said Skye Martin of the Rapid City Mayor’s Office. “It takes just a few seconds and it’s a great way to get into the spirit of the special America 250 holiday observance.” 

The display near the City’s finance office and lobby decorations were erected by a small group of staff members last week. The table display includes a large decorated banner with the theme ‘I Love America Because…’. Visitors are invited to fill out star-shaped stickers with their personal answers to the question and place the sentiments on the wall.

“It’s a simple way to share a feeling or sentiment about America,” said Skye Martin of the Rapid City Mayor’s Office. “It takes just a few seconds and it’s a great way to get into the spirit of the special America 250 holiday observance.”

Visitors to the table can also view a display board featuring the anchor events to Rapid City’s upcoming “Real America 250 Birthday Bash’ series of events July 1-5.

The lobby of Rapid City’s City Hall has been transformed and all decked out in celebration of America’s 250th anniversary, including a display table inviting building visitors and staff to share sentiments of why they love America.
