title: Perplexing plant problems? SDSU Extension Garden Hotline here to help
description: Got questions about what’s happening in your garden this summer? South Dakota State University Extension has added seasonal staff statewide to its Garden Hotline during the 2026 growing season.
_full_text:
Got questions about what’s happening in your garden this summer? South Dakota State University Extension has added seasonal staff statewide to its Garden Hotline during the 2026 growing season.

The Garden Hotline is a free service. Consumer horticulture assistants are on-site at the SDSU Extension region center in Rapid City, as well as in Pierre and Aberdeen, to help answer South Dakotans’ questions about their yards, lawns and gardens. In Rapid City, Kerry Pile is the consumer horticulture assistant. Rapid City’s SDSU Extension regional center is located at 711 N. Creek Drive.

The Garden Hotline is a resource for in-depth and quick questions, and for correcting misinformation. Some of the public’s most commonly asked questions focus on identifying weeds, accidental plant poisoning, and diagnosing why plants are dying.

In Rapid City, from now through October, contact sdsu.gardenswest@sdstate.edu or 605-394-6814 with gardening questions. Gardeners also can submit garden and yard questions at extension.sdstate.edu/garden-yard/problems-and-solutions.

Residents are encouraged to take photos of the plants in question or bring the plant in person to the regional sites if desired. Experts recommend one close-up photo and one photo of the entire plant. 

An SDSU Extension expert or Master Gardener will typically reply within 48 hours if the questions are submitted on a weekday.

The Garden Hotline provides the public with local experts who are knowledgeable about plants that thrive in their area.

“Just because a big box store sells blueberry bushes, it doesn't mean they are suitable for South Dakota,” said Sara Ogan, consumer horticulture assistant in Pierre. “Let us help point you in the right direction for fruit (and plants) that thrives in South Dakota.” 

The public can also get help with their garden questions from SDSU Extension Master Gardeners, including the Pennington County Master Gardeners at Black Hills Farmers Market at Market Park in Rapid City, and Northern Hills Master Gardeners at Neighbors 2 Neighbors Farmers Market, 1020 N. Third St. For more information, go to extension.sdstate.edu/garden-yard.

title: Grand opening of Chatku Art Center for Red Cloud Art Show brings in over 200 art pieces
description: PINE RIDGE — The 58th annual Red Cloud Art Show at the Chatku Art Center in Pine Ridge is a staple for the community to display local art and artists from across Turtle Island, giving visitors a chance to purchase one-of-a-kind art. In tandem with the annual art show, the center also celebrated its grand opening, marking the end of construction that began in 2024.
_full_text:
PINE RIDGE — The 58th annual Red Cloud Art Show at the Chatku Art Center in Pine Ridge is a staple for the community to display local art and artists from across Turtle Island, giving visitors a chance to purchase one-of-a-kind art. In tandem with the annual art show, the center also celebrated its grand opening, marking the end of construction that began in 2024.

 Chatku
A Keith BraveHeart artwork titled Cradle Song.  

According to a press release, opening day on June 6 brought in more than 1,000 visitors with guest speakers including Oglala Sioux Tribe President Frank Star Comes, artists Jhon Goes In Center, state Sen. Red Dawn Foster, Charlie Brave Heart and more.

There are more than 200 pieces submitted and currently displayed inside the art center, with all of the artwork available for purchase. The exhibit runs until Aug. 9. The center is located at 100 Mission Drive at Mahpíya Lúta High School.

Each year the center gives out awards for categories including painting, photography and digital art, drawing, graphics, mixed media, three-dimensional cultural art form and more. 

 Chatku
Executive Director for the Chatku Art Center Tawa Ducheneaux (Cherokee) poses in front of a piece at the Chatku Art Center in Pine Ridge. 

Center Executive Director Towa Ducheneaux (Cherokee) said two judges, one a curator or collections manager and the other an artist who is not competing or entering the show, select first and second place for each division. 

Of the various divisions, the Brother C. M. Simon, award is bought by the center and is used for next year's marketing poster.

"Each year the Brother Simon award is chosen. That award winner is featured on the poster for next year's show, Duscheneaux said.

Last year's winner was Maka Duta Win (Brittany Hill) for her ledger art titled Wahpe with my Winyans (Tea with my Ladies). 

This year's winner, whose work will be featured on the 59th annual Red Cloud art show poster, is Malina Two Bulls (Lakota) for her painting titled Lakota Skies.

 Chatku
"Lakota Skies," by Molina Two Bulls earned the Brother Simon award. This will be used for promotional material for Red Clouds 59th annual art show. 

Simon, who worked at Mahpíya Lúta, helped start the first show in 1969 because of his reverence for local art. When he passed away in 2006, the award was created for up-and-coming artists.

The Journal asked of all the exhibit pieces, what caught Ducheneaux’s eye. She said she was fond of all the pieces but couldn't not mention Dwayne "Chuck" Wilcox's three-dimensional dancer.

 Chatku
Dwayne Wilcox's three-dimensional art winning piece titled "Kuciyela." 

"Chuck had shared that he had this in his head for so long and he finally just had to do it. It was a solid few months of creating him. He's (the dancer) a version of himself," Ducheneaux said.

She said Wilcox used a mix of contemporary material with traditional materials such as the feathers of the headdress being made of paper and the moccasins being made of real hide and beadwork.

 Chatku
Artwork titled, "Something like Deja Vu," by Teslah "Sota" Knight. 

The figure is dressed in regalia for a style of dance called the chicken dance. The piece also won the Judge's Choice Award and the Founder's Award for most innovative technique. 

She also noted a piece by Jim Yellow Hawk titled Waktegli Wachipi (Victory Dance) that was bought by the Department of the Interior and will be added to the Sioux Indian Museum inside the Journey Museum in Rapid City.  

She clarified that all artist of 18 years and older are encouraged to submit their work to the exhibit.

"The special thing is that we're non-juried, meaning we accept from every emerging 18- to 19-year-old artist, because 18 is the youngest that we allow, and then upwards of all the legacy artists," Ducheneaux said.

2026 Awards

This year's winners first and second place division winners.

Painting:

Keith Braveheart - Sung Wapiyapi

Dennis R. Fox Jr. -Zig Jackson Tribute

Drawing:

Gerald Cournoyer - Thirsty

Donald Montileaux - Pro.Tec.Tor

Graphics:

Roger Broer - Finding Your True Self

Alice Crazy Bull - Chokecherry Constellations 

Photography & Digital Art

Nathan Blindman - Rita Long Visitor Holy Dance Oglala Lakota

Jawendjie Janis - Leaping Hooves

Mixed Media: 

Keith Braveheart & James Star Comes Out - C' atku el iyotaka ya

Malina Two Bulls - I dream in Lakota

Three Dimensional:

Dwayne "Chuck" Wilcox - Kuciyela 

Marty Two Bulls Jr. - Born in The USA

Cultural Art Forms:

Kevin Pourier - Be Fierce

Carol Wilcox - Horse Tail

Adornment:

Amy Deer- Rose Necklace

Mitchel Zephier - Medicine Wheel of the Universe (Concho Belt)

Chatku Art Center

"All pieces, no matter purchased or not, they'll all remain in the show until Aug. 9, and then after that we'll return unsold pieces to artists,” Ducheneaux said.

The purchased art will be shipped out after the exhibit ends in August. 

The Chatku (meaning Place of Honor in Lakota) Art Center was formally known as the Heritage Center before the construction of the dedicated art building was completed. Ducheneaux said the building provides 12,500 square feet for the use of exhibits, storage of permanent collections, additional storage space, offices and a gift shop. 

The new building has given them more resources to support their nearly 13,000 contemporary and historical collection. Ducheneaux said this makes the Chatku Art Center one of the biggest art collections in South Dakota.

title: Rapid City adjust office, landfill schedules for Juneteenth
description: City administrative offices will be closed next Friday, June 19, in observance of Juneteenth Freedom Day.
_full_text:
City administrative offices will be closed next Friday, June 19, in observance of Juneteenth Freedom Day.

The Rapid City Landfill will be closed as part of the holiday observance. Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday trash collections on City routes will be picked up one day early next week with Monday routes operating on a normal schedule, leave out until collected. For residents on the bi-weekly recycling schedule, recycling collection will continue as normal next week. Monday, Wednesday, and Friday recycling collections will be serviced during the holiday week; however, collection will occur one day earlier than usual in accordance with the holiday schedule.

Rapid Transit Services, including RapidRide and Dial-A-Ride services, will not be operating Friday, June 19, in observance of the national holiday. The Rapid City Public Library will be closed for the holiday. The Monument’s administrative offices will be closed but the venue will be open for scheduled events.

The Roosevelt Swim Center will operate regular hours from 5:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. with open swim scheduled on the holiday from 3:30-8:45 p.m. The outdoor swimming pools at Horace Mann, Parkview and Jimmy Hilton at Sioux Park will be open from noon to 6 p.m. The Roosevelt Swim Center’s 50-meter outdoor pool will be open on the holiday from 8 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

The Rapid City Airport will be open with administrative offices closed. Rapid City Police and Fire Departments will be operating on normal shift schedules with administrative offices closed.

Juneteenth commemorates and observes the official end of slavery in the United States, when three months after the Civil War ended and two and a half years after President Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation, word of freedom finally reached enslaved people in Texas.

 Juneteenth's roots go back to the document that declared freedom for the enslaved people in Texas
Among the orders issued as Union troops arrived in Texas at the end of the Civil War was one declaring that all enslaved people in the state were now free, and had “absolute equality.” (AP Video: Kendria LaFleur)

title: Joan Sutton
_full_text:
June 16, 1934 - March 11, 2026

Joan Fenner Sutton of Rapid City, SD died Wednesday, March 11, 2026, at Serenity Place, St. Martin's Village.

Joan was born Margaret Joan Deering, June 16, 1934, to Oscar and Ruth (Caton) Deering at the ranch ten miles north of Wasta, SD. Her birth was assisted by her Aunt Esther (Deering) Smith. Joan would tell everyone she was privileged to hold the spot of number five in the family of twelve; "Old enough to be one of the 'big' kids, but young enough to enjoy the little ones."

Very early in her life, her mom called her "Jan" or "Janny" and, except for legal documents, "Margaret" just never caught on. Joan began school in the Power's School District in the one room schoolhouse less than a mile up the road from the Deering place. When she began 5th grade she boarded in Wasta during the week to attend school, graduating in 1952 from Wasta High School as Valedictorian of her class of two.

On August 30, 1952, following a long courtship, Joan married Ivan L. Fenner, a cowboy from the Dalzell, SD community up the road. Joan and Ivan made their home in Rapid City for most of their nearly 45-year marriage, with the last few years in the town of Wasta.

Joan and Ivan's family increased to include daughter Shelli and three years later, son Ross. Their home was always filled with family and friends to enjoy a meal, including fresh baked bread and caramel rolls, good conversation, and even a place to stay. They welcomed with open, loving arms, son-in-law, Doug in 1972 and daughter-in-law, Joann in 1987.

Joan was a "stay-at-home" mom until Ross began school full time, when she bravely applied at the National Bank of SD (now US Bank) for a position in bookkeeping. Her affinity with numbers and love for helping people led her to a 25-year career, advancing into the teller line and eventually (after hours of correspondence banking classes) she was promoted to one of two operations officers. It wasn't unusual following an alarm at the bank late at night for Joan to find herself leading the local police through a dimly lit tunnel connecting the main bank to the drive-through.

After taking early retirement from the bank, she began another career using a life-long passion of hers: cleaning houses. It was an oft repeated quip that she may have been the only cleaning lady in Rapid City that drove a brand-new Buick Park Avenue. She loved rearranging furniture, not just in her own home, but throughout the rooms of her clients.

Joan joined the fledgling congregation of St. Andrew's Episcopal Church in 1959. It wasn't long until her beautiful singing voice captured the attention of the leadership, tapping her to be director for the youth choir. She remained active in a variety of roles through the years, including vestry, treasurer, funeral luncheon committee chair, delegate to Diocesan Convention, etc. She continued to sing in the choir every Sunday until a stroke November 2025.

Joan was also active in the larger Rapid City community through her memberships in Toastmasters, Altrusa, banking organizations, Minneluzahan Activity Center, the Elm Springs WTL Club and the Catalyst Club (where she was named 1999 "Good Neighbor"). She thoroughly enjoyed theater presentations (BHCT and BH Playhouse), Municipal band concerts in the park and the Black Hills Symphony.

Joan and Ivan enjoyed many trips to visit Fenner relatives on the west coast—or "reunions" in Reno or Las Vegas. Joan was a willing companion on fishing/camping excursions to various local spots (usually a prairie dam) or into Canada. She considered time spent with the four grandkids, here and in Idaho, heaven on earth. She enjoyed fun times with great grands as well, reliving hours spent on one sports bench or another, and watching plays or concerts.

A few years after Ivan's death in 1997, Clement Sutton danced into Joan's life at the Minneluzahan Activity Center. They joined their lives on February 17, 2001, enjoying their shared passions for dance and travel—and adult kids, grands and greats! Joan made many new and dear friends through Clem, but their time together was all too brief with his death in March of 2004.

Joan enjoyed singing, reading, feeding birds, playing cards, dancing and meeting people—she frequently described being "so fortunate" in one way or another almost every day of her life. Over the years she experienced travel destinations such as Canada, Italy, England, Scotland, Mexico, Hawaii, Alaska and various other scenic areas of the country.

Joan was preceded in death by Ivan, her husband of 44 years and Clem of 3 years; her parents, Oscar and Ruth Deering; siblings, Jean, Jim, David "Bud", Joyce, John, baby Dennis, Carolyn, George & Linda. In addition to beloved in-laws, nieces and nephews; her in-laws, Hack and Susie (Miner) Fenner and all that big loving Fenner family; son-in-law, Doug Vallis (September 2021).

Survivors and fortunate to have shared her life are her children: Shelli Vallis and Ross and Jo (O'Brien) Fenner. Grandchildren, Jocelyn (Jason) Woods, Meghan (Brett) Jones, Erin (John) Fenner-Eden, & Mac Fenner (Lucas White); great grandchildren: Aidan Jones, Emma Jones, Lauren Joan Woods, Gianna (Isaac) Jones-Hopke, Braden Woods, Veronica Jones, Felicity Jones, Marcianna Jones, Isabella Jones and Ephraem Jones; Sutton family: Joann (Jim), Linda and Dennis—their grandchildren—and the entire larger Sutton family who warmly welcomed Joan, keeping her close in thought, often traveling far to drop in for a visit.

In addition, Joan is survived by her siblings Kathryn Deering of Rapid City and Patrick (Frankie) Deering of Belle Fourche, SD. Peter Geyerman, special "nephew"/neighbor, John Kreber (her Rapid City "son"), Marty Garwood, her deacon, "the good daughter", and a host of beloved nieces, nephews and dear friends, including most recently her table mates at Serenity Place: Sid, Mary and Joyce, who brought special joy to her last four months, proving that not all angels have wings.

Services are scheduled for 10AM, Saturday, June 20, 2026, at St. Andrew's Episcopal Church, 910 Sioux San Drive, Rapid City, followed by inurnment at the Elm Springs, SD Cemetery, with a luncheon and time of sharing at the Wall Community Center, Wall, SD.

In lieu of flowers, the family requests memorials be given to The Club for Boys, Youth and Family Services, St. Andrew's Episcopal Church, Church Response (or a local food bank). We also wish to thank Joan's Stillwater Hospice caregivers and the staff at St. Martin's Serenity Place for their loving attention.

title: Council to hear Catalyst TIF amendment that would add Elevate Rapid City to project
description: During its Wednesday, June 10, meeting, the Rapid City Legal and Finance Committee voted 4-0 to approve an amendment to the Catalyst District Tax Increment Financing District that adds $19.4 million to the already approved $84 million TIF.
_full_text:
During its Wednesday, June 10, meeting, the Rapid City Legal and Finance Committee voted 4-0 to approve an amendment to the Catalyst District Tax Increment Financing District that adds $19.4 million to the already approved $84 million TIF.

The current Catalyst District plan includes infrastructure for the flagship development of a new sports complex, funded partially by the $84.1 million TIF. The project was approved by the Rapid City Council in September 2025.

How does a TIF work?
When a Tax Increment Financing District is established in a defined area, the value of the district is calculated. When infrastructure is improved or a development is added to the district, the value of that land increases. The property taxes generated beyond the base value are the increment. Rather than the city collecting those property taxes, the additional funds are diverted to pay for infrastructure, development or other costs. There are four TIF categories in South Dakota. Per the South Dakota Department of Revenue’s summary of the law, they are:
 Local: Local classification is the default classification. Unless the TIF district meets the definition of an Industrial, Economic Development, or Affordable Housing TIF district, it is a Local TIF district. Examples include public infrastructure improvements for housing that does not meet the Affordable Housing requirements. The projects usually benefit the local government instead of having a regional or statewide benefit.

 Industrial: Industrial classification includes an area where activities are recognized as industrial by zoning authorities. Examples include an animal processing plant or an ethanol plant.

 Economic Development: Economic development classification includes any area where there is or will be one or more businesses engaged in any activity defined as commercial or industrial by the governing body that has zoning authority over the land contained within the TIF district. Examples include public infrastructure improvements for commercial or retail development.

 Affordable Housing: Affordable Housing TIF examples include housing developments and workforce housing. The classification includes an area where:
The original selling price of any house in the district will be at or below the first-time homebuyer purchase price limit being used by the South Dakota Housing Development Authority as of the date the house is sold; OR

The monthly rental rate of all multifamily housing units in the district will be at or below the calculated rent for the state's eighty percent area median income as of the date the district is created, for a minimum of five years following the date of first occupancy.

Per the project plan, Phase II includes $9 million in TIF funding toward infrastructure that will support a $400 million private project. The money, "will be used for the construction of water and water reclamation mains and facilities necessary to provide services to a significant industrial client. The development of the infrastructure will allow further development along Deadwood Avenue, most of which is outside the proposed TIF boundaries. There is more than adequate water availability, however, the means of conveying the water to the sites with adequate pressure needs to be upgraded.”

In February, council members told the Journal there was discussion of a data center, but neither the plan documents nor council members identified the mystery client or the project.

That month, Black Hills Energy told the Journal the company owns property along Deadwood Avenue included in the Rapid City Catalyst TIFD.

“The property is the site of our Lange I and Lange II generating facilities. Lange II is currently under construction and scheduled to be online later this year. The remainder of the property is reserved for future resource development to meet customers’ needs,” a Black Hills Energy spokesperson said. “From our understanding, the $9M water investment through the TIFD will enhance growth opportunities along Deadwood Avenue which are currently limited by the lack of available water resources. The water need is not related to a Black Hills Energy planned project.”

 Elevate Rapid City
TIF boundary that is already included in the Catalyst District where Elevate Rapid City is looking to develop a business park and multi-family housing units. 

Elevate Rapid City’s recent request increases the TIF by $10 million in capital costs for street and utility improvements to North Maple Street north of Mall Drive, intersection improvements at the intersection of North Maple Street and Mall Drive as well as street and utility improvements to Mall Drive.

The request also includes $9,464,314 for financing costs for the improvements included in the TIFD request, bringing the increase to over $19 million and the total TIF to about $103 million.

 Catalyst District Boundaries
The boundaries of the Catalyst District are indicated with the yellow lines.  

According to city documents, the necessary infrastructure improvements would be toward the future development of a business park that would also include multifamily dwellings across 128 acres.

At the Wednesday meeting, local resident Mark Millar questioned whether the city is "self-financing" the project since it's a city TIF.

Senior Public Policy Director for Elevate Rapid City Garth Wadsworth then took to the podium to address the concerns posed by Millar.

"I do think it's worth just addressing some of the previous questions. I should state that the contingency fund that is included in the project plan, we do not touch that," Wadsworth said. "We are asking for an amendment, which is an additional projection on increment. We have to go out and get a loan for that money. We do not get that from the city. We protect the taxpayers by doing that. We're on the hook to pay that back in the event that things do not pan out."

From previous reporting by the Journal, Tax Increment Finance Planner Mike Dugan said the city does not write checks for the intended improvements by the TIF, the developer is taking the risk by taking a bank loan. After looking at all the invoices, the city reimburses the developer for the improvements.

The city will only cover only 7% of the bank loan’s interest rate. If the rate is higher, then the developer is responsible for those costs.

Dugan said if the amount spent for the improvements exceeds what was approved in the TIF the developer is also responsible for those costs. If a development does not generate enough increment to repay their bank loan after the development is completed, the developer is responsible for the loss, not the city, Dugan said.

On Wednesday, Wadsworth also mentioned Elevate, the Governor's Office of Economic Development (GOED), and Rapid City Commercial Real Estate gave letters about the project to the council.

In its letter, from Interim CEO Todd J. Kenner, Elevate said the current market condition is good for light industrial in Rapid City is needed with the Box Elder Industrial Park, Rushmore Business Park and the Black Hills Industrial Center.

The letter also includes a statement made by the GOED regarding the state considering giving $7.5 million in Revolving Economic Development and Initiative Fund financing to the project, as well as up to $1.5 million in grant funds to support infrastructure needs.

Councilman Lance Lehmann (Ward 4) asked Planning Director Vicki Fisher if Dugan could provide a presentation on the TIF to city council at its Monday, June 15 meeting.  Fisher said that would be at the discretion of Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun.

Lehmann replied, "I think we can certainly request that. It's our meeting, not the mayor’s."

The item will return for consideration at the June 15 council meeting.

title: South Dakota has seen vacation home purchases fall 62.3% since 2021
description: Vacation homes—also referred to as second homes or seasonal properties—are residential properties purchased primarily for leisure use rather than as a primary residence. While often associated with affluent buyers and resort destinations, this segment of the housing market can serve as a leading indicator of broader economic conditions. Because these purchases are typically discretionary, shifts in vacation-home demand can signal changes in consumer confidence, housing affordability, and the financial flexibility of higher-income households—factors that also influence the wider real estate market and local economies that depend on seasonal residents.
_full_text:
Vacation homes—also referred to as second homes or seasonal properties—are residential properties purchased primarily for leisure use rather than as a primary residence. While often associated with affluent buyers and resort destinations, this segment of the housing market can serve as a leading indicator of broader economic conditions. Because these purchases are typically discretionary, shifts in vacation-home demand can signal changes in consumer confidence, housing affordability, and the financial flexibility of higher-income households—factors that also influence the wider real estate market and local economies that depend on seasonal residents.

In recent years, higher mortgage rates, elevated home prices, and tighter financial conditions have made second-home purchases more difficult to sustain, particularly compared with the low-rate environment earlier in the decade. As a result, many prospective buyers are turning toward alternatives such as timeshares and short-term rentals, which offer access to vacation properties without the high upfront costs and unpredictable overhead of owning a vacation home.

 South Dakota Has Seen Vacation-Home Purchases Fall 62.3% Since 2021
South Dakota has seen vacation home purchases fall 62.3% since 2021. 

To better understand these shifting conditions and their effects, SellMyTimeshareNow—a global marketplace where people around the world connect to rent, buy, and sell timeshares—analyzed where the decline in vacation home purchasing is occurring, to what extent, and how the timeshare market is responding.

Here are the key takeaways from the analysis:

Vacation-home purchases fell 65.8% from their 2021 peak. U.S. second-home mortgage originations dropped from 257,549 in 2021 to 88,158 in 2025, while the second-home share of all mortgage originations also fell from 4.9% to 2.6% over the same period.
Florida saw the biggest drop in total vacation-home purchases. Between 2021 and 2025, Florida recorded 38,465 fewer vacation-home purchases with a mortgage, more than any other state. By percentage, Nevada saw the largest decline at 78.3%, followed by Hawaii (-77.8%) and Wyoming (-74.5%).
The U.S. timeshare industry expanded since pandemic-era lows. U.S. timeshare sales volume rose from $4.9 billion in 2020 to $10.5 billion in 2024, while rental revenue climbed from $1.3 billion to $3.2 billion. That amounts to gains of 114.3% and 146.2%, respectively.
Timeshare purchase interest in 2025 was heavily concentrated. On the SellMyTimeshareNow marketplace, the U.S. led with 14,942 purchase offers, far ahead of Mexico (3,373) and Aruba (1,598). Within the U.S., Florida ranked first with 3,506 offers, followed by Hawaii (2,219) and Nevada (1,755).

Trends in Vacation Home Purchases Over Time

Vacation home purchases fell by nearly two-thirds from 2021 to 2025 amid soaring prices and mortgage rates

Source: SellMyTimeshareNow analysis of FFIEC’s Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data | Image Credit: SellMyTimeshareNow

The U.S. vacation-home market has contracted sharply since its pandemic-era peak, reversing a surge driven by historically low borrowing costs and increased demand for remote-friendly living. Vacation-home purchases using a mortgage fell from 257,549 units in 2021 to just 88,158 in 2025, a decline of 65.8%. Similarly, the vacation-home share of total mortgage originations fell from 4.9% in 2021 to 2.6% in 2025. These drops followed a period when second-home demand expanded rapidly, particularly in resort markets and lower-density areas.

The decline aligns with a rapid deterioration in affordability. Mortgage rates rose significantly from pandemic-era lows, increasing borrowing costs and reducing purchasing power, even for higher-income households that typically drive second-home demand. At the same time, home prices in the U.S.—including many vacation-oriented markets—remained elevated, limiting the ability of buyers to re-enter the market after the initial pandemic surge. Taken together, these conditions appear to have significantly reduced the pool of buyers able or willing to purchase vacation homes outright. The scale and speed of the decline suggest that the vacation home segment—often more sensitive to financial conditions than primary housing—has been particularly affected by the post-pandemic economic conditions.

How Has the U.S. Timeshare Industry Fared in the Post-Pandemic Economy?

Despite persistent inflation, U.S. timeshare sales volume and rental revenues have both more than doubled since their 2020 lows

Source: SellMyTimeshareNow analysis of ARDA’s 2025 State of the Vacation Timeshare Industry data | Image Credit: SellMyTimeshareNow

While demand for traditional vacation homes has weakened, the U.S. timeshare industry has followed a markedly different path since the pandemic downturn. Data from the American Resort Development Association indicates that timeshare sales volume reached lows of $4.9 billion in 2020, while timeshare rental revenue was just $1.3 billion, reflecting the sharp disruption to leisure travel during the first year of the pandemic.

The industry recovered quickly in the years that followed. By 2024, timeshare sales had risen to $10.5 billion, up 114.3% from its 2020 low, while rental revenue increased to $3.2 billion, a gain of 146.2%. That rebound suggests that even as inflation and higher interest rates have made large real estate purchases more difficult, many consumers have continued to spend on vacation access through ownership models that typically require less long-term financial commitment than buying a second home outright.

What Are the Most Popular Destinations to Buy a Timeshare?

While Mexico and Aruba lead international interest, the U.S. dominates timeshare purchase offer volumes—driven by Florida, Hawaii, and Nevada

Source: SellMyTimeshareNow marketplace data | Image Credit: SellMyTimeshareNow

Despite broad growth in timeshare sales and rental activity, demand for timeshare ownership remains highly concentrated in a relatively small group of destination countries. On the SellMyTimeshareNow marketplace in 2025, the United States recorded the highest number of timeshare purchase offers by far at 14,942, with Mexico ranking a distant second at 3,373, followed by Aruba at 1,598. Other international markets saw significantly lower levels of activity, including Canada (398), the Netherlands Antilles (274), and Australia (258), indicating that interest is largely focused on a handful of established resort destinations.

Within the United States, activity was led by Florida with 3,506 offers, followed by Hawaii (2,219) and Nevada (1,755). A second tier of states—including California (1,284), South Carolina (1,156), and Colorado (1,063)—also recorded notable activity, though at lower levels. The concentration of demand in these markets reflects the role of established tourism infrastructure and consistent visitor demand in sustaining timeshare interest.

Where Are Vacation Home Purchases Declining the Most?

Florida led the U.S. with over 38,000 fewer vacation home purchases, but Nevada, Hawaii, and Wyoming saw the sharpest percentage declines

Source: SellMyTimeshareNow analysis of FFIEC’s Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data | Image Credit: SellMyTimeshareNow

Many of the same states that lead in timeshare demand also appear to be among those experiencing the sharpest pullbacks in traditional vacation-home purchases, pointing to a broader shift in how consumers access vacation properties. The decline in second-home buying has been widespread across the United States, though the scale and intensity vary significantly by state. In absolute terms, Florida recorded the largest decrease, with 38,465 fewer vacation-home purchases with a mortgage between 2021 and 2025, reflecting its outsized role in the second-home market during the pandemic-era surge.

Other high-volume vacation-home states also saw substantial declines in raw numbers. California recorded 13,516 fewer purchases, while Texas and North Carolina posted declines of 9,900 and 9,575, respectively. These figures suggest that states with the largest second-home markets during the pandemic boom have experienced the most pronounced pullbacks in absolute terms.

However, the steepest declines on a percentage basis were concentrated in smaller, tourism-dependent states—several of which also rank among the top timeshare destinations. Nevada saw the sharpest drop, with vacation-home purchases falling by 78.3%, followed by Hawaii (-77.8%) and Wyoming (-74.5%). These sharper contractions indicate that, in some destination markets, demand has fallen back more dramatically relative to its pandemic peak, underscoring the sensitivity of these regions to shifts in affordability and discretionary spending.

At the metro level, the sharpest declines were widespread across both large population centers and smaller destination markets. Among large metros, Austin, TX saw the steepest drop, with vacation-home purchases falling 80.4%, followed closely by major leisure markets such as Las Vegas (-79.4%), Orlando (-79.4%), and Miami (-78.8%). Similar patterns are evident in well-known vacation destinations, including Breckenridge, CO (-63.9%), Naples, FL (-76.1%), and Kahului, HI (-85.2%), all of which are heavily tied to tourism-driven housing demand. These declines suggest that even in large metropolitan areas and high-demand leisure markets alike, elevated costs and shifting consumer preferences have significantly curtailed second-home purchasing activity.

Here is a summary of the data for South Dakota:

Percentage change in second-home mortgages (2021–2025): -62.3%
Total change in second-home mortgages (2021–2025): -331
Total second-home mortgage originations (2025): 200
Total second-home mortgage originations (2021): 531
Second-home share of total mortgage originations: 2.2%
Median value of newly mortgaged second homes: $375,000
Share of housing used for seasonal, recreational, or occasional use: 3.2%

For reference, here are the statistics for the entire United States:

Percentage change in second-home mortgages (2021–2025): -65.8%
Total change in second-home mortgages (2021–2025): -169,391
Total second-home mortgage originations (2025): 88,158
Total second-home mortgage originations (2021): 257,549
Second-home share of total mortgage originations: 2.6%
Median value of newly mortgaged second homes: $495,000
Share of housing used for seasonal, recreational, or occasional use: 3.3%

For more information, a detailed methodology, and complete results, see U.S. Cities Where Vacation Home Demand Has Declined the Most on SellMyTimeshareNow.

title: FBI offers reward for information in 2022 Pine Ridge shooting case that killed child
description: Four years after 6-year-old Logan Warrior Goings was shot and killed in a drive-by shooting in Pine Ridge, the FBI has offered a $50,000 reward for information on the 2022 case.
_full_text:
Four years after 6-year-old Logan Warrior Goings was shot and killed in a drive-by shooting in Pine Ridge, the FBI has offered a $50,000 reward for information on the 2022 case.

The FBI Minneapolis Field Office announced the reward on Tuesday, June 9, for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the individual or individuals responsible for the murder of Warrior Goings.

According to the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety, officers responded to a call at approximately 9 p.m. on May 5, 2022, for a drive-by shooting at a home in the 2900 block of U.S. Highway 18.

 Logan Warrior Goings
Four years after 6-year-old Logan Warrior Goings was shot and killed in a drive-by shooting in Pine Ridge, the FBI offers $50,000 reward for information onto the 2022 case.  

When officers arrived, they learned an occupant of a vehicle had shot at the home and fled the scene prior to police officers' arrival. During the gunfire, Warrior Goings was shot and killed. Several other people, including children, were also inside the residence at the time. 

"This heartbreaking case remains an active priority for federal, tribal, and local law enforcement partners. Logan’s family deserves answers, and those responsible must be held accountable," the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety wrote on Facebook at the time.

The Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety has posted multiple requests for information on social media, asking anyone with information in the case to come forward.

If you have any information regarding this case, please contact the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI (225-5324) or submit a tip online at tips.fbi.gov.

title: Citizens for Liberty to host gubernatorial candidate forum in Rapid City
description: South Dakota Citizens for Liberty said it will host a Republican Party governor’s race candidate forum in Rapid City.
_full_text:
South Dakota Citizens for Liberty said it will host a Republican Party governor’s race candidate forum in Rapid City.

Gov. Larry Rhoden of Union Center faces Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden in the July 28 runoff election. Early voting begins on Friday, June 12, according to the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office. The voter registration deadline for the contest is July 13.

 052326-nws-sl-doeden-p1.jpg
Toby Doeden announces his candidacy for the Republican nomination for governor of South Dakota during an event on May 28, 2025, in Aberdeen. 

Doeden won the June 2 Republican primary but didn’t pass the 35% threshold to avoid a runoff. Doeden finished with 31%, followed by Rhoden at 25%. Doeden received the most votes in West River, with 14,536. Rhoden received 13,679.

Citizens for Liberty said it will host its GOP Governor Runoff Forum from 6 to 8 p.m. on Thursday, July 16, at the Rapid City Best Western Ramkota, 2111 N. Lacrosse St., in the Sylvan Room.

Per a release from the organization, the forum will feature candidates Rhoden and Doeden and will be moderated by Sioux Falls radio host and personality John Small.

The group said the purpose of the forum “is to provide the public with an opportunity to hear directly from the candidates and get to know them beyond campaign literature and prepared messaging.”

 'A BIG DEAL'
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden speaks during a ceremony celebrating a new $2 million expansion at South Dakota Wildland Fire’s Rapid City campus on Monday, April 20. 

“This is not a debate,” the group said. “This forum is designed to give South Dakota voters a respectful, structured opportunity to hear from the candidates and ask questions about the issues that matter to them.”

The evening will include candidate introductions, questions from attendees, and closing remarks from each candidate. Attendees will be able to ask questions from a center aisle standing microphone. Questions and responses will be timed to keep the forum moving and to avoid speeches or filibusters.

The emcee will determine when a topic has been exhausted, when a question has already been asked, and when a question is outside the scope of the forum.

Members of the public are encouraged to attend and participate respectfully.

SD Citizens for Liberty describes itself as a grassroots organization committed to civic engagement, constitutional principles and encouraging informed participation in local and state government. Per its bylaws, it does not endorse candidates.

title: 'A brighter future for Star Village': Community bands together to light up neighborhood and keep it safe
description: Under the soft glow of recently installed and strung up lights at every home, a neighborhood once overshadowed by neglect began to rewrite its own headline.
_full_text:
Under the soft glow of recently installed and strung up lights at every home, a neighborhood once overshadowed by neglect began to rewrite its own headline. 

Songs and laughter echoed down Kellogg Place in Rapid City as residents of Star Village and Rapid City community members banded together on Wednesday, June 10, for a transformative, full-day blitz aimed at reclaiming the neighborhood. The theme of the event, “Keeping Star Village Lit, Keeping Star Village Safe!”

Armed with tools, determination and community spirit, volunteers built a shed and installed lights in the recently constructed Star Village Community Garden, provided motion detector lights to residents and prepared for an entire day of festivities for residents to enjoy. 

 Ribbon cutting
Songs and laughter echoed down Kellog Place as residents of Star Village and Rapid City community members banded together on Wednesday, June 10, for a transformative, full-day blitz aimed at reclaiming the neighborhood. The theme of the event, 'Keeping Star Village Lit, Keeping Star Village Safe!' 

As children rushed to decorate their bikes with lights and reflective pieces and parents enjoyed the summer sun and ate a free meal from local food trucks, Star Village resident Mark Morris couldn’t help but smile at the overflowing sense of community for his beloved neighborhood. 

Morris has lived in Star Village for nearly 15 years and in Rapid City his entire life. He said when he was younger Star Village used to be a bustling neighborhood, where neighbors always helped each other out and there was no fear of crime. 

"It makes me feel good to see this (the event), because I grew up in Rapid City. I grew up in north Rapid, where north Rapid was a fine place and it was for young people," Morris said. "... It was the neighborhood where doors didn't get locked because you didn't need to lock it. All the neighbors looked out for each other. Everybody within five blocks knew who everybody was."  

Star Village's history dates back to the early 1950s when it was established as Signal Heights, a housing development for Air Force personnel and civilian defense workers. Applications opened in June 1952 for over 100 duplexes, according to Journal archives advertising for tenants. Two decades later, the name was changed to Star Village. By the 1980s, the number of military tenants at Star Village was at 30% and non-military affiliated residents could rent there.

 Mark Morris
Mark Morris has been living in Star Village for nearly 15 years and north Rapid City his entire life. He said when he was younger Star Village used to be a bustling neighborhood, where neighbors always helped each other out and there was no fear of crime.  

Star Village is now a low-income housing development under the management and ownership of Tzadik, a Florida company headed up by Adam Hendry. Tzadik purchased Star Village at the end of 2019, and residents said it went downhill from there. The company lists 18 Rapid City properties on their website, but its reach extends well beyond communities at the foot of the Black Hills.

As years passed, Morris witnessed his beloved neighborhood gradually deteriorate and be abandoned. He said it broke his heart watching what once used to be considered a vibrant budding community fall into disrepair. 

However, through efforts such as the Mayor's Love Your Block Grant through the Bloomberg Center for Public Innovation at John's Hopkins University, Fountain Springs Church's Love Your Neighbor Week and the ongoing efforts from the Rapid City Police Department, Morris said he is finally seeing the remnants of what made his neighborhood great. 

 Love your neighborhood
On Wednesday, June 10, community members gathered for an event themed, “Keeping Star Village Lit, Keeping Star Village Safe!” 

As soon as the police department settled at 1614 Kellogg Place, the department's community engagement center for Star Village, Morris said he has been actively making an effort to discuss changes and initiatives to transform the neighborhood and finally save it.  

Morris said his goal wasn't only to help the neighborhood, but to build a better future for the most vulnerable — the children. 

"The kids, they look at life through a kaleidoscope, but I want to change that and broaden their outlook," Morris said. "This is all they've seen in their lives, but I want to change it to a bright opportunities and colors."  

It was after dropping a friend off during the night that an idea struck Morris and a newfound determination to light up Star Village was born. Working together with other residents and community volunteers, Morris' dream became a reality on Wednesday. 

Attendees also got to enjoy youth tipi teachings and a gaga ball tournament, poster decorating contest, repairs by Black Hills Energy of seven light polls and installation of new LED lights in the neighborhood to promote public safety. 

 Police car
Songs and laughter echoed down Kellogg Place in Rapid City as residents of Star Village and Rapid City community members banded together on Wednesday, June 10, for a transformative, full-day blitz aimed at reclaiming the neighborhood. 

"We installed 80 solar lights today for all the residents at Star Village and handed out light bulbs for porches," RCPD Community Violence Intervention and Prevention Initiative Program Director Jamie Kirsch said. "... It's just to celebrate the importance of lighting and its impact on public safety."  

There was also a community dinner in the evening, followed by speeches from Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun and Rapid City Police Chief Don Hedrick. Hedrick said this really couldn't have happened without everyone in Rapid City joining together to build a better future for the neighborhood. 

"I think it's fitting that we're putting up lighting here tonight," Hedrick said. "... I think we're turning a corner with this lighting, and I think we can all just look to this as a way for a future being brighter for Star Village."

 BRIGHT SIDE LOGO.jpg

As dusk fell and the street lights turned on one by one in Star Village, men, women and children marched down Kellogg Place and circled the neighborhood, transforming the darkness into a festival of optimism.

For an area long plagued by infrastructure gaps and high crime rates, the glowing fixtures did more than just illuminate the pavement — it sparked a collective wave of change, proving that safety and pride could be built from the ground up by the very people who call it home.

title: Monument Health opens second ER in Rapid City on Wednesday
description: Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus opens Wednesday, June 10, 2026, at 1911 E. Mall Drive in Rapid City. The facility will offer 24-hour emergency care.
_full_text:
MH Emergency Services and Medical Campus.jpg
Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus opens Wednesday, June 10, 2026, at 1911 E. Mall Drive in Rapid City. The facility will offer 24-hour emergency care. 

Rapid City’s second emergency room opened on Wednesday, June 10. Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus will be open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, year-round.

Located at 1911 E. Mall Drive, Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus is situated along the Interstate 90 corridor on the growing east side of Rapid City. It’s part of Monument Health’s continued expansion in Rapid Valley and Box Elder, following the opening of Monument Health Rapid Valley Clinic and Urgent Care in September 2025, and Monument Health Box Elder Clinic in August 2025.

 MH new emergency services facility.jpg
Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus at 1911 E. Mall Drive in Rapid City will offer 24-hour emergency services, plus X-ray, lab, CT and other services. 

The one-story, 16,750-square foot medical facility is equipped with the full laboratory, plus X-ray and CT scan capabilities, a covered ambulance garage with easy access to a trauma room, eight emergency exam rooms, and two inpatient rooms for people who require overnight care.

 MH CT scan room.jpg
The CT scan room at Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus is pictured. The new facility in Rapid City includes CT scan and X-ray capabilities and full laboratory services. 

 MH emergency exam room.jpg
Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus in Rapid City includes eight emergency exam rooms. 

A designated isolation room is available for patients who might have infectious diseases such as tuberculosis.

Patients who require trauma surgery, cardiologists, and advanced services and testing will be transferred to Monument Health Rapid City Hospital, Eide said.

Like Monument Health Rapid City Hospital, Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus will be staffed by board-certified emergency medicine physicians 24 hours a day, with shorter hours for outpatient services.

“As emergency medicine specialists, we are proud to bring the same level of expert care available at Monument Health Rapid City Hospital to this new location,” Dr. Brook Eide, Emergency Department Chair, said in a news release announcing the new facility.

 MH inpatient room.jpg
Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus includes two inpatient rooms for people who require overnight care. 

“We have our same core of emergency physicians that will work at the main hospital and here,” he said. “The same with our nursing staff – there will be shared nursing staff so your ER nurse here tomorrow may be your ER nurse at the main hospital the next day, and so it’s nice we’ll have that continuity, understanding both places and really being able to tie them together.”

In addition to the main waiting area near the admission desk, the new facility has a separate waiting room, St. Barbara’s Chapel, for patients and families. The chapel is named in honor of the late Barbara Vidal Lien, who was a longtime Rapid City resident.

 MH waiting room chapel.jpg
St. Barbara’s Chapel is a separate waiting room for patients and families at the new Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus in Rapid City. The chapel is named for the late Barbara Vidal Lien, a longtime Rapid City resident. 

In choosing the location for this new standalone emergency services facility, Eide said a team from Monument Health studied how and where Rapid City is growing.

“We found there’s a lot of growth over here, a lot of new families here, so we really wanted to bring health care to where people are,” he said. “We wanted to be able to get emergency care to this side of town.”

“This facility allows us to provide critical emergency services to more patients closer to where they live and work. Every minute matters in emergency medicine, and this campus is going to make a real difference for this community,” Eide said.

 MH Dr. Brook Eide.jpg
Dr. Brook Eide is the Emergency Department Chair for Monument Health Rapid City Hospital and the new Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus in Rapid City. 

This new facility is the first completed phase of Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus. Eide said the facility was purposely located on property large enough to allow for expansion as the community grows.

“As Rapid City grows, we’ll see more resources here on this side of town with clinic space and other things, and there’s lots of things for those. We’re very excited to get this first step done,” Eide said.

“This campus was designed with the future in mind, with room for additional buildings and services as our community’s needs evolve,” said Paulette Davidson, Monument Health president and CEO.

Do you need emergency services or urgent care?

Knowing when an illness or injury requires emergency room care can be challenging for patients, Eide said.

“We want them to go to the right place for the right care,” he said, noting that urgent care is a good option for ailments such as minor lacerations, sprains, and sore throats.

“If you know you’ve got something minor, go to urgent care,” Eide said.

People who are suffering more serious or potentially life-threatening injuries or ailments should go to an emergency room.

“If you’re not really sure, usually I’ll tell you, ‘Go to the ER,’” Eide said. “If you’re (wondering) is this urgent care or is this emergency department, coming to the emergency department is fine.”

“The hope is that some of those emergencies that may have gone to the main emergency department can come here (to 1911 E. Mall Drive) and we can serve people in a different location with the same great care,” he said.

title: Deadline approaching to sign up for Rapid City’s America 250 parade
description: One week remains for businesses, organizations and groups to register for Rapid City’s America 250 Birthday Parade.
_full_text:
One week remains for businesses, organizations and groups to register for Rapid City’s America 250 Birthday Parade.

The community parade will be held Thursday, July 2, beginning at 7 p.m., through the streets of downtown Rapid City. The deadline to signup to participate is Thursday, June 18.

This is the first time in 35 years Rapid City and area residents will enjoy a downtown community parade during the Independence Day holiday period. The parade is one of several events planned as part of Rapid City’s “Real America Birthday Bash” July 1-4.

Organizing this year’s “Real America Birthday Bash” community parade is Connie Olson, long-time chair of Rapid City’s Festival of Lights parade, a traditional event held over the Thanksgiving holiday period that attracts nearly 100 parade entries and 30,000 people.

“We have received great interest and response from the community. We are inviting businesses, organizations, community, church, youth groups and others to join us in this historic celebration,” said Olson, a member of the “Real America Birthday Bash” steering committee. “Parades are part of Independence Day observances and traditions in communities around our nation. What a great way for Rapid City and the surrounding area to come together with family and friends and celebrate the 250th birthday of our country.”

To learn more about the parade, to volunteer and to register as a parade participant, visit festivaloflightsrc.com/americas250parade for more details.

The parade will be followed by the Sky Elements nationally-recognized patriotic drone show at 9:30 p.m. The drone show will be launched from near Memorial Park at the Central High School football field.

In addition to the parade and drone show, Rapid City’s “Real America Birthday Bash” includes multiple days of events from Main Street Square, along Sixth Street to Memorial Park. The slate of events features a downtown festival, a Mount Rushmore fireworks display viewing party from Main Street Square, a headline concert performance by country singer Chancey Williams, a concert by the Rapid City Municipal Band, the City’s fireworks display, a Kids’ Zone, Touch-A-Truck exhibits, interactive exhibits, a concert by the Air Force Academy Band, performances by local and regional bands, historical reenactments and patriotic readings, and culminating with a Freedom 5K Run.

To learn more about this summer’s “Real America Birthday Bash” events, visit realamericabirthdaybash.com or contact Visit Rapid City at 605-718-8484/800-487-3223.

Rapid City’s last community parade during the Independence Day holiday period was in 1991 as part of the celebration commemorating the 50th anniversary of Mount Rushmore National Memorial.

title: Rapid City police respond to trio of gunshot incidents in roughly 3 hours
description: The Rapid City Police Department had a busy night. From about 9:20 p.m. on Wednesday, June 10, and 12:35 a.m. on Thursday, June 11, the department responded the three different gunshot incidents. In one incident, a man sustained multiple injuries. In another, a person received a “superficial” injury. In another, no injuries were reported.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Police Department had a busy night. From about 9:20 p.m. on Wednesday, June 10, and 12:35 a.m. on Thursday, June 11, the department responded the three different gunshot incidents. In one incident, a man sustained multiple injuries. In another, a person received a “superficial” injury. In another, no injuries were reported.

First incident:

At around 9:20 p.m. on Wednesday, police were dispatched to the 200 block of Patton Street for a report of gunshots heard in the area. Police received information about an injured party who had just left the scene in a vehicle. The vehicle was located, and police found a man with gunshot injuries inside. He was subsequently transported to the hospital for the treatment of non-life-threatening injuries. Police located several shell casings in the roadway near the initial address of the call. Police continue to investigate the circumstances of the shooting.

Second incident:

While investigating the above gunshots call, police heard gunshots coming from the area of North 7th Street. On arrival at the location, police located spent shell casings, which were collected. No associated damage was located, and police received no report of injuries in relation to the incident. The case has been forwarded to the RCPD’s Criminal Investigation for further follow-up.

Third incident:

At around 12:35 a.m. on June 11, police were dispatched to the unit block of Saint Patrick Street — addresses below the number 100 — for a report of gunshots. Police located several shell casings in a nearby alleyway. Police located damage to a residence in the area. After speaking to witnesses, police learned an individual in the residence received a superficial injury as the gunfire occurred. Police continue to investigate the incident.

At this time, there is no evidence to suggest the three incidents are related, police said. Anyone with any information about any of the incidents or about the suspects responsible for the gunfire should contact Police Investigations at 605-394-4134.

title: Jacqeline Allen
description: September 21, 1931 - May 9, 2026
_full_text:
September 21, 1931 - May 9, 2026

Jacqueline Louise (Anderson) Allen was born September 21, 1931 to Martha Elizabeth Miner and Vernon Rudolph Anderson, in Aberdeen SD. She passed away after a full life of 94 years on May 9, 2026 at West Hills Village, Rapid City, SD.

Baptized in the Methodist church, she was an active Girl Scout, Jobs Daughter Queen, twirled baton and played percussion in the band, graduating in 1949. After 2 years at Northern State Teachers College, she taught 4th grade in Hot Springs, SD. She finished her BA in primary education at USD in 1954 where she was a Pi Beta Phi.

While working as a waitress at Custer State Lodge, she recognized a handsome man who had been washing dishes at the Pi Phi house. This man, Bruce Allen, became her husband in 1955. Following Bruce in his medical training, Jackie taught Kindergarten in Sioux City IA, Philadelphia, PA, and St. Paul MN. The first of four children was born in St. Paul, then Sherman TX, Detroit MI and lastly in Rapid City where she and Bruce decided to live the remainder of their lives.

Early years raising children meant driving to lessons, sports and musical activities with an occasional stop at the YMCA for water aerobics. The Esquire and Canyon Lake club were favorite dancing spots. Jackie learned to ski and enjoyed social and civic clubs, including leadership positions in the Medical Auxiliary, PEO, Questers, Symphony League, Rapid City Beautification committee, and volunteering with the Dahl Fine arts and Journey Museum. She was a 25-year member of the Sons of Norway. She and Bruce loved to entertain at home, hosting many a bridge club and Gourmet club. Her hobbies included hardanger, gardening (especially roses and orchids), scrapbooking, and genealogy. She was a lifelong learner collecting children's books, poetry, National Geographic magazines, watching movies, listening to music and traveling. She and Bruce were long time members of the New Horizons Band.

The First Presbyterian Church was the backbone of their marriage where they made many friends and she contributed in a variety of capacities.
