title: New data initiative helps Pennington County track vacation home rentals and improve compliance
description: Pennington County has hired a technology firm to help track the number of vacation rentals in the county.
_full_text:
Pennington County has hired a technology firm to help track the number of vacation rentals in the county.

The Pennington County Board of Commissioners voted unanimously to approve the Planning and Zoning Department to enter into an agreement with Deckard Technologies, a company specializing in short-term rental analytics and compliance services, to provide enhanced data regarding vacation home rentals and short-term rentals operating throughout Pennington County.

The county will gain access to data that helps identify active short-term rental properties and improve compliance with existing county regulations. The information will provide a more complete picture of the short-term rental market in Pennington County and assist the Planning & Zoning Department in facilitating VHR/STR’s.

“This service does strong data-mining for all VHRs in the county,” Planning and Zoning Director Brittney Hand told the commission during the Wednesday, June 3, meeting. “It also sends out notices to those that are not compliant with our current ordinance. Bringing all of those into compliance will counteract the cost of the software.”

Per Pennington County code, all vacation/short-term home rentals in the county outside the jurisdiction of incorporated municipalities are required to have a license. The maximum number of bedrooms if five, with a maximum occupancy of 14 “or the maximum capacity based on the onsite wastewater treatment system, whichever is smaller.” Rentals are limited to one per lot unless the property contains a multi-family/apartment dwelling or is located in a commercial zoning district.

The Deckard platform will use publicly available information to identify active short-term rental listings and provide insights such as booking trends, average rental rates, platform usage, property ownership information, and license status. The service will also assist the county in identifying properties that may be operating without the required license or advertising occupancy levels that exceed county regulations.

As part of this effort, the Planning & Zoning Department is encouraging vacation home rentals and short-term rental owners to apply for the required county license. Property owners will have six months from the Commission approval date of June 3 to submit their application before enforcement actions begin.

"We understand that some property owners may not be aware of the license requirement, and we want to give them a fair opportunity to come into compliance," Hand said in a release from the county "This six-month period is intended to provide additional time for Vacation Home Rental and Short-Term Rental owners to complete the process, pay the license fee, and ensure they are meeting county regulations before enforcement begins. Our goal is compliance through education first, and we encourage operators to work with our office during this process."

The Pennington County license fee is $150 and covers owners for 3 years. Operating a vacation home rental or short-term rental without the required license may result in a fine of $200 per day.

The license application and compliance checklist are available online at: https://www.pennco.org/services/planning/vacation_home_rentals.php

Applications may be submitted by email, mail, or in person.

State law currently requires the registration of rental homes but allows a home to be rented for 14 days without being registered with the state — colloquially known as the "Sturgis Rally rule." According to the South Dakota Department of Health, regulations on short-term rentals include a multitude of requirements such as proper pest control, installation of egress windows, and housekeeping maintenance. The initial license application fee at the state level is $100, with a yearly fee of $75 for license continuation.

In December 2025, the Rapid City Council approved a short-term rental ordinance that requires registration with the city to allow approval of vacation homes in residential and commercial zoning districts. It also requires a conditional use permit for larger-scale vacation homes in residential and commercial zoning districts. It defines larger scale as homes with five or more bedrooms.

title: Nebraska man dies in crash near Burke on U.S. Highway 18
description: A Nebraska man died in a single-vehicle crash near Burke.
_full_text:
A Nebraska man died in a single-vehicle crash near Burke.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol said the crash occurred around 7:24 p.m. on Tuesday, June 9, on U.S. Highway 18 near the 296-mile marker, about 10 miles east of Burke.

The patrol did not release the man’s name pending notification of family. He’s 71 and from Stuart, Nebraska, according to the patrol.

An investigation determined the man, driving a 1939 Chevrolet JB Coupe, was eastbound on Highway 18 when the vehicle left the roadway and entered the ditch. The vehicle struck an approach, went airborne and rolled. The driver died at the scene.

An investigation into the crash continues.

title: Hotel Alex Johnson renovates guest rooms, plans more updates
description: Hotel Alex Johnson in Rapid City has completed a full renovation of its guest rooms ahead of its 98-year anniversary on July 1.
_full_text:
Hotel Alex Johnson in Rapid City has completed a full renovation of its guest rooms ahead of its 98-year anniversary on July 1.

The hotel is a historic landmark in downtown Rapid City. Opened in 1928, it’s listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Hotel Alex Johnson blends distinctive architecture and regional character, according to management.

The renovation of its 143 guest rooms preserves the hotel’s character while providing guests with an updated, comfortable experience, according to a news release announcing the renovation.

 Curio-Hotel_Alex_Johnson-Bridal_Suite-Bedroom.jpg
Pictured is a newly renovated bridal suite at Hotel Alex Johnson, Curio Collection by Hilton, in downtown Rapid City. 

The guest room renovations are part of a broader plan to update the property. This fall, Hotel Alex Johnson will add enhancements to Starbucks, Paddy O’Neill’s Irish Pub & Grill and the hotel’s meeting and event spaces.

“This renovation was about getting the balance right,” Mitch McKeithan, general manager of Hotel Alex Johnson, said in the release. “We’ve preserved the details and character that make this place special while introducing thoughtful updates that improve the guest experience.”

Hotel Alex Johnson is one of more than 200 properties in 47 countries and territories that is part of the Curio Collection by Hilton. The Curio Collection hotels offer locally inspired design, food and beverages for travelers who want to explore a destination and who appreciate hotels that maintain the unique culture and spirit of that destination.  

“Hotel Alex Johnson is an important piece of our history and our future,” said Caleb Arceneaux, CEO of LIV Hospitality, which manages the property. “Our responsibility is to protect what makes it distinct while ensuring it continues to meet the expectations of today’s guests and remain relevant for years to come.”  

 Hotel Alex Johnson
One of the newly renovated guests rooms is shown at Hotel Alex Johnson, Curio Collection by Hilton, in downtown Rapid City. The hotel plans updates to other parts of its property this fall.

title: Central States Fair employee dies from injuries suffered in shooting
byline: SHALOM BAER GEE and MIKE BROWNLEE Journal staff
description: The man injured in a shooting at the Central States Fairgrounds has died.
_full_text:
The man injured in a shooting at the Central States Fairgrounds has died.

The Pennington County Sheriff’s Office said Wednesday, June 10, that Central States Fair Maintenance Manager Paul Nebel, 50, died from his injuries after being hospitalized following the shooting.

“We extend our deepest condolences to Paul’s family and friends, the Central States Fair family and all those affected by this tragedy. We also continue to keep the injured Oglala Sioux Tribe officer, his family and fellow officers in our thoughts. This incident has impacted multiple communities across western South Dakota,” the sheriff’s office said in a release.

John Troy Lee, 58, shot Nebel at the fairgrounds around 8:45 a.m. on Sunday, June 7, according to the sheriff’s office. Lee was also a fair employee and Nebel was addressing a “personnel issue” with Lee when the shooting occurred, the sheriff’s office said.

Amber Hultman-Webber, owner of TUF Productions who’s worked as a producer at the fairgrounds often, said in a Facebook post, “This is not the post I was hoping to make. Our beloved arena manager Paul has passed away. Being the amazing human being that he was, he did not deserve this. He deserved so much better.”

Hultman-Webber described Nebel as a kind, caring person.

“The unsung heroes are the ones in the background at events. The setup, the tear down, and our biggest relationships as producers. We will miss you my friend, so very much. All of our countless times together I will truly cherish. The big laugh, the smile, the excitement I felt just seeing his truck cross the parking lot to come check in. He always took care of us,” she said. “Hug your people. Tell them you are grateful and never take them for granted. It is not goodbye, but I will see you later my dear friend. Thankful for all the work you did so us horse crazy people to stay safe all of these years. The impact Paul made will not be forgotten. If more people could be like him, the world would be a better place. Rest easy in the hands of our Lord, your work here is done even though I so wish it wasn't.”

Lee fled after the shooting, and law enforcement asked for the public’s help in locating the suspect. Law enforcement released photos of the suspect and noted he was driving a white GMC pickup. Lee left the area, and law enforcement said he was believed to be armed and dangerous and he may have dyed his hair black and shaved his beard.

The Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety said the agency was informed on Sunday that Lee was possibly headed toward the reservation. After a search and coordinated law enforcement response, Lee was found on the southwest portion of the reservation after local residents tipped off OSTDPS. During the encounter, Lee shot at officers, hitting and injuring one, according to the law enforcement agency. During the encounter, law enforcement shot and killed Lee.

Oglala Sioux Tribe Acting Police Chief Iver Crow Eagle III said in a video shared to the OSTDPS Facebook page the officer Lee shot suffered non-life-threatening injuries.

“I’m happy to report this officer is good, in good spirits, good health,” Crow said.

Crow Eagle said an investigation into the officer-involved shooting continues, with the FBI and Bureau of Indian Affairs Division of Internal Affairs part of the investigation on the reservation.

Crow Eagle said numerous people called in to report spotting Lee on or near the reservation. The acting police chief said the agency works “hand-in-hand” with law enforcement throughout the area and beyond.

“To come on to Oglala … and think you’re going to hide out here is not the answer,” he said.

“We are fortunate to have such strong partnerships among our local, tribal, state and federal public safety agencies,” said Pennington County Sheriff Brian Mueller. “We are grateful for the cooperation and professionalism demonstrated by all those involved in these tragic circumstances.”

title: Black Hills Energy reminds customers of tree trimming safety and smart planting into the spring season
description: As vegetation begins to grow across South Dakota this spring, Black Hills Energy is reminding customers of the importance of smart planting and safe tree trimming practices that can help prevent system damages and power outages, improve safety and help reduce wildfire risk.
_full_text:
As vegetation begins to grow across South Dakota this spring, Black Hills Energy is reminding customers of the importance of smart planting and safe tree trimming practices that can help prevent system damages and power outages, improve safety and help reduce wildfire risk.

Trees that grow too close to power lines can cause service interruptions and safety hazards for homes and neighborhoods. Thoughtful planting and proper tree maintenance can help protect customers’ electric service and keep communities safe.

“Vegetation management plays a critical role in keeping our electric system and communities safe. When trees grow too close, they can cause power outages, safety hazards, and increase wildfire risk,” said Michael Pogany, General Manager of South Dakota Operations at Black Hills Energy. “By trimming trees near power lines and encouraging customers to make thoughtful planting decisions, we can all work together to keep our systems safe and reliable.”

 Vegetation managementy.jpg
As vegetation begins to grow across South Dakota this spring, Black Hills Energy is reminding customers of the importance of smart planting and safe tree trimming practices that can help prevent system damages and power outages, improve safety and help reduce wildfire risk. 

As part of this work, customers may see Black Hills Energy crews and contractors working in their neighborhoods trimming trees, removing vegetation, or conducting inspections near overhead power lines and poles.

A shared responsibility for safety

While Black Hills Energy is responsible for maintaining safe clearances around overhead distribution lines, customers play an important role on their own property, both above and below ground.

As customers plan projects and tree planting this spring, Black Hills Energy encourages the following smart planting and safety practices:

Never plant a tree that could grow within 25 feet of an overhead power line. If you're not sure how far away a tree should be planted from a power line, contact your electric utility company.

Regularly trim trees and remove dead or dry vegetation. Routine maintenance helps support safety, protects nearby utility systems, and reduces wildfire risk.

Never trim trees near power lines yourself. Hire a qualified line clearance certified arborist to trim trees near power lines.

Customers are responsible for maintaining vegetation around the service lines on their property.

Before starting any digging or landscaping project, customers should always call 811 to have underground utilities marked.

To learn more about tree safety and trimming, visit www.blackhillsenergy.com/safety/electric-safety/tree-safety-and-trimming

title: How a hospital is helping solve a hometown housing shortage in Hot Springs
byline: BART PFANKUCH South Dakota News Watch
description: HOT SPRINGS – In what could be a first-of-its-kind project in South Dakota, the small hospital in this southern Black Hills town is investing in a subdivision project to provide housing for its employees.
_full_text:
HOT SPRINGS – In what could be a first-of-its-kind project in South Dakota, the small hospital in this southern Black Hills town is investing in a subdivision project to provide housing for its employees.

Fall River Health Services, an independent nonprofit medical center in Hot Springs, is paying $2.3 million of the overall $3.4 million cost of infrastructure for a subdivision that could create 48 new affordable housing units a few hundred yards from the hospital campus..

 2026-5-27 Fall River Health Services sign_building.jpeg
The Fall River Health Services of Hot Springs, shown on May 27, 2026, is investing in a housing project in hopes of attracting new employees. 

Like many South Dakota employers, Fall River Health is enduring a long-range worker shortage that has put pressure on its existing staff and driven up costs due to hiring of expensive traveling, short-term medical employees.

As of May 29, the hospital had 19 job openings, most of them in direct patient care, a shortage of 10% of its needed workforce of 190. The hospital in recent years has lost about 70 prospective workers because they couldn't find affordable or suitable local housing, said Jesse Naze, chief financial officer at Fall River Health.

"You can't stop providing care, so we need workforce to care for our local population," Naze said. "It's not wages or benefits keeping employees away, it’s simply that housing just isn’t available."

Naze said he isn't aware of any South Dakota project in which an employer invested so much money on permanent housing that will benefit the business as well as the community at large for years to come.

 2026-5-27 Hot Springs city administrator portrait.jpeg
Hot Springs, S.D. City Administrator Aerial Allison outside City Hall on May 27, 2026. 

The private hospital with 25 beds saved money for years to be able to invest in the proposed housing project in which some homeowners could see a financial benefit if they take jobs at the hospital and stay for at least five years.

"The hospital is fronting the cash to get this infrastructure put in so we can get this project going," Naze said. "There's only so much local workforce, so we need to attract employees, and this should be a big help."

 South Dakota News Watch logo
Learn more about South Dakota News Watch at sdnewswatch.org. 

The South Dakota Housing Authority (South Dakota Housing) has high hopes for the Hot Springs project and in October approved a nearly $1.2 million grant to support the project. The money came from the $200 million Housing Infrastructure Financing Program approved by the Legislature in 2023.

Chas Olson, executive director of South Dakota Housing, said the authority had been in discussion with officials from Hot Springs and Fall River Health for several years to generate a plan for an affordable housing project.

“We knew they were having issues recruiting and keeping workers there because the (existing) housing is old and aging,” Olson said.

 2026-5-27 Hot Springs mural.jpeg
In what could be a first-of-its-kind project in South Dakota, the small hospital in this southern Black Hills town is investing in a subdivision project to provide housing for its employees. 

The current plan for the subdivision, located on the city’s south side east of Highway 71, is to build a mix of single-family and multi-family buildings that will create 48 total housing units with a wide range of square footages and prices, said Dennis Fischer, a former Hot Springs schools superintendent who now serves on the local hospital and housing boards.

Single-family homes of about 1,300 square feet should cost about $350,000, including the lot. Smaller villas, duplexes and townhomes could come in as low as $285,000, including lot costs, he said.

Project managers are working out details of a special mortgage for hospital employees who buy a home in which lot costs of up to $54,000 could be returned if they remain employed for five years, Fischer said.

 2026-5-27 Hot Springs house for sale.jpeg
This home on South Chicago Street in Hot Springs, S.D, shown on May 27, 2026, was one of the few homes on the market at that time. 

So far, the city of Hot Springs and its residents have been big supporters of the Cascade Hills project, said Aerial Allison, city administrator.

With no significant resident opposition and a unanimous city council vote, the city approved a $2.3 million tax increment financing (TIF) district to expedite development, she said.

Quality housing has been increasingly hard to come by as the city's reputation as a pleasant retirement community has grown. Adding to the demand is a large number of out-of-state people who moved to Hot Springs and bought homes during and since the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Not to blame them for anything, but we're really excited this project is focused on workforce housing," Allison said. "We're trying to get people of working age to come here and bring their family and put their kids in our schools and shop at our local stores."

South Dakota News Watch is an independent nonprofit. Read, donate and subscribe for free at sdnewswatch.org. Contact content director Bart Pfankuch: 605-937-9398/bart.pfankuch@sdnewswatch.org.

 2026-5-27 Hot Springs board member at site.jpeg
Dennis Fischer, a member of the housing and hospital boards in Hot Springs, S.D., stood on May 27, 2026, across Highway 71 from a proposed affordable housing development. 

 2026-5-27 Hot Springs mobile homes.jpeg
The city of Hot Springs, S.D., is working to fix up or remove properties in need of repair in order to bolster its housing stock, such as these aging mobile homes on Houston Avenue shown on May 27.

title: Turning emissions into opportunity: Mines startup advances carbon capture technology
description: For decades, scientists, engineers and industry leaders have pursued the same elusive goal, finding a carbon capture solution that is both environmentally sustainable and economically viable.
_full_text:
For decades, scientists, engineers and industry leaders have pursued the same elusive goal, finding a carbon capture solution that is both environmentally sustainable and economically viable.

From sprawling pipelines and deep underground storage wells to slow-acting enzymes, promising approaches have emerged, but none have achieved the right balance.

 1 Govil, Symes and team.jpg
Tanvi Govil, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Karen M. Swindler Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, and her research team with Merle Symes, Mines Entrepreneur in Residence and CEO of Carbon EnZero. 

Now, a multidisciplinary team at South Dakota Mines, led by Tanvi Govil, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Karen M. Swindler Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, may have found a breakthrough in an unexpected place. Deep beneath the Black Hills, microbes thriving in the extreme environment of the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) have inspired a technology that could help industries reduce carbon emissions without sacrificing the energy resources the world still depends on, a true win-win for both the economy and the environment.

“Dr. Govil and her team have developed technology that can convert fossil fuels into green energy – this is pretty eye-opening,” said Merle Symes, Mines Entrepreneur-in-Residence and CEO of Carbon EnZero, a company started by Govil to commercialize the technology. “We see this as the first win-win solution that should satisfy both sides of the aisle. It satisfies people who think fossil fuels are the way we should be going, and it satisfies the people who are concerned about climate change. I’ve been involved in a number of startups, but I’ve never been involved in one where all the moons are aligning like this one. Every factor is working toward this is the solution.”

The research team uses microbes, or tiny bugs, collected in SURF and other areas around the country to specially engineer high-performance enzymes capable of operating in harsh industrial environments, including high heat, pressure, acidity and exposure to toxic metals. Using these advanced enzymes as powerful biocatalysts, the process permanently captures carbon dioxide (CO2) from industrial flue gases and converts it into minerals. “These enzymes take 100 percent of the CO2 out of the flue gases,” Symes said. “Industrial flue gases make up 50 percent of carbon emissions, and 90 percent of those come from fossil fuel power plants.”

 2 Govil and her team underground.jpg
Tanvi Govil, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Karen M. Swindler Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, and her research team with Merle Symes, Mines Entrepreneur in Residence and CEO of Carbon EnZero. 

While using enzymes for the chemical reaction is not new technology, the specialized enzymes developed by Govil and her team greatly accelerate the process, reducing it from years to a few minutes. In addition, technology enables the removal of greenhouse gas emissions directly at the source.

Unlike many existing carbon-capture systems that require pipelines and underground storage wells, the enzyme process is designed to operate directly at industrial sites, significantly reducing infrastructure and transportation costs associated with traditional carbon sequestration.

“What we learned from these organisms helped us engineer enzymes that can efficiently remove CO2 directly from the industrial emissions,” Govil said.

 3 Group underground at SURF.jpg
Tanvi Govil, Ph.D., and team members sampling for microbes on the 1700 Level of the ground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility. 

In addition, the research addresses another major industrial waste stream – coal ash. Coal ash, a byproduct of coal-fired power plants, contains calcium that reacts with captured CO2 in the enzyme process to form calcium carbonate.

According to Symes, the resulting mineral can be used as a concrete-strengthening additive to extend the lifespan of bridges and other infrastructure.

While the original research focused on microbes themselves, the commercialization strategy shifted toward isolating and optimizing the enzymes those organisms produce.

“The workhorse behind all of this is the enzymes,” Symes said.

And those enzymes are what Carbon EnZero will be selling.

Earlier this spring, Govil won first place and $20,000 at the South Dakota Governor’s Giant Vision Business Plan Competition, providing momentum for pilot-scale development and commercialization efforts.

She also recently received a South Dakota Board of Regents (SDBOR) Competitive Research Grant to further her work with extremophiles, the tiny organisms that inspired the ground-breaking technology. This is the second SDBOR grant Govil has been awarded for this work.

 4 chemical reaction.jpg
Using these advanced enzymes as powerful biocatalysts, the process permanently captures carbon dioxide (CO2) from industrial flue gases and converts it into minerals. 

“We envision 2026 as being our beta launch year,” Symes said. “We utilized the Giant Vision money to really go out and start raising bigger money as well as continue the design and development work.”

Carbon EnZero’s business model centers on supplying the enzymes while partnering with established engineering firms, already working with power plants, that would design and install industrial-scale systems.

“We like to say we will sell the razor blade while engineering firms sell the razor,” Symes said.

The research team has already worked with regional industrial partners to obtain flue-gas samples and coal ash for laboratory validation. Black Hills Energy has provided industry insight during early development efforts.

The next step is construction of a mobile pilot-scale carbon scrubber that will allow them to test the system directly at industrial facilities.

Govil and Symes credit the university’s entrepreneurial culture, multidisciplinary department collaboration and support network for helping translate laboratory research into a commercial venture.

“We have a university president and administration that is really moving Mines toward being more entrepreneurial,” Symes said. “It has created an environment to allow this to happen. This is building a tremendous biological research capability at South Dakota Mines.”

Govil and Symes believe Carbon EnZero could eventually reach far beyond the United States, where thousands of fossil-fuel power plants continue operating worldwide.

“This has the potential of completely turning around the coal industry and making it the most desirable fuel in the country and the world again,” Symes said.

title: SD Vietnam veterans honored with national ceremony, traveling exhibit
description: After serving two tours of duty in the Vietnam War, SPC. Timothy M. Bjork spent much of his life battling health problems linked to the herbicide Agent Orange.
_full_text:
After serving two tours of duty in the Vietnam War, SPC. Timothy M. Bjork spent much of his life battling health problems linked to the herbicide Agent Orange.

Bjork, of Rapid City, died in March 2025. On June 20, he and South Dakota veterans Gregory J. Overholt of Piedmont, who died in 2025, and Theodore G. Knudsen of Rosholt, who died in 2024, will be inducted into the national In Memory Program. A traveling exhibit coming to South Dakota this week also is honoring Vietnam veterans.

In 2026, 768 Vietnam veterans, including Bjork, Overholt and Knudsen, will be inducted into the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund’s In Memory Program. On June 20, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund will host the In Memory ceremony on the East Knoll of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C., where each 2026 honoree’s name will be read aloud.

The In Memory Program honors veterans who weren’t killed in the line of duty but died later as a result of their service. VVMF believes all those who served in the Vietnam War should be honored and remembered for their service. The In Memory Program enables the families and friends of veterans who returned home but later died from their service the opportunity to have the veterans be forever memorialized, according to vvmf.org.

The 2026 In Memory ceremony will be streamed live on VVMF’s Facebook page, facebook.com/VietnamVeteransMemorialFund, on VVMF’s website, vvmf.org/live, at 8 a.m. MT on Saturday, June 20. The recorded video of the In Memory ceremony will be available to view shortly after the conclusion of the ceremony.

In Memory Program honorees’ names will be listed on a plaque on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial site. The plaque reads, “In Memory of the men and women who served in the Vietnam War and later died as a result of their service. We honor and remember their sacrifice.” The plaque that honors these veterans was dedicated as a part of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial site in 2004.

VVMF created a personal remembrance page for each honoree in the In Memory Honor Roll at vvmf.org/honor-roll. Since the In Memory Program was created in 1993, it has honored more than 8,300 veterans.

Bjork, an Army veteran, was drafted in 1968. He served his first tour of duty in 1969 and 1970, and served his second tour of duty in 1970 and 1971. Among his many duties in Vietnam, Bjork was involved in Operation Ranch Hand, which brought him into contact with powerful herbicides and defoliants such as Agent Orange.

Nine years later, at age 33, he suffered a heart attack. He eventually required an artificial heart and finally, a heart transplant, said his widow, Bonnie Bjork of Rapid City.  

“In the last four years of his life, he developed cancer and that metastasized in his lungs. It’s all related to Agent Orange,” Bonnie said.

Bonnie wants other veterans’ families to know the In Memory Program exists to honor veterans’ lives and service and give them the recognition they deserve. For more information about the In In Memory Program or to apply to have a veteran honored in 2027, go to vvmf.org/inmemory.

“There’s a lot of Vietnam veterans that have died as a result of their service” from causes such as PTSD-related suicide, and diseases linked to Agent Orange such as cancer, diabetes, and Parkinson’s disease, she said.

According to publichealth.va.gov/exposures/agentorange/conditions/index.asp, more than a dozen illnesses and cancers, and birth defects in veterans’ children, are linked to Agent Orange exposure.

The Wall That Heals

Vietnam veterans also are being honored with a digital exhibit called The Wall That Heals, which is traveling to South Dakota this week. It will be on display in Brookings at the Fishback Soccer Complex 24 hours a day starting June 11 and ending at 2 p.m. June 14. The exhibit is free to the public.

Bonnie Bjork said she will travel to Brookings to see The Wall That Heals. It features the names of 36 South Dakota veterans, according to information on the cityofbrookings-sd.gov/908/The-Wall-That-Heals-2026 website.

“The Wall That Heals” is a three-quarter scale replica of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, along with its Mobile Education Center. It will be The Wall's only visit to South Dakota in 2026. Like the In Memory Program, The Wall That Heals is operated by VVMF. It’s the only traveling exhibit connected to the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C.

The VVMF is the nonprofit organization that founded the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C. in 1982.

“For many Vietnam veterans, coming home from Vietnam was just the beginning of a whole new fight. Many never fully recovered, either physically or emotionally, from their experiences. As these veterans pass, it is our duty and solemn promise to welcome them home to the place that our nation has set aside to remember our Vietnam veterans,” said Jim Knotts, president and CEO of VVMF.

title: Scott Alex Cherry
description: November 17, 1951 - June 3, 2026
_full_text:
November 17, 1951 - June 3, 2026

Scott Alex Cherry, 74, of Millersville, PA, passed away on Wednesday, June 3, 2026. Scott was born in Flint, MI to the late Alex and Pauline (Hoffner) Cherry, and was the husband of Nancy (West) Cherry with whom he celebrated 47 years of marriage. He graduated from Kearsley High School in Flint, MI in 1969 before serving in the United States Army. He began his career as a Special Education Teacher in Durand, MI before completing his doctorate in Neuropsychology at Alliant University (formerly CSPP) in Fresno, CA. He retired as a Neuropsychologist in the Rehabilitation Department at Monument Health in Rapid City, SD after 29 years, where he specialized in FAA evaluations for pilots, brain trauma evaluations, pediatrics, and sleep disorders, among other things. He was also an Adjunct Professor for the Graduate Counseling Program for the SDSU extension in Rapid City for four years. Along with his professional accomplishments, Scott studied and taught martial arts. He also enjoyed golfing, fishing, tennis, pickleball, and traveling. Besides his wife, Scott is survived by his son Nathanial and his wife Cara (Walker) Cherry of Lancaster, PA; two siblings: Cheryl (Cherry) Look and her husband Martin Look and Kent Cherry and his wife Mary (Rubscha) Cherry, both of Davison, MI; sisters- and brothers-in-law: Lydia (West) and Chris Spafford of Beulah, MI, Bill and Pat (Bryant) West of North Fort Myers, FL, Della (West) and Tom Teeples of Stanfield, NC, Sarah (West) and Joe Diem of Montrose, MI, and Laura (West) and Eric Hall of Flushing, MI, as well as many cousins, nieces, nephews, and friends. In addition to his parents, Scott was preceded in death by his father-in-law and mother-in-law Howard and Verna (Wade) West and brother-in-law David West. Funeral services will take place at 12:30 PM on Tuesday, June 9, 2026, at Sharp Funeral Homes- Fenton Chapel, 1000 Silver Lake Rd, Fenton, MI. Visitation will be held from 10 AM until the time of service at the funeral home on Tuesday. Interment to follow at 2:30 PM at Great Lakes National Cemetery in Holly, MI. In lieu of flowers, please make a donation to the American Cancer Society or the Wolf Sanctuary of PA. Tributes may be shared at sharpfuneralhomes.com

title: Judy Wagenaar
_full_text:
July 18, 1944 - June 4, 2026

Judy Wagenaar, 81, of Rapid City died at Monument Health Home Plus Hospice on June 4th, 2026.

She was born July 18, 1944, in Rapid City, SD, the daughter of Elmer and Fran (Joyce) Riggert, joining an older brother, Billy. Her early childhood years were in the Viewfield, SD area where she attended Lost Nation School for three years.

The family moved to New Underwood, SD in 1954 where she continued her education and graduated from NUHS in 1962. After graduation, Judy worked at First Western Bank in New Underwood. She met David Wagenaar of Bruce, SD while he was working on construction of Interstate 90 near New Underwood. They were married on December 28, 1963, at St. John's Church, and then moved to Rapid City where their daughter, Vicky was born on October 4, 1964. Judy was employed by H&R Block for 40 years, retiring in April 2018.

A loving grandmother, Judy's two grandsons, Tad and Jared held a special place in her life. She enjoyed attending their school and sporting events and took them on extended vacations including a cruise to Alaska. A lifetime goal of visiting all 50 states was attained when she and David went on a cruise to Hawaii to celebrate their 50th wedding anniversary. Decorating her home and yard for every holiday brought her great joy as did the trips to Deadwood for a little gambling.

Judy is survived by her daughter, Vicky Litzinger (Ron Haney) of Douglas, WY; two grandsons, Tad (Jordan) Litzinger of Buffalo, WY and Jared (Shawna) Litzinger of Douglas, WY: four great-grandchildren, twins Brantley and Sawyer, Joe, and Truist Litzinger all of Buffalo, WY; three nieces, Robin Robertson, Patsy Besson, Carolynn Anderson; and several cousins.

Preceding her in death are her husband, David in 2016; brother, Billy in 2022; and her parents.

Visitation will be held from 5:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. Wednesday, June 10th at Kirk Funeral Home. Funeral Services will be held 1:00 p.m. Thursday, June 11th at the funeral home. Interment will be held at Mountain View Cemetery.

In lieu of flowers, memorials can be given in Judy's name to Monument Health Home Plus Hospice, 224 Elk Street, Rapid City, SD 57701.
