title: Rapid City man arrested in 2024 Sturgis Rally sex sting sentenced to federal prison
description: A Rapid City man arrested in the annual multi-agency sex sting held during the 2024 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally was sentenced to federal prison.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man arrested in the annual multi-agency sex sting held during the 2024 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally was sentenced to federal prison.

A federal grand jury charged Brockton Dominquez, 28, in August 2024, with attempted enticement of a minor. In February 2026, a superseding indictment charged him with attempted enticement of a minor, receipt of child pornography and possession of child pornography. He pleaded guilty to attempted enticement of a minor using the internet and receipt of child pornography on Feb. 17.

According to a United States Attorney’s Office press release, Dominquez used his Facebook account to begin an online conversation with someone he thought was a 14-year-old girl, who was actually an undercover police officer. On Aug. 2, 2024, Dominquez made arrangements with the girl to meet at West Middle School in Rapid City.

On June 1, U.S. District Judge Camela Theeler sentenced Dominquez to 20 years in federal prison, 10 years for the enticement of a minor charge and 10 years for the receipt of child sexual abuse material, followed by 10 years supervised release. Each sentence was ordered to run concurrently with the other.

The six other men, aside from Dominquez, who were arrested and charged in the 2024 sting cases are:

Eli Poorman, 20, Rapid City – Pleaded guilty to attempted receipt of child pornography and attempted transfer of obscene material to a minor. Poorman was sentenced May 19, to five years followed by five years of supervised release

Vance Coats, 25, Box Elder – Pleaded guilty to attempted receipt of child pornography. Coats was sentenced in January 2025 to five years in prison followed by five years of supervised release.

Corey Simon, 36, Rapid City – Pleaded guilty to attempted transfer of obscene material to a minor. Simon was sentenced in February 2025 to 10 years in prison followed by five years of supervised release.

Aaron Ray Williams, Jr., 23, Rapid City – Pleaded guilty to attempted enticement of a minor using the internet and receipt of child pornography. In September 2025, Williams was sentenced to 19 years and seven months in prison.

Brandon Bishop, 38, Rapid City — Was convicted by a federal jury in September 2025 for attempted enticement of a minor. Bishop was sentenced Jan. 12, to 10 years in prison followed by five years supervised release.

Dustin Day, 20, Piedmont — Pleaded guilty in October 2025 for attempted use of interstate facilities to transmit information about a minor. Day was sentenced Jan. 12, to two weeks in prison followed by five years of supervised release.

title: Rapid City father pleads not guilty to alleged murder of his infant son
description: RAPID CITY — A Rapid City father pleaded not guilty to a second-degree murder charge, in addition to a charge related to the improper disposal of a body, in connection with the death of his son.
_full_text:
RAPID CITY — A Rapid City father pleaded not guilty to a second-degree murder charge, in addition to a charge related to the improper disposal of a body, in connection with the death of his son.

Tyler Slow Bear, 33, appeared for his arraignment before Circuit Court Judge Matthew Brown at the Pennington County Courthouse on Thursday, June 18. Slow Bear was arrested on May 8.

 Tyler Slow Bear
Tyler Slow Bear 

The Rapid City Police Department was originally called to Slow Bear's residence at around 9:05 on Thursday, May 7, for a welfare check after someone called with concern for baby Melinko Bagola's safety.

 Melinko Bagola
Melinko Bagola 

Bagola was left in Slow Bear's care. When the reporting party attempted to make contact with the baby, he was nowhere to be found. Bagola was last seen on April 19.

Police made contact with Slow Bear and could not find the infant at the residence. Slow Bear told police a family member was watching the 9-week-old baby, but it was later discovered the family member lived on a different side of the state and did not have the baby.

Slow Bear was brought in for further questioning about the infant's disappearance. During the interview, it was determined that Slow Bear assaulted Bagola and the infant died at some point following the assault.

Following the infant's death, Slow Bear concealed Bagola's body at an undeveloped outdoor location in Rapid City. Police searched the location overnight and found the infant's remains.

In South Dakota, second-degree murder is a Class B felony with a mandatory minimum of life in prison and a possibility of a $50,000 fine. A permit required for the disposition of a dead body or fetus is a Class 1 misdemeanor with a maximum sentence of one year in jail and a $2,000 fine.

Slow Bear has a prior 2019 conviction for possession of a controlled substance. He was sentenced to five years in prison, according to South Dakota court records. He was released on parole and violated it in 2021. He was found guilty of the violation and given a suspended sentence. Slow Bear has several other convictions from 2022 to 2025 for domestic simple assault, resisting arrest and obstructing police, a jailer or firefighter, court records show.

Slow Bear’s next court appearance is set for 1:15 p.m. on July 30. He remains held on a $10 million cash-only bond at the Pennington County Jail.

title: Nigerian man sentenced in federal court for fraud and misuse of identification document
description: A Nigerian man was sentenced to time served for fraud.
_full_text:
A Nigerian man was sentenced to time served for fraud.

U.S. District Judge Camela C. Theeler sentenced Atuchukwu Markrufus Onyeanusi, 32, after his conviction on a fraud and misuse of visas, permits and other documents charge, according to an announcement from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for South Dakota. The sentencing took place on May 20, at the federal courthouse in Rapid City.

Onyeanusi was sentenced to time served — just under six months of custody — followed by one year of supervised release, and was ordered to pay a $1,000 fine and a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

Onyeanusi was indicted for fraud and misuse of visas, permits and other documents; false, fictitious, fraudulent document or writing and aggravated identity theft by a federal grand jury in December 2025. He pleaded guilty on Feb. 27, 2026.

Onyeanusi is an alien with lawful permanent status to be in the United States, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said. On Nov. 10, 2025, law enforcement in Oklahoma conducted a traffic stop on a vehicle Onyeanusi was driving for speeding. Onyeanusi possessed a Texas commercial driving license with his image but another person’s name.

Onyeanusi also possessed an employer’s identification for Great Plains Tribal Leaders’ Health Board located in Rapid City, with the same false name. This ID described Onyeanusi’s position as a “Cyber Threat Analyst.” Onyeanusi used the false Texas CDL, along with a false Social Security card with the same false name, to gain employment at Great Plains Tribal Leaders’ Health Board. Onyeanusi also falsely asserted on an employment immigration form that he was a United States citizen.

This case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations and the Craig County Sheriff’s Office in Vinita, Oklahoma. Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Schroeder prosecuted the case.

title: Lakota historian speaks about personal family involvement with the Battle of Little Bighorn ahead of 150th anniversary
description: Ahead of the 150th anniversary for the Battle of Little Bighorn (also referred to as the Battle of Greasy Grass), Racing Magpie hosted a Lakota historian to speak to community members about share Indigenous historical accounts from the time of the battle.
_full_text:
Ahead of the 150th anniversary for the Battle of Little Bighorn (also referred to as the Battle of Greasy Grass), Racing Magpie hosted a Lakota historian to speak to community members about share Indigenous historical accounts from the time of the battle. 

 Donovin Sprague
Donovin Sprague joined Racing Magpie on Monday, June 15 to tell Indigenous stories from the Battle of Little Bighorn. 

"At the very end of the battle on the Last Stand Hill, some of the women there, including Mary Crawler (also known as Moving Rogue Woman) and Kate Bighead said she seen the soldiers all laying there, and the men of our nation were circling the Last Stand Hill," Donovan Sprague told an audience on Monday, June 15, in Rapid City. "She had seen (Chief) Gall, Rain in the Face, (Chief) Hump and Crazy Horse and a group of Hunkpapa (Lakota) had the 7th cavalry flag."

Sprague, from Dupree on the Cheyenne River Sioux Reservation, belongs to both the Hump and Crazy Horse family.

 Donovin Sprague
Donovin Sprague, an instructor, author and historian spoke at Racing Magpie in Rapid City about the Battle of Little Bighorn on Monday, June 15. 

He has a bachelor's degree in social science and American Indian studies from Black Hills State University. He also has a master’s degree in political science from the University of South Dakota and has taught at numerous institutions, including Oglala Lakota College, the University of Iowa and Sheridan College in Wyoming.

Sprague said he spoke at the 125th anniversary of the battle, which was held at the battle site in Montana in 2001.

This year is the sesquicentennial anniversary of the battle in which notable U.S. military leader Lt. Col George Armstrong Custer was killed. The battle was a major conflict of the American Indian Wars.

 Hump
Sprague holds a family photo of his relatives involved in the Battle of the Little Bighorn. 

Sprague gave context about the lead-up to the infamous June 25-26, 1876, battle.

Before the battle 

On Nov. 27, 1868, Custer, along with the 7th Cavalry unit, attacked Southern Cheyenne Chief Black Kettle’s village on the Washita River in Oklahoma. This marked a notable victory in the Indian Wars for the U.S. government and established Custer’s reputation as a leader in conflicts against Indigenous people.

 Racing Magpie
More than 20 community members packed into Racing Magpie for a presentation made by Lakota historian Donovin Sprague. 

Earlier the same year, the U.S. and tribal leaders entered into the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, recognizing the Sioux Nation's right to the Black Hills. Shortly after the signing, the government seized the land when gold was discovered in the region. This prompted the U.S. to confine nearby tribal nations on reservations and in response some tribes banded together to fight a common enemy.

On June 17, 1876, the Battle of the Rosebud (also known as Where the Girl Saved Her Brother) took place, pitting the Lakota and Northern Cheyenne against U.S. soldiers allied with the Crow and Shoshone in Big Horn County, Montana.

Sprague said the Cheyenne described the story, saying, "A man looked like he was going to face certain death on the battlefield, and over the hill came this woman in her finest regalia, and the soldiers were firing, and she rode down through the middle and rescued him."

He said that woman's name was Buffalo Calf Road Woman. 

This tactical defeat would lead to a withdrawal of over 1,300 men led by Brig. Gen. George Crook as they made their way to Wyoming, which set up Custer with less men at the Battle of Little Bighorn.

"They went back, they were supposed to meet Custer and all of them in a three-prong attack at the Battle of the Little Bighorn eight days later. So that didn't happen because Crook went back, and so they say, maybe they would have won if Crook would have came up there with 1,300 more people," Sprague said.

The battle 

On June 25, 1876, tribal groups of the Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho were settled near the Little Bighorn River in Montana, making up an estimated 1,200 soldiers. Custer had less then 500 men with him.

 Battle of Little Bighorn
Historian Donovan Sprague showed a painting by Edgar Samuel Paxson titled “Custer’s Last Stand” during a presentation on the Battle of the Greasy Grass on Monday, June 15, in Rapid City. 

Custer’s Crow and Arikara scouts advised incorrectly on how many people were in the area.

Based on this information, Custer sought to attack the encampment with Col. Marcus Albert Reno attacking from the south. After Reno approached the area, he realizing they were outnumbered and laid down a defensive line 4 miles away from the camp.

Custer, at the same time, went around the area to attack from the north.  

After the conflict had begun, soldiers, including Lakota leader Crazy Horse, turned their attention north, intercepting Custer's approach.

Sprague said Reno was said to have abandoned Custer for not aiding when gunfire in the area was heard. Reno and his men retreated.

The exact number of casualties is unknown.

Aftermath and present day

This battle was a historic victory for the tribal nations as they killed Custer. Per the National Parks Service, however, the battle was “a momentary victory for the Lakota and Cheyenne." The death of Custer and his troops became a rallying point for the United States to increase their efforts to force Native people onto reservation lands. With more troops in the field, Lakota hunting grounds were invaded by Army expeditionary forces determined to conquer the Northern Plains Indians. Most of the declared "hostiles" surrendered within one year of the fight, and the Black Hills were taken by the US government without compensation to the Lakota.

In 1980, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the Sioux were entitled to $102 million (roughly over $1 billion in today’s dollars) for the wrongful seizure, but the nations have yet to accept compensation as they seek land ownership back.

Sprague, 150 years after the historic battle, brought a bow with him to Rapid City.

"I met the descendants of the Custer family ... they brought this in, it's a bow from out here, and they didn't know whose it was, but it's Lakota. They said this belongs with you out there. They said maybe you could share it with some people," Sprague said on the Custer family’s relations with Indigenous people.

 Lakota Bow
Sprague holds an old Lakota-style bow that was given to him by a descendant of George Armstrong Custer. 

He also said the only surviving horse of the conflict, named Comanche, ridden by Cap. Myles Keogh, was shot multiple times and was nursed back to health at Fort Abraham Lincoln in North Dakota. 

"There was a proclamation where this horse would never be ridden again, and it was wined and dined and had caviar, and it finally lived to 29 years old, and it's stuffed down at the University of Kansas. They said there was a tradition at the school museum that when your test is coming up and you go by Comanche, you take a little pinch of his hair as good luck for that test," Sprague said.

A week of activities commemorating the battle is planned at the Battle of Little Bighorn site in Montana next week.

"Our victory day is on the 25th, but a lot of people are celebrating this whole month and I think it's because you can't do everything in one day," Sprague said about celebratory events based on the Battle of Little Bighorn.

title: Sandra “Sandi” Kurry
description: October 1, 1949 - June 16, 2026

October 1, 1949 - June 16, 2026

Sandra Corine "Sandi" Kurry passed away at Monument Health Home Plus Hospice House on Tuesday, June 16, 2026, at the age of 76.

Sandra Corine Gustafson was born on October 1st, 1949, to Oscar Alfred and Stella Viola Gustafson. Sandra was the youngest of her two sisters, Noreen and Karen. They all lived on a farm south of Arnegard. They had a wonderful mom and dad and life together. When Sandra graduated high school, she moved to Minot, North Dakota, and worked at Midwest Federal for 10 years. There she met William Kurry and had their first daughter, Traci. William and Sandra then moved to Williston, North Dakota, and opened a mobile home business. A year and a half later their second daughter came, Jodi. William then died on February 8, 1980, due to an accident.

Sandra, Traci, and Jodi then moved to Hill City, South Dakota, in 1988. Sandra worked in Hill City, South Dakota, for several years. Then in the summer of 1996, Sandra moved to Oregon since both her daughters Traci and Jodi graduated from High School. Sandra lived and worked in Oregon until 2010, when she retired.

She then moved back to Rapid City, South Dakota, to enjoy her retirement and be close to family. During her retirement she was active in the local VFW and her church, Calvary Lutheran. Sandra also loved to read, travel, and spend time with family and friends.

Sandra is survived by her daughter, Traci (Casey) Eaton of Hermosa, SD; sister, Noreen (Chuck) VanNurden of Longview, WA; sister, Karen (Sherm) Heggen of Billings, MT; sister-in-law, Sharon (Fred) Randall of Georgetown, ME; sister-in-law, Debbi (Garritt) Toohey of Rye Beach, NH; grandsons, Benjamin and Bram; along with many nieces, nephews and cousins.

She is preceded in death by her husband, William Kurry; daughter, Jodi Kurry; parents, Oscar and Stella Gustafson; in-laws, William and Althea Kurry; and brother-in-law, Bob Kurry.

Celebration of Life Memorial Service will be Thursday, June 25, 2026, at 10 a.m. at Calvary Lutheran Church in Rapid City.

Burial will be at a future date at the Riverview Cemetery in Williston, North Dakota.

title: Richard Rudolph Goschke
_full_text:
June 11, 1931 - June 4, 2026

Lt. Col. Richard R. "Dick" Goschke age 94 (7 days shy of his 95th birthday), passed away peacefully in Camas, Washington on June 4, 2026, at his home with his family. He was born on June 11, 1931, in

Malta, Montana. At the beginning of WWII, his family relocated to Bremerton, WA where many family members joined the various branches of the military and some made their living working in the naval shipyards. Throughout high school, Dick worked in the Wardin family's stationery business. After years of superior work as an employee with exceptional integrity and performance, owners Stanley and Genevieve Wardin offered Dick a full ride to any university of his choice (Dick would often get a tear in his eye recounting this life changing gesture). When Dick graduated with a 4-year business degree from the University of Puget Sound, the Wardin family offered Dick to take over their flourishing family business. Instead, in 1954 he entered the USAF to complete a full 20-year career, retiring as a lieutenant colonel (Lt. Col.). Many would retire and relax. This turned out to be a springboard for his second career in business, politics and investing, including developing coffee farms in Hawaii with his son, and owning a few local businesses—CheckRite, the Fun Center, rentals and real estate.

From serving this country, to serving the Rapid City community, he offered his skills, time and expertise. He was the president of his children's school PTA, a board member at Canyon Lake United Methodist Church, a city councilperson, and a service club member of the Rapid City Lions and the Rapid City Rotary Club for many years. All of these hats he wore included raising five children along with his adventuresome wife of 51 years.

In closing this reflection on the rich life of Dick Goschke, his youngest daughter, raised by this man of service, offers this tribute:

"A Goodbye Letter to My Father"

Dad,

It is so hard to say good-bye to my number one (#1) fan! Tears are streaming down my face. My tears keep falling. So many years ago, I arrived on your birthday. We would spend so many of our shared birthdays together—especially as you grew older—until your 94th year —7 days shy of your 95th birthday.

When I was a young girl, you taught me how to fish. I always caught so many! One day, reasonably so, you said, "Genni, you are going to need to start cleaning them!" At that declaration, I was out! I would have none of that. Your son, my brother Rick, became your avid fishing and hunting buddy (Alaska, Canada, etc.). Then football came along--which you loved (being captain of your football team). I didn't like football either. However, what I did love, after researching thoroughly, was our infamous bets on the Super Bowl. Wow, did we have fun with that venture—every year. I even won often! What you did teach and role-model for me was honesty, confidence, financial independence and integrity! Through/with that, you knew I would flourish! And to this day, I am forever grateful!

Your words of wisdom and guidance still play a part in my daily living/life. I remember so clearly, "Genni, you must further your education so you can support yourself. " So I did, I completed my doctorate in clinical psychology.

After my stroke, when you and family came to stay with me, you told me, "this is only a chapter in your book/life." With those words resounding in my ears, I got back to work, doing what I love, practicing as a clinical psychologist.

Dad, after moving back from Minneapolis, I have been tending to, living and keeping up the "Rocking' R"—a place you so dearly loved! As promised, I/we will keep doing so and keep the embers burning, just as we so loved watching until the last coal would burn out. Dad, I am forever grateful for your years spent with us, your powerful and wise words, and the guidance you provided!

Love always,

your daughter (and

birthday-buddy)

Genni

PS. To those fathers with daughters, never underestimate the influence/impression that you may/do have on your daughters—like mine had on me.

Dick is survived by his daughters Sherri, Kally, and Genni; his son, Rick and his daughter-in-law Aza, who took impeccable care of him until he drew his last breath; his son-in-laws Norm and Sidi; and his many grandchildren: Zach, Carrie and Jess, especially Richy, Anna, Mae, and Elizabeth, who were at his side surrounding him with love and affection until the very end. He so did not want to leave them—he was deeply satisfied and full of gratitude for all of his living days! As he would so often reply, "On a good day like this you've got to be good!"—exemplifying his poignant, ever-ready positive nature and attitude.

He was preceded in death by his remarkable and accomplished wife Joan Goschke, his beloved daughter Laurie, his grandson Benjamin; his parents, all of his siblings and many extended family members.

In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in Dick's honor to the The Club for Boys Foundation or Storybook Island in Rapid City.

A celebration of life will be held at a future date.

title: SD Supreme Court: Conviction for Family Dollar killing holds up, self-defense claim doesn’t
description: The South Dakota Supreme Court has upheld the first-degree manslaughter conviction of a Rapid City man who shot and killed another man in a parking lot in Rapid City after a heated exchange.
_full_text:
The South Dakota Supreme Court has upheld the first-degree manslaughter conviction of a Rapid City man who shot and killed another man in a parking lot in Rapid City after a heated exchange.

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, including video evidence, Derrek Brave Heart, now 31, shot Jonathan Odom, 43, on Feb. 2, 2024, around 10:30 a.m. in the parking lot of 1445 Haines Ave. in Rapid City. At the time, the building housed a Family Dollar store.

After the incident, Brave Heart was indicted with one count of second-degree murder and three alternative counts of first-degree manslaughter. After a three-day trial in March 2025, the jury found Brave Heart guilty of one count of first-degree manslaughter, and he was sentenced in May 2025 to 30 years in prison. The maximum for the charge is life in prison.

Before Odom went to trial, the court considered Odom’s motion to have the charges against him dismissed based on South Dakota’s self-defense laws. Circuit Court Judge Joshua Hendrickson ruled against Brave Heart and concluded any threat of harm had dissipated before the fatal shot was fired.

The Supreme Court upheld the jury’s conviction and said the issue of the pretrial ruling is moot because of the conviction.

Justice Mark Salter wrote in the court’s opinion, “Though Odom had slapped Brave Heart several times, the video and the consistent testimony of eyewitnesses establishes that Brave Heart was not acting in self-defense when he shot the unarmed Odom who, by that point, had backed several steps away from Brave Heart, raised his arms to his side, and said, ‘Shoot me.’ We therefore affirm Brave Heart’s conviction.”

Chief Justice Steven Jensen and Justices Patricia DeVaney, Scott Myren and Robert Gusinsky, concurred with Salter’s written opinion.

 Derrek Brave Heart
Brave Heart 

The two men did not know each other before their interaction fatally escalated. Odom, per the supreme court’s summary of the case, added windshield wiper fluid to his vehicle in the parking lot that morning while Brave Heart sat in his truck parked next to Odom’s vehicle. After adding the windshield wiper fluid, Odom “appeared agitated” and threw the empty bottle before heading into the store. Brave Heart’s girlfriend, who had gone into the store, left the store around the same time as Odom went in. She got into the truck with Brave Heart.

When Odom left the store, he went to Brave Heart’s window and began yelling at him. Brave Heart testified he rolled down his window because he couldn’t hear what Odom was saying.

According to Brave Heart, Odom complained that Brave Heart had stared at him when he tossed the washer fluid container at the store. The girlfriend testified that she told Brave Heart the two should leave. At trial, Brave Heart disputed her testimony that she suggested leaving.

Bystanders saw Odom hit Brave Heart in the face twice through the open window. Brave Heart then got out of the vehicle. He testified Odom opened the door. His girlfriend testified Brave Heart opened the door himself.

When Brave Heart got out of the vehicle, he brought his concealed handgun with him. His girlfriend began recording on her cell phone. Brave Heart chambered a round, and Odom slapped him again.

The argument between the men continued, with Odom pushing Brave Heart, who raised his handgun and threatened to shoot Odom. Odom then stepped away, raised him outstretched arms and said, “Shoot me then,” before stepping forward and slapping Brave Heart again, stepping forward and saying, “What you going to do, shoot me then?”

Seconds later, Brave Heart shot Odom once in the chest. He died after he was transported to the hospital.

South Dakota Department of Corrections records show Brave Heart is serving his sentence at the South Dakota State Penitentiary in Sioux Falls.

title: Visit Rapid City launches ‘Where to watch’ page for drone, fireworks shows
description: If you’re looking for a good location to view two of the featured events of Rapid City’s upcoming America 250 Birthday Bash celebration — the patriotic drone show and the City’s fireworks show — Visit Rapid City has developed a convenient online page showcasing several options to maximize the viewing experiences.
_full_text:
If you’re looking for a good location to view two of the featured events of Rapid City’s upcoming America 250 Birthday Bash celebration — the patriotic drone show and the City’s fireworks show — Visit Rapid City has developed a convenient online page showcasing several options to maximize the viewing experiences.

Last week, Visit Rapid City launched a “Where to Watch” page on its website. The public is encouraged to visit Best Places to Watch the Drone Show & Fireworks in Rapid City | Visit Rapid City , which outlines a half-dozen locations for viewing the drone and fireworks shows, two of several must-see events of the upcoming Birthday Bash celebration.

The Real America Birthday Bash celebration is scheduled July 1-5. The Sky Elements Patriotic Drone Show at approximately 9:30 p.m. Thursday, July 2 after the community parade and the annual City fireworks show is scheduled for 9:30 p.m. Saturday, July 4.

 Rapid City Fireworks
Fireworks light up the sky during the Rapid City show in 2025. 

The “Where to Watch” page provides descriptive information and helpful recommendations for the sites, which include Memorial Park and downtown, Dinosaur Park and Skyline Drive, M Hill at Hanson-Larsen Memorial Park, Halley Park, Wilson Park and Horace Mann Park.

The site also provides “Before You Go” planning tips.

“If you’re looking at prime options for viewing these two great events, the ‘Where to Watch’ page is a valuable tool providing important information and recommendations,” said Visit Rapid City CEO Ally Formanek. “Both shows will light up the night skies in Rapid City and are must-see events. The page provides some viewing options to consider and some helpful hints.”

In addition to the drone and fireworks shows, the Birthday Bash celebration includes a community parade, downtown festival, a Mount Rushmore fireworks display viewing party, musical performances by Chancey Williams and Brandon Jones, a concert by the Air Force Academy Band, a Kids’ Zone, Touch-A-Truck exhibits, local and regional music performers, food vendors, exhibits, historical re-enactors and readings, and a Freedom 5K Run.

To learn more about this summer’s “Real America Birthday Bash” events, visit www.realamericabirthdaybash.com or call Visit Rapid City at 605-718-8484/800-487-3223.

title: Rapid City Council approves Catalyst District TIF amendment that adds Elevate Rapid City; adds $19 million to TIF
description: During the Rapid City Council meeting, a presentation about the Catalyst District Tax Increment Financing District was made for an amendment to add an additional project to the district, adding $19.4 million to the already approved $84 million TIF.
_full_text:
During the Rapid City Council meeting, a presentation about the Catalyst District Tax Increment Financing District was made for an amendment to add an additional project to the district, adding $19.4 million to the already approved $84 million TIF. 

The council voted 9-0 to approve the amendment. Councilman Rod Pettigrew absent at the meeting on Monday, June 15.

 Catalyst TIF
An overview of the TIF boundary with the new business park highlighted in a purple border.  

The current Catalyst District plan includes infrastructure for the flagship development of a new sports complex, funded partially by the $84.1 million TIF. The project was approved by the Rapid City Council in September 2025.

Per the project plan, Phase II includes $9 million in TIF funding toward infrastructure that will support a $400 million private project. The money, "will be used for the construction of water and water reclamation mains and facilities necessary to provide services to a significant industrial client. The development of the infrastructure will allow further development along Deadwood Avenue, most of which is outside the proposed TIF boundaries. There is more than adequate water availability, however, the means of conveying the water to the sites with adequate pressure needs to be upgraded.”

In February, council members told the Journal there was discussion of a data center, but neither the plan documents nor council members identified the mystery client or the project. 

That month, Black Hills Energy told the Journal the company owns property along Deadwood Avenue included in the Rapid City Catalyst TIFD.

 TIF example
This chart from the South Dakota Department of Revenue shows how a TIF works. 

“The property is the site of our Lange I and Lange II generating facilities. Lange II is currently under construction and scheduled to be online later this year. The remainder of the property is reserved for future resource development to meet customers’ needs,” a Black Hills Energy spokesperson said. “From our understanding, the $9M water investment through the TIFD will enhance growth opportunities along Deadwood Avenue which are currently limited by the lack of available water resources. The water need is not related to a Black Hills Energy planned project.”

City Tax Increment Finance Planner Mike Dugan gave a presentation to the council about the project addition Elevate is hoping to bring to north side of the city.

Elevate Rapid City’s recent request increases the TIF by $10 million in capital costs for street and utility improvements to North Maple Street north of Mall Drive, improvements at the intersection of North Maple Street and Mall Drive, as well as street and utility improvements to Mall Drive.

The request also includes $9,464,314 for financing costs for the improvements included in the TIFD request, bringing the increase to over $19 million and the total TIF to about $103 million.

According to city documents, the necessary infrastructure improvements would be toward the future development of a business park that would also include multifamily dwellings across 128 acres.

Before voting, Councilman John Roberts questioned whether the project had any guarantee for success, saying, "I'm just looking out for the citizens of Rapid City … that is my only concern. The project isn't bad, I think the project has a lot of merit. I just want to make sure 20 years from now if this TIF doesn't succeed, the taxpayers are not on the hook."

Councilman Kevin Maher (Ward 3) motioned for approval and then held the floor, saying he wished others viewed the Planning and Zoning Commission meeting where the presentation was originally given. 

Maher said the project area in north Rapid City lacks light industrial property, and he supports the amendment.

Roberts, who is a real estate agent and owns land within a mile of the project site, said there is plenty of land in the north side of the city and said the county already approved the $68 million Black Hills Marketplace TIF near land located generally south of Catron Boulevard, west of Fifth Street and east of Black Hills Boulevard. The project site is approximately 172 acres. 

Project details for the county TIF include construction of 400,000 square feet of retail, hospitality and restaurants, a 500-unit multi-family development and 130 single-family residential homes. Plans include sites for future retail and restaurants and industrial.

"Like I said, I'm just concerned about the taxpayers in the future," Roberts said as he cautioned that other industrial properties are still not being sold. 

Councilman Greg Strommen said he understood Roberts' concerns about whether this development would guarantee economic success, but he said he also supports economic growth and trusts Elevate Rapid City’s vision.

Per previous reporting by the Journal, Tax Increment Finance Planner Mike Dugan said the city does not write checks for the intended improvements by the TIF; the developer is taking the risk by taking a bank loan. After looking at all the invoices, the city reimburses the developer for the improvements.

The city will only cover only 7% of the bank loan’s interest rate. If the rate is higher, then the developer is responsible for those costs.

Dugan said if the amount spent for the improvements exceeds what was approved in the TIF, the developer is also responsible for those costs. If a development does not generate enough increment to repay their bank loan after the development is completed, the developer is responsible for the loss, not the city, Dugan said.

title: Red, Blue, and You blood drive unites first responders, community to save lives
description: Red, Blue, and You — formerly known as Rapid City’s annual Guns N’ Hoses Blood Drive — is bringing together first responders and the community to ensure blood is available for patients in need.
_full_text:
Red, Blue, and You — formerly known as Rapid City’s annual Guns N’ Hoses Blood Drive — is bringing together first responders and the community to ensure blood is available for patients in need.

Sponsored by Vitalant, the Red, Blue, and You community blood drive will take place from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Tuesday, June 23, Wednesday, June 24, and Thursday, June 25, at Uptown Rapid in the center court near Bath & Body Works. Donors will get the first Red, Blue and You shirts, while supplies last, when they donate at the event.

Scheduling an appointment to donate blood is encouraged. Appointments can be made by visiting vitalant.org/redblueyou, downloading and using the Vitalant Blood Donor App, or calling 877-25-VITAL (877-258-4825).

Every Vitalant donor who uses code JUNEGIFT-2026-V when scheduling an appointment will receive a $15 Donor Rewards gift card when they donate in June.

"The new name reflects what has always been at the heart of this event, joining together to help save lives." said Tori Robbins, communications manager for Vitalant. "Every blood donation represents someone in our community stepping up to help a neighbor they may never meet. Red, Blue, and You brings that spirit of teamwork and service together in one place.”

Donors of all blood types are encouraged to participate. Blood is needed every day for trauma patients, individuals undergoing cancer treatment, people with blood disorders, surgical patients, and many others facing serious medical conditions.

The need is especially great for type O blood. Type O negative blood can be transfused to most patients and is often used in emergency situations when there is no time to determine a patient's blood type. Type O positive blood is also the most transfused blood type and plays a critical role in maintaining hospital inventories. All blood types are being accepted, and you do not need to know your blood type to donate.

Vitalant is one of the nation’s largest nonprofit blood and biotherapies health care organizations, providing hospitals and patients nationwide with a safe blood supply, specialized laboratory services, transfusion medicine expertise and world-renowned research.

title: ‘It’s up to us’: Pine Ridge Bush Fellow advocates for Lakota language, culture to thrive
description: Elyssa Sierra Her Many Horses, 30, is already planning her legacy. The Pine Ridge resident dreams of a future where Lakota is spoken in homes, schools and communities as a living, thriving language.
_full_text:
Elyssa Sierra Her Many Horses, 30, is already planning her legacy. The Pine Ridge resident dreams of a future where Lakota is spoken in homes, schools and communities as a living, thriving language.

Her Many Horses (Cheyenne River Sioux, Oglála, Ojibwa and Taos Pueblo) is one of two 2026 Bush Fellows from South Dakota. She is a Lakota immersion educator. Since 2020, she’s worked at Mahpíya Lúta Owáyawa (Red Cloud School) in Pine Ridge as instructional support staff, where she also develops Lakota language curriculum.

Her goal is to continue to be a Lakota revitalization leader. When her two-year fellowship begins on Aug. 1, Her Many Horses plans to increase her Lakota language fluency, her understanding of Lakota culture and educate herself so she can help the Mahpíya Lúta Lakota immersion program grow and thrive.   

“I wanted to become a Bush Fellow ultimately because I knew this fellowship could help me travel to different Indigenous communities throughout the world and visit their programs. That’s ultimately where I want to grow more as a leader — understanding what other programs are doing, what’s working for them, what’s not working for them, and then bringing that back home to our program,” Her Many Horses said. “Our program is fairly new compared to some like in Hawaii and in New Zealand and Canada. They’ve been in this work for decades.”

“I’m young and I’m fairly new to it, so I just want to gain as much knowledge as I possibly can. That was really the big goal in what I wanted to do with this Bush Fellowship,” she said.

Her Many Horses believes restoring the Lakota language is the foundation for a strong education, identity and community life.

“Ultimately, (it’s up to) us to maintain our identity and keep true to being Lakota by speaking our language and knowing our ceremonies and teachings because no one else will be able to do it for us. This is all our knowledge that we have to carry within our own people and pass it on to our future generations,” Her Many Horses said.

She wants to spend time learning from community members and elders about cultural influences such as growing and using traditional plants, beading, sewing and traditional crafting.

“I have a lot of language knowledge, but cultural knowledge is where I need to grow, and then I can utilize the language in that way, and learn the language terminology with our traditional art and knowledge,” Many Horses said.

“Our language and our culture are our entire Lakota identity,” she said. “It’s what makes us unique as a people and a tribe. No other group of people in the world have these teachings, this language. It’s our responsibility to carry it on. Our ancestors fought so hard for it through colonization, through the boarding school era.”

She’ll also use her Bush fellowship to complete her doctorate in Indigenous language and culture revitalization. She’s earning her Ph.D through a hybrid program from the University of Hawaii at Hilo. Her Many Horses also holds a bachelor’s degree in English from Black Hills State University and a master’s degree in education from Arizona State University.

“Everything I’m going to gain from this journey being a Bush Fellow is all going to come directly back into my students and this program and my curriculum development. I ultimately just want to see Lakota thrive long beyond whenever I’m gone,” she said. “I want this to be a sustainable movement that continues to grow and grow, and I want to gain as much as I can that can help that sustainability.”

Her Many Horses began her Lakota immersion work a decade ago while she was earning her bachelor’s degree. She got a part-time job with a Lakota immersion daycare, which was originally offered through Thunder Valley CDC.  

“I fell in love with being in the classroom and learning a language and only speaking Lakota and developing curriculum, and all of that really excited me,” Her Many Horses said.

“I was a media consultant, so I helped with creating videos and using other people’s recordings and my colleagues’ translations and editing them into worksheets and books. That’s where I really got into it, and when I graduated (with my bachelor’s degree), that’s when I took a full-time job with that organization to continue my work as a media consultant and curriculu

 BRIGHT SIDE LOGO.jpg
Sharing the good news: We’re looking for upbeat stories and shout-outs worth celebrating. Send your story ideas to the Journal newsroom, news@rapidcityjournal.com, with "Bright Side" in the subject line. 

m developer. It kept growing from there,” she said.

Her Many Horses assisted in developing the first elementary Lakota immersion program at Mahpíya Lúta, where she teaches entirely in Lakota. She’s certified to teach the Lakota language, and she creates curriculum for the middle school immersion program, and materials such as books, videos and language resources for immersion program students from kindergarten through middle school.

She’s made thousands of educational resources that are available to other educators. She’s also helped develop curriculum for adult Lakota language learnings, and she assists in training immersion educators across the region.

“I love what I’m doing now. I’m in the classroom. I’m teaching the Lakota language … I’m developing curriculum daily as I go,” Her Many Horses said. “I love being in this role of constantly creating new things while also immediately being able to implement the curriculum I’m creating.”

Through her work with Lakota immersion students, she is already seeing children and teens grow up fluent and grounded in cultural knowledge. Her Many Horses’ inspiration for her Lakota immersion work came in part from her own siblings.

Her Many Horses was born in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and grew up in Albuquerque until, at age 13, her family moved to Pine Ridge. Much of her family is in South Dakota, including her grandparents, who live in Rapid City.

Her Many Horses is the oldest of 10 children, and she became intrigued when two of her sisters were learning Lakota in an immersion daycare.

“They’re first-language Lakota speakers, and I wanted to be on that journey with them,” Her Many Horses said. “Now I get to be part of their language journey every single day. They’re in middle school, and I work at the middle school, so it’s great to be on this journey with them.”

title: Pine Ridge man sentenced for assaulting deputy U.S. Marshal, threatening officers
description: A Pine Ridge man was sentenced to time in federal after his conviction for assaulting a federal officer and threatening a federal officer.
_full_text:
A Pine Ridge man was sentenced to time in federal after his conviction for assaulting a federal officer and threatening a federal officer.

U.S. Attorney Ron Parsons announced that U.S. District Judge Karen E. Schreier sentenced Franklin Long Black Cat, 32, to three years and five months in federal prison for the assault of a federal officer conviction to run concurrently with the threatening a federal officer conviction, followed by three years of supervised release. Long Black Cat was also ordered to pay a $200 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

In a release, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for South Dakota said Long Black Cat was indicted for assaulting a federal officer and two counts of threatening a federal officer by a federal grand jury in November 2025. He was found guilty following a two-day jury trial on Jan. 29.

On Nov. 18, 2025, Long Black Cat was in the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service at the federal courthouse in Rapid City in connection with a court hearing. Long Black Cat spat in the face of one deputy U.S. marshal and threatened to shoot two other deputy U.S. marshals.

This case was investigated by the FBI. Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Schroeder prosecuted the case.

Long Black Cat was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Pennington County warns residents again about fraudulent Planning & Zoning emails
description: The Pennington County Planning & Zoning Department is continuing to receive reports of fraudulent emails being sent to residents that falsely appear to originate from the department.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Planning & Zoning Department is continuing to receive reports of fraudulent emails being sent to residents that falsely appear to originate from the department.

The scam emails typically include invoices and detailed instructions directing recipients to take action or submit payment. These communications are not legitimate and are not being sent by Pennington County Planning & Zoning.

To help residents identify these fraudulent messages, the County is releasing an example of one of the scam invoices that has been reported. Residents are encouraged to review the example and remain cautious when receiving unexpected emails claiming to be from county offices.

"We want residents to know that these emails are still circulating and that they should remain cautious," said Brittney Hand, Director of Planning & Zoning. "If you receive an invoice or instructions from someone claiming to represent our department, do not assume it is legitimate. Contact our office directly so we can help verify the communication before any action is taken."

The Planning & Zoning Department does not routinely send invoices by email, and most payments and transactions are conducted directly through the department's office. Residents should be especially cautious of emails requesting payment, directing them to click links, download attachments, or follow instructions regarding county services.

An example of a reported fraudulent invoice is attached to this release for public awareness and educational purposes.

For additional information or to verify communications claiming to be from Planning & Zoning, please contact the Pennington County Planning & Zoning Department.

title: Pennington County Sheriff’s Office boat patrol on the water in the Black Hills
description: With summer in full swing, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office is returning to the waters for its annual summer boat patrol operation on Black Hills lakes.
_full_text:
With summer in full swing, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office is returning to the waters for its annual summer boat patrol operation on Black Hills lakes.

 IMG_8437.JPG
Pennington County Sheriff’s Office deputies set off from Sheridan Lake’s North Marina entrance with media for a tour around the lake. 

Through Labor Day, deputies will be patrolling Sheridan Lake, Pactola Reservoir and Deerfield Lake. Their intention is to broaden boater education, enforce regulations and monitor dangerous activity.

“Mostly what we’re doing is making sure everybody’s having a fun, safe day,” Pennington County Sheriff’s Deputy Janae Olson said. “Going around making sure people have life jackets and all the necessary things that they need.”

 Slow down
The PCSO will be making speed checks, checking for reckless behaviors and enforcing boating laws. 

Deputy Chris Brown said in addition to patrolling the waters, they will also be patrolling the shorelines, keeping an eye out for any suspicious activity. He said the main issue the patrol has dealt with is underage drinking from teens visiting the lakes. Brown encourages everyone to follow the law on and off the water, regardless of age.

“A lot of underage drinking. We do want to hit on that a little bit, especially up in Jenny Gulch, Pactola,” Brown said.

 Deputies out on the water
From Memorial Day to Labor Day, deputies will be patrolling Sheridan Lake, Pactola Reservoir and Deerfield Lake. Their intention is to broaden boater education, enforcing regulations and monitoring for dangerous activity. 

In addition, the deputies will be making speed checks, checking for reckless behaviors and enforcing boating laws.

title: Timothy R. "Tim" Wiese

November 14, 1947 - June 16, 2026

A Memorial Mass for Timothy R. Wiese, 78, Norfolk, will be 10:30 a.m. Monday, June 29, 2026, at St. Mary's Catholic Church in Norfolk. Reverend Vincent Germace will officiate, with burial in All Saints Cemetery in Columbus.

There will be a luncheon following the Mass at the Knights of Columbus Hall, 105 Elm Avenue, in Norfolk.

Visitation will be one hour prior to the service at the church.

Home for Funerals in Norfolk is in charge of arrangements.

Tim died Tuesday, June 16, at Faith Health in Norfolk.

Timothy Raymond Wiese, son of Raymond and Ollie (Coufal) Wiese, was born November 14, 1947, in Humphrey, Nebraska, while his family lived on a farm in Lindsay. He primarily grew up and attended school in Columbus. After high school graduation in 1966, he began school at Norfolk Junior College before attending Peru State, where he played baseball.

On June 14, 1969, he was united in marriage to Patricia McCarville. They were blessed with three children, Stephanie, Tim Jr., and Nick.

At age 15, Tim began working at a grocery store, a career that carried him through most of his life. His work took him to Grand Island, Columbus, Minot, ND, and Rapid City, SD. He was a hard worker who took good care of his family. He was a huge supporter of his children in their athletics through the years and was a loving and proud grandfather.

Tim loved the great outdoors and could often be found hunting, fishing, and camping in his free time. He was a longtime sports enthusiast with a special place in his heart for baseball and the Yankees, though he also was a fan of the Chicago Bears, and of course, the Huskers.

Tim is survived by his wife Pat; children, Stephanie (Brett) Heffes, Tim (Kate) Wiese Jr., and Nick (Nicole) Wiese; grandchildren, Madisen, Calvin, Tienna, Tavani, Imogen, Jamison, Gavin, and Collins; siblings, Pat (Susan) Wiese, Mary (Jeff) Searcy, Steve (Tracy) Wiese, Cindy Martin, Theresa (Tom) DeLaet, and Chuck (Julie) Wiese; in-laws, Debb Strate, Mike McCarville (Sheri Goodhard), Denis (Theri) McCarville, Mary Lu (Tim) Euler, Kevin (Joanie) McCarville, Jim (Stacie) McCarville, Teri (Ken) Petersen, Tom (Lisa) McCarville, and Mark (Rebecca) McCarville; and many nieces, nephews, and cousins.

He was preceded in death by his parents, Raymond and Ollie; parents-in-law, Mac and Emily McCarville; brother, Ted Wiese; and brothers-in-law, Alan Martin and Larry Strate.

Memorials may be directed to Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation (ADDF).

title: Monica Burgess
description: December 15, 1953 - June 21, 2026
_full_text:
December 15, 1953 - June 21, 2026

Monica Mellen Burgess, beloved wife, mother, grandmother, sister, business leader, and community champion, passed peacefully into the kingdom of heaven to be with her Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ. She was 72 years old.

Born on December 15, 1953, in Newark, NJ Monica was the daughter of Gregory Edward Mellen and Alice Eleanor Dooling Mellen. In 1957, her family relocated to Bloomington, MN where Monica's exceptional intellect quickly became evident. She graduated from Lincoln High School at just 16 years old, a remarkable achievement that foreshadowed a life defined by intelligence, determination, and excellence.

Monica continued her education at Macalester College, graduating with honors with a degree in Chemistry. Following college, she began her professional career at 3M through its Riker Labs division, where she started building a career that would place her at the forefront of technological innovation.

Guided in part by her father Greg, Monica later joined Unisys, where she helped engineer some of the largest mainframe computers of the era. As technology evolved, so did Monica. She transitioned into the personal computer division in San Jose, CA where she managed a manufacturing plant and further established herself as a highly respected leader in the technology industry.

Monica met Jim Burgess at the Minnesota State Fair—a chance encounter that almost never happened, as Jim had not planned to attend and only went at the urging of friends. That decision changed both of their lives forever. The two married in 1990, building a life centered on family, love, and shared purpose.

While Monica's professional accomplishments were extraordinary, some of her greatest joys were found on the water. She loved boating on the St. Croix River, where many of her happiest memories were made. Their shared love of boating became one of the foundations of Monica and Jim's relationship and remained a treasured part of their life together.

In 1994, Monica joined Dell Technologies as an Executive Director overseeing operations across the Americas, where she worked closely with Michael Dell. Her leadership, vision, and technical expertise made a lasting impact on those fortunate enough to collaborate with her. She retired in 2002, beginning a new chapter when she and her family relocated to Rapid City, SD where Monica became a partner in Black Hills Harley-Davidson.

Monica was also deeply involved with the United States Coast Guard Auxiliary, serving as an active officer in a flotilla based in Saint Paul. Her love of boats was matched by her mechanical confidence and willingness to tackle any challenge. Jim often recalled one of his favorite memories with admiration and affection: "Monica could crawl down into the engine compartment and change all 16 spark plugs and the oil." It was a perfect reflection of who she was—brilliant, fearless, practical, and never intimidated by hard work.

In 2020, Monica's son Nick met Sasha, who would soon become a cherished part of the family. They were married a year later, and a few years after that, Monica welcomed one of her greatest joys—her grandson, Ryker.

Becoming a grandmother brought Monica immense joy. She treasured the opportunity to build a special bond with Ryker, especially during a difficult season that allowed Monica and Jim precious time helping care for him. Those moments together became deeply precious, creating memories filled with love, laughter, and connection. Ryker brought tremendous joy to Monica's life, and the time they shared became one of her most treasured gifts.

Retirement did not slow Monica—it simply redirected her energy toward serving others. In 2008, recognizing the need to strengthen and expand opportunities for athletes with intellectual disabilities in Rapid City, SD Monica became a driving force in reimagining the local Special Olympics South Dakota program. Alongside Jason Alley, Dr. Mark Harlow, Jack Lynass, Steve Schacht, Stacey Fenske (Schaefer), Myles Kennedy, Tammy Barrows, and Lillie Pendleton, she helped create the Rapid City Flame, bringing renewed vision, leadership, and mission to the organization.

As Board Chair of Special Olympics South Dakota, Monica's leadership transformed possibilities into realities. She spearheaded the creation of the state's largest bocce complex, partnering with Rusty Wallace and the NASCAR Foundation, along with Rod Woodruff of the Buffalo Chip Campground, to raise the funds needed for construction. Her vision created a legacy that will benefit athletes and families for generations.

Monica's brilliance extended beyond business and nonprofit leadership. She was also instrumental in the development and design of augmentative communication devices, contributing to some of the earliest applications of predictive text technology—innovation that helped give voice and connection to countless individuals.

Monica lived a life of extraordinary achievement, but those who knew her best will remember more than her accomplishments. They will remember her sharp mind, adventurous spirit, determination, generous heart, and unwavering commitment to making things better—whether for her family, her community, or complete strangers whose lives she improved without seeking recognition.

As a young adult, Monica found joy in music and enjoyed playing the cello, where discipline and artistry came together in ways that reflected her character. Years later, that same love of music became part of her spiritual journey as she helped provide music for Taizé contemplative worship. In that community, she found prayer, reflection, and quiet connection. Monica also valued spiritual growth deeply and worked with a spiritual director in the Christian faith, intentionally nurturing a life of contemplation, discernment, and grace. These practices reflected the thoughtful and grounded spirit that guided how she lived, loved, and served others.

She is survived by her loving husband, Jim; sons Nick (Sasha) and Andrew; cherished grandson Ryker; brother Mike (Barb); sisters Roberta and Martha; mother-in-law Maxine; brothers-in-law Scott and Todd (Jill); and sisters-in-law Susan (Dan), Jane (John), and Carol.

She was preceded in death by her parents, Alice and Greg; her brother, Neal; and her father-in-law, Barry.

Monica's life was a testament to what is possible when brilliance is paired with purpose and success is measured by service to others. She leaves behind a remarkable legacy of innovation, leadership, love, and faith—one that will continue to inspire all who knew her.

She will be deeply missed and forever remembered.

Service will be held at Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church (the Cathedral) at 10:30 am Friday June 26, 2026

A celebration of life luncheon immediately following at Rushmore Hotel 445 Mount Rushmore Rd, Rapid City, SD.

In lieu of flowers, Monica's family requests memorial donations be made to the Rapid City Flame, P.O. Box 9780, Rapid City, SD 57709.

title: White House hasn’t confirmed president’s appearance at Rushmore fireworks
description: The White House has not yet confirmed if President Donald Trump will attend the July 3 fireworks at Mount Rushmore.
_full_text:
The White House has not yet confirmed if President Donald Trump will attend the July 3 fireworks at Mount Rushmore.

A White House press official declined to confirm if the president will attend when the Journal reached out to arrange press access, noting the office may provide information “once an event is confirmed.” As of Monday afternoon, June 22, the White House had not announced a Mount Rushmore visit.

As reported by the Bismarck Tribune, Trump will be in North Dakota on July 1, according to Freedom 250, an organization spearheading events throughout the country, including the Great American State Fair in Washington D.C.

Trump will visit the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora, North Dakota, ahead of its July 4 grand opening, the Tribune reported. Trump and others will participate in the facility's dedication.

 Trumps
President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump at Mount Rushmore in 2020 ahead of the fireworks display. 

“North Dakota transformed Theodore Roosevelt into a leader and conservationist who would leave an enduring mark on America. It’s where a young New Yorker found grit, purpose, perseverance and crafted a conservation vision that would shape America’s treasured places for generations,” U.S. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum said in a release from Freedom 250. Burgum was North Dakota’s governor before Trump tapped him for his current position.

“The dedication of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library will show how Roosevelt’s passion inspired the creation of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, dramatic expansion of our National Parks and the stewardship of our public lands,” Burgum said.

As for Rushmore, we await confirmation. C-SPAN expects him to be there, announcing in a June 18 release it’ll carry coverage of the America 250 celebrations at Mount Rushmore, “with remarks from President Trump.”

And NBC News reported earlier this month that — according to a senior White House official and a source familiar with the plans — Trump is considering a trip to the Black Hills on the inaugural flight of the new Air Force One jet, a gift from Qatar.

The president visited Mount Rushmore for a July 4 fireworks show in 2020.

title: Rapid City man arrested after pursuit through Star Village
description: A Rapid City man was arrested Sunday, June 21, after he evaded a police blockade and began a low-speed pursuit through Star Village.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man was arrested Sunday, June 21, after he evaded a police blockade and began a low-speed pursuit through Star Village.

Miles Makes Good, 35, was arrested on suspicion of ingesting a substance other than alcohol to intoxicate, driving under the influence, reckless driving, driving on the wrong side of the road, driving under suspension and possession of a revoked, altered or fictitious driver’s license.

At around 3:50 p.m. Sunday, police responded to a residence in the 100 block of Crescent Drive for a report of a man parked in an SUV in the driveway. The reporting party said the man was known to be huffing air duster.

Upon arrival, police found the SUV and identified Makes Good as the man inside it. Officers parked near the SUV in an attempt to pin it and keep the vehicle from leaving.

However, Makes Good drove around the police units, leading to a low-speed pursuit that went through Star Village. During the chase, the SUV drove through a yard in the unit block of East Signal Drive.

Police deployed spike strips to deflate the car’s tires at East Boulevard and Quincy Street. The car then drove back to Star Village, where it eventually stopped in the 100 block of East Signal Drive. Police detained Makes Good after he exited the car.

Police said they found a cold air duster in Makes Good’s possession.

As of Monday, Makes Good is being held at the Pennington County Jail with no bond set.
