title: Two new foster homes give kids chance to be ‘safe, secure and loved’
description: Abbott House Youth Services celebrated its two new foster homes in Rapid City on June 18 with ribbon cuttings, many smiles and some tears of joy.
_full_text:
Abbott House Youth Services celebrated its two new foster homes in Rapid City on June 18 with ribbon cuttings, many smiles and some tears of joy.

A year ago, Abbott House launched a $2.5 million capital campaign to build the two new therapeutic foster homes. Abbott House is a nonprofit organization. With the addition of the two new foster homes, Abbott House now runs six therapeutic foster homes in Rapid City for children and teens up to age 18 who have experienced trauma, abuse and neglect.

“Abbott House Youth Services does foster parenting differently. Instead of bringing children into your own home, Abbott House provides a beautiful home, vehicles, and everything needed to support a foster child. Bringing together the foster care services along with psychiatric residential treatment, addiction recovery and crisis care at Abbott House West is truly the optimal situation for young people struggling with trauma and/or addiction issues,” Abbott House said in a news release announcing the ribbon cuttings.

 062026-nws-newfosterhomes—Jodie Mathison foster home ribbon cutting.jpg
Abbott House Youth Services and Elevate Rapid City held a ribbon cutting on Thursday, June 18, at the Jodie Lynn Mathison foster home in Rapid City. Jodie, who worked with troubled kids, died of cancer in her 30s. Jodie’s mother, DeMaris Nesheim, is the vice president of the Abbott House board. Jodie’s brother, Jason Mathison, cut the ribbon at the Jodie Lynn Mathison foster home. Nesheim gave a brief presentation about her daughter before the ribbon cutting. Kris Garlick, chaplain at Monument Health Sturgis Hospital, gave a blessing and prayer over the home. 

“Now, more than ever, we have the opportunity to provide a continuum of care for South Dakota children who come from hard places,” said Eric Klooz, executive director of Abbott House Youth Services. “By investing in these children now, we’re building bridges to brighter futures.”

Most of the children and youth who come to Abbott House are referred by parents, extended family members or the South Dakota Department of Social Services. Abbott House's therapeutic foster homes offer weekly individual and family therapy and are the only ones of their kind in South Dakota.

During the June 18 ribbon-cutting ceremonies, Abbott House Executive Director Eric Klooz said there are about 500 children and teens in Rapid City who need foster care and only about 100 foster homes in the city to serve them.

“We provide a continuum of care that allows kids to heal, have a family, and graduate high school,” Klooz said of Abbott House’s foster homes.

“The primary reason kids come to our foster homes is they don’t have another place to go,” Klooz said. “There are so many kids that don’t have a home, and we’ve created a program that has worked really well, and the state continues to come back to us and ask us to provide more houses.”

 062026-nws-newfosterhomes-Fritz and Mary foster home ribbon cutting.jpg
Jim Scull cut the ribbon at the Abbott House Youth Services Fritz and Mary foster home on Thursday, June 18, in Rapid City. Scull is a longtime supporter of Abbott House programs. The new foster home is named to honor Scull’s stepfather and mother. Todd Lynch, a pastor at Fountain Springs Church, blessed and prayed over the new house. 

Abbott House runs a total of 12 therapeutic foster homes across the state of South Dakota.

Abbott House’s two newest foster homes in Rapid City opened in November 2025, according to Beth-Anne Ferley, assistant development director for Abbott House. Each new foster home can house six children and teens, plus foster parents who are employed by Abbott House to live in the homes 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

“It is exciting to see,” Ferley said. “We can play a part in making sure our kids’ lives are safe, secure and loved.”

title: Pennington County Commission adds more restrictions to wind and solar as it settles on rules
byline: SHALOM BAER GEE and FRANK ESPINOZA Journal staff
description: The Pennington County Commission voted 3-2, once again, on a wind and solar ordinance that bars utility-scale projects from agricultural land. The commission previously passed an ordinance on first reading, but restarted the process after making significant changes.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Commission voted 3-2, once again, on a wind and solar ordinance that bars utility-scale projects from agricultural land. The commission previously passed an ordinance on first reading, but restarted the process after making significant changes.

The most recent vote is the culmination of a monthslong process.

Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voted no on the amendments to the ordinance at the commission’s June 16 meeting. Ordinances need two readings before they officially pass, and the second reading is scheduled for July 7.

What’s changing?

The ordinance change shifts approval power for utility-scale wind and solar projects from the county Planning Commission to the Board of Commissioners, as well as including setbacks far exceeding the recommendations of county staff and the current zoning ordinance.

In a letter to the commission in support of the new ordinance, Derr wrote, “It does not prohibit distributed systems for homes, farms, and small businesses, which remain permitted across all zoning districts. Instead, it draws a commonsense line between private-use systems and utility-scale industrial projects.”

Utility-scale is defined as systems that go directly into the grid for further distribution. Distributed systems send power directly to a home, farm or small business.

The changes are to Section 317 of the county's zoning ordinance, which governs wind and solar, both on a utility scale and on a private scale. In addition to banning utility-scale wind and solar on agriculture land and confining it to industrial zones, the proposed ordinance expands setbacks significantly.

 Solar
Rows of solar panels stand inside a fence in New Underwood as part of Wild Springs Solar project, the largest solar project in South Dakota.  

A property line setback for solar panels of 1,000 feet (a forty-fold increase to existing code, which requires 25 feet or 1 ½ times the height of the structure, whichever is greater) and a buffer zone of 50 feet. The change for wind turbines puts the setback from property lines at 1.2 miles (up from 1 ½ times the height of the turbine of 1,000 feet, whichever is greater, in current code) and a 50-foot buffer zone. County staff had recommended solar be 50 feet from property lines and have a 25-foot buffer zone. Staff also recommended wind turbines be setback at three times the height of the turbines and a buffer zone of 25 feet.

Drewes said the amendments are overly restrictive. Rossknecht said he agreed.

The changes come more than a year-and-a-half after public interest led the county to form a task force on solar and wind energy, after the county passed a year-long moratorium on utility-scale wind and solar developments in November 2024. The commission extended the moratorium as the task force group researched the topic and considered future county regulations. The task force members include Commissioner Jerry Derr (District 4), attorneys, an appraiser and individuals from the ranching community, local government and energy sector.

Eileen Peterson, a member of the county's task force, spoke to the commission in May to ask for further changes to the proposed ordinance barring wind and solar on ag land. Peterson is the at-large representative on the task force. She holds two bachelor of science degrees from the South Dakota School of Mines, one in geological mining and the other in mining engineering. In her application for consideration on the task force, she wrote she is “committed to seeing fair and limited development on agricultural lands” and has concerns about health and safety issues.

On May 19, the commission approved the first reading of a wind and solar ordinance. In this case, the ordinance couldn’t move on to a second reading because the commission made significant changes to the ordinance, starting the process over.

Commissioner Deb Hadcock (District 3) added a ban on battery storage systems. Other changes included the expanded setback requirements and addressed roof systems.

Before they voted, Peterson asked the commission for a couple of tweaks to the proposed amendment, which included information on infrasound, setbacks and tighter bonding requirements. The commission voted to approve the ordinance without the additional changes proposed by Peterson.

The path from temporary moratorium to wholesale changes

The commission began laying the groundwork to ban wind and solar on agricultural land after more than 450 citizens petitioned for the moratorium, after the county’s Planning Commission issued conditional use permits in October 2024 for the Cheyenne River Ranch Wind and Solar Farm. The site is located 7 miles south of New Underwood, 30 miles southeast of Rapid City, and 3.5 miles north of Highway 44.

The project plan consists of 10 wind turbines and 175,000 solar panels on a 1,124-acre site. According to the site plan, the actual footprint of the solar farm is 331 acres. Residents told the commission they don’t want any more projects like the future Cheyenne River Ranch or the existing Wild Springs Solar Project.

Wild Springs, also located south of New Underwood, is the largest solar project in South Dakota. It boasts a 128-megawatt capacity, enough to power 37,000 homes each year, according to National Grid Renewables, which owns the farm. Cheyenne River Ranch will have a capacity of 142.8 megawatts, 56 megawatts from wind energy and 86.8 megawatts from solar.

The first step of codifying changes was an amendment to the county’s Comprehensive Plan-View to 2040, which passed with a 3-2 vote. Rossknecht and Drewes voted no. Utility-scale wind and solar systems are permitted in industrial districts in the plan. Pennington County Planning Director Brittany Hand told the Journal the county features approximately 970,000 acres for agricultural use and 1,500 acres for industrial use.

 Alternative energy
Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) (pictured) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voted against changes to regulations barring utility-scale wind and solar projects on agriculturally-zoned land in Pennington County. 

The county's comprehensive plan is defined as a guide for government officials, residents and developers in regard to "decision-making" for current and potential future development within the county. The plan specifically provides a framework for land-use decisions, public service expansions, economic development, resource management and the general growth of the county.

The Pennington County zoning ordinance serves as a regulatory framework indicating land use and development within the county, ensuring that land is utilized in a manner that aligns with community standards and environmental considerations.

It establishes specific zoning districts and outlines permitted uses, building height restrictions and setbacks, thereby promoting orderly development and mitigating potential conflicts between different land uses.

‘We need families to move in’

Derr said at the June 16 meeting that he and Cody Wiseman, marketing manager for the Pennington County Administration office, went out to already running utility-scale solar fields and felt it was unfit for the agriculture-based community, as well as future growth.

"We need families to move in, we need bodies in our school districts, we need kids and families to support the community. This is limiting this opportunity for that type of growth and that type of tax base to come in," Derr said.

Hadcock thanked the community for being involved in these changes over the last two years. She named key players such as Peterson and father-daughter duo Jerry and Lindsay Mader. Jerry Mader’s property is adjacent to the site on two sides. Lindsay Mader is on the task force.

title: ‘Be safe, have fun’: Sheriff’s Office reminds public about firework safety ahead of Black Hills for Fourth of July celebrations
description: With the Black Hills gearing up for America’s 250th birthday and what is expected to be its biggest Fourth of July celebration yet, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office is urging the public to put safety first this upcoming holiday.
_full_text:
With the Black Hills gearing up for America’s 250th birthday and what is expected to be its biggest Fourth of July celebration yet, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office is urging the public to put safety first this upcoming holiday.

“Be safe, have fun,” Pennington County Sheriff’s Office Deputy Hunter Rice said. “Make sure you follow the laws. Be safe with the fireworks, have parental supervision and have a water source around.”

For those who plan to set off fireworks in approved jurisdictions, Rice said to only set them off in safe, approved areas, make sure children are not handling them and have a sober, responsible adult in the area.

 Elks Lodge Fireworks
A child takes flight at the Elks Lodge Independence Day celebrations, held on Thursday night to kick off the holiday weekend.  

With fire season starting in March this year and the lower third of the state facing extreme drought conditions, Rice said everyone in the community has to do their part in promoting fire safety during festivities.

“Fireworks are dangerous to be around,” Rice said. “They have potential starting fires, specifically in the Black Hills Fire Protection District.”

The sheriff’s office said they will be posting further updates about firework-related preparations later in the week for the upcoming festivities.

Below is a list of jurisdictions and their respective fireworks restrictions.

Pennington County

Discharge of fireworks is permitted in Pennington County from Saturday, June 27, to Sunday, July 5 and Dec. 27 through January 1, 2027. The public is encouraged to be courteous of others and efficiently clean up fireworks litter after any discharge.

The sheriff's office asked for Rapid Valley to adhere to a voluntary curfew of 11 p.m. Deputies will have extra patrols in the area to ensure the safe and courteous discharge of fireworks.

 Elks Lodge Fireworks

Rice said the curfew is to encourage the public to be respectful of their neighbors and considerate of everyone’s needs.

Violations of the fireworks ordinance is a Class 2 misdemeanor punishable by up to 30 days in the Pennington County Jail and a $500 fine.

The following municipalities within Pennington County have ordinances governing fireworks discharge:

Rapid City

No discharge of fireworks is permitted inside city limits or one mile outside city limits, except novelty fireworks. Novelty fireworks include snaps, caps, pull-a-parts, fireworks you can toss on the ground, and sparklers. For further clarification, contact the Rapid City Fire Department's Fire and Life Safety Division at 605-394-5233.

Box Elder

Discharge of fireworks is allowed inside Box Elder city limits and on private property with the permission of the landowner between 9 a.m. and 11 p.m. from July 1 to July 4. If the grassland fire danger rating reaches the “very high” or “extreme” level, private or citizen use of fireworks is prohibited.

Hill City

No discharge of fireworks is permitted in Hill City limits, other than novelty fireworks. Novelty fireworks are party poppers, snappers, sparklers and toy caps.

 Elks Lodge Fireworks
A little girl displays a peace sign during a Fourth of July celebration at the Elks Lodge.  

Keystone

No discharge of fireworks is permitted in Keystone city limits, other than novelty fireworks. Novelty fireworks are party poppers, snappers, sparklers and toy caps.

Wall

No discharge of fireworks is permitted in Wall city limits, other than novelty fireworks. Novelty fireworks are party poppers, snappers, sparklers and toy caps.

Custer

No discharge of fireworks is permitted in the city of Custer.

New Underwood

Fireworks discharged in city limits are permitted from June 28 through July 5 and Dec. 28 through Jan. 1.

No fireworks sales are allowed before June 28 or after July 5. Retail sales are not allowed between 12 a.m. and 7 a.m.

A violation of the fireworks ordinance is a Class 2 misdemeanor. In dry years, the council may ban the use of fireworks within the city limits. For more information, call 605-754-6777.

Black Hills Fire Protection District

No discharge of fireworks is permitted. State law prohibits the sale and discharge of fireworks in this district, which is generally west of Highway 79, from Hot Springs to I-90 (Exit 61), including areas of east Black Hawk and Piedmont.

title: Local muralist completes America 250 project in Rapid City
description: When she set out to paint a mural on the side of one of Rapid City’s oldest buildings, Amber Hansen didn’t realize her biggest challenge to getting the project finished would be Mother Nature.
_full_text:
When she set out to paint a mural on the side of one of Rapid City’s oldest buildings, Amber Hansen didn’t realize her biggest challenge to getting the project finished would be Mother Nature.

On Monday afternoon, just a few hours before a rainstorm swept through areas of Rapid City, Hansen put the final touches on a mural depicting Rapid City’s America 250th birthday logo. The logo is etched on the south side of the office building that formerly housed Hooky Jacks/Phatty McGees restaurant and bar at the corner of Seventh Street and Apolda Street. The building is one of Rapid City’s oldest, constructed in 1896.

 Mural
The mural completes a patriotic theme to the building wall, sitting alongside the massive American flag mural that has adorned the side of the building for many years. 

The mural completes a patriotic theme to the building wall, sitting alongside the massive American flag mural that has adorned the side of the building for many years.

“It’s finished!,” Hansen announced on her business Facebook page Monday afternoon. Hansen, who owns her own studio in Rapid City, started the project June 11 and spent parts of the next week and a half balancing weather challenges, other commitments and occasional chats with curious onlookers.

 Rapid City America 250 mural
Amber Hansen takes a second to pose for a photo while working on the mural on Monday, June 22. 

Among those who stopped by to check on the progress of Hansen’s mural was Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun, who presented the artist with a challenge coin last week.

“Rapid City is the best in America. Our deep love and patriotism shine brightly through Amber’s beautiful mural, a lasting tribute to our city’s connection to America’s 250th birthday,” said Mayor Salamun. “Displayed alongside the massive American flag on a historic building, it will be enjoyed by residents and visitors for years to come. A wonderful tribute to our city and our nation!”

Throughout the project, Hansen kept her Facebook followers updated on the progress. Shortly after starting the project, she posted, “I’ll be refining the edges, adjusting proportions, and bringing everything together as the mural develops. It’s always fun to watch a large-scale painting take shape layer by layer.”

With the project finished, Hansen is now inviting residents and visitors to Rapid City to stop by and take a selfie of the mural.

title: Rapid City man arrested for soliciting minors
description: A Rapid City man faces charges for alleged “inappropriate acts” with underage victims, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office and Rapid City Police Department announced Tuesday morning.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man faces charges for alleged “inappropriate acts” with underage victims, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office and Rapid City Police Department announced Tuesday morning.

Jesse Victor Joseph, 44, was arrested on June 18 after a “lengthy investigation” by the two law enforcement agencies.

 Jesse Victor Joseph
Jesse Joseph 

The agencies said investigators determined Joseph communicated with and associated with multiple underage individuals and provided alcoholic beverages, vaping products, money “and other items over an extended period of time in an attempt to coerce them into inappropriate acts,” the agencies said in a release on June 23.

The investigative team executed search warrants related to the reports on June 17. Authorities arrested Joseph on suspicion of solicitation of a minor, contributing to the delinquency of a minor and furnishing an alcoholic beverage to a person under the age of 18.

“While this case has resulted in criminal charges and Joseph’s subsequent arrest, information garnered in the ongoing investigation leads investigators to believe there may be additional victims,” the agencies said in the release.

Anyone with information they believe may be related to the case is encouraged to contact Det. Karen Bicskei or Investigator Parker Frederick at 605- 394-6115.

The Rapid City Police Department and Pennington County Sheriff's Office said they are being assisted by the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force, the Department of Homeland Security, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and the Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office.

Joseph remains at the Pennington County Jail, held on a $50,000 cash-only bond, according to jail records. South Dakota court records show he made his initial appearance on Monday, June 22, and is due back in court at 1:30 p.m. on July 7. Sealed court filings show a pair of no contact orders.

No attorney was listed for Joseph as of Tuesday morning.

title: Helen Ackerson
_full_text:
May 6, 1938 - June 20, 2026

Helen Fern (Haugan) Ackerson was born on May 6, 1938, in St. Paul, Minnesota, to Helmuth and Anna Pegorsch. She grew up alongside her older sister, JoAnn, with whom she shared a very close bond. The sisters loved singing together in the choir at House of Hope Church and shared a lifelong passion for horses.

Helen attended Macalester College, where she earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in Religious Studies. To help support her education, she worked in Admissions at Miller Hospital. It was there she met Dr. Haakon Haugan, a radiology intern. They were married in 1961 and soon moved to the Black Hills of South Dakota to raise their family. They were blessed with three daughters: Joan, Ruth, and Mary.

The Black Hills became the backdrop for Helen's greatest joys. She and Haakon eventually purchased ranch land, and Helen devoted herself to family life and horsemanship. Her happiest years were spent training horses, supporting her daughters in riding, and traveling together to horse shows.

In 1988, the Westberry Trails fire devastated their forested ranch in the Black Hills. Following this loss, Helen and Haakon relocated to Williston, North Dakota, for a fresh start. Haakon worked as a radiologist at the local hospital, and Helen quickly built new friendships through her shared love of horses. Tragically, Haakon passed away in 1990.

In 1994, Helen returned to the Black Hills to be near her daughters. She once again found joy in the familiar landscape, spending cherished time with family, horses, and many adventures in the hills. She was especially proud of her three grandsons and loved supporting them at their soccer games and sharing her horses with them.

In 2004, Helen married her longtime friend, Ronald Ackerson. They began their life together in a cabin near Deadwood, South Dakota, and shared many adventures. Later, they moved to Spearfish, where they opened Yesterdays antique store and enjoyed several years as business owners, building friendships with the community.

Following a severe stroke in November 2025, Helen's health declined. In her quieter days, she found comfort in bird watching and spending time with her daughter's horses, Scout and Chief. We are grateful for all of those quiet days of reflection on a life well lived.

In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made in Helen's honor to Rainbow Bible Ranch, a summer camp in Sturgis, SD, dedicated to teaching horsemanship and Christian values.

Helen was preceded in death by her husband, Dr. Haakon Haugan of Rapid City; her sister, JoAnn Enstrom of California; and her daughter, Joan Pillen of Sturgis.

She is survived by her husband, Ronald Ackerson; daughters, Ruth Haugan and Mary (Alan) Anderson; son-in-law, Jubal Pillen; and grandsons, Haakon Anderson, Henry Anderson, and Holden Anderson.

A memorial service will be held at Kinkade Funeral Chapel on Friday, June 26th at 1:00 p.m. Please visit:

www.KinkadeFunerals.com

title: South Dakota Republican Party blocks journalist from attending Thune and Mullin speeches
description: The South Dakota Republican Party blocked journalists including Searchlight from attending speeches by U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Thursday night during the party’s state convention.
_full_text:
The South Dakota Republican Party blocked journalists including Searchlight from attending speeches by U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Thursday night during the party’s state convention.

South Dakota Searchlight completed an online registration days ago and received an email reply granting permission to attend. The party’s state convention started Thursday and lasts through Saturday at The Monument in Rapid City. 

An FAQ page on the party’s convention website includes the question, “Is there a place for press in Rushmore Hall and Lacroix?” The answer says, “Yes. There are areas set aside for the press in both rooms.” Thune and Mullin spoke in Rushmore Hall. The page also says reporters can apply for credentials.

Pennington County Republican Chairwoman Amy Wagner replied within minutes of receiving Searchlight’s form submission Saturday, writing in an email, “That opportunity is available. There will be a press box in both rooms. You will need to check in at the registration desk to get a press pass.”

At the event, Searchlight showed several party officials the email confirming permission to attend, and spoke with Wagner and other party officials and officeholders. Several said they were having problems with other people who registered as media but weren’t from what the state party considers legitimate outlets.

 062626-nws-sl-convention-p1.jpg
A view through the window of a closed door as U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks to the South Dakota Republican State Convention on June 25, 2026, at The Monument events center in Rapid City. South Dakota Searchlight completed an online press registration form and received a confirmation email but was denied entrance to speeches by Mullin and U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota. 

Wagner apologized to Searchlight and said, “I didn’t realize that they weren’t going to allow press tonight.” Wagner said it was the decision of “the chairman,” a reference to State Party Chairman Jim Eschenbaum.

Eschenbaum did not immediately respond to a text message Thursday night from Searchlight.

Friday evening’s schedule includes keynote speeches by the two candidates in the July 28 runoff election for the party’s nomination for governor — businessman Toby Doeden and Gov. Larry Rhoden.

Searchlight asked Wagner if journalists will be allowed to attend those speeches.

“I don’t know what his decision on that is,” Wagner said, referring to Eschenbaum. “It’s a possibility that we will. You might want to check tomorrow.”

title: ‘Sense of Service’: Gov. Rhoden appoints new Seventh Circuit Judge
description: Five months since now South Dakota Supreme Court Justice Robert Gusinsky left the halls of the Pennington County Courthouse and handed the reigns to Seventh Circuit Court Presiding Judge Heidi Linngren, the courthouse is preparing to welcome a new face to its roster.
_full_text:
Five months since now South Dakota Supreme Court Justice Robert Gusinsky left the halls of the Pennington County Courthouse and handed the reigns to Seventh Circuit Court Presiding Judge Heidi Linngren, the courthouse is preparing to welcome a new face to its roster.

On Thursday, June 25, South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden appointed Cassidy Stalley as a circuit court judge in the Seventh Circuit, which includes all of Pennington, Custer, Fall River and Oglala Lakota counties.

“Cassidy is a bright, talented, and highly respected professional who is deeply passionate about serving South Dakota,” Rhoden said. “It is my honor to appoint her to the Seventh Circuit. I trust she will lead her courtroom with excellence.”

Stalley is a civil attorney for Nooney & Solay whose represented individuals and businesses in state and federal court for 15 years.

“I was just very grateful for Gov. Rhoden in appointing me and trusting me to appoint me to the bench,” Stalley said. “It’s a great honor. I’m very grateful for my mentors, my partners that have got me to where I am in my career and to be able to step onto the bench.”

A Rapid City native, she graduated magna cum laude from the University of Mary and earned her law degree with honors from the University of South Dakota School of Law before serving as a judicial clerk for the Second Judicial Circuit for year.

“I fell in love with litigation and arguing, advocating for my clients, researching the law and figuring out the law,” Stalley told the Journal. “Especially in civil litigation, it’s kind of like a big puzzle and so you’re constantly putting together those puzzle pieces and figuring out the facts and how the facts apply to the law and how to best present that to either a jury or the judge or even opposing counsel to get a good resolution for your client.”

Stalley, along with her husband and children, moved back to Rapid City after her work as a judicial clerk. She’s been working in private practice since.

Stalley was named Outstanding Young Lawyer by the Pennington County Bar Association in 2019 and has been included in the Great Plains Super Lawyers Rising Stars list, as well as Best Lawyers in America — One to Watch since 2019.

Outside of the courtroom, Stalley is a coach for St. Thomas More High School girl’s soccer team. She also served two full terms as the president of the Rapid City Catholic School System Board, which ended in June. Stalley said she will be maintaining her position on the soccer field as she adjusts to her new position in the courtroom.

“My faith is important to me, but also my family,” Stalley said. “I was raised with a big sense of service to my community. So I’ve always showed up and given back for the things that I feel passionate about… I just have a strong sense of service to my community, which is Pennington County and Rapid City, which is why I’m going up to the bench. That sense of service drove me to want to be on the bench.”

Stalley is posed to join a new chapter at the Pennington County Courthouse. When Gusinsky moved on to the supreme court, he expressed excitement for a new era of judges, noting that everyone he started with has either moved on or died.

Stalley said she is thankful for Gusinsky, Linngren and all of the other judges for marking the path forward.

“I’m just so grateful for judges like him (Gusinsky) that have showed me — as a young lawyer learning from him, being in front of him — what it means to be a good judge,” Stalley said. “It’s people like Judge Gusinsky and Judge Linngren and many others that have really impacted how I view the bench and what I’m going to strive to be like.”

Stalley said she is not sure if she will be handling criminal or civil cases with her new position, her responsibilities are up to Linngren. Stalley’s state date is yet to be determined.

The Journal reached out to Linngren about Stalley’s state date and responsibilities, but did not receive a reply by the time of publication.

title: Oglala Tribe members reflect on Battle of Little Bighorn, look to future
description: CROW AGENCY, Mont. — On the eve of the sesquicentennial anniversary of the Battle of Little Bighorn (also known as Battle of Greasy Grass), during celebrations of victory for Indigenous people fighting for sovereignty and protecting their way of life during the American Indian Wars, members of the Oglala Sioux Tribe reflected on the past and looked to the future.
_full_text:
CROW AGENCY, Mont. — On the eve of the sesquicentennial anniversary of the Battle of Little Bighorn (also known as Battle of Greasy Grass), during celebrations of victory for Indigenous people fighting for sovereignty and protecting their way of life during the American Indian Wars, members of the Oglala Sioux Tribe reflected on the past and looked to the future. 

"For the 200th celebration, I'm not going to be here. These kids are going to be here, and they need to know why we're here, and why it's important, who we are, and being proud of being Native," Oglala Sioux Tribe Tribal Education Agency Director Dayna Brave Eagle said.

On June 24, hundreds of tribal members of various nations poured into the Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument in Crow Agency in Montana to celebrate the anniversary of the battle.

 Frank Star Comes Out
Oglala Sioux Tribe President Star Comes Out helps families and youth navigate the campgrounds.   

"We need to remind the United States government that we are here to stay; we're all survivors of what they tried to do to us in the past, that's commit genocide on our tribal nations here. Remember that. Be proud of who you are, represent your people with pride. You all have proud last names, proud family histories ... I hope you represent what you learned from what you're seeing today," OST President Frank Star Comes Out said. “You're going to carry that down to the youth behind you.”

The June 25, 1876, the battle was a major conflict of the American Indian Wars.

 Youth Camp
More than five tipis were set up for the youth camp, a separate area meant to keep the youth safe and in a learning environment, at the Battle of Little Bighorn site. 

This battle was a historic victory for the tribal nations as they killed Lt. Col George Armstrong Custer. Per the National Parks Service, however, the battle was “a momentary victory for the Lakota and Cheyenne." The death of Custer and his troops became a rallying point for the United States to increase their efforts to force Native people onto reservation lands. With more troops in the field, Lakota hunting grounds were invaded by Army expeditionary forces determined to conquer the Northern Plains Indians. Most of the declared "hostiles" surrendered within one year of the fight, and the Black Hills were taken by the U.S. government without compensation to the Lakota.

 Youth Camp
Quinlan Canty (Catawba) and Dayna Brave Eagle (Oglala) stand in front of the youth camp. 

 Celestine Stadnick
Little Wound School Principal Celestine Stadnick joined the Oglala camp at the Battle of Little Bighorn camp in Montana. 

 Youth Camp
The youth are joined by adults for days filled with activities and programs centered around Indigenous teachings and practices.  

In 1980, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the Sioux were entitled to $102 million (roughly over $1 billion in today’s dollars) for the wrongful seizure, but the nations have yet to accept compensation as they seek land ownership back.

Youth camp

For the 150th anniversary of the battle, tribes like the Oglala have been working in partnership with both tribes involved and not involved in the famous battle.

Brave Eagle said she invited all 20 schools on Pine Ridge to participate, and all but two schools showed up and she invited all the night tribes in South Dakota to participate. 

She also invited tribes outside the Plains region, with one tribal nation bringing in an estimated 24 students from the Catawba Nation.

 Youth Camps
A tipi setup at a sight on Crow Agency apart of small-scale reenactments of the Battle of Little Bighorn. 

Brave Eagle said she organized the youth camp at the Bighorn site to uphold Indigenous traditions and instill them into youth through programs. The camp features education from elders, lessons by Indigenous artists and lessons in making smudge kits, beading and shawl making.

“We're doing this all in a good way," Brave Eagle said.

Catawba Tribe Councilman Quinlan Canty, who traveled with a group of students from South Carolina, said the camp is about community for all tribal nations.

"Even though we are on the East Coast, it's important that we come together and show support. I think that's how things on Turtle Island are supposed to be, we're stronger together. We should work together, be together and share experiences and knowledge," Canty said. “All those things help our youth grow.”

Canty said it took six months of communication between the two tribes to coordinate getting two dozen students to Montana. 

"As I said, I won't be here for the 200th celebration, but these kids are going to be, and so we need to have them be experienced to what this is. So at the 200th celebration, Quinlan's kids and my grandkids will be here with their kids and grandkids, and they will say, ‘Remember when our dad and our grandma brought us here?" Brave Heart said.

Women in leadership

Little Wound Middle School Principal Celestine Stadnick, who is also running for state Senate in District 27 — which encompasses part of the Pine Ridge Reservation — also participated in the encampment near the Bighorn National Monument.

"This is the first time since the Battle of Little Bighorn, 150 years ago, where all of our tribes are uniting in this place. It's a historical moment, and to honor our ancestors and to be part of it is almost like a rebirth," Stadnick said while discussing her reason to travel to the camp.

She continued, saying, "There were not many nations in this world that defeated the United States Army, and we were one of them. It was this battle, one of the last moments where we were a free people. After that, my people, the Oglalas, had to move onto our reservation, which is technically considered a prisoner of war camp to this day.”

Stadnick said after the Oglalas were forced onto reservations after the Wounded Knee Massacre, a prophecy was foretold of how the future generation would thwart the dangers and harm from Western society.

"We are currently in the seventh generation and you see a lot of matriarchs rising, our people always were matriarchal in nature. But through colonization, we were taught that the leadership is with men," Celestine said emotionally. "So us finding that balance back is a really strong indicator that balance will be restored. One of those big things is finding a balance of traditional Lakota ways but also integrated with the new world that we're living in, and education is the highest, highest form of that."

She said her efforts to become a legislator are to aid the South Dakota Education system.

"We have to learn how to walk with our old ways, but also how to operate in a new world, and our education system in South Dakota is not good enough. It doesn't serve anyone; it doesn't matter if you're Native or not. And reforming our educational system in South Dakota is one of the big things that has to happen," Stadnick said.

She concluded by reflecting on the anniversary of the battle and what it means for the future. Stadnick said the people no longer fight in the same way they did 150 years ago, the real meaningful fight is by making sure everyone has an education to have a better chance at life.

"The lack of opportunity when it comes to education keeps us where we are. So, moving forward, it's taking on those barriers, imagine if we had more Indigenous legislators and lawyers. They would be the ones that are going to take down barriers with and for us," Stadnick said.

 PHOTOS: Tribes set up for the Battle of Little Bighorn 150th anniversary
It’s the 150th anniversary of the Battle of Little Bighorn (also known as the Battle of Greasy Grass) and more than a dozen tribal nations are participating in this year's sesquicentennial anniversary in Montana. This battle is notable as U.S. military leader Lt. Col George Armstrong Custer was killed in a period of U.S. history known as the American Indian Wars. As of Tuesday, June 23 there are an estimated 75 people already at the original campsite that the Arapaho, Northern Cheyenne and Lakota stayed in the 1876 battle, with more to come.

title: Mayday Health argues abortion law violates free speech in lawsuit; org and state await decision by federal judge
description: More than six months after launching a gas station ad campaign about the availability of abortion pills for South Dakotans, a nonprofit health organization is back in court with the state.
_full_text:
More than six months after launching a gas station ad campaign about the availability of abortion pills for South Dakotans, a nonprofit health organization is back in court with the state.

This time Mayday Health is arguing a law set to go into effect on July 1 violates the First Amendment.

House Bill 1274, which was signed by Gov. Larry Rhoden in March, prohibits the dispensing, distribution, sale or advertisement of certain articles or things for purposes of an unlawful abortion and provides a criminal and civil penalty therefor.

 Page A8 eedition image
Nonprofit Mayday health launched a four-week, statewide "ad blitz" on dec. 1, 2025, at gas stations in south dakota informing women about abortion pills. 

Both sides presented their arguments, followed by witness testimony, on Tuesday, June 23, at the Andrew W Bogue Federal Building in Rapid City.

“The state absolutely hates our speech,” Mayday’s attorney Jim Leach, of Rapid City, said during opening statements.

Leach argued the new law unconstitutionally targets free speech about abortion and that Mayday providing information about abortion pills isn’t a commercial transaction.

Attorney General Marty Jackley countered that Mayday’s website and its components, such as its since-removed chatbox called Charlie, "leads the user to abortion pills” and is not protected by the U.S. Constitution.

“The First Amendment does not protect a comment that elicits criminal conduct,” Jackley said.

On March 9, the state settled its lawsuit against Mayday Health, with the nonprofit agreeing to remove any advertisements still up in South Dakota and to not go forward with placing additional advertisements "within the physical borders of South Dakota that aid, abet or solicit illegal conduct as established by law."

As the case settled and the Legislature was on its way to approving House Bill 1274, the nonprofit — along with Nancy Turbak Berr, abortion rights advocate and former Democratic South Dakota lawmaker — filed a lawsuit challenging the new law.

Mayday Health

Starting on Dec. 1, 2025, Mayday Health launched a four-week, statewide ad blitz at gas stations informing women, "if you are pregnant and don't want to be, you still have a choice. Abortion pills are safe, FDA-approved, and accessible by mail — even in abortion-banned states like South Dakota."

As of June 24, the home page of Mayday Health asks in bold letters, “What do you need?” Underneath that is four buttons: “Abortion,” “Morning after pills,” “Birth Control” and “Gender-Affirming Care.”

The “Abortion” button routes to a page that links to five websites that offer abortion pills.

Among the most popular abortion pills are mifepristone and misoprostol, which are used in tandem, according to reporting by KFF, a nonprofit health policy research, polling and news organization.

In response to the ad campaign, on Dec. 9, 2025, Rhoden announced he'd asked Jackley to investigate the effort, "which appears to conflict with South Dakota's proud pro-life stance."

In Jackley’s cease-and-desist letter to Mayday the attorney general said, "Abortions are prohibited in South Dakota under SDCL 22-17-5.1, except for specific, extenuating circumstances."

"SDCL 22-17-5.1 specifically criminalizes administering to and prescribing or procuring for 'any pregnant female any medicine, drug, or substance ... to procure an abortion,'" he said.

South Dakota's abortion ban became effective after the U.S. Supreme Court's Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization decision in 2022 that overturned the 1973 Roe V. Wade ruled that solidified the right to abortion. The South Dakota exception allows abortions to preserve the life of a pregnant woman. It does not have exceptions for rape or incest.

 Andrew W. Bogue Federal Courthouse court
The Andrew W. Bogue Federal Building on Ninth Street in downtown Rapid City.  

"Your advertisement directs South Dakota consumers to resources that insinuate abortion-inducing pills are legal in South Dakota," Jackley said in the letter.

Some of the argument for the lawsuit is partially built upon Turbak Berry purchasing a sweatshirt from Mayday’s website that states “They don’t want you to know this: You can still get abortion pills in 50 states. Learn more at mayday.health.”

Turbak Berry said her goal was to spread awareness and provide information when she got the sweatshirt, however, with the new law she alleged the state could now label the shirt as abortion-pill advertising and prosecute her for wearing it.

“I’m not trying to attract customers. I’m trying to disseminate information,” Turbak Berry said.

She said she didn’t trust the attorney general to not prosecute her, highlighting the current political climate. Jackley said he has not charged Turbak Berry nor does he plan to, stating “this is a courtroom, not a political theater.”

Leach then brought on Mayday Health’s Executive Director Leo Raisner. Raisner co-founded Mayday Health in 2022 after seeing a survey about how many people in the United States were unaware that abortion pills are available.

Raisner said the goal of the nonprofit was to provide information. Mayday does not profit from the sales of pill companies, nor if the user clicks on any of the listed links Mayday has attached to its website.

“We want to be a source of up-to-date and accurate information about abortion pills,” Raisner said.

Raisner said Mayday has about $2.3 million in funds from grants, contributions and about 1% of that amount is from merchandise sales. He said selling T-shirts, sweatshirts and other merchandise is just another way to spread their message.

He said Mayday does not promote abortion nor do they encourage anyone to have an abortion.

The state

After hours of testimony from the plaintiff’s side, the state brought in their first witness to show Mayday’s website is more than just a clearinghouse of information, but a “scheme” for people to obtain illegal drugs.

Office of the Attorney General's Division of Consumer Protection Investigator Kayla Klemann testified she investigated Mayday’s website on June 15. She said the website provided several links to abortion pill providers.

Klemann said she interacted with the website’s chatbot called Charlie, where she would input that she was 14 years old and 23 weeks and four days pregnant. The site never asked what state she lived in or if abortion pills are legal in her area. The chatbot told her abortion pills were not the best option for her, however, Klemann was allowed to go back and change her responses.

Raisner testified on Tuesday that the chatbot had been removed as of Sunday, June 21, with no intention of installing another chatbot on the website. The removal of the chatbot caused heated debate between both sides in the courtroom.

Leach argued the judge should only consider the website’s current state when making a decision on whether to make an order against the new law. Jackley said the chatbot’s past existence plays a prevalent role in the case and there is no guarantee that Mayday will not install another one down the line.

Klemann said during her investigation she found information from Mayday advising people to use mail-forwarding services to receive abortion pills. Raisner testified that information has been removed from Mayday’s site for several years.

The state’s next witness was a retired OB-GYN, Dr. Patti Geibink, who testified that prescribing abortion pills online without an in-person consultation can lead to unexpected risks and potentially be dangerous for someone who may have conditions that could lead to further complications. Geibink considers herself “pro-life,” and said buying medication from online is “not with informed consent.”

 Federal Courthouse Rapid City - wide angle - court
The Andrew W. Bogue Federal Building and United States Courthouse in Rapid City. 

South Dakota Searchlight reported another retired OB-GYN, Dr. Marvin Buehner, was brought in to testify for Mayday and Turbak. Buehner, who won awards for his “pro-choice” advocacy, testified abortion pills occur in "astoundingly small numbers” and that abortion pills are safe and effective.

According to Searchlight, Leach said during closing arguments that the state failed to prove Mayday committed a crime or engaged in commercial activity involving abortion pills, or provided misleading information. Leach said Mayday has only provided information that is vetted by experts and takes no part in selling the pills.

Jackley argued Mayday selects the content and links on its page, highlighting how they describe pill providers as “trusted partners” and instruct users how to illegally obtain abortion pills in South Dakota.

With the new law set to take effect next week, Mayday and Turbak Berry are seeking a temporary injunction that would prevent the state from enforcing the new law as the lawsuit proceeds. However, Jackley said he does not intend to press charges against Mayday between Tuesday’s hearing and the judge’s ruling.

U.S. District Judge Camela Theeler gave both parties until June 30 to file additional briefs and until July 3 for responses to the briefs. The judge will make a decision after that.

title: Rapid City teen arrested after crashing stolen car into a guardrail
description: A Rapid City teen was arrested Wednesday, June 24, after crashing a stolen pickup truck into a guardrail and fleeing the scene.
_full_text:
A Rapid City teen was arrested Wednesday, June 24, after crashing a stolen pickup truck into a guardrail and fleeing the scene.

Jessina Left Hand Bull, 18, was arrested on suspicion of second-degree eluding, possession of a stolen vehicle, possession of a controlled substance, possession of drug paraphernalia, leaving the scene of an accident, driving without a valid license and littering, and is also held on a Department of Corrections warrant, parole hold and two additional warrants.

According to court records, Left Hand Bull has two warrants for not appearing in court for a no driver’s license charge and for the purchase, possession or consumption of alcohol by a minor. No public records were available about Left Hand Bull’s parolee status.

At around 6:55 p.m., police saw a pickup that was reported stolen in a parking lot in the 1300 block of Atlas Street. As police attempted to make contact with the driver, who was tossing an item out of the window, the woman then shifted gears and sped out of the parking lot over a non-roadway portion of the area.

Police later located the truck, abandoned behind one of the apartment buildings, after it struck a guardrail. Witnesses told police that the woman fled into a nearby apartment after driving past a nearby playground at a high rate of speed while children were present.

Officers made contact with the occupants inside the apartment and located the woman, identifying her as Left Hand Bull, and they detained her. A search of the bag that was tossed out the driver’s window turned up methamphetamine and associated paraphernalia.

As of Thursday, June 25, Left Hand Bull was in the Pennington County Jail, however, none of her charges were listed. None of the new charges were listed in state court records yet.

title: It's official: President Trump to attend Mount Rushmore fireworks celebration
description: President Donald Trump will attend the America 250 Mount Rushmore fireworks celebration.
_full_text:
President Donald Trump will attend the America 250 Mount Rushmore fireworks celebration.

South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden and U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds confirmed the visit on Thursday, June 25. The visit had long been expected but is now official.

“It is my honor to welcome President Trump to the great state of South Dakota — the freest state in a nation founded on the principles of freedom,” Rhoden said in a release. “Together, we will throw the biggest birthday party ever for our nation and celebrate America’s legacy of freedom, liberty, and justice for all.”

The fireworks celebration will be held on Thursday, July 3, in partnership with the U.S. Department of the Interior and the National Park Service. Rhoden and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum previously signed a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) to move forward with planning for the fireworks celebration, the governor's office said.

 Trump talks at Rushmore 2020
President Trump spoke in 2020 at Mount Rushmore ahead of the fireworks display. 

“I’m looking forward to attending the fireworks show at Mount Rushmore on July 3 with President Trump,” Rounds said in a release from his office. “In South Dakota, we don’t just climb mountains — we carve them. Thanks to President Trump and his team, fireworks will once again be displayed over Mount Rushmore for the first time since 2020, just in time for the 250th anniversary of America’s founding. There’s no better place to celebrate than at Mount Rushmore in South Dakota. Thank you to everyone who has been working hard to put on a great event."

“There’s no better place to celebrate the 4th of July than Mount Rushmore, and I’m looking forward to welcoming (the president) back to celebrate America 250,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune said in a Twitter post.

Tickets are required for attendance at the event, and they were distributed through a public lottery that ended on April 12. About 4,800 participants will be able to attend the event, according to the South Dakota Department of Tourism.

The department said "to enhance the visitor experience and prioritize safety and security," attendance has been reduced at the event, compared to the 2020 fireworks at Rushmore. Trump also attended in 2020.

The department also said the National Park Service has conducted an environmental assessment for the event. "Protection of the Black Hills and Mount Rushmore National Memorial remains central to planning efforts for the July 3 celebration. Planning partners continue to coordinate closely to ensure a safe and responsible event."

More information about the event, including FAQs, can be found on the National Park Service website.

title: Get ready for Rapid City’s Real America Birthday Bash
byline: MIKE BROWNLEE and TANYA MANUS Journal staff
description: Can you believe it’s almost July?
_full_text:
Can you believe it’s almost July?

Rapid City’s America 250 celebration team has been working on a series of events for a year, and on Wednesday, June 24, officials provided additional details about Rapid City’s Real America Birthday Bash.

“When I first became mayor, I started talking about, America's 250th birthday is going to be coming in 2026. I want Rapid City to be a premier destination to celebrate this great country of ours. And thanks to this great team behind me and a great community that we live in, it is possible,” Mayor Jason Salamun said during a media availability going over details of the events at Main Street Square in downtown Rapid City. “Rapid City is a special city, and so it's no surprise that Rapid City would celebrate the best of America right here in the Black Hills of South Dakota.”

 062526-nws-america-p2.JPG
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun discusses America 250 festivities in Rapid City during a media availability on Wednesday, June 24, at Main Street Square. 

The series of events will be held July 1-5, with the closure of Sixth Street between Main and Omaha streets during portions of the day July 2-4.

Per the city, the Birthday Bash includes a community parade, patriotic drone show, multi-day downtown festival, a headline concert by country music artist Chancey Williams, a Mount Rushmore fireworks display viewing party featuring regional performer Brandon Jones, a concert by the Air Force Academy Band, a Kids’ Zone, Touch-A-Truck exhibits, a concert by the Rapid City Municipal Band, local and regional music performers, food vendors, exhibits, historical re-enactors and readings, and a Freedom 5K Run.

“We're going to host a multi-day festival built around one of the most significant moments in our nation's history, America's 250th birthday, and there's no better place to celebrate it than right here in a city where presidents line our downtown streets and Mount Rushmore is right in our backyard,” Visit Rapid City CEO Ally Formanek said. “America only turns 250 one time, so we plan to give it the celebration it deserves.”

Speaking after Formanek, Bret Mattice with the city noted about the events, “They are totally free. They are family-friendly, so grab your lawn chairs, grab your blankets, grab your friends and get ready for an incredible couple of days filled with American spirit.”

The festivities kick off with a 7 p.m. performance by the U.S. Air Force Academy Band on Wednesday, July 1, at the Memorial Park Bandshell. The city will host a Fourth of July parade at 7 p.m. on Thursday, July 2, with a route through downtown Rapid City. The event features the same route as the annual Festival of Lights parade, with road closures and parking restrictions on Main Street and St. Joseph Street from Seventh Street to St. Patrick Street in the evening to accommodate parade staging and the parade itself.

 062526-nws-america-p3.JPG
“We're going to host a multi-day festival built around one of the most significant moments in our nation's history, America's 250th birthday, and there's no better place to celebrate it than right here in a city where presidents line our downtown streets and Mount Rushmore is right in our backyard,” Visit Rapid City CEO Ally Formanek said. “America only turns 250 one time, so we plan to give it the celebration it deserves.” 

“This is the first parade that has been offered in Rapid City since 2019 and we've had a phenomenal turnout. This year we will have over 100 floats that are from individuals, businesses, civic organizations, nonprofits, our community, coming together to celebrate this important event,” parade organizer Connie Olson, the Festival of Lights parade chair, said during Wednesday’s event. “(It) would not be possible for us to host a parade without the support that we received from the Rapid City Police Department and thousands of volunteers who are making this week possible.”

Salamun said organizers planned the Rapid City parade on July 2 to avoid conflicting with the annual Fourth of July parades in towns throughout the Black Hills.

A patriotic drone show, launching from Central High School, will begin at 9:30 p.m., with Memorial Park the best place to watch. Salamun told people to expect a “goosebumps moment” during the drone show.

 062526-nws-america-p5.JPG
“This is the first parade that has been offered in Rapid City since 2019 and we've had a phenomenal turnout. This year we will have over 100 floats that are from individuals, businesses, civic organizations, nonprofits, our community, coming together to celebrate this important event,” parade organizer Connie Olson, the Festival of Lights parade chair, said during Wednesday’s event. 

July 3 features an 8 p.m. performance by Brandon Jones and 9:30 p.m. Mount Rushmore Fireworks livestream watch party, both at Main Street Square. July 4 features a Main Street Square concert by headliner Chancey Williams at 8 p.m., with the Rapid City fireworks show starting at 9:30 p.m.

The Rapid City Council appropriated $250,000 to help pay for the Independence Day events, while fundraising had brought in around $230,000 to date, Rapid City Public Information Officer Darrell Shoemaker said.

 Mayor Jason Salamun
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun discusses America 250. 

Plus, the city’s America 250 committee is still looking for volunteers. Individuals can learn more and sign up at JustServe Rapid City America250 Volunteer Page. Go to justserve.org for more information.

“What's going to make it great is the American spirit that will be alive and well here in Rapid City. There is no country like America, there's no country left like America. This is an amazing place and so to celebrate 250 years of American independence and our freedoms right here in South Dakota is really tremendous,” Salamun said. “We are the best of America, and that in Rapid City, whatever your dreams are, it is possible here. And that's what the American dream is all about. That's what we're going to celebrate in a very big way all year long, but of course, culminating right here around the Independence Day holiday as we celebrate America's 250th birthday.”

title: James “Jamey” P. Brunsch
_full_text:
July 7, 1967 - June 21, 2026

BOX ELDER--James "Jamey" P. Brunsch was born July 7, 1967, in Martin, S.D., to Laurette Pourier and James P. Brunsch Sr. He was surrounded by loved ones when he made his journey to the Lord on Sunday, June 21, 2026, at the age of 58.

After graduating from Wall High School in 1985, Jamey enlisted in the US Navy (1986), where he traveled the world as an Anti-Submarine Warfare Aircrewman. Once separating from the military in 1992, Jamey went on to earn his degree in Electrical Engineering Technology at Southern Illinois University. After starting his family in San Diego, Jamey returned to South Dakota to continue growing his family and legacy. In 2001, Jamey founded Memsense, LLC, where he was able to continue his passion of design and engineering.

Throughout life, Jamey loved team roping, mountain biking, running, blasting his music, dancing, hiking, building (literally anything), spending time outdoors, and most importantly being with family. Many would describe Jamey as loving, compassionate, witty, hardworking, gearhead, jokester, fearless, brilliant, generous, and empathetic.

Jamey is survived by his loving wife, Tara and their children, Cade (Makayla), Kalena, Kayli, Logan (Amelia), America (Zack), Zach, Brock, and Tack. His memory lives on in his grandchildren, Mabel, Opal, Hazel, Boaz, Jamison, Rayel, Estelle, Laweson, Kade, and Silas.

Jamey is remembered by his father, Jim (Jill); father and mother-in-law, Mel and Beth; as well as his siblings, Tawney, Chad (Crystal), Grady (Kalee), Hayley, Jaimee (Neil), Katie, and Grant. He will also be remembered by many loving nieces, nephews, cousins, and friends.

Jamey was preceded in death by his late wife, Karen; his mom, Laurette; his uncle, Jack; grandparents; and many other loved ones.

Visitation will be held on Tuesday, June 30, from 5 tp 7 p.m., at the New Underwood Community Church, 300 S Baily Ave.

His Celebration of Life will be held Wednesday, July 1, at 11 a.m. at the New Underwood High School, 300 E Ash St.

Burial, with military honors rendered by the U.S. Navy and VFW Post 1273, will follow at New Underwood Cemetery, 16122 Highway 14/16.

title: Greg Bartron
description: August 15, 1950 - June 19, 2026
_full_text:
August 15, 1950 - June 19, 2026

Robert Gregory "Greg" Bartron, or known to his close friends as Black Bart, 75, passed away at his home in Rapid City on Thursday, June 18.

Greg was born on August 15, 1950, to Dr. Bob & Jean Bartron in Watertown, SD.

Greg lived a life marked by intelligence, service, humor, and a healthy appreciation for the outdoors. The youngest of three children, he graduated from Watertown Senior High School & went on to receive an undergraduate degree from the University of Colorado Boulder where he met and would later marry the love of his life, Mary Ellen Harman.

Greg continued his education at the University of South Dakota Law School, which led him to settle down in Watertown, raise a family and practice law for the next 20 years. During his time as an attorney, he had the opportunity to work as an assistant attorney general under Governor Bill Janklow, and was also appointed the states attorney for Codington County. He was passionate about helping others navigate difficult situations and believed that everyone deserved to be heard. Greg was intelligent, stubborn when he thought he was right, quick with an opinion, and never afraid of a spirited discussion. He had a sense of humor that could catch you off guard and a presence that filled a room.

Greg and Mary had always loved the Black Hills and decided to relocate to the Rapid City area in 1997 where Greg became deeply involved in the Rapid City community. Through his leadership with the West River foundation, he worked to support charitable initiatives and strengthen opportunities for people across western South Dakota. He was a dedicated member of many Alcoholics Anonymous groups in the Rapid City area, as well as being heavily involved with the Pennington County Sherrif's Office Friendship House, a residential treatment facility for people dealing with drug and alcohol addiction, where he generously shared his time, guidance, and encouragement with countless individuals on their recovery journeys.

Through his service, mentorship, and compassion, Greg positively affected many lives and earned the respect and gratitude of those who knew him. Greg found great joy in the outdoors, especially goose, pheasant & duck hunting. Greg loved the quiet before dawn, the company of good friends, and the excitement that comes with a flock appearing on the horizon. He enjoyed fishing on the Missouri River, watching the sunset over the beautiful Black Hills from his back deck, reminiscing about his childhood on Lake Kampeska, spending time with family and a good carrot cake.

Greg is survived by his children Ashley Romme (Scott) of Windsor CO and Grayson of Rapid City; sisters Lynn Schaefer (Larry) of Watertown and Stephanie Miscione of Carbondale CO; his grandchildren Sara, Sydney, Alex, Madi, Brekken & Addisyn; and many nieces & nephews. He was preceded in death by his wife of 56 years, Mary; parents Dr. Bob & Jean Bartron; and his beloved grandson Jack.

Though we mourn his passing, we celebrate a life well lived. Greg leaves behind a legacy of service, dedication, laughter, and love that will continue through those who knew him best.

A visitation will be held in Rapid City in honor of Greg at Kirk Funeral Home (1501 E Minnesota Street) on Thursday July 2, from 11-1pm. Greg will be laid to rest in Watertown at a later date.

title: Evanell Janousek
description: November 7, 1930 - May 24, 2026
_full_text:
November 7, 1930 - May 24, 2026

Evanell Sarah Kuglar Janousek passed away peacefully on Sunday, May 24, 2026 in Henderson, Nev. Evanell was born November 7, 1930 to Lawrence and Dorothy (Zurn) Kugler in Underwood, Minn. On April 8, 1953, Evanell married Raymond Janousek and moved to Rapid City, S.D.

In the 1960's she began oil painting and sculpting. She was especially proud of her smaller sculptures (called Uniques) and their inspirational accompanying poems. The opening for the Uniques was held at the Rapid City Civic Art Gallery and "Uniques by Evanell, Original Miniature Sculptures with Inspirational Poems" was later published. Her faith and love of God were ever present and guiding light through the years.

She contributed to the community as a Girl Scout leader, room mother, and was involved in Jaycettes, Beta Sigma Phi Sorority, Knights Ladies, Purple Hats and Dakota Artists Guild. For three years, she wrote "Life After 65" columns in the Rapid City Journal.

Evanell loved dancing with her husband, Raymond, well into their sixties and enjoyed October Fests with friends. They were especially proud of dancing in The Nutcracker production with their daughter, Karen, and granddaughter, Lindsey – three generations.

Evanell and Raymond were married seventy-two years.

Evanell is survived by daughters, Teri (Randy) Hammerquist, Billings, Mont., Karen (Steve) Waltman, Henderson, Nev.; and son, James (Cathy) Janousek, Libertyville, Ill.

Also surviving are grandchildren, Brad (Erika) Hammerquist, Bryan (Erin) Hammerquist, Lindsey (Ryan) LaBarge, Ashley Waltman, Sarah (Matt) Miotti, Jeff (Haley) Janousek, Laura (Alex) Janousek Blacketor; and great-grandchildren, Linnea, Evanelle, Maisy, Sawyer, Cassidy, Arlo, Miley, Addison, and Bennett. Evanell was preceded in death by her husband, Raymond, parents, three sisters and one brother.

A Funeral Mass was held at St. Francis of Assisi Catholic Church, Henderson, Nev., on Friday, June 26, 2026 at 10 a.m. Burial will follow at the Southern Nevada Veterans Memorial Cemetery, Boulder City, Nev.
