title: South Dakota GOP delegation shoots down proposed Thune censure
description: A resolution to rebuke and censure U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune failed in a voice vote on the 2026 South Dakota Republican Convention floor on Friday afternoon, June 26.
_full_text:
A resolution to rebuke and censure U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune failed in a voice vote on the 2026 South Dakota Republican Convention floor on Friday afternoon, June 26.

The party’s Resolutions Committee recommended the state’s delegates adopt the resolution, but the majority of delegates voted against. There was applause and whistling coming from the floor after the vote.

 Sen. John Thune censure vote during SDGOP convention
The South Dakota Republican delegation votes down a censure resolution aimed at Senate Majority Leader John Thune. 

The title of Resolution 012: “A resolution rebuking Senator John Thune of his performance as U.S. Senate Majority Leader, and censuring him until the SAVE America Act becomes law.”

“We all like story lines, even in politics, of how things progress, and this is sort of part of a stick and carrot situation,” said Minnehaha County delegate Michael Stangeland, who authored the stick, during the committee meeting. “The stick is the censure, and the possible failure is that the Save Act doesn't get passed, and Senator Thune has to deal with the fact that he is remembered as a senator who could not get it done, especially going into the upcoming election.”

What are party resolutions? 
Resolutions are formal statements or positions on policy, party principles, or issues—to be considered and potentially adopted by the convention delegates. Its objective is to ensure that resolutions reflect the party’s values, priorities, and strategic goals while fostering unity and clarity within the party.

The SAVE America Act would require voters to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections and photo identification when voting. The U.S. House has passed the bill, but it has yet to make it out of the Senate. Delegates on the floor on Friday in Rapid City spoke in favor of the SAVE America Act, even if they didn’t support the censure.

Todd Wilkinson, delegate from Kingsbury County, said on the floor, “I have faith that the people we put there are going to do their job, and if they're not, they're going to be voted out. That's the checks and balances.”

Other delegates expressed concerns for the message a censure sends and called for unity.

“It is the RNC's responsibility and duty to deliver a big win for President Trump in the midterms, and this only gives a very negative message coming out of our convention, and really does hand the Democrats a win in this,” said Heidi Engelhart, South Dakota Republican national commiteewoman.

Sandra Kading, Pennington County delegate, “There's really nothing that's going to be achieved by this resolution. In fact, it's going to harm in so many ways. The one thing you can say about the opposition party is they're united, where the Republicans party seems to circle, go into a circle and shoot inward, and that needs to stop, regardless of how you feel about John Thune.”

 Stangeland
Minnehaha County delegate Michael Stangeland appeared before the Resolutions Committee during the South Dakota Republican Party Convention to read a resolution to censure Sen. John Thune. 

Trump recently refused to sign a bipartisan housing reform bill until the SAVE America Act is passed, ABC News reported. The president has pushed Republicans in the Senate to eliminate or modify the filibuster to get the bill through, while Thune has maintained Republicans don't have the votes to do so.

In support of the resolution, Stuart Willett of Minnehaha County said on Friday, “We have the House, we have the Senate, we have the president, and here it is, 2026, and we still haven't passed this, which was our number one concern in 2020 through 2024. So we have to do something. That's why I support this.”

Filibustering is a tactic to delay a floor vote on a bill by prolonging debate. Under current law, it takes 60 senators to end a filibuster. If filibustering is taken out of lawmakers’ toolboxes, a simple majority will be all it takes to pass a bill. Republicans like Meade County Republican Party Chair Linn Hendrickson expressed concerns with removing the filibuster.

“If you nuke the filibuster, it opens the floor for all sorts of votes. The Democrats can bring as many votes as they want to on (any) number of items,” Hendrickson said during the resolutions committee meeting on Friday morning.

Hendrickson presented a different resolution, Resolution 015, titled, “Resolution to urge U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and the federal delegation to continue efforts to pass the SAVE America Act.”

 The floor
Delegates seated by county during the floor session on Friday, June 26. 

That failed in committee.

The South Dakota Republican Convention started in Rapid City at The Monument on Thursday, June 25, and it runs through Saturday, June 27.

Thune’s office did not immediately response to a request for comment about the resolution.

title: Letter from Custer's widow returns to Montana for battle's 150th anniversary
description: The cursive writing, with its large overlapping loops, can be difficult to read in places, but that’s to be expected. The author, Elizabeth Bacon Custer , was 85 years old when she wrote it.
_full_text:
The cursive writing, with its large overlapping loops, can be difficult to read in places, but that’s to be expected. The author, Elizabeth Bacon Custer, was 85 years old when she wrote it. 

 Elizabeth "Libbie" Custer
Elizabeth "Libbie" Custer lived almost to age 92, dedicating the years after her husband's death to keeping his memory alive. 

The long-widowed wife of Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer was penning a four-page missive to Ruth Renrick Gregory. Dated Aug. 7, 1927, Custer thanked Gregory for inviting her to the 50th anniversary commemoration of the Battle of the Little Bighorn the previous year.

“My dear Mrs. Gregory,” Custer began, “This last year has been such an eventful one for the loyal West has been paying tribute to my husband who opened the way and died for them and their struggles to make a safe place for those who came from the crowded East.”

‘Greatest crowd’

 Custer
Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer's decision to attack a large encampment of Lakota and Cheyenne along the Little Bighorn River resulted in a now famous battle. 

The 50th anniversary drew the “Greatest crowd in Montana history” to the battlefield, proclaimed the Kremlin (Montana) Chancellor newspaper in its July 9, 1926, edition.

The ceremony included veterans from both sides of the battle, “mingling arm and arm on the battle field where 50 years ago the Sioux and Cheyenne annihilated Gen. Custer’s immediate command,” wrote the Sioux City Journal on June 25, 1926.

The battle, known to the victorious tribes as the Battle of the Greasy Grass and to others as Custer’s Last Stand, was such a decisive defeat that then-president Ulysses Grant posthumously charged Custer with disobeying orders.

The Civil War veteran’s brash decision to attack the encampment of an estimated 7,000 Lakota, Cheyenne, Dakota and Arapahos resulted in the deaths of 260 soldiers and an estimated 60 to 100 warriors.

A circuitous route

 Letter from Libbie
Virginia Court received the four-page letter in the mail about six years ago encased in an embossed album. 

Now, as the 150th anniversary of the June 25-26, 1876, battle approaches — along with the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence — Elizabeth Custer’s 100-year-old letter has resurfaced and will be donated to the Big Horn County Historical Museum.

“I was so anxious to have the West know that tho I had not the courage to visit these harrowed scenes, my heart responded to everything done — on the anniversary of the Battle of the Little Bighorn — June 25th 1925,” Elizabeth Custer wrote to Ruth Gregory.

The letter’s route back to Bighorn County touches on many fateful incidents.

In about 2000, Gregory’s daughter-in-law, Jean Gregory, approached Virginia Court with a letter she had found while going through Ruth’s belongings.

At the time, Jean was a member of the Custer Battlefield Museum Association’s board and Court’s husband, Jim, was superintendent of the Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument.

Ruth Gregory died in 1991 at the age of 104, having lived on a ranch with her husband, Frank Gregory, on upper Rotten Grass Creek near Lodge Grass since 1928.

Court read the letter Jean Gregory had discovered and was amazed.

“It's incredible to think back in those years you could write a letter to Elizabeth Custer, and she would respond to you,” she said.

Most of Elizabeth Custer’s letters are about her trips abroad, or the love letters she exchanged with her husband. Many aren't dated or even signed.

“There are very few letters in existence written by Elizabeth Custer where she addresses her husband and how she felt about him,” Court added.

The museum board decided to auction the letter as a way to raise money for the preservation committee which wanted to buy and preserve land around the battlefield, Court said.

 Provenance
Philip Gates bought the Custer letter at auction in 2002, as this signed letter of provenance notes. 

On June 22, 2002, when the letter was being auctioned, Court attempted to buy it, hoping to donate the faded pages back to the museum. However, there was another bidder, a Floridian citrus grower with deep pockets — Philip Custer Gates.

After the bid hit $2,000, Court bowed out.

“That was a lot of money back then, you know,” she said.

A friend in need

 Jim and Virginia Court
Billings residents Jim and Virginia Court have been involved in the history of the Little Bighorn Battlefield since Jim was appointed superintendent of the national monument in 1978.  

Given their shared interest in history, the Courts and Gates became friends, taking several steamboat trips together. After Gates died in 2007 at age 83, Court asked his widow, Barbara, if she would consider giving her Elizabeth Custer’s letter for donation to the Big Horn County Historical Museum. The museum is located in Hardin, about 17 miles northwest of the battlefield.

About five years ago, a box arrived at Court’s Billings home. The package contained a green leather-bound album embossed in gold lettering that said: LIBBIE’S LETTERS on the top line. MRS. GEORGE A. CUSTER across the bottom.

Inside, held in place by plastic sleeves, was the four-page letter along with a signed letter of provenance which included Gates stating George Custer was his great-great-great-uncle — hence his middle name and interest in the letter.

In all the travels the Gates had taken with the Courts, this fact was never revealed, Virginia said.

After the box’s surprise arrival, life got in the way.

“This is terrible, but things have happened in our lives that I kind of forgot about it,” said the 81-year-old Court in a recent interview. “And then, you know, there's been such a to-do about the anniversary coming up, and I thought, ‘Hmm, why don't we do this. Why don't we give some publicity to the Big Horn County Museum?’”

She has made plans to turn over the letters this week.

“We are just so excited to get it,” said Beth Mehling, a longtime member of the museum’s board. “For us to receive that letter is such an honor.”

She also praised the Courts for their generosity not just with the donation, but all of their previous work on the museum, battlefield and preservation of 2,800 acres of land surrounding the site, for which Jim Court raised $6 million.

150th anniversary

 Custer letter
This is the last page of a four-page letter penned by Elizabeth Custer on Aug. 7, 1927, one year after the 50th anniversary of the Battle of the Little Bighorn. 

Festivities for the 150th anniversary of the battle begin on Thursday, June 25, when the gates to the national monument open at 7 a.m. followed by programs at 9:30 a.m. No entrance fee will be charged.

“With up to 10,000 visitors expected to attend the commemoration per day, be sure to plan ahead to ensure a safe and enjoyable experience,” the National Park Service advised on its website.

Tribal nations, descendants, historians, elected officials, authors, military representatives, and cultural organizations have activities planned, according to the agency, including a parade and fly over, opening prayer and talks. Tribal cultural demonstrations, cavalry descendant presentations and traditional drum groups are just some of the activities.

Unfortunately, the new visitor center, which has been under construction, will not be completed in time for the event. A tribally owned construction company is building the $14 million, 9,000-square-foot facility.

Custer lives on

 50th anniversary
This news article in the Sioux City Journal describes the 50th anniversary of the Battle of the Little Bighorn. 

Known to her acquaintances as Libbie, Elizabeth Custer died of a heart attack at age 91 — four days shy of her birthday — on April 4, 1933, in her New York City Park Avenue apartment. She never remarried, and the couple had no children. She was buried at West Point next to her husband.

“The last link with the romantic, stirring chapter of American history was broken on Tuesday with the passing away of Mrs. Elizabeth Bacon Custer,” The Evening News in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, announced in its April 8, 1933, edition.

“Although she rarely was seen in public, she led an active life,” The Great Falls Tribune reported on April 13, 1933. “She wrote three books on her experience in camp as the wife of a soldier,” including “Boots and Saddles,” “Tenting on the Plains” and “Following the Guidon.”

In her will, Elizabeth directed an executor of her estate to give all “souvenirs of General Custer, including ‘portraits and photographs, his army accoutrements, uniforms, souvenirs of war or frontier, books and illustrations and trophies of the chase’” to the “public museum or memorial which may be erected on the battlefield of the Little Big Horn in Montana,” according to a 1933 story in The Troy (Montana) Tribune.

A portion of the battlefield was designated a national cemetery in 1879. In 1940, the battlefield was transferred from the War Department’s administration to the National Park Service. In 1991, Congress changed the name of the battlefield and a new memorial dedicated to Native American participants was authorized.

In 2011, the Park Service decided to move the Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument’s more than 123,000 historical archives and some 26,000 historic objects, to a facility in Arizona for safekeeping as the visitor center deteriorated before being torn down.

But the Big Horn County Historical Museum houses a wealth of Custer memorabilia for visiting history buffs, including the dioramas that were originally at the battlefield, said Mehling, the museum board member.

“That little museum, honest to god, is one of the best kept secrets in Eastern Montana,” she added, noting the numerous buildings on the ground offer visitors a chance to step back in time.

Although Elizabeth Custer never made it to the site of her husband’s death in what is now Montana, she cherished those who helped keep his memory alive.

“I shall treasure your words as I try to recall more of my husband in the Civil War, as it were,” she wrote to Jean Gregory in 1926. “Continue to ‘love General Custer’ — he was worthy of your affection — Sincerely Elizabeth B. Custer”

title: Thousands show up for 150th anniversary of the Battle of Little Bighorn
description: LITTLE BIGHORN BATTLEFIELD NATIONAL MONUMENT, Mont.— On June 25, tribal members and leaders from across the country gathered to celebrate the sesquicentennial of the Battle of the Little Bighorn (also known as the Battle of the Greasy Grass), with the event drawing a crowd of thousands to the memorial site in Montana.
_full_text:
LITTLE BIGHORN BATTLEFIELD NATIONAL MONUMENT, Mont.— On June 25, tribal members and leaders from across the country gathered to celebrate the sesquicentennial of the Battle of the Little Bighorn (also known as the Battle of the Greasy Grass), with the event drawing a crowd of thousands to the memorial site in Montana.

The day’s events featured a chance to participate in a horse ride involving tribal nations who participated in the battle where Lt. Col George Armstrong Custer was killed.

 Bighorn
On June 25, more than 380 horseback riders featuring Arapaho, Northern Cheyenne and Lakota tribal members celebrated their victory anniversary against the U.S. Army.  

"The land is sacred with the people, and we're sacred with the land. We're here together today and back in 1876 because of our unity, there was no fear. We didn't allow the cavalry to come down all the way into the camp. We kept them back away, and eventually chased them up to the last stand hill, eliminated them eventually," said James Two Crow (Oglala Lakota).

For Indigenous people across the country, the battle is symbolic for tribal sovereignty, as tribal nations such as the Arapaho, Northern Cheyenne and Lakota defeated Custer and more than 200 7th Cavalry troops, along with the help of Arikara and Crow scouts.

The battle was a historic victory for the tribal nations. Per the National Parks Service, however, the battle was “a momentary victory for the Lakota and Cheyenne." The death of Custer and his troops became a rallying point for the United States to increase their efforts to force Native people onto reservation lands. With more troops in the field, Army expeditionary forces invaded Lakota hunting grounds, determined to conquer the Northern Plains Indians. Most of the declared "hostiles" surrendered within one year of the fight, and the Black Hills were taken by the U.S. government without compensation to the Lakota.

In 1980, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the Sioux were entitled to $102 million (roughly over $1 billion in today’s dollars) for the wrongful seizure, but the nations have yet to accept compensation as they seek land ownership back.

 Bighorn
Custer National Cemetery at the Battle of Little Bighorn Monument.  

"We need to remind the United States government that we are here to stay; we're all survivors of what they tried to do to us in the past, that's commit genocide on our tribal nations here. Remember that. Be proud of who you are, represent your people with pride. You all have proud last names, proud family histories ... I hope you represent what you learned from what you're seeing today," OST President Frank Star Comes Out said on June 24 at a youth camp meeting. “You're going to carry that down to the youth behind you.”

 Bighorn
Lt. Col. George Armstorng Custer's tombstone marker at the Battle of Little Bighorn Monument. 

Some of the horse riders from the three tribal nations involved in the battle made a journey from their reservations to the battlefield for the anniversary.

 Bighorn
The Battle of the Little Bighorn site in Montana has a dedicated Indian Memorial site for the associated tribes involved in the battle. 

A couple of those horses were owned by Two Crow.

"For me, it's another time of beauty, our people coming together. I'll say that was beauty, and that's what we mean whenever we say as Native Americans, our Lakotas, Nakotas, Dakotas, we're beautiful people when we unite," Two Crow said.

 James Two Crow.
James (Jim) Two Crow and his crew from the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota provided more than 200 tipi poles for the Oglala Sioux Tribe to use at the Crow Agency Reservation in Montana. The group erected nine tipis for the community to use on the Real Bird property. 

The three groups make up the Oceti Sakowin, which means the Seven Council Fires, a group of allied nations.

 Bighorn
Over 300 horseback riders from various tribal nations participated in the anniversary day. 

Over 300 horses and riders participated in the charge and roundup on the side of Last Stand Hill at the monument site that is not owned by the park service.

A day of prayer

On June 24, at dusk, Arvol Looking Horse (Lakota) and the keeper of the sacred White Buffalo Calf Pipe and Bundle, conducted a ceremony for the horses. No recording of any kind was allowed by the media.

 Bighorn
Native American warrior cutouts placed at the Bighorn monument, aiming arrows at the sky. 

The ceremony included a community gratitude to the Real Bird family (Crow) who own the land that the tribal communities had been using for the week to allow people to stay on the same land as the Arapaho, Northern Cheyenne and Lakota did 150 years ago.

The Curtis Real Bird family, owner of the land, said Star Comes Out reached out to him about organizing an event with fellow tribes. Real Bird said he drove Star Comes Out on his land and gave the blessing for camp to be set up for the tribal nations.

"You can see the good spirit, the positivity of being a Native. Just for several days, we're Indians. One nation where it doesn't matter if you're Oglala Cheyenne, Sioux, Blackfeet or Crow, we're one. That's always strong like that, we just all get together like this, good things can happen," Real Bird told the Journal.

After receiving a buffalo hide as a gift, Real Bird said it was an honor to be recognized in a good way.

"It was overwhelming, it was absolutely fabulous. Because that don't happen to me, I'm just a regular Indian boy that ventured off in the real world, working in shoeing horses. I've lived here all my life and to have this group of people to put me on a pedestal to honor me was out of this world," Real Bird said.

Thereafter, the horse riders circled the camp and victory dances closed out the ceremony for the day. 

 Bighorn
Thousands of visitors from across the nation and world came out to the monument to spend the day celebrating with Indigenous people. 

Victory day

On the early morning of June 25, members of the camp woke up at dawn to travel to the memorial site for morning prayers.

Buses then provided members of the public transportation to the battlefield site. Thousands of people from across the nation then stretched across the monuments’ walking path.

For non-Indigenous people, there were booths about the battle and the Plains people, as well as speakers from various tribal nations. The main event for Indigenous people was the horse riders.

 Bighorn
Horseback riders charge a hill just shy of the national park land. 

The horseback riders rode partway to the hill where Custer was killed, but instead of a reenactment, the horses circled the hill. After the flurry ended, a ceremony began with prayers, songs and other symbolic practices. In the midst of the crowd, there were tears, calls out to the riders and cheers.

 Bighorn
Horseback riders rode partway to the hill where Custer was killed, but instead of a reenactment, the horses circled the hill. After the flurry ended, a ceremony began with prayers, songs and other symbolic practices. In the midst of the crowd, there were tears, calls out to the riders and cheers. 

"This one here is a victory (day), we lost some battles, and we are still in continuous battles and we're still at war with the American government. We're always going to show resistance with these modern-day battles that we have with the government, over the Black Hills, or our lands with sovereignty or racism," Two Crow said as he reflected on the symbolic nature of the event.

Both Two Crow and Real Bird said the highlight of the week was seeing communities come together and making lasting, meaningful bonds. 

"I hope a lot of people get the opportunity to pursue their dreams, and make something right, and do the right stuff for the people. Help people and care and cherish one another. No hostility and to greet each other in a good way. That's how it should be," Real Bird said.

"Times changes … I think more changes are coming, but we'll always continue to exist, and we'll always continue to resist too, because that's how our ancestors taught us. They taught us to always lean to our Native ways and continue with our culture, our religions, our prayers, our artwork and especially our language," Two Crow said. "There are changes, but we understand each other, and that's what's important."

 Bighorn
Grave markers for the members of the 7th Calvary who fought and dies with Lt. Col. George Armstorng Custer.

title: South Dakota regulators approve Black Hills Energy, NorthWestern merger
description: South Dakota utility regulators unanimously approved the merger of Black Hills Energy and NorthWestern Energy on Wednesday in Pierre.
_full_text:
South Dakota utility regulators unanimously approved the merger of Black Hills Energy and NorthWestern Energy on Wednesday in Pierre.

The new utility will be named Bright Horizon Energy, with an estimated total value of $15.4 billion and 2.1 million customers in eight states.

Public Utilities Commission Chairman Chris Nelson said state law makes the approval of mergers the default unless there’s a serious problem discovered. 

“It says you shall approve these kinds of mergers, unless there’s a likelihood of significant adverse impacts to customers in this state,” Nelson said. “And I would submit that’s probably a fairly low bar. But that’s the bar that the Legislature has established. It’s not something we establish.”

Along with the merger, regulators approved two negotiated settlements addressing customer protections and labor concerns.

 062726-nws-sl-energy-p1.jpg
A sign stands outside Black Hills Energy’s corporate headquarters on June 24, 2026, in Rapid City, South Dakota. 

One settlement bars charging South Dakota customers for costs stemming from executive “golden parachutes” and other merger-related costs. It also delays rate increases and ensures the combined company keeps its headquarters in Rapid City for at least 10 years, and maintains a corporate office in or near Sioux Falls for at least five years.

The other settlement gives union and South Dakota-based contractors added consideration for projects. 

Frank Kloucek is the Democratic nominee for the Public Utilities Commission seat being vacated by Commissioner Gary Hanson, who is not seeking reelection. Kloucek criticized the merger during the public comment portion of Wednesday’s meeting, which happened after the vote. 

Kloucek said the merger creates a “super monopoly,” and he criticized the commission for not providing more time for public input and scrutiny. 

The companies announced the proposed merger in August. They said it would diversify the combined entity’s energy sources, help meet rising energy demands from data centers, and benefit investors.

NorthWestern Energy serves about 65,600 South Dakota electric customers and 51,200 South Dakota natural-gas customers. Black Hills Energy serves 78,976 South Dakota electric customers.

Among the states affected by the merger, Montana is the only one in which regulators have not yet approved it.

title: Stick or carrot? SDGOP considers censuring Sen. Majority Leader John Thune
description: A resolution to rebuke and censure U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune is headed for the 2026 South Dakota Republican Convention floor after the party’s Resolutions Committee chose the stick rather than the carrot.
_full_text:
A resolution to rebuke and censure U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune is headed for the 2026 South Dakota Republican Convention floor after the party’s Resolutions Committee chose the stick rather than the carrot.

All six voting members of the resolution committee — the chair only votes in the case of a tie — voted on Friday, June 26, to recommend party delegates censure the Murdo native and pass Resolution 012, titled “A resolution rebuking Senator John Thune of his performance as U.S. Senate Majority Leader, and censuring him until the SAVE America Act becomes law.”’

“We all like story lines, even in politics, of how things progress, and this is sort of part of a stick and carrot situation,” said Minnehaha County delegate Michael Stangeland, who authored the stick. “The stick is the censure, and the possible failure is that the Save Act doesn't get passed, and Senator Thune has to deal with the fact that he is remembered as a senator who could not get it done, especially going into the upcoming election.”

What does the Resolutions Committee do?
The Resolutions Committee for a state Republican convention is responsible for drafting, reviewing, and recommending resolutions—formal statements or positions on policy, party principles, or issues—to be considered and potentially adopted by the convention delegates. Its objective is to ensure that resolutions reflect the party’s values, priorities, and strategic goals while fostering unity and clarity within the party.

Reading from the resolution before the party’s Resolutions Committee, Stangeland said, “While there are many ways in which John Thune's performance as Senate Majority Leader has been found wanting, his failure in regards to the SAVE America Act is his most glaring and cannot be ignored.”

The SAVE America Act would require voters to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections and photo identification when voting. The U.S. House has passed the bill, but it has yet to make it out of the Senate.

 Stangeland
Minnehaha County delegate Michael Stangeland appeared before the Resolutions Committee during the South Dakota Republican Party Convention to read a resolution to censure Sen. John Thune. 

“Thune is from South Dakota. Thune is our senator. Thune is our senator to address and to deal with,” Stangeland said.

Trump recently refused to sign a bipartisan housing reform bill until the SAVE America Act is passed, ABC News reported. The president has pushed Republicans in the Senate to eliminate or modify the filibuster to get the bill through, while Thune has maintained Republicans don't have the votes to do so.

Filibustering is a tactic to delay a floor vote on a bill by prolonging debate. Under current law, it takes 60 senators to end a filibuster. If filibustering is taken out of lawmakers’ toolboxes, a simple majority will be all it takes to pass a bill. Republicans like Meade County Republican Party Chair Linn Hendrickson expressed concerns with removing the filibuster.

“If you nuke the filibuster, it opens the floor for all sorts of votes. The Democrats can bring as many votes as they want to on (any) number of items,” Hendrickson said.

Hendrickson presented a different resolution — the carrot — that was shot down by the resolution committee with a 5-1 vote to not recommend, with Charles Streeter, a delegate from Clay County, voting against. Resolution 015 is titled, “Resolution to urge U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and the federal delegation to continue efforts to pass the SAVE America Act.”

 Linn Hendrickson
Meade County Republican Party Chair Linn Hendrickson presented a resolution to encourage Sen. John Thune to continue working on the passage of the SAVE America Act. 

“People seem to think that since he's the majority leader, he dictates to the rest of the Senate Republican caucus,” Hendrickson said. “Trust me, there are 100 independent minds in the U.S. Senate, and corralling them all together is like herding cats, and John Thune has done an excellent job in herding them.”

Comments from delegates during the committee meeting and a vocal vote of the present delegates — which is not the official committee vote — were split.

The South Dakota Republican Convention started in Rapid City at The Monument on Thursday, June 25, and it runs through Saturday, June 27. A floor session began at 1 p.m. on Friday. As of about 3 p.m., the delegates had not yet addressed the Resolutions Committee recommendations.

Thune’s office did not immediately response to a request for comment about the resolution.

 Lining up
Delegates line up to comment on the potential censure of Sen. John Thune during the Resolutions Committee meeting held on Friday, June 26, the second day of the South Dakota Republican Convention.

title: Pennington County Sheriff’s Office on high alert with presidential visit, upcoming tourists for America’s Birthday Bash
description: With the promise of President Donald Trump coming to visit Mount Rushmore again and crowds in the Black Hills predicted to be at an all-time high for America’s 250th Birthday celebration, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, along with several agencies, are partnering together to ensure a fun and safe holiday week.
_full_text:
With the promise of President Donald Trump coming to visit Mount Rushmore again and crowds in the Black Hills predicted to be at an all-time high for America’s 250th Birthday celebration, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, along with several agencies, are partnering together to ensure a fun and safe holiday week.

“It’s the big 250th anniversary of the United States. We’re having some big celebrations not only in Mount Rushmore but throughout the Black Hills, from Rapid City to Custer, so the whole Black Hills is gonna be filled with a bunch of people celebrating the anniversary of our country here,” Pennington County Sheriff’s Office Patrol Division Capt. Casey Kenrick said.

Despite the predicted crowds and potential rowdiness that comes with tourism season, Kenrick said the office still only has one goal in mind — safety.

Kenrick said one of the major points of concern is traffic, as people attempt to stop on the road to get a glimpse of the surrounding festivities. He asked the public to take their travels slow, plan ahead and abide by road signs set by law enforcement and the cities in the Black Hills.

“Just try to make yourself have a lot of time to get there safely, so you’re not speeding,” Kenrick said. “Obviously, no drinking and driving, especially with all the traffic. It’s gonna be really busy in the Hills, so we’re just asking for people to be mindful of those things.”

Kenrick advised the public to be mindful of the heat by dressing appropriately for the weather, having water nearby and getting under shade to take a break from the sun’s rays.

Though the 250th Birthday Bash will be bringing in historic numbers of visitors, Kenrick said the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office will continue to work diligently with the South Dakota Highway Patrol, local law enforcement, fire departments and other emergency personnel like they do every year. “We’ve been working hard for the last few months to make sure we have the appropriate amount of staff in the Hills. To make sure we’re reaching our goal that everyone is safe,” Kenrick said.

Kenrick said the office will assist the Secret Service, which will be primarily focusing efforts on securing the Mount Rushmore area, in any way it can.

“It’s not abnormal to have dignitary visits, presidential visits, so we work well with Secret Service,” Kenrick said. “We help with whatever they need, they help us with what we need. So it’s just a partnership we have with them.”

Kenrick said the office learned a lot from Trump’s previous visit in 2020 and has addressed the learning curves that came with it.

During Trump’s 2020 visit to Mount Rushmore, a Rapid City man illegally purchased a rifle and told a deputy that he planned to climb to the top of Mount Rushmore and shoot the president during the July 3, 2020 fireworks event.

Lucian Celestine was ultimately detained and convicted in state and federal court for threatening to shoot Trump. Celestine entered a guilty plea in November 2024 to attempted threat of felony terrorism. Celestine was sentenced in March 2025 by the Pennington County Circuit Court to two and a half years in prison, and in federal court, he was sentenced to three years of supervised release.

In addition, there have been numerous concerns posted on social media about setting off fireworks at Mount Rushmore. Kenrick said the sheriff’s office will be working diligently with local fire departments to ensure a fire doesn’t break out.

“All these areas work together, we obviously all have the same goal in keeping people safe, keeping these situations and incidents as small as we can so they don’t effect everyone,” Kenrick said.

According to the South Dakota Department of Tourism, California-based Pyro Spectaculars will have a crew of 30 pyrotechnicians and specially trained highline operators handling the Rushmore show. The company did the 2020 show as well. In addition to fireworks, the “2026 contract includes lighting elements that can be utilized if environmental conditions require an alternative to fireworks,” the department said in a release about the show.

Kenrick said fire season is not only a concern for the holiday week and that everyone should be doing their part in ensuring safety during the summer.

Outside of the scheduled celebrations, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office gave a heads-up on firework safety for those who will be celebrating at home. Kenrick’s final note was to remind the public that safety is not solely the responsibility of law enforcement, but is a shared responsibility.

Further updates from the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office will be posted next week.

title: Rapid City announces street closures, parking restrictions for Birthday Bash parade

title: In Rapid City, Homeland Security Sec. Mullin joins Thune to discuss ICE’s work
description: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers are, “The best of the best, going after the worst of the worst” during a stop at a Rapid City Department of Homeland Security office with Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune.
_full_text:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers are, “The best of the best, going after the worst of the worst” during a stop at a Rapid City Department of Homeland Security office with Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

During a brief media availability on Thursday, June 25, Mullin and Thune, a Murdo native, said they met with ICE officials to discuss the office's recently concluded and ongoing cases. Mullin noted the office handles cases in South Dakota, North Dakota, Nebraska and Minnesota.

Mullin said 70% of ICE arrests “on a daily basis” are individuals with pending felonies or felony convictions.

 062726-nws-immigration-p2.JPG
“You think of a state like South Dakota, it's kind of removed from the borders, more rural, geographically dispersed … but we have, we got a lot of issues here too and these guys are getting after it every day trying to make our streets safer," Senate Majority Leader John Thune said at a Department of Homeland Security building in Rapid City on Thursday, June 25. 

“Everywhere we go, we try to one, go see the operations, and two, show them a little love and appreciation,” said Mullin, who was confirmed in the Senate in March to replace former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who previously served as governor of South Dakota.

Mullin said among the cases they heard about, “the grossest, and the ones that really keep you up at night are the sex trafficking, especially when you see child trafficking.” He commended South Dakota law enforcement agencies for entering into 287(g) agreements with ICE to assist with enforcement actions. Those agreements between federal and state or local agencies fall under Section 287(g) of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996. The program authorizes ICE to delegate "specified immigration officer functions" to state and local law enforcement officers, operating under the agency’s direction and oversight, according to ICE's website.

Last year, the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation and South Dakota Highway Patrol entered into 287(g) agreements with ICE.

“When you hear the amount of cases that are happening right here in South Dakota, it should concern all of us. But thank goodness we have cooperation, and this is what the 287(g) program is all about. We have cooperation with local, state, and federal … we work underneath President (Donald) Trump's initiative of making our streets safe again, making sure our cities are safe again, and getting rid of the criminals. And this is a prime example, right here in South Dakota.”

When asked, Mullin said he didn’t have statistics on the number of arrests ICE makes in the region or the percentage of those arrests that are tied to undocumented immigrants, noting they didn’t discuss that with ICE officials during the briefing.

 Mullin and Thune
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin discusses the purview of the Rapid City ICE office. 

Thune said “this past year” featured the lowest number of illegal immigrants crossing the border since 1970. According to Customs and Border Patrol data, there were 443,671 encounters at the Southern Border in Fiscal Year 2025, which ran from October 2024 to the end of September 2025. There were 201,780 encounters in 1970.

The highest recorded total was FY2023, with 2,475,669 encounters during the President Joe Biden Administration. Mullin criticized Biden’s administration multiple times while discussing immigration enforcement under Trump.

“This is a hard job, and as the secretary pointed out, we've had an opportunity to hear from some of the folks who are there day in and day out doing the really hard work,” Thune said. “You think of a state like South Dakota, it's kind of removed from the borders, more rural, geographically dispersed … but we have, we got a lot of issues here too and these guys are getting after it every day trying to make our streets safer.”

Mullin said, “Criminals think of some of these rural states as places they can go hide, they can't hide underneath the Trump Administration.”

 062726-nws-immigration-p1.JPG
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, left, discusses immigration enforcement work in the region during a stop in Rapid City with Senate Majority Leader John Thune. 

When asked, Mullin said there isn’t a need for an ICE detention center in the Rapid City area. The agency has agreements to keep detainees at the Pennington County Jail.

The secretary said ICE’s work in the area is, “not just immigration,” noting the majority of cases ICE agents discussed with Mullin and Thune “dealt with crimes that they were chasing” that led to immigration arrests.

“They (the criminals) will go after anyone they feel is weak and vulnerable, and some people that are here illegally” are targets to be taken advantage of. “We can't just simply look at one area, we got to look at all the above.”

title: Republican governor candidates spar over prison policy in dueling speeches
description: The two remaining Republican candidates for governor of South Dakota clashed over prison policy Friday night in what might have been the closest thing to a debate that voters will see before the party’s nomination is decided in a July 28 runoff election.
_full_text:
The two remaining Republican candidates for governor of South Dakota clashed over prison policy Friday night in what might have been the closest thing to a debate that voters will see before the party’s nomination is decided in a July 28 runoff election.

The candidates delivered back-to-back speeches to a crowd of hundreds during the Republican state convention at The Monument events center.

Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden said too many people in South Dakota return to prison after being released.

“Our recidivism rate has peaked at 50% — third worst in the country,” Doeden said. “We have a higher recidivism rate than almost every liberal state in the country.”

The 50% figure comes from the state Department of Corrections’ latest annual report, which says half of the people released from prison in South Dakota return within three years of their release.

 062926-nws-sl-candidates-p1.jpg
Toby Doeden, left, and Gov. Larry Rhoden deliver speeches to the South Dakota Republican Convention on Friday, June 26, at The Monument in Rapid City. 

Where South Dakota ranks nationally is difficult to ascertain due to differences in the ways that states define recidivism. Gov. Larry Rhoden has acknowledged the rate is “higher than any of our neighboring states.”

Rhoden responded to Doeden’s criticism, saying “he’s right: our recidivism rate is way too high.”

“And why is that? Because we have no room,” Rhoden said. “We have three prisoners stacked in rooms that are built for one. We have no room for programming.”

Rhoden said he’s solving that problem with a new men’s prison he convinced legislators to build. The $650 million facility, which is under construction in northeast Sioux Falls, will be funded without debt due to money lawmakers set aside for several years before approving the project in September. It will replace the oldest parts of the state’s 145-year-old Sioux Falls penitentiary.

Rhoden said he got the project approved despite dealing with lawmakers whose support was divided among the candidates for governor. There was a “Doeden camp” in the legislative prison debate, Rhoden said, and “the Dusty camp and the Hansen camp” — a reference to U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson and state House Speaker Jon Hansen, who finished third and fourth in the four-way June 2 primary race.

“All three of those candidates were lobbing bombs at me, because they didn’t want to see us get a win,” Rhoden said.

Neither Rhoden nor Doeden lobbed many verbal bombs in their speeches Friday, despite an ongoing feud between their campaigns about Rhoden’s refusal to debate. The two men participated in three debates with the other two candidates before the primary. Because nobody reached 35% in that election, the top two finishers — Doeden at 31% and Rhoden at 25% — advanced to a top-two runoff.

Doeden pledges to be unifying catalyst

The state Republican Party invited Doeden and Rhoden to speak at the convention and limited each of them to 15 minutes. By the flip of a coin, Doeden went first.

He spent the first part of his speech detailing what he described as the four principles that would guide him as governor: smaller and more efficient government, lower taxes, strong law and order, and quality educational opportunities for children.

After calling South Dakota “the greatest state in the country,” Doeden offered several critiques, including the recidivism rate. He said state government spending and taxes have increased too much, education in the state has “taken a step backwards,” and “people are living less affordable lives.”

Doeden, in his first run for elected office, pledged to be “the catalyst unifying this party to the strongest place it has been in decades.” He met several people at the convention, he said, who told him they were sorry for saying critical things about him on Facebook before the primary.

“I said it’s OK,” Doeden said. “The slate was wiped clean at midnight on June 2.”

Rhoden: ‘I’m that guy’

After Doeden finished, Rhoden began by saying that the first lady, Sandy Rhoden, is “always suggesting to me that there are things that people don’t know about me that I take for granted.” So Rhoden used the first part of his speech to talk about serving as an elder in his church, as president of a local cooperative board, as a coach of basketball and softball, as a six-year member of the National Guard, and as a school board member and legislator.

Rhoden was elevated from lieutenant governor in January 2025 when his predecessor, Gov. Kristi Noem, resigned to accept a job leading the federal Department of Homeland Security in President Donald Trump’s administration.

Rhoden described Noem as “the strongest person I know” and said “she was the right person for the job at that time,” referring to the COVID-19 pandemic years.

 Sen. John Thune censure vote during SDGOP convention
The South Dakota Republican delegation votes down a censure resolution aimed at Senate Majority Leader John Thune. 

But, Rhoden said, “when I took the reins, the water had gotten pretty choppy in our state.” The unsolved problems he inherited included what he described as the “three P’s”: a prison, a pipeline and property taxes.

In addition to getting the prison construction project across the finish line, Rhoden brought an end — for now – to a controversial carbon-capture pipeline proposal by signing a bill into law that bans such projects from using a court process known as eminent domain to gain access to private land. He also signed several bills into law that will lower property taxes for homeowners in the coming years, although two of them rely on higher sales taxes to bring property taxes down.

“We absolutely need somebody that can bring our party together and unify people and move an agenda forward,” Rhoden said. “And I’m that guy.”

State Republican party officials allowed media coverage of the speeches after blocking media access to U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s convention speech Thursday night. Several apologized to South Dakota Searchlight and said it was a “misunderstanding.”

 Photos from the South Dakota Republican Convention in Rapid City
The South Dakota Republican Convention is underway in Rapid City at The Monument. The convention began on Thursday, June 25, and concludes on Saturday, June 27.

title: GOP convention: Baxter to be South Dakota Secretary of State nominee
description: The South Dakota Republican Party chose its candidates for constitutional offices Saturday in Rapid City.
_full_text:
The South Dakota Republican Party chose its candidates for constitutional offices Saturday in Rapid City.

During the final day of the GOP convention at The Monument, delegates voted on a variety of offices, including Secretary of State and Attorney General.

Heather Baxter of Rapid City will be the Republican nominee for South Dakota secretary of state. Baxter netted 59.34% of the vote of GOP delegates to earn the nomination over current Secretary of State Monae Johnson, who was raised in Rapid City before moving to Pierre.

Baxter, a state representative who recently lost in the Republican primary, will face Democrat Terrence Davis of Sioux Falls in the general election. Democrats chose their candidates for constitutional offices during their convention on June 6 in Sioux Falls.

Johnson finished with 40.09% of the vote.

“The onus is on the Secretary of State's Office to inspire trust in the process and in the office by demonstrating integrity with full transparency. When this office runs well, you don't notice it. When it doesn't, you feel it everywhere,” Baxter said during her candidate speech on the convention floor. “I am running because I believe this office must be led by someone who understands its constitutional boundaries, respects its limitations, and executes its duties with precision and accuracy.”

Lance Russell of Edgemont will be the party’s nominee for attorney general. The former state legislator and current Fall River state’s attorney beat Austin Hoffman of rural McPherson County and John Fitzgerald of Spearfish. Hoffman is McPherson County’s state’s attorney and Fitzgerald is a former Lawrence and Butte County state’s attorney and was most recently a circuit court judge.

The nomination took two ballots, as Russell didn’t secure the 50% plus one required to advance. On the second ballot, Russell won with 57.14% of the vote, followed by Hoffman at 31.08% and Fitzgerald at 11.78%.

There is no Democratic nominee for attorney general.

title: Robert G Miller
_full_text:
June 26, 2026

Robert G. Miller departed peacefully on June 26, 2026, age 74.

Born and raised in Rapid City. He was preceded in death by his parents Clement and Cecile Miller, sister Glenda, and brother Mike.

Robert was a proud combat veteran of Vietnam. Following his military service, Robert pursued a career in wildland firefighting as a smoke jumper. Later, he formed a small business that sold original Native American Art.

Robert is survived by his devoted wife, Mary, and his stepson, John Winchester.

Robert was immensely proud of his Native American heritage, which imbued his life with a profound sense of identity and purpose. Rob wanted all to know that life is as exciting as you make it, but short, so call and visit your parents frequently, hug your kids every chance you get, and treat all you meet with kindness.
