title: Don’t drink and drive: Local law enforcement reminds public after string of DUI arrests
description: As the days count down for Rapid City’s busy Fourth of July celebration, the Rapid City Police Department has already made 10 DUI arrests from Thursday through Sunday ahead of this week’s festivities. The police department and the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office reminded the public to not drink and drive.
_full_text:
As the days count down for Rapid City’s busy Fourth of July celebration, the Rapid City Police Department has already made 10 DUI arrests from Thursday through Sunday ahead of this week’s festivities. The police department and the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office reminded the public to not drink and drive.

According to a joint press release from the PCSO and the RCPD, the Fourth of July holiday ranks as one of the deadliest periods on the nation’s roads. In 2024, there were 579 people killed in traffic crashes during the holiday period in the U.S. From 2020 to 2024, there were 1,724 driver fatalities, with 38% of those drivers driving drunk, the release noted, citing data from the U.S. Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.

“As we approach the 4th of July Holiday, law enforcement recognizes many of this weekend’s celebrations will include alcohol. It’s incredibly important that those choosing to celebrate the holiday with alcohol designate a sober driver,” the Rapid City Police Department said. “The week leading up to the 4th of July holiday is traditionally the busiest week of the year for the Rapid City Police Department, and extra officers will be on shift to handle the extra workload, including being vigilant for the signs of impairment.”

The sheriff’s office advises that when someone plans on drinking, they should preemptively plan to have a safe ride home by either asking a sober friend or using a ride share service.

“They shouldn’t wait until after drinking to plan how to get somewhere. Impairment clouds a person’s judgment and endangers others on the road,” the joint release said.

If a driver finds they are unable to drive, law enforcement encourages them to should give their keys to a sober driver so that person can get home safely. Friends should be proactive and take away the keys and help their friends get a sober ride home, law enforcement said. If anyone spots a drunk driver, contact local law enforcement.

Despite the warnings, there was a surge of arrests between 8 p.m. on Thursday, June 25 and 8 a.m. Monday, June 29. Below are some of the noteworthy incidents:

Thursday, June 25, 10:15 p.m.

A Rapid City man was arrested after crashing into two parked cars, a residence and a road sign while drinking.

Christopher Taylor, 40, was arrested on suspicion of DUI, open container in a motor vehicle, driving under suspension and three counts of hit and run.

Police responded to the area of 815 E. New York Street for a report of a pickup truck that had crashed into several objects, including two parked cars, a residence and a road sign.

Officers found the truck in the 500 block of East New York Street, disabled by damage. Police told Taylor to exit the vehicle, where they noted the strong smell of alcohol coming from him.

Following a DUI investigation, Taylor was determined to be too impaired to safely operate a motor vehicle.

As of Monday, June 29, Taylor was not found in the Pennington County Jail roster. His DUI case had not been entered in online court records as of early Monday afternoon.

Friday, June 26, 1:45 a.m.

A Rapid City man was arrested after crashing into a street sign while drinking.

Colton Jordan, 30, was arrested on suspicion of DUI, hit and run, driving under suspension and failure to surrender a suspended, revoked or canceled license.

Police responded to Catron Boulevard and Sheridan Lake Road for a report of a loud collision. Upon arrival, police found a large amount of debris on the roadway, along with a downed street sign.

Officers found the car involved in the collision parked at 5311 Sheridan Lake Road. Police said it had damage consistent with striking the sign.

Police made contact with Jordan, where they noted the smell of alcohol coming from him.

As of Monday, Jordan was not found in the Pennington County Jail roster. His DUI case had not been entered in online court records as of early Monday afternoon.

Friday, June 26, 1:05 p.m.

A juvenile male was arrested after a rollover crash at Skyline Drive.

Police responded to the area of Skyline Drive and Flormann Street for a report of a rollover crash. Police found the SUV on its roof and all of the occupants outside the vehicle.

Officers determined a boy was the driver at the time of the crash and noted the smell of alcohol coming from him.

The boy was subsequently detained and placed in the appropriate channels of the juvenile justice system.

Saturday, June 27, 4:10 p.m.

A Rapid City man was arrested after causing a disturbance at Kelly’s Sports Lounge.

Tana Tallon, 46, was arrested on suspicion of DUI, disorderly conduct and an open container in a motor vehicle.

Police responded to Kelly’s Sports Lounge at 825 Jackson Boulevard for a report of a man who was intoxicated and was causing issues with customers and staff.

Witnesses said Tallon entered a car, drove off and returned to Kelly’s parking lot. Police found the car in the parking lot and identified Tallon as the driver. Officers noted the smell of alcohol coming from him and slurred speech.

Tallon was determined to be too impaired to safely operate a motor vehicle and was placed under arrest.

As of Monday, Tallon was not found in the Pennington County Jail roster. Tallon’s due in court for a preliminary hearing at 1:30 p.m. on Aug. 13, according to South Dakota court records.

title: Opposition arises to rebuild of US 85 through the Black Hills
byline: BART PFANKUCH South Dakota News Watch
description: CHEYENNE CROSSING — Colorado tourists Kay and Dan Rider made a conscious decision to avoid interstates and busy highways on their way to a family vacation in western South Dakota.
_full_text:
CHEYENNE CROSSING — Colorado tourists Kay and Dan Rider made a conscious decision to avoid interstates and busy highways on their way to a family vacation in western South Dakota.

The decision to take the scenic route led them to a stretch of U.S. Highway 85 in the northern Black Hills on June 25 that would eventually take them through the Lead/Deadwood area on their way to Rapid City.

The couple stopped briefly to take a break in one of the many pull-offs that straddle the highway. The small parking areas provide motorists with a spot to soak in the beauty of the majestic pines and rocky ridges that frame the highway or to find calm in the gentle babble of Spearfish Creek that flows a few feet from the travel lanes in some areas.

"We've just been talking about how beautiful the drive is and what great shape the road is in," Kay Rider said of the highway.

The Riders were surprised to learn that the state of South Dakota has plans in 2030 for a major reconstruction of that 16-mile stretch of U.S. 85 from the Wyoming border on the west to its intersection with U.S. 14A at Cheyenne Crossing on the east.

 2026-6-25 US 85 signage close up.jpeg
U.S. 85 in the northern Black Hills on June 25, 2026, near Cheyenne Crossing, S.D. A 16-mile stretch of the highway is targeted for a rebuild by the state in 2029. 

The couple said it didn't make sense to them that the Department of Transportation would do anything that could alter the aesthetics of the highway.

"If I was paying taxes in South Dakota and that money was going to this project, I would be highly upset," Dan Rider said.

That sentiment is shared by more than a few residents and business owners in the Black Hills region.

"The scenery and the stream on one side of the road and the cliffs on the other side — there's nothing that can match that," said Paul Horsted, a renowned nature and landscape photographer from Custer who is opposed to the current plans to redo U.S. 85.

 2026-6-25 US 85 Colorado tourists.jpeg
Colorado tourists Kay and Dan Rider enjoyed a drive on U.S. 85 in the Black Hills of South Dakota on June 25, 2026, and do not support a reconstruction of the highway that could alter its aesthetics. 

Horsted said he and others are worried that the DOT could take the same approach to rebuilding U.S. 85 as it has with the ongoing project to reconstruct U.S. 385, another scenic road through the Black Hills.

That three-year, $72 million project that will conclude in 2027 is bringing wider lanes, extended road shoulders and fewer curves to the north-south highway between Deadwood and Hill City. To improve safety, the DOT has made more room for the highway by clearing trees, blasting rock and scraping away ridges.

DOT data show that U.S. 85 is in poor condition, has 20 curves with reduced speed limits and is marred by eroded roadway edges.

 2026-6-25 US 85 SD entry sign.jpeg
This image from June 25, 2026, shows the west end of the U.S. 85 rebuild project at the South Dakota/Wyoming border and reveals how the road shoulder and rumble strips used in Wyoming end at the South Dakota line. 

The preliminary $47 million plan is to resurface the roadway and widen traffic lanes from 11 feet to 12 feet in most areas and add 4-foot to 6-foot paved shoulders where ditches, rocky outcrops or the banks of Spearfish Creek mostly exist now.

The 16-mile stretch of two-lane highway had 140 crashes with three fatalities and 56 injuries reported during the decade from 2013 to 2022.

The crash rate on the road of 8.5 accidents per million vehicle miles traveled was nearly six times the state average of 1.5 accidents for similar highways over that decade, the DOT said.

Stevenson said the agency is considering construction of a short retaining wall to protect the creek.

"Having a safer highway and an aesthetically pleasing highway do not have to be mutually exclusive," she wrote.

 2026-6-25 US 85 degraded shoulder.jpeg
The shoulder of eastbound U.S. 85 in western South Dakota, shown on June 25, 2026, has fully worn away in spots and is one reason the state of South Dakota has proposed rebuilding the highway. 

Steve Paula, 74, lives in Brookings but spends a couple months a year at his cabin located on the north side of U.S. 85 a few miles west of Cheyenne Crossing.

Paula said he has witnessed two accidents in recent years that were caused in part by the poor condition and curvy configuration of the highway.

 2026-6-25 US 85 cabin resident.jpeg
Steve Paula of Brookings, S.D., shown on June 25, 2026, owns a cabin along U.S. 85 in the northern Black Hills of South Dakota and has witnessed a pair of motorcycle accidents on the highway over the past several years. 

Paula said he has been impressed with the DOT's willingness to receive public input and is hopeful the agency will find a way to improve safety without harming the aesthetics or damaging Spearfish Creek.

"We don't want it destroyed," he said. "But there's a reasonableness in play in that we want safe roads, and I do believe the DOT is sincere in saying that they don't want to screw it up either."

 South Dakota News Watch logo
Learn more about South Dakota News Watch at sdnewswatch.org. 

South Dakota News Watch is an independent nonprofit. Read, donate and subscribe for free at sdnewswatch.org. Contact content director Bart Pfankuch: 605-937-9398/bart.pfankuch@sdnewswatch.org.

title: Rapid City woman sentenced to probation for child abuse
description: A Rapid City woman convicted of child abuse was sentenced to four years probation.
_full_text:
A Rapid City woman convicted of child abuse was sentenced to four years probation.

Janelle Vela appeared for her sentencing before Circuit Court Judge Joshua Hendrickson Monday, June 29, at the Pennington County Courthouse. Hendrickson suspended imposition of Vela’s sentence, meaning if she finishes probation without any issues, the crimes will not be on her record. If she violates probation, the judge could send her to prison.

Vela was initially indicted on four counts of child abuse against a 14-year-old and an 11-year-old. In South Dakota, child abuse is a Class 4 felony with a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a $20,000 fine.

Through a plea agreement with the state, Vela pleaded guilty to one count of child abuse, with all other charges dismissed. In exchange for a guilty plea, the state agreed only to recommend local jail with probation.

The 14-year-old came up to the stand to give a victim impact statement. As she fought tears, she expressed blaming herself for the abuse and not wanting to impact Vela’s life negatively.

“I love her a lot and I miss her,” the 14-year-old said. “But I don’t miss this version of her.”

The 14-year-old said the abuse left a lasting impact on her, saying she constantly worried if she deserved it or not.

Assistant Chief Deputy State’s Attorney Olivia Siglin called the case “difficult and emotional.” Siglin said Vela’s actions left lasting impacts on both children, leaving one to blame themself for the abuse.

The state said that Vela would spank the children until it left marks and force them to skip school to do physical workouts as a punishment.

Siglin requested that the court consider a five-year suspended sentence.

Vela’s defense attorney, Angela Colbath, spoke on Vela’s behalf and told the 14-year-old that none of what happened was her fault. Colbath said Vela is extremely remorseful and took responsibility by attending anger management classes.

Colbath said Vela worked very hard “to have a different outcome in this case,” highlighting her consistency to maintain a job and her outstanding track record while out on bond.

She said Vela will already be facing unimaginable pain regardless of the case's outcome and asked the court to consider a suspended imposition of sentence.

Hendrickson credited this case as Vela’s first felony charge and noted her lack of criminal history. He also acknowledged the bravery it took for the 14-year-old to speak, sympathizing that she will be living with that trauma for a long time.

As a co-defendant in the case, Nicholas Floyd also is indicted for two counts of child abuse along with an additional charge of simple assault attempt to cause bodily injury, which is a Class 1 misdemeanor that carries up to one year in jail and a $2,000 fine.

Floyd’s next status hearing is set for Aug. 20 at 1 p.m. He posted a $500 cash bond on Sept. 11, 2025.

title: Starting July 5, Day One to launch initiative advocating for Black, Indigenous people nationwide
description: Multicultural leaders came together on June 29 in Rapid City to announce a nationwide effort supporting the rights and autonomy of Black and Indigenous people in the U.S., starting the day after Independence Day.
_full_text:
Multicultural leaders came together on June 29 in Rapid City to announce a nationwide effort supporting the rights and autonomy of Black and Indigenous people in the U.S., starting the day after Independence Day.

The announcement took place on former boarding school land that’s now owned by the Oglala, Rosebud and Cheyenne River Sioux tribes on the west side of town.

 Day One
The Day One movement said it is challenging U.S. history for its acts of genocide, slavery and land theft.  

The Day One website states, "The 4th of YOU LIE (July), 2026, marks 250 years of a fictional story this country has told about itself. Day One is telling the real story, history, and the start of another story. We're calling it Day One because that's what it is. July 5th, 2026, is the day after America's 250th and the first day of a better, more just and equitable world, unyielding solidarity between Black and Indigenous Peoples, the unflinching demand for genuine repair of past harms and a future that belongs to and includes all of us.”

Day One is made up of organizers from various communities. 

 Day One
Nick Tilsen spoke at the Monday, June 29, event about the importance of the multicultural and ethnic movement of Day One.  

NDN Collective CEO Nick Tilsen said he is part of the movement as an individual and not with NDN.

"I come here as a father, as a husband, as a community organizer here on my home lands. I'm not here talking on behalf of NDN Collective, I'm here talking as an individual, because this Day One movement is a movement that is not made up of organizations, it's made up of grassroots people across this country and across this nation," Tilsen said.

 Day One
As part of the movement’s launch, organizers unveiled a “Bill of Essential Rights,” offering a framework for future endeavors.  

Tilsen continued, saying, "In order for us to build a path forward, we have to acknowledge the past and our Indigenous relatives, our Black brothers and sisters, we experienced huge amounts of suffering, and we have to acknowledge that we cannot continue to perpetuate anti-blackness, we cannot continue to perpetuate Indigenous erasure if we're going to build a path forward, so we're here to build something new."

The movement is rolling out its first initiative with the "Bill of Essential Rights," a framework of changes they hope to create in the U.S.

The 10 listed rights, as listed on the Day One website, are to land-back, reparations, self-determination and sovereignty, consent, basic needs, religion and culture, dignity and bodily autonomy, safety, move freely and belong, regenerative food systems and a protected planet.

 Day One
Brenda Perez an immigrant labor rights activist from Tennessee, spoke at the Monday, June 29 announcement.   

Brenda Perez, an immigrant labor rights activist from Tennessee, said she is an immigrant from Mexico and is working to help more than just her community.

"On this cusp of 250 years, we know that the system has not worked for us, we know that there has been a division perpetuated, a false narrative between poor folks, between working-class folks, between Indigenous folks, Black folks and immigrants, and we know that our struggles are one, but we know that those in power continuously work towards pushing us apart," Perez said at the launch event. "So we are here to say that we are going to organize, we are going to heal, we're going to coordinate, and we're going to build a better future together."

 Day One
The announcement took place at camp Mni Luzahan in Rapid City on Monday, June 29.  

The group said there are no plans for a counter protest about America 250 or any Fourth of July celebrations, including President Donald Trump’s visit to Mount Rushmore for July 3 fireworks, as their goal is to organize and build toward a better future.

"We have to come together to display who is the majority in this country, and absolutely what this country will look like in the future," Tilsen said.

Tilsen said of Trump’s visit, "We're not really concerned. We kind of find Trump a little annoying, and we know how the system works. Trump comes and goes, but we'll still be here ... He'll leave, and we'll still be here afterwards."

 Day One
Erinn Carter, an organizer with Day One, speaks during a launch event on Monday, June 29. 

Erinn Carter, an organizer with the movement, said, "What we know is that the only way that we can move forward is to acknowledge the past, and the truth is that America is stolen land, and the truth is that America was built with stolen hands."

For more information visit Day One’s website.

title: Sober living home owned by Rapid City councilman caught up in reasonable accommodation questions
byline: SHALOM BAER GEE and FRANK ESPINOZA Journal staff
description: Amid city staff crafting an ordinance to address reasonable accommodations for those with disabilities, confusion arose regarding a sober living home owned by Rapid City Councilman Stephen Tamang.
_full_text:
Amid city staff crafting an ordinance to address reasonable accommodations for those with disabilities, confusion arose regarding a sober living home owned by Rapid City Councilman Stephen Tamang.

After a next-door neighbor complained about the number of people living in the Oxford House home, the councilman received a code violation letter. That led to the legal department of the organization leasing the house to respond with its own letter, and the city ultimately walked back the violation after learning more about how the house operates.

“I said, ‘Thank you very much,’” Tamang, who represents Ward 1, said about receiving the letter. He then contacted Oxford House and didn’t engage with city staff about the issue.

 Vicki Fisher
Community Development Director Vicki Fisher 

In the meantime, the Rapid City Council — with Tamang abstaining — voted on June 15 to delay the passage of an ordinance that aims address reasonable accommodations under the provisions of the federal Fair Housing Act (FHA) and Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Counsel for Oxford House said the homes fall under those federal disability and housing protections because the residents are disabled by alcoholism or other addictions.

Community Development Director Vicki Fisher said the work on the ordinance has been ongoing for about 18 months and is not a response to the house Tamang owns.

“We began noticing that a significant number of variances were coming before the Zoning Board of Adjustment due to a property owner with a qualifying disability needing a structural expansion to accommodate their needs and ensure quality of life. In all requests, the Zoning Board of Adjustment granted the setback, height or lot coverage variance, but the property owner also had to air their disability in a public meeting,” Fisher wrote the Journal.

She continued, “Along with creating an ordinance in compliance with the federal Fair Housing Act and Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act to affirmatively further fair housing and provide equal opportunities for those with disabilities, this is the catalyst that initiated putting this ordinance together.”

The ordinance, as currently written, establishes a procedure through an administrative process that doesn’t involve public hearings. A memo attached to the ordinance notes the city’s zoning ordinance does not include an administrative process to seek a modification to a zoning regulation to afford an individual with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a property, but the proposed administrative process meets FHA and ADA obligations. According to the memo, there is a reduced risk that an accommodation will be handled with discrimination when it’s handled administratively.

Fisher said, “Ongoing conversations are taking place regarding the required submittal information (for Tamang’s Oxford House).”

Oxford House is a nonprofit organization aiding in self-supporting, self-run recovery houses throughout the United States and internationally.

According to the Oxford House website, there are 3,500 Oxford houses across the country with 24,000 individuals in recovery living in the houses at any given time during the year. Six of those houses are in Rapid City. From previous reporting, Oxford Houses are not halfway houses, treatment facilities or homeless shelters. They are places where people in recovery from drug and alcohol addiction can live and find support while they re-establish their lives. Tamang, under an LLC registered in his name, purchased a house on Terracita Drive in Rapid City in October 2025 and leased it to Oxford House. The house is called “New Dreams.” It’s located in Tamang’s ward.

“They tend (the tenants of the homes) to do a very good job because everybody in there is sober and they have jobs. They just have a history of addiction, and so they stay together to maintain sobriety," Tamang said. "(It's) really a beautiful thing and it's definitely a net positive in there. (It's) also a form of affordable housing because they typically run six to nine people in the house and they pay a fraction of the cost for sharing the house."

The Oxford House website shows the home has a nine-person capacity and two vacancies.

In a letter to City Council obtained by the Journal, the next-door neighbor wrote she filed an official complaint with the city on Nov. 7, 2025, after finding out the house had been purchased to be used as an Oxford House for eight or nine people living in it. Under the city’s current zoning ordinance, no more than five unrelated adults may live in a home without obtaining a conditional use permit.

She wrote city staff informed her Tamang would be given 30 days to come under compliance with the city by applying for a CUP.

"In October, 2025, the Community Development Department received a complaint that the (residential property) was being used as an Oxford House. Community Development staff inspected the property and, subsequently, sent the property owner a code violation letter on Nov. 13, 2025,” Fisher said.

The letter stated that the use of the residence as a “group home” required the review and approval of a Conditional Use Permit by the Planning Commission. The letter gave Tamang 30 days to either reduce the number of residents or apply for a Conditional Use Permit for a group home.

“Upon receiving additional information from the property owner about the specific use of the structure as an Oxford House, it was determined that since no additional services beyond residential use was taking place within the residence, the use did not qualify as a ‘group home’ and a Conditional Use Permit was not needed," Fisher said.

A Jan. 20 letter from Oxford House’s general legal counsel, Steven Polin, explained Oxford House does not provide specialized attention or care, nor does it provide room and board, counseling, rehabilitative services and other services customarily provided by a group homes. Rather, its residents “relate to each other in the same manner as a traditional family.”

 Tamang
Rapid City Councilman Stephen Tamang (Ward 1), listens during the public safety roundtable at the Rapid City Public Library on Tuesday, April 7. 

Polin also explained the residents of Oxford House are individuals who are handicapped by alcoholism or drug abuse and cannot live independently, and it would be a reasonable accommodation for the city to waive the occupation limit and treat the individuals living in the home as a family.

“The city has a duty to provide a means of accommodating this request,” Polin wrote.

Tamang said Fisher is “wonderful” and he has a lot of respect for her, but they don’t discuss the topic.

“My job is to just abstain,” he said.

Fisher said she requested that the council delay the reasonable accommodation procedure vote by a month so her team can put a fact sheet to further explain the uses that will fall within a reasonable accommodation administrative approval and clarify the uses that will require a conditional use permit and/or variance. In addition, data is being gathered to determine if any nuisance violations and/or police calls have occurred at existing locations that will fall within the administrative approval allowance.

"The city desires to create a decision-making environment that guards against discriminatory community pressure that may infect a reasonable accommodation zoning decision,” Fisher said. “Reasonable accommodations for people with disabilities aim to give those people a fair and comparable chance to live in and enjoy a property. Courts across the U.S. have decided cases against local governments when neighborhood opposition that is rooted in fear, stereotyping or animus toward persons with disabilities has tainted the outcome of local government zoning decisions on reasonable accommodation requests. Those lawsuits are costly to local government taxpayers. A local government deciding upon a reasonable accommodation has a duty not to allow illegal prejudices of the majority to influence the decision-making process.”

Tamang said the creation of the procedures is the “right thing for the city to do.”

title: Black Hills Energy focus of Iowa safety probe
byline: ISRAEL SCHUMAN USA Today Network/Des Moines Register
description: An Iowa investigation of Black Hills Energy, a utilities provider for 1.3 million customers is being broadened as numerous safety issues have come to light.
_full_text:
An Iowa investigation of Black Hills Energy, a utilities provider for 1.3 million customers is being broadened as numerous safety issues have come to light.

The Iowa Utilities Commission announced what it said will be a "comprehensive investigation" on Monday, June 29, as the result of the issues, which were found in a probe of the company's Spencer unit. The Spencer operating area includes natural gas pipelines in 18 communities in northwest Iowa.

The initial investigation began in September 2025 after a routine inspection the previous June "identified more than 100 safety issues spanning 16 violation categories," the IUC said. It said none of the violations posed an immediate threat to the public, but because of their volume, it decided to evaluate whether civil penalties were warranted.

 The Black Hills Energy plant in Spencer, Iowa. The plant was found in a June 2025 routine inspection by the Iowa Utilities Commission to have committed scores of safety violations.
The Black Hills Energy plant in Spencer, Iowa. The plant was found in a June 2025 routine inspection by the Iowa Utilities Commission to have committed scores of safety violations. 

"However, as the IUC reviewed the data and looked at other Black Hills operations, the agency became increasingly concerned about potentially broader, company-wide safety issues that are not isolated to the Spencer Unit," the release said. "The sheer number of violations, delays in making necessary corrections, and the increased risk to public safety prompted the IUC to broaden its investigation."

The IUC said it is deferring a final decision on civil penalties for the Spencer Unit until it completes what said will be "a full evaluation of Black Hills’ safety and management practices" throughout the rest of Iowa. It said the company has 30 days to "address the root causes of these widespread violations, their delays in fixing known issues, and whether further corrective action plans are needed."

The IUC will hold a formal hearing Aug. 27 in Des Moines, where Black Hills will have to address its safety practices and compliance with regulations statewide, the release said. The IUC will review the company’s written response to the order and testimony at the hearing to evaluate what penalties and corrective actions are required, it said.

Based in Rapid City the company serves customers in that South Dakota as well as in Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and Wyoming.

This article originally appeared on Des Moines Register: Utilities provider Black Hills Energy focus of Iowa safety probe

Reporting by Israel Schuman, Des Moines Register / Des Moines Register

title: ‘Get prepared before you think you’ll need to’: Bush Fellow aims for robust disaster prep skills in tribal communities
description: Jessica “Jesse” Big Crow believes the best time to prepare for an emergency is before it strikes. Her mission, as a 2026 Bush Fellow, is to transform and improve disaster preparedness in tribal communities.
_full_text:
Jessica “Jesse” Big Crow believes the best time to prepare for an emergency is before it strikes. Her mission, as a 2026 Bush Fellow, is to transform and improve disaster preparedness in tribal communities.

“Get prepared before you think you need to,” Big Crow said. “Don’t wait until there’s a storm, fire or power outage. Know how you’ll communicate with people, where you’ll go, what supplies you’ll need. It starts with having a plan, and people around you know what the plan is.”  

Big Crow (Oglála Lakota) lives in her hometown of Pine Ridge, where she was born and raised. When she begins her two-year Bush Fellowship on Aug. 1, her work will focus on hazard mitigation and disaster preparedness that incorporates Indigenous culture.

Big Crow’s goal is to cultivate a new generation of Indigenous leaders who are able to shape disaster preparedness and resilience across tribal nations. Big Crow will use her Bush Fellowship to obtain leadership coaching and gain advanced training in designing programs and policies, according to a news release from the Bush Foundation.

“The Bush Fellowship will give me time and resources and space to help myself grow as a leader so I’ll be able to seek out trainings, education, mentorship, conferences and elders in the community I can work with,” she said. “I feel like I’m truly blessed with this opportunity.”

Big Crow is employed by the Oglála Sioux Tribe, where she already has a vital role in helping tribal communities cope with emergencies. When tribal communities risked losing access to emergency preparedness training, she organized a Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) Train-the-Trainer course. She later became a Master CERT Trainer herself.

She played a key role in securing statewide approval for a Hybrid CERT model, which expanded access to training across South Dakota’s rural and reservation communities.

Through her work with Oglála Sioux Tribe Emergency Management and Lakota Nation Disaster Resiliency, she designs and delivers trainings that integrate Lakota language, traditions and values.

Big Crow is excited about the fact that her Bush Fellowship will allow her to learn about preparedness measures that have successfully been used elsewhere, then adapt them for South Dakota’s tribal communities.

“I’ll be able to strengthen my skills, (which) will help me grow and become a stronger leader and get better at what I do,” she said.

When Big Crow began volunteering with OST Emergency Management in 2018, she saw a natural fit between Indigenous practices and the skills that can help individuals, families and communities cope in times of emergencies.

“Once I got involved with Emergency Management and we were about disaster preparedness activities and I was doing research, I started thinking about how, traditionally as Lakota people in general, we did things that already were considered disaster preparedness. If you do canning, that’s a disaster preparedness activity, but would you have thought canning was disaster preparedness?”

“Some of us already grew up doing this. We just didn’t call it disaster preparedness. We knew a storm was coming so we chopped wood. In case of water shortages, we were already using five-gallon (storage),” Big Crow said.

“Not just as Lakota people but in general, there are already people that do that,” she said. “We can’t prevent snow (for example), but leading up to it, watching the weather, what can we do to be ready for an event?”

“These are things we already do. I need to find ways to bring it back out to our communities and remind us we already do this, and these are other things we can do as far as disaster preparedness goes, and incorporating our culture back into it,” she said.

Food preparation, preservation and storage is an area of particular interest to her. Gathering traditional plants and foods, for example, is a form of disaster preparation. When high-tech resources aren’t available, or they fail, traditional methods of food preparation remain viable.

“One of the examples is the way we cut our meat real thin. It’s called ‘kabla’ and you hang it to dry. The result is like how you would make a jerky, but it’s not seasoned. That was one of the ways we preserved food,” Big Crow said. “We were able to store it and carry it with us.”

Oglala Lakota College offers a class on traditional plants and foods, but because not everyone has access to college classes, Big Crow wants to develop trainings about traditional food preparation, using whatever tools are available, that as many people as possible can access.

“I do plan to travel during my Bush Fellowship. I am working on reaching out to some communities and spaces that have strong food sovereignty and robust CERT programs already and seeing how they’ve done it,” she said. “I’m hoping it can help me with how I want our CERT programs to operate and be stronger and more culturally grounded.”

One of the resources where people can turn is the nonprofit organization Lakota Nation Disaster Resiliency, indresiliency.org, located on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation. Big Crow works with the organization, which has a website that offers information about disaster preparedness, disaster prevention, hazard mitigation, and recovery. 

A Facebook page for Lakota Nation Disaster Resiliency is in progress, Big Crow said, and it will be a resource that provides updates on weather and more to help people better cope with emergencies.

Big Crow credits her mother, Maretta Champagne, and her brother, Beau Big Crow, Sr., for helping spark her interest in disaster preparation, because both worked for FEMA. After a devastating hail storm, Champagne asked Big Crow to volunteer for OST Emergency Management, answering phones as people were calling in looking for help. Big Crow discovered she had a knack for documentation, paperwork and keeping track of things.

Through her career and as she begins her Bush Fellowship, Big Crow credits the support of her family, including her mother and brother, her daughter Asa A’pui Big Crow, her sons Cetan and Semni Big Crow. She also credits the influence of family members who have died but who still influence Big Crow — her father, Walter Big Crow, and her grandmother and great-grandmother.

“They are no longer here but they helped shape and guide me in the type of work that I do. I lean back on their lessons. My grandparents and my dad taught me how to be resilient, how to be prepared in disasters, how to get ready and that’s knowledge I’m grateful and blessed to have learned,” Big Crow said.

“It’s been a truly humbling experience and I’m really grateful for the opportunity,” she said. “I really am passionate about disaster resiliency and food sovereignty and our cultural knowledge and emergency preparedness and making sure our people are supported.”

title: Rapid City warns of return of email scam asking for application fees
description: An email scam similar to one from early June has surfaced this week in Rapid City. The emails appear official, even using City staff and signature blocks with invoice numbers and requesting immediate wire transfer of funds to the City’s Planning Commission. City of Rapid City officials are again issue a warning to the public of the email scam regarding the processing of development applications or seeking payment on fake invoices.
_full_text:
An email scam similar to one from early June has surfaced this week in Rapid City. The emails appear official, even using City staff and signature blocks with invoice numbers and requesting immediate wire transfer of funds to the City’s Planning Commission. City of Rapid City officials are again issue a warning to the public of the email scam regarding the processing of development applications or seeking payment on fake invoices.

City Planning officials have been notified of four incidences in recent days of businesses receiving emails seeking payment and providing fake invoices. The most recent emails end with @usa.com which are not City government emails.

The content of the emails is similar to an email that surfaced a month ago. In early June, City officials issued a warning to residents regarding an email that appeared to have been sent by the City’s Planning Commission. The detailed email included the City’s seal and indicated the correspondence was from the City of Rapid City – Planning Commission; with an invoice number, date, and indicating fees were due upon receipt. The correspondence included an invoice with line items of various fees and indicating failure to immediately remit payment would delay final administrative, processing, scheduling and approval actions with the application.

 Rapid City Hall
City Hall in Rapid City is located at 300 Sixth St. 

“The correspondence items appear legitimate with the use of the City’s seal, signature blocks and details that appear official in nature,” said Vicki Fisher, Director of Rapid City’s Community Development Department. “This is a scam. The City’s Planning Commission does not email or send out correspondence seeking payment. Although there are various fees associated with City permits and applications from the City’s Community Development Department, we would never seek immediate wire transfer of funds or threaten to delay work on the processing of applications without the wire transfer of funds.”

City officials advise the public that legitimate email messages from Rapid City government departments and staff will contain @rcgov.org (City offices), @rcplib.org (Rapid City Public Library) or @themonument.live (The Monument) as part of the sender’s address. Official correspondence will never be sent from the Rapid City Planning Commission. As a general rule, do not open links or attachments from unknown sources.

In addition, anyone receiving the Planning Commission wire transfer email request is advised to contact Community Development. Department staff are available to discuss the status of individual permits and applications with City customers.

title: Elevate Rapid City names Valentine new CEO
description: Elevate Rapid City announced Wednesday its board has appointed Jack Valentine as the new president and CEO of the organization, effective July 27.
_full_text:
Elevate Rapid City announced Wednesday its board has appointed Jack Valentine as the new president and CEO of the organization, effective July 27.

A U.S. Marine, former SWAT Team Leader, coach, mentor, and economic development executive, Valentine has “spent his career leading teams, developing people, building partnerships, and delivering results in complex and dynamic environments,” Elevate said in a release.

 Jack Valentine
Jack Valentine 

He brings extensive expertise in financial management, strategic planning, change management, and organizational leadership.

"I am deeply honored and excited for the opportunity to serve as president and CEO of Elevate Rapid City,” Valentine said in the release. “Rapid City is a remarkable community with great people, strong businesses, and tremendous opportunities. In this role, I am committed to building our community through strong partnerships and by helping deliver opportunities that strengthen our regional economy and the future of Rapid City and the entire Black Hills region."

In a letter to investors, Elevate board chair Tom Weaver said the announcement, “marks an important step forward for our organization and for the broader Rapid City region. Since 2019, Elevate has served as the primary economic development engine for the Black Hills, working to strengthen our business community, support job creation, advance workforce solutions, and build long-term regional prosperity. As we look ahead, the board believes Jack is the right leader to help Elevate continue that work with focus, energy, and a deep commitment to partnership.”

“Jack’s unique skillsets will help enhance Elevate’s ability to promote economic growth in the region while deepening relationships with its strategic partners,” Weaver said in the release.

 Helene Duhamel
Elevate Rapid City honored state Sen. Helene Duhamel at its 2025 annual meeting. 

Valentine most recently served as the operations division director for the South Dakota Governor’s Office of Economic Development, where he oversaw the organizational performance of the finance, marketing, and administrative teams.

"I am proud of Jack’s leadership throughout his career serving in the U.S. Marine Corps, law enforcement, and state government,” GOED Commissioner Bill Even said in the release. “I look forward to continuing our collaboration with Elevate Rapid City and the great work being done to grow the Black Hills economy."

Elevate said it had more than 200 qualified candidates identified through a national search process facilitated by Winner Partners.

“We were looking for a leader who understands economic development, values relationships, can strengthen organizational performance, and will continue building trust with investors, public partners, and the community. Jack stood out in each of those areas,” Weaver said in the letter to investors. “This is also a moment to thank Todd Kenner and Darren Haar for their steady leadership as Interim CEO and COO. They have helped guide Elevate through a critical period with professionalism, perspective, and a continued focus on the organization’s mission.”

Valentine replaces Tom Johnson, who left for a position in Texas in January.
