title: A brief history of Rapid City
description: Rapid City as its residents and visitors know it today didn’t exist 250 years ago when the country was founded. Compared to the country, the City of Presidents is relatively young, about 100 years younger. Here’s a brief history of the area, per the Rapid City Public Library:
_full_text:
Rapid City as its residents and visitors know it today didn’t exist 250 years ago when the country was founded. Compared to the country, the City of Presidents is relatively young, about 100 years younger. Here’s a brief history of the area, per the Rapid City Public Library:

Before the first survey laid out the town, the land was home to the Lakota and other American Indians for generations. In 1876, white settlers attracted to the Black Hills by the discovery of gold founded a community they called Hay Camp. Located at a natural entrance into the Black Hills, the community was later renamed Rapid City and became the largest city in western South Dakota.

Origins

Founders Park, located by the original campsite of the founding party pioneers of 1876, shares the historical significance of the founding of Hay Camp - later known as Rapid City.

Members of the founding party include John R. Brennan, Martin Persinger, Thomas Gerguson, W.P. Martin, Albert Brown, William Marston, J.W. Allen, James Carney, William Nuttal, Major Hutchinson, and Samuel Scott. These eleven founders laid out the original town site.

Unlike Black Hills communities that began as mining camps, Rapid City owes its beginning to a group of discouraged gold prospectors. John Brennan and Samuel Scott were part of the wave of white settlers who flocked to the region after the Custer Expedition discovered gold here in 1874. In February 1876, Brennan and Scott led a small party of men to the banks of Rapid Creek, where they laid out a square-mile business district for what is now Rapid City. Within six months, more than 100 people called Rapid City “home.”

 Founders Park Plaza
Founders Park was busy with locals enjoying the warm weather on Feb. 27, 2025. 

Founders Park, located by the original campsite of the founding party pioneers of 1876, shares the historical significance of the founding of Hay Camp - later known as Rapid City.

Members of the founding party include John R. Brennan, Martin Persinger, Thomas Gerguson, W.P. Martin, Albert Brown, William Marston, J.W. Allen, James Carney, William Nuttal, Major Hutchinson, and Samuel Scott. These 11 founders laid out the original town site.

Unlike Black Hills communities that began as mining camps, Rapid City owes its beginning to a group of discouraged gold prospectors. John Brennan and Samuel Scott were part of the wave of white settlers who flocked to the region after the Custer Expedition discovered gold here in 1874. In February 1876, Brennan and Scott led a small party of men to the banks of Rapid Creek, where they laid out a square-mile business district for what is now Rapid City. Within six months, more than 100 people called Rapid City “home.”

History

City founders billed the community as the “Gateway to the Black Hills,” and it quickly lived up to the moniker. Originally known as “Hay Camp,” Rapid City soon became a staging ground for wagons hauling supplies to miners in the Black Hills. Later it would also serve as a hub for rail traffic.

The population grew and shrank with several booms and busts between 1880 and 1920. The South Dakota School of Mines, formally established in 1889, provided a focus for higher education and after 1920, Rapid City population began to steadily rise. President Calvin Coolidge drew the nation’s attention on western South Dakota when he relocated his White House staff to the Black Hills in 1927. That same year Gutzon Borglum began carving Mount Rushmore, helping to spark a tourism industry that still powers the local economy.

During World War II, the War Department created the Rapid City Air Base (later renamed Ellsworth Air Force Base). After the war, the base and a growing economy fueled Rapid City’s development.

 2026 is Rapid's sesquicentennial
A painting of early Rapid City inside The Journey Museum. 

What may be the seminal event in Rapid City’s history began with a raindrop. On June 9, 1972, heavy rains caused massive flooding of Rapid Creek which would become the Rapid City Flood of 1972. As the worst natural disaster in South Dakota history, the flood claimed 238 lives. As documented on the Rapid City Public Library's Flood website and by National Weather Service, the flood caused $160 million in property damage.

The city rebuilt, creating a 12-mile-long bike path and public greenway along the creek’s banks that serves as both a memorial to the lost and a means of ensuring such a tragedy never happens again.

title: Pomp, circumstance and anti-communism punctuate Trump’s South Dakota visit
description: For the first time since 2020, President Donald Trump appeared in the Black Hills at Mount Rushmore. This time, Friday, July 3, it was the eve of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. A severe weather advisory and hail preceded his arrival and pageantry enveloped his approach. As he stepped onto the stage, the crowd of nearly 5,000 chanted “USA! USA! USA!”
_full_text:
For the first time since 2020, President Donald Trump appeared in the Black Hills at Mount Rushmore. This time, Friday, July 3, it was the eve of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. A severe weather advisory and hail preceded his arrival and pageantry enveloped his approach. As he stepped onto the stage, the crowd of nearly 5,000 chanted “USA! USA! USA!”

He centered his speech on the country’s birthday, while emphasizing American excellence and the “resurgence of the communist menace,” with a nod to fears about immigration as well. He also took the opportunity to push for the passage of the SAVE America Act and highlight the importance of the midterms.

 Evening crowd shot

“On this anniversary, we must remember, we have to remember, we can never forget that American liberty has not endured for 250 years merely because of words on paper. Liberty has prevailed here because of the culture and character of the people who declared it, defended it and preserved it,” Trump said.

Prior to Trump’s speech, Mount Rushmore National Memorial Superintendent Jennifer Carpenter welcomed the crowd, after the weather advisory lifted at 6:35 p.m. Country music artist Chancey Williams performed live music, as did the U.S. Air Force Academy Band. Williams is set to play a concert at Main Street Square in Rapid City on the evening of July 4, and the Air Force band played at the Memorial Park Bandshell on July 1. Gov. Larry Rhoden delivered a speech and introduced former North Dakota governor and current Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, who spoke before ultimately introducing the president.

 Presidential aircraft

Air Force One flew over the memorial twice before landing at Ellsworth Air Force Base around 7:50 p.m. President Trump took off for Mount Rushmore in Marine One around 8:15 p.m. He was greeted at the base by Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Ellsworth Commander Col. Jonathan A. Keller and Chief Master Sgt. Thomas Podgorski.

All said, the Rushmore festivities began at about 7 p.m. and concluded at about 10 p.m. after a barrage of fireworks surrounded the granite presidents’ faces. The crowd filed to their vehicles and traveled through dense traffic seldom seen in the Black Hills.

Trump touts the virtues of South Dakota pols, Americans, scolds use of term ‘stolen land’

The president called Senate Majority Leader John Thune, “a good friend of mine,” Sen. Mike Rounds a “great guy,” and thanked Rhoden.

“You live in a very special place. Congratulations, everybody,” Trump said. “From the snow-capped peaks of the Rockies to the white sand shores of the Gulf of America, right here in the Black Hills of the Dakotas, after 250 years of America, American freedom still rings.”

 President Donald Trump 1
President Donald Trump speaks at Mount Rushmore on Friday, July 3. 

Trump did not mention outgoing Rep. Dusty Johnson, who recently was beaten in the primary race for South Dakota governor by Rhoden and Toby Doeden. The two are competing in a run-off election on July 28. One will advance to the November general election.

Trump also did not mention former South Dakota Gov. Kristi Noem, who hosted Trump at Mount Rushmore in 2020 and gifted him a bust showing his face carved on the mountain. Noem served as Trump’s secretary of Homeland Security until Trump dismissed her this year, giving her the position of special envoy to the Shield of the Americas. The Associated Press reported Noem said Trump told her in 2018 that it was his dream to have his face carved in the monument. Trump posted a rendering of his face on the mountain to Truth Social ahead of the speech, Newsweek reported.

On Friday, however, he didn’t mention his likeness making it into the granite.

The president called the four presidents that are on Mount Rushmore — George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Abraham Lincoln and Theodore Roosevelt — “men of action, men of ambition, men of daring, men of destiny and men of truly great intelligence.”

“As for those who peddle Marxist lies about our heritage, tell our children that we live on stolen land, or that our heroes were oppressors, they're doing something much worse than slandering our past,” Trump said. “They are slandering and attacking our future.”

That was the president’s only reference to the complex history of Mount Rushmore, which is located on land the U.S. Supreme Court ruled was illegally seized in violation of the Fort Laramie Treaty.

Communism ‘a mortal threat’ worse than 9/11, Trump says

Aside from highlighting American inventions and freedom, Trump said American identity is being challenged by a “resurgence of the communist menace in our land, including from newcomers to our country.”

“Communism is a mortal threat to American liberty. It is the greatest threat to our country, including World War I, World War II, Pearl Harbor or even 9/11,” Trump said.

 Counter sniper team
A Secret Service Counter Sniper Team member keeps an eye on Mount Rushmore ahead of President Donald Trump’s arrival on Friday, July 3. 

Aside from the Cold War, the United States has a longstanding history of suspicion of communism and two specific Red Scare eras. According to the Encyclopedia Britannica, a Red Scare is a period of public fear and anxiety over the supposed rise of communist or socialist ideologies in a noncommunist state. The term is generally used to describe two such periods in the United States. The first occurred from 1917 to 1920, amid an increase in organized labor movements, immigration, urbanization, and industrialization. The second period, also called McCarthyism after U.S. Sen. Joseph McCarthy, took place from roughly 1947 to 1954.

“It's an ideology of mass theft, mass control, mass lies, and mass murder,” Trump said. “Such doctrines can be given no quarter in a democracy, because the first thing they do when they get into power is turn around and destroy it … You can be a communist, or you can be a patriot. You cannot be both.”

Trump weaves communism comments in with importance of SAVE America Act

After the president said, “We resolve and swear for all to hear that the citizens of the United States of America will vanquish communism quickly … and send them into exile,” he pivoted to the SAVE America Act before doubling down on communism again.

The president pushed for the elimination of the filibuster to pass the SAVE America Act. Filibustering is a tactic to delay a floor vote on a bill by prolonging debate. Under current law, it takes 60 senators to end a filibuster. If filibustering is taken out of lawmakers’ toolboxes, a simple majority will be all it takes to pass a bill.

The SAVE America Act would require voters to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections and photo identification when voting. Both are already required in South Dakota. The U.S. House has passed the bill, but it has yet to make it out of the Senate. Thune has consistently said there aren’t enough votes to pass the bill, telling Fox Business in June, "For me, it's a function of math.”

Trump said, “We will send them (communists) quickly away, and we will continue to build our country bigger and better and stronger than ever before. America will never be a communist country. We can only lose the midterms if we allow ourselves to lose the midterms, if we are foolish, stupid, and unwise. But if we terminate the filibuster as we should do and immediately vote for the SAVE America Act, we do that, we're not going to lose an election for 100 years. The Communist Party is made up of illegal immigrants, criminals, and everybody that doesn't want to work.”

Within minutes of Trump leaving the stage, the fireworks began. It’s been six years since a fireworks show at Rushmore.

 Firework 4

 070526-nws-ellsworth-p1.JPG
Air Force One lands at Ellsworth Air Force Base on Friday, July 3, carrying President Donald Trump. 

 Air Force One at Ellsworth Air Force Base
Air Force One taxis at Ellsworth Air Force Base after landing on Friday, July 3. 

 Photos from the America 250 events at Mount Rushmore
Have a look at what it was like at Mount Rushmore on Friday, July 3, the day before the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. A weather advisory sent attendees looking for shelter from hail. Admittance paused temporarily before resuming. Air Force One flew over the memorial on its way to Ellsworth Air Force Base, where the president landed before taking Marine One to Mount Rushmore and speaking for just shy of 30 minutes before a half-hour-long fireworks show.

title: Little Bighorn library letters: A glimpse into preparing for the 50th commemoration
description: “Don’t forget to keep a weather eye open for that prince of fakers, Alfred Chapman, the long-haired liar who claims he was Custer’s chief guide, and witnessed the massacre thru a spyglass from a hill a mile away.”
_full_text:
“Don’t forget to keep a weather eye open for that prince of fakers, Alfred Chapman, the long-haired liar who claims he was Custer’s chief guide, and witnessed the massacre thru a spyglass from a hill a mile away.”

This passage, close to the top of a June 1, 1926, letter written by cowboy poet Earl Alonzo Brininstool, was an admonishment to J.A. Shoemaker, secretary of the National Custer Memorial Association.

Shoemaker was helping coordinate the 50th anniversary commemoration of the Battle of the Little Bighorn, known to victorious Native American tribes as the Battle of the Greasy Grass. Their defeat of the 7th Cavalry on June 25-26, 1876, was being observed with great fanfare organized by a national committee led by Gen. E.S. Godfrey, National Commander Legion of Valor.

Custer commemoration

 Elizabeth "Libbie" Custer
Elizabeth "Libbie" Custer advocated for her husband long after his death, including as a member of the committee marking the 50th anniversary of the Battle of the Little Bighorn. 

At the top of the committee’s letterhead, just below Godfrey, was Mrs. George A. Custer, wife of Lt. Col. George Custer, who was killed while leading the 7th Regiment of the U.S. Cavalry against the Lakota Sioux, Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes camped along the Little Bighorn River in southeast Montana.

The letters, along with other documents that include 12 signed handwritten messages from Elizabeth Custer, are among artifacts contained in the Billings Public Library’s archives. Included are two letters from Elizabeth Custer to the librarian at the time, Elizabeth Garber, offering to send her books.

Elizabeth Custer wrote three books, two of which she signed when donating them to Billings and one of which has disappeared and was replaced by a donation.

“This could have very well been on the shelf for decades, and it just evaporated in the wind,” said Joe Lanning, Montana Room Librarian.

Where the correspondence and other documents came from is unknown.

“That’s a mystery, because provenance for most of it was a handshake,” Lanning said.

 I.E. O'Donnell
I.E. O'Donnell was a prominent Billings pioneer who helped organize the 50th anniversary commemoration of the Battle of the Little Bighorn. 

But Lanning suspects they may have been donated by one of the library’s original board members, Ignatius Daniel “I.D.” O’Donnell, a family friend and employee of Parmly Billings.

“Parmly was former president of the Northern Pacific and the largest private landowner in newly established Yellowstone County,” according to the Montana Cowboy Hall of Fame’s website, which inducted O’Donnell in 2018. “Parmly placed his various Yellowstone agricultural interests under I.D.’s supervision.”

 Letterhead
This 1926 letter from Earl Alonzo Brininstool is written on the National Custer Memorial Association's letterhead. 

Links to history

Lanning alerted the Billings Gazette to the artifacts after reading that Jim and Virginia Court were donating a 1927 letter from Elizabeth Custer they had acquired to the Big Horn County Museum. The donation took place as the 150th anniversary of the battle approached last month.

“There was correspondence between a lot of old members of different regiments here and there, really asking (O’Donnell), and kind of like making their case of, like, 'Hey, I was an important element of such and such unit,' maybe an invitation to come out, and 'I think maybe footing the bill for me traveling would be in order,'” Lanning said.

O’Donnell and Shoemaker were overwhelmed with such pleas and liked the idea of the “old timers” gathering but could only afford so much based on the event’s limited funds. Shoemaker’s handwritten list of invitees numbered into the 50s.

When finally launched, the 50th anniversary drew the “Greatest crowd in Montana history” to the battlefield, proclaimed the Kremlin (Montana) Chancellor newspaper in its July 9, 1926, edition.

“The fiftieth anniversary afforded a unique opportunity for a reunion of the aging combatants,” according to the Natural History Museum’s post quoting historian Douglas McChristian. “Promoters of the semi-centennial realized that the ranks of Little Bighorn survivors, both red and white, were thinning with each passing year. For the veterans, time had tempered some of the old animosities. It seemed a good time to reflect and symbolically ‘bury the hatchet’ while there was still time.”

In addition to Custer’s death, the battle resulted in the killing of 260 soldiers and an estimated 60 to 100 warriors.

Custer’s last charge

 Elizabeth Custer letter
The Billings Public Library has about a dozen letters from Elizabeth Custer. 

At age 84, Elizabeth Custer remained her husband’s greatest promoter, evidenced by her position on the 1926 committee.

“She was the number one supporter and salvager of Custer's image after the battle, right?” Lanning said. “She's the one that did the most work making sure that he was remembered as, like, a Western hero and not a failure, because there were plenty of people out there at the time that thought, well, maybe it's the latter, right?”

Elizabeth Custer wrote to Shoemaker requesting help with housing friends, praised those taking part in organizing the events and, in one instance, criticizing Major Marcus Reno for his actions in the battle.

Calling him “so great a coward,” she appealed to Shoemaker to ensure Reno wasn’t paid any tribute or “memorial of any kind to be placed on the sacred battlefield.”

“I beg you to try and avert any more in Congress that would glorify so faithless a soldier,” she wrote in the letter. “In writing this I feel almost my husband’s hand taking this pen away from me.”

In 1876, Reno led three companies across the Little Bighorn River toward the camp that contained an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 warriors. His troops were immediately attacked. Upon retreat, some soldiers were left behind, leading Reno to request a Court of Inquiry in hopes of exonerating his actions.

Propogating themes

 Elizabeth Custer signed book
Elizabeth Custer sent three of her signed books to the Billings Public Library in 1921. 

Lanning said in transcribing Elizabeth Custer’s letters, she hits on the same themes over and over again, which he called “some of the more interesting bits.” Those same themes – the ideology that United States settlers were destined by God to expand to the West – are in her books as well, he added.

“The language is very clear,” he said. “She is a believer in that cause.”

One letter Custer wrote noted her sorrow at not being able to attend the 50th anniversary and added how the West, so desolate before Euro-American arrival, was now “teeming with life.”

“In 2026 that's a rather controversial statement,” Lanning said. “I find powerful statements like that in every single letter I've looked through so far. I really think that that's the great part of these letters.”

 Dedication
Elizabeth Custer signed the books she wrote and donated. 

Odd bits

The library’s holdings also include a 1911 letter from John Burkman to Elizabeth Custer. Burkman, who as Custer’s orderly saddled the Lt. Col.’s horse on the day of the battle, wrote about his recollections of the day.

Burkman recounts Custer’s decision to attack, rather than wait for supporting troops, after the soldiers had been spotted by Native American scouts. He also complains about his deteriorating sight.

At age 86, nearly blind and in ill health, Burkman shot himself while living in Billings.

A Nov. 8, 1925, article in the New York Times noted his death.

“He was at one time caretaker of Custer's horses and blooded dogs,” the article said.

A 1916 handwritten letter in the library’s collection from Frederick Bond stated the writer could attest to the fact that the Lt. Col. did not have long hair at the time of the battle. While another letter writer claims to have arrived in the territory via steamboat and was the scout who sent dispatches about the location of Chief Sitting Bull’s camp on the Little Bighorn.

Are all the claims real? Lanning queried historians about one letter from a man saying he took messages from Gen. Alfred Terry to Reno during the battle calling for medical aid and reinforcements.

“When I first came upon it, I thought this seems like it might be a pretty big deal,” Lanning said, but after querying other historians, “Nothing else really backs it up.”

Native participants

 40th momento
Ribbons like this were printed for the 40th anniversary. 

Correspondence from 1926 in the library's possession from South Dakota provides a list of 40 Native American Greasy Grass combatants – including Puts on His Shoes, Did Not Go Home and Full Stomach – as now living on the reservation.

The reservation’s superintendent goes on to note that because of the “extreme age of these old braves, I believe that at least three of them will eliminate themselves by the time it is necessary” to commemorate the battle’s 50th anniversary.

One letter to O’Donnell sent by Nashua, Montana, resident Charles C. Sargent is typed on letterhead paper, the back of which contains advertisements. In the note, Sargent claims to “know about as much as anyone living about the affairs” of the battle, having talked to “nearly every one of the head mean of the Indians.”

According to his obituary, Sargent enlisted in the Union Army at the age of 15 and served for three years, six weeks of which was as a prisoner of war. “He enlisted again in January 1866, and came to Montana as a soldier to assist in building Fort Buford.”

He later settled on land that would become the Nashua townsite near the confluence of the Milk and Missouri rivers in northeastern Montana.

Fort Buford was built near the confluence of the Missouri and Yellowstone rivers, near present-day Williston, North Dakota, serving as a supply depot for western military actions. Sioux leader Sitting Bull surrendered at the fort in 1881 after avoiding U.S. Army capture for years by seeking refuge in Canada.

Digital future

Lanning plans on digitizing the letters and uploading them to the Montana History Portal so the public and researchers can easily access them.

The native southern Californian is a historian by training, with a graduate degree from Utah State University and undergrad at California State University, Fullerton. Lanning was hired to the library staff about eight years ago, working his way up to his current position, which he’s held almost five years.

“I'm just ridiculously lucky to have this position,” he said, calling the archives a “historian’s playground.”

Many of the library’s historic photos have already been uploaded to the Montana History Portal.

“Our photograph collection is phenomenal,” he said.

One last look back

In addition to warning organizers of the 50th Battle of the Little Bighorn commemoration to beware of “that prince of fakers,” Brininstool, in his letter from Los Angeles, also suggests who to include. He concluded by saying he hoped to make it to the event.

“Been in bed practically three weeks with flu or grip, and am just getting on my feet again, feeling rather wobbly,” he wrote.

Born in 1870, just six years before the battle, Brininstool was a “prolific author of books and articles on the Indian Wars,” according to the Nebraska State Historical Society. The society is home to a collection of his correspondence, manuscripts and articles between 1923 and 1935.

Interestingly, the author wrote a comment about a letter he published that was written by a U.S. Army colonel who vindicated Major Reno.

 Battle of Little Bighorn
Leading up the the 150th anniversary of the Battle of Little Bighorn, many tribal nations have set up infrastructure for their communities to utilize during their stay in Crow Agency, Montana. 

 Battle of Little Bighorn
Donovan Sprague a Lakota historian spoke at Racing Magpie on June 15, on the history of the Battle of Little Bighorn.

title: Jacqeline Allen
description: September 21, 1931 - May 9, 2026
_full_text:
September 21, 1931 - May 9, 2026

Jacqueline Louise (Anderson) Allen was born September 21, 1931 to Martha Elizabeth Miner and Vernon Rudolph Anderson, in Aberdeen SD. She passed away after a full life of 94 years on May 9, 2026 at West Hills Village, Rapid City, SD.

Baptized in the Methodist church, she was an active Girl Scout, Jobs Daughter Queen, twirled baton and played percussion in the band, graduating in 1949. After 2 years at Northern State Teachers College, she taught 4th grade in Hot Springs, SD. She finished her BA in primary education at USD in 1954 where she was a Pi Beta Phi.

While working as a waitress at Custer State Lodge, she recognized a handsome man who had been washing dishes at the Pi Phi house. This man, Bruce Allen, became her husband in 1955. Following Bruce in his medical training, Jackie taught Kindergarten in Sioux City IA, Philadelphia, PA, and St. Paul MN. The first of four children was born in St. Paul, then Sherman TX, Detroit MI and lastly in Rapid City where she and Bruce decided to live the remainder of their lives.

Early years raising children meant driving to lessons, sports and musical activities with an occasional stop at the YMCA for water aerobics. The Esquire and Canyon Lake club were favorite dancing spots. Jackie learned to ski and enjoyed social and civic clubs, including leadership positions in the Medical Auxiliary, PEO, Questers, Symphony League, Rapid City Beautification committee, and volunteering with the Dahl Fine arts and Journey Museum. She was a 25-year member of the Sons of Norway. She and Bruce loved to entertain at home, hosting many a bridge club and Gourmet club. Her hobbies included hardanger, gardening (especially roses and orchids), scrapbooking, and genealogy. She was a lifelong learner collecting children's books, poetry, National Geographic magazines, watching movies, listening to music and traveling. She and Bruce were long time members of the New Horizons Band.

The First Presbyterian Church was the backbone of their marriage where they made many friends and she contributed in a variety of capacities.

Jackie was preceded in death by her parents, her brother Jon, her beloved husband Bruce, and daughter Dianne. She is survived by Karen Allen Failinger, Susan (Brian) Sheehan, Richard (Claire) Allen, 15 grandchildren and 6 great grandchildren. Our thanks to the staff at West Hills Village who took care of Jackie and Bruce during the final years of their life.

A celebration of life will be July 11, 2026 at 10am, First Presbyterian Church in Rapid City, Rev. Adam Knutson officiating. Interment will be at Mountain View Cemetery. Memorials can be made to The First Presbyterian Church and/or West Hills Foundation, both in Rapid City, SD. Condolences can be sent to www.osheimschmidt.com.

title: Mia Cipriaso
description: December 7, 2020 - June 29, 2026
_full_text:
December 7, 2020 - June 29, 2026

With hearts deeply broken we announce the unexpected passing of Mia Linn Cipriaso, age 5, on June 29, 2026, in Spearfish, S.D. Mia was born to Kaycee Jo (Johnson) and Mario Cipriaso on December 7, 2020.

Though her time with us was far too short, Mia filled every day with laughter, happiness, just the right amount of sass and so much love. Her smiles and giggles were infectious with wild, untamed red hair to match her personality. Mia's love of adventure and discovery of new things should be something we all aspire to. She loved dresses, dancing, arts and crafts, picking flowers for her mama, being outside, riding bikes with her dad, playing with Luca, making friends everywhere she went and most of all, her family.

Her parents, Kaycee and Mario, along with her brothers, Luca (age 2) and Leo (age three months) are devastated by her loss but grateful for their time with her. Luca will forever have his sissy as she watches over her whole family. Equally blessed to share Mia's love are her grandparents, Jennifer and Brooke Leighty, Allyson and Austin Stephens, Jamie Johnson, Barry and Cynthia Cary, Mario and Marie Cipriaso; and her great-grandparents, Jane and Bill Dunbar, Susan Johnson, and Ron Leighty. She was deeply cherished by her Aunties, Ericka Cary, Jasmine Marriner, Javoni Cary, Letrice Tate and Charlene Cary as well as Uncles, Daulton and Brecken Johnson, Maddox and Nicco Stephens, and Trey Cary. Mia had several great aunts, uncles, cousins, and friends who she also shared her endless joy with.

Mia was met in Heaven and will be forever comforted by her great-grandparents, Peggy Cressman, Betty Essick, Opal and James Dunbar, Mary and Floyd Meek, Mac, Jean and Ed Johnson, Lola and Bruce Miller, Toni Leighty, Evelyn and Bob Cooper and other close family members.

While we struggle to understand this unimaginable loss, we take comfort in remembering the love she freely gave in her five beautiful years. She will forever be our Mia Beans, Sissy, Stinker Butts, Little Turd and Beautiful Girl. Mia brought so much life and love to her family, her loss is shattering. Mia Linn is forever loved, forever missed, forever five.

A service will be held at 10 a.m., Tuesday, July 7, 2026, at Fidler-Isburg Funeral Chapel.

Arrangements are under the care of Fidler-Isburg Funeral Chapel & Isburg Crematory of Spearfish. Online condolences may be written at https://www.fidler-isburgfuneralchapels.com/.

title: Pennington County buildings operational tomorrow, sheriff’s office says cybersecurity incident still under investigation
description: The Pennington County Sheriff’s Office said county operations will be open on Tuesday, July 7, but with limited services. Though public-facing county buildings will reopen, the sheriff’s office said an investigation into a cyberattack that led to closures on Monday continues.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Sheriff’s Office said county operations will be open on Tuesday, July 7, but with limited services. Though public-facing county buildings will reopen, the sheriff’s office said an investigation into a cyberattack that led to closures on Monday continues.

Pennington County officials said the county is working closely with the South Dakota National Guard Cyber Incident Response Team, the South Dakota Fusion Center, the Cyber Infrastructure Security Agency and other partners as the investigation continues.

Because this is an active investigation, there is very limited verified information available at this time.

“We’re just very appreciative of all the help that we’ve had,” Sheriff Brian Mueller said at a press conference on Monday, July 6. “We’re not going to be able to discuss a lot of details yet because this is an ongoing investigation and right now our focus is on assessing our current systems, working on getting them back online and doing the best we can to protect everyone’s personal information.”

The cyber security incident occurred over the Fourth of July weekend, and the sheriff’s office, along with local and federal entities, have been working on the case for several days. Mueller said it’s still being investigated as to how the incident occurred in the first place.

Mueller said he was unable to share whether the cybersecurity incident is malicious or not as of this time, but more information will be released once the office has a better idea of what they’re dealing with. Though the county buildings will be operational, Mueller asked the public to be patient as some of the services will be limited.

“Anything that’s really technology-based, as we slowly bring our systems back online, there might be a little bit of lag on our end,” Mueller said. “So I just ask for the public’s patience over the next couple of days as we get everything back to fully functioning.”

Mueller said the county already has protections in place for cybersecurity threats and will be thoroughly looking to further strengthen the system as the investigation continues.

“Cybersecurity is an ever-growing threat across the country,” Mueller said. “It’s been an issue all the way across the country in the private and the government sector. That’s something that we continue to monitor and try to be proactive in protecting that type of information. That’s just going to be an ever-growing challenge for us in today’s environment.”

Here are the latest updates since the incident. Although Pennington County offices will be open beginning July 7, many public services will be significantly impacted, the county said.

The Pennington County Commission meeting will take place as scheduled.

Vital Records services remain available through neighboring counties, by phone at 605-773-4961 or online at VitalChek.com for birth, death and marriage certificates.

Vehicle registration services remain available online at my605drive.sd.gov and at self-service kiosks.

Critical public safety services, including 911, the Pennington County Jail, 24/7 program, emergency response operations and court operations remain fully operational.

Treasurer’s Office: Staff will be available to answer questions related to vehicle titles and other Treasurer’s Office matters. However, the office cannot process vehicle registrations or accept payments of any kind. Vehicle registration renewal services remain available online at my605drive.sd.gov and at self-service kiosks.

Auditor’s Office: Early voting remains available. However, the office is unable to process lien payments at this time.

Register of Deeds: Beginning tomorrow, birth, death, and marriage certificates may be obtained through the office on site. Those records are also available online through VitalChek.com. Register of Deeds can also take real estate recordings.

For the most up-to-date information on available County services, please follow the Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office Facebook page, or contact the appropriate County department before visiting an office.

title: Advanced CT imaging in Rapid City a ‘game changer’ for health care
description: New CT imaging technology — the first of its kind in South Dakota — is now in use at Sanford Health Black Hills Imaging Center in Rapid City.
_full_text:
New CT imaging technology — the first of its kind in South Dakota — is now in use at Sanford Health Black Hills Imaging Center in Rapid City.

In June, Sanford Health Black Hills Imaging Center implemented the use of the new NAEOTOM Alpha with Quantum Technology. This is the latest generation of photon‑counting CT imaging, and the most advanced CT imaging technology in the state, according to a news release from Sanford Health.

This technology’s benefit, for medical professionals and patients, is that it provides sharper, more detailed images while exposing patients to lower radiation.

 070426-nws-CTscan-demonstration
Sanford Health Black Hills Imaging Center staff members demonstrate the use of the NAEOTOM Alpha® with Quantum Technology, the latest generation of photon‑counting CT imaging. This new technology at the imaging center in Rapid City is the first of its kind in South Dakota. It will provide clearer, more detailed images for use in treating patients. 

“This provides a more precise image with 30% to 60% less radiation on average. That reason alone is why we pursued this and why Sanford Health is investing in this technology,” said Kyle Wiese, president and CEO of Sanford Black Hills. “This is the type of machine I’d want my grandmother, my family and my friends to use.”

Because of the lower radiation doses, the new CT technology supports safer, frequent follow-up imaging, which can be especially beneficial for patients who have chronic or long-term conditions.

“This investment reflects Sanford Health’s commitment to bringing leading-edge, patient-centered care close to home,” Wiese said. “This is a major step forward in cardiovascular care for our region, and we are proud to provide this advanced technology to our patients.”  

Previously, Sanford Health Black Hills Imaging Center used conventional CT technology, which reconstructs images indirectly and produces lower-resolution images. Photon-counting CT uses a QuantaMax detector that directly measures each X-ray photon and captures its energy, producing images with high spatial resolution and reduced noise, according to a news release.  

“The conventional CT is great but this (new technology) … gives you more precise answers off a single scan,” Wiese said. “Imagine a bucket catching rain. That’s kind of like a conventional CT catching X-ray energy. It can tell you a lot about the rain but not each individual drop of rain.”

“With this new photon-counting technology, this is more like counting individual raindrops as they fall and even measuring the size of each one. Each X-ray photon is getting detected and sorted,” he said.

 070426-nws-CTscan-machine
Sanford Health Black Hills Imaging Center in Rapid City is implementing the NAEOTOM Alpha® with Quantum Technology, the latest generation of photon‑counting CT imaging. This technology is the first of its kind in South Dakota. It will provide clearer, more detailed images for use in treating patients. 

Physicians are very excited about the new technology, Wiese said. These sharper, richly-detailed images can provide more answers in a single scan, helping medical care teams as they make decisions about the best treatment for patients.

This advanced CT imaging will play a critical role in cardiovascular care, said Wiese, who calls it “a game changer for most heart doctors.”

“It operates at such a remarkable speed that it captures the heart in a single beat and when needed, it can scan the chest, abdomen and pelvis in nearly one second,” Wiese said.

“Its enhanced resolution gives finer detail even in the most small, complex areas, which supports more precise and earlier diagnoses,” he said. “You’re going to get a better answer to what’s ailing you, which should give you a better fix to the problem.”

The advanced CT imaging also will strengthen diagnostic capabilities in emergency care, oncology, pulmonary care, and more. For example, this advanced technology provides better images of fractures that aid orthopedic surgeons in treating traumatic injuries. It could be used for pulmonary care to look into a patient’s lungs, and in oncology to examine tumors in more detail to tell whether they’re growing.

“When you think about all those uses, this is the right step forward for technology in our community,” Wiese said. “I’m proud to be part of making a significant investment in technology. It’s one of the reasons (Black Hills Imaging Center) is excited to join Sanford Health.”

Sanford Health Black Hills Imaging Center is located at 215 Anamaria Drive, on the campus of Sanford Black Hills Surgical Hospital.

title: FBI offers $25K for information about 2023 Pine Ridge murder
description: The FBI said it’s offering a reward of up to $25,000 for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the person or persons responsible for the 2023 murder of Patrick Carlow Sr., 73.
_full_text:
The FBI said it’s offering a reward of up to $25,000 for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the person or persons responsible for the 2023 murder of Patrick Carlow Sr., 73.

On the morning of May 19, 2023, Carlow was found murdered in his home near Oglala on the Pine Ridge Reservation. An investigation revealed the murder likely happened overnight, according to the FBI. Investigators found no signs of forced entry and the investigation determined the death was a homicide, the FBI said in a release. Investigators believe the person(s) responsible likely knew Carlow and were familiar with the layout of his home.

“The FBI is dedicated to finding justice for all crime victims,” FBI Minneapolis Field Office Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson said in the release. “It only takes one person to do the right thing for a grieving family. There is no better time than now to come forward with information that will answer the outstanding questions about Mr. Carlow’s death.”

 070926-nws-fbi-p1.pdf
A poster released by the FBI about Patrick Carlow Sr.

This reward is part of the FBI’s surge of resources into Indian Country investigations under Operation Steadfast Promise and Operation Not Forgotten.

The FBI is requesting anyone with information regarding Carlow’s death to contact the FBI at 800-CALL-FBI or by submitting information to tips.fbi.gov. You may also contact the nearest American Embassy or Consulate. A poster is available at fbi.gov/wanted/seeking-info/patrick-carlow-sr.

The FBI said Operation Steadfast Promise is “a comprehensive surge of resources to address a wide range of violent crime threats, including gangs and criminal enterprises, violent crimes against children and fugitive apprehension cases while working to improve public safety in Tribal communities.”

Under this surge, Operation Not Forgotten seeks justice for victims of unresolved crimes. The goal of Operation Not Forgotten is to move cases closer to resolution, provide services for victims, and to bring offenders to justice, who have so far escaped it,” the FBI said.

title: A look back at Gov. Larry Rhoden’s Mount Rushmore speech
description: KEYSTONE — To the sound of the “Rawhide” theme song — which goes, ‘Rollin’, rollin’, rollin.’ — South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden took the stage below the Mount Rushmore National Memorial.
_full_text:
KEYSTONE — To the sound of the “Rawhide” theme song — which goes, ‘Rollin’, rollin’, rollin.’ — South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden took the stage below the Mount Rushmore National Memorial.

“Welcome to the greatest free state in a nation that was founded on the principles of freedom. Here in South Dakota, we still honor America, our freedoms, our founding fathers. If you need proof of that, just look up. Above us now are four leaders carved in granite. Their image is built to last for generations. Their leadership will not be forgotten,” Rhoden told a crowd of almost 5,000 during the fireworks and visit by President Trump on Friday, July 3. “More importantly, the principles, the values, and the freedoms that they stood for carry just as much weight as they did 250 years ago.”

Rhoden was one of a few selected speakers to take the stage before Trump, including the monument’s superintendent and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, the former North Dakota governor.

Rhoden quoted President Calvin Coolidge, who said at the 150th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, “There is a finality that is exceedingly restful. It is often asserted that the world has made a great deal of progress since 1776, that we may therefore very well discard their conclusions for something more modern. But that reasoning cannot be applied to this great charter. If all men are created equal, that is final. If they are endowed with inalienable rights, that is final. If government derive their just power from the consent of the governed, that is final. No advance, no progress can be made beyond these propositions.”

 Rhoden at Rushmore
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden speaks at Mount Rushmore on Friday, July 3. 

In his own words, Rhoden said, “Ladies and gentlemen, America is not just a piece of land. America is an ideal, a set of values, a shining city on a hill, an example to the world of freedom. But freedom doesn’t defend itself. That’s our job.”

The governor highlighted his family’s history of service in the U.S. military, dating back to the Revolutionary War and up to his service in the South Dakota National Guard and his son’s service flying Black Hawk helicopters.

“Defending freedom requires the sacrifice of brave men and women in uniform, but it also takes everyday Americans, it takes elected leaders who know their duty and who put American freedom,” Rhoden said. “It just so happens we have just such a leader here with us tonight. We are joined by our 45th and 47th president, President Donald J. Trump.”

Rhoden said the president puts the American people and freedom first and called him “a leader who says what he means and does what he says. Ever since he’s been back in the White House, it has been like a light switch has turned back on.”

He also touched on his role as governor of South Dakota, stating his mission is to, “Keep our state strong, safe, and free. Like America is to the world, South Dakota has been a beacon of hope for what is possible when we keep government limited, when we remain true to American values and to our freedoms. Here, we recognize that our rights, liberties, and freedoms are not given to us by government, but by God, and government has no authority to take those rights away.”

Rhoden is currently in a race to stay in the governor’s office. Rhoden and Toby Doeden are headed for a runoff election on Tuesday, July 28 to determine who will be the Republican nominee for governor in the general election. The winner will face Democrat Dan Ahlers in November.

Rhoden, Doeden, U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson and South Dakota Speaker of the House Jon Hansen competed in the primary. Although the two beat out Johnson’s 31,925 votes (23%), neither met the 35% threshold needed to avoid a runoff, with Doeden receiving 41,791 votes (31%) and Rhoden pulling in at 34,379 votes (25%).

title: ‘I love America’: Patriotic sentiments on display at Rapid City Hall
description: The “I Love America Because…” display in the lobby of Rapid City’s City Hall received several dozen sentiments from visitors in the three weeks the public was encouraged to stop and share heartfelt messages as the community prepared to observe America’s 250th birthday.
_full_text:
The “I Love America Because…” display in the lobby of Rapid City’s City Hall received several dozen sentiments from visitors in the three weeks the public was encouraged to stop and share heartfelt messages as the community prepared to observe America’s 250th birthday.

In mid-June, a small group of staff members erected a patriotic display table with banners, inviting the public to express brief sentiments on red, white and blue star-shaped stickers that could be affixed to a large display board displaying the theme “I Love America Because…” Approximately 100 “message stars” were placed on the board.

 PHOTO Love America display 070626a.jpg
The “I Love America Because…” display in the lobby of Rapid City’s City Hall received several dozen sentiments from visitors in the three weeks the public was encouraged to stop and share heartfelt messages as the community prepared to observe America’s 250th birthday. 

Of the sentiments, many expressed they love America and were thankful for various freedoms, the flag, for liberty, the military, democracy and family. Others expressed their love of America for opportunities, for veterans, the beauty of our people, for education and diversity. There were sentiments expressed their love of nature, mountains and the forest, the freedom to be different, land is protected for wildlife and public use. Others loved America for everything from motocross and apple pie; rock and roll, roller skates and Johnny Cash; to Raising Cane’s Chicken, Nintendo and the Savannah Bananas!

“It was a great response from the public,” said Skye Martin of the Rapid City Mayor’s Office, one of the staff members who organized the effort. “For those visiting City Hall, it was a simple way to share a feeling or sentiment about America. It took just a few seconds to fill out a star but a great way to get into the spirit of the special America 250 holiday observance.”

The “I Love America Because…” table is expected to remain in the lobby for the next several days.

title: Rapid City offers ‘cool’ options for upcoming heat wave
description: With triple-digit heat in the forecast starting this weekend, Rapid City Parks and Recreation officials offered some suggestions for cool relief, relaxation and fun in the city’s parks system.
_full_text:
With triple-digit heat in the forecast starting this weekend, Rapid City Parks and Recreation officials offered some suggestions for cool relief, relaxation and fun in the city’s parks system.

“No matter the temperature, our city parks and facilities offer a great number of options to relax, cool off and enjoy time with family and friends,” City Parks and Recreation Director Jeff Biegler said in a release from the city. “There are opportunities throughout the city to beat the heat.”

According to the National Weather Service office in Rapid City, the high on Friday is 94, with the high reaching 101 on Saturday. Beyond Saturday, Accuweather predicts a high of 101 on Sunday and a high of 96 on Tuesday.

City officials offered 10 suggestions for the public when seeking relaxing, comforting and cool options during stretches of hot weather:

• The City has nearly 40 parks, many with playground areas and all serving as great places for lawn chairs, blankets and areas to enjoy a picnic lunch. Park hours are 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. Check out the Park’s page on the City’s website for a list of city parks and select a park you haven’t visited in a while or ever.

• The City has three outdoor pools – Parkview, Horace Mann and Jimmy Hilton at Sioux Park, along with the outdoor 50-meter pool and indoor pools at the Roosevelt Swim Center - to enjoy and catch some cool relief. Concessions at the pools offer cold beverages and treats on these hot days

• The Rapid City Public Library provides the opportunity to escape from the outdoor heat and peruse books, check out makerspace, and catch a variety of scheduled programs that will entertain the entire family.

• Various parks offer beautiful floral gardens for a quiet, relaxing stroll. Halley Park includes the First Nations Sculpture Garden, providing a leisurely walk to view statues of Native artists and intellectuals. Various parks offer gazebos, picnic shelters and tree canopies for shade.

• From swing sets and slides, horseshoe pits and disc golf, kids bike park and playland areas, there’s a lot of opportunities to relax during the hot days of July

• Dino at Dinosaur Park and the characters at Storybook Island would welcome a visit from people of all ages!

• Wading opportunities at Canyon Lake Park as you enjoy a picnic lunch, play cornhole or dip a fishing line into the water.

• Rapid Creek offers some great recreational opportunities, from fishing, wading and kayaking to paddle boarding and inner tubing. Always use additional caution in the creek waters and have a good time.

• Among the city parks is Braeburn Dog Park, where you can let your four-legged canine friends frolic with their friends and take a dip in Rapid Creek. Braeburn Park is one of six off-leash dog parks in Rapid City along with Wilderness Park, Vicki Powers Park, Robbinsdale Park, Memorial Park East and the Knollwood Drainage Area.

• Rapid City offers a 10-mile bike path and various trails to experience. With the intense heat, be sure to pack water, sunscreen and take some breaks along the way.

For more information, visit the parks and recreation and library pages at www.rcgov.org , or call City Parks and Recreation Department at 605-394-4175 and the Rapid City Public Library at 605-394-6139.

title: Fitgerald Stadium disposal site containers to be moved for tournament
description: Effective this week, the yard waste and recycling containers located adjacent to Fitzgerald Stadium will be removed for several days for the Dave Ploof Legacy baseball tournament.
_full_text:
Effective this week, the yard waste and recycling containers located adjacent to Fitzgerald Stadium will be removed for several days for the Dave Ploof Legacy baseball tournament.

Containers will be removed Wednesday for the American Legion baseball tournament. Containers will return on Monday, July 13.

In February, the City Council approved a request from the Rapid City Sports Commission to remove the yard waste and recycling containers from the remote yard waste site located adjacent to Fitzgerald Stadium during four baseball tournaments scheduled for the summer baseball season. It is the fourth consecutive season the containers have been removed to provide additional parking for the tournaments, which draw large audiences.

The City Council approved removing the containers for the Veterans Classic June 4-7, the Firecracker Tournament July 1-5, the Dave Ploof Legacy Tournament July 9-12, and the State Tournament July 26-August 2. The removal dates include a day or two before and after the tournaments to allow for removal of the containers, cleanup of the area and resetting of the containers.

During the temporary closure of the Fitzgerald Stadium remote site, the public is advised to drop off materials at the Nickel Street site, at the Rapid City Landfill or schedule drop off of materials before or after the tournament periods.

title: Box Elder man arrested after shooting from inside a pickup
description: A Box Elder man was arrested after firing shots out the window of a pickup truck near the 100 block of Monroe Street in Rapid City.
_full_text:
A Box Elder man was arrested after firing shots out the window of a pickup truck near the 100 block of Monroe Street in Rapid City.

Joseph Stevens, 22, was arrested on suspicion of discharging a firearm from a moving vehicle, DUI and obstruction, according to the Rapid City Police Department.

At around 4:25 a.m. on Tuesday, July 7, police responded to the 100 block of Monroe Street for a report of gunshots. A reporting party said they saw a pickup in the area with a person firing shots out the window.

Police later found the pickup in a parking lot in the 100 block of Waterloo Street and saw a man exit the driver’s seat with a handgun before running north. As the man left the car, police saw a bullet casing fall to the ground from inside the pickup.

Police chased the man on foot. At one point, the man, later identified as Stevens, fell to the ground and dropped the gun. Stevens attempted to reach for the gun but officers were able to grab the weapon and throw it away from him beforehand.

Stevens was detained and the gun was secured. Police noted Stevens was exhibiting signs of alcohol impairment. Ammunition in Stevens’ possession matched shell casings recovered from the original area where the gunshots were reported.

As of Tuesday, the Journal was unable to confirm if Stevens is in the Pennington County Jail due to the cybersecurity incident that occurred over the Fourth of July weekend.

title: Biberdorf, Seachris, Maher, Roberts and Armstrong sworn in at Rapid City Council meeting
description: Four incumbents and a former councilwoman were sworn in at the Rapid City Council meeting on Monday, July 6.
_full_text:
Four incumbents and a former councilwoman were sworn in at the Rapid City Council meeting on Monday, July 6.

 City Council
From left to right Lara Armstrong (Ward 5), Josh Biberdorf (Ward 1), Lindsey Seachris (Ward 2), Kevin Maher (Ward 3) and John Roberts (Ward 4) were sworn in on Monday, July 6. 

All five won in the June 2 election. According to the city, this was the first race since 2002 with contests in each of the city’s five wards.

In Ward 1, Councilman Josh Biberdorf retained his seat. Biberdorf received 1,881 votes (71%) against challenger Murray Lee (770 votes, 29%).

In Ward 2, Councilwoman Lindsey Seachris (775 votes, 54%) beat challenger Chris Vanderhoof (652 votes, 46%).

In Ward 3, Councilman Kevin Maher (1,921 votes, 58%) beat challenger Andrea Schaefer (1,392, 42%).

In Ward 4, Councilman John Roberts (870 votes, 52%) beat Valeriah Big Eagle (737 votes, 44%). Ardin Jay Cychosz, who announced he was dropping out of the race months ago but still appeared on the ballot, received 65 votes (4%).

And in Ward 5, former Councilwoman Laura Armstrong (1,589 votes, 56%) beat former Councilman Pat Roseland (1,229 votes, 44%).

Finance Director Daniel Ainslie officiated the swearing in, requesting the five repeat the oath, " I will faithfully and impartially perform the duties of the office of Alderperson for the city of Rapid City, South Dakota, according to the law, and to the best of my ability, so help me God."

 Daniel Ainslie officiates swearing
Finance Director Daniel Ainslie officiated the swearing in for the incumbents and Armstrong.  

Ward 5 Councilman Rod Pettigrew did not seek reelection and was honored at the meeting. Salamun thanked Pettigrew for his service in the council. 

Councilman Greg Stromen said, "He's a common-sense guy who was not afraid to buck the trend if it needed to be done, and I just think he showed really great leadership, and we did get some really significant things accomplished recently with his leadership. I want to thank him for that.”

In addition to swearing in members, the council also chose a president and vice president. 

 City Council
The Rapid City Council poses for a photo on Monday, July 6. 

Councilman Bill Evans (Ward 2) nominated Stephen Tamang (Ward 1) as council president, while Seachris nominated Maher as president. The council voted 6-4 to chooose Tamang as president. He takes the helm from Pettigrew.

Evans then nominated Councilwoman Callie Meyer as vice president. Meyer then nominated Armstrong, who declined the nomination. Meyer, with the sole nomination, was elected vice president.

title: Carol Cameron
description: February 25, 1940 - July 6, 2026
_full_text:
February 25, 1940 - July 6, 2026

Carol Cameron was born to Marian B. and Dr. James E. Graham on February 25, 1940, in Springfield Illinois. She was the second oldest of six children. Her ancestors on both sides were Scotch Irish Catholics, traceable back to the 1700s. She was privileged to receive an excellent education by the Ursuline sisters and the Dominican nuns in both grade school and high school, graduating with a degree in psychology and French from Washington University in St. Louis. She extended her studies in France after doing graduate studies at Georgetown University.

While in Washington DC, she worked at the Turkish Embassy and married Dave Morrison. Mike Morrison and Ann Morrison Eads were both born in Fredericksburg, Virginia. The family moved to Rapid City, SD, in 1972 after the flood. Carol became a single Mom and had the good fortune of working in the advertising department at The Rapid City Journal, as an outside salesperson with Nauman Printing and in the Marketing department of the Alex Johnson Hotel. She and her husband, Douglas E. Cameron, founded the local tour company, Affordable Adventures, which they ran successfully for 15 years. In 1994, she was reunited with twin girls she had given up for adoption, Maura Mayer and Kate Tracy Blattner, both of St Louis. Carol's passion in life was travel, starting at age 5 with her parents and siblings. She loved to cook, participate in the theater arts and be in the presence of friends. Later in life she married Gene Britt and they continued traveling. She completed two bucket lists.

She is survived by her four children, grandchildren, brother, Tony Graham, sister-in-law, Carolyn Graham, and numerous Buoy & Graham cousins.

title: ‘Mission accomplished:’ Rapid City reflects on Real America Birthday Bash
description: On July 4, 2025, Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun stood in front of the bronze statue of Thomas Jefferson at the corner of Seventh and Saint Joseph streets and declared, “My hope is that it (Rapid City) will be the premier destination for the great American birthday bash.”
_full_text:
On July 4, 2025, Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun stood in front of the bronze statue of Thomas Jefferson at the corner of Seventh and Saint Joseph streets and declared, “My hope is that it (Rapid City) will be the premier destination for the great American birthday bash.”

A year and four days later, when asked if it went how he envisioned it, the mayor said, “Mission accomplished … I’m tickled pink about how it went.”

Salamun and others involved in the planning and execution of the Real America Birthday Bash held a press conference at The Hive in Main Street Square on Wednesday, July 8, to take a look back at the festivities.

The Real America Birthday Bash was an amalgamation of events held from July 1-5 in Rapid City in celebration of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. The festivities started with the U.S. Air Force Band playing at the Memorial Park Bandshell on July 1. Just a couple days later, on July 3, the band played at Mount Rushmore ahead of President Trump speaking at the first fireworks show at the monument in six years.

 Laugh
From left: Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun, Rapid City Chief of Staff Leah Braun, Rapid City Grants Division Manager Jamie Toennies, and Rep. Mike Derby (R-Rapid City), laugh at a Wednesday, July 8, press conference looking back at Rapid City’s Real America Birthday Bash. Derby served as a liaison to the South Dakota America 250 committee. 

“There was speculation, of course, that we might have the president, but we planned this, not knowing any of that buzz. Regardless of what happened at Mount Rushmore, we were going big,” Salamun said.

A parade on July 2 went ahead in downtown Rapid City despite rain and hail. The parade was followed by a drone show that featured Rapid City’s logo, replete with Dinosaur Hill’s most visible dinosaur. Musical acts like country music artist Chancey Williams — who also played at Rushmore — and Brandon Jones played the Main Street Square stage. Other events included a Mount Rushmore fireworks show watch party, kids’ zones, historical re-enactments, dance performances, the city fireworks show and more. The festivities capped off with the America 250 Freedom 5k on Sunday morning, July 5.

 Map
A map at a post Real America Birthday Bash press conference held at The Hive in Rapid City on Wednesday, July 8, shows where visitors came from. 

“In a time where people are often divided about many things, we all united under the red, white and blue in celebration of our nation and, of course, with the great spirit of community that we had. To me, that was what it was all about. Absolutely outstanding, incredibly proud. (I’m) still reflecting on it,” Salamun said

The mayor made abundantly clear the events could not have happened without the community coming together. Those who were involved include Rapid City Chief of Staff Leah Braun, Visit Rapid City, The Monument, T-N-T Event & Marketing Management, the Rapid City Police Department, Rapid City Fire Department, the Birthday Bash committee and JustServe, a volunteer organization.

It’ll take some time before the city has exact estimates of how many people attended the festivities, but Salamun said it’s in the tens of thousands. Visit Rapid City will be able to track cellphone data to determine how many people were in the area and where they came from, but it will take a few weeks to compile that.

 America’s 250th Birthday drone show over Memorial Park
After the parade and live music, attendees of the Rapid City’s America’s 250th Birthday celebration was concluded with a drone show over Memorial Park on Thursday, July 3. 

Visit Rapid City CEO Ally Formanek said the visitor center in Rapid City, from July 1-5, had visitors from 47 states and five countries — Australia, Canada, France, Germany and Ireland.

“July 3 was actually the busiest single day we've had at a visitor center since we opened our doors in 2024, which is amazing,” Formanek said.

She also noted hotel occupancy from June 28 through July 4 averaged at 77%, which is up about 9% over the same week last year.

“We're hearing from a lot of downtown business owners, which is wonderful. Several have told us they were busier than they've ever been throughout the festivities, and the few said it may have been their best single day of sales they've ever had, which is amazing to hear,” she said. “We put Rapid City in front of the entire country.”

Rapid City Finance Director Daniel Ainslie estimated the costs for the celebration came out to about $500,000, half of which came from the Rapid City Council, which allocated $250,000 from its contingency funds. Rapid City Grants Division Manager Jamie Toennies said 45 local businesses contributed to the efforts. Over $228,000 were raised, with about $160,000 of that coming in as cash to support things like musical acts and safety and security needs.

“We also had about $67,000 that was in-kind support, helping with the marketing, helping with printing signs, and that's all on top of, of course, the amazing in-kind support that we had from our partners around the table and our staff,” Toennies said.

 Rapid City drone show (Copy)
Rapid City’s logo shined in the night sky during the drone show on July 2, the second day of the Real America Birthday Bash, held from July 1-5. 

Ainslie said, “When you look at the sales tax return that comes back to the community, the community will have made its investment back easily, but really that's due to all the significant work from Visit Rapid City, as well as everyone else.”

Rapid City Council Vice President Callie Meyer said although it’s hard to speak for the whole council, “I feel confident that everyone’s excited about the community spirit that was generated from this.”

Scott Sitts, assistant chief with the Rapid City Police Department, said from a public safety and law enforcement perspective, “the celebration couldn’t have gone better.”

“We had a couple of missing kiddos that got separated from their parents, but we had a strong volunteer presence. We had a strong law enforcement presence. We were able to gather those kids up and reunite them really quickly,” Sitts said, adding the only other issue was congestion, which is to be expected.

Rapid City Fire Chief Jason Culberson said “ditto” to Sitts’ comments.

“Really happy with all that planning, that we really had no major incidents down here. We gave a grand total of six — six — band aids, so it was pretty awesome,” he said.

Salamun said it may not be as big next year, but he hopes to make an America Birthday Bash a tradition in the city, “We're all exhausted right now, it's probably the last thing everybody wants to think about. But I will say this: I think it would be a great thing for our community to keep bringing us together, that this is a place to celebrate America, each and every year, in the City of Presidents, in one of the greatest cities in the United States, Rapid City, South Dakota.”

 A half a dozen photos from the drone show in Rapid City on July 2
After the sun set on Rapid City on Thursday, July 2, a dazzling drone show launched from Central High School as part of the city’s Real America 250 celebrations.

title: Rapid City Fire Department responds to 12 fire incidents over 4th of July weekend
byline: MADISON WILLIS and MIKE BROWNLEE Journal staff
description: The Rapid City Fire Department said it responded to 338 calls for service between July 2 and July 5. The 338 calls also include EMS responses, hazardous materials incidents, public assists and other emergency calls. Due to the cybersecurity incident that occurred over the Fourth of July weekend , the department was unable to provide the exact breakdown of calls by category, outside of how many fire calls the department responded to.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Fire Department said it responded to 338 calls for service between July 2 and July 5. The 338 calls also include EMS responses, hazardous materials incidents, public assists and other emergency calls. Due to the cybersecurity incident that occurred over the Fourth of July weekend, the department was unable to provide the exact breakdown of calls by category, outside of how many fire calls the department responded to.

There were 12 fire incidents during that time, of those, five were directly related to fireworks activity, including three grass fires, one tree fire and one dumpster fire, the department told the Journal.

“We are not aware of any reported fireworks-related injuries,” RCFD Public Information Officer Tessa Jaeger said in an email. “While several small fires were attributed to fireworks, crews responded quickly and prevented them becoming larger incidents. We do not have damage estimates to report.”

Jaeger said, “We did see an increase in calls this year compared to last year.” Jaeger did not immediately respond when asked for last year’s numbers.

The Journal communicated with Monument Health to learn how many fireworks-related injuries were treated at its facilities and awaits a response.

The Journal also asked the Rapid City Police Department about their calls for service over the weekend, however, because of the Pennington County cybersecurity incident, the department said they won’t be able to pull up that type of report until later in the week. The police department and Pennington County Sheriff’s Office share a building.
