title: 'Heartbreaking': Hot Springs residents gutted over Jalapeños Grill fire
description: Hot Springs head football coach Ben Kramer was speeding along on a treadmill when he received an alarming text: Jalapeños Grill, the town's Mexican eatery, had just weathered a fire. The exterior was black, smoke was rising, and the windows were busted.
_full_text:
Hot Springs head football coach Ben Kramer was speeding along on a treadmill when he received an alarming text: Jalapeños Grill, the town's Mexican eatery, had just weathered a fire. The exterior was black, smoke was rising, and the windows were busted.

It was a gutting, stark contradiction from the images Kramer typically correlated with the beloved joint on Highway 18. His prized Macho Burrito. His wife's chicken chimichangas. Wall-to-wall clatters of conversation. And who could forget the birthday celebration?

"If somebody was celebrating a birthday," Kramer began, "they would make a big scene out of it, and slap a pie in your face, and put a sombrero on your head."

But now, after seeing the image, Kramer can't help but compare it to a "tragedy."

According to Fall River County, the fire initially broke out before business hours on Monday, July 6. It began in the kitchen and percolated into the attic, according to KOTA. In a release, Fall River County said the Hot Springs Police Department evacuated two individuals from the building. 

The Hot Springs Volunteer Fire Department and Jalapeños Grill didn’t immediately responded to interview requests. 

 Hot Springs restaurant fire
According to Fall River County, the fire at Jalapeños Grill initially broke out before business hours on Monday, July 6. Hot Springs Police Department evacuated two individuals from the building.  

"From the bottom of our hearts, we want to express our deepest gratitude to everyone who has supported us during this incredibly difficult time," Jalapeños Grill posted to its Facebook page. "We are especially grateful to the firefighters from Hot Springs, Edgemont, Custer, Argyle, and the VA Fire Department, along with the police, first responders, Black Hills Power, and the gas company, who responded so quickly and worked tirelessly to contain the fire. We cannot thank you enough for your courage, dedication, and hard work."

The restaurant added, "While this has been a heartbreaking and difficult experience, we are deeply thankful that we are not facing it alone."

Originally from Goodland, Kansas, the restaurant moved to Hot Springs after a customer mentioned it. Years later, it's the lone sit-down Mexican restaurant in the southern South Dakota town.

"Heartbreaking. Some of the best Mexican food in the black hills and such kind people," one West River resident commented on Facebook. 

The restaurant posted to its Facebook page, "This is not the end of our story. As we take things one day at a time and begin to figure out what comes next, we will share more when the time is right. One thing we know for certain is that we will be back, stronger than ever. From our family to yours, thank you. Truly, from the bottom of our hearts."

 Below the Facebook post was a comment that said, "I know I speak for a lot of us when I say, we can’t wait to have you back! The community is here to support you throughout this difficult time. We’re glad you all are safe!"

title: Unexploded homemade explosive delays firefighters’ response to Black Hills wildland fire
description: The Rapid City Fire Department responded to a fire on Thursday, Sept. 18 on Nowlin Street.
_full_text:
Nowlin Street fire
The Rapid City Fire Department responded to a fire on Thursday, Sept. 18 on Nowlin Street. 

As firefighters responded to a small wildland fire burning in the Black Hills National Forest, units were met with an unexploded homemade explosive on Tuesday, July 7.

The Custer County Sheriff’s Office said the explosive not only endangered the responders, but it also temporarily delayed suppression efforts while authorities dealt with the device.

After inspecting the device, authorities were able to determine the explosive was some type of homemade Tannerite, a brand of binary explosive targets used for firearms practice and sold in a kit. The device was handled in a controlled explosion at a safe location, the sheriff’s office said.

The sheriff’s office said the incident serves as a good reminder that just like campfires and fireworks, exploding targets are illegal in the Black Hills Fire Protection District.

Despite some vegetation beginning to bloom in the Black Hills, officials reminded the public that the Black Hills are still very dry and capable of providing fuel for wildfires.

 Unexploded homemade explosive in Black Hills
As firefighters responded to a small wildland fire burning in the Black Hills National Forest, units were met with an unexploded homemade explosive on Tuesday, July 7.

title: Continuity on the RCAS Board: Stephenson, Swan start new terms; leadership remains the same
description: The new Rapid City Area Schools Board looks quite familiar.
_full_text:
The new Rapid City Area Schools Board looks quite familiar.

On Tuesday, July 7, the now old board adjourned just moments before Area 5 Representative Christine Stephenson and Area 4 Representative Walt Swan took oaths of office to start new three-year terms on the board. Neither Stephenson or Swan’s positions were challenged in the recent election cycle, so they were automatically up for new terms. Both joined the board in 2023.

 Stephenson takes the oath
Area 5 Representative Christine Stephenson takes her oath of office for a new three-year term at the Tuesday, July 7, Rapid City Area Schools Board meeting. 

Both swore to support the laws and constitutions of South Dakota and the United States and to faithfully and impartially perform the duties of the offices they hold.

Chief Financial and Operations Officer Coy Sasse administered the oaths. In addition to Stephenson and Swan rejoining the board, the board voted to elect officers.

 Walt Swan
Area 4 Representative Walt Swan on Tuesday, July 7, heads back to his seat on the Rapid City Area Schools Board after taking his oath of office for another three-year term. 

Continuing in the same spirit of continuity, the board re-elected Board President and Area 2 Representative Troy Carr to his position as president of the board. The board also opted to keep First Vice President and Area 6 Representative Jamie Clapham in her position, and Second Vice President and Area 7 Representative Katy Urban retained her leadership position as well.

Stephenson said board leadership is, “a really important role because there are times in the district where the board needs to know something and the leadership team has to know it first, and then has to disseminate that information.”

 Stephenson
Area 5 Representative Christine Stephenson walks back to her seat on the Rapid City Area Schools Board after taking the oath of office on Tuesday, July 7, for another three-year term. 

“I think the three of you have done a nice job of that. I’m quite pleased that you’re willing to serve in leadership, especially you, President Carr. This is not an easy job, and I know it takes a lot of time, and it takes a lot of flexibility on your part,” she said.

There were no opposing nominations for the leadership positions.

“'I’d like to thank each board member for your confidence and your support,” Carr said. “I don't make any assumptions, and I don't take it for granted. So I appreciate your support.”

Addressing the community, Carr thanked it “for keeping this board together. We are excited about the work that we have to do. It’s no secret that we are offering up a bond. And the fact that we all are together still brings strength and support to that effort.”

A $107 million Rapid City Area Schools bond question is set to appear on the Nov. 3 ballot. The tax levy will be dedicated to school improvements and construction. 

The district's most recent bond attempt came in 2020 — with a price tag of $189.5 million. It accrued a vote of 56%, short of the required 60%. Voters in the district have not passed a bond since the 1976. 

Next year, Urban’s and Area 1 Representative Donna Moore’s terms will be up for election. There are seven positions on the board, with terms overlapping.

title: Rapid City man arrested in sting sentenced for attempted enticement of a minor
description: A Rapid City man convicted of attempted enticement of a minor faces 10 years in prison.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man convicted of attempted enticement of a minor faces 10 years in prison.

U.S. District Judge Camela C. Theeler sentenced Elmer Hopper, 37, to 10 years in federal prison for attempted enticement of a minor using the internet, followed by five years of supervised release, according to the U.S. Attorney

Hopper was indicted for the charge by a federal grand jury in August 2025. He pleaded guilty on March 30, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.

During the 2025 Sturgis Bike Rally, Hopper initiated communications on the internet-based application Plenty Of Fish with someone he thought was a 14-year-old girl. The girl, in fact, was a Rapid City Police Department detective operating in an undercover capacity on Plenty Of Fish, an app used for dating and sexual encounters. Hopper and the undercover persona started communicating through texting. Hopper told her that he wanted someone to lie in bed with him. Later, Hopper explained that he meant that he wanted someone to have sex with, not lie in bed with. Hopper and the undercover persona agreed to meet at West Middle School in Rapid City. When Hopper arrived at the school, he was arrested, the office said.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice, the U.S. Attorney's Office said. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc.

This case was investigated by the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation’s Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force, the Rapid City Police Department, and the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office. Former Assistant U.S. Attorney Heather Knox and Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Patterson prosecuted the case.

The sentencing took place on June 15 at the federal courthouse in Rapid City. Hopper was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Hot Springs man sentenced to 7 years in connection to standoff with authorities
description: A Hot Springs man was sentenced to federal prison for possessing a firearm as a felon.
_full_text:
A Hot Springs man was sentenced to federal prison for possessing a firearm as a felon.

U.S. District Judge Camela C. Theeler sentenced Cecle Crist, 53, to seven years in federal prison after his conviction of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person, the U.S. Attorney's Office for South Dakota announced. The sentence will be followed by three years of supervised release.

Crist was indicted for possession of a firearm by a prohibited person by a federal grand jury in November 2025, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office. He pleaded guilty on March 9.

In November 2025, several officers with the Fall River County Sheriff’s Office and the Hot Springs Police Department attempted to arrest Crist on a federal arrest warrant pertaining to another firearm charge, the office said. When the officers entered the camper Crist lived in, he hid in a closet, threatened to kill law enforcement and said he had a gun.

The officers exited the camper and called in the Rapid City Special Response Team (SRT). After SRT fired several rounds of OC powder into the camper, Crist exited the camper and was placed under arrest. Officers thereafter located in the camper three loaded rifles, a pellet gun and several rounds of ammunition, which Crist knew were in his possession.

Crist is a previously convicted felon who knew he was prohibited from possessing firearms.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, the Rapid City Police Department, the Fall River County Sheriff’s Office, and the Hot Springs Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Patterson prosecuted the case.

The sentencing took place on June 22 at the federal courthouse in Rapid City. Crist was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Rapid City man pleads guilty to possessing child sexual abuse material
description: A Rapid City man pleaded guilty on Thursday, July 9, to two counts of possession of child sexual abuse material.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man pleaded guilty on Thursday, July 9, to two counts of possession of child sexual abuse material.

Levi Johnson, 21, appeared for his change of plea hearing before Presiding Circuit Judge Heidi Linngren at the Pennington County Courthouse.

Johnson was initially indicted for three counts of possession of child sexual abuse material, after allegedly having multiple videos and photos on his phone on Feb. 14, 2025.

However, through a plea agreement with the state, prosecutors dismissed the third charge. The state agreed to suggest a concurrent sentence.

In South Dakota, possession of child pornography is a Class 4 felony with a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a $20,000 fine, there is also a mandatory minimum of one year in prison.

Johnson’s sentencing is set for 8:30 a.m. on Aug. 14.

title: Pennington County cyber incident investigation continues
description: Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story’s headline was incorrect regarding early voting. Early voting is still available. The Journal regrets the error.
_full_text:
Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story’s headline was incorrect regarding early voting. Early voting is still available. The Journal regrets the error.

Pennington County said Thursday, July 9, officials continue working with state and federal partners to investigate the recent cybersecurity incident “while safely restoring county systems and services.”

“Protecting County data remains our highest priority,” the county said in a release.

Because an active investigation continues, “we are unable to discuss specific details regarding the incident at this time,” the county said.

As restoration efforts continue, some county services remain limited.

Treasurer’s Office

Staff is available to answer questions related to vehicle titles and other Treasurer’s Office matters.

The office is currently unable to process vehicle registrations or accept payments of any kind.

Vehicle registration renewals remain available online at my605drive.sd.gov and at self-service kiosks.

Individuals whose temporary license plates expire within the next week should visit the Treasurer’s Office at 900 Concourse Drive for options.

Auditor’s Office

Early voting remains available.

The office is unable to process lien payments at this time.

Register of Deeds

Birth, death and marriage certificates remain available online through VitalChek.com or by calling 605-773-4961

The Register of Deeds Office is currently accepting real estate recordings; however, they cannot be fully processed at this time.

Planning & Zoning

Staff is now able to manually process building permits.

The Planning & Zoning Commission will meet as scheduled on July 13 to elect officers. All other agenda items will be continued to the July 27 meeting.

County Commission

County Commission meetings will continue as scheduled. Due to the cybersecurity incident, meetings may not be livestreamed. They will be recorded and posted as soon as systems allow.

For the latest information regarding County services, please visit PennCo.org or follow the Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office Facebook page.

title: Real estate, car dealerships, bitcoin and a TIF: A look into Toby Doeden's empire
byline: MOLLY WETSCH South Dakota News Watch
description: Businessman Toby Doeden, whose campaign for governor has hinged largely on the elimination of all property taxes for South Dakotans, has links to real estate investment companies that would save more than half a million dollars every year under that plan, according to public records. That number reflects the sheer size of the candidate's reach and business experience in the state's third-largest city.
_full_text:
Businessman Toby Doeden, whose campaign for governor has hinged largely on the elimination of all property taxes for South Dakotans, has links to real estate investment companies that would save more than half a million dollars every year under that plan, according to public records. That number reflects the sheer size of the candidate's reach and business experience in the state's third-largest city.

Though Doeden has frequently referred to his experience in the business world as his primary qualifier for the office of governor, little was known about the full extent of his ventures and wealth.

In addition to a vast portfolio acquired through multiple real estate investment and development companies, Doeden also owns the Aberdeen Chrysler dealership in Aberdeen and Redfield Ford in Redfield. He also has ties to land next to the Aberdeen dealership that company Plaza Rentals and his son had rezoned in 2020 to allow for bitcoin mining. And that's only a few of the two dozen LLCs with links to Doeden.

Searches of the Better Business Bureau, court records and the state of South Dakota's consumer protection portal paint a generally positive picture of the empire: Doeden's companies are in good standing and have not had any major outstanding legal or civil issues. All but one of his limited liability companies remain active on the South Dakota Secretary of State's website, Scotty's Diner, LLC, which closed in 2024.

 2026-06-15 214 S. Kline St, Plaza Rentals-owned apartments.jpeg
The Roosevelt Apartments at 214 S. Kline St. in Aberdeen, S.D., on June 15, 2026. Doeden's Plaza Rentals owns and operates the 32-unit building. The property was originally purchased and renovated in 2013 by Roosevelt Apartments LLC. Brown County Register of Deeds records indicate Plaza Rentals took out a mortgage on the property in 2021. 

Doeden declined a phone interview with News Watch to clarify his current status at the companies but provided a statement.

“I am extremely proud of the work my team and I have been able to accomplish over the years at Doeden Investment Group. Being able to give back to the people and state that have given me so much has been the honor of a lifetime," Doeden said in the statement. "We have created thousands of jobs, grown countless businesses, and invested 100% of that money back into our communities right here in South Dakota. I look forward to bringing that much needed business experience directly to Pierre as Governor."

Doeden Investment Group is the mechanism behind much of Doeden's real estate and business portfolio. It describes itself as "a leading investment firm dedicated to identifying and nurturing business opportunities that drive growth and prosperity within communities" and says it has " a diverse portfolio spanning various industries."

Dozens of properties make up real estate portfolio in northeastern SD

Companies Plaza Rentals LLP, Tenth Street Properties LLC and Five-Star Management LLC, all with links to Doeden through years of annual reports filed with the South Dakota Secretary of State's office, own more than $30 million of property in and around Aberdeen.

That includes single-family homes, commercial buildings and multi-family buildings, according to data from the Brown County Equalization Department.

Doeden told the Aberdeen Insider on June 17, though, that categorizing him as a major property owner in Aberdeen is incorrect because he is no longer deeply involved with the companies' business dealings. Several other individuals are involved in the day-to-day management of those real estate companies, including sons Jonathan and Jackson and daughter Josie.

 South Dakota News Watch logo
Learn more about South Dakota News Watch at sdnewswatch.org. 

“But I hear, ‘Toby owns all the property…’ Well, Toby doesn’t hardly own any property in Aberdeen, and I haven’t for a long time. That property was put into a trust many years ago. I don’t control it. I don’t manage the companies. They’re trying to connect me to things that (I’m not even) involved with anymore, that I don’t even own anymore. And it’s unfortunate,” Doeden told the Insider.

But that doesn't jibe with his current Statement of Financial Interest submitted to the South Dakota Secretary of State's Office in April 2026, which lists him as an owner, employee and shareholder, partner or shareholder of 24 companies and funding sources.

Doeden is the registered agent for Tenth Street Properties and was the registered agent for Plaza Rentals until Tuesday, June 16, when the company's annual report removed him and listed Mariah Bloom-McNeece, who serves as general counsel for Doeden Investment Group, as the new registered agent. He is still listed as a partner in the company along with the "Trustees of 4J 2023 Trust." The trust was added to annual reports for Plaza Rentals starting in 2024.

Designating a registered agent is required for the formation of an LLC. The registered agent is the individual who is authorized to receive legal, tax and other government correspondence on behalf of the LLC and is usually a member of the LLC – though not necessarily the owner – or an individual through a professional registered agent service.

 2026-06-15 Aberdeen Chrysler Center.jpeg
Aberdeen Chrysler Center, which Toby Doeden took over ownership of in 2020, in Aberdeen, S.D., on June 15, 2026. 

Doeden was also identified explicitly as a partner in Plaza Rentals both on his candidate statement of financial interest and in 2023, when the city of Aberdeen implemented a Tax Increment Financing (TIF) district for several apartment buildings that the company purchased and redeveloped on North 2nd Street in Aberdeen, now called 4J Commons after Doeden's four children. The TIF's purpose is to "redevelop and repurpose a dilapidated apartment complex" and is estimated to mature in 2043.

Doeden also runs a charitable organization called the 4J Foundation.

A copy of the agreement signed by Toby Doeden on behalf of Plaza Rentals to incorporate its land on North 2nd Street in Aberdeen, S.D., into a Tax Increment Financing (TIF) district in 2023.

At least 75 properties in Aberdeen and Groton are linked to Plaza Rentals, Tenth Street Properties and Five-Star Management, with a current taxable portfolio value of at least $34,246,283 and a property tax commitment this year of at least $558,129, according to public records from the Brown County director of equalization's office.

Tenth Street Properties is the deed holder to the building housing Street Corner Urban Market – another LLC tied to Doeden – in Aberdeen, as well as Legends Liquor and Casino. Mulligan's Sports Bar and Casino is also located in the complex owned by Tenth Street Properties.

Bitcoin mining

Real estate is not Doeden's only business venture.

One of his businesses was involved in the zoning of a building for 150 bitcoin mining units near his Aberdeen dealership. That zoning permit, which was issued to son Jackson Doeden and company Plaza Rentals, was initially granted in February 2022 for 70 units and was upgraded to 150 units in June 2022, according to Aberdeen News and minutes from the Aberdeen Board of Zoning meetings.

Aberdeen Community Development planner Eric Miller told News Watch that as far as he knew, the mining operation was still active today. But since no extended licensing is required to continue operation of the facility, he could not confirm whether it is still taking place.

 2026-06-15 Street Corner Urban Market, Legends.jpeg
Street Corner Urban Market in Aberdeen, S.D., a company for which Doeden is the registered agent, on June 15, 2026. Legends Liquor and Casino also recently opened in the building. 

Bitcoin mining units are large, complex computers that generate units of cryptocurrency through computing efforts. A large-scale center like the one in Aberdeen can become a mostly passive income stream after the initial investment of the mining units, which can cost up to several thousand dollars per machine, depending on the model.

Because of the largely-opaque nature of cryptocurrency and how it is produced and sold, it is unclear what the Plaza Rentals facility's bitcoin output is per year, and therefore how much it earns from the operation.

Doeden did, however, disclose "digital assets" as a source of funding on his April 2026 candidate statement of financial interest. Examples of digital assets, according to the IRS, include convertible virtual currencies and cryptocurrencies like bitcoin, stablecoins and non-fungible tokens (NFTs).

Business experience key to campaign

Doeden has spoken about his experience in business frequently and touts it as his biggest qualification for governor, often calling himself the "outsider" and the "businessman" in the governor's race.

Doeden came out on top in the June 2 Republican primary election with 31%, followed by Gov. Larry Rhoden with 25%. U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson was third with 23% and state House Speaker Jon Hanson fourth with 21%.

Because no one received 35% of the vote, Doeden and Rhoden are headed to a July 28 runoff election for the Republican nomination for governor. The winner will meet Democrat Dan Ahlers in the Nov. 3 general election.

 2026-04-10 Toby Doeden candidate financial statement of interest.jpeg

Doeden backed up his promise to largely self-fund his campaign by loaning it another $2 million this year, in addition to the $2 million he put up in 2025, according to the latest campaign reports.

Of that latest $2 million, roughly $1.4 million has gone to advertisements, while he has also spent $210,000 on salaries for campaign staff.

Doeden's campaign website says that he is "one of South Dakota’s most successful self-made business owners." His campaign ads, too, tout years of business experience and his creation of "thousands of jobs" in South Dakota.

"No one is able to outwork me," he said in one ad.

In 2023, Doeden told the Aberdeen Insider that the growth of other enterprises he is linked to and his success in the business world can be entirely credited to his work at Aberdeen Chrysler.

“Aberdeen Chrysler is a very successful business,” Doeden said. “That afforded me the ability to start these other companies. Without Aberdeen Chrysler, none of these things would have happened.”

One comment made at an event before Doeden announced his gubernatorial run illustrates just how much the Doeden name means in Aberdeen.

"Here's how to measure Toby's success," Brown County GOP chair Richard Hilgemann joked at the 2025 Brown County Lincoln Day Dinner. "When he buys up enough of Aberdeen that we get to name the town 'Aber-Doeden,' that's when we know he's successful."

Post-pandemic lucrative era for Doeden

Doeden's fast rise to success seems to have started roughly six years ago.

The South Dakota Secretary of State's office shows that he took over Plaza Rentals as its registered agent in 2020. That's also when Doeden took ownership of the Aberdeen Chrysler Center after serving as general manager for nine years and gradually purchasing stock.

Roger Gray was the prior owner of Aberdeen Chrysler and also was the registered agent for Plaza Rentals when it was founded in 2007.

All but two of the 27 companies Doeden is linked to were incorporated in or after 2020. Doeden credits his innovative thinking to his success during the pandemic, citing a risk-taking approach and careful planning.

“You can either suffer or find a way to come out the other end,” Doeden said of the pandemic to the Aberdeen Insider in 2023. “We got together, had a plan and had a fantastic three years.”

The Aberdeen businessman boosted Republican populist candidates in last year’s legislative primaries and is exploring his own run in 2026.

 071026-nws-sdnw-doeden-p5.JPG
A Toby Doeden campaign sign in a parking lot on Fifth Street near the intersection with Kansas City Street in Rapid City. 

Doeden's business activity during the pandemic, though, has also come under scrutiny on the campaign trail.

During a gubernatorial debate in April, The Dakota Scout's Jonathan Ellis asked Doeden why he thought it was appropriate to "personally benefit from federal PPP (Paycheck Protection Program) funds and leverage those programs to grow your businesses" when the candidate has come out against government-led economic development programs.

Doeden railed against Ellis' questioning.

"I don't appreciate you saying that I used it to further my business interests. That is a flat out lie, and as a moderator, you should apologize to the people here tonight because it's a flat out, utter lie," Doeden said during the debate.

Aberdeen Chrysler is a member of the Rydell Automotive Group. PPP data shows that Aberdeen Auto Center, also known as Aberdeen Chrysler, received $1.1 million in loans in 2020. Doeden said during the debate that 150 jobs were saved at his company from the program. Doeden said during the debate that 150 jobs were saved at his company from the program.

PPP loans were sent directly to businesses and were largely intended to cover employee salaries during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Where would our state economy be today if we hadn't fought to keep our companies open? I'm proud of that one loan," Doeden said.

Other loans in Plaza Rentals' holdings include 77 mortgages on properties in and around Aberdeen since 2020, according to information from the Brown County Register of Deeds' office.

But long-term debt certainly is not part of the Plaza Rentals business plan.

Many of those mortgages were taken out on five-year terms – a relatively short lifespan. At least 20 of them have been fully satisfied, with several others partially paid. Notably, records show a $4 million mortgage for the 4J Commons complex from American Bank & Trust was fully satisfied in just one year, between 2023 and 2024.

Mortgages for Plaza Rentals properties have come from regional banks Dacotah Bank, American Bank & Trust, First Interstate Bank and Dakotaland Federal Credit Union.

Doeden has in the past credited strong, trusting relationships with lenders as a reason for his ability to acquire large amounts of property in a short period of time.

What we don't know

Though public records can illustrate a broad picture of how Doeden came to his financial success and status as a top vote-getter in the gubernatorial campaign, there are still some portions of the story that are unclear.

The trust industry is largely a hidden one, especially in South Dakota. The state's privacy statute prevents any trust information from being revealed to the public in court proceedings, and trusts by nature are opaque.

We do not know whether the trust Doeden refers to is revocable (a living trust), which can be altered, or irrevocable, which are established trusts that cannot be altered and essentially cede ownership of property.

Information that is also unavailable to the public is who the beneficiaries of that trust are – though the trust is ostensibly named after Doeden's children – and how many properties are actually in trust.

It is also unclear how much real financial stake and income Doeden maintains in and from the companies he is linked to.

title: Sanford Health introduces dermatology outreach in Spearfish
description: SPEARFISH — Two Sanford Health dermatology clinicians have started outreach services this week in Spearfish.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Two Sanford Health dermatology clinicians have started outreach services this week in Spearfish.

Alexander Reid, M.D., and Mindy Rowe, APRN, CNP, who practice at the Sanford Health Tower Road Clinic in Rapid City, are now offering dermatology services at Sanford Health Spearfish Clinic. The clinic is located at 120 E. Michigan St. Reid and Rowe will serve patients with medical and cosmetic needs and will provide non-surgical and surgical treatments.

 070926-nws-AlexanderReid
Dr. Alexander Reid 

Reid is a board-certified dermatologist and fellowship-trained Mohs micrographic surgeon who provides comprehensive medical, surgical and skin cancer care. He will be providing outreach at Sanford Health Spearfish Clinic every Tuesday.

After completing his dermatology residency at the University of Iowa, Reid completed fellowship training in Mohs micrographic surgery and dermatologic oncology at Geisinger Health System, where he received advanced training in skin cancer treatment and facial reconstruction. Originally from Spearfish and a graduate of Spearfish High School, Reid is excited to provide care in his hometown.

 070926-nws-MelindaRowe
Melinda Rowe 

Rowe is a certified nurse practitioner who evaluates and treats a wide range of skin conditions, including acne, eczema, psoriasis, rashes, rosacea, scars, skin lesions and warts. Rowe will be providing outreach at Sanford Health Spearfish Clinic every Tuesday and Wednesday.

As a Spearfish resident, she is excited for the opportunity to serve patients in her own community and help expand access to dermatology care close to home.

To schedule appointments, go to sanfordhealth.org or call 605-508-3000 ext. 6.

title: Rapid City hosting 'cool pool' specials for heat wave
description: With temperatures forecasted to reach the triple digits for multiple days beginning this weekend, Rapid City Parks and Recreation officials are reminding the public of some ‘cool pool’ options at the three City outdoor pools.
_full_text:
With temperatures forecasted to reach the triple digits for multiple days beginning this weekend, Rapid City Parks and Recreation officials are reminding the public of some ‘cool pool’ options at the three City outdoor pools.

The City’s Parks and Recreation Department offers a pair of convenient specials including "Sunday for Funday" with half-price admission of $4 per person on Sundays, and "Quick Dip Hour Passes," which are half-price $4 passes daily from 5-6 p.m. The special offerings apply to the Parkview, Sioux Park and Horace Mann pools.

All three outdoor pools also offer "cool" treats and drinks among their concession offerings.

The three outdoor city pools at Parkview, Horace Mann and Jimmy Hilton are open from noon to 6 p.m. daily. In addition, the Roosevelt Park’s 50-meter outdoor pool is open from 8 a.m.-7:45 p.m. Monday-Friday, 8 a.m.-5:30 p.m. Saturdays and Noon to 5:30 p.m. Sundays.

Daily swim passes are $8 for adults and youth, and $7 for senior citizens 62 years and older.

title: Rapid City man sentenced for shooting in an apartment on Anamosa Street
description: A Rapid City man was sentenced to four years in prison for second-degree burglary and simple assault for a shooting and fleeing incident that occurred at the beginning of the year.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man was sentenced to four years in prison for second-degree burglary and simple assault for a shooting and fleeing incident that occurred at the beginning of the year.

Tristin Black Elk, 20, appeared for his sentencing before Presiding Circuit Judge Heidi Linngren on Thursday, July 9, at the Pennington County Courthouse.

The state alleged that Black Elk, who was 19 at the time of the Jan. 24 incident, shot several rounds inside an apartment near the 700 block of East Anamosa Street after “a minor verbal disagreement.”

Deputy Pennington County State’s Attorney Emily Toms said Black Elk then fled after the shooting. He was later found that day walking in the 1700 block of North Seventh Street with a handgun. After police attempted to make contact with him, he ran again and attempted to throw the gun on top of a roof before hiding in a resident’s garage.

Toms asked the court to consider a six-year jail sentence.

Black Elk’s attorney Bryan Anderson highlighted Black Elk’s young age and lack of criminal history. He said probation would not only hold Black Elk accountable but also ensure he stays on track in getting mental health resources.

Before sentencing, Linngren called Black Elk’s actions a “significant danger to the community.”

As Black Elk was being transported back to the Pennington County Jail his family members called out to him, telling him how much they loved him.

title: South Dakota to receive $410K in deceptive cash app practices settlement
description: South Dakota will receive $410,946.38 as the state’s share in a $45 million, 46-state settlement with Block, Inc. The settlement resolves allegations that Block, Inc. misled consumers about the safety of Cash App, a peer-to-peer payment platform, and failed to protect users from fraud, according to a release from the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office.
_full_text:
South Dakota will receive $410,946.38 as the state’s share in a $45 million, 46-state settlement with Block, Inc. The settlement resolves allegations that Block, Inc. misled consumers about the safety of Cash App, a peer-to-peer payment platform, and failed to protect users from fraud, according to a release from the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office.

“Block, Inc. did not provide the fraud protection it promised and required by law,” South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley said in a release. “Consumers were left vulnerable to fraud, and the company failed to help consumers when fraud occurred.”

The AG’s office said Block, Inc. told Cash App users their money was safe – “implying that the app worked like a bank, with the same protections, which wasn't true.” At the same time, Block, Inc. knew fraud on its platform was rising sharply – and instead of warning users or strengthening protections, it doubled down on its marketing, the office said.

“For years, Block, Inc. actively promoted direct deposits of paychecks and government benefits into Cash App. It made a particular push to reach unbanked and underbanked consumers — people who would often rely on Cash App as their primary financial account, and who were especially vulnerable to fraud,” the office said in the release. “Block, Inc. grew its user base without making sure it could support those users when problems arose.”

South Dakota’s share will go to the Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Division to fund future consumer protection efforts, according to the release.

As part of the multistate settlement, Block, Inc. will distribute between $75 million and $120 million to compensate South Dakotans and consumers nationwide as part of a settlement with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the AG’s office said.

South Dakota consumers who believe they are entitled to compensation should click onto: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/enforcement/actions/block-inc/ and https://cashappcfpbsettlement.com/.

Other states that are part of the agreement are: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, and Wisconsin.

title: Mertz to be honored with statewide school library award
description: Doris Ann Mertz is the only western South Dakota recipient of a 2026-2029 School Achievement Through Libraries award.
_full_text:
Doris Ann Mertz is the only western South Dakota recipient of a 2026-2029 School Achievement Through Libraries award.

The award recognizes outstanding school library programs and school library professionals, and provides guidance about best practices in school librarianship. Mertz works at Custer Elementary and Custer High schools and Hermosa Elementary School. Mertz and School Achievement Through Libraries award recipients from 15 other South Dakota schools will be formally recognized this fall.

 070926-nws-DorisAnnMertz
Doris Ann Mertz 

The School Achievement Through Libraries award honors schools that demonstrate exemplary and accomplished practice in all three pillars of school librarianship: program, place, and professional. Through its rigorous application process, school libraries are required to submit 15 items of evidence that demonstrate their excellence and commitment to providing collaborative programs and environments that support the whole child’s academic and personal growth.

“School librarians and libraries far exceed the reputation of providing a place to read,” said Scottie Bruch, School Achievement Through Libraries training coordinator. “They instill confidence, promote literacy, and support the development of our students, preparing them for lifelong learning.”

For more information about the SATL Award and school library excellence in South Dakota, go to School Achievement Through Libraries, library.sd.gov/LIB/SLC/satl.aspx.

title: Rapid City man sentenced to 11 years for meth distribution
description: A Rapid City man faces more than a decade in prison on methamphetamine charges.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man faces more than a decade in prison on methamphetamine charges.

U.S. District Judge Camela C. Theeler sentenced Lucius Muldrow, 40, to 11 years in federal prison, followed by four years of supervised release, for conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for South Dakota.

Muldrow was indicted by a federal grand jury in September 2025. He pleaded guilty on March 16 as part of an agreement with prosecutors, according to court documents.

Between November 2021 and September 2025, Muldrow was part of a conspiracy to distribute at least 200 grams of methamphetamine in Western South Dakota. Muldrow routinely received methamphetamine from co-conspirators within the community and sold it from his home and other areas throughout the community, the office said.

This case was investigated by the Unified Narcotics Enforcement Team, which is comprised of law enforcement from the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, the Rapid City Police Department, the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation, the South Dakota Highway Patrol, and the South Dakota National Guard. Assistant U.S. Attorney Edward Tarbay prosecuted the case.

The sentencing took place on June 15 at the federal courthouse in Rapid City. Muldrow was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Homeowners near Black Hawk sinkhole lose state Supreme Court case
byline: BART PFANKUCH South Dakota News Watch
description: BLACK HAWK — A group of homeowners whose properties were impacted by a large sinkhole just west of Rapid City have lost a major legal battle now that the South Dakota Supreme Court has ruled against them in their lawsuit against the state.
_full_text:
BLACK HAWK — A group of homeowners whose properties were impacted by a large sinkhole just west of Rapid City have lost a major legal battle now that the South Dakota Supreme Court has ruled against them in their lawsuit against the state.

The court issued a unanimous decision on Thursday in favor of the state, which argued it was not responsible for damages caused by the opening of the large sinkhole above a former underground gypsum mine in April 2020.

Roughly a dozen homes in the Hideaway Hills subdivision in Black Hawk were condemned and still sit vacant in the neighborhood. Those property owners were joined by about 150 other homeowners in Hideaway Hills in filing a $60 million class-action lawsuit against the state.

In its ruling, the high court affirmed the ruling of a circuit court judge who said the state had sovereign immunity and, therefore, could not be sued by the homeowners.

 sinkhole 5 jpeg.jpg
Exposed earth in the backyard of a Hideaway Hills property shows the bumper of a vehicle in this June 2021 photo. 

The plaintiffs had argued the state was responsible for damages because it operated a gypsum mine on the site for more than 60 years before selling it to a private owner in 1994, after which the land was developed into a subdivision. They also said the state was responsible because it retained the underground mineral rights after the sale.

The origins of the sinkhole date back to the early 1900s when a company called Dakota Plaster dug underground mine shafts in search of gypsum, which slows the hardening of concrete.

When the state of South Dakota opened its own concrete plant in Rapid City in 1925, it began mining for gypsum, including on the future subdivision site. Lawyers for the state said mining was done only on the surface and that no underground mining was undertaken, though blasting did occur.

In the 1990s, the state ended mining operations, reclaimed it for grazing and sold it in 1994 to a private owner. That owner lived and ranched on the land before selling it to a developer who obtained permission from Meade County to build a subdivision in the early 2000s.

 RCJ sinkhole photo side view.jpg
In this May 2020 photo, a sinkhole on East Daisy Lane in Black Hawk exposes that part of the Hideaway Hills community was built over an abandoned gypsum mine. 

In July 2024, a class-action lawsuit was filed against the state, arguing that the gypsum mining operation was not properly reclaimed by the state when it sold the land. A circuit judge ruled in favor of the state in September 2024, and the homeowners appealed the case to the Supreme Court, making oral arguments in fall 2025.

With representation by the national law firm of Fox Rothschild, the homeowners argued that the state improperly filled in areas where it had mined with overly soft materials that led to the sinkhole. They argued that the state's failure to properly close its mining operation is akin to an "inverse condemnation," or a taking of their land similar to the use of eminent domain.

 South Dakota News Watch logo
Learn more about South Dakota News Watch at sdnewswatch.org. 

Other attempts by the homeowners at legal remedies over the past six years have been unsuccessful.

Lawyers for the state had argued that the prior owner’s underground mining on the site led to the sinkhole, and that the state had only mined on the surface. They also said the developer knew of the underground mine before building the homes, but did not alert the homeowners.

Retired Supreme Court Justice Janine Kern, who wrote the court’s opinion, said the state’s position was supported by previous case law and the state Constitution.

“Plaintiffs maintain that selling the surface property to private owners while retaining the mineral rights to the property to the present date renders the State strictly liable for any damage to their private property that has occurred or will occur in the future as a result of the prior mining activities on the property,” Kern wrote.

 2026-5-12 Sinkhole fencing.jpeg
Fences and signage warn people to stay away from the immediate area around the sinkhole in the Hideaway Hills subdivision in Black Hawk, S.D., shown on May 12. 

“The Plaintiffs have failed to establish that the State’s retention of the mining rights to the property is a 'public use' under the damaging clause of the South Dakota Constitution.”

Near the end of the 23-page ruling, Kern sympathized with the homeowners.

“While we acknowledge the devastating and sympathetic circumstances in which Plaintiffs find themselves, our review is limited to the claims before us, and Plaintiffs have not presented viable claims against the State in the present action,” Kern wrote.

Attorneys with Fox Rothschild did not immediately respond to News Watch contacts seeking comment.

title: Ahead of gubernatorial runoff election, legislators and community members push Pennington County to hand-count ballots
byline: FRANK ESPINOZA, SHALOM BAER GEE and MIKE BROWNLEE Journal staff
description: A group of locals, including area politicians, have asked the Pennington County Board of Commissioners to look at hand-counting votes, and the board’s obliged.
_full_text:
A group of locals, including area politicians, have asked the Pennington County Board of Commissioners to look at hand-counting votes, and the board’s obliged.

The commission heard the public voice concerns with tabulating machines at its Tuesday, July 7, meeting, after what Commissioner Ron Weifenbach (District 2) said was months of requests for discussion about “election integrity.” The commission voted 3-2 to have the county look into the legality of hand-counting every ballot in the post-election audit of the upcoming gubernatorial runoff election between current Gov. Larry Rhoden and Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden.

Weifenbach and Gary Drewes (District 1), voted against.

"I'm just going to reiterate the fact that one of the reasons this was put on the agenda is because some of the hand-count people have come here on several occasions and they wanted to be heard in more of a public forum, so that's what we're doing," Weifenbach said at the meeting.

 Elections
Amid public concerns about election integrity, the Pennington County Board of Commissioners approved looking at hand-counting the audit of the July 28 gubernatorial runoff election. 

Doeden received 31% of the votes in the June 2 Republican governor's primary but fell short of the required 35% to avoid a runoff election. Rhoden came in second at 25%. The runoff election is scheduled for Tuesday, July 28, and winner will face Democrat Dan Ahlers in the November general election.

Normally, 5% of precincts are hand-counted in post-election audits, but a vocal group wants all votes hand-counted.

Roughly 10 speakers presented arguments in support of hand-counting ballots. The speakers included outgoing Sen. John Carley, outgoing Rep. Heather Baxter, R-District 34, Sen. Greg Blanc, R-District 35, Tonchi Weaver and Pennington County Auditor-elect Tina Mulally. Blanc won the Republican primary in June and will uncontested in November.

Baxter is the Republican Party nominee for South Dakota secretary of state. She’ll face Democrat Terrence Davis in the November general election. The office, among other duties, administers elections in the state.

Commissioner Jerry Derr (District 4) asked current Pennington County Auditor Sabrina Green if, after running the ballots through the tabulating machines, they could then complete a post audit of the election of the precincts and compare that with the tabulating machines’ results.

 Elections
Tonchi Weaver with South Dakota Citizens for Liberty voiced her concerns about tabulating machine errors in reading ballots through her personal experience from working in elections. 

Green explained that in elections, the office runs ballots through the tabulator and then there’s a post-election audit that is hand-counted. The audit counts 5% of randomly-selected precincts. If one of the chosen precincts doesn’t have 100 ballots, additional precincts are selected until that number is met.

The state law on the matter is SDCL 12-17B-20, which notes, "The post-election audit must be conducted in 5% of the precincts in the county by manually counting all votes cast in two contests and comparing the results of the manual count to the results for those precincts at the county canvass. The county auditor shall select the precincts for the audit at random without the use of a computer in public during the meeting of the county canvassing board.”

Deputy Pennington County State’s Attorney Tyler Sobczak gave his input on the legalities of doing a hand-count and using a machine for the full election.

"When the ballots are counted, they're sealed, and essentially you would be lifting that seal to recount them again, which would be a Class One misdemeanor for anybody tampering with the box. So I'm not sure that plan works for that reason," Sobczak said about using tabulating machines and then hand-counting all of the ballots.

Sobczak gave his opinion to the commission, saying, "I think there's two ways you can cut that audit language. On one hand, you can say the audit must be conducted in exactly 5% of the precincts, because there's no language that says it must be conducted in at least 5% of the precincts ... I know we heard some conflicting information that that audit could be the entirety of that, but that's not the whole election … That's not necessarily how I read that statute."

Commissioner Deb Hadcock (District 3) said she believes that hand-counting ballots can also be tampered with and that no system is without flaws or reason for doubt.

"I'm not against hand-counting, and I'd love to do the comparable. I'm just that kind of person. I'd like to see the hand-count, just to see what it comes out to, and I like it to be a comparable to the machine," Hadcock said.

Carley, who lost in the June Republican primary for District 29, gave his reasons for a hand-count.

“First one is, the president is encouraging it. We just had him here at Mount Rushmore,” Carley said before reading a Truth Social post by President Donald Trump about voting.

Trump, since losing the 2020 Presidential Election against now-former President Joe Biden, continues to this day to claim elections have been “rigged” in the country, especially his in 2020, through mail-in ballots, tabulating machines and lax voter I.D. requirements. These claims have not been proven.

According to the Campaign Legal Center, Trump and his surrogates filed around 60 such lawsuits, all of which were dismissed on their merits or withdrawn. The Campaign Legal Center is a nonpartisan legal organization “dedicated to solving the wide range of challenges facing American democracy,” according to its website.

Per the South Dakota Secretary of State, tabulators used in the state operate as isolated pieces of technology without internet capability. They are tested at federally accredited labs before the U.S. Election Assistance Commission certifies the equipment. The commission is an independent, bipartisan commission whose mission is to help election officials improve the administration of elections and help Americans participate in the voting process,” per its mission statement . Testing includes running 1.5 million consecutive ballot positions through the tabulator to make sure they’re read correctly, reviewing three million lines of source code and a full security audit of the election management software.

Trump fires all EAC commissioners
On July 9, Trump ousted all three commissioners at the EAC just months ahead of the midterm elections, NBC and Reuters reported. A White House official confirmed with the outlet the commissioners are gone and will be replaced. Presidential appointments to the EAC are subject to Senate confirmation. There are four commissioner positions at the EAC, normally held by two Republicans and two Democrats. One Republican, Don Palmer, resigned this year, leaving it with three members. NBC also reported the remaining Republican commissioner Christy McCormick received a call and was asked to resign.

Weaver, who is with the conservative-leaning South Dakota Citizens for Liberty, requested a recount after her race for Republican Precinct Committeewoman for Precinct 5-3. She was opposed by Leigha Carsrud, who received 151 votes. Weaver received 149. The recount resulted in the same numbers, Weaver told the Journal later. She posited, however, that hand-counting could have found errors the machine was unable to detect and expressed concern that the county Auditor’s Office didn’t grant her request for a hand-count.

Weaver questioned the use of machines in counting, regardless of internet access, and said the final goal of the group is to shift South Dakota elections to only hand-counting. Baxter’s secretary of state platform includes such a shift.

"I have personally been involved in recounts of ballots, about this time last year, there was a school board election that we had a recount, and we did find a vote that the machine missed in one of the precincts. Now, in a very close election, like I just lost one by two votes for precinct committeewoman, that can matter," Weaver said at the commission meeting.

Rapid City School Board member Jamie Clapham won her seat in a 546-544 vote against Brian Johnson after a recount. The initial results had the race at 546-543.

Election audits are conducted by hand-count. South Dakota state law has various thresholds for allowing a recount. In local elections, votes within a 2% margin are eligible. Recounts are done with a mix of tabulation and hand-count.

Baxter, who lost in the Republican District 34 primary race, said she would like to see the gubernatorial runoff election be hand-counted.

"I'm in favor of counting the governor's race … just having maybe one race on the ballot (would be) simple. I've offered, five years prior to being a legislator, to come in and help. I'm still willing to help,” Baxter said, adding she has other people who are her constituents who would help.

She continued, saying, "I do like that voter intent is available to see on hand-count. With this being a Republican election only ... That means you only have to have Republicans in the room to do the hand-counting, so you don't have to worry about finding other people from the (other) party."

 Elections
State Rep. Heather Baxter, R-District 34, who’s the Republican nominee for secretary of state, argued the county has the ability to do a hand-count of elections. 

Baxter cited SDCL 12-17B-3, which states governing bodies that supervise elections are free to use, abandon or experiment with automatic tabulating or electronic ballot marking systems that are approved for use by the State Board of Elections.

Mulally and Blanc said if there's an issue of needing volunteers there shouldn't be a shortage. Mulally said she has volunteered to help with elections in the past, but has never been selected. 

Blanc, who won in District 35 to advance to an uncontested general election, questioned the commission about what the harm is of conducting a hand-count.

"I think most of you know the Bible says that there's wisdom in a multitude of councils, so I'm grateful that you're willing to receive our input. The question for me is, what is the value of having the trust of the voters?" Blanc said on the added cost of paying vote counters.

Derr motioned to give direction to county staff to reach out to the Secretary of State’s Office, Attorney General’s Office and the South Dakota Public Assurance Alliance for their input on doing a complete hand-count audit post-election.

Weifenbach cautiously disagreed with the motion, saying, "You're not going to get a definitive answer, because we can do whatever we want until somebody brings effect to it, and when they bring effect to it, then it goes to the court. The court decides. So, if we do that, it's not legal, then it can be invalidated. That's what I'm telling you guys. I've seen this. Nobody can give you an opinion that can stand on a gold standard."

Derr said if there's no response from any of those government offices, then the county will not proceed with a total hand-count and will stick with the 5% canvass audit.

title: Pennington County once again delays passage of alternative energy ordinance
byline: FRANK ESPINOZA and SHALOM BAER GEE Journal staff
description: The Pennington County Commission has delayed voting on the second reading of an ordinance that would bar utility-scale wind and solar projects from agricultural land to allow time for more amendments. This comes after a litany of delays and amendments.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Commission has delayed voting on the second reading of an ordinance that would bar utility-scale wind and solar projects from agricultural land to allow time for more amendments. This comes after a litany of delays and amendments.

It’s been nearly two years since the county started the process with a moratorium on utility-scale wind and solar projects and formed a task force to research wind and solar.

A timeline of the alternative energy saga
Oct. 28, 2024: Pennington County Planning and Zoning Commission approves conditional use permits for the Cheyenne River Ranch Wind and Solar Farm, located 7 miles south of New Underwood, 30 miles southeast of Rapid City, and 3.5 miles north of Highway 44. In response, more than 450 citizens petitioned for a moratorium on such projects.
 Nov. 19, 2024: Commission votes unanimously to enact a year-long moratorium on all utility-scale wind and solar projects in the county.
 Dec. 12, 2024: Moratorium goes into effect.
 March 4, 2025: Commission forms an alternative energy task force to research the effects of such projects and future county regulations. The members include attorneys, an appraiser and individuals from the ranching community, local government, and the energy sector. From March-July 2025, the task force meets eight times.
 Oct. 21, 2025: Commission votes unanimously to extend the moratorium to Nov. 18, 2026.
 Jan. 20, 2026: Commission passes the first reading of comprehensive plan amendments to lay the groundwork for zoning amendments to ban utility-scale wind and solar on agricultural land, sequestering in to industrial zones.
 March 3, 2026: Commission passes the second reading of the comprehensive plan amendments. The foundation for zoning amendments is in place.
 April 7, 2026: Commission opts to delay a vote on updates to the zoning ordinance, including limiting projects to industrial zones and shifting the approval power from the planning commission to the board of commissioners.
 May 19, 2026: Commission votes 3-2, Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voting no, on the first reading of the ordinance. They made significant changes, which meant the ordinance would need to be re-advertised and go through first reading again. Those changes included significant setback requirements.
 June 16, 2026: Commission votes 3-2 again, with Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voting no, on the second first reading of the ordinance.
 July 7, 2026: Commission votes 5-0 to delay the vote on the second reading to Aug. 4 for more amendments, such as a definition of infrasound and guidelines for decommissioning bonds for utility-scale wind and solar developments. The county must re-advertise the ordinance again.

The commission must approve the ordinance on two readings to officially adopt the law. At its Tuesday, July 7, meeting, the commission continued voting on the second reading to Aug. 4. The commission passed the first reading of the ordinance on May 19 and, after additional amendments were made at that meeting, passed the first reading again on June 16.

The commission voted 5-0 on July 7 to delay a second reading vote due to additional amendments that include a definition of infrasound and guidelines for decommissioning bonds for utility-scale wind and solar developments.

 Alternative energy
At the Tuesday, July 7, Pennington County Board of Commissioners meeting, the commission voted to add additional amendments to an ordinance barring utility-scale wind and solar on agricultural land. 

Infrasound concerns come from wind turbines that emit low-frequency sound that could disturb wildlife and livestock in the area, task force member Eilleen Peterson told the commission previously. The commission said the bonding language will require companies to have plans in place to cover the cost of decommissioning utility wind and solar developments.

According to the U.S. Department of Energy, on average, land-based, utility-scale wind turbines produce sounds that fall in the range of 35–45 dB when heard from 300 meters away (the closest distance a wind turbine is typically placed to a home or building). That means they are no louder than a typical refrigerator (50 dB) and create far less noise pollution than average city car traffic (70 dB).

“Although concerns about potential impacts on human health from neighboring wind turbines are often topics of discussion when new wind energy projects are proposed, a wide body of scientific evidence suggests no direct relationship between human exposure to wind turbines and human health issues,” per the department.

The county must re-advertise the ordinance. Commissioner Deb Hadcock (District 3) told the Journal the commission doesn’t have to take the issue back to a second reading because of the new changes.

What does the ordinance do?

The ordinance shifts approval power for utility-scale wind and solar projects from the county Planning Commission to the Board of Commissioners and includes setbacks far exceeding the recommendations of county staff and the current zoning ordinance.

Utility-scale is defined as systems that go directly into the grid for further distribution. Distributed systems send power directly to a home, farm or small business.

The changes are to Section 317 of the county's zoning ordinance, which governs wind and solar, both on a utility scale and on a private scale.

 Deb Hadcock
Commissioner Deb Hadcock (District 3) suggested adding further guidelines for utility-scale wind and solar projects. 

The Pennington County zoning ordinance serves as a regulatory framework indicating land use and development within the county, ensuring that land is utilized in a manner that aligns with community standards and environmental considerations.

It establishes specific zoning districts and outlines permitted uses, building height restrictions and setbacks, thereby promoting orderly development and mitigating potential conflicts between different land uses.

The new ordinance includes a property line setback for solar panels of 1,000 feet (a forty-fold increase to existing code, which requires 25 feet or 1 ½ times the height of the structure, whichever is greater) and a buffer zone of 50 feet. The change for wind turbines puts the setback from property lines at 1.2 miles (up from 1 ½ times the height of the turbine of 1,000 feet, whichever is greater, in current code) and a 50-foot buffer zone. County staff had recommended solar be 50 feet from property lines and have a 25-foot buffer zone. Staff also recommended wind turbines be setback at three times the height of the turbines and a buffer zone of 25 feet.

The changes come more than a year-and-a-half after public interest led the county to form a task force on solar and wind energy after commissioners passed a year-long moratorium on utility-scale wind and solar developments in November 2024. The commission extended the moratorium as the task force group researched the topic and considered future county regulations. The task force members include Commissioner Jerry Derr (District 4), attorneys, an appraiser and individuals from the ranching community, local government and energy sector.

More changes

The original proposal of these additional changes were brought up by Peterson, who spoke to the commission in May to ask for further changes to the proposed ordinance barring wind and solar on ag land. Peterson is the at-large representative on the county’s task force. She holds two bachelor of science degrees from the South Dakota School of Mines, one in geological mining and the other in mining engineering.

At the July 7 meeting, Matt Hasvold, another member of the task force and VP of Markets & Origination at Accelergen Energy LLC, disagreed with the changes at the meeting. According to Accelergen Energy's website, they are a developer of utility-scale battery energy storage systems and hybrid solar storage systems.

Hasvold specifically disagreed with the ban on battery storage systems used by wind and solar.

 Wind and Solar
One of several panel fields belonging to Wild Springs Solar is visible from 161st Avenue just south of New Underwood. 

"We know it's not agriculture, and I agree it's not industrial. Industrial, to me, that's manufacturing, so something in between," Hasvold said to the commission on the zoning changes. "I would really favor zoning that wouldn't be industrial ... it's basically death by overregulation."

Hadcock mentioned the concerns of fire dangers of the wind turbines and battery systems.

Hasvold told the commission that the fire safety of battery energy storage systems has progressed to be safer from fires.

"The battery chemistry that you talked about, that has a big (fire risk), is (made of) nickel magnetic manganese cobalt, which again is the battery chemistry that's in your phone and electric cars," Hasvold said. "The industry now switched over to lithium iron phosphate … You can look at the incidence of fires and battery storage projects just straight going down as the new lithium iron phosphate technologies."

 BESS Graph
A Battery Energy Storage Systems graph of fire incidents prepared by Matt Hasvold. 

Hadcock disagreed, saying the materials in the turbine and battery systems are concerning if there were to be a fire. Hadcock previously told the Journal she had concerns about battery storage, which she said can have a technical issue that overstresses the lithium batteries, potentially causing thermal runaway.

Per reporting from North Dakota Monitor, thermal runaway occurs “when a small portion of a battery unit fails and captures more heat than it can dissipate,” the outlet reported, quoting a fire safety engineer for a battery storage company.

The wind turbines, Hadcock said, also have areas of concern as they have hydraulic oil and lubricants, composite material, insulation and polymers, which are flammable materials.

Commissioner Ron Weifenbach (District 2) concluded the discourse, saying, "Putting solar panels out in the middle of an agricultural field to me is kind of like defies all common sense, other than the fact that people are going to make a lot of money. I'm not against that, but the only people that are making that money are the solar farm people themselves. It really hasn't provided anything for the community that's substantial."

title: Woman dies in truck crash on Highway 248 near Lyman
description: A Reliance woman died in a two-vehicle crash near Lyman.
_full_text:
A Reliance woman died in a two-vehicle crash near Lyman.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol said the crash occurred around 6:47 p.m. on Thursday, July 9, on South Dakota Highway 248 at the 257-mile marker, 2 miles east of Lyman. The patrol did not release the names of those involved in the crash pending notification of family members.

A preliminary investigation determined the 63-year-old woman, driving a 1998 Suzuki VDD51TON mini-truck was traveling southbound on 324th Avenue. At the same time, a 2006 Freightliner semi-truck was traveling westbound on Highway 248. The driver of the Suzuki entered the intersection without stopping and collided with the Freightliner, the patrol said.

The force of the crash ejected the woman from her vehicle and she suffered fatal injuries, the patrol said. Medics took the driver of the Freightliner, a 57-year-old man from Reliance, to a Chamberlain hospital for treatment of non-life threatening injuries.

Neither person was wearing a seat belt, the patrol said. An investigation into the crash continues.

title: Spearfish’s DeWeese wins national aerospace education award
description: SPEARFISH -- Civil Air Patrol Lt. Col. Buck DeWeese of Spearfish has received the 2026 national Frank G. Brewer Memorial Lifetime Aerospace Education Award.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH -- Civil Air Patrol Lt. Col. Buck DeWeese of Spearfish has received the 2026 national Frank G. Brewer Memorial Lifetime Aerospace Education Award.

“Being chosen for the Brewer Award Lifetime winner across all of Civil Air Patrol reflects the profound impact of your commitment, skill, and selfless contributions,” said Maj. Gen. Regina Aye, CAP’s national commander. “Your unwavering devotion to our missions and the communities we serve sets a standard of excellence for all members and embodies the very spirit of Civil Air Patrol.”

 Buck DeWeese
Buck DeWeese 

DeWeese joined CAP in 1998 after careers with the U.S. Air Force and as a pilot for Delta Airlines. He has served CAP in a variety of local unit and state-level positions, up to CAP’s state vice commander. Throughout these many roles, DeWeese has maintained a high emphasis on aerospace education leadership and training, which is one of the principal national program areas of Civil Air Patrol.

DeWeese’s award nomination said that since 2000, he has transformed CAP aerospace education across the state through innovative programming, educator outreach, hands-on STEM experiences and sustained mentorship of CAP youth and adult members.

“His leadership, vision, and personal commitment have directly advanced CAP’s aerospace education mission and established enduring programs that continue to shape aerospace education within the South Dakota Wing of CAP,” said Maj. Lori Fussell, who submitted DeWeese’s award nomination.

DeWeese has been invited to CAP’s national Conference in August to receive this award. He previously won comparable awards at the state level and a seven-state regional level.

title: Charles Loos
_full_text:
March 12, 1937 - July 11, 2026

Charles Michael Loos was born on March 12, 1937, in Delmont, S.D. He was the fourth of seven children born to Mathias and Gertrude Loos, second generation immigrants from Germany and Ireland, respectively.

Charlie, as he was widely known, spent his youth attending school and working hard on the family homestead, which included a passion for raising ducks and geese. He was an avid outdoorsman, spending many days hunting and fishing. The Loos clan was musical, and all the children played an instrument; Charlie was notable for guitar, banjo, and trombone (his song-writing skills would blossom later in life). And all were fervent Catholics, steeped in the faith instilled by their parents.

Upon graduation from high school, Charlie followed in the footsteps of his older siblings and enrolled at Creighton University. He wanted to be a game warden, so he got an undergraduate degree in Biology. Nearing the end of his studies, he inquired about opportunities in that realm but was told he'd have to wait ten years to get such a coveted position, so he was forced to pivot. He narrowed it down to the priesthood or medical school. He decided that a career in medicine would be intellectually challenging and allow him to be of great service to many people. That's a noble pursuit, true, but it also allowed him to marry the love of his life, a young nursing student by the name of Kay—the priesthood offered no such perks. They fell in love and married in 1963.

Charlie's medical career began with a stint in Public Health in Phoenix, Ariz., part of his military obligation. After three years there, he settled his growing family in Chamberlain, S.D., where he perfected the broad-spectrum clinical skillset required of a busy rural doctor. He was the trauma specialist, obstetrician, psychiatrist, minor surgeon…he did it all, sometimes in exchange for eggs or a side of beef. When in 1973 the opportunity to join a bigger clinic in Rapid City came up, he jumped at the chance to mitigate his nearly 24/7 call obligations. It was here that Charlie and Kay decided to plant their roots, raise their boys (five!), and build their life.

True to his calling, he indeed impacted the lives of many, many people in his thirty-five years practicing medicine. He was the primary caregiver for thousands, and it's estimated that he delivered over 2000 babies. Lord only knows how many high school physicals he performed. He was an excellent physician, the perfect blend of supreme competence, empathy, compassion, and integrity.

Outside of work, he continued to be an ardent sportsman, participating in regular hunts of pheasants, ducks, geese, and deer, and pursuing walleye and pike on the Missouri River. He also found another love in the game of golf; he most certainly put in the required 10,000 hours it is said to be a master at something. Cards and poker seemed to go hand-in-hand with the golfing life at the country club, and he got pretty darn good at those games as well.

Ultimately, Charlie was a man of deep faith and unflinching principle. What he did mattered to him, but more importantly, how he did it seemed to be more important. His faith was instilled early, and it only strengthened throughout the course of his lifetime. This provided a steadfast moral compass for he and his family to follow, and he never wavered from it. He always did the right thing. He always was kind. He always lent a hand. He never judged. If you want to witness what a devout man of faith looks like, look no further than Charlie's life as an example—he truly walked the walk.

The most important things to Charlie were his faith, his family, and his career. His faith informed and infused the other two, which led to remarkable successes by any measure. He exemplified how to live well, and in turn, how to die well. He was absolutely at peace with his fate, and lived to the very end without fear, regrets, or complaints of any kind--a last gift of grace which made coming to terms with his passing much easier for his family to bear. At his death, he was surrounded by the fruits of his life's labor, as a room full of his children and grandchildren sang him off to heaven. His legacy will live on in the values he has instilled in the next generations, and in generations yet to come.

He is survived by his wife of 63 glorious years, Kay; his siblings, Paul, Mary, and Pat; and his children, Mike (Heather, children, Ireland and Grady), Steve (Kristen, children, Henry, Eden, and Ava), Greg (Susan, children, Macy and Katie), Chuck (Chris, children, Isabel and Xander), and Jeremy (children, Dylan and Max). He is preceded in death by his parents, brother, Bob; and sisters, Corrine and Fran.

Vigil service 6:30 p.m. Wednesday, July 15, at Blessed Sacrament Catholic Church in Rapid City. Mass of Christian Burial will be 11 a.m. Thursday, July 16 at the church. Private family inurnment with full military honors will be at the Black Hills National Cemetery. Online condolences at www.osheimschmidt.com

In lieu of flowers or gifts, please consider a donation to the Neurofibromatosis Foundation. One of Charlie's grandchildren is living with this condition, and he would consider that a true blessing. Here's that link: https://www.nfnetwork.org/contribute/contribute-online/
