title: Patricia Kay Deeg
_full_text:
July 10, 2026

RAPID CITY, SD - Patricia Kay Deeg passed away peacefully in her home with her daughters.

Born and raised in Rapid City, SD the daughter of Vince and Edna Boland, Pat completed training at St. John's McNamara School of Nursing. She married Larry C Deeg then after their daughters were born the family adventures took them across the US. Pat cherished the friendships she made along the way and remained in touch with folks far and wide.

Her favorite place, however, was back home in the Black Hills sitting next to Rapid Creek "having an orange" and visiting with friends. She was a generous soul; rarely did a visitor leave without a bloom, a potted plant, cake or bag of cookies she pressed into their hands.

Preceded in death by her parents, Vince H and Edna R Boland as well as her husband, Larry C Deeg. Survivors include daughters, Kristin Regan; Karin Wommack (Eddie) and grandchildren, Sarah and Vince Wommack.

Services will be held at Osheim & Schmidt on Thursday, July 16. There will be a short visitation at 12:30, followed by memorial at 1:30 then 2:45 graveside at Pine Lawn Memorial Park.

In lieu of flowers, the family requests donations be made to St. Joseph's Indian School stjo.org/flowers

title: Rapid City man arrested for assault on officer
description: A Rapid City man faces charges for alleged simple assault on a police officer.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man faces charges for alleged simple assault on a police officer.

The Rapid City Police Department said Jeremy Hollen, 38, was arrested on Saturday, July 11, after an incident that started around 2:10 p.m. Officers were dispatched to the 1600 block of Space Avenue for a report of a man attempting to force his way into an apartment building. Police arrived and made contact with Hollen and attempted to detain him, but he pulled away and began allegedly resisting the officer.

At one point, he attempted to kick the officer, the department said. He also attempted to give the police a false name.

Officers arrested Hollen on suspicion of obstruction, simple assault on law enforcement and impersonation to deceive law enforcement, and on a warrant. Police said officers took him to the Pennington County Jail. The online jail roster is currently unavailable because of a cyberattack against the county.

South Dakota court records show Hollen made his initial appearance in court on Monday, July 13. A preliminary hearing is scheduled for 2 p.m. on July 28.

title: Hill City 1880 Train derails near Keystone, tickets remain on sale
description: Known for connecting Hill City and Keystone on a 20-mile round trip through the Black Hills, the 1880 train derailed Saturday, July 11.
_full_text:
Known for connecting Hill City and Keystone on a 20-mile round trip through the Black Hills, the 1880 train derailed Saturday, July 11.

The recreational train offers a two-hour narrated ride through National Forest land, past old mines and mountain views. At 68 years running, it’s the oldest continuously operating standard-gauge excursion train in the world, according to the 1880 Train website.

One of the passengers of the train posted on Facebook and described the experience as “terrifying.” Several posts, including from Black Hills Shootists, said there were no reported injuries. The derailment did result in the cancellation of the Train Robbery event scheduled on Sunday, July 12.

 1880 Train derailed
Known for connecting Hill City and Keystone on a 20-mile round trip through the Black Hills, the 1880 train derailed Saturday, July 11, about 4 miles from the Keystone depot. 

“On Saturday, July 11, the 1880 train had a delay when the rear axle of the last coach derailed at a crossing near Old City Hill Road. No one was injured and passengers were returned to the depot,” Leah Hicks, vice president of marketing for the train’s parent company, World Choice Investments, said in a statement to Journal.

The 1880 train resumed operations on Monday, July 13, Hicks said.

NewsCenter1 reported the location of the incident was around 4 miles from the Keystone depot. The station also reported crews worked over the weekend to remedy the situation. Equipment included a crane to help lift the derailed car.

title: A look at Gov. Larry Rhoden's career, legislative record, campaign finances
byline: MOLLY WETSCH South Dakota News Watch
description: Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden has spent a quarter of a century in state government, much of it as a representative from rural Meade County.
_full_text:
Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden has spent a quarter of a century in state government, much of it as a representative from rural Meade County.

Rhoden and businessman Toby Doeden meet in a July 28 runoff election that will send one of them to a general election contest against Democrat Dan Ahlers.

Rhoden ran for U.S. Senate in 2014, losing to Mike Rounds in the GOP primary, but became more well-known statewide when he was chosen as former Gov. Kristi Noem's lieutenant governor and took her role after she was tapped to join the Department of Homeland Security.

 04-13-26 Larry Rhoden SDPB debate.jpg
Gov. Larry Rhoden speaks at the South Dakota Public Broadcasting studios in Sioux Falls, S.D. during a gubernatorial debate on April 13, 2026. 

Rhoden was first elected to the state House of Representatives in 2000 and served there until 2008. His focus areas have been agriculture, education and taxes, which tracks with his history.

The governor owns a ranch in Union Center, which was his primary source of income throughout his political career, according to candidate financial disclosure records. He also served on the Meade 46-1 school board before running for the Legislature.

Some of his prominent bills are those that have altered property tax procedure in the state, a topic that has remained a key part of the highly contested governor's race.

In 2008, while serving as House majority leader, Rhoden brought forth as the prime sponsor three House Bills that changed both agricultural property tax structure as well as the state's contribution to school funding.

Rhoden would spend the rest of his legislative career switching between the Senate, where he served from 2008 to 2015, and back to the House, where he again represented District 29 from 2015 until 2019, when he was sworn in as Noem's lieutenant governor.

This year, Rhoden signed two bills authorizing what his office called "the largest property tax cut in South Dakota history."

 Rhoden-hugging-Noem--DHS-photo.jpg
Gov. Larry Rhoden hugs former South Dakota Gov. and then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem at her office in Washington. Noem was dismissed from the role by President Donald Trump on March 5, 2026. 

Julie Bartling, a former Democratic legislator from Burke who now serves as the Gregory County auditor, said that much of Rhoden's legislative career was centered around bringing light to rural issues – and that he often had to persuade other legislators of why they were important.

"I'm from a rural area, Larry's area there at Union Center is even more rural," Bartling said. "Sometimes you had to kind of convince what I call the 'urban legislators' to see how important a bill is.”

For most of his state legislative campaigns, Rhoden rarely raised more than a few thousand dollars from individual and political action committee (PAC) donations.

Contributing PACs to his gubernatorial campaign, however, is much shorter and the numbers much larger.

 Rhoden 2026 campaign finances (1).png
Campaign finance records from Gov. Larry Rhoden's campaign, which illustrate donations from in- and out-of-state political action committees. 

Records from the South Dakota Secretary of State's office show the Strong, Safe, and Free PAC, a pro-Rhoden group led by state legislator Mike Derby, has made several donations totaling at least $269,000 to the campaign. The South Dakota Realtors PAC gave $10,000. Those donors and some others make up the hundreds of thousands of dollars brought into his campaign through PAC spending.

The Free American Fund, though, is perhaps the most elusive: Rhoden received a total of more than $244,000 from the PAC and is the only candidate to receive direct funding from the group this year.

 South Dakota News Watch logo
Learn more about South Dakota News Watch at sdnewswatch.org. 

While the PAC is legally a federal committee and is based in Missouri, some of its major recent contributors are South Dakotans. Banker and philanthropist Denny Sanford gave the largest amount to the PAC at $50,000. Beal Distributing, led by Republican state Rep. Arch Beal of Sioux Falls, gave $10,000. Both of those donations were filed in December.

Ian Fury, Rhoden's campaign manager, told News Watch that "nearly all" of the dollars sent to the PAC are from South Dakota. The group's second-quarter disclosures with the FEC have not yet been filed, so contributor data is only available through March 31. As of that day, Sanford and Beal were the only South Dakotans in the group of five donors, though their contributions make up two-thirds of the donations to the PAC.

Rhoden has reported raising a total of $571,853 and spending $914,052 in 2026, though that only reflects his disclosure statement filed before the June 2 primary election and not for any pre-runoff financial activity. That brought his campaign total to just over $1 million raised and just under $1 million spent.

A screenshot from the only website linked to the Free American Fund, a donation site managed by WinRed.

Campaign finance statements from Rhoden's 2004 campaign for South Dakota House of Representatives. 

 Rhoden 2006 House run.png
Campaign finance statements from Rhoden's 2006 campaign for South Dakota House of Representatives.

title: Police: Woman drove through backyard during Rapid City chase
description: A 19-year-old woman was arrested after she allegedly fled from police through the backyard of a residence.
_full_text:
A 19-year-old woman was arrested after she allegedly fled from police through the backyard of a residence.

The Rapid City Police Department said officers arrested Josiah Hornbeck of Rapid City after an incident that started around 12:40 p.m. on Sunday, July 12.

Police said officers were dispatched around that time to the 1300 block of Atlas Street for a report of a vehicle that was occupied by a juvenile runaway. On arrival, police located the suspect vehicle in a parking lot.

As officers attempted to make contact with the driver of the vehicle, later identified as Hornbeck, she allegedly put the vehicle in drive and sped off through a nearby yard. Police said officers located Hornbeck in the vehicle in the alleyway between North 7th Street and Northeast Drive. Hornbeck fled through the alley at a high rate of speed before striking an officer’s patrol car, police said.

The chase continued. The department said Hornbeck drove through a fence and into the backyard of a residence. Hornbeck then fled the vehicle on foot before being apprehended a short time later.

Officers located the juvenile runaway safe and arrested Hornbeck on suspicion of reckless driving, felony vandalism, misdemeanor vandalism, obstruction and underage consumption of alcoholic beverages, along with on a warrant and a probation hold. Police said officers took her to the Pennington County Jail. The online jail roster is currently unavailable because of a cyberattack against the county.

The case was also not available in South Dakota online court records as of late morning Monday, July 13. Records show Hornbeck has a pending driving under the influence-first offense case tied to a May 2023 arrest. She’s due in court on that case for a dispositional conference on July 13 and a status hearing on July 17.

title: South Dakota court system eyes 3rd circuit consolidation in 50 years, raising concerns about ‘mega circuit’
description: South Dakota’s court system intends to merge the Fourth and Seventh judicial circuits, creating one that will cover nearly a third of the state’s land area.
_full_text:
South Dakota’s court system intends to merge the Fourth and Seventh judicial circuits, creating one that will cover nearly a third of the state’s land area. 

The Fourth Judicial Circuit encompasses the northwestern quarter of the state, including Butte, Corson, Dewey, Harding, Lawrence, Meade, Perkins and Ziebach counties. The Seventh Judicial Circuit includes the southwestern corner: Custer, Fall River, Oglala Lakota and Pennington counties.

The merged circuit would have the largest population and geographic footprint of any in the state, and the second-largest caseload.

The merger of the Fourth and Seventh circuits would “increase operational efficiencies” within the system, according to a news release from the Unified Judicial System.

The merger would result in one presiding judge, one chief court services officer and one deputy chief court services officer for the combined circuit, said court system spokeswoman Alisa Bousa. Each county would retain its own clerk of court.

If approved by the state Supreme Court, it would be the third circuit consolidation since the system was implemented more than 50 years ago. At least one state’s attorney in northwestern South Dakota worries the consolidation will hurt access to justice for rural residents.

 071426-nws-sl-courts-p1.jpg
Ziebach County Courthouse in Dupree. 

“The way circuits are set up right now makes sure rural counties are always properly served with the right amount of resources so we can do what we need to do,” said Shane Penfield, state’s attorney for Perkins, Dewey, Ziebach and Corson counties. “I think there could be some potential pitfalls with a circuit that large in geographic size.”

The system has not yet presented a formal rule proposal to the state Supreme Court, State Court Administrator Greg Sattizahn said in an email. Sattizahn declined an interview request. He said the system is “focusing on providing information to the public” through in-person forums planned for Aug. 26:

8:30 a.m. at the Pennington County Courthouse in Rapid City.

11 a.m. at the Meade County Courthouse in Sturgis.

3:30 p.m. at the Lonesome Dove Conference Center in Lemmon.

History of consolidation

The Unified Judicial System consists of the Supreme Court and seven circuits, each of which includes more than one county.

The term “unified” stems from the system’s setup, in which the state serves as the administrative overseer while counties manage and fund many day to day operations. Prosecutors and public defenders are paid for by counties; judges, court services officers and clerks of court are paid by the state.

The system was established by constitutional amendment in 1972, originally with nine circuit courts and 37 judges. The Supreme Court reduced that number of circuits to eight in 1976 and to seven in 2000, after an internal report recommended equalizing court costs and workloads to balance declining rural populations with growing urban areas, according to Rapid City Journal reporting at the time.

Neil Fulton, dean of the University of South Dakota’s Knudson School of Law, worked in the Sixth Circuit during the 2000 reorganization. 

“In general, these have been responses to the balance of workload,” said Fulton, who characterized the proposed consolidated operations for western South Dakota as a “mega circuit.”

Some circuits, like the Second Circuit serving the Sioux Falls metro area, handle significantly higher caseloads than rural districts, which cover a larger geographic area that involves more travel time. Fulton said the allocation of cases among judges was more balanced after the 2000 consolidation.

“It makes the work of the judiciary more sustainable,” Fulton said. “If we run our judges to the bone then they won’t be able to do things. That consolidation made coverage more reliable and regular so you saw a more predictable schedule in those courthouses.”

Balancing rural population shifts and representation

Currently, South Dakota’s circuit court system has 46 circuit court judges among its seven circuit courts. 

The Seventh Circuit has eight judges serving 144,356 residents and reported 21,042 criminal filings and 9,213 civil filings during fiscal year 2025, according to the annual report. The Fourth Circuit has four judges serving 84,181 residents. It had 11,185 criminal filings and 4,622 civil filings in fiscal year 2025 — the second-fewest in the state.

The proposed merger is a “reflection of reality,” Fulton said.

“We have to consolidate services more in some areas to get judges, clerks and court service officers needed to deliver services,” Fulton said. “You see that with a lot of stuff: healthcare and education, to a degree. I’m not surprised court services is in the same boat.”

Fulton added that the consolidation would expand the pool of potential judges, since there are more lawyers in Rapid City than in the rural northwest.

“I’m 100% confident that UJS’s goal is to provide effective administration of justice for all South Dakotans,” Fulton said. “I think everyone has a shared goal, so let’s be patient working toward that.”

Penfield is open, but more skeptical.

Rapid City may have more lawyers, but Penfield argues it is culturally and economically distinct from the northern Black Hills and northern plains. A larger Rapid City presence could mean more Rapid City-based judges, who he said have different perspectives than those from less populated counties.

“Combining those two would be a disservice not only to folks in the northern plains but to folks in the northern hills as well,” Penfield said.

If finding lawyers to serve as judges is the issue, Penfield said, the court system should increase salaries and offer judges additional staffing.

 Ground shot of courthouse
The Pennington County Courthouse is located at 315 Saint Joseph Street, Rapid City.  

The merger “sends a mixed message,” Penfield said. The court system has invested in incentive programs to draw lawyers to rural areas for over a decade, through the Rural Attorney Recruitment Program and Public Service Pathway pilot program. But the rural-urban divide for South Dakota lawyers has worsened over the past decade.

When Penfield moved back to Lemmon from Rapid City in 2007, he was the fifth lawyer in town. When Lemmon had a circuit judge in the 1980s, there were more. Now there are two lawyers in town, he said.

“If there was still a judge seated in Lemmon, I’m guessing there’d be a few more lawyers in town,” Penfield said. “There were other economic changes, but those things have impacts and send messages.”

Penfield said he doesn’t see “where the numbers justify” the consolidation.

The Fourth Circuit has a greater population than the Fifth Circuit, which includes Aberdeen, and a comparable caseload. Its workload and population also exceed those of the Sixth Circuit, which serves Pierre.

Penfield worries that the Seventh Circuit’s existing criminal caseload could create problems for representation in smaller counties and result in reduced services.

“My criminal caseload in my four counties is just a blip — probably not even a week’s worth of cases in Pennington County or a couple of days,” Penfield said. “I see that getting lost.”

Penfield plans to research the impact of the 1976 and 2000 consolidations, and said he plans to keep an open mind about the process.

Written comments on the proposed merger may be submitted by email to comment@ujs.state.sd.us or by mail to the State Court Administrator’s Office. The comment period ends Oct. 1.

title: Crews put out fire that damaged Box Elder commercial building
description: A fire severely damaged a commercial building in Box Elder.
_full_text:
A fire severely damaged a commercial building in Box Elder.

The City of Box Elder said crews reported to the structure fire on Tuesday, July 14, at a building near Box Elder Road West and Johnson Drive.

Fire crews were able to successfully knock down the fire. The fire spread beyond the building, and affected about 1.66 acres, according to Watch Duty.

The city thanked the owners of The Hangar Pub of Box Elder, who opened their doors as a cooling shelter for first responders and provided ice water during the incident. Midco supplied Gatorade to crews working throughout the response.

A fire severely damaged a commercial building in Box Elder on Tuesday, July 14. 

“We would like to thank the Box Elder Police Department and the Box Elder Volunteer Fire Department for their quick response and continued efforts throughout the incident,” Box Elder said. “We also extend our sincere appreciation to the many agencies that assisted throughout the incident.”

Assisting were fire departments from Summerset, Black Hawk, Ellsworth, Rapid City, Rapid Valley, New Underwood, North Haines, Piedmont and Whispering Pines, in addition to the South Dakota Highway Patrol and Pennington County Sheriff’s Office.

“Today's response demonstrated the strength of the Black Hills community,” the city said. “The coordination between fire, EMS, law enforcement, city staff, and community partners was instrumental in supporting an effective response.”

title: Pennington County continues cybersecurity investigation, several services unavailable or limited
description: Pennington County said Tuesday, July 14, it continues making “steady progress” in its response to the recent cybersecurity incident. An investigation into whether personal information was affected continues.
_full_text:
Pennington County said Tuesday, July 14, it continues making “steady progress” in its response to the recent cybersecurity incident. An investigation into whether personal information was affected continues.

“County staff and cybersecurity experts remain focused on restoring operations within a safe and remediated network environment. We apologize for the operational disruption that this event may have caused, or continue(s) to cause, until a safe restoration of services has been completed,” the county said in a release.

The county first announced the impact of the incident on Sunday, July 5.

An investigation into the incident continues, with county teams “working closely with state and federal partners, as well as forensic experts.”

“The comprehensive assessment is ongoing, and part of the assessment includes an analysis of whether personal information was affected. At this time, no action is required from members of the public. If we determine that personal information was involved in the incident, we will notify those individuals directly,” the county said.

Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office Public Information Officer Katy Urban said its office is finding workarounds as it continues to conduct business, and noted the court has been accommodating “as we work through this.” A message to the Pennington County Public Defender's Office wasn’t immediately returned. The cyberattack has led to a delay of jury trials.

Pennington County Sheriff’s Office PIO Helene Duhamel said deputies have shifted to paper citations instead of its usual computer-based citations but the office has not made any changes in is arrest discretion because of the computer outages. She said Pennington County has also released inmates when scheduled. The office’s online jail roster remains unavailable.

Department updates, per from the county’s release:

Treasurer’s Office

Staff is available to answer questions related to vehicle titles and other Treasurer’s Office matters.

The office is currently unable to process vehicle registrations or accept payments of any kind.

Vehicle registration renewals remain available online at my605drive.sd.gov and at self-service kiosks.

Individuals whose temporary license plates expire within the next week should visit the Treasurer’s Office at 900 Concourse Drive for options.

Auditor’s Office

Early voting remains available.

The office is unable to process lien payments at this time.

Register of Deeds

The Register of Deeds Office is now able to process vital records requests; however, they can only accept cash at this time. Vital records are also available online through VitalChek.com or by calling 605-773-4961.

The Register of Deeds Office is currently accepting real estate recordings; however, they cannot be fully processed at this time.

Planning & Zoning

The Department is providing its usual services; however, some processes may take longer than normal, and they are only able to accept cash or checks at this time.

Board of Commissioners

County Commission meetings will continue as scheduled. Due to the cybersecurity incident, meetings may not be livestreamed. They will be recorded and posted as soon as systems allow.

For the latest information regarding County services, please visit PennCo.org or follow the Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office Facebook page.

title: South Dakota Mines names new academic leaders ahead of fall semester
description: As South Dakota Mines prepares for the start of the fall semester, five longtime faculty members are stepping into new leadership roles across the university’s academic departments.
_full_text:
As South Dakota Mines prepares for the start of the fall semester, five longtime faculty members are stepping into new leadership roles across the university’s academic departments.

“This new cohort of departmental leaders was already all well-known and respected within our academic programs and have been selected to help South Dakota Mines to continue pushing the boundaries of both academic and research excellence that we’re known for,” said James Stone, Ph.D., provost and vice president of academic and student affairs.

The new leadership appointments include:

Kenneth Benjamin, Ph.D., will be taking over as head of the Karen M. Swindler Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering. Benjamin has been with Mines since 2007, previously serving as interim department head from 2020 to 2023.

 Kenneth Benjamin.
Kenneth Benjamin. 

Following the departure of Robert Hall, Ph.D., who led both the mining engineering and management and geology and geological engineering departments, the university has established separate leadership for the two programs. Rudra Mitra, Ph.D., will serve as interim head of mining engineering and management, while Kurt Katzenstein, Ph.D., has been appointed interim head of geology and geological engineering. Mitra, a Syd & Felicia Peng Professor in Mining Engineering, has been with Mines since 2022, and Katzenstein, recently selected as the Mickelson Professor, has been a faculty member since 2008.

 Rudra Mitra
Rudra Mitra 

 Kurt Katzenstein
Kurt Katzenstein 

Marc Robinson, Ph.D., assumed leadership of civil and environmental engineering, succeeding Stone after his appointment to provost and vice president for academic and student affairs. Robinson joined the Mines faculty in 2009.

 Marc Robinson
Marc Robinson 

Adam Piper, Ph.D., has returned to Mines as head of the industrial engineering department. He previously spent more than a decade in the Mines faculty before serving the past two years as a teaching professor at Mississippi State University.

 Adam Piper
Adam Piper 

“They have been tasked to further integrate experiential learning into their academic programs to best prepare our students for the grand challenges that await them in the workforce of tomorrow,” Stone said. “I’m looking forward to seeing their departments and programs continue to thrive under their leadership.”

title: Authorities investigates shooting death of woman near Kyle
description: The Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety is investigating the death of a woman who was found dead inside a vehicle west of Kyle.
_full_text:
The Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety is investigating the death of a woman who was found dead inside a vehicle west of Kyle.

Law enforcement responded to a report of suspicious activity in an area west of Kyle. Upon arrival, officers found an unresponsive woman inside a vehicle and a young child walking alone nearby, the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety. The child was immediately brought to safety and evaluated by medical personnel, the department wrote on Facebook.

Despite life-saving efforts, the woman succumbed to her injury, which was determined to be the result of a gunshot wound. The department did not release the woman’s name. The incident occurred on June 27.

A coordinated search of the surrounding area was conducted with assistance from multiple OST Department of Public Safety units and K-9 support, according to the department. Officers located and detained the individuals connected to the incident. All subjects involved have been apprehended.

The department did not immediately respond to the Journal's messages seeking information on the detained individuals, including their names and potential charges.

This was an isolated incident, and there is no ongoing threat to the public, the department said.

The incident remains under investigation in cooperation with the appropriate agencies.

title: Authorities release name of woman killed in crash near Lyman
description: Authorities have released the name of a Reliance woman who died in a two-vehicle crash near Lyman.
_full_text:
Authorities have released the name of a Reliance woman who died in a two-vehicle crash near Lyman.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol said Gayle V. Mohr, 63, died from injuries suffered the crash. The wreck occurred around 6:47 p.m. on Thursday, July 9, on South Dakota Highway 248 at the 257-mile marker, 2 miles east of Lyman.

A preliminary investigation determined Mohr, driving a 1998 Suzuki VDD51TON mini-truck was traveling southbound on 324th Avenue. At the same time, a 2006 Freightliner semi-truck was traveling westbound on Highway 248. Mohr entered the intersection without stopping and collided with the Freightliner, the patrol said.

The force of the crash ejected Mohr from her vehicle and she suffered fatal injuries, the patrol said. Medics took the driver of the Freightliner, a 57-year-old man from Reliance, to a Chamberlain hospital for treatment of non-life threatening injuries.

Neither person was wearing a seat belt, the patrol said. An investigation into the crash continues.

title: Mines team completes prestigious NSF I-Corps Program as the only Great Plains and northwestern U.S. rep
description: A research team from South Dakota Mines is advancing to the next phase of commercialization of its NanoGuard product, an invisible, nanometer-thin shield that protects devices from biological buildup and corrosion, after recently completing the prestigious National Science Foundation (NSF) National Innovation Corps (I-Corps) program.
_full_text:
A research team from South Dakota Mines is advancing to the next phase of commercialization of its NanoGuard product, an invisible, nanometer-thin shield that protects devices from biological buildup and corrosion, after recently completing the prestigious National Science Foundation (NSF) National Innovation Corps (I-Corps) program.

The NSF I-Corps program is an immersive, entrepreneurial training program that facilitates the transformation of invention to impact. The seven-week training prepares scientists and engineers to broaden their focus beyond the university laboratory, accelerating the economic and societal benefits of NSF-funded and other research projects poised for commercialization.

 1 - NanoGuard team in lab.jpg
A research team from South Dakota Mines is advancing to the next phase of commercialization of its NanoGuard product, an invisible, nanometer-thin shield that protects devices from biological buildup and corrosion, after recently completing the prestigious National Science Foundation (NSF) National Innovation Corps (I-Corps) program. 

“The I-Corps experience pushed us to think beyond the laboratory and listen directly to potential customers,” said Sunith Varghese, doctoral candidate and entrepreneurial lead for the NanoGuard team. “Through more than 100 interviews, we learned where fouling and corrosion create the most urgent pain points, especially for sensors, submerged devices and high-value assets. Those insights are now shaping our target markets, product design and next steps of commercialization.”

The Mines team was the only participant from the Great Plains and Northwestern regions selected for a national cohort that includes teams from institutions such as the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley.

“Being the only team representing the Great Plains and Northwestern U.S. regions was both humbling and energizing,” said Venkataramana Gadhamshetty, Ph.D., Mines professor of civil and environmental engineering and co-director of the 2D-Best Center on campus. “It showed that innovative research developed at South Dakota Mines stands alongside innovations emerging from institutions such as MIT, Columbia University, UC Berkeley and other leading institutions. It also reinforces the importance of bringing technologies developed in our region into national conversations on infrastructure resilience, defense readiness, environmental monitoring and advanced manufacturing. We are small, but mighty, all because of collegial, talented and convergence tech-focused faculty and students.”

With the NanoGuard coating invisible and thousands of times thinner than the human hair, it provides strong protection without getting in the way of how a device works. “It can protect delicate sensors, microelectronics and other high-value components without changing their size, shape, sensitivity or performance,” Gadhamshetty said. “It acts like an invisible shield that protects the device without interfering with its job.”

The idea for NanoGuard traces back to Gadhamshetty’s time at the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory at the Tyndall Air Force Base and has been advanced over more than 15 years of research. “I-Corps gave us the opportunity to connect this research foundation with customer needs, market opportunities and a commercialization pathway,” Gadhamshetty said.

 2 -NanoGuard team.jpg
The NanoGuard team includes, from left to right, Manoj Tripathi, Ph.D., research scientist, Jim Quinn, industry mentor, Sunith Varghese, doctoral candidate, and Venkataramana Gadhamshetty, Ph.D., professor of civil and environmental engineering. Not pictured, Ramesh Devadig, Ph.D., former Mines doctoral student. 

As part of the I-Corps program, the Mines team received $50,000 to support customer discovery and advance early-stage commercialization efforts. Through intensive entrepreneurship training and market research, the team evaluated the commercial viability of NanoGuard, exploring its potential as an innovative antifouling and anticorrosion coating solution.

 3 - NanoGuard Graphic.jpg

The team will now focus on advancing NanoGuard beyond Technology Readiness Level 5 by expanding testing beyond the laboratory and validating the coating's performance across a wider range of real-world applications and operating environments.

Their goal is to help customers reduce the need for frequent cleaning, replacement, recalibration and chemical treatments by providing durable, low-maintenance surface protection that saves both time and money.

title: Grants to fund after-school, summer programs for four years
description: Two grants awarded to Black Hills Special Services Cooperative will support after-school and summer learning programs for students in Rapid City and Philip.
_full_text:
Two grants awarded to Black Hills Special Services Cooperative will support after-school and summer learning programs for students in Rapid City and Philip.

BHSSC received the two Nita M. Lowey 21st Century Community Learning Centers grants through the South Dakota Department of Education, according to a news release from BHSSC. Over the next four years, the grants will support after-school and summer learning programs serving students at South Middle School in Rapid City. The grant funds will also allow Philip Elementary School to launch a new program.  

Both grants will help ensure students have access to safe, engaging learning environments outside of regular school hours.

In Rapid City, the grant funds will aid South Middle School Club Hub and Club Five, which serves students in partnership with South Middle School.

 071426-nws-Club Hub South Middle School.jpg
Students sew during South Middle School’s Club Hub. Grants from the South Dakota Department of Education will expand local high-quality afterschool and summer learning opportunities for students in the South Middle School Club Hub and the Club Five program. 

“This grant will provide additional opportunities to enhance programming, strengthen student supports, and expand enrichment experiences for our South Middle School students over the next four years,” said Kellsie Judge, BHSSC 21st Century project director. 

In Philip, the grant funds will enable Philip Elementary School to introduce a new program, Promoting Achievement and Wonder with Scotties (PAWS), which will provide an engaging after-school program during the school year, and six-week summer learning experiences for Philip students. These programs will incorporate academic support, hands-on enrichment activities, and experiences designed to promote both learning and personal growth.

BHSSC is an educational agency with a mission is to build stronger communities by helping individuals and organizations reach their full potential. In awarding the grants to BHSSC, the South Dakota Department of Education recognized the Rapid City and Philip programs for their commitment to meeting the needs of students and families.

"These grants represent an exciting opportunity to invest in students beyond the school day," said Dr. Pam Lange, BHSSC deputy executive director. "We are grateful to the South Dakota Department of Education for their support and proud to partner with our local schools to create welcoming environments where students can learn, explore new interests, build relationships, and thrive."

title: Helmsley trust investing $500k to aid BHACF’s Beautiful Black Hills Initiative
description: Black Hills residents are passionate about enjoying and preserving their parks, trails and outdoor spaces. The Black Hills Area Community Foundation has received a $500,000 investment that will perpetually help support nature-focused nonprofits in the region.
_full_text:
Black Hills residents are passionate about enjoying and preserving their parks, trails and outdoor spaces. The Black Hills Area Community Foundation has received a $500,000 investment that will perpetually help support nature-focused nonprofits in the region.   

BHACF announced on June 28 that it received the $500,000 investment from The Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust. With that money, plus significant matching funds from local donors, BHACF is making its Beautiful Black Hills Initiative a permanent grant-making program. The $500,000 investment from the Helmsley Trust will be distributed to BHACF over a three-year period.

“We have a three-year $500,000 indirect match where local donors can work to direct grants to nonprofits they want to support,” Zimmer said, because donors can give to Beautiful Black Hills Initiative and specify which nature-focused nonprofits they want their funds to benefit.

The Beautiful Black Hills Initiative provides grants that support healthy outdoor spaces and recreation. The initiative also aims to enrich communities by bringing people together through their shared love of the outdoors. Beautiful Black Hills Initiative was introduced in 2024 as a result of the ongoing Thriving Communities effort, which invites the public to vote about where they’d like to see grant funds invested to improve local communities.

“The Black Hills are a place of extraordinary beauty and significance. They inspire a deep connection to the land and to one another. By supporting efforts to protect natural spaces, expand opportunities for outdoor recreation, and promote mental, spiritual, and community wellbeing, (Beautiful Black Hills) is helping cultivate a culture of stewardship that is rooted in place and driven by local voices,” said Walter Panzirer, trustee of The Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust, in an excerpt of a written statement on behalf of the Trust.

Eric Zimmer, BHACF’s vice president of philanthropy and special projects, credits Kathleen Fitzgerald-Ellis, BHACF’s director of philanthropy for the Northern Hills, for helping obtain the Helmsley Trust funding. She met Helmsley Trust staff at a conference, and that ultimately led to BHACF being invited to apply for funding.

Amid increasing growth and development in the Black Hills, this funding to preserve and protect the region’s natural resources is especially vital, Zimmer said.

“Recent years have brought historic growth and change to the Black Hills region,” Zimmer said. “The Beautiful Black Hills Initiative meets the moment by sustaining healthy outdoor spaces for future generations to enjoy. We’re deeply grateful to The Helmsley Charitable Trust and many other donors for making this permanent support for our land, water, and wildlife possible.”

In 2026, more than $200,000 in grants were awarded to nonprofits throughout the Black Hills. The Beautiful Black Hills Initiative will invest in nature-focused nonprofits on an annual basis in three focus areas: healthy outdoor spaces, community building, and outdoor recreation, perpetually.

Healthy natural spaces grants promote healthy land, water, and wildlife. Grantees in 2026 include the Black Hills Watershed Collaborative, the Norbeck Society, Dakota Rural Action, Black Hills State University Science Education, Montana Conservation Crops, and the Spearfish Museum.

Outdoor recreation grants expand access to the outdoors. Grantees in 2026 include the Highpointers Foundation, the Nordic Ski Club, Spearfish Trails Coalition, the South Dakota Parks and Wildlife Foundation, and the South Dakota Wildlife Federation.

Community building grants inspire collaborations between nature-focused nonprofits and also aim to connect locals through their shared passions for the outdoors. Grantees in 2026 include the Black Hills Environmental Coalition, The Journey Museum, the Rapid City Arts Council, the Thunder Valley Community Development Corporation, the Cheyenne River Youth Project, the Black Hills Parks and Forests Association, and the Badlands National Parks Conservancy.

All three focus areas contribute to an overarching goal of the Beautiful Black Hills Initiative — to promote unity and community around a shared love of the Black Hills. Whether people like to hike, camp, fish, hunt, ski, bike, or simply enjoy the beauty of the region, nature can be an issue where people find common ground.

“One of the goals of the Beautiful Black Hills Initiative is to highlight for everybody in the community — in what I think is an age where too many people feel lonely, too online and mad at each other — a reminder that the Black Hills is one thing we all love and we all care about, even if it’s for very different reasons,” Zimmer said.

“For the Black Hills Area Community Foundation, part of our role and part of our work in the community is to lead the efforts that bring people together. This is a way to get people gathering together on their terms in the place that they love, talking about the things they agree on rather than the things they don’t agree on,” he said.

“The longer-term goal of the Beautiful Black Hills Initiative is to build up and deepen a culture of outdoor stewardship in the Black Hills,” Zimmer said. “There’s a lot of people here that love this place but I don’t think we have the deep culture around conservation and stewardship and place that other parts of the Mountain West do. This is our time to be able to work together to maintain the character of this place amid growth and development.”

Anyone interested in supporting the Beautiful Black Hills Initiative or learning more about it can go to bhacf.org/beautiful-black-hills and contact Zimmer or Fitzgerald-Ellis.

title: Mary K "Kitty" Ryan
description: December 19, 1941 - June 11, 2026
_full_text:
December 19, 1941 - June 11, 2026

In Loving Memory of Mary K. "Kitty" Ryan

Surrounded by her daughters, Mary K. "Kitty" Ryan passed away on June 11, 2026, in Denver, Colorado.

Her journey began in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, where she was born. She grew up in Belle Fourche, South Dakota and graduated from Belle Fourche High School in 1959. Kitty went on to attend South Dakota State University in Brookings, earning her Bachelor of Science in Science & Applied Arts in June 1963. It was there that she met John L. Ryan. The two were married on November 23, 1963, beginning a partnership that lasted for over 60 years.

Together, she and John had two children: Maggie and Katy. As a family, they moved all across South Dakota, Nebraska, Minnesota, and Iowa. They eventually settled in Lakewood, Colorado. After John's retirement, their moves continued as they lived in California, South Dakota, and Wyoming, before finally returning home to Denver.

In addition to raising her children and being a homemaker, she had eight years of work with the U.S. Park Service. An avid reader, she also loved gathering around a table to play Whist, Mahjong, Bridge, and work on ceramics. Kitty enjoyed planning holiday neighborhood parties and progressive dinners. Upon John's retirement, she and John took trips and cruises to such places as Australia, Ireland, and Hawaii with family and friends.

Kitty will be missed by her family and all who knew her. She is survived by her two daughters, Maggie and Katy; two grandchildren, Megan and Connor in California and Colorado, and two great-grandchildren, Adeline and James; her older brother, Jim Olsen in Illinois; her younger sister, Sue Broyles in Wyoming; and sister-in-law, Alice Maturkanich in California. Following her cremation, she will be laid to rest alongside John on July 24, 2026, 11am, at Mountain View Cemetery in Rapid City, South Dakota, bringing her journey full circle back to the state she always loved.

A vehicle crash extrication exercise by the Rapid City Fire Department.

 Skyline drive fire
The fire that burned through 2.1 acres on Flormann Street and Skyline Drive was caused by a catalytic converter, the Rapid City Fire Department said on Wednesday, July 15. 

“Catalytic converters can reach extremely high temperatures during normal vehicle operation. Please make sure you keep your vehicle's exhaust system properly maintained,” the department said.

Fire crews have completed operations. The department said there were no homes lost in the fire. However, one residence sustained minor structural damage. There are no reported injuries.

The fast-moving timber and grass fire was reported at around 6:30 p.m. on Tuesday, July 14, on a hillside off Flormann and Skyline Drive. Within an hour, crews were able to contain the fire.

Crews monitored the scene throughout the night and into the Wednesday, July 15, to ensure the fire remained contained.

“Thank you to our firefighters, our partner agencies, and the community for your continued cooperation as crews complete their work,” the department said.

title: City to tear down 28 buildings at Star Village amid continued issues with management
description: Rapid City officials shared plans to demolish 28 garages and sheds in Star Village after Tzadik Management failed to meet the deadline of a myriad of code enforcement violations and tear down the condemned buildings itself. Mayor Jason Salmaun pleaded with the management group to come into compliance, meet the needs of the residents and live up to the expectations placed on them as property owners.
_full_text:
Rapid City officials shared plans to demolish 28 garages and sheds in Star Village after Tzadik Management failed to meet the deadline of a myriad of code enforcement violations and tear down the condemned buildings itself. Mayor Jason Salmaun pleaded with the management group to come into compliance, meet the needs of the residents and live up to the expectations placed on them as property owners.

 Jason Salamun
Mayor Jason Salamun spoke on July 14 on the city’s plan to demolish structures in Star Village as Tzadik Management fails to meet deadlines and pay debts to the city. 

"Time and time again, we've provided opportunities to make things better, and time and time again, we've been let down. For me, this is about the people who live in these neighborhoods," Salamun said at a Tuesday, July 14, press conference that included city officials and others.

Per previous Journal reporting, Star Village is a low-income housing development under the management and ownership of Tzadik, a Florida company headed up by Adam Hendry. Tzadik purchased Star Village at the end of 2019. The company lists 18 Rapid City properties on its website.

Lon Schnittgrund with the city's Building Service Division said the city ordered the management company demolish more than 30 structures in three phases starting in November of 2025. He said they completed demolition of an estimated nine structures in the beginning of 2026, but failed to continue to meet the deadlines of two more demolition phases.  According to a press release from the city, those deadlines were Nov. 13, 2025 and Feb. 20, 2026.

 Lon Schnittgrund
Lon Schnittgrund, with the city's Building Service Division, said Star Village management has failed to meet deadlines and demolish 28 structures. 

Schnittgrund said the city sent a notice of the failure to meet code enforcement to Tzadik.

"They said, ‘We're doing stuff for the community. We don't like deadlines,’ basically. Just kind of a ‘We're going to do things our own way.’ That's kind of how I felt they were (saying it)," Schnittgrund said of the management's response.

The Journal reached out for comment from several Tzadik representatives and did not immediately hear back.

City Public Information Officer Darrel Shoemaker said Tzadik has racked up an estimated $533,096 in unpaid utility bills and more than $10,000 in code enforcement abatements for Star Village and other properties they own in Rapid City. The bulk of the unpaid utility bills, $344,000, is for Star Village.

"We have not proceeded with our traditional course of action, which would be to turn off the utilities. Obviously, we're not doing that because the residents who live in those structures are paying. The really sad part is that those payments are not coming back to the city, and so we have not been proceeding with turning off the services because we don't want to have that impact on those tenants who are paying their bills," City Finance Director Daniel Ainslie said.

The Rapid City Public Works Committee approved three contracts for contractors to demolish the structures, and the issue will now go to final approval from the Rapid City Council on Monday, July 20. The council will vote on whether to approve the $133,500 price tag to demolish the structures from Aug. 10-21. Those costs will be assessed to the owner.

City Attorney Carla Cushamn said Tzadik will pay for the price tag through added property taxes, noting, "These kind of abatements ... are put onto the taxes of the properties, so we have a mechanism to certify them at the City Council and then send them over to the county, and they're collected on the properties in the same way that taxes are."

 Mark Morris
Mark Morris, a resident of Star Village, shares his positive experience with law enforcement and continued community partnerships in his neighborhood. 

Fifteen-year Star Village resident Mark Morris said, "Star Village was a nice place when I was a child growing up, and it just has depleted throughout the owners taking over control of the property."

Schnittgrund described the condition of the structures as having degraded roofs, ceilings, assemblies, roof drainage, cracked paint, missing siding, compromised doors and holes that impact structural integrity. Residents have previously described the conditions in the units as “third world” to the Journal, reporting issues with plumbing, sanitation and heat.

The Journal asked Schnittgrund how long the properties have been without regular upkeep, and he said it’s has been roughly 15 years.

Rapid City Police Department Capt. Christian Sigel said the community has also seen an uptick in crime in recent years.

 Christian Sigel
Rapid City Police Department Capt. Christian Sigel spoke on crime in Star Village. 

“When it comes to crime, Tzadik Management is often number one or number two as far as criminal activity, both violent crime and reactive calls for service that occur on their properties alone, compared to all the other apartment complexes throughout the city,” Sigel said.

In the summer of 2025, there were two murders and a robbery within weeks at Oxford Square Apartments, another Tzadik property. It’s located on East Watertown Street in north Rapid City.

To alleviate some of these issues, the city has been awarded community grants dating back to 2024. The Love Your Block grant for 2026 gave Star Village a $100,000 for a 2-year period for a focused intervention project at Star Village.

"I was robbed two years ago, so that's why I got involved in this Love Your Block grant, as I wanted to try to make it a safer community. And since they've been involved, the crime has gone down," Morris said.

 Kellogg Drive in Star Village
Kellogg Drive in Star Village on Monday, June 2, 2025.
