title: What to know about the 1880 Train derailment
description: The local- and tourist-favorite 1880 Train that takes passengers on a scenic trip through the Black Hills from Keystone to Hill City derailed on Saturday, July 11 .
_full_text:
The local- and tourist-favorite 1880 Train that takes passengers on a scenic trip through the Black Hills from Keystone to Hill City derailed on Saturday, July 11.

The recreational train offers a two-hour narrated ride through National Forest land, past old mines and mountain views. At 68 years running, it’s the oldest continuously operating standard-gauge excursion train in the world, according to the 1880 Train website.

“On Saturday, July 11, the 1880 train had a delay when the rear axle of the last coach derailed at a crossing near Old City Hill Road. No one was injured and passengers were returned to the depot,” Leah Hicks, vice president of marketing for the train’s parent company, World Choice Investments, said in a statement to Journal.

“What a terrifying experience this afternoon … We were in the last car on our way back to Keystone when we derailed crossing the road. Thank goodness for that tree. God was looking out for us and kept everyone safe. No one was hurt. There were several babies in our car. So thankful,” passenger Dawn Stevens said in a Facebook post on Saturday.

1880 Train resumed operations on Monday, July 13, Hicks said.

 1880 Train derailed
Known for connecting Hill City and Keystone on a 20-mile round trip through the Black Hills, the 1880 train derailed Saturday, July 11, about 4 miles from the Keystone depot.

title: Rapid City Legal and Finance Committee to look at sports complex land gift
description: The Rapid City Legal and Finance Committee will consider and discuss a proposed real estate agreement involving property for the new sports complex.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Legal and Finance Committee will consider and discuss a proposed real estate agreement involving property for the new sports complex.

The proposed agreement between Pete Lien & Sons and the City of Rapid City would donate 22.65 acres of property located between Seger Drive, E. Mall Drive, N. Lacrosse Street and Tish Boulevard, the city said in a release, with the land to be used for the construction of a sports complex. The agreement, as listed in the committee’s meeting agenda, notes substantial completion of construction at the complex on or before Dec. 31, 2029.

If the Legal and Finance Committee approves the agreement, the item will move on to the Rapid City Council for consideration at its Monday, July 20.

 Sports Complex
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun, left, and Rapid City Sports Commission Executive Director Domico Rodriguez, right, speak during a media availability about the sports complex on Wednesday, Jan. 21. 

“The agreement and donation of property are important steps in the process to build the new sports complex, a key component to the future growth and quality of life for Rapid City and its residents,” Mayor Jason Salamun said in the release. “We appreciate the work of everyone in this process as we continue to move forward towards a facility that will positively impact Rapid City for decades.”

As part of the proposed property agreement, the publicly-owned facility would be developed, operated and maintained by or on behalf of the City of Rapid City for the purposes of hosting recreational, educational and competitive athletic activities, the city said.

The complex location is within the Catalyst District TIF, which the council approved in September of 2025, with the total including partial funding of the sports complex. The TIF is now for $103.5 after a recent amendment. Also in September 2025, the council passed the $125 million Destination District TIF, which would have been located near the sports complex. Of those $125 million, $10 million was dedicated to infrastructure that both developments would utilize.

After voters struck down the Destination District (which would’ve included Libertyland) in January, the city in February announced it was looking at other locations, including near The Monument, Executive Golf Course or Roosevelt Swim Center.

At a February Rapid City Council meeting, Salamun said the Lien family was still willing to donate the land, and there were cost-cutting opportunities since the Destination District won't be developed, leaving "some real possibilities at the original location." 

"We are determined to bring this to life," Salamun said at the meeting.

The City’s Legal and Finance Committee meets on Wednesday, July 15, at 12:30 p.m. in Council Chambers of City Hall. Officials are scheduled to provide additional details on the effort on Thursday, July 16.

title: South Dakota firefighters sent out to assist in Colorado wildfires
description: A ferocious wildfire has devoured 36,965 acres of southwestern Colorado , flames consuming Montrose, Gunnison and Ouray Counties. A devasting march that turned tragic on Sunday, July 12, when the Gold Mountain Fire claimed the life of a helicopter pilot battling the flames from above.
_full_text:
A ferocious wildfire has devoured 36,965 acres of southwestern Colorado, flames consuming Montrose, Gunnison and Ouray Counties. A devasting march that turned tragic on Sunday, July 12, when the Gold Mountain Fire claimed the life of a helicopter pilot battling the flames from above.

Three Fairburn firefighters from Fairburn Volunteer Fire Department, along with several others from the Black Hawk, Piedmont and Rapid City fire departments, set off June 27 to answer the call for help at the Gold Mountain Fire.

As of Tuesday, July 14, the fire is 12% contained.

 Fairburn firefighters at Gold Mountain Fire
Three Fairburn firefighters from Fairburn Volunteer Fire Department, along with several others from Bthe lack Hawk, Piedmont and Rapid City fire departments, set off June 27 to answer the call for help at the Gold Mountain Fire. 

After the assistance from Colorado firefighters in containing the Qury Fire that claimed 9,161 acres in the Black Hills near Custer, Fairburn Volunteer Fire Department’s District Treasurer Moritz Espy said there was no doubt in anyone’s minds that they wouldn’t go help their neighboring state.

“If your neighbor comes over and helps you, you should go back and help your neighbor,” Espy said.

Espy said the crews have been proactively preparing the areas that are forecasted in the fire’s path. Their work includes readying homes and essential infrastructure by implementing fire protection measures.

This involves the setup of hose lays to ensure water supply to strategic points around properties and the installation of sprinklers to protect assets. These fire mitigation systems are backed by portable tanks and pumps, which require meticulous setup and testing to ensure effectiveness.

The crews have been working about 16-hour days for a little over three weeks to help contain the fires. Taking in jobs out of state helps maintain volunteer fire departments' infrastructure and resupply so they can continue to assist in local fires, Espy said.

 Fairburn firefighters at Gold Mountain Fire
The crews have been proactively preparing the areas that are forecasted in the fire’s path. Their work includes readying homes and essential infrastructure by implementing fire protection measures. 

Though the crews are paid, Espy said it requires a sense of purpose rather than an incentive to face that level of danger. Each firefighter is motivated by the overwhelming community support.

“It’s helping people, it’s wired in our DNA to help people and everyone wants to help somehow,” Espy said.

With most of the Midwest facing heat waves and drought conditions for the past several months, Espy said the Gold Mountain Fire is not the only one Fairburn Volunteer Fire Department is assisting in. Espy himself is helping fight against another Colorado wildfire — the Ferris Fire has claimed 64,868 acres and is 29% contained.

Canadian helicopter pilot dies in fire

The Gunnison County (Colorado) Sheriff’s Office confirmed on Sunday, July 12, the pilot who died after his K-MAX helicopter crashed into Silver Jack Reservoir was identified as 56-year-old Nicholas Dale of Sooke, British Columbia, Colorado.

Dale was the only occupant in the helicopter and was engaging in wildfire suppression efforts in support of the Gold Mountain Fire when the aircraft went down at 5:17 p.m. in the southwest region of Gunnison County. The Montrose County Sheriff’s Office Dive Team recovered his body from the submerged helicopter later that evening and he was transferred to the Gunnison County Coroner’s Office.

“The Gunnison Sheriff's Office offers its deepest condolences to Mr. Dale's family, friends, and fellow wildfire-fighting personnel during this incredibly difficult time,” the department wrote on Facebook.

The helicopter crash investigation is being conducted by the National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration.

title: Rapid City woman sentenced to prison for conspiracy to commit money laundering
description: A Rapid City woman was sentenced to just over a year in prison for conspiracy to commit money laundering.
_full_text:
A Rapid City woman was sentenced to just over a year in prison for conspiracy to commit money laundering.

Federal Judge Karen E. Schreier sentenced A’Aliyah LeClaire, 30, to one year and one day in federal prison, followed by two years of supervised release, according to a release from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for South Dakota.

LeClaire was indicted for conspiracy to commit money laundering by a federal grand jury in March 2025. She pleaded guilty on April 17, 2026.

LeClaire was involved with moving money generated from a cocaine conspiracy that spanned from Texas to Rapid City, the office said. A source in Texas supplied cocaine through the mail to an individual in Rapid City. LeClaire assisted that individual with moving the money by helping make deposits and by allowing her accounts to be utilized to transfer the money to help hide the nature and ownership of the money.

“Whether you’re moving the drugs or moving the drug money, you can expect to hear from us sooner or later,” U.S. Attorney Ron Parsons said in a release.

“It doesn’t matter how big or small a person’s role is when it comes to assisting drug traffickers, IRS-CI will be relentless in pursuing those who bring drugs into our communities. Our special agents will follow the money to a criminal’s door,” IRS-CI St. Louis Special Agent in Charge William Steenson said in the release. “Every prison sentence is a result of the incredible coordination between federal, state and local law enforcement and it’s a victory for the people of South Dakota.”

This case was investigated by the Unified Narcotics Enforcement Team (UNET) the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), and Division of Criminal Investigation. UNET is comprised of law enforcement from the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, the Rapid City Police Department, the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation, the South Dakota Highway Patrol, and the South Dakota National Guard. Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Hodges prosecuted the case.

LeClaire has been ordered to self-surrender. The sentencing took place on June 26 at the federal courthouse in Rapid City.

title: South Dakota Mines student earns 4 national awards for Hardrocker athletics creative pieces
description: A South Dakota Mines student is earning national acclaim for his award-winning creative work. Carter Aispuro, a senior computer engineering major and student worker for Hardrocker Athletics, captured four awards in the College Sports Communications (CSC) Creative & Digital Design Contest, setting a new record for the university’s program. He received the honors at the 2026 CSC Convention in Las Vegas, Nev.
_full_text:
A South Dakota Mines student is earning national acclaim for his award-winning creative work. Carter Aispuro, a senior computer engineering major and student worker for Hardrocker Athletics, captured four awards in the College Sports Communications (CSC) Creative & Digital Design Contest, setting a new record for the university’s program. He received the honors at the 2026 CSC Convention in Las Vegas, Nev.

“I am super proud of Carter for these well-deserved awards,” said Luke Kotcher, assistant athletic director of athletic communications. “CSC is the most respected organization in our profession and to be recognized is unbelievable. Carter represents our student group, Hardrocker Athletics and South Dakota Mines proudly in his everyday work and fully deserves these awards.”

The awards came from two different pieces Aispuro created - a Hardrocker Volleyball hype video and a Rocker Recap.

 Carter Aispuro
Carter Aispuro, a senior computer engineering major from Santa Clarita, Calif., and student worker, earned four College Sports Communications (CSC) Creative & Digital Design Contest awards, the most in the university’s athletics program. Aispuro was honored during the 2026 CSC Convention in Las Vegas, Nev. 

“I’m super proud to be honored like this on a national level,” said Aispuro, who has been working with the university’s athletics program for two years. “I believe we're truly just scratching the surface of what's possible with our content. If I can achieve this with just my videos, think about what we can do with a team of students all working towards making the best athletics videos possible.”

His 2025 volleyball hype video received three recognitions in the highly competitive hype/pregame video category. Aispuro earned the second-best ranking in NCAA Division II, the fourth highest mark among student workers and seventh in the entire College Division.

His March 4 edition of Rocker Recap earned the third-best mark among student works in the College Division.

Overall, CSC saw 2,565 total entries in the Creative & Digital Design Contest, including 1,585 in the College Division. Nearly 90 contest reviewers judged the entries this past year.

“I’m so thankful for Luke and the rest of the administrative team that was willing to put their trust in me and our other students to make this happen,” Aispuro said.

Check out Aispuro’s award-winning videos at gorockers.com.

title: Local news briefs
description: The fire that burned through 2.1 acres on Flormann Street and Skyline Drive was caused by a catalytic converter, the Rapid City Fire Department said on Wednesday, July 15.
_full_text:
Crews contain wildfire off Floormann, Skyline Drive

The fire that burned through 2.1 acres on Flormann Street and Skyline Drive was caused by a catalytic converter, the Rapid City Fire Department said on Wednesday, July 15.

“Catalytic converters can reach extremely high temperatures during normal vehicle operation. Please make sure you keep your vehicle's exhaust system properly maintained,” the department said.

Fire crews have completed operations. The department said there were no homes lost in the fire. However, one residence sustained minor structural damage. There are no reported injuries.

The fast-moving timber and grass fire was reported at around 6:30 p.m. on Tuesday, July 14, on a hillside off Flormann and Skyline Drive. Within an hour, crews were able to contain the fire.

Crews monitored the scene throughout the night and into the Wednesday, July 15, to ensure the fire remained contained.

“Thank you to our firefighters, our partner agencies, and the community for your continued cooperation as crews complete their work,” the department said.

Crews put out Box Elder fire

A fire severely damaged a commercial building in Box Elder.

The City of Box Elder said crews reported to the structure fire on Tuesday, July 14, at a building near Box Elder Road West and Johnson Drive.

Fire crews were able to successfully knock down the fire. The fire spread beyond the building, and affected about 1.66 acres, according to Watch Duty.

The city thanked the owners of The Hangar Pub of Box Elder, who opened their doors as a cooling shelter for first responders and provided ice water during the incident. Midco supplied Gatorade to crews working throughout the response.

“We would like to thank the Box Elder Police Department and the Box Elder Volunteer Fire Department for their quick response and continued efforts throughout the incident,” Box Elder said. “We also extend our sincere appreciation to the many agencies that assisted throughout the incident.”

Assisting were fire departments from Summerset, Black Hawk, Ellsworth, Rapid City, Rapid Valley, New Underwood, North Haines, Piedmont and Whispering Pines, in addition to the South Dakota Highway Patrol and Pennington County Sheriff’s Office.

“Today's response demonstrated the strength of the Black Hills community,” the city said. “The coordination between fire, EMS, law enforcement, city staff, and community partners was instrumental in supporting an effective response.”

Firefighters extinguish hot spots in Custer attic fire

The Custer Volunteer Fire Department said crews extinguished hot spots after a homeowner reported smoking coming from their attic.

Firefighters were paged at 10 p.m. Tuesday, July 14, for smoke coming out of an attic space in a large building.

“After smelling smoke, the homeowner opened the access panel to the attic and upon seeing smoke, immediately shut it which is exactly what we want people to do as that helps deprive the fire of oxygen,” the department said.

Crews were able to find the area of concern and extinguish the hot spots rather quickly. Afterwards they spent time ensuring the fire was out. Custer Volunteer Fire Department responded with five apparatus and nine personnel.

Units were backed by Hill City Volunteer Fire Department, Hot Springs SD Volunteer Fire Department, Argyle Volunteer Fire Department, South Dakota, Pringle VFD, Custer Ambulance Service, Inc., Custer County Sheriff and Black Hills Energy.

Cohort aims to strengthen early learning

Early Learner Rapid City invites the community to help shape future of early learning by joining the Early Learner Rapid City Family Engagement Cohort.

The first meeting of the ELRC Family Engagement Cohort will be from 5:30 to 7 p.m. Monday, July 20, at the United Way of the Black Hills office, 621 Sixth St., Suite 100, in Rapid City. A light meal will be provided. Virtual participation will be provided upon request.

ELRC Family Engagement Cohort is a new opportunity for families, caregivers, providers and community partners to help strengthen early learning in the community.

To attend the first meeting, RSVP to earlylearnerrc@gmail.com or call 605-343-5872.

Early Learner Rapid City is an initiative led by the John T. Vucurevich Foundation, United Way of the Black Hills, the City of Rapid City, and Early Childhood Connections.

Police say hotel death suspicious

The Rapid City Police Department is investigating the death of a person at the Rodeway Inn at 1313 N. LaCrosse St.

Officers were dispatched to the hotel at around noon on Tuesday, July 14, for a report of a dead person inside a room. When they got to the hotel, they found the body, “believed to be an adult male,” police said.

Based on information at the scene, police are investigating the individual’s death as suspicious in nature.

An autopsy has been scheduled in the ongoing investigation in an effort to identify the person and determine a cause of death.

The Pennington County Sheriff’s Office and the police department are teamed up on the investigation.

Authorities investigate Kyle woman’s death

The Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety is investigating the death of a woman who was found dead inside a vehicle west of Kyle.

Law enforcement responded to a report of suspicious activity in an area west of Kyle. Upon arrival, officers found an unresponsive woman inside a vehicle and a young child walking alone nearby, the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety. The child was immediately brought to safety and evaluated by medical personnel, the department wrote on Facebook.

Despite life-saving efforts, the woman succumbed to her injury, which was determined to be the result of a gunshot wound. The department did not release the woman’s name. The incident occurred on June 27.

A coordinated search of the surrounding area was conducted with assistance from multiple OST Department of Public Safety units and K-9 support, according to the department. Officers located and detained the individuals connected to the incident. All subjects involved have been apprehended.

The department did not immediately respond to the Journal's messages seeking information on the detained individuals, including their names and potential charges.

This was an isolated incident, and there is no ongoing threat to the public, the department said.

The incident remains under investigation in cooperation with the appropriate agencies.

title: Helmsley trust investing $500k to aid BHACF’s Beautiful Black Hills Initiative
description: Black Hills residents are passionate about enjoying and preserving their parks, trails and outdoor spaces. The Black Hills Area Community Foundation has received a $500,000 investment that will perpetually help support nature-focused nonprofits in the region.
_full_text:
Black Hills residents are passionate about enjoying and preserving their parks, trails and outdoor spaces. The Black Hills Area Community Foundation has received a $500,000 investment that will perpetually help support nature-focused nonprofits in the region.   

BHACF announced on June 28 that it received the $500,000 investment from The Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust. With that money, plus significant matching funds from local donors, BHACF is making its Beautiful Black Hills Initiative a permanent grant-making program. The $500,000 investment from the Helmsley Trust will be distributed to BHACF over a three-year period.

“We have a three-year $500,000 indirect match where local donors can work to direct grants to nonprofits they want to support,” Zimmer said, because donors can give to Beautiful Black Hills Initiative and specify which nature-focused nonprofits they want their funds to benefit.

The Beautiful Black Hills Initiative provides grants that support healthy outdoor spaces and recreation. The initiative also aims to enrich communities by bringing people together through their shared love of the outdoors. Beautiful Black Hills Initiative was introduced in 2024 as a result of the ongoing Thriving Communities effort, which invites the public to vote about where they’d like to see grant funds invested to improve local communities.

“The Black Hills are a place of extraordinary beauty and significance. They inspire a deep connection to the land and to one another. By supporting efforts to protect natural spaces, expand opportunities for outdoor recreation, and promote mental, spiritual, and community wellbeing, (Beautiful Black Hills) is helping cultivate a culture of stewardship that is rooted in place and driven by local voices,” said Walter Panzirer, trustee of The Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust, in an excerpt of a written statement on behalf of the Trust.

Eric Zimmer, BHACF’s vice president of philanthropy and special projects, credits Kathleen Fitzgerald-Ellis, BHACF’s director of philanthropy for the Northern Hills, for helping obtain the Helmsley Trust funding. She met Helmsley Trust staff at a conference, and that ultimately led to BHACF being invited to apply for funding.

Amid increasing growth and development in the Black Hills, this funding to preserve and protect the region’s natural resources is especially vital, Zimmer said.

“Recent years have brought historic growth and change to the Black Hills region,” Zimmer said. “The Beautiful Black Hills Initiative meets the moment by sustaining healthy outdoor spaces for future generations to enjoy. We’re deeply grateful to The Helmsley Charitable Trust and many other donors for making this permanent support for our land, water, and wildlife possible.”

In 2026, more than $200,000 in grants were awarded to nonprofits throughout the Black Hills. The Beautiful Black Hills Initiative will invest in nature-focused nonprofits on an annual basis in three focus areas: healthy outdoor spaces, community building, and outdoor recreation, perpetually.

Healthy natural spaces grants promote healthy land, water, and wildlife. Grantees in 2026 include the Black Hills Watershed Collaborative, the Norbeck Society, Dakota Rural Action, Black Hills State University Science Education, Montana Conservation Crops, and the Spearfish Museum.

Outdoor recreation grants expand access to the outdoors. Grantees in 2026 include the Highpointers Foundation, the Nordic Ski Club, Spearfish Trails Coalition, the South Dakota Parks and Wildlife Foundation, and the South Dakota Wildlife Federation.

Community building grants inspire collaborations between nature-focused nonprofits and also aim to connect locals through their shared passions for the outdoors. Grantees in 2026 include the Black Hills Environmental Coalition, The Journey Museum, the Rapid City Arts Council, the Thunder Valley Community Development Corporation, the Cheyenne River Youth Project, the Black Hills Parks and Forests Association, and the Badlands National Parks Conservancy.

All three focus areas contribute to an overarching goal of the Beautiful Black Hills Initiative — to promote unity and community around a shared love of the Black Hills. Whether people like to hike, camp, fish, hunt, ski, bike, or simply enjoy the beauty of the region, nature can be an issue where people find common ground.

“One of the goals of the Beautiful Black Hills Initiative is to highlight for everybody in the community — in what I think is an age where too many people feel lonely, too online and mad at each other — a reminder that the Black Hills is one thing we all love and we all care about, even if it’s for very different reasons,” Zimmer said.

“For the Black Hills Area Community Foundation, part of our role and part of our work in the community is to lead the efforts that bring people together. This is a way to get people gathering together on their terms in the place that they love, talking about the things they agree on rather than the things they don’t agree on,” he said.

“The longer-term goal of the Beautiful Black Hills Initiative is to build up and deepen a culture of outdoor stewardship in the Black Hills,” Zimmer said. “There’s a lot of people here that love this place but I don’t think we have the deep culture around conservation and stewardship and place that other parts of the Mountain West do. This is our time to be able to work together to maintain the character of this place amid growth and development.”

Anyone interested in supporting the Beautiful Black Hills Initiative or learning more about it can go to bhacf.org/beautiful-black-hills and contact Zimmer or Fitzgerald-Ellis.

title: Parasite causing gastrointestinal distress reaches South Dakota
description: A parasite spreading across the country causing severe diarrhea has reached Pennington County.
_full_text:
A parasite spreading across the country causing severe diarrhea has reached Pennington County.

The South Dakota Department of Health’s Infectious Disease Dashboard shows three cases of cyclosporiasis, which is caused by the cyclospora cayetanensis parasite, in South Dakota. There are two cases in Pennington County and one in Clay County, according to the department.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it has received reports of 1,645 confirmed domestic cases of cyclosporiasis and is aware of more than 5,100 cases that require further analysis to confirm the illness as domestically acquired. But CDC data lags behind individual state counts, with the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services alone reporting 4,312 cases, with 102 hospitalizations, in the state as of Thursday, July 16.

The CDC said the most common symptoms include watery diarrhea, “which can be frequent,” loss of appetite, weight loss, bloating, nausea and fatigue. Less common symptoms include low-grade fever and vomiting. Without treatment, symptoms can follow a remitting-relapsing course that can last from a few days to a month or longer, according to the CDC. Illness can be severe, but is not usually life-threatening.

Reuters reported shredded iceberg lettuce supplied to Taco Bell restaurants by California-based supplier ​Taylor Farms has been identified by investigators as a potential source ‌of contamination. The restaurant chain had already preemptively removed some ingredients from its menu amid the outbreak.

Ways to avoid cyclosporiasis, according to the CDC, include:

Wash all fruits and vegetables thoroughly under running water before eating, cutting, or cooking.

It is important to thoroughly wash produce even if it is labeled as pre-washed.

Scrub firm fruits and vegetables, such as melons and cucumbers, with a clean produce brush.

Cut away any damaged or bruised areas on fruits and vegetables before preparing and eating.

Per the Michigan health department, precautions to take also include:

Lettuce/leafy greens: Buy whole heads of lettuce (rather than prewashed, bagged lettuce or salad mixes), throw away the outer two–three layers of leaves and wash the inner leaves under running water. For leafy greens that can be cooked, cooking is the safest option.

Cilantro, basil: Wash thoroughly under running water, separating the leaves. Safest when cooked.

Green onions: Trim the root end and remove the outer layer, wash thoroughly under running water. Safest when cooked.

Raspberries: Their bumpy surface makes them especially hard to clean; the parasite can hide in the tiny crevices. Safest when cooked (pies, jams etc.). Consider frozen raspberries as an alternative. Freezing may reduce but does not guarantee elimination of the parasite.

Snow peas: Wash under running water and rub the surface. Safest when cooked.

title: ‘Somebody’s not coming tonight:’ Citizens for Liberty Rhoden-Doeden forum features half of the equation
description: South Dakota Citizens for Liberty hosted a Republican governor runoff forum in Rapid City on Thursday, July 16. The event was missing just one thing: Gov. Larry Rhoden (or one of his surrogates).
_full_text:
South Dakota Citizens for Liberty hosted a Republican governor runoff forum in Rapid City on Thursday, July 16. The event was missing just one thing: Gov. Larry Rhoden (or one of his surrogates).

“Somebody’s not coming tonight,” said Tonchi Weaver, president of South Dakota Citizens for Liberty.

Rhoden, a Union Center native, and Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden are going head-to-head in a runoff election on Tuesday, July 28. Doeden won the June 2 Republican primary but didn’t pass the 35% threshold to avoid a runoff. Doeden finished with 31%, followed by Rhoden at 25%. Doeden received the most votes in West River, with 14,536. Rhoden received 13,679.

The forum was held at the Rapid City Best Western Ramkota, 2111 N. Lacrosse St., in the Sylvan Room.

“We are not an organ of any party, but we are a conservative organization that promotes informed voters and active citizenship, and that’s why we put on events like this,” Weaver said.

Weaver has personally endorsed Doeden.

 Doeden
Aberdeen businessman and South Dakota governor candidate Toby Doeden speaks at a Republican governor candidate forum in Rapid City on Thursday, July 16. His opponent, who he faces on July 28, did not attend. 

Weaver said she contacted both campaigns “right after” the Republican primary on June 2, and Doeden confirmed “right off the bat,” and Rhoden’s office acknowledged the invite.

“I said, ‘Well, this is how we’ll proceed. We will expect both candidates to be there unless we hear different.’ We never heard different, but yesterday there was a spontaneous event that cropped up on the governor’s schedule,” Weaver said.

Rhoden posted on his Facebook page at 8 a.m. on Wednesday, July 15, that he would be holding a telephone town hall, starting at the same time of the Citizens for Liberty event. The town hall offered voters a chance to enter their phone number and receive a call connecting them to the event. The Journal didn’t receive the call when it entered its information.

Rhoden campaign manager Ian Fury told the Journal Rhoden, “has been very clear for a month now, he has debated Toby Doeden three times and will not be doing so a fourth time.” The two participated in three debates ahead of the June 2 Republican primary.

Asked about Citizens for Liberty billing the event as a forum, not a debate, Fury said, “The rules were very much structured as a debate. Opening/closing statements, rebuttal, etc.”

"(Rhoden) held a telephone town hall tonight that was attended by thousands of South Dakotans and he answered about a dozen questions,” Fury said.

Weaver said Rhoden’s office informed Citizens for Liberty on the day of the forum that he would not be attending. His office did not respond to a question about whether Rhoden would send a representative on his behalf, according to Weaver.

“I don’t think it’s disrespect to CFL (Citizens for Liberty), I think it’s disrespect to the people that came here to hear the candidates,” Weaver said.

Fury did not answer a question about the timing of the Rhoden campaign’s response to Citizens for Liberty.

Doeden took a shot at Rhoden for not attending, saying, “Larry's hiding in the mansion in Pierre right now … I'm here. No notes. No script. And I will answer any question you can throw at me.”

A recently released poll by KELO Media showed Rhoden with a commanding 62% lead, to Doeden’s 32%, with 7% undecided. The KELO/Emerson College poll of 500 Republican likely primary voters and had a margin for error of 4.3%.

title: Authorities identify man found dead at Rapid City hotel, 3 arrested
description: The Rapid City Police Department released the name of the man who was found dead at the Rodeway Inn in Rapid City. Three people are in custody on suspicion of improper disposal of a body.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Police Department released the name of the man who was found dead at the Rodeway Inn in Rapid City. Three people are in custody on suspicion of improper disposal of a body.

Police were dispatched to the hotel, at 1313 N. LaCrosse St., around noon on Tuesday, July 14, for a report of a body in a room. When they got to the hotel, they found the body, “believed to be an adult male,” police said.

In an update on Thursday, July 16, the department identified the man as 33-year-old Jason Horned Eagle, of Rapid City. Based on evidence at the scene, detectives believe he had been left in the hotel room for several months. An autopsy has been completed, and law enforcement is awaiting toxicology results and additional forensic testing in an effort to determine cause of death.

According to the Rapid City Police Department, detectives identified three people who knew about Horned Eagle’s death and made attempts to conceal his body in the hotel. Police arrested those three suspects:

51-year-old Barbara Diaz, of Rapid City, was arrested on three charges: unauthorized dissection of body, failure to furnish information and failure to notify the coroner or sheriff of a death within 24 hours. All three charges are misdemeanors. Court records show Diaz appeared in court on July 16 and is set to reappear on July 24.

29-year-old Diana Hairy Shirt, of Rapid City, was placed under arrest for improper disposal of a body, the police department said. No recent cases appeared under her name in South Dakota court records as of 4:20 p.m. on Thursday, July 16.

50-year-old Walter Cordon, of Rapid City, was placed under arrest for improper disposal of a body, the police department said. No recent cases appeared under his name in South Dakota court records as of 4:20 p.m. on Thursday, July 16.

The Pennington County Sheriff’s Office and the police department are teamed up on the investigation. Law enforcement asks anyone with any information relevant to the ongoing investigation to contact Det. James Halterman at 605-394-4134.

 Rodeway Inn
A person was found dead at the Rodeway Inn on LaCrosse Street in Rapid City on Wednesday, July 14. The hotel is located across the street from the northside Walmart.

title: Rapid City’s VFW Post 1273 earns All-American honor
description: Rushmore VFW Post 1273 in Rapid City has been recognized for the second consecutive year as an All-American Post.
_full_text:
Rushmore VFW Post 1273 in Rapid City has been recognized for the second consecutive year as an All-American Post.

The honor comes from the Veterans of Foreign Wars of the United States. Being recognized as an All-American is one of the organization's highest honors. The All-American designation is awarded to VFW Posts that demonstrate exceptional performance in membership growth, community service, youth and veteran programs, volunteerism, and support for fellow veterans. Only Posts that meet rigorous national standards receive this distinction.

Earning All-American status for the second consecutive year is a testament to the dedication of the Post's volunteers and members who live the VFW's mission: “No one does more for veterans.”

 VFW
The war mural at Rushmore VFW Post 1273 in Rapid City features soldiers representing World Wars I and II, and the Korean and Vietnam Wars. The Post announced July 6 it has been honored for the second consecutive year as an All-American Post, which recognizes exceptional performance in membership growth, community service, youth and veteran programs, volunteerism, and support for fellow veterans. 

"This recognition belongs to every member of Post 1273," Post 1273 leadership said in a news release. "It reflects the countless hours our volunteers dedicate to serving veterans, honoring those who have served, supporting our community, and ensuring that the VFW remains strong for future generations."

Rushmore VFW Post 1273 is located in downtown Rapid City at 420 Main St. It has 800 members and is the largest VFW Post in South Dakota. Throughout the year, members of Post 1273 volunteer countless hours in support of veterans and the Rapid City community.

The Post conducts military funeral honors, hosts community events, supports youth scholarship programs, organizes patriotic ceremonies, partners with local nonprofit organizations, provides assistance to veterans and their families, and serves as a gathering place for camaraderie and service.

Rushmore VFW Post 1273 was founded on Oct. 13, 1932. The Post remains committed to growing its membership and expanding its impact throughout the Black Hills region. The Post encourages eligible combat veterans to learn more about the VFW and the opportunities available to serve their fellow veterans and the community.

To learn more about Rushmore VFW Post 1273, go to vfw1273.org or facebook.com/vfw1273

title: Rapid City Council to vote on solidifying sports complex location on July 20
description: Nearly a year after the original approval of a Tax Increment Financing District that includes the flagship development of a sports complex in Rapid City, the city is set to accept a land donation from Pete Lien & Sons for the facility. The city considered alternative locations for the complex, but ultimately landed on the north Rapid City land.
_full_text:
Nearly a year after the original approval of a Tax Increment Financing District that includes the flagship development of a sports complex in Rapid City, the city is set to accept a land donation from Pete Lien & Sons for the facility. The city considered alternative locations for the complex, but ultimately landed on the north Rapid City land.

At its Wednesday, July 15, meeting the Rapid City Legal and Finance Committee voted unanimously to approve agreements on the facility management, engineering services and land donation.

 Rapid City sports complex sign
The Rapid City sports complex will be located in the general area of Seger Drive and 143rd Avenue.  

"What you have before you here at the committee, as well as the council meeting on Monday, is the efforts of many months and, quite frankly, years of work," Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun told the committee during public comment.

City documents state the total anticipated project cost for the development of the sports complex will be $76.2 million. The city has secured approximately $66 million in committed funding, Salamun said, including $24.58 million from the Catalyst District TIF. An estimated $28.28 million will come from the Hotel Business Improvement District, $6.2 million in land donation value and $5 million from the Vision Fund, per city documents.

The documents state there are negotiations over the primary naming rights sponsorship that will include a substantial upfront capital contribution and an annual payment. Salamun wrote in a column the naming rights sponsorship is “soon-to-be-announced.”

 071826-nws-complexfacts-p1.JPG
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun speaks at a press conference about the sports complex on Thursday, July 16.  

Of the details provided by the city, the 180,000 square foot facility will include an indoor walking track, indoor playground and "specialized spaces" to host regional and national sporting events, including volleyball and basketball. The building is also set to include pickleball.

The land donation agreement states substantial completion of construction at the complex on or before Dec. 31, 2029.

Resident Mark Millar expressed skepticism to the Legal and Finance Committee about the selection of the facility operator.

In the agreement, Sports Facilities Management, LLC, based out of Florida, is named as the proposed operator for the sports complex, pending city council approval.

Rapid City Sports Commission Executive Director Domico Rodriguez responded to Millar's comments, stating four interviews were conducted with other management groups before SFM was chosen. He did not name the other groups.

Rodriguez told the Journal, “They mange the most similar facilities in the United States, about 120 different facilities.”

 Catalyst District Boundaries
The boundaries of the Catalyst District are indicated with the yellow lines.  

Earlier in the year, the city announced it was looking at other potential locations within the TIF boundary, including areas near The Monument, Executive Golf Course and Roosevelt Swim Center.

The TIF was approved in August and then reapproved in September after a clerical error by the city, and the sports complex will be developed on the 22.7 acres donated by Pete Lien & Sons on the intersection of Seger Drive and 143rd Avenue. Pete Lien & Sons is a Rapid City-based construction and mining company.

“Our family business is happy to make Rapid City a better place, and this is a way we could do that,” Pete Lien, owner of the company, said at a city press conference on Thursday, July 16.

The site was to be developed in tandem with the $125 Destination District TIF, which included the anchor development Libertyland, a development with an America-themed amusement park. The TIF, which Rapid City voters shot down at the ballot box in January, included an estimated $10 million in shared infrastructure funds that would've benefited the Destination and Catalyst Districts.

The final approval of the sports complex will go before the City Council on Monday, July 20.

In June, the council approved an amendment to add Elevate Rapid City to the Catalyst District, adding $19 million in infrastructure improvements for a future business park. This park would also include multifamily dwellings across 128 acres. This increased the TIF amount to $103.5 million.

title: Rapid City Sports Complex: What you need to know
description: Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun and the Rapid City Sports Commission Executive Director Domico Rodriguez have recently made one fact clear: The Rapid City sports complex will be built .
_full_text:
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun and the Rapid City Sports Commission Executive Director Domico Rodriguez have recently made one fact clear: The Rapid City sports complex will be built. 

"Rapid City, this is for you," Salamun said at a press conference on Thursday, July 16.

 Rapid City Council to vote on solidifying sports complex location on July 20
"What you have before you here … is the efforts of many months and, quite frankly, years of work,” Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun said.

Here are important facts regarding the project:

The total projected cost, per city documents, is $76.2 million. Salamun said, "to date, we have secured more than $66 million through the Hotel BID fee, the Catalyst TIF district, the land donation, Vision Funds, and a soon-to-be-announced naming rights partnership," in a recent op-ed for the Journal. The sports complex was originally priced at $55 million in June 2025. 

Salamun said it's "safe" to expect the first games to be played in 2029.

Salamun said the sports complex will be constructed even if there's a change in leadership. Salamun's seat is up for re-election in July of 2027. "This is a project that's beyond one mayor," Salamun said.

Rodriguez estimates it will be 180,000-200,000 square feet. Amenities will include eight basketball courts that can double as 16 volleyball courts or 32 pickleball courts; an indoor soccer field that can be used for football and lacrosse; a performance center similar to Monument Health's Sports Performance Institute; and a walking track. 

The sports complex will be funded and completed without the Libertyland TIF, which would’ve included $10 million in shared infrastructure work before Rapid Citians voted it down on Jan. 20. Rodriguez said, “We just had to get creative to find ways to address needed infrastructure without the funding.” One of those adjustments included removing a road from the plan.

The Rapid City Council is set to approve the intended location, donated by Pete Lien & Sons, on Monday, July 20.

title: Without funding, RCFD says it can’t provide EMS in Pennington County; Board of Commissioners explore options
description: The Rapid City Fire Department has notified Pennington County it will no longer be able to provide Emergency Medical Services for rural areas after the end 2026. The Pennington County Board of Commissioners has expressed its support for funding rural medical response and is looking into where to find the money.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Fire Department has notified Pennington County it will no longer be able to provide Emergency Medical Services for rural areas after the end 2026. The Pennington County Board of Commissioners has expressed its support for funding rural medical response and is looking into where to find the money.

Under South Dakota law, EMS is currently not considered an essential service that must be funded by local governments. In 2025, House Bill 1043 would have required counties and municipalities to fund Emergency Medical Services, but the bill was shot down in committee. In 2026, Senate Bill 89 created the Emergency Medical Services Funding Task Force to look into whether EMS is an essential service. What the task force finds, and if any laws will come from it, is still to be determined.

 Jerry Derr
Pennington County Board of Commissioners voted 5-0 to work with RCFD to discuss funding needs to continue EMS services in rural communities.  

In the meantime, the commission voted unanimously on July 7, to formally send a letter to RCFD Chief Jason Culberson to express support for proper funding to continue services outside of Rapid City limits.

According to Commissioner Jerry Derr (District 4), the RCFD notified the commission ambulance service outside the Rapid City municipal limits will cease, effective Dec. 31, 2026, if further funding cannot be found to meet the growing needs. 

Culberson told the Journal, "The ambulance service is funded through an enterprise fund run through the city. Revenue was/is generated when a patient is transported ...No funding has stopped, we are asking for funding to continue to provide the service. We are no longer able to provide services outside the city without funding."

According to the city's 2026 budget, ambulance enterprise funds were approved at $7.2 million for the year. An enterprise fund is self-supported through user fees.

Derr's said the department needs an estimated $800,000 to continue ambulance coverage for the unincorporated areas, and he said there were about 2,655 calls made in 2025 for ambulance services in unincorporated areas of the county. 

Culberson said, "We do not want to expand. We are already providing services to these areas. Again, we are asking for agreements and a funding mechanism to continue to provide the service in the areas. Ultimately, we are unable to provide the service the way it has been done."

Derr stated in a memo to the board the affected areas are primarily rural areas of District 4, which encompasses much of eastern Pennington County, including New Underwood. Derr represents the district. He also stated the RCFD has advised him this issue comes as the service "cannot continue to bear the financial burden" of medical services without further funding. 

The letter to Culberson is the beginning of a discussion on steps to take between the two entities to ensure future services for rural county residents. 

The letter asks the RCFD:

What estimated level of funding would be required to continue ambulance service into 2027?

What geographic service area would that funding support?

Would that service area include New Underwood and the other rural areas currently served by Rapid City Fire? 

Would Rapid City Fire be willing to enter into a short-term agreement while a permanent funding model is established?

What terms, conditions, or commitments would Rapid City Fire require in order to continue providing service during that transition period?

"No resident of Pennington County should ever wonder whether an ambulance will come when they call 911. Sustainable EMS service is a public safety necessity, not a luxury," Derr's informative presentation read.

Culberson notified the commission of the changes by writing a letter in Dec. 2025, stating the city since 2003 has provided some EMS to many county residents with no subsidy and has been without a contract with the county since 2007.

Derr's presentation looked at three possible solutions for continuing services, which included a direct county levy with a rate of either a .251 mill rate for full property value (based on value of the entire property within the taxing area) or .329 mills for owner occupied only (based on value of each owner occupied property within taxing area) year to contract with RCFD.

A mill levy is a property tax based on the assessed value of a property; one mill is equal to one dollar per $1,000 of assessed value. The levy is calculated by determining the amount of revenue each jurisdiction needs to fund its budget for public services, such as schools, parks and libraries.

If a home in the county were valued at $300,000 and the mil levy was approved at .251 then the cost to fund services would be $75.30 a year. If the county approves the owner-occupied rate of .329 for an estimated home value of $300,000, then the yearly cost would be $98.70.

Derr's also noted the county could look at a special assessment of collecting $119 for each owner-occupied home regardless of value or using funding from the county's general fund.

They are also not limited partnering with RCFD as they can create an ambulance district to contract with other agencies.

"The counties are not mandated to provide ambulance services. The fact of the matter is it is really part of what we should be doing is helping create ambulance districts and find out how they get funded," Commissioner Ron Weifenbach (District 2) said.

title: Scrubs & Stethoscopes: Teens get interactive lessons about working in health care
description: Teens learned to suture, experienced physical therapy, watched EKGs of their own hearts and more during Scrubs & Stethoscopes in Rapid City.
_full_text:
Teens learned to suture, experienced physical therapy, watched EKGs of their own hearts and more during Scrubs & Stethoscopes in Rapid City.

Sanford Health’s Scrubs & Stethoscopes Health Care Career Minicamp was hosted Wednesday, July 14, at Black Hills Surgical Hospital. Sixteen students from Rapid City Stevens and Central High Schools, St. Thomas More, Douglas High School and Hill City High School who are interested in health care careers spent half a day getting a glimpse of their possible future jobs.

 071626-nws-ScrubsandStethoscopes-vein
Danni Honner, RN Inpatient at Black Hills Surgical Hospital, right, helps a teen learn how to find a vein as the process of drawing blood was explained. The activity was part of Sanford Health’s Scrubs and Stethoscopes Health Care Career Minicamp on July 14 in Rapid City. 

The interactive event allowed the teens to get hands-on training in the basics of suturing wounds, blood draws and physical therapy, as well as go through some activities patients might experience. The teens also had the option to be hooked up to EKG machines so they could watch their own heart rhythms while using a stethoscope to feel their heart beating.

The minicamp included a tour of Black Hills Surgical Hospital and the neighboring Black Hills Imaging Center to see the radiology equipment. The minicamp ended with a forum where health care professionals explained what their jobs entailed and answered teens’ questions.

This week’s Scrubs & Stethoscopes is the second Sanford Health has hosted, with more planned in the fall. The first minicamp, held in June, attracted teens from Rapid City, Hill City, Wall and Pierre. The minicamps are designed based on feedback from the teens themselves, said Colleen Bsharah, Sanford Health senior career development consultant for the Black Hills Region.

“I went out and talked to classroom students and said, ‘What would you want to experience, where would you want to experience it,’ and the answers we got were they wanted to be in a facility. So we brought them to Black Hills Surgical Hospital because they wanted to see what does it feel like to be in a facility where hopefully one day they’re going to work,” Bsharah said.

The students requested hands-on activities they could touch and engage with, she said, which inspired the interactive portions of the minicamp. Students also wanted to meet and spend time with staff members and learn more about what’s involved in their jobs.

 071626-nws-ScrubsandStethoscopes-suture
Amber Johnson, RN Inpatient at Black Hills Surgical Hospital, taught students the step-by-step process of suturing a wound during Sanford Health’s Scrubs and Stethoscopes Health Care Career Minicamp on July 14 at Black Hills Surgical Hospital. The minicamp gave teens hands-on experiences and a chance to learn about careers in health care. 

“We’re hoping more hands-on hopefully sparks that interest and gets them excited about a future in health care,” Bsharah said.

By the end of each minicamp, while students were learning, they were also noticeably more comfortable spending time in a health care environment.

“The biggest thing is, with Sanford Health coming out here, they really prioritize getting students hands-on experiences and opening their doors for students to be here. Health care is such an important field in our area. We’re such a hub. These are great jobs for students,” Bsharah said. “If they have an interest and a passion for it, you really can’t go wrong around here getting into health care, exploring those different fields and finding what does light that passion for them.”

 071626-nws-ScrubsandStethoscopes-EKG
Teen participants in Sanford Health’s Scrubs and Stethoscopes Health Care Career Minicamp could volunteer to be hooked up to an EKG machine. Danni Honner, RN Inpatient at Black Hills Surgical Hospital, explains what the teens are seeing on the machine. The July 14 minicamp in Rapid City gave teens a chance to learn more about careers in health care. 

 071626-nws-ScrubsandStethoscopes-heartbeat
Kandace Wauer, RN Inpatient at Black Hills Surgical Hospital, helps a teen listen to his heartbeat with a stethoscope while he is hooked up to an EKG machine. The activity was part of Sanford Health’s Scrubs and Stethoscopes Health Care Career Minicamp on July 14 in Rapid City. 

 071626-nws-ScrubsandStethoscopes-suturecloseup
A teen practices suturing techniques during Sanford Health’s Scrubs and Stethoscopes Health Care Career Minicamp on July 14 in Rapid City. 

 071626-nws-Scrubs and Stethoscopes-balancecoordination.jpg
Standing on one foot on a spongy surface while using a light to point to numbers, letters and symbols on a board in front of them was one of the exercises teens practiced. They were learning about physical therapy during an educational session with Madeline Basso, DPT, with Sanford Health Black Hills Orthopedic and Spine Center. The activity was part of Sanford Health’s Scrubs and Stethoscopes Health Care Career Minicamp on July 14 in Rapid City. 

 071626-nws-ScrubsandStethoscopes-openingbottle.jpg
Teens not only learned about physical therapy but tried some exercises during Sanford Health’s Scrubs and Stethoscopes Health Care Career Minicamp on July 14. The teens were given props to mimic disabilities such as hearing loss, vision loss and neuropathy. Here, a teen attempts to open a pill bottle while wearing gloves that limit her dexterity like neuropathy might. 

 071626-nws-ScrubsandStethoscopes-injectingneedle
A teen practices injecting a needle while learning about the process of drawing blood. The activity was part of Sanford Health’s Scrubs and Stethoscopes Health Care Career Minicamp on July 14 in Rapid City.

title: Carolyn Joy Mollers
_full_text:
April 26, 1936 - July 13, 2026

Carolyn Joy (Claussen) Mollers, 90, died Monday, July 13, 2026, in Missoula, Montana.

Carolyn was born in Carroll, Iowa, on April 26, 1936, to Joyce and Melbourne Claussen. She grew up in Storm Lake, Iowa, and graduated from Buena Vista University with a BA in Speech and English. She later earned an MA in Communication from the University of South Dakota. She married Mark J. Mollers on September 8, 1959.

Carolyn enjoyed teaching at South Dakota State University, Arlington High School, and Rapid City High School for a number of years. Later, she found great satisfaction in helping with the family automobile business and in her many civic activities. She was active in the First Presbyterian Church, AAUW, the Rapid City Concert Association, the South Dakota Humanities Foundation, Rushmore Rotary, and the Mount Rushmore Society and its Preservation Fund Committee.

Carolyn worked at Mount Rushmore as a college girl and fell in love with the Memorial and the Black Hills. She was grateful to spend much of her later life in Rapid City and treasured many wonderful experiences throughout the area. In later years, she and her husband spent winters in Naples, Florida, where they made many happy memories with friends. Finally, they chose to make their home in Missoula, Montana, close to their oldest daughter and the families of their three grandsons.

Carolyn will be remembered as a loving wife, mother, grandmother, sister, and friend. She is survived by her husband, Mark Mollers; daughters, Catherine Mollers and Cari Lynn (Patrick) Verlanic; grandsons, Alex (Noelle) Verlanic, Andrew (Tina) Verlanic, and Connor (Haley) Verlanic; three great-grandchildren; and her sister, Marolyn McDiarmid, and her family.

Visitation will be from 4:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. on Tuesday, July 28, 2026 at Osheim & Schmidt Funeral Home.

Carolyn's Funeral Service will be at 11:30 a.m. on Wednesday, July 29, 2026 at First Presbyterian Church (710 Kansas City St. Rapid City).

Interment will follow at 1:30 p.m. at Black Hills National Cemetery.

title: Majority of Pennington County Commissioners say ‘no’ to hand-count ahead of meeting
byline: MIKE BROWNLEE and FRANK ESPINOZA Journal staff
description: Members of the Pennington County Republican Party are pushing for a full hand-count of ballots in the gubernatorial runoff election and have started recruiting vote counters for election night. But four Pennington County Commission members said they don’t expect that to happen.
_full_text:
Members of the Pennington County Republican Party are pushing for a full hand-count of ballots in the gubernatorial runoff election and have started recruiting vote counters for election night. But four Pennington County Commission members said they don’t expect that to happen.

“I don't know where they got that,” Commissioner Ron Weifenbach told the Journal on Friday, July 17. “Trying to do a hand count is going to be, would be, very difficult. … I don’t think that’s going to happen.”

The party sent an email to members announcing the Pennington County Commission will approve a hand-count of the July 28 matchup between Gov. Larry Rhoden and challenger Toby Doeden, who won the June 2 GOP primary. The party is recruiting 46 five-person counting teams, in line with South Dakota state law, for counting boards that would count the ballots at polling sites after voting ends at 7 p.m., according to the email. The email was first obtained by Dakota War College, and Tonchi Weaver confirmed to the Journal the party had sent an email. That would put the number of counters needed at 230, plus alternates, though Weaver estimated 170 because the counters can do multiple precincts at the same polling site.

At its July 7 meeting, the commission voted 3-2 on a motion to have county legal counsel look into the legality of hand-counting every ballot in the post-election audit. The discussion and eventual vote came after a push by a group of citizens, including South Dakota Republican Secretary of State nominee Heather Baxter, Pennington County Auditor-elect Tina Mulally and Weaver, to examine hand-counting votes.

Per state law, a post-election audit must be conducted in 5% of the precincts in the county “by manually counting all votes cast … and comparing the results of the manual count to the results for those precincts at the county canvass. The county auditor shall select the precincts for the audit at random without the use of a computer in public during the meeting of the county canvassing board.”

The agenda for the board’s Tuesday, July 21, meeting includes a discussion of the July 7 motion, with the option to review or update the standing motion based on advice from counsel.

“I'm going to try to limit it to that conversation (at Tuesday’s meeting),” said Weifenbach, the board’s president. “The conversation is about whether we can do 100% hand-count vote after we do the tabulation. That's what the conversation is about, whether it's legal or not, going over our attorney's opinion after he gathered the information, just like we talked about, nothing changed.”

Weaver pointed to SDCL 12-18-1.5, which allows for the creation of counting boards. Election Day poll workers turn over ballots to the counting board. Weaver said the party has recruited enough counters to cover the five per polling site requirement. She said they continue to recruit alternates as a contingency.

Commissioner Ron Rossknecht said, per guidance from the Pennington County Auditor’s Office, the counting effort would require training those counters in time for the election. He also said they’d be paid $25 per hour and estimated each would work three hours. Weaver estimated two hours for counting.

“All volunteers would have to be trained and certified within six to seven days, which to me poses a problem as county operations continue to struggle with the cybersecurity incident,” Rossknecht told the Journal in an email, referencing ongoing issues the county is dealing with (and the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office is investigating) after a cyberattack around the July 4 holiday weekend.

Commissioner Jerry Derr said, based on advice from the Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office, the best move would be to stick to the 5% post-election audit count. He also mentioned the cybersecurity incident and said entering more than 200 new employees into the system to count at polling sites would be untenable.

“For the upcoming run-off election, I feel that we should be doing only the 5% post-election requirement. What are we proving with doing only a hand-count and not being able to compare the results with the tabulators?” Rossknecht said. “With all the issues that Pennington County is currently dealing with, I feel that only employing the 5% post-election requirement is the best solution going forward for the July 28th runoff.”

“If anything,” he said in concluding his email, “I would probably support a hand count for the general election in November or the 100% post-election audit. This gives our auditor’s office more time to prepare and make sure that everything is done correctly and in order.”

 Alternative energy (Copy)
Commissioner Ron Rossknecht (District 1) said he’s not in favor of hand-counting the July 28 Republican gubernatorial runoff election. 

Weaver said hand-counting ensures chain of custody, with the ballots not leaving the polling site until they’re counted.

“I think it will be faster and more efficient and more trustworthy. By trustworthy, I'm not saying I don't trust (County Auditor) Sabrina (Green),” she said. “I just don't trust what I can't see in the machine.”

Per the South Dakota Secretary of State, tabulators used in the state operate as isolated pieces of technology without internet capability. They are tested at federally accredited labs before the U.S. Election Assistance Commission certifies the equipment. The commission is an independent, bipartisan commission whose mission is to help election officials improve the administration of elections and help Americans participate in the voting process, per its mission statement. Testing includes running 1.5 million consecutive ballot positions through the tabulator to make sure they’re read correctly, reviewing three million lines of source code and a full security audit of the election management software.

 Email to Pennington County GOP members

Derr said in a perfect world the county would be able to do a 100% hand count in the post-election audit to alleviate any concerns.

“I don't want to discount, you know, the concerns the public has,” he said about the group pushing for hand-counting. “If you go through that process, then you might get more participation in the electorate coming forward to cast a vote.”

Asked how he’d vote if there’s a motion at Tuesday’s meeting to conduct the polling site hand-count, Commissioner Gary Drewes said, “My vote would be ‘no.’”

“I’m not going to put her (Green) in that type of position,” Drewes said, while echoing Rossknecht’s concern about getting counting boards trained in time for the runoff. “In my opinion, if you're doing a hand-count, there's a lot more chance of an error there than there is if you're doing it by the tabulation.”

Commissioner Deb Hadcock said she’d be in favor of hand-counting ballots at the polling sites.

“Do I want to do it all the time? No. But let’s try it,” Hadcock said.

title: Judge temporarily blocks South Dakota’s abortion-pill advertising ban as lawsuit continues
description: A new South Dakota law that criminalizes the advertising of abortion pills cannot be enforced while a lawsuit against it continues, a federal judge ruled Friday.
_full_text:
A new South Dakota law that criminalizes the advertising of abortion pills cannot be enforced while a lawsuit against it continues, a federal judge ruled Friday.

Nancy Turbak Berry, who formerly served as a Democratic state legislator from Watertown, and New York-based nonprofit Mayday Health filed the lawsuit in May against Gov. Larry Rhoden and Attorney General Marty Jackley, who are both Republicans. Rhoden signed the legislation in March after legislators approved it, but it wasn’t scheduled to take effect until this month.

 Mayday Health argues abortion law violates free speech in lawsuit; org and state await decision by federal judge
Mayday Health is arguing a law set to go into effect on July 1 violates the First Amendment.

South Dakota already had a near-total ban on abortion, except when it’s necessary “to preserve the life of the pregnant female.”

The new law prohibits the dispensing, distribution and advertising of abortion pills and other abortion-related items, and makes violations punishable by felony prosecutions and fines.

Mayday Health and Turbak Berry say the law illegally restricts Turbak Berry’s free speech. As an example, the lawsuit says the prohibition on advertising would prevent her from wearing a sweatshirt sold by Mayday. The sweatshirt says abortion pills can be obtained in all 50 states and encourages people to learn more on Mayday’s website.

“Unless this court grants relief, Turbak will be deterred from wearing the sweatshirt,” and thereby deterred from engaging in First Amendment-protected speech, the lawsuit says.

Mayday also posted advertisements at South Dakota gas stations last year directing people to the organization’s website for information on abortion pills.

 071826-nws-sl-mayday-p1.jpg
Mayday Health posted signs like this one at gas stations around South Dakota in December 2025 as part of a campaign to spread awareness about the availability of abortion pills. 

Jackley said during a hearing in Rapid City last month that the state is not attempting to criminalize the wearing of a sweatshirt. He said the state is targeting the way Mayday uses its website to connect South Dakotans with abortion-pill providers, which he said is not legal in a state that bans abortion.

“What the First Amendment doesn’t do is protect an illegal drug transaction in South Dakota,” he said.

A Mayday official said during the same hearing that the organization only provides information and does not encourage anyone to obtain abortion pills.

Judge Camela Theeler wrote in her ruling that the state’s lawyers have “not shown that Mayday advertises with the specific intent that another person engage in specific criminal conduct and thus have not shown that Mayday’s advertising is integral to criminal conduct.”

Mayday and Turbak Berry, along with their lawyer, Jim Leach, of Rapid City, will now seek a permanent order blocking the law’s enforcement.

Jackley issued a statement saying the state will continue to defend the new law.

“Protecting and defending innocent life is and remains important to our Legislature, governor, attorney general and citizens,” Jackley said.

title: Key takeaways from the Citizens for Liberty GOP governor runoff forum
description: South Dakota Citizens for Liberty hosted a Republican governor runoff forum in Rapid City on Thursday, July 16.
_full_text:
South Dakota Citizens for Liberty hosted a Republican governor runoff forum in Rapid City on Thursday, July 16.

Both Gov. Larry Rhoden, a Union Center native, and Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden were invited to the forum hosted by the conservative group. Doeden attended. Rhoden did not. The forum was held at the Rapid City Best Western Ramkota, 2111 N. Lacrosse St., in the Sylvan Room.

Here’s some key takeaways and things to know about the upcoming race:

Runoff to choose the Republican primary candidate

Rhoden and Doeden are going head-to-head in a runoff election on Tuesday, July 28. Doeden won the June 2 Republican primary but didn’t pass the 35% threshold to avoid a runoff. Doeden finished with 31%, followed by Rhoden at 25%. Doeden received the most votes in West River, with 14,536. Rhoden received 13,679.

Whoever wins the runoff will head to the general election ballot and face Democrat Dan Ahlers.

Rhoden opted to hold telephone town hall instead of attending forum

Rhoden campaign manager Ian Fury told the Journal Rhoden, “has been very clear for a month now, he has debated Toby Doeden three times and will not be doing so a fourth time.” The two participated in three debates ahead of the June 2 Republican primary.

Asked about Citizens for Liberty billing the event as a forum, not a debate, Fury said, “The rules were very much structured as a debate. Opening/closing statements, rebuttal, etc.”

Tonchi Weaver, president of Citizens for Liberty, said both candidates were invited to the forum “right after” the June primary. Doeden confirmed and Rhoden neither confirmed nor turned down the invite, but his office did acknowledge the invitation, Weaver said. On the day of the forum, Weaver said she received word Rhoden would not be coming.

 Toby Doeden
Aberdeen based businessman Toby Doeden is seeking election as governor for South Dakota against incumbent Gov. Larry Rhoden. In what was planned as a forum for the two candidates, Rhoden failed to attend leaving Doeden with ample time to answer questions from the public. 

Doeden digs into plan to eliminate property taxes

“I think all property tax is bad. If you ask me, I think it's unfair and I think it's unjust,” Doeden said. “I believe we have to start with owner-occupied homes for South Dakota residents, and I'll go down even a little deeper. We need to start with fixed-income seniors and veterans. They are struggling more than any group of people in the state today. If I have to meet one more fixed-income senior that had to sell their home because of property taxes, I'm going to scream.”

Doeden has run on eliminating property taxes, with language from his website stating, “Toby Doeden will fight to reduce and ultimately eliminate your property taxes, so that you can raise your family, operate your farm or ranch, and grow your business free from crushing property taxes.”

Rhoden has launched a website in criticism of Doeden’s tax plan, framing Doeden’s campaigning materials as a plan to “blow a $1.8 billion hole in the state budget — gutting education, roads and public safety.”

South Dakota Searchlight reported, in response to that criticism, Doeden’s campaign spokesperson Matt Hurley said this week that Doeden’s plan has never applied to any classes of property beyond owner-occupied homes. They produce about $815 million in local tax revenue. Eliminating property taxes for homeowners — and nobody else — has “always been the plan,” Hurley said.

In response to whether his plan would mean an income tax, Doeden said, “As long as I’m upright, South Dakota will never have a state income tax.”

 Julie Frye-Mueller
Julie Frye-Mueller, a former South Dakota state senator, posed questions over concerns of property taxes to Doeden. 

Polls show Rhoden in the lead, Doeden calls it ‘completely fictitious’

A recent poll released by KELO Media showed Rhoden with a commanding 62% lead, to Doeden’s 32%, with 7% undecided. The KELO/Emerson College poll of 500 Republican likely primary voters and had a margin for error of 4.3%. It was conducted July 12-13.

“And I promise you, fake polls or not, I'm winning on July 28, and then everybody's going to endorse me,” Doeden said in Rapid City, claiming his internal polls show he’s in the lead.

Also during the forum, Doeden billed himself as a law and order candidate, saying he would deputize law enforcement as ICE agents if he is elected governor and expressing strong opposition to recreational marijuana.

Under Rhoden’s governorship, South Dakota law enforcement agencies entered into 287(g) agreements with ICE to assist with enforcement actions. Those agreements between federal and state or local agencies fall under Section 287(g) of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996. The program authorizes ICE to delegate "specified immigration officer functions" to state and local law enforcement officers, operating under the agency’s direction and oversight, according to ICE's website.

According to Rhoden’s office, South Dakota State Troopers have assisted in more than 204 immigration-related arrests involving individuals unlawfully present in the United States who were encountered during routine patrols across South Dakota.

The South Dakota National Guard deployment of seven guardsmen to assist ICE has continued since fall 2025. These active-duty soldiers in Sioux Falls and Rapid City are “helping process deportations, acting as a force multiplier for South Dakota ICE officers,” per Rhoden’s office. Through July 2, 2026, the South Dakota National Guard has assisted directly in processing 807 illegal immigrants who have been deported out of South Dakota. The guard costs have been paid directly with federal funds.

 Tonchi Weaver
South Dakota Citizens for Liberty President Tonchi Weaver kicked off the event with opening remarks on Gov. Larry Rhoden’s absence. 

 Citizens for Liberty sign
South Dakota Citizens for Liberty’s hosted a South Dakota Republican governor runoff forum on Thursday, July 16. Per the organization’s president, Tonchi Weaver, “We are not an organ of any party, but we are a conservative organization that promotes informed voters and active citizenship, and that’s why we put on events like this.”

Rob Schleiffarth, M.D. 

Schleiffarth is a board-certified otolaryngologist who treats allergies, sleep apnea, nasal obstructions and sinus issues. He is an expert in using the Inspire implant to treat sleep apnea and in the VivAer procedure for nasal obstruction. Before joining Sanford Health, Schleiffarth practiced at Rapid City Medical Center for 12 years.

Same-day nose and throat appointments are a unique service for the Black Hills region that allow patients to be seen quickly when allergies and sinus issues arise without warning.
