title: Good Samaritan locations in Rapid City earn national awards
description: Good Samaritan Society St. Martin Village skilled nursing location and Good Samaritan Society Echo Ridge assisted living/basic care location, both in Rapid City, received 2026 Silver Achievement in Quality awards.
_full_text:
Good Samaritan Society St. Martin Village skilled nursing location and Good Samaritan Society Echo Ridge assisted living/basic care location, both in Rapid City, received 2026 Silver Achievement in Quality awards.

The Silver Achievement in Quality awards are presented by the American Health Care Association and National Center for Assisted Living. Silver winners are long-term care locations with the best quality metrics and survey results in the United States.

The Silver award distinction is part of the AHCA/NCAL National Quality Award Program. The program honors long term and post-acute care providers across the nation that have demonstrated their dedication to enhancing quality care for the residents they serve. The AHCA/NCAL National Quality Award Program is a rigorous three-level process in which organizations are reviewed and evaluated by trained experts.

 071926-nws-samaritan 002.JPG (Copy)
Good Samaritan Society St. Martin Village skilled nursing location, pictured, and Good Samaritan Society Echo Ridge assisted living/basic care location, both in Rapid City, have received 2026 Silver Achievement in Quality awards. 

“At Good Samaritan, we are continually inspired by the residents, families and communities we serve,” said Nate Schema, Good Samaritan president and CEO. “It is a privilege to care for seniors in the rural communities they call home, and with that comes a deep responsibility to deliver personalized, meaningful care. Being recognized through AHCA/NCAL’s rigorous awards program is both an honor and a reflection of that commitment.”

“Congratulations to this year's Silver recipients on reaching this level in the Quality Award journey,” said Clif Porter, AHCA/NCAL president and CEO. “These providers have built strong systems, embraced continuous improvement, and are making a measurable difference in the lives of those they serve. As we look to a future that will ask more of providers as demand for care increases, this commitment to excellence will serve as a critical foundation.”

The AHCA/NCAL National Quality Award recipients will be celebrated during the AHCA/NCAL Convention & Expo, October 11-14, 2026, in Boston.

For more information about Good Samaritan, go to good-sam.com.

title: Mary Lou Saugstad
description: January 2, 1934 - February 4, 2026
_full_text:
January 2, 1934 - February 4, 2026

Mary Lou Saugstad, age 92, of Breese, formerly of Rapid City, SD, died at 5:30 a.m. Wednesday, February 4, 2026 at Cedarhurst of Breese. While our hearts grieve her loss, we give thanks for a life well lived and deeply loved.

She was born January 2, 1934 in Huron, South Dakota, the daughter of the late Earl and Mary Maxine (Austin) Knickrehm.

She graduated from Huron High School. After graduation she worked at Weir Music Store where she met the love of her life, Wayne Saugstad. They were married May 9, 1954 and celebrated 57 years together.

Mary Lou enjoyed riding her bike with her faithful companion, Sandy Dog in the basket. She was also an accomplished seamstress. Her love of sewing also turned into a love of quilting and counted cross-stitch. She was also an avid bowler for over 50 years.

Mary Lou is survived by two daughters: Peggy (Gary) Myers of Lebanon, IL and Penni (William) Liebig, also of Lebanon, IL; three grandchildren: Kelley (Justin) Kocher of Portage, MI, and Nicole and Matthew Liebig of Highland, IL; three great-grandchildren: Hannah, Gavin and Noah Kocher of Portage, MI; two sisters: Karen (Robert) Nelson of Billings, MT and Bonnie (Wayne) Gutzmer of Black Hawk, SD; and her adopted daughter, Mary (Chuck) Medina of Anaheim, CA, along with many nieces and nephews.

Besides her parents and husband, she was preceded in death by a granddaughter, Stephanie Myers; son-in-law, Gary Myers; and a brother-in-law, Robert Nelson.

Burial will be at Black Hills National Cemetery in Sturgis, SD on July 24, 2026 at 3:00 pm.

title: Update: Crews contain Oakland Street house fire in Rapid City

The Journal arrived on scene around 3:35 p.m. and saw multiple flames coming out of windows and the front door. Fire personnel arrived on scene shortly thereafter. The house is across the street from St. Thomas More High School.

Witnesses on scene said occupants and pets in the home had escaped safely. The Rapid City Fire Department confirmed no injuries were reported.

The department said the fire call came in at 3:30 p.m. and crews arrived to find heavy fire coming from windows on two sides of the home. Crews quickly attacked the fire and were able to bring the fire under control, the department said.

The resident was home when the fire started. All occupants have been displaced as a result of the fire and the American Red Cross has been notified to assist those affected, the department said.

title: Sturgis man sentenced for possession of child sexual abuse material
description: The U.S. Attorney’s Office for South Dakota said U.S. District Judge Camela C. Theeler has sentenced a Sturgis man convicted of receipt of child pornography.
_full_text:
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for South Dakota said U.S. District Judge Camela C. Theeler has sentenced a Sturgis man convicted of receipt of child pornography.

Luke Basche, 21, was sentenced to seven years in federal prison, followed by five years of supervised release, according to the office.

Basche was indicted by a federal grand jury in February 2025. He pleaded guilty on March 31, 2026.

According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office:

Between December 2022 and January 2025, Basche used Mega, an internet-based chat application, to search for, download and view sexually explicit visual depictions of child pornography on his cellular phone. After Basche received and downloaded child sexual abuse material to his Apple iPhone, he stored many of the depictions in his Dropbox and Google accounts, which are cloud-based internet storage services. Investigators found over 2,500 images and 445 videos of child pornography on his phone. Basche also stored child pornography on computers and a hard drive. The victims depicted in child pornography he received included infants and toddlers.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, go to https://www.justice.gov/psc.

This case was investigated by the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation’s Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force, the Rapid City Police Department, and the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office. Former Assistant U.S. Attorney Heather Knox and Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Schroeder prosecuted the case.

The sentencing took place on June 29. Basche was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Summer school graduates adds baker’s dozen to Rapid CIty graduation rolls
description: For most of the Rapid City Class of 2026, graduation is fading in the rearview. But on Friday, July 17, a baker’s dozen graduates were added to the rolls.
_full_text:
For most of the Rapid City Class of 2026, graduation is fading in the rearview. But on Friday, July 17, a baker’s dozen graduates were added to the rolls.

Rapid City Area Schools District held its 2026 summer school graduation at Rapid City Alternative Academy on Friday to celebrate students who completed their high school degrees, 10 from Rapid City Central High School and three from Rapid City Stevens High School. Five of the students attended the in-person graduation ceremony.

 Principal Jesse Sporrer
Rapid City Area Schools Summer School Principal Jesse Sporrer delivers the commencement address on Friday, July 17, to five students who attended summer school graduation. 

Summer School Principal Jesse Sporrer said 210 students participated in summer school this year, earning 337 half-credits.

“It was really awesome to see those kids come in and take the opportunity that they had, run with it and work towards graduation,” Sporrer told media after the graduation. Summer school is not required in the district. In addition to Sporrer, summer school staff consists of six teachers, a counselor and two secretaries.

In his commencement address, Sporrer emphasized the “power of choice” to the five graduates sitting in the front row, who he thanked for showing up. “I’m tickled pink,” he said.

“You chose to do summer school, and not all of you were dealt the same deck of cards. We all have different things that happen in life, but you chose to finish. Don't lose track of that because at some moment in time, you know, it could be today, it could be tomorrow, it could be when you're 35, you're going to have the opportunity to do something because you finished this,” he told the graduates sitting in the front row.

One of those students was Jayson King, who received his Central High School diploma on Friday.

“I'm glad to do all the work I've done to get to this point,” King said. “I was afraid that I wouldn't be able to do graduation right now … Because of me getting this done, I was able to graduate at the same time my friends graduated, just a little bit later.”

King said he plans to get into welding or plumbing.

 Jayson King
Jayson King, a graduate of Rapid City Central High School, stands with his diploma after graduating on Friday, July 17. 

Sydney Jerred, who earned her Stevens High School diploma, said it’s surreal to be done with high school and she’s still working out what she wants to do now.n

About her summer school experience, she said, “It was good. I love the teachers and the principal was amazing.”

Jerred said she went through a lot of changes throughout school, and, “It’s just kind of crazy being here … I didn’t think I was actually going to graduate until they emailed me telling me, ‘Congratulations, you’re graduating.’”

“I wouldn't be here without all my friends and family, with the support that they’ve given me,” Jerred added.

 Sydney Jerred
Sydney Jerred, a graduate of Rapid City Stevens High School, left, stands with her diploma for a photo with Summer School Principal Jesse Sporrer, right, after graduating on Friday, July 17. 

In addition to Sporrer’s commencement address, the festivities included the national anthem and a traditional honoring song, sung by Marlin Medicine Horse. Guests of honor included RCAS School Board President Troy Carr, Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson, Assistant Superintendent Cory Strasser, Human Resources Director Nicole Wojcik, Federal Programs Director Justin Conroy and Director of Indian Education and School Improvement Gina Curran.

 Jesse Sporrer, summer school principal
Jesse Sporrer, summer school principal, speaks to media after the summer school graduation on Friday, July 17, at Rapid City Alternative Academy. 

 Dulce Iron Horn
Dulce Iron Horse, a graduate of Rapid City Central High School, stands with her diploma for photos with family after graduating on Friday, July 17. 

 Graduates
RCAS Summer School students stand at their graduation on Friday, July 17.

description: Pennington County said the Pennington County Courthouse is set to reopen today.

Pennington County Courthouse set to reopen today

Pennington County said the Pennington County Courthouse is set to reopen today.

The courthouse was closed half-day on Friday and on Monday because the chillers in the AC unit in the complex were causing issues last week that persisted into the weekend.

“We’re still working on it today. We thank the public for their understanding and patience,” the county said in a release on Monday, July 20.

The Courthouse is set to reopen at 8 a.m. on Tuesday, July 21.

Per the National Weather Service, high temperatures are forecast to dip into the 80s as the week goes on before things ramp back up on Friday through the weekend.

2 shot during ‘confrontation’ between juveniles

Two minors were shot and taken to the hospital with serious injuries on Saturday, June 18, in what the Rapid City Police Department said was a “confrontation between two groups of juveniles.”

The department said officers responded to 965 E. Omaha St. in Rapid City around 8:10 p.m. on June 18. Sagebrush Flats, an apartment complex, is located at that address.

Police detained several juveniles after the incident and said the age range of the group members range from 13 to 17.

On Sunday, June 19, the department said in an update police believe there were two shooters, one from each group. One shooter was shot. Police found the other a short time later and detained the minor.

One of the shooters has been placed in the juvenile justice system, according to police. Police said the investigation is ongoing and other juveniles involved in the incident will face “similar consequences.”

Juvenile charges and courts are not open to the public, so the Journal is unable to locate what charges the minor faces.

Woman found dead at car dealership

A woman was found dead in Rapid City on Sunday, July 20, the Rapid City Police Department said.

Police responded to 1400 Cambell Street, a car dealership, at around 6:30 a.m. for a report of an unresponsive woman. When police arrived, they determined the woman was dead. There were no obvious signs of trauma or significant injury that would contribute to her death, but the department ordered an autopsy to determine the cause of death.

The department is withholding her identity while next of kin is notified.

Anyone who may have any information about the incident is encouraged to contact the RCPD’s Criminal Investigations Division at 605-394-4134.

title: T. Denny Sanford
description: December 23, 1935 - July 18, 2026
_full_text:
December 23, 1935 - July 18, 2026

Philanthropist Thomas "Denny" Sanford of Sioux Falls passed away peacefully on July 18, 2026. He was 90 years old. Denny, as he was known to many, was born Dec. 23, 1935, in St. Paul, Minn., to William and Edith (Hill) Sanford. Denny always said he wanted to live a life of significance and gave generously. His philanthropy impacted millions of lives and transformed the landscape of South Dakota and beyond.

Denny lost his mother to breast cancer when he was four and he began working at his father's garment shop at the age of eight. These early years instilled in him a desire to help others, a commitment that lasted throughout his life. After graduating from the University of Minnesota in 1958 with a degree in psychology, Denny began a successful career in sales, marketing and materials distribution. His experiences led him to establish Contech, Inc., a Minneapolis-based company that manufactured sealants, coatings and adhesives.

After selling the company, Denny purchased a bank in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, in 1986. He renamed it First PREMIER Bank and expanded into the credit card sector with PREMIER Bankcard. Today, PREMIER is considered one of the nation's strongest financial organizations, which allowed Denny to focus on philanthropic endeavors in his later years.

He was a champion for charitable organizations that benefit children, health care, higher education, workforce development and the arts. His first significant donation was a $2 million gift in 1999 to Children's Home Society of South Dakota. In 2007, he made history with his $400 million gift to the Sioux Valley Health System, which became Sanford Health. Additional gifts to Sanford Health were used to establish specialty facilities, including the Edith Sanford Breast Center, Sanford Children's Hospital, Sanford Imagenetics and Sanford Health's Virtual Care Initiative. Passionate about the power of education, Denny funded numerous scholarships including South Dakota's Build Dakota and Freedom scholarship programs. He was also instrumental in construction of the Denny Sanford PREMIER Center in Sioux Falls and provided significant gifts to the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) and Crazy Horse Memorial in the Black Hills of South Dakota.

Over the course of his life, Denny provided more than $4 billion in gifts to charitable organizations. While he focused largely upon South Dakota initiatives, he also funded projects in communities where he felt a strong connection. He was instrumental in establishing the Sanford Consortium for Regenerative Medicine in San Diego and the Sanford-Burnham-Prebys Medical Discovery Institute in La Jolla, California, the University of California-San Diego, and Rady Children's Hospital. Denny's passion for social and emotional research and education led to the development of the Sanford Harmony and Inspire Programs at Arizona State University, and the Sanford College of Education at National University in San Diego.

The magnitude of Denny's overall charitable contributions has been recognized in various news sources, including the Chronicle of Philanthropy which named him one of the 50 most generous philanthropists. He has also been the recipient of many prestigious awards, among them the Horatio Alger Association Distinguished American Award.

title: Rapid City Council votes to accept land that’ll house sports complex
description: The Rapid City Council unanimously approved a land agreement that’s a big step toward bringing a sports complex to Rapid City.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Council unanimously approved a land agreement that’s a big step toward bringing a sports complex to Rapid City.

Nearly a year after the original approval of a Tax Increment Financing District that includes the flagship development of a sports complex in Rapid City, the City Council voted 10-0 on a land donation agreement with Pete Lien & Sons.

 Rapid City sports complex sign
The Rapid City sports complex will be located in the general area of Seger Drive and 143rd Avenue.  

The TIF was approved in September 2025 and the sports complex will be developed on the 22.7 acres donated by Pete Lien & Sons at the intersection of Seger Drive and 143rd Avenue. Pete Lien & Sons is a Rapid City-based construction and mining company.

City documents state the total anticipated project cost for the development of the sports complex will be $76.2 million. The city has secured approximately $66 million in committed funding, Salamun said, including $24.58 million from the Catalyst District TIF. An estimated $28.28 million will come from the Hotel Business Improvement District, $6.2 million in land donation value and $5 million from the Vision Fund, per city documents.

 Catalyst District Boundaries
The boundaries of the Catalyst District are indicated with the yellow lines.  

The documents state that negotiations are underway for the primary naming rights sponsorship, which will include a substantial upfront capital contribution and an annual payment. Rapid City Mayor Salamun wrote in a column the naming rights sponsorship is “soon-to-be-announced.”

Of the details provided by the city, the 180,000 square foot facility will include an indoor walking track, indoor playground and "specialized spaces" to host regional and national sporting events, including volleyball and basketball. The building is also set to include pickleball.

The land donation agreement notes substantial completion of construction at the complex on or before Dec. 31, 2029. In the agreement, Sports Facilities Management, LLC, based out of Florida, is named as the proposed operator for the sports complex, pending city council approval.

title: Mayor Salamun presents $312 million 2027 Rapid City budget
byline: SHALOM BAER GEE and FRANK ESPINOZA Journal staff
description: Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun’s 2027 city budget proposal is hot off the press.
_full_text:
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun’s 2027 city budget proposal is hot off the press.

Salamun presented the $312.33 million budget to the Rapid City Council on Monday, July 20. It features a 7.4% reduction compared to 2026 ($337.3 million), investment in roads, sports complex funding, an increase to firefighter and ambulance personnel and updates to parks like Main Street Square.

 Jason Salamun
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun, left, on Monday presents his budget to the Rapid City Council.  

“With this budget in particular, I really looked at it like stewardship,” Salamun said at a Tuesday, July 21, press conference, held the morning after the presentation. “Stewardship means just leaving it better than you found it, not just giving (it) back the way you got it, but leaving it better.”

The mayor highlighted the city’s strong sales tax revenue. Year-to-date collection trends in 2026 are running 5.6% above the 2026 budget projection, indicating stronger-than-expected economic activity, according to Rapid City Finance Director Daniel Ainslie. Rapid City’s general sales tax collections have increased 21.3% since 2022.

“We see that with our sales tax revenue, and because of that strong economy with our sales tax revenue, it allows us the opportunity to make historic investments in roads. It allows us the opportunity to not take any property tax increases to help affordability for taxpayers in our community.” who said this?

The mayor added sales taxes make the city able to invest in a combination fire-police-library building to be located on Homestead Street on the east side of the city.

The bulk of the city’s revenue comes from sales taxes ($98.74 million), followed by utility fees ($56.87 million) tickets, leases and user fees ($27.55 million) and property taxes ($26.86 million).

“You can tell a tree by its fruit, and what you see is our people investing in Rapid City,” Salamun said.

Historic road investments

The mayor’s budget prioritizes road improvements with more than $65 million budgeted for road improvements. The highest ticket categories are $27.86 million in new road construction through Tax Increment Financing projects, including East Anamosa Street, Healing Way and Highway 79/Old Folsom Road, $17 million in new road construction through the strategic growth fund, and $16.74 million in road reconstruction through the Capital Improvement Projects Program, including Wonderland Drive, Skyline Drive and work in the Dakota and Robbinsdale neighborhoods.

The other investments are a $450,000 budget for a proactive road crew and $3 million for mill and overlay projects to rehabilitate roads before full reconstruction is needed.

 Salamun
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun speaks about his proposed 2027 city budget at a press conference held at City Hall on Tuesday, June 21. 

Mike Theis, Rapid City public works director, said of the projects, “We look at a multitude of factors, everything from the utilities underneath the street, traffic flow, the condition of the pavement at the surface, and try to balance all those out on prioritizing those items.”

Salamun said he wishes the city could do everything at once, but even with all the money in the world, that’s not possible.

“We have all sides of the city that are aging, and that's always kind of a challenge,” Salamun said. “ … There's only so much concrete and asphalt, and workers and construction crews and equipment. So we'll do everything that we can, work on that priority list.”

Public safety prioritization

“We are going to invest a great deal into public safety,” Salamun said. “You're seeing us make sure that we're fully staffed and that we're staffing even for the future, and that takes great planning. Thanks to our chiefs that are planning for that, that takes a lot of work on all of our parts to make sure that we're serving the citizens of Rapid City.”

That includes $3.2 million to complete the Northside Police Precinct using TIF, general and CIP funds, $9 million to complete the Homestead Fire, Police and Mini-library building through TIF funds and $1.61 million for the addition of 15 firefighters and six ambulance personnel. The fire department’s proposed 2027 budget is $21 million, a $1.3 million reduction from the 2026 budget. There will also be a new city park near the combination fire-police-library building.

Salamun said about funding the additional staff, “We hope to relieve that pressure with grants … They may not all be hired at the same time. They might distribute that throughout the year.”

The Rapid City Police Department’s budget remains steady at about $30.62 million in 2027, compared to $30.6 in 2026. Last budget cycle, the Rapid City Council approved the addition of 12 police officers to the department. Police Chief Don Hedrick said the department is working on training officers to fill those positions, so he didn’t request more positions this year.

 Hedrick
Rapid City Police Chief Don Hedrick speaks at a 2027 city budget press conference held at City Hall on Tuesday, June 21. 

Hedrcik said it’s historic for the fire department and police department to share a building, referencing the planned Homestead Street building. He called it, “something we can really hold up as a community win.”

“When (Rapid City Fire Chief Jason Culberson) and I took our positions in 2020, the police department and fire department had good working relationships, but I can remember us sitting there that day waiting to be sworn in, and we just kind of looked at each other and said we're going to make the relationships between our departments even better,” Hedrick said. “I think it's really cool and amazing, something our entire community can be proud of. And that’s just what we do here in our community, we work together.”

 Culberson
Rapid City Fire Chief Jason Culberson, center, speaks at a 2027 city budget press conference held at City Hall on Tuesday, June 21. 

Rapid City Fire Chief Jason Culberson, said the building will be a significant benefit to the community that will increase response times on the eastern side of the city. Plus, the park will be good for his grandkids.

“I live out in that area, so having that park out there is going to be awesome for my grandkids,” Culberson said.

Economic growth and quality of life: Sports complex and parks

Salamun also emphasized $76.2 million in funding for the city’s budding, first-ever sports complex, and $6 million in funding to go towards two new parks — Knollwood in north Rapid City and the Homestead park — and the refurbishment of Main Street Square and Robbinsdale Park.

The 180,000-square-foot sports complex will include an indoor walking track, an indoor playground and "specialized spaces" to host regional and national sporting events, including volleyball and basketball. The building is also set to include pickleball.

The city has secured approximately $66 million in committed funding, Salamun said, including $24.58 million from the Catalyst District TIF. An estimated $28.28 million will come from the Hotel Business Improvement District, $6.2 million in land donation value and $5 million from the Vision Fund, per city documents.

The Rapid City Council on Monday, June 20, voted unanimously to accept a 22.7-acre land donation from Rapid City-based construction and mining company Pete Lien & Sons for the complex. The land is located at the intersection of Seger Drive and 143rd Avenue in north Rapid City.

“That sports complex will be great for our community, for our quality of life, but also for our visitor industry,” Salamun said.

As for the Main Street Square refurbishments, Salamun said some updates are needed as the square reaches 15 years old. Those updates include the concrete underneath the turf and ice rink, as well as updates to the stage’s technology. The mayor is asking for $500,000 in 2027 and $500,000 in 2028.

“If you don't take care of something, it eventually fades into something else. I just want to say, not on my watch. At least I gave it a fighting chance to make sure that this remains a gem,” Salamun said.

No comments were made by the council about the budget at the meeting.

The next series of meetings start with the department heads, kicking off July 27 with the Fire and Police departments, July 28 with The Monument and Public Works departments, July 29 with the Human Resources and Information Technology, Mayor’s Office, Parks and Recreation departments and July 30 with the City Attorney’s Office, Community Development, Rapid City Regional Airport, Rapid City Public Library and (Finance) departments.

The department budget sessions will include presentations and an opportunity for council members to ask questions. 

The council must approve two formal readings of the budget by Sept. 30 of each year.

title: Transportation department announces Sturgis-related speed limit changes
description: The 86th Annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally is scheduled for Aug. 7-16, 2026. With increased traffic volumes expected during the annual Rally, the South Dakota Department of Transportation said it will activate temporary traffic signals and place speed limit reductions.
_full_text:
The 86th Annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally is scheduled for Aug. 7-16, 2026. With increased traffic volumes expected during the annual Rally, the South Dakota Department of Transportation said it will activate temporary traffic signals and place speed limit reductions.

The DOT reported 537,459 vehicles entered the city during the 10-day event in 2025, up 11.3% over 2024.

Temporary traffic signal locations

S.D. Highway 34/79 and Ft. Meade main entrance;

S.D. Highway 34/79 and Glencoe Drive;

S.D. Highway 34 and S.D. Highway 79 east of Sturgis;

S.D. Highway 34 and Ft. Meade Way (Buffalo Chip);

S.D. Highway 44 and U.S. Highway 385;

U.S. Highway 16 and U.S. Highway 385 east of Hill City;

S.D. Highway 34/79 and 11th Street in Sturgis; and

Interstate 90 exit 55 eastbound ramp.

The temporary traffic signals will be in full operation from Friday, July 31, through the end-of-the-day on Monday, Aug. 17, the DOT said.

Speed limit reductions

Speed limits will be reduced on the following highways from Thursday, Aug. 6, through Sunday, Aug. 16:

The Interstate 90 speed limit will be reduced from 75 mph to 65 mph from west of Exit 55 (Deadwood Avenue) in Rapid City to west of Exit 30 (Lazelle Street) in Sturgis.

The S.D. Highway 34 speed limit will be reduced from 65 mph and 45 mph to 35 mph from Blanche Street in Sturgis, east approximately four miles (east of Buffalo Chip).

 Sturgis Main Street
A pair makes their way down Main Street in downtown Sturgis during the 2025 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. 

The S.D. Highway 79 speed limit will be reduced from 65 mph to 45 mph from the junction of Highway 34 north approximately 2 miles (north of Iron Horse Campground) and from one-half mile south of the intersection with Bighorn Road north approximately 1 mile, near the Full Throttle Saloon and Drag Pipe Saloon approaches.

Message Boards: The SDDOT will also deploy message boards and speed trailers at various locations along with the permanent dynamic message boards on the Interstate to display messages regarding traffic conditions, crashes causing delays, extreme weather events, and other messages as needed.

U.S Highway 385 project information

Construction on U.S. Highway 385 (Pactola Dam to Calumet Road) will be paused starting on Wednesday, Aug. 5, and will resume on Tuesday, Aug. 18. Motorists are asked to remain alert for any traffic adjustments should they become necessary during the rally, the DOT said.

title: South Dakota Highway Patrol announces August sobriety checkpoints
description: The South Dakota Highway Patrol will conduct sobriety checkpoints in 12 counties throughout August. Checkpoints are planned for Brown, Brookings, Campbell, Codington, Davison, Hand, Jackson, Jerauld, Lyman, Meade, Stanley, and Yankton counties.
_full_text:
The South Dakota Highway Patrol will conduct sobriety checkpoints in 12 counties throughout August. Checkpoints are planned for Brown, Brookings, Campbell, Codington, Davison, Hand, Jackson, Jerauld, Lyman, Meade, Stanley, and Yankton counties.

Meade County is home to the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, which runs Aug. 7-16.

 August 2026 sobriety checkpoints

The patrol said the enforcement effort is aimed at reducing impaired driving and improving roadway safety. Funding for the checkpoints is provided by the South Dakota Office of Highway Safety, and operations will be carried out by the patrol in coordination with local law enforcement agencies.

"Motorists are reminded to make responsible choices and avoid driving after drinking alcohol, whether or not a checkpoint is planned in their area. Drivers who plan to drink should arrange for a designated sober driver or use public or commercial transportation," the patrol said in a release.

Both the South Dakota Office of Highway Safety and the South Dakota Highway Patrol are agencies of the South Dakota Department of Public Safety.

title: New White House Rose Garden statue created by Trump sculptor
description: How does the White House Rose Garden grow? With Washington and Hamilton and Franklin and Jefferson all in a row.
_full_text:
How does the White House Rose Garden grow? With Washington and Hamilton and Franklin and Jefferson all in a row.

President Donald Trump’s remaking of the Rose Garden continues apace with sculptures lining one side of the paved-over garden, facing the Oval Office. Statues of founding fathers have popped up in recent months.

Last week, a new one was added: Thomas Jefferson.

 A sculpture of Thomas Jefferson by George Lundeen at the University of Missouri next to the David R. Francis Quadrangle. Another edition has been placed in the White Rose Garden.
A sculpture of Thomas Jefferson by George Lundeen at the University of Missouri is seen next to the David R. Francis Quadrangle. Another edition of the piece has been placed in the White House Rose Garden. 

Ben Franklin, the oldest founding father and polymath, stands across from George Washington, the first president of the United States. Alexander Hamilton, the first U.S. secretary of the Treasury, stands next to a sculpture honoring Revolutionary War heroes called Freedom's Charge.

Unlike the other statues, which are all on loan to the People’s House, the statue of Jefferson, the nation’s third president, was a gift created by Colorado-based sculptor George Lundeen, a White House official told USA Today. Also unlike other statues, Jefferson is portrayed sitting on a bench.

With a quill in his hand, he's seen writing the Declaration of Independence.

 A statue of Ben Franklin in the Rose Garden.
A statue of Ben Franklin is seen in the Rose Garden. 

Lundeen also created a life-size bronze statue of Trump titled the Defiance Monument, capturing the moment Trump pumped his fist in the air immediately following the 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania. A life-sized bronze casting of the scene can be found at Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Florida.

At the end of Trump's term, the National Archives could transfer the statue to the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library in Miami, a White House official told USA Today. Other options include the Trump library loaning or donating it back to the White House.

In the case of a donation, the sculpture would become the property of the White House and be maintained by the White House Usher's office and the National Park Service.

Other editions of the life-size bronze statue, including one featured at Sorrel Sky Gallery in New York, have an asking price of $90,000. There is one located at the University of Missouri next to the David R. Francis Quadrangle, as well as one at Booth Western Art Museum in Georgia, according to auction site invaluable.com

 A sculpture named Freedom's Charge at the Rose Garden. It depicts soldiers of the Revolutionary War.
A sculpture named Freedom's Charge is on display at the Rose Garden. It depicts soldiers of the Revolutionary War. 

The Jefferson statue currently faces the Truman Balcony with its back toward the Oval Office. This placement is temporary since the location picked by the president has to be shored up before installing the statue, the White House official said.The statue will face the Rose Garden and Oval Office when the installation is complete.

Trump, who has had a long career in real estate, has been putting his design stamp on all manner of things at the White House, from decking out the Oval Office with portraits of presidents, military flags and golden flourishes to paving over the Rose Garden lawn. Workers are in the middle of building a 90,000-square-foot ballroom, for which Trump decided to demolish the East Wing, drawing scorn from critics.

He's also remaking DC with projects such as the Triumphal Arch and the Reflecting Pool renovation.

 A statue of Alexander Hamilton at the White House Rose Garden.
A statue of Alexander Hamilton is seen at the White House Rose Garden. 

 A statue of George Washington at the Rose Garden.
A statue of George Washington is seen at the White House Rose Garden in Washington.

title: Amid Alzheimers battle, RC Stevens legend finds hope through new business
description: Michael Jones was a man in motion before the diagnosis that changed his life. He won three state titles at Rapid City Stevens, dazzled for University of Wyoming football and taught across and pastored across Georgia, Michigan, Kansas, Minnesota and the Rocky Mountains while raising a family.
_full_text:
Michael Jones was a man in motion before the diagnosis that changed his life. He won three state titles at Rapid City Stevens, dazzled for University of Wyoming football and taught across and pastored across Georgia, Michigan, Kansas, Minnesota and the Rocky Mountains while raising a family.

“Just throw it in his area code and he’ll catch it,” teammates quipped of the future Raiders Hall of Famer. 

But on a church Saturday in 2022, Jones, then a pastor, couldn’t tie his tie. He settled on the edge of his bed, stared directionless for 10 minutes and turned toward the Lord.

“God, I need help tying my tie. I need to go preach. I need to get ready,” Jones prayed.

His prayers were answered. He tied his tie. But the moment largely spurred the rounds of medical tests that eventually led to an early-onset Alzheimer’s Diagnosis at 51.

Four years later, Jones, 55, can’t drive or work. Daily tasks are becoming increasingly difficult. But as life changes in unpredictable increments, the husband and father of two has been anchored by his faith and launched Bnana Bones: a company he started that produces and sells dehydrated fruit.

“I don't want to just sit there at home. I want to do something,” Jones said, sitting at Rapid City’s Perkins Restaurant in February, tears beginning to well.

 Mike Jones.jpg
Mike Jones prepares to ship a batch of his Bnana Bones in 2023.  

***

It's become a regular part of his life and a source of joy for Aquarius, Jones’ wife, as she collects voice recordings and takes care of him while working a full-time job.

“Probably three months ago, we were in bed and we were talking, and he said, 'I'm glad it's me and not you or the boys,’” Aquarius said.

Tristan, Jones’ 15-year-old son, grew up playing driveway hoops with his doting father, but has begun to eat more to cope with the circumstance.

“As I've seen things get worse, I just try and not think about it and just fall back on something that comforts me,” Tristan said.

“Very brave to share,” Aquinas said, looking at him.

 Mike Jones 8.JPG
The Jones family from left to right: Aquinas, Michael, Josiah and Tristan at Michael's Rapid City Stevens Hall of Fame induction ceremony in February 2026. 

For Jones, meanwhile, Bnana Bones has become one variable in a larger equation to make the most of his changing reality.

“The person that he is has not changed. He's still persistent. He's still a giver, and he's just still seeking ways to benefit and bless people,” Aquarius said.

Up until his diagnosis, he was a multi-faceted force of nature. Yes, there was his athletic career — the fifth-most receptions in University of Wyoming history and state titles at Rapid City Stevens in track and field, football and basketball in the late 1980s — but there were the decades spent as a teacher and pastor that molded his life.

While substitute teaching at an underfunded school in western Michigan, Jones used his part-time salary to purchase pencils and various school supplies for students.

“That’s his heart,” Aquarius said, “That’s who he is.”

 Banana Bones Photo 1.jpg
A batch of Bnana Bones.  

While working at the school, he challenged teens involved in high-risk behavior to pick up hoops. The best way to enact change, he felt, was to meet them on their level and gain their respect.

Sweat-dripping, the raw ability he utilized for the 1989 Rapid City Stevens state title-winning squad coming out, Jones hit bucket after bucket — trash-talking along the way.

“I chummed them,” Jones quipped.

 Mike Jones 7 copy.jpeg
Michael Jones poses at his Hall of Fame induction ceremony in February 2026.  

After a teaching career in which he helped many underprivileged children, he became a pastor in 2005, most recently working in Georgia. He logged upwards of 50 hours a week. The congregation, made up of various walks of life, was drawn to his uplifting messages and storytelling.

Which is what made it difficult when, inexplicably, his sermons were interspersed with involuntary noises. They were sharp. They were random. He didn’t know what it was. Then came the day he struggled with his tie, sought some medical tests and everything began to make sense.

***

After his diagnosis, he stepped down from his job. He relinquished his driver’s license. He can recall vivid details of breakfasts with teammates at Perkins on Mount Rushmore in the 1980s, but can lose his train of thought mid-sentence. He and his family moved from humid Georgia to Chester, S.D. to be closer to family.

Amid this unplanned, uncontrollable stretch, Jones became focused on what he could do — not what he couldn’t — which is what led him to Banana Bones.

It began when he learned a healthy diet could help reverse or slow cognitive decline. He was a lifelong, self-described “sugar-holic.” So, hoping to steer away from artificial sugar, he fished out a dehydrator he gifted Aquarius and began making dehydrated fruit.

He was hooked — not just on the taste — but the process and the idea of what it could become. He believed in taking life and squeezing it to the last drop. Why not start a business based on that same concept?

“I wanted to help people,” Jones said.

He collaborated with a local small-business developer in Sioux Falls. Aquarius, who helps out with the administration side in between her job, regularly sees him working on it. Eyes wide, smile stretched ear to ear, excited to tell her about the next creation. 

The reviews have been strong.

 MIke Jones 11 .JPG
Michael Jones, left, and his brother Paul Hendry, right, at Michael's Rapid City Stevens Hall of Fame induction ceremony in February 2026. 

He recently went to a funeral in Sioux Falls and former colleagues asked about it. At church, fellow congregants routinely ask if he’s brought any. Whoever wants some, he’s happy to send some their way.

Name it, he’s dehydrated it. Dog treats. Apples. Watermelon. Peaches.

“My husband is a dreamer,” Aquarius said, “I'm just like, ‘Babe, let's just stick with Bnana Bones.’ But that's not my husband.”

title: Gerald LeRoy Hazledine
description: March 15, 1929 - April 15, 2026
_full_text:
March 15, 1929 - April 15, 2026

Gerald LeRoy Hazledine passed away peacefully, age 97, at Gordon Countryside Care in Gordon, NE, on April 15, 2026, with his family by his side.

He was born March 15, 1929, during a spring snowstorm in Deadwood, SD, to Earl and Florence (Klinger) Hazledine of Spearfish. Florence had been staying with relatives in Lead. Earl and 6-year-old big brother Jimmy met Gerry a few days after his birth when roads were passable.

Gerry grew up in Spearfish, graduating from High School in 1947. His childhood and teen years were spent at his dad's Hazledine Drug Store, and finding mischievous adventures all over Spearfish and the surrounding area. In high school he lettered in football, basketball, and track. His senior year he took up golf, he was senior class president and was on Spearfish's first American Legion baseball team.

He attended South Dakota State and Black Hills State universities and worked at the Homestake Sawmill in Spearfish before going into the US Army in August of 1951. He was discharged in July of 1953, a few days after the official end of the Korean War. Gerry was stationed during that time in the army in Stuttgart, Germany. After returning from Germany, he was a member of the South Dakota National Guard.

In January of 1954, Gerry began dating Pat Sears, who was teaching in Belle Fourche, and they were married in Spearfish at the United Methodist Church on November 21, 1954. To this union were born four children; Linda, Lawrence, Sandra, and Michael.

They owned Gerry's Hardware store in Spearfish, and he worked at the Minute Man Missile warehouse between Spearfish and Belle for a time before managing a motel in Minot, ND.

Returning to Spearfish in 1964, Gerry graduated with a degree in Education in 1966 from Black Hills State University. He would later get his master's degree from Western New Mexico University in Silver City. He taught high school business classes and drivers Ed enforce Forsyth, Montana, Douglas, AZ, and Thermopolis and Rawlins, Wyoming. He coached high school wrestling, tennis, and golf.

Retiring from teaching at Rawlins in 1991, Gerry and Pat divided their time between Wyoming and Casa Grande, AZ, and later between Spearfish and Casa Grande. They traveled to Canada, Mexico and Europe, but also loved just spending time at their cabin at Iron Creek Lake after moving to Spearfish full time, reconnecting with family and old friends.

In 2017, Gerry and Pat moved to Rushville, NE, where their son Mike and his family reside.

Gerry's interests and hobbies were hunting, fishing, camping, golf, and woodworking. He and Pat loved packing the camper and, with their dogs, going to craft fairs where they sold his wood projects and she painted some of them. He liked history and Western books and movies, puzzles, and game shows. He won office furniture on The Price is Right game show while visiting California. Gerry and Pat were both decades long Dodgers baseball fans and Denver Broncos football fans.

Gerry loved very much and always had great pride in all of his children, grandchildren, and great-grandson. He had a great interest in keeping up with their activities, achievements, endeavors, hopes, and dreams.

He is preceded in death by his parents, his father in law and mother in law, John and Eva Sears, his brother and sister in law Jim and Alta Hazledine, his son Lawrence, his granddaughter Sophia Rose Jones-Hazledine, his sister in law and brother in law Shirley and Harry Bickel, their daughter Deb Meginness, and Deb's daughter Joy Austin. Gerry is also preceded in death by his loving wife of 68 years, Pat. At the time of Gerry's passing, they had been apart nearly 4 years. And that was quite enough.

Gerry is survived by daughter Linda (John) Nemec of Midland, SD, daughter Sadra Lowery of Spearfish, and son Michael (Cate Jones-Hazledine) Hazledine of Rushville, NE. Grandchildren Jessica Gamotis, Heather Lowery, Rachael Lowery, Evan Jones-Hazledine, Stella Jones-Hazledine, Ivy Jones-Hazledine, his great grandson Leon Gamotis, and by his nephews, nieces, and their families. Gerry is also survived by his longtime friend Arne Koski of Spearfish.

Memorial services will be July 25, 2026 at 10 am at Spearfish United Methodist Church. Inurnment with military honors will follow at Spearfish Rose Hill Cemetery followed by a light luncheon back at the church.

In lieu of flowers a memorial to the newly open Spearfish Museum has been established in Gerry's name. Gerry was loved and is so missed.

title: Elmer L Karl
description: January 23, 1932 - July 15, 2026
_full_text:
January 23, 1932 - July 15, 2026

Elmer L. Karl passed away peacefully on July 15, 2026, at the age of 94 in Gregory, South Dakota. He leaves behind an extraordinary legacy of faith, family, entrepreneurship, community service, generosity, and love.

Elmer was born January 23,1932 to Edward and Mary (Jamber) Karl on the family farm north of Gregory. Growing up on the farm, he learned the values that guided him throughout his life: work hard, keep your word, treat people fairly, help your neighbors, and leave things better than you found them. He attended a one-room country school and later graduated from Gregory High School.

After high school, Elmer worked on the family farm before serving his country in the United States Army during the Korean War. His military training in electronics changed the direction of his life. Following his service, he attended DeVry Technical Institute in Chicago and worked as a television technician before returning home to Gregory.

In 1956, Elmer founded Karl's TV & Appliance with a small loan co-signed by his father, a knowledge of electronics, and a firm belief that customers in rural communities deserved quality products and dependable service. His business philosophy was straightforward: treat customers honestly, stand behind what you sell, and provide exceptional service after the sale.

What began as a small television sales and repair business in Gregory grew into one of the nation's leading independent appliance and electronics retailers while remaining proudly headquartered in Gregory. Through seven decades, Karl's became known not simply for the products it sold, but for the relationships it built with customers, employees, vendors, and the communities it served. Despite its growth, Elmer never forgot its small-town roots or the people who made its success possible.

On June 1, 1957, Elmer married Kay Joyce Snider in Gregory. To this union three children were born—Michael, Cindi, and Sandi. For the next 57 years, Kay was Elmer's partner in marriage, family, travel, community life, and business. Together they built not only a successful company, but a family and a way of life grounded in faith, hard work, loyalty, and generosity.

Family was at the center of Elmer's life. He was proud of his children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and all those welcomed into the family through marriage, friendship, and love. He treasured family gatherings, followed the lives and accomplishments of each new generation, and enjoyed sharing stories from the early years of Karl's and life in Gregory.

After Kay's unexpected passing in 2015, Elmer was blessed to find companionship and happiness again with Karen Stukel. Their marriage brought love, friendship, and an expanded family into Elmer's later years. He warmly welcomed Karen's children, grandchildren, and extended family into his life.

Although Elmer's business accomplishments were considerable, he never measured success only by sales, stores, or recognition. He believed that successful businesses had an obligation to support their employees and strengthen the communities they served. Gregory was never simply where Elmer lived or operated a business—it was home.

Elmer devoted decades to public and civic service. He served two terms as Mayor of Gregory and two terms on the Gregory City Council. For more than 30 years, he was a member of the Gregory Volunteer Fire Department, giving his time to help protect the community and its residents.

He helped organize and lead Gregory's local business development efforts and worked to create economic opportunities for the community. Elmer invested his time, leadership, and personal resources in projects that helped preserve local businesses, attract new enterprises, create jobs, and keep Gregory strong. He firmly believed that rural communities could thrive when their residents were willing to work together and invest in their future.

Elmer was an active member of Rotary and a longtime Mason. He was also a member of the El Riad Shrine and the Independent Order of Odd Fellows Lodge. Through these organizations, he formed lasting friendships and supported charitable, and community causes throughout South Dakota.

His leadership extended throughout the retail and appliance industries. Elmer served as president of the Midwest Appliance and Retail Dealers Association and as president of the South Dakota Retailers Association. He was respected by fellow retailers, manufacturers, vendors, and business associates for his experience, judgment, loyalty, and willingness to help others succeed.

Throughout his career, Elmer received numerous business, industry, and community honors recognizing both his leadership and integrity. Among them were South Dakota Retailer of the Year, the American Heritage Award from the Anti-Defamation League, South Dakota Sales & Marketing Executive of the Year, and many additional industry recognitions. He also served as President of the Midwest Appliance and Retail Dealers Association and the South Dakota Retailers Association. He considered his induction into the South Dakota Hall of Fame one of the greatest honors of his life.

Although he appreciated these recognitions, Elmer never sought attention for himself. He remained approachable, practical, and grounded. Whether speaking with an industry leader, a longtime employee, a customer, or someone he had just met, he treated people with genuine interest and respect. His handshake mattered, his word could be trusted, and he rarely forgot where he came from. Those who knew him will also remember the unmistakable twinkle in his eye and his wonderful sense of humor. He always seemed to have a quick one-liner or gentle joke at the ready, using humor to put others at ease. His laughter was genuine, his wit effortless, and he had a remarkable gift for making everyone feel welcome.

One of Elmer's proudest accomplishments was helping secure the future of Karl's TV & Appliance as an employee-owned company. He believed the employees who helped build the business deserved to share in its success. Perhaps more than anything else, Elmer wanted Karl's to remain an independent, family-oriented company whose culture would endure long after he was gone. Employee ownership made that possible.

Elmer was preceded in death by his parents, Edward and Mary Karl; his sisters, Dorothy Berger and Agnes Novotny; his brother, Edwin Karl; his beloved first wife of 57 years, Kay Karl; his daughter, Cindi Nikodym; and his son-in-law, Jay Wernke.

He is survived by his loving wife, Karen Karl; his children, Michael (Joni) Karl of St. Cloud, Minnesota, and Sandi Wernke of Gregory, South Dakota; son-in-law Roger Nikodym of Sioux Falls, South Dakota; and sister-in-law Ellen Sargent of California.

He is also survived by his grandchildren, Matthew (Jessica) Nikodym of St. Cloud, Minnesota; Ariann (Dan) Lenihan of Omaha, Nebraska; Adam (Joni) Nikodym of Sioux Falls, South Dakota; Abby Mock of Minneapolis, Minnesota; Andrew (Kelsey) Karl of Maple Grove, Minnesota; and Shane (Taylor), and Dane Wernke of Sioux Falls, South Dakota.

Elmer's eleven cherished great-grandchildren are Jackson, Derek, and Ryan Nikodym; James, Josie, and Katherine Lenihan; Henry, Harvey, and Leni Nikodym; and Isaac and Addi Karl.

He is also survived by foreign exchange daughter Annelie Strath of Sweden; Karen's children and their families, Cal (Ann) Stukel and family, Kimberly (Allen) Veskrna and family, and Kurt (Kellie) Stukel and family; along with many nieces, nephews, cousins, extended family members, treasured friends, loyal customers, business associates, and generations of Karl's employees and employee-owners.

Those who knew Elmer will remember far more than the business he built. They will remember his steady handshake, quiet confidence, generous spirit, the unmistakable twinkle in his eye, and his unwavering belief in people. They will remember his stories, his one-liners, and the easy smile that so often accompanied them. He believed a person's word was their bond, that customers deserved honesty, that employees should be treated like family, and that successful businesses have a responsibility to strengthen the communities they serve. Those principles became the foundation of Karl's TV & Appliance and the guiding values by which he lived every day.

While his passing leaves an immeasurable void for his family, friends, employees, and community, his example will continue to inspire all who had the privilege of knowing him. His legacy lives on through his family, the employee-owners of Karl's TV & Appliance, the community of Gregory, and the countless lives he touched through nearly a century of faith, service, generosity, leadership, humor, love, and quiet example.

In lieu of flower, memorials may be sent to the Gregory Community Foundation Pool Project, Gregory United Methodist Church, or the Shriners Children's c/o El Riad Shrine Sioux Falls SD.

title: Chance Dooley
_full_text:
April 3, 1998 - July 17, 2026

Chance Daniel Dooley was born on April 3, 1998, to Danny and Eleisha Dooley. Chance grew up in Custer with his younger siblings, Wyatt and Kadense. They were his best friends and co-conspirators. The three had a special bond, even when they disagreed on life.

Chance was always very active and involved in sports from a young age. He wrestled from AAU into high school, played baseball, took golf lessons, played football in middle and high school. But most of all he enjoyed running, which came naturally to him. Chance was a two-time state champion in the 2-mile in track and in his senior year he also captured the Class A Cross Country Championship. His passion for running was passed down to both Wyatt and Kadense. It has been said he was a pleasure to coach, a great teammate and a fierce competitor.

After graduating from Custer High School in 2016 Chance ran both Cross Country and Track and Field for Black Hills State University and went on to earn his bachelor's degree there. He was the first in his immediate family to graduate from college and that was a great accomplishment for him; his siblings followed suit. After college Chance continued to live in and work in Spearfish until his death.

Chance enjoyed being outdoors, hunting, fishing, gardening, running, animals, creating, painting. He was an artist with a specific taste. Chance was quick-witted and gave unique nicknames to most he crossed paths with. When he found something he was passionate about he worked hard. He took pride in Wyatt and Kadense and all their accomplishments. Chance often told his parents how proud he was of them. He had a special bond with his Nana Lawana and Grandpa Jeff. Chance loved and cared deeply.

Chance passed away July 17, 2026. He is survived by his loving and heartbroken parents, Danny and Eleisha Dooley of Custer; brother; Wyatt of Spearfish; sister, Kadense (Miles) of Sioux Falls; his grandparents, Jeff and Lawana Gramm of Mesa, Ariz., Dan Dooley of Huntley, Mont., Hoby and Peggy Bruce of Sturgis, S.D.; aunts and uncles, Jim Dooley, Trent (Nicole) Bruce, Jamie (Derek) Barnhurst, Jason Lembke, Frank (Mindy) Dooley; cousins, Kennedy and Oscar Bruce, Carter, Grady and Henley Lembke, and Ayden and Easton Dooley; as well as numerous extended family, friends, classmates, teammates and coaches.

He was preceded in death by his grandma, Jennie Dooley; great-grandma, Jeanette Auen; great-grandma, Allie Becker; great-grandma, Ethel Gramm; great-grandparents, Don and Rose Bruce; great-great-grandma, Gladys Raver; and other extended family who knew and loved him.

Chance will forever be remembered for his smile, quick wit, his passion, and the love and support he provided.

A celebration of life is scheduled for 2 p.m. at the track in Custer on Friday July 31st followed by a gathering at Mt Rushmore Brewing Company where you will have an opportunity to reflect or tell any great stories about Chance at that time.

You may sign his online guestbook at www.kinkadefunerals.com.

title: Pennington County passes 0.5% sales tax increase for property tax relief
byline: MIKE BROWNLEE and FRANK ESPINOZA Journal staff
description: Sales tax in Pennington County is set to increase 0.5%, with the money destined for property tax relief.
_full_text:
Sales tax in Pennington County is set to increase 0.5%, with the money destined for property tax relief.

The Pennington County Board of Commissioners voted unanimously on Tuesday, July 21, to approve an ordinance that implements the gross receipts tax and use tax. The move comes after Senate Bill 96, passed during the 2026 legislative session, allowed counties to pass such a tax for property tax relief.

The tax goes into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

In a letter to the board, Assistant Chief Deputy State’s Attorney Tyler Sobczak told the board the ordinance, per the state law, requires governments to deposit revenue generated by the tax into a property tax reduction fund. All money in the fund must be used to provide owner-occupied properties with a tax credit against the county portion of their property tax bill. Sobczak noted counties can retain 2% of the funds in the initial year after implementation and up to $20,000 in subsequent years for administrative costs.

A document from the state included in the board’s agenda packet estimates that the 0.5% sales tax will generate $25,941,668 for Pennington County, based on a total owner-occupied taxable valuation of $9,461,388,757 in the county.

“This is not an added tax. It is a shift. It's a shift from owner-occupied property to a sales tax, which we hope that the tourists will pick up a big bit of this. The county hasn't had a sales tax before,” Commissioner Ron Weifenbach (District 2) said.

Critics have argued the new tax shifts additional burden onto low-income and middle-income residents, not tourists. Per research by John T. Vucurevich Foundation Research and Reporting Director Lee Strubinger, of that roughly $26 million generated, 20% would come from tourists, based on visitor spending data from the South Dakota Department of Tourism.

The ordinance notes depositing the monies collected to the property tax reduction fund, but does not provide guidance on the distribution to owner-occupied homeowners.

Commissioner Ron Rosskencht (District 1) noted the board can revisit the matter in the future.

“It's not perpetual by no means,” he said.

Per previous reporting, the Governor's Office released an interactive map showing the savings from the bill. As an example of the property tax relief provided by the bill, if a home in Pennington County were assessed at $325,000, its property taxes would decrease by 22%.

The 2026 levy rate for Pennington County is 2.488 and a home valued at $325,000 would have a property tax of $808.60. The estimated 22% decrease in property tax brought on by SB 96 would then decrease the cost to roughly $603.70.

A mill levy is a property tax based on the assessed value of a property. One mill is equal to one dollar per $1,000 of assessed value. The levy is calculated by determining the amount of revenue each jurisdiction needs to fund its budget for public services, such as schools, parks and libraries.

Pennington County Director of Equalization Shannon Rittberger told the Journal in March residents might not feel relief efforts until 2028 or 2029.

title: 14 people arrested after multi-agency law enforcement drug bust
description: For more information on the Rapid City PD tip line, go to https://shorturl.at/ShAIX. For Pennington County, go to https://shorturl.at/Gya1r.
_full_text:
Crime tip submissions for Rapid City, Pennington County
For more information on the Rapid City PD tip line, go to https://shorturl.at/ShAIX. For Pennington County, go to https://shorturl.at/Gya1r. 

From Black Hills communities to Colorado, 14 people were arrested Tuesday, July 21, after a multi-agency law enforcement operation investigated a multi-state cocaine trafficking organization responsible for importing kilograms of cocaine into western South Dakota, including to communities within the Pine Ridge Reservation.

Operation Black Book is a federal investigation under Operation Take Back America, with the intended goal of protecting communities from “perpetrators of violent crimes.” Through the investigation, law enforcement seized over 37 firearms, more than $61,000 and approximately five kilograms of cocaine intended for distribution in South Dakota.

“Operation Black Book is the latest chapter in our mission to carry out this administration’s directive to completely dismantle and eliminate drug trafficking organizations and to protect our communities from violent crime,” United States Attorney Ronald Parsons Jr. said at a joint press conference on Tuesday.

The first phase of the operation happened in Colorado on Tuesday, June 16, where authorities arrested three people allegedly responsible for supplying to the South Dakota drug trafficking organization with cocaine. Parsons said the second phase began in the early morning hours of June 21 and continued until the afternoon. By the end of it, authorities arrested 14 “targeted fugitives.”

Parsons said no one was injured during the arrests.

The following is a list of the defendants arrested in connection with Operation Black Book:

Wuttichai Chankaeo, 32, of Commerce City, Colorado.

Joseph Valdez, 49, of Westminster, Colorado.

Amber Bravo, 42, of Westminster, Colorado.

Zeno Rendon, 31, of Box Elder, South Dakota.

Deja Guthmiller, 23, of Rapid City, South Dakota.

Mason Martin, 23, of Rapid City, South Dakota.

Dylan Sanchez, 34, of Rapid City, South Dakota.

Jarrian Ribitsch, 31, of Pine Ridge, South Dakota.

Laci Ribitsch, 32, of Pine Ridge, South Dakota.

Sara Clifford, 33, of Rapid City, South Dakota.

Ryan Jopnes, 38, of Rapid City, South Dakota.

Caleb Allard, 35, of Rapid City, South Dakota.

Savannah Backward, 31, of Pine Ridge, South Dakota.

Evan Sanchez, 33, of Rapid City, South Dakota.

“The arrests today in this case, highlight the extensive and aggressive efforts to secure our communities across the territory, including the Rapid City area and the tribal lands of the Oglala Sioux from the clutches of those who seek to poison our communities with deadly drugs and spread violence throughout these neighborhoods,” FBI Minneapolis Field Office Special Agent in Charge Christopher Dotson said at the meeting.

Parsons said the defendants have all been federally indicted for conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance, with some members of the drug trafficking organization facing additional federal charges related to financial crimes and firearms offenses for their conduct in furtherance of the drug trafficking organization. The investigation remains ongoing and additional charges may be considered.

“All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty, but I can promise you that our drug prosecutors at the U.S. Attorney’s Office intend to do precisely that. Prove them guilty in federal court in this building in short order,” Parsons said.

The investigation was spearheaded by the FBI Badlands Safe Trails Task Force in conjunction with the Drug Enforcement Administration and IRS-Criminal Investigation.

title: Pennington County to run runoff as usual; Commission folds on full hand-count audit idea
description: After the Pennington County Board of Commissioners entertained hand-counting every vote in a post-election audit, some conservatives thought a full hand-count at the precinct level was in hand and started gathering vote counters. The commissioners have now abandoned the idea completely — at least for now.
_full_text:
After the Pennington County Board of Commissioners entertained hand-counting every vote in a post-election audit, some conservatives thought a full hand-count at the precinct level was in hand and started gathering vote counters. The commissioners have now abandoned the idea completely — at least for now.

On Tuesday, July 21, the board voted 3-2 to rescind their July 7 vote to seek an opinion from counsel on the legality of hand-counting 100% of votes in the required post-election audit after the July 28 GOP gubernatorial runoff election.

The vote came after the county received legal guidance and halted the board’s exploration of a full hand-count in the upcoming runoff.

Commissioners Deb Hadcock (District 3) and Ron

 Hand Count
Deputy Pennington County State’s Attorney Tyler Sobczak gives input to the Pennigton County Board of Commissioners on election state laws during the board’s Tuesday, July 21, meeting. 

Rossknecht (District 1) voted against rescinding the item.

“We're just going to decide whether it's legal or not legal, and that's going to be talked through,” Chair Commissioner Ron Weifenbach (District 2) said before public comment opened.

Over 10 speakers stood before the commission, including residents, outgoing Rep. Heather Baxter, R-34 (who’s also the Republican nominee for South Dakota secretary of state) Rep. Mike Derby, R-34, and conservative leader Tonchi Weaver.

The runoff pits Gov. Larry Rhoden of Union Center against Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden. The winner will face Democrat Dan Ahlers in the November general election.

Weifenbach stated the item for discussion was for the post-election audit legality and said a full hand-count on election day at polling sites could be done legally but was not up for discussion.

Resident Cindy Cooke said election integrity doubt comes from President Donald Trump's recent comments challenging tabulators.

 Hand Count
State Rep. Heather Baxter, R-District 34, who’s the Republican nominee for secretary of state, argued the county has the ability to do a hand-count of elections. 

“President Trump spoke last Thursday on this, which was kind of ironic. And based on data from whitehouse.gov, we have foreign agents that are interfering in our elections. It's not speculation. It's not a conspiracy. This is official and comes from the highest office,” Cooke said.

Trump, since losing the 2020 Presidential Election against now-former President Joe Biden, continues to this day to claim elections have been “rigged” in the country, especially his in 2020, through mail-in ballots, tabulating machines and lax voter I.D. requirements. These claims have not been proven.

According to the Campaign Legal Center, Trump and his surrogates filed around 60 such lawsuits, all of which were dismissed on their merits or withdrawn. The Campaign Legal Center is a nonpartisan legal organization “dedicated to solving the wide range of challenges facing American democracy,” according to its website.

Weifenbach clarified at the Tuesday meeting tabulator machines are not connected to the internet.

Per the South Dakota Secretary of State, tabulators used in the state operate as isolated pieces of technology without internet capability. They are tested at federally accredited labs before the U.S. Election Assistance Commission certifies the equipment. The commission is an independent, bipartisan commission whose mission is to help election officials improve the administration of elections and help Americans participate in the voting process,” per its mission statement. Testing includes running 1.5 million consecutive ballot positions through the tabulator to make sure they’re read correctly, reviewing three million lines of source code and a full security audit of the election management software. 

 Mike Derby
Sen. Mike Derby, R-Rapid City, poses a question for the commission over hand-count laws. 

Baxter, who lost in the Republican District 34 primary race, read a list of state laws pertaining to elections.

Baxter cited SDCL 12-17B-3, which states governing bodies that supervise elections are free to use, abandon or experiment with automatic tabulating or electronic ballot marking systems that are approved for use by the State Board of Elections.

The state law on the matter is SDCL 12-17B-20, which notes, "The post-election audit must be conducted in 5% of the precincts in the county by manually counting all votes cast in two contests and comparing the results of the manual count to the results for those precincts at the county canvass. The county auditor shall select the precincts for the audit at random without the use of a computer in public during the meeting of the county canvassing board.”

Election audits are conducted by hand count. South Dakota state law has various thresholds for allowing a full recount. In local elections, votes within a 2% margin are eligible. Recounts are done with a mix of tabulation and hand-count.

Deputy Pennington County State’s Attorney Tyler Sobczak said regarding to legality of a full hand count in the post-election audit, “We got in contact with the election hotline from the SDPAA (South Dakota Public Assurance Alliance), who did indicate that it's a strict 5% on the post-election audit.”

He continued, saying SDCL12-17B-20 specifically states the post-election audit only applies to a primary and general election, but not the primary runoff.

“I think what we're faced with is the fact that the statute does not refer to what we're trying to do,” Weifenbach said. “That can be fixed in the next legislative session, if so be it. But my opinion is based on what I've heard in talking to legal counsel, (which) is ‘You should proceed as you've always done in the past.‘ Do the tabulation and do what you've done in the past, keep your eye on the ball.”

Weaver, who is with the conservative-leaning South Dakota Citizens for Liberty, said she has been collecting signatures for registered Republicans to volunteer for a full hand-count at polling sites on election day, and felt the commission should vote on this action instead of a post-election audit. In an email to members, the Pennington County GOP said it had the support of the commission to do a full hand-count at polling sites. Four of the five commissioners told the Journal on Friday, July 17, they didn’t support such a count, apparently to Weaver’s surprise.

“I just want to give a little background because there was a newspaper article (referencing the the Journal’s reporting), and I think that it needs some explanation — after the last meeting, in private conversations with each one of you, we discussed the legalities, and we did talk about the fact that the law allows one or the other; both are legitimate methods to count an election,” Weaver said.

County Auditor Sabrina Green clarified that election workers (including counters) would have to be made up of Republicans and Democrats.

“In statute, with looking and speaking with SDPAA and other county auditors, there is no statute saying that we (could) have only Republicans. So we still have to remain at the Republican-Democrat split for hand-counting precincts,” Green said.

Commissioners Jerry Derr (District 4), Gary Drewes (District 5) and Weifnebach noted the short timeline to train volunteers and the recent cyberattack against the county as factors contributing to their no vote for a hand count at the precincts.

Deb Hadcock (District 3) was not in favor of this opinion.

“My intent the whole time, and I think Ron Rossknecht was on the same page, was to do a hand-count,” Hadcock said.

Rossknecht told the Journal last week he supported sticking with the 5% post-election audit because of the need to train and pay counters and because of “all the issues that Pennington County is currently dealing with.”

Weifenbach challenged Hadcock, requesting her to make a substitute motion to do a hand-count at the precincts. Hadcock did not make a motion.

Derr concluded, saying, “I'm just going to do a follow-up comment that I believe even Sabrina Green, our auditor, said if we're going to do this, then she would be open to looking at a general election.”

The commission didn’t discuss the matter further.

title: ‘Hectic, wonderful’ opening expected for Rapid City’s Natural Grocers store
description: “Hectic in a wonderful way” is what Natural Grocers staff predict for the store’s grand opening in Rapid City on Wednesday, July 22.
_full_text:
“Hectic in a wonderful way” is what Natural Grocers staff predict for the store’s grand opening in Rapid City on Wednesday, July 22.

In fact, it’s typical for crowds to stretch out the doors each time Natural Grocers hosts a grand opening, said Katie Macarelli, Natural Grocers director of public relations.

The Rapid City store, at 855 Omaha St., is the second Natural Grocers store in South Dakota. On Wednesday at 8:10 a.m., before the store officially opens with a ribbon cutting at 8:27 a.m., Natural Grocers will present a $2,500 donation to Feeding South Dakota, Macarelli said. Natural Grocers’ Sioux Falls location also donates to Feeding South Dakota.

 072226-nws-NaturalGrocers-exterior
Natural Grocers’ Rapid City helds its grand opening on Wednesday, July 22. The store is located at 855 Omaha St. 

Additionally, anytime customers bring a reusable bag when they shop, Natural Grocers donates 5 cents per transaction to Feeding South Dakota.

Giveaways are planned throughout Wednesday, including gift cards for the first 150 customers in line (18 and older), and hand-woven backpacks made by artisans in Pechugue, Ecuador, for the first 500 shoppers.

From noon to 5 p.m., customers can try the Prize Wheel for a chance to win prizes from Natural Grocers. At 5 p.m., the store will put out samples “like trick-or-treating for grown-ups,” Macarelli said.

 072226-nws-Natural Grocers-produce.jpg
An assortment of organic produce is displayed at Natural Grocers in Rapid City. 

Store hours are 8:27 a.m. to 8:36 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and 8:27 a.m. to 7 p.m. Sunday.

Sales, special events and giveaways will continue into August to celebrate the Rapid City store’s opening and the Natural Grocers’ chain’s 171 anniversary. Giveaways will include a Toyota RAV4 Hybrid.

 072226-nws-Natural Grocers-checkout.jpg
Customers shopped and browsed during a private event on July 21 at Rapid City’s new Natural Grocers store. The store’s grand opening was Wednesday, July 22. Anytime customers bring a reusable bag when they shop, Natural Grocers donates 5 cents per transaction to Feeding South Dakota. 

Natural Grocers is a family-owned chain that began in 1955 as a door-to-door business and now has 174 stores in 22 states. Natural Grocers specializes in 100% organic and GMO-free produce, pasture-based dairy products, antibiotic- and hormone-free meats, plus supplements, face and body care products, pet food, and more. Products come from a variety of regional, national and international sources.

“We’ve been doing organic (since) before it was cool,” Macarelli said. “We are here for you and you shouldn’t have to have a doctorate in food science to understand what’s in your food. We are big on consumer transparency, we are big on education, and we are very friendly. If you ever have questions, our crew is educated in the fashion that they can answer them or find the answer.”

Customers eager to explore Rapid City’s new Natural Grocers store browsed and shopped during a private event on July 21 ahead of the store’s grand opening on July 22.
