title: South Dakota severe weather snapshot
byline: ELENA TITTEL South Dakota News Watch
description: South Dakota is no stranger to severe weather events. The latest proof: a 131 mph wind gust on June 29 in Highmore that was one of the strongest recorded in U.S. history and the second-highest gust recorded in South Dakota.
_full_text:
South Dakota is no stranger to severe weather events. The latest proof: a 131 mph wind gust on June 29 in Highmore that was one of the strongest recorded in U.S. history and the second-highest gust recorded in South Dakota.

The National Weather Service issued a severe thunderstorm warning at the time of the storm and confirmed the winds did not come from a tornado, according to a fact brief published by News Watch.

 2026-6-29-Highmore-storm-damage.JPG
Extreme winds caused significant property damage and knocked down power lines in the town of Highmore, S.D., June 29, 2026. 

Laura Edwards, SDSU Extension state climatologist, said winds exceeding 130 mph are "uncommon," but with the right ingredients, it can occur.

"I think they had just the right perfect conditions with the strengthening storm as it was approaching that area," she said.

It was the latest of several recent wind-related events.

In December, a record-breaking winter windstorm swept across Custer, Fall River and Pennington counties, causing widespread damage.

According to a press release from Gov. Larry Rhoden, the storm produced sustained winds and gusts exceeding 90 mph, bringing down power lines, snapping off and topping trees, damaging public infrastructure and leaving thousands of residents without power. It prompted Gov. Larry Rhoden to request a presidential disaster declaration, which was received in April.

16 federal disasters in past decade

Over the past nine years, there have been 16 federal major disaster declarations, not including the COVID-19 pandemic, in the state of South Dakota, according to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Federal disaster declarations are determined by the president.

The reasons include winter storms, flooding, thunderstorms, tornadoes and straight-line winds.

 Wind graphic.png

State disaster declarations, on the other hand, are issued by the governor. Executive orders related to state disasters from the previous decade include severe winter storms, flooding, droughts and straight-line winds.

Drought-like conditions in South Dakota

Aside from the two recent major wind-related storms, South Dakota has also seen a lack of precipitation in the southern parts of the state.

Andrew Kalin, senior service hydrologist for the National Weather Service in Sioux Falls, said in the northwest and other parts of the state, precipitation levels are closer to normal.

Data from the U.S. Drought Monitor shows approximately 48% of the state is in moderate to extreme (D1-D4) drought, affecting an estimated 557,792 people. These drier conditions, primarily concentrated within the southern parts of the state, are causing a lack of soil moisture, especially following a drier winter that had less snow, Clabo said.

 Precipitation graphic.png

Edwards said that there has been an ebb and flow of drought in the state over the past five or so years, especially along the southern part of the state. She predicts improvement will be relatively local, meaning it will not be uniform across the state.

"I think the improvement that we'll see will be relatively local, and I think we're going to continue to see this ebb and flow of worsening and improvement," Edwards said.

Staying informed: Weather alert services

In instances of severe weather, South Dakotans have multiple options to stay informed. One of these are weather sirens, which are designed to alert people who are outdoors.

Sometimes, though, not everything goes according to plan.

Back in early June, weather sirens in Aberdeen and Viborg experienced troubles ahead of tornado season ramping up.

Tanner Jondahl, chief of police for the city of Aberdeen, said the backup plan is still working. The sirens are being tested every Wednesday at 6 p.m. and they expect the new primary system to be up and running sometime in August.

 2025-12-23 Custer wind damage.JPG
Significant wind damage at Custer State Park, S.D., as pictured Dec. 23, 2025. 

In the southeast South Dakota town of Viborg, the sirens on the west side stopped working after a control board burned out. It has been replaced and the sirens are working again, said maintenance superintendent Jody Nelsen.

Aside from weather sirens, there are multiple ways to stay informed during potentially life-threatening situations. The most widespread weather alert system is NOAA Weather Radio, a nationwide radio station network, providing 24/7 weather alerts. Aside from tuning into the radio, people can also enable wireless emergency alerts on their iPhone or Android's settings.

However, it's wise not to rely solely on one weather alert system, due to potential unpredictability.

Looking forward, a forecast from the NOAA Climate Prediction Center, the next one to three months are projected to have warmer than average weather in the west, south and eastern parts of the state, whereas the north-central part of the state may experience near- to below-average temperatures.

title: Reptile Gardens is rising from the ashes with new tortoise building after tragic fire
description: Reptile Gardens was buzzing with activity on Thursday, July 23. Families meandered along pathways lined with curated garden beds and visited the campus’ signature glass dome filled with yet more foliage and a host of frogs, snakes, birds, lizards, alligators and crocodiles. In the outdoor tortoise enclosure, gentle giants munched on carrots as young children cautiously approached them to bestow gentle pets.
_full_text:
Reptile Gardens was buzzing with activity on Thursday, July 23. Families meandered along pathways lined with curated garden beds and visited the campus’ signature glass dome filled with yet more foliage and a host of frogs, snakes, birds, lizards, alligators and crocodiles. In the outdoor tortoise enclosure, gentle giants munched on carrots as young children cautiously approached them to bestow gentle pets.

A casual tourist wouldn’t know nine months ago, just off from the public-facing portion of the destination, tragedy struck. At about midnight on Nov. 21, 2025, an off-exhibit building housing 47 alligators and 53 tortoises caught fire. None of the animals survived. The giant tortoises were not affected, but the fire devastated Reptile Gardens staff and the community.

 Tortoise in a hardhat
Children pet Hugo, one of Reptile Gardens’ giant tortoises on Thursday, July 23, during a groundbreaking for the new tortoise building. Hugo wears a SECO Construction hardhat. SECO is the contractor on the project. 

“We had so many people reach out to us. People from Rapid City, from the Black Hills, from South Dakota, from all over this country, offering their condolences and wanting to know what they could do to help us here at Reptile Gardens. It was an outpouring of support that just warmed our hearts. It was so, so special,” said Reptile Gardens Public Relations Director John Brockelsby — the son of the park’s founder Earl Brockelsby, who established Reptile Gardens in 1937.

Now, the Black Hills institution is rising from the ashes.

On Thursday, Reptile Gardens held an official groundbreaking for a new $2.1 million, 3,200 square-foot tortoise building in the same place where the animals perished. Damon’s Tortoise House is being built in memory of those animals and Damon Mueller, the great-grandson of Earl Brockelsby. Damon died at 9 years old in August 2025 after battling cancer.

“One of his favorite places in the whole world was Reptile Gardens and the giant tortoises. And I spent a lot of time with that young man … to my dying day, he will always be a huge inspiration to me, so we are naming this Damon's Tortoise House,” said Reptile Gardens Animal Department Curator Terry Phillip.

The facility will not only house tortoises, but it’ll also include exhibits and provide a space for visitors to interact with and learn about the tortoises during the shoulder seasons — spring and fall.

“It's climate-controlled, odor-controlled, and it's going to be like literally a state-of-the-art cool thing. I had to chase down some expertise from some friends of mine in Florida that had done some similar projects and get some advice too,” Phillip said.

 Reptile Gardens Animal Department Curator Terry Phillip
Reptile Gardens Animal Department Curator Terry Phillip on Thursday, July 23, points to a photo of himself and Damon Mueller, the great-grandson of Earl Brockelsby. Damon died from cancer in 2025. He is the namesake of Damon’s Tortoise House, for which the gardens held a groundbreaking on Thursday. 

Officials labeled the cause of the fire last year as electrical, but the exact source couldn’t be determined. Phillip said he takes responsibility for the fire because his job is to mitigate risk.

“I had zero tolerance for any hardening of wires or darkening of sockets … That's all I did every day, is walk through and risk mitigate. And so, what did I miss? Did I miss something? I don't know … I’ll torture myself forever about it,” Phillip said.

When the fire hit the old building, Philip said he came down to Reptile Gardens with his wife, “and I literally sat here from 1:30 in the morning until 10 a.m. and just watched the building burn. And there’s nothing you could do about it.”

The new building, though, is designed to further mitigate fire risk. Reptiles need supplemental heat, like from heat lamps, to regulate their bodies.

“In this building now, instead of a lot of electrical components for the supplemental heat, we're doing a gas line and doing gas heaters,” Phillip said, adding he consulted with everybody he could about preventing a fire, including “reptile people, engineers, construction. Anything we can do to reduce that (fire risk), we’ve done.”

Brockelsby noted, “There were no blueprints that we could follow.”

 Reptile Gardens Public Relations Director John Brockelsby
Reptile Gardens Public Relations Director John Brockelsby — the son of the park’s founder Earl Brockelsby, who established Reptile Gardens in 1937 — said at the Thursday, July 23, groundbreaking for a new tortoise building that the community showed support after the November 2025 fire. 

Brockelsby said Tallgrass Design out of Custer, Rapid City’s SECO Construction and the animal experts at Reptile Gardens got together and meet weekly for months and changed plans until the final design emerged.

Ethan Hudson with Seco Construction said he’s never done a tortoise building before, but, “That’s why Reptile Gardens is one of our favorite customers because they have interesting needs.”

With the design ready, Brockelsby said the next step was financing from Pioneer Bank.

“Thankfully, they agreed that it was a project worth funding, and so they agreed to fund it for us. We're greatly appreciative of Pioneer Bank for that,” Brockelsby said.

The target date for opening the new building is March 2027. In the meantime, Reptile Gardens’ summer hours are 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. until Sept. 7. Fall hours are 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. from Sept. 8 to Oct. 31. Winter hours are 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., Nov. 1-30.

“Reptile Gardens is a great place to be on a hot day, on a cold day, on a rainy day, and during a rally day when it's nice and slow for the tourist attractions out here. Come on down, see us,” Philip said. “That's my sales pitch.”

 Damon’s Tortoise House
A display at Reptile Gardens details the plans for Damon’s Tortoise House. The groundbreaking for the tortoise house was held on Thursday, July 23, nine months after a fire killed 47 alligators and 52 tortoises.

title: Less travel for families: Rapid City Hospital breaks ground on children’s expansion
description: Monument Health took the latest step on a project many have been waiting for, breaking ground on a children’s expansion at Rapid City Hospital.
_full_text:
Monument Health took the latest step on a project many have been waiting for, breaking ground on a children’s expansion at Rapid City Hospital.

“This 63,000 square-foot edition is designed around one idea: Families should not have to leave home or move between units to receive the care that they need,” Monument Health Dr. Kyle Lemley said during the groundbreaking ceremony.

The $48 million project includes 19 labor, delivery, recovery and postpartum rooms, meaning new moms will stay in the same room throughout the birthing process and postpartum recovery. The expansion also includes taking the neonatal intensive care unit from an open bay environment to 25 private and semi-private rooms (made up of 17 private rooms and four twin bays), Monument Health officials said at the event.

The expansion will connect to the existing hospital building, taking up a portion of parking lot on the hospital’s north side.

 Rapid City Hospital children’s expansion
Officials held a ceremonial groundbreaking of the children’s expansion at Rapid City Hospital on Thursday, July 23. 

Stephanie Battell, director of nursing for women and children with Monument Health, said the rooms will be bigger as well, meaning more family members and others will be able to visit new mothers and families with babies in the NICU. Providing additional privacy was important as well.

Battell told media the labor, delivery, recovery and postpartum rooms is a change from the current process of taking new mothers from the labor room to a separate recovery room.

“Our current postpartum rooms are very small. It's hard when you're a new mom and you have family coming to see you. It's a tight space. You bring a lot of your stuff from home because you want to be comfortable as you're bringing a new one into the world,” she said. “So this will provide a lot of comfort, especially in those recovery days.”

 Groundbreaking
Nursing staff members throw dirt during a ceremonial groundbreaking on a children's expansion at Rapid City Hospital on Thursday, July 23. 

Battell said labor/delivery and recovery/postpartum nurses will help guide the process as the changes are implemented.

“Right now, they're pretty separate. You have L and D nurses and you have postpartum nurses. This will make it where they have to work a lot closer together,” she said. “They will help design what it looks like.”

During his remarks, Lemley noted, “As labor and delivery and the NICU move into the new space, we're able to backfill and expand our current children's area. This benefits our pediatric intensive care unit, our inpatient pediatrics, as well as our outpatient pediatric services, like pediatric sedation and infusions.”

 Groundbreaking
Monument Health celebrated a planned $48 million children's expansion at Rapid City Hospital with a groundbreaking on Thursday, July 23. 

Monument Health CEO Paulette Davidson said the hospital has “been planning on this day” for a long time.

“We realize that our region continues to grow, the need for specialized care for babies and children continues to grow. We understand the burden that families have when they need to leave our community,” Davidson told a crowd of around 100 people at the event. “If they have to travel, if they have to separate from their own family members for months at a time, if they have to leave their jobs … we understand traveling is tough. And for us, to continue to make the investment in our children, in our families here in Rapid City, can help alleviate much of that burden for our families.”

 Groundbreaking
Monument Health CEO Paulette Davidson said the hospital has “been planning on this day” for a long time. 

The Monument Health Foundation began raising funds for the children’s expansion in 2022 and hit a fundraising goal of $7.1 million to put toward the project.

“This achievement reflects years of extraordinary support and generosity from our donors and our supporters,” foundation Vice President of Philanthropy Ross McKie said during the ceremony. “This campaign is all about one thing: It's about caring for our children and supporting our families. “

Construction is expected to start in August, with completion expected in February of 2028.

“This is something that the community really needs,” Battell said.

The groundbreaking was held about 16 months after Lemley announced the hospital would break ground on a women and children's expansion project in about a year. Lemley made the announcement at a March 2025 press conference celebrating a $2 million grant from the Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust used to purchase state-of-the-art NICU equipment.

 Groundbreaking
A youngster hams for the camera at the groundbreaking. 

 Groundbreaking
Officials applaud after breaking ground on a children's expansion at Rapid City Hospital. 

 Rapid City Hospital children’s expansion groundbreaking
Stephanie Battell, director of nursing for women and children with Monument Health, speaks at a groundbreaking for a children’s expansion at Rapid City Hospital on Thursday, July 23.

title: Public can drop off items for 911 cell phone bank at Rapid City Hall
description: Rapid City officials remind the public the City Hall lobby in Rapid City is serving as a permanent drop-off location for cell phones, tablets, chargers and cords for the 911 Cell Phone Bank.
_full_text:
Rapid City officials remind the public the City Hall lobby in Rapid City is serving as a permanent drop-off location for cell phones, tablets, chargers and cords for the 911 Cell Phone Bank.

In December and January, the lobby in City Hall served as a temporary drop-off location for cell phones and related items. A total of 419 phones were donated by the public and Victim’s Specialist Program turned the items over to the 911 Cell Phone Bank. Working with the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office Victim’s Specialist Program, City Hall became a permanent drop-off location in May.

 PHOTO Cell phone donation box May 2026.jpg
The donated items are repaired, refurbished, recycled and securely erased, then provided to partnering agencies to be given to victims of violent crimes. 

The donated items are repaired, refurbished, recycled and securely erased, then provided to partnering agencies to be given to victims of violent crimes.

“We are pleased to serve as a permanent location for donations of cell phones for this worthwhile effort,” said Kelly Langenbau with the City of Rapid City. “The phones are literally a life line for victims of violent crimes. We are encouraging the public to drop off the phones, tablets and accessories they no longer will use and know the items will continue to provide a great service.”

Donations are also accepted at the Public Safety Building, 300 Kansas City Street.

For more information, contact Rebecca Elger or Jeanne Mann with the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office at 605-394-6115.

title: RCAS Board of Education approves $214 million 2027 budget
description: The Rapid City Area Schools Board voted unanimously Tuesday, July 21, to approve the district’s $214.76 million fiscal year 2027 budget, an about 10% ($19.7 million) increase from 2026 expenditures.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Area Schools Board voted unanimously Tuesday, July 21, to approve the district’s $214.76 million fiscal year 2027 budget, an about 10% ($19.7 million) increase from 2026 expenditures.

The budget approval comes as the district is contending with steady decreases in enrollment, building updates, a 2.5% increase to wages and new state laws shifting the funding burden from majority local property taxes to state aid fueled by sales taxes.

Despite those factors, Chief Financial and Operations Officer Coy Sasse said, “I think the overriding theme here being that despite a lot of these really complex financial pressures that we deal with coming into the year, all our funds are in good condition.”

Sasse presented the budget to the school board on Tuesday, July 21. He noted it was developed with the involvement of RCAS Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson, as well as the Finance Committee, which consists of Board Members Christine Stephenson, Troy Carr and Katy Urban.

“Of course, the district's strategic plan and the board's goals and objectives served as the overriding framework for the development of the budget,” Sasse said.

“I feel good voting to approve this budget,” Stephenson said.

 RCAS Education Center
The Rapid City Education Center 

The budget consists of 17 funds. Over 90% stems from four key funds: The General Fund ($97.16 million), which pays for day-to-day educational programs and essential services; the Special Education Fund ($28.33 million); the Capital Outlay Fund ($48.98 million), which pays for maintaining and upgrading facilities, and the Health Insurance Fund ($20.5 million), which supports health insurance coverage for employees.

“This is a very fiscally conservative budget, which is positive in terms of the impact on our constituents, but has somewhat of a concern as we always need to balance the needs of our taxpayers with the needs of our students and providing them with a high-quality education. I believe we can still do that, and we'll be doing it in a fiscally responsible manner,” Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson said.

Shifts in funding sources

The 2026 South Dakota State Legislature voted to reduce property taxes, increase the state sales tax, and pull money from reserves to make local entities whole. The legislature also passed a bill to allow counties to implement a 0.5% sales tax to offset property taxes, which the Pennington County Commission did on Tuesday. That impacts how school districts like RCAS are funded.

Before the changes, 57% of the district’s revenue came from local property taxes, with the remaining coming from state aid. After the implementation of property tax relief, that nearly flips the equation with 53% set to come from state aid and 47% from local property taxes.

Sasse said this shifts the burden to sales taxes, which are a more “volatile” source of funding, as it fluctuates more drastically with economic conditions than property valuations.

“Of course, that all remains to be seen,” Sasse said.

Although the district will be relying on property taxes less going into the new fiscal year, those taxes still have an impact. Sasse noted that property valuations in the district continue to grow, with a $770 million increase last year, bringing the total valuation to $14.5 billion.

 Coy Sasse (Copy)
Chief Financial and Operations Officer Coy Sasse answers questions about employee negotiations at the Tuesday, April 21, Rapid City Area Schools Board meeting. 

Enrollment, which directly affects the state aid formula, continues to trend downward. The district’s last bump in enrollment was in 2022, when it went from about 12,700 to 12,800; otherwise, enrollment has been declining for the past decade. The count for RCAS that the state looks at for funding — taken on the last Friday of September of the most recent school year — is 11,948, a 2% decline from last year.

Per Sasse’s presentation, enrollment will largely dictate the district’s financial condition moving forward. If enrollment grows, the district will be able to continue to offer wage increases and accelerate facilities improvements. If it declines, revenue will continue to lag and major budget modifications will likely follow with wage increases coming “increasingly difficult to sustain.”

The district spends $84 million — about 87% of the General Fund — on salaries and benefits. The district approved a 2.5% wage increase for its employees, effective July 1.

“In any case, the district is well positioned to take on whatever challenges lie ahead — with strong reserves, clear priorities, and a committed leadership team.”

Managing the deficit, investing in facilities and tax levy

“The tricky piece of managing a deficit is always not allowing it to get to a point where we don't feel like we can pull it back in without major restructure of funds and of our system in general,” Sasse said.

In the final version of the budget, the General Fund showed a deficit of $3.3 million (3.4%), down from the 5% deficit shown in the preliminary budget. That reduction in the deficit came from moving property insurance premiums to the Capital Outlay Fund. The remainder of the deficit will be covered by cash reserves if needed

The Capital Outlay Fund budget for 2027 ($48.98 million). About 58% of the budget is dedicated to facility projects during the fiscal year, including the Rapid Valley Elementary School expansion project, multiple secure entrances and Horace Mann HVAC upgrades.

The board also approved the tax levy rates for the fiscal year. Overall, property taxes will decrease.

From 2026 to 2027, the owner-occupied tax levy will drop from 2.518 to .669, a reduction of $1.849 per $1,000 of valuation. For a home assessed at $400,000, the owner-occupied burden shifts from $1,007 to $268. The district is requesting a Capital Outlay levy increase. For a $400,000 home, the tax burden will go from $920 to $1,006.

Overall, the total tax request for a $400,000 home will go from $2,512 to $1,854.

The 2027 budget is available through the RCAS website.

Board Member Jamie Clapham said she often hears comments from people about not knowing where the district’s money goes, and she noted there is a public budget hearing every year and it is fully accessible to the public.

“There is no effort not to be transparent,” Clapham said.

title: Eixenberger family celebrates immigrant’s role in South Dakota history
description: A celebrated immigrant to the Black Hills, Peter Eixenberger, inspired a reunion that honored him and his contributions to South Dakota history.
_full_text:
A celebrated immigrant to the Black Hills, Peter Eixenberger, inspired a reunion that honored him and his contributions to South Dakota history.

More than 200 of Eixenberger’s descendants gathered in the Black Hills June 16 and 17 to observe the 150th anniversary of Eixenberger immigrating to the United States. The family provided much of the information in this article.

Eixenberger was a U.S. Army veteran who became “one of the best and most well-known musicians that ever entered the Black Hills,” according to his obituary. Eixenberger was known for exceptional musical talent and leadership. He started several bands, a local orchestra, and he taught music.

In 1885, under Eixenberger’s leadership, the Deadwood Brass Band played at the opening of the original Deadwood Bandstand, which is now Outlaw Square. A plaque at the corner of Main Street and Deadwood Street recognizes Peter for leading the band during that opening celebration.

 072126-nws-Mary and Peter Eixenberger.jpg
Mary and Peter Eixenberger. Descendants of the couple, who lived in the Sturgis and Deadwood areas, held a reunion on June 16 and 17. 

Born in Munich, Bavaria, Germany, Eixenberger was a musician from an early age. He learned to play the violin when he was a young boy. When Eixenberger left Germany, the beginnings of the industrial revolution were creating economic and financial hardships, and many immigrants from Germany, Italy, and Ireland arrived in the United States looking for opportunities.

Eixenberger was 15 when he traveled alone to the United States. His father had recently died, and his mother had died a few years earlier. According to Eixenberg family lore, Peter didn’t want to burden his family so he left his younger brother and stepmother behind in Germany. Eixenberger served as a working hand aboard the SS Donau steamship to pay for his journey to New York.

Eixenberger started his journey in late 1875. When he arrived in New York City, he was met by an Army recruiter, Lt. John Babcock, who talked him into enlisting as a musician. Eixenberger arrived in the Black Hills in 1876 amid the gold rush that began in 1874. Eixenberger remained in the Black Hills until his death in 1917, according to his obituary.

Eixenberger served for 10 years in the U.S. Army and was a member of the 7th Cavalry Regiment. Eixenberger’s obituary notes he was stationed at Fort Meade most of that time as sergeant of the band.

 072126-nws-Eixenberger—7thCavalryband1870's.png
Peter Eixenberger was a bugler in the 7th Cavalry Regiment band, shown here in this 1870s photo. 

In 1876, Eixenberger was assigned as an Army musician — a bugler — to the 7th Cavalry led by Lt. Col. George A. Custer, with Felix Vinatieri as the leader of the band. They were stationed at Fort Abraham Lincoln. Vinatieri was a conservatory-trained musician from Italy, and Eixenberger’s musical skills grew while he was in the military.  

The 7th Cavalry departed Powder River Depot near Terry, Montana, in June 1876. Due to a shortage of horses, Eixenberger and 15 other Army musicians missed the Battle of Little Bighorn.

Historical records document the band played the songs “Garry Owen” and “The Girl I Left Behind Me” as Custer and his troops rode away. The musicians traveled on foot to help with the aftermath of the battle. After the Battle of Little Bighorn, “Garry Owen” became a popular military song that is still played today by the U.S. Army.

Fort Meade, near Sturgis, was created in 1878. Eixenberger and some other musicians were reassigned there. Eixenberger re-enlisted in the Army in 1880 for an additional five years and was honorably discharged in November 1885. A few days later, he married Mary Auchenbach.   

Peter and Mary lived in the Sturgis and Deadwood areas. They also acquired 160 acres of land near Bell Tower, Montana, under the Homestead Act and tried farming. The Eixenbergers and other families in the Bell Tower area were very religious and built a small wooden church on the homestead land. 

Peter and Mary Eixenberger had seven sons and two daughters; two sons and a daughter died as children. The surviving six children, Frank, Arthur, Joseph, Charles aka “Carl,” Clarance, and Marie had families of their own. Frank, Joe and Carl married three sisters from the Gergen family in Sturgis. Arthur married Elizabeth Schummer, daughter of Nick Schummer who built historical buildings in Sturgis. Many Eixenberger descendants still live in the Black Hills.

 072126-nws-Eixenberger-reunion
Descendants of Peter and Mary Eixenberger gathered for a group celebration at Outlaw Square in Deadwood on June 16. As part of the celebration, the Northern Hills Community Band performed historical brass band music. The event continued with a presentation about Deadwood history, an outdoor barbecue, group photos and more. The reunion celebrated the 150th anniversary of Peter Eixenberger immigrating to the United States and ultimately to the Black Hills, where he was an Army veteran and musician. 

The Black Hills and American West were still rowdy places during this era. These were difficult times financially for Peter and Mary Eixenberger. While Peter played for formal musical events, he also had side jobs playing music in the local hotels, halls, and saloons. He continued to pursue his love for music, and according to local newspaper articles and promotional artifacts, Eixenberger created several local bands and the first orchestra in South Dakota such as the Redmen Band and A La Gungl Orchestra, which had 40 to 50 participants.

Tim Eixenberger, one of Peter and Mary’s great-grandsons, grew up in the Black Hills. He said the Eixenberger family reunion attracted people from about a dozen states. Family members wore specially designed matching T-shirts and, for many, it was the first time meeting some other Eixenberger descendants.  

With the help of Outlaw Square, City of Deadwood, Deadwood Historical Office, Deadwood Alive, City of Spearfish, Elkhorn Resort, local catering businesses and hotels, Eixenberger family members held group events at Outlaw Square and Elkhorn Resort and Campground in Spearfish. Reunion participants also visited family gravesites, Fort Meade Calvary Museum and Deadwood historical sites.  

“The 150-year commemorative celebration is a significant milestone in the Eixenberger Family ancestry. However, it also provided an opportunity to reflect on the story of how a single individual, with his pursuit for a better life, musical talents, resilience and pure luck coincide with American Western history,” the family said.

Family members note the “X” in the spelling of the Eixenberger name is unusual, and anyone with that name spelling is likely related. It is estimated about 500 to 1,000 people in the United States have the surname Eixenberger. There are descendants of Peter and Mary Eixenberger with other surnames due to marriage, and the vast majority live in the western United States.

title: Goodwill hosts back-to-school sales
description: Families can get a head start on affordable back-to-school shopping when Goodwill hosts two weekends of sales at its Rapid City stores.
_full_text:
Families can get a head start on affordable back-to-school shopping when Goodwill hosts two weekends of sales at its Rapid City stores.

Goodwill is expanding its back-to-school sale to two weekends to help families whose budgets are tight as they prepare for a new school year. Goodwill’s stores at 611 Lindbergh Ave. and 611 Timmons Blvd. will offer sales on Saturday, July 25, and Saturday, Aug. 1. Store hours are 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Sunday.

Sale prices will be 99 cents for all kid-sized clothing, $1.99 for all regularly-priced shirts and $2.99 for all regularly priced pants.

Anyone who has clothing that is clean and in good condition to donate to Goodwill can take donations to Rapid City’s Goodwill stores seven days a week.

Every dollar spent at Goodwill does double duty. Purchases help pay for job training and employment opportunities. For more information and a complete list of items that can and cannot be donated to Goodwill, go to goodwillgreatplains.org.

title: Barbara Dean Cunningham
description: August 29, 1950 - July 18, 2026
_full_text:
August 29, 1950 - July 18, 2026

The family of Barbara Dean Cunningham is deeply saddened to announce her sudden passing on July 18, 2026, at the age of 75.

Barbara, an enrolled member of the Oglala Lakota Tribe and a descendant of the Cherokee and Wichita Tribes, was born on August 29, 1950, in Pine Ridge, South Dakota, the daughter of Bill and Vivian (Conroy) Cunningham.

Barbara's early education began at Saint Patrick's Mission School in Anadarko. Following the family's move to Lawrence, Kansas, she graduated from Lawrence High School in 1968, attended the University of South Dakota in Vermillion, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in Education, and later obtained her Master's Degree in Counseling from the University of North Dakota in Grand Forks.

Barbara began her teaching career and service to the Bureau of Indian Affairs with brief stints at Dunseith Indian Day School in Dunseith, North Dakota, and Cheyenne-Eagle Butte Boarding School in Eagle Butte, South Dakota. Then, following in the footsteps of her grandpa, John Conroy, Barbara was hired to work at Flandreau Indian School and taught at the elementary school for several years. She then moved to Lawrence, Kansas, and worked at Haskell Indian Nations University as a counselor and classroom instructor, as well as in many other roles and positions. Barbara poured herself into her work; she enjoyed working with young people, loved her students, and saw them as her own. In 2005, she retired as a GS-15, the highest non-executive grade in the U.S. federal civil service, a career milestone, of which Barbara was extremely proud.

Barbara was always a very hard worker. She held multiple jobs from the age of 16, including working at the bakery at Dillon's in Lawrence, at various places in Flandreau, at Sears in Overland Park, Kansas, and, after she retired from Haskell, back at Dillon's in Lawrence. After moving to Gracemont and Anadarko, she also worked at Walmart for a few years.

Barbara especially loved sewing and was an exceptionally talented seamstress. In her spare time, she meticulously created everything from elaborate Halloween costumes to beautiful ribbon skirts to numerous other projects that she saw as a labor of love.

Barbara loved traveling. She sponsored many student dance groups to powwows across the United States, even taking them to Russia and Germany to perform. She was known for taking spontaneous road trips "up north," but most enjoyed going places with her good friend, Inez, and spending time with the Falcon girls.

Again, following in the footsteps of her grandpa, John - or Popo, as she called him - who was a 32nd Degree Mason, Barbara became a member of the Order of the Eastern Star. In addition, throughout her career and 35 years of dedicated service to the B.I.A., she received numerous service awards, honors, and recognitions.

Barbara was the best big sister and took her role very seriously. She was always caring for those around her and ended every conversation with "Love you." She had the biggest heart, she was very generous and always had the best interest of her family and others in mind.

Remaining to cherish Barbara's memory are her brother, John Monroe Cunningham; sisters, Coleen Cunningham and Cassie Melton and her husband Michael; nephew, Kyle Cunningham, his wife Luena, and their children, Evelyn and Cassian; nephew, Tyler Melton, his wife Hannah, and their daughter, Camila; her uncle, Walter John Conroy, cousin Michelle Kobrick, and her daughter Jenifer; her aunt Betty (Cunningham) Shirley; her cousin Jodene (Irving) Smith, her husband Gary, and their daughter Autumn; her best friend and special sister, Inez Crawford; special granddaughters Hannah, Mia, Summer Sky, and Jaella Falcon; Victoria Houghton and family; her tiny beloved fur baby Finney; and a host of other relatives and friends.

Preceding Barbara in death are her parents, Bill and Vivian (Conroy) Cunningham; her grandparents, John and Marjorie (Lamar) Conroy, and James Monroe and Bessie (Pendleton) Cunningham; her sister-in-law LaDonna (Chalepah) Cunningham; her aunt Elfrieda (Conroy) Irving and her husband Seth; her cousin Francis "Sonny" Irving; her aunt Wanda (Cunningham) Robinson and her husband Arnold; and her uncles Homer Cunningham and Kenneth Cunningham.

The family would like to give special appreciation to Dr. Jay Belt, whom Barbara thought the world of and considered not only her doctor but also a friend, for his compassionate care and friendship.

title: Delma Jones
description: December 17, 1933 - July 22, 2026

title: Black Hills Stage 2 fire restrictions in effect due to weather and drought
description: A torch is used to light fire to fuel in burnout operations. Burnouts create fireflies to stop uncontrolled spread of a wildfire.
_full_text:
Burnout operations for Qury Fire
A torch is used to light fire to fuel in burnout operations. Burnouts create fireflies to stop uncontrolled spread of a wildfire. 

The U.S. Forest Service warned residents and visitors of the Black Hills National Forest that it will be entering Stage 2 fire restrictions on Monday, July 27, due to severe fire weather and extended drought.

“These restrictions are in place to protect public safety and natural resources. Violations can result in fines up to $5,000 for individuals and $10,000 for organizations, plus possible jail time,” the service said on Facebook.

According to service’s website, the restriction will take effect on all national forest lands in Bearlodge, Northern Hills, Mystic and Hell Canyon Ranger Districts on the Black Hills National Forest between the state of South Dakota and Wyoming. The restrictions will begin at 12:01 a.m. on July 27.

Stage 2 restrictions prohibit the following:

Building, maintaining, attending or using a fire, campfire, charcoal barbecue or grill, except if using a device solely fueled by liquid or gas that can be turned on and off in an area barren or cleared of all flammable materials within three feet of the device.

Smoking, except in an enclosed vehicle or building.

Welding or operating an acetylene or other torch with open flame.

Using an explosive.

Possessing or using a motor vehicle off national forest system roads, except when parking in an area devoid of vegetation within 10 feet of the motor vehicle.

Though the hot temperatures gave a brief reprieve over the week, the triple-digit weather will be returning in full swing on Saturday, July 25, National Weather Service Rapid City office Warning Coordination Meteorologist Aaron Woodward said.

“We’re going to see temperatures in the upper 90s across much of the area today (Friday), but the heat really turns on Saturday and Sunday,” Woodward said.

He said Saturday will have a heat index value ranging from 100 to 107 degrees, with Sunday following a similar pattern of remaining in the triple digits. Humidity levels ranges from 10 to 20%, along with 20 to 30 mph winds, are predicted this weekend.

“This time of year we can see warm temperatures and hot temperatures,” Woodward said. “I will say seeing the extended string of triple-digit heat is uncommon for this area, although it does happen.”

On top of these conditions, Woodward said there is a threat of thunderstorms with low precipitation, which can result in a dry lightning risk. There will be a red flag warning in effect from noon to midnight on Saturday.

Through collaboration with local fire departments, fire dispatch and emergency management organizations, Woodward said a decision is made about fire restrictions based on the weather, drought conditions and potential fuels in the area. He said with the lack of snow during the winter and continuous dry weather, the Black Hills have been in the thrall of fire season since late February.

Woodward advises the public who may be spending the weekend outdoors to stay cool and hydrated as the temperatures continue to rise.

title: South Dakota universities’ Native American enrollment rises to pre-pandemic level
description: Native American student enrollment at South Dakota public universities has returned to its pre-pandemic level, according to a new report .
_full_text:
Native American student enrollment at South Dakota public universities has returned to its pre-pandemic level, according to a new report.

Black Hills State University in Spearfish had 227 Native American students during the 2025-26 school year, up 49 from 178 the year before. That 28% increase was a major factor in the 6% systemwide growth in Native American students compared to the prior year. 

The university’s student body typically has the highest percentage of Native American students of the six institutions in the system. Urla Marcus, director of the Center for American Indian Studies at the university and a member of the Northern Cheyenne Tribe, said the recent numbers are a sign that new programs are working to recruit and retain more students.

Higher enrollment leads to a “ripple effect,” Marcus added.

“They can go back to their communities and make an impact, set that example that more people are attaining these degrees,” Marcus said.

In 2019, the Legislature required the South Dakota Board of Regents, which oversees the public universities, to develop programs aimed at increasing Native American student enrollment and retention. The board submits a report by July 1 each year detailing activities and progress made.

Systemwide, Native American enrollment decreased during the COVID-19 pandemic and stayed lower for several years afterward despite increases at some universities. 

 072626-nws-sl-enrollment-p1.jpg
A sign marks an entrance to Black Hills State University in Spearfish, South Dakota, on Aug. 28, 2024. 

The Native American percentage of the systemwide student body also dipped below 3% for several years but now stands at 3.2%. South Dakota’s overall population is 9% Native American.

Black Hills State’s latest increase pushed systemwide Native American enrollment to 1,155 — nearly reaching the 1,157 recorded in 2017. Native American enrollment increased this past school year by 16 students at South Dakota Mines and 15 at the University of South Dakota, but decreased by five at South Dakota State University, four at Northern State University and two at Dakota State University.

This is the first year since the pandemic that Native American enrollment decreased at South Dakota State. The university has played a significant role in increasing Native American enrollment within the South Dakota public university system in the last decade. President Barry Dunn, a member of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe, launched the Wokini Initiative in 2017 to recruit, retain and support Native American students. Enrollment of Native Americans at the university grew from 259 in 2017 to a peak of 329 in 2024.

Scholarships and financial aid awarded to Native American students across the state have nearly doubled since the 2022 school year, driven largely by a near doubling in Pell Grants and scholarships from institutions and private foundations.

Black Hills State has not yet recovered its own pre-pandemic Native American enrollment numbers, despite the recent gains. Students at the time of the pandemic, Marcus said, were “very cautious,” and many chose not to enroll outside tribal land, with some opting for tribal colleges instead. Those schools offered incentives that the university did not, such as tuition discounts and supplies.

Between 2015 and 2022, the latest data available from the National Center for Education Statistics, enrollment at Oglala Lakota College on the Pine Ridge Reservation fell by 189 students and at Sinte Gleska University in Rosebud by 103. Sisseton Wahpeton College on the Lake Traverse Reservation gained 55 students over the same period.

As the pandemic receded and tribal college incentive programs ended, Marcus said more students have shown interest in enrolling at Black Hills State. Marcus said the university’s location in the Black Hills, an area of historical and spiritual significance for several tribes, is a draw for students. The school has Native faculty and staff working with the center.

“Students see a lot of opportunities for them to grow and be successful,” Marcus said.

In addition to more targeted recruiting efforts, Marcus said the center has strengthened or created new programs to support students, including mentorship and scholarship programs.

The Native Scholars program is in its third year. Students in the program regularly engage with advisers and the center’s administration, participate in cultural activities and mentor their peers. Graduates receive a stole and star quilt. The program graduated six students last spring and expects to graduate another 13 next spring.

The peer mentor program grew organically before being formalized in recent years, Marcus said. The center pairs upperclassmen with freshmen and sophomores who share similar fields of study and home regions.

“We have a lot of silent leaders in our center,” Marcus said. “These students have taken some years getting closer and closer to graduation. Younger students look up to them, ask them questions and allow upperclassmen to share what they’ve learned and what they’ve stumbled on.”

title: William Henry Young
_full_text:
March 18, 1941 - July 22, 2026

William (Bill) H. Young, 85, of Custer, SD, died July 22 at his home. He was born March 18, 1941 to William & Lorene (Neville) Young in Madison, SD. He grew up on a farm in Winfred, SD, with his brother Mark. In 1952 the family moved to Custer, SD, when his mother became a resident of Sanator for a time. He graduated from Custer High School in 1959, went on to become a multisport athlete at Black Hills State College and graduated in 1963. He also received his Masters of Education from Black Hills State in 1969. In the summer of 1966, he met his wife, Linda Poe, and they were married in September. They had four children.

Bill was a life-long high school math and science teacher and coach, who was loved and respected by his students. He taught three years in Broadus, MT, where he started the wrestling program in 1963; one year in Glendive, MT; two years in Spearfish, SD; seven years in Custer, SD; one year at New England St. Mary's, 21 years back at Custer and five years at St. Thomas More in Rapid City, SD. During that time, he received many awards; Golden Apple Award, Regional Coaching Track Assistant Award, South Dakota Wrestling Hall of Fame (2004), and the Custer High School Hall of Fame (2017). In 2021, the Custer Invitational Wrestling Tournament, which he started in 1970, was renamed the "Bill Young Invitational" to recognize Bill's dedicated service to building the Custer wrestling program.

Bill also enjoyed many summers working for the Forest Service. For several years, he led a trails crew in the Black Elk Wilderness trails system. He spent many summers fighting wild land fires, including being a member of the Helitack crew. Bill was recognized by the state of South Dakota naming "Bill Young Day" on September 25, 2020, for 61 years of outstanding service to the state fighting wild land fires over the span of eight different decades.

Bill retired from teaching in 2004. He continued coaching middle school wrestling at Custer. He also assumed new duties with Chamberlain McColley's Funeral Home and Rocky Knolls Golf Course in Custer.

He was an active member of St. John the Baptist Catholic Church, Knights of Columbus, St. John's Finance Committee, Pringle Fire Department, 1881 Courthouse Museum volunteer, a lifetime member of SD Coaches Association, Custer County Library Board Member, Custer Regional Hospital Board Member, Custer Youth and Alumni Foundation Board Member, and past member of NEA and SDEA.

After his semi-retirement, he enjoyed spending time with family and friends. He especially enjoyed a trip to Italy with his wife and friends from their church in 2011, an all-family trip to Kauai, Hawaii in 2012, a trip to Mexico for their daughter Kathy's wedding in 2014, and an all-family trip to Myrtle Beach, SC, in 2025.

Bill was preceded in death by his parents, sister-in-law Nancy Maynard, son-in-law Stacey Bauer, and niece, Kim (Maynard) Miiller.

He is survived by his wife of 59 years, Linda; children, Tracy Bauer of Rapid City, SD; Christy (Miles) Mettler of Colorado Springs, CO; Kathy Young (Bill Schaefer) of Custer, SD; and Steve (Tara) Young of Sioux Falls, SD; and grandchildren, Austin, Chandler (Olivia) and Logan Bauer; Zachary, Maria (Aric) Kedge, Matthew (Meghan) and Anna Mettler; Jessica (Matt) Goth, Katelyn (Graydon) Fritz and Jordyn Larsen (Kyle Virtue); Will, Jonah, Lucas and Ellie Young; brother Mark Young, Sioux Falls, SD; brother-in-law Frank Maynard, Hot Springs, SD; five great-grandchildren and several nephews.

Christian Funeral Vigil will be held at St. John the Baptist Catholic Church 7:00 p.m., (Catholic Rosary at 6:00pm) Friday, July 31, 2026, with a Mass of Christian Burial at St. John's at 10:00 a.m., Saturday, August 1, 2026, followed by Christian Funeral Committal at Custer Cemetery.

In lieu of flowers, charitable donations can be made to the Pringle Fire Department and St. John the Baptist Catholic Church to be directed toward a new and expanded gathering area.

title: Spearfish man dies from motorcycle crash injuries
description: A Spearfish man died Sunday from injuries sustained in a single-vehicle crash near Spearfish.
_full_text:
A Spearfish man died Sunday from injuries sustained in a single-vehicle crash near Spearfish.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol said the crash occurred around 5:45 p.m. on Saturday, July 25, on Interstate 90 near mile marker 19, 1 mile east of Spearfish.

The patrol did not release the man’s name pending notification of family members.

The patrol said a preliminary crash investigation determined the 56-year-old man, driving a 1995 Harley Davidson, was traveling west on I-90 when he started to lose control of the motorcycle and laid it down. In the process, he became separated from the motorcycle. The driver was taken to a Spearfish hospital before being transferred to a Rapid City hospital, the patrol said. He was not wearing a helmet, according to the patrol.

The man died from his injuries on Sunday, July 26. An investigation into the crash continues.

title: Rapid City Parks and Recreation Director Jeff Biegler announces retirement
description: After serving 13 years as Parks and Recreation director for Rapid City, Jeff Biegler is set to step down on Sept. 18.
_full_text:
After serving 13 years as Parks and Recreation director for Rapid City, Jeff Biegler is set to step down on Sept. 18. 

"It has been an honor and a privilege to serve alongside such a brilliant team of dedicated professionals, all working for the betterment of Rapid City and its residents,” Biegler said in a release from the city. “I am confident the department will continue to do great things under new leadership and wish the staff at Parks and Recreation continued success.” 

 Jeff Biegler
Parks and Recreation Director Jeff Biegler leads the Flood Memorial Walk in 2022 at Memorial Park in Rapid City. The walk was hosted by Rapid City Parks and Recreation, and included speakers from the National Weather Service. 

According to the release, Biegler took on the position of director in December of 2012 and is the longest-serving director across the city's department heads. His career in public service spans 42 years as he’s worked in parks and recreation positions in Michigan, Idaho and California in addition to South Dakota.

As of December 2025, Biegler was making an estimated $162,582 a year as director for Parks and Recreation. 

“Through his many years of dedicated service, Jeff has fulfilled and promoted the department’s mission to make Rapid City a better place to live, work and play,” Mayor Jason Salamun said. “Jeff and his staff effectively manage 1,700 acres of greenway in our city, 10 miles of bike path and over 30 parks, as well as numerous recreation programs and facilities, all for the enjoyment of both community residents and visitors.”

Salamun said a search for a new parks and recreation director will begin soon. Department directors are appointed by the mayor and confirmed by the Rapid City Council. All other personnel decisions, including termination, fall under the mayor.

title: Rapid City Council members scold Star Village owners for failure to meet ‘basic obligations’
description: "I think it's worth saying publicly that this company has repeatedly failed to meet its basic obligations to its residents and to its community, yet it has found the resources to retain professional advocacy when accountability finally arrives," Rapid City Council President Stephen Tamang said about Tzadik Management, a property owner and management company that owns over a dozen properties in the city, including Star Village.
_full_text:
"I think it's worth saying publicly that this company has repeatedly failed to meet its basic obligations to its residents and to its community, yet it has found the resources to retain professional advocacy when accountability finally arrives," Rapid City Council President Stephen Tamang said about Tzadik Management, a property owner and management company that owns over a dozen properties in the city, including Star Village.

This comes after Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun on Tuesday, July 14, held a media advisory announcing the city would demolish 28 garages and sheds in Star Village after Tzadik failed to meet the deadline for a myriad of code enforcement violations.

During its Monday, July 20, meeting, the council unanimously voted to approve three contracts with Ridgeline Construction LLC, MMI LLC and HC LLC for the demolition of structures in Star Village — if Tzadik doesn’t knock down the buildings by Aug. 10. The approval consists of a $133,500 price tag to demolish the structures from Aug. 10-21. Those costs will be assessed to Tzadik. The city said original deadlines for Tzadik to demolish the structures were Nov. 13, 2025 and Feb. 20, 2026.

 Rapid City Council
On Monday, July 20, the Rapid City Council voted to move forward with demolition agreements for 28 structures at Star Village. 

Per previous Journal reporting, Star Village is a low-income housing development under the management and ownership of Tzadik, a Florida company headed up by Adam Hendry. Tzadik purchased Star Village at the end of 2019. The company lists 18 Rapid City properties on its website.

According to the city, Tzadik has racked up an estimated $533,096 in unpaid utility bills and more than $10,000 in code enforcement abatements for Star Village and other properties they own in Rapid City. The bulk of the unpaid utility bills, $344,000, is for Star Village.

Tamang said, "You can't hold certain people accountable that don't have the capacity unless there is a serious public danger. Tzadik management has demonstrated tremendous amounts of capacity. It has the capacity to retain professional advocates. It has the capacity to repeatedly reassure the city that its violations will be corrected, only for those assurances to go unfilled. It has the capacity to advertise, manage public image, use social media to tell a story. It has the capacity to protect someone's interests, but what it has repeatedly failed to do is to use that same capacity to meet its most basic obligations to residents and to this community.”

At the council meeting, Community Development Director Vicki Fisher said Tzadik submitted 18 of the 28 permits needed for demolition after the July 14 press conference.

As of July 23, officials with Tzadik applied for demolition of the remaining structures. Lon Schnittgrund of City Building Services told the Journal the department is in the process of issuing permits to Tzadik for the demolitions.

 Love your neighborhood
On Wednesday, June 10, community members gathered for an event themed, “Keeping Star Village Lit, Keeping Star Village Safe!” 

Council Member Callie Meyer (District 5) followed up on Tamang's comments, saying, "I think it's just good to put on record that these are people who have things like sewage backup in their yards, and you've got people on different blocks and they're sharing water in one house because they don't have running water, and I find that incredibly disturbing."

Star Village residents have described conditions in the neighborhood as “third-world” to the Journal.

Meyer shared data from city staff stating that in the first half of 2025, Star Village reported 105 violent crimes. The Rapid City Police Department said last year the neighborhood has the highest violent crime rates and police calls for service in the city.

Chief of Police for RCPD Don Hedrick concluded the discussion, saying, "I just have to mention that we have just tremendous amounts of problems on these properties, problems we don't have elsewhere."

From previous reporting, in the summer of 2025, there were two murders and a robbery within weeks at Oxford Square Apartments, another Tzadik property. It’s located on East Watertown Street in north Rapid City.

A Tzadik representative declined to comment when reached by the Journal.

title: All smiles at Rhoden election night watch party in Rapid City
description: On Tuesday, July 28, more than 50 supporters of Gov. Larry Rhoden gathered inside Paddy O'Neill's Irish Pub and watched as their candidate faced off against Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden for the Republican nomination in a runoff election.
_full_text:
On Tuesday, July 28, more than 50 supporters of Gov. Larry Rhoden gathered inside Paddy O'Neill's Irish Pub and watched as their candidate faced off against Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden for the Republican nomination in a runoff election.

 Larry Rhoden Watch Party
Over 50 supporters of Gov. Larry Rhoden poured into Paddy O'Neill's Irish Pub in downtown Rapid City on Tuesday, July 28. 

Within minutes after the polls closed, a member of the media cautiously announced that the AP News called the race in Rhoden’s favor.

The Associated Press called the race for Rhoden, a Union Center native, against Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden at 7:08 p.m., just minutes after polls closed at 7 p.m. According to results from the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office, Rhoden is at 71% of the vote to Doeden’s 29% with 561 of 649 precincts reporting, as of 9:25 p.m. Four of Pennington County’s 46 precincts were reporting at 9:25 p.m., showing a percentage split of Rhoden with 72% of the vote and Doeden with 28%. 

 Mike Derby
Sen. Mike Derby-Rapid City, District 34, said he's been a longtime supporter of Gov. Larry Rhoden.  

“We're not done yet. We've got a general election. We still need to move forward. So we're going to take a little time, we're going to rest. We're going to give the people of South Dakota a break from the advertising and everything that's going on,” said Rep. Mike Derby, R-34 of Rapid City, who hosted the event, “but we've got to get the machine put back together and win the general election.”

Derby, a self-proclaimed longtime supporter of Rhoden, said after the four-man June 2 Republican primary election — where Doeden came in first with 31% of the vote, followed by Rhoden at 25% — he felt there was some doubt about Rhoden’s ability to win, but he held his faith.

“I think people had doubts, and it might sound a little overboard for me to say I never had a doubt because I knew the gentleman, I knew the people, I knew the cabinet, I knew who he was doing the media strategy, and really it was an amazing team,” Derby said.

Since neither candidate cleared the 35% threshold statewide to secure the party nomination, they headed for a runoff election, the first in state history.

“I’m very excited with the result, and we had hoped to be in the runoff. That was kind of our goal, was to be in the runoff, and here we are,” Derby said with a grin.

Meade County resident and Rhoden’s neighbor Gary Cammack said that after growing up together, he believes Rhoden is an honest and committed man. 

 Gary Cammack
Union Center resident and Gov. Larry Rhoden neighbor Gary Cammack came to Rapid City's gubernatorial runoff election watch party in support of Rhoden. 

“He was always a very passionate individual. No matter what he was doing, he always went 100% with everything … he's a proven legislator, proven leader and he doesn't promise anything that he can't follow through,” Cammack said.

He continued, saying, “He's never forgotten where he came from, but having said that, he's always been really concerned about the rural areas, concerned about the people that are in agriculture, (made) sure that agriculture had a fair shake, and so those roots have never left him. He's always been good at following through on that.”

After AP News called the election, Cammack said he was going to enjoy time with long-time friends and then go back to work the next day.
