title: Former Rapid City priest among list of naturalized citizens the Justice Department wants to strip of citizenship
description: The Justice Department has moved to revoke the citizenship of 10 naturalized citizens, and one of them is a former Rapid City priest who was convicted of stealing from three Rapid City parishes and of illicit sexual conduct in a foreign place for a case involving a minor.
_full_text:
The Justice Department has moved to revoke the citizenship of 10 naturalized citizens, and one of them is a former Rapid City priest who was convicted of stealing from three Rapid City parishes and of illicit sexual conduct in a foreign place for a case involving a minor.

Marcin Garbacz, 47, is a native of Poland. He became a lawful permanent resident in 2008 and naturalized U.S. citizen in 2014. Garbacz worked as a high school chaplain in the Catholic Diocese of Rapid City between 2012 and 2018, according to court documents. During that time, he stole $260,000 from donations to three different parishes. He deposited some of that money into back accounts and bought items such as gold-plated chalices, bronze statues, a $10,000 diamond ring and a grand piano, according to court documents. Garbacz also secretly recorded a 17-year-old showering during a church trip to Poland.

Garbacz was sentenced in November 2020 to seven years and nine months in federal prison after a jury convicted him of 65 felony counts for the financial crimes. In March 2022, he was sentenced to five years in prison for illicit sexual conduct in a foreign place, which he pleaded guilty to.

The Justice Department claims Garbacz concealed that criminal conduct throughout the naturalization process. He was arrested in 2019, five years after he obtained citizenship. He is no longer a priest.

 Marcin Garbacz (Copy)
Marcin Garbacz 

Per the Justice Department, the government alleges Garbacz, “illegally procured his citizenship by lacking the good moral character required for naturalization, providing false testimony under oath during the naturalization process, and procuring U.S. citizenship through the concealment of material facts and willful misrepresentations.”

Federal law allows a revocation of a naturalized U.S. citizen’s citizenship if the naturalization was illegally procured or procured by concealment of a material fact or by willful misrepresentation.

The government filed the complaint asking for to naturalization revocation on July 6. Garbacz is serving his sentences at Engelwood, a low security federal prison in Littleton, Colorado.

“We refuse to give a free pass to criminals who cheated their way into American citizenship,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “Under this administration, if you defrauded the naturalization process, you will face the full force of the Justice Department. We’ve only scratched the surface — many more complaints are coming.”

The other nine naturalized citizens the Justice Department listed are from Mexico, Pakistan, Cuba and Peru. Garbacz is the only person from Poland and the only person with ties to South Dakota.

The complaints were filed in the Southern District of Florida, Northern District of Georgia, Southern District of Iowa, District of Maryland, Western District of Pennsylvania, Northern District of Texas, Southern District of Texas, District of Utah, and Western District of Washington. Here are those cases, per the Justice Department:

Yoskmaikel Rodriguez Perez (Age 45/Cuba):

Rodriguez Perez, a native of Cuba, became a lawful permanent resident in 2004 and naturalized as a U.S. citizen in 2018. Before obtaining citizenship, however, Rodriguez Perez operated a purported medical clinic and submitted false and fraudulent claims to Medicare in excess of $886,694. Rodriguez Perez later pleaded guilty and was convicted of conspiracy to commit healthcare and wire fraud. On June 18, 2026, the United States filed a four-count denaturalization action in the Southern District of Florida. The complaint alleges that Rodriguez Perez illegally procured his citizenship because he lacked the good moral character required for naturalization given his crime of moral turpitude, unlawful acts, and false testimony under oath during the naturalization process; and because he procured U.S. citizenship through the concealment of material facts and willful misrepresentations.

Ceflo Luviano-Mojica (Age 60/Mexico):

On July 14, 2026, the United States brought a denaturalization action against Ceflo Luviano-Mojica, a native of Mexico, who misrepresented his prior arrest for Carrying a Concealed Firearm and for Grand Theft, for which he spent 30 days in jail. In 1998, Luviano pleaded guilty and was convicted in the Northern District of Georgia of, inter alia, Providing False Information in a Naturalization Application, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 1015. Luviano admitted he had made a false statement both on his naturalization application and during his interview, when he testified under oath that he had never been arrested, charged, or imprisoned for breaking or violating any law. The United States filed a two-count denaturalization action in the Northern District of Georgia alleging that Luviano illegally procured his citizenship by lacking the good moral character required for naturalization and procuring U.S. citizenship through the concealment of material facts and willful misrepresentations.

Urbano Vazquez Ortega (Age 53/Mexico):

On July 10, 2026, the United States brought a denaturalization action against Urbano Vazquez Ortega, who sexually assaulted children while employed as a priest in a Washington, D.C. church. Mr. Vazquez Ortega is a native of Mexico and was naturalized as a U.S. citizen on July 11, 2017. Mr. Vazquez Ortega was charged with and convicted in the Superior Court for the District of Columbia of multiple counts of Second-Degree Child Sexual Abuse. In 2019, Mr. Vazquez Ortega was sentenced to fifteen years in prison and is presently incarcerated. The United States filed a five-count complaint against Mr. Vazquez Ortega to revoke his naturalized citizenship as he committed these crimes before, during, and after his naturalization as a U.S. citizen.

Murtaza Ali (Age 65/Pakistan):

Ali is a native of Pakistan who filed multiple applications for immigration benefits under different aliases until he obtained a grant of an immigration benefit under the alias “Muhammad Iqbal.” Ali, through the grant of the immigration benefit, obtained permanent residency under the alias “Muhammad Iqbal” and thereafter naturalized under this alias in 2009. Following Ali’s naturalization, a fingerprint expert determined that the fingerprints provided with immigration benefits applications filed under the names “Mortaza Ali” and “Muhammad Iqbal” were made by the same person. As a result, the United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas charged Ali with making False Material Statements to an Agency of the United States in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 1001. In 2014, Ali pleaded guilty as charged, admitting that he had filed three separate applications for immigration benefits using three different identities. On July 14, 2026, the United States filed a four-count denaturalization action in the Northern District of Texas alleging that Ali procured his citizenship by committing immigration fraud, engaging in unlawful acts that reflect adversely on his moral character, providing false testimony under oath during the naturalization process, and procuring citizenship through the concealment of material facts and willful misrepresentations.

Jimmy Aguero (Age 51/Peru):

Mr. Aguero repeatedly sexually abused a child prior to naturalizing as a U.S. citizen on October 6, 2015. A jury found Aguero guilty on eight counts of the sexual abuse of a minor, and he was sentenced to ten years of imprisonment. The Department of Justice filed a complaint alleging that Mr. Aguero was statutorily barred from showing that he was a person of good moral character because of his convictions. The Department also alleged that he procured his naturalization by concealment of material facts.

Antonio Alcantara-Ruiz (Age 53/Mexico): On June 23, 2026, the United States brought a denaturalization action against Antonio Alcantara-Ruiz, a/k/a Emiliano Quintana-Gonzalez, a/k/a Antonio Quinn Alcantara. Prior to the naturalization process, Alcantara allegedly purchased identity documents from a fellow Mexican citizen and used those documents to secure a replacement permanent resident card which contained Alcantara-Ruiz’s picture and fingerprint. Alcantara-Ruiz then used the false documents in support of his naturalization. The United States filed a 4-count complaint against Alcantara-Ruiz seeking to cancel his naturalized citizenship.

Omar Cantu-Montalvo (Age 44/Mexico):

Cantu-Montalvo was admitted to the United States in March 1996 and subsequently obtained permanent residence. When he applied to naturalize in July 2005, Mr. Cantu-Montalvo stated in his application that he had never committed a crime or offense for which he had not been arrested. He later repeated that claim during his naturalization interview. His application was approved, and he naturalized in December 2005. In April 2016, however, Mr. Cantu-Montalvo pleaded guilty in federal district court to conspiracy to possess with the intent to distribute more than 5 kilograms of cocaine—a conspiracy he joined in April 2005, just a few months before he applied for naturalization. For his crime, the court sentenced Mr. Cantu-Montalvo to 100 months of imprisonment followed by a five-year term of supervised release. On June 15, 2026, the United States filed a complaint seeking to revoke Mr. Cantu-Montalvo’s citizenship because he illegally procured his citizenship as he was unable to demonstrate good moral character in light of his commission of a controlled substance offense. Additionally, the government claims, Mr. Cantu-Montalvo is subject to denaturalization because he willfully misrepresented or concealed his offense while seeking United States citizenship.

Francisco Montano (Age 59/Mexico):

Montano was legally admitted to the United States in February of 1987, but when he applied to naturalize in 1997, Montano failed to divulge that he had sexual abused a child during the mandatory five-year good moral character period prior to the naturalization process. Montano was later convicted in a Texas State court of two counts of Aggravated Sexual assault and four counts of Indecency with a Child that occurred during the five-year period. As Montano should not have been naturalized, the United States filed a complaint on June 30 in the Southern District of Texas to revoke his illegally-obtained citizenship.

Martin Garcia Cardie (Age 60/Mexico): On July 6, 2026, the United States filed a Complaint in the District of Utah seeking the denaturalization of Martin Garcia Cardiel. Garcia Cardiel was admitted to the United States in December 2000 and subsequently obtained permanent residence. When he applied to naturalize in 2011, Mr. Garcia Cardiel wrote in his application that he had never committed a crime for which he had not been arrested. He further indicated in his application that he had never given false or misleading information to any United States government official while applying for any immigration benefit. He naturalized in October 2011. However, in 2022, a petit jury in the State of Utah convicted Mr. Garcia Cardiel of nineteen counts of aggravated sexual abuse of a child based on acts the defendant committed in 2007. Garcia Cardiel was sentenced to consecutive terms of imprisonment of 15 years to life.

title: Box Elder man charged with attempted murder after Rapid City shooting
description: A Box Elder man is in custody for allegedly shooting a man in Rapid City.
_full_text:
A Box Elder man is in custody for allegedly shooting a man in Rapid City.

The Rapid City Police Department said officers were called around 3:10 a.m. on Monday, July 27, to the area of Van Buren Street and Dilger Avenue on a report of an individual who’d just been shot. Officers found a man walking in the roadway, suffering from a gunshot wound. Police told the Journal the man is in his 30s. Officers administered first aid and medics took the man to the hospital.

 IMG_0835.jpeg
The Rapid City Police Department detained multiple individuals at this residence after a shooting in the early morning hours on Monday, July 27. 

An investigation determined residents at apartments in the 700 block of North Seventh Street had been involved in the incident, police said. Officers detained several individuals at the location, including 23-year-old Mario Moran of Box Elder.

Officers arrested Moran on suspicion of possession of a controlled substance after finding methamphetamine on him. After interviews with witnesses, police determined Moran was the alleged shooter and arrested him on suspicion of attempted murder.

South Dakota court records show Moran is charged with aggravated assault-bodily injury with a dangerous weapon. That charge is in the alternative, meaning he couldn’t be convicted of both the assault and attempted murder charges. He was set to appear in court at 10 a.m. on Tuesday, July 28.

 North Seventh Street
Mario Moran, 23, is in custody on an attempted murder charge for a shooting in Rapid City on Monday, July 27. He was arrested at a residence North Seventh Street after police were called to the nearby intersection of Dilger Avenue and Van Buren Street. 

Court records show Moran’s most recent arrest on state charges, before the shooting, was in June 2025 on drug and weapons charges. He ended up pleading guilty to possession of a controlled substance in August 2025 and was sentenced to three years in prison, all suspended. The sentence also included a 180-day sentence at the Pennington County Jail, with credit for 105 days served and the rest suspended.

 Van Buren and Dilger
The Rapid City Police Department said officers were called around 3:10 a.m. on Monday, July 27, to the area of Van Buren Street and Dilger Avenue on a report of an individual who’d just been shot. Officers found a man walking in the roadway, suffering from a gunshot wound. 

The 2025 arrest violated his supervised release in a federal case. He was arrested in July 2022 and ultimately convicted of federal possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. He was sentenced to nine months in prison in August 2025. Federal prison records show he was released in June of this year.

An investigation into the shooting incident continues, police said. The Pennington County Jail online roster remains down after a cyberattack on the county, so his bond was unavailable.

title: How a strategic security degree prepares leaders for the age of AI
byline: Sponsored content by Mary McHugh, Brand Ave. Studios contributing writer
description: Artificial intelligence can analyze enormous amounts of information in seconds. It can identify unusual patterns, flag potential threats and generate insights faster than ever before.
_full_text:
nau stock img 6.25.26

Artificial intelligence can analyze enormous amounts of information in seconds. It can identify unusual patterns, flag potential threats and generate insights faster than ever before.

But when a corporate executive receives a credible threat, a workplace violence incident unfolds or an organization faces a major security crisis, technology alone cannot determine the best course of action. These situations still require experienced professionals who can interpret information, weigh competing risks and exercise sound judgment when the stakes are high. Human leaders are best equipped for determining what information matters, how risks should be assessed and what actions should be taken to safeguard people, organizations and critical assets.

“In a rapidly changing world, organizations need professionals who can evaluate risk, interpret complex information and make sound decisions under pressure,” said Barbara Burke, Ph.D., dean of Henley-Putnam School of Strategic Security at National American University. “Technology will continue to evolve, but the need for leaders who can protect people, organizations and critical assets remains constant.”

Security leadership in an AI world

While many discussions about AI focus on technology and cybersecurity, the impact of AI reaches far beyond digital systems.

Organizations increasingly face challenges involving misinformation, workplace violence, executive threats, insider risk, reputational attacks and rapidly evolving crises. AI can help identify patterns and process information, but organizations still need professionals who can evaluate intelligence, understand human behavior, communicate risk and lead effective responses.

Today’s security professionals work in a wide range of roles, including executive protection, corporate security, intelligence analysis, investigations, emergency management and public safety leadership.

As AI becomes more sophisticated, the ability to transform information into action may become one of the most valuable skills employers seek.

Many security professionals begin their careers in military service, law enforcement, executive protection, private security, emergency response or related fields.

At Henley-Putnam, students study intelligence management, counterterrorism, and strategic security and protection management, or SSPM, a discipline that combines executive protection, protective intelligence, investigations, risk management and organizational security into a broader leadership framework.

Rather than focusing solely on how threats emerge, students learn how executive protection teams conduct advance work before major events, how protective intelligence professionals identify potential threats before they escalate and how security leaders evaluate risks that could impact employees, facilities, operations or organizational reputation.

They also develop skills in intelligence analysis, investigations, crisis preparedness and strategic communication — capabilities that help organizations navigate uncertainty and make informed decisions during high-pressure situations.

“AI can rapidly analyze data and identify patterns, but strategic security ultimately depends on professionals who can turn information into action, assess risk and make decisions when people’s lives and business operations are on the line,” Burke said.

Preparing for what’s next

The future of security will not belong to technology alone. It will belong to professionals who understand how to combine technology, intelligence, leadership and human judgment to protect people and organizations.

For more information, visit national.edu/schools/henley-putnam.

title: Here’s what Pennington County operations look like 3 weeks after cyber incident
description: For more information on the Rapid City PD tip line, go to https://shorturl.at/ShAIX. For Pennington County, go to https://shorturl.at/Gya1r.
_full_text:
Crime tip submissions for Rapid City, Pennington County
For more information on the Rapid City PD tip line, go to https://shorturl.at/ShAIX. For Pennington County, go to https://shorturl.at/Gya1r. 

A little over three weeks ago Pennington County was affected by a cybersecurity incident that caused several public-facing county offices to “look for innovative ways to continue serving the public,” the county said in a release. As of Monday, July 27, officials said the county is still responding to the incident as law enforcement investigates.

At this time, no action is required from members of the public. If the investigation determines that protected personal information was affected, impacted individuals will be notified directly.

According to Monday’s press release from the Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office, all county offices remain open and operational, although there are a few services that remain limited and processing times may be longer than usual as systems are safely restored.

“County Information Technology staff, together with state and federal partners, continue to make progress in the investigation and remediation effort. Because the investigation remains active, we cannot comment on specific technical details. While we understand the public's desire for additional information, protecting the integrity of the investigation remains a priority. We appreciate the patience and understanding of our residents, as well as the extraordinary efforts and flexibility of County employees throughout this response,” the press release stated.

Below is a list of offices and their services:

Treasure’s Office

Motor Vehicle
The Treasurer's Office is once again processing motor vehicle transactions and accepting all forms of payment. Due to ongoing system limitations, the office currently has four to six processing stations available at any given time, compared to nine under normal operations. Transactions are being processed, but customers should expect longer wait times.

To help expedite service, only transactions that have been reviewed and determined to be complete will be moved to the processing line.

All completed transactions from last week that required next-day pickup are expected to be distributed by Wednesday of this week.

All vehicle registration renewal requests received by mail have been processed and mailed back to customers as of Thursday, July 23.

Residents are encouraged to use the self-service kiosks or the State's online portal at My605Drive.sd.gov whenever possible for eligible registrations and other transactions. Those services remain fully operational and can help reduce wait times.

Real Estate
At this time, there are no new updates regarding the queue system. Restoring this functionality remains a high priority for County Information Technology staff; however, access has not yet been restored.

The queue system will be reevaluated once both the real estate and motor vehicle systems are fully operational. Until then, customers will be served on a first-come, first-served basis.

Payments accepted are cash, checks, or credit cards With proper ID

Auditor’s Office

Early voting is available at the Pennington County Administration Building today until 5 p.m. Tomorrow is Election Day, and voters should report to their assigned polling location to cast their ballots.

The office is currently unable to process lien payments.

Register of Deeds

The Register of Deeds Office is now processing requests for vital records. Records also remain available online through VitalChek.com or by calling 605-773-4961.

The office is accepting real estate recordings; however, those documents cannot be fully processed until systems are restored.

Planning & Zoning

The department continues providing its normal services, although some processes may take longer than usual.

Board of Commissioners

County Commission meetings will continue as scheduled.

Due to the cybersecurity incident, meetings may not be livestreamed. They will be recorded and posted as soon as systems allow.

County emails remain unavailable, but county phone lines are operational.

title: Red Ribbon Skirt Society opens space honoring MMIW victims at Minneluzahan Center in Rapid City
description: A new addition to community services at Minneluzhan Senior Citizens Center is a space dedicated to Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women (MMIW).
_full_text:
A new addition to community services at Minneluzhan Senior Citizens Center is a space dedicated to Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women (MMIW).

"Families really need to have a place where they can go and spend time in prayer and to be able to heal. A big part of it for us is to make sure that those girls aren't forgotten," said Lily Mendonza (Lakota), founder of the Red Ribbon Skirt Society.

The space opened to the public on July 20, after months of planning by the center and Mendoza.

The Red Ribbon Skirt Society is a local nonprofit, based in the Black Hills. It serves victims' relatives and loved ones, striving to bring a sense of healing.

 Lily Mendoza
Red Ribbon Society founder Lily Mendoza speaks during the opening of a space honoring Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women inside the Minneluzahan Senior Citizens Center on Monday, July 20. 

Mendoza previously owned a bookstore, the Bird Cage, in downtown Rapid City, which closed in 2023. The store held a space like the one at the senior center, with dresses and items that brought awareness of MMIW.

Since the closure, she’s had to store many of the items of remembrance away in boxes.

"People can come in and put names on that (red dresses) and this is especially for those that are still missing. Families haven't had closure, so where do they go visit? They don't have a grave site to go visit," Mendoza said.

According to the Bureau of Indian Affairs, a 2016 study by the National Institute of Justice found that more than four in five American Indian and Alaska Native women have experienced violence in their lives, including 56.1% who have experienced sexual violence. Overall, the study found that 1.5 million American Indian and Alaska Native women have experienced violence in their lifetime.

As of July 22, the South Dakota Missing Persons Clearinghouse reports there are 99 American Indian and Alaskan Native missing persons cases in the state.

Mendoza said she has acquired so many items since starting the organization in 2016 there isn’t enough space to display them all.

 Red shirt and dresses
A display of red dresses and clothing items highlights regional MMIW cases at the Minneluzhan Center in Rapid City. 

Among the many dresses, shirts and obituary cards on the walls is a shirt memorializing Sahela (Different Cheyenne Woman) Sangrait-Dubray, a Cheyenne River Lakota woman, who was allegedly murdered on Aug. 11, 2024 on Ellsworth Air Force Base. She was 21 years old. 

Sangrait-Dubray's body was found on March 4, 2025, outside of Hill City, 40 miles from Box Elder. Quinterius Charles Chappelle, a 24-year-old airman, is charged with first-degree murder in federal court. 

A star quilt, also displayed, was donated by the family of Cole Brings Plenty (Lakota). The 27-year-old was reported missing on April 1, 2024. He was found dead four days later in a wooded area of Johnson County, Kansas — about 40 minutes from Indian Nations University, where he was a student.

 Star Quilt
A star quilt donated by Cole Brings Plenty's family is on display at the Red Ribbon Skirt Society’s MMIW memorial space inside the Minneluzahan Senior Citizens Center in Rapid City. 

He was most well-known for his role as Pete Plenty Clouds in the “Yellowstone” prequel series “1923.” He had also been featured in “Into the Wild Frontier” and “The Tall Tales of Jim Bridger.”

Kansas law enforcement said there is no foul play suspected in Brings Plenty’s death, but the family continues to advocate for further investigation. 

Mendoza said the community can come in and pray, contribute names of MMIW victims by posting them on red dresses, give obituary cards and even donate to the nonprofit.

"I plan to be down here in my little office area. I do plan to be down here at least every day," Mendoza said.

The center is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m.

title: Trailhead Scholars offers college savings accounts for qualifying Custer, Hermosa kindergarteners
description: Families of qualifying Custer and Hermosa kindergartners will have a chance to start a college savings account through a new program, Trailhead Scholars.
_full_text:
Families of qualifying Custer and Hermosa kindergartners will have a chance to start a college savings account through a new program, Trailhead Scholars.

Trailhead Scholars, offered by Black Hills Area Community Foundation, opens a $500 529 college savings account for each eligible Custer School District kindergartner who qualifies for free and reduced-price meals. The 529 account is provided at no cost to each student’s family. Funds in the account grow tax-free until the student graduates from high school or completes their GED.

BHACF announced the Trailhead Scholars program on July 28. To become eligible for the Trailhead Scholars program, families must complete the Custer School District’s free and reduced-price meal application by August 25.

After families qualify for free and reduced-price meals, they will receive a yellow envelope in the mail instructing them to claim the $500 for their child. BHACF will open, own and manage the savings account through My529, a secure, nationally recognized savings platform. Parents are encouraged to open their own My529 account alongside the Foundation’s to contribute to their child’s college savings.

The Trailhead Scholars program is made possible by support from a local donor. After the student graduates from high school or earns their GED, the funds in their 529 account can be used for tuition, fees, and books, at any accredited college, university, or technical school. When a Trailhead Scholars student graduates from high school or completes their GED, BHACF will contact the family to begin the process of directing the funds to a post-secondary school within two years. Any unused funds will be recycled back into the program to support future Trailhead Scholars students.

The Custer School District 16-1 serves about 900 students across Custer County, Fall River County, and Pennington County in southwestern South Dakota.

“This (Trailhead Scholars) program is about opening possibilities for every child in the Black Hills. Postsecondary education, whether at a college or trade school, sets families and children up for success. Trailhead Scholars is starting off in Custer and Hermosa, and we hope to expand this program to kindergartners throughout the Black Hills with support from local donors,” said Chris Huber, president and CEO of the Black Hills Area Community Foundation.

Research shows that children with a college savings account, even a small one, are three times more likely to enroll in education after high school, BHACF said in a news release. A small head start like the Trailhead Scholars gift is an early incentive that can offer students and families a tangible reason to envision themselves continuing their education.

"Our mission in the Custer School District is to educate every student to their full potential, and the Trailhead Scholars program aligns perfectly with that goal. We are incredibly grateful for this generous support, which breaks down obstacles and creates new opportunities for our kindergarten students, showing them that college or trade school is truly accessible to everyone. We encourage all eligible Custer and Hermosa families to complete their meal applications by August 25, so they don't miss out on this terrific opportunity,” said Tim Frederick, Custer School District Superintendent of Schools.

This year’s Trailhead Scholars program is fully funded. BHACF is actively seeking donations to continue and expand the program. Donors can contribute to Trailhead Scholars to help support more kindergartners in the Custer School District or throughout the Black Hills.

BHACF is a 501(c)(3) public charity that invests $8 to $15 million in Black Hills communities each year. Based in Rapid City, BHACF awards grants to nonprofits, facilitates donor gifts, and leads programs such as Trailhead Scholars that strengthen the region. Anyone who would like more information about Trailhead Scholars or BHACF is encouraged to contact BHACF staff at 605-718-0112.

description: A house in Spearfish was apparently struck by lightning on Wednesday, July 29, before lighting on fire.
_full_text:
A house in Spearfish was apparently struck by lightning on Wednesday, July 29, before lighting on fire.

Upon arrival, firefighters confirmed there was an active fire in the attic.

At about 5:36 p.m., the Spearfish Fire Department was paged out to the area of Seventh and Elgin streets for a report of a house that was struck by lightning with smoke coming out of the roof, according to the department.

“Firefighters made an aggressive interior attack, and although efforts were impeded by difficult access to void spaces behind knee walls, the fire was contained to the attic and roof structure of the home,” the department said in a social media post.

All residents and pets were safely evacuated from the home with no injuries to civilians or firefighters on scene.

The Spearfish Fire Department was assisted by the Deadwood Volunteer Fire Department, Whitewood Volunteer Fire Department, Spearfish Police Department, Spearfish Fire Auxiliary, Whitewood Voluntary Fire Department Auxiliary Lawrence County Emergency Management, Black Hills Energy, and MDU.

title: Oglala Lakota Nation Fair returns for 40th annual celebration after 2024 shooting on powwow grounds
description: PINE RIDGE — "Still here. Still Strong," is this year's theme for the 40th annual Oglala Lakota Nation Fair, Rodeo and Horse Races after officials canceled last year’s event to honor a community member who was shot on the powwow grounds in 2024.
_full_text:
PINE RIDGE — "Still here. Still Strong," is this year's theme for the 40th annual Oglala Lakota Nation Fair, Rodeo and Horse Races after officials canceled last year’s event to honor a community member who was shot on the powwow grounds in 2024. 

 grass dance
Junior men's grass dancers compete on June 8, 2024 during the Oglala Lakota Veterans Wacipi at the Pine Ridge powwow grounds. 

“We took last year off to heal from the events that happened, but this year we expect this to be one of the largest ones so far,” said Valeire Adams, public relations coordinator for the Oglala Sioux Tribe. 

On Aug. 2, 2024, 57-year-old Francis "Tom" Thunder Hawk was shot at the 39th annual powwow and died two days later at Monument Health Rapid City Hospital. His Sioux Funeral Home obituary shows he left behind 12 children, 20 grandchildren and eight siblings.

 Honoring
An honoring for Francis "Tom" Thunder Hawk was held Sunday night, July 26, during the Oglala Nation Fair, Rodeo and Horse after his death that morning. 

A suspect was arrested immediately after the shooting, but the shooter's name has not been made public.

Thereafter, the Oglala Sioux Tribal Council voted to cancel the 2025 event, a major economic driver for the tribe. This year, Adams said security has been increased with several security teams, an on-site ambulance and additional entry-point restrictions.

“The significance of this, this is the largest gathering of everybody, in terms of dance prizes offered. The rodeo is an INFR (Indian National Finals Rodeo). The horse races bring in teams from everywhere,” Adams said.

She said this year's event is also dedicated to Yvonne Jane “Tiny D” DeCory and Chris Eagle Hawk, two community members who passed away.

Highlighted events:

Thursday, July 30 - Social dance at powwow grounds at 7 p.m. A flag raising and ground blessing was held on Thursday morning.

Friday, July 31 - Rodeo pageant at 8 a.m., rodeo events at 6 p.m. and powwow grand entry at 7 p.m.

Saturday, Aug. 1 - The community parade begins at 10 a.m., grand entry starts at 2 p.m., Toby Classic Skateboarding at 3:30 p.m. and rodeo events at 6 p.m.

Sunday, Aug. 2 - Powwow grand entry starts at 1 p.m. and a memorial honor run for Tom Thunder Hawk will begin at 5 p.m.

 Flyer
Flyer for the 40th annual Oglala Lakota Nation Fair list of events. 

“I lived off the rez over 20 years, and I always came back to Oglala Nation. It's a part of our culture in terms of each of these aspects that we embody,” Adams said. “It's always been a positive, grounding feeling. There’s nothing like being among your own people. There's so much history in that. Dancers have come here for years. Many of the best drum groups come here. With this being the largest event on the reservation, that's significant.”

Day pass tickets are $15 with weekend passes at $40. Tribal members who show their tribal I.D are discounted $5.

Free camping, water and showers are provided, as well as two meals daily. A military flyover will be conducted on Saturday, Aug. 1.

title: Pennington County works to improve emergency access and safety on dead-end roads
description: One of the Pennington County Commission's most important responsibilities is protecting the health, safety, and welfare of our residents while planning responsibly for future growth. As our county continues to develop, we must also ensure that our road network can safely serve the people who live here today and those who will call our communities home in the future.
_full_text:
One of the Pennington County Commission's most important responsibilities is protecting the health, safety, and welfare of our residents while planning responsibly for future growth. As our county continues to develop, we must also ensure that our road network can safely serve the people who live here today and those who will call our communities home in the future.

One area receiving increased attention is development along dead-end roads. Current fire code generally limits a dead-end road to serving no more than 40 dwelling units (Subdivision Regulations Ordinance - Section 904 & Zoning Ordinance - Section 204) unless additional access is provided. This standard exists for an important reason: during emergencies such as wildfires, severe weather, or other disasters, emergency responders need reliable access to homes, and residents need dependable evacuation routes if a single roadway becomes blocked.

Many neighborhoods throughout the county were legally developed before these standards were adopted. This effort is not about penalizing existing property owners or requiring immediate changes. Instead, it is about understanding where long-term opportunities may exist to improve public safety as our communities continue to grow.

To assist with that effort, the County has partnered with consultant Avid4 to conduct a comprehensive review of dead-end road systems throughout the county. The study will evaluate existing road networks, identify areas where emergency access may be limited, and help prioritize locations where additional planning or future improvements could provide the greatest public safety benefit. Currently, Avid4 has done the preliminary analysis and is working on the prioritization.

The recommendations from this study will help guide future discussions with property owners, developers, fire districts, and other stakeholders. Potential solutions will vary depending on each area's unique circumstances and may include future roadway connections, emergency access routes, or other mitigation strategies where appropriate. The study will also position the County to pursue grants and other funding opportunities should infrastructure improvements be identified.

This study represents the first step in a thoughtful, long-term planning process. By understanding where challenges exist today, we can make informed decisions that improve emergency response, support responsible growth, and help ensure that residents have safe and reliable access to their homes for years to come.

title: Rapid City Area Schools schedules bond info meetings in the months leading up to vote
description: In about three months, on Nov. 3, voters in the Rapid City Area Schools District will decide on a $107 million bond referendum. In the interim, the district is holding several informational sessions to inform the public.
_full_text:
In about three months, on Nov. 3, voters in the Rapid City Area Schools District will decide on a $107 million bond referendum. In the interim, the district is holding several informational sessions to inform the public.

“Our goal is to make sure that accurate information is accessible to everyone across the community. We know that people have questions, and we want to make sure that we can answer them directly,” said RCAS Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson.

The tax levy will be dedicated to school improvements and construction. The district's most recent bond attempt came in 2020 — with a price tag of $189.5 million. It accrued a vote of 56%, short of the required 60%. Voters in the district have not passed a bond since the 1976. In April, the RCAS school board voted to place the bond on the ballot.

RCAS bond informational session schedule
Thursday, Aug. 6, Virtual (Zoom), 7–8 p.m.

Thursday, Aug. 27, South Park Elementary 6–7:30 p.m.

Thursday, Sept. 10, Virtual (Zoom), 7–8 p.m.

Thursday, Sept. 24, Valley View Elementary, 6-7:30 p.m.

Thursday, Oct. 15, Virtual (Zoom), 6–7:30 p.m.

Thursday, Oct. 29, Stevens High School Theatre, 6–7:30 p.m.

 The district said virtual meeting links will be shared prior to each online session.

Thompson said each of the informational sessions will include a presentation explaining the bond referendum, information on why the projects were chosen, a breakdown of each project, financial and tax information, time to answer questions and resources to take home.

“We want to make sure that everyone leaves these sessions feeling informed, regardless of how they ultimately vote on the proposal,” Thompson said.

 Jami Jo Thompson
Rapid City Area Schools District Superintendent Jami Jo Thompson speaks with media on Thursday, July 30, about upcoming bond referendum informational sessions scheduled over the next few months. 

The bond, if approved, will finance school improvements, including constructing, renovating and improving school facilities, including but not limited to:

HVAC energy and efficiency upgrades at Horace Mann Elementary, Meadowbrook Elementary, and North Middle School ($32 million)

Safety and security upgrades at Black Hawk, Grandview, Knollwood, Southwest Middle, and West Middle schools ($3 million)

Renovation and an addition to South Park Elementary ($12 million)

Construction of a new elementary school on the Parkview property ($40 million)

Safety and security improvements at Stevens High School ($20 million)

Furnishing and equipping the improvements

Paying the costs of issuance for the bonds

RCAS Chief Financial and Operations Officer Coy Sasse said the district worked to prioritize projects and be responsive to the community’s concerns during the formation of the upcoming bond, which is $82 million less than the failed 2020 bond. The reduced amount shifts the tax burden from about $.85 per $1,000 of taxable value to about $.49 per $1,000 of taxable valuation. If the proposed bond passes, a homeowner with a house at a taxable value of $400,000 would owe an estimated $196 a year for the levy, about $16.33 a month. Under the 2020 bond, that cost would have been $340 a year, or $28.33 a month.

“A couple of the areas in particular that we heard great concern on last time around were the overall ask, or the the amount of the bond, and then the tax impact,” Sasse said. “As we have worked through this process, one of the focus points has been how do we get this package to a point where we're hitting all of our critical needs, or the majority of our critical needs, and we are lowering the tax impact and the burden on our property holders and our stakeholders in this city, and we feel like the package that we're presenting does a really good job of combining all those interests.”

 Coy Sasse
Rapid City Area Schools District Chief Financial and Operations Officer Coy Sasse on Thursday, July 30, speaks with media about an upcoming bond referendum. Sasse’s bruises come from practicing martial arts. 

In the event the bond doesn’t pass, Sasse said the district’s needs won't change, but the timeline of the projects and the costs associated with them will.

“It means that students wait for better, more secured facilities. It means that we all, as stakeholders and property holders of this community, will pay more for these facilities and these projects. As we push projects into the future, one thing we all know is they don't ever get cheaper; they get more expensive,” Sasse said. “The path to getting these projects accomplished will be much longer, much windier, and much more expensive as we move into the future.”

More information about the bond can be found at rcas.org/bond-information. The webpage includes a tax calculator, where voters can see an estimate on how much the bond would cost them.

 RCAS CFO Coy Sasse
Rapid City Area Schools District Chief Financial and Operations Officer Coy Sasse speaks on Thursday, July 30, about a school bond referendum.

title: Rapid City police arrest Pine Ridge man after foot pursuit
description: Police arrested a Pine Ridge man on burglary and assault charges after a brief foot pursuit.
_full_text:
Police arrested a Pine Ridge man on burglary and assault charges after a brief foot pursuit.

The Rapid City Police Department said officers were called around 12:50 a.m. on Thursday, July 30, to an apartment in the 200 block of East Knollwood Drive for a report of a man who had forced his way into the apartment before threatening the resident with a handgun.

An investigation led to the arrest of Aaron Brown, 18, on suspicion of first-degree burglary and aggravated assault.

Police said when officers arrived on scene the resident told them the suspect, later determined to be Brown, had just fled the residence. While searching the area, police located Brown and attempted to make contact, but he instead allegedly ran off.

After a brief foot pursuit, officers detained Brown. A witness positively identified him as the burglary suspect, and a search of the path he took while running turned up a handgun, police said.

Officers took Brown to the Pennington County Jail. Online jail records remain down as the county deals with a cybersecurity incident.

title: Steel Across America visits Mount Rushmore National Memorial
description: New York and local first responders along with Mount Rushmore crowds gathered in front of the Sculptor Studio at Mount Rushmore as the 9/11 steel beam rode in on Tuesday, July 28.
_full_text:
Steel Across America at Mount Rushmore
New York and local first responders along with Mount Rushmore crowds gathered in front of the Sculptor Studio at Mount Rushmore as the 9/11 steel beam rode in on Tuesday, July 28. 

Nearly a quarter-century after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, a piece of the World Trade Center steel arrived in the Black Hills as a physical reminder of a national promise to never forget.

The Tunnel to Towers Foundation’s Steel Across America on Tuesday, July 28, brought a steel beam recovered from the World Trade Center to one of the most historic landmarks in the United States — Mount Rushmore. It was the 26th stop on a nationwide tour in honor of the 25th anniversary of 9/11.

 073026-nws-steelacrossamerica-p7.JPG
The tour began on May 2 at Lower Manhattan, New York City, and will end on Sept. 11, at Brooklyn New York. The four month long journey is planned to cover 10,500 miles, 21 states and 35 cities. During the tour stops visitors are able to view the 9/11 steel, which is 21 feet and nine inches long and weighs 16,900 pounds, up close and connect with and learn from individuals who lived through the tragic events. 

The tour began on May 2 at Lower Manhattan, New York City, and will end on Sept. 11, in Brooklyn, New York. The four-month-long journey is planned to cover 10,500 miles, 21 states and 35 cities. During the tour stops visitors are able to view the 9/11 steel, which is 21 feet and 9 inches long and weighs 16,900 pounds, up close and connect with and learn from individuals who lived through the tragic events.

As dozens of community members lined up to touch and pray over the steal beam, while speaking with retired firefighters who helped during the tragic event, Stephen Siller Jr. looked at the event with a smile on his face.

Siller’s father, Stephen Gerard Siller, was one of the many brave men and women who raced into the World Trade Center to help rescue survivors. Siller was only 9 months old when his father went in and never came back.

“I say the South Tower, that’s where my father was when he lost his life,” Siller said. “He’s one of about 1,000 men whose bodies were never recovered that day. Who he is, is engrained in that steel.”

On Sept. 11, 2001, Siller’s father Stephen just finished his shift and was on his way to play golf with his brothers when he got a report of a plane hitting the North Tower of the World Trade Center. Siller said his father immediately gathered his things and raced to go help those in need.

 073026-nws-steelacrossamerica-p19.JPG
Nearly a quarter-century after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, a piece of the World Trade Center steel arrived at Mount Rushmore National Memorial on Tuesday, July 28, as a physical reminder of a national promise to never forget. 

“My father, a FDNY firefighter, was actually off duty, he loved being a fireman, it was his passion in life,” Siller said.

Siller said his dad drove his truck to the entrance of the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, but it was closed for security purposes.

“He parked his car outside of the tunnel, called my mother and brought about 75 pounds of gear and ran two miles to the South Tower of the World Trade Center, where he ultimately lost his life,” Siller said. “His actions that day inspired the Tunnel to Towers Foundation.”

The Tunnel to Towers Foundation was created by Siller’s mother and his late father’s seven siblings. Siller said it initially started as a 5K race to honor those who made the ultimate sacrifice and the families who will be forever impacted.

Siller said the foundation has since grown and now not only honors the past but also honors current active duty members and first responders.

Celebrating his one-year retirement anniversary from a 43-year career between the New York Fire Department and Police Department, Joseph LaPointe recalled when he first heard about the incident back on Sept. 11, 2001.

LaPointe said he was off duty working a side job that day when a delivery guy came into the store saying a plane hit the World Trade Center. LaPointe said he figured it was a small private plane that accidentally hit the tower, but when another person came in to inform him of the destruction, he knew the situation was much more dire than he realized.

It was one of two times in history where the entire city of New York had a total recall of first responders, LaPointe noted — the other time was in July 1945 when a B-25 bomber crashed into the Empire State Building. LaPointe could only describe the harrowing event as “surreal.”

“Every member of the FDNY (Fire Department of New York City) was pulled back and responded and spent days down there into weeks, months, in rescue recovery,” LaPointe said. “You know there was a point where you’re rescuing people but then it’s not (a rescue situation). It’s similar to when they have earthquakes, it gets to a point where you don’t think you’re going to have any survivors.”

LaPointe said the work didn’t end there, after rescue and recovery was completed there was time spent preparing funerals and ceremonies for the ones that lost their lives from the incident.

“This was the first time in history for the FDNY where we weren’t able to recover our members, because more than half the people were never found and that’s what makes this steel so sacred, because the souls and the spirit of those people … We’ve seen many of family members go up, and it’s a really powerful moment when they get up and get a chance to touch the steel.”

LaPointe said he lost many good friends during the incident and many more who are still tackling the mental and physical scars they acquired since that day.

After the viewing, attendees were directed to a ceremony where they heard a performance of the national anthem by the Shrine of Democracy Chorus, followed by an invocation and blessing of the steel delivered by Father Andrzej Wyrostek. LaPointe then formally introduced the steel beam, led the audience in a moment of silent reflection and oversaw the retirement of colors.

 073026-nws-steelacrossamerica-p5.JPG
The Tunnel to Towers Foundation’s Steel Across America on Tuesday, July 28, brought a steel beam recovered from the World Trade Center to one of the most historic landmarks in the United States — Mount Rushmore. 

Jennifer Carpenter, superintendent of Mount Rushmore National Memorial, delivered remarks on the significance of welcoming the Steel Across America tour to Mount Rushmore, and of the ideals that have defined the American spirit across generations.

“Mount Rushmore National Memorial honors the leaders and ideals that have shaped our nation,” Carpenter said. “We are honored to welcome the Tunnel to Towers Foundation’s Steel Across America tour and help preserve the memory of those whose courage and sacrifice continue to inspire Americans.”

 073026-nws-steelacrossamerica-p2.JPG
The Tunnel to Towers Foundation was created by Stephen Gerard Siller’s mother and his late father’s seven siblings. Siller said it initially started as a 5K race to honor those who made the ultimate sacrifice and the families who will be forever impacted. 

Siller gave Carpenter a steel flag, a gift bestowed to those who demonstrate honorable dedication to the work and mission of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation.

"There is no more fitting backdrop for this steel than the faces of the presidents who shaped this nation carved into the mountain behind us," Siller said. "Each of those leaders understood that freedom is not free, and that the greatness of America has always been built on the backs of those willing to give everything in its defense. The heroes of September 11th gave everything. Steel Across America is our promise to each and every one of them that this Foundation, and this country, will never stop honoring their sacrifice."

 PHOTOS: Steel Across America at Mount Rushmore
Steel Across America is a national tour in honor of the 25th anniversary of 9/11. On Tuesday, July 28, the steal beam relic from the twin towers visited Mount Rushmore National Memorial.

title: Flappin’ jacks: Minneluzahan Senior Center, Troop 605 invite you to a pancake breakfast
description: Minneluzahan Senior Center, in partnership with Troop 605, invites the community to enjoy a delicious pancake breakfast while supporting programs that enrich the lives of local seniors and veterans.
_full_text:
Minneluzahan Senior Center, in partnership with Troop 605, invites the community to enjoy a delicious pancake breakfast while supporting programs that enrich the lives of local seniors and veterans.

The fundraiser will be held from 9 a.m. to noon on Sunday, Aug. 9, at Minneluzahan Senior Center, 315 N. Fourth Street in Rapid City.

Guests will enjoy pancakes, sausage, juice, and coffee for a $10 suggested donation, Minneluzahan said in a release. All proceeds will directly support the expansion of Minneluzahan Senior Center's programs and services for seniors and veterans throughout the community.

"This is more than a pancake breakfast — it's an opportunity for our community to come together in support of those who have contributed so much to Rapid City," Laura Armstrong, Rapid City Council liaison for Minneluzahan Senior Center, said in a release. "Every breakfast purchased helps us expand meaningful programs that promote connection, wellness, arts, culture, history, and lifelong learning."

 Minneluzahan Senior Citizen Center (Copy)
The Minneluzahan Senior Citizen Center is located at 315 N. Fourth St. in Rapid City. 

The event is made possible through a collaboration with Troop 605, whose Scouts continue to demonstrate their commitment to community service through volunteerism and civic engagement, the center said.

“The partnership also highlights the value of intergenerational connections, bringing together youth, seniors, veterans, families, and community members to share a meal, build relationships, and strengthen the fabric of our community,” the center said.

Minneluzahan Senior Center is also seeking additional volunteers to assist with the event. Civic groups, businesses, churches, service clubs, and other local organizations are encouraged to lend a hand, whether by helping prepare and serve breakfast, greeting guests, or assisting with cleanup. Events like this provide meaningful opportunities for organizations and individuals of all ages to volunteer side-by-side while supporting a shared community mission.

Everyone is welcome to attend. Bring your family, friends and neighbors for a hearty breakfast while making a meaningful investment in programs that serve seniors and veterans and foster intergenerational engagement throughout Rapid City.

For more information or to volunteer, please contact Minneluzahan Senior Center at 605-394-1887.

title: Sarah June Wilkinson
_full_text:
June 28, 1926 - July 17, 2026

Sarah June "Sally" Wilkinson, 100, passed away peacefully on July 17, 2026. She was lovingly honored during her funeral service and celebration of life on July 23, 2026.

Sally was born on June 28, 1926, on a farm outside of Gregory, South Dakota, to John and Lydia (Jenner) Burr. On June 12, 1949, in Dallas, South Dakota, she married Edward Carr Wilkinson. They shared 57 wonderful years of marriage until Ed's passing in 2006.

Together, Sally and Ed made their home in Rapid City, South Dakota. After the heartbreaking loss of their oldest daughter, Barbara Ann Wilkinson, in 1976, they opened their hearts and home to Shaun and Laura, raising them with the same unconditional love and devotion as their own.

Sally worked for Wells Fargo for more than 20 years, where she was known for her dedication and strong work ethic.

Family was Sally's greatest joy. She had an adventurous spirit, a wonderful sense of moxie, and a zest for life that inspired everyone around her. She loved dancing at weddings and family celebrations, cheering on her favorite football teams, taking trips to Deadwood, canning pickles, making homemade salsa, and creating cherished memories with those she loved.

Sally is survived by her children, Paula Wilkinson Smith and her husband Steven; Craig Wilkinson; Catherine "Sam" Swaney; Shaun Wilkinson and his wife Amy; and Laura Borders. She was also blessed with 13 grandchildren, Michelle (Corey), Brooke (Patrick), Lee (Stephanie), April (Hans), Dusty (Chelsea), Andy (Megan), Kelly (Violeta), Miranda (Colby), Toni, Mirissa, Kayla, Kyle, Christina, 21 great-grandchildren and 7 great-great-grandchildren. She was preceded in death by her husband, Edward Wilkinson; her daughter, Barbara; her daughter-in-law, Alexandra Wilkinson, her parents, John and Lydia Burr and her 5 brothers and 4 sisters, Edwin Burr, Christina Burr, John Burr, Elsie Burr, Ruth Burr, Magdalena Burr, Willis Burr, Fritz Burr, Arthur Burr.

Phyllis Ann Weaver passed away on July 25, 2026, in Summerset, S.D.

She was born October 5, 1936, in Rapid City, S.D., the youngest child of William and Ruth Anderson. She attended high school in Rapid City and got her teaching degree from Black Hills State University. She married Jack Weaver on December 26, 1957, and had two sons.

Phyllis is survived by sons, Daniel Weaver of Denver, Colo., and Donald Weaver and family of Alamogordo, N.M.

She was preceded in death by her parents; and husband; as well as by her brothers, Wayne Anderson and Donald Anderson; and her niece, Barbara Lewis.

She taught elementary school for over 50 years in Wyoming, Montana, South Dakota, and New Mexico. Phyllis enjoyed going to church services and functions. She liked baking and was considered very good at it, as well as crafts like pottery, macrame, and embroidery. She enjoyed music, from classical to Elvis Presley. Phyllis loved animals and her pets were always an important part of her life.

Funeral services will be held at Trinity Lutheran Church, 402 Kansas City Street in Rapid City on Wednesday August 5, 2026, at 10 a.m., with visitation beginning at 9 a.m. She will be missed by all who knew her.

Burial will follow at Mountain View Cemetery.

title: Lynne Marie Carlson

title: Edward Aaron Himrich
description: January 13, 1934 - July 29, 2026
_full_text:
January 13, 1934 - July 29, 2026

It is with heavy hearts and cherished memories that we announce the passing of Edward Aaron Himrich, who departed this life peacefully on July 29, 2026, at the age of 92 from late-onset Parkinson's Disease. His wife and daughter were by his side as he passed away. Born on January 13, 1934, in Selby, South Dakota, Ed was the beloved son of Edward and Emily Himrich. He was one of nine children who grew up working on a farm operated by his family. Ed was preceded in death by his parents, several siblings, and his sons, Mark Himrich and Matthew Himrich.

Ed's journey was marked by service, dedication, and a profound impact on all who had the privilege of knowing him. He was a devoted husband to Frances Kae Manke, whom he married on August 11, 1957, after a long courtship that included many letters while they were separated. Their union, a testament to a lifelong commitment to love and partnership, spanned an incredible 69 years, filled with unwavering support and shared joys as they raised their three children, Mark, Connie, and Matthew.

A proud graduate of Selby High School, Ed attended South Dakota State University for one year before answering the call to serve his county. From 1953 to 1955, he served as a military police officer in the army, stationed in Georgia, Louisiana, and Texas. This experience instilled in him a sense of duty and discipline that would guide his future endeavors and leadership.

Following his military service, Ed completed his education at the University of South Dakota and later graduated from the University of Minnesota's Dental School in 1960. Many people admired Ed's strong work ethic and when asked about attending three different colleges and where he learned the most, his answer was, "I learned the most growing up in a hardworking family of nine kids on the farm". Armed with skill and compassion, he embarked on a career in dentistry, initially practicing in Perham, Minnesota before establishing the Himrich Dental Clinic in Custer, South Dakota in 1962. For more than 25 years, he served his community with dedication, earning a reputation as a compassionate and skilled dentist who cared deeply for his patients, many of whom drove distances to receive his care.

Ed's commitment to his community extended far beyond his professional life. As an active member of the Custer Community Church since 1962, he served in numerous roles, including on the Board of Trustees and as Church Moderator. His leadership and generosity were also evident through his involvement with the Jaycees, the Rotary Club, the Custer Golf Club, and the Custer Community Hospital where he served as a Board member for many years. Notably, he was highly responsible for the construction and opening Colonial Manor Skilled Nursing Facility, demonstrating his dedication to the betterment of his community.

A man of many passions, Ed found joy in hunting, fishing, and golfing, pursuits he lovingly shared with his sons and grandsons. In the fall, his main hunts were for pheasants and deer. For many years, in both spring and fall, he went to Three Lakes Camp in Saskatchewan, Canada, always sharing this trip with family and friends.

He and Fran also delighted in travel with friends and family, creating countless memories and stories to share. Their destinations included Mexico, Australia, Great Britain, and four trips to Europe, including attending the 2006 Winter Olympics in Turin, Italy. They took five trips to Hawaii which included a six-week retirement celebration in 1989 where they hosted family and friends on the beautiful island of Maui.

In 1990, Fran and Ed became snowbirds, spending their winters in Arizona City, AZ. They purchased two properties and for seven years, they rented a condominium at a golf course. During those years, Ed designed and had a house built on Paradise Lake. He was instrumental in creating and chairing the committee to obtain the title to Paradise Lake and helped form the Paradise Lake Association and write their bylaws. He and Fran spent every winter in that house until they sold it in 2025. In the summer of 2025, their doctor advised them that they needed assisted living care. They moved to Valdosta, Georgia to be near their daughter Connie and son-in-law, Mike.

Ed's kindness, generosity, and wisdom left an indelible mark on the lives he touched. Quick with a friendly joke and always ready to share his knowledge, he was a beacon of warmth that touched many lives.

Ed is survived by his cherished wife, Fran, their daughter Connie and her husband Michael Porcaro, his daughters-in-law Lorraine Himrich, and Tammy Allen (Troy), his brother John Himrich, and sisters, Millie Carmen and Mavis McGill, along with numerous nieces and nephews. His legacy continues through his grandchildren: Aaron Himrich (Anna), Galen DeReu (Kyle), Alexander Keintz (Alexa), Cameron Keintz, Adam Himrich (Kourtney), and Haley Himrich, as well as seven great-grandchildren (Mackenzie, Emmy, and Marlee Himrich; Adaleigh, Matthew, and Karson Himrich; Quinn Keintz) who will grow up hearing stories of his remarkable life.

Donations in memory of Ed Himrich can be made to the Custer Community Church or the Custer Care and Rehabilitation Center. A service will be held at Custer Community Church, planned for September 12, 2026, at 11:00 a.m.

title: ‘Our system is very secure’: Rapid City officials address wastewater cyberattack
description: Rapid City said a recent cyberattack targeted one of the city’s lift stations, which are part of the city’s wastewater system.
_full_text:
Rapid City said a recent cyberattack targeted one of the city’s lift stations, which are part of the city’s wastewater system.

In a Friday, July 31, release, the city said officials “discovered the attempt quickly and precautions were taken to protect the system.”

The city said water and wastewater infrastructure systems were never in jeopardy and assured residents the city’s water supply remains safe and protected.

“We continually take steps to ensure the continued security and reliability of our water and wastewater systems,” Rapid City Public Works Director Mike Theis said in the release. “We want to assure residents our city water system remains safe and we are continuing to remain vigilant in monitoring for cyberattacks across city systems.”

Working with federal agencies

The city said it’s working with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and other federal agencies. CISA issued a nationwide alert on Thursday, July 30, saying the agency has seen a “significant increase” in cyber threat actors targeting programmable logic controllers in water and wastewater systems. Programmable logic controllers are industrial computers used to automate machinery and processes, according to manufacturer Rockwell Automation.

During a press conference on Friday that featured Theis, Rapid City Information Technology Director Jim Gilbert and Rapid City Reclamation Superintendent Jeremy Casteel, Casteel said the wastewater lift station is part of the city’s sewage collection system.

“A lift station is a low point in the city. All the wastewater flows to that low point, and then there's pumps that pump it out to another gravity section, and then it flows by gravity to the wastewater plant,” Casteel said, before adding — and emphasizing — the water system wasn’t targeted. “So it was not the water system; it was actually the water reclamation wastewater system.”

Casteel said had the attack been successful, one problem could’ve been an overflow of sewage out of the station if pumps were turned off.

 080126-nws-cyber-water-p1.JPG
From left, Rapid City Reclamation Superintendent Jeremy Casteel, Rapid City Public Works Director Mike Theis and Rapid City IT Director Jim Gilbert discuss a cyberattack on Friday, July 31, at City Hall. 

Theis, when asked if people should worry about the city’s water system, said, “Our system is very secure, and again, it's the work that Jim and his team have done with training our employees that has helped make that happen. It's the security that they've set up, but there has been no risk to our water sewer systems. So our system is very safe, and it's because of the diligence that we've taken ahead of events like this to make sure that we know what to do.”

Gilbert said someone with the water department reported suspicious activity on a programmable logic controller that was running the lift station.

“We were … able to come to the conclusion that our measures that we have in place were adequate at that time to ensure the safety of the water,” Gilbert said, “and we took additional measures as was pointed out by our partners.”

Gilbert noted the difference between information technology (think email) and operational technology, like the systems that run a lift station pump.

Gilbert said cyber criminals test systems all over the country, “So the idea that it was targeted at Rapid City is probably not accurate. It was targeted at a known issue or suspected issue, and they just cast a really wide net because it doesn't cost them anything to to send out. It's just like spam.”

CISA urged water and wastewater system operators to remove publicly exposed programmable logic controllers and other operational technology from the internet “as soon as possible.”

“Threat actors targeting exposed (programmable logic controllers) have modified passwords to lock out operators and disconnected the PLCs by changing their IP addresses. This activity has resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations,” CISA said.

Asked about actions taken by the city, Gilbert said, “I’m not going to get into the specifics about how we secure our environment. Those lift stations were, it's fair to say that they were cellularly connected, and we are taking the appropriate steps to address those issues as put out by CISA.”

Attackers likely foreign

Gilbert said the attack “certainly” didn’t originate in the United States. The CISA alert came on the heels of the state of Minnesota reporting a coordinated cyberattack against operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems on July 26 and 27.

Minnesota officials said an investigation into the attack continues, but noted in a Thursday update, “At this time, there are no active requests from Minnesota communities for residents to modify their drinking water use.”

The New York Times reported U.S. officials and investigators believe Iran is likely behind the Minnesota attack.

The FBI and Environmental Protection Agency said in an alert also issued Thursday that at least seven states have reported similar incidents, “and some of that activity degraded water operations.” Problems from the incidents reported to the FBI have included loss of pressure and flooding.

“Pressure loss in water systems could potentially allow untreated groundwater to seep into pipes,” the FBI and EPA said.

Gilbert said he’s limited in what he can say when asked if the FBI is involved in the Rapid City case, but noted, “It's always fair to say that if we mention CISA, they are in touch with those federal partners that are important.”

The incident comes as Pennington County continues to recover from a cyberattack reported around the July 4 holiday that’s left county employees without email, while some county services are altered or unavailable. Gilbert said the attacks are not related.

 Gilbert asked about Pennington County cyberattack
Rapid City IT Director Jim Gilbert is asked if the cyberattack against a city wastewater lift station is related to a cyberattack against Pennington County.
