title: Applications open for fall Deadwood Fund grants
description: Applications are being accepted through Oct. 1 for the next round of the Deadwood Fund grant program. The Deadwood Fund grant program encourages restoration or rehabilitation of historic properties by individuals, organizations, or public agencies.
_full_text:
Applications are being accepted through Oct. 1 for the next round of the Deadwood Fund grant program. The Deadwood Fund grant program encourages restoration or rehabilitation of historic properties by individuals, organizations, or public agencies.

Grant applications must be for work starting no earlier than Jan. 1, 2027. Grant application forms are available online at history.sd.gov/preservation/fundingopportunities.aspx. Grants will be awarded in amounts ranging from $1,000 to $25,000. The grant amount must be matched on at least a dollar-for-dollar basis by non-federal and non-state sources. Nonprofit organizations will be allowed to use in-kind services for one half of their match.

The Deadwood Fund grant program is funded by a portion of the gaming revenue generated in Deadwood that is earmarked by state law for historic preservation projects throughout the state. The grant funds are distributed by the South Dakota State Historical Society.

The Deadwood Fund Grant program awards projects annually, with two application deadlines on Feb. 1 and Oct. 1. The first round of 2026 applications were awarded to properties in Lake City, Zeona, Tabor, Custer, Canton, Mitchell, Alcester, and Madison counties, with projects totaling $95,000. In Custer County, the Camp Bob Marshall cabins received $15,000 for a roofing repair project.  

For more information about the South Dakota State Historical Society’s Deadwood Fund grant program, contact the State Historic Preservation Office at the Cultural Heritage Center, 900 Governors Drive, Pierre, SD 57501-2217, call 605-773-3458 or contact shpo@state.sd.us.

title: Experts: Cyberattack on Pennington County likely by foreign adversary
byline: BART PFANKUCH South Dakota News Watch
description: Based only on the little information released by authorities so far, two cybersecurity experts said it is likely that a malicious foreign entity is behind the recent cyberattack that crippled communications and other computer-based systems in Pennington County government.
_full_text:
Based only on the little information released by authorities so far, two cybersecurity experts said it is likely that a malicious foreign entity is behind the recent cyberattack that crippled communications and other computer-based systems in Pennington County government.

Two federal agencies, meanwhile, have recently warned state and local governments across the U.S. that cyberattacks are increasingly likely, and that such attacks are likely to originate in Iran, China or Russia.

On July 5, Pennington County announced that a "cybersecurity incident" had occurred and affected parts of the county's computer network. The county shut down public access to government services for a day and has since embarked on a major multi-agency investigation. The county continues efforts to bring back communication and other computer-based systems.

County officials said critical county services such as the sheriff's office, courts, 911 dispatch and jails have remained operational since the incident. Several county functions, such as computer-based communications, internet access and providing record-keeping and registration services to the public, were slowed or otherwise affected by the incident and response.

 2026-07-28 Line at Pennington office.jpeg
A line of about three dozen people waited to obtain in-person services from the Treasurer's Office at the Pennington County Administration Building in Rapid City, S.D., on July 28, 2026. 

"Unfortunately, there's not a lot I can say because it's an ongoing investigation," Pennington County State's Attorney's Office spokeswoman Katy Urban told News Watch. "If anyone's personal information has been compromised, we will contact them directly as required by state law."

Elements of the cyberattack point to an adversarial foreign government as the responsible party, said John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, a Sturgis-based company that is an industry leader in cybersecurity.

Strand told News Watch in an interview that cyberattacks on American government entities typically originate from one of two sources: international organized crime groups that seek money from victims or international adversaries that either seek intelligence on U.S. networks and systems or intend to disrupt daily life in America.

Since county officials have not discussed any demands for ransom from the cyberattacker, it is more likely that a foreign adversary of the U.S. is behind the attack, possibly Iran, China or Russia, Strand said.

The New York Times on July 30 quoted anonymous state and federal sources in an article indicating that Iran is the likely culprit of a major cybersecurity attack that sought to disrupt water systems in more than 30 communities across Minnesota in late July. The Times said federal officials were concerned the cyberattacks could be a new salvo by Iran in its ongoing war with the United States.

 2026-07-28 Pennington admin building.jpeg
Pennington County offices in Rapid Valley, S.D., remained open on July 28, 2026, though some services were being provided more slowly than usual. 

A more aggressive cyberattack could not only disrupt critical services in the U.S. but could interfere with systems that keep people safe, Strand said.

For example, a cyberattacker could contaminate or limit access to drinking water, send sewage to places it shouldn't go, disrupt medical or prescription drug information or even affect safe operation of traffic lights, he said.

"The biggest concern that I have is a cyberattack that leads directly to a loss of life or multiple people losing their lives," Strand said.

Both governments and private industry should expect more cyberattacks in the future, said Bryce Austin, a cybersecurity expert and the CEO of TCE Strategy, a Minnesota-based firm that provides cybersecurity protection.

The "one-two punch" of cyberattacks in South Dakota and Minnesota within the same month is concerning but not overly surprising, he said.

Several signs point to cyberattacks by Iran, which may be trying to make a statement as it continues to battle the U.S. in war, Austin said.

 2026-07-28 Pennington TV screen.jpeg
A television that was offline at the Pennington County Administration Building in Rapid City, S.D., on Tuesday, July 28. 

"I think we’re cannon fodder in the Iran war," he said. "It's like they're trying to send a message that they can attack us from halfway around the world."

Strand, who launched his family-run company in his basement near Deadwood in 2008, has grown the firm to 160 employees who conduct 950 security assessments annually across the world.

He complimented Pennington County on how it has handled the security breach so far but said it would be a "tragic mistake" if the county doesn't release a full accounting of the attack and its response at some point.

"Just trying to hide it and bury it is almost always the wrong answer," Strand said. "We better get used to it because this is the new normal."

title: Hideaway Hills homeowners ask SD Supreme Court to reconsider sinkhole decision
description: A few weeks after the South Dakota Supreme Court ruled the state is not liable for the plight of Hideaway Hills in Black Hawk, the homeowners are trying again.
_full_text:
A few weeks after the South Dakota Supreme Court ruled the state is not liable for the plight of Hideaway Hills in Black Hawk, the homeowners are trying again.

On July 9, the court delivered a unanimous opinion that the state’s role as the mineral rights owner doesn’t constitute public use or make it liable for the unstable ground the neighborhood was built on. On Thursday, July 30, the attorneys representing Hideaway Hills homeowners filed a petition asking the Supreme Court to rehear the case.

“The class action lawsuit seeks to hold the state responsible for its ineffective attempts at remediation after closing the gypsum mines that supported a for-profit cement company,” the homeowners’ legal representation said in a press release.

The request for rehearing is based on the court’s “failure to acknowledge that the state’s remediation work was the direct cause of current and ongoing damage to surface owners of land and homes at Hideaway Hills.” The court’s opinion also misapplied the “public use” standard, according to the filing.

The homeowners argued the property is being used for "public use,” and the state is responsible for its integrity. The Supreme Court said that’s not the case and applied its “use by the public test.”

“Under the public use test, South Dakota citizens and the public do not have the right to use the mining rights retained by the state or to appropriate any of the gypsum should the state ever decide to mine gypsum from this location in the future,” Justice Janine Kern wrote in the court’s opinion.

Kern also wrote the state’s prior mining operations were for proprietary and commercial use, not public use.

Hideaway Hills was completed around 2005 on top of an old, underground gypsum mine for which the state retains mineral rights. Issues began to arise in 2008, with residents noticing foundational issues like cracking and settling in the walls and basements of their homes. Later that year, small sinkholes began to open.

Those issues reached a crisis point in April 2020 when a large, 30-foot-deep sinkhole opened up on East Daisy Drive in Hideaway Hills, forcing 13 homes to be evacuated. The subdivision is currently home to 150 homeowners and the 13 evacuated homes remain vacant.

 Abandoned
A sign on the porch of 6903 East Daisy Drive in Hideaway Hills on Monday, July 27, reads, “Abandoned like #hideawayhillsmine.” The home is one of 13 that were evacuated when a large sinkhole opened up in April 2020. 

Although the state, developer, homebuilders and realtor who sold the properties knew about the mine underneath the surface before the notorious sinkhole sunk in, the homebuyers did not.

The land was first mined in the early 1900s by Dakota Plaster, which supplied the state’s cement plant with gypsum, a component used to control the speed at which concrete hardens. The underground mining activities weren’t fully documented, but it appears the company mined for almost 30 years, per court documents.

US Gypsum bought the mine in 1930. Because the state didn’t have a state mine inspector from 1926 to 1936, there are no records on the company’s mining activities during those years. A private individual purchased the property in 1945 and lived in a house on it until the late 1980s. Hills Materials strip mined the property in 1946, supplying over 2 tons of gypsum to the state’s Cement Plant and over 10 tons of the material to Iowa. The Cement Plant purchased the land in 1985 and strip mined it throughout the 1980s and 1990s. The state claims it did not mine underground, and the homeowners’ experts agreed there’s no documents showing the state mined underground.

After the state mined on the surface, 16 acres of the land were backfilled, sloped and reseeded. Part of that process included using gypsum to backfill areas. The homeowners argue the state did not properly reclaim the land because gypsum dissolves when exposed to water, creating piping through the soils, which allows more water to enter the subgrade and leads to further instability.

 Mailboxes
Tall weeds grow around mailboxes on East Daisy Drive in Hideaway Hills on Monday, July 27. In the background, a door to the garage of an abandoned house sits open. 

The state sold the land in 1994 but retained the mineral rights. The man who bought it, Raymond Fuss, later transferred it to his son Larry Fuss. The younger Fuss knew about the mine, and when developer Bryon Kuchenbecker approached him in 2000 about turning the pastureland into a residential community, Fuss suggested a manufactured home park because he was concerned about the underground mine. Kuchenbecker first submitted an application to the Meade County Planning Commission for a manufactured home park, but later changed his plans and went forward with a standard subdivision. Fuss sold the property shortly after for $250,000. A disclaimer in the property agreement showed Kuchenbecker acknowledged “there may be excessive rock, underground cavities, foundations and junk underground,” and Fuss sold the property as-is with no guarantee it was suitable for any development.

Kuchenbecker went ahead with development, discovering “several large underground voids while scraping the land and digging utility trenches,” per the Supreme Court opinion. He filled in the holes and continued on. He contracted with real estate agent Ron Sjodin on an exclusive listing basis to sell the lots to individual homebuilders, who were informed of the underground mine and purchased the lots as is. Sjodin represented the homebuilders in the sales to homebuyers, who were not informed of the mine.

South Dakota Searchlight reported multiple lawsuits against Meade County, the land’s developers and the real estate agent who represented the homebuilders were dismissed.

Homeowners have also reached out to governor candidates — including current Gov. Larry Rhoden, who recently won the Republican runoff and is headed for the general election ballot to face Democrat Dan. Ahlers — about if they’ll help the residents.

Rhoden said his staff is looking into what the options are and if — or how — the state can help.

“I have zero information about what our options might be. That’s what we’re going to do, is see,” Rhoden said.

Ian Fury, Rhoden’s campaign manager and member of the governor’s executive team, said the day the South Dakota Supreme Court ruling came down, Rhoden instructed his team to look into what the options are.

Ahlers issued a statement that read, in part, “We need to work with these families, local leaders, and other stakeholders to find a fair path forward that helps make this situation right. Whether through legislative action, targeted assistance, or other solutions, we have a responsibility to stand with South Dakotans when they face extraordinary circumstances.”

 Sinkhole progression
Left: A spring 2020 photo courtesy of Dan Austin shows the fresh sinkhole that opened up in April 2020 in Hideaway Hills. Right: A photo of sinkhole on July 27, 2026, by Mike Brownlee, Journal staff. The sinkhole has progressed in size over the past six years.

title: Stop sign violation in Rapid City leads to 4 arrests, seizure of drugs and guns
description: Four people are in custody after police tried to pull over a SUV that ran a Rapid City stop sign.
_full_text:
Four people are in custody after police tried to pull over a SUV that ran a Rapid City stop sign.

According to the Rapid City Police Department, police saw a silver SUV fail to stop at the intersection of Anamosa Street and North Seventh Street. The SUV then pulled into the parking lot of Hainesway Apartments at 1314 Atlas St., “nearly striking another vehicle” that was making its way through the parking lot.

Police pulled the SUV over, and it stopped in front of 1330 Atlas Street, also a Hainesway building. When the vehicle stopped, the driver and two passengers jumped out and ran. One passenger stayed inside the vehicle. She was identified as 21-year-old Daiondra Tyon, of Oelrichs, and police arrested her on suspicion of possession of a controlled substance.

Police said they found methamphetamine and associated paraphernalia in the vehicle, along with a loaded pistol magazine.

Two of the people who ran away were connected with a nearby apartment, police said. After getting a search warrant, police entered the apartment and found 22-year-old Cylis Chipps, of Rapid City, 20-year-old Damon Milk, of Rapid City, and “a number of drug(s) and firearms items.” Police allege Chipps was the driver and Milk was one of the passengers. Along the path the runners took toward the apartment, police found two handguns.

The other passenger who ran away is at large. A spokesperson for the department said, “it appears we are still working to determine the identity of the second fleeing passenger.”

Chipps was arrested on suspicion of obstruction, possession of a firearm with a prior felony drug conviction, possession of a controlled substance, possession of drug paraphernalia, driving without a valid license, careless driving and a stop sign violation. Court records show Chipps was convicted in December 2023 of possession of methamphetamine and sentenced to three years of probation and a five-year suspended prison sentence. His probation is that case runs through April 7, 2027. In March 2024, he was convicted of grand theft of a firearm and sentenced to two years of probation and a two-year suspended prison sentence. His probation in that case concluded on April 9 of this year.

Milk was arrested on suspicion of obstruction, possession of a firearm with a prior felony drug conviction, possession of a controlled substance and on an existing bench warrant. Court records show Milk was convicted in February of possession of methamphetamine and impersonation to deceive law enforcement. He was sentenced to two years of probation and a 93-day suspended jail sentence with 87 days time served.

Police also arrested 55-year-old Tanya Bettelyoun, who was also inside the apartment, on suspicion of a controlled substance and an existing bench warrant in a pending 2022 methamphetamine possession case. She was not involved in the vehicle situation.

title: Man found dead in West Boulevard, police investigating as ‘unattended death’
description: A man was found dead on Sunday, Aug. 2, in the West Boulevard neighborhood of Rapid City, police said.
_full_text:
A man was found dead on Sunday, Aug. 2, in the West Boulevard neighborhood of Rapid City, police said.

The Rapid City Police Department said officers were dispatched to the intersection of West Boulevard and Saint Charles Street for a report of an unresponsive man lying in the grass. The man was “obviously deceased.”

Police didn’t observe any signs or trauma or other foul play, but an autopsy has been scheduled in order to determine the man’s cause of death and the investigation continues.

title: Crews battle apartment complex fire in Mission
description: Mission Volunteer Fire & Rescue said crews put out a fire involving two apartment units at Sunrise Apartments in Mission.
_full_text:
Mission Volunteer Fire & Rescue said crews put out a fire involving two apartment units at Sunrise Apartments in Mission.

Firefighters arrived around 5:35 p.m. on Saturday, Aug. 1, at the 700-numbered block of apartments and found heavy fire pushing from two apartment units, along with smoke coming from the roof and adjoining apartment units. Information indicated that the block was abandoned, the department said in a social media post.

 080426-nws-mission-p1.jpg
Fire damages an apartment complex in Mission on Saturday, Aug. 1. 

With limited personnel and the fire spreading, crews searched the adjoining apartment units before transitioning to a defensive strategy, which pulled all crews back from the building for safety, the department said.

The Valentine (Nebraska) Volunteer Fire Department responded with an engine, aerial ladder, and manpower to supplement the Mission crews. At the height of the incident, both the Mission and Valentine departments had aerial master streams in service, prompting the City of Mission Maintenance Department to boost municipal water pressure to support firefighting efforts, Mission Volunteer Fire & Rescue said.

 080426-nws-mission-p2.jpg
Mission Volunteer Fire & Rescue said crews put out a fire involving two apartment units at Sunrise Apartments in Mission. 

Firefighters remained on scene throughout the evening, mopping up and managing hotspots with the assistance of a backhoe from the city’s maintenance department. The last fire department unit was back in service at 10:09 p.m. on Saturday, the department said.

No injuries were reported by the department.

Agencies that responded to this incident include Mission Volunteer Fire & Rescue, Valentine (Nebraska) Volunteer Fire Department, Rosebud Sioux Tribe Ambulance Service, Mission Police Department, Todd County Sheriff’s Office, Rosebud Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services, City of Mission Maintenance Department, and Cherry-Todd Electric.

 080426-nws-mission-p3.jpg
With limited personnel and the fire spreading, crews searched the adjoining apartment units before transitioning to a defensive strategy, which pulled all crews back from the building for safety, the department said.

title: Sioux Falls woman dies in motorcycle crash near Rochford
description: A woman died in a motorcycle crash near Rochford.
_full_text:
A woman died in a motorcycle crash near Rochford.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol said the Sioux Falls woman, 67, was a passenger in a 2025 Canam Spyder RT that crashed 5 miles west of Rochford at South Rochford and Seven Hills roads.

The patrol said around 11 a.m. on Saturday the driver of the Spyder, a 72-year-old man from Sioux Falls, was traveling on South Rochford Road near Seven Hills Road when he failed to negotiate a curve. The Spyder left the road and rolled.

The passenger died from her injuries, the patrol said. The driver was taken to a Rapid City hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

The patrol did not release the driver and passenger’s names pending notification of family.

Both were wearing a helmet, the patrol said. An investigation into the crash continues.

title: Florence May Orr
description: July 2, 2026
_full_text:
July 2, 2026

Florence May Orr, 97, passed away at the Poudre Valley Hospital in Ft. Collins, Colorado, on July 2, 2026. She was born on July 7, 1928, in Coalmont, CO to Anson Lafette Mahan and Effie Estella Chedsey Mahan. Florence lived in Coalmont, Walden, and Laporte, Colorado during her youth; and in Ephraim, Utah, Rapid City, South Dakota, Zapata, TX and Fort Collins, CO, thereafter. She and her husband, Howard, raised their family in Rapid City, SD. Inurnment will be held at the Grandview Cemetery in Fort Collins at a later date. Condolences may be expressed at goesfuneralcare.com.

title: Rapid City police teams up with Cody Two Bulls once again for school supply drive
description: The Rapid City Police Department is hosting its annual “Fill a Patrol Car with School Supplies” effort, and the department is once again teaming up with Backpacks & Baseball founder and Citizen Honor Award recipient Cody Two Bulls, of Oglala.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Police Department is hosting its annual “Fill a Patrol Car with School Supplies” effort, and the department is once again teaming up with Backpacks & Baseball founder and Citizen Honor Award recipient Cody Two Bulls, of Oglala.

Two Bulls, a recent graduate of Mahpíya Lúta High School, has been collecting school supplies and baseball supplies for students in need since his freshmen year of high school. Two Bulls was honored this year by the Congressional Medal of Honor Society in Washington with a Citizen Honor Award for his efforts.

This year’s drive will be held on Wednesday, Aug. 5, from noon to 6 p.m. at both Rapid City Walmarts. The partnership started when Rapid City Police Lt. Tim Doyle saw Two Bulls' Facebook post about the drive and threw the department's support behind the effort.

 Two Bulls
Cody Two Bulls, of Oglala, at a press conference on Tuesday, Aug. 4, ahead of a school supply drive. 

“For the past several years, we’ve been honored to partner with Cody as he works to garner school supplies for area students in need,” Rapid City Chief of Police Do

n Hedrick said in a statement. “It’s inspiring to see a young member of our community work so hard to put the needs of others first, and we’re excited to support him as he does everything he can to help ensure other students have the gear they need to succeed in the classroom.”

Just last year, the drive netted about 400 backpacks filled with supplies. Some were distributed at a baseball clinic Two Bulls hosted in Oglala. Others went to the Rapid City Police Department Community Outreach Team, which distributed them to Rapid City youth.

Jamie Kirsch of the outreach team said the bulk of the backpacks will go to Two Bulls, who will then distribute them on the Pine Ridge Reservation. The outreach team will keep the rest on hand to provide to Rapid City kids who need them.

 Jamie Kirsch
Jamie Kirsch of the Rapid City Police Department’s Community Engagement Team on Tuesday, Aug. 4, told media she’s grateful for the partnership with Cody Two Bulls on gathering school supplies. 

“I'm really grateful for the partnership with Cody to be able to provide things like that to kids throughout the entire school year. We'll also identify young people in both of the neighborhoods that we currently work in who are also needing some of that support,” Kirsch said.

Those neighborhoods are currently Star Village and Knollwood, both of which experience high crime rates.

Suggested school supplies for donation include color pencils, crayons, pencil cases, pens, pencils, folders, three-ring binders, paper, notebooks, ¼ inch graph paper, headphones, glue sticks, dry-erase or regular markers, scissors, calculators, and tissue boxes.

Kirsch and Two Bulls said the supplies that tend to get overlooked are highlighters, three-ring binders and pens.

 Cody Two Bulls wearing medal
Cody Two Bulls, of Oglala, wears his Citizens Honor medal, on Tuesday, Aug. 3. Two Bulls is the 2026 Youth Service Honoree. 

 Medal
Cody Two Bulls holds the medal he received on March 25, 2026 from the Congressional Medal of Honor Society. 

 Jamie Kirsch
Jamie Kirsch of the Rapid City Police Department’s Community Engagement Team, speaks about the importance of school supplies on Tuesday, Aug. 4, ahead of a drive.

title: How South Dakota hospitals fared in the latest quality ratings
byline: BART PFANKUCH South Dakota News Watch
description: Two hospitals in South Dakota were rated "below average" in 2026 based on a regular review of patient care and medical outcome benchmarks set by the federal government.
_full_text:
Two hospitals in South Dakota were rated "below average" in 2026 based on a regular review of patient care and medical outcome benchmarks set by the federal government.

But those poor results were far from the norm, as most hospitals statewide received average or better grades in the annual Overall Hospital Quality Star Ratings determined by the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

The ratings range from 1 star on the low end to 5 stars at the top and are based on categories including mortality, safety of care, readmission, patient experiences and timely and effective care.

The two South Dakota hospitals rated 2 stars in 2026 were Avera St. Mary's in Pierre and Huron Regional Medical Center. Both had some positive and negative findings in their overall reviews, but they had lower-than-average recommendation rates by patients.

 2024-4-17 Monument Health signage.JPG
Monument Health's Rapid City Hospital, shown in April 2024, has seen improvement in its CMS ratings in recent years but slid back one spot to a 3-star rating in 2026. 

Five hospitals received top 5-star marks in 2026, up from three last year.

Tim Rave, CEO of the South Dakota Association of Healthcare Organizations, called the ratings "an important benchmark" and added they are far from the only metric hospitals and the public should use to evaluate the quality of patient care.

"While the overall star rating provides helpful information for consumers, hospital leaders rely on much more detailed data to identify opportunities for improvement and ensure they are providing safe, high-quality care," Rave said in an email to News Watch.

Here is a look at how each South Dakota hospital that was rated fared in 2026, with the 2025 Star Rating included in parentheses where applicable.

5 stars (much above average):

Avera Heart Hospital, Sioux Falls (5 stars in 2025)

Avera St. Benedict Health Center, Parkston (no rating in 2025)

Sanford USD Medical Center, Sioux Falls (4 stars in 2025)

VA Medical Center, Sioux Falls (5 stars in 2025)

VA Healthcare System, Sturgis (4 stars in 2025)

4 stars (above average):

Avera McKenna H/UMC, Sioux Falls (3 stars in 2025)

Avera Queen of Peace, Mitchell (no rating in 2025)

Avera St. Luke's, Aberdeen (5 stars in 2025)

Brookings Health System, Brookings (4 stars in 2025)

Monument Health, Spearfish (no rating in 2025)

Sanford Medical Center, Aberdeen (4 stars in 2025)

3 stars (average):

Avera Sacred Heart, Yankton (4 stars in 2025)

Monument Health, Rapid City (4 stars in 2025)

Prairie Lakes Healthcare, Watertown (4 stars in 2025)

2 stars (below average):

Avera St. Mary's, Pierre (3 stars in 2025)

Huron Regional MC, Huron (no rating in 2025)

1 star (much below average):

No South Dakota hospital at this rating

Cale Feller, director of corporate communications for Avera Health, said the CMS ratings use data from as far back as 2021 and there is a slim margin between star rating levels.

"Avera’s commitment to deliver safe, effective and compassionate care remains steadfast," Feller wrote to News Watch in an email.

Monument Health representatives said they have taken numerous steps toward improving patient care and outcomes at Rapid City Hospital, which raised its star rating from a 1 in 2023 to a 4 in 2025. The Rapid City hospital fell to a 3-star rating this year.

"Many of our quality outcomes remain strong and continue to improve," Melissa Haught, director of communications at Monument Health, wrote to News Watch in an email.

 Avera-St.-Mary-s-in-Pierre-from-FB-1.jpg
Avera St. Mary's Hospital is the primary healthcare provider in Pierre, S.D. 

Both Feller and Haught said their health systems have used the CMS ratings as motivation to improve, and that both systems took specific actions to improve patient care and potentially boost future ratings.

Destiny Price, chief operating officer at Huron Regional, said the independent hospital voluntarily entered into the CMS evaluation system last year.

"We recognized the value of being transparent to identify where we’re not hitting all the targets so we can start working on those things," Price said.

For example, before the 2-star rating was announced, leaders of the 25-bed hospital recognized issues in sepsis care and took steps to minimize infections and improve outcomes, Price said.

Huron Regional has also created a multi-disciplinary team that meets daily with each hospitalized patient, added a chronic care nurse and community health worker, and has a renovated birthing center and a new robot to aid in orthopedic surgeries.

"The quality of care we deliver now is not reflected in the rating," she said.

South Dakota News Watch is an independent nonprofit. Read, subscribe for free and donate at sdnewswatch.org. Contact content director Bart Pfankuch: 605-937-9398/bart.pfankuch@sdnewswatch.org.

 Rapid City Hospital expansion
Monument Health Dr. Kyle Lemley speaks during a groundbreaking ceremony on Thursday, July 23.

"Still here. Still Strong," is the theme for the 40th annual Oglala Lakota Nation Fair, Rodeo and Horse Races. Officials canceled the 2025 event to honor Francis "Tom" Thunder Hawk, who was shot at the 39th annual powwow in 2024 and died two days later at Monument Health Rapid City Hospital. title: After 2-2 vote, Pennington County Commission’s alternative energy ordinance kicked down road — again
byline: MIKE BROWNLEE, FRANK ESPINOZA and SHALOM BAER GEE Journal staff
description: The Pennington County wind and solar saga continues.
_full_text:
The Pennington County wind and solar saga continues.

A deadlocked Pennington County Board of Commissioners voted 2-2 on a second reading of an ordinance that would bar utility-scale wind and solar projects on agricultural land during its meeting on Tuesday, Aug. 4.

Board Chair Ron Weifenbach, who likely would've been the third vote to approve, was absent from the meeting. As they've done throughout the process, Commissioners Deb Hadcock (District 3) and Jerry Derr (District 4) voted "yes" on the changes while Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voted "no."

With the tie vote, the matter is continued to the commission's Aug. 18 meeting.

"If Chairman Weifenbach were here we would have a third vote today. If not today, it will be at the next commission meeting. If we're in the interest of doing the county's business, even though we don't always agree, your opposition is duly noted, but I would ask for a third vote today to make this through,” Derr said ahead of the vote while trying to get the nays to switch their decision.

 080526-nws-solar-p3.JPG
Pennington County Planning Director Brittney Hand speaks at the Pennington County Board of Commissioners meeting on Tuesday, Aug. 4. 

But Rossknecht and Drewes held true to their position on the topic.

“I will continue to oppose this based on a couple different reasons. First of all, I'd like to have seen the wind and the solar separated for two different ordinances, and the other reason is I believe that this ordinance is just far too restrictive relative to the alternative energy,” Rossknecht said.

The ordinance shifts approval power for utility-scale wind and solar projects from the county Planning Commission to the Board of Commissioners and includes setbacks far exceeding the recommendations of county staff and the current zoning ordinance.

It also includes a property line setback for solar panels of 1,000 feet (a forty-fold increase to existing code, which requires 25 feet or 1 ½ times the height of the structure, whichever is greater) and a buffer zone of 50 feet. The change for wind turbines puts the setback from property lines at 1.2 miles (up from 1 ½ times the height of the turbine of 1,000 feet, whichever is greater, in current code) and a 50-foot buffer zone. County staff had recommended solar be 50 feet from property lines and have a 25-foot buffer zone. Staff also recommended wind turbines be setback at three times the height of the turbines and a buffer zone of 25 feet.

 080526-nws-solar-p2.JPG
From left, Pennington County Commissioners Jerry Derr and Gary Drewes. The two are divided on the green energy zoning changes. 

The commission passed the first reading of the ordinance on May 19 and, after additional amendments were made at that meeting, passed the first reading again on June 16. On July 7, the commission voted 5-0 to delay a second reading to the Aug. 4 meeting for more amendments, including a definition of infrasound and guidelines for decommissioning bonds for utility-scale wind and solar developments.

Infrasound concerns come from wind turbines that emit low-frequency sound that could disturb wildlife and livestock in the area, task force member Eileen Peterson told the commission previously. The commission said the bonding language will require companies to have plans in place to cover the cost of decommissioning utility wind and solar developments.

 080526-nws-solar-p1.JPG
Pennington County Commissioner Ron Rossknecht (District 1) has been a consistent "no" vote on efforts to bar utility-scale alternative energy from land zoned agricultural. 

According to the U.S. Department of Energy, on average, land-based, utility-scale wind turbines produce sounds that fall in the range of 35–45 dB when heard from 300 meters away (the closest distance a wind turbine is typically placed to a home or building). That means they are no louder than a typical refrigerator (50 dB) and create far less noise pollution than average city car traffic (70 dB).

“Although concerns about potential impacts on human health from neighboring wind turbines are often topics of discussion when new wind energy projects are proposed, a wide body of scientific evidence suggests no direct relationship between human exposure to wind turbines and human health issues,” the department said.

During Tuesday’s meeting, Drewes said Robert’s Rules of Order note a 2-2 tie kills an action item. But Assistant Chief Deputy State’s Attorney Tyler Sobczak explained that, per state law, a tie vote moves the vote to the next meeting. Sobczak said when state law and Robert’s Rules conflict, state law wins out.

A timeline of the alternative energy saga
Oct. 28, 2024: Pennington County Planning and Zoning Commission approves conditional use permits for the Cheyenne River Ranch Wind and Solar Farm, located 7 miles south of New Underwood, 30 miles southeast of Rapid City, and 3.5 miles north of Highway 44. In response, more than 450 citizens petitioned for a moratorium on such projects.
 Nov. 19, 2024: Commission votes unanimously to enact a year-long moratorium on all utility-scale wind and solar projects in the county.
 Dec. 12, 2024: Moratorium goes into effect.
 March 4, 2025: Commission forms an alternative energy task force to research the effects of such projects and future county regulations. The members include attorneys, an appraiser and individuals from the ranching community, local government, and the energy sector. From March-July 2025, the task force meets eight times.
 Oct. 21, 2025: Commission votes unanimously to extend the moratorium to Nov. 18, 2026.
 Jan. 20, 2026: Commission passes the first reading of comprehensive plan amendments to lay the groundwork for zoning amendments to ban utility-scale wind and solar on agricultural land, sequestering in to industrial zones.
 March 3, 2026: Commission passes the second reading of the comprehensive plan amendments. The foundation for zoning amendments is in place.
 April 7, 2026: Commission opts to delay a vote on updates to the zoning ordinance, including limiting projects to industrial zones and shifting the approval power from the planning commission to the board of commissioners.
 May 19, 2026: Commission votes 3-2, Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voting no, on the first reading of the ordinance. They made significant changes, which meant the ordinance would need to be re-advertised and go through first reading again. Those changes included significant setback requirements.
 June 16, 2026: Commission votes 3-2 again, with Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voting no, on the second first reading of the ordinance.
 July 7, 2026: Commission votes 5-0 to delay the vote on the second reading to Aug. 4 for more amendments, such as a definition of infrasound and guidelines for decommissioning bonds for utility-scale wind and solar developments. The county must re-advertise the ordinance again.

 Pennington County Commission
Pennington County Commissioner Gary Drewes (District 5) discusses his opposition to a utility-scale alternative energy ban on ag land on Tuesday, Aug. 4.

title: Rapid City Council makes steps towards realizing eastside police-fire-library building and northside police precinct
description: The City of Rapid City is moving forward with plans to expand public safety service on the east and north sides of the city.
_full_text:
The City of Rapid City is moving forward with plans to expand public safety service on the east and north sides of the city.

The Rapid City Council on Monday, Aug. 3, unanimously passed a rezone request for two parcels of land on the east side of the city that are set to house public services and voted to allow city staff to advertise for bids to renovate the old Sewing Center on Knollwood Drive to house a new police precinct.

Eastside rezones

The council voted to rezone a 1.99 acre parcel at 4121 Homestead Street from general commercial to public. The city plans to develop a fire station at the address that includes space for the Rapid City Police Department and the Rapid City Public Library.

The other rezone — also from general commercial to public — applied to 3.23 acres at 1225 Neel Street, adjacent to the Homestead Street land. The city intends to develop a park there. The city owns both parcels.

In Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun’s proposed 2027 budget, he earmarked $9 million to complete the Homestead building through Tax Increment Financing funds. Both Rapid City Police Chief Don Hedrick and Rapid City Fire Department Chief Jason Culberson spoke in favor of the new project at a July 21 budget press conference. Hedrick said it’s historic for the fire department and police department to share a building, calling it, “something we can really hold up as a community win.” Culberson said the building will be a significant benefit to the community that will increase response times on the eastern side of the city.

Northside police precinct

In April 2025, the city announced it had made an offer on 120 Knollwood Drive for $1.8 million dollars, and the city voted that same month to approve the purchase. The building previously housed The Sewing Center and is set to be the location of a new police precinct.

Currently, the Rapid City Police Department occupies its main station in the Public Safety Building at 300 Kansas City St. and a southwest precinct on the corner of Sheridan Lake Road and Catron Boulevard, which opened in 2023. The department also has two substations on the northside — one on Knollwood Drive right next door to 120 Knollwood Drive and another in Uptown Rapid Mall.

 120 Knollwood Drive North Rapid City Police Precinct Location
The city purchased 120 Knollwood Drive for a north Rapid City police precinct. 

There are key differences between a substation and a precinct.

Police use substations as a space to type reports and complete other minor activities. Operating out of a substation requires officers to start and end their day at police headquarters downtown Hedrick previously told the Journal. A precinct, on the other hand, is a permanent facility where officers start and end their day. It provides a constant presence that allows for quicker response times and increased community engagement.

The estimated cost of renovations is $1.86 million.
