title: Culture exchange through travel: Students from Japan, Rapid City learn from trips across the world
description: It would be a stretch to say 16-year-old Sanami Iimi and 17-year-old Anna Boyle come from different worlds, but they do come from different continents. Both girls, and other teens like them, recently had the chance to learn a little bit more about each other’s countries by crossing an ocean.
_full_text:
It would be a stretch to say 16-year-old Sanami Iimi and 17-year-old Anna Boyle come from different worlds, but they do come from different continents. Both girls, and other teens like them, recently had the chance to learn a little bit more about each other’s countries by crossing an ocean.

Iimi is one of seven students from Nikko, Japan, who recently visited Rapid City for a 10-day trip through the Rapid City Sister City Partnership Association. Boyle is one of five Rapid City students who just returned from a 10-day trip to Nikko. The trips are part of the ongoing relationship between the two sister cities.

Iimi said the people in Rapid City are “very friendly.” When asked to describe Nikko, Iimi said, “beautiful nature.”

“Everybody there was so sweet, so nice to us Rapid City kids,” Boyle said. “It was just such an interesting perspective to view how they live through our eyes and see the difference.”

 Sanami Iimi
Sanami Iimi, 16, of Nikko, Japan, holds a challenge coin at the Monday, Aug. 2, Rapid City Council meeting. Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun presented students visiting from Rapid City’s sister city at the meeting. 

Rapid City and Nikko’s sisterhood began in the early 1990s with the city of Imaichi. In March 2006, Imaichi combined with four other cities to form Nikko, and Rapid City was selected as its sister city. It’s located in the Tochigi Prefecture, about 95 miles north of Tokyo. Per the Japan National Tourism Organization, “Nikko's beautiful setting and sacred mountains have been the backdrop of Shinto and Buddhist worship since at least the 8th century. Its most famous shrines and temples, among the most magnificent in Japan, are a UNESCO World Heritage site. The surrounding national park is a destination for hikers of all levels.”

The trips haven’t taken place for years, but this year’s were the first since the COVID pandemic.

The students attended the Rapid City Council meeting on Monday, Aug. 4, introduced themselves to the council and presented a gift to Mayor Jason Salamun, who presented the students and their chaperones with challenge coins.

 Group photos
Students from Nikko, Japan, Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun (center), Rapid City students and members of the Rapid City Sister City Partnership Association pose for a group photo at the Monday, Aug. 4, Rapid City Council meeting. 

“One of the traditions that we have here at City Hall is we have something called a challenge coin, and this is a challenge coin that we give for when we see something remarkable, and I'm going to give this to each of our guests here today as a token of our appreciation and a token of our friendship between Rapid City and Nikko City, and I exchange it with a handshake,” Salamun said.

Laurie Knight, board member of the Rapid City Sister City Partnership Association, told the council the Nikko students visited Mount Rushmore and participated in a Native American day, which included visits to the Children’s Memorial, Oyate Health and Oaye Luta Okolakiciye (OLO). The nonprofit offers ceremonies, traditional medicines, cultural identity development and cultural community-based approaches to addiction and behavioral health.

 Salamun
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun opens a gift from students visiting from Nikko, Japan, at the Monday, Aug. 3, Rapid City Council Meeting. 

Ashok Kumar, a member of the Rapid City Rotary Club and a host parent, said in the past, students from Japan said they wished they had been able to spend more time with Native Americans.

“This year they made sure that we had a Native American day,” Kumar told the Journal.

Other activities included visits to the Rapid City Police Department and Rapid City Fire Department. Iimi said her favorite part of the trip was the visit to the police department. Knight said the students asked “very excellent questions.”

“They (the students) were so impressed,” the group’s translator said.

 Gift
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun, right, poses for a photo with a student from Nikko, Japan, at the Monday, Aug. 3, Rapid City Council meeting. The two hold a gift the student presented to Salamun. 

The trip to Nikko included visits to multiple Buddhist temples, Shinto shrines and theme parks. Boyle said one of the theme parks featured miniatures of landmarks from different countries, including the Twin Towers and the White House.

“Me and my sister, in particular, we got to go to a castle with our host family on host day and that was really cool. We just got to experience all the culture and it was really interesting, world-changing,” Boyle said.

title: State drops charges in case of missing, presumed dead Belle Fourche woman
description: It took over 22 years after 43-year-old Beverly Ann Ozuna-Ulrich went missing from Belle Fourche for two men to face charges for her presumed death. The state has dropped the charges, at least for now.
_full_text:
It took over 22 years after 43-year-old Beverly Ann Ozuna-Ulrich went missing from Belle Fourche for two men to face charges for her presumed death. The state has dropped the charges, at least for now.

“Following a review of the evidence currently available, the Butte County State’s Attorney’s Office has determined that the state does not presently have sufficient admissible evidence to prove the charged offenses beyond a reasonable doubt,” the office said in a statement sent to the Journal on Thursday, Aug. 5.

Ozuna-Ulrich’s estranged husband Steven Urlich, 69, and Max Piekkola, 42, were both arrested in November 2025 and indicted in December 2025.

 Beverly
This photo of Beverly Ulrich was taken in 2002. 

Urlich was charged with first-degree murder and, in the alternative, second-degree murder. Piekkola was charged with aiding and abetting first-degree murder and, in the alternative, aiding and abetting second-degree murder. He also faced accessory charges and misprision of felony, which is having knowledge of a felony and failing to report it.

Both men’s charges were dropped without prejudice on Wednesday, Aug. 5. When charges are dismissed without prejudice, the state can bring them forward at a later date. The Butte County State’s Attorney’s Office said the investigation into Ozuna-Ulrich’s disappearance remains open and will continue.

Ozuna-Urlich was last seen on Oct. 17, 2003, about 22 years ago. At the time, she was living in Belle Fourche and had separated from Urlich for about 18 months, but continued to visit to cook and clean for her children. 

According to previous reporting by the Journal, Urlich told police at the time he had seen her at the home and watched her drive off. Ozuna-Urlich's sister Rose Grusing told the Journal in 2005 that Ozuna-Urlich was known to take trips by herself, but she would always let someone know her location. 

Ozuna-Urlich was reported missing by family members 10 days after she was last seen.

title: Sanford Health deepens Rapid City roots with sports complex naming rights
description: Under bright sun Thursday, Aug. 6, with a (for now) empty field in the background, Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun stood at a podium and announced a $10 million partnership with Sanford Health for the naming rights of the city’s future sports complex. The move adds to the health company’s growing involvement in the community, including a planned medical complex and partnerships with existing clinics.
_full_text:
Under bright sun Thursday, Aug. 6, with a (for now) empty field in the background, Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun stood at a podium and announced a $10 million partnership with Sanford Health for the naming rights of the city’s future sports complex. The move adds to the health company’s growing involvement in the community, including a planned medical complex and partnerships with existing clinics.

The sports complex will be developed on the 22.7 acres donated by Pete Lien & Sons at the intersection of Seger Drive and 143rd Avenue. Pete Lien & Sons is a Rapid City-based construction and mining company.

On top of naming rights, Sanford Health will have a dedicated space within the complex for sports medicine, sports performance and Sports Academy activities, among other recognition rights and privileges, including input in the design phase and participation in the programming.

“That's a really good deal for Rapid City. It's a great deal for them too. That's a win-win, and when everybody wins, we all win, and that's what it is all about.” Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun said.

 Mayor Jason Salamun
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun officially announced on Thursday, Aug. 6, that Sanford Health will have the naming right for the city’s future sports complex. 

City documents state the total anticipated project cost for the development of the sports complex will be $76.2 million, including $24.58 million from the Catalyst District TIF. An estimated $28.28 million will come from the Hotel Business Improvement District, $6.2 million in land donation value and $5 million from the Vision Fund, per city documents. The $10 million from Sanford Health adds to that.

Kyle Wiese, Sanford Black Hills president and CEO said Sanford Health is, “so very glad to be part of this.”

He added, “This is my home too, and every time I think about what's ahead, the lights turning on at this complex and the doors opening at that hospital, I feel great pride, gratitude, excitement for this community's future.”

 Rapid City Council Vice President Callie Meyer
Rapid City Council Vice President was one of three council members who attended a press event Thursday, Aug. 6, where it was announced that Sanford Health will have the naming rights for the city’s future sports complex. 

Sanford Health announced in November 2025 it plans to build the Sanford Black Hills Medical Center campus in Rapid City. The campus will be located in southwest Rapid City, adjacent to the Black Hills Orthopedic & Spine Center. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027, with completion expected by 2030. The company said Denny Sanford made a $300 million philanthropic gift to Sanford Health to help establish the center, which is estimated to cost more than $500 million. In the last couple of years, the company has also joined with Black Hills Orthopedic & Spine Center, Black Hills Urgent Care, Black Hills Surgical Hospital, Creekside Medical Clinic, Black Hills Plastic Surgery and some providers from Rapid City Medical Center.

Sanford has been involved in athletic development for more than 25 years. The efforts include operating the 500-acre Sanford Sports Complex in Sioux Falls and partnering on the 400,000-square foot Fargo Parks Sports Center at the Sanford Sports Complex in Fargo.

“These investments in the community are part of Sanford Health's belief that care begins often before the hospital, through wellness and taking care of yourself. And this complex is going to give our young youth a place to grow as athletes,” Wiese said.

 Sanford Black Hills President and CEO Kyle Wiese
Sanford Black Hills President and CEO Kyle Wiese said Sanford Health is, “so very glad to be a part of this,” on Thursday, Aug. 6, at a press conference announcing Sanford Health will be contributing $10 million to the future Rapid City sports complex in exchange for exclusive naming rights. 

Sanford Sports, which will occupy a space at the complex, operates sports performance, sports academy and sports events in South Dakota, North Dakota and Minnesota. Annually, Sanford Sports has more than one million athlete contacts, runs more than 250 club teams and hosts nearly 100 tournaments and spectator events ranging from youth and high school to major college and professional, per information from the City of Rapid City.

Steve Young, president of Sanford Sports, said, “We focus on providing experiences for those we serve. Those experiences have to do two things. Number one, they have to encourage a transformation. People have to get better. Number two, they have to enhance community well-being. This facility, this vision, this investment helps us do just that.”

 Sanford Sports President Steve Young
Sanford Sports President Steve Young said at the naming rights announcement on Thursday, Aug. 6, that he is both personally and professionally excited. 

Rapid City Sports Commission Executive Director Domico Rodriguez, who has been working towards new sports facilities in Rapid City for years it’s been a long journey, and the naming rights is just one additional piece to help make the sports complex come to fruition.

“This partnership with Sanford Health, I've seen it firsthand from an athletic and competitive standpoint, and partnering with strong advocates for sport and youth throughout the state makes us and makes this facility successful from the very beginning,” Rodriguez said.

 Rodriguez
Rapid City Sports Commission Executive Director Domico Rodriguez, center, smiles as he talks with his son, left, and Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun, right, on Thursday, Aug. 6, at the Rapid City sports complex naming rights announcement. Rodriguez has been advocating for more sports facilities in Rapid City for years. 

Along with an agreement with Scull Construction to serve as the construction manager at risk, the naming agreement is subject to approval by the Rapid City Legal and Finance Committee at its Wednesday, Aug. 12 meeting, and by the Rapid City Council at its following meeting. If given those official stamps of approval, the naming right agreement will begin in 2027 and stretch for 20 years.

In spring 2027, Sanford Health will pay $2 million to go towards the construction of the facility. Each year for the following 19 years, the company will contribute just over $421,052 for the ongoing costs of operating the facilities.

“We really do not want the property taxes or sales tax to have to go to continue to pay for the operations of it, and so Sanford really stepping up is helping to pay for the initial construction, but honestly, more importantly, the ongoing costs of operating the facility,” Rapid City Finance Director Daniel Ainslie told the Journal.

Of the details provided by the city, the 180,000-square-foot facility will include an indoor walking track, indoor playground and "specialized spaces" to host regional and national sporting events, including volleyball and basketball. The building is also set to include pickleball.

The land donation agreement notes substantial completion of construction at the complex on or before Dec. 31, 2029. In the agreement, Sports Facilities Management, LLC, based out of Florida, is named as the proposed operator for the sports complex.

 Salamun, Wiese, Young and Rodriguez
Foreground from left, wearing suit jackets: Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun, Sanford Black Hills President and CEO Kyle Wiese and Sanford Sports President Steve Young at the Thursday, Aug. 6, announcement that Sanford Health will have naming rights of Rapid City’s future sports complex. 

 Rodriguez on sports complex naming rights
Rapid City Sports Commission Domico Rodriguez on Thursday, Aug. 6, speaks at the naming rights announcement for the city’s future sports complex. 

 Salamun on sports complex naming rights
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun on Thursday, Aug. 6, speaks at the naming rights announcement for the city’s future sports complex. 

 Wiese on sports complex naming rights
Kyle Wiese, Sanford Black Hills president and CEO on Thursday, Aug. 6, speaks at the naming rights announcement for the city’s future sports complex.

title: Pennington County Emergency Management to coordinate rural ambulance plan
byline: MIKE BROWNLEE and FRANK ESPINOZA Journal staff
description: The Pennington County Emergency Management Office will be the county's lead coordinating office for regional EMS planning.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Emergency Management Office will be the county's lead coordinating office for regional EMS planning.

The Pennington County Commission voted 3-1 at its on Tuesday, Aug. 4, meeting on a resolution to have the office coordinate with the City of Box Elder, the City of New Underwood, the Rapid City Fire Department and “affected jurisdictions, state partners, and any potential consultant hired by the City of Box Elder” to develop options for maintaining sustainable EMS coverage in Pennington County.

The move comes after Rapid City Fire Chief Jason Culberson told the commission during its July 7 meeting the department will no longer be able to provide Emergency Medical Services for rural areas after the end of 2026 without external funding. During that meeting, the commission discussed seeking funding to keep the service alive into 2027 and beyond.

Culberson told the Journal at that meeting, "The ambulance service is funded through an enterprise fund run through the city. Revenue was/is generated when a patient is transported ... No funding has stopped, we are asking for funding to continue to provide the service. We are no longer able to provide services outside the city without funding."

Culberson notified the commission of the changes by writing a letter in Dec. 2025, stating the city since 2003 has provided some EMS to many county residents with no subsidy and has been without a contract with the county since 2007.

According to the city's 2026 budget, ambulance enterprise funds were approved at $7.2 million for the year. An enterprise fund is self-supported through user fees.

At the July meeting Commissioner Jerry Derr (District 4) said the department needs an estimated $800,000 to continue ambulance coverage for the unincorporated areas, and he said there were about 2,655 calls made in 2025 for ambulance services in unincorporated areas of the county. 

According to a study by the Maine Rural Health Research Center, South Dakota is one of eight states with fewer than three ambulances covering every 1,000 square miles of land area. The study, which gathered data from 41 states, showed South Dakota has 1.6 ambulance stations per 1,000 square miles, fifth-worst among states that participated in the study.

 080526-nws-solar-p2.JPG (Copy)
From left, Pennington County Commissioners Jerry Derr and Gary Drewes at the commission meeting on Tuesday, Aug. 4. 

Under South Dakota law, EMS is currently not considered an essential service that must be funded by local governments. In 2025, House Bill 1043 would have required counties and municipalities to fund Emergency Medical Services, but the bill was shot down in committee. In 2026, Senate Bill 89 created the Emergency Medical Services Funding Task Force to look into whether EMS is an essential service. What the task force finds, and if any laws will come from it, is still to be determined.

In a letter to the board, Derr noted the county’s working with Box Elder, which has applied for a South Dakota Department of Health grant that would fund a consultant to help study the issue and develop a plan for EMS coverage among the county, the small towns and the Rapid City Fire Department.

“The purpose is to better understand the path forward and to avoid a piecemeal approach where each community is forced to solve the issue on its own,” Derr wrote in the letter, which was part of the Aug. 4 meeting agenda packet. “A regional study would allow stakeholders to evaluate service areas, response needs, funding options, governance models, taxing authority, contractual options and long-term sustainability.”

Pennington County Emergency Management Director Dustin Willett told the commission his office is able to take on the coordinating responsibilities, noting his purview as director includes strategic planning for a “defined disaster or emergency.”

“I think it could be argued the potential loss of ambulance service to citizens of Pennington County would constitute a state of emergency,” Willett told the commission. “That's a significant thing. If somebody calls 911 and doesn't get an ambulance, that's a bad day.”

Commissioner Deb Hadcock (District 3) voted against the resolution after taking issue with Derr communicating with Box Elder about the grant application without bringing the matter to the full board.

“There is no financial obligation. Pennington County did not sign any grant paperwork. Pennington County is not on the hook for a consultant,” Derr said at the meeting.

title: Patrol releases name of woman killed in Pennington County rollover crash
description: Authorities have released the name of a woman who died in a single-vehicle crash near Scenic.
_full_text:
Authorities have released the name of a woman who died in a single-vehicle crash near Scenic.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol said Kristina Yellowhawk, 18, of Wall, died in a crash that occurred around 7:55 a.m. on Monday, Aug. 3, on Bombing Range Road near Sheep Mountain Road, about 4.5 miles south of Scenic.

The patrol said Yellowhawk was driving a 2008 Chevrolet Impala northbound on Bombing Range Road when the vehicle left the roadway. Yellowhawk attempted to correct and lost control of the vehicle, which rolled. Yellowhawk sustained fatal injuries in the crash, the patrol said.

Medics took a 19-year-old man from Pierre, who was a passenger in the vehicle, to the hospital for treatment of non-life-threatening injuries. Neither were wearing a seat belt, the patrol said. An investigation into the crash continues.

The Pennington County Commission discussed Bombing Range Road during its Tuesday, Aug. 4, meeting, at the request of a citizen who expressed concern about the safety of a 7-mile stretch of the roadway south of Scenic. In a letter to the board discussed at the meeting, Highway Superintendent Joseph Miller said reconstruction of Bombing Range Road has been on the Highway Department’s radar for several years. In 2024, the county applied for but did not receive federal funding that would’ve assisted with the engineering and design costs on the reconstruction.

Miller said reconstruction is estimated at $15 to $20 million and at this time the county hasn’t identified a funding source to take on the work. The project remains part of Pennington County’s Five-Year Transportation Plan, but is contingent on finding a funding source.

“As the department develops long-range capital improvement plans, projects are prioritized using a variety of factors, including roadway condition, traffic volumes, safety considerations, available funding opportunities, and overall system needs,” Miller wrote in the letter.

In the meantime, Miller noted the county continues to perform routine asphalt maintenance on Bombing Range Road “to preserve the roadway and maintain safe travel conditions.”

A June 2025 study determined 1,222 drivers used the road daily, according to Miller.

During the commission meeting, Miller said, quoting state data, there were 36 total crashes from 2015 to the present on Bombing Range Road. That includes 25 injury accidents and three fatal accidents. Miller said the state has called for a road safety audit, which will include the Highway Department, Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, South Dakota Highway Patrol and South Dakota Department of Transportation.

As part of that process, “We’ll learn what type of funding is available,” Miller said.

Asked about lowering the 50 mph speed limit on the road, Miller said he didn’t believe that would make a difference. He said a traffic study determined 85% of people are driving 67 mph on the road and about 93% of people speed on the road.

“It’s a fairly wide open road,” Miller said, noting it gives the sense you can drive fast before hitting rough patches that cause issues.

The commission did not take action on the agenda item.

title: The Revival on Main celebrates creativity, independent business in downtown Sturgis
description: An art gallery meets a garage party at The Revival on Main, a downtown Sturgis destination where artists and craftspeople are reigniting the spirit of creativity.
_full_text:
An art gallery meets a garage party at The Revival on Main, a downtown Sturgis destination where artists and craftspeople are reigniting the spirit of creativity.

The Revival on Main is located at Sturgis Jewelry’s longtime storefront, 1049 Main Street. Leather, custom jewelry, art, vintage clothing and more from 17 independent businesses will be featured in a curated retail space that gives visitors a unique shopping experience.

“It's our response to the changes we've seen on Main Street over the years, and our way of celebrating the creativity and craftsmanship that have always been part of motorcycle culture,” said owner Jo Willers.

 080626-nws-rally-The Revival-McKaylaLindvintage.jpg
McKayla Lind stands beside a curated collection of vintage items that will be sold at The Revival on Main. The shop in the Sturgis Jewelry storefront at 1049 Main St. will be open during the Sturgis motorcycle rally. 

The Revival on Main opened Aug. 5 and will be open through Aug. 16. The Revival is hosting a grand opening party from 6 to 9 p.m. Aug. 6. The party is open to those who sign up to be on the guest list. Go to sturgisjewelry.com/revival-grand-opening-join-guest-list to sign up. The grand opening party will be an evening of live music by Josh Rogan, an exclusive giveaway and a chance to meet artists who are part of The Revival on Main.

“Main Street in Sturgis has evolved over the years, and many small, independent businesses have disappeared from the street,” Jo said. “Sturgis Jewelry has watched that change from its store at 1049 Main since 2000. Now led by a new generation of the Willers family, the company is bringing together the next generation of makers, artists and independent businesses for the Sturgis Rally.”

Jo’s father, master jeweler John Willers, first began selling his original, hand-crafted jewelry at the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally in 1988. He opened Sturgis Jewelry’s storefront at 1049 Main St. in 2000.

The Revival on Main hours
Aug. 5-6: 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.
 Aug. 7-15: 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.
 Aug. 16: 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

John died in 2025, but Jo Willers is confident her father will be at The Revival on Main in spirit to enjoy this new venture. The Revival on Main’s wares will include sterling silver and solid gold jewelry made from John’s original designs inspired by a lifetime of motorcycle culture. Sturgis Jewelry is now handcrafted by a family-owned company in Los Angeles.

The Revival on Main aims to recapture a time when Main Street Sturgis was “the heart of shopping in the motorcycle community,” Jo said. “There was so much handmade stuff, small businesses, artisans, and things you couldn’t get anywhere else, and that’s part of what was so exciting about it and so much fun.”

 080626-nws-rally-The Revival-HeideFowler.jpg
Heide Fowlers stands beside a display of her crocheted accessories, photography and more at The Revival on Main at 1049 Main St. in Sturgis. The shop will showcase the work of 17 artists and craftspeople during the Sturgis motorcycle rally. 

“Over the years the rally’s changed. That’s something that we’ve seen,” Jo said. “My first year working here was 2009, and we watched a lot of smaller vendors disappear. … We kept dreaming about how could we bring back these smaller businesses and give them a presence on Main Street.”

“It’s that hub of creativity that I was missing personally, and we had heard from a lot of people that they were missing as well,” Jo said.

 080626-nws-rally-The Revivaldisplay.jpg
Clothing and art that celebrates motorcycle culture is on display at The Revival on Main. The shop inside Sturgis Jewelry’s storefront will be open during the Sturgis motorcycle rally until Aug. 16. 

Shoppers will find items such as original artwork by tattoo artists and riders, photography, paintings, knives, accessories, crocheted items, and motorcycle-themed vintage from local vintage curators. There will be live music in the store daily through Aug. 16.

 "My dad came to Main Street in Sturgis because it was the heart of creativity in the riding community. The Revival is our way of reigniting that spirit,” Jo said. “We want people to come, find something unexpected and stay awhile.”

For more information, go to sturgisjewelry.com.   

 080626-nws-rally-The Revivalclothing.jpg
Clothing and accessories on are display at The Revival on Main, located in Sturgis Jewelry’s storefront at 1049 Main St. in Sturgis.

title: Slow down, enjoy the ride: Medical facilities ready to care for Sturgis rallygoers
description: Slow down, enjoy the scenery, and save lives. Resisting the urge to speed is the top safety tip Monument Health and Sanford Health officials recommend during the 86th annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.
_full_text:
Slow down, enjoy the scenery, and save lives. Resisting the urge to speed is the top safety tip Monument Health and Sanford Health officials recommend during the 86th annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

The rally officially begins Aug. 7, but motorcycles are already lining the streets in Sturgis ahead of opening day. Statistically, the rally tends to draw bigger crowds for its “milestone” years, such the 85th anniversary in 2025 – but years like 2026 when rally crowds may be smaller can still create hazards on the roads, according to Dustin Calhoun, business continuity coordinator/emergency manager for Monument Health.

When the roads are less crowded, drivers may be more likely to speed — and that can lead to disaster.

“These ‘off years’ are when we see more patients come in. People drive faster. The roads aren’t congested,” Calhoun said. “You’re here on vacation. Slow down and enjoy the sights and scenery around you. Enjoy your time here at Sturgis. Take in the sights.”

When non-life-threatening illnesses or injuries occur during the rally, Calhoun encourages locals and visitors who need medical help to use urgent care locations, and Monument Health’s Nurse Triage Line as much as possible. That can alleviate pressure on Monument Health Rapid City Hospital’s emergency department.  

Monument Health Emergency Services and Medical Campus, a second emergency department, opened in June at 1911 E. Mall Drive, just minutes off Interstate 90. It’s open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, year-round.

Anyone experiencing chest pains, stroke symptoms or serious injury should call 911 to get medical help immediately.

Monument Health has urgent care locations in Box Elder at 375 Berky Drive and in Rapid Valley at 2625 Elderberry Boulevard; those are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. In Rapid City, the urgent care at 1303 N. Lacrosse St. is open from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. Urgent care locations at 2820 Mount Rushmore Road and 2116 Jackson Boulevard in Rapid City are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Monument Health Sturgis Clinic offers same-day and walk-in appointment care from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. weekdays at 2140 Junction Avenue in Sturgis, adjoining the Monument Health Sturgis Hospital, where 24-hour emergency care is available. For information or appointments, call 605-720-2600.

For more information or to schedule an appointment online, go to monument.health/site-search/locations/.

Monument Health’s Nurse Triage Line, 605-755-1350, offers patients with non-COVID-19 illnesses the opportunity to talk directly to a trained registered nurse who can help them understand the urgency of their illness or injury and help them get the most appropriate type of care. This could include their primary care doctor, an urgent care clinic or the hospital emergency department, if needed. Calls to the Nurse Triage Line are free. Nurses are available weekdays from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. and weekends from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Calhoun said Monument Health begins planning in January for each year’s rally, relying on data from previous years to ensure Monument Health locations have enough medical supplies for the rally. Monument Health also increases staff during rally week.

“The nice thing is the rally happens every year so we know what to expect,” Calhoun said. “We’re welcoming everybody to the Black Hills. They can feel confident Monument Health stands ready to take care of them.”

Sanford Health operates two urgent care locations in Rapid City — Sanford Health Baken Park Clinic, 741 Mountain View Road #A1, and Sanford Health Haines Avenue Clinic, 1730 Haines Avenue. Hours at both locations are 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. weekdays, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturdays and Sundays. For information or to make an appointment online, go to bhucare.com/our-locations/.

Locals and visitors who aren’t sure where to seek medical care can call My Sanford Nurse, 800-445-5788, anytime to contact an experienced provider who can assess their symptoms and guide them toward the right medical care.  

All local urgent care locations typically treat a wide variety of health concerns, according to Dr. Christopher Wenger, medical director of Sanford Black Hills Urgent Care. Sanford Health urgent care locations each will have two providers and staff available, and they’ve stocked up on extra medical supplies for rally week.

“We get a lot of minor wrecks, people tipping bikes over, or burns from motorcycle exhaust,” Wenger said.

“We have the ability to do IV fluids if someone’s dehydrated. We X-ray in-house that we get reports in 20 minutes. We do have lab in-house so we can check blood tests and other things very quickly,” he said. “We tend to be able to take care of whatever can show up.”

“Our ultimate goal is to keep things out of the (Monument Health Rapid City Hospital emergency room) that can be safely kept out and try to take the load off, because they’re busy with trauma (injuries). Anything we can do to help off-load, that is the plan,” Wenger said.

Wenger offered gratitude to all the first responders who are working overtime and will be extra busy as the 86th annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally amps up.

Staying safe during the rally

Although South Dakota law doesn’t require motorcyclists to wear helmets, Wenger and Calhoun both recommend helmets to help prevent injuries.

Goggles might be smart, too. Wenger said Sanford urgent cares sees patients during the rally who suffer injuries, including scratched corneas, when bugs fly in their eyes.

“Drive slow, wear a helmet, stay hydrated, wear sunscreen, be safe,” said Wenger, who suggests about two liters, or about 67 ounces, of water per day to stay hydrated.

With temperature forecasts in the 80s and 90s during rally week, rallygoers should take precautions against sunburns and heat exhaustion as well. Drink plenty of fluids, wear loose-fitting clothing, and stay indoors during the hottest times of day.

Altitude-related sickness can also be a problem that tends to catch visitors by surprise.

“We see a lot of people who struggle with the altitude. They come from sea level locations and they don’t realize we’re 5,000 to 7,000 feet here,” Wenger said.

If feeling unwell for any reason, don’t hesitate to seek medical attention.

title: Loren "Bat" Pourier
description: January 13, 1952 - August 1, 2026
_full_text:
January 13, 1952 - August 1, 2026

Loren Baptiste Pourier, known to many as Bat, passed away peacefully on August 1, 2026, at Regional West Medical Center in Scottsbluff, Nebraska, at the age of 74. Born January 13, 1952,to Loren and Isabelle (Rooks) Pourier in Rapid City, South Dakota, Bat will always be remembered for his unwavering commitment, boundless generosity, and enduring love for his family, friends, and community.

Bat grew up with his cousins in the Bad Lands of South Dakota between Interior and Scenic, graduating from Rapid City Central High School, where he earned himself a position on the All State Football team in 1969. He went on to attend South Dakota State University and later earned his banking certificate from The Schools of Banking, Inc. in 1985.

In 1974 Bat married Vicky (Cathey) Morford and they had two sons Corey and Tye. In 1983 Bat married the love of his life Patty (Pich) Pourier.

From an early age, Bat displayed a remarkable sense of purpose and leadership. In 1976, he testified before the United States Senate Committee on Indian Affairs, advocating for locally controlled school boards, a testament to his dedication to education and tribal sovereignty. His commitment to his people only deepened as he took on the role of Director of Administration for Native Americans with the Oglala Sioux Tribe from 1981 to 1984.

Bat's entrepreneurial spirit, paired with his passion for community development, led him into the world of business and finance. As a loan officer at Stockman's National Bank and manager of the Stockman's National Bank Insurance Company from 1984 to 1990, he cultivated skills and vision that would shape the rest of his professional life. In 1989, Bat and his wife Patty founded Muddy Creek Oil and Gas Corporation and constructed the Longhorn Food n Fuel in Rushville, Nebraska. This bold step laid the foundation for a legacy that would touch countless lives.

The opening of the first Big Bat's Convenience Store in Pine Ridge, South Dakota, in 1990 marked another significant milestone. Under Bat's direction, the business flourished. By 1995, Big Bat's had evolved into a wholesale fuel marker, acquiring its first fuel transport. In 1996, Bat and Patty opened a second Big Bat's location in Chadron, Nebraska, followed by third and fourth stores in Hot Springs, South Dakota in 1997. In 2004 Bat and Patty started the Lakota Country Times focusing on local Lakota news. Then in 2007 Bat and Patty tried to retire and sold their four stores to sons, Corey and Tye, and nephew Kevin Kelso. At that time 3 more locations were purchased. Bat and Patty then purchased Pine Ridge Oil in Pine Ridge, SD expanding their contributions to the regional economy.

Bat's dedication was felt far beyond his businesses. In 1991, he and his brothers and nephew created Pourier Tiyospe, a collaboration that brought propane services to Pine Ridge and supported his passion for ranching in Kyle, South Dakota. His work extended into advocacy, as seen when Muddy Creek Oil and Gas sued the State of South Dakota for the return of fuel taxes to South Dakota Indian Tribes, resulting in a victory in 2003, ensuring that future fuel tax proceeds collected on the reservation would be returned to the individual tribes.

Bat and Patty's achievements and service were widely recognized: Small Business of the Year awards in 1993 for both South Dakota and Region 8, and BIA Small Business of the Year in 2000. Bat further committed his time and talents to guiding and supporting youth and education by serving on the Red Cloud Indian School Foundation Board, National Board of Trustees for American Indians, and Little Wound School Board.

Behind his impressive career and advocacy, Bat was cherished for his warmth, humor, and genuine spirit. Anyone who crossed his path soon learned to expect witty remarks, spirited teasing, and plenty of laughter. His quick wit, frank honesty, and perfect timed comments endeared him to all. If Bat gave you a hard time, it was his way of showing he cared. Even when projecting a tough exterior, Bat's compassion for his loved ones was unmistakable.

What truly brought Bat joy were the moments spent with his family, especially his grandchildren, who were the light of his life. His keen attention to detail, his pride in his work, and his deep affection for those around him including his beloved dog, Mister.

Bat's legacy continues through his loving family. He is survived by his wife Patty Pourier, sons Corey (Sheila) Pourier and Tye (Nichole) Pourier, brother Warren "Bim" Pourier, sisters Patty Kelso, Peggy Pourier, Karla (Rod) Longwell, and Shelly Pourier. His legacy is further carried by his grandchildren: Nate Dodd, Ahlaura (Louis) Pourier, Katarina (Sam) Rischling, Taurie (Austin) Anderson, Josslyn Pourier, Kenzie Pourier, Raylie Pourier, and Tyson Baptiste Pourier, as well as great-grandchildren Lauren, Kaizen, Ryker, and Cameron. Bat will be remembered fondly by a host of nieces and nephews: Kevin Kelso, Darty Saunders, Stevie Kjerstad, Vicki Saunders, Tawney Brunsch, Chad Brunsch, Grady Brunsch, Hayley Brunsch, Warren Pourier Jr., Nicole Pourier, Josh Mousseau, DJ Pourier, Isabelle Pourier, Travis Muir, Kourtney Muir, Trent Remiley, Abagail VanVleit, Elizabeth VanVleit, and Alexandra VanVleit and numerous great nieces and nephews & great-great nieces and nephews.

He was preceded in death by his father Loren, mother Isabella, sister Laurette Pourier, nephew Kelly Kelso, nephew Jamie Brunsch, and niece Kim Kelso.

The community is invited to remember and celebrate Bat's life during the wake at Chamberlain Chapel, 1700 US-20, Chadron, Nebraska, on August 6, 2026, beginning at 7:00 p.m. Funeral services will be held at Lakota Tech High School, 14 New Wolf Cr, Pine Ridge, South Dakota, on August 7, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Burial to follow at Greenwood Cemetery in Chadron Nebraska.

Bat's legacy of leadership, dedication, and love will live on in all those whose lives he brightened. He will be deeply missed but never forgotten.

title: Barbara Ann Alton
description: Barbara Ann Alton, 90, of Collierville, Tennessee, passed away on August 3, 2026.
_full_text:
Barbara Ann Alton, 90, of Collierville, Tennessee, passed away on August 3, 2026.

Barbara devoted 22 years to education, teaching kindergarten and later Title I Reading. In her younger years, she enjoyed horseback riding, attending horse shows, and performing horseback acrobatics with her father. She was an avid reader and found her greatest joy in spending time with her family.

She was preceded in death by her husband, George Edward Alton; her sister, Sandra Kearns; and her brother, Duke Goodell.

Barbara is survived by her daughter, Keely Jo Burton; her son, Chad Edward Alton; her sister, Connie Denker; her granddaughter, Elizabeth Ann Downey; and her great-granddaughters, Lyla Kate Downey and Emory Grace Downey.

She will be dearly missed by all who knew and loved her.

title: How a Black Hills adult store benefits from the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally
description: Dick and Jane’s owner David Eliason sees a few sales spikes every year at his chain of Black Hills-based adult stores: Valentine’s Day for lovers. October for costumes and otherwise. Christmas for gag gifts. But nothing – truly, nothing – is remotely close to the annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. The 86th rendition kicks off Friday, Aug. 7, and runs through Sunday, Aug. 16.
_full_text:
Dick and Jane’s owner David Eliason sees a few sales spikes every year at his chain of Black Hills-based adult stores: Valentine’s Day for lovers. October for costumes and otherwise. Christmas for gag gifts. But nothing – truly, nothing – is remotely close to the annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. The 86th rendition kicks off Friday, Aug. 7, and runs through Sunday, Aug. 16.

“Sturgis treats us well,” said Eliason, who opened the chain’s first store in Sturgis.

 072826-nws-dickandjanes-p5.JPG
A sign at Dick and Jane's Rapid City location.  

Compared to the other 10 months of the year, Eliason said sales are roughly 50% higher in July and 110% higher in August – sometimes more. The sales spike plays a role in Eliason offering health insurance, along with dental and vision benefits, to his longtime employees.

Their billboards dot the I-90 Highway leading up to rally grounds. Preparation begins in May. Days are a blur of sales and hoping – maybe praying – stock doesn’t run out. Just to keep up, workers regularly log overtime. 

Customers range in age from 18 to 70-plus. Bailee Hoffman, an employee, said she’s helped members of the LGBTQ+ community and some walking in “wearing Trump stuff.” They work in various industries and hail all the way from Gillette, Wyoming, to Australia, London and Ireland.

 072826-nws-dickandjanes-p3.JPG
Bailee Hoffman, an employee, poses next to a sign at the Rapid City on Monday, July 20. 

“Isn't it about time for you to have your seven bonus Valentine's Days?” a colleague recently asked Eliason at a trade show in Los Angeles, referring to the rally.

"Yes, my seven bonus Valentine's Days are just around the corner,” Eliason responded.

Dick and Jane’s is hardly the only business swept up in the “Sturgis Bump” bottom trawl.

Sara Brunsell, general manager of Sturgis Lodge & Suites, estimates "30-45%" of the hotel's yearly revenue comes from the Rally. Rod Bradley, who co-owns Oasis — a bar and restaurant in the heart of downtown Sturgis — with his wife, said 28% of the bar's overall revenue in 2024 came from the Rally. Peter Schmid, who runs the Phillips 66 on Mount Rushmore Road, estimated sales are “90%” higher during rally time compared to regular months.

 Rod Bradley
Rod Bradley, co-owner of Oasis, poses outside the restaurant and bar in downtown Sturgis on Saturday, Aug. 10, 2025.  

But compared to bars, hotels and gas stations, Dick and Jane's products are more niche than gas, food, alcohol and a place to sleep.

Which begs the question: Why the uptick?

Eliason believes the open-minded, free-spirited side of biker couples lends well to the nature of his products.

“They're open to trying new things and to keeping the relationship healthy and progressive,” Eliason said.

It’s something he feels outsiders in the rut of their routines – and struggling to break them – can learn from.

“I have friends who … go to work, they come home, they watch television,” Eliason said, “and they don't go to concerts, they don't do things, and eventually I think it just becomes monotonous.”

For one, the chain, which has locations in Sturgis (Dick and Jane's Naughty Spot), Rapid City (Dick and Jane's Super Spot) and Box Elder (Bonnie and Clyde's Adult Supercenter), appeals to the NSFW jokester side of bikers.

Hence the uptick in sales of suction-cup products.

“They want to put them on their headlight, their taillight, their gas tank and they want to drive down the street with a phallic shape hood ornament or bike ornament … so we see an unusual surge in suction cup-based products,” Eliason said. “It's hard to say that with a straight face.”

 072826-nws-dickandjanes-p2.JPG
Bailee Hoffman, an employee, poses outside the Rapid City location on Monday, July 20. 

The bulk of Dick and Jane’s sales during the rally, Hoffman noted, come from the shop’s vast line of corsets and lingerie sets. It’s a form of creative expression for attendees and a go-to for bartenders and waitresses. Knowing that Dick and Jane’s has what they’re looking for, Hoffman noted they have several repeat buyers. One particular enjoyable moment was helping some find products for a VA theme night in 2025.

 072826-nws-dickandjanes-p1.JPG
Baile Hoffman enjoys helping customers who are attending the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. 

“We had a whole bunch of red, white, and blue stuff left over from the Fourth of July, and that one was just fun to help dress a couple of the girls up,” Hoffman said. “I'm like, look at this bikini! Look at this! Look at this! And it's so easy because it's just what they're looking for.”

 072826-nws-dickandjanes-p4.JPG
Bailee Hoffman gives a customer's dog a free treat on Monday, July 20.  

But Hoffman observes another key appeal for Dick and Jane’s is tailoring lingerie and corsets to women of all shapes and sizes.

“Everybody deserves to feel sexy,” Hoffman said. “We should be able to present them with something that will make them feel complete and comfortable in their own skin, in their body.”

On numerous occasions, she’s watched plus-size women walk in, palpably self-conscious with their shoulders hunched when shopping for something revealing.

“They have no expectations to find anything,” Hoffman said.

In these situations, Hoffman noted that it’s vital to make customers feel comfortable by sharing some of her own difficulties.

“I'll straight up grab my belly and be like, ‘I'm not happy with this.’ I gotta point out my flaws, too,” said Hoffman, a mother of two who helps moms with postpartum body image struggles. “I know what I struggle with. Maybe they're struggling with the same thing, and they don't have to tell me.”

But after showing them an array of options and finding something that complements their features, Hoffman watches a transformation take place: Shoulders roll back with confidence paired with a smile.

“You can see life brought into their face,” Hoffman said. “Their face gets a little bit more blushed, and they just look happy overall.”

title: Check out the city's map for free motorcycle parking in Rapid City
description: The City of Rapid City is offering free motorcycle parking in designated areas for the upcoming 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.
_full_text:
The City of Rapid City is offering free motorcycle parking in designated areas for the upcoming 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

Effective now, parking spaces in seven specific locations will be reserved for free motorcycle parking through Aug. 16. The locations include:

 Rally_parkingRC_2026.jpg
The City of Rapid City is offering free motorcycle parking in designated areas for the upcoming 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. 

• Downtown Parking Structure: Northeast section of the Lower Level of parking structure reserved for motorcycles.

• Hotel Alex Johnson: Four vehicle parking spaces reserved for motorcycles on the west side of Sixth Street in front of the Hotel Alex Johnson between Main Street and St. Joseph Street

• Prairie Edge: Three vehicle parking spaces reserved for motorcycles on the east side of Prairie Edge Trading Post, located on the west side of Sixth Street between Main Street and alley.

• Rapid City Visitor Center: Three vehicle parking spaces reserved for motorcycles in front of the Rapid City Visitor Center, on the north side of Main Street between Sixth Street and Seventh Street.

• Tinder Box: Three vehicle parking spaces reserved for motorcycles in front of Tinder Box on the east side of Seventh Street between Main Street and St. Joseph Street.

• FourFront Design: Three vehicle parking spaces reserved for motorcycles in front of FourFront Design on the west side of Seventh Street between Main Street and St. Joseph Street.

• Murphy’s Pub & Grill: Three vehicle parking spaces reserved for motorcycles in front of Murphy’s Pub & Grill on the south side of Main Street between Mount Rushmore Road and 9th Street.

City officials remind the public to drive with caution with a higher-than-expected volume of motorcycle traffic for the 86th annual Sturgis Rally event.

title: Authorities release name of motorcycle passenger killed in crash near Rochford
description: Authorities have released the name of a Sioux Falls woman who died in a motorcycle crash near Rochford.
_full_text:
Authorities have released the name of a Sioux Falls woman who died in a motorcycle crash near Rochford.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol said Dawn Hillman, 67, was a passenger in a 2025 Canam Spyder RT that crashed 5 miles west of Rochford at South Rochford and Seven Hills roads.

The patrol said around 11 a.m. on Saturday, the driver of the Spyder, a 72-year-old man from Sioux Falls, was traveling on South Rochford Road near Seven Hills Road when he failed to negotiate a curve. The Spyder left the road and rolled.

Dawn Hillman died from her injuries, the patrol said. The driver was taken to a Rapid City hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

Hillman and the driver were each wearing a helmet, the patrol said. An investigation into the crash continues.

title: No one injured after Deadwood Trolley catches fire on Interstate 90 near Sturgis
description: A Deadwood Trolley caught fire on Interstate 90 Wednesday morning.
_full_text:
A Deadwood Trolley caught fire on Interstate 90 Wednesday morning.

The City of Deadwood said one of the popular trolleys was on the way to Rapid City for repairs when it stalled and began smoking. The driver was the only person on the trolley and was able to exit and call emergency services, the city said. A passerby reported seeing the fire around 11 a.m.

No one was injured in the incident.

The Meade County Sheriff’s Office said the “scene was handled safely, traffic kept moving, and the incident was cleared as quickly as possible.”

The City of Deadwood thanked the Sturgis Police Department, Meade County Sheriff’s Office, South Dakota Highway Patrol, Sturgis Fire Department, SD Wildland Fire and Sturgis Ambulance Service.

title: YMCA of the Black Hills announces fall programming
description: The YMCA of the Black Hills announces the release of its all-new Fall Program Guide, offering a wide variety of activities and programs designed to keep individuals and families active, connected, and thriving across the Black Hills this season.
_full_text:
The YMCA of the Black Hills announces the release of its all-new Fall Program Guide, offering a wide variety of activities and programs designed to keep individuals and families active, connected, and thriving across the Black Hills this season.

From youth and tiny tot sports and swim lessons to group exercise classes and wellness workshops, the Fall Program Guide highlights opportunities for every age and interest. Families can look forward to engaging childcare programs, enriching arts and education activities, and seasonal events that bring the community together.

“Our Fall programs are about more than just activities — they’re about building connections, developing skills, and supporting overall health and well-being,” said Kristy Lintz, Chief Operations Officer. “Whether you’re trying something new or returning to a favorite class, the Y is here to help you grow in spirit, mind, and body.”

 YMCA

Key highlights from the Fall Program Guide include:

Youth Sports: Basketball, soccer, flag football, and martial arts classes designed to teach teamwork and build confidence.

Aquatics: Swim lessons for all ages and abilities, plus open swim times for family fun.

Wellness & Fitness: Group fitness classes, personal training, and wellness programs to support healthy lifestyles.

Award-Winning Childcare & Afterschool: Safe, engaging spaces where kids can learn, grow, and thrive after school.

Special Events: Seasonal family nights, Halloween celebrations, and community gatherings.

The Fall Program Guide is available now online at: https://shorturl.at/wZGZ0 Registration for programs is open, and members and community participants are encouraged to sign up early as spaces fill quickly.

For more information, visit www.ymcabh.org or call your local YMCA branch location in Rapid City, Box Elder (Liberty Center), Custer or Edgemont.

title: Edward Schuh
description: December 5, 1945 - August 3, 2026
_full_text:
December 5, 1945 - August 3, 2026

Edward William Schuh, a proud Wisconsin farm boy, Vietnam veteran, devoted Catholic, and deeply loved husband, father, brother, brother-in-law, uncle, grandfather, and great-grandfather, passed away peacefully on the morning of August 3, 2026, just after the sun rose. In that quiet morning light, Edward was reunited with his beloved wife, Theresa, as well as his parents, siblings, and others who have gone before him.

Edward was born on December 5, 1945 to Edward and Ottilia (Miller) Schuh, the 10th of 13 children, at Holy Family Hospital in Manitowoc, Wisconsin. He graduated from Reedsville High School in 1963. His roots on a Wisconsin farm shaped the man he became. He was hardworking, humble, resilient, and most at home with his hands in the soil. He carried those values throughout his life, first in service of his country during the Vietnam War and later through a career dedicated to caring for the land on the Pine Ridge Reservation and serving others.

As a young adult Edward enlisted in the military and was awarded a Purple Heart after being honorably discharged from the US Army. Edward then attended the University of Wisconsin - Stevens Point and graduated with a bachelor's degree in forestry. He later attended South Dakota State University for another bachelor's degree in Range Management and Soil Conservation. He worked with the Washington State forest service and the Department of Interior - Bureau of Indian Affairs as a soil conservationist; a career that brought him to Pine Ridge, SD where his life changed forever when he met and married Theresa. Together they built a beautiful life and made Pine Ridge their home.

Their home was filled with daughters and a son, creating a lively household full of love, laughter, faith, and family. Over the years, that same home welcomed many grandchildren and great-grandchildren. Through every season of life, Edward proudly embraced one of his most cherished roles: being "Papa."

Edward found great joy in being outdoors and working around the property. He was never afraid of hard work and was happiest when tending to the land, completing a project, or spending time in his garden, which reflected so much of who he was; patient, steady, nurturing, and always willing to put in the work necessary for something meaningful to grow.

Edward's legacy lives on in the family he loved so deeply, the land he cared for, the lessons passed down, and the countless memories made within the home he and Theresa created together. He will be remembered as a proud veteran, a faithful servant, a devoted family man, and above all, a proud Papa. Though his passing leaves an ache that words can hardly hold and an emptiness that will be felt in every place his love once filled, there is comfort knowing that as the sun rose on his final morning, he was gently called home to God. There, he was welcomed into the arms of his beloved Theresa and reunited with the parents and siblings he had carried in his heart for so many years. There is peace in knowing that after a lifetime of faith, service, and devotion, he is finally home.

Edward will be greatly missed by his children: Jody Twiss, Julie Yellow Cloud, Jeannie Cuny, Thetna (Lionel) Weston, James Schuh, as well as two special daughters: Lynn Pourier and Suzette Brown: his grandchildren: Quent and Joseph (Zadia) Bourne, Cody and Jesse Ferguson, Catlin (Jordan) and Kyle (Kateri) Clifford, Alaina (Gerome) Gutierrez, Joshua (Peppermint) and Riley Yellow Cloud, Michael, Marlee, Lala, and Tiaunni Kelly, Kristin (Greg) Weston, Tori (Gabriel) Old Man, Jeila, T'Rese (Trevin), Jamesson, Joel, and Samantha Schuh; his great grandchildren: Quent, Carson, Molly, Tya, Mia, Adam, Ava, Ziya, Aiyanna, Amarri, Wylder, Lynx, River, Payson, Keegan, Gatlin, Rylan, Phoenix, Zepplin, Motley, Araya, Joshie, Samuel, Talayah, and Janayah; his brothers and sisters; Don and Leon (Carolyn) Schuh, Bernice Brochtrup, Corrine Staudinger, Florence Braun, Germaine (Bill) Hoyer, Irene (John) Nenahlo: brother-in-law: Lloyd Twiss; sister-in-law: Nancy (Bill) Mathes; and son-in-law: Gaylon Kelly; as well as numerous nieces, nephews, and godchildren.

He was preceded in death by his wife, Theresa (Merrival) Schuh, parents, Edward and Ottilia Schuh, Brothers: Harlan and Kenneth Schuh; Sisters: Alice Maney, Eleanore Brunig, and Mary Schuh; Brothers-in-law: Jon Maney, Kenneth Brochtrup, Norbert Braun, Paul Staudinger, Donald Brunig, Donroy Merrival; sisters-in-law: Joyce Schuh, Gloria Steinfest, Greta Brown, Ila Twiss, Bonita Merrival, Doris Clifford, and Lema Merrival, and numerous other loved ones.

title: Duane Baumgartner
_full_text:
April 19, 1932 - July 19, 2026

Duane E. Baumgartner, 94, passed away peacefully at his home in Casper, Wyoming, on July 19, 2026.

Born on April 19, 1932, in Scottsbluff, Nebraska, Duane was the youngest of four children born to Casper Baumgartner and Myrtice A. Baumgartner. He grew up with his brothers and sister and carried throughout his life the warmth, humor, and easygoing spirit that made him so dearly loved by his family.

Duane earned his master's degree and built a life centered on creativity, learning, and service. He taught college-level art in Texas and North Dakota before spending the majority of his career at Stevens High School in Rapid City, South Dakota, where he taught art and journalism. He shared his love of art with generations of students, encouraging them not only to create, but to see the world with curiosity and imagination.

His influence extended far beyond the classroom. Duane was deeply involved in the Rapid City community, serving on several boards, including the City's Historic Preservation Board, and supporting organizations such as the Dahl Art Museum and the Dakota Artists' Guild. His dedication to the arts and to his community was recognized in 1999, when he was named an Honoree of the Rushmore Cultural Arts Honors.

To his family, Duane was more than an educator and artist - he was the fun-loving uncle, the one whose presence brought laughter, warmth, and fond memories. He also had a true love for animals, especially his beloved Westie dogs and cats. He will be remembered for his kind heart, his lively spirit, and the genuine joy he brought to family gatherings and to the lives of those around him.

Duane was preceded in death by his brothers, Richard and Jerold, and his sister, Patricia.

He is survived by his sister-in-law, Lorna Baumgartner, and by seven nieces and one nephew, who will cherish the memories they shared with him and remember him always with love.

A Celebration of Life will be held on August 22, 2026, from 11 am to 2 pm, at Hotel 21 & CO., 2605 10th St., Gering, Nebraska.

Duane will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered by his family, friends, former students, and all whose lives were brightened by his kindness, humor, and generous spirit.

title: Police arrest 2 after downtown Rapid City stabbing
description: Two young men were arrested on Thursday, Aug. 6, after a stabbing in downtown Rapid City.
_full_text:
Two young men were arrested on Thursday, Aug. 6, after a stabbing in downtown Rapid City.

Per the Rapid City Police Department, officers were called to the 400 block of Mount Rushmore Road around 11:25 p.m. on Thursday for a report that someone was stabbed. When police arrived, they found the stabbed person and learned the stabbing took place a block away, in the 500 block of Mount Rushmore Road, after several people got into a verbal argument. That block includes parking lots, Press Start and Bukoju Ramen.

After gathering a description of two suspects from a witness, police found 21-year-old Jacorey Vega and 22-year-old Ross Cloud Man Jr., both of Rapid City, walking north in the alleyway of the 900 block of Main Street, which is near West Boulevard. Witnesses identified them as the men involved in the stabbing. Cloud Man was arrested on suspicion of aggravated assault and Vega was arrested on suspicion of accessory to aggravated assault. Both were taken to the Pennington County Jail.

Due to a cybersecurity incident affecting the county, the jail roster and accompanying bond information is not available.

title: Road deaths stack up before official start of 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally; law enforcement says to slow down
description: Over the course of one day in the Black Hills — Thursday, Aug. 6, the day before the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally officially started — five people died in crashes involving motorcycles. That’s in addition to a motorcycle crash less than a week ago that took a Sioux Falls woman’s life and a vehicle rollover near Scenic that killed an 18-year-old girl.
_full_text:
Over the course of one day in the Black Hills — Thursday, Aug. 6, the day before the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally officially started — five people died in crashes involving motorcycles. That’s in addition to a motorcycle crash less than a week ago that took a Sioux Falls woman’s life and a vehicle rollover near Scenic that killed an 18-year-old girl.

Each year, roughly half a million vehicles enter Sturgis, per the South Dakota Department of Transportation. Although Sturgis is the namesake and the epicenter of the rally, it touches the entire Black Hills area, as riders travel along the winding roads and take in the scenery. What is an enjoyable time for many, however, can and does end in tragedy.

During the 2025 rally, four people died in crashes and 66 were injured. In 2024, there were three deaths and 35 injuries.

Since the recent crashes all took place before the official start date of this year’s rally, Aug. 7, they won’t be included in the South Dakota Department of Public Safety’s “Sturgis Rally Tally.” The tally lists daily crashes, deaths, arrests, citations and other information.

In light of the recent fatal crashes in Pennington County and the increased traffic the rally brings to the Black Hills, Lt. Jason Mitzel of the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office met with media on Friday, Aug. 7, at the Public Safety Building in Rapid City and urged the public to slow down.

“We welcome everybody to come to Pennington County and the Black Hills for the rally, we just ask people to slow down, give yourself a little bit of distance, and you know, pay attention to those speed limits and make sure you're wearing your safety gear as well,” Mitzel said, noting that some people come to South Dakota because there isn’t a helmet law.

 Mitzel
Lt. Jason Mitzel, with the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, urged the public to slow down during the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally during a Friday, Aug. 7, press conference at the Public Safety Building in Rapid City. Mitzel is wearing a highlighter-yellow shirt that the public can expect to see deputies wearing throughout the county during the rally. 

Mitzel said some of the factors that cause crashes are speed, alcohol and distraction. He said the more protective gear riders wear, the less likely they are to be injured. He also encouraged motorists driving other vehicles to, “slow down, give themselves space, keep your head on a swivel, watch your blind spots.”

“Welcome, everybody, to Pennington County and the Black Hills. We want to make sure everybody has a safe and fun Rally, and again, slow down. Give yourself some extra time. Enjoy the scenery,” Mitzel said.

On Thursday, Aug. 6, five people die in three crashes:

1 p.m.: A 46-year-old Sioux Falls woman was traveling eastbound on U.S. Highway 14A on a 2013 Suzuki Gladius 650. At the same time, a 77-year-old man from Wrentham, Massachusetts, was driving a 2013 Victory Jackpot westbound on the highway and failed to negotiate a curve. The Victory Jackpot crossed into the eastbound lane and struck the Suzuki, the patrol said. The driver of the Suzuki sustained fatal injuries. The driver of the Victory was transported to a Sturgis hospital with serious, non-life-threatening injuries. Both were wearing helmets.

1:51 p.m.: A 69-year-old man and 69-year-old woman, both from Emden, Illinois, died from injuries suffered in a crash on U.S. Highway 385 at mile marker 89, 8 miles northeast of Hill City. The 1953 Harley-Davidson motorcycle they were riding collided with a 2011 Toyota 4Runner. The motorcycle caught fire, as did the Toyota. Both occupants of the Toyota were wearing seatbelts and survived. The pair on the motorcycle were wearing helmets.

6:27 p.m.: A 54-year-old woman and a 59-year-old man, both from Frederick, Colorado, died in a two-vehicle crash 4 miles east of Deadwood. The man was driving a 2020 Harley Davidson Street Glide. The woman was the passenger. The driver failed to negotiate curve on U.S. Highway 14A near mile marker 47 as it was traveling east. At the same time, a 2009 Jeep Grand Cherokee was traveling westbound. The Harley Davidson crossed into the westbound lanes and collided with the Jeep. The motorcyclists were not wearing helmets. The driver of the Jeep was a 15-year-old girl from Sturgis. She was wearing a seatbelt. The two passengers were a 67-year-old man from Lead and a 59-year-old woman, also from Lead. It’s under investigation whether the passengers were wearing seatbelts.

Pennington County sees other deaths

In addition to the Thursday crash northeast of Hill City that took the lives of the two people from Illinois, two others died on Pennington County roads recently.

At around 11 a.m. on Saturday, Aug. 1, a 2025 Canam Spyder RT crashed 5 miles west of Rochford at South Rochford and Seven Hills roads. The South Dakota Highway Patrol said the driver of the Spyder, a 72-year-old man from Sioux Falls, was traveling on South Rochford Road near Seven Hills Road when he failed to negotiate a curve. The Spyder left the road and rolled. Dawn Hillman, a 67-year-old Sioux Falls woman who was the passenger on the motorcycle, died from her injuries, the patrol said. She was wearing a helmet.

Also in Pennington County, on Monday, Aug. 3, Kristina Yellow Hawk, 18, of Wall, died in a crash near Scenic. Per the South Dakota Highway Patrol, she was driving a 2008 Chevrolet Impala northbound on Bombing Range Road when the vehicle left the road. She attempted to correct and lost control of the vehicle, sending it into a roll. Yellow Hawk’s 19-year-old passenger was taken to a Rapid City hospital with serious non-life-threatening injuries.

Mitzel said Pennington County deputies will be out and about throughout the rally the public shouldn’t hesitate to ask questions. If deputies are working a crash, however, Mitzel asked the public to give them space to do their work.

“We spread our deputies out across Pennington County. We have them on both vehicle and foot patrols in our contract towns in Keystone and Hill City. Our vehicle patrols are out on the county roads and state highways. So we try to stay as visible as possible. Obviously, with our highlighter yellow shirts, you'll see us around,” Mitzel said.

Pennington County Highway Superintendent Joseph Miller said at a recent Pennington County Commission Meeting quoting state data, there were 36 total crashes from 2015 to the present on Bombing Range Road, where Yellow Hawk died. That includes 25 injury accidents and three fatal accidents. Miller said reconstruction of the road is estimated at $15 to $20 million and at this time the county hasn’t identified a funding source to take on the work. The project remains part of Pennington County’s Five-Year Transportation Plan, but is contingent on finding a funding source.

title: 2 suffer fatal injuries after motorcycle collides with Toyota near Hill City
description: Two people died in a crash involving two motorcycles in Pennington County.
_full_text:
Two people died in a crash involving two motorcycles in Pennington County.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol said a 69-year-old man and 69-year-old woman, both from Emden, Illinois, died from injuries suffered in a crash that occurred around 1:51 p.m. on Thursday, Aug. 6, on U.S. Highway 385 at mile marker 89, 8 miles northeast of Hill City.

The patrol said an investigation determined the 69-year-old man was driving a 1953 Harley-Davidson, with the woman as a passenger. They were traveling northbound on Highway 385, as was a 72-year-old Glendale, Arizona man on a 1956 Harley Davidson FLE 74CI.

A 67-year-old woman, traveling northbound on Highway 385 in a 2011 Toyota 4Runner with a 62-year-old woman as a passenger, was stopped and waiting for oncoming traffic to pass so she could turn onto Wrinkle Valley Road, the patrol said. A fourth vehicle was between the Toyota and motorcycles and passed the Toyota on the shoulder.

Upon approaching the Toyota, the motorcyclists attempted to stop and their brakes locked, the patrol said. The man on the 1956 Harley laid his bike down on the road. The man and woman in the 1953 Harley collided with the Toyota and the motorcycle caught fire, which spread to the Toyota, according to the patrol.

Medics took the 72-year-old man from Arizona to the hospital for treatment of serious, non-life-threatening injuries. The driver of the Toyota was not injured.

The man and woman from Illinois were wearing helmets, the patrol said. The agency is investigating whether the Arizona man was wearing a helmet. The Toyota driver and passenger were each wearing a seat belt.

The patrol did not release the names of those involved pending notification of family.

An investigation into the crash continues.

title: Rapid City man arrested for shooting at residence
description: No one was injured when a Rapid City man allegedly fired a gun at a residence Saturday night.
_full_text:
No one was injured when a Rapid City man allegedly fired a gun at a residence Saturday night.

The Pennington County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded to a shots-fired call at a residence north of Rapid City on 225th Street around 11 p.m. on Aug. 8. Deputies found evidence that multiple rounds had struck the residence.

The resident was able to locate and identify the suspected vehicle and provided that information to law enforcement, the office said. Rapid City Police Department officers located the vehicle a short time later at a residence in Rapid City.

Investigators executed search warrants and recovered evidence connected to the incident, the sheriff’s office said. Authorities arrested Jaycias Flying Horse, 18, of Rapid City, and a juvenile. Flying Horse, 18, of Rapid City, was arrested on suspicion of aggravated assault, discharge of a firearm at an occupied structure, receiving stolen property and underage consumption.

South Dakota court records show Flying Horse faces charges related to a May 2026 arrest. Flying Horse is charged with possessing a loaded firearm while intoxicated, obstructing an officer and underage drinking.

In addition to Rapid City police, the South Dakota Highway Patrol assisted as well during the Aug. 8 incident. An investigation into the incident continues. “There is no indication of an ongoing threat to the public,” the office said in a release.

title: Patrol reports fatal crash as local authorities provide Sturgis Rally updates
description: A 72-year-old man died from injuries suffered in a crash on U.S. Highway 85 on Saturday, Aug. 8.
_full_text:
A 72-year-old man died from injuries suffered in a crash on U.S. Highway 85 on Saturday, Aug. 8.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol issued an update on Sturgis Motorcycle Rally crashes and arrests, covering a time frame from 6 a.m. on Aug. 8 through 6 a.m. on Aug. 9. In addition to the fatal crash, there were another seven injury accidents.

The patrol said around 4:41 p.m. the 72-year-old man, driving a 2003 Harley-Davidson Electra Glide motorcycle, was traveling north on Highway 85 near mile marker 35 when he braked while approaching a motorcycle in front him that was turning. The driver lost control of the vehicle and became separated from the motorcycle, the patrol said. Medics took the man to Monument Health Spearfish Hospital, where he later died.

The patrol did not release the man’s name, pending notification of family, and did not immediately respond to a request for the man’s hometown.

It’s the first fatal crash of the rally, which officially started Friday, Aug. 7, that the patrol has been the lead agency on. Per stats released by the patrol, there were two fatal crashes during the same timeframe in 2025.

 081026-nws-rally-dailystats-p1.jpg

In a release issued by the City of Sturgis, the patrol encouraged riders to check out ridesafesd.com.

Highway Patrol Capt. Zac Bader, speaking at the Rally daily news conference on Saturday, said the agency is making the website a focus of its safety messaging during Rally week following a difficult pre-Rally period on South Dakota roads, the release noted.

Bader said three fatal crashes on Thursday, Aug. 6, resulted in five deaths. Among the problems troopers have seen in pre-Rally crashes are motorcycles leaving their lanes and motorists following too closely.

“We’re really going to be pushing out those messages and that website,” Bader said in the release while discussing RideSafeSD.com. “They’ve got some good safety tips.”

During the same 6 a.m. on Aug. 8 through 6 a.m. on Aug. 9 timeframe, the Sturgis Police Department reported four injury accidents, four driving while intoxicated arrests, two assaults and seven drug arrests. Officers responded to eight fight calls/disturbances/assaults.

In total, the police department reported 23 non-traffic arrests and 20 traffic arrests during the timeframe. Over two days, the department has made 80 arrests, down from 100 over the same time period in 2025.

Injury crashes from the South Dakota Highway Patrol:

At 9:19 a.m. Saturday, US Highway 16A, mile marker 33: A 2017 Harley-Davidson motorcycle operated by a 68-year-old male (Unit 1) was driving westbound on US 16A near MM 33. He was life-flighted to Rapid City Monument Health with serious injuries.

At 11:46 a.m. Saturday, US Highway 14A, mile marker 32: A 2018 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 59-year-old male, was driving eastbound on Highway 14A near mile marker 32. The driver was transported to Lead-Deadwood Monument Health for treatment of his injuries.

The driver of Unit 1 was transported to Monument Health for treatment of his injuries.
