title: Update: 2 arrested for firing shots from overlook on Skyline Drive
description: In an afternoon update, the Rapid City Police Department said it has identified two suspects accused of shooting guns from the Stonewall Overlook on Skyline Drive.
_full_text:
In an afternoon update, the Rapid City Police Department said it has identified two suspects accused of shooting guns from the Stonewall Overlook on Skyline Drive.

The suspects fired the shots around 6:30 a.m., police said, leading many to call authorities to report the incident.

The department said officers arrested 20-year-old Wicapiiyoyinpa Richards and 29-year-old Miranda Marks, both of Rapid City, for reckless discharge of a firearm and possession of a loaded firearm while intoxicated. Police said officers executed a search warrant at their residence in the 1900 block of Twin Elms Drive and recovered the handgun allegedly used during the incident.

The department said early Sunday, Aug. 9, it received multiple reports of gunshots heard from the area of Skyline Drive. Police were able to review camera footage from the area and observed two individuals fire a handgun in the area of the Stonewall Overlook. Police said the shots were fired from the overlook in the direction of the neighborhood to the west of the location.

 image005.png
Video footage from a shooting incident on Skyline Drive. 

No reports of damage or injuries were reported. “Several persons of interest have been identified and steps are being taken to hold them accountable for their dangerous and reckless actions,” the department said in its initial release about the incident.

There are no records for Richards and Marks in available online South Dakota court records. The Pennington County Jail roster remains unavailable online because of the cyberattack against the county.

An investigation into the shooting remains active with additional charges pending as the investigation progresses, police said.

Anyone with any information on the incident or the suspects involved should contact police at 605-394-4131. Should damage from the gunfire be discovered, it should be reported to police at the same number. An anonymous tip can also be submitted by texting the letters “RCPD” and the information to 847411.

 image003 (2).png
The Rapid City Police Department is investigating after these suspects allegedly fired shots from the area of Skyline Drive.

title: Renee Plumb
_full_text:
June 30, 1952 - July 31, 2026

The lure was too great when Renee received an invite to join the fishing group that had been assembled. Bill had her rod and reel, bait and tackle ready on the boat. Aunt Daisy and Uncle Al were joining in to say, "The fishin' is great!" It was an invite she could not pass up. For the family that loved her dearly, this news is sudden and shocking.

Renee Lynn Plumb was born to Alvin and Daisy (Merrill) Plumb on June 30, 1952. She grew up in Huron, SD, and attended Huron High School. In high school Renee was a member of the school paper staff, the National Honor Society, and a cheerleader. She went on to study at South Dakota State University in Brookings, SD attaining a degree in Social Work. She began her career working for the Watertown Department of Social Services. She also spent many years working for the Alex Johnson Hotel, in Rapid City. After her move to Pierre, SD she worked for the Kings Inn Motel, later being employed by the State of South Dakota, in Pierre, where she retired from.

Bill Opsahl was the true love of Renee's life. When she met Bill, she knew she had found the love of her life. They enjoyed many fishing trips together, so Pierre was the perfect location for them to make their home. Good weather or bad, they could usually be found in their boat on Lake Oahe; fishing the day away. They also enjoyed spending time with their dog Brandy, their faithful companion. They lived together in Pierre until Bills death on January 13, 2021.

Renee is preceded in death by her fiance, Bill Opsal and his son Michael Opsahl, her parents Alvin and Daisy Plumb, maternal and paternal grandparents, along with many loved aunts and uncles, cousins and friends. Renee is survived by a contingent of family members from Renee and Bill's family along with Bill's family: Brother Jerry (Wendy) Opsahl, sister Cindy (Steve) Closset, sons Robert Procko (Kimberly), Bryan Procko (Joyce), three grandchildren (Emily, Verdani and Michael) and one great-grandchild (Landon) and dear friends that are all mourning the loss of one of their own.

A Celebration of Life will be held at a site on the Missouri River where her ashes and those of her beloved fiance Bill and their cherished dog Brandy will be released over the waters that played such an important role in her life.

You may sign her online guestbook at www.kinkadefunerals.com.

title: UPDATE: Authorities release names of the 2 who died from fatal injuries in crash near Deadwood
description: The South Dakota Department of Public Safety released the names of the man and woman from Colorado who died in a two-vehicle crash 4 miles east of Deadwood around 6:27 p.m. on Thursday, Aug. 6.
_full_text:
The South Dakota Department of Public Safety released the names of the man and woman from Colorado who died in a two-vehicle crash 4 miles east of Deadwood around 6:27 p.m. on Thursday, Aug. 6.

Shawn Lee Rector, 59, and Susan Renee Rector, 54, of Frederick, Colorado died after a car-vs-motorcycle collision on Thursday. The department released their names on Monday, Aug. 10.

Per the South Dakota Department of Public Safety, preliminary crash information indicates the driver of a 2009 Jeep Grand Cherokee was traveling westbound on U.S. Highway 14A near mile marker 47. At the same time, the driver, Shawn Rector, of a 2020 Harley Davidson Street Glide was traveling east and failed to negotiate a turn. The Harley Davidson crossed into the westbound lanes and collided with the Jeep.

Both the driver and passenger of the Harley Davidson sustained fatal injuries. One of the Jeep’s passengers sustained minor injuries. Neither of the Rector’s were wearing helmets.

The driver of the Jeep was a 15-year-old girl from Sturgis. She was wearing a seatbelt. The two passengers were a 67-year-old man from Lead and a 59-year-old woman, also from Lead. It’s under investigation whether the passengers were wearing seatbelts.

U.S. Highway 14A was closed for approximately three hours. The investigation is ongoing. All information released is preliminary.

title: Yungblud embraces rally, rocks Sturgis Buffalo Chip
description: Yungblud committed to the Sturgis Rally thing. On the last stop of his North America tour, the British artist, Grammy award winner, UK chart-topper and Ozzy Osbourne protege played the Sturgis Buffalo Chip on Sunday, Aug. 9 — but not without giving motorcycle riding a go first (which was featured in a pre-show hype video played on a large screen before he took the stage).
_full_text:
Yungblud committed to the Sturgis Rally thing. On the last stop of his North America tour, the British artist, Grammy award winner, UK chart-topper and Ozzy Osbourne protege played the Sturgis Buffalo Chip on Sunday, Aug. 9 — but not without giving motorcycle riding a go first (which was featured in a pre-show hype video played on a large screen before he took the stage).

 Yungblud
Yungblud put on an energetic performance at the Sturgis Buffalo Chip on Sunday, Aug. 9. 

And he didn’t overlook Rapid City. In social media posts ahead of the concert, Yungblud posted a video riding down Quincy Street in front of the Performing Arts Center. Sources reported his tour buses stopped at Hardee’s in downtown Rapid City, and his crew bunked at the Hotel Alex Johnson.

Dirt bike riding around Camp Zero at The Chip a couple hours before the 10:30 p.m. concert apparently didn’t go so well. Yungblud told the crowd, “I think I nearly broke by (expletive) leg, man,” but with the help of a steroid injection and against a doctor’s advice, the 29-year-old rock star powered through with a subtle limp.

That didn’t stop the artist, whose lesser-known name is Dominic Harrison, from delivering an energetic performance, jumping around the stage and engaging and flirting the crowd.

“Does anybody want to kidnap me and take me home with them?” he asked coyly.

At one point during the show, Yungblud brought an audience member holding a sign that said, “Can I play Fleabag,” onto the stage. The man, who introduced himself as Dakota from Nebraska, held a guitar and played a portion of the song while Yungblud sang.

 081126-nws-yungbuld-p1.JPG
Dakota, from Nebraska, holds a sign asking to play “Fleabag” at the Sunday, Aug. 9 Yungblud concert at the Sturgis Buffalo Chip. The artist later invited him to come onto the stage and play. 

Hayley, a 25-year-old from Alliance, Nebraska, told the Journal ahead of the show she came to Sturgis to see Yungblud for a second time after seeing him in Denver.

“I loved it, that’s why I’m back,” she said.

 Hayley
Hayley, left, and her friend take a photo with a poster of Yungblud at the Sturgis Buffalo Chip on Sunday, Aug. 9, ahead of his concert. 

Brandon, a 33-year-old Minnesota man working at a vendor booth at The Chip, told the Journal he’s indifferent about Yungblud.

“I’ve heard of him before, but I’ve never listened to his stuff,” he said.

 PHOTOS: Yungblud at the Buffalo Chip
Have a look at a few (well, more than a few) photos of three-time Grammy nominee and Ozzy Ozbourne mentee Yungblud’s Sturgis Buffalo Chip performance on Sunday, Aug. 9. 

Larry Thomas, a 55-year-old, also from Nebraska, said he knows of Yungblud as an up-and-coming artist who was Ozzy Osbourne’s protege.

“It’ll be interesting to see what kind of performance he puts on,” Thomas said from the back of the crowd."

That smattering of takes from people at The Chip is consistent with what the artist pointed out to The Guardian’s Alexis Petridis, who reported, “Beyond his famously rabid fanbase, who call themselves the Black Hearts Club, people may know the name Yungblud, but would struggle to name one of his songs.”

 Yungblud
British artist Yungblud sings at the Buffalo Chip on Sunday, Aug. 9. 

The crowd’s reaction to Yungblud was similar. Some were clearly there for him, knew the lyrics to his songs, and sang along enthusiastically. Others seemed to look at the young artist through an observational lens.

As reported by Petridis in January, “Yunglud’s fourth studio album, Idols, entered the UK charts at No 1, outselling its nearest competitor by 50%. The same month, the annual festival he curates and headlines, Bludfest, drew an audience of 30,000 to The National Bowl in Milton Keynes. In July 2025, he played at Back to the Beginning, the farewell performance by Black Sabbath, whose frontman Osbourne died 17 days after the gig.”

Yungblud played tribute to Osbourne with a performance of “Changes,” saying the artist got him through “so much.” Yungblud’s performance of the song at Back to the Beginning earned him his first-ever Grammy in the Best Rock Performance category. His 2025 album “Idols” and his song “Zombie” received nominations.

In a brief social media video after Yungblud’s Sturgis show, he said he, “can’t wait to be back.” It’s yet to be determined if and when Yungblud will find his way back across the pond and to the Black Hills.

 081126-nws-yungbuld-p35.JPG
A large crowd cheers on Yungblud at Sturgis Buffalo Chip. 

 Yungblud at the Buffalo Chip
Yungblud playing the Sturgis Buffalo Chip on Sunday, Aug. 9.

title: Police: SUV ran a Rapid City stop sign before fatal crash with motorcycle
description: For more information on the Rapid City PD tip line, go to https://shorturl.at/ShAIX. For Pennington County, go to https://shorturl.at/Gya1r.
_full_text:
Crime tip submissions for Rapid City, Pennington County

A motorcycle rider died on Friday, Aug. 7, after colliding with an SUV that allegedly ran past a stop sign, the Rapid City Police Department said in an update on Monday, Aug. 10.

The driver, 82-year-old Richard Lennon, received a stop sign violation. The Rapid City Police Department said the crash is still under investigation by its Critical Accident Reconstruction Team, and the results of the investigation will be sent to the Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office. As of Monday, Aug. 10, there are no court records showing Lennon facing criminal charges from the incident.

The crash happened around 1:10 p.m. Friday at the intersection of Highway 16 and Enchantment Road.

After speaking with witnesses, police determined a Ford SUV was westbound on Enchantment Road when it attempted to make a left-hand turn to head south on Highway 16. A northbound motorcycle struck the SUV in the intersection.

A review of security video in the area showed the SUV driver did not stop at the stop sign at the intersection before turning, police said.

Hours later, police were informed that the motorcycle rider died at the hospital from his injuries. His identification is being withheld until police notify the next of kin.

title: Staying past closing time: Rapid City man faces sixth DUI, weapons charges after late-night park arrest
description: A Rapid City man was arrested for a sixth DUI offense and weapons charges after parking past Canyon Lake Park’s closing time.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man was arrested for a sixth DUI offense and weapons charges after parking past Canyon Lake Park’s closing time.

Paul Verhelst, 59, was arrested on suspicion of sixth DUI offense, possession of a loaded firearm while intoxicated, no proof of insurance, and trespassing in a closed park.

Around 11 p.m. on Friday, Aug. 7, police were conducting an extra patrol at Canyon Lake Park when they found a pickup truck parked at the west Rapid City park past closing time. Rapid City parks hours are from 5 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Police found Verhelst and noted the smell of alcohol coming from him, along with other indicators of alcohol impairment, according to the department. Police determined he was too impaired to drive, so they arrested him.

During a pre-tow inventory of the truck, police found several firearms, some of which were loaded.

title: Rapid City police say Nebraska man pointed rifle at someone before he was arrested
description: A Nebraska man was arrested Sunday, Aug. 9, in Rapid City after allegedly pointing an AR-15 style rifle at another passenger in a vehicle.
_full_text:
A Nebraska man was arrested Sunday, Aug. 9, in Rapid City after allegedly pointing an AR-15 style rifle at another passenger in a vehicle.

Kendrell Cuveas, 21, of Rushville, Nebraska, was arrested on suspicion of aggravated assault and obstruction.

Around 9:25 p.m. on Sunday police responded to the 3700 block of Arizona Street for a report of an assault with a weapon. After speaking with the reporting party, police determined Cuveas was in a car when he pointed a rifle at another occupant in the vehicle.

The suspect vehicle drove off with Cuveas inside. However, it was found a short time later during a traffic stop in the area of Fifth Street and Stumer Road. The car stopped and Cuveas fled from the car on foot.

Police eventually caught up to Cuveas after he tripped and fell to the ground. Police detained him at taser-point and he was taken into custody. A search of the vehicle turned up an AR-15 style rifle in the area where Cuveas had been sitting.

title: Patrol releases name of pair killed in crash near Hill City
description: Two people died in a crash involving two motorcycles in Pennington County.
_full_text:
Two people died in a crash involving two motorcycles in Pennington County.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol released the names of a man and woman from Emden, Illinois, who died from injuries suffered in a crash that occurred around 1:51 p.m. on Thursday, Aug. 6, on U.S. Highway 385 at mile marker 89, 8 miles northeast of Hill City.

Kurt D. Klokkenga, 69, and Regina K. Klokkenga, 69, died in the crash, the patrol said on Monday, Aug. 10.

The patrol said an investigation determined Kurt D. Klokkenga was driving a 1953 Harley-Davidson, with Regina as a passenger. They were traveling northbound on Highway 385, as was Kendall Klokkenga, 72, of Glendale, Arizona, on a 1956 Harley Davidson FLE 74CI.

A 67-year-old woman, traveling northbound on Highway 385 in a 2011 Toyota 4Runner with a 62-year-old woman as a passenger, was stopped and waiting for oncoming traffic to pass so she could turn onto Wrinkle Valley Road, the patrol said. A fourth vehicle was between the Toyota and motorcycles and passed the Toyota on the shoulder.

Upon approaching the Toyota, the motorcyclists attempted to stop and their brakes locked, the patrol said. Kendall Klokkenga laid his bike down on the road. Kurt and Regina Klokkenga collided with the Toyota and the motorcycle caught fire, which spread to the Toyota, according to the patrol.

Medics took Kendall Klokkenga to the hospital for treatment of serious, non-life-threatening injuries. The driver of the Toyota was not injured.

Kurt and Regina Klokkenga were wearing helmets, the patrol said. The agency is investigating whether Kendall was. The Toyota driver and passenger were each wearing a seat belt.

The Journal awaits a response from the patrol on how the Klokkengas are related.

An investigation into the crash continues.

title: Updated: Patrol releases name of Sioux Falls woman who died in Sturgis crash, charges pending
description: A Sioux Falls woman died from injuries suffered in a two-vehicle crash near Sturgis.
_full_text:
A Sioux Falls woman died from injuries suffered in a two-vehicle crash near Sturgis.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol said on Monday, Aug. 10, that 46-year-old Angelee Kay Glammeier, 46, died from injuries suffered in the crash.

Glammeier was traveling eastbound on U.S. Highway 14A on a 2013 Suzuki Gladius 650 around 1 p.m. on Thursday, Aug. 6, according to the patrol. At the same time, Darry Warnock Stuart, 77, of Wrentham, Massachusetts, was driving a 2013 Victory Jackpot westbound on the highway and failed to negotiate a curve.

Stuart crossed into the eastbound lane and his motorcycle struck Glammeier’s Suzuki, the patrol said. Stuart was transported to a Sturgis hospital with serious, non-life-threatening injuries. Eastbound lanes on the highway were closed for about an hour that day.

The patrol told the Journal charges against Stuart are pending.

Both motorcyclists were wearing helmets. An investigation into the crash continues.

title: Juvenile tries to steal manual transmission SUV, crashes
description: A juvenile unsuccessfully tried to steal a manual transmission vehicle in Rapid City on Monday, Aug. 10, police said.
_full_text:
A juvenile unsuccessfully tried to steal a manual transmission vehicle in Rapid City on Monday, Aug. 10, police said.

The Rapid City Police Department said someone watching CCTV video of a parking lot at 312 Main Street saw a male enter a parked SUV and attempt to drive it off. That attempt was unsuccessful when he couldn’t get the manual transmission into gear properly, fumbling the theft and crashing the SUV into a nearby truck.

The owner of the SUV went out to confront the unruly youth, who ran away on foot. Police detained him in the 600 block of Main Street. A witness identified him as the one who tried to get away with the SUV. He’s since been entered in the juvenile justice system, which is not open to the public.

title: Medicine Wheel Ride marks 7th annual event to bring awareness to Missing and Murdered Indigenous People
description: STURGIS — Starting from the western shores of the United States through the chasms of Zion National Park, the Medicine Wheel Riders trekked for nine days to reach Bear Butte State Park. The ride’s purpose is to bring awareness to missing and murdered Indigenous people.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Starting from the western shores of the United States through the chasms of Zion National Park, the Medicine Wheel Riders trekked for nine days to reach Bear Butte State Park. The ride’s purpose is to bring awareness to missing and murdered Indigenous people.

"We do those trips every single year in honor of our missing and murder Indigenous women, and the reason why we do that is because we believe in building community .... We go into different communities and make them aware of what's going on in our communities and hopefully bring them in as allies to help us in these efforts that we're working toward," said Medicine Wheel Ride Executive Director and Co-Founder Lorna Cuny, Oglala Lakota.

With over 100 riders gathered on Aug. 9 at the base of Bear Butte, a sacred site to the Lakota, community members spoke about personal losses.

 MMIW
Medicine Wheel Ride Executive Director Lorna Cuny speaks on the mission of the Medicine Wheel Ride organization at Bear Butte on Sunday, Aug. 9. 

According to the National Criminal Justice Training Center, Native American women are 10 times more likely to be murdered than all other ethnicities, with murder the third leading cause of death for Native women. More than 84% have experienced violence, more than 56% have experienced sexual violence, more than 55% have been physically abused by an intimate partner, and 40% of all sex trafficking victims are Native women.

Community member Delany Apple, Lakota, gave a prayer before stories from victims' families were shared.

 Delaney Apple
Delaney Apple, of Rapid City, shared words over loss and sang songs for healing. 

"Each and every one of us is affected in some way or another. We've all experienced loss ... We walk in a sacred way because we're at our most vulnerable. Because we can't be ourselves in public. We carry an empty space in our heart for a loved one who has gone on," Apple said. "Even though we can't see those relatives, they're here beside us. When our bodies are done on this earth, our spirit lives on.”

He continued, saying, "They prayed for each one of you to do what you need to do today, to do what you need to do to make our future better for our children."

Darlene Gomez, an attorney who works on MMIP cases for the Medicine Wheel Ride, said her friend Melissa Ann Montaya (Jicarilla Apache) has been missing since 2001.

 MMIW
Darlene Gomez is an attorney with the Medicine Wheel Ride. 

"I want all of you guys to know that when you donate to the Medicine Wheel Ride, you are donating directly to these families. There is very little funding that's available for missing and murdered Indigenous people," Gomez said.

Hillary Dubray attended the event. She is the mother of Sahela (Different Cheyenne Woman) Sangrait-Dubray, a 21-year-old Cheyenne River Lakota woman who was killed on Aug. 11, 2024, allegedly at Ellsworth Air Force Base.

 MMIW
The Medicine Wheel Ride organization provides services to MMIW/MMIP victims' families and works to bring awareness to the issue. 

Her body was later found on March 4, 2025, outside of Hill City, 40 miles from Box Elder.

Quinterius Charles Chappelle, a 24-year-old former airman, is charged with first-degree murder in federal court. His jury trial is scheduled to begin at the federal courthouse in Rapid City on Nov. 2. According to federal court documents, Drew Durand of Rapid City is charged with accessory after the fact and misprision of a felony in connection with the case.

Dubray thanked the Medicine Wheel Ride organization for working on her daughter's case.

Belle Brings Plenty, Lakota, presented a blanket design honoring her brother, Cole Brings Plenty.

 MMIW
Belle Brings Plenty, sister of late actor Cole Brings Plenty, presented her blanket design that honors her brother.  

Brings Plenty was named the winner of the 2025 Tribal College Blanket Design Competition for her blanket titled Journey. Pendleton included this design in their Woolen Mills’ American Indian College Fund blanket collection.

Cole Brings Plenty, Lakota, was reported missing on April 1, 2024. He was found dead four days later in a wooded area of Johnson County, Kansas — about 40 minutes from Indian Nations University, where he was a student.

He was most well-known for his role as Pete Plenty Clouds in the “Yellowstone” prequel series “1923.” He had also been featured in “Into the Wild Frontier” and “The Tall Tales of Jim Bridger.”

 MWR
On Aug. 9, members of the Medicine Wheel Ride Organization concluded their journey from California to Sturgis S.D, to bring awareness of MMIW/MMIP. 

Kansas law enforcement said there is no foul play suspected in Brings Plenty’s death, but the family continue to advocate for further investigation.

"I wanted to honor my brother in a good way and make this blanket for him,” Brings Plenty said.

She said her family's birth dates are incorporated on the blanket, including her brother's date of death. There are stars incorporated to reflect the Lakota belief that after death, a person is returned to the stars from which they came.

The use of red and blue in the blanket is also intentional. Brings Plenty said that the use of red represents the day someone is born, and the use of blue represents the day someone passes away.

She concluded by singing a song with her family members.

title: Bear Butte Fire near Sturgis now 90% contained
description: South Dakota Wildland Fire said the Bear Butte Fire is now 90% contained.
_full_text:
South Dakota Wildland Fire said the Bear Butte Fire is now 90% contained.

According to the South Dakota Department of Public Safety and Watch Duty, the fire affects about 457 acres. It’s located west of South Dakota Highway 79, about a mile south of Bear Butte, and was reported around 2 p.m. on Monday, Aug. 10.

The Meade County Sheriff’s Office said the grass fire near Highway 79 featured a response by multiple agencies on Monday, including a helicopter. The Journal observed a helicopter over the fire around 2:30 p.m. that day. The department said forward progress of the fire was stopped around 2:50 p.m.

Fire crews made their way to the fire amid heavy Sturgis Motorcycle Rally traffic.

"Thank you to all who stayed away from the area and allowed the fire trucks get to where they needed to be. And all the other folks who pulled over to the right and stopped so they could get out here, thank you," the Meade County Sheriff's Office said on social media. "Can't fight a fire if they can't get there!"

 PHOTOS: Bear Butte Fire near Sturgis
The Bear Butte Fire affected more than 456 acres and was 50% contained as of late Monday, Aug. 10, according to Watch Duty. Forward progress was stopped, according to authorities.

title: Partners in law and life: The story behind Rapid City's Colbath & Sperlich
description: The courtroom hummed with a quiet, restless anticipation in July 2025 as defense attorney Angela Colbath stepped forward to deliver closing statements in the high-profile case of a woman was accused of killing her 7-week-old niece .
_full_text:
The courtroom hummed with a quiet, restless anticipation in July 2025 as defense attorney Angela Colbath stepped forward to deliver closing statements in the high-profile case of a woman was accused of killing her 7-week-old niece.

Behind Colbath stood five grueling days of emotional testimony and meticulously dismantled evidence, much of it expertly dissected by her and her husband and legal co-counsel Gregory Sperlich. Operating as a formidable courtroom power couple, Sperlich’s surgical cross-examinations set the stage for Colbath’s compelling final push, weaving their complementary talents together and leading to Courtney Martinez’s acquittal.

The Martinez case is one of many high-profile cases they’ve defended, with notable ones including the acquittal of Allac “A.J.” Dismounts Thrice and the recently overturned conviction of Dion Bordeaux. The couple also defended Ezekiel Mayweather, who was sentenced to life in prison for the revenge killing of 24-year-old Esther Wolfe.

 Angela Colbath and Sperlich
Angela Colbath and Gregory Sperlich are criminal defense attorneys in Rapid City with over 40 years of combined legal experience. 

That shared courtroom confidence and natural sync didn’t just help defend cases, it sparked their relationship. After years representing clients in Pennington County, their professional chemistry blossomed into a romantic partnership, leading to their marriage in 2014.

“I think part of the reason we work well together is we both have a very strong belief that to do the best job we can do, our goal needs to be to know our case better than anyone else,” Colbath said.

By 2019, the couple decided to combine law firms, which is now known as Colbath & Sperlich Attorneys at Law. Together, the criminal defense attorneys have over 40 years of combined legal experience.

A match made in the courtroom

Long before they were a dynamic defense team, Colbath and Sperlich built their foundation on opposite sides of the aisle. Meeting for the first time in the high-stakes arena of the courtroom in 2004, the two faced off in the trial of a Rapid City Hardee’s assistant manager who faced charges after he was involved in a nationwide strip search hoax.

On one side of the courtroom was Colbath, born in Yankton and from an extensive family lineage of lawyers and paralegals. She was partnered with and under the tutelage of former defense attorney Randy Connelly, who was representing the assistant manager. The man was charged with kidnapping and second-degree rape.

On other side was Sperlich, who was a Pennington County deputy state’s attorney at the time. He grew up in Rapid City and earned a bachelor of arts degree in economics before finding his calling at law school.

 Ground shot of courthouse
The Pennington County Courthouse is located at 315 Saint Joseph Street, Rapid City.  

The assistant manager was accused of conducting a strip search on a 19-year-old female employee in a locked office of the downtown Hardee’s restaurant. The woman remained there for nearly three hours. Much of that time, he was on the telephone with a caller who claimed to be a police officer investigating a report of a stolen purse. The caller said the woman was a suspect in the case.

The Hardee’s assistant manager was acquitted on all charges after days of a trial testimony.

The wave of phone calls spanned between 1994 to 2004, with and the Louisville Courier Journal in Kentucky reported investigators identified roughly 70 confirmed incidents across the nation, confirming 53 fast-food chains and nine sit-down restaurants and eight retail stores fell victim to the hoax calls.

A Fountain, Florida man named David Stewart was arrested five months later and accused of being the caller. He was found not guilty of impersonating a police officer, soliciting sodomy and soliciting sexual abuse for a phone call and strip search at a Mount Washington, Kentucky, McDonald’s in April 2004. According to court records, Stewart was never charged in Pennington County.

According to the Journal’s archives, R.A. Dawson, a private investigator with Phoenix Investigations in Rapid City, looked into the calls for the defense in the Rapid City case. He is convinced that Stewart was on the other end of the line during the Hardee’s incident.

Sperlich would eventually leave the state’s attorney’s office in the summer of 2004 and enter private practice.

“I just wanted to make a change,” Sperlich said.

Regardless of the results of the case, Colbath and Sperlich said they built a great amount of respect for one another since that trial and began to frequently see each other in the courthouse. Their growing respect for each other and consistent interactions eventually led them to dating in 2013 and marrying the next year.

An inspiration in the courtroom

Criminal defense attorney Kyle Beauchamp joined the dynamic duo’s team in the fall of 2022. Beauchamp was born and raised in the Black Hills, beginning his career at Reptile Gardens where he discovered his passion to connect with people and be able to teach. The passion later blossomed further when Beauchamp achieved his dream by graduating from law school, where he became a judicial clerk for the Seventh Circuit — which includes Pennington, Custer and Fall River counites— and later on a defense attorney.

“The defense in western South Dakota is strong, but I thought it could be stronger,” Beauchamp said. “And I thought that started with just more individuals wanting to get in and help out and so I think it was a combination of both that wanting to join a great bar, but also knowing that I probably could help contribute to make it greater.”

During Beauchamp’s clerkship, he continued to hear about Colbath and Sperlich and the work they’ve done together. It wasn’t until Beauchamp witnessed Colbath prepare for a murder trial that he knew he needed to put his hat in the ring and join their firm.

“I just saw how she got up and just passionately advocated for her client and she wasn’t just going through the motions,” Beauchamp said. “She was zealously advocating for her client, you know, the way that everything was kind of going. She took great issue with it; she was quite upset, and just seeing how passionate she was about the law and protecting individuals’ rights. That’s the first time that I thought ‘that’s somebody that I absolutely want to learn more from.’”

Four years later Beauchamp said it has been “incredible” working for them. He said the pair has always had the drive to help their staff regardless of the situation and teach whenever someone has a question. Beauchamp said they’re one of the reasons that he is the attorney he is today.

Beauchamp said what makes the two so special and an overwhelming force in the courtroom is how much they compliment one another. He said the number one thing he learned from Colbath is to always be passionate and empathetic for every case, while Sperlich taught him the importance of having faith in the legal system.

Rapid City will always be home

Together the pair’s family consists of one 13 year-old, four adult children and their spouses, along with a granddaughter. They’ve built that family in Rapid City, and both Colbath and Sperlich said Rapid City will forever be home.

“For me it’s totally home. I can’t imagine living anywhere else,” Colbath said.

Over the years they’ve not only built a home a personal life but a strong legal foundation within Pennington County. Sperlich said it is an attorney’s duty to educate people about the system and become involved in it. He said the system is something that is carefully put together through years of dedication and care.

Sperlich said being a defense attorney is one piece in a big picture in ensuring the law not only protects but remains fair and balanced. He said everyone from the judge to the rivaling attorneys plays a part in making the system better. Pennington County is no exception.

As the two reflected on their careers so far and look forward to the endless possibilities the future may hold, Colbath and Sperlich said they are honored and proud to serve the community.

title: Stanford Mark Adelstein
description: August 10, 2026
_full_text:
August 10, 2026

KEYSTONE - Stanford Mark Adelstein, a former South Dakota State Senator, philanthropist and businessman, died peacefully on August 10, 2026. He is survived by his beloved wife, Lynda Clark Adelstein; his sons: Daniel Adelstein (Judy), James Adelstein, Jonathan Adelstein (Karen); his grandchildren: Adam and Alexis, Shirley (Joshua Sanderlin), Michael (Laura Molnar) and Danielle as well as his great-granddaughter, Lea Sanderlin. He is also survived by his brother, Robert Adelstein (Carol) and his cousin, Jerry Mizel (Liora).

Stan had a profound love for Rapid City, the State of South Dakota and a passion for public service. He served in the state legislature between 2001 - 2013, first in the House of Representatives, then as a state senator. He relished the fight for good causes and often said representing the people of District 32 was the best job he ever had.

Stan is well known for his charitable giving and leadership in civic and public service organizations including: The Rushmore Plaza Civic Center, St. John's McNamara Hospital, the Journey Museum, the Dahl Fine Arts Center, the Black Hills Symphony, the Black Hills Playhouse, Lutheran Social Services, the Performing Arts Center of Rapid City, the Club for Boys, and South Dakota Public Broadcasting among many other organizations. Stan continually asked the question, "how can I help?" He committed his time, money and expertise to friends and strangers alike, changing many lives for the better.

The son of Morris and Bertha Adelstein, Stan was born in Sioux City, Iowa and grew up in Rapid City. Stan earned bachelor's degrees in civil engineering and business administration from the University of Colorado at Boulder. He met his first wife Ita Korn Adelstein (1930- 2009), a fellow student at the university. Ita and Stan married in 1952 and had three sons, Daniel, James and Jonathan. Stan's love for his sons was fierce. He delighted in their successes and proudly celebrated their achievements to anyone who had the patience to listen. His five grandchildren and his great-granddaughter were a great joy for him and represented his hope for the future.

Stan took great pride in his Jewish faith, participating in national and international Jewish organizations and was a staunch advocate for Israel. He was a national leader for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, American Jewish Committee, Jewish Institute for National Security Affairs, and the Republican Jewish Coalition. He was often called upon to represent the Jewish community at public events, such as helping to establish the Hanukkah menorah at the State Capitol in Pierre. He spearheaded the move of The Synagogue of the Hills from Ellsworth Air Force Base to Rapid City where it found a permanent home in a building he donated.

Stan proudly served his country as a lieutenant in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (1955-1957) and as a captain in the South Dakota Army National Guard (1957-1961). As a civilian, he was a reservist for the National Defense Executive Reserve and was appointed as a reservist for the Federal Emergency Management Agency. In 1999, he was appointed as Civilian Aide to the Secretary of the Army and in 2001 was awarded the Distinguished Service Award from the Association of the U.S. Army. He was also a member of the American Legion.

After his military service, Stan assumed the role of engineer and estimator at Northwestern Engineering Company, founded in 1924 by his father. He became president of the company in 1968 and later assumed the role of Chief Executive Officer, overseeing its growth into one of the region's largest highway and heavy construction companies. He later led the company's transition into real estate acquisition and development.

Stan was incredibly fortunate to meet Lynda Clark in 1998; they were married in 2011. Together, they traveled the world and shared an appreciation for art, music, their beloved dogs and above all else, each other. Lynda filled Stan's days with joy and meaning. His children are profoundly grateful for Lynda's unwavering devotion, care and compassion during the difficult final chapter of Stan's life.

Stan's family would like to thank the staff at Good Samaritan St. Martin Village for the loving care they gave Stan during his last few years. We also wish to thank the doctors, nurses and therapists at Custer Hospital for their excellent care of Stan during a critical stage of his illness. They gave Stan the precious gift of additional time to spend with family and friends.

In lieu of flowers, donations honoring Stan's memory may be made to The Synagogue of the Hills, The Journey Museum, South Dakota Public Broadcasting or The Club for Boys.

description: September 30, 1933 - August 12, 2026
_full_text:
September 30, 1933 - August 12, 2026

Mary Katherine "Kathy" Garness, 92, of Spearfish, SD, passed away on Wednesday, August 12, 2026.

Mary Katherine McNeill was born September 30, 1933, to James and Mary Anna McNeill in St. Onge, South Dakota. She attended grade school at a one-room country school (Todd School) grades 1 through 8 before attending and graduating from Spearfish High School in 1951. She worked for Dr. Ward after graduation.

On October 18, 1951, she was united in marriage to Robert Dean Garness at St. John's Catholic Church in St. Onge. They were blessed with five children. The growing family lived together in Spearfish, SD, until Bob was drafted into the Army. They moved to Ft. Riley, KS, and Ft. Sheridan, IL. After returning to Rapid City, Kathy was employed at Fenske Printing, Mr. Print, and the Rapid City Journal, retiring in 1995. She worked part time for the Quik Quarter for 16 years.

Kathy belonged to Our Lady of Perpetual Help Cathedral, Women of the Moose, and Catholic Daughters of the Americas Americas Court St. Rita #916 for 66 years. She bowled 52 years on the same league, Rapid Robins, attending many State and several National Tournaments, and was awarded a 50-year plaque at a party at Robbinsdale Bowling Alley in 2016. Kathy enjoyed traveling with her husband and friends in their convertibles and she loved her family.

Kathy is survived by her five children, Ken (Jane) Garness, Cheryl (Larry) Atencio, Alan (Norma) Garness, Randy Garness, and Susan Kidd; twelve grandchildren; 26 great-grandchildren; six great-great-grandchildren; niece Lori Lewis; nephews, Jim McNeill, Danny and Chris Garness, Scott and Anthony McNeill, Jr., and Larry Anderson.

She was preceded in death by her husband of 68 years, Bob Garness; her parents, James and Mary Anna McNeill; two brothers, Anthony and Danny McNeill; sister Patricia Yanzick; brothers-in-law, Wayne Garness and Robert Yanzick; sisters-in-law, Jackie Garness, and Thelma McNeill; son-in-law Gary Ball; aunt Agnes Mayer; cousin Norma Jean Mayer; nieces, Carol Ann Anderson, Michelle McNeill, Novi Garness, and Rita Cole; and nephew Michael Yanzick.

Her family would like to express thanks to the staff of Stillwater Hospice and Spearfish Canyon Healthcare for their loving care.

A visitation will be held at Kirk Funeral Home on Tues. Aug 18 from 6-8pm with a Vigil starting at 7pm. Mass will be held at the Cathedral of Our Lady of Perpetual Help in Rapid City on Wed. Aug 19 at 11am with a reception to follow. Burial is scheduled for Black Hills National Cemetery on Wed. Aug 19 at 2:30pm.

title: Donald Kechely
_full_text:
July 27, 1935 - July 30, 2026

Don Kechely, 91 years, passed on to enter his heavenly home of our Lord on July 30, 2026.

Don was born on July 27, 1935, to LeRoyce W. Kechely and Josie May Kechely, along with a twin sister, Donna Jean Kechely. Don grew up in Cheyenne, graduating from Cheyenne High School in 1954. He attended the University of Wyoming in Laramie, Wyoming. He graduated in 1957 with a Bachelor of Science degree in Education. In 1956 Don and Marlene were married. Two daughters were born in this marriage, Kelly Jo 1959, Karol Lee 1961. Don and Marlene were high school sweethearts, married seventy years as of January 2026.

Don taught two years of Industrial Arts in Rock River, Wyoming. Don's next teaching assignment was in Rapid City, South Dakota. He taught Industrial Arts at South Junior High, for two years. The next twenty-six years were spent teaching Auto Mechanics at Stevens and Central High school. Don enjoyed teaching and being with his students. He felt having Vocational Education available was very important. He enjoyed being in this area with the other instructors, Purpur, Andy, Bert, and Verlyn. Don retired from teaching in 1991.

Don and Marlene owned the Cherry Avenue Mobile Home Park for 37 years. Don spent a lot of time at the park, taking care of things that needed to be done.

Don loved old cars. He and his friend, Ken, drove to Denver to answer an ad and came home with a 1924 Model T. Don was a member of the Black Hills Model T Club of America and the Black Hills Model T Club in Spearfish.

We know that Don is reunited with his mom Josie, his dad Roy, his twin sister Donna Jean, his brother Robert, his daughter Kelly, and his grandson Chris.

We will celebrate Don's life and will miss his positive attitude, his sense of humor, his laughter, and love. Those of us left behind have wonderful memories to share with each other. We are: Marlene, Don's wife, Karol, Don's daughter, Casey, his grandson, LeeAnn, Casey's wife, Josie, his granddaughter, and Josie's husband, Karl, as well as family and friends.

The Celebration of Life will be August 22, 2026, at 10:30 a.m., at the Dahl Arts Center, Rapid City, South Dakota.

In lieu of flowers, if you so wish, please make donations to First Congregational Church of Keystone, Keystone, South Dakota, or a place of your choice. Please join us for lunch after the service.

title: Rapid City to implement year-round water restrictions
description: The City of Rapid City is elevating the storage condition status for Pactola Reservoir from “concern status” to “alert status,” meaning water restrictions will be in effect year-round.
_full_text:
The City of Rapid City is elevating the storage condition status for Pactola Reservoir from “concern status” to “alert status,” meaning water restrictions will be in effect year-round.

On Tuesday Aug. 11, City Public Works Director Mike Theis spoke at the Public Works Committee meeting sharing that Pactola Reservoir water low inflow is causing concern, leading to an upgrade to “alert status,” which implements year-round water restrictions. Normally, restrictions end on Sept. 30.

"(This) doesn't change things drastically for customers in Rapid City (other) then that it extends that beyond the September 30 deadline," Theis said at the meeting.

Pactola is nearly 4.5 feet lower than it was a month ago (comparing data from July 15 to Aug. 14), according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

The current “concern status” restrictions restricts watering to be allowed between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. daily. Odd-numbered addresses are allowed to water outside those time restrictions on odd-numbered calendar days. Even-numbered addresses are allowed to water on even-numbered calendar days. No outside watering is allowed on the 31st day of any month. The “concern status” designation is used when Pactola Reservoir contains less than 48,950 acre feet of water or the inflow to Pactola Reservoir is less than 90% of the mean monthly average.

 Pactola
Sand bars not normally seen on Pactola Reservoir, S.D., in the Black Hills of South Dakota were visible in April 2025 due to unusually low water levels. The reservoir is a water source for the Rapid City region. 

Manual watering with a handheld hose or with a bucket, sprinkling can or other similar container is allowed at all times.

According to Theis's presentation the “alert status” is implemented when Pactola contains less than 26,950 acre feet of water or the inflows are less than 50% of the mean monthly average. Theis said the mean monthly inflow average is what is triggering the status change. Theis's presentation stated the current water level in Pactola is 41,070 acre-feet.

Water flowing out of Pactola to hydrate the city is at 66 cubic feet per second, per the city’s Aug. 13 update. For context, data from May 23-June 30 shows outflows ranged from 27 cubic feet per second to 60 cubic feet per second. The output ramped up in July and August, ranging from 55 cubic feet per second on the low end on July 27 and peaking on Aug. 3 and Aug. 5 at 90 cubic feet per second.

Since the 1990s, the City of Rapid City has instituted mandatory water conservation measures, generally implemented June 1-Aug. 31 each year under "normal status" conditions. Status conditions include normal, concern, alert and critical stages and are determined by the water levels and inflows to Pactola Reservoir.

Pactola water levels can be tracked through the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Theis said a full press conference is scheduled next week to address further information on the status change.

Councilwoman Laura Armstorng (Ward 5) asked Theis if water restrictions are coming then the city should be leading by example. Theis said the city's parks department has made changes in watering grass in city parks but would also have further information at the future press conference.

A Rapid City man who allegedly threatened another driver with a knife was arrested at the drive-thru of a Wendy’s.

Quitan Chee, 35, was arrested on suspicion of aggravated assault and driving without a valid license, the Rapid City Police Department said.

title: Sturgis Rally racks up 3 more injury crashes, patrol says
description: The South Dakota Highway Patrol’s latest rally tally reported two motorcyclists were transported to Monument Health in Custer after nearly colliding into each other at Custer State Park’s Wildlife Loop near mile marker five. The crash occurred at 11:28 a.m. Wednesday, Aug. 12.
_full_text:
The South Dakota Highway Patrol’s latest rally tally reported two motorcyclists were transported to Monument Health in Custer after nearly colliding into each other at Custer State Park’s Wildlife Loop near mile marker five. The crash occurred at 11:28 a.m. Wednesday, Aug. 12.

According to the report, a 71-year-old man driving a 2004 Harley-Davidson motorcycle was northbound on the loop, while a 69-year-old man driving a 2019 Harley-Davidson motorcycle was southbound at the same location. The 69-year-old man was entering the corner at the center of the roadway when the other motorist entered the southbound lane attempting to avoid a collision, the patrol said. From there the 2019 bike swerved to the right, also attempting to avoid the other motorcyclists. Both units overturned and the drivers sustained non-life-threatening injuries. The patrol did not say if either driver was wearing a helmet.

No fatalities were reported as of Thursday, Aug. 13.

Just an hour after noon on Wednesday, the patrol reported another singular motorcycle crash on U.S. Highway 16A at mile marker 31. The report said a 62-year-old man driving 2015 Harley-Davidson was traveling eastbound when he lost control of the motorcycle during a left curve. The driver was wearing a helmet and sustained minor injuries. He declined transportation and rode the motorcycle away from the scene.

At around 12:45 a.m. Thursday, a 58-year-old man driving a 1993 Harley-Davidson was driving eastbound on I-90 near mile marker 45 in rainy conditions. The man lost control and left the roadway into the median. The man was wearing a helmet and was transported to Monument Health in Rapid City with minor injuries.

As of Thursday, the patrol reports 82 total DUI arrests, 214 drug arrests, 26 injury accidents and three fatal accidents. There were 87 DUI arrests, 236 drug arrests, 50 injury accidents and three fatal accidents during the same time frame in 2025.

The Sturgis Police Department reported a total of 13 injury accidents since opening day on Friday, Aug. 7, through 6 a.m. on Thursday. The department has made 27 DUI arrests and 81 drug arrests, while last year they made 59 drug arrests and 35 DUI arrests during the same time from in 2025.

In the report, the department made 130 non-traffic arrests, 119 traffic arrests and 84 parking citations within the past six days.

Rain didn't deter the crowds in downtown Sturgis on Wednesday, though many did take precautions to stay dry.

title: William Lyman Ostermeyer
description: April 24, 1945 - August 3, 2026
_full_text:
April 24, 1945 - August 3, 2026

William Lyman Ostermeyer, 81, of Kilbourne, Illinois, passed away on Monday, August 3, 2026.

Born on April 24, 1945, in Crawford, Nebraska, Bill was the son of Ralph and Dorothie Ostermeyer. He grew up on the family farm and could often be found with the animals or on a tractor. He graduated from Crawford High School, where he was active in athletics, music, and student leadership. After the death of his father in 1961, Bill assumed greater family responsibilities while completing his education.

Following graduation, Bill proudly served four years in the United States Navy, including two years stationed in Kodiak, Alaska, before receiving an honorable discharge.

Bill spent his career in the computer software industry, supporting national defense programs for government contractors while holding Confidential, Crypto, and Top Secret security clearances. His work included projects associated with Cheyenne Mountain in Colorado Springs, Colorado, and White Sands, New Mexico. He later retired from Caterpillar Inc.

Bill enjoyed hunting, fishing, camping, mountain man rendezvous, and historical reenactments. One of his favorite adventures was returning to Alaska for a moose hunting trip. He was also an accomplished artist, especially in chalk and pencil drawing.

A lifelong Lutheran, Bill was baptized, confirmed, and married at Bethlehem Lutheran Church in Crawford, Nebraska, where his grandparents, the Ostermeyer and Rauscher families, were among the founding members.

Bill is survived by his daughters, Wendy Koza of San Diego, California, and Taunya Rapley of Stuart, Florida; his grandchildren, Alyssa Koza, Reid Koza, Ryan Rapley, and Sawyer Rapley; and his sisters, Saundra Peterson and Cheryl McDuffie, both of Alliance, Nebraska.

In lieu of flowers, memorial donations in memory of Bill Ostermeyer may be made to the Wounded Warrior Project, P.O. Box 758516, Topeka, KS 66675.

Bill will be remembered for his love of family, his faithful service to his country, his adventurous spirit, and his quiet strength.

title: South Dakota Mines to receive $25M to expand mining ed
description: South Dakota Mines is slated to receive $25 million in federal funding to expand mining education and workforce development.
_full_text:
South Dakota Mines is slated to receive $25 million in federal funding to expand mining education and workforce development.

The United States is working to strengthen its domestic critical minerals supply chain and address a growing shortage of skilled professionals.

President Donald Trump announced Friday a combined federal investment of more than $180 million aimed at strengthening the nation’s critical minerals workforce and increasing domestic production of minerals that are essential to national security, energy technologies, advanced manufacturing and infrastructure.

 081326-nws-Mines-funding
South Dakota Mines is set to receive $25 million in federal funding to expand mining education and workforce development, according to an announcement made by President Donald Trump on Aug. 7 during an event hosted at the U.S. State Department. 

As part of the investment, three universities, including South Dakota Mines, are set to receive a share of $80 million in Department of War funding to educate and train the next generation of geologists, metallurgists, and mining engineers.

Trump made the announcement during a roundtable at the U.S. State Department attended by educational leaders from universities across the country, along with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, and Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick. Rudra Mitra, Ph.D., interim head of the university’s Department of Mining Engineering and Management, represented South Dakota Mines at the roundtable.

The investment also includes a $100 million Department of Energy grant to expand the nation's mining and critical minerals workforce. The program aims to significantly increase the number of students earning degrees in these fields over the next two years. Funding will support scholarships and other workforce development initiatives. Universities, community colleges, trade schools, industry organizations and other eligible partners will be able to apply for grants.

The $25 million funding for South Dakota Mines will establish the Critical Minerals Merit Scholars Consortium, a workforce development initiative involving South Dakota Mines, the University of Kentucky, and Missouri University of Science and Technology.

The consortium will create four integrated workforce development programs designed to attract more students to critical minerals fields, expand educational opportunities, and prepare graduates for high-demand careers.

“We are deeply grateful for President Trump’s announcement of major federal investments in mining education and workforce development,” Mitra said. “South Dakota Mines is proud to be selected for $25 million in funding to establish the Critical Minerals Merit Scholars Consortium. This investment will allow us to expand opportunities for students while strengthening the workforce needed to develop and secure America’s critical mineral resources.”

The investment comes as the United States faces a significant shortage of professionals trained in mining, geology, metallurgy and related fields. U.S.-accredited mining programs currently graduate fewer than 170 mining engineers annually, compared with more than 3,000 in China. At the same time, a significant portion of the U.S. mining workforce is approaching retirement.

“This investment recognizes the critical role that institutions like ours play in training the next generation of mining engineers, geologists, metallurgists and related STEM professionals who are essential to America’s energy security, national defense and economic competitiveness,” said Andrea Brickey, Ph.D., professor of mining engineering and management, and principal investigator for the award.

The investment builds on South Dakota Mines’ longstanding role in educating professionals for the mineral industries, and recent investments in critical minerals education and research.

South Dakota Mines recently opened the Nucor Mineral Industries Building, a state-of-the-art facility supporting mining engineering, metallurgy, geological engineering and materials science. The facility was made possible through strong support from the state of South Dakota, industry partners and alumni, reflecting a shared commitment to preparing the next generation of mineral industry professionals. South Dakota Mines has also added new critical minerals minors and continues research in areas including rare earth elements, advanced mineral processing and materials technologies.

“This funding accelerates our longstanding mission of producing highly skilled graduates ready to strengthen domestic critical minerals supply chains,” said Mines President Brian Tande, Ph.D. “It is an investment not only in South Dakota Mines, but in the students who will become the engineers, scientists and technical leaders our country needs to responsibly develop the resources that underpin our national security and economic strength.”

Tande said the investment will also help Mines attract more students to high-demand mineral STEM fields and build on the university’s strong graduate outcomes.

“By investing in scholarships, education and hands-on workforce development, we can attract more talented studejnts to Mines, increase enrollment and graduation in high-need mineral STEM fields, and build on the outstanding outcomes our graduates already achieve,” Tande said. “Our graduates are highly sought after by companies, government agencies and organizations across the country, and this investment will help us prepare even more students for these critical careers.”

The university’s interdisciplinary approach — connecting geology and geological engineering with mining engineering, materials science and metallurgy — positions Mines to educate students across the mineral lifecycle. This expertise will be showcased at the university’s second annual 4M Expo.

4M Expo

South Dakota Mines invites the community to the family-friendly 4M Expo on Saturday, Oct. 3, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Attendees can hear from industry leaders, learn about workforce development, explore South Dakota’s critical minerals story, and discover the connections among the 4Ms: mining, materials, munitions and manufacturing.

The 4M Expo will feature activities all day from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., including: cookie mining; panning for gold; pyrotechnics in munitions; crafts; blacksmithing; engineering and mining experiment station tours; scanning electron microscopy demonstration; water erosion; rock and mineral identification; sandbox mining; mining and military equipment displays; and the Museum of Geology. Go to sdmines4mexpo.my.canva.site for more information.
