It was the second time during the 2026 rally that a biker endured non-life-threatening injuries after colliding with a deer.

Roughly two hours earlier that Tuesday evening, a 29-year-old man traveling eastbound on Highway 34, near mile marker 13, lost control of his 2013 Harley-Davidson motorcycle and crashed after turning left into a private drive. According to the report, the driver was separated from the motorcycle and sustained non-life-threatening injuries. He was transported to Monument Health in Spearfish.

No fatalities were reported on Tuesday, Aug. 11. This comes after a slew of fatalities in the Black Hills in the lead-up and beginning of the rally.

So far this rally, the patrol reports 69 total DUI arrests, 186 drug arrests, 23 injury accidents and three fatal accidents. There were 70 DUI arrests, 141 drug arrests, 41 injury accidents and three fatal accidents during the same timeframe in 2025.

Although only three deaths are counted in the official tally, five people died in motorcycle crashes in the Black Hills on Thursday, Aug. 6, the day before the rally officially began. Also, a week before the rally, on Saturday, Aug. 1, a Sioux Falls woman died in a motorcycle crash near Rochford.

title: ‘With open arms’: Black Hills welcomes Sturgis Motorcycle Rally crowds
description: A thunderous wall of sound has rolled over western South Dakota yet again as thousands of motorcyclists pour into the Black Hills for the 86th annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. What begins as a deep, metallic rumble along Main Street quickly reverberates across the region, echoing through the granite pigtail bridges of Iron Mountain Road and the lush, winding turns of Spearfish Canyon.
_full_text:
A thunderous wall of sound has rolled over western South Dakota yet again as thousands of motorcyclists pour into the Black Hills for the 86th annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. What begins as a deep, metallic rumble along Main Street quickly reverberates across the region, echoing through the granite pigtail bridges of Iron Mountain Road and the lush, winding turns of Spearfish Canyon.

 081326-nws-sturgis-keystone-p1.JPG
From customized v-twin cruisers to vintage choppers, riders from around the globe are firing up their engines to trade interstate miles for the legendary, sun-drenched canopy of the Black Hills National Forest. 

From customized v-twin cruisers to vintage choppers, riders from around the globe are firing up their engines to trade interstate miles for the legendary, sun-drenched canopy of the Black Hills National Forest.

Tallying her sixth visit to the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, motorcycle rider Victoria Curtis said what always convinces her to make the trip from Wyoming is visiting family and getting to explore “God’s Country.”

“It’s just beautiful,” Curtis said. “So when you think of the phrase of ‘God’s Country,’ to me that is the Black Hills. There’s nothing more beautiful than being up here.”

Curtis said she always makes an effort to stop in Keystone before she treks her favorite route — Needles Highway. She said the communities in the Black Hills are always welcoming and embrace the biker culture.

Traveling all the way from New York with his son and making his fifth visit to the rally, Jim Purcell echoed the same sentiment.

 081326-nws-sturgis-keystone-p14.JPG
Traveling all the way from New York with his son and reigning in his fifth visit for the rally, Jim Purcell stopped at Keystone for refreshments before he hits Mount Rushmore. 

“We really like Keystone, we’re not at downtown Sturgis,” Purcell said. “We like to ride, we like to have fun. We just did Iron Mountain Road and now we’re going to Mount Rushmore.”

Despite the tidal wave of traffic, high-octane commotion and sudden gridlock, Black Hills residents and shopkeepers aren’t flinching. They’re rolling out the red carpet or, for Keystone business owner Lisa Toskin, a red garter cocktail.

 Ruby
Red Garter Saloon owner Lisa Toskin has been serving attendees of the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally for nearly 30 years. 

Toskin’s Red Garter Saloon has been nestled in the heart of Keystone for over 50 years and has been taking in customers from the rally for just as long. Toskin said for the towns anchored in the Black Hills, the annual chaos isn’t just an event; it’s a cherished homecoming and a welcomed sight for businesses.

“We love the Sturgis Rally,” Toskin said. “We are the hotspot for the southern hills and so most everybody who goes riding to the pigtails or Iron Mountain, they (congregate) right up here. And then of course we have Mount Rushmore, so hopefully out of the 400,000 to 500,000 people that are here, we get at least one or two of them during the day for at least five minutes to have a drink.”

Toskin said the rally crowds that fill up her saloon, leased out restaurant and leather goods store are considered regulars as they always make an effort to visit every year. She said she’s never raised prices during the rally as she prides herself on serving the community with affordable cocktails.

Though the rally brings in a swell of people to Keystone, Toskin said the town reaches a peak season three times a year — summer break for families, Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, and tourist season in the fall. She said her establishment doesn’t shy away from the waves of people but instead welcomes each new face with a smile and a menu of either cocktails or food.

 081326-nws-sturgis-keystone-p4.JPG
Thousands stop at Keystone as they make their way to popular spots such as Mount Rushmore or Needles Highway. 

Toskin’s words held true as her saloon is filled wall-to-wall with motorcyclists itching for a taste from the saloon’s menu as they listened to live music. Laughter and conversation among motorists could be heard outside the saloon doors.

While the rally continues throughout the week, the Black Hills will continue to welcome the community with open arms.

title: Work begins on affordable rental housing project in Spearfish
description: SPEARFISH — Work began Aug. 7 on Stone Ridge Commons, a 94-unit affordable housing project in Spearfish. The mix of townhome- and flat-style rentals will be open to local residents and full-time college students.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Work began Aug. 7 on Stone Ridge Commons, a 94-unit affordable housing project in Spearfish. The mix of townhome- and flat-style rentals will be open to local residents and full-time college students.

“Today is really a recognition, step in the right direction. We’ve heard, we’ve recognized that the lack of housing in our community is having a significant impact on our young professionals, our graduates from Black Hills State University, as well as our business recruitment efforts but also, and probably most importantly, our existing businesses,” said Kory Menken, executive director for the Spearfish Economic Development Corporation, during a groundbreaking announcement ceremony on Aug 4.

Stone Ridge Commons will be built and owned by Lloyd Companies. Menken estimated Stone Ridge Commons will be completed in about 18 months.

The rental units will be available to residents earning up to 80% of the Area Median Income, according to Black Hills Area Community Foundation. Data from the U.S. Census Bureau indicates that, as of 2024, the median household income in Spearfish was $65,688.

“They will be open to whoever would like to live here,” said Mark Quasney, president of development at Lloyd Companies. “We partnered with Black Hills Area Community Foundation to ensure rents never go above 80% of the area median income. There is no income verification required (to live at Stone Ridge Commons).”

 081326-nws-StoneRidgeCommons-Spearfish
A new affordable housing project in Spearfish, Stone Ridge Commons, was announced during a groundbreaking ceremony on Aug. 4 on the property where 94 townhome-style units will be built. From left, Kory Menken, executive director of Spearfish Economic Development, Greg Litton, Black Hills Area Community Foundation’s director of Strategic Housing, and Mark Quasney of Lloyd Companies pose with golden shovels after the announcement was made about the new housing project. 

This multi-family housing project will be a mix of one-, two- and three-bedroom units in five buildings. The project plan indicates Stone Ridge Commons will include 23 garage stalls, a management office, a play area for children, open green space, and a dog park. The plan calls for Stone Ridge Commons to connect to Platinum Drive and Paramount Drive.

The below-market-rate housing project is made possible from a TIF through the City of Spearfish, housing infrastructure financing dollars from the state of South Dakota, Black Hills Area Community Foundation’s Affordable Housing Initiative, with support from the South Dakota Ellsworth Housing Authority, according to Greg Litton, director of strategic housing at Black Hills Area Community Foundation.

Stone Ridge Commons will fill a need for “missing middle housing.” While most Black Hills communities primarily have single-family housing or multi-family apartment buildings, the types of townhomes and flat-style condo units at Stone Ridge Commons are “demanded and requested in basically every community that we work in,” Litton said.

“The ability for us to come together and do the things that we are doing today matters,” Litton said during the groundbreaking announcement on Aug. 4. “If we think about the folks in our community, whether that is nurses, teachers, educators, first responders, those folks are being priced out of our communities.”

The lack of affordable housing is a challenge for existing residents and for Spearfish’s future growth.

“It’s really hurting (businesses’) efforts for talent attraction when they are unable to find housing for their employees,” Menken said. “That’s why Spearfish Economic Development Corporation always identified this as a major initiative for our group, for our community.”

“We’ve actually heard stories from some of our largest employers that they’ve lost really good, quality candidates because they were unable to secure appropriate housing. (The job candidates) would love to come to Spearfish, they would love to work at that organization or that business, but unfortunately they just couldn’t swing it,” Menken said.

“Spearfish is a great community. It’s beautiful, it’s vibrant, there’s a lot of population growth in Spearfish and a lot of need for housing,” Quasney said at the groundbreaking announcement on Aug. 4. “A lot of housing that’s been developed in Spearfish has been more for folks at the upper end of the income levels, and you see a lot of service economy developing around folks that are here in Spearfish, and you see all of the other parts that you need for a thriving community that aren’t at those income levels, and their housing needs are just not being met.”

“The combination of a city that’s doing all the right things to grow and be vibrant with the need for housing allows Lloyd Companies to see there’s definitely a demand and an opportunity to do something here,” Quasney said. “The Black Hills Area Community Foundation and the City of Spearfish were obviously strong advocates for the project.”

title: Tamang’s liquor bottle litter crusade gains traction with Legal and Finance vote
description: During its Wednesday, Aug. 12, meeting, the Rapid City Legal and Finance Committee voted 4-1 to instruct the City Attorney’s Office to bring forward ordinance amendments to address alcohol-related litter in Rapid City.
_full_text:
During its Wednesday, Aug. 12, meeting, the Rapid City Legal and Finance Committee voted 4-1 to instruct the City Attorney’s Office to bring forward ordinance amendments to address alcohol-related litter in Rapid City.

Councilman John Roberts (Ward 4) voted against the request, saying he believes the underlying issue of alcohol addiction needs to be better addressed at a state level with support for addiction services, rather than a city ordinance.

Councilman Stephen Tamang (Ward 1) brought the request before the committee after making a Facebook post on July 30 and submitting a column to the Journal addressing the issue of discarded mini liquor bottles found left on the ground in the city.

"This morning, while walking with my daughter, as usual, we found cheap vodka shooters lying in the neighborhood," Tamang wrote in his post. "I’m frustrated that this has become normal. These products contribute not only to alcohol related harm, but they’re also routinely discarded throughout our neighborhoods, and probably yours!"

Tamang, a doctor and director of addiction medicine and community health service at Monument Health, wrote in his column his efforts are not about stopping responsible adults from enjoying a drink, “The concern is the repeated sale and immediate consumption of cheap, potent, portable alcohol that contributes to public intoxication, public consumption, litter, and repeated demands on public services.”

Rapid City municipal code addresses litter, with a violation of any provision punishable by no more than 30 days in jail or a fine of no more than $100, or both.

There are no specific amendments being considered yet. First the Rapid City Council must vote to instruct the attorney’s office to draft an ordinance. If that happens, the Legal and Finance Committee will consider the ordinance, which must also pass the full council.

 Stephen Tamang
Councilman Stephen Tamang (Ward 1), right, and Councilman Lance Lehmann (Ward 4) at the April 1, 2026, Legal and Finance Committee meeting.  

During public comment, Journey On's Executive Director Stephanie Kor spoke in favor of Tamang's request. 

Kor said, "Journey On appreciates Dr. Tamang for starting this conversation. We encourage the city to look at an array of solutions, maybe stronger enforcement of existing ordinances, partnerships with retailers, better education, targeted strategies in areas experiencing higher volumes of alcohol related litter and maybe examining other approaches that have worked in communities facing the same challenges."

Resident Mark Millar voiced his support to the council of addressing the littering of mini liquor bottles. He proposed the city ban the sale of the mini liquor bottles.

Tamang gave context to the issue of the mini liquor bottles with the state-wide issue of alcohol related deaths by quoting data from the South Dakota Department of Health. 

SDDH's website states an estimated 178,000 people die from excessive drinking each year, and in 2024, the state had the third-highest age-adjusted rate for alcohol-related deaths at 31.4 per 100,000, compared to the national average of 12.1 per 100,000 from 2019-2023.

"These are things that maybe the council has some consideration on, and then the body can take a look at that and decide what's worthy of going forward. And so that's the spirit behind this alderman item. And what my request today would be not to say yay or nay, it would just be to send to the full council because all 10 people should get to weigh in on this," Tamang said.

Councilman Kevin Maher (Ward 3) said he believes this issue needs to be addressed by lawmakers rather than the city. Roberts agreed on addressing the issue, but not at the city level.

"I think that a lot of the help with this mitigation is going back to Pierre again to get funding for long-term treatment for West River, for both alcohol and drugs. I think that we need a West River mental health facility. I think there's a lot of things that we need to help us with this problem, but limiting the size of alcoholic bottles sold is going to do absolutely nothing," Roberts said.

Councilman Josh Biberdorf (Ward 1) said, "We've never tried anything since I've been on the council, so how about we try something and see if the ball moves? We all know it's a big issue, but basically the council isn't asking for anything in particular. It's to explore options and opportunities, and to come with an open mindset as opposed to a fixed mindset.”

The item will need approval from City Council on Aug. 17 before city staff can draft ordinance options for consideration.

title: Highway 16B bridge in Rapid City now honors Kadoka soldier who died during World War II
description: U.S. Air Force 1st Lt. Laurence E. Radlinger grew up in Kadoka and was assigned to a unit in Rapid City. After his unit was called into service during World War II, he served with a firefighting platoon and was stationed in France.
_full_text:
U.S. Air Force 1st Lt. Laurence E. Radlinger grew up in Kadoka and was assigned to a unit in Rapid City. After his unit was called into service during World War II, he served with a firefighting platoon and was stationed in France.

Radlinger never came home. But his memory lives on, and will be on display for all to see on a bridge on U.S. Highway 16B in Rapid City. On Monday, Aug. 17, South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden and others held a bridge naming ceremony at the Minneluzahan Senior Center in Rapid City.

During the ceremony, Staff Sgt. Jonathan Wright with the South Dakota National Guard told the crowd about Radlinger’s heroism.

 081826-nws-bridge-p1.JPG
Debbie Radlinger, left, helps unveil the 1st Lt. Laurence E. Radlinger Memorial Bridge sign during a ceremony on Monday, Aug. 17, at the Minneluzahan Senior Center in Rapid City. 

“His unit had a very specific mission: When an aircraft crashed or caught fire, it went forward. Their job was to stabilize the people inside. On Dec. 9, 1944, in an airfield north of France, that mission would demand everything from Lt. Radlinger and his soldiers. A B26 bomber returning from a combat mission stalled approaching the runway. The aircraft crashed,” Wright recounted. “There was another danger — the bomber was still carrying a payload of 250-pound demolition bombs. Lt. Radlinger and his firefighting crew knew exactly what that meant. They knew aircrew members were still trapped inside, and they went anyway,” he said, noting the crew was able to pull two airplane crew members out before the bombs exploded.

“These men were not killed crossing a beach or fighting from a foxhole. They were doing something equally heroic,” Wright said. “They ran toward a burning aircraft.”

During his remarks, Rhoden noted the state’s Fallen Heroes Bridge Dedication Program started in 2019 under then-Gov. Kristi Noem and has honored “countless” soldiers who were killed in action or classified as missing in action across the state.

 081826-nws-bridge-p6.JPG
“These men were not killed crossing a beach or fighting from a foxhole. They were doing something equally heroic,” Staff Sgt. Jonathan Wright with the South Dakota National Guard said about 1st Lt. Laurence Radlinger and his unit. “They ran toward a burning aircraft.” 

“Bridges are strong. They're structures that are intended to reconcile and hold things together. Lt. Radlinger and his fellow brothers and sisters in arms possess uncommon strength, and it's their service that holds our country together,” Rhoden said. “My hope is that whenever someone drives across that bridge, it causes them to pause, if only for a minute, and think of the price of freedom that we enjoy and all too often take for granted as Americans. The lives of all those who fought to protect freedom should never be forgotten.”

 081826-nws-bridge-p1A.JPG
The 1st Lt. Laurence E. Radlinger Memorial Bridge is on Highway 16B in Rapid City. 

Rhoden closed his remarks by saying, “I thank you all for gathering today to honor the life of Lt. Radlinger. May we live lives worthy of his sacrifice, and may we each do our part to preserve the blessings of liberty for the next generation.”

Radlinger’s niece Debbie Radlinger, nephew Charlie Ray and Charlie’s wife, Gwen, spoke briefly during the ceremony, thanking the state for honoring an uncle they never knew.

“It means everything,” Debbie Radlinger told the Journal after the event. “I wish I would have met him.”

 081826-nws-bridge-p3.JPG
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden speaks during a bridge naming ceremony in Rapid City. 

 081826-nws-bridge-p2.JPG
From left, Laurence Radlinger's nephew Charlie Ray, Charlie’s wife, Gwen, and Debbie Radlinger speak during the ceremony. 

 PHOTOS: Ceremony naming the Lt. Laurence E. Radlinger Memorial Bridge
Gov. Larry Rhoden and others participated in the the Lt. Laurence E. Radlinger Memorial Bridge naming ceremony on Monday, Aug. 17.

title: South Dakota expands drought mitigation strategies
description: Gov. Larry Rhoden has signed an executive order aimed at helping rural fire departments during the prolonged drought.
_full_text:
Gov. Larry Rhoden has signed an executive order aimed at helping rural fire departments during the prolonged drought.

The order expands South Dakota Wildland Fire’s assistance and resources to help rural fire departments outside the Black Hills Forest Fire Protection District, the governor’s office said in a release. In addition, the governor extended the provisions of an earlier executive order related to flexibility for hay hauling.

“As a volunteer firefighter, I understand that every second counts when attacking a fire. And as a lifelong rancher, I recognize the difficulty feeding livestock during this ongoing drought,” Rhoden said in a release. “Supplementing local resources with approved state assistance will improve response time, saving lives and property.”

Over 90% of South Dakota is suffering from abnormally dry or moderate to extreme drought conditions, the office noted. According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, the southwest corner of the state is in extreme drought, including the western half of Pennington County, all of Lawrence, Custer and Fall River counties, the western edge of Oglala Lakota County and the southwest tip of Butte County.

Rhoden previously signed an executive order that allows for the deployment of firefighting airplanes and helicopters to assist with fires within the Black Hills Forest Fire Protection District. The new order extends those resources to any fire in the state if needed to protect lives and property, the governor’s office said.

 South Dakota drought

This year, the governor has verbally declared an emergency to exist for the 79 Fire in April and the Bear Butte Fire in August because those fires were outside the Black Hills Forest Fire Protection District. The Bear Butte Fire affected more than 400 acres near Sturgis during the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. It was started by a cigarette, according to the South Dakota Highway Patrol.

This order approves similar future deployments to assist local fire departments immediately.

As drought conditions continue to negatively impact feed availability for livestock across South Dakota, this order also extended the expiration date so the provisions of EO 2026-08, which increase access to hay for farmers and ranchers, lasts through the end of the season. Hay hauling can continue for two hours before sunrise and two hours after sunset from now until Nov. 15.

 Bear Butte Fire
The Bear Butte Fire affected more than 400 acres near Sturgis during the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. It was started by a cigarette, according to the South Dakota Highway Patrol. 

These haulers must be properly equipped with warning lights, and they cannot run overweight. Permits are available to allow oversize movement of hay up to 12 feet wide and to extend the time allowed for movement of vehicles from 4 a.m. to 10 p.m., provided the load has reflectorized or lighted oversize load signs on the front and back of the vehicle(s). The permits are free and available by contacting the South Dakota Highway Patrol Permitting Office at 605-698-3925.

Earlier this spring, Rhoden activated the state Drought Task Force to monitor drought conditions across South Dakota and be available to quickly respond to emergencies like this. The Drought Task Force endorsed these waivers at their meeting on Tuesday, Aug. 18, when presented by the Governor’s Office and the Department of Agricultural and Natural Resources.

 PHOTOS: Bear Butte Fire near Sturgis
The Bear Butte Fire affected more than 456 acres and was 50% contained as of late Monday, Aug. 10, according to Watch Duty. Forward progress was stopped, according to authorities.

title: Rapid City Council approves future sports complex naming agreement with Sanford Health
description: The Rapid City Council voted on Monday to approve the naming recognition agreement between the city and Sanford Health for the future Rapid City sports complex, a partnership that includes a $10 million contribution by Sanford Health.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Council voted on Monday to approve the naming recognition agreement between the city and Sanford Health for the future Rapid City sports complex, a partnership that includes a $10 million contribution by Sanford Health.

The council voted 9-0, with Councilman Stephen Tamang (Ward 1) abstaining. Tamang told the Journal his reason for abstaining is due to his role at Monument Health Rapid City Hospital as director of addiction medicine and community health services, which could be seen as a conflict of interest in voting on another healthcare service provider.

City documents state Sanford will be contributing $2 million in March of 2027, as well as an annual contribution of $421,052.63 for 20 years.

 Mayor Jason Salamun
Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun officially announced on Thursday, Aug. 6, that Sanford Health will have the naming right for the city’s future sports complex. 

The move adds to the health company’s growing involvement in the community, including a planned medical complex and partnerships with existing clinics.

The sports complex will be developed on the 22.7 acres donated by Pete Lien & Sons at the intersection of Seger Drive and 143rd Avenue. Pete Lien & Sons is a Rapid City-based construction and mining company.

In addition to naming rights, Sanford Health will have a dedicated space within the complex for sports medicine, sports performance and Sports Academy activities, among other recognition rights and privileges, including input in the design phase and participation in the programming.

From previous reporting, the total anticipated project cost for the development of the sports complex will be $76.2 million, including $24.58 million from the Catalyst District TIF. An estimated $28.28 million will come from the Hotel Business Improvement District, $6.2 million in land donation value and $5 million from the Vision Fund, per city documents, in addition to the $10 million from Sanford.

title: Bart "Bubba" Boos
description: November 22, 1947 - August 7, 2026
_full_text:
November 22, 1947 - August 7, 2026

Bart "Bubba" Boos, 78, passed away on August 7, 2026, following a short battle with cancer. He was born on November 22, 1947, in Fulda, Minnesota, to Bart Boos Sr. and Lorraine Boos.

Bart was a devoted father, grandfather, great-grandfather, brother, and friend. He is survived by his children, Tara King (Tyler), Joshua Boos, and his brother, Mike "Mikey" Boos of Rapid City.

Family was central to Bart's life. He was a proud grandfather to Taylor Boos and his wife, Mackenzie; Marisa King; Connor King; and Megan King. He was also a loving great-grandfather to Maverick Mason and Skye Lorraine, and he cherished every moment spent with them.

Bart had a lifelong love of all sports, especially baseball. He set a bucket-list goal to visit every Major League Baseball stadium and came close, missing only eight. All of those trips were shared with his grandchildren and became life long family memories.

In his younger years, Bart enjoyed staying active and social. He played pool and golf, always bringing a competitive edge, and enjoyed Harley Davison motorcycles, classic cars, and gambling for fun, valuing the excitement and time spent with others.

For 13 years, Bart drove the bus for Post 22, covering many miles and creating countless memories. He often joked about the miles driven and the surprisingly few bruises on the buses. Whenever he traveled in the state he loved to play the mile marker game. He could tell you exactly where you were at if you told him what mile marker you were on. His humor and easygoing nature made him a favorite among those he worked with.

Bart will be remembered for his love of sports, his humor, his adventurous spirit, and above all, his love for his family. Whether at a ballgame, on the road to another stadium, spending time with his Post 22 family, or simply with loved ones, he made the most of every moment.

He was preceded in death by his parents, Bart Boos Sr. and Lorraine Boos; Helen (Hill) Boos; and his grandson, Mason Boos.

A funeral service celebrating Bart's life will be held at 10 a.m. on August 22, 2026, at Dave Ploof Field at Black Hills Surgical Hospital Ballpark, The "Fitz". Please wear your favorite baseball attire to the baseball-themed service honoring one of his greatest passions. Any current or past Post 22 players/coaches please wear your Hardhat if you still have it.

Bart "Bubba" will be deeply missed by his children, brother, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, extended family, and many friends. His stories, laughter, and love of life will live on in all who knew him.

So, as Bart would have wanted, we tip our caps, remember the good times, and send him off to his final ballpark.

Take me out to the ballgame, Bubba. Your final inning is complete, but your story lives on.

Online condolences can be sent at www.OsheimSchmidt.com

title: Patients wary of governments, companies pushing AI as a rural healthcare solution
byline: ARIELLE ZIONTS and DARIUS TAHIR KFF News
description: HOT SPRINGS, S.D. — Two of the nation’s most powerful health officials predict artificial intelligence will play a key role in solving rural America’s health challenges.
_full_text:
HOT SPRINGS, S.D. — Two of the nation’s most powerful health officials predict artificial intelligence will play a key role in solving rural America’s health challenges.

Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told a panel of U.S. senators that AI nurses can provide “concierge care” to rural patients. Mehmet Oz, who leads the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, has said “the best way to help some of these communities is going to be AI-based avatars” that connect rural patients to mental health services.

And many state health leaders agree. They are using some of their funding from the $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program to expand AI among rural health organizations.

AI is computer technology that performs tasks that typically rely on human intelligence by finding patterns or generating words. It has the potential to improve the healthcare system by automating back-office work or identifying patients at risk, but several reports contend there’s little evidence AI can improve access to care and patient health in rural areas. It’s unclear how well states will track and share outcomes of the tech they invest in.

Meanwhile, some rural Americans are skeptical, according to interviews with people in Hot Springs, South Dakota, a city of about 3,400 residents at the southern end of the Black Hills.

“I get artificial intelligence for certain things, but for personal healthcare — no,” Tara Haffner said while standing outside the American Legion.

Haffner said she’s worried about AI making mistakes and wants healthcare to stay between her and her doctor.

But Phillip Mues, who oversees technology at Cherry County Hospital and Clinic in rural Valentine, Nebraska, said AI is already helping clinicians save time, reduce burnout, and focus more on patient care.

“I think it will help reduce burden on actual staffing,” he said. “It won’t replace people, but I think it will help in rural communities.”

Still, Mues said, AI can’t fix every challenge. Rural hospitals at risk of closing or ending certain services probably can’t use AI to save enough money to prevent those consequences, he said.

Congressional Republicans created the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program last summer as a last-minute sweetener to President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The funding was intended to offset concerns about the outsize fallout anticipated in rural communities from the law, which is expected to reduce overall Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade.

The Word on the Street

Hot Springs, which has a 25-bed independent hospital and a Department of Veterans Affairs hospital, is known for its sandstone buildings, veterans’ services, and, yes, hot springs. Residents must drive at least an hour for more advanced care.

Six people interviewed there by KFF Health News said the biggest problem in rural healthcare is the cost or long wait times caused by staffing shortages.

Doug Nikkila, a heavy equipment operator, said AI and other technology come with benefits and risks.

“If it’s not utilized correctly, it becomes a burden,” he said.

Nikkila, who’s concerned about nursing home residents being neglected amid staffing shortages, said he thinks AI should send reminders to staff when their residents are due for diaper changes or other care. He also wondered whether AI-powered video monitors could send alerts when they detect falls or illness symptoms.

The healthcare industry is rapidly adopting AI despite the tools being “poorly evaluated,” according to a recent report from ARISE, a Stanford- and Harvard-led group that evaluates health-related AI. The report says that while some AI has been successful in controlled settings, there’s less evidence it can perform in the real world. It also said few studies track patient outcomes.

Evidence is especially lacking in rural areas. A recent academic paper found that only 26 peer-reviewed studies about AI in rural healthcare were published from 2010 through April 29, 2025. Few analyzed implementation or outcomes.

Despite the dearth of results, some states appear interested in bold experiments — such as using AI to suggest diagnoses or recommend treatments. Utah officials said in their application to the rural health program that they are interested in funding a controversial experiment in AI-powered prescription refill requests.

Even tools proven to work in urban settings may not work in rural ones, said Qian Huang, an assistant professor at the Center for Rural Health and Research at East Tennessee State University.

She said the technology is usually tested at large, academic hospitals and trained on data from urban patients, who may not have the same health issues and obstacles — such as a lack of transportation — as rural patients.

A KFF Health News review of states’ plans for the Rural Health Transformation Program shows they’re interested in using AI to automate time-consuming, behind-the-scenes tasks, such as medical charting, coding, referrals, and prior authorization requests. Some states also mentioned ways AI can save money, such as Washington, which discussed tools that “identify and recover” money it’s owed.

Mues said the Valentine clinic has been using AI scribes that record appointments and generate notes describing the visit. He said surveys of clinicians before and after they started using the technology show the scribes have helped reduce burnout by letting providers focus on patient care with “eye contact on the patient, not the computer.”

States also mentioned funding AI that directly affects patient care, such as tools that recommend possible diagnoses and treatment options to clinicians. Mississippi wants to use predictive AI algorithms to “guide” emergency medics with “triage, routing, and treatment decisions.”

Several states want to use AI to analyze patients’ medical charts and remote monitoring devices to identify immediate or future health risks. North Dakota’s plans mention AI to “detect early signs of chronic disease and behavioral health conditions,” while New Hampshire’s discusses AI that identifies patients “at high risk of adverse drug events.”

Some states plan to give patients access to chatbots or wearable devices that transmit data to their clinicians. Utah is interested in funding AI-powered fetal-monitoring devices, while Kentucky will explore using AI chatbots to “deliver personalized nudges and education” through “health coaching, gamified incentives, and rewards.”

Whether the technology appeals to consumers is another matter. Hot Springs resident Stephanie Keller wears a smartwatch to track her fitness but has no interest in an AI chatbot using her data to encourage her to reach her health goals.

“I don’t have the time to chat with AI every day. I mean, are you kidding me? I don’t want to spend my time on a cellphone,” she said.

Rural health facilities also face challenges in implementing AI.

Huang, who has written about AI in rural healthcare, said rural hospitals and clinics may not have the hardware or IT staff needed to support the technology. She said clinicians and staff may already be doing three jobs at once and not have time to go through AI training.

Rural health facilities may not have fast-enough internet to use AI, while patients may have slow connections at home — if they have internet at all — or may not feel comfortable using AI, Huang said.

“In rural communities, trust and a personal relationship is essential,” she said.

Roy Ehlers, a Hot Springs resident, said he doesn’t trust AI in healthcare, or anywhere else.

“I’m old-fashioned. I don’t believe in it. Technology is not my forte,” Ehlers said.

Mues said that while some rural patients are “scared of AI,” most have let their clinicians at the Valentine facility use the scribing technology to record patients’ visits.

Will States Share AI Results?

Despite questions about implementation, the boom is on. Jordan Everson, an assistant professor at the Georgetown University Department of Family Medicine, said both urban and rural health facilities are rushing to use AI.

“The risk of signing contracts that rural healthcare organizations come to regret is pretty high,” said Everson, who previously worked in the information technology office at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

Several states are addressing that risk by using their rural health funding to create groups that will help rural health facilities vet, select, or monitor AI tools while offering training, ongoing assistance, or funding for upfront costs.

CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster said the agency doesn’t have any AI-specific reporting requirements but is working on a form for states to report their overall progress and outcomes.

Abraham Pritzker, who works at Julota, a company that helps health organizations track data, said states should measure more than how often AI programs are used.

For example, states can measure whether the tech reduces falls, 911 calls, or hospital admissions, said Pritzker, a former paramedic. Huang said it’s also important to ask clinicians and patients about their experiences using AI.

Yet many states’ applications to the rural health program mention tracking only AI adoption metrics, not what happens after facilities deploy the tech. Some of these states may add further reporting requirements down the road.

Vermont spokespeople did not respond when asked why their state’s funding opportunity for AI scribes requires organizations to report only how many clinicians and patients are served by the tech, not how much time they save.

States requiring recipients to report outcomes include Connecticut, which will track how often AI-powered patient monitoring devices trigger accurate alerts. Texas will require organizations to track cost savings, while Wisconsin lists “patient outcomes” and “productivity and efficiencies” as possible metrics.

Huang said that after collecting results, states need to share them so other states and healthcare organizations can learn from their experiences.

“We do not have a lot of resources to waste on tools that don’t work in rural areas,” she said.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

title: Stacy Ann Reynolds
description: July 21, 1957 - August 11, 2026
_full_text:
July 21, 1957 - August 11, 2026

Stacy Ann Reynolds came into this world accompanied by her twin sister, Susan, on July 21, 1957. They joined twin brothers, Larry and Chris. Growing up in the greater Los Angeles area, the two girls embarked on a childhood journey only possible in the mid 60's America. With all the antics and associated adventures, Stacy immediately assumed the role of the "evil" twin (in a very loving capacity).

In their late teens both the girls migrated to Nebraska. Stacy returned numerous times over the years to California, the last time to provide end of life care for her mother. Upon her return to Nebraska, Stacy co-owned and operated a tavern in Morrill for nearly a decade. When Susan opened the "Our Place" restaurant, Stacy moved to Custer and went to work for her sister. That occupation and her unique ability as a people person brought her a true fulfillment in life. For the next 16 years when one of her customers would suffer a loss or could no longer make it into the café, she would visit with homemade goodies, the joke of the day and a compassion to listen and lift the spirit of all involved. She became the consummate care-giver to any that were involved with her interaction.

Her other passion in life was fishing. There was never any better thrill than feeling the "tug on the pole". While her methods were simplistic her success was uncanny. Limits were sometimes optional!

She enjoyed travel throughout the years, visiting Greece and on multiple occasions, the islands of Hawaii. In 2007, as the free spirit she was, she did the unthinkable (in her own words) and married Mike Carter. Together they spent the next 19 years at their home in Custer. Stacy lived life to the fullest, giving a large portion of it to those in need. Never afraid to have a good time, she lived life as she saw it.

At the young age of 69 she passed after a brief illness, at Monument Health Hospice on August 11, 2026.

We all have an epitaph, her's definitely comes from her favorite TV series, Lonesome Dove. In the immortal words of the character, Augustus McRae - My God it's been quite a party, hasn't it!

Blessed to share in her life were her husband, Mike Carter and their fur baby, Cheyenne. In addition, she is survived by her brother, Lawrence (Ana) Reynolds of Hawaii and Brazil; her surviving aunt, Faith (Joe) Finotti of Washington State; cousin, Maria (Steve) Costa of Mesa, CA; half sister, Chris of Georgia; fishing buddy, Wanda of Custer and a host of friends whose lives she touched through the years, too numerous to mention.

The family requested in place of a memorial, that any contributions be made to St. Judes in Stacy's name.

Arrangements have been placed in the care of Chamberlain McColley's Funeral Home in Custer, SD.

title: Ila Vivian Gluhm
description: January 3, 1931 - August 14, 2026
_full_text:
January 3, 1931 - August 14, 2026

Ila Vivian Gluhm, 95, passed away August 14, 2026, at Westhills Village Health Care, in Rapid City, South Dakota.

Ila was born January 3, 1931, in Highmore, South Dakota, the youngest child of Herman and Alvina (Koepsell) Gluhm. She grew up on the family farm north-east of Harrold, South Dakota. Ila attended Harrold School, grades one through twelve, graduating as valedictorian in May 1948. On June 1, 1948, she enrolled in the National School of Business (NSB) in Rapid City, South Dakota. Upon graduation from NSB in 1949, she was employed by Montana-Dakota Utilities Company in Rapid City.

With a desire to explore and seek employment beyond South Dakota, she was referred to the Barnes School of Commerce in Denver, Colorado in 1951, and was immediately employed in Denver by the then Carter Oil Company, a subsidiary of Standard Oil of

New Jersey.

Upon reading a most interesting and entertaining book written by journalist, Herb Caen, covering the City of San Francisco, California, she moved to that city in 1952. One week after arriving in San Francisco, she was employed by Shell Oil Company.

After 20 years with Shell in San Francisco, she transferred with the Company to Houston, Texas in 1972, where she remained to complete 38½ years of service. During those years, she worked in all aspects of Shell's Human Resources Department. After retiring in 1991, Ila moved to Port Ludlow, Washington in 1993 to enjoy a cooler and more moderate climate.

In May 2013, Ila returned to her native State of South Dakota to reside at Westhills Village Retirement Community in Rapid City.

In her early years, Ila enjoyed snow skiing (Utah, Colorado and California), ice skating, participating in local theater and tap dance. At Westhills she enjoyed line dance, chorus, bridge, mah-jong, all card and other games.

Ila was a "people person" and believed "life is what you make it." As she would say: "Don't judge a book by the cover. You will learn something from every person you meet". She also maintained that travel, domestically and abroad, adds a whole new dimension to one's life. She traveled extensively in Europe and Asia.

She was preceded in death by her parents and two brothers, Clarence and

Wilbur Gluhm. She is survived by nieces and nephews, including grand and great-grand.

Ila was a member of Peace Lutheran Church in Rapid City. A Memorial Service will be on Thursday, August 20, 2026, at 1:00pm at Kirk Funeral Home. Inurnment will be at the Highmore, South Dakota, Protestant Cemetery at a later date.

Memorials in Ila's name may be directed to Westhills Village Foundation, 255 Texas Street, Rapid City, South Dakota 57701.

title: Donald Kechely
_full_text:
July 27, 1935 - July 30, 2026

Don Kechely, 91 years, passed on to enter his heavenly home of our Lord on July 30, 2026.

Don was born on July 27, 1935, to LeRoyce W. Kechely and Josie May Kechely, along with a twin sister, Donna Jean Kechely. Don grew up in Cheyenne, graduating from Cheyenne High School in 1954. He attended the University of Wyoming in Laramie, Wyoming. He graduated in 1957 with a Bachelor of Science degree in Education. In 1956 Don and Marlene were married. Two daughters were born in this marriage, Kelly Jo 1959, Karol Lee 1961. Don and Marlene were high school sweethearts, married seventy years as of January 2026.

Don taught two years of Industrial Arts in Rock River, Wyoming. Don's next teaching assignment was in Rapid City, South Dakota. He taught Industrial Arts at South Junior High, for two years. The next twenty-six years were spent teaching Auto Mechanics at Stevens and Central High school. Don enjoyed teaching and being with his students. He felt having Vocational Education available was very important. He enjoyed being in this area with the other instructors, Purpur, Andy, Bert, and Verlyn. Don retired from teaching in 1991.

Don and Marlene owned the Cherry Avenue Mobile Home Park for 37 years. Don spent a lot of time at the park, taking care of things that needed to be done.

Don loved old cars. He and his friend, Ken, drove to Denver to answer an ad and came home with a 1924 Model T. Don was a member of the Black Hills Model T Club of America and the Black Hills Model T Club in Spearfish.

We know that Don is reunited with his mom Josie, his dad Roy, his twin sister Donna Jean, his brother Robert, his daughter Kelly, and his grandson Chris.

We will celebrate Don's life and will miss his positive attitude, his sense of humor, his laughter, and love. Those of us left behind have wonderful memories to share with each other. We are: Marlene, Don's wife, Karol, Don's daughter, Casey, his grandson, LeeAnn, Casey's wife, Josie, his granddaughter, and Josie's husband, Karl, as well as family and friends.

The Celebration of Life will be August 22, 2026, at 10:30 a.m., at the Dahl Arts Center, Rapid City, South Dakota.

In lieu of flowers, if you so wish, please make donations to First Congregational Church of Keystone, Keystone, South Dakota, or a place of your choice. Please join us for lunch after the service.

Online condolences can be left at www.OsheimSchmidt.com

title: 6 men arrested in sex sting during 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally
description: A multi-agency sex trafficking sting during the 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally resulted in six men arrested, the U.S. Attorney’s office announced on Monday, Aug. 17.
_full_text:
A multi-agency sex trafficking sting during the 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally resulted in six men arrested, the U.S. Attorney’s office announced on Monday, Aug. 17.

The state’s Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force conducted the rally operation from Friday, Aug. 7 through Wednesday, Aug. 12, agents and detectives posed as children and/or as traffickers offering children for prostitution.

According to a press release, law enforcement officers posted ads and created profiles on various sites and social media platforms to provide offenders the opportunity to communicate with whom they believe to be minors or traffickers.

“This week’s operation is a strong reminder of the importance of our local, state and federal partnerships, including agreements such as our 287 (g) immigration authority, in locating and removing dangerous individuals from our communities,” Attorney General Marty Jackley said in the release. “This operation is about protecting our children and was a success thanks to the hard work and dedication of our ICAC Task Force.”

Arrested, all on state charges are listed below:

Johan Vazquez-Garza, 33, of Rapid City was arrested on suspicion of solicitation of a minor. Vazquez-Garza, who has been deported five times since 2009, may face additional federal immigration related charges. As of Tuesday, the Journal could not find Vazquez-Garza’s case in state court records.

Bo Bo Aung, 38, of Box Elder is charged with first-degree human trafficking, attempted first-degree human trafficking and attempted fourth-degree rape. Aung, initially from Myanmar, allegedly illegally absconded from a work visa program in Texas seven years ago and may face federal deportation proceedings following the conclusion of state proceedings. Aung’s arraignment is set for Sept. 10 at 9 a.m.

Adrian Tomas Randles, 39, of Rapid City is charged with solicitation of a minor and attempted distribution of scheduled one or two drug to a minor. Randles is a registered sex offender resulting from a 2013 conviction for solicitation of a minor. Randles next preliminary hearing is set for Aug. 27 at 4 p.m.

Steven Clay Brown, 62, of Sturgis is charged with solicitation of a minor and attempted sexual exploitation of a minor. Brown’s arraignment is set for Sept. 3 at 10:15 a.m.

Kevin Orlanda Tassion Brown, 30, of Dillion South Carolina was arrested on suspicion of first-degree human trafficking, attempted first-degree human trafficking and attempted fourth-degree rape. As of Tuesday, Brown’s case was not found in court records.

Jay Anderson, 39, of Hot Springs is charged with solicitation of a minor. Anderson’s next court appearance is scheduled on Aug. 27 at 2:30 p.m.

This is the 14th consecutive year of the ICAC operation during the Sturgis rally. Since its inception, the operation has arrested 104 offenders. This operation is a unified unit between local, state and federal law enforcement agencies.

“The Sturgis Motorcycle Rally brings thousands of people together, and with that comes a shared responsibility to keep the community safe. HSI (Home Security Investigations) is grateful for the hard work and vigilance of our federal, state, and local partners, who stood with us to find and stop those who world exploit the vulnerable or harm children,” HSI St. Paul Acting Special Agent in Charge Tonya Price said. “This effort shows what strong law enforcement partnerships can do: protect victims, remove predators from our communities, and make clear that child exploitation will not be tolerated.”

Each of the men are being prosecuted by the South Dakota Attorney' General’s office in partnership with the Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office, stated the release.

title: Rapid City watering restrictions now year-round
description: Watering restrictions already in place for Rapid City residents and businesses will continue throughout the year.
_full_text:
Watering restrictions already in place for Rapid City residents and businesses will continue throughout the year.

The city has elevated the storage condition status for Pactola Reservoir from “concern status” to “alert status,” meaning restrictions already in place will continue past the original end date of Sept. 30.

Per the city, no watering is allowed between the hours of 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. daily. Odd-numbered addresses are allowed to water on odd-numbered calendar days. Even-numbered addresses are allowed to water on even-numbered calendar days. No outside watering is allowed on the 31st day of any month.

Manual watering with a handheld hose or with a bucket, sprinkling can or other similar container is allowed.

“The change from the ‘concern’ to the ‘alert’ status has no immediate impact to customers at the present moment,” Rapid City Water Superintendent Eric Boyda said during a press conference on Wednesday, Aug. 19, at Sioux Park, next to Rapid Creek.

 Rapid City Water Superintendent Eric Boyda
Rapid City Water Superintendent Eric Boyda speaks to media during a press conference on Wednesday, Aug. 19, at Sioux Park, next to Rapid Creek. The city announced it has extended watering restrictions indefinitely. 

The upgrade to “alert” status comes because of low inflows to Pactola Reservoir, not because of the storage level at the reservoir. The mean monthly inflows this summer have been “dramatically” lower than average, the city said. Boyda said the August mean monthly inflow is 50.05 cubic feet per second (cfs), but inflows were at 18.5 cfs as of Wednesday morning and were as low as 12.2 cfs earlier in the month.

“Even though we got some record-breaking precipitation here in Rapid City, those storms didn't occur in the upper watershed,” Boyda said.

He noted all of Pennington County is in a drought. According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, the western half of Pennington County is in extreme drought, while the eastern half is in either severe or moderate drought.

“The upper watershed is under extreme drought conditions,” Boyda said.

Water levels at Pactola Reservoir — also referred to as storage levels — are over 40,000 acre feet, according to the city. Boyda noted Pactola is a 73.6% of its storage level and Deerfield Reservoir is at 92%.

“So we still have multiple years of surface water storage in both of these reservoirs, and remember that the whole point of reservoirs is to have multiple years of storage so that we can weather through droughts like we're going through right now,” he said.

Boyda said Pactola Reservoir water levels were lower during previous drought periods, specifically 1988-1991 and 2005-2008. Ron Bengs with the South Dakota Bureau of Reclamation noted the lowest level since 1956 at Pactola came in February 1962, when the reservoir was at 7.3% full (4,089 acre feet).

The low point during the late 80s/early 90s drought was in February 1991, when the reservoir was at 42.8% full (23,957 acre feet) and during the mid-2000s drought the reservoir was at 49.9% full (27,984 acre feet) in February 2008.

 Ron Bengs with the South Dakota Bureau of Reclamation
Ron Bengs with the South Dakota Bureau of Reclamation speaks to media on Wednesday, Aug. 19, at Sioux Park. 

Earlier this spring, the elevated storage condition status from “normal status” to “concern status” was due to the water levels at Pactola and the lack of inflows due to no snowpack in the watersheds above the reservoir, according to the city. That move led to the conservation measures currently in place, which are normally implemented yearly on June 1, beginning instead in late March.

During the press conference, Boyda noted residents who are installing sod or seeding their yards can apply for a waiver that would allow them to irrigate every day, though still within the 6 p.m. to 9 a.m. timeframe.

How to help

Boyda offered conservation tips for homeowners:

Plant low-water use native plants.

Irrigate in the early morning, during the lowest temperatures, to reduce evaporative loss.

Lift lawnmower blades for longer grass, which tolerates higher temperatures better.

Sharpen lawnmower blades to cleanly cut the grass.

Keep grass clippings “in a mulch fashion” on the lawn to reduce evaporative losses “by not having the sun directly contact the soil.”

Monitor and adjust sprinkler heads — “Make sure they’re not sprinkling on the sidewalk, on the street.”

“We always encourage people to irrigate longer to allow water to penetrate deeper in the lawn, encourage healthy, deep roots in the lawn. Water longer, less frequently,” Boyda said.

Boyda mentioned the city’s billing portal for water allows people to look at their historic usage, which lets them to see how much water they are using and, in theory, work to use less.

Other water users

Boyda said the rules also apply to businesses.

The city has taken steps as well, including planting native plants that benefit pollinators to “create a landscape that doesn't require additional supplemental irrigation versus a mowed grass area.”

 Rapid Creek at Sioux Park
Rapid Creek flows at Sioux Park on Wednesday, Aug. 19. 

“Parks and Rec has been doing a systematic upgrade of facilities, including updating their controllers, replacing irrigation pipes to prevent leaks,” he said.

The city is also using leak detectors to identify small leaks in the water utility system. City Hall will update its landscaping next year with more focus on low water use native plants, and the city restored filters and other equipment at its Mountain View water treatment plant to help conserve water, among other measures taken.

What if people don’t comply?

Boyda noted that often when a resident or business is violating the rules, it’s because they don’t know about the restrictions. He said if someone sees a neighbor or business irrigating outside of the allowed hours or on a restricted day, call Rapid City Public Works at 605-394-4165. Generally, he said, a Public Works compliance officer will go to the violator and either speak with them or leave a flier with information on restrictions.

 Rapid City Water Superintendent Eric Boyda
Rapid City Water Superintendent Eric Boyda speaks to media about watering restrictions in Rapid City. 

“We mostly get corrections by just talking with the property owner,” he said.

Boyda said habitual offenders could face a fine, but noted, “We haven’t gotten to that point yet.”

Pactola outflows

On Tuesday, the city decreased the water flows from Pactola Reservoir from 48 cfs to 42 cfs to comply with requirements to maintain sufficient supply for downstream water rights.

“We're monitoring almost on a daily basis, working with city staff who operates Pactola for us under contract. We work with the downstream users. We have contracted water needs and water rights downstream that we need to legally fulfill,” Bengs said.

He explained those water rights belong, in part, to irrigators (agriculture) in the Rapid Valley area, in addition to the Rapid Valley Sanitary District.

title: ‘We need change’: U.S. House candidate Gronli campaigns in Black Hills
description: Nikki Gronli said she believes South Dakotans are open to new leadership. The Democratic candidate for South Dakota’s U.S. Congressional House seat stopped in Rapid City and Lead on Wednesday to campaign and to listen to people’s concerns.
_full_text:
Nikki Gronli said she believes South Dakotans are open to new leadership. The Democratic candidate for South Dakota’s U.S. Congressional House seat stopped in Rapid City and Lead on Wednesday to campaign and to listen to people’s concerns.

Gronli attended the Great Plains Tribal Chairmen’s Association meeting in Rapid City, then traveled to Lead for the Lawrence County Democrats picnic on Wednesday evening. In western South Dakota, Gronli said, health care, housing, protecting public lands and the future of tourism are among locals’ top concerns.

“I’ve been out all over the state doing community meetings and sitting with people who are struggling with affordability, and the thing that keeps coming up is, ‘We need change.’ People are looking for change, and I think you see that in the results of the governor’s race (and Dusty Johnson’s loss),” Gronli said. “People are open to new leadership at this point. What we have isn’t working for South Dakotans.”

“I will continue to be out doing town halls and … if there’s a community that would like me to come and visit, I would love it,” she said.

Gronli will face Sturgis native Marty Jackley, currently the South Dakota attorney general, in the November general election. Gronli did not have a primary challenger, while Jackley beat challenger James Bialota 80.2%-19.8% in the June Republican primary.

Gronli, who lives in rural Dell Rapids, led the USDA Rural Development in South Dakota from 2022 to 2025, overseeing millions of dollars in investments supporting rural housing, broadband, infrastructure, and community facilities. She has nearly 30 years of experience in marketing, communications and leadership.

Her top priorities in her campaign for U.S. House are economic opportunity, education, disability inclusion, agriculture, health care, public safety, and tribal sovereignty, according to her website, nikkigforsd.com. On her website, she lists her plans aimed at creating a statewide economy that “works better for all residents,” and by addressing costs that place the “greatest strain on families” – housing, child care, health care, energy, and everyday goods.

Gronli told the Journal on Wednesday that affordable and accessible healthcare are top concerns she’s heard from residents in western South Dakota and across the state. At the Lawrence County Democrats picnic, she planned to talk about healthcare and some of the other biggest concerns for South Dakotans.

“One of the most important ones for me is health care and the variety of issues that we’re seeing in health care. That is everything from affordability and people just being able to get health care access (to) the fact that prescription drugs have gotten so expensive and we’ve got a lot of citizens are struggling with the ability to pay for their prescriptions,” she said.

“Often, insurance companies are moving the goal post, where year after year (the cost) ticks up and ticks up. I’m hearing from families who are trying to figure out, ‘How are we going to continue to deal with these increases?’ when everything else is so unaffordable. Health care is top of mind because it seems to be the thing that comes up the most.”

“I worry about our rural areas and accessibility to health care,” she said, citing examples of small towns that are without care after their only dentist retires, for example, or who can’t hire a doctor because there’s no available housing. Many rural areas have lost places to deliver babies.

“All these things are coming together, and it makes South Dakota more dangerous to be in,” Gronli said.

A lack of affordable housing is another top issue that’s affecting South Dakotans of all ages. Gronli said she’s heard from young adults who fear they’ll never be able to afford a home, and from senior citizens on fixed incomes who struggle with rising rental costs in addition to rising healthcare and food prices.

“The average first-time home buyer is now 40 years old,” Gronli said. “It doesn’t matter what part of the state you’re in. … You have young adults and seniors struggling with different types of housing, and at the same time I don’t see anybody addressing the fact that it is hard for developers to develop affordable housing” due to costs of lumber and materials.

Gronli said Congress needs to make sure incentives such as tax credits are put in place for developers to develop affordable housing. Tax credits also could be incentives for landlords and companies to keep rentals well-maintained.

Western South Dakotans worry about protecting public lands and making sure they’re not used for mining, Gronli said.  

“I’ve heard concerns about whether public lands could be used for data centers, especially when looking at water usage in western South Dakota. That seems to be (an issue) that really gets brought up (often),” she said. “We want to protect our lands because they are the lands for all of us.”

Tariffs, particularly concerns over tariffs on Canada, have sparked worries, too. Gronli said she’s talked with business owners who say the rising and changing costs of materials make it hard for them to give customers accurate estimates for projects and services.

Tariffs and tensions between the United States and Canada have fueled local worries about the tourism industry, which is especially vital to the Black Hills region. Gronli has heard from area residents who are concerned that Canadians who have vacationed here might, in the future, choose to visit elsewhere instead of returning to the Black Hills. Gronli has also heard that tourism numbers have particularly affected some industries, such as restaurants.

“We as a Congress need to address the tariff situation,” she said. “Congress has a right to have a say in that. The Constitution gives them that right.”

Gronli said she will return to western South Dakota this fall to continue meeting with the public at the Black Hills Pow Wow and other events.

title: Safety at the Central States fair: Law enforcement, lighting, cameras enhance security
description: Making the Central States Fair a safe environment for family fun takes months of planning and teamwork. Local law enforcement, Black Hills Energy and the City of Rapid City have joined forces to create a more secure, well-lit environment at the fair.
_full_text:
Making the Central States Fair a safe environment for family fun takes months of planning and teamwork. Local law enforcement, Black Hills Energy and the City of Rapid City have joined forces to create a more secure, well-lit environment at the fair.

The 81st annual Central States Fair opens Friday and continues through Aug. 29. The Pennington County Sheriff’s Office and the Rapid City Police Department will maintain a joint presence outside of and on the fairgrounds throughout the fair. The PCSO and RCPD announced their security measures at a press conference on Thursday morning.

The PCSO will provide the majority of law enforcement services inside the fairgrounds. Clad in high-visibility yellow gear, PCSO deputies will be easy to spot amid the fair festivities.

A law enforcement Regional Command Post is already set up on the fairgrounds near the carnival.

“This is a good place to find us if you need help or you’re just looking for directions, or maybe (looking for) a missing family member. This is a good place to start,” said Capt. Casey Kenrick with sheriff’s office.

 Fair press conference
From left, Patrol Lt. Darren Soucy with the Rapid City Police Department, Rapid City Public Works Director Mike Theis, Black Hills Energy General Manager Michael Pogany and Pennington County Sheriff’s Office Capt. Casey Kenrick discuss safety measures to protect fairgoers while they’re enjoying the Central States Fair during a press conference on Thursday, Aug. 20. 

The Rapid City Police Department will cover external parking areas and provide law enforcement outside the fair, according to Patrol Lt. Darren Soucy. He said the public can expect to see RCPD patrolling the area around the fair on bike patrol, foot patrol and more.

“We’ll be visible,” Soucy said. “If (PCSO) law enforcement has a need on the interior, we can move in to help, and if we have a need on the exterior, they can move outside to help us, too.”

This year, improved lighting and security cameras will enhance safety at the fair. Soucy praised a partnership with Black Hills Energy, which provided labor and materials to improve lighting and security, and the efforts of multiple City of Rapid City departments. The Public Works Department provided generators to ensure adequate power for the added lighting.

Soucy described lighting and security cameras as “crime prevention 101.”

“One of the things we are really encouraged about this year is we have better lighting out there, a better camera system out there to monitor what’s going on. … This was just a basic need we identified. We want to be able to make sure you’re safe getting out of your car and walking into the fairgrounds with your family.”

“Black Hills Energy and the city really helped us a lot with some lights to make sure we have some safe areas just outside of the fairgrounds into the parking lot,” Kenrick said.

“We want to provide the best, safest environment that we can for fairgoers. This should be a fun family event and not stressful at all,” Soucy said.

No kid alone at the fair

Kenrick urges families not to send unaccompanied kids and teenagers to the fair. Especially in light of events such as shootings at the fairgrounds in recent years, Kenrick said kids and teens should have supervision while enjoying the fair.

In 2025, for example, a shooting on the fairgrounds left a boy about 16 years old with non-life-threatening injuries. Police found the handgun they believe was used in the shooting, which they said those involved tried to discard. The shooting occurred as a result of a dispute between two groups, police said at the time.

“Obviously, we want kids supervised,” Kenrick said. “If we have kids causing issues, we’ll deal with those on a case-by-case basis. Our message is if you’re going to send your kids to the fair, please come with them or send some sort of supervision.”

 Central States Fair
A Central States Fair snapshot taken on Aug. 15, 2025, which included a day with youth livestock shows, mutton bustin' and the carnival. 

Kenrick encourages fairgoers to follow the Central States Fair’s safety rules and code of conduct, which can be found online at centralstatesfairinc.com/privacy-terms-cookies. In particular, Kenrick discouraged the wearing of gang colors, an issue he said occurs every year at the fair.

“Some of the rules that the fairgrounds established that we’re going to enforce on behalf of the Central States Fair is there’s no gang colors. If we see that, if you’re going to come here and wear that, just leave it in your car, and that’s what you’re going to be asked to do at the gate is leave it in the car,” Kenrick said.

“The big thing we see every year is unsupervised kids. You get a few of them together and some bad decisions can be made, and maybe it turns to something more serious,” Kenrick said. “What we don’t want is to create some kind of situation where we have families in the middle of something else, so we’re trying to avoid that completely.”

Finally, Kenrick urged adults who plan to drink alcohol at the fair to do so responsibly and to make sure they have a ride so they get home safely without putting themselves or others at risk.

“This is the end-of-summer bash that we all look forward to all year, and we’re looking for a safe family-fun event to end the summer, and end on a high note,” Kenrick said.

title: Rapid City’s Seed & Sparrow Collective: A place for small businesses to shine
description: Seed & Sparrow Collective is downtown Rapid City’s newest chic, cozy shopping hub, where local small businesses have teamed up to sell an array of unique hand-crafted goods and plants.
_full_text:
Seed & Sparrow Collective is downtown Rapid City’s newest chic, cozy shopping hub, where local small businesses have teamed up to sell an array of unique hand-crafted goods and plants.

The collective is located at 529 Main St., in a building with huge windows overlooking Main Street Square.

Seed & Sparrow Collective is co-owned by Sydney Riendeau and Amanda King. Riendeau owns Uprooted, a plant and plant care business, and King owns Scarlet Sealed Crafts, an apparel and jewelry business. In addition to showcasing their own products, Riendeau and King primarily share the storefront with Kacey’s Natural Creations and Bakes Two to Tango.

Kacey’s Natural Creations, owned by Kacey

 081826-nws-SeedSparrow-owners.jpg
Amanda King, left, and Sydney Riendeau co-own Seed & Sparrow Collective in downtown Rapid City. In their new storefront, they sell products from their own individual small businesses, as well as products from Kacey’s Natural Creations, Bakes Two to Tango, and an array of other small locally owned businesses. 

Hill, specializes in all-natural skincare and wellness items.

Alexia Drifmeyer, owner of Bakes Two to Tango, sells cinnamon rolls and other baked goods during pop-up shops at the storefront. Drifmeyer announces the days she’ll be there on her Facebook page and on Seed & Sparrow Collective’s page.

Drifmeyer also runs Tulip Tea Co. and sells small-batch loose-leaf tea blends at Seed & Sparrow Collective.

Tote bags, candles, soaps, macrame, crocheted beanies and headbands, embroidered items, pots, and much more from a variety of other locally owned small businesses complement the products from Uprooted, Scarlet Sealed Crafts, Kacey’s Natural Creations, and Bakes Two to Tango.

 081826-nws-SeedSparrow-boutique.jpg
Amanda King sells hypoallergenic jewelry, custom clothing, and more at Seed & Sparrow Collective in downtown Rapid City. 

Together, the shop owners and vendors have curated an atmosphere that focuses on hand-crafted items, natural products and ingredients, in an atmosphere that encourages shoppers to linger, relax, and stay awhile.

“We’re trying to keep it light and airy and where it flows and feels natural, and where it’s not just random items coming together,” Riendeau said.

The four business owners each were looking for different and more permanent locations that would give their businesses greater visibility. Teaming up to form Seed & Sparrow Collective allowed them to afford a prime downtown location in a historic building across from Main Street Square.

 081826-nws-SeedSparrow-macrame
Macrame made by Kacey Hill of Kacey’s Natural Creations is displayed at Seed & Sparrow Collective in downtown Rapid City. 

“That’s a huge thing to me — having that community that we’re part of by being a downtown business,” Riendeau said.

“I never thought in my wildest dreams this would be an opportunity, and it’s really awesome,” King said. “We’ve heard so many great things about how the space looks and how it feels. It’s been very encouraging.”

Beyond a shopping experience, Riendeau and King hope to use Seed & Sparrow Collective to host workshops and for small private events such as baby showers that bring the community together.

Seed & Sparrow Collective is open from Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Follow Seed & Sparrow Collective on Facebook and Instagram, and at seedandsparrowcollective.square.site for more information.

 081826-nws-SeedSparrow-Uprooted.jpg
Sydney Riendeau’s business, Uprooted, offers a potting station and live plants at Seed & Sparrow Collective in downtown Rapid City. 

 081826-nws-SeedSparrow-tea.jpg
Alexia Drifmeyer owns Bakes Two to Tango and Tulip Tea Co. An assortment of custom blended teas is always available at Seed & Sparrow Collective in downtown Rapid City.

title: County kicks off the 81st annual Central States Fair with proclamation recognizing the nine-day event
description: The Pennington County Board of Commissioners celebrated the Central States Fair ahead of the starte of the regional staple, which runs Aug. 21 through Aug. 29.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Board of Commissioners celebrated the Central States Fair ahead of the starte of the regional staple, which runs Aug. 21 through Aug. 29.

 Ron Jefferies
Central States Fairgrounds General Manager Ron Jefferies joined Assistant General Manager Ashely Solano to speak at the Pennington County Commission meeting on Tuesday, Aug. 18. 

"We're just here to invite you and the public to come out and enjoy the 81st annual Central States Fair. We've got plenty of fun and exciting things lined up," Central States Fairgrounds General Manager Ron Jefferies said at the commission's Tuesday, Aug. 18 meeting.

 Central States Fair music promises country hits, polka and more
Jo Dee Messina is among the acts coming to Rapid City for the fair.

The fair will host popular events such as PRCA Xtreme Broncs Finals, PRCA Range Days Rodeo, mutton bustin’, youth agriculture exhibits, country-western concerts, demolition derby, ArenaCross, Freestyle MotoX and the carnival.

Tickets to the fair are available online at CentralStatesFair.com, in-person and at Runnings of Rapid City.

Ticket prices:

ArenaCross & Freestyle MotoX: $50 for adults 13 and older, $20 for youth 7-12.

Mountain States Ford Demolition Derby: $50 for adults 13 and older, $20 for youth 7-12.

Sip & Saddle Wine Tasting: $30

PRCA Range Days Rodeo: $50 for adult 13 and older, $20 for youth 7-12.

PRCA Xtreme Broncs: $75 for adult 13 and older, $20 for youth 7-12.

Concerts: $75 for ages 7 and older.

Passes price:

VIP $350: Includes grounds admission, VIP seating for all 9 arena events, free parking via Campbell St. entrance, tailgate party access, and VIP food & drinks. All ages require pass. Ages 0–6 not free. 

Premier $175: Includes grounds admission, Premier seating for all 9 arena events, free parking via Campbell St. entrance, tailgate party access, and early seating access.

Grandstand $100: Includes admission for all 9 nights of Fair entertainment. Includes grounds admission and admission to all grandstand events and concerts.

Jefferies said the first day of the event, Friday Aug. 21 will feature  a ribbon cutting ceremony at the Monument Community Health Stage at 3 p.m. 

Assistant General Manager Ashely Solano gave a breakdown of events, saying, "We'll kick it off with the ArenaCross and the freestyle motocross (Aug. 21). Then we'll go into the Mountain States Ford Demolition Derby (Aug. 22) We did move around Xtreme Bronx and the Range Days Rodeo this year. So Sunday, Monday, Tuesday will be the Range Days Rodeo. Wednesday is going to be the Xtreme Bronc Finals, and then Thursday (Aug. 27) we've got Jo Dee Messina, Friday (Aug. 28) Billy Currington and Saturday (Aug. 29) Gary Allen."

 Central States Fair
The 81st annual Central States Fair opens Aug. 21 and runs through Aug. 29. 

Commissioner Ron Weifenbach (District 2) said the fair has the support from board and said the event is a substantial economic driver for the region.

Commissioner Deb Hadcock (District 3) read the proclamation, saying, "whereas the 81st anniversary of Central States Fair brings together a generation of young and old together to gather and celebrate agricultural heritage, foster community spirit, and create lasting memories for years to come."

Commissioners Hadcock, Weifenbach, Ron Rosskencht (District 1) Jerry Derr (District 4) and Gary Drewes (District 5) thanked the organizers and volunteers for their work in bringing the event together. They also acknowledged the loss of a staff member.

Central States Fair Maintenance Manager Paul Nebel, 50, was shot on Sunday June 7, by another fair employee. Nebel died from his injuries after being hospitalized on June 10.

The shooter, identified as John Try Lee, 58, traveled to the Pine Ridge Reservation after the shooting, where tribal officers located Lee. Lee fired at officers and was killed in the exchange.
