title: Meade County Sheriff's Office investigating security personnel incident at Sturgis campground
description: The Meade County Sheriff’s Office said Thursday it's investigating an Aug. 15 incident at the Sturgis Buffalo Chip during an evening concert.
_full_text:
The Meade County Sheriff’s Office said Thursday it's investigating an Aug. 15 incident at the Sturgis Buffalo Chip during an evening concert.

The office said it has received and reviewed numerous social media posts, videos, photographs and other information related to an incident that involved Buffalo Chip security personnel and several patrons at the venue.

The office did provide details about the incident.

"Additional information regarding other alleged incidents at the campground have also been forwarded to our office for review," the office said in a release.

A message sent by the Journal to Buffalo Chip seeking comment wasn’t immediately returned.

The sheriff's office said it has identified the security personnel involved in the incident and continues to gather and review evidence and information from those involved and other witnesses.

Videos of incidents from the Chip have made the rounds on social media.

"The Meade County Sheriff’s Office is aware of the significant public interest surrounding this incident and the considerable amount of information and commentary circulating on social media. We want to assure the public we take these allegations seriously," the office said in the release. "At the same time, our responsibility is to conduct a thorough, comprehensive, and impartial investigation based upon the facts and available evidence. Social media can provide valuable information and evidence, but conclusions regarding criminal conduct must be based upon a complete investigation and the applicable law."

Anyone who may have firsthand information, photographs or video related to the incident and has not already provided that information to law enforcement is encouraged to contact the Meade County Sheriff’s Office.

The office said it won't be commenting further on the matter until an investigation is complete.

title: Rapid City Council passes reasonable accommodations ordinance spurred in part by sober-living home discussion
description: The Rapid City Council voted 8-1 to approve an ordinance to update the city's municipal code regarding accommodations for those with disabilities, in a discussion spurred in part by a complaint about an Oxford House home owned by Councilman Stephen Tamang (Ward 1).
_full_text:
The Rapid City Council voted 8-1 to approve an ordinance to update the city's municipal code regarding accommodations for those with disabilities, in a discussion spurred in part by a complaint about an Oxford House home owned by Councilman Stephen Tamang (Ward 1).

Councilman Kevin Maher (Ward 3) voted against the measure, while Tamang abstained during the council’s Monday, Aug. 17, meeting.

A next-door neighbor to the home filed a complaint with the city in November of 2025 stating concerns about an Oxford House home owned by Tamang operating in her neighborhood. Oxford House is a nonprofit organization aiding in self-supporting, self-run recovery houses throughout the United States and internationally.

Under the city’s current zoning ordinance, no more than five unrelated adults may live in a home without obtaining a conditional use permit. The Oxford House website shows the home has a nine-person capacity and four vacancies.

City staff said the new ordinance looks to address the issue as the city is seeking to comply with the federal Fair Housing Act (FHA) and Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), as the housing falls under those federal disability and housing protections because the residents are disabled by alcoholism or other addictions.

The ordinance, as currently written, establishes a procedure through an administrative process that doesn’t involve public hearings. A memo attached to the ordinance notes that the city’s zoning ordinance does not include an administrative process to seek a modification to a zoning regulation to afford an individual with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a property, but the proposed administrative process meets FHA and ADA obligations.

According to the memo, there is a reduced risk that an accommodation will be handled with discrimination when it’s handled administratively.

Before the council voted, the neighbor spoke to the council, saying, "I want to thank the City Council, the City Attorney's Office, and the Community Development office and their staff for working through this issue and trying to find a solution that is best for the city as a whole. I understand that it may not always be the solution for every neighborhood, or what I personally would prefer. However, I am still concerned about loopholes being left open, particularly the lack of a reasonable occupancy limit for a residential dwelling."

A user of Oxford House, Carl Hodson, said he faced addiction but was helped in his sobriety journey by Oxford House.

 Carl Hodson
Carl Hodson, a past resident of an Oxford House, shared his experience of the self-run and peer-supported housing for those suffering from addiction. 

"These Oxford Houses are driven by peer-to-peer support for substance use recovery. We provide mutual encouragement, practical help, and understanding to one another as equals," Hodson said. "Because there are six to 10 people per house, chances are you're going to have shared life experiences with others fighting the same battles as yourself, and you're going to build relationships through equality instead of traditional top-down dynamics of modern clinics. We empower each other, focus on personal strength and goals instead of simple symptoms like other facilities do."

According to the Oxford House website, there are 3,500 Oxford Houses across the country, with 24,000 individuals in recovery living in them at any given time during the year.

Seven of those houses are in Rapid City. Oxford Houses are not halfway houses, treatment facilities or homeless shelters. They are places where people in recovery from drug and alcohol addiction can live and find support while they re-establish their lives.

Tamang, under an LLC registered in his name, purchased a house on Terracita Drive in Rapid City in October 2025 and leased it to Oxford House. The house is called “New Dreams.” It’s located in Tamang’s ward.

 Tamie Hopp
Tamie Hopp, director for Black Hills Works and a member of the Rapid City Disability Awareness and Accessibility Committee, spoke in favor of an ordinance looking to create reasonable accommodation procedures for people with disabilities. 

Tamie Hopp, with Black Hills Works Foundation and a member of the Rapid City Disability Awareness and Accessibility Committee, voiced her support for the ordinance to the council.

Hopp said, "People with disabilities or their representatives should not have to disclose the nature of their disabilities at a public hearing just to get equal use of their own homes. In addition, we know that the public hearing requirement exposes Rapid City to the risk of lawsuits based on Americans with Disabilities Act and Fair Housing Act violations. This is not a new revelation."

Maher said he thinks the proposed ordinance needs to address occupancy limits, spacing requirements and consideration for nearby neighbors.

 Rapid City
On Monday, Aug. 17, the Rapid City Council voted 8-1, with abstention from voting by Councilman Stephen Taamng (Ward 1), on the first reading of an ordinance amending the Rapid City Municipal Code to create a reasonable accommodation procedure for those with a disability.  

Community Development Director Vicki Fisher said, “Whether it's for an Oxford home or Black Hills Works or any other residential use to accommodate those with a qualifying disability because of mental or physical challenges, they are deemed a family. Whatever occupancy we would put on those uses ... we would have to put universally on every family in the city of Rapid City."

City Attorney Carla Cushman added, "If we had a requirement in the zoning code where these kinds of uses required notification to the neighborhood, that may be appropriate in these cases. But we don't have that requirement about notification to the neighbors with similar types of uses, and so if we put it into place when a reasonable accommodation is requested, that's the definition of discrimination."

Before the council voted, Greg Strommen (Ward 3) said the council would still have a chance to suggest changes before the ordinance's second reading.

Second reading of the ordinance will occur on Tuesday, Sept. 8.

title: Police search for suspects after gunshots near Hainesway Apartments
description: The Rapid City Police Department is searching for four suspects after several gunshots were fired from a car at Hainesway Apartments.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Police Department is searching for four suspects after several gunshots were fired from a car at Hainesway Apartments.

At around 7:40 p.m. on Friday, Aug. 21, police responded to multiple reports of several gunshots being fired from a car in the parking lot of Hainesway Apartments at 1314 Atlas St. Witnesses told police the suspect vehicle was occupied by four Native American males.

 Suspect vehicle
At around 7:40 p.m. on Friday, Aug. 21, police responded to multiple reports of several gunshots being fired from a car in the parking lot of Hainesway Apartments at 1314 Atlas St. Witnesses told police the suspect vehicle was occupied by four Native American males. 

Police haven’t received any reports of injury or damage caused by the gunfire and preliminary witness information suggests the shots were fired into the air, police said.

The suspect vehicle is described to be a silver or gray Chevrolet Impala. Police said the incident is actively being investigated.

Anyone with any information on the whereabouts of the suspect vehicle or the occupants involved in the shooting, should contact the police immediately at (605)394-4131.

title: ‘We have to take action now’: South Dakota tribal leaders, victim families call for help from state, feds
description: Confronting a surge in violent crime and crippling law enforcement shortages, dozens of tribal leaders and impacted families from South Dakota, North Dakota and Nebraska came forward to demand urgent state and federal intervention, insisting that the government partners uphold long-standing treaty obligations to protect Native communities.
_full_text:
Confronting a surge in violent crime and crippling law enforcement shortages, dozens of tribal leaders and impacted families from South Dakota, North Dakota and Nebraska came forward to demand urgent state and federal intervention, insisting that the government partners uphold long-standing treaty obligations to protect Native communities.

At the start of a two-day long forum hosted by the Great Plains Tribal Chairmen’s Association, Oglala Sioux Tribe President Frank Star Comes Out joined tribal chairpersons Ryman LeBeau, Peter Lengkeek, Chelaine Knudsen and Lonna Jackson-Street — alongside victims’ families — to testify about the critical need for increased federal funding for tribal law enforcement across the Dakotas and Nebraska.

"We have a major issue going on here in South Dakota and throughout the country with our law enforcement issues, we have a lot of problems. We have a lot of unsolved cases. We have a lot of families that have a lot of questions, and it's getting out of hand now," Oglala Sioux tribe President and Chairman for the Great Plains Tribal Chairmen’s Association, Frank Star Comes Out said during a Wednesday, Aug. 19, press conference held at the Hilton Garden Inn on Mall Drive in Rapid City.

The media event was held ahead of a Thursday, Aug. 20, conference held by Great Plains with a number of tribal representatives, Gov. Larry Rhoden and representatives of the states’ congressional delegation, among others.

 Frank Star Comes Out
Oglala Sioux Tribe President Frank Star Comes Out led speaks on Wednesday, Aug. 19, highlighting violent crime on reservations and the lack of resources and man power to tackle the issue. 

In the midst of a surge in violent crime and crippling law enforcement shortages within reservations, dozens of tribal leaders and impacted families from South Dakota, North Dakota and Nebraska came forward Wednesday, Aug. 19 to demand urgent state and federal intervention, insisting that the government partners uphold long-standing treaty obligations to protect native communities.

The GPTCA created two resolutions previously in July, calling to fully fund public safety, law enforcement and the administration of justice on tribal lands. The first resolution states, “Whereas, Indian nations and tribes have inherent sovereign authority to make our own laws and be ruled by them, including public safety, law enforcement, corrections, tribal courts and the administration of justice."

The resolution continues, "GPTCS calls on Congress and (the President Donald Trump) administration to fully fund Indian country public safety, law enforcement, corrections, tribal courts, drug and alcohol misuse treatment, and the administration of justice at our actual needs of $3.5 billion.”

A separate resolution additionally calls for fund of youth programs and juvenile justice. The GPTCA resolution calls for the Department of the Interior to contribute $50 million to juvenile justice and for the Department of Justice to set aside 10% of its $375 million budget for Indian country block grants, in addition to $25 million for youth treatment, rehabilitation and community re-entry.

"We have to take action now. Our people, tribal nations here in the Great Plains regions, has suffered far too long when it comes to crime, the violence, drugs, alcohol, missing and murdered Indigenous peoples, unsolved cases. We need action now. We need results," Star Comes Out said.

The Great Plains Tribal Chairmen’s Association is made up of 16 tribal nations representing over 100,000 tribal citizens in North and South Dakota, Nebraska, Montana and Iowa. The association advocates for tribal sovereignty, treaty rights and the safety and welfare of tribal citizens.

 Attendees
Residents from tribes spanning from North Dakota, South Dakota and Nebraska gathered for the Great Plains Tribal Chairmen’s Association’s public safety meeting to discuss the need for more resources in the tribes and address public safety concerns. 

According to data by the CDC, Native Americans experience homicide five times higher than non-Hispanic whites.

Tribal officials cited Bureau of Indian Affairs reports in estimating the annual need of $3.5 billion.

Tribal leaders identified the need for 2.8 officers per 1,000 people, per federal guidelines. Star Comes Out said there are 27 officers on the Pine Ridge Reservation, covering a population of 18,850, as counted by the U.S Census. Pine Ridge would need roughly 53 officers to cover the 2.8 per 1,000 guideline. The reservation encompasses 2.1 million acres, a land area larger than Delaware and Rhode Island combined.

Knudsen, the chairwoman of the Yankton Sioux Tribe, said on her reservation there are currently five tribal officers.

"We have an issue with competitive pay and retirement benefits as barriers to recruitment and retention. Another issue is being competitive with the surrounding towns and other agencies … (Officers) do find better jobs elsewhere because we're not providing that competitive pay to retain our officers," Knudsen said.

Lengkeek, chairman of the Crow Creek Sioux tribe, said, "My people are suffering. Our children are bearing the brunt of the lack of the federal government's treaty responsibilities. They are being traumatized by the violence and the crime within our communities and retraumatized by the very system that is meant to protect them."

Lengkeek said in 2023 the Crow Creek Reservation declared a Public Safety State of Emergency over violence. He also added the law enforcement in his community has been without a facility for more than 20 years and is operating out modular homes.

"When we have violent crime occur, we have to leave the reservation. Our law enforcement has to pick up that violent offender and take them to the next reservation, hoping that there's room (so) they can put this violent offender in. And a lot of times there is no room, so the law enforcement brings them back into the community and lets them go," Lengkeek said.

Jackson-Street, chairperson of the Spirit Lake Sioux Tribe, discussed her reservation in North Dakota, saying she could not address all of her community's needs in one statement.

"I speak on behalf of the Spirit Lake Tribe, our families, and all those who have been forced to carry this burden of underfunded and unstable public safety systems," Jackson-Street said.

She continued, "The United States must honor its treaty and trust responsibilities to our tribal nations. Public safety in Indian country is not charity, and it is not a temporary grant priority. It is a legal and moral obligation.”

LeBeau, chairman of the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe, said, "We do need the Congress to act. We need the Senate to act. We need the President of the United States to act on behalf of these tribal nations because it is their trust and treaty responsibility to provide these services for our for the tribes."

The tribal leaders cited that it is the United States’ obligation to uphold any treaty obligation, which includes the U.S. need to provide protection and law enforcement. The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie recognized the Sioux Nation's right to the Black Hills, which was later violated after settlers discovered gold in the hills. 

In 1980, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the nations were entitled to $102 million (roughly over $1 billion in today’s dollars) for the wrongful seizure, but the nations have yet to accept compensation as they seek land ownership back.

Family testimony

 Lisa Carlow
Lisa Carlow shares her story about losing her father and how it took 13 days to learn the investigation transitioned to a homicide. 

Lisa Carlow of the Pine Ridge Reservation shared that her father, Patrick Carlow Sr., was murdered in 2023 and despite her persistent push for answers, the case remains unsolved

"Three years is too long. My whole world was shattered that day. Getting out of bed every day is a chore," Carlow said.

Carlow, 73, was found dead inside his home on May 19, 2023, and investigators ruled the death a homicide.

"It's very frustrating because the people of Oglala are scared to tell what they know or what they've heard because there's not enough law enforcement to protect them, and they're worried about retaliation because it happens so much on the reservation. We need law enforcement. We need extra officers. We need extra people there looking out for our people," Carlow said.

 Hilda Kills Small
Hilda Kills Small is brought to tears as she explains how family members died due to violent crime and how it took hours for law enforcement to respond. 

Hilda Kill Small said in 2004 while law enforcement was in pursuit of a vehicle her daughter was in the back of, she fell out while the officer chased the vehicle. She died of her injuries.

She said her relative Ona Two Eagles was found dead on June 6 from apparent homicide and is still left with no answers.

Emmanuel Black Bear spoke on his nephew Alton Mesteh, 54, who was killed Jan. 27, 2024, from multiple gunshots from a vehicle striking through his home in Kyle. 

"I had a nephew. He was a good man, he worked hard, he was a father, he was a veteran, he fought for this country, for our people and he was murdered. Someone pulled up late at night and shot his trailer up, from side to side. They took his life in front of his children," Black Bear said.

 Janie Ducheneaux
Janie Ducheneaux detailed how she lost her ex-husband and son to violent crime and expressed concern that, along with the court system, has yet to provide justice. 

Janie Ducheneaux said her ex-husband and son were victims of homicide in separate cases. 

After her ex-husband was found dead in November 2022, she and her son sought answers for his death just east of Eagle Butte. She said his home where he was found dead was ransacked and showed signs of theft of his possessions. 

"I know that there was no justice in his death," Ducheneaux said.

Tragically in 2024, her son was killed, she said.

"My son Dylan on November 29, 2024, was killed. The only one who stood by me to continue to fight for justice for his dad. His life was taken, without going into great detail with that," Ducheneaux said before stepping away.

Day one of the event hosted tribal leaders, law enforcement officials, victims and families. Day two of the forum hosted tribal leaders and representatives, along with officials including Rhoden, Bureau of Indiana Affairs Office of Justice Services Director Charles Addington and representatives from the offices of U.S. Sens. John Thune and Mike Rounds, among others.

title: Officials break ground on Rapid City police precinct-fire station-city park
description: Work on the newest park, fire station and police precinct is now officially underway in Rapid City.
_full_text:
Work on the newest park, fire station and police precinct is now officially underway in Rapid City.

“Another day, another win in Rapid City. What I love about this project, it represents so much about the spirit of cooperation and teamwork that we have these days,” Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun said during a groundbreaking for the new station, precinct and park at the corner of Homestead Street and Neel Street on Monday, Aug. 24.

According to the city, the project will cost about $10 million and was made possible when the Rapid City Council approved funding the project, with the monies coming from Tax Increment Financing funds. Construction will start this month and is expected to be completed in December 2027.

Police Chief Don Hedrick said the precinct will serve initially as a place where officers can stop to file reports and the like, though it won’t be manned 24-7. He said as Rapid City continues to grow and expand eastward, that’ll change.

“We're planning ahead for the future here … As we continue to grow, and we continue to outgrow our downtown space, at that point we’ll then operate here on more of a full-time basis,” Hedrick said. “It’s a foothold for the future.”

 New fire station, police precinct and city park
A rendering of the city's police precinct-fire station-park on display at a groundbreaking on Monday, Aug. 24. 

Rapid City Fire Chief Jason Culberson said the fire station will be fully staffed right away. The department’s looking to hire 21 new crew members to accommodate the additional station. Staff at Station No. 9 will be a mix of new and seasoned firefighters, Culberson said, while the department will also move its Hazardous Material Team to the Homestead building.

Those 21 new positions are part of the department’s request in the 2027 city budget, which is still going through the approval process.

The park will provide green space, walking paths and recreational areas that will connect surrounding housing developments and create additional opportunities for residents to enjoy the area, the city said.

“This is going to be a spectacular location for a park,” City Parks and Recreation Director Jeff Biegler said during the ceremony. “It's going to be a big addition to this neighborhood.”

Culberson noted, “Projects like this don't happen because of one person, one department. They require vision, planning, funding, cooperation and a lot of work behind the scenes,” thanking city, police and fire staff, in addition to the design and construction team — TSP, Wag Co Construction and EMG Engineering are involved in the project.

During his remarks, Hedrick said he’s proud of the collaboration between city departments on the project.

“Police and fire, we make jokes, we have this brotherly or sisterly rivalry, we tease each other. But I got to tell you when the emergency happens, all of that goes out the window. We form as a team and come together and make sure that the community's services are put first. And we do it every single day.”

Bringing the three entities together — a fire station, police precinct and park — is something Culberson said is going to strengthen the bond between those agencies and Rapid Citians.

“Fire stations and police stations are traditionally places people associate with emergencies. This site will be different,” Culberson said during the ceremony. “Families will come here to use the park. Kids will play here. People will walk by the station, see our firefighters and our police officers, and hopefully get to know those men and women behind the uniform.”

title: Cliffside Park reopens after explosive device found near trashcan
description: Cliffside Park in west Rapid City has been reopened to the public after law enforcement extracted something with “the appearance of a improvised explosive device,” per Rapid City Police Department spokesperson Brendyn Medina.
_full_text:
Cliffside Park in west Rapid City has been reopened to the public after law enforcement extracted something with “the appearance of a improvised explosive device,” per Rapid City Police Department spokesperson Brendyn Medina.

 Cliffside Park
Cliffside Park features cliffs located right above it. 

Medina said a Rapid City Parks Department employee found the small, water-bottle-sized item next to a trashcan at the park and called law enforcement around 11 a.m. on Tuesday, Aug. 25. Authorities closed the park immediately.

“This is a good example of see something, say something. If you encounter something suspicious in our public areas that doesn't seem like it belongs, definitely give authorities a call,” Medina said.

 Trash can at Cliffside Park
On Tuesday, Aug. 25, a Rapid City Parks Department employee reported a suspicious item next to this trash can. Law enforcement ultimately removed the item. 

The Rapid City Police Department enlisted the help of South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation, which has “personnel with the subject matter expertise on how to identify and safely remove explosive devices,” Medina said.

The park, which is located at West Highway 44 and Dark Canyon Road, was closed while law enforcement checked the device. The park reopened at about 12:20 p.m. after law enforcement took the item and moved it out of the park for safe disposal.

 082626-nws-device-p1.JPG
Cliffside Park is located at West Highway 44 and Dark Canyon Road in Rapid City. 

Medina told the Journal it is under investigation whether the device was intended to cause any harm.

“That facet of it still remains under investigation. That's a question that we currently have right now, and that we'll be digging into,” Medina said.

title: After 4-year-old falls out of window, Rapid City woman pleads guilty to child abuse
description: A Rapid City woman pleaded guilty Tuesday, Aug. 25, to child abuse after a 4-year-old child fell out of an apartment window. The child survived the fall.
_full_text:
A Rapid City woman pleaded guilty Tuesday, Aug. 25, to child abuse after a 4-year-old child fell out of an apartment window. The child survived the fall.

Andrea Jumping Eagle, 37, appeared for her change of plea hearing before Circuit Court Judge Jeffrey Connolly at the Pennington County Courthouse Tuesday. Jumping Eagle was released on a personal recognizance bond on March 25.

Jumping Eagle was initially indicted for child abuse for a victim under the age of 7 and nonsupport of a child by parent, but ultimately pleaded guilty to a lesser version of child abuse. The initial charge, child abuse of a victim under the age of seven, is a Class 3 felony with a maximum sentence of 15 years in prison and a $30,000 fine. Nonsupport of child by parent is a Class 1 misdemeanor with a maximum sentence of one year in jail and a $2,000 fine.

Through a plea agreement with the state, Jumping Eagle pleaded guilty to a version of child abuse without the aggravation of the victim being under 7, knocking it down to be a Class 4 felony and a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a $20,000 fine.

Discussing the facts of the case, Connolly said Jumping Eagle was intoxicated on Nov. 2, 2025, when a 4-year-old child fell out of the window of an apartment she was in. Connolly highlighted how Jumping Eagle was notified of the window potentially being a problem prior to the incident and did not act.

In exchange for a guilty plea, the state asked for a 10-year sentence, with five years suspended.

Jumping Eagle’s sentencing is set for 10 a.m. on Sept. 29.

title: 3-2 vote from Pennington County Commission final step in barring utility-scale green energy projects on ag land
description: The Pennington County utility-scale wind-and-solar saga comes to an end.
_full_text:
The Pennington County utility-scale wind-and-solar saga comes to an end.

The Pennington County Board of Commissioners voted 3-2 to approve the second reading of an ordinance amendment that bars utility-scale wind and solar projects on agricultural land during its meeting on Tuesday, Aug. 18.

Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voted "no."

The ordinance shifts approval authority for utility-scale wind and solar projects from the county Planning Commission to the Board of Commissioners and includes setbacks that far exceed the recommendations of county staff and the current zoning ordinance.

It also includes a property line setback for solar panels of 1,000 feet (a forty-fold increase to the existing code, which requires 25 feet or 1 ½ times the height of the structure, whichever is greater) and a buffer zone of 50 feet. The change for wind turbines puts the setback from property lines at 1.2 miles (up from 1 ½ times the height of the turbine of 1,000 feet, whichever is greater, in the current code) and a 50-foot buffer zone. County staff had recommended solar be 50 feet from property lines and have a 25-foot buffer zone. Staff also recommended wind turbines be setback at three times the height of the turbines and a buffer zone of 25 feet.

 Energy
Commissioner Ron Rossknecht (District 1) has been a vocal "no" vote on an ordinance that bars utility-scale wind and solar projects from ag land. The ordinance passed its second reading 3-2 last week. 

Before voting, Rossknecht said, "I believe that it's over restrictive. I'm not really crazy about solar farms myself, but I am pretty crazy about people's property rights. And I think with this support as presented, we're not addressing the property rights of the folks that might want to develop these."

Rossknecht asked whether rezoning utility-scale wind and solar to just industrial should be more specific to light industrial or heavy industrial.

Pennington County Planning Director Brittney Hand said, although light and heavy industrial are two different defined uses, the ordinance, as written, gives the utility scale wind and solar an either-or choice.

 Energy
Commissioner Deb Hadcock (District 3) has been a proponent of changes that bar utility-scale wind and solar projects from ag land. 

Commissioner Deb Hadcock (District 3) said she has been a skeptic over these projects and has concerns about the safety of the agricultural community.

"I think we did a service to the community, and again, protecting our citizens and... protecting our (agricultural) land was our goal. I think for most of us commissioners," Hadcock said.

Commissioner Ron Weifenbach (District 2) said the commission changed the comprehensive plan to give residents and future residents an outline of what they can expect to be or not be developed in their zoning district.  

"If you go and buy a piece of land in the county, you have an expectation that we’re going to live up to the comprehensive plan, and the comprehensive plan says agricultural. It's as simple as that for me," Weifenbach said.

The commission passed the first reading of the ordinance on May 19 and, after additional amendments were made at that meeting, passed the first reading again on June 16. On July 7, the commission voted 5-0 to delay a second reading to the Aug. 4 meeting for more amendments, including a definition of infrasound and guidelines for decommissioning bonds for utility-scale wind and solar developments.

At the Aug. 4 meeting, the second-reading decision was delayed after a 2-2 split vote. Weifenbach was absent from the meeting, delaying action again until the Aug. 18 meeting.

This lengthy saga to bar such projects from agricultural land came in two parts as the commission first approved changes for the county's comprehensive plan, a tool used by the county as a guide for government officials, residents and developers in regard to "decision-making" for current and potential future development within the county.

A timeline of the alternative energy saga
Oct. 28, 2024: Pennington County Planning and Zoning Commission approves conditional use permits for the Cheyenne River Ranch Wind and Solar Farm, located 7 miles south of New Underwood, 30 miles southeast of Rapid City, and 3.5 miles north of Highway 44. In response, more than 450 citizens petitioned for a moratorium on such projects.
 Nov. 19, 2024: Commission votes unanimously to enact a year-long moratorium on all utility-scale wind and solar projects in the county.
 Dec. 12, 2024: Moratorium goes into effect.
 March 4, 2025: Commission forms an alternative energy task force to research the effects of such projects and future county regulations. The members include attorneys, an appraiser and individuals from the ranching community, local government, and the energy sector. From March-July 2025, the task force meets eight times.
 Oct. 21, 2025: Commission votes unanimously to extend the moratorium to Nov. 18, 2026.
 Jan. 20, 2026: Commission passes the first reading of comprehensive plan amendments to lay the groundwork for zoning amendments to ban utility-scale wind and solar on agricultural land, sequestering in to industrial zones.
 March 3, 2026: Commission passes the second reading of the comprehensive plan amendments. The foundation for zoning amendments is in place.
 April 7, 2026: Commission opts to delay a vote on updates to the zoning ordinance, including limiting projects to industrial zones and shifting the approval power from the planning commission to the board of commissioners.
 May 19, 2026: Commission votes 3-2, Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voting no, on the first reading of the ordinance. They made significant changes, which meant the ordinance would need to be re-advertised and go through first reading again. Those changes included significant setback requirements.
 June 16, 2026: Commission votes 3-2 again, with Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voting no, on the second first reading of the ordinance.
 July 7, 2026: Commission votes 5-0 to delay the vote on the second reading to Aug. 4 for more amendments, such as a definition of infrasound and guidelines for decommissioning bonds for utility-scale wind and solar developments. The county must re-advertise the ordinance again.
 Aug. 4, 2026: Commission votes 2-2 on the ordinance, which delays it to the Aug. 18 meeting. With Commissioner Ron Weifenbach absent, the "yes" side doesn't have enough votes.
 Aug. 18, 2026: With all five commissioners present, the ordinance amendment passes 3-2.

The plan provides a framework for land-use decisions, public service expansions, economic development, resource management and the county's overall growth.

The amendment barred utility-scale wind and solar from agricultural to industrial zoned land usage. Commission approved this change on March 3, with the same 3-2 vote.

The purpose of the zoning amendment is to further set specific setback and regulations for these projects.

The amended Section 317 states, "These provisions are intended to establish minimum standards for solar energy systems, wind energy facilities, and battery energy storage systems in order to minimize impacts on neighboring properties, ensure compatibility with surrounding land uses, protect environmental resources, and promote the safe, responsible, and coordinated development of renewable energy while safeguarding the public health, safety, and general welfare."

Commissioner Jerry Derr (District 4) said before voting, "In my mind (we) kicked this can down the road. Solar panel, wind turbine, whatever you want to call it, and we need to get the motion approved today so that we're not working up against the timeline of our moratorium."

The county's moratorium for utility-scale wind and solar is to end Nov. 18.

title: Bonnie Edwards
description: April 15, 1949 - August 23, 2026
_full_text:
April 15, 1949 - August 23, 2026

Bonita Allene Edwards (77) died on August 23, 2026, in Rapid City, South Dakota, from pancreatic cancer. Bonnie was born on April 15, 1949, in Sioux Falls, S.D., to Warren Allen and Ruth Eleanor (Barrett) Scott. She grew up in Rowena, S.D., with her older sister, Ruthie. She attended grade school in Rowena and graduated from Brandon Valley High School in 1967. She met her husband, Jack Marshall Edwards on a blind date while attending Dakota Wesleyan University in Mitchell, S.D. They were married on August 2, 1968, in Sioux Falls. They were blessed with two wonderful children, Julie Marie and Scott Marshall.

Bonnie was employed as a legal secretary for the law firm of Morrill, Thomas, Nooney and Braun. Prior to her retirement, she was an office assistant at Regional Home Care and Hospice.

Music was a very important part of her life. At the age of four, her mother and accompanist took her singing in nursing homes for the grandmas and grandpas. Singing duets with her "'Nother Mother", Jane Anderson, singing in the First Congregational UCC Choir for over 50 years, bell choir, and later piano/organ duets added great joy to her life.

Bonnie loved her grandson, Jackson, whom she called "her best boy." She especially enjoyed the Thursday afternoons chatting, playing games, going to movies. He could always make her laugh with his original turns of phrase and his unique look on life.

Bonnie and Jack enjoyed many camping trips to the Bighorn Mountains and the fly-fishing trips to Alaska. She also traveled to Canada and Mexico with Jack. With friend, Georgia O'Connor, she visited England, Italy, Wales and Ireland. With her sister Ruthie, she traveled to Norway and Italy.

Bonnie was a member of First Congregational Church UCC, P.E.O. Chapter BR-SD, and was Secretary of Black Hills Flyfishers for many years.

She survived by her husband, Jack Marshall Edwards; her daughter, Julie Marie Edwards (Scot Singpiel), Salt Lake City, Utah; her son, Scott Marshall Edwards (SO Cathy Wilson), Rapid City S.D.; her grandson, Jackson Scott Edwards, Rapid City S.D.; sister, Ruth Marie Schemmel, Rapid City S.D.; brother-in-law, Douglas Edwards, Deerfield S.D.; and many other relatives and friends.

She was preceded in death by her precious granddaughter, Lilah Jane Edwards; her parents, Warren and Ruth Scott, brother/cousin, Raymond Barrett and his wife, Jackie; brother-in-law, Ronald Schemmel; in-laws, Jack and Jane Charline Edwards; brother-in-law, Robert Edwards; and her best friend, "Nother Mother" Jane Anderson.

Bonnie especially wants to thank her good friends and supporters through this journey Chuck and Sybil Rounds, and Susan Kelts.

Her family and friends would also like to thank Hospice House and their wonderful staff for the exceptional care she received at the end of her journey.

A memorial service is planned at First Congregational Church UCC, 1200 Clark Street, Rapid City, S.D., on Monday, August 31 2026, at 11 a.m., with visitation one hour before the service. Private inurnment will occur at a later date.

In lieu of flowers, a memorial to First Congregational Choir, or in memory of all the cats in her life to A Place for Meow Pet Rescue, 6345 Tittle Springs Place, Rapid City SD 57702.

"And she left her body and flew through the sky and we whispered 'See you later' instead of goodbye" (Joanne Boyle).

title: Randy Brink
_full_text:
May 12, 1951 - August 23, 2026

Randy Brink, 75, passed away peacefully on August 23, 2026. Born on May 12, 1951, Randy lived a full and meaningful life marked by hard work, adventure, generosity, and an unmistakably independent spirit.

Randy graduated from Rapid City High School in 1969. After graduation, he immediately began working for his father and the family company. He worked his way up to foreman before, in 1978, branching out with his brothers to build a second successful company in Colorado. Fifteen years later, they returned to the parent company, where Randy continued to grow professionally, eventually becoming vice president before retiring in 2007.

Randy was remarkably self-taught and innovative, qualities that served him well in a highly technical industry. His ability to learn, adapt, and find creative solutions was a testament to his determination and intelligence. He took great pride in his work and in everything he accomplished alongside his family.

Randy had a deep love for the outdoors and found great joy in fishing, hunting, and waterskiing. His and Monica's cabin at Pactola Lake held a special place in his heart—a treasured retreat, where he especially enjoyed being out on his boat.

Randy met Monica Bower-Brink at their high school reunion, and from that meeting began a life together filled with travel, adventures, and shared experiences. For 26 years, Randy and Monica enjoyed many activities together and built a life rich with love, laughter, and unforgettable memories. Their love and companionship were an important part of Randy's life and brought him tremendous happiness.

Generosity was another defining part of Randy's legacy. He continued his family's tradition of supporting others by generously giving to numerous charities and causes, including the Children's Home. He believed in helping his community and, often without fanfare, made a meaningful difference in the lives of many through his generosity.

Randy will be remembered for his rebellious spirit, kindness, generosity, and straightforward, to-the-point way of communicating. He knew his own mind, lived life on his own terms, and never hesitated to be himself. Beneath his independent nature was a man who cared deeply for the people around him.

Above all, Randy loved his family. He loved each of his grandchildren deeply, and that love was returned to him in abundance. The special bond he shared with them brought him tremendous happiness and will remain one of the most treasured parts of their memories of him.

He will be deeply missed by his wife Monica Bower-Brink, daughters Heidi (Adam) Malbrough, Jenna Brink, and son Ryan Brink (Ashley Byrd); step-daughters Niki (Aaron) Studer, Brandi (Shane) Tipton, Tyna (Jesse) Jurrens and grandchildren Jade, Rachel, Tyrus, Izabelle, Haiden, Asa, Quincy, Garet, Jackson, Dylan T., Dylan B., Cole, Morgan, Gresen, Hudson, and Haizley, brothers Doug (Ginger) Brink, Lyle (Cathie Brink) and sister Kay (Rod) Everson. He will be profoundly missed by his family, and his friends who were important to him.

Randy's presence, strength, humor, independence, and generosity will be profoundly missed by his family, friends, and all who were fortunate enough to know him. His adventurous spirit, unwavering love for his family, and commitment to helping others will remain part of his lasting legacy. The many lives he touched—and the memories he created along the way—will keep his spirit close for years to come.

title: South Dakota to receive at least $52 million from Meta settlement
description: South Dakota will receive a minimum of $52,612,676 from the $17.1 billion multistate settlement with Meta Platforms, Inc.
_full_text:
South Dakota will receive a minimum of $52,612,676 from the $17.1 billion multistate settlement with Meta Platforms, Inc.

The South Dakota Attorney General’s Office announced the total on Wednesday, Aug. 26.

“Today’s historic settlement marks a significant milestone in our efforts to protect children online,” Attorney General Jackley said in a release. “We have secured a record monetary award and meaningful safeguards for children and parents, setting the new national online standard.”

 South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley
Attorney General Marty Jackley, shown in this file photo, announced on Wednesday, Aug. 26, that South Dakota will receive a minimum of $52 million from the $17.1 billion settlement with Meta Platforms, Inc. 

In the settlement, South Dakota, along with 47 other states, will receive monies that will be distributed over a 10-year span. This marks one of the state's largest settlements since the Big Tobacco settlement of the 1990s, the AG’s office said.

South Dakota’s share will be paid out over the next 10 years. South Dakota’s share of the settlement could grow to $73,480,057 upon certain conditions being met, the office said. As part of a presentation on the settlement, the office said 30% of the 17.1 billion would be paid to states when other social media industry participants — namely, TikTok, YouTube, and Snapchat — enter into agreements with the states similar to Meta’s agreement.

The settlement is contingent on the approval of the agreement by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California which is hearing a lawsuit filed against Meta by South Dakota and 28 other states.

Meta will roll out safety features for children on Instagram and Facebook after the company was found to have knowingly exposed children to mental harm and misled the public over safety concerns, the AG’s office said.

Safety features

● Hard cap daily time limits and “Productive Pauses” for children: For its two platforms, Instagram and Facebook, a combined two-hour daily time limit with mandatory pauses after 15 minutes of continuous use and again at 60 and 90 minutes to interrupt endless scrolling. These limits remain in effect for five years. If Snapchat, TikTok, and YouTube adopt comparable terms, the daily limit on each platform will drop to 60 minutes for 10 years.

● “Nighttime blocks” restricting children’s access from 12 a.m. to 6 a.m.

● Limited school-time access for children, eliminating push notifications on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. during the school year.

● Robust age assurance measures to more effectively verify the age of young users.

● Safer, age-appropriate content controls, including stronger safeguards against bullying, content promoting eating disorders, and content related to suicide and self-harm.

● Stronger, more user-friendly parental controls.

● Limits on social comparison features, including beauty filters and visible “like” counts, that have been linked to poor mental health outcomes in kids and teens.

● Both the implementation and efficacy of the features will be regularly assessed by an independent auditor and the settling states.

A bipartisan and nationwide investigation, it was found that Meta implemented addictive features and internally documented its harm toward children, but failed to give parents warnings. Thirty-three attorneys general sued Meta as part of a multistate coalition.

Additionally, the release states that the settlement resolves the states’ claims against Meta’s for for sharing non-public information about Facebook users with third parties, such as Cambridge Analytica.

title: Rapid City man arrested after crash, BAC was 5 times legal limit
description: A man driving with a blood alcohol content more than five times the legal limit crashed in Rapid City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, police said.
_full_text:
A man driving with a blood alcohol content more than five times the legal limit crashed in Rapid City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, police said.

According to the Rapid City Police Department, 40-year-old Tyler Janis, of Rapid City, was driving a black passenger vehicle around 5 p.m. Tuesday at the intersection of East Omaha and Cambell streets when he struck “at least two vehicles,” a Rapid City Police Department spokesperson said. One person went to the hospital with minor injuries.

When police arrived and found Paris, they noted a strong smell of alcohol coming from him. A breathalyzer test read his blood alcohol content at .426%, more than five times the legal limit of .08%.

Police arrested Paris on suspicion of DUI and driving under revocation. This is not the first time he’s had alcohol-related brushes with the law. Paris has four DUI convictions in his past.

In 2003, he picked up his first DUI and was sentenced to a 10-day suspended jail sentence, and the court suspended his license for 30 days.

Paris picked up another DUI in 2006, for which he received a 90-day jail sentence with 83 days suspended. His license was also revoked for a year in that case. Also in 2006, he was convicted of possession of alcohol by someone under 21 and maintaining a place to violate beverage laws. His license was suspended in that case for 30 days.

After a nearly 20-year intermission, Paris was convicted of two DUIs in December 2025, one stemming from May 2025 and the other from August 2025. He was sentenced to 180 days in jail with 160 days suspended. The sentence also included a driver’s license suspension for one year, starting on Dec. 23, 2025. He was under the revocation during the Tuesday incident.

title: Box Elder man sentenced for possession of child sexual abuse material
description: A Box Elder man was sentenced to 10 years in prison followed by five years of supervised release for possession of child sexual abuse material and attempted enticement of a minor using the internet.
_full_text:
A Box Elder man was sentenced to 10 years in prison followed by five years of supervised release for possession of child sexual abuse material and attempted enticement of a minor using the internet.

Christopher Teagle, 41, appeared for his sentencing hearing before U.S. District Judge Camela Theeler on Tuesday, Aug. 25.

Teagle was initially indicted for attempted enticement of a minor, distribution of child pornography, possession of child pornography, obstruction of justice and forfeiture.

Through a plea agreement with the government, Teagle pleaded guilty to attempted enticement of a minor using the internet and possession of child pornography. In exchange of a guilty plea the government agreed to dismiss all other charges and request a 10-year sentence, followed by five years of supervised release.

Both parties asked the court to follow the agreement, with Teagle’s defense attorney Paul Andrews highlighting Teagle’s prior service in the Air Force.

According to the factual basis statement in court documents, on Aug. 6, 2024, Teagle contacted an undercover law enforcement officer, who he believed was a 14-year-old girl at the time, for sexual relations. Upon further investigation, law enforcement were able to find 17 images of child sexual abuse material on one phone and 55 videos on another phone.

Before sentencing, Theeler acknowledged Teagle was raised in an environment of heavy alcohol abuse and experienced physical and emotional abuse at a young age. She said Teagle would be intoxicated before engaging in the criminal behavior.

Theeler also said Teagle contacted a mother and requested sexual relations with her and her underage child. Though Teagle did not physically harm a child himself, Theeler said he had clearly supported an industry that leaves these children “vulnerable and completely traumatized for the rest of their lives.”

Theeler sentenced Teagle to 10 years in prison, followed by five years of supervised release for each count. The sentences will run concurrently.

title: South Dakota state, federal partners reply to regional tribal leaders’ pleas for funding, assistance
description: Great Plains tribal leaders and families delivered an urgent plea over two days of discussion about how rising violent crime is outpacing their ability to protect their people, leaving chronically understaffed and overworked police departments on reservations to make impossible choices between active crises.
_full_text:
Great Plains tribal leaders and families delivered an urgent plea over two days of discussion about how rising violent crime is outpacing their ability to protect their people, leaving chronically understaffed and overworked police departments on reservations to make impossible choices between active crises.

Gathering on Wednesday, Aug. 19 and Thursday, Aug. 20, dozens of community members and officials representing reservations across South Dakota, North Dakota and Nebraska called on state and federal partners to fulfill long-standing treaty obligations and supply critical law enforcement resources.

Oglala Sioux Tribe President Frank Star Comes Out said the goal of the two-day forum at the Hilton Garden Inn on Mall Drive in Rapid City was to not only address the crisis but also establish better understanding and communications between the tribal nations and their state and federal partners.

 Rhoden part 2
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden speaks during a meeting with tribal leaders on Thursday, Aug. 20, at the Hilton Garden Inn in Rapid City. 

“We would just like to see a change in South Dakota for the better,” Star Comes Out said.

The Great Plains Tribal Chairmen’s Association is made up of 16 tribal nations representing over 100,000 tribal citizens in North and South Dakota, Nebraska, Montana and Iowa. The association advocates for tribal sovereignty, treaty rights and the safety and welfare of tribal citizens.

‘Reset our relationship:’ Rhoden talks about public safety

On Thursday, those federal and state partners finally responded, with South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden taking the lead.

“When I took office, my very first speech in the Legislature, I talked about what Frank (Star Comes Out) already mentioned, the need for us to reset,” Rhoden said. “Reset our relationships with the tribes and I hope that you’ve seen that promise (become) reality.”

Rhoden said the cornerstones of his administration is openness, responsiveness and stability. He said law enforcement has been a key focus for him since he took over as governor in early 2025.

“Our law enforcement deserves respect at all levels. But for too many years, law enforcement officers have not had the full protection under South Dakota law,” Rhoden said. “This year we changed that.”

 Gov. Larry Rhoden
Gov. Larry Rhoden said the cornerstones of his administration are openness, responsiveness and stability. He said law enforcement has been a key focus for him since he started his administration. 

South Dakota Searchlight reported that Rhoden signed House Bill 1007, which recognizes tribal police who are helping with their state and local counterparts as law enforcement officers under South Dakota law.

Although tribal officers routinely assist state counterparts at crime and crash scenes outside reservation borders, state law did not formally recognize them as law enforcement officers, leaving them without key legal protections, such as classifying simple assault against them as a felony. Simple assault is normally a misdemeanor.

House Bill 1007 addresses this gap by extending state-level legal protections to tribal officers whenever they assist in public safety operations anywhere in the state.

Rhoden signed House Bill 1084, which protects law enforcement officers and public servants from doxxing. He also mentioned he established the Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force, which will assess the programming needs of the inmate population, explore options for faith-based and Native American-focused programs, study best practices for re-entry models and make recommendations on how to best use the expanded space of the new prison facility in Sioux Falls.

“If we can get inmates the opportunity for true rehabilitation, then we can end this never-ending revolving door in our prisons,” Rhoden said.

At the end of his speech, Rhoden encouraged all of the tribes to meet with his administration and consider signing a law enforcement agreement through the 287(g) program, which is a formal partnership between U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and state or local law enforcement agencies. He said the agreement would provide additional training to tribal law enforcement. The South Dakota Highway Patrol and South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation have both entered into such agreements with ICE.

“Crime does not recognize borders or even things like saturation patrols. There’s so many things that we can do to work together, provide safety for our communities,” Rhoden said. “… To reduce crime throughout South Dakota and our reservations we must look past the politics. We must focus on working together. And for as long as I’m governor, it will always be my mission to keep South Dakota strong, safe and free.”

Tribal leaders didn’t directly engage with Rhoden on the 287(g) suggestion.

After Rhoden’s speech, tribal leaders were given the floor to ask him questions. A common question was how can tribal nations benefit from some of the funding the state receives from the federal government?

Rhoden acknowledged that tribal nations want to protect their sovereignty while seeking aid from partners, and he suggested they sign a memorandum of understanding with the state where they can receive some benefits and back out whenever the tribal nation sees fit.

 Group photo
Oglala Sioux Tribe President Frank Star Comes Out said the goal of the two-day forum is to not only address the crisis but also establish better understanding and communications between the tribal nation and their state and federal partners. 

“I think that we can demonstrate that we can work (together),” Rhoden said.

Rhoden said he believes the federal delegation would be more than willing to help, if both the state and the tribes show they are willing to work together.

Another hot topic from Thursday’s discussion was whether the two-day event will push the state and federal government into action or if this will be the latest in an endless cycle of conversations that lead nowhere.

“What we’re talking about here has been talked about over and over and over again, and we start the dialogue and when that gets tough, we stop coming,” Rosebud Reservation Treasurer Louis Wayne Boyd said. “We stop talking to each other, and then we wake up and somebody new comes in and starts over again.”

Rhoden said he appreciates the honest feedback, but said he’s taken a different approach than his predecessors when working with the tribes.

“I think previous administrations, quite frankly, tried too hard in reaching out to the tribes and I’ve been a lot more reserved as far as trying not be forceful and not push myself onto the tribes,” Rhoden said. “I do have a heart that believes we could cover a lot of ground by working together and showing a little trust.”

A crisis that cannot be ignored

According to data from the CDC, Native Americans experience homicide rates five times higher than non-Hispanic whites.

Tribal officials cited Bureau of Indian Affairs reports in estimating an annual need from the government of $3.5 billion.

Tribal leaders identified the need for 2.8 officers per 1,000 people, per federal guidelines. Star Comes Out said there are 27 officers on the Pine Ridge Reservation, covering a population of 18,850, as counted by the U.S Census. Pine Ridge would need roughly 53 officers to cover the 2.8 per 1,000 guideline. The reservation encompasses 2.1 million acres, a land area larger than Delaware and Rhode Island combined.

Oglala Sioux Tribe Police Chief Jason Lone Hill expressed hope that the discussions will yield real solutions, noting that while the data is critical to showing state and federal partners the severity of the crisis, the true urgency lies beyond the numbers — in the lives shattered by violent crime.

 Oglala Sioux Tribe Police Chief Jason Lone Hill
Oglala SIoux Tribe Police Chief Jason Lone Hill expressed hope that the discussions will yield real solutions, noting that while the data is critical to showing state and federal partners the severity of the crisis, the true urgency lies beyond the numbers — in the lives shattered by violent crime. 

“We need to find a solution and numbers and data are very, very paramount to our agreements, but we forget about our people suffering and that’s the true data, that’s the true numbers and (solutions) should be built with them in mind,” Lone Hill said.

Lone Hill said the United States government has neglected its responsibilities and said the tribal nation is always pushed to do more with less.

The lack of resources and manpower has caused the few tribal law enforcement members to be overworked and underpaid, Lone Hill said, often pushing them to make impossible decisions in picking which crisis to respond to.

“We do our best. We do our best with what we have and been doing our best with what we have for years,” Lone Hill said. “We keep going to the same people for funding year after year, when we should be looking for different solutions to these problems.”

Some tribal residents testified on Wednesday about their harrowing experiences after losing their loved ones from violent crime and often waiting hours for help to come.

 Law enforcement
Tribal leaders identified the need for 2.8 officers per 1,000 people, per federal guidelines. Star Comes Out said there are 27 officers on the Pine Ridge Reservation, covering a population of 18,850, as counted by the U.S Census. Pine Ridge would need roughly 53 officers to cover the 2.8 per 1,000 guideline. 

The tribal leaders cited said Wednesday that it is the United States’ obligation to uphold any treaty obligation, which includes the country’s obligation to provide protection and law enforcement. The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie recognized the Sioux Nation's right to the Black Hills, which was later violated after settlers discovered gold in the hills.

In 1980, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the nations were entitled to $102 million (roughly over $1 billion in today’s dollars) for the wrongful seizure, but the nations have yet to accept compensation as they seek land ownership back.

‘What are you doing for us?’ tribes challenge BIA

Tensions flared Thursday over whether the Bureau of Indian Affairs has done enough to boost base funding and address critical tribal needs amid a wave of state-of-emergency declarations across the Great Plains.

BIA Office of Justice Services Director Charles Addington said the agency is doing everything they can to support the tribal nations. Addington highlighted that they have been trying to orchestrate as many operations in Indian Country as possible to impact traffic flow and crime rates in the area. With six major operations completed so far this year, the goal is to increase BIA law enforcement staff to better assist tribal officers.

“We know resources are a big issue and we’re committed to getting resources on the ground the best we can,” Addington said.

BIA is a United States federal agency within the Department of the Interior that manages programs, land and services for Native Americans and Alaska Natives.

Addington said they are actively looking for ways to better assist tribes by improving communications and asking for feedback. He highlighted that another goal was to communicate with the Bureau of Indian Education to look at possible school resource officer issues and safety in schools.

Though some attendees appreciated the sentiment of Addington’s promise for BIA to maintain a better relationship with the tribes, Oglala Sioux Tribe Finance and Credit Director Courtney Two Lands addressed what was on everyone’s minds — “How are you going to help the tribes in the Great Plains region to increase their base funding?” Two Lands asked the question several times in the two-hour-long discussion with federal partners.

Addington said it all depends on Congress giving out funding. He said it’s looking positive after conversations with Congress that there may be more funding coming BIA’s way to give out to the tribes. However, he couldn’t promise how much funding will come and if it will at all.

“We are hoping our good friends in Congress provide us dollars, will increase dollars, for us to be able to provide for the tribes,” Addington said. “There’s also discussions going on within the department of how we can leverage internal resources to help drive. We’ll have to wait and see kind of what what the budget ends up checking out.”

Tribal leaders said South Dakota’s congressional delegation was invited to the event. No one representing Sens. John Thune and Mike Rounds and Rep. Dusty Johnson spoke during the public portion of the forum. An initial release about the event said video comments from Johnson and Attorney General Marty Jackley were to be shown. Jackley is running to replace Johnson in the U.S. House after Johnson sought the governorship.

Field Operations Deputy Associate Director Joel Chino said BIA can better represent the tribal nation in D.C. if the office and the tribes actively work together to gather reports — such as violent crime and crashes — and communicate.

“What we can do is we can work together,” Chino said. “We can work together in the technical assistance to provide the training so that way we are telling our story of what is going on within Indian Country.”

Not satisfied with that answer, several tribal members came forth expressing resentment towards BIA and said the office is not adequately advocating for them in D.C. because they are not personally experiencing the struggles many residents face on a day-to-day basis.

Two Lands, followed by several other tribal members, said the BIA’s funding formula is severely flawed and only reflects numbers based on outdated data. Addington after Congress determines whether to increase BIA’s budget the formula is utilized to determine how much money goes to each tribe. He said that can either be one-time funding or base funding.

“It’s got the violent crime piece, it’s got the land-base piece, it’s got the unmet needs,” Addington said. “So we submit the unmet needs report to Congress.”

Addington said the funding formula has been discussed at several meetings over the years.

“We have told the tribes many times if everybody can get together and come up with a different kind of formula, we would be more than happy to use a different formula, but it has to be agreed upon by all the tribes,” Addington said.

As discussions continued, Anna Halverson, one of Oglala Sioux Tribes representatives, challenged Addington’s role in representing the tribes, especially regarding the public safety crisis. She said people are dying from violent crime and there is no time for discussions that lead to zero actions.

“Why aren’t you speaking up for us as tribes?” Halverson said. “You know the challenges tribes are facing with public safety. You know the problems with the inadequate funding. You know the problems that we’re facing with these formulas that leave our tribe struggling to meet these responsibilities that we’re given — the responsibilities to keep our people and our tribe safe.”

Addington said he was offended by Halverson's insinuation that he was not making every effort to bring resources to Indian Country, highlighting how he was able to raise $6 million in base funding under the Trump Administration.

“That was an increase to the tribes. I know it may not be much as is needed, but that’s pretty significant when we got in 2024 and in 2025 … flat budgets from Congress under the previous administration,” Addington said.

He said public safety is the top priority as they continue to show Congress, who determines how much funding is given, what the unmet needs are.

“It’s not my fault that you’re offended, and I don’t mean to offend you if that’s the way you took it, but in order for our Oglala Sioux Tribe to try to be properly adequate with public safety , we’ve (previously) requested $31.1 billion for public safety and the BIA allocated $4.2 million. So you should understand the frustration that we have as tribal leaders when we’re telling you that we’re underfunded.”

There are two ways tribes receive funding for law enforcement. One is by receiving law enforcement services directly from the BIA, which is the case for 23 agencies, but Pine Ridge’s law enforcement funding comes from the second option, the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA), which provides the ability for tribes to take over services administered by the Secretary of Interior, including law enforcement. 

If a tribe opts for law enforcement funding through ISDEAA, they receive a lump sum that is not less than what the Secretary of Interior would spend on that service. The Oglala Sioux Tribe has contracted law enforcement through ISDEAA for 40 years.

Addington agreed there’s a great need to fix the crisis, but it’s up to Congress and all BIA can do is to continue providing reports and advocating for more funding.

Despite the heated debates with federal partners, Star Comes Out said he hopes these conversations continue to grow so that one day action can occur.

As the two days of tense debate and impassioned testimony drew to a close on Thursday, quiet murmurs of resolve and skepticism lingered in the hallways.

For many tribal residents, the words spoken by government officials offered a glimmer of hope, yet familiar doubts quickly crept back in — leaving a fractured community to wonder whether real, lasting change is on the horizon or if these hearings were simply the latest chapter in a long cycle of endless conversations.

title: Mary Mitchell
description: August 2, 1940 - August 26, 2026
_full_text:
August 2, 1940 - August 26, 2026

Mary Ellen Mitchell, 86, of Rapid City, South Dakota, passed away on August 26, 2026, in Rapid City after a long battle with Alzheimer's disease. She was born on August 2, 1940, in Faulkton, South Dakota.

Mary built a life centered on faith, family, and service to others. She earned an associate degree in Elementary Education from Northern State Teachers College in 1960 and went on to teach fourth grade in Fort Pierre, South Dakota. While she valued her work as an educator, most of her life was devoted to raising her six children and helping care for her beloved grandchildren. That devotion remained one of the defining gifts of her life.

She was a deeply family-focused woman whose proudest accomplishments included raising her six children, helping to raise her 14 grandchildren, and sharing 65 years of marriage with her husband, Jerry. To those who knew her best, Mary was the moral compass of her family. Sunday Mass was a constant in her home and in her life, and her faith guided not only her own path but also the lives of those around her. Even while traveling, that devotion never wavered. Alongside her strong convictions, she was remembered for a wonderful sense of humor and a joyful laugh that brought warmth to family gatherings and everyday moments alike. Mary loved all children, and her many grandchildren were a lasting source of happiness and pride.

Her days were also filled with many interests and acts of generosity. Mary was an avid bowler and spent many years in the Wednesday morning women's league with the Halo Hangers team. Later in life, she took up golfing and joined both a women's league and a couples league. She enjoyed reading, sewing, and walking with her friend group. She gave her time freely, volunteering for her children's and grandchildren's many activities and becoming a dedicated presence in causes and organizations that mattered deeply to her. She was very active in right to life and Birthright organizations, as well as the Catholic Daughters, where she received numerous awards for her work. At her local Catholic church, she served faithfully by teaching religious education classes, baking for funeral dinners, and working with the Dusting Angels cleaning crew. In every role, Mary offered steady care, quiet strength, and a willing heart.

She is survived by her husband, Jerry Mitchell; her children, Linda and Roger Williams, Ron and Tonya Mitchell, Dale and Nancy Mitchell, Susan and Brian Wiedmeier, Brian Mitchell, and Mark and Tara Mitchell; her brother, Terry Myers, and sister-in-law, Lucila Myers; her sisters, Kathy Rea and Karen Eissinger; and her brother-in-law, Ron Jeitz. She leaves behind a family shaped by her example, strengthened by her faith, and blessed by her enduring love.

She was preceded in death by her parents, Florence and Leo Myers; her sister, Jean Jeitz; and her granddaughter, Romy Mitchell. Their memories remained part of her life and of the family story she cherished so dearly.

A visitation will be held on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, from 6:00 to 7:00 p.m. at St. Therese Catholic Church, 532 Adams Street, Rapid City, South Dakota, followed by a Wake Service at 7:00 p.m. A Mass will be celebrated on Wednesday, September 2, 2026, at 10:30 a.m. at St. Therese Catholic Church. A luncheon will follow at the church from 11:45 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. Burial will take place that afternoon from 2:30 to 3:00 p.m. at Black Hills National Cemetery, 20901 Pleasant Valley Drive, Sturgis, South Dakota.

Mary Ellen Mitchell's life was one of steadfast love, faithful service, and joyful devotion to the people entrusted to her care. She will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered.

Her online guestbook is available at www.osheimschmidt.com.
