title: Rapid City officials drafting ordinance barring hyperscale data centers
description: Rapid City’s mayor and city officials are looking at an ordinance that would give city officials oversight of future data centers.
_full_text:
Rapid City’s mayor and city officials are looking at an ordinance that would give city officials oversight of future data centers.

"It's very reasonable and responsible, and it's better than what we have right now, which is not much of anything," Mayor Jason Salamun told the Journal on Aug. 25.

This comes after Salamun took to Facebook on April 20, stating that city staff is working on an ordinance requiring a Conditional Use Permit for data centers. Now the ordinance is nearly ready to be sent to city government for approval.

If the ordinance is approved, this would give the city the ability to hold hearings, demand studies and attach conditions.

Currently, the city has little oversight in the approval process for data centers.

 Salamun
Mayor Jason Salamun, right, during a 2026 Rapid City Council meeting. At left is Councilman Stephen Tamang. 

Per previous reporting, Rapid City Community Development Director Vicki Fisher said after Sequitor Edge's February announcement about its data center, the next step for a center’s development plans would be the approval of a building permit. Fisher said no action is needed by the Planning Commission or by the City Council, because building permits are administratively approved by the City's Building Officials after review by the City's Development Review Team.

Now, after months of planning, research and discussions with council members, an ordinance is being drafted to give the city oversight of such developments.

"The basic framework of what's going to be proposed is this: hyperscale data centers will be prohibited,” Salamun said.

He explained that hyperscale centers would be defined as centers with a peak power demand of 50 megawatts or more and using more than 10,000 gallons of water per day.

“Number two, the proposal says that a large-scale data center will need to have a conditional use permit, and we define that as a data center with a peak demand of more than 10 megawatts and less than 50 megawatts of power, with a maximum of 10,000 gallons of water per day, exclusive to the initial fill," Salamun said.

Salamun said a micro data center would be defined as, “a facility that will have a peak demand of a maximum of up to 10 megawatts of power, but no more than 4,000 gallons of water per day, exclusive to the initial fill."

The initial submission for the city government's approval process starts at the Planning Commission’s Sept. 10 meeting. Details of the ordinance are subject to change. But Salamun said he is looking to give the city oversight for future approval processes.

"It's still being edited, so I always hate to get information out that's going to be changed. But I think, from what I understand, at least those three categories are pretty solid," Salamun said of the size definitions of data centers.

Salamun said he has looked at other communities' ordinances addressing the data center review process.

Fisher told the Journal the other communities they looked into for data centers included Cheyenne, Wyoming, Fairfax County, Virginia, Frisco, Texas, and San Jose, California.

 Vicki Fisher
Community Development Director Vicki Fisher 

"Data centers … are ever evolving. What we knew two years ago is not what we know today, and what we know today is what we won't know two years from now. Things keep changing, but I think putting the guardrails in place helps us ensure that things that are done here in our community are done openly and fairly to all parties," Salamun said.

Sequitor Edge's data center will be located at the Black Hills Industrial Center, located south of Old Folsom Road and east of Highway 79.

Fisher told the Journal the city has not yet received a building permit or any updates for the Sequitor Edge data center.

"Depending upon the water and electric usage, the Sequitor Edge data center may require a Conditional Use Permit. However, the proposed ordinance proposes to allow a micro-data center with a peak demand of 10 megawatts and no more than 4,000 gallons of water per day as a permitted use. Strict compliance standards are being proposed for permitted and conditional data centers," Fisher said on future actions of the approval process.

 Data Center
A map shows where the Sequitor Edge data center will be located within the Black Hills Industrial Center.  

Victoria Blatchford, vice president of business development for Sequitor Edge's Great Plains operation, said on Feb. 11, the facility will use 2 megawatts initially, with a maximum of 10 megawatts. The facility would be closed loop, with a one-time use of around 20,000 gallons of water to fill its cooling pool.

A study by the International Energy Agency estimated a 100-megawatt U.S. data center would consume roughly the same amount of water as 2,600 households, accounting only for direct water consumption and averaged across the various cooling strategies, according to the service report.

According to a release from Elevate Rapid City, Sequitor Edge, “will support industries that depend on secure, fast, and reliable data processing, including advanced manufacturing, healthcare, defense-related industries, financial services, and other technology-enabled operations."

According to Darrell Shoemaker, the city's Public Information officer, after the possible approval of the ordinance, it would then head to Legal and Finance Committee on Sept. 16 and then would require two readings by the City Council.

title: A few chickens and a duck: 4-H poultry show at fair holds on, participants see value in feathered friends
description: There certainly weren’t flocks of chickens at the Central States Fair on Thursday, Aug. 27, but that didn’t stop a few 4-H kids from putting in the effort to show their poultry, or from a dedicated judge from taking the opportunity to impart kernels of her decades of wisdom on young chicken (and duck) tenders.
_full_text:
There certainly weren’t flocks of chickens at the Central States Fair on Thursday, Aug. 27, but that didn’t stop a few 4-H kids from putting in the effort to show their poultry, or from a dedicated judge from taking the opportunity to impart kernels of her decades of wisdom on young chicken (and duck) tenders.

“It's a good way for kids in 4-H or kids in general to learn responsibility. They have to feed those hens. They have to go out and get the eggs. Very good. And it gives them confidence when they get up in front of other kids,” said poultry judge Barb Uhrig.

“I’m an excellent judge. Go get your chicken,” the judge with 60 years of experience clucked to one participant in the time between egg judging and chicken judging.

 Barb Uhrig
Barb Uhrig, a poultry judge, carefully looks over eggs on Thursday, Aug. 27 during the 4-H poultry show at the Central States Fair. 

During judging, Uhrig took the time to speak directly with each child, asking them about the different parts of their chickens, and giving them tips on how to improve their showmanship as she encouraged them to come back next year.

“I look at the comb size, the ears, the waddles, the beak, the breastbone, the wings, the back, the legs, the tail — everything has to be characteristic of that breed,” Uhrig explained.

Jesse Rieb, whose 15-year-old daughter Payton Rieb showed three chickens and a duck, shared that same sentiment. He said 4-H has helped Payton become comfortable speaking in front of people. She started showing chickens when she was 5 years old.

“She was so shy. She would stand with her head down, and once she started doing this, she blossomed,” Rieb said.

 Payton Rieb
Payton Rieb holds a hen on Thursday, Aug. 27 during the 4-H poultry show at the Central States Fair. Rieb has shown chickens since she was 5 years old. 

Payton was one of three youth to show poultry on Thursday. She was the only participant in the senior category. Two participated in the beginner category, Oakley Keffler and Asher Grimmett. Payton and Oakley also showed eggs.

“This is the first year in three years it's been not only me,” Payton said. “I guess kids don't want to do it anymore.”

 Asher Grimmett
Asher Grimmett, reserve champion in the beginner category, shows his chicken on Thursday, Aug. 27 during the 4-H poultry show at the Central States Fair. 

Uhrig, who judges in other counties as well, said participation depends on the area.

“It depends on location because different counties, there might be more rural kids. Lawrence County has a lot of rural kids. Their show was 120 birds, and tons of kids. And Meade County was probably what 50 birds, 60 birds,” she said.

But Rapid City’s recently-passed backyard chicken ordinance, which allows for those within city limits to own up to six hens, could potentially change poultry participation.

“We hope that will help a lot,” said SDSU Extension Pennington County 4-H Educator Kimberly Suckow. “We have a family that helped fight for that, and I know that they will have poultry then and be able to show it. That (the previous restriction) really does limit us because a lot of our kids are inside city limits.”

Rieb added it’s a misconception that 4-H is just for rural kids.

“I don't think people understand that 4-H ain't just for ranch kids. Like they have shooting, archery. You can be cooking, gardening.”

Another factor that contributes to lower poultry, and rabbit, show participation is the closure of the fair’s poultry and rabbit barns, Suckow said.

“I’ve seen it really decline since Central States Fair shut down their barns,” she said.

 Oakley Keffler
Oakley Keffler shows a hen on Thursday, Aug. 27 during the 4-H poultry show at the Central States Fair. Keffler won champion in the beginner category. 

Central States Fair General Manager Ron Jeffries couldn’t remember exactly when the fair closed its rabbit and poultry barns, but it’s been about a decade.

“Well, the bird flu is what stopped it, and we just didn't revive it,” Jeffries said of the poultry barn. As for the rabbit barn, Jeffries said it was shut down because the fair wasn’t doing a rabbit show anymore and it was mostly displays.

“They still do it on the 4-H side, and we encourage everybody to participate and have their kids participate there. But we don't do it on the on the fair side,” Jeffries said.

Jeffries added there are still rabbits and baby chicks at the fair. Rabbits are at the petting zoo in the red barn, and chicks are located in the Ag Adventure Zone in the GenPro Energy Pavilion.

“It's (chickens) not a display anymore. It's part of the educational program,” Jeffries said. “It's work and effort and energy to do a display, and I can incorporate that (rabbits) into an animal nursery and say, ‘Hey, here's something for you to come see all kinds of animals.’”

The poultry and rabbit barns are currently used as storage. Although there’s not currently any plans to revive the buildings, Jeffries said, “We're not opposed (or) saying, ‘Hey we hate chickens,’ or anything like that. Chickens or rabbits. But you just gotta have the right circumstances to get enough people involved and do a show.”

 Photos from the 4-H poultry show at Central States Fair
Pennington County 4-H held a poultry show on Thursday, Aug. 26. Here’s some photos of the feathery friends, their eggs, tenders and judge.

title: Mushroom seller launches Black Hills Producers Market after his ouster from Black Hills Farmers Market
description: A vendor kicked out of the Black Hills Farmers Market has launched a new farmers market that will open this weekend in Rapid City.
_full_text:
A vendor kicked out of the Black Hills Farmers Market has launched a new farmers market that will open this weekend in Rapid City.

Black Hills Producers Market will hold its first market day on Saturday, Aug. 29, from 3 to 7 p.m., at 721 Mount Rushmore Road in the parking lot of the Bob’s 66 gas station. The market’s founder, Alan Carner, confirmed that at least five vendors will be there.

“We're starting a new weekly farmers market in the Black Hills, and we're looking for local people who want to build it together. Farmers, ranchers, produce growers, food businesses, makers, small businesses, nonprofits, and community organizations are all welcome,” Carner stated last week on the Black Hills Producers Market’s Facebook page.  

 082926-nws-farmers-market-Carner
Alan Carner, owner of Black Hills Mushrooms, has launched Black Hills Producers Market, a new farmers and producers market in Rapid City. 

Carner owns Black Hills Mushrooms, an urban mushroom farm in Rapid City that “sells gourmet mushrooms and forages certified wild mushrooms in the surrounding Black Hills,” according to blackhillsmushrooms.com.

In a post, Carner further described his goal for Black Hills Producers Market as “something that works for the people actually participating in it. We want open and transparent communication from the beginning, with vendors having a voice in how the market develops. We're looking for founding vendors who want to help decide what days, locations, rules, and structure make the most sense.”

“I would love to see my neighbor come down to the market if they have an excess load of produce, be able to distribute that produce,” Carner told the Journal, noting he wants Black Hills Producers Market to focus on local foods and locally produced items.

Carner said local individuals and business owners have contacted him to express interest in Black Hills Producers Market. Some, like Carner, are also frustrated with Rapid City’s longstanding Black Hills Farmers Market, he said.

 Black Hills Producers Market
Scott and Amanda Sellers of Rapid City and their daughters Aurora, 8 months, and Ruth, 4, paint signs for the new Black Hills Producers Market on Friday, Aug. 21 at Rapid City Public Library. The family owns Good Ground Living, growing and selling pesticide-free organic produce. They hope to have enough produce to become vendors at Black Hills Producers Market next year. Black Hills Producers Market founder Alan Carner invited artists and potential vendors to gather and make signs for the market, which will have its first day in operation on Saturday, Aug. 29. 

“We want to build this community around an open market,” Carner said, saying he wanted to launch Black Hills Producers Market without “creating issues with other existing markets.”

Carner is seeking vendors for Black Hills Producers Market, taking suggestions and input, and promoting Black Hills Producers Market through its Facebook page, its Facebook group and its What’s App chat. Carner can also be reached by email at blackhillsproducersmarket@gmail.com. He invites the community to view a proposal for the Black Hills Producers Market posted on Facebook and make suggestions.

Farmers market kerfuffle

Carner’s business, Black Hills Mushrooms, began in 2018. He had been a vendor at Black Hills Farmers Market, but his membership there was revoked this month. Carner publicly announced the loss of his membership on social media on Aug. 20. He reposted a letter, dated Aug. 19, he received from Black Hills Farmers Market telling him his membership was revoked. Carner said he has made a formal appeal via email to the Black Hills Farmers Market Board of Directors.

“Black Hills Mushrooms had been part of the Black Hills Farmers Market since 2019. We’ve had a disagreement with market management over scheduling and communication,” Carner told the Journal last week.

 Black Hills Producers Market
Signs handmade by local vendors and artists for use at the Black Hills Producers Market. 

“On Aug. 19, they sent me a letter revoking my membership and ability to sell at the market. The letter says it identified multiple violations of rules and communication policies and code of conduct but it doesn’t actually identify those violations. I believe I (should) have the opportunity to know exactly what I’m accused of or what I supposedly violated,” he said.

The letter mentions an Aug. 18 special meeting of the market’s board. It notes on Aug. 5 Carner asked to be removed from future Black Hills Farmers Market days. The board approved the request on Aug. 11, and then that same day Carner asked to be added back to the schedule, the board said in the letter.

“In the days that followed your August 11, 2026 request to be added back to all future BHFM market days, the Board identified multiple instances where you violated the BHFM Rules and Regulations, Communication Policy, and Code of Conduct,” the board said in the letter. “Further review by the board identified additional communication issues beyond this instance.”

In an Aug. 23 email to the Journal, Black Hills Farmers Market Board President Heather Maude, speaking on behalf of herself and the Board of Directors, said they could not publicly share communication between the board and a vendor. Maude answered questions from the Journal after consulting with the full board.

 Black Hills Farmer's Market
During the winter months, the Black Hills Farmers Market is open 9 a.m. to noon on Saturdays. 

Though Maude would not address specific infractions committed by Carner, she said, “The issues were communication-related, and there was communication that was found to be in violation of the rules and the communication policy, and that was all included in the letter that was provided to Alan.”

“The incident and timeframe of communication the board reviewed was included in the letter to Alan, as was a notation that the board also took time to review additional communication between Alan and board members and/or BHFM employees,” Maude said. “In the instance of Black Hills Mushrooms, the board determined the communication in question was in violation of rules and policies, which then required the board to establish a penalty in response to the infraction. The BHFM Board’s decision was to revoke membership and privilege to sell at BHFM.”

Maude did not disclose the nature of the communication between Carner and the market that was deemed an infraction. Carner told the Journal he believed the conflict with BHFM involved his requests for schedule changes.

In a Friday, Aug. 28, social media post, Carner said he filed a formal complaint about communication and other concerns ahead of his removal. He also said he’s heard no response on his appeal seven days after filing it.

Revoked memberships are rare

Hundreds of vendors have participated in the Black Hills Farmers Market since it began in 1989. Personal and professional changes in vendors’ lives often contribute to vendor turnover, Maude said. Only three vendors have had their memberships revoked because of violating the market’s rules and regulations, and those all have occurred in the past 11 years, Maude said.

“This is abnormal,” Maude said. “One (revoked membership) was a sexual harassment issue, (Carner’s) was a communication issue, and one was in violation of what they were allowed to sell. These are really rare. … Those three issues have occurred while several hundred vendors have had no issues.”

 Black Hills Farmer's Market
The Black Hills Farmers Market operates in Market Park in Rapid City. 

Black Hills Farmers Market is a vetted market, meaning individuals and businesses that want to be vendors must apply and be approved to sell at the market, Maude said. Maude and the board said Black Hills Farmers Market allows anyone to sell produce at the market if vendors meet general requirements to sell there, including having insurance and a sales tax identification number.

Approved vendors can communicate with the Black Hills Farmers Market board by following guidelines listed on blackhillsfarmersmarket.org. Additionally, Black Hills Farmers Market sent a survey to vendors and customers in fall 2025 seeking feedback about how to improve the market for vendors, and to see what new products customers would like, Maude said. The board plans to survey vendors and customers again this fall.

Black Hills Farmers Market currently has more than 60 approved vendors, and in the past year it has nearly doubled its number of active vendors, Maude and the board of directors said. Booth spaces are currently full for upcoming Saturday markets.

Maude said Black Hills Farmers Market’s goal is to provide as much variety as possible in products offered, always allowing room for additional produce vendors. Preference is given to local, home-raised and homemade food products and products that are complementary to growing, cooking and consuming food. The market board of directors always ensures there is room for additional produce.

“The market manager is always willing to visit with potential new vendors, especially those wanting to sell produce,” the email said.

title: Iann S Collins
description: March 12, 1943 - August 20, 2026
_full_text:
March 12, 1943 - August 20, 2026

Iann S. Collins, age 83, of Spearfish, South Dakota, passed away Thursday, August 20, 2026, at Monument Health Hospice, Rapid City surrounded by the quiet strength and grace that defined her life.

A private burial will take place in the Faulkton Cemetery.

Iann Schreiner Collins, was born in 1943 at Faulk County Memorial Hospital, she grew up ten miles west of town on her family's dairy farm, the youngest of four children. Her parents instilled simple but enduring values - be good and do good - principles she carried faithfully throughout her life.

A bright student, Iann attended Latham rural school, skipping the second grade, and graduated from Faulkton High School in 1960. Unsure of her path, she enrolled at Northwest College of Business in Huron, later beginning a long career in administrative and payroll work.

Iann married in 1967 and became the devoted mother of three sons. She worked steadily outside the home, serving utility companies, gold mines, and eventually spending twenty years working for Doug Lueder at Lueders Food Centers and his modular home dealership—handling payroll with her trademark reliability and precision.

Her greatest pride was her family. Her eldest son, Andrew, retired from the DEA and the Navy Reserves as an Admiral. His wife, Andrea, works at Rapid City Christian School; their daughter Lily will attend BHSU this fall, and their son Jack attends Central High School. Her second son, Nick, retired from the U.S. Forest Service after years supervising a Hotshot crew; he and his wife Becky share a love of the outdoors and their French Bulldog, Gin. Her youngest son, Joe, owns his own professional home inspection company near Seattle.

In 2021, Iann suffered a fall that led to a diagnosis of Primary Lateral Sclerosis. Though the disease gradually took her voice, it never dimmed her spirit. She embraced a quieter world with courage, positivity, and deep attentiveness, becoming - by her own words - "a great listener" to her wonderful friends at Saint Martin Village in Rapid City.

Iann is survived by her beloved sons, daughters in law, grandchildren, and extended family. She will be remembered for her resilience, her work ethic, her gentle humor, and her unwavering devotion to those she loved.

Luce Funeral Home of Faulkton has been entrusted with Iann's arrangements. (www.luceluzereck.com)

title: Authorities release name of Summerset man killed in Black Hawk motorcycle crash
description: Authorities have released the name of a Summerset man who died in a Wednesday, Aug. 26, single-motorcycle crash near Black Hawk.
_full_text:
Authorities have released the name of a Summerset man who died in a Wednesday, Aug. 26, single-motorcycle crash near Black Hawk.

Francis M. Bierman, 44, died in the crash, the South Dakota Highway Patrol said in a Saturday, Aug. 29, press release.

Bierman was riding a 2010 Triumph motorcycle westbound on Erikson Ranch Road near the Escape Lane intersection when he laid the motorcycle down after the curve, left the roadway and separated from the motorcycle. The patrol did not say what caused him to lay the bike down.

The crash occurred around 7:08 a.m. about 1 mile northwest of Black Hawk, according to the patrol.

Bierman sustained fatal injuries. He was wearing a helmet, the patrol said.

An investigation into the crash continues.

title: Motorcyclist stopping in Sturgis to raise awareness about kids with hemophilia
description: Richard Williams is traveling through the Black Hills this weekend to save children.
_full_text:
Richard Williams is traveling through the Black Hills this weekend to save children.

Williams, 75, will be in Sturgis on Saturday, Aug. 29, and Sunday, Aug. 30, as part of Save One Life's Wheels for the World campaign. Williams will visit the Sturgis Motorcycle Museum and Hall of Fame during his time in Sturgis. He’ll also stop in Oacoma on Sunday, Aug. 31.

Wheels for the World is a cross-country fundraising journey supporting children living with hemophilia and other bleeding disorders in developing countries.  

Williams began his journey from his hometown of Billings, Mont., and he will be riding vintage 1980 Honda Gold Wing motorcycle nearly 5,000 miles through more than a dozen states for Wheels for the World. He’ll end his trip in Maine.

For Williams, this journey is deeply personal. Doctors once told Williams his son, Trevor, might not live past age 18. Williams and his family suffered a devastating loss years ago when one of his twin sons died before birth due to uncontrolled bleeding. The surviving twin, Trevor, was diagnosed at age 5 with severe Hemophilia A.  

 082926-nws-WheelsfortheWorld
Richard Williams, 75, of Billings, Montana, will stop in Sturgis Aug. 29 and 30 as part of a cross-country journey for Wheels for the World, which raises funds and awareness to help children with hemophilia. 

To keep his son alive, Williams spent decades navigating insurance challenges and changing jobs in order to ensure Trevor had uninterrupted insurance access to the life-saving medications he needed. Today, Trevor is 37 years old and thriving because that treatment was available.

However, in countries with limited healthcare resources, children with hemophilia often go undiagnosed, untreated, and face preventable disability or death from bleeding episodes that would be manageable in the United States.

Williams’ ride across the United States aims to raise awareness and support for those children through Save One Life, an international nonprofit serving families affected by bleeding disorders in resource-limited countries.

“Our family’s experience was extremely difficult, but with a lot of education, treatment, and patience, we found a way. I can only imagine how hard it must be for parents in countries where those same options aren’t available for their children. Your chances of surviving hemophilia shouldn’t depend on what country you were born in, which is why raising awareness through Wheels for the World is so important,” Williams said in a press release from Save One Life.

For more information or to support Williams’ ride, go to https://runsignup.com/Race/107621/Donate/Nf98m0lhaHlKVfX5

title: Gerry Ray Feddersen
description: September 5, 1951 - July 25, 2026
_full_text:
September 5, 1951 - July 25, 2026

Gerry Ray Feddersen, 74, passed away on Tuesday, July 25th at his home in Vivian, S.D. A remembrance of life will be held on Saturday, September 5th at 11 a.m. CDT at Isburg Funeral Chapel in Pierre with a visitation with family and refreshments one hour prior to the service.

Gerry was born on September 5th, 1951 to Herman and Ada (Stotts) Feddersen at the Kadoka Memorial Hospital in Kadoka, S.D. He attended school in Wasta, S.D., Arkansas, Valentine, Neb., and in 1964 the family settled in Keystone, S.D. He attended school until the 8th grade in Keystone before graduating from high school in Hill City, S.D. in 1969.

After graduation he had summer jobs in the Keystone area before he was hired to a road construction crew. While working road construction he helped build the Keystone Wye on Hwy 16A and the I90 interstate east of Murdo.

Gerry met his wife Bonnie Heil while working in Keystone and they were married on July 27, 1974. Their marriage was full of travel and adventures. They made their home in Alaska, Montana and California. While they lived in Alaska, he worked on the Alaskan Pipeline and was a hunting guide, this is also where he and Bonnie welcomed their son Jess. While living in Montana and California he entered the world of retail construction and was involved with the building of 100's of Starbucks. He was the superintendent of construction and was involved from start to finish overseeing the jobs.

In 2016 Gerry and Bonnie retired and moved home to South Dakota where they settled in Vivian. After 51 years of marriage Gerry lost Bonnie on March 10th, 2026.

Gerry is survived by his son, Jess (Keeley) of Long Beach, Calif.; brother, Lonnie of Hill City, S.D.; sisters, Karla (Mike) Rohde of Rockerville, S.D., Linda (Doug) Perry of Presho, S.D. and Ronda Hunter of Gillette, Wyo. He is also survived by sisters-in-laws, Karen (Clint) Kobly of California, Cheryl (Dave) Potts of Rapid City, S.D., Darla (Bob) Heil of Bishop, Calif.

He was preceded in death by his wife, Bonnie; his parents; infant brother, Herman; his sister, Galene Meza; brother-in-law, Dale Hunter; and sister-in-law, Patty Feddersen.

In lieu of flowers the family requests memories of Gerry and Bonnie be sent to P.O. Box 124, Vivian, SD 57576.

title: Terry Howard Fiero
description: April 20, 1946 - August 24, 2026
_full_text:
April 20, 1946 - August 24, 2026

Terry H. Fiero, a longtime Newark resident, died on August 24, 2026 at age 80. He was active until the last days of his life, loving his family and living life to the fullest.

Terry was born April 20, 1946 in Ontario, Oregon to Bailey and Kathryn (Lale) Fiero. His mother married Nicholas Evans in February 1949 following the death of his father in November 1947. He attended grade and high schools in North Dakota, Montana, and South Dakota, graduating from Rapid City High School (South Dakota) in 1964. He married his high school sweetheart Pamela Steinmetz at Blessed Sacrament Catholic Church in Rapid City. Together, they raised two beloved daughters, Christina (Tina) and Tracy.

Terry attended Colorado State University (Fort Collins) and the South Dakota School of Mines and Technology (Rapid City), graduating with a Bachelor of Science degree in Chemical Engineering in June 1970. He was a member of the Triangle Fraternity, the only social fraternity exclusively for men majoring in engineering, architecture, and the sciences. While at the Mines, he was also a member of the university choral group, the Singing Engineers. One of his proudest awards was the "Raben" Lifetime Achievement Award given by the RCHS Class of 1964.

After graduation, they moved to Midland, MI with their family to start his 28-year career with the Dow Chemical Company in 1970. They transferred to Newark, Ohio in 1984. While at Dow, he held a number of senior technical and business leadership positions in six technology areas that included specialty chemicals, plastics, and fabricated products. He was the inventor/co-inventor on three U.S. patents for paints and coatings materials, food additives, and fabricated products, and was involved in many professional organizations throughout his career. He retired from Dow Chemical in 1998. He then joined Renaissance Worldwide in Columbus, OH, where he was a Senior Business Management Consultant until 2001. In 2002, he was named the President and Chief Operating Officer for BizCarta Inc., a professional services company in Columbus, Ohio specializing in strategic planning, business processes, and information technology. There, he developed the proprietary ADEPT6SM business processes that were used to deliver these professional services. He retired from BizCarta in 2008.

Terry was preceded in death by his parents, Bailey and Kathryn; and stepfather, Nicholas Evans.

He is survived by his wife, Pam; two daughters, Christina (Tom) Gwynn and Tracy (Ron) Byerly; grandsons, Brandon and Ryan Byerly; sister, Pamela Evans Ph.D.; and brothers, William Evans and Dr. Duane Evans.

Visitation will be held at Reed-Egan Funeral Home, 141 Green Wave Drive, Newark, 4-7 P.M., Wednesday, September 2, 2026, with a Vigil Service held at 6:30 P.M. title: Staff cuts discussed at emotionally-charged Rapid City Council budget meeting
description: The Rapid City Council made substantial changes to the mayor's $312.33 million proposed 2027 budget, including reducing council contingency funds, decreasing the mayor's office budget by $100,000 and increasing compensation for Rapid Transit System drivers.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Council made substantial changes to the mayor's $312.33 million proposed 2027 budget, including reducing council contingency funds, decreasing the mayor's office budget by $100,000 and increasing compensation for Rapid Transit System drivers.

In July, Mayor Jason Salamun presented his proposed budget to the Rapid City Council, which featured a 7.4% reduction compared to 2026 ($337.3 million), investments in roads and the sports complex, an increase for firefighter and ambulance personnel, and updates to parks, including Main Street Square.

The changes were discussed during a special meeting on Wednesday, Aug. 26. The council is holding meetings to discuss and revise the budget before the state’s Sept. 30 deadline.

Councilors question Mayor’s Office positions

In the most-discussed item of the night, Councilman Greg Strommen (Ward 3) moved to cut the Mayor's Office employment budget by $200,000, specifically the chief of staff position held by Leah Braun and the communications and marketing position held by Bret Mattice. The proposed Mayor’s Office budget is $890,619, a decrease of 24.5% compared to 2026’s budget of $1,179,506.

Strommen said he has been asked by other council members and constituents about the pay for the two staff positions, as people are unclear about their duties and their contributions to the city.

"I look at our chief of staff's salary, right around $132,000 (a year), that's more than what the lieutenant governor of South Dakota (Tony Venhuizen) makes, which is $129,000. The governor of South Dakota (Larry Rhoden) only makes $148,000,” Strommen said.

 City council
Councilman Greg Strommen (Ward 3) motioned to cut two staff positions within the Mayor's Office that sparked lengthy discussion during a Wednesday, Aug. 26, special Rapid City Council meeting. 

According to South Dakota public records, Venhuizen makes $128,969 per year, while Rhoden makes $148,522 and has his housing provided.

"I think we have enough people that are doing publicity and public information … I don't think that it's providing the same value to the city as what the salary is," Strommen said, explaining his reasoning.

Councilman Josh Biberdorf (Ward 1) said he did not support the cut to the chief of staff, noting she had done a great job coordinating services for the city.

"As chief of staff, you're human beings, not human doing. So, to slash this right out of the blue is something I'm definitely not supportive of," Biberdorf said.

 Leah Braun
Leah Braun 

Councilwoman Laura Armstrong replied, "In response to my colleague, Mr. Biberdorf, we're not a business. We're a municipality, and we have to be very responsible with taxpayer dollars. I think what we're doing here tonight, we're taking very seriously."

Armstrong said the position did not exist within the mayor's office prior to Salamun's appointment as mayor in 2023. Councilman Kevin Maher (Ward 3) said the mayor needs the support of a chief of staff to properly manage day-to-day operations and work with other entities in the city.

Strommen fired back, saying, "I don't think all the publicity is that important. I don't think that's important for the mayor and the chief of staff and the marketing position. Which I don't even know why the city even has a marketing (position) because as Councilwoman Armstrong said, we’re a municipality, we are not a private business that's marketing anything."

Strommen said the city already works with Visit Rapid City and Elevate Rapid City for marketing needs.

Biberdorf responded, saying, "I would hope we're marketing our city when our biggest asset and revenue generator is sales tax. Whether you call it a municipality or a business, everybody wants to run their municipality like a business... I sure hope we take marketing in this town seriously, or why build a sports complex cause nobody is going to come."

 Josh Biberdorf
Councilman Josh Biberdorf (Ward 1) defended the chief of staff and marketing positions within the Mayor's Office. 

Rapid City Finance Director Daniel Ainslie clarified that the chief of staff position has been included in the city budget since 2023, with responsibilities that include coordinating with the 12 city departments, the City Council and community groups, as well as fielding community concerns. Braun has been acting as chief of staff since April 2025.

Strommen again rebutted, saying the chief of staff doesn't need to be handling conflicts between the various departments.

"I don't think the chief of staff needs to get in there and try to mediate conflict between them; that's what the mayor is elected to do. He's supposed to be running the city," Strommen said.

The back-and-forth among council members reached a point where Dr. Stephen Tamang (Ward 1) reminded the council to refrain from making emotionally-charged statements that may offend city employees.

"I sense there (are) emotions that are brewing here, so I just want, as a friendly reminder, not directed at anyone, that we will maintain professionalism tonight,” Tamang said.

Councilwoman Lindsey Seachris (Ward 2) alternatively motioned to reduce the Mayor's Office budget by $100,000 and cautioned against personal attacks.

Before voting, Tamang said Braun was one of the finest executives he's worked with and Mattice is one of the most technically gifted in his role as well. The substitute motion was approved 6-4 with Maher, Councilwoman Callie Meyer (Ward 5), Tamang and Biberdorf voting no.

Salamun, Braun and Mattice did not address the topic with the council during the meeting.

"The City Council has the authority to set the city’s budget. I respect that process," Salamun told the Journal when asked about the discussion of cutting his office’s budget.

"A budget hearing is the right place to debate spending. It is not the place to take cheap shots at members of our team. You can disagree with a budget without tearing down the people who serve our city,” Salamun said. “The disrespect shown to our chief of staff crossed the line. She is a dedicated public servant doing the job this council previously approved, and the city is better for it. The same is true of the rest of this office. Our team deserves the same respect we expect for every other public servant.”

The mayor concluded by saying he will wait until the budget approval process is complete before determining any further actions.

America 251

Another lengthy topic of the night was defunding the 2027 Independence Day celebration budget, with the council reducing it from $500,000 to $100,000.

Ainslie said the budget item was originally listed at $500,000 — a mistake, because it should have been $250,000, the same as the 2026 budget for the U.S. celebration of America 250.

The year prior, 2025, the fireworks budget was set at $30,000, according to Mattice.

Biberdorf disagreed with the motion, saying, “There are very few things … where somebody calls you and gives you an 'attaboy' and gives you more than one 'attaboy’… lots of ‘attaboys’ for the work that was done for the celebration.”

 City council
The Rapid City Council held a special budget meeting on Wednesday, Aug. 26. The council made a number of changes to the mayor's proposed FY2027 budget. 

He said the cost of the Fourth of July celebration is small, given the success it brought to the city, noting that even people from both political spectrums agreed it was a positive experience for the community.

Councilman Bill Evans (Ward 2) said he agreed with Biberdorf.

Roberts said next year's celebration will not be as big because this was the 250th anniversary milestone of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. He said he agreed it could be worth raising money in other ways to give a smaller-scale celebration to the community. Roberts suggested the money be raised from the private sector.

The changes were approved 8-2, with Maher and Biberdorf voting no.

Cut to council contingency fund

The first action the council took was a recommendation by Armstrong to reduce the council contingency fund to $100,000. This is a $700,000 reduction in their total contingency fund for the use of undesignated cash. According to Mattice, the 2027 budget included an $800,000 council contingency fund.

Armstrong’s motion was approved 9-1, with Seachris voting no. Seachris said she voted against the change because she preferred that the funds go to a specific place and preferred a reduction to $200,000.

Seachris then requested adding a new position for the Community Development Department, for an additional planner and code enforcement officer, using the contingency funds the council removed. Tamang said the position would cost an estimated $93,443. The council approved the motion 10-0.

Councilman John Roberts (Ward 4) requested a new planner be added to the Community Development Department. Ainslie said creating this position would cost an estimated $145,946, including salary and benefits. The council approved the motion 10-0.

Also at the meeting, Strommen motioned to increase the Canyon Lake Activity Center and the Minneluzahan Senior Center budgets by $50,000 each. This was approved 9-1, with Seachris voting no.

Armstrong, who voted “yes” on the increase, previously served a one-year contract position as the Minneluzahan Senior Center Executive Director. That position ended in June 2026.

According to the mayor's proposed budget, the activity center and senior center were each set to receive $20,250.

Meyer moved to add $182,523 from undesignated funds to enhance Rapid Transit System driver compensation. This was approved with no opposition.

Mattice said the average hourly wage for RTS drivers is $23.18, and the approved changes would increase the rate by 9%.

The council also approved an additional $124,000 to fully fund four new employees, to be shared between the parks department and The Monument.

The council voted to approve $120,000 for the parks department for professional services and $7,423 for emergency planning.

title: Rapid City hosting session on housing, infrastructure, development
description: The City of Rapid City’s Community Enrichment Division will host a public meeting next week discussing housing and community development priorities.
_full_text:
The City of Rapid City’s Community Enrichment Division will host a public meeting next week discussing housing and community development priorities.

title: Rotary-supported literacy initiative for Native children launches in Rapid City and Pine Ridge Reservation
description: A new culturally grounded literacy initiative, Friends of the Children – He Sapa, is helping Native children in Rapid City and on the Pine Ridge Reservation strengthen their reading skills while connecting learning with Indigenous culture, identity and storytelling.
_full_text:
A new culturally grounded literacy initiative, Friends of the Children – He Sapa, is helping Native children in Rapid City and on the Pine Ridge Reservation strengthen their reading skills while connecting learning with Indigenous culture, identity and storytelling.

“At Friends of the Children – He Sapa, we believe that schools and caregivers should be equal partners in their child’s education,” Tyresha Grey Horse, executive director of Friends of the Children – He Sapa, said in a release. “Literacy is a powerful pathway to breaking cycles of generational poverty. When youth are stronger readers, they are better equipped to navigate systems, advocate for themselves and create the futures they deserve.”

Friends of the Children – He Sapa recently launched its first summer Literacy Camp in Rapid City and Rockyford with support from a Rotary Foundation Global Grant that involved nine Rotary districts and several individual Rotary clubs in eight states and India.

 Friends of the Children–He Sapa
Keith Ferguson, program manager for Friends of the Children — He Sapa, congratulated students with a certificate of reading achievement during a graduation ceremony/naming ceremony on Aug. 5. The ceremony concluded the first Friends of the Children – He Sapa summer Literacy Camp. 

During the Literacy Camp, about 120 reading-fluency assessments were administered to establish a baseline for each student and measure progress. By the end of the camp, 20% of participating students had increased their reading fluency by a full grade level, while 57% demonstrated measurable growth in reading fluency, according to project organizers.

Students participated in reading, writing, observation, storytelling and hands-on discovery in a culturally responsive learning environment, project organizers said in a news release. The broader initiative will provide culturally relevant reading materials, interactive learning technology and welcoming learning spaces that honor Indigenous culture while encouraging educational achievement.

The initiative also recognizes that a child’s reading development extends beyond the classroom. Friends of the Children – He Sapa is holding Family Engagement Nights to give children and their caregivers practical ways to make reading part of everyday life at home.

 Friends of the Children–He Sapa
Members of the Rapid City Rotary Club and the leadership team from Friends of the Children — He Sapa participated in a graduation ceremony/naming ceremony on Aug. 5. The ceremony concluded Friends of the Children – He Sapa’s first summer Literacy Camp. 

At the first Family Engagement Night on Aug. 13, families received “I Tell You That I Love You” by Indigenous author Tanaya Winder as the first selection in the Red Book Bag program. Board member Dr. Whitnee Coy and literacy specialist Stacy Cole led the event with the organization’s professional mentors. Additional Family Engagement Nights are planned.

“Our professional mentors build deeply supportive relationships with youth and caregivers to create lasting change in the lives of families and the larger community,” Grey Horse said.

Friends of the Children – He Sapa is the first Indigenous-led, culturally specific chapter in the national Friends of the Children network. It combines the organization’s evidence-based, long-term mentoring model with Lakota values and culturally grounded learning.

 Friends of the Children–He Sapa
Stacy Cole, literacy specialist, partnered with Dr. Whitnee Coy (not pictured) to create an effective and fun learning environment for the Friends of the Children — He Sapa young reader group. Friends of the Children – He Sapa recently launched its first summer Literacy Camp in Rapid City and Rockyford. 

The program identifies children ages 4 to 6 who face significant obstacles and pairs each child with a professional mentor. Mentors spend four hours a week with each child — two hours during school and two hours outside school — and develop individualized plans with specific goals.

The literacy initiative’s long-range goal is to help Native youth graduate from high school or earn a GED and become scholars, leaders and lifelong learners. It also seeks to empower parents and caregivers to take an active role in their children’s reading through the Raising a Reader program.

The Rotary grant was coordinated by Dr. Ashok Kumar, past president of the Rotary Club of Rapid City. The project grew from a vision shared by Kumar and Jeanne W. Clark, a Kentucky Rotary leader who had long sought an opportunity to support Native children and families.

“Every child deserves the opportunity to feel valued, supported and empowered to reach their full potential,” Clark said. “I hope this Rotary Global Grant gives Friends of the Children – He Sapa the resources to inspire confidence, hope and a stronger sense of possibility for Oglala Lakota children.”

The project’s core committee includes Kumar, representing Rotary International District 5610; Grey Horse, an Oglala Lakota leader; and Clark, past governor of Rotary International District 6740 in Kentucky.

title: 21 local professionals named to Elevate Leadership Institute Class of 2027
description: Elevate Rapid City will empower 21 local professionals to strengthen their leadership and management skills through the Elevate Leadership Institute Class of 2027.
_full_text:
Elevate Rapid City will empower 21 local professionals to strengthen their leadership and management skills through the Elevate Leadership Institute Class of 2027.

The Elevate Leadership Institute Class of 2027 is a nine-month program that begins Sept. 10. Participants will enhance their abilities to manage people and teams while gaining a deeper understanding of Rapid City’s businesses, challenges and opportunities. Elevate Leadership Institute will provide the Class of 2027 participants with interactive experiences, community engagement, and opportunities to better understand the people, organizations and issues that are shaping Rapid City.

Class of 2027 participants also are encouraged to become more engaged leaders within their workplaces and community.

Elevate Leadership Institute Class of 2027 is: Mark Adcock, United States Air Force; Lorrae Aker, Monument Health; Karlee Baumann, Monument Health; Arika Beals, Black Hills State University – Rapid City; Michael Boyle, Purple Wealth; Pamela Carpino, FourFront Design, Inc.; Casey Cuny, Scull Construction; Aidan Goetzinger, Gunderson, Palmer, Nelson & Ashmore, LLP; Roxanne Hammond, Northwestern Mutual; Corinne Heiberger, South Dakota Mines; Adam Karschnik, Malone Engineering, Inc.; Brent Kastner, Omnitech; Heather Knox, Black Hills Energy; Pomaikai Lindenthal, Visit Rapid City; Crystal Ortbahn, John T. Vucurevich Foundation; Angela Ratliff, Liberty Superstores; Greg Robinson, SDN Communications; Kylie Tucker, Monument Health; Briana Vande Pol, South Dakota Governor’s Office of Economic Development; Kaelixte Wagner, Dakota Credit Union Association; and Karen Linn, Rustic Nook Bakery.

Linn also is the recipient of the Linda Rabe Women in Leadership Scholarship. Rabe spent more than 30 years with the Elevate Rapid City Chamber, and Rabe was the first woman to serve as the chamber’s chief executive. Throughout her career, she helped break barriers and create opportunities for women in leadership.

“We look forward to welcoming the ELI Class of 2027,” said Bailey Sadowsky, program director. “Our goal is for them to leave the program better equipped to lead their teams and make a meaningful impact in our community.”

Elevate Leadership Institute builds on the legacy of Leadership Rapid City, which served the community for decades.

title: Saying goodbye: Demolition of Rapid City’s St. John’s church coming in September
description: The bell has tolled for the last time at Church of St. John the Evangelist in Rapid City. The small brick church that served parishioners for 35 years is set to be demolished in September.
_full_text:
The bell has tolled for the last time at Church of St. John the Evangelist in Rapid City. The small brick church that served parishioners for 35 years is set to be demolished in September.

St. John’s was built in 1941 at 802 Dilger Ave., and was used until 1976, when St. Therese Catholic church was built. St. John’s is located across a parking lot from the much larger St. Therese the Little Flower Catholic Church, 532 Adams St.

The condition of St. John’s has deteriorated to the point that it is being torn down. The land on which the building stands will be repurposed as green space for the children of St. Therese to play.

 St. John’s Church from Dilger Avenue
The front of the Church of St. John the Evangelist as seen from Dilger Avenue in Rapid City on Aug. 25, after crosses and other sacred items were removed in preparation for demolition. 

Father Mark McCormick, the new priest at St. Therese of the Little Flower, arrived July 1. One of his first duties was shepherding his flock through the imminent loss of St. John’s. On July 19, McCormick led a procession from St. Therese Church to the front steps of St. John’s. Parishioners sang and prayed over the space.

“We blessed the inside and the outside,” McCormick said. “The bell rang for the last time. A lot of people enjoyed it. (There were) some good tears.”

The previous priest for St. Therese and St. John’s, Father Kerry Prendiville, began a new assignment on July 1 as the pastor for St. Ambrose Parish in Deadwood and St. Patrick Parish in Lead.

Before the processional service, St. Therese Church posted on its Facebook page to give parishioners and the public more information about the church’s demolition.  

This spring, Prendiville worked with Bishop Scott Bullock of the Diocese of Rapid City to complete the proper paperwork necessary to move forward with the demolition of St. John’s Church. St. John’s had already been relegated from a sacred church space to secular but not profane use.

 Foundation cracking
Cracks were visible in the Church of St. John the Evangelist’s foundation on Aug. 25. 

All sacred items from St. John’s have been removed, McCormick said, and after St. John’s was relegated to secular use, it was used as a storage space.

McCormick told the Journal that although St. John’s exterior still appears to be a solid brick church, inside the building is falling apart. Restoration is not fiscally prudent.

 Deacon Don Moore
St. Therese the Little Flower Church Deacon Don Moore said the footprint of the Church of St. John the Evangelist will become a grassy area for children to play. The church was dedicated in 1940 before St. Therese the Little Flower Church was dedicated as its replacement in 1976. 

“The basement is full of mold. The structure is falling apart. It’s not really fitting for a church,” McCormick said. “Now it’s to the point where there’s no return. We have a beautiful church at St. Therese. St. John’s is nice from the outside but when you go inside, it’s dirty. It’s moldy. It’s falling apart, and I think it’s hard for people to understand that.”

Quinn Construction will handle demolition of St. John’s. The white cross from the top of the church, the bell, and two faux stained glass windows from the front doors have been preserved, along with the St. John’s cornerstone. According to the Diocese of Rapid City, sacramental records are permanently stored at St. Therese.

Decades of memories

Amid news of the church’s demise, former parishioners have shared fond memories and sadness over the loss of St. John’s.

“People were saying, ‘Father Mark, I was baptized at that church. I made my confirmation,’ and then you start getting the tears,” McCormick told the Journal, describing the July 19 processional service. 

 St. John’s Church, northwest corner
The northeastern corner of the Church of St. John the Evangelist as seen from Dilger Avenue in Rapid City on Aug. 25. 

“I would say, ‘Lord, what do you want me to say to them? I have no idea,’” McCormick said. “I heard the Holy Spirit say, ‘Tell them about their baptism, what happened to them in their baptism. It’s something that happened in their heart. Tell them when they made their first communion, when they received Jesus, it’s something in their heart.’”

McCormick reminded parishioners that God’s people are the church.

 St. John’s Church bell tower and St. Therese the Little Flower Church
St. Therese the Little Flower Church, background, was dedicated on May 1976, as the replacement for the Church of St. John the Evangelist, foreground, which was dedicated in April 1940. 

“I found myself praying over people, saying, ‘There’s nothing special that happened to you by your baptism, your confirmation, your first communion, your wedding that can be contained in the physical structure of a church, because it’s in your heart,’” he said.

Some people shared their memories on Facebook, saying their parents or family members were married at St. John’s. Others recalled activities, including their first communion or ringing the bell in the bell tower. Amid the daily bustle of parish life, some events remain unforgettable, such as the memorial service at St. John’s for the six Rapid City High School cheerleaders who died in a plane crash in 1968.

 Bell tower
The bell tower at the Church of St. John the Evangelist as seen on Aug. 25. The bell was rung for the last time in the bell tower on Aug. 18 before it was removed. 

Gretchen Hutter Cooney of Spearfish told the Journal she and her brothers, John and Bob Hutter, had many recollections of St. John’s. They attended St. John’s in the 1960s. Cooney was in high school. She recalls memories she said would apply to many parishes of that era, including wearing hats, mantillas, white gloves and patent leather shoes at Easter.

“The main memory I have is how full the church always was. Many people had to stand in the side aisles. It made getting to Mass early a priority!” Cooney said. “Also, we went to confession every other week. I remember standing in line with a lot of other kids.”

 Stair cracks
Bricks around the front steps of St. John’s Church show cracks on Aug. 25, ahead of demolition. 

John Hutter was a lector who remembers, in the mid 1960s, that Mass was held in a school gym, with religious education classes afterward, to ease some of the overcrowding.

Bob Hutter served as an altar boy.

“My brother got to be an altar server, and I was not pleased that I couldn’t,” Cooney said. “He brought home a cool laminated card to learn the Latin responses. I was jealous!”

For those who want one final memento of the place that holds a spot in their minds and hearts, some bricks from St. John’s will be available as keepsakes after the church is demolished.

 Ivy
Ivy grows on the side of the Church of St. John the Evangelist on Aug. 25.

title: Groundbreaking held for affordable housing project in Rapid City
description: Infrastructure work will begin in September on East Creek Village, an affordable housing development in Rapid City.
_full_text:
Infrastructure work will begin in September on East Creek Village, an affordable housing development in Rapid City.

A groundbreaking event on Aug. 24 introduced East Creek Village, which will be located at 1727 Creek Drive. East Creek Village is a joint venture between RCS Construction and Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity.

The infrastructure work starting in September will include curbs, gutters, sidewalks, street, sewer and water. Construction on Phase 1 of East Creek Village will begin in 2027.

East Creek Village will be a mixed-income “attainable” homeownership opportunity for 40 qualifying individuals and families who earn up to 120% of the Area Median Income, which currently ranges from $40,200 to $123,600 in Pennington County, according to a news release from Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity.

This development will consist of townhomes ranging in sizes from 1,500 to 2,000 square feet. Each townhome will have its own garage and parking and will be purchased with its own plat of land.

East Creek Village in an infill development that will replace 4.25 empty acres near Cambell and E. St. Patrick streets. The housing project leverages existing city infrastructure while providing housing that’s close to amenities such as a grocery store, restaurants, bike path, softball fields, public transit and employment opportunities, according

 East Creek Village
An empty 4.25 acres of land near Cambell and E. St. Patrick Streets is the future site of East Creek Village affordable housing. The project is a joint venture between RCS Construction and Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity. 

to Habitat.

The East Creek Village project was conceived and developed by Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity’s former executive director, Scott Engmann, who left his position in July after serving for more than 20 years. He now works as a consulting advisor to Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity.

"From day one, we envisioned the East Creek Village development as a way to provide much needed affordable infill housing that was unique in character, walkable to retail shopping and banking, with easy cycling on the bike path,” Engmann said. “It has been important to us to create something that is appropriate for singles and families, meeting a critical need for the workforce of our region. The fact these will be purchased and occupied by homeowners who live and work in our community will make it durable and a great neighborhood for years to come."

Engmann and more than 75 individuals attended the groundbreaking ceremony on Aug. 24. Sen. Mike Rounds spoke briefly at the event. According to Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity, support for East Creek Village comes from federal, state and local resources, donors and community partners.

“This is a win for families and a win for our entire community,” said Barbara O’Malley, acting executive director of Black Hills Area Habitat for Humanity. “East Creek Village offers a unique homeownership opportunity. We are grateful to the many supporters who don’t just talk about the affordable housing crisis, they are doing something about it.”

RC Scull, president of RCS Construction, said RCS Construction is proud to be part of the East Creek Village affordable housing project.

“This development represents more than new housing. It is an investment in people, families, and the future of our community. We are excited to help create a place where residents can thrive and feel a true sense of belonging,” Scull said.

title: ‘This isn’t justice’: Man sentenced for 2022 Rapid City bar shooting, victim’s family outraged
description: Overcome with grief and indignation, the family and friends of 30-year-old Dallas Quick Bear condemned the Seventh Circuit Court on Monday, Aug. 31, calling a five-year prison sentence an insulting penalty for the 2022 shooting death of Quick Bear inside a former Rapid City bar. But prosecutors said their options became limited, while defense attorneys cited a lack of evidence.
_full_text:
Overcome with grief and indignation, the family and friends of 30-year-old Dallas Quick Bear condemned the Seventh Circuit Court on Monday, Aug. 31, calling a five-year prison sentence an insulting penalty for the 2022 shooting death of Quick Bear inside a former Rapid City bar. But prosecutors said their options became limited, while defense attorneys cited a lack of evidence.

Timothy Huante of Rapid City appeared for his change of plea and sentencing before Circuit Court Judge Matt Brown at the Pennington County Courthouse.

 Timothy Huante
Timothy Huante 

Huante was initially indicted in March 2022 for first-degree murder in connection to the shooting death of Quick Bear inside of Teddy’s Sports Grill around 1 a.m. on Feb. 20, 2022. Through an agreement with the state, Huante entered an Alford plea to accessory to a crime, a Class 5 felony with a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $10,000 fine. He avoids a potential life sentence.

An Alford plea is a guilty plea in which a defendant maintains their innocence but admits the prosecution’s evidence would likely result in a guilty verdict if brought to trial. It functions the same as a guilty plea.

The plea follows more than four years of extensive litigation as the state sought to hold Huante accountable for Quick Bear’s death, including an appeal to the South Dakota Supreme Court that resulted in a ruling favorable to the state.

One of Huante’s defense attorneys, Greg Sperlich, said there was no physical evidence indicating Huante as the shooter.

Huante was sentenced to five years in prison. After applying time served and South Dakota parole eligibility statutes, Huante will serve 60 days.

Family expresses outrage, defense sites lack of evidence

Quick Bear’s family described him as a “respectful, gentle soul” who was stolen away from them too soon. A friend of Quick Bear’s said he had a smile that lit up the room and always made an effort to make the people around him laugh.

About a dozen family members came forward to testify on Quick Bear’s behalf at the sentencing. They not only expressed their resentment with Huante but also with the Seventh Circuit Court. Several family members stated the justice system is biased and “a white man can get away with murdering a Native American.”

A family friend of Quick Bear’s said the Native American community is often left “to pay the price” while the justice system only “serves for the white man.”

According to the South Dakota Department of Corrections 2025 annual report, the jurisdictional population — offenders in state correctional and contracted facilities — as of June 30, 2025, consisted of 39% Native Americans, 46% White, 9% Black, 5% Hispanic or Latino and 2% other inmates.

According to the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office 2025 annual report 7,211 inmates of the Pennington County Jail’s population are Native American, good for 63.56%. The rest are white (32.65%, 3,704 inmates), African American (3.53%, 400 inmates) and Asian (0.27%, 31 inmates).

Quick Bear’s sister, Sheila Quick Bear, said she felt betrayed by the system, questioning how Huante could “get away with murder.”

“Maybe you guys can make a board game and make steps on how to get away with murder,” Quick Bear said to the court, prosecution and defense.

Several family members testified they didn’t expect to be brought up to speak, let alone attend Huante’s change of plea and sentencing. Before the hearing began, Sheila Quick Bear asked when the trial would begin and when the jury would be brought in. Before the plea agreement, Huante’s trial was set to begin on Monday.

She said whenever the name Quick Bear is brought to court it always leads to a lengthy sentence, while Huante faces a shorter sentence than most people who are arrested on drug charges.

Quick Bear’s family called Huante “a coward.”

“This isn’t justice, my son should be here and I hope you see the other side of a gun and feel the pain I felt,” Quick Bear’s mother, Moriah Gankin, said with tears in her eyes.

 Ground shot of courthouse
The Pennington County Courthouse is located at 315 Saint Joseph Street, Rapid City.  

Sperlich told the Journal there was no evidence, such as video, pictures or witness testimony, that narrowed Huante as the shooter. He said the only thing the state had was Huante’s “false confession” during a police interview about a night he doesn’t remember after drinking.

He said Teddy’s had eight cameras inside the establishment and the shooting occurred within the blind spot of all eight of them. Sperlich added that the majority of witness statements given to police described the shooter inconsistently, with conflicting details regarding race, age and physical appearance.

If the trial was going to continue, Sperlich said the defense was going to bring in one witness who told police three times who the shooter was. Sperlich did not disclose the name but said the witness never described the shooter “to be a white guy.”

Huante’s other defense attorney, Angela Colbath, said during the sentencing there was “a good reason” the charge was changed, “so that the real person who is responsible for Dallas’ death can be held accountable.”

Colbath asked the court to consider granting credit for time served in its sentencing decision.

As Deputy States Attorney Adam Shiffermiller attempted to give a closing argument at sentencing, members of Quick Bear’s family continued to interrupt by questioning Brown and stating the proceeding was an injustice. Brown said he respected the family’s feelings, but asked there to be order so court proceedings could continue smoothly. Family members continued to make comments.

Shiffermiller asked the court to consider the maximum sentence of five years.

A press release from the Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office said the discrepancies in eyewitness accounts and a ruling barring testimony from a key state witness, along with expected testimony from a defense expert calling into question the reliability of admissions made by Huante, further impacted the evidence prosecutors would have been able to present to a jury and, ultimately, the state’s ability to prove the murder charge beyond a reasonable doubt.

“Dallas Quick Bear and his family have remained at the center of our efforts throughout this case,” Pennington County State’s Attorney Lara Roetzel said in the release. “The fact that this case did not ultimately resolve with a murder conviction does not diminish the work that law enforcement and our prosecutors have put into seeking justice for Dallas. Prosecutors also have an ethical responsibility to continually evaluate the evidence in a case and pursue only those charges we believe can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. As the evidence available to present to a jury changed, so did our assessment of the charge we could responsibly pursue.”

Before the sentencing, Brown sympathized with the family and agreed Quick Bear did not deserve to be shot and killed.

“I’m known for being rather long-winded and in this case I feel the more the court has to say the more pain the court will cause to the community that loved Dallas,” Brown said.

Though he acknowledged the family’s claims of injustice, Brown said he doesn’t agree with it. Despite that, he said he knows the decisions made on Monday will only continue to divide the community.

“It does pain me because this system is intended to be color blind, intended to be unbiased,” Brown said.

Huante has been incarcerated in the Pennington County Jail since his arrest in 2022. Following Monday’s sentencing, he was remanded for transportation to the South Dakota State Penitentiary to serve the remainder of his five-year sentence — 60 days.

Huante also faces a federal charge for possession of a firearm by a prohibited person.

As Huante was being escorted out of the courtroom, family members yelled after him with only one message — “Don’t forget Dallas’ name!”

Background of the case, Supreme Court decision

Huante was initially scheduled to go to trial in July 2024. After a Pennington County judge ruled a Rapid City psychiatrist could testify as a defense expert about false confessions, the state appealed and the Supreme Court eventually weighed in. According to the Supreme Court's opinion, Huante confessed to the killing after multiple police interrogations, despite having poor memory of the night due to heavy drinking.

According to Journal archives, the Rapid City Police Department and Pennington County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division interviewed dozens of witnesses, including Huante, who wanted to speak with police the morning of the shooting.

During the interview, police learned few details and the investigation continued. Law enforcement was alerted to a handgun that was discarded in the 400 block of 7th Street.

Investigators interviewed Huante on Tuesday, Feb. 22, 2022, and showed him still images of video from the crime scene. He denied any involvement. On Wednesday, Feb. 23, 2022, he voluntarily submitted to a polygraph examination.

According to law enforcement, the polygraph results showed signs of deception. Huante at first continued to deny he was involved. Then Rapid City Police Department Det. Andrew Randazzo told Huante the polygraph, "told us that you know you shot him," and Huante said he did. Polygraph tests are not admissible in court.

"He explained that the people he went to the bar with told him that Quick Bear 'needed to go,' though he did not know why. Huante then described how he approached Quick Bear’s left side and shot him under the chin," according to the Supreme Court opinion's characterization of the interaction.

Huante's defense attorneys filed for a motion to suppress the statements, arguing he was coerced. Sperlich said on Monday that evidence showed Quick Bear was actually shot in the back of the head.

A hearing was held to address the motion. Circuit Court Judge Matt Brown allowed the psychiatrist, Stephen Manlove, to testify as an expert on false confessions and interrogation tactics.

The Supreme Court overturned the judge's ruling, writing in its opinion that the circuit court judge should not have allowed Manlove to testify as an expert about false confessions at the hearing addressing the motion.

"Dr. Manlove could not accurately convey the frequency or incidence of false confessions; nor did he marshal his qualifications as a forensic psychiatrist to explain under any reliable methodology why, when, or how false confessions occur or to identify characteristics unique to false confessions," Justice Mark Salter wrote in the court's majority opinion.

The defense was allowed to still address false confessions, just not through Manlove. The majority opinion consisted of Chief Justice Steven Jensen, Justice Patricia Devaney and retired Justice Janine Kern. Justice Robert Gusinsky did not participate because he was not a member of the court when the action was under consideration.

Justice Scott Myren was the only one to dissent from the majority's opinion.

"Huante intended to draw the jury’s attention to instances during the interview when law enforcement falsely suggested to him that the polygraph demonstrated that he knew he killed Quick Bear, and other instances where they falsely indicated they had evidence of his guilt," Myren wrote.

title: LaVonne Castleman
description: January 20, 1932 - July 6, 2026
_full_text:
January 20, 1932 - July 6, 2026

LaVonne Ruby Castleman, 94, of Happy Valley, California, passed away at home on July 6, 2026. Her family and her Chihuahua, Gidget, were at her side.

LaVonne was born on January 20, 1932, in Alexandria, South Dakota, to Vera Taylor and Dennis Wood. She attended school in Chamberlain, South Dakota, and later moved to Rapid City where she met her future husband, Bennie Franklin Castleman, who was stationed at Ellsworth AFB. They were married on May 16, 1953 and had two children – Gail Lynette and Marshall Allen (Mark).

While Bennie was in the Air Force they lived in Rapid City SD, Okinawa, Myrtle Beach SC, and Clovis NM, eventually retiring to Sturgis, SD. LaVonne worked in civil service most of her career, and was a Contract Specialist at the Fort Meade VA when she retired. She lived in Tilford and Sturgis until she moved to California in 2024 to be closer to her son, Mark, and his wife.

LaVonne loved animals, especially her dogs. She enjoyed sewing and was an excellent seamstress, something she perfected while living in Okinawa. And she loved nothing more than having friends or family stop by for coffee.

Survivors include her son and his wife, Mark and Diane Castleman of Happy Valley, California, and her daughter and her husband, Gail and Craig Johnson, of Colorado Springs, Colorado. She is also survived by three grandchildren, Ciarra, Keith, and Brittany, as well as her cousin Donna Ennis and her husband Duane of Lead, South Dakota.

LaVonne's parents, her husband, Bennie, and a granddaughter, Amanda Castleman, preceded her in death.

LaVonne will be interred at Black Hills National Cemetery on Monday, September 14, at 10:00 AM. The family invites you to join them for a Celebration of Life/Wake and refreshments at the Sturgis Vet's Club at 11:30 AM following the interment.

You may sign her online guestbook at www.kinkadefunerals.com.

title: Shirley Wolff
description: January 24, 1942 - August 28, 2026
_full_text:
January 24, 1942 - August 28, 2026

The memorial service for Shirley J. Wolff, 84, of Eureka, SD, will be 10:30am, Friday, September 4, 2026 at Salem Emmanuel Lutheran Church in Long Lake, SD with Pastor Tim Vander Vorst officiating. Burial will be at Emmanuel Lutheran Cemetery in Long Lake. Visitation will be one hour prior to the service. Shirley died Friday, August 28, 2026 at Eureka Healthcare Center, following a courageous battle with Parkinsons disease.

Shirley was born on January 24, 1942, to Edwin & Theresa (Bertsch) Heupel. After graduation, Shirley was united in marriage to Gary T. Wolff of Long Lake, SD, at the Eureka Baptist Church. Shortly after that, they moved to Rapid City where they started their life together. In 1962, Gary started working for a mobile home mover, and it was then that Shirley would learn how to manage the business. Shortly thereafter, they bought a trailer home park. In 1975, they bought a second mobile home park. Now Shirley had her hands full not only managing the parks, but with working on the ground to extend the park to over a hundred mobile homes.

Shirley and Gary owned the Long Lake Café from 2007-2014. Here was where Shirley showed another talent for being a very good cook, learning yet another business and how to manage it. They sold the café in 2014 and farmed part time. Shirley was seen many times helping out in the fields.

Throughout Shirley's life, she enjoyed many activities outside the business. She was a terrific crafter. She especially liked working on puzzles, of which she had several framed and hanging in her room. She had done some beautiful things in her lifetime for herself and others. She also enjoyed knitting and made many knitted pieces for her nieces. She enjoyed making candy with her friends and family. The Christmas gatherings of the Heupel family were a time she always looked forward to.

Shirley and Gary enjoyed themselves taking vacations. They went to Alaska and spent one whole summer there. They also went to Florida where they watched a NASCAR race in person and visited with friends. Shirley loved dogs & cats, especially her cat Foxy.

Grateful for having shared Shirley's life are sisters: Sylvia (Don) Heinrich, Donna Heinrich, and Patty (Rick) Trupe; many nieces and nephews; and special friends: Reid & Gwen Gray, Kevin & Tammy Heupel, Rod & Donna Hoffman, Larry Sullivan, and Hazel Vilhauer.

Preceding Shirley in death are her husband Gary; parents Edwin & Theresa Heupel; niece Dawn Quenzer; brothers-in-law Derrold Follmer and Lester Heinrich.
