title: Patrols increased for Labor Day weekend celebrations
description: As part of a multi-agency initiative called “Drive Sober or Get Pulled Over,” there will be extra law enforcement patrols out on the roads during the Labor Day weekend.
_full_text:
As part of a multi-agency initiative called “Drive Sober or Get Pulled Over,” there will be extra law enforcement patrols out on the roads during the Labor Day weekend.

Through Monday, Sept. 7 the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, Rapid City Police Department, South Dakota Highway Patrol and the U.S. Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration will be working together to deter drunk driving during the Labor Day holiday weekend.

“With the upcoming holiday weekend the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office is just trying to urge the public to be careful,” PCSO Lt. Thad Mason said.

Mason encourages the public to be mindful of following the speed limits as they travel throughout the Black Hills and to not drink and drive during the celebrations.

According to the press release from the PCSO, during the 2025 Labor Day holiday there were 505 traffic crash fatalities nationwide. Of these 505 fatalities, 34% involved a drunk driver. About 77% of the impaired drivers killed had a blood alcohol concentration of 0.15% or higher. The legal limit is 0.08%.

The South Dakota Office of Accident Records reported over the past five Labor Day weekends — 2021 to 2025 — impaired driving crashes have resulted in six fatalities and 51 injuries on South Dakota roadways.

Mason said if a driver intends to drink during Labor Day, he or she should plan ahead for a safe ride home by securing a designated driver or calling a taxi or rideshare. Planning shouldn’t wait until after drinking has started, as impairment clouds a person’s judgment and endangers others on the road.

If a driver finds they are unable to drive, they should give their keys to a sober driver so they can get them home safely. Law enforcement encourages the public to contact them if a drunk driver is spotted on the roadway.

title: Back-to-school wake-up call: Local law enforcement warns parents after students bring prohibited items to school
description: After a series of children bringing prohibited items to school during the first week back, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office is urging parents to speak with their children.
_full_text:
After a series of children bringing prohibited items to school during the first week back, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office is urging parents to speak with their children.

PCSO Sgt. Jeremy Milstead said with archery season kicking off on Tuesday, Sept. 1 and a recent string of incidents within the first week of school, the office wanted to encourage parents to talk with their children about what is allowed and not allowed at school grounds. Milstead the goal isn’t to scare parents but to make sure they’re informing their children and ensuring there’s no forgotten items in cars or backpacks that shouldn’t be brought to school.

“We’ve seen a few things that have happened over the last week in some of our schools out in the county, one of those things being different items being brought to school,” Milstead said. “Prohibited items that we don’t want to see in and around our schools.”

Milstead said prohibited items include fireworks, toys that resemble any weapon, any type of knife, including pocket knives or box cutters, and guns. He said the best practice is to have a sit down discussion with the child and to double check their backpacks or cars to ensure there aren’t any forgotten items.

“The big thing is just staying involved in the kids’ lives. That helps prevent a lot of these things,” Milstead said.

Lastly, Milstead warns the public to be extra precautious in leaving hunting gear and rifles in cars during hunting season. He said law enforcement responds to many calls about a student forgetting their guns or knives in backpacks or cars.

One particular incident that caught law enforcement’s attention was a student bringing in an airsoft gun to East Middle School on Monday, Aug. 31.

Rapid City Area Schools District said they were aware of a report of an item that resembled a firearm and was later able to determine it was a airsoft gun with the help of the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office.

“We do not tolerate items of this nature on our school campuses and take these situations seriously,” Community Relations Manager Bobbi Shaefbauer told the Journal. “The matter is being handled in accordance with district policy, the student handbook, and the district’s discipline matrix. The safety of our students and staff remains our top priority.”

Due to student privacy laws, the Rapid City Area Schools said they cannot disclose more information about the incident.

Milstead said, whether its a toy that looks like a weapon or the real deal, local law enforcement takes each case seriously and will respond appropriately.

title: 10 Rapid City schools to close early for heat on Thursday
description: Citing high temperatures and heat conditions, the Rapid City Area Schools District said 10 schools will let out early on Thursday, Sept. 3. The schools are:
_full_text:
Citing high temperatures and heat conditions, the Rapid City Area Schools District said 10 schools will let out early on Thursday, Sept. 3. The schools are:

Grandview Elementary

Horace Mann Elementary

Meadowbrook Elementary

Rapid Valley Elementary

Robbinsdale Elementary

Pinedale Elementary

South Canyon Elementary

South Park Elementary

Wilson Elementary

North Middle School

The Rapid City Area Schools District said buses will run on an adjusted schedule, and after-school activities at the 10 schools are cancelled.

 Swing
A student at swings in the sun at a Rapid City elementary school on Monday, Aug. 24. 

Per the National Weather Service’s Rapid City office, the Thursday forecast shows a high of 93 and a low of 64, with southwest wind 7 to 11 mph. Gusts could reach 26 mph.

The 10 schools that are closing early either don’t have air conditioning or have limited air conditioning. The Rapid City Area Schools Board is putting forward a $107 million bond referendum on the November ballot. The plan for the bond, if it passes, dedicates $32 million to HVAC energy and efficiency upgrades at Horace Mann Elementary, Meadowbrook Elementary and North Middle School, along with other facilities improvements.

The district's most recent bond attempt came in 2020 — with a price tag of $189.5 million. It accrued a vote of 56%, short of the required 60%. Voters in the district have not passed a bond since the 1976. In April, the RCAS school board voted to place the bond on the ballot.

The district is holding bond information sessions as the vote approaches. The next session will be held over Zoom on Sept. 10 from 7 p.m. Visit rcas.org/page/bond-information for more information about the bond.

As Labor Day weekend approaches, early release is also scheduled districtwide for Friday, September 4.

“Thank you for your flexibility and understanding as we work to keep our students and staff safe and comfortable during the heat,” the district said in a statement.

title: Baer Gee to take over as executive editor of the Rapid City Journal
description: Veteran South Dakota journalist and editor Shalom Baer Gee will be the next top editor of the Rapid City Journal.
_full_text:
Veteran South Dakota journalist and editor Shalom Baer Gee will be the next top editor of the Rapid City Journal.

Baer Gee, an award-winning journalist who currently serves as the Journal’s assistant editor, will take command of the newsroom on Sept. 28. The Kalispell, Montana, native has worked at the Journal for more than four years, starting in April 2022.

Baer Gee began as a reporter on the public safety beat, providing extensive coverage of crime and the court system as she became one of the best-sourced journalists in the Black Hills. She later shifted to coverage of local government, and then the education beat when she took on the assistant editor role in April 2025.

 Shalom Baer Gee
Shalom Baer Gee 

Regardless of her beat, Baer Gee approaches topics with curiosity and compassion to provide thorough, engaging stories to readers, current Rapid City Journal Editor Michael Brownlee said.

Baer Gee will succeed Brownlee, who will be moving to the executive editor position at the Billings Gazette, a sister paper of the Journal in Montana.

“I’m eternally grateful for the trust members of this community have put in me during my time here so far. Journalism is truly impossible without relationships, and the value of the people who make up our community is not lost on me,” Baer Gee said. “In this new position, I’ll dedicate everything I have to empower our newsroom to continue to provide accurate, contextual and fair stories. When I was a child, my local newspaper was my window to the world, and I hope I’m able to give that to this community while I’m at the helm.”

Baer Gee is a graduate of Minot State University in Minot, North Dakota, where she earned a degree in journalism. She worked at the Minot Daily News before heading south to work at the Journal. She lives in Rapid City with her husband and daughter, who is currently the youngest member of the newsroom — replete with a press badge.

“Shalom is going to excel in this role. I’m beyond thrilled for her,” Brownlee said. “I had high hopes for Shalom when she took over as assistant editor, and she exceeded them exponentially. I expect the same as she takes the top role in the newsroom. Journal readers, your newspaper is in great hands.”

title: Rapid City man pleads not guilty to several sexual abuse charges
description: A Rapid City man pleaded not guilty on Thursday, Sept. 3 to several sexual abuse charges against a minor younger than 13 years old.
_full_text:
A Rapid City man pleaded not guilty on Thursday, Sept. 3 to several sexual abuse charges against a minor younger than 13 years old.

Steven Dillon, 37, appeared for his arraignment hearing before Presiding Circuit Judge Heidi Linngren at the Pennington County Courthouse on Thursday.

Dillon is indicted for first-degree rape, possession of child sexual abuse material, solicitation of a minor and sexual exploitation of a minor. Dillon faces another sexual abuse charge — the Journal is not specifying the charge to protect the victim’s identity.

In South Dakota, first-degree rape is a Class C felony with a maximum sentence of a life in prison and a $50,000, there is a mandatory minimum of 15 years for the first offense. Possessing child pornography and solicitation of a minor are Class 4 felonies with a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a $20,000 fine. Sexual exploitation of a minor is a Class 6 felony with a maximum sentence of 2 years in prison and a $4,000 fine.

Dillon’s next court appearance is set for 2:15 p.m. on Oct. 29. Defense attorney Ellery Grey said they will address bond at that time.

title: Martin man arrested after 1 injured in Anamosa Street shooting
description: Rapid City police arrested a 20-year-old Martin man on Wednesday, Sept. 2, after an officer heard gunshots and saw muzzle flashes while responding to an unrelated call on Anamosa Street. One person was injured in the shooting.
_full_text:
Rapid City police arrested a 20-year-old Martin man on Wednesday, Sept. 2, after an officer heard gunshots and saw muzzle flashes while responding to an unrelated call on Anamosa Street. One person was injured in the shooting.

Per the Rapid City Police Department, around 10:45 p.m. on Wednesday an officer was on a call in the 700 block of East Anamosa Street when he heard the gunfire coming from the area of 743 E. Anamosa St., the address of LaCrosse Estates Apartments. Police saw the shooter run into an apartment and then formed a perimeter around that apartment.

In the meantime, police found a wounded man nearby who was injured by the gunfire. He was taken to the hospital with serious, non-life-threatening injuries.

Police ordered four people to come out of the apartment, including 20-year-old Cesar Shangreaux, of Martin.

According to the department, witness interviews pointed to Shangreaux as the shooter.

He was arrested on suspicion of aggravated assault and taken to the Pennington County Jail.

After obtaining a search warrant for the apartment, police found a gun they believe was used in the shooting. At this time, police believe Shangreaux and the victim were known to each other at the time of the shooting, and the incident does not appear to be random in nature.

State court records have yet to reflect charges against Shangreaux, and the Pennington County Jail roster is not available due to a recent cybersecurity attack on the county, making bond information unavailable at this time.

title: 10 years later, Rapid City runs to remember Tom Pfeifle
description: Whether breaking stride on the cinder track or rocky paths, commanding the stage under theater lights, opening discussions about conservation efforts for national parks or penning prose thanking those he cared for, 19-year-old Tom Pfeifle seemed to master whatever world he chose to step into.
_full_text:
Whether breaking stride on the cinder track or rocky paths, commanding the stage under theater lights, opening discussions about conservation efforts for national parks or penning prose thanking those he cared for, 19-year-old Tom Pfeifle seemed to master whatever world he chose to step into.

Yet, for those who knew him best, his rarest gift was neither on paper nor field — it was the effortless, magnetic grace that managed to capture the heart of not only those who were close to him, but the entire Black Hills community.

His mother Jane Wipf Pfeifle said he carried his remarkable gifts with an easy, infectious grin and an irrepressible sense of fun. Always quick with a joke, up for an impromptu adventure and charging into every single day with the wide-eyed eagerness of someone determined to wring every drop of wonder from life.

“He loved to be outside, he loved to hike, run, climb, swim, and he really liked to bring people along with him,” Wipf Pfeifle said. “He was hyper-friendly. He was funny. He liked to play pranks on his friends. He just really had a wide group of friends, all kinds of stuff, and we’ve heard lots of people say, ‘Tom was my best friend.’”

That boundless spirit came to a devastating, sudden halt in August 2016. After summiting Granite Peak — Montana’s highest and most unforgiving point — with his three best friends, Tom fell 20 to 30 feet along the rugged rock face on Aug. 8, 2016.

Rushed by emergency crews to a Seattle hospital, he succumbed to his injuries days later, cutting short a vibrant life and a future brimming with limitless potential.

A decade after his passing, the ache never truly faded for his parents, Wipf Pfiefle and Craig Pfeifle. Yet through enduring an unimaginable loss, Tom’s legacy remains anything but dim. Ten years later, Tom’s memory continues to shine on in the heart of Rapid City at Raider’s Park.

A friend never forgotten

Bradley Drake first met Tom not as friends but as competitors in an 8th grade track race. With their middle schools rivaling against each other, Drake said both he and Tom gave everything they had in the 1-mile race. Though Drake came out on top in the race, he said it wasn’t the win or the medals that he remembered the most from that day, it was Tom’s sporting personality as he ran over to shake Drake’s hand.

A fierce track rivalry quickly blossomed into brotherhood when they reunited at Stevens High School. Along with Jackson Dorsey and Eric Sanderson, the group formed an inseparable quartet bound by trail hikes and outdoor adventures.

Drake, Dorsey and Sanderson were with Tom on Granite Peak during that fatal descent, an ordeal that left them forever scarred as they learned to navigate life without him.

“It was a two-day trip to the summit of the peak. We had made it to the summit and on our descent is when Tom fell,” Dorsey said, noting the difficulty scale was Class 3. “Some rocks went loose and Tom fell and we organized a rescue operation with the helicopter evacuation on the side of the mountain.”

In the wake of Tom’s passing, the boys mourned together, piecing together the void their best friend left behind. Drake, motivated to not let Tom’s memory to be left on a sad note, approached his friends and Tom’s parents about an idea to keep Tom’s memory alive.

“The summer after Tom passed away, we were grieving together and wanted to do something to turn that into a positive association, something to remember Tom by,” Drake said. “So then we had this idea putting on a 5K.”

Dorsey said Tom’s will requested people donate to two different charities in the event of his death: The Wilderness Land Trust and The Wilderness Society. Wanting to honor his wishes while encompassing his love for the outdoors and running, both Dorsey and Drake hosted the first-ever Tom Pfeifle Memorial 5k Run/Walk in 2017.

“He (Tom) really kind of focused on being outside and engaging with the outdoors and I felt like Tom always pushed me to expand my horizons when it came to recreations, outdoors,” Dorsey said.

Drake said they expected only about 30 attendees, but were blown away when 300 participants came to celebrate Tom’s memory. Together, they made over $10,000 in donations to be split between each charity.

Though it was a smashing success during the first year, Drake and Dorsey knew they couldn’t feasibly maintain the race as they continued on to college. With the Pfeifles’ permission, the 5K was then given to Diane and Bill Tschetter, who transformed the race into a cornerstone event in Rapid City.

In 2019, plans to develop Raider Park into a multi-purpose educational and community space recieved a $50,000 boost thanks to a donation from Tom Pfiefle Memorial 5K, Inc. The $50,000 was raised through sponsorships, donors, grants and from the annual 5K.

The donation was accepted by Seth Keene and Tom Keck, the two Stevens math teachers who are leading the efforts to transform 38 acres of property on public-school land across from Stevens High School. Tom’s parents said the park was the perfect fit to honor their son’s passion for outdoor exercise and the environment.

Seven years after the creation of Raider Park, attendees from all over the Black Hills come to race in the annual 5K. Craig Pfeifle said every year is a testament to how many lives Tom impacted and the sense of community that was created after his passing.

“One of the things we like about the annual memorial run is the ability to talk about Tom and tell stories,” Pfeifle said. “It’s a good reminder in asking the community on how impactful he was even though he died a very young age.”

The 10th annual race

Crowds filled Raider Park once more as the morning sun broke over the park on Saturday, Aug. 29, marking a decade since Tom’s passing. Clad in matching sky-blue shirts, runners, walkers, family and friends stretched and swapped heartfelt stories beside Stevens High School — Tom’s magnetic presence still echoing across the field where his legacy took root.

Drake and Dorsey led the run. They said they always make sure that either one of them or Sanderson makes it out to the 5K.

 090126-nws-5k-p1.JPG

Though the three of them have grown up into men with varying careers, Dorsey and Drake said being Tom’s friend is what helped shape them into the people they are today and they will always be grateful for that.

Dorsey and Drake reflected back on their favorite memories of Tom. Dorsey mentioned their adventures in national parks in Utah, where they would enjoy breathtaking sights, but also quiet moments.

For Drake, it was the day before Tom’s passing, where they watched a sunset at the summit while having a heart-to-heart conversation, excited about what the future holds.

After the race, participants were welcomed with several slices of pie ranging from apple to blueberry. Though winded and covered in sweat as the morning sun transitioned to afternoon, each participant had a smile on their face as they laughed and cheered.

 090126-nws-5k-p4.JPG
Crowds filled Raider Park once more as the morning sun broke over the park on Saturday, Aug. 29, for an annual 5K in Tom Pfeifle's honor. 

Wipf Pfeifle said it’s a sight her son would’ve loved to see. The Pfeifles told the Journal their son was an amazing young man.

“It never goes away, but the pain becomes less sharp and he feels very present to us in many ways, and we’re very happy about that,” she said.

title: Oaye Luta Okolakiciye rallies for support towards cultural services tackling addiction and recover
description: In the face of the vicious cycle of addiction, Rapid City-based Oaye Luta Okolakiciye — which means "Moving Forward in a Sacred Way" — has been using cultural medicine practices geared toward the Indigenous community. The organization, along with supporters, believes their treatment model needs support from the South Dakota Legislature for Medicaid to cover their services.
_full_text:
In the face of the vicious cycle of addiction, Rapid City-based Oaye Luta Okolakiciye — which means "Moving Forward in a Sacred Way" — has been using cultural medicine practices geared toward the Indigenous community. The organization, along with supporters, believes their treatment model needs support from the South Dakota Legislature for Medicaid to cover their services.

On Aug. 26, OLO gathered officials, including South Dakota Secretary of Health Melissa Magstadt, Oglala Sioux Tribe President Frank Star Comes Out (Lakota), Johns Hopkins Center for Indigenous Health Co-Director Donald Warne (Lakota), senior research sssociate at the Johns Hopkins Center for Indigenous Health Jordyn Gunville-Pourier (Lakota), Rep. Mike Derby R-34, Rep. Peri Pourier R-27 (Lakota) and others to learn about OLO's services to the community.

"We work extra hard here, and we take on a lot because the relatives that come our way, they carry a lot. They're looking for ways to be who they are intended to be. I'm not saying the western way is not effective, but it's just not working for us," OLO Founder and Executive Director OLO Gene Tyon (Lakota) said.

 Gene Tyson
Oaye Luta Okolakicive Executive Director and Founder of Gene Tyon speaks during an event calling for support for his nonprofit organization. 

OLO was founded in 2015 as an Indigenous-led organization based in Rapid City, with the goal of fostering and supporting mentoring relationships and promoting wellness, prevention and healing for youth, adults, families and the community.

They go about these services in a manner that is tied to traditional Lakota practices.

“Western medicine and behavioral health services have an important role, but they can be strengthened when they respect and work alongside Indigenous knowledge and traditional ways of healing,” reads an OLO handout.

The nearly daylong event started with an educational tour that shared Lakota beliefs at the Crazy Horse Memorial. The event concluded with a visit to the OLO site in Rapid City, featuring presentations on the need for culturally-oriented addiction treatment and OLO's effectiveness as an organization.

State health data

According to American Indian Health Data from the South Dakota Department of Health from 2023 — the latest year with available data — Native Americans in South Dakota face higher rates of alcohol-related deaths, overdose-related deaths, lung cancer, maternal deaths, infant deaths, syphilis infection and other health issues compared to other groups.

"In the Department of Health, we gather a lot of data, a lot of data. A part of what we want to do is be able to tell the story about what our data says about us in the state of South Dakota, and unfortunately, a very precious group of people have some of the most (despairing) outcomes in the state of South Dakota," Magstadt said.

According to the state data, the median age of death in Oglala Lakota, Bennett and Todd counties ranges from 58 in Oglala Lakota County to 67 years in Bennett County. Pennington, Oglala Lakota, Jackson, Bennett, Todd and Millette Counties experience a higher social vulnerability. The data defines those vulnerabilities as poverty, lack of access to transportation and/or crowded housing.

 Melissa Magstadt
South Dakota secretary of Health Melissa Magstadt speaks during a gathering of officials with Oaye Luta Okolakiciye staff on Wednesday, Aug. 26. 

Magstadt stated Dr. Joshua Clayton, who is South Dakota’s epidemiologist, found that 50% of white South Dakotans reach age 80. In contrast, 50% of Native Americans in South Dakota reach age 58.

"It's a 22-year difference between two populations who share the same state and often are just one zip code away or one county away,” Magstedt said. "I said until those two numbers are the same, where our Native Americans and fellow South Dakotans live to the ripe old age of 80 as well, we have not completed our mission in the Department of Health."

According to the state's data, American Indian alcohol-related death rates were seven times higher than white death rates (120.9 vs 16.3), overdose-related death rates were 6.2 times higher than whites, suicide rates 2.6 times higher than whites, and reported higher rates of infant (4 to 5 times higher) and pregnancy-associated deaths (4 times higher) than the white population.

OLO treatment data

According to OLO, the organization provides low-barrier healthcare that treats trauma and addresses severe substance use and behavioral health.

The organization utilizes five levels of care ranging from one-on-one peer mentoring and specialized group programs to elder-led traditional assessments and ceremony-assisted treatment.

From Jan. 1, 2026 to Aug. 26, 2026, OLO reported it provided 1,200 meals, logged 1,500 walk-in visits and recorded nearly 500 attendances at healing sessions. The total number of people who used their services during that time frame was 381.

 Frank Star Comes Out
Oglala Sioux Tribe President Frank Star Comes Out, a United States Marine veteran, gave personal testimony about recovery from PTSD after his combat service in the Persian Gulf War and his post-service struggles. 

Of the 71 individuals who participated in OLO’s ceremony-assisted treatment program, 75% remained sober from drugs and alcohol, according to the organization.

Tyon said the Lakota ceremonies are the most effective way for the Indigenous community to seek support and treatment.

According to the National Library of Medicine, cultural interventions toward treating addiction in Native Americans have been shown to be effective.

"Yesterday, they gave me a little birthday cake because I celebrated 27 years of recovery. That was pretty cool for me. I never thought I could do this. I'm trying to help those that went through what I went through, and this is the way that helped me," Tyon said.

 Richard Two Dogs
Richard Two Dogs (Lakota), an elder with traditional knowledge of Lakota practices and beliefs, shares with the OLO group about Oglala Lakota leader Crazy Horse. The group attended Crazy Horse Memorial on Wednesday, Aug. 26. 

OLO argues that they provide a critical service by providing accessible, culturally grounded recovery care for Native Americans.

Aside from services, OLO’s programs are backed by an ongoing clinical trial funded by the National Institutes of Health, in partnership with researchers at Avera Health Research Institute and the University of Michigan.

The trial is scheduled for completion in early 2027, with data on culturally grounded care and its effectiveness in measurable health improvements, long-term alcohol abstinence and additional insights into OLO’s practices.

Coming together in a good way

In the midst of the discussion, Derby asked what legislators like him could do to help the cause.

Tyson replied, "To be a resource in the behavioral health department, the substance abuse addiction treatment programs."

Warne said section 1115 of the Social Security Act could reimburse programs like OLO for their “demonstration projects" that are likely found to assist in promoting objectives of the Medicaid Program.

In 2024, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services approved 1115 waivers in Arizona, California, New Mexico, and Oregon, allowing state Medicaid agencies to cover American Indian and Alaska Native traditional healthcare practices. The states allow coverage of certain traditional healthcare practices.

 OLO
From left to right: Jordyn Gunville-Pourier (Lakota), a senior research associate at the Johns Hopkins Center for Indigenous Health, and Donald Warne (Lakota) co-director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Indigenous Health.  

"We're just spending who knows how many billions of dollars for programs that are not working. We have a program here that's effective that doesn't get any of those resources, so it's tenuous, right?" Warne, with the Johns Hopkins Center for Indigenous Health, said... "So, it's not like South Dakota (is doing) something outside the norm or outside of what's possible because it's basically following the template."

Derby responded, saying, "I'm here because I want to help, and you have to help me help you, and there needs to be specific legislation brought forth by a secretary or another representative that could help do that, but time is of the essence."

Derby asked for further data on addiction recovery through ceremonial practices to present to legislative committees to drum up support for a bill.

Star Comes Out, a United States Marine veteran, gave personal testimony about recovery from PTSD after his combat service in the Persian Gulf War and his post-service struggles.

 Mike Derby
Rep. Mike Derby, R-34, attended the OLO group day event, asking how, as a legislator, he could help the organization.  

"I'm a living product of how our culture and spirituality work. Ten (to) 15 years ago, I was in real bad shape. I started at a young age, 19. I joined the service, boot camp, straight to war, right to the front lines. So, in the infantry, I experienced a lot. I've seen a lot of death."

He continued saying, "Once I got into inipi, I talked to a spiritual leader. He gave me the confidence of taking that first step, and that's the very first step that is the hardest, realizing you have a problem."

Inipi is a purification ceremony consisting of sweating out in an enclosed fixture.

Star Comes out said at one point he was taking different medications to address his ailments. He said the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs utilizes Native American culture and practices to aid in their Native American clients.

"We have evidence. There is proof and it works. Ask any veteran who goes through that in-house treatment,” Star Comes Out said.

The discussion ended with the group members coming together joyfully, with the expectation that talks supporting the Medicaid change will be pursued. 

Next steps

An OLO representative told the Journal the organization is looking at various options to push for Medicaid to help pay for cultural services, including the legislative route or arguing the services fall under religious freedom.

Currently, Tyon, with other partners, is looking to form a committee to advocate for a bill during the 2027 legislative session for this Medicaid change. Other avenues include advocating that Native American beliefs are equal to Christian denominations, something Rep. Pourier said, or claiming tribal sovereignty for culturally based practices.

title: Marilyn Opitz Dieken
description: February 25, 1955 - August 30, 2026
_full_text:
February 25, 1955 - August 30, 2026

Marilyn Opitz Dieken, born February 25, 1955, in Eden, S.D., to Vernon and Arlene Opitz, lived a life defined by fierce determination, courageous spirit, and a love that never wavered. She passed away on August 30, 2026, surrounded by the family she devoted her life to.

Marilyn grew up with a strength that was unmistakable — the kind that showed in the way she protected her loved ones, faced challenges head on, and built a life rooted in grit, generosity, and devotion. She shared a lifelong bond with her brother Vern (wife Brenda), whose presence remained a steady and cherished part of her life.

Marilyn married Kevin Stahl, and to that union were born her two children, Nicole (husband Bart) and Cody. Becoming a mother was one of her greatest joys, and nothing brought her more pride than watching her children grow into the people she loved so fiercely.

Later, Marilyn married Kenny Dieken, and with that marriage she gained three more children, Kristin, Karri, and Klint, whom she welcomed with the same open heart and steady devotion that defined her life. Together, Marilyn and Kenny poured their determination into building a trucking company, a testament to her entrepreneurial spirit and her willingness to take on new challenges with courage and conviction.

Marilyn was also a grandmother whose love was felt in every warm meal, every gathering, and every moment spent around her table. Her unforgettable grandma magic in the kitchen created comfort, healing, and tradition. Her grandchildren, Levi, Mesa, Lane, Mattie, Macy, Bionca, and Sterling, along with her niece, Mckenzie and nephews, Connor and Hayden Opitz, each held a special place in her heart, and she poured her love into them with the same fierce devotion that shaped her life.

Marilyn was preceded in death by her parents, her husband, Kenny Dieken, and her beloved granddaughter, Bionca.

A graveside burial will be held at Rose Hill Cemetery in Spearfish on September 10, 2026, at 3 p.m. A celebration of Marilyn's life will immediately follow at her home, 10784 Chicken Creek Rd, Spearfish.

Marilyn's legacy is one of strength, love, and tradition, a woman who stood firm when life demanded it, who loved without hesitation, and who created moments in the kitchen and beyond that her family will cherish for generations.

She will be deeply missed by her family, friends, and all who were touched by her unwavering heart.

Online condolences may be written at www.fidler-isburgfuneralchapels.com.

title: Richard E. (Dick) Kahler
description: March 14, 1930 - August 22, 2026
_full_text:
March 14, 1930 - August 22, 2026

Richard E. (Dick) Kahler, 96, died August 22, 2026, in Rapid City, SD. Dick was born in Sioux Falls, SD, on March 14, 1930, to E.J. (Ernie) and Millie I. Kahler.

Dick grew up in Sioux Falls and graduated from Washington High School in 1948. He left Sioux Falls to attend the University of Missouri Journalism School in Columbia, MO, graduating with a Bachelor of Journalism degree in 1952. He obtained high honors in ROTC while attending the university and entered military service in August 1952 as a Second Lieutenant in the Army Field Artillery.

In early 1953, Dick was deployed to Japan and then to Korea as a Forward Observer with the 24th Infantry Division Artillery. It was considered one of the deadliest assignments in the military, as the duties included going behind enemy lines, gathering information, and directing artillery fire in support of the infantry. At the last minute before deploying, the commanding general of his division reassigned him as his Public Information Officer because of his journalism background. This reassignment probably made the difference in whether Dick survived the war. He held the rank of First Lieutenant at the time of his honorable discharge in 1954.

Dick married Beverly J. Murphy in Columbia, MO, on June 14, 1952. In 1954, they moved to Rapid City. Dick and Bev were blessed with three children, Rick, David, and Jan. Bev was the love of his life, and they celebrated 72 years of marriage on June 14, 2024. She died 12 days later.

Dick began his employment with the Rapid City Journal in the advertising department, becoming the classified manager in 1957. In 1959, he joined R. Doc Baumann Real Estate. He became a full partner in 1962 and sole owner of Kahler Realtors in 1970. In 1973, Dick was the recipient of South Dakota's Realtor of the Year award. Dick retired in 1995 and sold the firm to his two sons. It operates today as Keller Williams Realty.

Throughout his career Dick was active in community organizations, including Cub Scouts (Cub Master), Boy Scouts, Rapid City Multiple Listing Service (President two terms), Black Hills Board of Realtors (President), South Dakota Real Estate Commission (Chairman), Rapid City Masonic Lodge #220, NAJA Shrine, NAJA Flag Unit (President), Rapid City Elks Club Lodge #1187, the Rapid City Chamber of Commerce Military Affairs Committee, and the Rapid City Cosmopolitan Club (Club President, Federation Governor, and International President).

He was a charter member of Westminster Presbyterian Church, an active board member of South Canyon Baptist Church, and most recently a member of Rimrock Evangelical Free Church. He served on that church's Financial Team for several years. In 2006, he was appointed to the Rapid City Christian School Board. He served a three-year term, helping the school build and move into its new Hart Ranch campus.

If you ever attended any events at the Rushmore Plaza Civic Center and Theater in the past forty-four years, you most likely met Dick. He, with his wife Bev at his side, served as the head usher and ticket taker in his very visible yellow Cosmopolitan Club jacket, greeting eventgoers with a hearty "Howdy" and his signature big smile. As a 67-year member of the Rapid City Cosmopolitan Club, he attended weekly service club meetings until a few years before his death. He was also a strong advocate for the new Summit Arena at The Monument, writing letters to the editor and speaking in public forums.

Advocacy ran deep with Dick. As a Realtor, he consistently put his clients' financial wellbeing above his own, to the extent that he refused to buy investment property for himself. His view was that to do so would put him in competition with his clients.

One of Dick's most notable achievements is something very few people knew, because he seldom talked about it. As a boy, Dick had a severe stutter. While there is no cure for this condition, through determination and hard work he completely overcame his speech disability.

Dick and Bev enjoyed traveling, especially in their motor home van. They visited 49 states, including Alaska several times. They were able to visit Canada, Mexico, Australia, New Zealand, Great Britain, and many European countries. Dick also enjoyed an annual tradition of going to the NCAA Men's Final Four games with his son Rick. He attended 21 Men's Final Fours between 1992 and 2016.

Raised in an alcoholic family, Dick counted 1973 as the highlight of his life. That year he became a Christian, ending his lifelong relationship with alcohol and beginning his deep relationship with his Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ. Dick's deeply held hope was that all his children and grandchildren have a personal relationship with Jesus Christ. Being a part of his grandchildren's and great-grandchildren's lives was a crowning point of his life.

In January 2023, Dick was found to have stage four lung cancer and given five or six months to live. Treatment with a new drug gave him another three and a half years cancer-free. Dick wanted to ensure his obituary conveyed his profound gratitude for the compassion and support shown by the staff at The Courtyard and Westhills Healthcare during the final years of his and Bev's lives.

He was preceded in death by his parents, Ernie and Millie Kahler; his wife of 72 years, Beverly J. Kahler, who died June 26, 2024; his two brothers, Jack and Steve Kahler; and his daughter-in-law, Renaye (Dave) Kahler.

He is survived by his three children: son Rick Kahler (Marcia), and grandchildren London/Seth and Davin; son Dave Kahler (Renee), and grandchild Joshua Montgomery (Talya) and great-grandchild Lynk, grandchild Jeremy (Amanda) and great-grandchildren Lucas, Madelyn, and Gwenyth, and grandchild Brianna Satterfield (Dan) and great-grandchildren Sophia, Aidall, Olive, and Benjamin; and daughter Jan Kahler, and grandchild Tyler Blumenthal (Laura) and great-grandchildren Leah, Colby, and Dane, and grandchild Nikki Davis (Kyle); and many nephews, nieces, extended family, and very close friends.

The visitation will be from 4 to 6 p.m., Monday, October 12, 2026, at Osheim & Schmidt Funeral Home in Rapid City, SD.

The memorial service will be at 11 a.m., Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at South Canyon Baptist Church, 3333 West Chicago Street, Rapid City, SD.

The burial service will be at 3 p.m., Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at Black Hills National Cemetery near Sturgis, SD with full military honors.

Arrangements with www.osheimschmidt.com

Memorials may be made to the Rapid City Christian High School Endowment Fund; Love, Inc.; and Young Life.

title: Pennington County employees told to stay home after cyberattack will lose vacation time or go without pay
description: The Pennington County Board of Commissioners voted not to compensate county employees who were told not to report to work after a July cyberattack ground some county services to a halt.
_full_text:
The Pennington County Board of Commissioners voted not to compensate county employees who were told not to report to work after a July cyberattack ground some county services to a halt.

If employees wanted to receive pay, they had to use vacation time. Those who reported to work, as instructed, were paid their normal wages. If the county had declared an emergency, which it did not, those workers would have received time-and-a-half.

 Ron Rossknecht
On Tuesday Sept. 1 the Pennington County Board of Commissioners voted to make no changes for employee leave and further compensation for county employees told not to report for duty after the July cybersecurity breach. 

According to a county document, a cybersecurity incident was discovered over the Independence Day weekend. The county's IT staff then requested that county systems remain offline to assess the cyberattack.

On the evening prior to the first scheduled workday after the incident — Monday, July 6 — a countywide employee notification advised employees not to report to work, while also directing them to contact their supervisors regarding work expectations, per a memo from Commission Office Director Jordan Neeb. The memo did not directly quote the information that went out to employees.

The county paused some services on July 6 and has since been involved in a multi-agency investigation into the security incident. The breach continues to affect county services.

 Neeb Memo from Sept. 2 Pennington County Commission agenda packet
A memo from Commission Office Director Jordan Neeb to the Pennington County Commission was included in the Sept. 2 commission agenda packet. Neeb explains the situation surrounding payroll on July 6, a day some county employees were told to stay home in the wake of a cyberattack. 

Pennington County Commission Office Communications Manager Cody Wiseman said he couldn’t comment when asked about the wording in the message because it’s related to the cyberattack.

Department heads made decisions on staffing, per the memo. The county has more than 800 employees, according to its human resources department. It’s unclear exactly how many employees were told to stay home.

Ron Weifenbach (District 2) told the Journal an estimated 75% of employees showed up for work.

According to county documents, no formal declaration or authorization to close county facilities under the County's Emergency Facility Closure policy was made.

 Lara Roetzel
Pennington County State's Attorney Lara Roetzel voiced her support to have employees who used leave time to have leave restored and those who used unpaid time to be compensated for the day. 

In the event the procedure is enacted, employees instructed to work during the emergency are paid time-and-a-half, and nonexempt employees instructed not to work are given paid leave for the shifts they miss.

“The chair of the board (Weifenbach) has since indicated that it was not his intent to declare an emergency facility closure related to the cybersecurity incident,” per the Neeb memo.

According to county documents, the commission looked at four options: Making no changes, restoring leave used by employees, providing compensation for those who used unpaid time and/or giving employees who worked time-and-a-half pay.

The estimated financial impact for the four options ranged from $0 to $133,000.

After the board reviewed those options, Commissioner Jerry Derr (District 4) made a motion to make no changes to how employees were paid or not paid. That motion passed with a 3-2 vote. Commissioners Ron Rossknecht (District 1) and Gary Drewes (District 5) voted against.

Drewes made an alternate motion to qualify employees who used leave to have their hours restored, while employees who took unpaid time would receive equivalent paid compensation, but no time-and-a-half. That motion failed 2-3, with Deb Hadcock (District 3), Weifenbach, and Derr voting no.

Before the board voted, department heads made their case on whether employees should get coverage for the day.

Officials weigh in

Pennington County Sheriff Brian Mueller said he supported the option to not recognize the day as an emergency closure.

 Brian Mueller
Pennington County Sheriff Brian Mueller told the county he agreed with their decision to make no further changes.  

"To just pay the ones that (didn’t) come to work … I think is problematic for three-quarters of the employees from Pennington County that came to work that day," Mueller said. "But also at the same time, I think the financial impact of paying everybody time-and-a-half for coming in and doing their regular work doesn't necessarily seem right for me."

Pennington County State’s Attorney Lara Roetzel voiced her support for compensating employees.

"I think that (it) needs to be clear for the record that our people were heeded not to report, and many of them live paycheck to paycheck, and even one day of leave impact matters," Roetzel said.

Natural Resources Department Director Scott Guffey said he supported keeping things as they are.

Equalization Director Trevor Abernathie said he was the only person to report for duty in his department, but supported restoring the leave time for employees who used it and compensating those who used unpaid time for the day.

"I think that with this being a factor, our leave and our vacation pay is so broad and so lucrative to employees that I'm fine with option A," Weifenbach said about making no changes.

Hadcock said, "The bottom line, (this) comes down to the complexity and the anomaly for what happened (the cyberattack), hopefully at this point we've learned something."

title: ‘A duty to never forget’: Rapid City Fire Department reflects on 9/11
description: Fresh off a grueling 24-hour private ambulance shift on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, future Rapid City Fire Chief Jason Culberson expected quiet after his 6-year-old headed off to kindergarten. Instead, an urgent phone call from his father to turn on the news revealed the smoking silhouette of the World Trade Center, instantly transforming a routine Tuesday into the defining tragedy of a generation.
_full_text:
Fresh off a grueling 24-hour private ambulance shift on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, future Rapid City Fire Chief Jason Culberson expected quiet after his 6-year-old headed off to kindergarten. Instead, an urgent phone call from his father to turn on the news revealed the smoking silhouette of the World Trade Center, instantly transforming a routine Tuesday into the defining tragedy of a generation.

In an interview with the Journal on Wednesday, Sept. 3, reflecting on the milestone nearly 25 years later, Culberson recalled how the initial shock rapidly gave way to a singular, consuming drive to serve.

He said several firefighters and EMS from South Dakota Wildland, Rapid City Fire Department and the many volunteer fire departments pushed to go help in New York. Culberson said being in this line of work creates a family that relies on one another regardless of state lines.

 Jason Culberson and Dexter with 9/11 memorial statue
Rapid City Fire Department Fire Chief Jason Culberson and Department’s Mascot Dexter stand in front of the 9/11 memorial statue New York City gifted Station 1 for South Dakota efforts after the World Trade Center was attacked. 

According to KOTA, the Rapid City Fire Department attempted to send out 12 firefighters to help in New York, but the deployment was canceled. However, that didn’t stop other volunteers from South Dakota from going to help with the cleanup.

Culberson said that pull wasn’t reserved for those wearing a badge or carrying turnout gear. It was an innate, collective reflex that swept across the country, as ordinary citizens stood shoulder-to-shoulder with firefighters, paramedics and police officers to help during tragic times. He said it was the most united he’s ever seen the nation.

“That first year, of course, you felt a lot of unity amongst the community and the country felt unified,” Culberson said. “Everybody rallied together for a common cause and what we wanted to accomplish and protect each other and help each other.”

 Sign close up
The Fire Department of New York gifted a statue to the citizens of Rapid City for their support during the City of New York’s time of need. 

Though the attack on the World Trade Center left many scars throughout the nation, Culberson said it helped push a new frontier of communication, command structures, training and health standards across the country.

Culberson said 9/11 highlighted severe radio communication failures between first responders. Since then, the FirstNet Authority was created, making a high-speed public safety broadband network for first responders to better communicate during emergencies.

As a new generation of firefighters steps onto the rigs to face today’s calls, many carry no personal memory of 9/11, some were not even born yet. For them, the history comes in fragments, passed down by a veteran generation that swore to never forget, and Culberson said the fire department is doing just that.

Coming up on Friday, Sept. 11, on behalf of the Ellsworth Firefighters Association and the Rapid City Firefighters Association, there will be a day of remembrance as the community marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

 Close up of the statue
A piece of the World Trade Center sits in front of Rapid City Fire Department’s Station 1 as a reminder to never forget what happened on Sept. 11, 2001. 

“Of course, we’re coming up to the 25th anniversary of 9/11. Which is definitely an important time to sit back and remember for us,” Culberson said. “About the nearly 3,000 people that died, which include 343 FDNY members, but we want to also remember those that survived; the families that still carry that loss and the responders who continue to suffer from the illnesses they’ve contracted since working at (Ground Zero).”

Culberson said the event is to recognize not only those who made the ultimate sacrifice, but also those who were impacted after the incident.

Throughout the day there will be several events for the community to be a part of:

A memorial ceremony at Founders Park at 8 a.m. honoring those who lost their lives on 9/11. Guest speakers such as South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden, Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun, Culberson and SD Wildland Firefighter Mike Reed, who assisted in the cleanup in New York, will be speaking at the event.

A ruck march bringing together first responders, military personnel, veterans and community members. This M-Hill Stair Climb, symbolizes the 110 stories FDNY firefighters climbed at the World Trade Center. March begins up M-Hill at 9:11 a.m.

The 9/11 Memorial Golf Tournament at Meadowbrook Golf Course, raising funds to support first responders, veterans and the Children’s Hospital Colorado Burn Center. The tournament starts at noon.

“It’s very important to us to continue to remember that. To preserve that history, tell the story accurately and ensure the lessons and the sacrifices, so that they are never forgotten,” Culberson said.

title: SD Highway Patrol promoting school bus safety
description: The South Dakota Highway Patrol will conduct a three‑day School Bus Safety Outreach event Sept. 8–10 to increase public awareness and reinforce safe driving behaviors around school buses statewide.
_full_text:
The South Dakota Highway Patrol will conduct a three‑day School Bus Safety Outreach event Sept. 8–10 to increase public awareness and reinforce safe driving behaviors around school buses statewide.

During the outreach period, troopers will partner with school districts to observe bus routes, monitor loading zones, and ensure motorists follow state school bus stopping laws. Patrol vehicles will be visible near school bus stops, loading areas, and along high‑traffic routes where children board and exit buses.

The Highway Patrol’s goal is to remind drivers of safety requirements, reduce dangerous driving behavior, and help protect South Dakota students as they travel to and from school.

“School bus safety is a shared responsibility,” said Captain Jon Stahl. “Our presence during these three days is meant to educate drivers, support school districts, and reinforce that stopping for school buses isn’t optional—it’s essential for protecting children.”

Troopers will take part in several activities including:

Following select school buses along their routes to observe motorist behavior

Positioning marked patrol vehicles near loading zones to increase visibility

Conducting targeted safety operations to identify violations and encourage compliance; and

Providing safety reminders and information to community members and media

The Highway Patrol encourages all motorists to remain alert, slow down near school buses and always stop when red bus lights are flashing. Small actions behind the wheel can prevent tragic outcomes.

South Dakota Highway Patrol troopers are available for interviews to discuss details of the event and share important information on bus safety.

The Highway Patrol is an agency of the South Dakota Department of Public Safety.

title: Wells drying up at homes and ranches in West River due to heat and drought
byline: BART PFANKUCH South Dakota News Watch
description: CAPUTA — Each morning this summer, Gordon and Connie Howie have awoken on their cattle ranch in central Pennington County and turned on the kitchen faucet, unsure if any water will come out.
_full_text:
CAPUTA — Each morning this summer, Gordon and Connie Howie have awoken on their cattle ranch in central Pennington County and turned on the kitchen faucet, unsure if any water will come out.

“We can’t do laundry or dishes or take showers other than with a little trickle,” said Connie Howie, 76. “Other times we have a little water because it seems to come and go.”

Like many ranchers and residents in rural areas of western South Dakota, the Howie family relies on a well to provide them with water for their lives and livelihood.

 2026-08-20 Dry wells Howie feeding bills.jpeg
Gordon Howie inserts bills to pay for fresh water at J&J Asphalt in Rapid City, S.D., on Aug. 20, 2026. 

But this year, perhaps the worst in recent memory, many shallow wells are running slow or have gone completely dry, forcing people to go to great lengths and expense to provide clean water for themselves or their livestock.

Experts say several consecutive years of limited winter snow pack and a shortage of rainfall have combined with increased consumption of water to cause a decrease in the levels of some underground aquifers that are a main source of water for a large swath of the Black Hills region. The problem is most acute in areas outside the reach of pipes from municipal and rural water systems.

High heat during the summer of 2026 has exacerbated the problem as people, crops and animals all require more water than usual to survive.

“We have a well at the house, but it’s just not keeping up because the aquifer is dry,” said Gordon Howie. “For 20 years you could trust that well 24/7, and it never quit on us, but now it’s not providing enough water for everything we need.”

 2026-08-20 Dry wells Howie on ladder.jpeg
Rancher Gordon Howie of Caputa, S.D. connects his tank to a water hose at J&J Asphalt in Rapid City, S.D., on Aug. 20, 2026, to gather fresh water needed for his cattle. 

The Howies are buying bottled water for drinking and positioning jugs of fresh water throughout the house for daily uses.

“I’ve lived here my whole life and I’ve never seen it this dry, this hot, this long,” said Gordon Howie, who served in the Legislature from 2009-2011 and ran for governor in 2010.

All across the plains of western South Dakota, residents who rely on shallow wells — generally 1,000 feet deep or less — are being forced to find alternative water sources.

 South Dakota News Watch logo
Learn more about South Dakota News Watch at sdnewswatch.org. 

Some are utilizing a somewhat obscure system of obtaining water in which users insert quarters or bills into a vending machine that triggers a hanging water spout to provide fresh water that is collected in tanks in pickups or on trailers. Such water stations are available in Black Hawk, Deadwood, Piedmont, Rapid City, Spearfish and Sturgis.

Those self-serve water stations are much busier than usual this summer, particularly in Rapid City, where the spout at J&J Asphalt is the only bulk water available in town and is often accessible only after a long wait.

 2026-08-20 Dry wells old man tanker.jpeg
Amanda Rivera and Ralph Bifulco fill a tank with fresh water at J&J Asphalt in Rapid City, S.D., on Aug. 20, 2026. 

"Everybody is hauling water these days,” said Nick Randall, shop foreman at J&J Asphalt, whose shop and water station are located in an industrial area off Dyess Avenue.

Many rural residents have clean water delivered by truck, which requires planning and expense.

Businesses such as Frontier Water in Rapid City are extremely busy this summer.

“With all these shallow wells going dry, it’s really boosted my business,” said Darin Klapperich, the owner of Frontier who also ranches northwest of Rapid City.

Klapperich gathers purified fresh water from municipal systems across the Black Hills and delivers it to customers.

 Dry wells woman inspects flow
Amanda Rivera monitors drinking water flowing into a tank at J&J Asphalt in Rapid City, S.D., on Aug. 20, 2026. 

On arrival, the water is dumped into a cattle tank or a holding tank for household use. At some locations, he fills underground concrete cisterns people use to store water on their properties and occasionally drains the water into a well to fill it part way, Klapperich said.

To avoid future dry spells, the Howies plan to drill a new, deeper well to replace the 30-foot well that has run dry. The couple will continue to use a reverse osmosis system in the house to purify the well water for drinking and other uses.

Until then, he'll continue his twice-weekly water-gathering ritual, positioning his trailer below the J&J spigot, climbing a ladder to connect an extension pipe to the spout, unfurling bills into the payment slot and filling the tank on his trailer.

“I let every last dribble go in, because those cattle have got to have water,” he said.

 2026-08-27 Wells Black Hawk water station.jpeg
The self-serve water stations around the Black Hills region, such as this one in Black Hawk, S.D., on Aug. 26, 2026, are nothing fancy but serve a major purpose for people whose wells run slow or not at all.

title: South Dakota Supreme Court will not rehear Hideaway Hills sinkhole case
description: The Hideaway Hills sinkhole case appears to have reached a dead-end in the South Dakota Court system.
_full_text:
The Hideaway Hills sinkhole case appears to have reached a dead-end in the South Dakota Court system.

On Aug. 27, the South Dakota Supreme Court denied the Black Hawk neighborhood’s homeowners’ request for a rehearing of their case against the state.

On July 9, the court delivered a unanimous opinion that the state’s role as the mineral rights owner doesn’t constitute public use or make it liable for the unstable ground the neighborhood was built on. On July 30, the attorneys representing Hideaway Hills homeowners filed a petition asking the Supreme Court to rehear the case.

Hideaway Hills was completed around 2005 on top of an old, underground gypsum mine for which the state retains mineral rights. Issues began to arise in 2008, with residents noticing foundational issues like cracking and settling in the walls and basements of their homes. Later that year, small sinkholes began to open.

 Sinkhole through the fence
A view of the largest Hideaway Hills sinkhole through a fence on Monday, July 27. The South Dakota Supreme Court recently ruled the state is not liable for the damage to the neighborhood, which sits on an old gypsum mine for which the state retains mineral rights. 

Those issues reached a crisis point in April 2020 when a large, 30-foot-deep sinkhole opened up on East Daisy Drive in Hideaway Hills, forcing 13 homes to be evacuated. The subdivision is currently home to 150 homeowners and the 13 evacuated homes remain vacant.

Although the state, developer, homebuilders and realtor who sold the properties knew about the mine underneath the surface before the notorious sinkhole opened up, the homebuyers did not.

The lawsuit against the state is not the only one the homeowners have unsuccessfully raised.

South Dakota Searchlight reported multiple lawsuits against Meade County, the land’s developers and the real estate agent who represented the homebuilders were dismissed.

The homeowners have also reached out to governor candidates — including current Gov. Larry Rhoden, who recently won the Republican runoff and is headed for the general election ballot to face Democrat Dan Ahlers — about if they’ll help the residents.

In July, Rhoden said his staff is looking into what the options are and if — or how — the state can help.

“I have zero information about what our options might be. That’s what we’re going to do, is see,” Rhoden said.

Ian Fury, Rhoden’s campaign manager and member of the governor’s executive team, said the day the South Dakota Supreme Court ruling came down, Rhoden instructed his team to look into what the options are.

Ahlers issued a statement that read, in part, “We need to work with these families, local leaders, and other stakeholders to find a fair path forward that helps make this situation right. Whether through legislative action, targeted assistance, or other solutions, we have a responsibility to stand with South Dakotans when they face extraordinary circumstances.”

title: Jim Sutton
description: April 20, 1935 - September 3, 2026
_full_text:
April 20, 1935 - September 3, 2026

Jim Sutton, 91, passed away Thursday, September 3, 2026. Visitation will be held 10:00-11:00am, Monday, September 14, 2026 at the Sully Buttes Gymnasium with a Funeral Celebration of Life following begining at 11:00am. Interment will follow at the Onida Cemetery. Condolences may be conveyed to the family and his service may be viewed online at www.feigumfh.com.

James Louverne Sutton, Jr. was born to James and Flossie (Nystrom) Sutton April 20th, 1935, in Hughes County. He grew up on the Sutton Ranch beside the Missouri River and was educated in Sully County rural schools, Onida High School, and South Dakota State University.

High school sweethearts, Jim, and Julie (Nelson) Sutton were married in June 1953. They lived in Brookings, while Jim was attending SDSU to play basketball and rodeo. Their daughter, Teri and son, Steve, were born there. He joined ROTC and served as a second lieutenant in the artillery at Ft. Sill, OK. Jim received a degree in Animal Husbandry at SDSU where he was an all-conference basketball player for two years and was the national free-throw champion for percentage shot.

The Minneapolis Lakers drafted Jim and he attended their preseason training camp. However, he believed following his father and grandfather in the ranching business made more financial sense than a basketball career.

In 1968, Jim and Julie joined Jim's father, James, in creating the Sutton Rodeo Company. Edwin Sutton, Jim's grandfather, produced the first rodeo on the home ranch in 1926. Their daughter, Tanya was born while living at the ranch. They supplied stock from their Agar, S.D., ranch to rodeos across South Dakota and the Northwest. By the late 1970s, Sutton's were raising more than 90% of their own bucking stock and developed a breeding program that is one of the best in the business.

The program produced three PRCA Horse of the Year winners: saddle bronc horse Deep Water (1979), bareback horse Big Bud (1985), and saddle bronc horse Chuckulator (2012). Chuckulator also won Top Saddle Bronc Horse of the National Finals Rodeo in 2012. The program also earned Sutton four nominations for PRCA Stock Contractor of the Year, with Sutton Rodeo stock selected to perform at every National Finals Rodeo since it started in 1959 but two.

Jim and Julie won the PRCA Donita Barnes Lifetime Achievement Award in 2017. The award, created to recognize PRCA members who have dedicated their lives to the rodeo industry for their commitment, work, and contributions. Jim and Julie were perfect candidates for this honor.

Jim served as Director and past president of Miss Rodeo America and on the PRCA's Executive Council as Rodeo Committee Representative. He valued the friendships made with rodeo committees, personnel, and sponsors. Jim was inducted into the ProRodeo Hall of Fame Class of 2020, for Stock Contractor.

Jim is past president and Director of SD American Quarter Horse Association and National AQHA.

Jim is preceded in death by his parents James and Flossie, wife Julie, daughter Teri, siblings Delores, Lorraine, and Lyle. Jim and Julie enjoyed 68 years of marriage. They were blessed with children: Teri (Monte) Melvin, Steve (Kim) Sutton, Tanya (Todd) Yackley; grandchildren: Amy (Steven) Muller, Blake (Kayla) Yackley, Brent (Roz) Sutton, Sasha Yackley, Brice (Alyssa) Sutton, Wayne Yackley (Rozlynn Murrow); and great grandchildren: Shaden Muller, Shally Muller; Jett Yackley, Nathan Nelson, Lakyn Yackley, Tracen Yackley, Wesley Yackley; Sid and Scottie Sutton; Briggston, Bevin Bertsche; Ruby Sutton, Stella Sutton, Waylon Sutton; and Vera Jo Yackley.

In lieu of flowers, Jim would like memorials sent to SDSU Athletic-Rodeo/Basketball, Casey Tibbs Hall of Fame, Ft Pierre, SD and ProRodeo Hall of Fame, Colorado Springs, CO.

title: Minnesota man arrested after stabbing in Deadwood gaming resort’s parking lot
description: A Minnesota man was arrested after allegedly stabbing a 44-year-old man on Main Street in Deadwood.
_full_text:
A Minnesota man was arrested after allegedly stabbing a 44-year-old man on Main Street in Deadwood.

Preston Wolowicz, 20, was arrested on suspicion of attempted first-degree murder and aggravated assault.

On Sept. 6, Sunday, at 2:02 a.m., Lawrence County Dispatch received multiple reports of a stabbing at Cadillac Jack’s Gaming Resort’s parking lot at 360 Main Street in Deadwood.

The suspect had fled the scene as officers from the Deadwood Police Department responded. A short time later, officers located an individual matching the suspect’s description near Whitewood Creek, across from 402 Main Street.

Police said Wolowicz and the 44-year-old man — also from Minnesota — had been involved in an altercation in the parking lot of the resort, resulting in Wolowicz allegedly stabbing the man multiple times before fleeing.

The injured man was evaluated by emergency personnel and transported to a local hospital where he remains in critical condition.

This investigation remains active and ongoing, investigators said they believe this is an isolated incident. Anyone with information concerning this case is asked to contact Detective Sergeant Sally Sprigler at 605-578-2623.

title: Lookout Fire at 443 acres; no containment declared
description: The Lookout Fire burning near Spearfish is at 443 acres per a Tuesday, Sept. 8 update. Containment has not been declared on the fire.
_full_text:
The Lookout Fire burning near Spearfish is at 443 acres per a Tuesday, Sept. 8 update. Containment has not been declared on the fire.

The wildfire is just east of Interstate 90 on the north side of Lookout Mountain near Spearfish. Watch Duty, which tracks wildfires, first shows a report of the fire at 2:53 p.m. on Monday, Sept. 7. By 5:15 p.m. on Monday, the fire was at 100 acres before growing to an estimated 300 acres by 6:47 p.m. Monday.

The fire is at 443 acres as of a Tuesday morning update from the South Dakota Department of Public Safety.

 Lookout Fire Map for September 8. 2026

According to the department, fire lines held steady overnight Monday with no significant growth. The goal Tuesday is to keep the fire at its current footprint.

Specific objectives include keeping the fire South of Kerwin Lane, North of Lookout Peak, East of Interstate 90, and West of Lookout Mountain Lane.

Crews stopped forward progress of the fire to the north on Monday night and began working on the southern end of the fire, putting in place a dozer line across the south end, up and over the ridge. There are residences, businesses and churches on the south base of Lookout Mountain.

State, federal, local, and out-of-state resources are assisting in the interagency firefight. Significant aerial resources played a key role in Monday’s effort and will continue that support again today.

 Spearfish wildfire (Copy)
Traffic is closed in one lane of I-90 northbound between mile marker 10 and 12 due to the Lookout Fire. 

Some intersections, lanes closed; flight restrictions in place

There are temporary flight restrictions over the perimeter of the fire and the public is warned not to fly any unauthorized aircraft of the fire.

Traffic is closed in one lane of I-90 northbound between mile marker 10 and 12. Traffic is closed at the following intersections: Kerwin Lane and Highway 85, Kerwin Lane and Lookout Rd., and Lookout Mountain Rd and Airport Rd. The public is asked to avoid the area due to ongoing active fire suppression activity including personnel and equipment.

Evacuations in place, but not mandatory

Lawrence County Emergency Management ordered evacuations at 3:48 p.m. Monday in the immediate area of Lookout Mountain, Kerwin Road, Lookout Vista Road and surrounding areas.

Per the Spearfish Police Department on Monday afternoon, law enforcement was conducting evacuations of residences that may be threatened by the fire.

The South Dakota Department of Public Safety said in its Tuesday update there are no mandatory evacuations in place, but voluntary evacuations remain in place for some residences in the vicinity of the fire.

title: Patricia Shank
description: March 17, 1929 - September 2, 2026
_full_text:
March 17, 1929 - September 2, 2026

RAPID CITY - Patricia "Pat" Marie (Hardy) Shank was born on March 17, 1929 and died on September 2, 2026 at the age of 97.

Her parents were Arthur and Irmgard (Lehmann) Hardy from Sturgis, SD.

Pat loved that she was born on St. Patrick's Day. Her parents had chosen another name for her but the delivery nurse said "you have to name her Patricia" and so they did. Because her birthday was on a holiday, everyone remembered and she always received lots of cards and phone calls and celebrated the entire week.

Pat grew up on a farm near Sturgis and loved the country life and helping her father Art who she adored. Pat was an only child for about six years until Shirley and Maxine were born. The Hardy Girls were a force of nature. They loved each other, had so much fun together and stayed close their whole lives.

After High School, Pat got a teaching certificate and taught in a Rural K-12 school for a year. She married Tillman Shank of Rapid City in 1948 and they had three children, Char Lii (Robert) Eastwood of Anselmo, NE, Cathy (Stephen) Meradith of Lincoln, NE and Bryan (Nancy) Shank of Lincoln, NE. While her children were growing up, she was a stay-at-home Mom who was lots of fun and a great cook. Her pies were always in demand. Till worked for Northwestern Bell Telephone and his job moved them from Rapid City to Omaha to North Platte and finally back to Omaha. After her children were grown, Pat worked for many years running estate sales in Omaha and later got her real estate license. When Till retired in the late 1980's they decided to move back home to the beautiful Black Hills of South Dakota. They had several years in Rapid City before Till died in November of 1996.

Pat remained in Rapid City and we were so proud of the way she made a new life for herself. She loved her home and stayed busy with many activities like attending "the Broadways" at the Civic Center and dining/shopping excursions but most of all being a part of Maxine's family. She was always included in whatever the Sieler family was doing. She thought of Maxine's children (Julie & Jay) as her second family and loved Julie & Todd's boys (Ian, Calvin and Brennan) like they were her own. She was also close to Shirley's girls Tammy & Kim and Tammy's children Nathaniel (Nate) Goodman & Kiva Goodman.

Since she remained in Rapid City, she had to come to Nebraska every Fall to visit her children and very special and only grandchild Cole. She would stay for 2 to 3 weeks of shopping, eating, movies and plays and sitting around in the evenings drinking red wine and talking for hours. At the end of the visits, we had to beg Maxine to get her back to Rapid City because we were exhausted!

In her later years, she met a special friend, Jim Randash and had the opportunity to take many exciting trips within the US and abroad which is something she had never done before and she loved it. She also spent several wonderful holidays with Jim's family in Denver. We appreciate their kindness and generosity to her.

As her health began to fail, she sold her home and moved into assisted living at Echo Ridge and later to Saint Martin Village. We would like to thank the staff of these 2 facilities for the care they provided her.

Pat was preceded in death by her parents, husband, sister Shirley Walters of Tucson, AZ and brother-in-law David Sieler of Rapid City.

She is survived by her children, grandson Cole Patrick Crawford Shank of Boulder, CO, dear sister Maxine Sieler of Rapid City, nieces Julie (Todd) Brink of Rapid City, Tamara Walters of Tucson, AZ, Kimberly (Tom) Jordan of Fort Collins, CO, nephew Jay Sieler of Minneapolis, MN and the great niece and nephews listed above.

We love you so much Mom and will miss having you in our lives but we know you are in Heaven where you wanted to be.

Memorials can be made to either the Theatre 605 Black Hills Playhouse in Custer, SD, a charity of your choice in Pat's honor or to the family for future designation.

Visitation will be 12:00 to 1:00 PM Monday, September 14 at Osheim & Schmidt Funeral Home with the Funeral Service at 1:00 PM. Burial will be at 2:30 PM at Black Hills National Cemetery near Sturgis, SD.

Arrangements with www.osheimschmidt.com
