title: Betty Jean Halstead
description: April 9, 1934 - September 1, 2026
_full_text:
April 9, 1934 - September 1, 2026

Betty was Born in Newell South Dakota, April 9, 1934, to Jacob and Katie (Hinkel) Jordan. She grew up there in the Newell and Nisland area, attending school there and working on various farms with her family, growing sugar beets, corn and cattle. In 1950, she moved to Belle Fouche, where she took a job working at Belle Telephone as a telephone operator. In 1951, she married Richard Vincent Justice. To this union she was blessed with two sons, Richard and Robert.

After her first husband passed in 1970, she worked at John Burns Memorial Hospital. In 1972, she married Pat Halstead, who had three grown daughters, Alice, Donna, and Paula. She and Pat lived on the ranch west of Spearfish. She enjoyed ranch life and all that it entailed, such as hay season, calving season, lambing season, cattle drives, rodeo. She spent 51 years on the ranch and loved all the adventures ranch life offered and she especially loved being a wife, mother, grandmother and great (great) grandmother. And doing crafts, playing the piano, and working in her yard and taking care of her animals.

On March 20, 2000, Pat passed away and Betty remained on the ranch property. On April 16, 2006, at Cheery Easter Service at the St Onge church, Betty married Buck E.R Brengle. They remained married until Buck passed away in June of 2013.

Betty then remained on the ranch alone until 2023, when health issues caused her to move to Highgate Assisted Living Facility in Billings MT closer to family. Betty passed away on September 1st, 2026, at the age of 92.

She is grateful for sharing her life with her two sons, Richard and wife Helen, and their six children Kathy, Stephen, Chrissy (Gene), Sarah (Chris), Amy, Christa (Dave), 17 great grandchildren of Washington State. Robert and Dixie with their daughters Patti (Jay), Stanfill and Linda (Jeff) Johnson and seven great grandchildren of Montana. As well as three stepdaughters Alice Sprauger, Donna Halstead and Paula Halstead of South Dakota, one stepson John Brengle of Texas, two step grandchildren Tammy (Chad) Wojtalewicz and Tanya (Todd) Johnson, and three step great grandchildren. Three very close and loving nieces, Diane, Sharon and Janet as well as their wonderful families.

Betty was preceded in death by her parents Jacob and Katie Jordan, brother Ervin, sister Dorothy Zorn, brother-in law John Zorn, grandchildren Kathy and Stephen Justice and three loving husbands.

Funeral services will be held at 10:00 AM on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, at Connection Church Belle Fourche, SD located at: 613 6th Avenue, Belle Fourche, SD with a visitation being held one hour prior to the service. Burial will follow at Pine Hills cemetery. Arrangements are under the care of Fidler-Isburg Funeral Chapel. Online condolences may be written at https://www.fidler-isburgfuneralchapels.com/.

title: Updated: Rapid City drug call ends with officer bit, suspect dying in custody; DCI investigating incident
byline: MADISON WILLIS and SHALOM BAER GEE Journal staff
description: For the second time in a year, a person placed in a full-body WRAP restraint system has been found unresponsive in the back of a patrol vehicle, following a struggle between the man and Rapid City police late Tuesday night. The investigation into the incident last year determined the WRAP was not the cause of death. The state’s investigative arm is looking into the recent incident.
_full_text:
For the second time in a year, a person placed in a full-body WRAP restraint system has been found unresponsive in the back of a patrol vehicle, following a struggle between the man and Rapid City police late Tuesday night. The investigation into the incident last year determined the WRAP was not the cause of death. The state’s investigative arm is looking into the recent incident.

At around 11:15 p.m. Tuesday, Sept. 8, police responded to an apartment complex at 28 Racine Street for a report of an unknown man who was acting erratically. It was reported the man appeared to be under the influence of drugs.

Upon arrival police made contact with the man, where police said the man admitted to have taken drugs. Police said the man “became uncooperative and began physically fighting with officers.”

The man bit an officer, breaking skin and an officer used a stun gun to get the man under control, the department said. The suspect was ultimately taken into custody and was placed into the WRAP safety restraint device due to his uncooperative behavior.

What is a WRAP system?
The WRAP system is manufactured by Safe Restraints. It features a locking shoulder harness, leg restraint, ankle strap and the option of carrying handles.
 Per Rapid City Police Department’s rules and procedures, the WRAP is designed as a temporary restraining device. The rules and procedures document reads, “Used properly, it can increase officer safety and reduce the risk of liability due to injuries and in-custody deaths.”
 In most cases when applying the WRAP, the suspect is placed prone, faced down with hands cuffed behind their back. Officers “will minimize the time subject is restrained face down to reduce the risks associated with respiratory fatigue,” per RCPD rules and procedures.

Following standard law enforcement practice after a stun gun deployment, a medical unit evaluated the man and told police his vitals were good.

The man was then transported to the Pennington County Jail, where jail staff located the unresponsive man in the patrol car. Emergency CPR was administered by jail staff, an ambulance was called and the man was taken to the hospital.

Police said the man died at the hospital. The man’s name is being withheld until proper notification to next of kin can be made.

Due to the in-custody nature of the man’s death, the investigation into the incident has been handed over to the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation, with the assistance of the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office.

Less than one year ago

Last year, the Rapid City Police Department experienced a similar situation after Tyrell Larson, 43, of Wolsey, died after being arrested and restrained on Sept. 19, 2025. The WRAP was used 65 times in 2025 and 36 times year-to-date in 2026, according to the police department.

In a Sept. 22, 2025 update, DCI said a medical examiner performed an autopsy and the department is awaiting a toxicology report. That October, DCI’s answer to a string of questions about the incident from the Journal was that, “DCI has completed its investigation and found no criminal laws were violated” and the investigation report was turned over to Rapid City police for review.

On Wednesday, Sept. 9, Rapid City police told the Journal that investigation determined "the officers involved in his arrest acted appropriately, based on his combative and resistive demeanor during the interaction with law enforcement."

An autopsy determined Larson died due to an enlarged heart, the presence of methamphetamine and his recent physical altercation in a fight, police said, noting, "The cause of death was identified as sudden cardiac death."

"The DCI investigation and administrative review showed that the leg restraint system was used correctly as designed, and did not play a role in Mr. Larson’s death. We are confident that the DCI will conduct an equally thorough review of this most recent incident," police spokesman Brendyn Medina said.

The police department said at the time an officer spotted the man, who had active warrants for his arrest, around 11 p.m. on Friday, Sept. 19, 2025, in the 1300 block of Mount Rushmore Road.

Police said the man ran from officers. He was apprehended after a short foot pursuit but the suspect was allegedly combative with officers.

Police said officers found syringes and suspected illegal narcotics on the man. The police department said because the suspect was combative he was placed in a WRAP safety restraint system, a spit mask and a padded helmet prior to transport to the Pennington County Jail.

Police said “upon arrival at the jail, he was determined to be unresponsive.” Law enforcement staff rendered emergency life-saving measures and he was transported to the hospital where he was declared dead.

“The investigation was closed after review by the (South Dakota Attorney General’s) Office with no criminal conduct found. Autopsy results showed he died as a result of an enlarged heart and the presence of methamphetamine during his altercation with RCPD,” a spokesperson for DCI told the Journal on Wednesday, Sept. 9.

The Rapid City Police Department's rules and procedures on the use of the WRAP system.

title: Exceeding federal requirements, RCFD trains all firefighters on aircraft rescue, fire response
description: The Rapid City Fire Department holds Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting (ARFF) training every year, but this year the training was expanded to all of the department’s firefighters, and it took place at the department’s very own training facility on Creek Drive.
_full_text:
The Rapid City Fire Department holds Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting (ARFF) training every year, but this year the training was expanded to all of the department’s firefighters, and it took place at the department’s very own training facility on Creek Drive.

“We've been getting our companies from in town involved for years, but this is the first year we decided, let's get everybody in one shot,” said Neill Goodart, ARFF battalion chief. “… We try to bring our in-town folks in to teach them their part of the job because there's no way we handle that scenario by ourselves. It's going to take the whole community.”

 Putting out a fire
One firefighter stands outside the aircraft simulator while another directs the hose to a roof fire. 

ARFF training entails an aircraft simulator that catches fire, simulated fuel fires and rescue practice. The fire department has an ARFF station (Station 8) at the Rapid City Regional Airport and 15 ARFF qualified firefighters.

Commercial airports are required by federal law to provide Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting, and those firefighters must be trained yearly. The rest of the department’s 160 firefighters, however, aren’t required to undergo ARFF training.

In the past, condensed trainings took place at Ellsworth Air Force Base for the ARFF qualified firefighters. When the base was no longer an option a few years ago because it was undergoing work to the training area, the department trained at the airport. Other firefighters who weren’t ARFF qualified participated, but the training would sometimes hit the same shift each year, Goodart said. That meant some firefighters were trained repeatedly, while others were missed.

The Creek Drive property, which also features West River’s only training tower outside Ellsworth, afforded the department the space and time to train everyone.

“It just provides more reps for us to get good practice,” Goodart said.

 ARFF Training
Pans of propane outside the aircraft simulator were set ablaze to simulate fuel spill fires. 

ARFF Specialist is the company that provides the aircraft simulator. Its owner, Louis Kurtz, commended the Rapid City Fire Department for training all of its firefighters.

“They're being visionaries trying to bring more education to some guys who wouldn't necessarily see that, and again, it gives them a whole new skill set and abilities that they wouldn't have leading into this,” Kurtz said.

Kurtz said the company owns five aircraft simulators, and he sees approximately 185 department and 4,200 firefighters a year.

“We're at major airports, but I choose to be here in Rapid City and participate as the owner with something, again, that's so progressive with bringing a whole city component into this. It's very unique,” Kurtz said. “One out of 100 at best try to bring this much training in such a short period of time and incorporate so much.”

 Victim
A Rapid City Fire Department firefighter carries a training mannequin to safety during Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting on Tuesday, Sept. 8.
